Introduction
Fleet Lifecycle 9.1.1.0200 | 12 OCT 2026 | Build 25801070
Check for additions and updates to these release notes.
What's New
This release contains various security enhancements and delivers fixes as described in the Resolved Issues section.
Applying the Patch
You apply this patch by using VCF Operations. See Upgrade or Patch an Individual VCF Component.
Resolved Issues
Domain Lifecycle content fails to load in VCF Operations
After navigating to Build > Lifecycle and selecting a domain or refreshing the page, the Lifecycle content might fail to
load and the loading indicator might continue to spin. As a result, users cannot access the Upgrades page for the domain.
Deployment spec validation now rejects non-native Single Sign-On domains for the administrator username
When you submit a deployment spec, the system now validates that the value belongs to the
adminUserSsoUsername
vCenter native or local Single Sign-On (SSO) domain, as reported by the vCenter SSO configuration API. If the username
belongs to a federated or external domain, the system rejects the submission and displays a validation error that instructs
you to provide a native SSO account. This change prevents misconfigurations that could occur when a federated domain
account was previously accepted for the administrator username.
Missing VSP services runtime binaries cause VCF Automation deployment or upgrade to fail
When you deploy or upgrade VCF Automation on an existing SDDC, the operation fails with a generic, unactionable error
if the requested VCF services runtime installation binaries are not downloaded in SDDC Manager. The failure occurs after
the bootstrap task has started.
Incorrect IP pool size is not reported as an error in the UI when a fleet task runs
When an IP pool has an incorrect size, the VCF services runtime task detects and reports the error, but the fleet task does
not show this error in the UI. As a result, users may not be aware that the IP pool size is invalid, and the operation may
appear to succeed or fail without a clear error message.
Fleet lifecycle component installation or patch fails in multi-VCF deployments because of an invalid SDDC
Manager certificate
In a multi-VCF deployment, upgrading SDDC lifecycle on a secondary VCF instance after upgrading fleet lifecycle on a
primary VCF instance can fail. The fleet lifecycle refresh step encounters
refresh_fleet_lcm_component_task_ref
an unexpected error, and the subsequent step also fails. The root cause is that
post_upgrade_inventory_sync
an invalid SDDC Manager certificate is sent during component install or patch operations. This failure affects both
component patching and component install workflows.
Upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1.x requires the source and target clusters to reside on the management
datastore
Broadcom 707

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
When you upgrade to VCF Automation 9.1.x from 8.x or 9.0.x, both the source cluster and the target cluster must reside
on the same datastore, and that datastore must be the management datastore. An arbitrary non-management datastore
that is visible to the management cluster does not satisfy this requirement. If the source and target clusters do not both
reside on the management datastore, the upgrade to 9.1.x is not supported.
Fleet lifecycle installs dependency components at base version instead of latest express patch
Fleet lifecycle 9.1.1.0 and 9.1.1.0100 always install dependency components at version 9.1.1.0, regardless of the
latest available express patch release. This behavior prevents customers from installing the latest express patch for
migration service engine and VCF services runtime when deploying VCF Automation, and for real-time metrics store when
deploying real-time metrics.
Deployment validation does not detect an invalid identity broker IP address until late in the process
During deployment, the validation checks do not detect when the identity broker IP address is not part of the VCF services
runtime network. Because the misconfiguration goes unchecked, the deployment proceeds for approximately three hours
before it fails with an error. This delays detection of the invalid network configuration and wastes deployment time.
Deployment wizard forces vCenter selection when using an existing VCF Operations instance
When deploying VCF 9.1.1, customers who select the option to use an existing VCF Operations 9.1 instance find that the
wizard automatically selects the option to use an existing vCenter instance. Customers cannot clear this selection. This
affects customers who want to reuse their existing VCF Operations instance but do not want to reuse an existing vCenter
instance.
Known Issues
VCF services runtime component upgrade task fails during database failover
During a VCF services runtime upgrade, the Conductor task that upgrades the VCF services runtime component can fail if
a PostgreSQL database failover or database read timeout occurs while Conductor is updating the task state.
Because the task state update fails in the database, the task is not returned to the queue and is lost. When the Conductor
sweeper thread finds that the component upgrade task is stuck in progress, has not received any new task updates,
and hits , it marks the task as failed. Conductor has a repair mechanism to fix a lost task, but this
responseTimeout
mechanism is only invoked once during startup in VCF 9.1 and 9.1.1, not periodically. As a result, a lost task is not
automatically recovered.
The underlying VCF services runtime task that upgrades the VCF services runtime cluster continues to make progress
without interruption. Only the Conductor task tracking fails. Retrying the failed fleet lifecycle task completes quickly.
Workaround: Retry the failed task.
Transport Node Collection creation fails during Brownfield Import for VCP clusters
When you perform a Brownfield Import of a VMware vCenter® instance running version 8.0.3Ue or later that contains
VCP clusters with hosts running version 8.0.3 or later, joining an existing NSX Manager cluster in pinned mode during
upgrade from 4.2.x to 9.x causes Transport Node Collection creation to fail for those VCP clusters. The operation returns
the following error:
vLCM Config Manager is enabled on this cluster. Applying Transport Node Profile is not allowed. (error code
26219)
Workaround:
1. Complete the NSX Manager upgrade finalize process.
2. Retry the Brownfield Import.
Certificate replacement fails when a component certificate's Common Name contains special characters
After a component certificate is replaced outside SDDC Manager, the Non-Disruptive Certificate (NDC) replacement
workflow fails. The error is . SDDC Manager can then no longer connect to the
CS_APPLIANCE_CERT_ALIAS_INVALID
affected component, because the new certificate is not added to its trust store.
When a component certificate is replaced directly in the product (out of band) and the new certificate's Common Name
(CN) contains special characters, SDDC Manager builds a trust-store alias from that CN. The alias is rejected if it contains
anything other than:
Broadcom 708

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• letters (A–Z, a–z) and digits (0–9);
• period ( ), underscore ( ), hyphen ( ) and colon ( ).
. _ - :
The alias is also rejected if it contains consecutive periods ( ) or exceeds 255 characters. A common example is a
..
space, as in .
CN=Root CA
Workaround: Re-issue the component certificate with a CN that uses only letters, digits, periods, underscores, hyphens
and colons, and has no consecutive periods. Then re-run the NDC workflow.

What Is VMware Cloud Foundation?
VMware Cloud Foundation ® (VCF) is a private cloud platform that delivers public cloud scale and agility with on-premises
security, resilience and performance, while lowering total cost of ownership.
VMware Cloud Foundation can help you accelerate digital innovation with faster infrastructure modernization, a unified
cloud experience, along with stronger cyber resilience and platform security.
VCF delivers a consistent private cloud experience across any environment whether it is a customer-managed data
center, edge location, or any cloud endpoint. VCF supports both traditional as well as modern workloads such as
containers and AI/ML workloads, and brings modern applications faster to the market with self-service Infrastructure as a
Service (IaaS) consumption experience for the application teams.

VCF Installer Overview
VCF Installer is a dedicated virtual machine that helps you plan, configure, and deploy VCF and vSphere Foundation
components.
Use the VCF Installer to perform the following operations:
• Download the binaries to deploy VCF or vSphere Foundation.
• Plan the desired size and configuration of your VCF or VMware vSphere Foundation deployment.
• Deploy and configure a new VCF or VMware vSphere Foundation platform. You can also reuse existing VCF
Operations and VCF Automation instances for new VCF fleets.
• Use existing virtual infrastructure to converge them to a VCF or vSphere Foundation platform.
• Extend an existing VCF fleet by deploying an additional VCF Instance.
• Deploy VCF management services and license server to complete the vSphere Foundation upgrade to 9.1.
• Review historical deployment process details, download passwords, and download JSON specifications from VCF or
vSphere Foundation deployments.
VCF Installer works with major, minor, and maintenance releases, but does not support patch or express patch releases.
After the VCF Installer workflows complete, you can apply patches manually.
VCF Installer is part of the SDDC Manager appliance and the binaries for both reside in the
VCF-SDDC-Manager-
file.
Appliance-9.x.x.ova
VCF Installer Modes
For VCF deployments, depending on where you deploy VCF Installer, it can deploy multiple VCF platforms, or it can
become the SDDC Manager instance for the target VCF Instance that you deploy.
VCF Installer mode If you deploy the VCF Installer appliance on an ESX host that is not part of the management domain for the
target deployment, then the appliance stays in installer mode after the deployment completes. In this mode,
you can deploy additional VCF Instances and perform convergence workflows.
VCF Installer to SDDC If you deploy the VCF Installer appliance on a host that is part of the management domain, during the
Manager mode deployment, the appliance switches to SDDC Manager mode. Once in SDDC Manager mode, the
appliance can no longer work in installer mode. As a best practice, deploy the appliance on a local
datastore, then during the deployment workflows, the appliance migrates to the primary datastore. For FC
storage, the appliance can initially be deployed on the FC datastore.
VCF Installer Documentation
For more information about the VCF Installer and the options for deployment, convergence, and upgrade to VCF and
vSphere Foundation it provides, see Deployment, Convergence, and Upgrade.
Broadcom 719

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSphere Overview
Virtualize physical infrastructure into managed CPU, storage, and networking resources.
The two core components of VMware vSphere® are VMware ESX® and VMware vCenter®. ESX is the virtualization
platform where you create and run virtual machines and virtual appliances, Kubernetes workloads, and AI/ML workloads.
vCenter is the service through which you manage multiple hosts connected in a network and pool host resources.
vSphere manages large collections of infrastructure, such as CPUs, storage, networking, GPUs, and DPUs as a seamless
and dynamic operating environment, and also manages the complexity of a data center.
Lifecycle Management of vSphere
• Lifecycle management is achieved using pre-staging ESX images, remediating hosts in parallel, and by applying
updates in parallel across clusters.
• vSphere can manage infrastructure images to patch, update, or upgrade clusters using a desired state model.
• vSphere can reduce maintenance windows using reduced downtime upgrades for vCenter and live patching for ESX
for near zero downtime for security patches.
Workload Performance
• With its GPU support, vSphere improves workload performance for modern AI workloads
• vSphere on DPUs (VMware vSphere® Distributed Services EngineTM) helps accelerate infrastructure network
functions on the Data Processing Unit (DPU) by using available CPU cycles to achieve higher workload consolidation
per host.
• Distributed Resource Scheduler (vSphere DRS) enables automatic load balancing of resources that are allocated to
workloads in a vSphere cluster. Storage DRS optimizes VM data placement as the VM is created and used over time.
Business Continuity
• High Availability with vSphere automatically restarts your VMs following physical machine failure.
• Fault Tolerance provides continuous availability of any application if a hardware failure with no data loss or downtime
occurs.
• vMotion enables live migration of virtual machines with no disruption to users or loss of service, eliminating the need to
schedule application downtime for planned server maintenance. Storage vMotion avoids downtime for planned storage
maintenance.
Built-in Security
• Identity federation with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), ADFS, and Okta: Secure access and account
management.
• Virtual Machine Encryption: Data-at-rest encryption for virtual machine data and disks.
• vSphere Trust Authority: Remote attestation for sensitive workloads.
vSphere Documentation
For information about the built-in vSphere capabilities, see the vSphere documentation.
vSAN Overview
VMware® vSAN™ aggregates local or direct-attached capacity devices of all ESX hosts in a cluster and creates a single
storage pool that is shared across all ESX hosts in the vSAN cluster.
You can use vSphere features that require shared storage, such as vSphere HA, vSphere vMotion, and vSphere DRS,
without the need for external shared storage.
Broadcom 720

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Performance Across Workloads
vSAN delivers high throughput and low latency storage. For best performance, you can use vSAN Express Storage
Architecture™ (vSAN ESA) with high performance NVMe-based TLC flash devices.
Agile Scaling for Deployments of All Sizes
vSAN offers flexible scaling ranging from clusters as small as two nodes (plus witness) to clusters with up to 64 nodes.
Whether scaling out by adding nodes to a cluster, scaling up by adding drives to nodes or scaling compute and storage
resources independently with disaggregation, vSAN enables you to customize performance and capacity to optimize
storage resources and drive down costs. Disaggregation in vSAN decouples compute and storage resources. As a result,
compute and storage resources can be scaled independently within your environment. Disaggregation enables the use of
dedicated storage-only clusters.
Unified Operations and Lifecycle Management
vSAN provides operational consistency from edge to cloud, with complete visibility and lifecycle management of compute
and storage from a single UI.
Storage Capacity and Efficiency
Improve storage efficiency with optimized compression methods. A single-tier architecture option eliminates the need for a
cache tier, further enhancing storage efficiency. vSAN enables you to store data using RAID 5 or RAID 6 for efficiency with
performance at the speed of RAID 1.
Integrated File Services
vSAN enables provisioning of file shares with a single workflow and provides a unified storage control plane for both block
and file storage. vSAN file services can integrate Active Directory and support Kerberos network authentication and the
most common protocols. vSAN file services can be used in two-node deployments and stretched cluster deployments.
VM-Centric Policy-Based Management
You can perform consistent, VM-centric operations by using policy-based management. Within the vSAN ESA, per-VM
policies increase flexibility of management, enabling compression policies, or customize data services on a per-VM basis.
vSAN Documentation
For more information about the built-in vSAN capabilities, see the vSAN documentation.
NSX Overview
VMware NSX® simplifies network connectivity, consumption, and operations with scalable multi-site connectivity, efficient
infrastructure utilization, and self-service for application teams. It uses a software-defined approach to networking that
spans data centers, clouds, and application frameworks.
NSX brings networking services closer to the application, whether running on virtual machines (VMs), containers, or
physical servers. This allows for a cloud operating model where networks can be provisioned and managed independently
of the underlying hardware.
NSX replicates the entire network model in software, enabling any network topology—from simple to complex multi-
tier networks—to be created and provisioned in seconds. Users can create multiple virtual networks with diverse
requirements, leveraging a combination of the services offered over NSX or from a broad ecosystem of third-party
integrations to build inherently more agile and secure environments. These services can then be extended to various
endpoints within and across clouds.
Layer 2 - Layer 7 Network Stack and Overlay Services
NSX provides a complete set of logical networking capabilities and services, including logical switching, routing,
distributed load balancing, virtual private network (VPN), quality of service (QoS), and monitoring. These services are
Broadcom 721

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
provisioned in virtual networks. Virtual networks are deployed non-disruptively over the networking hardware and can
extend across data centers, private clouds, and container platforms.
• Switching. Enable logical Layer 2 overlay extensions across a routed (Layer 3) fabric within and across data center
boundaries.
• Routing. Dynamic routing between virtual networks that is performed in a distributed manner in the hypervisor kernel,
and scale-out routing with active-active failover with physical routers. Static routing and dynamic routing protocols are
supported, including support for IPv6.
• Virtual routing and forwarding (VRF). Complete data plane isolation among tenants with a separate routing table,
network address translation (NAT), and edge firewall support in each VRF on the NSX Tier-0 gateway.
• NSX gateway. Support for bridging between VLANs configured on the physical network and NSX overlay networks, for
seamless connectivity between virtual and physical workloads.
• VPN. Site-to-site and unmanaged VPN for cloud gateway services.
Multi-Site Networking and Disaster Recovery
By using NSX, you can move workloads between racks and data centers by decoupling them from the underlying
networks. You can use network overlays and a consistent policy framework across different infrastructures without the
need for any changes to the network when moving workloads. This capability supports workload mobility for disaster
recovery and workload balancing, ensuring continuous availability and optimal application performance.
• Federation. Centralized policy configuration and enforcement across multiple locations from a single pane of glass,
enabling network-wide consistent policy, operational simplicity, and simplified disaster recovery architecture.
• Multi-cloud networking. Enable consistent networking and security across data center sites, and across private cloud
boundaries, irrespective of underlying physical topology or cloud platform.
Network Automation with Declarative APIs
NSX can manage the provisioning, deployment, operations, and retirement of software defined networking infrastructure
and applications from a central control pane. You can automate infrastructure operations and offload manual tasks with
workflows and agile templating using tools such as VCF Automation, Terraform, and Ansible. NSX abstracts network
services from the underlying hardware, enabling programmable infrastructure through APIs. You can implement policies
and workflows to automate tasks like network provisioning, security enforcement, load balancing, streamlining operations,
and improving efficiency.
Self-Service Networking with VPCs and Multi-Tenancy
VPCs provide isolated network environments within a shared infrastructure. You can use Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
constructs to provision and manage network resources to business units or project teams independently, with granular
control over networking policies and resource allocation.
By creating projects, you can isolate security and networking objects across tenants in a single NSX deployment. You
enable multi-tenant deployment and consumption of NSX services for the provider administrator and the tenants or
organizations. The provider administrator can create projects, assign users and groups, and allocate quotas to restrict the
configurations available to the tenants.
NSX Documentation
For more information about the built-in NSX capabilities, see the NSX documentation.
VCF Operations Overview
VMware Cloud Foundation Operations® (formerly VMware Aria Operations) or VCF Operations helps your organization
build, manage, operate, and secure your private cloud infrastructure by deploying and maintaining its fleet-level
components, providing visibility and enhanced performance across the workload and infrastructure stack, and helping
your organization stay compliant with regulatory standards and organizational guidelines.
VCF Operations has the following main functional areas, reflecting the main categories of operations in a VCF private
cloud:
Broadcom 722

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Build Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
• Manage Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
• Operate Your Private Cloud in VCF Operations
• Protect Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
Build Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
By using VCF Operations, you can add infrastructure to your private cloud as workload domains or standalone vCenter
instances and can manage the lifecycle of your private cloud by providing the ability to patch and upgrade your
infrastructure.
VCF Operations is also the central hub for managing software binaries using software depots . VCF Operations also
enables extensibility by providing developers with access to APIs and SDKs through its developer center area.
Workload Domain Creation
You can create workload domains or import vCenter instances as workload domains in a VCF Instance from the VCF
Operations inventory. Accordingly, VCF Operations deploys a vCenter instance, an NSX Manager instance (which can be
shared with other workload domains) and adds a default vSphere cluster with ESX hosts to vCenter and NSX Manager,
optionally with enabled Supervisor functionality.
For more information, see the Managing VCF Domains in VMware Cloud Foundation documentation.
For information about VCF logical constructs, see VCF Taxonomy.
Lifecycle Management and Software Depot
The fleet lifecycle component provides a unified framework to upgrade, patch, back up, restore, and maintain VCF
Operations, VCF management services, and VCF Automation. You can also deploy additional components after the initial
VCF deployment or convergence. Similarly, you use SDDC lifecycle management to perform lifecycle management on the
components running on VCF Instances. Component binaries are stored in one or more software depots - one at the fleet
level and optionally one or more software depots at the instance level.
For more information, see the Upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x, Lifecycle Management, Adding or Removing
VCF Components Post Deployment, and Component Backup and Restore of VMware Cloud Foundation documentation.
Manage Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
In VCF Operations, you can make your infrastructure compliant and standardized using automated updates across
all workload domains, including identity-based access, license entitlement, and fleet-wide certificate and password
maintenance.
Licensing
With a unified view in VCF Operations, you can easily manage licensing for your VCF and vSphere Foundation
infrastructure. VCF Operations provides a comprehensive overview of VCF license allocation and usage in a private
cloud. VCF Operations also provides a view of the older licenses that are pre-version 9.0.
VCF provides license management in two modes - for connected environments and disconnected environments. You can
upgrade your licenses and you can choose when and how to monitor VCF assets across the entire VCF stack.

Fleet Management
By using the fleet management functionality of VCF Operations, such as identity and access management, management
of certificates and passwords, you can centrally manage your VCF components.

Certificate Management VCF Operations introduces a unified, non-disruptive TLS certificate management system,
allowing centralized control of certificates across most of the components in the VCF
private cloud. The system provides automated workflows, integration with various certificate
authorities, and auto-renewal capabilities.
Features include viewing certificates and alerts, auto-renewal for VMCA, MSCA, and
OpenSSL CA, replacing default certificates with enterprise CA certificates, CA configuration
and CSR generation, and certificate expiry notifications.
For more details on how to use certificate management, see the Managing Certificates in
VMware Cloud Foundation documentation
Identity and Access Management You can use single-source configuration in VCF Operations for identity and access
management. In this way, you can use the same identity configuration across VCF
components and across multiple geolocations, offering Single Sign-On (SSO) and centralized
management of federated access, enhancing both flexibility and user experience.
For simplified access management of VCF users, you can use VCF roles across VCF
components, such as vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations, VCF Automation, and other. You can
assign predefined VCF roles for functions such as admin, viewer, and other.
For more details on how to use identity and access management, see the Managing Identity
and Access With VCF Single Sign-On documentation.
Tag Management By using unified tag management, you can manage tags across vCenter instances from a
central location.
By using the tag management capabilities you can perform the following tasks:
• Create, edit, or delete categories and tags from a single pane of glass.
• Unify existing tags across vCenter instances, assign and view tag assignments, and
define consistent tagging practices at scale.
• Import tags and categories from converged or upgraded environments. For legacy VCF
Operations (formerly VMware Aria Operations) users, legacy tags continue to be available
independently.
• Create tags and categories.
• Push tags and categories
• Assign tags to vCenter instances.
For more details on how to use tag management, see the Tags and Categories Overview
documentation.
Configuration Management Unified configuration management provides features like scheduled drift detection for vCenter
and cluster objects through VCF Automation or VCF Operations orchestrator., enabling
proactive detection of configuration deviations from the desired state.
You can manage global templates across vCenter instances, integrate with Git, and schedule
drift detection through VCF Automation or VCF Operations orchestrator.
For more details on how to use configuration management, see the Managing the
Configuration of your Environment documentation.

Password policy enables you to be compliant with enterprise security standards for managing

are most suitable to use capacity management for optimal utilization of your resources.

Operate Your Private Cloud in VCF Operations
The comprehensive observability hub in VCF Operations, delivers a single pane of glass for monitoring operational health
and performance. To enable proactive troubleshooting and quick root-cause analysis across the entire infrastructure,
it synthesizes critical information, including system metrics, logs, and network traffic flows. Additionally, it provides
environmental analytics through sustainability scores, allowing organizations to align infrastructure performance with
energy-efficiency goals.
Core Monitoring
The Inventory of VCF Operations is a collection of all objects in your VCF fleet that are discovered and monitored by VCF
Operations. The inventory includes objects in all VCF Instances in your environment, including management domains
and workload domains, and all standalone vCenter instances. The inventory is the primary entry point for observability
and health assessment. It provides real-time visibility into object health across the VCF fleet to surface active alerts,
performance bottlenecks.

Diagnostics and Analysis
This functional area integrates disparate data types, including structured metrics, unstructured logs, and network flow
data, into unified workflows. Instead of isolated monitoring, these features prioritize data correlation to isolate the root
cause of performance degradations or system failures across the management and workload domains.
Diagnostics and Analysis Capability Description
Workbench Provides teams with the ability to collaborate, build a knowledge base of issue
investigations which can be saved for future reference, and can enhance
troubleshooting by viewing real-time data. For more details on Workbench, see the
Troubleshooting with the Workbenchdocumentation.
VCF Health Continuously monitors the operational state of VCF components in your environment
to ensure they are functioning as expected. By proactively identifying potential issues
such as expired certificates, NTP drifts, DNS misconfigurations, and configuration
errors, you can take preventative actions before these issues escalate into significant
problems. By using proactive monitoring, you can maintain a stable, secure, and
efficient environment, reducing the risk of downtime and operational disruptions.
For more information on how to use VCF Health, see the Monitor Your Environment
and Prevent Issues with VCF Health documentation.
Diagnostics Automatically detects known issues and critical vulnerabilities within the VCF software
stack, providing detailed descriptions, root cause insights, and actionable remediation
steps to resolve problems and mitigate risks.
The Diagnostic Findings feature offers a consolidated view of known product issues,
VMSA-based security exposures, and best-practice recommendations across your

operations.

Sustainability
Green Score is used to measure sustainability in digital operations through data center virtualization. Green Score
consists of multiple parameters for effective measurement of the score. Virtualization plays a crucial role in optimizing
resource utilization, helping reduce hardware footprints in data centers and further enabling savings in power consumption
and floor space. This improves the overall efficiency and curbs carbon emissions resulting from IT infrastructure and
operations.
For more information, see the Configuring Green Score documentation.
Workload Operations
Workload operations ensure that critical applications are running properly by monitoring their performance, availability,
and end-user experience. For container-based applications, VCF Operations provides native integration with vSphere
Supervisor which enables automatic monitoring of Supervisor instances and vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters
at a granular level, shortening troubleshooting time.
A business application consists of a set of interconnected applications or services running on one or more virtual
machines which together offer a service to users.
For more information, see the Workload Monitoring and Observability documentation.
Protect Your Private Cloud with VCF Operations
VCF Operations provides continuous, real-time assessment of the infrastructure's security posture by monitoring
encryption readiness and critical security advisories. This defensive stance is extended by robust auditing and compliance
validation against industry benchmarks.
Security Operations
The Security Operations dashboard is designed to provide a comprehensive view of your security posture in VCF. This
dashboard consolidates elements that are related to user and infrastructure security to help you identify areas that might
require attention and tightening based on your security exposure. The dashboard covers host encryption, host mode
compliance, vSAN cluster encryption, advisories for CVE violations, certificate health, and VM encryption status.
For more information on how to use security operations, see the Monitoring Security Operations documentation.

VCF Automation Overview
VMware Cloud Foundation Automation® (formerly VMware Aria Automation) or VCF Automation enables IT teams and
cloud service providers (CSPs) to deliver a self-service private cloud for AI, Kubernetes, and VM-based applications. The
solution simplifies the process of provisioning and scaling a multi-tenant private cloud with out-of-the-box Infrastructure
as a Service (IaaS) offerings, accelerating the time to market for applications while maintaining control using policy-based
governance.
VCF Automation has the following capabilities:
• Cloud Services. Provides a set of cloud services to meet the needs of application teams.
• Provider Management. Supports IT teams and cloud service providers to effectively manage, deliver, and scale cloud
services across multiple vCenter and VCF instances.
• Organization Management. Provides capabilities that enable the organization administrator of a Line of Business or a
tenant to further organize and govern resources allocated to them among application teams.
• vSphere Supervisor. Provides the capability to run Kubernetes workloads directly on ESX hosts and to create
upstream Kubernetes clusters within dedicated namespaces.
Cloud Services Overview
VCF Automation provides a set of cloud services which are accessible on a self-service basis using multiple interfaces,
including UI, CLI, and API.
With this interface, users can provision the following types of workloads:
• VMs
• Kubernetes workloads
• Networking
• Volumes
• Secret stores
• Databases
• Harbor container registries
• External DNS
• Certificates
• AI workloads
Additionally, application teams can also provision resources on a self-service basis from Catalogs which are backed by
pre-configured workload templates. These self-service options help developers focus on application development instead
of managing the underlying infrastructure.
For more information about cloud services, see the Building Cloud Applications documentation.
Provider Management Overview
IT teams and CSPs can model multi-tenancy by using the concept of Organizations in VCF Automation, effectively
allocating resources and managing users specific to each Organization.
Broadcom 734

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This capability provides isolated environments with dedicated network setup. IT Teams and CSPs can monitor resource
usage, control permissions, and provide managed services while ensuring security through comprehensive network
isolation.
For more details on provider management, see the following resources:
• Provider Management documentation. Explains how to use provider management.
Organization Management Overview
VCF Automation improves governance for users and resources by enabling organization administrators create and assign
projects and vSphere Namespaces tailored for different application teams.
Organization administrators can set resource limits and policies while delegating network management through Virtual
Private Clouds (VPCs) for application teams. Additionally, Policy as Code enables organization administrators to enforce
instance-centric policies for Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) resources from a central location for compliance and
reducing the risk of human error.
For more details on organization management, see the following resources:
• Organization Management documentation. Explains how to use organization management.
vSphere Supervisor Overview
VMware vSphere Supervisor ® is the foundation of VCF consumption and can be enabled during workload domain
creation or directly in vCenter.
It transforms vSphere clusters into modern application platforms by embedding a platform-level Kubernetes control plane
directly into ESX hosts, exposing a unified declarative API surface. This integration allows end users to provision and
manage workloads, including VMs, containers using vSphere Pods, full Kubernetes clusters through VKS, OCI image
registries, and data services through a consistent API interface.
vSphere Supervisor maintains enterprise-grade governance, security, and operational consistency through vCenter, VCF
Operations, and VCF Automation. Its vSphere Namespaces provide the foundation for multi-tenancy, enabling GitOps-
based workflows, and delivering cloud-like self-service in private data centers.
For an overview of vSphere Supervisor concepts and how they apply in VCF Automation, see the vSphere Supervisor
Platform and Building Cloud Applications documentation.
What Is vSphere Foundation?
VMware vSphere Foundation (vSphere Foundation) is an enterprise-grade workload platform for modern infrastructure
delivering virtualized benefits, simplified management, cost efficiency, scalability and serves as the core foundation for
VCF.
vSphere Foundation provides the following capabilities:
• Intelligent operations management for visibility and infrastructure optimization.
• Hyperconverged infrastructure integrating compute and storage virtualization for resource management.
• Simplified deployment and scalability enabling faster application delivery and future ready infrastructure.
• Unified service-oriented platform, VCF management services, for centralized lifecycle management and operational
functionality.
In a vSphere Foundation environment, VCF management services provide lifecycle management of VCF Operations
and license server, and log analysis.
• Unified workload platform for running consumer VMs and containers side by side in a native Kubernetes runtime.
vSphere Foundation does not include the cloud management and integrated automation capabilities that are available in
VMware Cloud Foundation. See What Is VMware Cloud Foundation?.
For a feature comparison and differences between VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation, see
Feature Comparison & Upgrade Paths on vmware.com.

VCF Domains
A VCF domain in a VCF Instance consists of the following components:
• One vCenter instance.
• One or more vSphere clusters with vSphere HA and vSphere DRS enabled.
• At least one vSphere Distributed Switches per cluster for system traffic and NSX segments for workloads.
• One NSX Manager instance, either specifically for the VCF domain or shared between VCF domains, for configuring
and implementing software-defined networking.
• Optional. One or more NSX Edge or Virtual Network Appliance clusters, added after you create the workload domain,
that connects the workloads in the workload domain for logical switching, logical dynamic routing, and load balancing.
• One or more shared storage allocations as principal or supplemental storage.
Table 4: Types of VCF Domains
VCF Domain Type Description
Management domain The management domain is created during the deployment or convergence process by the
VCF Installer. The management domain contains the components of the VCF Instance and,
in the first VCF Instance, License server, VCF Operations, VCF management services, and
VCF Automation.
In addition to the components that are common for each VCF domain, the management
domain includes the SDDC Manager appliance that adds workflows for infrastructure
management automation to the VCF Operations instance for the VCF fleet, and VCF
management services that are working on the instance level.
Workload domain You create workload domains in VCF Operations to run consumer workloads.
For the first workload domain in your environment, in the management domain, VCF
Operations deploys a vCenter instance , and if required by your organization, an NSX
Manager instance. For each additional workload domain, VCF Operations deploys an
additional vCenter instance. New workload domains can share the same NSX Manager
cluster with an existing workload domain or with the management domain, or you can deploy
a new NSX Manager cluster.

You start building a VCF platform by deploying a new platform, converging your existing virtual infrastructure to VCF, or
upgrading existing your VCF platform. After you deploy your VCF Instances and VCF fleet, you can continue with adding
workload domains and integrating them in VCF Automation for end-user consumption.

Upgrade Your Management Domain to VCF. • In a VCF 5.2.x environment, the high-level upgrade process is as follows:
– Upgrade the existing VMware Aria components and SDDC Manager. Then,
deploy VCF management services and the license server component. Upgrade

Aria and management domain components and deploy the rest of the VCF fleet
components that you need.
• In a VCF 9.0.x environment, the high-level upgrade process is as follows:
Upgrade VCF Operations and SDDC Manager in the VCF Instances in your fleet.
Then, deploy VCF management services and the license server component.
Upgrade the rest of the fleet components and the management components of the
VCF Instances.
Add Workload Domains to a VCF Instance
After you deploy the VCF fleet and VCF Instances, you can start adding workload domains with infrastructure for
consumer workloads to the VCF Instances in one of the following ways:
• Deploy new workload domains.
As part of workload domain deployment, you can enable vSphere Supervisor with NSX VPC on the initial cluster of the
workload domain. You can then add the initial infrastructure of the workload domain to VCF Automation.
• Import vCenter instances, managing consumer workloads, as workload domains.
You can import components that are compatible with VCF 5.x and upgrade to version 9.1 after you import them as a
workload domain.

Add a vCenter Instance to the VCF Fleet
You can add virtual infrastructure under a vSphere Foundation license to a VCF fleet. See vSphere as a data source in
VCF Operations.

Complete the Configuration of the VCF Fleet, VCF Instances, and Workload Domains
After you deploy the VCF fleet or VCF Instance or add a workload domain to a VCF Instance, complete its configuration
by performing the following tasks in VCF Operations or the vSphere Client. Assigning a license must be done right after
you complete deployment.
• Assign a license to the VCF fleet, VCF Instance or workload domain in VCF Operations.
• Configure software depot settings in VCF Operations.
• Configure identity and access management in VCF Operations.
• Configure backup of the management components in VCF Operations.
• Configure certificate management in VCF Operations and the vSphere Client.
• Configure password management in VCF Operations.
• Add clusters and individual ESX hosts to your VCF domains in the vSphere Client.
Add Workload Domains to Your Cloud Organization Structure
You can add workload domains to an organization in VCF Automation Provider Management for consumption by end
users. You can create two types of organizations in VCF Automation - All Apps Organizations for workload domains with
Supervisor clusters that run both containers and VMs, and a VM Apps Organization for workload domains with clusters
that run only VMs.
1. Set up network connectivity in the workload domains and create Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs) in vCenter.

Getting Started with vSphere Foundation
You can start building a vSphere Foundation private cloud by deploying a new platform оr converging your existing virtual
infrastructure to vSphere Foundation. After you deploy VCF Operations, VCF management services, and license server
using a new or existing vCenter instance, you can continue with adding vCenter instances to the cloud.
In this article:
• Deploy VCF Operations
• Add vCenter Instances to VCF Operations
• Complete the Configuration of vSphere Foundation
• What to Do Next
Deploy VCF Operations
The first step in building a vSphere Foundation platform is deploying VCF Operations, VCF management services, and
the license server component in one of the following ways:
• Deploy a new vSphere Foundation platform.
• Deploy VCF Operations, VCF management services, and license server on an existing vCenter instance.
If you have an existing VMware Aria Operations and vCenter instance with managed vSphere clusters, upgrade VMware
Aria Operations to VCF Operations 9.1 and vCenter to version 9.1.
Add vCenter Instances to VCF Operations
After you deploy or upgrade to VCF Operations, you can start adding vCenter instances with infrastructure running
consumer workloads. See vSphere as a data source in VCF Operations.
Complete the Configuration of vSphere Foundation
After you deploy VCF Operations or add a vCenter instance to it, complete the platform's configuration by performing the
following tasks. Assigning a license must be done right after you complete deployment.
• Assign a license.
• Configure software depot settings in VCF Operations
• Configure backup of the management components.
• Configure certificate management in VCF Operations.
• Deploy and configure vSphere Supervisor.

VCF Fleet Deployment Models
This section outlines the VCF Fleet Deployment Models and available design options, offering guidance on selecting the
most appropriate deployment model to meet your specific requirements.
Understanding the VCF Fleet Construct
A VCF fleet represents a unified operational framework that enables organizations to deploy, manage, and operate one
or more VCF Instances as a cohesive infrastructure ecosystem. The VCF fleet construct serves as the foundational
organizational model that provides:
Broadcom 754

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Centralized Management Plane: A single control point for managing multiple VCF Instances across geographic
locations.
• Unified Operations Framework: Consistent operational practices, policies, and governance across all instances.
• Standardized Lifecycle Management: Coordinated deployment, upgrade, and maintenance procedures across the
fleet.
• Integrated Monitoring and Analytics: Comprehensive visibility into performance, capacity, and health across all
instances.
• Consistent Automation Capabilities: Standardized automation templates and workflows deployable across the entire
fleet.
Common Elements Across VCF Fleet Deployment Designs
This section highlights the common elements that are shared across the four fleet deployment designs. Each design
is built on a unified framework for operating and managing a VCF fleet across single or multiple instances, leveraging
centralized management and automation capabilities. These designs provide a consistent approach to deploying,
consuming, and automating virtual machines, Kubernetes, and other infrastructure resources, ensuring scalability and
operational efficiency.

VCF Fleet Deployment with Site High Availability (Across Zones) Design
The VCF Fleet Deployment with Site High Availability (Across Zones) Design enhances the VCF Fleet Deployment Basic
Design by introducing fault domains that distribute resources across multiple physical hardware groups. This architecture
protects workloads from localized failures—single availability zone power outages, network disruptions, cooling system
issues, and hardware breakdowns.
The design maintains operational continuity when these failures occur by ensuring workloads remain available across
zones. Built on vSphere HA best practices, it supports three cluster models: Single-Rack, Multi-Rack, and Stretched
configurations. Organizations can select the appropriate model based on their infrastructure requirements and availability
targets.
Deploy this design when minimizing downtime and maintaining continuous availability are operational priorities.

VCF Fleet Deployment with Disaster Recovery (Across Regions) Design
The VCF Fleet Deployment with Disaster Recovery (Across Regions) Design protects organizations from site-wide failures
through integrated disaster recovery capabilities. Building on the VCF Fleet Deployment Basic Design, this architecture
uses VMware Live Recovery to enable seamless failover and failback between sites or regions.
The design replicates critical workloads across locations, reducing downtime and data loss during outages. Both Single-
Rack and Multi-Rack configurations are supported, providing deployment flexibility based on infrastructure requirements.
Organizations gain a resilient foundation that is built on fault tolerance and disaster recovery best practices—essential for
maintaining business operations when disruptions occur.

Fault domains distribute resources across physical hardware groups to minimize the impact of localized failures—
power outages, hardware breakdowns, or network disruptions within a single zone. Disaster recovery features, including
replication and failover, protect workloads against site-wide outages by enabling recovery across regions.
The design supports Single-Rack, Stretched, and Multi-Rack configurations, and follows vSphere HA, fault tolerance, and
disaster recovery best practices. Deploy this architecture when critical operations require protection from both localized
hardware failures and large-scale site disruptions.

VCF Automation Models
A VMware Cloud Foundation platform uses VCF Automation as the central provisioning console for your VCF fleet to
provide users self-service consumption of Kubernetes and cloud infrastructure resources "as a Service", while maintaining
control, security, and compliance, all available in a self-service portal.
VCF Automation runs on containers within a Kubernetes cluster, which is deployed on dedicated virtual appliances. The
VCF Automation infrastructure is visible in the vCenter inventory as individual nodes. During installation the dedicated
Kubernetes cluster is to orchestrate the deployment of the VCF Automation component containers and services.

vSphere Supervisor uses storage policies to integrate with storage available to vSphere. The policies represent datastores
and manage storage placement of vSphere Supervisor objects. Storage policies support vSphere cluster principal and
supplemental datastores configured.
When assigning storage for vSphere Supervisor, availability and performance considerations should be made in relation
to the underlying storage that supports the vSphere Zones that are used by vSphere Supervisor.

Storage Topologies for vSphere Zones
vSphere Supervisor supports different datastore topologies for vSphere Zones. These topologies define how storage is
presented to hosts in each zone and how workloads behave during a zone failure.
Figure 15: Zonal datastore
A zonal datastore is local to a single vSphere Zone and is only available to workloads in that zone.
Figure 16: Multi-zone datastore
A multi-zone datastore topology uses separate datastores per zone; each zone has its own datastore, with no storage-
level replication or automatic failover between zones, so application-level resilience is required.
Broadcom 774

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 17: Cross-zone datastore
A cross-zone datastore is a single logical datastore shared across multiple zones, providing infrastructure-level
availability and protection against the failure of an entire zone.
Broadcom 775

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Zone Datastore Type Description
Zonal datastore • The Zonal datastore is local to a single vSphere Zone.
• Datastore is attached to all the hosts that are part of the underlying vSphere cluster.
• Datastore is only accessible by workloads running within that vSphere Zone.
• This configuration provides high availability at the vSphere cluster level.
Multi-zone datastore • Multiple vSphere Zones, each with its own availability zone paired with a dedicated datastore.
• Datastore is attached to all the hosts that are part of the underlying vSphere cluster.
• Datastore is only accessible by workloads running within that vSphere Zone.
• Does not provide replication or failover capability. The application must provide HA functionality
Cross-zone datastore • A single logical datastore shared across multiple vSphere Zones, with the datastore spanning multiple
availability zones.
• This configuration provides high availability and fault tolerance at the infrastructure level, protecting
workloads from the failure of an entire availability zone.

Network Consumption Models
Network Consumption Models are the methods cloud users use to deploy and manage networking and security
capabilities withVMware Cloud Foundation. Different capabilities are supported according to the selected Network
Consumption Model.
VCF Automation All Apps Orgs Consumption Model
When the goal is to use the VMware Cloud Foundation infrastructure using VCF Automation via an All Apps Orgs, where
the management of compute, storage, and network is centralized via single UI/API, the cloud user should not interact
directly with the NSX UI/API other than for troubleshooting purposes. The cloud user should create and administer Virtual
Private Clouds (VPCs) via the VCF Automation API/UI.
Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Consumption Model
A VPC is a cloud networking construct, a secure, isolated virtual network within a cloud environment. VPCs bring the
same characteristics and consumption model of the public cloud to VMware Cloud Foundation.
The VPC is a foundational and required component for designs requiring VCF Automation All Apps Orgs, but it is also
the recommended network consumption model for any network topology aimed at supporting the manual deployment of
workloads, VCF Automation VM Only Orgs, or third-party automation tools.
VPCs can be configured and managed from the vCenter making the vSphere client the single user interface for managing
compute, network, and storage for simple single-tenant deployments. Multi-tenant deployments that do not require the
full capabilities of VCF Automation All Apps Org can leverage the NSX multi-tenancy framework to provision self-service
network and security services via the NSX UI or API.
NSX Segment Consumption Model
This model leverages NSX objects such as Tier-0/Tier-1 gateways and segments to deploy network topologies. This
model allows the network administrator to leverage all of the advanced NSX network capabilities but requires more
extensive networking and NSX-specific knowledge.
This model does not support VCF Automation All Apps Orgs, and while it does support VMware vSphere Kubernetes
Service (VKS), it is recommended that new deployments of VKS embrace the VPC-based topology.
The NSX Segment Consumption Model should be considered when the capabilities it provides compared to the VPC
Consumption Model are critical to meeting the design requirements. Among those, the ability to extend network topologies
across workload domains respective NSXinstances in different VMware Cloud Foundation instances via NSX Federation
is a primary use case.
VLAN Networking Consumption Model
In this model, the only VMware Cloud Foundation component participating in the networking functionalities is the vSphere
Distributed Switch, responsible for switching the traffic between the VMs running in the hypervisor and the physical
uplinks. Once the packets are delivered to the upstream physical switch, it is the responsibility of the physical network
fabric to deliver them to the appropriate destination. Virtual machines are connected to vSphere Distributed Port Groups
or NSX VLAN segments.
This model lacks the benefits provided by the NSX network virtualization which decouples the physical network from
the topology requirements of the applications and services that run on top of it. With NSX network virtualization, the
underlaying physical network fabric can be designed and operated based on a simpler and more stable model that does
not require following the application's lifecycle. The role of adapting to the ever-changing application requirements is
offloaded to the NSX network virtualization layer while the physical network fabric design can be centered on maximizing
throughput and high availability, minimizing latency, and optimizing operational efficiency.
The VLAN Networking Consumption Model is supported in VMware Cloud Foundation and may be appropriate for
specific use cases, but it is not recommended for the majority of scenarios as it lacks the benefits provided by network
virtualization.

network services. Each Workload Connectivity Model presents different capabilities regarding simplicity, performance,
service availability, and scalability.

for VCF management components.
VCF Management Services Component Models
VCF 9.1 introduces VCF management services to provide a unified architecture for centralized lifecycle and operational
functionalities. The VCF services runtime instance of the first VCF Instance hosts the fleet-level VCF management
services components that perform global operations and the instance-level components for that VCF Instance. Every
VCF Instance has a VCF services runtime instance that hosts the instance-level VCF management services that run local
tasks. This foundation allows for a unified architecture, simplified lifecycle management, and streamlined backup and
recovery of all hosted components.
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple VCF Management Services Models that provide different levels of
availability.
When deploying a new VCF Instance, you choose a component model and a deployment model for VCF management
services based on the profiles and needs of that instance.

VCF Management Network Models
VMware Cloud Foundation provides flexibility for the deployment of the VCF management components including (VCF
management services, VCF Operations, and VCF Automation) to different network types. Either vSphere distributed port
groups or NSX segments can be used.
Using VCF Installer by default the VCF management components are deployed to the VM management network,
the same network that is used to deploy vCenter, NSX Manager, and SDDC Manager. Or they can be deployed to a
dedicated distributed port group on a dedicated VLAN, known as the VCF management network.
Alternatively, custom networking can be selected which defers the deployment of VCF Operations and VCF Automation so
that an NSX segment or different vSphere distributed port group can be used. You must configure these networks after the
initial VCF Installer deployment is complete and before deploying the deferred VCF management components with VCF
Installer.
Note:
The VCF management services must always be deployed to a vSphere distributed port group. The full list of VCF
management services are described here VCF Management Services Models
NSX segments are required or if there are plans to stretch the network between VCF Instances using NSX Federation.
This might be the case if disaster recovery is implemented for the VCF management components.
Note:
The cloud proxy is a VCF Instance level management component and is always deployed to the VM
management network by VCF Installer.

VCF Operations Models
VMware Cloud Foundation utilizes VCF Operations as the central console for operating your VCF fleet. It provided
dashboards, log analysis, issues reporting, and licensing. VCF Operations also provides fleet management capabilities
such as fleet extension, lifecycle, certificate, and password management.
Broadcom 795

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations Models
Use the VCF Installer to deploy your new VCF fleet, which includes vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations, VCF Automation, and
SDDC Manager. At deployment time you must select one of the VCF Operations Models based on your organizational
objectives.
vCenter and SDDC Manager are always deployed as single node. You have the flexibility to choose whether to deploy
NSX Manager, VCF Operations, VCF Automation, and VCF Management Services as single node deployments, or as

Identity Broker Models
VMware Cloud Foundation provides identity and access management services to VCF fleet components. You build your
authentication design by using three main components - your external Identity Provider (IdP), identity broker, and VCF
Single Sign-On.
Your corporate identity provider is the centralized source of digital identities for your enterprise, which provides
authentication and identity assertion. You connect the corporate identity provider to your VCF fleet components by using
identity broker. Identity broker enables a VCF Single Sign-On implementation and streamlines authentication across
different VCF fleet components, except for SDDC Manager. The third component of this design is VCF Single Sign-On,
which provides centralized authentication, identity federation, and user management.
Identity Broker Models
The identity broker component acts as the single broker for VCF Single Sign-On that all components in a VMware Cloud
Foundation platform can authenticate to. It connects to your identity provider or directory, maintains Single Sign-On tokens
and validates users as they log into VCF fleet components. Identity broker is consumed as an embedded service, running
on vCenter, or deployed as an instance. Instance model is the recommended deployment for production environments.

VCF Domain Models
When deploying a VCF Instance within a VCF fleet, you determine the VCF Domain Models according to your objectives
for availability, networking, and security.
A VCF domain represents a logical unit of application-ready infrastructure that groups ESX hosts managed by a vCenter
instance with specific characteristics according to VMware recommended practices. A VCF domain can have one or more
vSphere Cluster Models.

VCF Instances that are upgraded from an earlier version may have shared vCenter Single Sign-On domains.

vSphere Cluster Models
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple vSphere Cluster Models that provide different levels of availability to the
workloads running in a workload domain.
vSphere Cluster Models
A vSphere Cluster Model is defined and implemented per vSphere cluster and describes the maximum level of availability
that can be provided to virtual machines on that vSphere cluster. Each workload domain or VCF Instance can contain a
combination of the defined vSphere Cluster Models. You can also select to deploy a single vSphere Cluster Model in a
workload domain or VCF Instance according to your availability objectives.

zone that can be tagged as a vSphere Supervisor management and workload zone.

Distributed Switch Models
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple Distributed Switch Models that provide different levels of network availability,
performance, resilience, and scale.
Distributed Switch Models
VMware Cloud Foundation uses vSphere Distributed Switches to provide many network services, infrastructure networks,
virtual networking, etc. A vSphere Distributed Switch acts as a single switch across all associated ESX hosts in a vSphere
cluster to provide centralized provisioning, administration, and monitoring of networks.
vSphere Distributed Switches provide several services to ESX hosts and virtual machines. You can enable two types of
network services in ESX:
• Connecting virtual machines to the physical network and to each other.
• Connecting VMkernel services (such as management, vSphere vMotion, vSAN, and NSX host TEP) to the physical
network.
When you design vSphere cluster networking, consider the configuration of the vSphere Distributed Switches, distributed
port groups, and VMkernel adapters in the VMware Cloud Foundation platform. VMware Cloud Foundation provides a
flexible approach to vSphere Distributed Switch deployment options, the Distributed Switch Models are chosen based on
the design qualities, availability, manageability, performance, recoverability and security. The following table shows some
of the most common Distributed Switch Models, each with its benefits and implications listed.

between clusters in a VCF domain.

Storage Models
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple Storage Models that provide different levels of availability to workloads
running within a VCFdomain.
Principal and Supplemental Storage
• Principal storage is used during the creation of a VCF domain or a vSphere cluster and is capable of running
workloads.
• Supplemental storage can be added after the creation of a VCF domain or a vSphere cluster and can run workloads or
be used for data at rest storage (such as virtual machine templates, backup data, and ISO images).

Important:
vSAN Datastore Sharing (also known as "HCI Mesh") is permitted on all vSAN storage models within a VCF
domain. This allows multiple independent vSAN HCI Clusters to consume storage of adjacent vSAN storage
resources. This represents a flexible cross-cluster capacity sharing capability between vSAN clusters.
Figure 30: vSAN Storage
vSAN aggregates local, direct-attached storage devices across a vSphere cluster to create a single datastore that all
hosts and virtual machines in a vSAN cluster can access.
vSAN can be deployed in multiple different topologies such as single rack, multi-rack, stretched or as separate storage
and compute clusters.

Table 42: vSAN Storage Model Attributes
Attribute Detail
vSAN HCI Cluster A cluster that provides both compute and storage to virtual machines.
vSAN Storage Cluster A vSAN cluster that provides disaggregated storage for vSAN and vSphere clusters.
vSAN Compute Cluster A vSAN Compute Cluster is a vSphere cluster that does not have local vSAN storage, but instead, it
mounts a remote vSAN datastore.
vSAN Stretched Cluster A vSAN Stretched Cluster is a vSAN cluster topology that extends a single logical vSAN cluster
across two availability zones. A vSAN Stretched Cluster can tolerate a site failure.
vSAN Multi-Rack Cluster A vSAN multi-rack vSAN cluster is a vSAN cluster topology spread over different physical racks,
enhancing resilience and scalability. A multi-rack cluster can use vSAN fault domains to tolerate a
rack failure.
vSAN Datastore A distributed datastore that supports features that require shared storage.
vSAN Physical Networking Host network interfaces can be dedicated or shared with other traffic types.
vSAN Availability Workloads are protected by synchronously replicating objects in a vSAN cluster.

NSX Manager and Control Plane Models
NSX Manager and Control Plane is contained within the NSX Manager nodes. These manage and configure virtual
networking, including logical switches, Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), and transit gateways through a user interface and
API.
The NSX Manager nodes serve as the control plane for VMware Cloud Foundation networking by managing traffic flow
and network topologies.

NSX Global Manager Models
NSX Global Managers establish a centralized management plane to orchestrate consistent networking and security
policies across an NSX Federation. In contrast, NSX Local Managers provide management and control plane services
unique to a single VCF Instance or networking workload domain. While local managers maintain localized objects and
traffic flows, global managers enable the extension of segments and security groups across workload domains residing
within the same or different VCF Instances.

NSX Edge Cluster Models
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple NSX Edge Cluster Models, you determine the form factor, number of nodes
and placement according to the requirements for network services in a VCF instance. NSX Edge nodes can be shared
across workload domains where such workload domain shares an NSX Manager cluster.
An NSX Edge node is an appliance that provides centralized networking services which cannot be distributed to
hypervisors. Some services, such as Tier-0 gateways, are limited to a single instance per NSX Edge node. However,
multiple instances of most services can coexist in these nodes.
NSX Edge Form Factor
An NSX Edge node can be deployed as a virtual appliance, or installed on bare-metal hardware. The NSX Edge node on
bare-metal hardware can have better performance capabilities at the expense of more challenging deployment and limited
deployment topology use cases.

NSX Edge Cluster Models

During NSX Edge node deployment, the NSX Edge node supports either centralized password management
via VCF Operations or locally configured passwords. VCF Operations supports the password management
task 'update', which requires the current password before a new one can be configured. When centralized
password management is selected during a fresh NSX Edge node deployment, randomized passwords are
generated. These passwords can be retrieved, for example, via the SDDC Manager API (GET /v1/credentials),
and subsequently used to update the passwords through VCF Operations.

Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models, you determine the form factor,
node count, and placement based on the requirements for stateful network services within distributed VPC environments
running in a VCF domain.
A Virtual Network Appliance node is an appliance that provides stateful network services such NAT or VNA load balancer
which cannot be distributed to hypervisors running the Distributed Transit Gateway. North-South traffic that is sourced
from or destined to the hypervisor that requires stateful network services such as NAT are redirected to the Virtual
Network Appliance node.
Virtual Network Appliance Form Factor
Virtual Network Appliance  nodes can only be deployed as virtual appliances; other form factors are not available.

Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models
Virtual Network Appliance  nodes are grouped in one or more Virtual Network Appliance clusters, representing a pool of
capacity for stateful network services consumed by VPCs connected to a Distributed Transit Gateway.
Important:
Centralized password management via VCF Operations is the only supported option; local credentials cannot
be configured during the Virtual Network Appliance node deployment. VCF Operations supports the password
management task 'update', which requires the current password before a new one can be configured. A fresh
Virtual Network Appliance node deployment generates randomized passwords, which can be, for example,
retrieved via the SDDC Manager API (GET /v1/credentials) and subsequently used to update the passwords
using VCF Operations.
Broadcom 826

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
When using the Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model and a Virtual Network Appliance cluster is required, the
Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model is not supported. The external VLAN is, by design, stretched across
racks, which inherently implies a Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model. This limitation does not apply when
using the Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1.
Note:
The Virtual Network Appliance cluster provides a pool of capacity and runs one or more service instances for
stateful network services. One service instance is automatically configured per VPC when a stateful network
service is configured. When two or more Virtual Network Appliance nodes are part of the Virtual Network
Appliance cluster, the service instance is deployed in active/standby High Availability mode; active/active mode is
not supported. Each service instance is connected to exactly one of the four data plane fastpath interfaces, and
multiple service instances are distributed across all four data plane fastpath interfaces.
Note:
This section is exclusively for the use of Virtual Network Appliance nodes for stateful network services such as
NAT and not when the Virtual Network Appliance node is used as an EVPN Route Controller. The design section
for the EVPN Route Controller including the Virtual Network Appliance nodes is covered within the Workload
Connectivity Models section for VPC with EVPN integration.

Network Fabric Models
The data center network fabric facilitates communication between ESX hosts and VMware Cloud Foundation components
within and across VCF Instances. It also provides networking services to workload virtual machines via VLANs and Virtual
Networking.
Data Center Network Fabric Options
The Network Fabric Models define the physical and logical topologies that present Layer 2 and Layer 3 networking to
ESX hosts. There are four primary network topologies, each with implementation-specific advantages and integration
requirements:
• Campus-style Network Fabric (Core–Aggregation–Access)
• CLOS Network Fabric (Leaf-Spine/Superspine)
• Hardware SDN - Standards Based BGP-EVPN
• Hardware SDN - Proprietary Fabric
Each deployment has unique performance requirements based on design objectives, vSphere Cluster Models, Network
Consumption Models, and Storage Models. Key considerations include latency, bandwidth, MTU settings, gateway and
switch availability, and inter-site networking capacity, all of which must be properly sized for the specific design. To fully
leverage the VMware Cloud Foundation platform, the fabric must be highly performant data center-grade ethernet fabric
that meets the design availability goals.
VMware Cloud Foundation is generally agnostic to physical networking configurations, offering customers flexibility
in selecting their preferred topology. However, certain data center network fabric options and vendor-specific
Broadcom 828

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
implementations may affect the deployment of supported topologies and configurations. A thorough review of network
fabric requirements detailed in the design library section should be conducted in collaboration with the network fabric
vendor.
VMware Cloud Foundation supports optional integration with standards based EVPN-VXLAN fabrics to connect the Virtual
private clouds (VPCs) to the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric. In this model, VCF components setup BGP-EVPN
exchange between EVPN Route Controller and the physical fabric EVPN gateway to advertise internal prefixes directly
into the fabric's control plane. This integration utilizes BGP-EVPN Type-5 routes (IP Prefix routes) to advertise workload
prefixes associated with tenant VPCs. Utilizing Type-5 routes allows the physical fabric to dynamically learn the location
of workloads without requiring broad Layer 2 extension or manual static route configuration on the ToR switches. See
Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 for more details.
Network Fabric Models
The Network Fabric Models describe the physical and logical topologies to present Layer 2 and Layer 3 networking
to your ESX hosts. You must select the appropriate Network Fabric Model based on your specific requirements for
vSphere cluster scale, physical fault isolation, and availability spanning single racks, multiple racks, or multiple data center
availability zones.

Use Cases
In order to enable businesses to provide edge infrastructure everywhere, edge compute, network technologies, and
architectures will be required as business applications and workloads develop and spread beyond data centers and the
cloud to the sites where data is produced and consumed.
For customers looking to deploy edge solutions for use cases within retail, banking, energy, healthcare, and utilities,
VMware Cloud Foundation is a scalable solution that enables the ability to support secure, edge solutions using the full
stack or required elements of VMware Cloud Foundation.

and the level of abstraction of the underlying virtual infrastructure are the key factors in selecting the most appropriate
