Design Blueprints for VMware Cloud Foundation
This section contains an overview of the design blueprints that can be consumed when designing your VCF private cloud
with VMware Cloud Foundation.
• Infrastructure Modernization
Broadcom 836

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Application Modernization
• Security Modernization
Infrastructure Modernization
Build and Deploy Private Cloud infrastructure On-Premises
VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal The VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint is an infrastructure blueprint
Footprint where the management domain of the first VCF Instance is deployed with a minimal
footprint. All management and workload components are deployed in a single vSphere
cluster.
VCF Fleet in a Single Site The VCF Fleet in a Single Site is an infrastructure blueprint, where the management
domain of the first VCF Instance is deployed with high availability for management
components. Workloads are isolated to a separate workload domain. All components
are located within a single data center and a single availability zone.
VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region is an infrastructure blueprint,
Region where the management domain of the first VCF Instance is deployed with high
availability for management components. Workloads are isolated to a separate
workload domain. Multiple sites exist and stretched clusters are used to increase
availability across sites.
VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions is an infrastructure
Regions blueprint, where the management domain of the first VCF Instance is deployed with
high availability for management components. Workloads are isolated to a separate
workload domain. Multiple sites exist in different regions.
VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region Plus Additional Region(s) is an
Region plus Additional Region(s) infrastructure blueprint, where the management domain of the first VCF Instance is
deployed with high availability for management components. Workloads are isolated
to a separate workload domain. Multiple sites exist, where some sites co-exist in the
same region, and other sites exist in a different region.
Optimize Infrastructure and Operations
VCF Fleet Management Blueprint VCF Operations helps build, manage, and scale your private cloud infrastructure while
providing that consistency across each of its components.
VCF Monitoring and Alerting Blueprint This blueprint provides comprehensive guidance for monitoring a VMware Cloud
Foundation platform by using the monitoring components Real-time metrics, Log
management, and VCF Operations for networks. Effective monitoring is crucial for
maintaining the stability, performance, and health of the SDDC infrastructure.
VCF Troubleshooting Blueprint This blueprint is intended to help troubleshooting efforts for typical scenarios
experienced in an enterprise environment. The blueprint focuses on incident
management - identifying the cause of an occurring problem, and determining potential
solutions.
Extend Data Center to the Edge, Public, and Sovereign Clouds
VCF Edge: Single Node with Argo CD Design A single-node VCF Edge deployment consolidates the ESX hypervisor, vSphere
Blueprint Supervisor, and workload plane onto one physical host.
VCF Edge Design Blueprint for Government This blueprint focuses on federal use cases for a VCF Edge to address the unique
and Defense Use Case operational, security, and compliance needs of federal agencies on and off the
battlefield.
VCF Edge Design Blueprint for Manufacturing This blueprint focuses on manufacturing use cases for a VCF Edge to address the
Use Case unique operational, security, and compliance needs.
Application Modernization
Enable Self-Service Infrastructure and Cloud Services for App Teams
Self-Service Multi-Tenant Private Cloud The Self-Service Multi-Tenant Private Cloud Consumption blueprint provides guidance
Consumption Design Blueprint for implementing a self-service, multi-tenant private cloud. The blueprint delivers a
robust, scalable, and automated platform that offers agility and efficiency in resource
consumption, while adhering to commonly adopted design patterns.
Broadcom 837

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Build, Run, and Manage Kubernetes and Other Modern Workloads
VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service The VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service Consumption Blueprint provides
Consumption Blueprint architectural guidance for selecting and implementing the appropriate VMware
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) consumption model within VMware Cloud
Foundation platforms.
Build, Run, and Manage Private AI Apps
Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint The Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint describes the design selections
and architectural components required to deploy and operate a GenAI platform on
VMware Cloud Foundation. It is intended to be used in conjunction with an underlying
infrastructure blueprint.
Security Modernization
Bolster Lateral Security and Intrusion Detection and Prevention
Lateral Security with vDefend The Lateral Security with vDefend blueprints describes the architectural components
and design selections required to provide centralized, enterprise-grade security
services for a VMware Cloud Foundation platform using VMware vDefend.
Accelerate Recovery from Ransomware and Other Disasters
VCF Component Backup and Restore The VCF Component Backup and Restore blueprint provides guidance on ensuring the
resilience and continuity of your VCF private cloud. In the event of data loss or system
failure, having up-to-date backups allows for efficient restoration of critical services,
minimizing downtime and maintaining operational integrity. Implementing a consistent
backup strategy protects your infrastructure against unforeseen disruptions.
VCF Instance Backup and Restore The VCF Instance Backup and Restore blueprint provides guidance on the recovery of
an entire VCF Instance that has failed, and must be recovered in the same site.
VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery This VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery protection blueprint provides the ability to handle a
VCF Instance, or site failure, and recover components in another location, where that
location is typically outside metro radius.
Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud This Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation protection blueprint provides a
Foundation clean room environment on a vCenter instance that allows you to inspect, analyze, and
recover infected virtual machines before restoring them to a production environment.
Infrastructure Modernization
Broadcom, through its portfolio of VMware products, delivers a proven path to infrastructure modernization — helping
enterprises replace fragmented, legacy environments with a unified, software-defined platform. VMware solutions
consolidate compute, storage, and networking into a streamlined architecture that supports private cloud, hybrid
deployments, and modern application frameworks. The result: reduced operational overhead, stronger security posture,
and the agility to scale on demand — all without disrupting business continuity.

Expansion after Infrastructure Blueprint Deployment
The included infrastructure blueprints are starting points for the initial deployment and cover either a management domain
only, or a management domain and the first workload domain. All VCF deployments may be expanded in the following
ways and are subject to the limits defined in VMware Configuration Maximums.
Note:
Type of Expansion Method of Expansion Description
Resource Expansion Add hosts to an existing vSphere cluster. Adds compute capacity (and storage if using vSAN)
with automated workload balancing and failover within
the scope of the entire cluster. All ESX hosts in a
cluster must have the same configuration and access
to resources (networking, storage).
Add vSphere clusters to an existing VCF domain. Adds compute capacity (and storage if using vSAN)
in an isolated scope from workloads in other clusters.
Can have different configuration, networking and/or
storage from other clusters. Automated failover and
workload balancing does not span across clusters.
Add workload domains to an existing VCF Instance. Provides separate management and control plane
(vCenter) from other workload domains, allowing
for different configurations or to support separate
locations or access.
Add VCF Instances to an existing VCF fleet. Provides separate management and networking from
other instances, allowing for different configurations
or to support separate locations, while maintaining a
common consumption instance (VCF Operations, and
VCF Automation.
Availability Expansion Add Interconnected Site (in the same region) Steps are required to create additional availability
by deploying new or modifying the configuration of
existing vSphere clusters in that site.
Add Interconnected Site (in another region) Steps are required to create additional availability
by deploying new or modifying the configuration of
existing vSphere clusters in that site.

The consumption layer for the VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint infrastructure blueprint represents
the top-most tier of a modern data and application architecture, serving as the primary interface between end users
and underlying systems. This layer is where business value is realized through direct interaction with processed data,
applications, and services.

authentication.

Instance Identity Broker Model Attributes
The Instance Identity Broker Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Service Location Identity broker runs as a service on VCF Management Services.
Deployment mechanism An identity broker is automatically deployed during the installation or upgrade to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 in the first management domain. Additional identity brokers can be
deployed in each VCF Instance as part of a day 2 operation.
Number of Nodes multi-node cluster.
Scale considerations • Scale up: Identity broker supports small, medium, and large sizes to match different
configuration demands.
• Scale out: Support for multiple identity broker instances to increase redundancy and
throughput.
• Recommendations:
– Scaling up is preferred over scaling out when a single large-size identity broker meets
security, resilience, and performance standards, as it reduces operational complexity
and simplifies SSO management.
– Schedule scale-up operations within a maintenance window, as these activities can
impact active services.
Supported services For support directories and IdPs, see Identity Providers and Protocols Supported for Single
Sign-On.
Backup and restore Use VCF management services backup and restore process.
Resiliency Resiliency is provided by a distributed multiple-node deployment running each node on
separate vSphere hosts.
Operational Impacts As an isolated, external service, operational tasks performed on vCenter do not impact the
authentication stack of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
Migration path Migrating from the appliance to embedded requires a reset of the VCF Single Sign-On
configuration. Users must be re-added to components.

Scale Low Scale - A single identity broker services all VCF Instances in your VCF fleet.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services,
and workloads within an organization's Software-Defined Data Center. This essential layer provides the fundamental
capabilities required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which
higher-level services and applications are constructed.

vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Table 84: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.
Broadcom 879

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 881

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 87: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Single Distributed Switch Model Options
A Single Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) • Use a single 2-port NIC (no NLR).
• Use two separate 2-port NICs.
– Each traffic type is spread across two separate NIC to avoid single point of failure.
– Results in unused ports on NIC.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.

Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Attribute Detail
Virtual Machine Storage policies vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN 9.1 automatically configures vSAN Auto-RAID policy on new vSAN ESA clusters.
vSAN Auto-RAID policy manages the resilience for data residing in a cluster, regardless of
the size or topology of the vSAN cluster. vSAN Auto-RAID creates a single policy within the
vCenter server,

Physical Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint
The physical infrastructure layer constitutes the hardware and facilities that provide the foundational computing, storage,
and networking resources.
Single-Rack Network Fabric Model
The VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint infrastructure blueprint uses the Single-Rack Network Fabric Model.
Selected Model Additional Information
Single-Rack Network Fabric Model The data center network fabric provides connectivity to the
vSphereclusters. The selected vSphere Cluster Models and
Storage Models determine which data center availability model
can support the connectivity and availability in the cluster. This
section describes the requirements to support a Single-Rack
vSphere Cluster Model. Depending upon the storage type chosen,
additional VLAN requirements may apply.
The data center network fabric provides connectivity to the vSphere clusters. The vSphere Cluster Models and Storage
Models chosen will determine which data center availability model is required to support the connectivity and availability
within the cluster. This section describes the requirements to support a Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model. Depending
upon the storage type chosen, additional VLAN requirements may apply.

VCF Fleet in a Single Site
The VCF Fleet in a Single Site is an infrastructure blueprint, where the management domain of the first VCF Instance is
deployed with high availability for management components and workloads are isolated to a separate workload domain.
All components are located within a single data center and a single availability zone.

Management Domain Design Selection
The following models were selected for the management domain to align with the design profile of the VCF Fleet in a
Single Site infrastructure blueprint.
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Consumption High Availability VCF Automation Model The High Availability VCF Automation Model consists
of a three-node deployment. This model provides
resiliency at both the application level through the
clustered deployment and the vSphere cluster level
through vSphere HA and vSphere DRS functionality.
Tenancy Deployment Model 2: Shared Workload This model offers a multi-tenant VMware Cloud
Domain for Multiple Organizations in a VCF Instance Foundation platform where multiple organizations share
a single workload domain. Isolation is achieved through
vSphere Namespaces and network segmentation.
Operations High Availability VCF Operations Model The High Availability VCF Operations Model deploys a
three node cluster for the analytic engine, and a single
cloud proxy appliance. To achieve high availability
after the initial deployment, an additional cloud proxy
appliance should be deployed and then combined in a
collector group.
VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance The first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet runs a VCF
Model management services cluster with a combination of fleet
level and instance level components for managing all
VCF Instances in the fleet.
High Availability VCF Management Services Model The High Availability VCF Management Services Model
deploys multiple control plane nodes and multiple
worker nodes, and uses vSphere HA as an availability
mechanism.
Single License Server Model The Single License Server Model is the default
configuration for VMware Cloud Foundation platform,
designed to provide centralized license management
for the entire fleet. It is suitable for most deployments
where reduced operational overhead is prioritized.
High Availability VCF Operations for Networks Model The High Availability VCF Operations for Networks
Model consists of a three-node deployment. This
model provides increased performance and scalability.
Availability is provided by the native vSphere HA
functionality within the vSphere cluster.
Broadcom 909

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
High Availability Log Management Model The High Availability Log Management Model consists
of a three-node deployment behind an internal load
balancer. This model provides resiliency at both the
application level through the clustered deployment
and the vSphere cluster level through vSphere HA and
vSphere DRS functionality.
Security Instance Identity Broker Model Deploys the Identity Broker component on the VCF
Governance and Management Services instance in the management
Compliance domain.
VCF Fleet Level Single Sign On Model Single Identity Broker deployment. A user can log in
once and can gain VCF Single Sign-On capabilities for
all components across all VCF Instances in the same
VCF fleet.
Virtual Management Domain Model The management domain in a VCF fleet hosts the
Infrastructure management components of the VCF Instance where
it is deployed and the management components of the
fleet.
VCF Management Shared VLAN Network Model VCF management components can be deployed to
the same vSphere Distributed Switch port group used
for the VCF Instance level management components
( vCenter, NSX Manager, and SDDC Manager). This
can be achieved using VCF Installer during initial
deployment of the VCF fleet or more instances in the
fleet.

Shared Design Selection Across Management Domain and Workload Domain
The following models are shared across both the management domain and workload domain in the VCF Fleet in a Single
Site infrastructure blueprint.
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Virtual vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high
Infrastructure availability, and identity domain isolation of the vCenter
instances for the VCF domains in a VCF fleet.
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your
VMware Cloud Foundation platform, consider the
resources, networking, and security policies that
are required to support the virtual machines in each
VCFdomain vSphere cluster.
Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model The Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model is the simplest
form of protection where workloads are deployed to a
vSphere cluster in the same physical rack, in a single
availability zone.
Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model in
VMware Cloud Foundation provides separation of
storage traffic from all other network services running on
the vSphere cluster.
Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model vSAN ESA uses a single-tier architecture that utilizes
high-performance flash storage devices. vSAN ESA
supports only NVMe high-performance storage devices.
High Availability NSX Manager Model This model addresses use cases requiring the highest
scale, optimized operations, and maximum availability
requirements.
Physical Single-Rack Network Fabric Model The data center network fabric provides connectivity
Infrastructure to the vSphere clusters. The vSphere Cluster Models
and Storage Models chosen will determine which data
center availability model is required to support the
connectivity and availability within the cluster. This
section describes the requirements to support a Single-
Rack Cluster Model. Depending upon the storage type
chosen, additional VLAN requirements may apply.

The security governance and compliance layer refers to the framework of policies, procedures, and controls that
organizations establish to manage security risks while meeting regulatory, legal, and industry standards around
authentication.

Instance Identity Broker Model Attributes
The Instance Identity Broker Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Service Location Identity broker runs as a service on VCF Management Services.
Deployment mechanism An identity broker is automatically deployed during the installation or upgrade to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 in the first management domain. Additional identity brokers can be
deployed in each VCF Instance as part of a day 2 operation.
Number of Nodes multi-node cluster.
Scale considerations • Scale up: Identity broker supports small, medium, and large sizes to match different
configuration demands.
• Scale out: Support for multiple identity broker instances to increase redundancy and
throughput.
• Recommendations:
– Scaling up is preferred over scaling out when a single large-size identity broker meets
security, resilience, and performance standards, as it reduces operational complexity
and simplifies SSO management.
– Schedule scale-up operations within a maintenance window, as these activities can
impact active services.
Supported services For support directories and IdPs, see Identity Providers and Protocols Supported for Single
Sign-On.
Backup and restore Use VCF management services backup and restore process.
Resiliency Resiliency is provided by a distributed multiple-node deployment running each node on
separate vSphere hosts.
Operational Impacts As an isolated, external service, operational tasks performed on vCenter do not impact the
authentication stack of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
Migration path Migrating from the appliance to embedded requires a reset of the VCF Single Sign-On
configuration. Users must be re-added to components.

Scale Low Scale - A single identity broker services all VCF Instances in your VCF fleet.

Availability Low Availability per Private Cloud - A single identity broker servicing all VCF Instances in

VCF Instances within the same VCF fleet.

• Failure Scenario 1

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet in a Single Site
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.

Shared Design Selection between Management and Workload Domain
Shared Design Selections between Management and Workload Domain are the models that are the same across the VCF

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet in a Single Site
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.
vCenter Model
The vCenter Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet in a Single Site infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high availability,
and identity domain isolation of the vCenter instances for the VCF
domains in a VCF fleet.
vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Broadcom 961

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Table 148: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.

ESX Model
The ESX Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet in a Single Site infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, consider the resources, networking, and
security policies that are required to support the virtual machines
in each VCF domain vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 964

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 151: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model Attributes
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Number of vSphere Distributed Switches Two (2)
Number of Physical NICs per ESX Host Four (4)
Bandwidth • Shared for Management, vSphere vMotion, NSX workloads.
• Dedicated for IP storage.
Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model Options
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric • Single (all traffic on same fabric).
• Dual (storage traffic isolated to dedicated fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across different network cards.
NLR:
• Use two or more network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across separate network cards to avoid single point of failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.
Shared vDS (VCF 9.1.1 onwards for • No - Dedicated vDS per cluster
Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model Attributes
A Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Single Tier All data is stored on the same type of storage device, regardless of access frequency or
importance.
Storage Pool All NVMe Flash Storage.
Data Services • Compression (enabled by default).
• Encryption. (in transit and at rest)
• vSAN Global Deduplication
Restriction:
vSAN Global Deduplication is not currently compatible with vSAN Stretched Clusters
and Two Node vSAN Clusters.
• Integrated vSAN File Services.
• vSAN iSCSI Target Service.
• vSAN Storage Clusters.
• Stretched Cluster.
• Fault domains.
• Kubernetes persistent storage services (block and file).
• Native scalable snapshots
Virtual Machine Storage policies vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN 9.1 automatically configures vSAN Auto-RAID policy on new vSAN ESA clusters.
vSAN Auto-RAID policy manages the resilience for data residing in a cluster, regardless of
the size or topology of the vSAN cluster. vSAN Auto-RAID creates a single policy within the
vCenter server,

Physical Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet in a Single Site
The physical infrastructure constitutes the tangible hardware and facilities layer that provides the foundational computing,
storage, and networking resources upon which all digital services depend. This layer encompasses the actual physical
assets—servers, storage arrays, network equipment, and supporting facilities—that form the bedrock of modern IT
operations.

VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region
The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region is an infrastructure blueprint, where the management domain of the
first VCF Instance is deployed with high availability for management components and workloads are isolated to a separate
workload domain. Multiple sites exist and stretched clusters are used to increase availability across sites.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Management Domain Design Selections
The following models in the design align with the objectives for deploying the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single
Region infrastructure blueprint.
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Consumption High Availability VCF Automation Model The High Availability VCF Automation Model consists
of a three-node deployment. This model provides
resiliency at both the application level through the
clustered deployment and the vSphere cluster level
through vSphere HA and vSphere DRS functionality.
Tenancy Deployment Model 2: Shared Workload This model offers a multi-tenant VMware Cloud
Domain for Multiple Organizations in a VCF Instance Foundation platform where multiple organizations share
a single workload domain. Isolation is achieved through
vSphere Namespaces and network segmentation.
Operations High Availability VCF Operations Model The High Availability VCF Operations Model deploys a
three node cluster for the analytic engine, and a single
cloud proxy appliance. To achieve high availability
after the initial deployment, an additional cloud proxy
appliance should be deployed and then combined in a
collector group.
VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance The first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet runs a VCF
Model management services cluster with a combination of fleet
level and instance level components for managing all
VCF Instances in the fleet.
High Availability VCF Management Services Model The High Availability VCF Management Services Model
deploys multiple control plane nodes and multiple
worker nodes, and uses vSphere HA as an availability
mechanism.
Single License Server Model The Single License Server Model is the default
configuration for VMware Cloud Foundation platform,
designed to provide centralized license management
for the entire fleet. It is suitable for most typical
deployments where reduced operational overhead is
prioritized.
Broadcom 995

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
High Availability VCF Operations for Networks Model The High Availability VCF Operations for Networks
Model consists of a three-node deployment. This
model provides increased performance and scalability.
Availability is provided by the native vSphere HA
functionality within the vSphere cluster.
High Availability Log Management Model The High Availability Log Management Model consists
of a three-node deployment behind an internal load
balancer. This model provides resiliency at both the
application level through the multi-replica deployment,
VCF management services to restart replicas, and
vSphere HA to restart nodes in the event of an ESX
host or log management component failure.
Security Instance Identity Broker Model Deploys the Identity Broker component on the VCF
Governance and management services instance in the management
Compliance domain.
VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model Single Identity Broker deployment. A user can log in
once and can gain VCF Single Sign-On capabilities for
all components across all VCF Instances in the same
VCF fleet.
Virtual Management Domain Model The management domain in a VCF fleet hosts the
Infrastructure management components of the VCF Instance where
it is deployed and the management components of the
fleet.
VCF Management Shared VLAN Network Model VCF management components can be deployed to
the same vSphere Distributed Switch port group used
for the VCF Instance level management components
( vCenter, NSX Manager, and SDDC Manager). This
can be achieved using VCF Installer during initial
deployment of the VCF fleet or more instances in the
fleet.

Selected Model Additional Information
Single License Server Model The Single License Server Model is the default configuration
for VMware Cloud Foundation platform, designed to provide
centralized license management for the entire fleet. It is suitable
for most typical deployments where reduced operational overhead
is prioritized.
Table 185: Single License Server Model Attributes
Attribute
Detail
Use Cases This is the typical license server deployment model for VMware Cloud Foundation and is
suitable for most VCF deployments.
Deployment mechanism One license server per VCF fleet. A license server is automatically deployed as part of the
installation or upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.
Backup and restore Backup is not required. If the original license server becomes unavailable, deploy a new
license server instance and migrate the licenses within 90 days.
Lifecycle The upgrade and patch management of the license server is managed through VCF
Operations.
High Availability High availability is provided by vSphere HA.
License Scope A single license server provides licensing management for the whole VCF fleet.

Instance Identity Broker Model Attributes
The Instance Identity Broker Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Service Location Identity broker runs as a service on VCF Management Services.
Deployment mechanism An identity broker is automatically deployed during the installation or upgrade to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 in the first management domain. Additional identity brokers can be
deployed in each VCF Instance as part of a day 2 operation.
Number of Nodes multi-node cluster.
Scale considerations • Scale up: Identity broker supports small, medium, and large sizes to match different
configuration demands.
• Scale out: Support for multiple identity broker instances to increase redundancy and
throughput.
• Recommendations:
– Scaling up is preferred over scaling out when a single large-size identity broker meets
security, resilience, and performance standards, as it reduces operational complexity
and simplifies SSO management.
– Schedule scale-up operations within a maintenance window, as these activities can
impact active services.
Supported services For support directories and IdPs, see Identity Providers and Protocols Supported for Single
Sign-On.
Backup and restore Use VCF management services backup and restore process.
Resiliency Resiliency is provided by a distributed multiple-node deployment running each node on
separate vSphere hosts.
Operational Impacts As an isolated, external service, operational tasks performed on vCenter do not impact the
authentication stack of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
Migration path Migrating from the appliance to embedded requires a reset of the VCF Single Sign-On
configuration. Users must be re-added to components.

VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model Attributes

Attribute
Detail
Scale Low Scale - A single identity broker services all VCF Instances in your VCF fleet.
Resources requirements Low Resource Footprint - A single identity broker deployment is required for one VCF fleet.
Operational Overhead Low Operational Overhead - An identity broker per VCF fleet will need to be managed
separately for operational tasks such as backup and restore.
Availability Low Availability per Private Cloud - A single identity broker servicing all VCF Instances in
your VCF fleet.
Blast Radius Large Blast Radius - An outage of one identity broker instance will impact logins for a single
VCF fleet.
Single Sign-On Realm Large SSO Realm - Users do not need to re-authenticate when moving between different
VCF Instances within the same VCF fleet.
Disaster Recovery Supported DR scenarios:
• Failure Scenario 1
• Failure Scenario 2 (Restoration Option 2a only): Because the identity broker is hosted
on the primary VCF instance, VCF instance restoration is required; Option 2b is not
applicable.
• Failure Scenario 3

required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.
vCenter Model
The vCenter Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high availability,
and identity domain isolation of the vCenter instances for the VCF
domains in a VCF fleet.
vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Table 214: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.

Foundation
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.

Selected Model Additional Information
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, consider the resources, networking, and

ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 1053

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 217: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Stretched vSphere Cluster Model
The Stretched vSphere Cluster Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region infrastructure
blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
Stretched vSphere Cluster Model The Stretched vSphere Cluster Model allows you to protect
workloads on vSphere clusters in your environment against
a failure of a single fault domain by implementing a stretched
vSphere cluster across multiple availability zones.
Broadcom 1056

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 95: Stretched Cluster Model
VCF Instance
Availability Zone 1 Availability Zone 2
Rack Rack
Workload Domain 1
Stretched Cluster
Stretched Cluster Model Attributes
A Stretched Cluster Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Datacenters Multiple datacenters
Cluster rack mapping • Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, each zone in a single rack.
• Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, with Layer 2 multi-rack clusters
in each zone.
Resilience • vSphere HA protects workloads against host failures.
• Multiple availability zones protect against availability zone failures.
Bandwidth • When using VMware vSAN™ stretched clusters, the bandwidth between the zones must
be at least 10 Gbps and the round-trip latency must be less than 5 ms.
• When using storage array based stretched clusters, you must work with your storage
vendor to define the bandwidth and latency requirements.
Management Domain Requirements Having the management domain on a stretched cluster is a prerequisite to configure and
implement stretched cluster in a workload domain. In this way, the critical management
components managing the workload domains are still available if an availability zone failure
occurs.
Availability Zones • You can have up to two availability zones associated with a given stretched cluster.
– In the case of vSAN stretched clusters, a third, independent fault domain is required to
host the vSAN witness appliance.
Stretched Cluster Model VLANs and Subnets
Function VLANs and Subnets
VM management Shared across availability zones
ESX management Unique per availability zone
vSphere vMotion Unique per availability zone
vSAN* Unique per availability zone
Host overlay Unique per availability zone
NFS* Depends on stretched storage design
Note:
*Optional based on principal storage choice for the cluster

Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model Options
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric • Single (all traffic on same fabric).
• Dual (storage traffic isolated to dedicated fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across different network cards.
NLR:
• Use two or more network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across separate network cards to avoid single point of failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.
Shared vDS (VCF 9.1.1 onwards for • No - Dedicated vDS per cluster
Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Stretched vSAN Storage Model
The Stretched vSAN Storage Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region infrastructure
blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
Stretched vSAN Storage Model A Stretched vSAN Storage Model is a cluster configuration where
the ESX hosts, that comprise a single vSAN cluster, reside in two
availability zones.
Figure 97: Stretched vSAN Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
Stretched vSAN Storage Model depicting three availability zones for vSAN. Two availability zones are designated for
vSAN data nodes and a third availability zone is designated for a vSAN witness node.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stretched vSAN Storage Model Attributes
A Stretched vSAN Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Fault Domain / Avilability zone • Stretched vSAN clusters comprise of three (3) Fault domains. A fault domain comprises of
one or more vSAN nodes.
• A fault domain or availability zone can represent a physical location. Fault domains /
availability zones can either be two distinct data centers in a metro distance, or two safety
or fire sectors (data halls) in the same large-scale datacenter.
vSAN Traffic Type • Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Traffic type for data traffic.
• Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Witness Traffic type for vSAN meta-data traffic.
Note:
Stretched vSAN Storage clusters (ESA) can be configured to use vSAN Storage
Cluster Client traffic for vSAN compute client clusters. See Stretched vSAN Storage
Cluster Storage Model.
vSAN Witness Appliance A witness node is a pre-configured appliance that runs ESX and is distributed as an OVA file.

This design requires stretching a minimum number of VLAN segments between each availability zone. The physical
network fabric stretches these segments to provide a single Layer 2 domain across zones, enabling virtual machine
mobility during an availability zone outage. For these fabric-stretched VLAN segments, the first-hop gateway must remain
highly available across both availability zones. You must give special consideration to VLAN segments for NSX Edge
uplinks when using the Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge vSphere HA Recovery Model, as BGP peering from
the NSX Edge node to the fabric occurs over these networks.
Note:
VLAN IDs are switch-level numerical labels identifying a Layer 2 domain. In some fabric configurations, the same
VLAN ID may identify different domains, or different VLAN IDs may identify the same domain. A distributed port
group can be associated with a single VLAN ID. Any distributed port groups supporting virtual machines must
have the same VLAN ID and Layer 2 domain mapping across the entire vSphere cluster. You may use different
VLAN IDs for separate vSphere clusters that do not share a common vSphere Distributed Switch.

IP Connectivity and Symmetry
Traffic must be routed between availability zones for all VLAN segments that require cross-site communication. For
example, vSAN networks in each availability zone must have a route to each other to support synchronous data
replication.
For VLAN segments that stretch between availability zones, the physical network fabric determines the ingress and
egress paths. In most cases, to simplify troubleshooting, symmetrical routing is recommended.
For workloads, the ingress and egress path depends upon the Network Consumption Models chosen. For the Centralized
Connectivity Modelingress and egress paths depend on the specific NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability
Zonesand routing model:
• Static Routing: The physical network fabric determines the ingress and egress paths.
• eBGP: A combination of the physical fabric and the NSX Edge gateway determines the ingress and egress paths.
For all stretched VLAN network segments (infrastructure networks, VLAN Networking Connectivity Model or Distributed
VLAN Connectivity Model), or Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0, the physical network fabric must
provide a highly available Layer 3 gateway at the first hop. This ensures that virtual machines maintain connectivity on the
same IP address when moving between availability zones.
Broadcom 1089

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Witness Location
For vSAN stretched cluster, an independent witness site is required. This requires independent network paths from each
availability zone to the witness site, such that the failure of an individual availability zone does not impact the traffic path
from the other availability zones to the witness site.
When configured with vSAN Witness Traffic Separation (WTS), the vSAN witness traffic flows between the ESX
management VMkernels and the vSAN Witness node. This traffic uses the MTU of the ESX management VMkernels.
Availability Zone Data Center Interconnect
The data center inter-connect between the availability zones must be appropriately sized to handle all infrastructure,
workload, and storage replication traffic. The interconnect is important to the operations of the vSAN Cluster. It should
have the appropriate level of resilience to achieve business objectives.

The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions an infrastructure blueprint, where the management domain
of the first VCF Instance is deployed with high availability for management components and workloads are isolated to a
separate workload domain. Multiple sites exist in different regions.

Multiple Regions infrastructure blueprint.
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Consumption High Availability VCF Automation Model The High Availability VCF Automation Model consists of
a three-node deployment. This model provides resiliency
at both the application level through the clustered
deployment and the vSphere cluster level through
vSphere HA and vSphere DRS functionality.
Tenancy Deployment Model 2: Shared workload This model offers a multi-tenant VMware Cloud
domain for multiple organizations in a VCF Instance Foundation platform where multiple organizations share
a single workload domain. Isolation is achieved through
vSphere Namespaces and network segmentation.
Operations High Availability VCF Operations Model The High Availability VCF Operations Model deploys a
three node cluster for the analytic engine, and a single
Cloud Proxy appliance. To achieve high availability
after the initial deployment, an additional Cloud
Proxyappliance should be deployed and then combined
in a collector group.
VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance The first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet runs a VCF
Model management services cluster with a combination of fleet
level and instance level components for managing all
VCF Instances in the fleet.
VCF Management Services in an Additional VCF Additional VCF Instances in a fleet run a VCF
Instance Model management services cluster with instance level
components for managing that instance only.
High Availability VCF Management Services Model The High Availability VCF Management Services Model
deploys multiple control plane nodes and multiple
worker nodes, and uses vSphere HA as an availability
mechanism.
Single License Server Model The Single License Server Model is the default
configuration for VMware Cloud Foundation platform,
designed to provide centralized license management for
the entire fleet. It is suitable for most typical deployments
where reduced operational overhead is prioritized.
Broadcom 1092

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
High Availability VCF Operations for Networks Model The High Availability VCF Operations for Networks
Model consists of a four-node deployment. This model
provides increased performance and scalability.
Availability is provided by the native vSphere HA
functionality within the vSphere cluster.
High Availability Log Management Model The High Availability Log Management Model consists
of a three-node deployment behind and internal load
balancer. This model provides resiliency at both the
application level through the clustered deployment
and the vSphere cluster level through vSphere HA and
vSphere DRS functionality.
Security Identity Broker Model Deploys the Identity Broker component on the VCF
Governance and management services instance in the management
Compliance domain.
VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model Single Identity Broker deployment. A user can log in
once and can gain VCF Single Sign-On capabilities for
all components across all VCF instances in the same
VCFfleet.
Virtual Management Domain Model The management domain in a VCF fleet hosts the
Infrastructure management components of the VCF Instance where
it is deployed and the management components of the
fleet.
VCF Management Shared VLAN Network Model VCF management components can be deployed to
the same vSphere Distributed Switch port group used
for the VCF Instance level management components (
vCenter, NSX Manager, and SDDC Manager). This can
be achieved using VCF Installer during initial deployment
of the VCF fleet or more instances in the fleet.

Consumption Single Management Zone with Combined Workload A Single Management Zone with Combined Workload

Virtual Network Appliance Load Balancer Model The Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) load balancer can

Virtual Workload Domain Model As you expand your VCF fleet, you can add workload

Selected Model Additional Information
Virtual vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high
Infrastructure availability, and identity domain isolation of the vCenter
instances for the VCF domains in a VCF fleet.
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your
VMware Cloud Foundation platform, consider the

Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model The Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model is the simplest
form of protection where workloads are deployed to a
vSphere cluster in the same physical rack, in a single
availability zone.
Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model A Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model in
VMware Cloud Foundation provides a separation of
workload traffic running on NSX segments from all other
network services running on the vSphere cluster.
Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model vSAN ESA uses a single-tier architecture that uses
high-performance flash storage devices. vSAN ESA
supports only NVMe high-performance storage devices.
High Availability NSX Manager Model The High Availability NSX Manager Model addresses
use cases requiring the highest scale, optimized
operations, and maximum availability requirements.
Physical Single-Rack Network Fabric Model The Single-Rack Network Fabric Model describes the
Infrastructure VLAN and gateway requirements to support the Single-
Rack vSphere Cluster Model.

the top-most tier of a modern data and application architecture, serving as the primary interface between end users
and underlying systems. This layer is where business value is realized through direct interaction with processed data,
applications, and services.

Security Governance and Compliance Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions
The security governance and compliance layer refers to the framework of policies, procedures, and controls that
organizations establish to manage security risks while meeting regulatory, legal, and industry standards around
authentication.

Instance Identity Broker Model Attributes
The Instance Identity Broker Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Service Location Identity broker runs as a service on VCF Management Services.
Deployment mechanism An identity broker is automatically deployed during the installation or upgrade to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 in the first management domain. Additional identity brokers can be
deployed in each VCF Instance as part of a day 2 operation.
Number of Nodes multi-node cluster.
Scale considerations • Scale up: Identity broker supports small, medium, and large sizes to match different
configuration demands.
• Scale out: Support for multiple identity broker instances to increase redundancy and
throughput.
• Recommendations:
– Scaling up is preferred over scaling out when a single large-size identity broker meets
security, resilience, and performance standards, as it reduces operational complexity
and simplifies SSO management.
– Schedule scale-up operations within a maintenance window, as these activities can
impact active services.
Supported services For support directories and IdPs, see Identity Providers and Protocols Supported for Single
Sign-On.
Backup and restore Use VCF management services backup and restore process.
Resiliency Resiliency is provided by a distributed multiple-node deployment running each node on
separate vSphere hosts.
Operational Impacts As an isolated, external service, operational tasks performed on vCenter do not impact the
authentication stack of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
Migration path Migrating from the appliance to embedded requires a reset of the VCF Single Sign-On
configuration. Users must be re-added to components.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.

components of the VCF Instance where it is deployed and the
management components of the fleet.

Attribute Details
Availability Model • Host level redundancy only.
• Single shared storage.
• This design cannot ensure continuous service availability for north-south communication
and centralized network services during a complete rack failure.
NSX Edge Node Mobility Mobility is not required when a compute policy type Best Effort Restart (BER) is configured.
Optional during ESX host maintenance by disabling the VM/host rule.
BGP Peering Establish BGP peering solely with the local ToR switches located within the same rack that
hosts the NSX Edge node.
NSX Edge Node and Link Failover • Fast NSX Edge node High Availability detection for NSX Edge node failures.
Mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for BGP.
North-South Bandwidth Growth • Add hosts to the single existing vSphere cluster or preferably transition to a rack fault
tolerant design with two or more vertical Layer 2 clusters in separate racks.
• When deploying more NSX Edge nodes on existing hosts, ensure each host has sufficient
CPU, memory, and importantly, additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain maximum
packet forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.
vCenter Model
The vCenter Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high availability,
and identity domain isolation of the vCenter instances for the VCF
domains in a VCF fleet.
vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Broadcom 1146

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Table 292: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.

ESX Model
The ESX Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, consider the resources, networking, and
security policies that are required to support the virtual machines
in each VCF domain vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 1149

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 295: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model Options
A Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric • Single (all traffic on same fabric).
• Dual (workload traffic using NSX and VPC networks isolated to a dedicated fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across different network cards.
NLR:
• Use two separate 2-port network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across two separate network cards to avoid single point of
failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.
Shared vDS (VCF 9.1.1 onwards for • No - Dedicated vDS per cluster
Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Attribute Detail
Virtual Machine Storage policies vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN 9.1 automatically configures vSAN Auto-RAID policy on new vSAN ESA clusters.
vSAN Auto-RAID policy manages the resilience for data residing in a cluster, regardless of
the size or topology of the vSAN cluster. vSAN Auto-RAID creates a single policy within the
vCenter server,

Physical Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites Across Multiple Regions
The physical infrastructure layer constitutes the tangible hardware and facilities layer that provides the foundational
computing, storage, and networking resources upon which all digital services depend. This layer encompasses the actual
physical assets—servers, storage arrays, network equipment, and supporting facilities—that form the bedrock of modern
IT operations.

VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s) infrastructure blueprint, where the
management domain of the first VCF Instance is deployed with high availability for management components and
workloads are isolated to a separate workload domain. Multiple sites exist, where some sites co-exist in the same region,
and other site(s) exist in a different region.
Broadcom 1178

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

The VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s) infrastructure blueprint is well suited to
customers who are looking for the following design profile for their VMware Cloud FoundationVMware Cloud Foundation
platform.
Attribute Value
Consumption • Self-service consumption via VCF Automation supporting modern workloads like VKS,
Data Services, AI Services, and so on. with multi-tenancy.
• Direct vCenter consumption supporting modern workloads like VKS, Data Services, AI

• Self-Service Multi-Tenant Private Cloud Consumption

Attribute Value
Availability • Tolerates failure of a single ESX host
• Tolerates failure of an individual network path
• Tolerates failure of a single rack

• Tolerates failure of a single availability zone
Isolation • Hypervisor-based (logical isolation)
• Network traffic type isolation
• Cluster-based (physical isolation)
