Management Domain Design Selections Region
The following models in the design align with the objectives for deploying this VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single
Region plus Additional Region(s) infrastructure blueprint.
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Consumption High Availability VCF Automation Model The High Availability VCF Automation Model consists of
a three-node deployment. This model provides resiliency
at both the application level through the clustered
deployment and the vSphere cluster level through
vSphere HA and vSphere DRS functionality.
Tenancy Deployment Model 2: Shared workload This model offers a multi-tenant VMware Cloud
domain for multiple organizations in a VCF Instance Foundation platform where multiple organizations share
a single workload domain. Isolation is achieved through
vSphere Namespaces and network segmentation.
Operations High Availability VCF Operations Model The High Availability VCF Operations Model deploys a
three node cluster for the analytic engine, and a single
Cloud Proxy appliance. To achieve high availability
after the initial deployment, an additional Cloud
Proxyappliance should be deployed and then combined
in a collector group.
VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance The first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet runs a VCF
Model management services cluster with a combination of fleet
level and instance level components for managing all
VCF Instances in the fleet.
VCF Management Services in an Additional VCF Additional VCF Instances in a fleet run a VCF
Instance Model management services cluster with instance level
components for managing that instance only.
High Availability VCF Management Services Model The High Availability VCF Management Services Model
deploys multiple control plane nodes and multiple
worker nodes, and uses vSphere HA as an availability
mechanism.
Broadcom 1180

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Layer Selected Model Additional Information
Single License Server Model The Single License Server Model is the default
configuration for VMware Cloud Foundation platform,
designed to provide centralized license management for
the entire fleet. It is suitable for most typical deployments
where reduced operational overhead is prioritized.
High Availability VCF Operations for Networks Model The High Availability VCF Operations for Networks
Model consists of a four-node deployment. This model
provides increased performance and scalability.
Availability is provided by the native vSphere HA
functionality within the vSphere cluster.
High Availability Logs Management Model The High Availability Log Management Model consists
of a three-node deployment behind and internal load
balancer. This model provides resiliency at both the
application level through the clustered deployment
and the vSphere cluster level through vSphere HA and
vSphere DRS functionality.
Security Identity Broker Model Deploys the Identity Broker component on the VCF
Governance and management services instance in the management
Compliance domain.
Single VCF Instance Single Sign On Model With the Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model
each VCF Instance will utilize its own dedicated identity
broker. The VCF Single Sign-On scope will be limited to
the VCF Instance. VCF management components, such
as VCF Operations and VCF Automation, can connect to
only one of identity broker instances for Single Sign-On.
Virtual Management Domain Model The management domain in a VCF fleet hosts the
Infrastructure management components of the VCF Instance where
it is deployed and the management components of the
fleet.
VCF Management Shared VLAN Network Model VCF management components can be deployed to
the same vSphere Distributed Switch port group used
for the VCF Instance level management components (
vCenter, NSX Manager, and SDDC Manager). This can
be achieved using VCF Installer during initial deployment
of the VCF fleet or more instances in the fleet.

blueprint represents the top-most tier of a modern data and application architecture, serving as the primary interface
between end users and underlying systems. This layer is where business value is realized through direct interaction with
processed data, applications, and services.

Instance Identity Broker Model Attributes
The Instance Identity Broker Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Service Location Identity broker runs as a service on VCF Management Services.
Deployment mechanism An identity broker is automatically deployed during the installation or upgrade to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 in the first management domain. Additional identity brokers can be
deployed in each VCF Instance as part of a day 2 operation.
Number of Nodes multi-node cluster.
Scale considerations • Scale up: Identity broker supports small, medium, and large sizes to match different
configuration demands.
• Scale out: Support for multiple identity broker instances to increase redundancy and
throughput.
• Recommendations:
– Scaling up is preferred over scaling out when a single large-size identity broker meets
security, resilience, and performance standards, as it reduces operational complexity
and simplifies SSO management.
– Schedule scale-up operations within a maintenance window, as these activities can
impact active services.
Supported services For support directories and IdPs, see Identity Providers and Protocols Supported for Single
Sign-On.
Backup and restore Use VCF management services backup and restore process.
Resiliency Resiliency is provided by a distributed multiple-node deployment running each node on
separate vSphere hosts.
Operational Impacts As an isolated, external service, operational tasks performed on vCenter do not impact the
authentication stack of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
Migration path Migrating from the appliance to embedded requires a reset of the VCF Single Sign-On
configuration. Users must be re-added to components.

Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model Attributes
The Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Scale High Scale - A single identity broker service for each VCF Instance.
Resources requirements Large Resource Footprint - Each identity broker deployment will require additional
compute / memory / storage resources.
Operational Overhead High Operational Overhead - Each identity broker will need to be managed separately for
operational tasks such as backup and restore.
Availability High Availability per Private Cloud - A single identity broker servicing each VCF Instance.
Blast Radius Small Blast Radius - An outage of one identity broker instance will only impact logins for the
VCF Instance associated with it.
Single Sign-On Realm Small SSO Realm - For each identity broker deployment users will have an additional Single
Sign-On realm. Moving across instances will require re-entering credentials.
Disaster Recovery Supported DR scenarios:
• Failure Scenario 1
• Failure Scenario 2 (Restoration Option 2a only): Option 2b is not a viable option because
restoring across different SSO realms is not supported.
• Failure Scenario 3
Note: local accounts and VCF SSO emergency access client (for API access) continue to
work during outages.

The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.

Dual Availability Zone Design Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model Attributes
The Dual Availability Zone Design Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Details
Availability Model • Host and availability zone redundancy.
• Independent shared storage per vSphere cluster when using vSAN or single shared
storage.
• This design ensures continuous north-south communication and centralized network
services even if one availability zone completely fails.
NSX Edge Node Mobility • Mobility is not supported across racks/availabilty zones when using multiple instances of
the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model.
Mobility is not supported across availability zones when using the vSphere Stretched
Cluster Model.
• Mobility is not required within a single availability zone when a compute policy type Best
Effort Restart (BER) is configured. Optional during ESX host maintenance by disabling the
VM/host rule.
BGP Peering Establish BGP peering solely with the local ToR switches located within the same availability
zones that hosts the NSX Edge node.
NSX Edge Node and Link Failover • Fast NSX Edge node High Availability detection for NSX Edge node failures.
Mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for BGP.
North-South Bandwidth Growth • Add more hosts to both vSphere clusters simultaneously or scale out the stretched
vSphere cluster with additional hosts in each availability zone.
• When deploying more NSX Edge nodes on existing ESX hosts, ensure each ESX host
has sufficient CPU, memory, and importantly, additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain
maximum packet forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
The virtual infrastructure layer represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.
vCenter Model
The vCenter Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
vCenter Model The vCenter design considers the location, size, high availability,
and identity domain isolation of the vCenter instances for the VCF
domains in a VCF fleet.
vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Broadcom 1238

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 361: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.

ESX Model
The ESX Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, consider the resources, networking, and
security policies that are required to support the virtual machines
in each VCF domain vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 1241

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 364: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Stretched vSphere Cluster Model
The Stretched vSphere Cluster Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional
Region(s) infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
Stretched vSphere Cluster Model The Stretched vSphere Cluster Model allows you to protect
workloads on vSphere clusters in your environment against
a failure of a single fault domain by implementing a stretched
vSphere cluster across multiple availability zones.
Broadcom 1244

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 146: Stretched Cluster Model
VCF Instance
Availability Zone 1 Availability Zone 2
Rack Rack
Workload Domain 1
Stretched Cluster
Stretched Cluster Model Attributes
A Stretched Cluster Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Datacenters Multiple datacenters
Cluster rack mapping • Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, each zone in a single rack.
• Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, with Layer 2 multi-rack clusters
in each zone.
Resilience • vSphere HA protects workloads against host failures.
• Multiple availability zones protect against availability zone failures.
Bandwidth • When using VMware vSAN™ stretched clusters, the bandwidth between the zones must
be at least 10 Gbps and the round-trip latency must be less than 5 ms.
• When using storage array based stretched clusters, you must work with your storage
vendor to define the bandwidth and latency requirements.
Management Domain Requirements Having the management domain on a stretched cluster is a prerequisite to configure and
implement stretched cluster in a workload domain. In this way, the critical management
components managing the workload domains are still available if an availability zone failure
occurs.
Availability Zones • You can have up to two availability zones associated with a given stretched cluster.
– In the case of vSAN stretched clusters, a third, independent fault domain is required to
host the vSAN witness appliance.
Stretched Cluster Model VLANs and Subnets
Function VLANs and Subnets
VM management Shared across availability zones
ESX management Unique per availability zone
vSphere vMotion Unique per availability zone
vSAN* Unique per availability zone
Host overlay Unique per availability zone
NFS* Depends on stretched storage design
Note:
*Optional based on principal storage choice for the cluster

Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model Attributes
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Number of vSphere Distributed Switches Two (2)
Number of Physical NICs per ESX Host Four (4)
Bandwidth • Shared for Management, vSphere vMotion, NSX workloads.
• Dedicated for IP storage.
Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model Options
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric • Single (all traffic on same fabric).
• Dual (storage traffic isolated to dedicated fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across different network cards.
NLR:
• Use two or more network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across separate network cards to avoid single point of failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.
Shared vDS (VCF 9.1.1 onwards for • No - Dedicated vDS per cluster
Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Stretched vSAN Storage Model Attributes
A Stretched vSAN Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Fault Domain / Avilability zone • Stretched vSAN clusters comprise of three (3) Fault domains. A fault domain comprises of
one or more vSAN nodes.
• A fault domain or availability zone can represent a physical location. Fault domains /
availability zones can either be two distinct data centers in a metro distance, or two safety
or fire sectors (data halls) in the same large-scale datacenter.
vSAN Traffic Type • Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Traffic type for data traffic.
• Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Witness Traffic type for vSAN meta-data traffic.
Note:
Stretched vSAN Storage clusters (ESA) can be configured to use vSAN Storage
Cluster Client traffic for vSAN compute client clusters. See Stretched vSAN Storage
Cluster Storage Model.
vSAN Witness Appliance A witness node is a pre-configured appliance that runs ESX and is distributed as an OVA file.

Physical Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
The physical infrastructure layer constitutes the tangible hardware and facilities layer that provides the foundational
computing, storage, and networking resources upon which all digital services depend. This layer encompasses the actual
Broadcom 1274

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
physical assets—servers, storage arrays, network equipment, and supporting facilities—that form the bedrock of modern
IT operations.
Multi Availability Zone Network Fabric Model
The Multi Availability Zone Network Fabric Model was chosen for the VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus
Additional Region(s) infrastructure blueprint.
Selected Model Additional Information
Multi Availability Zone Network Fabric Model This section describes the VLAN and gateway requirements to
support a vSphere cluster within multiple availability zones.
This design requires stretching a minimum number of VLAN segments between each availability zone. The physical
network fabric stretches these segments to provide a single Layer 2 domain across zones, enabling virtual machine
mobility during an availability zone outage. For these fabric-stretched VLAN segments, the first-hop gateway must remain
highly available across both availability zones. You must give special consideration to VLAN segments for NSX Edge
uplinks when using the Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge vSphere HA Recovery Model, as BGP peering from
the NSX Edge node to the fabric occurs over these networks.
Note:
VLAN IDs are switch-level numerical labels identifying a Layer 2 domain. In some fabric configurations, the same
VLAN ID may identify different domains, or different VLAN IDs may identify the same domain. A distributed port
group can be associated with a single VLAN ID. Any distributed port groups supporting virtual machines must
have the same VLAN ID and Layer 2 domain mapping across the entire vSphere cluster. You may use different
VLAN IDs for separate vSphere clusters that do not share a common vSphere Distributed Switch.

IP Connectivity and Symmetry
Traffic must be routed between availability zones for all VLAN segments that require cross-site communication. For
example, vSAN networks in each availability zone must have a route to each other to support synchronous data
replication.
For VLAN segments that stretch between availability zones, the physical network fabric determines the ingress and
egress paths. In most cases, to simplify troubleshooting, symmetrical routing is recommended.
For workloads, the ingress and egress path depends upon the Network Consumption Models chosen. For the Centralized
Connectivity Modelingress and egress paths depend on the specific NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability
Zonesand routing model:
• Static Routing: The physical network fabric determines the ingress and egress paths.
• eBGP: A combination of the physical fabric and the NSX Edge gateway determines the ingress and egress paths.
For all stretched VLAN network segments (infrastructure networks, VLAN Networking Connectivity Model or Distributed
VLAN Connectivity Model), or Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0, the physical network fabric must
provide a highly available Layer 3 gateway at the first hop. This ensures that virtual machines maintain connectivity on the
same IP address when moving between availability zones.
Broadcom 1276

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Witness Location
For vSAN stretched cluster, an independent witness site is required. This requires independent network paths from each
availability zone to the witness site, such that the failure of an individual availability zone does not impact the traffic path
from the other availability zones to the witness site.
When configured with vSAN Witness Traffic Separation (WTS), the vSAN witness traffic flows between the ESX
management VMkernels and the vSAN Witness node. This traffic uses the MTU of the ESX management VMkernels.
Availability Zone Data Center Interconnect
The data center inter-connect between the availability zones must be appropriately sized to handle all infrastructure,
workload, and storage replication traffic. The interconnect is important to the operations of the vSAN Cluster. It should
have the appropriate level of resilience to achieve business objectives.

Virtual Infrastructure Layer for VCF Fleet with Multiple Sites in a Single Region plus Additional Region(s)
Virtual Infrastructure Software represents the foundational technology stack that underpins all applications, services, and
workloads within an organization's computing environment. This essential layer provides the fundamental capabilities
required to run, scale, and manage modern enterprise systems, serving as the building blocks upon which higher-level
services and applications are constructed.

vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.

Selected Model Additional Information
ESX Model In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, consider the resources, networking, and
security policies that are required to support the virtual machines
in each VCF domain vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 1280

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 396: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric • Single (all traffic on same fabric).
• Dual (workload traffic using NSX and VPC networks isolated to a dedicated fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across different network cards.
NLR:
• Use two separate 2-port network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across two separate network cards to avoid single point of
failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.
LAG • Enabled
– Requires LACP configuration on the physical switches
• Disabled
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.
Shared vDS (VCF 9.1.1 onwards for • No - Dedicated vDS per cluster
Greenfield Deployments) • Yes - Shared between clusters

Broadcom 1295

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Attribute Detail
Virtual Machine Storage policies vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN 9.1 automatically configures vSAN Auto-RAID policy on new vSAN ESA clusters.
vSAN Auto-RAID policy manages the resilience for data residing in a cluster, regardless of
the size or topology of the vSAN cluster. vSAN Auto-RAID creates a single policy within the
vCenter server,
Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model Options
A Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
Deduplication vSAN Global Deduplication is supported with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 and can be
enabled as a day 2 operation.
Data In Transit Encryption Data In Transit is supported to be enabled as day 0 or day 2 operation.
Data at Rest encryption Data at Rest Encryption is supported as a day 2 operation.
vSAN Networking vSAN ESA can utilize 10GbE , 25GbE or higher. See Table 764: vSAN Host Network Model
Options.

Physical Infrastructure Layer
The physical infrastructure layer constitutes the tangible hardware and facilities layer that provides the foundational
computing, storage, and networking resources upon which all digital services depend. This layer encompasses the actual
physical assets—servers, storage arrays, network equipment, and supporting facilities—that form the bedrock of modern
IT operations.

VCF Fleet Management Blueprint
Fleet management in VCF Operations helps build, manage, and scale your private cloud infrastructure while providing that
consistency across each of its components.
Introduction
This document defines the operational guidelines for fleet management functions in VCF Operations , serving as
the authoritative benchmark for achieving security and operational excellence at scale. By moving beyond siloed
administration toward a global governance model, this blueprint provides prescriptive guidance on the following core
capabilities:
1. Identity and Access Management
2. Certificate Management
3. Account and Password Management
4. Fleet Configuration Management
5. VCF Tag Management for vSphere
These guidelines are recommended for new or transforming environments, ensuring infrastructure is aligned for
standardization, automation, and predictability.
Deviation from guidelines and best practices in this blueprint is permissible to meet unique business needs, but any such
deviation:
• Requires evaluation of the impact on long-term supportability.
• May diverge from operational efficiency goals and could impair subsequent automation, lifecycle management, and
platform consistency.
Audience
Platform engineers: Implement and maintain fleet-wide infrastructure components such as SSO, certificate, password,
and configuration management. They operationalize automation frameworks, APIs, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
pipelines.
Cloud Operations Engineers: Execute daily operations across VCF instances and fleets, perform routine compliance
validations, and ensure audit readiness.
Cloud and Infra Architects: Define the overarching VCF fleet architecture, ensuring that designs align with enterprise
governance, scalability, and automation principles. They make key design decisions on topology, identity, certificate, and
configuration models.
Fleet Management Objectives
Maximize Operational Efficiency: Reduce administrative overhead through standardized fleet-wide operations,
automated lifecycle management, and centralized governance.
Ensure Unified Governance & Consistency: Enforce consistent policy application and lifecycle management across all
fleet instances.
Broadcom 1310

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Scale with Automation: Standardize architectural design to support robust, API-driven automation and predictable
scalability.
Fleet Management Foundational Principles
Centralization Strategy: VCF Operations acts as the single management interface for fleet-wide services, providing a
unified view for operations and compliance.
Automation-First: Day 2 operations should be executed via API or workflow automation through VCF Operations or
integrated automation platforms to reduce human error and dependency on individual operator accounts.
Governance & Consistency: Unified configuration baselines should be enforced across the Fleet. Administrators should
utilize VCF continuous configuration drift detection to verify the infrastructure configuration remains synchronized with the
central validated baseline. Inconsistent configurations should trigger timely remediation alerts or automated correction.
Identity and Access Management
VCF Identity and Access Management (IAM) defines the framework for centralized identity governance and access control
across a VCF Fleet. It enables operational teams to design and manage access to VCF Operations, VCF Automation,
vCenter, NSX, and so on, at fleet scale.
Prerequisites
The guidance in this section assumes the following environmental state:
• A VCF Fleet where all management components are deployed and operating normally, and VCF SSO is deployed and
enabled.
• An authoritative external Identity Provider (IdP) is available to manage user and group identities and to perform
authentication for access to the VCF Fleet.
• Network connectivity is established to allow secure communication between the Identity Broker and the external IdP.
When System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) is used, the inbound connectivity from the external
Identity Provider to the identity broker should be allowed to support real-time provisioning events.
• [Optional] Log Management is recommended for centralized collection, retention, and auditability of identity-related
events across the VCF Fleet.
Scope
This section provides operational guidance for the following use cases:
Use Case Number Description
UC 1.1 How to choose between specific Modern Identity Providers (such
as Okta, Ping Identity, or Microsoft Entra ID) and generic SAML
2.0 or OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP when configuring IdP.
UC 1.2 How to select an appropriate user and group provisioning
approach for VCF SSO, based on environment constraints and
identity lifecycle requirements.
UC 1.3 How to design roles and manage role assignments to achieve
consistent access control across the VCF Fleet, enabling
standardized operations while supporting intentional scoping
aligned with organizational responsibilities.
UC 1.4 How to structure programmatic access using API clients and
tokens to support automation and system integrations, while
minimizing operational dependency and access risk.
To implement the recommendations and best practices discussed in this section, refer to Managing Identity and Access
With VCF Single Sign-On and the relevant portions of the fleet management guide for procedural guidance.
Broadcom 1311

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuring VCF SSO
VCF SSO enables unified identity management across the entire VCF fleet. The SSO configuration is a multi-steps
process.
Choosing an Identity Provider Type
VCF SSO supports several types of Identity Providers (IdP), ranging from directory-based services like AD or LDAP to
modern IdPs such as Okta and Microsoft Entra ID, as well as generic SAML 2.0 or OIDC options. It is recommended to
select the IdP type that most closely matches your specific provider. For instance, although Okta supports both SAML 2.0
and OIDC protocols, you should choose the Okta IdP option rather than generic SAML 2.0 or OIDC IdP option. Use the
generic IdP options only if your specific provider is not listed. This approach ensures that the environment uses a more
deeply validated integration.
VCF SSO User and Group Provisioning Options
VCF SSO supports several user and group provisioning options: AD/LDAP On-demand Provisioning, AD/LDAP pre-
provisioning, Just-in-Time (JIT) users and groups on-demand provisioning, group pre-provisioning, and SCIM 2.0.

Important:
No single user and group provisioning method is universally applicable across all VCF deployments.
Environmental constraints such as regulatory requirements, network security policies, and identity lifecycle
expectations influence which provisioning approach is feasible and operationally sustainable. The considerations
that are outlined are intended to help organizations evaluate trade-offs and select a provisioning strategy that
aligns with their fleet architecture, governance model, and compliance requirements.
Roles and Assignments for Consistent Access Control
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is the access control model that is used in VCF. VCF supports defining and
managing roles at fleet scope, enabling consistent role usage across systems. Predefined VCF-level roles are provided
for common administrative functions, and custom roles can be created to meet specific operational requirements.
VCF Custom Role Definition
Custom roles enable operational teams to align access permissions with their organizational structure and support model.
Important:
You can only choose built-in roles from NSX, VCF Operations HCX, VCF Operations orchestrator when defining
a VCF custom role. Custom roles from VCF Operations, VCF Automation, and vCenter are available for VCF
custom role definitions.

VCF API Token Management
VCF API access is granted through two identity types—SSO users (for humans) and API clients (for systems). Both
generate API tokens that are exchanged for short-lived bearer access tokens that are used across the VCF Fleet.
Operational teams should manage these tokens to ensure automation reliability and contain security risks.
Important:
API token permissions are inherited exclusively from the access levels that are assigned to SSO users or API
clients at the VCF level. Tokens do not inherit SSO user permissions that are configured directly at the component
level.
For example, an SSO user might be assigned the VCF Viewer role at the fleet level while holding a vCenter
Administrator role directly on a specific vCenter. In this case, any access tokens that are generated by the user
only reflect the VCF Viewer permissions.

Certificate Management
Certificate management ensures secure communication and authentication integrity within a VCF Fleet. This section
provides guidance on certificate management for VCF management components such as VCF Operations, VCF
Automation, vCenter, NSX, and SDDC Manager, and infrastructure components (ESX hosts).
Prerequisites
The guidance in this section assumes the following environmental state:
• A VCF Fleet where all management components are deployed and operating normally
• An enterprise Certificate Authority (CA) is available for integration.
• [Optional] A defined governance model for certificate lifecycle operations, including approval policies, certificate
standards, and CA issuance controls.
• [Optional] Log Management is recommended for the audit trail required for certificate-related compliance validation
across the fleet.
Scope
This section provides operational guidance for the following use cases:

VCF Certificate Lifecycle Automation
VCF fleet administrators should select a certificate management automation approach that balances efficiency with other
factors.
Evaluate the following decision drivers:
• Operational Scale: As fleet size increases, manual intervention becomes a reliability risk. For large-scale fleets, Auto-
Renewal or API-Based Automation is preferred to standardize execution.
• Automation Maturity: API-Based Automation assumes that the organization is able to design, operate, and govern
custom certificate lifecycle workflows. This includes ownership of workflow logic, failure handling, validation, and
auditability across the fleet. Organizations should assess whether they can sustainably maintain this operational
responsibility before adopting this approach.
• Regulatory and Compliance: Regulated environments often mandate strict issuance policies or manual approval gates.
Since native auto-renewal relies on post-event auditing, organizations requiring pre-event approval (change control)
should use API-Based Automation to enforce these checks before issuance.
• Key Custody: If security policies require private keys to be generated externally (for example, on a Hardware Security
Module), API-Based Automation is the only viable path. Native Auto-Renewal relies on VCF generating the keys.

VCF Service Accounts
In VCF, accounts are categorized into three distinct types:
• OS Account: These accounts are provisioned directly within the operating system of a virtual appliance and are
primarily used for Secure Shell (SSH) access. A common example is the vCenter Server root account.
• Application Account: These accounts are designed for interactive logins, granting users access to the VCF component
UI and API. A typical example of a user account is the vCenter administrator@vsphere.local account.
• Inter-Component Account: These accounts that are used for one VCF component to communicate with another VCF
component. An example of an inter-component account is svc-ops-vc-vcf-ops-cluster-uid@vsphere.local
that is used for communication from VCF Operations to vCenter.
Starting with VCF 9.0, the VCF platform offers the capability to manage inter-component accounts for component

Fleet Configuration Management
VCF Configuration Management can provide configuration consistency and operational integrity across a VCF Fleet. By
using vCenter configuration templates and vSphere cluster templates, administrators can establish standardized baselines
to monitor vSphere infrastructure configuration at scale. While current capabilities are focused on drift detection, this
approach significantly reduces reliability risks by providing clear visibility into manual or unintended changes that occur as
the fleet size increases.
Prerequisites
The guidance in this section assumes the following environmental state:
• A VCF Fleet where VCF Operations is deployed and operating normally.
• One or more vSphere Clusters are managed with vSphere Configuration Profiles in a vCenter instance that serves as
the authoritative source for the cluster template.
• All target vCenter Server instances and vSphere clusters are under the VCF Operations management.
•
[Optional] Log Management is configured as the central logging platform to provide the audit trail for configuration
changes.

tagging that is confined to individual components like vCenter Server, enabling VCF Fleet-wide tag visibility and
orchestration. This ensures that tags that are used for policy enforcement are consistent across all managed vCenter
instances.

VCF Monitoring and Alerting Blueprint
This document provides guidance for monitoring a VMware Cloud Foundation platform using the monitoring components
Real-time metrics, Log management, and VCF Operations for networks. Effective monitoring is crucial for maintaining the
stability, performance, and health of the SDDC infrastructure.
Extending Monitoring Capabilities with Components
During the initial installation or converge of a VMware Cloud Foundation platform, VCF Operations is installed as the
default monitoring solution. It provides monitoring, alerting, capacity planning, and charge-back capabilities for the
platform. VCF Operations can be used as is or extended with extra capabilities, services, and also consumed through API,
or integrated with 3rd-party monitoring systems. The components in this section are part of the VMware Cloud Foundation
license entitlement and are highly recommended additions to the initial installation.
Log Management
Log Management collects, analyzes, and visualizes logs across your VMware Cloud Foundation platform. In VMware
Cloud Foundation 9.1 this component runs on top of VCF management services and is deployed using VCF Operations.
VCF Operations for Networks
VCF Operations for Networks delivers intelligent operations for software-defined networking and security. It helps
customers build an optimized, highly-available, and secure network infrastructure across multi-cloud environments. VCF
Operations for networks accelerates micro-segmentation planning and deployment, enables visibility across virtual and
physical networks, and provides operational views to manage and scale the NSX component.
Broadcom 1343

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Real-Time Metrics
Real-time metrics allows you to collect the real-time, granular data from the underlying core infrastructure, such as
vCenter, ESX, NSX, and vSAN. To collect detailed performance data for effective troubleshooting, you can configure
different tiers of metric collection within your monitoring policies. Essentials metrics are always enabled by default and
cannot be turned off.
Adding Components to VCF Operations
Note:
If you navigate to a UI section that requires Log management, Real-time metrics, or VCF Operations for Networks
you will see a button "Install <Component_Name>" that will land you in the component management page, where
you can install the required component.
Prerequisites:
The Software depot service should be populated and the desired install binaries should be downloaded.
Workflow:
1. Login into VCF Operations as a user with administrator privileges
2. Navigate to: Build -> Lifecycle -> VCF Management -> Components
3. Click on “ADD COMPONENT” and select the component that you want to install
4. Follow the wizard to install the component.
5. Enable components for the desired VCF Instances/resources if necessary.
More details could be found in the "Completing the Deployment of Your Platform".

VCF Operations provides effective monitoring through a collection of pre-built, curated dashboards. These dashboards
are organized into distinct sections. They are designed to align with key operational areas, offering comprehensive
visibility into both the SDDC infrastructure and the associated workloads, making them the essential starting point for your
monitoring efforts.

domains, vCenter instances, NSX instances, vSAN, and ESX hosts.

The dashboards that are frequently used could be added to the "Favorites" section by clicking the star in the tile or

Alerts
Alerts are a way to be notified of anything that is new or an issue that could be potentially dangerous to your environment.
Whenever there is a problem in the environment, alerts are generated. You can also create alert definitions so that the
generated alerts inform you about the problems in the monitored environment.
Alerts in VCF Operations
The alerts in VCF Operations have tree main components:
• Symptoms: A symptom might be "CPU Usage > 90%" or "vCenter Heartbeat Lost". Also an alert might be triggered
when a specific combination of symptoms occurs simultaneously.
• Alert Definitions: Defines the "criticality" of the alert (e.g. Info, Warning, Immediate, or Critical) and determines which
objects (e.g. aVM, vCenter, or all production clusters) the alert applies to.
• Recommendations: Alerts in VCF Operations could include a list of human-readable steps or automated Actions to
resolve the issue.
Broadcom 1345

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Checking Open Alerts
You could see the active alerts in the VCF Operations UI under: Operate -> Alerts -> Alerts. This view by default is
filtered to show only the Active alerts, you could filter further, expand groups, and go through the other tabs in the Alerts
section.
Configure Event Notifications
Notifications are alert notifications that meet the filter criteria in the notification rules before they are sent outside VCF
Operations. You can configure notification rules for the supported outbound alerts so that you can filter the alerts that are
sent to the selected external system.
Why I may need an event notification
Since each environment may have different critical components, the administrator of the environment should map and
analyze it. This analysis should be used to create a plan for proactive notifications. The recommended way is to start
with fewer notifications and gradually increases them based on learning and analysis. If you decide to send all alerts as
notifications, your notification channel is overloaded and you are risking missing the important messages.
Some common areas that could provide a starting point for defining the critical points in your notification plan:
1. Availability & "Hard" Failures ("Is it Up?")
These are the most common high-priority notifications. They trigger immediately because they represent a service
outage.
a. Host Not Responding / PSOD: An ESXi host has crashed or lost network connectivity.
b. VM Unexpected Reboot: Useful for identifying hardware issues or underlying storage drops that caused a Guest
OS to restart.
c. Management Component Down: Critical VCF-specific alerts for when SDDC Manager, a vCenter Service, or an
NSX Edge Node becomes unreachable.
2. Performance & Contention ("Is it Slow?")
These are often "Symptom-based" alerts. Instead of triggering the moment that a spike happens, they usually wait for
a Wait Cycle (e.g., 3 consecutive collections) to ensure that the problem is persistent.
a. CPU/Memory Contention: Alerts when a VM is "starving" for resources because the physical host is over-
committed.
b. Disk Latency: Triggers when storage response times exceed a threshold (e.g., >20ms), often used to identify
"Noisy Neighbors" on a shared Datastore.
c. vSAN Health Alarms: High-level notifications when vSAN disk groups are degraded or resyncing.
3. Capacity & Planning ("Will it fit?")
These are Intelligent Alerts. VCF Operations uses AI to "look ahead" and notify you before the failure actually
happens.
a. Days Remaining Alert: A notification that says, "Based on your current growth, Datastore X will be full in 14 days".
This is far more useful than a simple "Disk Full" alert.
b. Snapshot Accumulation: Notifies you if a VM has a snapshot older than a week, or larger than a specific size,
preventing storage exhaustion.
4. VCF Infrastructure ("Management")
Unique to VCF environments, these alerts monitor the health of the management connections between SDDC
components.
a. Password or Certificate Expiration: Notifies you 30–60 days before an SDDC Manager or vCenter certificate
expires (a common cause of VCF upgrade failures).
b. NSX Controller Stability: Alerts if the NSX management cluster loses its "stable" status or if a Controller node
goes down.
c. BGP/Routing Peering Down: Critical for networking teams to know if the physical-to-virtual network link has been
severed.
How to Create an Event Notification
Broadcom 1346

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In this section, we go over a scenario for creating a notification that will be send to the team that is responsible for the
support of vSphere infrastructure. The example creates a single notification for any critical alarm for an ESX host and it
could be used as a template to create more notifications.
Configure the Desired Protocol
As part of the notification strategy you should decide what will be the best way to present the information the the
interested parties. You could choose between several options including Email; SNMP Trap; Webhook; Slack ServiceNow.
Choose the one that the recipient of the notification pays attention to. If different teams prefer different channels, you
could configure multiple protocols and could choose them later based on the recipient.
In this example, we decided to send an email to the infrastructure team mailbox, so we must configure the respective
plugin (if it is not configured).
Procedure:
1. Login into VCF Operations as a user with administrator privileges
2. Navigate to: Operate -> Administration -> Configurations -> Alerts -> Outbound Settings -> Outbound Instances
3. Click “ADD” and in “Plugin Type” select “Standard Email Plugin”
4. Fill in the details and click “Test” - if the configuration is correct a test email is sent to “Receiver Email Address”
5. Confirm that the email is received and click “Save”
Create a Notification Rule
The notification rule is used as a filter for alerts. Only the alerts that match this filter are sent as a notification with the
selected protocol.
Procedure:
1. Login into VCF Operations as an user with administrator privileges
2. Navigate to: Operate -> Administration -> Configurations -> Alerts -> Notifications
3. Click “ADD”
4. In “Notification” tab fill-in Name (e.g. “CRITICAL - ESX Host”), fill in Description to help you identify the notification
later and click Next
5. In “Define Criteria” tab fill-in:
a. In Criteria: Select “Object Type”; in “Select an Object Type” dropdown go to “vCenter->Host System” or directly
type “Host System”.
Selected the ESX host as the object for the filter.
b. In Alert Scope we will choose:
Category: <Do not change>
By default all the categories will be matched. If this generates too many alerts we will reconsider this in the future
and choose a subset of categories.
Criticality: Critical
We want only the Critical alarms to trigger notification. The other states are triaged as a dayly routine, since they
are with less priority.
Control State: Open
Filter only alarms that are in an open state.
c. In Notify On select:

The message is sent only for new events.
d. We will not enable "Notification Heartbeat" since this will send a new notification for each collection cycle leading
to multiple notifications for the same object.

a. Recepient(s) - the mailbox for the infrastructure team.

Pause Alerts and Notifications
Alerts and notifications could be paused during expected downtime - e.g. hardware upgrade that requires servers
downtime, power maintenance, servers relocation. Doing so will not create an "alert storm" that could mask some real
issues in the environment. When an object is identified as being in maintenance mode, VCF Operations does not collect
metrics from the object or generate anomalies or alerts for it. In addition, VCF Operations cancels any active symptoms
and alerts for the object.
Manual Maintenance
Manual maintenance mode is used during single events like hardware or software maintennace. In the below example we
need to add aditional hardware in a single host.
Procedure:
1. Login into VCF Operations
2. Navigate to: Operate > Inventory and select the VCF instance that contains the ESX host which we want to manage.
3. Click the Environment tab.
4. Use the filter on the right side of Environment tab and type the ESX hostname or part of it.
5. Select the ESX host name (you could select several hosts if needed) and click Start Maintenance from the tool bar in
the Objects tab.
Tip:
In this example we will choose to end maintenance on a specific date - tomorrow. In this way even if we forget to
end maintenance after the host is up and running VCF Operations will do it for us. Choose the right option for your
case.
6. Select End Maintenance on and choose the date.
7. Confirm with OK. No
8. Use your procedure to enter host in Maintenance Mode through vCenter and to Shutdown the ESX host.
9. Complete hardware maintenance, run hardware tests if needed, and put the host back in service through vCenter.

Scheduled Maintenance
You could also create a scheduled maintenance window for periodical processes, avoiding false alarms during a known
maintenance windows.
In the example below we create a scheduled maintenance for one of our remote clusters in a production plant. Every
quarter the power of the facility is stopped for a day to perform an equipment maintenance. During this period, the
connection to the main datacenter is lost and we have alarms in VCF Operations, that we want to prevent.
We must perform three steps in order to attach a scheduled maintenance to a resource:
1. Create the Scheduled Maintenance.
2. Create a custom profile with the Scheduled Maintenance.
3. Attach the Custom Profile to a resource.
Procedure (create Scheduled Maintenance):
1. Login into VCF Operations.
2. Navigate to: Operate > Administration > Configurations and click on Maintenance Schedules tile under Others.
3. Click ADD.
4. Populate a Schedule Name that will help you to identify the schedule (e.g. "Production plant maintenance").
5. Select the right time zone for the Schedule.
6. Maintenance happens at the last day of each quarter and finishes for a working day, so we enter the following values:
Recurrence: Monthly
Start on: 3/31/26 at: 7:30AM
Stop after: 12 hours
Repeat every: Mar; Jun; Sep; Dec
Days: Last
Expires on: 12/31/30
7. Click SAVE and check the values in the table.
Scheduled Maintenance shold be attached to a Custom Profile in order to be used.
Procedure (create a Custom Profile):
1. Login into VCF Operations.
2. Navigate to: Operate > Administration > Configurations and click on Policy Definition tile under Policies.
3. Click ADD.
4. In Create New Policy enter a name and description that will help you to identify this policy on a later stage. For this
example we will use:
Name: "Production Facility Maintenance"
Description: "Power outage in production plan at the end of every quarter"
5. Select the policy that you want to be used as a temlate and click Create Policy. For this example "Default Policy" has
the corect atributes so we select it in the Inherit From dropdown.
6. Click on the Maintenance Schedule tile
7. We want the maintenance to be applied on the cluster, ESX hosts, datastores, and VMs.
a. In the "Select Object Type" dropdown, type "Cluster Compute Resource" and select: vCenter > Cluster
Compute Resource, click on the padlock in front of "Maintenance Schedule" and select the Maintenance
Schedule that we created in the previous step (e.g. "Production plant maintenance").
b. In the "Select Object Type" dropdown, type "Datastore" and select: vCenter > Datastore, click on the padlock in
front of "Maintenance Schedule" and select the Maintenance Schedule that we created in the previous step (e.g.
"Production plant maintenance").
c. In the "Select Object Type" dropdown, type "Host System" and select: vCenter > Host System, click on the
padlock in front of "Maintenance Schedule" and select the Maintenance Schedule that we created in the previous
step (e.g. "Production plant maintenance").

d. In the "Select Object Type" dropdown, type "Virtual Machine" and select: vCenter > Virtual Machine, click
on the padlock in front of "Maintenance Schedule" and select the Maintenance Schedule that we created in the

8. (Optionally) Click on "View Unsaved Changes" and check that the correct objects and attributes are set.
9. Click on Save.
The custom profile should be attached to a resource.

1. Login into VCF Operations.
2. Navigate to: Operate > Inventory
3. Navigate to the object that you want to assing policy to. In our example it is a cluster so VCF instances > "The name

4. In the top right corner click on "Policy" dropdown and select "Assign Policy"

Create a Custom Dashboard
Custom dashboards allow administrators to consolidate relevant information from various VCF components into a single,
focused view that is tailored to specific roles or operational needs.
Why I may need a custom dashboard
VCF Operations comes with dozens of powerful out-of-the-box dashboards, they are designed to be "one size fits most".
Users could move toward custom dashboards to transition from generic monitoring to targeted operations.
Why I may want a custom dashboard:
1. Unified Visibility
Standard dashboards often focus on a single layer (e.g., vSAN or just NSX). A custom dashboard can bridge these
gaps:
a. The Full Stack View: You can place a widget for Physical Switch health right next to a widget for VM Latency. This
allows an admin to see if a networking issue is the root cause of an application performance drop without switching
tabs.
b. Multi-vCenter Aggregation: While OOTB dashboards often drill into one vCenter at a time, a custom dashboard
can show "Top 10 most stressed VMs" across your entire global VCF footprint on one screen.
2. Role-Specific Personalization
Different teams care about different metrics. Custom dashboards allow you to strip away the "noise":
a. Executive/Manager View: High-level "Green/Yellow/Red" health scores and "Money Saved" via rightsizing,
without the technical weeds of IOPS or CPU cycles.
b. App Owners: A view filtered strictly to the VMs and databases that belong to their specific application, rather than
the entire infrastructure.
c. Help Desk: A simplified "search-and-status" dashboard where they can quickly type in a VM name and see its
current health and recent alerts.
3. Resource & Cost Optimization
Create custom views to justify spending or prove efficiency:
a. Rightsizing Dashboards: Specifically highlighting VMs that are over-provisioned (wasted money) or under-
provisioned (performance risk).
b. Showback/Chargeback: Visualizing resource consumption by department so IT can show business units exactly
what they are using in terms of VCF resources.
4. Focused Troubleshooting
Broadcom 1350

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a. Incident Dashboards: Build a "War Room" dashboard that displays only the specific components that are involved
in a recurring issue (e.g., specific Edge Nodes, Load Balancers, and Backend Web Servers) with high-frequency
data collection.
b. Additional troubleshooting options and ideas in the Trobleshooting Guide.
5. Branding and Reporting
a. NOC Displays: Creating "Wallboard" dashboards with large, high-contrast widgets that are designed to be
displayed on large monitors in a Network Operations Center.
b. Custom Labels: Using "Views" within dashboards to translate technical metric names into business-friendly
language (e.g., instead of sys|uptime_latest, labeling it as Service Availability).
Tip:
• If you want to create a custom dashboard you could use an existing dashboard as a template. To do so, clone
the existing dashboard and edit the clone. Editing an existing dashboard is not a good practice, since it could
be used by other users or teams.
• You could export Dashboards and could import them in other VCF Operations. This approach provides a
uniform configuration across environments.
• Consider using a source control for your exported configurations for a better version management and
reverting to a previous working verstion if needed.
VCF Troubleshooting Blueprint
The troubleshooting guide is intended to help guide troubleshooting efforts for typical scenarios experienced in an
enterprise environment. The focus of the guide is on incident management - identifying the cause of an actively occurring
problem, and determining potential solutions.
Overview
This guide assumes typical enterprise workloads running on a VMware Cloud Foundation platform, with VCF Operations
9.1. A subset of the described capabilities may be available in prior versions.
It will leverage the data and analysis capabilities from:
• VCF Operations
• Log Management
• VCF Operations for Networks
• Real-Time Metrics
Having all of these components installed and configured will provide the best capabilities for troubleshooting effectively,
however, it is still possible to troubleshoot with a subset of the capabilities. At a minimum VCF Operations is required.
Example scenarios:
• An application is performing slower than typical
– What process should be followed to find the cause
– What data points and which areas should be used to help
• A workload is not able to connect to a database
– Where should the investigation start
– What are some of the tools that can help pinpoint the issue
• Sometimes a file transfer operation fails
– How to investigate when the symptoms are not occurring
– What additional measure to take to capture details during a recurrence
• Unplanned reboot/crashes
– How to investigate a crash/reboot scenario
Broadcom 1351

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Components for VCF Troubleshooting
Before experiencing an incident that requires investigation, it is important to have the appropriate data collection and
analysis tools deployed and configured to capture metrics and data that will be important during an investigation. For the
purposes of this guide, the following components should be installed:
• VCF Operations
– This component is core to VCF 9, and provides the central User Interface for the other components referenced
in this guide. It also provides capabilities for environment configuration and management, which are covered in a
separate guide.
– All VCF 9 deployments will have one instance of VCF Operations per VCF Fleet. If you have multiple Fleets in your
environment, each will have its own VCF Operations instance, managed through its own UI. As of VCF 9.1, the core
inventory and metrics from multiple VCF Fleets’ Operations can be connected together and viewed in a single VCF
Operations instance, providing easier visibility. However, for more advanced troubleshooting including logs, network
and real-time data, each VCF Operations instance will need to be accessed directly. Therefore the steps in this
guide should be considered incompatible with the Federation feature of VCF Operations.
– VCF Operations collects inventory data for the entire fleet, as well as a number of metrics for each inventory object
pertaining to its performance, health and activity, which are stored to various resolutions - higher for shorter periods
of time and lower resolution data retained over extended periods.
• Log Management
– This component collects the contents of log files for components in the VCF Fleet, as well as any external
components that have been configured to send their log (syslog) data to the logs collector.
– Log messages contain valuable information on what is occurring in a system, and sometimes includes performance
information as well (either through data embedded in messages or by analyzing the time stamps for logs identifying
specific states or actions). Logs are also a key component for root cause analysis through event re-creation.
– Log data needs to be retained for the period of time where troubleshooting may need to refer back to. Longer
retention provides more history, but it also consumes more storage capacity and can make searching through logs
slower and more difficult. Older logs rarely provide significant value, but can help determine when an issue first
started occurring, or confirm if it happened previously.
• VCF Operations for Networks
– This component tracks network flows - communication sessions between 2 endpoints over the network. It is useful
for understanding what workloads are connecting to and how much data they are sending or receiving to those
endpoints.
– Traffic is categorized into “flows” which is traffic part of the same session, or generally the same “conversation”.
It includes the source, destination, protocols used and the type of traffic. It does not contain the actual data being
exchanged in most cases, unless that data is encoded in the network packet header. It also tracks the number and
size of packets, which can provide the total amount of data sent and received.
• Real-time data
– This component is new for VCF 9.1, and provides high-resolution metrics from ESX hosts, vSAN, and NSX Edges
for detailed troubleshooting. It allows tracking the different counters on the hypervisor (ESX) that describe a VM’s
activities and how its performance is affected by available resources, and how the host’s resources are being
allocated.
Troubleshooting Concepts
Methodologies and Glossary of concepts used in this guide and for Incident Management in general.
Workbench
Workbench is a module in VCF Operations that provides a framework to guide the troubleshooting process as a session.
Based on a selected context (such as a VM or other vSphere object), you can refine details like the time range, or
expand to related objects. You are shown potential evidence - metrics, events, or changes that stand out, and can
expand to additional metrics, events, flows, and logs within the defined context. You can add text notes or save charts
or graphs to the notes, and save the investigation to refer to later on and compare to other data points that are identified
as the investigation proceeds. It also enables sharing the session with others so that they can assist or take over the
troubleshooting process, making collaboration on an incident much easier.
Broadcom 1352

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
While it is optional, in this guide we recommend using Workbench for all incidents of significance. It provides a solution to
track and share what was captured and reviewed during the troubleshooting process, which can help resolve the incident
more quickly and make hand-offs between team members easier. It also retains this history for post-incident review and
for future recall comparing against new similar incidents that can also help with problem management and root-cause
identification.
Best Practices when using Workbench
• Define Precise Time Windows: Start by narrowing the scope of the workbench analysis to the exact period when the
issue was detected. This focus filters out "noise" from unrelated system events, allowing the tool to surface the most
relevant evidence and configuration changes.
• Start with top-level impacted object for scope: Workbench can automatically identify all related objects and expand
or collapse using relationship mapping. For example, selecting an impacted VM will identify the dependent host,
network, datastores, etc. to include in the analysis.
• Prioritize Root Cause Evidence: Rather than manually scanning individual logs, focus on the "Potential Evidence"
tab. Use the workbench to automatically correlate metric spikes with recent configuration changes, which frequently
point directly to the source of the problem.
• Leverage Metric Correlation: Use the workbench to compare multiple metrics simultaneously. If a virtual machine is
underperforming, correlate its CPU and memory usage with the underlying host's resource availability to determine if
the issue is contained within the VM or stems from the physical hardware.
• Review Recent Configuration Changes: Infrastructure instability often follows a change in the environment. Check
the workbench for "Events" that indicate new patches, setting updates, or hardware reconfigurations.
• Compare with Regular Performance: Review metrics for periods when the issue was not occurring to understand the
baseline and use that to identify variances to "normal" behavior.
• Incorporate Log Insight Integration: While the workbench excels at high-level correlation, use its integrated view of
log data once the issue has been narrowed down to a specific component or timestamp.
Isolation
Isolation can have two distinct meanings in troubleshooting:
Isolation (segregated environment): When the environment or workload with the issue is prevented from
communicating or interacting with external components. This method is typically used on a clone of the production
environment that can then be tested in ways that cannot be done on a live environment without fear of impact. This is
often done as part of an issue reproduction (see below) or when the problem cannot be identified sufficiently on the live
environment. In cases of malware infection, a live environment may need to be isolated to prevent the spread of the
malware to other environments while it is investigated and cleaned.
Isolation (Narrow the scope): This is a process where the source or cause of the issue is focused on a more specific
area - ruling out various services and components so the investigation can concentrate on a smaller area. It’s important to
isolate an issue to specific components at the start of the troubleshooting process to know where to look more closely. A
number of methods may be used to rule out components (for example other services sharing the same components but
are not affected by the same problem) or where the issue can be triggered across different workloads by using a common
infrastructure component.
Problem Theory Development
Once the issue has been isolated to a specific component or area, the observed symptoms and configuration are matched
to possible chains of actions that could fully represent the problem. A theory may start out being relatively vague, and
then through observing additional configurations, logs or behaviours from the impacted systems, can be refined to a full
chain of events scenario that encompasses all the symptoms and observations of the problem scenario within the affected
environment’s configuration.
Problem Theory Validation
Once a theory for the cause of the problem has been identified, it needs to be validated through testing to confirm that the
theory is actually the source of the issue. A full validation test requires confirming both making a change causes the issue,
and reversing the change causes the issue to stop. The detail of the theory as to the full chain of the problem and aligning
all symptoms to it will help prepare more accurate validation tests. This step is critical to ensure that the theory is properly
validated. If the theory is too vague when validation is performed, it may lead to a scenario where it is validated correctly
but does not accurately confirm the full problem chain.
Broadcom 1353

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Issue Reproduction
It may be helpful in some scenarios to create a different environment in a controlled fashion that mimics the configuration
of the impacted environment and attempt to reproduce the issue in this test environment. This is necessary when
the production environment is not suitable for testing - either in high security, high availability, or extremely critical
environments, or when more destructive/impactful configurations need to be put in place to help trace difficult to identify
issues (for example debug logging on a busy production environment may generate too much data to capture, or
cause a performance impact itself). A Reproduction environment is generally kept fully isolated from the live production
environment to avoid cross-contamination of data used for testing.
Incident Management
Incident management addresses the process of identifying and resolving an impactful problem to the environment. It aims
to restore functionality to eliminate or reduce the impact to customers, end users and applications.
Problem Management
Problem management delves deeper into issues at a wider, more systemic level and works to reduce the likelihood of a
recurrence of issues and/or prevent future similar or related issues in the original or other systems. It is generally done
after an incident has been resolved, and includes root-cause analysis of prior incidents.
Troubleshooting Scenarios
Sample scenarios that walk through a typical problem situation and use the available VCF components to scope, analyze,
and resolve an issue.
Workload Performance Issue
The primary challenge with identifying the cause of a performance issue is to sift through the layers of data to identify
the root cause. Often the overloaded components will be easily identifiable in metrics, but the reason for the increased
demand can be many layers deep, and each layer needs to be peeled back one at a time until the underlying cause is
identified. In some cases this will just be a scale limitation, where the design’s limits have finally been reached. It can also
be a misconfiguration that results in a high-load operation being performed too frequently.
Another challenge with performance issues is that they can also be intermittent issues. That scenario is covered under its
own section.
Resources
VCF Operations (required), VCF Operations Networks (optional), Real-time Data (optional)
[other]:
Sample scenario:
Customers report a 2-tier app called WorkDataApp is very slow to respond after clicking a button in its UI. Reports
of this slowness are coming in from all locations. They said that it was working fine yesterday, but this morning it is
unusably slow.
Step 1: Initial Triage and Isolation
1. Set clear performance expectations: This should identify the scope of the problem (what is affected), and the
definition of what a “good” state is. The goal for incident management is to address a specific performance issue,
not to engage in performance optimization of an application or system. The target should be based on what the
performance was prior to the incident (or as close as can be determined when not known).
2. Isolate the Impact: Determine the scope of the performance degradation. Is it affecting a single VM, a specific ESXi
host, an entire cluster/fleet, or a particular application/service?
3. Determine the timeline: Did the issue start on a particular date/time? Is it consistently better or worse at specific
times of day or days of the week?
4. Establish a Baseline: If possible, compare current performance against historical metrics (before the issue started) to
quantify the degradation and identify the resource under stress (CPU, Memory, Disk, Network).
Broadcom 1354

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. Use VCF Operations Workbench: Create a new Workbench entry for the incident. Attach initial charts showing the
degraded metrics, relevant logs, and a description of the symptoms for collaboration and historical tracking. If you
don’t know the exact scope of the issue, enter the most specific object you know is impacted (or choose one if multiple
are impacted). For example, select a VM that is part of the impacted application. Workbench will provide all the related
objects to help you further narrow the scope.

Identify the VMs involved in this application:
Web/App Server: WDA-App1
DB Server: WDA-DB1
Start a workbench session and enter the App VM as the scope.
Enter the Time Range for a confirmed period when the issue was occurring, or enter one for a time a bit earlier
than when the issue was known to have started to capture the transition.

• Review the last 7 days of performance graphs for the impacted object(s) (VM or Host) based on what was identified in
Step 1. Use the Troubleshoot an Application view to see the typical metrics that apply to an application across multiple
