• Pinpoint the time the degradation started and check for any correlated configuration changes or increases in workload
by comparing against other metrics.
• Compare against related components: for example high load on a database server correlating to high load on
application servers, or different load on different servers performing similar tasks. To accomplish this, leverage the
Correlation tool on the metrics graphs for the affected workloads to compare across other metrics on the same
workload, or the same metric on other workloads for the same time period.

times. This can help to define the scope of the issue, and trace back to a root cause - for example, an application
misconfiguration creating a large number of network connections impacting an entire network segment or host.
• The goal of the analysis is to develop a problem theory, which can then be tested in the next step. Continue to look for
matching data points to support or disprove the interim theories.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Log Analysis
*Requires Log Management.
Logs are the least likely source of information for performance issues, as most applications don’t self-monitor or report
on performance issues, however there are some logs that might provide indications that are observed as performance
issues:
• Repeated service or VM restarts. If a VM or an application service fails and restarts, that can produce performance
impacts as the affected node will be unavailable to process data while it is restarting. Look for messages containing the
words restart, reboot, failure, crash as examples.
• Connectivity issues - if there are intermittent connectivity losses between application components, this can also be
observed as slow performance, as the application will be stalled while the connection re-establishes. High packet loss
on a connection can also lead to performance issues as the data will need to be re-transmitted resulting in delays.
Look for connections being terminated and/or re-established, for example to databases. Terms such as disconnect,
reconnect, timeout, drop can be indicators of such an issue.
• Some systems can log messages at performance thresholds - for example the vDefend IDS/IPS system can log when
different utilization thresholds are hit, and if any packets are dropped due to oversubscription of inspection capacity.

the Logs search panel, and adjust the timeframe to the 5PM start time. While the search turns up some standard
housekeeping log entries from services like fdm (vSphere HA), and some messages from Hostd about monitoring
and metrics tracking, nothing in the logs appears to indicate any abnormalities in this case.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Step 3: Problem Theory and Validation
Once the data points converge on a suspected bottleneck (e.g., high storage latency, high CPU ready time, or high
network flow counts):
1. Formulate a Problem Theory: Example Theory: "The performance issue is caused by high CPU Ready Time on Host
X, which is driven by a resource-intensive nightly backup job running on VM Y, confirmed by a spike in historical CPU
metrics at 1:00 AM."
2. Validate the Theory: Test the theory. In the example above, try disabling or rescheduling VM Y's backup job. If
performance immediately improves, the theory is validated. If the issue persists, the investigation must pivot to the
next most likely cause.
[other]:
Sample scenario:
We can theorize that there is a task running every 10 minutes on the VM WDA-DB1 that is transferring data over
the network on port 22. If we start a workbench for WDA-DB1 and look at the same metrics, we can see that there
is both Disk Read and Write traffic, as well as Network Transmit in a pattern that matches what we saw on WDA-
App1. To further validate our theory and identify the task, we will need to look at the guest OS itself, and observe
what processes are generating the disk and network I/O.
In this case, we observe that there is a cron job scheduled every 10 minutes under the root account that is
generating data to disk, transferring that data to WDA-App1 and then deleting it from disk. We’ll need to identify
the administrator who created this job to understand what the goal was, and find an alternative solution that does
not impact the performance of the application.
Connectivity Problem
This is when an endpoint is not able to communicate with an external entity. Sometimes this can appear intermittent, or
may only affect certain communications. All these details can be valuable clues to isolating where the problem is.
The most important thing to keep in mind when dealing with a connectivity issue is that in order for a connection to be
established, all points in the path must be operating. This includes the application service at the destination. If a database
service isn’t running, then a remote client will not be able to connect to it, and that failure to connect is most often returned
as a “connection error”. This does not imply a network problem. This is why isolation of the issue should be the first
step with a connection issue - start at the destination and validate each component, validating one step towards the
source until the entire end-to-end chain is validated. Many application services have a proxy service that establishes the
connection to the external clients, so ensure to validate if this is the case - it can be possible to establish a connection to
this proxy service, but the proxy cannot then reach its back end application because of an issue with the application. This
is often seen as an error 502 - bad gateway, because the proxy cannot reach its gateway (the application).
When troubleshooting a connectivity problem, the objective is to methodically isolate the failure point along the path from
the source to the destination, which involves checking application, operating system, hypervisor, virtual network, and
physical network layers.
Resources
VCF Operations (required), VCF Operations Networks (optional but recommended), Log Management (optional)

Step 1: Initial Triage and Isolation
1. Start with a clear problem definition: Define exactly when the problem started (did this work previously?), what
is affected (certain types of communications, traffic between specific endpoints, etc.), what the type of desired
communication is/are, and any other defining characteristics of the problem.
2. Start at the Destination (Application Layer): Before investigating network components, confirm the target service is
running and accessible locally.
– Actionable Step: Log into the destination VM/server and confirm the target application service (e.g., database, web
server) is active and listening on the expected port (e.g., using netstat or service status checks).
– Problem Theory: If the service is down, the connection failure is an application issue, not a network problem.
3. Test Local Connectivity (OS Layer): Verify the source VM's OS can reach its default gateway and itself.
– Actionable Step: Use simple connectivity tests (e.g., ping or traceroute or nc) from the source VM to its own virtual
IP and its gateway.
4. Work from the destination back to the source: Test at each accessible point until the spot where the communication
fails is identified, and then focus on that component.

On the Logs tab of the Workbench, there are a few terms we can search for to find entries from firewall rules that
might be dropping the traffic. “DROP” will find any logs of rules that are dropping traffic. “REJECT” is another

In the logs, we can see a firewall rule dropping traffic from 10.11.19.21, which is our source VM’s IP, destined

determine what the reason for that rule is and whether it can be removed.
Metrics (Utilization/Congestion Check)
*Requires VCF Operations.
Review Network Metrics to rule out congestion masquerading as a connectivity issue.
• Actionable Step: Check Network Throughput and Packet Loss/Drops for the affected VM's virtual NIC and the
corresponding ESXi host's pNIC.
• Problem Theory: High packet loss or drops often indicate a severe bottleneck (saturation) either at the physical switch
or the host's pNIC, making it appear as if the connection is failing intermittently.
Step 3: Problem Theory and Validation
1. Formulate a Problem Theory: Based on the flow analysis, metrics, and logs, pinpoint the single most likely point of
failure.
Broadcom 1364

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Example Theory: "Connectivity is failing because an explicit NSX Distributed Firewall DENY rule is blocking TCP port
1433 between the application and database segments, as confirmed by firewall logs and the absence of established
flows in VCF Networks."
1. Validate the Theory: Take action on the suspected component and immediately retest the connection.
• Example Validation: Disable the suspected NSX rule (or create an explicit ALLOW rule) and retest the connection.
If the connection immediately succeeds, the theory is validated, and the resolution is a policy fix. If it fails, pivot the
investigation.
[other]:
Sample scenario:
Our sample scenario had a vDefend Distributed Firewall (DFW) rule blocking the desired traffic. When we had the
NSX ipfix data being collected, this gave an explicit report of what the issue was. In cases where the traffic was
being blocked by either an external firewall or a Guest OS-based firewall, we would have seen the connection
being initiated by the source, but no flow established. This would require some additional steps to test the traffic
from the source and isolate where it was being blocked, but the troubleshooting process would follow the same
process.
Intermittent Problems
This type of issue refers to a problem that only appears on occasion, and at other times presents no symptoms. The
challenge with this type of issue is that much or all of the isolation and reproduction efforts must be done by looking at
historical information - logs, metrics, network flows rather than observing live systems.
The process for troubleshooting intermittent issues should follow the same general process based on the incident type
(e.g. intermittent connectivity should follow the connectivity issue process, intermittent performance should follow the
performance issue process). On top of that some additional considerations are required:
1. Create a workbench session. While using workbench is a good practice for any type of issue, it’s especially important
for intermittent issues so that when they do occur, all the prior information gathered can be immediately at hand.
2. Create a detailed timeline and history. Since the incident is not constant, it’s important to understand when the issue
does occur to address 2 main situations:
a. Is there a pattern to when it is triggered?
b. Identifying the times when it has occurred to review other datasets at those times to look for similarities that can
point to the source of the problem.
Reboot or Crashing problems
This type of issue is where a system hits an unrecoverable error that causes the system to halt operations. It is referred to
a BSOD (Blue Screen of Death) or PSOD (Purple Screen of Death) as the systems generate a core dump and display it
on the console with a background of Blue for windows OS and Purple for ESX. The core dump contains an image of the
memory and system registers at the time of the crash, which can help to determine what occurred just prior to the failure
to help isolate the issue to a specific module and/or scenario.
Resources
VCF Operations (required), Log Management (optional)

2. Record the time and host/resources that experienced the crash to identify any patterns.
3. Track the resolution - does a reboot resolve the issue? A full power disconnect/reconnect?

VCF Edge: Single Node with Argo CD Design Blueprint
VMware Cloud Foundation Edge (VCFE) extends the centralized management capabilities of the platform to
geographically dispersed edge locations. Common edge use cases that are supported by VCF Edge are remote office /
branches, manufacturing factories, retail stores, or mission-critical battle vehicles for the Tactical edge. Design Library
for VMware Cloud Foundation outlines the most commonly adopted and recommended infrastructure design options to
accommodate those use cases.
In a traditional fleet deployment, vCenter "pushes" configurations to the edge. For Edge sites that only have intermittent
connectivity, if the WAN link is down, the configuration update fails as Edge ESX hosts are not reachable. A GitOps-
based approach uses a "Pull" model that is inherently resilient to the intermittent connectivity typical of edge sites can be
a good alternative. Configuration updates for workloads are staged in a central Git repository, and Edge sites retrieves the
workload update only when there is connectivity.
To enable easier adoption of GitOps, VCF bundles the Broadcom-built Argo CD Operator. Unlike the upstream Argo CD
Operator, this operator is purpose-built by Broadcom to integrate directly into the VCF platform. This Operator can be
consumed in the datacenter and edge, enabling seamless lifecycle management, namespace-level access control, and
native support for hybrid workloads. Argo CD Operator can be used across all VCF edge designs patterns. The following
patterns are the most applicable to one-node integration:
VCF Edge Pattern 8: Single Host vSphere Supervisor at the Edge in a VCF Instance
VCF Edge Pattern 9: Leveraging Existing VCF Operations for Far Edge Expansion
VCF Edge Option 1: VCF Operations with vCenter for Distributed Edge
Those designs unlock a wide range of GitOps-driven workflows across infrastructure and application layers on a single
edge node:
• Create, update, and configure VKS clusters.
• Declarative Virtual Machine provisioning, updating or scaling.
• Deployment of containers as vSphere Pods to simplify the deployment abstraction.
• Application deployment and configuration into VKS clusters using version-controlled manifests.
Single Host Design Criteria
A single-node VCF Edge deployment consolidates the ESX hypervisor, vSphere Supervisor, and workload plane onto one
physical host. Every hardware and software decision must account for the absence of HA failover between hosts. The
following criteria govern a production-grade single-host edge design.

Central Management with Remote Edge hosts consists of the following major components:
• Centralized Management Domain
– A Central management domain is used to host a dedicated set of management components for the Edge sites.
Customers have the flexibility to host the management domain either locally at the edge location or at a central data
center. Management components are tasked with managing the inventory and lifecycle of the remote edge clusters
across the WAN. For the one node design, Required management components consist of:
• vCenter: Resource and LCM management of vSphere Cluster
• VCF Ops: Monitoring and licensing of Edge
SDDC Manager and NSX manager are not required for the one node architecture, but can be used to manage thick
Edge locations.
– The WAN link must satisfy the following latency and bandwidth requirements:
• Up to 300ms RTT between vCenter and ESX (Please refer official Latency details for each component.)
• Bandwidth: Minimum 10-Mbps throughput
• Remote Edge Clusters: Each edge site is represented by a single vSphere Cluster. Characteristics of the edge cluster
include:
– vSphere Cluster: Single-Node with vSphere DRS and HA enabled.
– vSphere Supervisor: vSphere Supervisor enables the deployment and management of Kubernetes workloads
directly on the ESX host.
– Workloads: Supports a mix of traditional Virtual Machines (VMs), native Containers, and vSphere Pods.
– Edge Services to support GitOps Integration: ArgoCD and Harbor that is deployed as part of the Supervisor
Services.
Single Node Management Design
The Management Domain is a foundational component of the VCF architecture. It is highly flexible and can be tailored to
accommodate the environmental constraints of an Edge deployment.
The design of a Management Domain factors in edge security requirements, WAN bandwidth, latency, and the overall
scale of the edge locations. Hosting Edge management components begins with placement. If the latency between the
central data center and the edge is below 300ms, centralizing the Management Domain at the central DC is the most
efficient and simplest approach. For locations where latency exceeds 300ms, deploying the Management Domain closer
to the edge locations is a viable alternative. Regardless of the placement strategy, the following design recommendations
apply to all Management Domain architectures.

Single Node Cluster Design
A core tenet of edge design is the ability to support VM and Kubernetes workloads at the edge that offers operational
predictability and simplified lifecycle management.
The fundamental unit of resources for each edge site is a vSphere cluster. Even with a single node edge, each host must
be a member of a single node vSphere cluster. This cluster must have both vSphere HA (no admission control) and DRS
must be enabled as these features are required by VKS. Storage on the one node can be VMFS based on local disk or
external storage using FC or NFS.
A single VDS with a minimum of two NICs is required for link level redundancy on a single node. NIC speed can be GE or
higher.

Adding a single host to an existing vCenter environment is a manual step. For larger-scale edge onboarding or

Single Node vSphere Supervisor Design
Single node vSphere Supervisor is crucial for edge use cases due to several factors that align with the unique demands
and constraints of edge deployments:
• Get the most out of a single physical server by efficiently running both virtual machines and containerized applications,
managed by a unified control plane
• Process data and run applications directly at the source, crucial for real-time analytics, AI/ML inference, and critical
operational control at the edge.
• Native integration with vSphere Content Library, Argo CD, and Harbor to deliver pull and desired state-based
orchestration for Containers and Virtual Machines workloads.

GitOps Components Placement
The following components are the minimum components that are needed for GitOps:
• Argo CD - Argo CD is used to implement a GitOps-based continuous delivery model by synchronizing application
configurations stored in Git repositories with edge clusters. Two placement choices for Argo CD Operator and instance
across edge sites: A per edge site design versus A centralized Argo CD instance. The appropriate approach depends
on factors such as network reliability, scale of edge sites, operational overhead, and organizational governance
requirements.
• Git Repository - Git repositories serve as the source of truth for infrastructure and application configurations in a
GitOps workflow. A decision must be made whether to host these repositories using a third-party git platform as a
service or through an internally managed solution.
• Content Caching - Two types of Content Caching: Content Library stores VM OVAs and Container registries store. In
distributed or edge environments, organizations often evaluate whether to rely on a third-party cloud-based container
registry or deploy an internally managed private registry with caching or replication capabilities. Organizations also
must determine if VM OVAs must be centrally managed or must reside locally at the edge.
Argo CD Placement
Two placement choices for Argo CD across multiple edge sites: a per edge site design versus a centralized ArgoCD
instance.
Argo CD communication involves periodically checking Git repositories for configuration updates and communicating with
each cluster to detect configuration drift. Depending on the placement of the Argo CD server, if deployed at the edge, Git
repository access requires WAN bandwidth, and configuration drift checks require LAN bandwidth. If deployed centrally,
configuration drift check requires WAN bandwidth and Git repository access does not require bandwidth from the edge.
The total amount of network traffic depends on the size of the applications and the number of clusters at the edge site.
In general, configuration drift check generates a high volume of traffic compared to repository access. The configuration
check is low bandwidth because only the Git commit hash id is used to determine if the branch has been updated. If the
commit SHA remains unchanged, ArgoCD does not fetch the repository content again.
Local Argo CD Instance Per Edge - Distributed Argo CD
In the per Edge Site design, each edge site hosts its own dedicated Argo CD instance managing VKS clusters
or Supervisor namespaces local to the edge location. This design works well in environments with limited WAN.
Credentials required to manage the edge site can be scoped locally (see section on Authentication design). If VM
images and application binaries are also hosted locally using the Content Library and Harbor container registry, workload
bootstrapping does not need to leave the site. Since each site is independent, local Argo CD also helps reduce the blast
radius by isolating failures to individual sites.
For thin edges that support only a handful of edge applications, capacity planning of the Argo CD instance can also be
simplified. There are typically no sharding requirements of Argo CD Application controllers, lots of the parallelism and
concurrency settings can be left at default or even reduced for thin edge sites to minimize consumption and configuration
management overhead (see section on sizing).
While this approach simplifies Argo CD sizing and tuning, especially as the number of sites increases to thousands. Since
each site requires its own Argo CD instance, complexity in monitoring and number of deployment steps increase as site
counts gets larger. Although both can be managed effectively through deployment automation and monitoring. VCF Edge
Automation is developed to reduce deployment complexity. The automation framework addresses the ease of on-ramp by
simplifying deployment of Supervisor and services with idempotent deployment. VCF Edge Automation is available on the
Powershell Gallery and on Github.com (Open Source).
Central Argo CD for all Edge Sites - One Argo CD managing all remote Namespaces and Clusters
The centralized Argo CD setup involves a single Argo CD instance managing remote VKS clusters or Supervisor
namespaces across edge sites. The centralized approach allows for simpler control, since there is only a single Argo CD
endpoint, one place to add repository credentials, API keys, Argo CD CLI/API and etc.
The steps to add remote VKS clusters to Argo CD are similar to the distributed setup. However it’s important to make
sure the Argo CD has direct access to the Kubernetes API server at each location and there is sufficient WAN bandwidth.
Argo CD relies heavily on communication with each Kubernetes cluster to capture data to ensure that the desire state is
always maintained. In a centralized setup, this communication must traverse the WAN. The larger the edge location (more
Broadcom 1374

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
applications), the more bandwidth is consumed by Argo CD. Careful bandwidth monitoring is critical in the centralized
deployment as any issues with the WAN at the central instance could impact configuration updates for all sites.
Attention:
Managing remote namespaces requires creating an additional service account and role binding in each
namespace before it can be added to ArgoCD. Currently this step is manual and must be centrally maintained.
Performance tuning is also a key consideration in this architecture. Cluster states, can grow significantly over time.
Sharding Application Controller replicas across clusters to improve performance can be complex and often requires
manual intervention at scale. As the number of sites and applications increases, careful resource planning and ongoing
performance optimization become essential.
Key Considerations:
•
Local Argo CD design ensures better fault isolation and easier scalability at a high number of locations. Simple Local
Network design. Works well with limited WAN. Overhead of monitoring and patching are high as each site must be
managed separately.
• Centralized Argo CD carries the risk of failure impacting all sites, and it needs careful attention to performance and
resource management. Complex Network design. Does not operate well with limited WAN, edge connectivity. Day-2
activities such as monitoring and patching are centralized.

Git Repository and Container Registry Placement
This section outlines the architecture and operational considerations for implementing GitOps for Edge sites. It focuses
on placement impact of key GitOps components and configurations that enable scalable, reliable, and secure GitOps
workflows.
GitOps Infrastructure Design
The Supervisor enables the deployment and management of workloads in a declarative manner through Supervisor
services, supporting modern, containerized applications and must be enabled at each edge site. This section reviews
three possible design patterns:
Infrastructure Design 1: Local Argo CD at Edge with Public Git Repository and Container Registry
Git repositories and container registries are consumed as services from GitHub, GitLab, Docker, Artifactory, or other third-
party hosted platforms. ArgoCD is deployed at each Edge site for simplified performance, RBAC, and networking design.
Infrastructure Design 2: Local Argo CD at Edge with Private Git Repository with Local Harbor Registry
Private Git repositories are deployed in the central VCF instance or a mirror copy of the central Git repository are
deployed in the management domain of the VCF instance. ArgoCD is deployed at each Edge site for simplified
performance, RBAC, and networking design. Harbor registry and Content library are also deployed at each edge site to
service virtual machine or VKS cluster deployment.
Git Repository and Container Registry Placement Design 1
Git repositories and container registries are consumed as services from GitHub, GitLab, Docker, Artifactory, or other third-
party hosted platforms. ArgoCD is deployed at each Edge site for simplified performance, RBAC, and networking design.

Git Repository Design
Repository design stands out as one of the most critical elements for operational scalability, maintainability, and team
efficiency. A well-structured repository enforces a clear separation between source code and deployment code, which is
essential for managing environments and automating deployments effectively. For smaller projects, a monorepo approach
can be a simple starting point. However, as systems grow and multiple teams manage different applications, adopting a
multi-repo strategy can be more effective.
One of the most important best practices is to maintain a clear separation between source code repositories and
deployment configurations (defined using YAML). Combining source code and deployment configurations in a single
repository introduces unnecessary coordination across teams and makes auditing changes difficult. Keeping them
separate helps prevent accidental deployment and simplify access control.
Mono Repository
Use a single Git repository for all Argo CD deployments, infrastructure, and applications. This repository does not contain
any source code. Instead, it stores the deployment definitions for all applications, even when those applications are
unrelated to each other. Monorepo is a logical choice when starting out with GitOps. Using one repository simplifies
maintenance and improves overall visibility. However as the edge environment grows and more teams and applications
are involved in the GitOps process, this approach introduces coordination challenges and deployment conflicts.
Git Repository Per Team
Broadcom 1382

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A single Repository works great as a starting point, another approach is to group applications into groups, based on team
or projects. Each team would have a dedicated repository. Members of each team would be given write access to the
repository while read access or no access are provided to members of other teams.
Broadcom 1383

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Broadcom 1384

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A minimum of two repositories are created when starting out: one for application and another for Infrastructure. The
infrastructure repository contains workload configurations that run directly on top of the virtualization layer, such as VM
and VKS. The application layer includes both App Configuration and App monitoring deployment definitions. Over time as
edge applications grow, more application repositories can be created to align with each application development team,
and a common repository to share dependencies required by all teams. With a dedicated repository, devOps engineers
can check out only the Git repository that contains the relevant components. This approach helps avoid Git conflicts and
makes it easier to apply extra security constraints without running into cross-organization challenges.
Key Considerations:
• Mono Repository design works well when it’s desirable to view all changes across all environments and services in
one place. But it’s harder to scale to large projects with multiple teams.
• Multi Repository provides autonomy. Each team manages its own pipeline, approvals, and dependency. It provides
scoped access control, but much harder to apply updates across services. Global changes must be repeated across
repositories. Tracking deployment and changing history across repositories can be cumbersome.
Table below is a summary comparison of the two approaches:
Table 439: Repository Approaches
Mono Repository Multi Repository
Change Isolation Change in one directory can impact others Each repo is isolated. Misconfiguration is
isolated to each repository.
Change Visibility All changes are tracked at one place, Changes are spread across repos, harder
including history. to get full visibility
Scalability Harder for large teams and projects Scales better across many teams.
Team Autonomy Must coordinate changes across multiple Changes can be coordinated within a team.
teams
Access control RBAC Hard to limit permission per team. Simple. Team controls who gets access to
the repository
Repository structure to Model Edge Sites
Software Development organizations are familiar with using Git branches to represent a release and promote a branch
only after it passes all automated tests. When adopting GitOps, it may seem natural on paper to extend the same
branching strategy that is used for application release management to edge configuration management. However in
practice managing each environment as a separate branch is highly complex and should be avoided.
The best practice in GitOps is to map all environments to a single branch and use dedicated folders to represent each
environment. This "environment-per-folder" approach is similar to how Helm operates - a set of base configuration that
can be shared, and a site-specific folder that contains parameters unique to each deployment. Configuration updates are
done by creating a short-lived branch, modify configuration in the site-specific folder, and immediately commit back to
main for deployment. Long lived branches should not be used to model edge environments.

and changes always merge back to the long lived environments across multiple
main branch. branches are difficult and hard to maintain.
View Site specific configuration Simple. If implemented correctly, only Complex - Complexity in associating
configuration deltas are maintained in each branch to environment. Lacks consistency
folder. in addressing environment-specific
configuration delta.
Change Auditing Simple. All change histories are maintained Complex - Change histories are specific to
in a single place a branch & environment
Base and Overlay
Broadcom 1385

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In GitOps, configuration readability and maintainability are critical. Less configuration, reduces the likelihood to introduce
configuration errors and is easier to understand the configuration delta between sites.
Configuration optimization is often accomplished with the Kustomization operator using base and overlays. Base consists
of defining a set of base configuration that applies to all edge locations, and overlays are site-specific modifications
of the base configuration. The Kustomize operator traverses base configuration manifests to add, remove, or update
configuration in line, without requiring templates. More details can be found here. The following figure is an example using
base and overlay to define the configuration for a VM:

for Windows and Large for Linux. Kustomization YAML is used to override the base configuration. In this scenario, Site 1
deploys Small flavors for both Linux and Windows VMs, while Site 2 deploys a Large Linux VM and a Small Windows VM.

Bootstrap and Operational Flow
Edge site activation involves configuration ESX host into a single node vSphere edge cluster, activate the Supervisor
service, and install Argo CD and register the Git Repository with Harbor.
The Day 0 Bootstrap phase establishes the foundation by provisioning ESX hosts using Zero Touch Provisioning or
manual ISO installation, followed by enabling the vSphere cluster and Supervisor through vCenter. Once the infrastructure
is ready, the Broadcom Argo CD Operator is deployed via the Supervisor catalog, and the Git repository is securely
registered to trigger the initial synchronization.
Day 1 Ongoing Operations, the environment shifts to a continuous delivery model where platform operators push manifest
updates directly to Git, which Argo CD continuously monitoring for state drift. Argo CD automatically detects and applies
Broadcom 1389

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
configuration updates. This GitOps approach streamlines lifecycle maintenance, allowing workloads to self-recover after
central VCF-driven events.

Argo CD Application Components Design
In Argo CD, the journey from deploying a single application to managing a global fleet of edge sites is bridged by three
progressive concepts: the Application, the App-of-Apps pattern, and the ApplicationSet.
At its foundation, an Application is the core building block that connects one specific Git directory to one target cluster
and namespace. However manually creating these individual resources becomes a tedious bottleneck. The App-of-Apps
pattern was created to bootstrap an entire edge cluster's application from a single root manifest. For multiple cluster
environments, the ApplicationSet uses "generators" (example: scan Git repo for application folders) to dynamically
template and spawn dozens or hundreds of individual Applications on the fly.

deploys other Applications. without clicking through the UI a single cluster.
many times.

generates multiple Argo CD multi-tenant environments, and 20 clusters, or auto-deploying

and rules. Git folder with new Apps is

App-of-AppSets is another design pattern for more advanced use cases and we cover it in a later update to the design
guide if necessary.

Argo CD Component Design Pattern #2
The App-of-App design involves defining a parent application referencing a directory in a Git repository that holds the
definitions of other child applications. Instead of manually deploying each application, the root Argo CD application
automatically detects and deploys all the child applications. The parent application tracks changes and propagates
updates, configurations, and policies to its child applications, without manually accessing the Argo CD UI or CLI. This
design pattern uses the Application controller, and is installed by the Argo CD operator by default. App of App is typically
used for Argo CD bootstrapping, and a programmatic way to control application startup dependencies. A typical directory
folder structure looks similar to the following diagram:

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Argo CD Example Repository layout for App-of-App
When a cluster is created, a parent Application is created in argo CD pointing to the bootstrap YAML. The bootstrap YAML
references applications defined in the Application folder. Each site has a separate bootstrap App of App YAML referencing
applications that are required for each location.

kind: Application
metadata:
name: site1-bootstrap
namespace: demo1
spec:
project: default
source:
repoURL: https://github.com/xiaoGaoBroadCom/argocd-example.git
path: argocd/application/site1
targetRevision: HEAD
destination:
server: https://192.168.30.161:443
namespace: demo1

Argo CD Component Design Pattern 3:
When managing many edge sites spread across many geographically diverse sites, creating and mapping Argo CD
application YAMLs can be repetitive. ApplicationSet significantly reduces the manual effort that is involved in building Argo
CD Application YAML files. It uses a template to define the base configuration for applications, which is then combined
with parameters from a generator to produce multiple Argo CD Applications.
The ApplicationSet controller currently supports several types of generators, each offering different ways to define
and generate application parameters. The Cluster generator can be powerful in a centralized Argo CD design with lots
of edge clusters deploying identical sets of Apps. If Argo CD is deployed at an edge site, the Git generator could be
more appropriate to deploy multiple application workloads to a site. To add dependency or order of boot-up sequence,
ProgressiveSync feature was introduced in Argo CD v.2.6.0, but is in an early stage of adoption, not ready for production
deployments.
The ApplicationSet controller is bundled with the VMware Argo CD Operator, but must be explicitly enabled.
ApplicationSet Design Pattern
Broadcom 1396

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Below YAML is an example design. This design assumes that the Git generator is used. Instead of creating Application
YAML, ApplicationSet YAML is used to auto generate all applications, in this case VKS clusters, and virtual machines.
ApplicationSet Design Pattern Example
Broadcom 1397

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Git Directory generator generates parameters using the directory structure of the Argo CD repo. The application
metadata name is derived from indexing array elements making up the directory path (3 and 1 in this example). Source
is set to the directory path that matches path “apps/*/overlays/site1” deploying to the destination cluster specified in the
destination server endpoint.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
name: site1-appset
namespace: argocd
spec:
goTemplate: true
goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
generators:
- git:
repoURL: https://github.com/xiaoGaoBroadCom/argocd-example.git
revision: HEAD
directories:
- path: apps/*/overlays/site1
template:
metadata:
name: '{{index .path.segments 3}}-{{index .path.segments 1}}'
spec:
#Referto https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues/18643 when adding repo to project.
project: default
Broadcom 1398

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
source:
repoURL: https://github.com/xiaoGaoBroadCom/argocd-example.git
targetRevision: HEAD
path: '{{.path.path}}'
destination:
server: https://10.50.12.202:443
namespace: argocd
This ApplicationSet automatically discovers every directory under repoURL that matches the pattern apps/*/overlays/site1
and creates a separate Argo CD Application for each one and dynamically names the generated application. Some of the
key parameters:
• metadata.name: '{{index .path.segments 3}}-{{index .path.segments 1}}':
The path.segments variable breaks the matched directory path into parts that are separated by "/".
For a path like apps/vmapp/overlays/site1:
• Index 1 is vmapp (since the path starts with apps).
• Index 3 is site1.
The final name for the VM application is vmapp-site1
Argo CD Resources Design
Scalability of Argo CD deployment is a function of configuration options for its three core components: the application
server, repository server, and API server.
For the Application controller, factors that influence the sizing includes:
• Number of applications
• Number of clusters under management
• Rate of APIs requests (Client QPS)
• Tuning configurations regarding parallelism, operational processors, etc
• Number of shards (If applicable)
Argo CD Repo server handles Git repository operations. Operations such as cloning, syncing, and manifest generation.
Variables to consider include:
• Size of the manifest
• Type of tooling (Helm vs. Kustomization)
• Parallelism / Concurrent processing
The primary function of the Argo CD API server is to expose platform functionalities to users via UI, API, and CLI.
Each Service is configured with a default resource Request / Limits based on the K8s resource specification definition.
The following table outlines the default resource limits associated with each service.
CPU Limit Memory Limit Ephemeral Storage
Repo Server 1 0.5G 5G
Argocd-Server 1 0.25G 1G
Redis 1 0.25G 1G
Notification 1 1G 1G
application-controller 2 2G 1G
applicationSet-controller 2 1G 1G
The above settings are a good starting point for PoC with a limited number of applications and clusters. Platform
administrators are expected to monitor actual usage based on their deployment and configure appropriate resource
Broadcom 1399

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
requests and limits for their production edge deployments. Options to reduce CPU and memory utilization involve reducing
the number of parallel operations:
• Reposerver.parallelism.limit - Default value is 0, which means no limit. In environments with many applications,
introducing a limit can prevent performance degradation and OOM kills.
• Controller.kubectl.parallelism.limit - Default value is 20, which means Argo CD can use 20 concurrent kubectl
sessions to interact with the K8s cluster. Decreasing this value reduces resource utilization, but might slow down sync
operations.
• controller .operation.processors and controller.status.processors - Both settings control parallel processors for
reconciliation and sync operations. Decreasing this value reduces cpu and memory utilization, but slows down sync
performance.
• ArgoCD_K8S_Client_QPS and ARGOCD_K8S_CLIENT_BURST - Both parameters can indirectly impact Argo CD
utilization
Networking Resource Design
In environments with infrequent changes, and where self-healing is not enabled, WAN bandwidth usage is minimal when
Argo CD is deployed at the edge. However, in scenarios with frequent application updates, Argo CD tuning may be
required to reduce the frequency of configuration manifest downloads.. Argo CD design options that can help reduce WAN
usage include:

timeout.reconciliation the frequency of automatic sync attempts

according to the characteristics of the

Network capacity should match the number of clusters and users involved. It is important to monitor the right set of Argo
CD Application metrics reflecting the deployment architecture.
Argo CD Authentication Design
The VMware distribution of the Argo CD Operator supports authentication using either local accounts or Single Sign-
On (SSO) using the OpenID Connect (OIDC) protocol. Protocols such as SAML and LDAP requires external delegation
capabilities and can be accomplished using VCF Automation.
Design Option 1 (Central OIDC Provider)
This design assumes reliable external access from the edge to either the Internet or intranet. In Central OIDC Provider
setup, Argo CD is configured to redirect all UI and CLI access requests to a centralized Identity Provider (IdP). IdP
can be hosted either on-premises or in the cloud. List of certified OIDC-compliant providers are listed on the ArgoCD
documentation page. A sample integration with Okta is listed in the Appendix.
Design Option 2 (Local Accounts)
In scenarios where external connectivity is unavailable and only a small group of users, local Argo CD accounts are the
best alternative that can be used to ensure uninterrupted access. Local accounts are typically created as part of the Argo
Broadcom 1400

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
CD instance creation, and can be updated via kubectl patching and Argo CD CLI. JWT tokens are still used even for local
accounts. When a local user is authenticated, a non-expiring JWT token is signed and issued by the Argo CD API server.
This token can be revoked by updating the user password.
Important:
Based on this blueprint design, to deploy and onboard single-host edge sites, including Argo CD integration,
customers can use the VCF Edge at Scale automation script to simplify and streamline edge deployments.
VCF Edge Design Blueprint for Government and Defense Use Case
This design focuses on the Defense Use Case for VCF Edge to address the unique operational, security, and compliance
needs of federal agencies on and off the battlefield.
Broadcom 1401

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 165: VCF Edge Reference Design for Defense Use Case
This design blueprint focuses on government, federal, and defense use cases for VMware Cloud Foundation Edge. The
Blueprint addresses the unique operational, resiliency, and compliance requirements of mission environments both within
centralized facilities and at remote or tactical edge locations.
The architecture is designed to support operational environments where connectivity may be intermittent, degraded, or
fully disconnected. Type of deployments include operating in remote field locations, mobile operational environments,
forward operating sites, and other mission-critical edge scenarios.
This reference design demonstrates the integration of centralized infrastructure services, localized edge operations,
Kubernetes and VM-based workloads, and security controls into a unified operational model. This model supports both
connected and disconnected states. Key design objectives of this architecture include:
• enabling localized operational autonomy at the tactical edge
Broadcom 1402

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• maintaining centralized governance and policy control where connectivity permits
• supporting mission continuity during WAN or SATCOM disruption
• securing sensitive workloads through segmented networking and layered security controls
• supporting sovereign and compliance-sensitive operational environments
• enabling scalable deployment of mission applications and AI-enabled workloads at the edge
• supporting both VM and Kubernetes-based application platforms in constrained edge environments
This architecture also supports multiple operational deployment models depending on mission and site requirements,
including:
• centrally managed edge operations
• regionally autonomous edge hubs
• fully disconnected or degraded edge operations
• lightweight edge deployments with constrained infrastructure footprints
• locally managed edge environments requiring operational independence
The design blueprint progressively decomposes the architecture into the specific domains, including the infrastructure,
networking, security, lifecycle management, and workload.
Operational Context
VMware Cloud Foundation Edge (VCFE) extends the centralized management capabilities of the platform to
geographically dispersed edge locations supporting a wide range of use cases and verticals. VCFE edge locations can
be as small as one node, two node cluster with vSAN witness or external storage, or multi-node ESX clusters up to
256 Cores per edge location. A typical VCFE customer can start with as little as 10 physical locations and can scale to
thousands of sites. There’s no upper adoption limit on the total number of edge sites that can be deployed. The number of
edge locations are driven by the use case.
This guide focuses on various Military use cases and focuses on the thin edge design, which supports vSphere cluster
deployments ranging from a single host up to four ESX hosts. The document addresses these deployment scenarios by
detailing three common architectures.

Government or Federal Use Cases
Military platforms, from heavily armored tanks and high-performance fighter jets to the individual soldier's wearable
gear, rely on highly specialized, mission-critical applications to achieve operational success. These software systems,
collectively known as C4ISR (Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Intelligence, Surveillance, and
Reconnaissance), must function with absolute reliability in the harshest environments. Application stacks that are
hosted on this platform provide real-time situational awareness and precise targeting, whether the asset is traversing
rugged terrain, flying at supersonic speeds, or operating in a Disconnected, Intermittent, and Limited (DIL) bandwidth
environment. Use cases that are applicable to this guide:

Design Options
This section expands on the three options that are outlined in the overview section.
Design Options:
• Central Management with Remote Edge Hosts and Intermittent Connectivity
• Remote Management with Multiple Hosts
Central Management with Remote Edge Hosts and Intermittent Connectivity
Central Management with Remote Edge hosts consists of the following major components:
• Centralized Management Domain
– A dedicated set of management components hosted near the edge locations. Management Domain components
are tasked with managing the inventory and lifecycle of the remote edge clusters across the WAN. The WAN link
must satisfy the following latency and bandwidth requirements:
• Latency: Up to 300ms RTT between vCenter and ESX
• Bandwidth: Minimum 10-Mbps throughput
• Remote Edge Clusters: Each edge site is represented by a single vSphere Cluster. Characteristics of the edge cluster
include:
– vSphere Cluster: Single-Node or Multi-Node ESX hosts with DRS and HA enabled.
– vSphere Supervisor: vSphere Supervisor enables the deployment and management of Kubernetes workloads
directly on the ESX host. A "Control Plane VM" and Load Balancer are deployed for the Supervisor functionality.
– Workloads: Supports a mix of traditional Virtual Machines (VMs), native Containers, and vSphere Pods. Native
Containers running within the vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) cluster. Virtual Machine and vSphere Pods run
directly on top of the hypervisor.
– GitOps Integration: Argo CD deployed as part of the Supervisor Services. Argo CD enables declarative application
deployment directly to the edge cluster. Deployments can be infrastructure or applications running inside the
infrastructure.
A core tenet of this design is the standardization of the edge deployment. By maintaining a uniform host configuration,
network topology, and storage configuration across all remote sites ensures operational predictability and simplified
lifecycle management. This standardized approach is a foundational best practice for distributed edge infrastructure and is
assumed throughout this document.
Management Component Design
The management domain is based on the design options that are published in the VCF9.1 Design Library. Management
component design to support the edge must be aligned with the specific functional requirements of the edge. Sites that
do not require multi-layer routing and security addon with vDefend can extend existing Fleet with a new edge vCenter and
can share VCF Operations for licensing and monitoring. This approach is documented as Edge Pattern #9.

Edge Core Service Design
The availability of foundational services such as DNS, NTP, and workload templates are critical for autonomous
operations. Provided the services themselves do not consume excessive CPU or memory capacity that are intended for
workloads, deploying close to the edge is recommended. In addition, deploying foundational services at the edge reduces
WAN bandwidth contention between workloads and the control plane.
Broadcom 1415

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To support the disconnected mode of operation required for autonomous operations, infrastructure services that are
required to support the workload runtime dependencies must be available.
• Network and Foundational Services: STIG-compliant infrastructure relies on FIPS-validated encryption and a robust
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to ensure session integrity and data-in-transit security. Modern cloud-native workloads
have deep, systemic dependencies on these foundational services:
– DNS: Service discovery in both traditional and modern applications relies heavily on DNS. If DNS is unavailable,
edge applications may fail to operate.
– NTP: Encryption is highly sensitive to temporal accuracy. If the system clock drifts even slightly, certificate validation
may fail. STIG compliant infrasturcture relies on encryption and certificates to ensure session integrity.
– Availability Requirements: Because both DNS and NTP services are pre-requisites for the rest of the stack,
they must be architected for high availability to prevent a single point of failure from cascading through the entire
environment.
• Artifact Repository: Local Artifact repository enables fast provisioning without WAN dependency and offline
operations during WAN disruptions.
– Local Content Library: Content libraries are vSphere container objects for storing and sharing OVF and OVA
packages, VM templates, vApp templates, and other types of files.
– Container Registry: If a Kubernetes pod crashes or a node reboots while the WAN link is down, the host
(depending on imagePullPolicy) pulls an image from its configured registry. If the registry is central and can't be
reached, the workload stays down (ImagePullBackOff). With a local Harbor registry, the Images can be stored
at the edge. Hosts pull images over the high-speed local LAN rather than the restricted WAN link. Harbor can
be consumed as a supervisor service or deployed as a VM appliance. Harbor replication policies can be used to
control image distribution between instances, or used as a pull-through proxy for local caching. In both scenarios,
an image is retrieved from the central registry once and served locally to all endpoints within the edge cluster. This
architectural approach prevents bandwidth saturation, and significantly accelerates application startup times by
using high-speed local LAN connectivity.
• Pull based Configuration Updates: In a traditional fleet deployment, vCenter "pushes" configurations to the edge.
For Edge sites that only have intermittent connectivity, if the WAN link is down, the configuration update fails as
Edge ESX hosts are not reachable. A GitOps-based approach uses a "Pull" model that is inherently resilient to
the intermittent connectivity typical of edge sites. Configuration updates for workloads are staged in a central Git
repository, and Edge sites retrieves the workload update only when there is connectivity.
Broadcom 1416

With services running locally, even without vCenter connectivity, the following actions remain operational at the host level.
• ESX Host Resilience: A physical host can be rebooted. Once initialized, the hypervisor remains in its last known good
configuration and resumes managing local resources.
• VM Workload Continuity: Existing Virtual Machines can be restarted and resumed. Because the VM configuration files
(.vmx) reside on shared or local storage, the ESX host can power them on without vCenter intervention.
• VKS / Containerized Workloads: vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) workloads can be restarted provided vCenter
assisted operation is not required. An example of such operation is Persistent Volume (PV) attachment to containers.
This is contingent on the host having access to the container image repository to pull images if necessary.
The following limitation applies when operating in disconnected mode:
• Administrative and maintenance tasks that rely on the vCenter API must be deferred and scheduled once connectivity
is restored.
• Any workload requiring the creation, attachment, or modification of Persistent Volumes.
• Any operation specifically requiring vCenter, Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) balancing, creating VMs, or
modifying virtual networks.
Edge Compute Hardware and Network Design
Broadcom 1418

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Military edge compute hardware must be ruggedized to tolerate extreme temperatures and environmental fluctuations.
Depending on the specific use case, systems may be required to adhere to MIL-STD-810H for environmental survivability
and MIL-STD-461G for electromagnetic compatibility, ensuring signal stealth in contested environments. Beyond physical
durability, the hardware must be optimized to support VMware ESX in alignment with the DISA STIG framework. This
includes a hardened BIOS and hardware-assisted virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V), TPM 2.0 modules to satisfy
CCI-000366, which mandates hardware-rooted Secure Boot and host attestation. If shared storage is required, the
hardware should ideally be vSAN ReadyNode certified. If vSAN ReadyNode is not available, at a minimum, edge
hardware should be listed on the VMware Compatibility Guide (VCG) for VCF 9.
Depending on the edge requirements, edge hardware must be equipped with sufficient disk count and capacity to support
ESX host imaging and persistent data storage. To accommodate use cases requiring strict network isolation, servers must
also feature enough of physical NICs, each providing sufficient throughput to meet application performance requirements.
Edge workloads using external storage such as NFSv3 and FC can also be used as primary storage. Refer to VCF9
documentation for external storage support.

Edge Compute Node Design
The fundamental unit of resources for each edge site is a vSphere cluster. Since edge sites are geographically separated
and follow a traditional hub-and-spoke topology, resources are localized to each site, making a single-site cluster design
the most appropriate. Depending on the host count, number of uplinks, and storage profile, each cluster type follows a
specific design pattern.
• Single-Node Edge: vSphere cluster settings even in a single node requires vSphere HA (no admission control) and
DRS, as these features are required by VKS. Local VMFS storage volume using local disks is sufficient for a Single
Node configuration. A single vDS with a minimum of two NICs is required for link level redundancy. NIC speed can be
GE or higher.
• Two-Node Edge: A two-node edge cluster can use both vSAN or third-party external storage such as NFS or Fibre
Channel. If a two-node vSAN design is used for storage, then a witness node is required to maintain quorum and
store metadata. VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) at the edge fully supports both dedicated witness and shared
witness models. Witness appliance can be local or remote, in the cloud or at the Edge. Both vSAN OSA and ESA are
supported. A single vDS with a minimum of two NICs is required as a starting point. Multiple vDS with redundant NICs
is required to support use cases that require physical isolation between workloads.
• Three+ Node Edge: Similar to the two-node design, three-node edge vSphere cluster can use both vSAN or third-
party external storage such as NFS or Fibre Channel. Cluster using vSAN as storage can use both OSA and ESA
depending on the type of disks and network connectivity. A single vDS with a minimum of two NICs is required as
a starting point. Multiple vDS with redundant NICs is required to support use cases that require physical isolation
between workloads.
In all cases, data must be encrypted both in transit and at rest, adhering to FIPS 140 requirements. Traffic isolation is
achieved through dedicated physical interfaces (where hardware permits) or VLAN tagging when constrained to a single
interface.

When sharing a common uplink for all traffic, classifying and tagging traffic is essential for maintaining both cluster stability
and deterministic performance. By assigning vSAN traffic to a dedicated VLAN with High NIOC priority, you protect the
storage backplane from latency spikes that could cause host desynchronization. vMotion and Management traffic are
isolated on their own VLANs to prevent bulk data transfers from saturating the link, ensuring that administrative functions
to the hosts remain accessible. Finally, categorizing VM traffic with a lower relative priority ensures that a surge in
application demand or a guest-level network issue cannot starve critical infrastructure services of bandwidth. The following
table outlines the recommended VLAN and QOS marking based on traffic type:
Table 445: VDS VLAN Tagging and QoS Marking
Traffic Type VLAN Recommendation Priority (NIOC)
vSAN Dedicated High
vMotion Dedicated Standard
MGMT Dedicated Standard
VM Traffic App Specific Low/Standard
Edge Access Security Design
Security for virtual infrastructure is a defense-in-depth model where each layer must be individually hardened to prevent
lateral movement and unauthorized access. This layered approach starts at the hypervisor and moves up through the
management and network control planes.
While the vSphere stack is secure by default, mission-critical environments, especially at the Edge require more
configurations to meet DISA STIG standards.
Edge environments lack the protection of a traditional data center. This section focuses on hardening security at the ESXi
layer and management components that resides at the edge. Ensuring that even when unauthorized physical access is
gained, the integrity of the host and its data remains intact is critical. Key security decisions include:
• Secure Boot & TPM 2.0: In the DISA STIG for vSphere, Secure Boot and TPM 2.0 form the foundation of the
Hardware Root of Trust. Secure Boot ensures that only digital signatures that it trusts are loaded. If an attacker
attempts to replace the ESX bootloader with a malicious version, Secure Boot detects the absence of a valid
VMware signature and refuses to start the server. The TPM 2.0 chip enables Remote Attestation, allowing vCenter
to cryptographically verify that the hypervisor has not been compromised by unauthorized kernel-level modifications.
Together, these technologies ensure that the boot process and the operating state of the host remain untampered and
compliant with the federal security mandates.
• VIB Acceptance Levels: For DISA STIGs, VIB Acceptance Levels are critical because they establish the "Chain
of Trust" for every piece of code running at the kernel level. If an attacker can inject a malicious VIB, they gain total
control over the hypervisor and all hosted Virtual Machines. To prevent the execution of unauthorized code set to a
minimum of PartnerSupported. In high-security or tactical environments, acceptance level is often restricted further to
VMwareCertified.
• Encryption in Transit: vSphere now runs in FIPS-compliant mode by default. Both TLS1.2 and TLS1.3 are available.
TLS1.3 protocol is on by default and falls back to TLS1.2 as well to support legacy product integration.
• Access control and Account Security: Lockdown restricts access to ESX host. At the Edge, where physical security
may be lower than in a central data center. Limiting ESX host access with lockdown mode is vital. Normal Lockdown
Mode allows specific users to access the DCUI, while Strict Lockdown Mode disables the DCUI entirely, forcing all
management through vCenter.. Implementing Active Directory for centralized identity management. Enable ESX Shell
and SSH services only when required for troubleshooting
Broadcom 1424

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Traffic & Network Isolation: infrastructure stability and security depend on the strict logical and physical separation
of critical system traffic. Administrators must classify Management, vSAN, and vMotion traffic into dedicated VLANs to
prevent unauthorized interception and "noisy neighbor" contention. To mitigate the risk of MAC spoofing and packet
sniffing, vSwitch security policies must be set to Reject for Promiscuous Mode, MAC Address Changes, and Forged
Transmits. The DISA STIG for VMware ESX mandates a "Least Privilege" approach to network security. For every
enabled service (like SSH, vMotion, or Web Access), you must disable the "Allow connections from any IP address"
setting. Limiting firewall ports on ESX hosts to a specific set of hosts prevents attack surface

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Edge Cluster Activation
Edge activation starts at the edge location. With the introduction of Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP) in VCF 9, new
edge hosts can be imaged, provisioned, and brought into service using VCFE PowerShell automation without manual
intervention.
The transition of a new host from power-on to an active member of the remote cluster follows a highly orchestrated
automated workflow. The process initiates at the edge when a device powers on and requests an IP address with DHCP.
The DHCP server provides an IP along with a global vCenter boot URL. The edge ESX server uses this boot URL to
securely retrieve its boot configuration. vCSA uses values from SMBIOS data from the Edge server to decide which
cluster and image to assign. If DHCP is not used, this boot URL can be statically programmed in the BIOS. The activation
process varies between deployment scenarios.
Scenario 1: vCenter only and basic L2 connectivity at edge location.
• Design 1: Central vCenter with remote edge vSphere cluster, no NSX
• Design 2: Edge vSphere cluster with vCenter local to the cluster, no NSX
Scenario 2: vCenter and NSX at the edge with multi-layer routing/switching.
• Design 1: Central vCenter and NSX manager, remote edge cluster with 3+ hosts
• Design 2: Remote edge cluster with 3+ hosts, vCenter, and NSX local to the cluster

Once Edge activation and vSphere infrastructure configuration are complete, having critical services available locally even
when there's no external connectivity is a critical part of DoD autonomous operations requirement.
Day 2 Operations
Maintaining consistent ESX host configurations is critical. Even a minor drift in key settings such as firewall rules,
password policies, DNS configuration, or NTP can have far-reaching consequences. Once the edge stack is activated,
Desired State Configuration (DSC) enables version control of the intended configuration of edge locations. In doing so,
it is possible to continuously enforce consistency and ensure that all environments remain aligned with the desired state
configurations. This desired state enforcement happens at two layers:
• vSphere Layer: The vSphere Configuration Profile (VCP) delivers desired state configuration across vSphere clusters.
Administrators can:
– Set the desired configuration at the cluster in the form of a JSON document.
– Check that hosts are compliant with the desired configuration.
– If non-compliant, remediate hosts to bring them into compliance.
Broadcom 1437

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Workload Layer: ArgoCD synchronizes the runtime state of the workload with the desired state configuration that is
defined in Git. Configuration changes are made in Git and Argo CD updates the runtime state to reflect the Git. With
Argo CD:
– Set the source of workload desired state by pointing to a git Repo
– Monitor workload runtime compliance by using the Argo CD UI
– Update the Git Repo to change the desired state

Local Management with Multiple Hosts
Local Management with Multiple hosts is an air-gapped architecture that is designed for total self-sufficiency. Edge
cluster consists of three or more hosts and the management control plane is runs directly on the edge cluster. This "Local
Management" design ensures that the edge cluster remains fully operational and secure without any external connectivity.
Broadcom 1438

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 170: Local Management Design
The Local Management Design is built around a vSphere cluster that provides foundational infrastructure, networking,
storage, and lifecycle management in a unified platform. Networking is delivered through one or more vSphere Distributed
Switches (VDS), sized according to uplink capacity and service isolation needs. Storage is powered by vSAN (OSA or
ESA), with architecture determined by disk types and networking. Lifecycle management is handled through vLCM using a
single cluster image.
Broadcom 1439

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The vSphere management plane runs as virtual appliances within the same cluster as workloads. Management
components include vCenter for ESX resource management, and NSX for deployments needing advanced network
services and multi-layer routing/switching. Depending on the type and duration of the mission, VCF Ops and fleet
management components may run local to the cluster or remotely.
Modern container workloads and traditional VM applications are both fully supported at the edge by enabling the VCF
Supervisor. Modern applications can run as vSphere Pods directly on ESXi or within VMware Kubernetes Service (VKS)
clusters for standard Kubernetes cluster deployments. Traditional virtual machines operate alongside containers within the
same namespace boundaries. Workload management is based on the operational model. Either directly through vSphere
or GitOps-based using Argo CD.
Management Components
Management components to support the "local Management with Multiple Hosts"design must be aligned with the
functional requirements of the Edge.
Edge sites that do not require hypervisor-based security only needs a new edge vCenter, license server, and VCF
Operations for license management and monitoring. The management component layout is similar to Edge Option #1, but
for a single location. Management domain is also used for workloads.

Edge Service Design
The availability of foundational services such as DNS, NTP, and workload templates are critical for autonomous
operations. Deploying those services at the edge is required.
To support the disconnected mode of operation required for autonomous operations, infrastructure services that are
required to support the workload runtime must be deployed locally.
• Network and Foundational Services: STIG-compliant infrastructure relies on FIPS-validated encryption and a robust
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to ensure session integrity and data-in-transit security. Modern cloud-native workloads
have deep, systemic dependencies on these foundational services:
– DNS: Service discovery in both traditional and modern applications relies heavily on DNS.If DNS is unavailable,
edge application fails to operate.
Broadcom 1443

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– NTP: Encryption is highly sensitive to temporal accuracy. If the system clock drifts even slightly certificate validation
may fail. STIGs compliant infrasturcture relies on encryption and certificates to ensure session integrity.
– Availability Requirements: Because both DNS and NTP services are "pre-requisites" for the rest of the stack,
they must be architected for high availability to prevent a single point of failure from cascading through the entire
environment.
• Artifact Repository: Local Artifact repository enables fast provisioning without WAN.
– Local Content Library: Content libraries are vSphere container objects for storing and sharing OVF and OVA
packages, VM templates, vApp templates, and other types of files.
– Container Registry: If a Kubernetes pod crashes or a node reboots in a disconnected environment, the host
(depending on imagePullPolicy) will try to pull an image from its configured registry. With a local registry, required
images are always available at the Edge. VMware Harbor is a CNCF compliant container registry and can be
consumed as a supervisor service or deployed as a VM appliance.
• Pull based Configuration:
– In a traditional VCF Edge deployment, vCenter "pushes" configurations to the infrastructure. A GitOps-based
approach uses a "Pull" model that allows configuration updates to be staged in a Git repository, and applied as
infrastructure code update instead of manual "pushes". ArgoCD is a CNCF Continuous Delivery (CD) tool that
follows the GitOps methodology and can be consumed as a supervisor service.

Edge Cluster Design
Edge cluster design consists of the following aspects:
• Edge Hardware:
– Environmental and Electromagnetic Compliance: Select hardware that meets rigorous standards for
environmental survivability and electromagnetic compatibility.
– Hardware-Rooted Security: Implement security foundations that are based on TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot to ensure
platform integrity.
• vSphere Cluster:
Broadcom 1445

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– Compute Design: Define the CPU core and memory requirements necessary for both the management plane and
edge workloads.
– Storage Architecture: Determine the optimal shared storage strategy that is based on the disk configuration of the
compute
– Network Configuration: Develop a VDS design based on the available number of physical NICs and the required
traffic isolation for management and workload data.
– Availability and Optimization: DRS (Distributed Resource Scheduler) automation levels and establish affinity rules
to support the most optimal resource utilization. vSphere HA settings to ensure management stack failover under a
single-node failure.
• Security and Compliance Alignment
– STIG Compliance: Ensure full alignment with the DISA STIG implementation guidelines for all cluster components.
– Traffic Isolation: Implement robust traffic isolation based on service type to prevent lateral movement.
– Identity and Access Management: Restrict cluster access using Strong Identity, Credential, and Access
Management (ICAM)
– FIPS-Validated Cryptography: Use FIPS validated cryptographic modules for both vSAN data-at-rest encryption
and data-in-transit protection.

Management At Edge Activation
Edge activation starts in a staging environment and shipped to the field at the start of each mission. With the introduction
of Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP), the transition of a new host from power-on to an active member of the remote cluster
follows a highly orchestrated automated workflow. Along with PowerShell automation scripts, new edge hosts can be
imaged, provisioned, and brought into service without manual intervention. The process is initiated at the central staging
data center. Once a mission starts, vSphere cluster LCM is frozen until mission completion and equipment is returned
back to the staging environment. Based on the desired topology, there are three activation approaches:
Scenario 1: vCenter only to manage edge deployments requiring only basic L2 connectivity and standard vSphere security
at edge locations.
Scenario 2: Deploy a new VCF instance and power-off components that are not required for a mission. This approach
requires a pre-existing VCF Ops instance and assumes that the cluster may rejoin the fleet for LCM after each mission.
Scenario 3: Deploy a new VCF fleet where central VCF ops for continuous infrastructure monitoring, patching, and ESX
LCM are mandatory. This approach allows administrators to have a full set of day-2 operational capabilities including
centralized monitoring, logging, LCM of cluster image, management certificate, password, and identity.

Example Day 2 Deployment
Modern naval vessels are an example of a multi-node air gap use case. Modern navy ships rely on highly resilient edge-
computer architectures to support mission-critical operations. Unlike conventional terrestrial data centers, shipboard
IT infrastructure must maintain continuous availability under stringent operational constraints, including hardware
degradation, power transients, and the potential for kinetic impact. The onboard compute hosts a diverse set of workloads
essential to the operation from combat and navigation systems to engineering telemetry and logistical support.
To optimize resource allocation without sacrificing operational integrity, applications are classified into three distinct tiers
based on mission criticality:
Table 455: Application Classifications & Recovery Patterns
Classification Pattern Recovery
