Infrastructure Platform Orchestration
To operationalize the high-availability and failure recovery patterns that are previously defined, the underlying hardware
must be abstracted and managed by a robust VCF fleet architecture. In this design, a locally managed edge deployment
model based on four nodes is used. This model is explicitly engineered for environments that anticipate severe network
degradation or complete physical isolation.
Figure 173: Independent Fleet
To provide the highest availability, architecture is based on two sets of fully autonomous management planes. As
illustrated in the deployment diagram, two physical failure domains (Domain A and Domain B) are provisioned. Each
physical Failure Domain is provisioned with an independent, self-contained VCF Fleet management stack and operates
independent of each other.
• Independent Infrastructure: Each domain operates its own localized instance of SDDC Manager, vCenter Server,
and NSX Manager
• Localized Operations: VCF Operations (monitoring, logging, and performance analytics) are isolated to their
respective domains.
Broadcom 1452

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
By deploying an independent locally managed control plane, the architecture ensures that if one failure domain suffers
catastrophic physical destruction, the resources in the failover domain experiences zero interruption.
The distribution of workloads across these autonomous VCF instances directly correlates to the application availability
tiers defined in the Application Classification table.
• Mission-Critical Instantiation (Tier 0 & 1): The highest-priority workloads, example Combat/C2 (Tier-0), Navigation
(Tier-1), and Engineering Control(Tier-0), are symmetrically instantiated across both Failure Domain A and B.
Symmetrical instantiation ensures an active-active or hot-standby placement that are required by Tier 0/1 applications
execute continuous state replication or autonomous local control.
• Routine Instantiation (Tier 2): Conversely, lower-priority business and administrative workloads do not require
redundant instantiation across all domains. Email server application, for example, does not determine the mission
outcome and can reside exclusively in Domain A or Domain B. In a failure event, these Tier 2 applications can be
manually restarted based on the availability of compute and network.
Because the infrastructure layers are independent, data must be replicated at the vSphere layer or natively within the
application. An alternative deployment model uses a synchronously stretched storage fabric to reduce the need for
vSphere replication.
Stretched Fleet Design
Figure 174: Stretched Fleet
As depicted in the diagram, this configuration consolidates the VCF Fleet management stack entirely within Failure
Domain A. Failure Domain B acts as a compute and storage extension. The foundational element of this design is
the Stretched vSAN cluster, which aggregates the local storage of both Domain A and Domain B into a single, logical
Broadcom 1453

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
datastore. Deploying a Stretched vSAN configuration offers specific advantages, primarily by shifting the burden of high
availability from the application layer to the underlying infrastructure:
• Zero Recovery Point Objective (RPO): Stretched vSAN implements synchronous, block-level I/O replication across
the two failure domains. Every write operation is committed to both physical domains simultaneously, ensuring zero
data loss if an entire compartment is destroyed.
• Infrastructure-Level High Availability: This model facilitates seamless vSphere High Availability (HA). If Failure
Domain A experiences a failure, virtual machines can be automatically restarted on the surviving hardware in Failure
Domain B without requiring complex, application-specific failover implementation.
• Legacy Application Support: Applications that lack native clustering or state replication capabilities can achieve
high availability purely through the infrastructure layer, simplifying the deployment of legacy or off-the-shelf (COTS)
software.
• Single Pane of Operations: VCF Operations (monitoring, logging, LCM, and performance analytics) for the entire
vessel, across Failure Domains A and B.
VCF Edge Design Blueprint for Manufacturing Use Case
This design blueprint provides architectural guidance for deploying VMware Cloud Foundation Edge in manufacturing
environments where IT and OT workloads must operate together within resilient, secure, and low-latency edge
infrastructure. The blueprint focuses on workload isolation, industrial network segmentation, operational resiliency, and
supporting both traditional industrial applications and modern Kubernetes-based workloads at the manufacturing edge.
Figure 175: Manufacturing VCF Edge reference design
Manufacturing VCF Edge reference design supporting converged IT/OT operations, real-time industrial workloads, and
resilient edge infrastructure for factory and industrial environments.
Broadcom 1454

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This design focuses on manufacturing and industrial edge use cases for VMware Cloud Foundation Edge and
addresses the operational, resiliency, segmentation, and low-latency requirements of converged IT and OT (Operational
Technology) environments.
Manufacturing environments often require infrastructure platforms capable of supporting both traditional enterprise
workloads and sensitive industrial control systems operating under strict performance, availability, and network isolation
requirements. These environments may include real-time industrial communication protocols, segmented production
networks, deterministic workloads, manufacturing execution systems, historian platforms, SCADA systems, and edge
analytics platforms operating close to production systems.
This reference architecture demonstrates how centralized operational governance can be combined with localized
industrial edge infrastructure to support resilient and scalable manufacturing operations across distributed factory
environments.
The architecture illustrates how:
Broadcom 1455

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• centralized VCF operations integrate with manufacturing edge sites
• IT and OT networks remain logically segmented while operating on shared infrastructure
• real-time and non-real-time workloads can coexist within the same VCF workload domain
• industrial protocols and deterministic traffic patterns can be isolated through dedicated networking constructs
• operational continuity can be maintained during WAN degradation or disruption
• modern application platforms and Kubernetes workloads can be integrated into manufacturing edge environments
Key architectural themes that are represented in this design include:
• convergence of IT and OT operational environments
• segmentation between industrial and enterprise workloads
• support for real-time and deterministic industrial workloads
• resilient edge infrastructure for manufacturing operations
• industrial network isolation using VLAN and distributed switch segmentation
• operational continuity during a network disruption or degraded connectivity conditions
• support for industrial telemetry, analytics, and manufacturing application platforms
This architecture also demonstrates how manufacturing edge environments can support multiple workload classes within
the same operational framework, including:
• real-time industrial workloads
• non-real-time operational workloads
• manufacturing execution systems
• SCADA and historian platforms
• HMI workloads
• industrial telemetry and analytics platforms
The design patterns and implementation models presented throughout this document progressively decompose this
architecture into infrastructure, networking, workload isolation, resiliency, lifecycle management, and operational design
considerations required for manufacturing and industrial edge deployments.
Industrial Operational Context
For OT and IT Infrastructure administrators and architects, selecting the right design pattern for a stable and resilient VCF
Workload Domain capable of running sensitive real-time workloads can be challenging due to numerous options. The
optimal choice depends on factors such as the specific use case, budget, and workload sensitivity.
Begin by familiarizing yourself with the general VCF architecture and terminology. Refer to the VCF Product Overview and
review the VCF Release Notes. For information on deploying, converging, or upgrading VCF, consult the Overview of VCF
Deploy, Converge, and Upgrade Guide.
These Design Options cover the most common use cases, though not every configuration option is detailed. Architectures
that align with official documentation, such as the maximum settings within the Hardware Compatibility List (HCL), are
supported.
Design Options
Edge Design Options for Manufacturing
This section explores design options, focusing primarily on replacing traditional Physical Logic Controllers (PLCs) with
virtual PLCs (vPLCs) hosted in data centers. While PLCs are most commonly found on the shopfloor, this approach is
also applicable to other environments like building control or logistics centers. Establishing a scalable, future-proof Edge
Infrastructure is essential for global manufacturing organizations. VCF 9 supports diverse Edge Deployment scenarios,
managed through a comprehensive Management Plane.
Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) for Shopfloor IPC Replacement
Broadcom 1456

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VDI offers an alternative to traditional Shopfloor Industrial PCs (IPCs), which are used for tasks such as worker guidance,
device control (e.g., documenting and applying torque), and as Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs). This involves
centralizing the IPC functionalities on virtual machines (VDI Desktops) within a data center.
This transition yields significant Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) savings, as Thin Clients are substantially cheaper than
IPCs. Furthermore, Thin Clients prove more cost-effective over time because IPCs frequently require replacement due to
the demanding production environment.
(Note: VDI use cases are mentioned for context only, as they are not the primary focus of this specific design.)
Core vPLC Design Leveraging VCF 9
This design capitalizes on VCF 9's enhancements to support real-time workloads, such as vPLCs, on a VCF
infrastructure. The typical architectural approach involves creating a separate Workload Domain for each location to
ensure operational and physical separation and clearly defined responsibilities. Each domain generally comprises two
clusters: one dedicated to real-time workloads (vPLCs) and another for non-real-time workloads (e.g., Engineering
Solutions, HMIs).
Networking utilizes the Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP), which needs two distinct LAN Fabrics, referred to as LAN A
and LAN B. LAN A is typically the LAN which connects to other Services on the network.

Real-Time Platform Design Considerations
To effectively execute real-time workloads, it is crucial to establish a cluster that guarantees deterministic performance.
The platform design is composed of several layers, each requiring distinct considerations during the planning phase of the
target platform.
Server Design and Settings
Reliable Realtime Workload Platform performance hinges on properly configured ESXi Hosts. Incorrect configurations can
lead to timing issues in Realtime VMs, causing PLC and production stops. To prevent this, a valid server configuration is
crucial.
For easy integration, a single-socket server with at least 32 cores is recommended. This setup avoids NUMA architecture
complexities and provides enough cores to run up to 12 PRP vDANs, which is the current maximum supported.

Parallel Redundancy Protocol Design
Industrial networks require low latency and minimal jitter, standard Active/Passive redundancy methods are inadequate
for maintaining production continuity during component failures. To address industrial networks requirements, the IEC
62439-3 Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) was developed to ensure fault tolerance for network traffic.
Parallel Redundancy Protocol Overview
Industrial networks require low latency and minimal jitter. Because standard Active/Passive redundancy methods are
inadequate for maintaining production continuity during component failures, the IEC 62439-3 Parallel Redundancy
Protocol (PRP) was developed to ensure fault tolerance for network traffic.
Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) is a Layer 2 redundancy protocol designed to eliminate service interruptions,
packet loss, and delays. Unlike traditional protocols like spanning tree that take time to reconverge after a failure, PRP
achieves instant failover by transmitting identical data simultaneously across two separate active networks. One network
is designated as LAN A and another as LAN B. To manage this dual-traffic, PRP uses sequence numbers to identify and
drop duplicate frames. Latency between the two networks must be matched. If one network is slower than the other, the
sequence tracking fails and the connection can drop.
Key PRP Components:
• DAN (Dual Attached Node): A PRP node that connects to both LAN A and LAN B simultaneously.
• SAN (Single Attached Node): Standard devices (like PCs or servers) that do not natively support PRP.
• RedBox (Redundancy Box): Often an industrial switch with PRP support (or a specialized NIC adapter), this allows
SANs to join a PRP network.
Broadcom 1459

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VMware Industrial vSwitch (IvS) Architecture
Available since VCF 9, the Industrial vSwitch (IvS) can function as a RedBox, enabling virtual machines to establish
redundant PRP connections.
The IvS comprises two primary components:
1. The IvS incorporates a VMware Distributed Switch, which is configured at the vCenter level. Each ESXi Host within the
IvS contains a Data Plane, which is optimized for stringent latency demands and offers support for Profinet and PRP.
2. NSX Manager facilitates the creation and management of the IvS configuration, including all network-related settings.
This encompasses NIC failover settings, establishing security and functional boundaries through Transport Zones,
and segmenting each production cell with isolated VLANs. activate or deactivate PRP is based on the NSX Segment
Profile using the NSX Manger.
Both the physical and virtual layers must strictly control latency and jitter. The IvS, designed for the virtual layer, aims
to maintain latency within 250 microseconds with a jitter of ±10%. These exact same rules must be applied to the
underlying physical layer to ensure stability.
Broadcom 1460

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 177: Parallel Redundancy Protocol Topology Overview
Broadcom 1461

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The general architecture, illustrated in the preceding diagram, routes each ESXi host uplink belonging to the IvS to either
LAN A or LAN B.
The following guidelines are important for PRP design:
• Minimum Requirement: PRP requires at least one uplink that is connected to LAN A and one connected to LAN B.
• Best Practice: For enhanced redundancy and to eliminate single points of failure, two uplinks per LAN are
recommended.
• Uplink Limitations: You can use a maximum of two uplinks per LAN. Because the IvS only supports failover mode for
redundant NICs per LAN, these dual uplinks operate in an active/standby failover sequence.
• PRP Management: PRP can be dynamically activated or deactivated using NSX Segment Profile. More about
Segment Profiles here
Parallel Redundancy Protocol Use Cases
Not all industrial network connections need PRP. The specific design choice depends on the needs of your particular use
case. Furthermore, each production cell should be isolated with its own dedicated VLAN to create distinct security and
responsibility boundaries.

Traffic Routing and Configuration Details
• Non-PRP Traffic Handling: Typically, LAN A serves as the primary connection, handling all traffic, including non-PRP
traffic originating from SANs located behind a RedBox. Although LAN B is technically identical, using both LAN A and
LAN B to connect to standard services adds unnecessary complexity for operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting.
• Virtual Machine SANs: Virtual machines without PRP support (such as Windows VMs used for HMI) only
communicate on LAN A. In the event of a persistent failure on LAN A, this non-vDAN traffic can be manually changed
to LAN B (see command syntax in Troubleshooting).
Industry vSwitch Integration with vSphere Details
The IvS is composed of the following key components:
• vDS (vCenter Level): The foundational distributed switch. Must be version 9 or later.
• VLAN Transport Zone (NSX): Defines the scope for VLAN-backed segments.
• Uplink Profile (NSX): Decouples the vDS uplink from the NSX uplink and specifies the active and failover uplinks.
• Segment Profiles (NSX): One or more profiles that are created, which may include Parallel Redundancy Protocol
(PRP) settings.
• Transport Node Profiles: Defines, which Hosts shall inherit the IvS Configuration
• NSX Segments: Created and assigned a specific IvS Segment Profile, segregated via VLANs
Refer to the official VCF Documentation to create an Industrial vSwitch. Refer to the Appendix for Host and NSX config
details.

vPLC Storage Design
Virtual PLCs (vPLCs) must offer the same resilient features as their physical counterparts to ensure continuous
production. Physical PLCs utilize a dedicated hardware capacitor to detect power loss and locally store transient data.
Because vPLCs lack this physical capacitor, vendors have developed a software-based method to achieve similar
availability.
The most intensive storage requirement involves saving "retain and remanent" data to disk. Remanent data captures the
state and position of downstream I/O devices before a vPLC failure. This data is critical because it allows downstream
devices to seamlessly resume operations without requiring a manual reset. To ensure this availability, vPLCs continuously
save this information directly to disk after each program cycle, based on parameters defined by the PLC software
developer.
The constant saving of remanent data results in a continuous, 100% I/O write pattern per vPLC. Current data indicates a
write rate of approximately 1 Gb/s per host.
In scaled-up environments, this constant data stream can significantly load the storage backend. To manage storage
cluster fragmentation, mitigate contention, and reserve capacity for supplementary workloads (like non-real-time VMs),
you must adhere to the following constraint:
• Scale Limit: Access to the Storage Cluster is limited to a maximum of 20 hosts.
Disk latency thresholds are typically dictated by the vPLC vendor, as they depend entirely on how their specific Retain
Data mechanism is implemented.
Every storage technology presents unique advantages and disadvantages. Your selection depends on performance
requirements, staff skill sets, site technology, and organizational processes.
Note:
While VCF 9 is compatible with any supported storage solution, VMware typically recommends vSAN due to its
operational advantages and because all platform testing was conducted using it. Consolidating both platform and
storage operations under a single team significantly accelerates time-to-resolution for troubleshooting.
For discussing different Storage models, also consult our documentation.

The manufacturing edge design features two distinct clusters:

Edge Deployments
Edge Deployments use standard VCF Edge Deployment procedures. For comprehensive deployment instructions,
consult our Edge Design Guides. A key consideration is determining the necessity of a dual-site deployment versus the
sufficiency of a single-site deployment.
Modern multinational manufacturers operate on a massive scale, relying on numerous distributed edge locations that
span across multiple geographical regions to power their global operations. To navigate the operational complexities,
manufacturers employ a sophisticated dual-level management approach that seamlessly combines high-level centralized
control with dedicated regional administration to optimize both enterprise-wide efficiency and scalability. This strategy
features localized control within each specific region, ensures compliance with strict regional data regulations but also
enhances operational resilience against potential inter-region network disruptions. Ultimately, this robust architectural
framework guarantees the reliable, ultra-low latency performance that is required directly on each distributed factory floor
to support advanced, real-time manufacturing use cases. Edge Pattern 4 is most suited for this design.

Deploying industrial workloads across multiple availability sites is crucial because it significantly enhances service
availability. This multi-site deployment provides robust protection against various disasters, ensuring continuous operation
and minimizing downtime.
When utilizing multiple locations, it is not always necessary to establish a single management plane, workload domain, or
clusters across these sites. However, this approach is worth considering. A disaster could bring down a centralized, non-
stretched alarming system, leading to alarming outages and impacting downtime. Details about multiple Site Deployments
can be found here.
Another valid approach is to operate workloads for different production lines in separate locations, while still allocating
resources for a manual failover in the event of a disaster. Consider those Architectural decisions.

data across an Inter-Site Link could negatively impact other
workloads.
• Stateless Operation: vPLCs can be treated as stateless
machines. Upon power-on, the project is loaded into the vPLC.
Having cold-standby vPLCs per site allows a fast restart of the
production.
Networking • Network Consistency: All sites must have access to all
networks and VLANs, including storage and industrial
networks.
• Inter-Site Bandwidth: Sufficient bandwidth is required
to handle all replication traffic within specified timeframes
(synchronous vs. asynchronous).
• Firewall Rules: Firewall rules are necessary to allow
management and monitoring systems to access workloads
across all sites.
Storage • High-Performance Inter-site Link: The necessity of a high-
performance link between sites is contingent on the specific
storage technology employed.
• vSAN Implementation:
– Storage Profiles: When utilizing vSAN, it is recommended
to create multiple storage profiles tailored to diverse
workload requirements. For instance, synchronous
mirroring for vPLCs is only beneficial if the remanence data
is deemed critical also for disasters.
– Availability: To meet availability demands with vSAN, a
minimum of three locations is required. Further details can
be found here.
• Synchronous Mirroring: Designing for synchronous mirroring
of remanence data needs careful attention to the potential
I/O load on both the disks and the inter-storage link. Each
virtual PLC (vPLC) contributes significantly to this load, with
approximately 1000 IOPs and typically 6-7MB of throughput,
all of which are write operations. These figures are subject
to variation based on the vPLC vendor, technology, and
data volume. This combined activity results in an I/O load of
nearly 1 Gb per host. Therefore, deploying a high number of
vPLCs across multiple hosts risks generating enough traffic
to potentially saturate the storage link that connects the sites.
A saturated Storage Link leads to higher Disk Latency and
therefore potential PLC Stops or inconsistent data.
Network Design Overview
To prevent production outages, a reliable network is crucial when separating PLCs from their PROFINET IO Devices.
Reliability is achieved by using the PRP Protocol, enabling full active/active networking. Also, if a Safety vPLC is used, a
separate IVS-backed network handles the Time Services.
For management, monitoring, and connecting to SCADA systems for production planning and data collection, a regular
Non-realtime Network is employed.
Broadcom 1470

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 181:
In a typical manufacturing setting, the logical network connectivity features an industrial network connection that links
the production cell (or line) to an industrial vSwitch. This vSwitch, which is not considered a PROFINET Device, supports
PROFINET as a bus protocol and includes PRP for redundancy. A vPLC, located elsewhere, is also connected to this
industrial vSwitch.
Broadcom 1471

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A second industrial vSwitch facilitates the transmission of a time signal between the vPLC and a dedicated Time Server.
Both components are supplied by the same PLC vendor and are essential for Safety vPLCs. The vendor also provides the
detailed implementation for the time service.
Network Feature and Traffic Details
Industrial vSwitch The Industrial vSwitch facilitates deterministic PROFINET
communication and end-to-end monitoring between a virtual PLC
and PROFINET Devices on dedicated industrial networks. A
maximum of two Industrial vSwitches are permitted per Host. See
Configuration Maximum Tool
Within the production cell, an industrial Switch with PRP Support,
functioning as a RedBox (Redundancy Box), is deployed. SCADA
Systems, which are used for monitoring and production planning,
are also connected via Profinet, depending on the specific solution
implemented. That may include OPC/UA Traffic, like Pub/Sub
traffic.
PRP Support PRP (Parallel Redundancy Protocol) requires two independent
network fabrics, which are designated as LAN A and LAN B.
Network traffic is transmitted simultaneously over both paths.
Each LAN can accommodate multiple Network Interface Cards
(NICs) configured for failover. Currently, only one Industrial
vSwitch per Host supports PRP.
Regular Network Traffic Non-Realtime network traffic (VM Traffic, vSAN, vMotion, and etc).
This includes OPC/UA Traffic, like pub/sub. See Network Fabric
Models
Setup Real-time VMs
Achieving Deterministic Behavior in Manufacturing Edge Designs
Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) demand deterministic behavior to maintain consistent speed and latency for their
operations. Failure to meet this requirement can lead to PLC program halts, production downtime, and significant financial
losses.
The entire technology stack must support the deterministic execution of PLC programs. To guarantee deterministic
behavior, virtual machine resources must be configured with guaranteed allocation. Real-time capabilities are built upon
guarantee the following three fundamental pillars:
• Networking
• CPU
• Memory
Real-time and PRP Networking Prerequisites:
For real-time networking, the prerequisites include a VMXNet3 Adapter and the latest driver (version 1.9.0 or higher). This
driver is integrated into the upstream Linux Kernel and should be included with all current Linux distributions (from Kernel
6.14 onward). Deterministic networking becomes available for a specific VM when its network adapter is connected to the
Industrial vSwitch.
It is important to note that only Linux VMs equipped with this updated VMXNET3 driver are fully compatible with a PRP
network. Systems such as Windows VM or linux VM using older VMXNET3 drivers or different virtual NIC types are not
PRP capable. Non PRP capable systems can only be connected to a single LAN fabric. In most OT designs, only LAN A
of the PRP network as LAN-B is typically isolated.
For virtual machines using industrial bus protocols not supported by IvS (e.g., EtherCAT, EtherNet/IP), DirectPath I/O
(PCI passthrough) of a dedicated physical NIC (VMNIC) is required. However, PCI passthrough introduces architectural
constraints. Standard vSphere capabilities such as VM snapshot, HA, and vMotion are not available for VM with
passthrough NICs. In addition, large number of passthrough NICs imposed a large constraint on the number of available
physical NICs on a single host.
Operating System Considerations:
Broadcom 1472

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Guest Operating System requires a real-time Kernel to achieve fully deterministic performance. As of now, only
Linux RT-Kernel has been validated. Windows-based vPLC isn't available from PLC partners and has not been validated
against the iVS Switch.
When tuning a linux based VM for real-time workload, The following settings are the most important for optimizing latency:
• Real-Time (RT) Kernel: Install the Linux RT Preemptive Kernel to ensure predictable behavior for time-sensitive
applications.
• Tickless (NO_HZ): Implement the tickless feature in the Linux Kernel to reduce kernel overhead. This can significantly
improve both performance and application latency. Refer to your specific Linux Distribution's Manual for detailed
instructions.
• Tuned Profiles: Use the tuned utility, which offers pre-defined profiles such as "latency-performance" or "real time."
This tool can also help isolate workloads to specific virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and prevent Linux Kernel scheduling that
adds latency. For maximum optimization, a customized tuned profile may be necessary.
• Large Pages: Using Large Pages (up to 2 MB) at guest OS Level and Application helps eliminate latency that is
associated with memory allocation operations.
For more comprehensive information, consult Broadcom's Performance Whitepaper.

Safety Time Source Redundancy Design Options
vPLC Design Option for Safety vPLCs
Human safety PLCs require a redundant time source to prevent time drift from compromising program reliability. In
physical installations, this often involves using specialized PLCs equipped with a secondary, built-in PTP clock to serve as
a fail-safe.
In a virtualized setting, a virtual PLC (vPLC) initially relies on the underlying ESXi host for its primary time reference.
Therefore, a secondary time source must be introduced through an external application. The approach to implementing
this redundancy differs based on the vPLC vendor, generally falling into one of two design and implementation models.
• Design 1: dedicated Time Service IvS for time service and dedicated IvS for Profinet-PRP
• Design 2: Single IvS for time service and Profinet-PRP
Broadcom 1473

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Both approaches have their pros and cons. Design 1 requires more CPUs to support a second IVS switch, but it offers
better protection against latency spikes. This is because time-synchronization processing is mapped to a dedicated CPU
on the second IvS, minimizing the risk of slowing down the PROFINET processing. Conversely, Design 2 carries a higher
risk of latency spikes but is more resources and operationally efficient, as the same resource pool supports multiple
application flows. Refer to the following sections for details on both design options.
Design 1 - Dedicated Time IVS with Time Service VM with PTP passthrough
This design uses a dedicated physical network adapter to obtain a PTP time signal. The adapter, which is attached to
a PTP grandmaster clock, is passed through directly to the Time Service VM (TSA). The TSA VM then uses the NIC
hardware oscillator to acquire a qualified PTP time signal,. Once PTP time signal is acquired, the TSA distributes it across
a VMXNET3 vNIC attached to a dedicated Time Service IvS instance. The primary difference between the Time Service
IvS and the Profinet-PRP IvS is their NIC composition: the Time Service IvS can be deployed with zero NICs if TSA
redundancy is not required, or with two NICs for host-level TSA redundancy.
Also attached to the Time Service IvS switch are vPLCs local to the host. Each vPLC configured to receive PTP traffic
from the local TSA, and for redundancy, a remote TSA server running on a different Real-time host. PTP signal from the
local TSA is preferred over redundant TSA running on another host. Synchronization between the TSA and vPLC are
based on PTP, but the actual PTP implementation can be vendor-specific.
From a resource perspective:
• Two IvS switches per Host
– One Time-Service IvS
– One Profinet PRP IvS
• 1 Time Service VM
• 12 vPLCs VMs, each connects to a unique Profinet VLAN.
• All vPLC VMs share the Time Service VLAN on the second Time-Service IvS
• A total of 5 ENS LCores required to support 12 vPLC
Below is a high-level diagram of Option 1:
Figure 182: Time Service Design Option 1
Time Service VM with PTP passthrough
Broadcom 1474

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design 2 - Single IVS, different Port group for Time Service
Instead of a dedicated IVS switch, this approach uses the same IVS switch to obtain the PTP time signal. Similar to the
previous design, a dedicated network adapter that is attached to a PTP grandmaster clock is passed through directly to
the Time Service VM (TSA). The TSA VM then uses the NIC hardware oscillator to acquire a qualified time signal. The
acquired time signal is then distributed by the TSA across a VMXNET3 vNIC attached to the IvS.
In this design, the same Industrial Virtual Switch (IvS) used for Profinet-PRP is used, vLAN, and port group is used to
segregate the time service and Profinet-PRP traffic. Each vPLC has two VMXNET3 vNICs attached to the IvS switch, one
vNIC for PRP and a second vNIC for PTP Time service. For redundancy, vPLC is configured to receive PTP traffic from
the local TSA and from a redundant TSA server running on a different Real-time host. PTP signal from the local TSA is
preferred over redundant TSA running on another host. Synchronization between the TSA and vPLC are based on PTP,
but the actual PTP implementation can be vendor-specific.
From a resource perspective:
• One IvS Switch per Host
– 12 vPLC, each connects to a unique Profinet VLAN
– All vPLC VMs share Time Service VLAN, Port group
• 1 Time Service VM per Host
• A total of 4 ENS LCores required to support 12 vPLC

Organizations are evolving application platforms to support Kubernetes-based workloads, self-service infrastructure
consumption, AI-enabled services, and modern private cloud operating models. This section provides architectural
blueprints and design guidance for designing and operating modern application platforms on VMware Cloud Foundation
environments. The following blueprints provide deployment patterns, operational models, and design considerations for
different application modernization scenarios and platform requirements.

Self-Service Multi-Tenant Private Cloud Consumption Design Blueprint
This blueprint aims to provide a structured design guide for implementing a self-service multi-tenant private cloud solution
using VMware Cloud Foundation. The primary objective is to empower customers with a robust, scalable, and automated
platform that offers agility and efficiency in resource consumption, while adhering to commonly adopted design patterns
within the VCF private cloud enviornments.
Use Case and Objective
This guide provides the most widely used design patterns for deploying and operating VMware Cloud Foundation
(VCF) with VCF Automation across Enterprise and Cloud Service Provider (CSP) environments. It is intended for cloud
architects, platform engineers, and operations teams responsible for designing scalable, multi-tenant cloud platforms.
• Define and differentiate the primary tenancy models that are supported by VCF with VCF Automation
• Establish reference network topologies that are aligned to tenancy and consumption patterns.
• Provide prescriptive IdP (Identity Provider) design guidance for tenant onboarding scenarios.
• Detail chargeback and billing model for single-tenant and multi-tenant environments.
• Design patterns for VKS (VMware Kubernetes Service) with VCF Automation, covering single and multi-region
deployments.
• PAIS (Private AI Service) integration patterns with VCF Automation
• DSM integration pattern with VCF Automation

Before initiating the design for a self-service multi-tenant private cloud, potential tenants or cloud administrators must
assess their deployment needs against existing, validated VCF infrastructure blueprints. This ensures the foundational
infrastructure meets the necessary scale, availability, and geographic requirements.

confirmed prior to starting the multi-tenant design work.

There are multiple VCF fleet design blueprints available, and the appropriate choice depends on factors such as
geographic footprint, availability requirements, and organizational scale (for example, single site, multi-site, or multi-region

Selecting the right fleet model is the first foundational decision, as it establishes the underlying infrastructure architecture
on which all higher-level platform services are built.
Once the fleet architecture is defined, organizations can then determine how to deploy and expose VCF Automation to
enable private cloud consumption. This includes decisions around domain topology, external access, and how tenants and
application teams will interact with the platform.

Pre-Requisite Design Choices for VCF Automation Deployment
Before deploying VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation, architects and platform engineers must evaluate and
document a defined set of infrastructure design choices across several interdependent components. These pre-requisite
decisions are not optional post-deployment configurations - they are foundational commitments that shape the topology,
scalability, security posture, and operational model of the entire VCF platform for consumption. Getting these decisions
right before Day 1 significantly reduces rework, avoids architectural debt, and ensures the platform is fit-for-purpose from
the outset.
The scope of these design choices varies depending on the deployment model being adopted. A single-enterprise
deployment - where VCF Automation manages a single vSphere environment and a single organizational boundary -
requires fewer integration touchpoints and simpler identity and network models. A multi-enterprise deployment, where
multiple business units or tenants share the platform, introduces additional considerations around federated identity,
cross-domain networking, namespace isolation, and centralized governance. Deployments operating within regulated
industries or subject to compliance frameworks such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or SOC 2 must also incorporate security
hardening, audit logging, encryption, and DFW policy decisions from the start.
Each design area includes a summary of the key decision points, a structured design-choice table with recommended
options and justification, and a reference to the detailed section of this guide where full configuration guidance can
be found. For environments with unique constraints -such as air-gapped deployments, regulated data residency
requirements, or existing brownfield network topologies - require additional design considration.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

VCF Automation Deployment Topologies
The placement and network exposure of the VCF Automation platform are critical design decisions that directly impact
security, accessibility, and tenancy model support. While VCF Automation can be deployed in various configurations,
the choice is usually driven by whether the platform is intended for internal consumption only or for external, multi-tenant
public access.
This guide details three primary deployment patterns, focusing particularly on the External-Facing Deployment as it is
essential for the self-service multi-tenant cloud blueprint.

As outlined in the table above, there are multiple deployment patterns available for customers to choose from based
on their requirements. However, for the context of this design guide, we focus on a comprehensive deployment model
where customers require segregation of the VCF Automation deployment for security and compliance reasons, while also
exposing VCF Automation for external (internet-facing) access to end users.
This model is referred to as:
External-Facing Deployment (Deployment Pattern 3)
Figure 187: External Facing Deployment of VCF Automation
For a Self-Service Multi Tenant Private Cloud environment (both Enterprise with strict governance, and especially the
CSP Multi-Organization Model), the VCF Automation platform must be externally accessible to tenants while maintaining
robust isolation from the VCF Management Network.
Key Design Elements:
1. Dedicated Network Segment: VCF Automation components are placed on a dedicated VPC overlay subnet that is
isolated from the VCF Management Network. Any required connectivity to management services is controlled through
explicit routing, firewall policies, and least-privilege access rules rather than direct flat network adjacency. AVI Service
Engines are placed in a separate DMZ VPC subnet to isolate north-south application traffic from management and
automation components.
2. Public Access Exposure:
3. Security Gateways: Strict DFW and Gateway Firewall policies are enforced to ensure that:
– Only necessary inbound ports (443, 80) are permitted to the VCF Automation public VIPs.
– No inbound traffic from the tenant public segment is allowed to the VCF Management Network.
– Outbound communication from VCF Automation to VCF components (vCenter, NSX, SDDC Manager) is restricted
to required API calls only.
Broadcom 1491

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This pattern is critical for Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) as it allows external customers to access the self-service
catalog without compromising the core infrastructure management plane.
Important:
Current Platform Constraint: At the time of this design, deployment of the VMware Avi Load Balancer Control
Plane that is integrated with NSX requires the Avi Management segment to be connected through a Tier-1 (T1)
segment. This is currently the supported deployment model for Avi Control Plane communication and integration
with NSX networking services.
However, as illustrated in the architecture diagram, Avi Service Engine traffic handling ingress, and egress
application flows can still be deployed within a dedicated DMZ VPC subnet. This enables separation between
the Avi management/control plane traffic and externally exposed application traffic paths, improving network
segmentation and security isolation for tenant-facing services.
Tenancy Deployment Models
This section details the various VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) tenancy deployment models available, providing a
foundational understanding for architects and implementers. Although the VCF design library contains a broad range of
patterns to meet various organizational requirements, we have picked the two most widely used deployed tenancy models
in this blueprint: the Single Organization Model and the Multi-Organization Cloud Service Provider (CSP) Model.
These two primary models are the central focus of the subsequent detailed design guidance.
The choice of a VCF tenancy model is a critical decision dictating:
• Resource allocation.
• How tenants are separated.
• The operational model for management and consumption of the cloud environment.

While the VCF supports multiple deployment models to address complex enterprise and sovereign cloud requirements,
this design blueprint focuses on the two most widely adopted patterns. These following two patterns represent the
fundamental architectural divergence between internally consumed IT services and externally provided cloud services:
• Single Organization - Single Tenant (Tenancy Deployment Model 1): This model prioritizes resource sharing and a
unified operational plane for different internal business units. The focus is on logical isolation (VPC Subnets, vSphere
namespaces) within a single trust domain. This pattern is elaborated in the Enterprise – Single Organization section
below.
• Multiple Organizations - Multi-Tenant or Cloud Service Provider (Tenancy Deployment Model 2): This model
prioritizes operational and identity isolation between distinct external customers. The focus is on mapping each
Broadcom 1493

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
customer to a dedicated Aria Organization and ensuring strict separation via network segmentation (Tier-1 per tenant)
and per-tenant IDP federation. This pattern is elaborated in the Cloud Service Provider – Multiple Organizations
section below.
Single Organization - Single Tenant
In the Enterprise model, a single organization owns and operates the VCF stack. All workloads, management
components, and platform services belong to one administrative domain. While multiple business units or projects may be
isolated using virtual constructs (VPC Subnets, vSphere namespaces, or VCF Automation Projects), there is a single root
of trust and a centralized operations model.
Key Characteristics
• Centralized identity federation via a corporate IdP (Active Directory / LDAP / SAML).
• Shared physical infrastructure with logical isolation per team or department.
• Chargeback reports or internal cost center allocation using VCF Operations.
• Platform services (VKS, PAIF) deployed in a shared or dedicated namespace per BU.
When to Use
• Single-enterprise IT operating model with a central cloud team.
• Regulatory environments where a single audit scope is required.
• Environments where shared services (DNS, NTP, monitoring) span all workloads.
Multiple Organizations - Multi-Tenant or Cloud Service Provider
In this model, a single infrastructure stack is partitioned to serve multiple distinct organizations (tenants). Each tenant is
operationally isolated and may have independent IdP integration, dedicated network segments, private compute domains,
and separate billing. The CSP operator maintains a shared infrastructure plane while tenants interact only with their own
resource pools.
Key Characteristics
• Multiple Organizations, each mapped to a distinct company.
• Tenant-specific IDP federation (per-tenant SAML / OIDC providers).
• Resource and network isolation is enforced at per tenant.
• Independent chargeback with metered billing per tenant.
• Shared or dedicated physical clusters depending on compliance/isolation requirements.
Broadcom 1494

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Multi-Tenancy Consumption Patterns
While the Tenancy Deployment Model defines the physical and operational separation between organizations, the
Consumption Design defines how tenants, business units, application teams, and end users consume infrastructure,
networking, and platform services within the private cloud environment.
These consumption patterns describe different approaches for implementing logical isolation, network segmentation,
organizational boundaries, and shared versus dedicated resource models across VPCs, Supervisor Zones, gateways, and
workload domains.
The appropriate pattern depends on factors such as:
• organizational structure and tenant boundaries
• required level of network and resource isolation
• scalability and operational management requirements
• regional deployment strategy
• shared versus dedicated infrastructure preferences
• governance and compliance considerations
The following patterns illustrate common multi-tenancy consumption models that can be implemented using VCF
Automation for a modern private cloud architectures.

Network Consumption Model:
However, the ability to implement these patterns effectively depends heavily on the underlying software-defined
networking architecture.
Networking is not just an implementation detail - it is the control plane for isolation, connectivity, and policy enforcement
across tenants. The choice of networking model directly impacts how well you can achieve:
• Tenant isolation (organization vs line of business)
• Scalability across Supervisor Zones and regions
• Operational simplicity vs flexibility
• Shared vs dedicated services
VMware Cloud Foundation provides multiple networking constructs - such as VPCs, VRFs, shared and dedicated
gateways, and VPC - based subnets that enable these consumption patterns.

Foundation. In practice, these approaches can be broadly categorized into two representative deployment models:
• Centralized Connectivity Model
• Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model

The model uses an NSX Edge cluster with Tier-0 gateway to provide VPC-compatible workload construct with network
connectivity established via a Centralized Transit Gateway.

Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model
The Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model enables rapid adoption of VPC network virtualization without requiring NSX
Edge VM deployment. It uses a Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) that connects via external VLANs in the physical
network fabric, utilizing a distributed forwarding model at the ESX host level, achieving close to host pNIC line rate.

This architecture illustrates a single-organization or tenant deployment model in VCF Automation where a tenant
organization within a Cloud Service Provider (CSP) environment requires strict separation between:
• internet-facing external connectivity
• private enterprise or on-premises data center connectivity
To achieve this separation, the design uses:
• two dedicated Centralized Transit Gateways (CTGWs)
• separate connectivity domains for Internet and private DC traffic
• dedicated Tier-0 (T0) gateways or isolated VRFs
• separate VPCs aligned to workload communication requirements
This architecture enables the tenant organization to securely consume public Internet services while simultaneously
maintaining private MPLS, Direct Connect, or enterprise WAN connectivity back to their own data center environment.
Design Justification
This design is intended for tenant organizations operating within a CSP hosted VCF Automation environment that require
different connectivity and security boundaries for internet-facing workloads versus enterprise-connected workloads.
By separating these connectivity domains through independent Transit Gateways and dedicated routing constructs,
organizations can:
• enforce different security policies for public and private traffic
• isolate routing domains between external and internal workloads
• reduce security exposure between Internet-facing and enterprise-connected applications
• maintain private enterprise WAN connectivity while still supporting external-facing services
• support hybrid application architectures spanning cloud and enterprise data center environments

This architecture illustrates a single-organization or tenant deployment model in VCF Automation where multiple
connectivity types are consolidated through a shared Centralized Transit Gateway (C-TGW). Instead of deploying
separate transit gateways for each connectivity domain, this design uses one shared C-TGW to provide unified routing
and network services across multiple VPCs.
The tenant organization may require connectivity to:
• Internet or CSP networks
• Private data center or MPLS networks
• Remote access VPN users
• Out-of-band management networks
To support these requirements, the design uses:
• Multiple Tier-0 gateways for upstream connectivity domains
• A shared C-TGW for centralized routing and network services
• Separate VPCs for public, private, remote access, and management workloads
• Segmented subnets aligned to workload and access requirements
The shared C-TGW provides common services such as gateway firewall, NAT, DHCP, route distribution, policy routing,
and VPN services. Each VPC remains logically separated, but connectivity is centralized through a common transit layer.
Design Justification
This design is intended for customers who want a simplified connectivity model while still supporting multiple types of
north-south access for a tenant organization.
By using a single shared Transit Gateway, organizations can:
• reduce the number of gateway constructs to deploy and manage
• centralize routing and policy enforcement
• simplify connectivity between VPCs and upstream networks
• provide a common services layer for NAT, DHCP, firewall, route distribution, and VPN
• support multiple workload zones such as public, private, remote access, and management VPCs
This model is well suited when the tenant requires multiple connectivity paths, but does not require strict separation of
routing domains through dedicated transit gateways.

This architecture illustrates a multi-tenant VCF Automation deployment model where each tenant is provided with one
or multiple dedicated Transit Gateway (TGW) that connects to multiple external connectivity domains through shared
provider infrastructure.
The design enables tenant environments to simultaneously access:
• Public Internet connectivity
• Shared enterprise services (e.g., DNS, NTP)
• Private data center (DC) connectivity
This is achieved by integrating tenant-specific TGWs with multiple upstream Tier-0 gateways located in the provider
space.
Architecture Overview
In this model:
• Each tenant (e.g., Blue and Green) is assigned dedicated TGWs
• Each TGW provides:
– NAT services
– Gateway firewall (N-S policy enforcement)
– Routing and connectivity control
• TGWs connect upstream to:
– Internet Tier-0 gateway for public access
– Shared Services Tier-0 gateway for platform services (DNS/NTP)
– Tenant Private Tier-0 gateway for DC/MPLS connectivity
Within each tenant:
• Multiple VPCs are deployed
• Each VPC contains:
– Public and private subnets
– Integrated NAT, firewall, and load balancing capabilities
• Workloads are isolated per tenant and per VPC
Design Justification
This architecture is designed for multi-tenant environments where each tenant requires:
• Independent network control and policy enforcement
• Access to multiple external connectivity domains
• Secure and isolated communication paths
By using dedicated TGWs per tenant, the design enables:
• Tenant-level isolation of routing and security policies
• Controlled and secure access to shared and external resources
• Separation of tenant traffic while still leveraging shared provider infrastructure

VPC VLAN Extension with VCF Automation
VPC VLAN Extension is a VMware Cloud Foundation networking capability that enables Layer 2 (L2) and Layer 3 (L3)
connectivity between traditional physical network VLANs and VCF-managed Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) subnets. This
capability allows workloads running inside VPC-based environments to integrate directly with existing enterprise VLAN-
backed network architectures without requiring immediate network redesign or large-scale IP renumbering efforts.
By extending VLAN-backed network connectivity into VPC-managed environments, organizations can support
coexistence between traditional VM-based applications and modern VPC or cloud-native workload constructs within the
same operational framework. This enables a gradual transition toward VPC-based consumption models while preserving
compatibility with existing enterprise networking and operational dependencies.
Migration Use Case: Transitioning Traditional VM Workloads into VCF Automation Constructs
One of the primary use cases for VPC VLAN Extension is enabling migration of traditional virtual machine workloads into
VCF Automation consumption constructs without requiring immediate rearchitecture of the existing network environment.
In many enterprise environments, traditional workloads are tightly coupled to existing VLAN-backed network designs,
static IP addressing schemes, firewall policies, routing dependencies, and operational processes. Replatforming these
workloads into VPC-based automation environments often introduces operational risk if applications must be immediately
re-IPed or migrated into entirely new network segments.
VPC VLAN Extension helps address this challenge by allowing existing VLAN networks to be extended into VPC-
managed environments so that workloads can retain their existing network context during migration.
Example Workflow
1. A provider administrator creates a VPC subnet associated with an existing enterprise VLAN and IP range.
2. The subnet is exposed to a tenant organization within VMware Aria Automation.
3. Existing virtual machines are migrated or imported into the tenant namespace or VPC construct.
4. The migrated workloads continue operating within the same IP addressing and network context as the original VLAN-
backed environment.
5. Over time, workloads can be progressively modernized or transitioned into fully cloud-native VPC networking models if
desired.
Broadcom 1509

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 191: VPC VLAN Extension with VCF Automation - Migration Use Case
Best Fit Scenarios:
• VPC VLAN Extension bridges the gap between brownfield VLAN-based infrastructure and greenfield VPC-based deployments.
• It enables customers to modernize incrementally without forklift migrations or re-IP exercises.
• Direct L2 adjacency between physical VLANs and VPC subnets eliminates the need for NAT, firewall hairpins, or complex routing
overlays in hybrid workload scenarios.
• VM Migration: Lift-and-shift VMs from physical hosts to VCF without re-IP. VMs retain their physical VLAN X IPs and default
gateway.
• Legacy Application Compatibility: Apps with hardcoded IP/GW configurations that cannot tolerate re-IP (ERP systems, license
servers, etc.).
Identity and Access Management Design
Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a foundational pre-requisite for VCF Automation deployment. Configuring
authentication correctly determines who can access the platform, at what level of privilege, and through which identity
source. VCF Automation enforces a two-tier access model built around two distinct personas - the Provider and the
Tenant / Line-of-Business (LOB) - each with its own authentication requirements, supported identity providers (IdP), and
portal scope. These personas do not share authentication configuration; each must be independently integrated with an
enterprise identity provider before operational use begins.

Chargeback and Billing
Chargeback is a cost management solution that is designed to help service providers accurately track and distribute
expenses within a private cloud environment. Enabling both providers and tenants to gain insights into resource usage
and ensures fair cost allocation-based on consumption. As a plug-in for tenants, Chargeback provides a metering and
billing interface that simplifies usage tracking, measurement, and invoicing for services delivered through VCF Automation
and VCF Operation.
For more design information, refer to the VCF Automation Design Library section on Chargeback and Billing.
Platform Protection and Multi Tenant Workload Protection Design
Backup/ Restore and Disaster Recovery (DR) for a VCF private cloud must address two distinct protection domains:
the platform infrastructure itself, and the tenant workloads running on that platform. These are not the same problem.
Platform DR protects the management and control plane components such as - VCF Fleet, vCenter, NSX Manager,
VCF Automation, and the Identity Broker - that the platform cannot function without. Tenant workload DR protects the
application VMs running in tenant Supervisor Namespaces and VPCs, governed by per-tenant SLA commitments that
may have very different RPO and RTO requirements from one tenant to the next.
Both protection domains must be designed before production go-live. A platform that can recover tenant workloads but
not its own management plane cannot execute that recovery. Equally, a platform that can recover its management plane
Broadcom 1516

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
but has no tenant workload replication cannot meet the SLA obligations made to tenant organizations. This section covers
both domains and documents the design choices, recommended technologies, and pre-requisite steps for each.

Multi Tenant DR Design Choices
Multi-tenant workload Disaster Recovery (DR) in VCF Automation is the capability to protect, replicate, and orchestrate
the recovery of tenant application VM workloads across two independent VCF Instances within a single VCF Fleet - a
primary instance where workloads run day-to-day, and a recovery instance at a geographically separate site that is ready
to receive and run those VM workloads in the event of a primary site failure. This section describes how that capability
is designed, what technologies deliver it, what design decisions must be made per tenant, and what the pre-requisite
configuration looks like within the VCF Automation architecture.
In VCF Automation, tenant workloads are isolated by design - each tenant has their own vSphere Namespace, their own
Project, their own VPC, and their own Transit Gateway. This isolation model is not abandoned at the DR layer; it is carried
through it.
Protection and Recovery for VCF Automation Topologies
Protection and recovery for VCF Automation allows authorized Organization users to replicate VM Service VMs across
regions that each have a region quota within a vSphere Supervisor namespace.The most basicprotection and recovery
topology is where VMs residing in a vSphere namespace from a single organization are replicated between two regions
(for example, region A and region B) of a VCF fleet.
Broadcom 1517

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 194:
In the diagram above, the contents of protected VMs registered in namespace A are replicated over the network to
storage capacity in namespace B. Replicas of protected virtual machines can be used to recover VMs in Namespace B.
Workload Protection Design Scenario#1 :One VCF Fleet with Two VCF Instances Across Multiple Regions
A commonly supported and recommended topology for protection and recovery in VCF Automation is a single VCF fleet
spanning multiple regions, where each region is backed by its own independent VCF instance. Within each region, both a
management domain and one or more workload domains are deployed.
While this approach requires deploying a dedicated management domain per region, it is intentionally designed to isolate
failures and limit the blast radius of any disaster event to a single region.
In the event that a management domain hosting VCF Automation becomes unavailable, the service can be restored in
another region’s management domain. This enables continued access for organization users and allows for the recovery
of workloads without dependency on the affected region.

VCF Service Consumption: Extending the Foundation
The design and architecture documented each section of this blueprint design establish a complete, production-grade
private cloud with VMware Cloud Foundation Automation. That foundation - the Supervisor cluster, VPC networking,
Transit Gateway, VCF Automation multi-tenant model, IAM, load balancer, and disaster recovery design -is not the end
state. It is the starting point.
Once your foundation is in place, VMware Cloud Foundation exposes a rich catalog of platform services that your tenant
users and application developers can consume directly through the same self-service model established in this design
guide. Each of these services - VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), Data Services Manager (DSM), and Private
AI infrastructure - runs on the vSphere Supervisor you have already designed and deployed. There is no separate
infrastructure to build. The network, security, identity, and governance model you have already defined automatically
extends to every service you add.
This section explains how the foundational architecture supports service consumption, describes the primary VCF
services available, and provides the reference table of Design Libraries and Implementation Blueprints that guide the
deployment of each service.
Whether you have designed VCF Automation for a single enterprise with internal teams, or for multiple independent tenant
organizations sharing the same infrastructure, the consumption architecture is the same. The difference is the scope of
isolation - not the capability. Both deployment models have access to the full VCF service catalog.
The following table catalogs the dedicated Design Libraries and Implementation Blueprints available for each VCF
service. Each Design Library is the authoritative architectural reference for the service - it defines the design decisions,
prerequisites, and configuration guidance that is required to deploy the service on VMware Cloud Foundation.

Transition Scenario – Aria Automation to VCF Automation (All Apps Model)
This section addresses customers who are currently using Aria Automation with a VM-based consumption model and
are looking to transition to VCF Automation to enable a more modern private cloud experience with self-service, multi-
tenancy, and Kubernetes-native consumption.
In these environments, Aria Automation is typically used for VM provisioning with limited or externally implemented
tenancy and governance constructs. As organizations evolve toward platform-centric operating models, there is a need
to move beyond VM-only consumption and adopt a unified model that supports both virtual machines and modern
application workloads.
VCF Automation introduces the All Apps consumption model, which provides:
• Built-in multi-tenancy using organizations and projects
• Policy-driven governance with quotas and RBAC
• Self-service catalog and API-driven provisioning
• Native support for Kubernetes through VKS
• Integrated networking using NSX VPC-based constructs
For customers transitioning from Aria Automation, this shift represents not just a tooling change, but an operational model
transformation-from infrastructure-centric provisioning to platform-based consumption.
The following guidance outlines recommended approaches for:
• Transitioning existing VM-based workloads and automation workflows
• Introducing multi-tenant constructs using organizations and projects
• Enabling self-service consumption for both VM and Kubernetes workloads
• Designing VPC-based networking aligned with modern application architectures
Customers can adopt this model incrementally by continuing to operate existing VM workloads while enabling new
application deployments through the VCF Automation All Apps model, allowing a phased transition toward a fully
integrated private cloud platform.
Note:
For detailed design information, refer to the Bimodal Consumption Design for VM Apps and All Apps Workloads

Design Context
This architecture illustrates a transitional adoption model for organizations migrating from existing VMware Aria

operations and enabling gradual adoption of modern application consumption models.
In these scenarios, organizations may already operate existing Aria Automation environments using either:
• traditional VLAN-backed networking through a VDS-based architecture
• or existing NSX-backed networking and segment-based workload connectivity models
Following the transition to VCF Automation:
• existing workloads continue operating on their current networking and infrastructure constructs
• existing VLAN-backed or NSX-backed networking configurations remain unchanged
• existing workloads continue to be consumed through the VM App organization model
• operational disruption to existing workloads, routing models, firewall policies, and application connectivity is minimized
This design enables organizations to preserve existing operational and networking models while incrementally introducing
modern platform consumption capabilities through the VCF Automation All App model.

Apps workload VMs between a pair of supervisors,
within two region quotas, in the same VCF
Automation instance and organization.
After you have deployed and configured
Protection and Recovery for VCF Automation,
you can start creating VMs, configuring
replication, and protecting / reprotecting VMs.

For each new Organization for All Apps you will:

Securing VCF Automation Deployment Pattern 3 with vDefend and Avi
This runbook, describes how to deploy VCF Automation on an external network using Avi as the external load balancer.
Overview
The VMware Cloud Foundation design library has a section that covers different VCF Automation Deployment Patterns for
VCF private clouds. For the first 2 deployment patterns listed:
• Deployment Pattern 1: VCF A in a VCF Instance with Single Domain and Multiple Clusters.
• Deployment Pattern 2: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with multiple domains.
VCF Automation is deployed in the same network as the other management components reside(to include: vCenter,
NSX Manager, SDDC Manager, VCF Operations Manager, etc.). Securing such architecture is covered in detail in the
published Detailed Design for Lateral Security for VMware Cloud Foundation with VMware vDefend.
The final design model, Deployment Pattern #3: External-Facing Deployment of VCF Automation, details implementing
VCF Automation to seamlessly interact with external networks or services in a secure manner while minimizing the attack
surface, containing potential security breaches, and providing the necessary controls for meeting various security and
compliance standards for VCFA. In this document, we will be covering how to secure this deployment pattern.
Deployment Overview
Before proceeding with the technical details of securing the VCF Automation, we need to ensure that the environment is
configured per VMware recommendation. The following diagram illustrates the architecture covered in this run book:
The following sections will go into detail but here are the highlights In this model:
1. VCF Automation is deployed as an appliance - in a single node (Simple) or 3 node (High Availability) model within a
VPC specifically created as the DMZ for VCF Automation (DMZ VPC). The VPC includes:
a. An external IP block defining the publicly facing IP range available for this deployment.
b. Subnets.
Broadcom 1530

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a. A manually configured VPC public subnet for VCF Automation components.
a. IP addressing is pulled from the external IP block.
b. Must be a /28 or larger CIDR range.
b. An automatically created VPC services subnet (private) where the Avi service engines providing load balancing
services for VCF Automaton are deployed.
2. The Avi controllers, the management and control plane components of the Avi Load Balancers - are connected to a
VLAN-backed management subnet (VCF Management). It must be fully routed to an overlay-backed NSX segment
that is connected to the NSX T1 gateway where the Service Engine management NICs reside. This T1 gateway will be
used for securing Avi controllers to Avi Service Engine communications with gateway firewall (GFW) functionality.
3. The Avi Service Engines, which runs the advanced load balancer that is used for load balancing traffic for VCF
Automation, is connected to the VPC services subnet in DMZ VPC. The one-arm load balancing function for VCF
Automation will be hosted here. This is the same VPC that has the subnet for VCF Automation. Please note that:
a. The VPC services subnet is a private subnet.
b. The VPC subnet where the VCF Automation components are located e is a VPC public subnet.
4. The DMZ VPC has one public VPC subnet:
a. The public VPC subnet will provide all IPs used to deploy VCF Automation and configure the AVI-based virtual
service.
b. The public VPC subnet is part of the external IP block and is connected to the transit gateway (TGW) for onramp/
offramp function. This TGW will also provide gateway firewall (GFW) services.
5. VCF Management components - such as vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations etc. - are connected to a VLAN-backed
management subnet. vDefend DFW will be used here for security services.
The next section, we will cover summary order of Operations, assumptions and pre-requisites related to installation and
configuration.
Order of Operations Summary
The following list summarizes the order of operations for integrating VCF Automation and Avi:
1. Create a NSX project with a VCF Automation Subnet for the DMZ VPC for this deployment
a. Recommend that this is a dedicated NSX Project for the VCF Automation DMZ VPC.
b. Recommend assigning an external IP block to the NSX Project that is at least a /27 (32 IPs).
c. From that external IP block, you will need a public subnet that is at least a /28 (16 IPs) as all the IPs used will be
public IPs.
2. Deploy Avi and integrate with the target management domain
3. In Avi, pre-VCF Automaton installation
a. In Avi
a. Create a virtual service for the target VCF Automation FQDN.
b. Configure the virtual service to allow L4 passthrough on port 443 to allow for VCF Automation installation.
Important:
Post install it is recommended to reconfigure the virtual service to support HTTP/HTTPS with SSL offloading
leveraging either the self-signed certificate created at VCF Automation install or a custom certificate (also applied
to VCF Automation).
b. In the Management Domain NSX Manager, ensure Avi SEs are added to the distributed firewall exclusion list in the
target NSX Manager
Important:
VCF Management Components are automatically in an exclusion list.You will remove them from the exclusion list
in a later step.
4. Deploy VCF Automation via VCF Operations fleet management API (see section 1.2 VCF Automation Deployment
Procedure for more information)
5. Once VCF Automation is deployed following these documents for configuration
a. For provider-level configuration, refer to the Provider Management guide.
b. For organization-level configuration, refer to the Organization Management guide.
Broadcom 1531

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. Secure the VCF Automation deployment
a. In Avi
a. Reconfigure virtual service to support HTTP/HTTPS with SSL offloading.
b. Configure WAF rules for the virtual service.
b. In NSX Manager
a. Remove VCF Management Components from the distributed firewall exclusion list.
b. Configure gateway and distributed firewall rules to secure communication with VCF Automation.
Assumptions
for the VCF Automation application cluster. For more information on VCF Automation design refer to the VCF Automation
Design Library section of the VCF Design Guide.
The following is a list of assumptions for how the target environment should be configured:
• VCF 9.1 Fleet infrastructure.
– Deployed and configured.
– VCF Automation is NOT deployed with the base VCF Fleet deployment.
• Avi
– Installed in the target VCF management domain through VCF Operations fleet management.
– Integrated with the VCF management domain instance.
• VCF Automation
– Will be deployed as a Day-2 activity.
– Will be deployed in a network separate (i.e. DMZ network) from the other VCF Fleet components.
– The target separate network will be a VPC subnet.
• The VCF Fleet, Avi, and vDefend Security component licenses can be entitled.
VCF Automation Deployment Procedure
Deploying VCF Automation with external load balancer integration requires:
• VCF Automation is installed as a day-2 activity after initial VCF Fleet deployment.
• VCF Automation is deployed through VCF Operations fleet lifecycle API.

• Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDN) registered and resolvable.
• IP addresses are defined.

Node Sizing and High Availability

Optional - Split DNS and Network Configuration
The VCF Automation default design calls for a single FQDN/VIP combination that is then exposed both internally and
externally. Additionally, the default example used in this guide assumes the FQDN/VIP combination is on the same overall
IP range as the internally facing VCF Automation components (Node IPs, VCF Automation service runtime, and the load
balancer virtual service IP Pool).
Depending on your organization’s security posture, the default deployment could potentially expose the internally facing
VCF Automation components, previously mentioned, unnecessarily. This issue can be mitigated by deploying VCF
Automation using a split DNS and network configuration.
What is Split DNS and Networking Configuration?
The overall concept is to split the communication between internal users and external users so that the internally facing
VCF Automation components are not directly exposed to external access.
The overall process:
1. Assigning VCF Automation components to separate network ranges within the external IP block
2. Separate internal and external DNS configurations for the target VCF Automation FQDN.
3. Internally the VCF Automation FQDN will resolve to the virtual service IP Pool addresses.
4. Externally the VCF Automation FQDN will resolve to the virtual service VIP address.
Creating a Split DNS & Network Configuration
Important:
This uses the IP structure from the JSON example in Example CURL Command with Example JSON
Payload section of this guide.
Process
1. Configure Split Networking - Configure two separate ranges in the external IP block for the DMZ VPC.
For example:
a. External IP block range #1
a. 172.16.49.0/24.
b. Used for internally facing VCF Automation components (Node IPs, VCF Automation service runtime, and the
load balancer virtual service IP Pool).
b. External IP block range #2
a. 10.200.0.0/24.
b. Used for external IP block for the VCF Automation FQDN/VIP.
2. Configure Split DNS
a. Internally facing DNS - Configure the internally facing DNS to resolve the VCF Automation FQDN to the IP Pool IP
addresses.
For example: vcfa01.rainpole.io resolves to 172.16.49.43,172.16.49.44, and 172.16.49.45 for internal usage.
Important:
The VCF Automation service runtime FQDN will only be advertised by the internally facing DNS.
Broadcom 1539

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
b. Externally facing DNS - Configure the externally facing DNS to resolve the VCF Automation FQDN to the IP Pool
IP addresses
For example: vcfa01.rainpole.io resolves to 10.200.0.100
3. Secure Deployment - Follow guidance in this guide to secure VCF Automation network traffic through WAF and
firewall configuration.
Result
1. All users access VCF Automation through the same FQDN (in this example vcfa01.rainpole.io).
2. Internal users will resolve the FQDN to the “internal” IP Pool IP addresses associated with the load balancer virtual
service.
3. External tenants will resolve the FQDN to the “external” virtual services VIP address associated with the load balancer
virtual service.
Important:
The JSON file for the split DNS configurations is the same as the standard JSON (non-split DNS). During the
deployment of the split DNS configuration, the system will assign the IP Pool IPs as the VCF Automation FQDN
within VCF Operations. This will ensure that the VCF Fleet components communicate with VCF Automation using
the “internal” path. External users will still access VCF Automation through the externally facing IP address.
