Network Traffic Segregation with vDefend and Avi Load Balancer
In the following section, we will go into detailed design and methodologies to secure the deployment pattern #3 , including
the scope, conventions as well as detailed implementation steps.
• Network Traffic
• Configuration Inventory
Network Traffic
External Traffic
An external connection defines how a transit gateway (TGW) in Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connects to networks outside
of NSX and into the outside environment as well as services it supports. This runbook is based on using centralized
TGW (CTGW) connection, where the transit Gateway uses a Tier-0 gateway provisioned on NSX for external connection.
Distributed TGW (DTGW) connection, where the transit gateway connects directly to VLANs provisioned in the fabric is
not in the scope.
Tenant Traffic
External traffic, originating from the Tenant Organizations into VCF Automation. This traffic traverses through NSX
T0 Gateway, NSX Transit Gateway (TGW) and DMZ VPC Gateway into the VPC subnet that hosts the load balancer
services.
Management Traffic
Internal traffic includes bi-directional communication channels between VCF Automation and other required entities.
This includes VCF management components, e.g. vCenter, NSX Manager etc for access to the underlying resources.
as well as VCF Automation user interface for the VCF Automation provider to perform configuration and administrative
activities. The traffic in this case traverses through the NSX T1 gateway for Avi management and TGW gateway for the
Broadcom 1541

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
rest. vDefend distributed firewall (DFW) controls traffic to the management network segment that hosts VCF management
components mentioned, such as vCenter, NSX manager, VCF Operations etc.
Please see the diagram in the Deployment Overview Section at the beginning of this blueprint.
Configuration Inventory
Before implementing firewall policies and rules, we will utilize various inventory management options available in NSX to
organize and give uniformity to the various elements used.
Groups and Service
In order to secure VCF Automation, NSX objects are created to provide structure and streamline the process by
organizing various components into logical groups. This includes creating dynamic groups using attributes or properties,
such as IP, VM name etc as well as static groups that aggregates similar objects, e.g. VCF Management Components.
This will ensure that the constructs are defined once and used in various areas, such as the NSX gateway firewall as well
as NSX distributed firewall. The following section covers the convention and logic used to create those components:
• Groups: NSX allows logically grouping various objects into groups. The groups used in this document start with grp-
and include name to indicate what it includes, e.g.
– Groups, grp-vcenters and grp-nsx-managers include vCenter servers and NSX Managers respectively.
– Group, grp-vcf-a includes all of the VMPS management IPs used by VCF Automation
– Groups, grp-vcf-fleet includes every VCF Operations component, such as VCF Ops, VCF Fleet Management,
SDDC manager etc.
– Groups, ext-* for any component used for external traffic, e.g. ext-tenant-one for traffic sourced from external tenant,
tenant-one
• Services: NSX includes pre-defined services that cover most of the common protocol+port combination. Any new
services created to formally organize and re-use new services are created with svc- followed by the services e.g.
– Service, svc-vsphere-supervisor to identify TCP:6443 used by vSphere Supervisor
– Service, svc-vc-webconsole to identify TCP:902 used for web console to the VM form VCF Automation
Naming Convention
Firewall Policies & Rules: vDefend firewall policies and rules follow the guidelines below where applicable:
• Policy names use the convention policy- to identify what the policy is created for, e.g. Policy-Avi is related to Avi vs
Policy-VCFA for VCFA Automation
• Rule names use the convention [allow | deny | reject]-<serviceName> to identify what the rule action (allow, deny or
reject) will be for a given service, e.g. allow-web to allow HTTP/HTTP traffic with TCP 89/443 and allow-ssh to allow
SSH service
If the same security policy needs to be in multiple places - TGW FW, T1 GFW and DFW - names for groups, services and
FW policies and rules are reused for consistency.
Configuring Security Policies and Rules
In the following sections, we will cover how to use vDefend firewall as well as Avi WAF rules to provide secure channels
for relevant traffic.
• Protecting Tenant Traffic with vDefend Gateway Firewall on TGW
• Protecting Tenant Traffic with vDefend and Avi
• Avi Virtual Service Configuration
• Avi HTTP Configuration
• Avi Web Application Firewall (WAF) Configuration
• Protecting Management Traffic
Protecting Tenant Traffic with vDefend Gateway Firewall on TGW
In this design, along with the ingress and egress to the VPC, the Transit Gateway (TGW) also provides security with its
built-in gateway firewall (GFW) functions to control and isolate the internal, management traffic from that of the external,
tenant traffic. This TGW has a VPC for DMZ where a public VPC subnet, Avi Services hosts the Avi Load Balancers. The
Broadcom 1542

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
services that provide external tenant network traffic into VCF Automation flows through this subnet in DMZ VPC and into
TGW. The firewall security policies on this TGW allow only the required services access into the VCF Automation user
interface. The following table shows sample firewall policies required in the transit gateway’s gateway firewall:

Protecting Tenant Traffic with vDefend and Avi
The native load balancer deployed with VCFA provides only layer 4 services. In this deployment pattern, an external
VMware Avi Load Balancer will be used with VCFA deployment for advanced layer 7 LB features. This Avi Load Balancer
will:
• Provide a Virtual Service that will SNAT for the external traffic to the VCF Automation appliances.
• Provide SSL termination.
• Provide certificates in addition to those assigned at deployment for the VCF Automation tenant users to access the
service portal.
•
Front-end traffic to the internal load balancer configured at VCF Automation deployment.
Broadcom 1543

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Provide security filtering using the Avi WAF engine.
• Provide analytics on the traffic destined for the VCF Automation portal.
• Prevent tenant users from accessing the provider portal via redirection.
• (Optional) Prevent tenant users from accessing other tenant’s portals.
– This requires knowing the client source IPs of the tenant users.
WAF protection of the VCF-A VIP
• Prevent client subnets from getting to provider portal.
• Prevent Tenant 1 subnets from getting to Tenant 2 portal when we know the source IP (no possibility if we don’t know
client subnet).
• Configure VIP and pool with HMs appropriate to VCF-A, use the new 9.1 deployment model to have 3 internal VIPs
and configure those to be the pool members.
Best Practices:
• Static IP must be configured via Avi CLI.
High level requirements:
• A Certificate on vip with matching FQDN SAN.
• Persistence, using HTTP cookie.
• WAF configurations.
• SEs in NSX exclusion list.
• HTTP policies to prevent access based on source IP to provider portal.
– Also other tenant portals as an option, would be cumbersome in a large deployment and does require known source
IP ranges.
Important:
All objects should be created in the tenant corresponding to the VPC that VCF Automation is deployed in.

Avi HTTP Configuration
IP/String Group Configuration for HTTP Policies
We will utilize IP groups for configuring HTTP Policies, as well as string groups for WAF positive security model rules.
Reference for String Group
Reference for IP Group
• IP group for Provider Portal users, this should be the subnet where management stations will be sourced.

^[0-9A-Za-z._ \t:,!?+*=@#\-\$\(\)\&\'\/\[\]]*$

Protecting Management Traffic
The VCF Automation nodes are deployed in a private VPC subnet - VCF Automation Subnet in the same VPC as the
Service Subnet where Avi Load Balancer resides. The VCF Automation nodes provide ingress via a built-in native load
balancer to the VCF Automation services.This design with public VPC subnet for Avi Load Balancer data traffic and
private VPC subnet for management traffic maintains a separation between the tenant organization traffic from that of
the internal application network for VCF Automation. There are two main types of management traffic that needs to be
secured in this design::
• Avi management traffic
• VCF Automation Management Traffic

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Protecting VCF Automation Management Traffic
VCF Installer creates an User Excluded Groups called “VCF-Created-Virtual-Machines” in NSX by default. This group’s
members include all VCF Management applications including VCF Automation. From NSX web interface, navigating to
Security > Distributed Firewall : Settings > User Excluded Groups shows the members of this group as seen here:
Broadcom 1550

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Being a member of this group means that the following security posture is applicable:
1. All of the VCF management components are automatically excluded from any of the firewall rules created in DFW
2. Inter-communication between all of those components are unrestricted
However, VCF Automation management network in this pattern is different from the rest of the management components;
it's hosted in a VPC subnet in DMZ VPC whereas the rest are in a management network segment, VCF Automation traffic
needs a communication channel to the VCF management components. TGW FW configuration covered in section 2.3.1
explicitly allows those communication channels.

VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service Consumption Blueprint
The VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service Consumption Blueprint provides architectural guidance for selecting and
implementing the appropriate VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) consumption model within VMware Cloud
Foundation platforms.
The guide focuses on the architectural, operational, networking, governance, and multi-tenancy considerations that
influence how organizations should consume Kubernetes services using VKS. Rather than presenting deployment
steps alone, this document provides a design decision framework intended to help architects align VKS consumption
patterns with organizational operating models, governance requirements, scalability objectives, and private cloud
strategies.VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service Consumption Blueprint.
VKS Consumption Adoption Journey
Before selecting a specific VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service consumption model or deployment architecture, it is
important to recognize that Kubernetes platform adoption is typically an incremental operational journey rather than a
single deployment event.
Organizations often evolve their platform strategy over time based on operational maturity, existing infrastructure
investments, governance requirements, modernization goals, and long-term private cloud strategy. As a result, VKS
adoption may occur at different stages of operational and architectural maturity depending on the organization.
The following adoption journey illustrates a common progression path organization may follow as they transition from
traditional virtual infrastructure operations toward modern Kubernetes-enabled and private cloud operating models.
Broadcom 1553

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 200: VKS Consumption Adoption Journey
Broadcom 1554

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This figure illustrates a progressive adoption journey for organizations transitioning from traditional VMware vSphere
environments toward a modern Kubernetes-enabled private cloud platform using VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
and VMware Cloud Foundation.
The journey demonstrates how organizations can incrementally modernize their infrastructure and operational model
without requiring an immediate transition to a full private cloud architecture on day one.
Stage 1 – Existing vSphere Environment
The journey begins with an existing vSphere 8.x environment operating traditional virtualized workloads that are managed
through VMware vCenter.
At this stage:
• infrastructure operations remain VM-centric
• Kubernetes services are not yet enabled
• operational management is focused on traditional virtualization administration
This phase represents the baseline operational state for many existing enterprise environments.
Stage 2 – Platform Foundation Modernization
Organizations begin modernizing the platform by upgrading to newer platform services and introducing foundational
operational components.
Typical activities include:
• upgrading to vSphere 9.1
• deploying VCF Operations capabilities
• integrating centralized licensing services
This phase establishes the operational foundation required for future Kubernetes and private cloud adoption.
Stage 3 – VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Enablement
After the foundational platform services are established, organizations enable vSphere Supervisor for VKS to begin
consuming Kubernetes services directly on the existing infrastructure platform.
At this stage:
• Kubernetes workloads can coexist with traditional VM workloads
• organizations begin operational adoption of Kubernetes platforms
• platform teams gain operational experience with Kubernetes lifecycle management
This phase represents the transition from traditional virtualization operations toward modern application platform
operations.
Stage 4 – Full Private Cloud Operating Model
As platform maturity increases, organizations can expand toward a more complete private cloud operating model by
introducing additional VMware Cloud Foundation services and operational capabilities.
This may include:
• VCF Automation
• NSX
• SDDC Manager
• Fleet management services
• platform governance and automation capabilities
At this stage, organizations evolve toward a fully integrated private cloud platform capable of supporting both traditional
and modern application workloads under a unified operational model.
Key Architectural Message
The primary architectural message of this journey is that organizations do not need to adopt the full private cloud stack
immediately in order to begin consuming Kubernetes services.
Broadcom 1555

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Instead, organizations can progressively evolve:
• from traditional virtualization operations
• toward Kubernetes-enabled infrastructure platforms
• and eventually toward a fully integrated private cloud operating model based on their operational maturity,
organizational readiness, governance requirements, and modernization strategy.
Consumption Patterns
The adoption journey that is outlined above demonstrates that organizations may adopt VMware vSphere Kubernetes
Service at different stages of operational and platform maturity.
As organizations progress through this journey, selecting the appropriate VKS consumption model becomes a critical
architectural decision that influences networking architecture, governance models, operational workflows, and long-term
platform strategy.
The following sections provide a design decision framework for evaluating the available VKS consumption patterns within
VMware Cloud Foundation.
Broadcom 1556

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 201: Consumption Patterns
Design Context
This design blueprint focuses on the architectural decision framework for consuming and operating VMware vSphere
Kubernetes Service within VMware Cloud Foundation 9 environments.
Broadcom 1557

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The reference design shown above represents the operational and architectural models available for deploying and
consuming VKS across different organizational structures, operational models, governance approaches, and infrastructure
consumption patterns.
Within VCF 9 and later, organizations can consume VKS through two primary consumption models:
• Model 1 – vCenter Consumption Pattern
• Model 2 – VCF Automation Consumption Pattern
These patterns represent fundamentally different operational consumption approaches and platform operating models
for Kubernetes services. The architecture also illustrates how supporting platform services including networking, load
balancing, identity integration, governance controls, quota management, and Kubernetes lifecycle operations -integrate
into the overall VKS consumption architecture.
Design Philosophy
The core design principle of this guide is that VKS architecture decisions should be driven primarily by:
• operational ownership and consumption model requirements
• organizational operating structure and governance boundaries
• desired level of infrastructure abstraction
• lifecycle and operational management approach
• standardization and automation requirements
• scalability of operational processes and platform consumption models
• long-term platform operating strategy and organizational growth
The decision between vCenter-based VKS consumption and VCF Automation-based VKS consumption is fundamentally
an operational architecture decision rather than purely a technical implementation choice. Both approaches can support
varying levels of governance, isolation, and automation depending on how the environment is designed and operated.
The appropriate model should therefore be selected based on the desired operational experience, organizational
structure, lifecycle management approach, and long-term platform strategy rather than on individual technical features
alone.
As a result, selecting the appropriate consumption model early in the design process is critical, since networking
architecture, governance models, operational workflows, lifecycle boundaries, and consumption experiences are directly
influenced by this decision.
Model Comparison
Characteristic Model 1: vCenter Model 2: VCF Automation
Organization Support Typically aligned to a single operational Designed for single or multiple
organization or centralized infrastructure organizational consumption models
team
Multi-Tenancy Model Can be implemented operationally through Natively organization, project, quota, and
infrastructure segmentation, namespaces, policy-driven organizational abstraction built
RBAC, or external governance models into the platform
Self-Service Consumption Can be implemented through custom Built-in catalog-driven consumption
automation, APIs, or external self-service experience with integrated workflows and
platforms integrated with vCenter API-driven provisioning
Network Options VDS, NSX Classic or NSX (VPC) NSX VPC-based networking model
Load Balancer Foundation Load Balancer or Avi Load NSX default Load Balancer or Avi Load
Balancer Balancer
Consumption Interface vCenter UI/API VCF Automation Portal/API
Resource Governance Operationally managed through Integrated policy-based governance with
infrastructure administration processes and quotas and organizational controls
controls
Greenfield and Brownfield Deployment Considerations
This document distinguishes between two deployment scenarios that carry different constraints and recommendations:
Broadcom 1558

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Greenfield: Net-new VCF deployments with no existing VKS infrastructure. Architects have maximum freedom to
choose the optimal pattern and networking model from Day 1.
• Brownfield: Brownfield deployments include existing VMware vSphere 8.x environments that may already be running
VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, as well as environments planning to adopt VKS after upgrading to VMware
Cloud Foundation 9 or later. The upgrade and adoption journey may vary depending on the existing networking, load
balancer architecture, and target operational model.
The selected consumption pattern determines how administrators, platform teams, and developers interact with the
vSphere Supervisor platform and its downstream Kubernetes workload clusters. This consumption model is distinct from
how Kubernetes workloads themselves are operated after deployment.
Operational models such as:
• GitOps workflows
• Helm-based deployments
• Argo CD operations
• CI/CD integration pipelines remain consumption-pattern agnostic and can operate across both vCenter-based and
VCF Automation-based VKS environments.
Greenfield Scenarios
Following this section, the design guide presents:
• Example consumption patterns for both vCenter-based and VCF Automation-based VKS consumption
• Deployment models and architectural patterns that map these consumption approaches to real-world design scenarios
Pattern 1: Single Organization -VKS Consumption with vCenter and VLAN based network
Pattern 1 enables direct consumption of VKS Clusters through the VMware vCenter interface and is designed for
organizations operating under a single administrative and operational model.
Broadcom 1559

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 202:
This architecture illustrates the logical design for consuming VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service directly through a
VMware vCenter-based operational model.
In this consumption pattern, Kubernetes services are provisioned and managed directly through vCenter and vSphere
Supervisor constructs without introducing additional platform abstraction layers such as VCF Automation.
This model aligns closely with traditional infrastructure-centric operational practices where virtualization administrators
manage Kubernetes infrastructure alongside existing virtual machine operations.
The architecture uses VLAN-backed networking through a VMware vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) and integrates
Kubernetes workloads directly into existing enterprise Layer 2 and Layer 3 networking environments.
Broadcom 1560

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Pattern 2: Single Organization - VKS Consumption with vCenter and VPC Networking model
Figure 203:
This architecture illustrates the logical design for consuming VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service directly through a
VMware vCenter-based operational model while leveraging NSX VPC-based networking.
In this consumption pattern, Kubernetes services are still provisioned and managed directly through vCenter and vSphere
Supervisor constructs, without introducing additional platform abstraction layers such as VCF Automation. However,
unlike the VDS-based model, networking is implemented using NSX VPC constructs, enabling a more modern and flexible
networking architecture.
This model maintains an infrastructure-centric operational approach - where virtualization administrators retain direct
control - while introducing enhanced networking capabilities such as logical isolation, scalable segmentation, and policy-
driven connectivity for Kubernetes workloads.
The architecture uses NSX VPC-based networking to provide:
• logical network isolation for workloads within a single organization
• abstraction from traditional VLAN-based networking constructs
• integrated routing and connectivity through NSX gateways
• support for modern application networking patterns within Kubernetes environments
This approach is well suited for organizations that want to retain vCenter-based operational control while adopting more
advanced, cloud-like networking capabilities for Kubernetes workloads.
Broadcom 1561

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Pattern 3: Single Organization– VKS Consumption with VCF Automation
Figure 204:
This architecture illustrates the logical design for consuming VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service using VMware Cloud
Foundation Automation within a single-organization model, where VPC-based networking is the default and required
construct.
In this consumption pattern, Kubernetes services are provisioned and managed through the VCF Automation platform
rather than directly via VMware vCenter. The vSphere Supervisor still provides the underlying Kubernetes control plane,
but all consumption, governance, and lifecycle operations are abstracted through VCF Automation constructs such as
organizations, projects, and policies.
This model introduces a platform-centric operational approach, where infrastructure is abstracted and consumed through
standardized workflows, APIs, and catalog-driven provisioning, enabling consistent governance and operational control
even within a single organization.
The architecture uses NSX VPC-based networking as the default model, providing:
• logical network isolation through VPC constructs
• integrated routing and connectivity via TGW and NSX gateways
• built-in NAT capabilities for workload egress
• policy-driven networking aligned with project and organizational boundaries
• abstraction from underlying VLAN or traditional network constructs
Kubernetes workloads are deployed within VPC-backed subnets and are logically grouped under organizational and
project constructs, enabling structured consumption and governance even in a single-organization environment.
This approach is best suited for organizations that want to:
• standardize Kubernetes consumption through a platform layer
Broadcom 1562

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• introduce governance, quotas, and policy-driven operations
• adopt cloud-like networking and application delivery models
• prepare for future multi-tenancy expansion without redesigning the architecture
Even in a single-organization setup, this model establishes a foundation for scalable, governed, and automated
Kubernetes platform operations, aligning closely with modern private cloud operating models.
Pattern 4: Multiple Organization– VKS Consumption with VCF Automation
Figure 205:
This architecture illustrates the logical design for consuming VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service using VMware Cloud
Foundation Automation in a multi-organization (multi-tenant) model.
In this consumption pattern, Kubernetes services are provisioned and governed through VCF Automation constructs
such as organizations, projects, and policies, rather than direct interaction with VMware vCenter. The vSphere Supervisor
provides the shared control plane, while VCF Automation enforces logical separation and operational boundaries across
multiple tenants.
This model introduces a true multi-tenant platform architecture, where each organization is isolated at the networking,
policy, and consumption layers while sharing underlying infrastructure resources.
The architecture uses NSX VPC-based networking as the default, enabling:
• Tenant-level isolation through dedicated VPCs per organization
• Independent networking domains with separate subnets, routing, and NAT policies
• Dedicated connectivity paths via TGW and Tier-0 gateways per tenant
Broadcom 1563

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
•
Policy-driven segmentation aligned with organizational and project boundaries
• Secure multi-tenant access to upstream networks through controlled egress
Kubernetes workloads are deployed within organization-specific namespaces and mapped to VPC-backed subnets,
ensuring that each tenant operates within a logically isolated environment while leveraging a shared Supervisor and
infrastructure platform.
This approach is best suited for environments that require:
• Strong multi-tenancy and tenant isolation (e.g., enterprise business units, service providers)
•
Centralized platform governance with decentralized consumption
• Chargeback / showback models aligned to organizations and projects
• Scalable onboarding of multiple tenants without infrastructure redesign
Key Takeaway
VCF Automation enables multiple organizations to safely share the same underlying VKS platform while maintaining strict
isolation, independent networking, and controlled access - making it the preferred model for scalable, multi-tenant private
cloud environments.

Load Balancer Decision Tree
Broadcom 1566

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Load Balancer Selection
The load balancer selection depends on the VKS consumption model, the vSphere Supervisor networking model, and the
level of application delivery capability required. The design decision should be viewed in two layers:
1. vSphere Supervisor load balancer selection
2. VKS workload load balancer continuation
The vSphere Supervisor load balancer is selected as part of the platform design. Once selected, it becomes the default
aligned load balancer option for VKS workloads. However, customers may choose to bring their own load balancer for
Kubernetes workloads using the BYOLB model. This BYOLB option applies only to VKS workloads and does not replace
or change the load balancer used by the vSphere Supervisor.
vCenter-Based VKS Consumption:
For vCenter-based VKS, the primary design decision is whether the environment requires basic vSphere Supervisor and
Kubernetes service exposure or advanced application delivery.
The Foundation Load Balancer is appropriate when the primary requirement is basic vSphere Supervisor and VKS
service exposure with minimal operational complexity. This model is best suited for foundational VKS enablement, small
dev environments, or simpler Kubernetes deployments where advanced application delivery services are not required.
When Foundation Load Balancer is selected for the vSphere Supervisor, it also becomes the default aligned option for
VKS workloads. Customers can continue to use Foundation Load Balancer for VKS workload exposure. Alternatively, they
may use Bring Your Own Load Balancer (BYOLB) for VKS workloads only, if they have a separate Kubernetes workload
load balancing requirement.
Avi Load Balancer should be selected for vCenter-based VKS when the customer requires production-grade Kubernetes
ingress, advanced L7 services, application analytics, autoscaling, GSLB, WAF, or stronger application delivery control.
When Avi Load Balancer is selected for the vSphere Supervisor, Avi also becomes the default aligned option for VKS
workloads. Customers can continue with Avi for both vSphere Supervisor and VKS workload load balancing, or they can
use BYOLB for VKS workloads only. In this case, the underlying vSphere Supervisor load balancer remains Avi.
VCF Automation-Based VKS Consumption:
For VCF Automation-based VKS, the load balancer decision is tied to NSX VPC-based tenant networking and the level
of application delivery required by tenants or application teams.
The NSX Default Load Balancer is appropriate when the customer needs basic L4 load balancing integrated with NSX
VPC-based tenant networking and VCF Automation consumption. This model aligns well with standard tenant Kubernetes
clusters where platform-provided networking services are sufficient.
When NSX Default Load Balancer is selected for the vSphere Supervisor, it also becomes the default aligned option
for VKS workloads. Customers can use NSX load balancing for VKS workload exposure. Alternatively, they may use
BYOLB for VKS workloads only. In this case, the underlying vSphere Supervisor load balancer remains NSX Default Load
Balancer.
Avi Load Balancer should be selected for VCF Automation-based VKS when tenants or application teams require
advanced self-service application publishing, Kubernetes ingress, L7 routing, app visibility, WAF, GSLB, or enterprise-
grade application delivery.
When Avi Load Balancer is selected for the vSphere Supervisor, Avi becomes the default aligned option for VKS
workloads. Customers can continue with Avi for workload load balancing or use BYOLB for VKS workloads only. The
underlying vSphere Supervisor load balancer remains Avi.
VKS Workload Load Balancer Alternatives:
For VKS workloads only, customers may use workload-specific alternatives instead of continuing with the selected
Supervisor load balancer.
Supported workload-level options include:
• Istio
• Contour
• OR Bring Your Own Load Balancer (BYOLB)
Broadcom 1567

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
These options are useful when application teams have existing Kubernetes ingress standards, service mesh
requirements, third-party load balancer preferences, or specialized application delivery patterns.
However, BYOLB does not replace the load balancer required by the vSphere Supervisor. The vSphere Supervisor must
still use the platform-supported load balancer choice based on the selected consumption and networking model.
A key design consideration is that BYOLB is a workload-level option, not a vSphere Supervisor load balancer
option.

vSphere Supervisor Design for VKS Consumption
The vSphere Supervisor is the foundational control plane that enables VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service consumption
within a vSphere environment. It provides the Kubernetes API endpoint, namespace abstraction, and integration with
underlying vSphere infrastructure required to provision and manage Kubernetes workload clusters.
Designing the Supervisor correctly is critical, as it directly influences networking architecture (VDS vs NSX VPC), load
balancing, resource isolation, and operational scalability. The Supervisor design also determines how Kubernetes
workloads are exposed, secured, and integrated with enterprise networking and platform services.
The following scenarios explore different Supervisor deployment models and design patterns based on networking
choices, operational requirements, and consumption models.

Deployment Models
After selecting the appropriate consumption pattern for VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, the next critical step is
defining the deployment model of the vSphere Supervisor.
The Supervisor deployment model determines how Kubernetes control plane services are integrated with the underlying
networking architecture, how workloads are connected and exposed, and how operational responsibilities are structured
across infrastructure and platform teams. It also directly impacts key design areas such as network segmentation, load
balancing, scalability, and workload isolation.
In VCF environments, two primary Supervisor deployment models are commonly used:
• VDS-based networking model, which leverages traditional VLAN-backed networking using vSphere Distributed
Switch and aligns with existing enterprise network architectures
• VPC-based networking model, which uses NSX VPC constructs to provide cloud-like network abstraction, enhanced
isolation, and platform-oriented networking capabilities
The following sections describe these deployment models in detail and provide guidance on when to use each approach
based on operational requirements, networking strategy, and long-term platform design objectives.
Broadcom 1573

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 210: vSphere Supervisor Deployment Model for VKS Consumption Using VDS-Based Networking
Architecture Details
This architecture illustrates the deployment model for vSphere Supervisor and VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
consumption using a traditional VDS-backed networking architecture within a VMware Cloud Foundation enviornment.
In this model, Kubernetes services are deployed on top of existing VLAN-backed networking infrastructure using a
vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) architecture rather than NSX VPC-based networking. The design enables organizations
to consume VKS while preserving existing Layer 2 and Layer 3 networking constructs commonly used in traditional
enterprise virtualization environments.

Brownfield Scenarios
Many organizations adopting VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service within VMware Cloud Foundation environments are
not starting from a net-new infrastructure deployment. Instead, they are evolving existing environments that may already
contain established VKS deployments, networking architectures, operational processes, workload clusters, automation
platforms, and governance models.
These brownfield environments introduce unique architectural considerations because existing operational models,
networking dependencies, load balancer integrations, and workload placement strategies often need to be preserved
during the modernization journey.
Brownfield adoption scenarios may include:
• existing vSphere environments with no Kubernetes deployments
• existing VKS deployments operating on VLAN-backed networking
• existing NSX-backed Kubernetes environments
• environments requiring coexistence between existing workloads and new modern workloads with VCF Automation
The following sections outline common brownfield deployment scenarios and describe architectural considerations,
transition models, networking implications, and operational design choices associated with each approach.
Attention:
Note: The brownfield scenarios described in this document provide high-level design and transition guidance
for moving to VCF 9 or later. They are intended to help architects understand possible upgrade paths, design
considerations, and target-state options.
This section is not a step-by-step upgrade guide and does not replace the official product upgrade documentation.
When planning an actual upgrade, refer to the official VCF upgrade documentation and follow the prescribed
upgrade procedures, compatibility checks, and sequencing guidance.
Broadcom 1577

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Scenario 1: vSphere 8.x + VKS + VDS Networking + Avi Essentials
Current State:
This brownfield scenario represents an existing VMware vSphere 8.x environment operating:
• vSphere 8.x
• vSphere Supervisor
• VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS)
• VDS-based VLAN-backed networking
• Avi Essentials load balancing
The existing environment consumes VKS using a VLAN-backed networking architecture integrated with Avi Essentials for
Kubernetes services.
Transition Path to Target State:
The target architecture modernizes the environment to a vSphere 9.x and VCF 9.x-aligned deployment model while
preserving the existing VDS-based networking architecture and Supervisor/VKS operational model.
In this scenario, Avi Essentials must be upgraded to VMware Avi Load Balancer Enterprise to align with VCF 9.x
capabilities and support production-grade load balancing features.
High Level Upgrade Workflow:
• Plan the platform and Avi upgrade strategy prior to upgrading to vSphere 9.x.
• Upgrade Avi Essentials to Avi Enterprise, ensuring licensing and feature compatibility.
• Upgrade vCenter from 8.x to 9.x.
• Upgrade ESX hosts to 9.x.
• Existing Supervisor and VKS workloads are preserved but it is still recommended to keep a workload backup before
you plan for the transition.
Broadcom 1578

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Existing VLAN Backed networking retained
• Deploy VCF Operations.
• Deploy License Server for centralized license management.
Scenario 2: vSphere 8.x + VKS + NSX Overlay Networking + NSX Load Balancer
Current State:
This brownfield scenario represents an existing VMware vSphere 8.x environment operating:
• vSphere 8.x
• vSphere Supervisor
• VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS)
• NSX overlay networking
• NSX Load Balancer
The existing environment consumes VKS using NSX-based overlay networking, where Kubernetes workloads are
integrated with NSX overlay segments and leverage the NSX Load Balancer for ingress and service exposure.
Transition Path to Target State:
The target architecture upgrades the existing environment to a VMware Cloud Foundation 9 or later full-stack
deployment model.
In this scenario, because the environment is already based on NSX overlay networking, the supported and recommended
path is to transition to a full VCF stack rather than a phased or incremental modernization approach as described above in
the VKS consumption adoption journey section.
This requires converging or upgrading the existing environment using the VCF Installer and following the official VCF
upgrade process.
Broadcom 1579

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
High Level Upgrade Workflow:
• Follow the official product upgrade guide and plan the transition to VCF 9.x full-stack and validate compatibility of all
components, including NSX, vCenter, ESX, Supervisor, and VKS.
• Use the VCF Installer to converge or upgrade the existing environment into a VCF 9.x deployment.
• Upgrade vCenter and ESX as part of of the VCF Upgrade workflow.
• Upgrade NSX components (NSX Manager and Edge nodes and Load Balancer Services) as part of the VCF upgrade
workflow.
• Supervisor upgrades are done as a separate step and need to be done after the brownfield import.
• Existing Supervisor and VKS workloads are preserved but it is still recommended to keep a workload backup before
you plan for the transition.
• Existing NSX Overlay network and NSX Load Balancer retained.
Important:
After upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 or later, you can choose to consume VMware vSphere
Kubernetes Service using the VCF Automation (All Apps) model.
However, this requires deploying a new vSphere cluster with vSphere Supervisor enabled using VPC-based
networking.
This can be achieved by either:
• adding a new cluster within the existing vCenter, or
• deploying a new workload domain with a dedicated vCenter and NSX instance
Existing clusters and workloads remain unchanged and cannot be directly converted to the VPC-based All Apps
consumption model. Please refer Scenario 5 for more information.
Scenario 3: vSphere 8.x + VKS + NSX Networking + Avi Load Balancer
Current State
This brownfield scenario represents an existing VMware vSphere 8.x environment operating:
Broadcom 1580

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• vSphere 8.x
• vSphere Supervisor
• VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
• NSX overlay networking
• VMware Avi Load Balancer (Avi Essentials or Enterprise)
The environment is already tightly integrated with NSX for networking and uses Avi Load Balancer for Kubernetes ingress
and service exposure. Kubernetes workloads are deployed on NSX overlay segments and rely on NSX and Avi for
networking, routing, and load balancing services.
This architecture reflects a modern NSX-based deployment model that is aligned with cloud-like networking constructs
and is well-positioned for transition into a full VCF stack.
Transition Path to Target State
The target architecture upgrades the existing environment to a VMware Cloud Foundation 9 or later full-stack
deployment model.
In this scenario, because the environment is already based on NSX overlay networking, the supported and recommended
path is to transition to a full VCF stack, rather than a phased or incremental modernization approach as described earlier
in the VKS consumption adoption journey.
This requires converging or upgrading the existing environment using the VCF Installer and following the official VCF
upgrade process.
During this transition:
• Existing vSphere Supervisor and VKS workloads are preserved
• NSX overlay networking is retained
• Avi Load Balancer continues to provide Kubernetes ingress and service exposure
• Platform services such as VCF Operations and License Server are introduced as part of the VCF stack
High-Level Upgrade Flow
Plan and validate compatibility of all components, including vCenter, ESX, NSX, VMware Avi Load Balancer, vSphere
Supervisor, and VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service.
Note:
If Avi Essentials is deployed, upgrade to Avi Enterprise prior to any platform upgrade.
• Upgrade the Avi Load Balancer (Controller and Service Engines) to a version compatible with the target VCF release.
• Validate Avi integration with vSphere Supervisor and ensure Kubernetes ingress and service exposure are functioning
correctly.
• Prepare the environment for VMware Cloud Foundation conversion, including networking, DNS, NTP, and resource
requirements.
• Use the VCF Installer to converge or upgrade the existing vSphere environment into a VCF 9.x deployment.
• Upgrade NSX components (NSX Manager and Edge nodes) as part of the VCF upgrade workflow.
• Upgrade vCenter and ESX hosts to versions aligned with the VCF release.
• Validate NSX overlay networking, transport nodes, and connectivity.
• Validate vSphere Supervisor and VKS cluster health post-upgrade.
• Validate Kubernetes workloads, ingress connectivity, and application functionality.
Broadcom 1581

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Scenarios 4: VCF 5.x + VKS + NSX Networking + Avi Enterprise
Current State
This brownfield scenario represents an existing VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x environment operating:
• VCF 5.x platform (SDDC Manager, vCenter, NSX)
• vSphere Supervisor
• VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
• NSX overlay networking
• VMware Avi Load Balancer (Essentials or Enterprise)
The environment is already deployed as a full VCF stack with integrated lifecycle management through SDDC Manager.
Kubernetes workloads run on NSX-backed networking and leverage Avi Load Balancer for ingress and service exposure.
Transition Path to Target State
The target architecture upgrades the environment from VCF 5.x to VCF 9.x (or later) using the standard VCF Upgrade
process.
Since the environment is already operating on a full VCF stack:
• Existing VKS clusters and workloads are preserved
• NSX overlay networking is retained
• Avi Load Balancer continues to provide Kubernetes ingress and service exposure
However, to align with VCF 9.x lifecycle and platform requirements:
• Avi Essentials must be upgraded to Avi Enterprise (if applicable)
High-Level Upgrade Flow:
• Plan and validate compatibility of all VCF components against the target VCF 9.x Bill of Materials (BOM).
Broadcom 1582

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• If Avi Essentials is deployed, upgrade to Avi Enterprise as the first step.
• Upgrade the VMware Avi Load Balancer Controller and Service Engines to a version compatible with the target VCF
release.
• Validate Avi integration with vSphere Supervisor and ensure Kubernetes ingress and service exposure are functioning
correctly.
• Follow the VCF upgrade sequencing defined in the upgrade guide
• Validate NSX overlay networking, transport nodes, and connectivity.
• Validate vSphere Supervisor and VKS cluster health post-upgrade.
• Validate Kubernetes workloads, ingress connectivity, and application functionality.

Broadcom 1584

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The target architecture upgrades the environment to VMware Cloud Foundation 9 and introduces multi-tenant VKS
consumption using VCF Automation (All Apps) while preserving existing workloads.
In this scenario:
• Existing VKS clusters and workloads remain unchanged
• Existing networking architecture carries forward
• No replatforming or migration of existing workloads is required
Multi-tenancy is introduced by deploying new infrastructure alongside the existing environment, rather than modifying
the existing cluster.
Recommended Approach:
After upgrading or converging the environment into VCF 9:
Step 1 – Preserve Existing Environment
• Existing vSphere cluster continues to run current VKS workloads
• No changes to Supervisor or networking are required
• Existing workloads remain operational (“stay as-is”)
Step 2 – Introduce Multi-Tenant VKS (All Apps)
Customers can choose one of the following deployment models:
Option A – Same Workload Domain (Side-by-Side Cluster)
• Deploy a new vSphere cluster in the existing vCenter
• Enable vSphere Supervisor with VPC networking
• Integrate with VCF Automation (All Apps)
Use this cluster for:
• Multi-tenant VKS consumption
• New application workloads
Option B – New Workload Domain (Dedicated vCenter + NSX)
Deploy a new workload domain with:
• A dedicated vCenter
• A dedicated NSX instance
• Deploy a new vSphere cluster in this domain
• Enable Supervisor with VPC networking
• Integrate with VCF Automation (All Apps)
Important:
Scenario 5 represents a side-by-side consumption pattern for brownfield VKS environments and VCF Automation
All App model. This approach enables customers to deploy and consume new VKS clusters through the VCF
Automation All Apps consumption model while existing brownfield VKS environments continue to operate
separately. It does not provide an in-place migration path for existing VKS clusters into the VCF Automation All
Apps model. Migration support for brownfield VKS environments into VCF Automation All Apps is planned for a
future release.
Post-Deployment Operational Enablement
After selecting a VKS consumption pattern and successfully deploying the VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service platform,
organizations can enable additional application delivery and platform operations capabilities.
These capabilities are independent of the chosen consumption model (vCenter-based or VCF Automation-based) and can
be layered on top of the deployed Supervisor and downstream Kubernetes workload clusters.

Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint
The Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint describes the design selections and architectural components required to
deploy and operate a Generative AI platform on VMware Cloud Foundation. It is intended to be used in conjunction with
an underlying infrastructure blueprint.
Blueprint Objectives
This blueprint is designed to address a specific set of business outcomes enabled by the Private AI platform running on
VMware Cloud Foundation. Each objective maps a concrete business driver to the platform capability that satisfies it,
giving stakeholders a clear view of the value delivered. Use this table to validate that the blueprint scope aligns with your
organization's AI strategy before proceeding with this design selection.
Business Objective Capability Enabled
Accelerate Generative AI application development Self-service deployment of model endpoints and agents via GUI/API, minimal
Kubernetes, or VM expertise required
Enable private, sovereign AI inference On-premises LLM inference via OpenAI-compatible APIs, data never leaves the
datacenter boundary
Ground AI responses in enterprise knowledge Automated RAG pipeline: ingest, chunk, embed, and retrieve from corporate
data sources (Google Drive, Confluence, SharePoint, S3, MCP servers)
Deliver enterprise conversational AI Stateful agents with session management, automated RAG, and MCP tool
integration for acting on live systems
Reduce MLOps operational complexity Platform abstracts VM, Kubernetes, and microservice management. Engineers
operate at the knowledge base and model endpoint level
Broadcom 1586

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 212: Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint
Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint Components
The table below presents the function of the main components part of the Private AI Services Consumption Blueprint.
Component Function
VCF Automation Identity Provider Authenticates the Organization Admin and ML/AI Platform Admin personas to
the VCF Automation portal.
Private AI Services Identity Provider Authenticates the GenAI Developer persona to the Private AI Services UI and
API.
Harbor Model Gallery Central registry for AI model artifacts, organized into public projects (open-
weights models) and private projects (fine-tuned and custom models).
Open-weights LLM Completion model served by the Model Runtime; generates text responses via
an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint.
Open-weights Embedding Model Embedding model served by the Model Runtime; produces vector
representations used for semantic search operations.
Fine-tuned LLM Completion model variant stored in a private Harbor project; consumed by the
Model Runtime.
Custom LLM Customer-provided completion model stored in a private Harbor project;
consumed by the Model Runtime.
Postgres DB with PG Vector External PostgreSQL database with the pgvector extension; stores and
retrieves vector embeddings produced by the embedding model.
Data Sources (Google Drive, S3, Confluence, External content repositories indexed by the Data Indexing and Retrieval
SharePoint, MCP) module; documents are split into chunks and embedded as vectors.
Private AI Services PodVMs (API, Ingress, Retrieval, Runtime components of the Private AI Services application; collectively
Indexing) implement model serving, data retrieval, and agent orchestration.
VCF Operations Provides infrastructure-level visibility for VI admins; correlates Private AI
Services workload demands with cluster capacity and GPU resource utilization
across namespaces.
Broadcom 1587

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Component Function
Grafana Visualizes Prometheus metrics through pre-built dashboards that display GPU
hardware metrics alongside vLLM inference performance and pod health.
OpenTelemetry Collects OpenTelemetry-compliant LLM trace data,including request flows,
prompt/completion pairs, and token-level timing, for consumption by an external
observability platform such as Phoenix or Langfuse.
Personas
Successful deployment and operation of the Private AI platform spans multiple organizational roles, each with distinct
responsibilities across the infrastructure and application layers. This table defines the personas involved, from the Cloud
Admin who provisions the underlying VCF fleet to the GenAI Developer who consumes model endpoints and builds
AI-powered applications. Understanding these role boundaries is essential for planning access control, onboarding
sequences, and operational handoffs. In some organizations, the role of multiple personas is fulfilled by the same
individual.
Persona Responsibilities
VI Admin • Deploys and operates the VCF fleet, VCF instances, and workload domains
• Set up virtual infrastructure and accelerators
• Create the VCF Automation Organization and assign resource quotas to it (It should include
GPU VM Classes)
Organization Admin • Create a VCFA Project and associate a Namespace with GPU and non-GPU VM Classes with it
• Assign the ML/AI Platform Admin user to the VCF Automation Project
ML/AI Platform Admin • Deploy PostgreSQL Database via VCF Automation Data Services
• Collect OIDC Identity Provider Details for Private AI Services
• Enable Private AI Services
• Integrate Private AI Services with observability tools
• Deploy Completion and Embeddings Models
GenAI Developer • Configures Private AI Services agents with session management and MCP tool connections.
• Builds LLM-powered applications consuming Private AI Services endpoints and agents
Infrastructure Dependencies
The Private AI Services blueprint is not a standalone design; it builds on an existing VCF infrastructure blueprint and
inherits its design attributes and its storage, compute, and connectivity models. This table identifies the underlying
infrastructure components and the specific models that are compatible with the Private AI Services blueprint. These
requirements ensure that prerequisite design selections are in place before Private AI Services are enabled.
Underlying Infrastructure Compatible Models
Infrastructure Modernization • VCF Fleet in a Single Site with Minimal Footprint
Blueprint • VCF Fleet in a Single Site
Network Consumption • VCF Automation All Apps Orgs Consumption Model
Workload Connectivity • Centralized Connectivity Model
• Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model
vSphere Supervisor • Single Management Zone with Combined Workload Zone Model
vSphere Cluster • Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model
Blueprint layering
The following diagram illustrates how the Private AI Services blueprint layers additional components on top of an existing
infrastructure blueprint. In this case, the VCF Fleet in a Single Site blueprint is presented. In the management domain, the
Cloud Admin deploys the Data Services Manager appliance alongside the existing Fleet and VCF Instance management
components.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The workload domain cluster already hosts Supervisor cluster VMs. Depending on the selected workload connectivity
model, it also hosts either NSX Virtual Network Appliances (VNAs) for the Distributed VLAN model, or NSX Edge nodes
for the Centralized Connectivity model.
Within the workload domain cluster, the Cloud Admin adds the NVIDIA vGPU driver (VIBs) to the cluster vLCM image.
The Cloud Admin then enables the following Supervisor Services: Harbor, Contour, Data Services Manager, and Private
AI Services.
The Private AI Services application and its PostgreSQL database are then deployed trough VCF Automation by the ML/AI
Platform Admin. The components added by the Private AI Services blueprint are highlighted in purple.

GPU communication overhead,
offers simpler deployment and
better fault isolation. Single
replica failure reduces capacity
but does not crash the entire
system (vs tensor parallelism,
where one GPU failure brings
down the model). Tensor
parallelism requires high-
speed interconnects (NVLink/
NVSwitch) and introduces
latency from GPU-to-GPU
communication every forward
pass.

Security Modernization
To assist with choosing a protection and recovery model for your specific business and technology requirements, the
protection blueprints section provides a set of pre-defined architecture topologies, based on specific design profiles. To
deliver a ready-to-consume solution, providing the full set of capabilities (end-to-end design) offered by the VMware Cloud
Foundation platform, each protection blueprints provides a prescriptive set of requirements and implementation steps.
Bolster Lateral Security and Intrusion Detection and Prevention
Lateral Security with vDefend The Lateral Security with vDefend blueprint describes the architectural components
and design selections required to provide centralized, enterprise-grade security
services for a VMware Cloud Foundation platform using VMware vDefend security
solutions.
Accelerate Recovery from Ransomware and Other Disasters
VCF Component Backup and Restore The VCF Component Backup and Restore blueprint provide guidance on ensuring the
resilience and continuity of your VCF private cloud. In the event of data loss or system
failure, having up-to-date backups allows for efficient restoration of critical services,
minimizing downtime and maintaining operational integrity. Implementing a consistent
backup strategy protects your infrastructure against unforeseen disruptions.
VCF Instance Backup and Restore The VCF Instance Backup and Restore blueprint provides guidance on the recovery of
an entire VCF Instance that has failed, and must be recovered in the same site.
VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery This VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery protection blueprint provides the ability to handle a
VCF Instance, or site failure, and recover components in another location, where that
location is typically outside metro radius.
Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud This Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation protection blueprint provides a
Foundation clean room environment on a vCenter instance that allows you to inspect, analyze, and
recover infected virtual machines before restoring them to a production environment.
VCF Component Backup and Restore
Regularly backing up the management components of a VMware Cloud Foundation platform is essential to ensure the
resilience and continuity of your VCF private cloud. In the event of data loss or system failure, having up-to-date backups
allows for efficient restoration of critical services, minimizing downtime and maintaining operational integrity. Implementing
a consistent backup strategy safeguards your infrastructure against unforeseen disruptions.
Overview
This Protection Blueprint applies to both the management domain and workload domains where you must recover one or
more management components.
After you deploy a VCF fleet, backing up management components ensures that you can keep your environment
operational if a data loss or failure occurs. You implement backups to prepare for:
Broadcom 1615

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• A critical failure of any management component.
• An upgrade of any management component.
• A certificate update of any management component.
You take the following backup types:
• Scheduled backups, which ensure that at any given point in time, you can restore from a recent backup.
• Manual backups before a system update, which ensure that if the operation is unsuccessful, you can restore to a point
in time immediately before the operation.
• Manual backups after the recovery of a failed part of the system.

VCF Instance Backup and Restore
VCF Instance Backup and Restore involves the recovery of an entire VCF Instance that has failed, and must be recovered
in the same site.
This Protection Blueprint applies to both the management domain and workload domains where you must recover all
management components.
Example Failure Scenarios
• Complete VCF Instance failure.
• Datastore corruption.
Supported Topologies
Several topologies of VCF exist according to the number of availability zones and VCF Instances. See Design.
Broadcom 1620

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The following topologies are supported for recovery using this guidance.
Supported Topology
• Single VCF fleet.
• Workload domains with a single or multiple vSphere clusters.
• vSphere clusters with a single or multiple vSphere Distributed Switches.
• Workload domains deployed in a single availability zone.
• vSphere Supervisor with a single or multiple zones.
• vSphere content libraries running on NFS storage.
VCF Components to Back Up
All important data in a VMware Cloud Foundation platform should be backed up to a remote backup site, or local backups
should be duplicated to an offsite location. Include all virtual machines in the management domain and virtual machines in
workload domains that require data protection.
After initial deployment, the management domain contains a core set of virtual machines to manage the VCF fleet. When
you deploy a workload domain, VCF deploys additional virtual machines to manage the workload domain.
Note:
If you have other virtual machines deployed in the management domain that require backup, for example,
Microsoft SQL servers, Microsoft Active Directory servers, backup software virtual mahines, and so on, plan to
back them up too. These components will not be restored as part of the Instance Recovery process and need to
be carried out manually
Follow the VCF Component Backup and Restore protection blueprint to ensure all required management components are
backed up.
Documenting the System Configuration of VCF
Keeping detailed as-built documentation on the system configuration eases the recovery process if a failure in your
VMware Cloud Foundation platform occurs.
While the processes in this guidance retrieve much of the information below, keep a record of the following items. Save
this information on a secure secondary storage.
• Topology diagrams of the VMware Cloud Foundation platform
– Physical networking
– vSphere Distributed Switch networking
– NSX networking
– Workload domain configuration
– Cluster configuration for each cluster in a workload domain
– ESX hosts assigned to each cluster
– vSphere Supervisor configuration
• Networking information
– ESX host vmnic-to-switch port mappings
– VM virtual NIC to distributed port group mappings
– IP address information of the VMkernel interfaces on the ESX hosts
– IP address information of virtual machines
– DNS, NTP, AD, and other well-known services used by the VMware Cloud Foundation platform
Note:
The Planning & Preparation workbook used to deploy the platform is a good source for capturing this detail.
Broadcom 1621

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery
This VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery blueprint, provides the ability to handle a VCF Instance, or site failure, and recover fleet
components in another location, where that location is typically outside metro radius.
Architecture
You use a combination of Protection and Recovery and restore from backup to implement disaster recovery between two
VCF Instances for the management domain and workload domains in the VCF fleet.
Figure 215: VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery Architecture
Broadcom 1625

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Objective Description
Main objective Provide disaster recovery capabilities for VMware Cloud Foundation fleet
components in a multi-instance environment.
VMware Cloud Foundation architecture support Multiple VCF Instances with IP mobility
VCF domain type support • Management domain
• Workload domain
Scope of guidance • Deployment and initial configuration of site protection and disaster recovery
components for the management domain.
• Operational guidance for the site protection and disaster recovery components
such as failover and failback of management applications.
Scope of implementation Deployment and configuration of solution components:
• Protection and Recovery
Configuration for failover and failback for VMware Cloud Foundation components:
• VCF Operations
• VCF Operations for networks
Backup & restore is used for the following components
• VCF Automation
• VCF management services
Planning for VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery
Before implementing the VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery blueprint, verify that the environment meets all compute, storage,
and networking prerequisites, and that all required external services are accessible to the solution components.
Use the Planning and Preparation Workbook to capture environment-specific input values that are required during the
implementation.
Implementation of VCF Fleet Disaster Recovery
To provide disaster recovery of VCF fleet components, you use the following recovery methods.
Fleet Component Recovery Method
• VCF Operations • Protection & Recovery Replication & Recovery Plan *

restore from backup
Note:

• Fleet lifecycle

• Log management

Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation
This Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation protection blueprint provides a clean room environment on a vCenter
instance that allows you to inspect, analyze, and recover infected virtual machines before restoring them to a production
environment.
Architecture
You use Protection and Recovery to protect business critical workloads with remote vSAN snapshots against cyber
threats.
After a cyber attack or ransomware attack, virtual machine snapshots might also be infected. An isolated network in a
clean room is used to perform analysis, remediation, and validation of compromised virtual machines without risking
infection of other production workloads.
Once the virtual machines are validated as clean, they can be recovered and reprotected to production.
Broadcom 1632

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Protected Instance Recovery Instance
VCF Instance VCF Instance

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 has the following main elements:
Protected instance The protected VMware Cloud Foundation or VMware vSphere Foundation platform provides business-
critical data center services.
Recovery instance The recovery VMware Cloud Foundation platform is an alternative infrastructure where business critical
workloads are replicated.
It consists of the following
• Management domain
• Isolated clean room (Isolated Recovery Environment)
Clean room A cloud component used to create isolated clean rooms in the recovery instance.
orchestrator
Isolated clean room • An isolated workload domain in the recovery instance.
• In the event of a ransomware attack, the business critical workloads are recovered to the isolated clean
room in the recovery instance for forensic analysis and validation.
• Contains integrated Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) used by the cyber response team to
verify, cleanse, and recover business-critical workloads.
• Provides push-button network isolation to apply different isolation rules to one or more virtual machines
under validation.
– In VCF 9.1.0, push-button network isolation is available by using VMware vDefend Firewall.
– In VCF 9.1.1, push-button network isolation is available by using VMware vDefend Firewall or NSX
VPC networking.
• Workload domain consists of the following clusters.
– 1x Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
– 1x Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model
– 1x Host Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model
Or
– 1x Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model
– 1x Host Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model
• vSphere Compute cluster
– Provides a dedicated, secure network environment that enables you to safely power-on
ransomware-infected virtual machines.
• vSAN Storage cluster
– Backed by vSAN ESA, it provides a high-performance enterprise storage system.
– The replicated business-critical workloads are stored on the storage cluster's datastore, which is
mounted remotely to the vSphere cluster.
Replication of virtual You configure remote replication of business-critical workloads using the integration of Protection and
machine data Recovery.
You configure Protection and Recovery to use the multiple-point-in-time snapshot feature providing more
flexibility for data recovery of protected business critical workloads on the recovery instance.
vSAN Protection groups Place virtual machines in a protection group to schedule and manage snapshots for all VM members of the
group and to replicate virtual machines to the recovery VCF Instance.
Recovery plans A recovery plan specifies how Protection and Recovery recovers virtual machines in the protection groups.
Endpoint Detection and Access to the EDR portal to perform security analysis on ransomware-infected virtual machines.
Response (EDR)

in the protected site.

Planning for Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation
Before implementing the Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation protection blueprint, verify that the environment
meets all compute, storage, and networking prerequisites, and that all required external services are accessible to the
solution components.
Use the VMware Cloud Foundation Planning and Preparation Workbook to capture environment-specific input values that
are required during the implementation.
Implementation of Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation
To provide ransomware recovery for business critical workloads within VMware Cloud Foundation, you deploy the
protection and recovery appliances across the protected and recovery instances. Then, you configure replication and
create recovery plans.
To implement the Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation protection blueprint, follow the procedures in the
following table.
Before implementing Cyber Recovery for VMware Cloud Foundation, onboard to the service and verify that the clean
room vCenter instance meets the NSX requirements. See the Onboard to Cyber Recovery and NSX Requirements.

Lateral Security with vDefend
The Lateral Security with vDefend blueprints provides centralized enterprise-grade security services for a VMware Cloud
Foundation platform using the VMware vDefend security solutions.
Understanding the Lateral Security with vDefend Blueprints
A blueprint is:
• A prescriptive end-to-end security design created to accelerate time-to-value when protecting the VCF private cloud
platform.
• Has a prescriptive selection of deployment and configurations models that are chosen from the design library to
conform to the design profile of the blueprints.
• Provides a set of planning, implementation, and design elements (requirements and recommendations) based on the
chosen deployment models.
Choosing Lateral Security with vDefend Blueprint
This design guide covers the following pre-defined blueprints:
• License Hub for vDefend and Avi Load Balancer
•
Security Services Platform for VMware Cloud Foundation
• Management Domain Security
• Workload Domain Security
• Distributed Virtual Patching
vDefend Distributed Firewall for VMware Cloud Foundation
VMware vDefend is built into the VCF private cloud, which is activated by providing a valid license key. vDefend Firewall
configurations for your workloads are done through the respective NSX Manager instances for the workload domains. An
NSX instance can manage a single or multiple workload domains. To provide security services, vDefend addresses the
configurations for the respective workload domains.
Broadcom 1646

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
Starting VCF 9.1, the management domain NSX Manager can be shared with workload domains.
Architecture Overview
vDefend Distributed Firewall (DFW) provides complete Layer 2 to Layer 7 visibility and enforcement with automated policy
delivery for VMware Cloud Foundation private cloud workloads and management components. The DFW is implemented
as a software-defined architecture, with a centralized management plane, hybrid control plane, and distributed data plane.
This software-defined architecture enables firewalling at the scale and speed that is required for dynamic private cloud
environments. The DFW delivers lateral security for different workload types: virtual machines, containers, and bare metal
workloads.
Broadcom 1647

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 217: Lateral Security with vDefend for VMware Cloud Foundation
Broadcom 1648

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
The DFW operates on every virtual NIC (vNIC) of each VM, monitoring every packet entering or exiting without
hairpinning or network re-architecture. Attached to the VM's vNIC, the DFW policy, and state seamlessly follow
the VM during vMotion events, maintaining its security posture. Kubernetes clusters running the Antrea Container
Network Interface (CNI) plugin can be easily integrated with NSX, thus providing an efficient centralized security
management policy for container workloads using VMware vDefend. Applications running on a Bare Metal server
can also be protected with the vDefend DFW. The latter is facilitated by the Security Services Platform, which
implements a new, horizontally scalable architecture designed to support, alongside advanced security services,
micro-segmentation for Bare Metal servers.

Foundation using the VMware vDefend security solutions.

License Hub for vDefend and Avi Load Balancer
License Hub for VMware vDefend and VMware Avi Load Balancer is a centralized licensing platform that manages and
distributes subscription-based licenses for VMware vDefend and VMware Avi Load Balancer. The License Hub is a
mandatory component when using the VMware vDefend and Avi Load Balancer add-ons. This section provides the design
details and decisions for deploying License Hub on VCF.
Broadcom 1649

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Architecture Overview
License management for VMware vDefend and VMware Avi Load Balancer involves using digitally signed subscription
license keys to activate features corresponding to the purchased license editions. License utilization reports are
instrumental in monitoring product usage and consumption across diverse deployments.
Figure 218: License Hub Architecture
Broadcom 1650

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
License Hub Core Components
Component Component Details
Avi Cloud Console A cloud-based platform that serves as the source for VMware vDefend and VMware Avi Load
Balancers licenses.
License Hub appliance This appliance manages the License Hub service. You can perform tasks such as upgrading the
License Hub service or viewing diagnostic information.
License Hub service Also known as License Hub. This service is started by the License Hub appliance. You can manage
licenses and perform related tasks through this service.
License Edition See the vDefend Feature and Edition Guide for feature entitlement details for VMware vDefend
products.
Endpoints Endpoints are the downstream components that consume license from the License Hub:
• NSX Manager Cluster
• Security Services Platform
• Avi Controller Cluster
Operating Modes
Mode Details
Connected Mode • The License Hub has Outbound HTTPS Internet access to the Avi Cloud Console portal. The
License Hub supports Proxy configuration for secure Internet communications.
• Registration is automatic, and licenses are polled from the Avi Cloud Console to the License Hub
every 15 minutes without file exchange.
• License usage report is consolidated and provided to the Avi Cloud Console every 24 hours.
Disconnected Mode • No direct connectivity to Avi Cloud Console.
• Suitable for isolated or air-gapped environments.
• Registration is file-based: the file is manually exported from the License Hub and uploaded to the
Avi Cloud Console.
• The activation file is downloaded from Avi Cloud Console and imported to the License Hub.
• The license file is downloaded from the Avi Cloud Console and manually imported to License
Hub.
• In order to avoid license expiration, the license must be manually uploaded at least once every
six months.
Private Mode • For highly secure, classified, or operationally sensitive environments where even manual Internet
access for licensing is restricted. This mode is only for Broadcom-certified private customers.
System Requirements
The License Hub appliance has the following system requirements.
vCPU Memory, GB Storage, GB
6 12 256
Networking Requirements
Any supported network type, including DVPG, NSX Segment (VLAN or Overlay), and VPC subnet, can be used to deploy
the License Hub as long as it has Layer 3 connectivity to the endpoints that needs to be licensed.
• Three IP addresses:
– Single IP address for appliance management.
– One address pool with two contiguous IP addresses for the License Hub service. It is not required that the
management IP address and the IP address pool be on the same subnet as long as they are reachable.
• Two DNS records:
Broadcom 1651

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– One FQDN for the appliance. This FQDN must map to the management IP address of the appliance (for example,
licensehub20.example.com maps to 172.16.111.39).
– One FQDN for Kafka. This FQDN must map to the second IP address of the IP address pool (for example,
licensehub-kafka.example.com maps to 172.16.111.41).
• Latency:
– Network latency between License Hub and the endpoints is 150 ms or less.
– Storage latency is 10 ms or less.
• Ports and Protocols:
– License Hub management port - TCP/5480.
– License Hub Services - TCP/443 and TCP/9092
– Refer to the Ports and Protocols web page for the full list of the ports and protocols that are required by the License
Hub Service.
• License Hub endpoint connectivity types:
– Dynamic - connection type for the endpoints that are not behind a load balancer or NAT.
– Static - connection type for the endpoints that are behind a load balancer or NAT.
• Avi Cloud Console connectivity:
– When in Connected mode, License Hub connects to Avi Cloud Console, which needs Internet access. If the
management network can't connect directly to the Internet, a proxy can be set up.
Scale
• A single License Hub supports up to 120 endpoints to be connected, where endpoints could be a mix of NSX Manager
Clusters, vDefend Security Services Platform, Avi Controller Clusters.
• Multiple License Hub can be deployed when the number of endpoints to license is above 120.
