Security Services Platform for VMware Cloud Foundation
The Security Services Platform for VMware Cloud Foundation blueprint covers the design details and decisions, planning
and preparation, and implementation steps for deploying the vDefend Security Services Platform on VCF.
Architecture Overview
The Security Services Platform (SSP) is VMware vDefend next-generation solution that provides visibility and advanced
security capabilities in VMware Cloud Foundation. SSP is a high-performance, scalable platform that runs vDefend
security services, including Security Intelligence, Network Detection and Response, Malware Prevention, and more.
Security services provided by the Security Services Platform:
• Segmentation and Advanced Threat Prevention Score along with Security Assessment Report to help users assess
their security posture.
• vDefend Security Journey: Built-in automated workflows to speed-up DFW and Advanced Threat Prevention(ATP)
deployments.
• Firewall Rule Analysis: Identify potential security gaps in the DFW configuration and manage the DFW rules more
efficiently.
• Security Intelligence: Visibility about the security posture and the applications network behavior, and streamlines
Distributed Firewall Security Policies configuration thanks to a recommendation engine.
• Network Traffic Analysis (NTA): Detects abnormal network behaviors, such as DNS tunneling, Data Exfiltration, or port
scanning
Broadcom 1661

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Network Detection and Response (NDR): Collects, scores, and correlates atomic security events from IDPS, NTA, and
Malware Prevention into campaign blueprints. This feature enables security teams to reduce the Mean Time To Detect/
Respond and focus on the incidents that really matter.
• Malware Prevention Service (MPS): Detects malware being transferred over the network and prevents them from
writing to the disk. An optional cloud sandboxing can also be used to analyze Day-0 malware activity.
• Security Metrics: Collects and stores metrics coming from various platform components - used for multiple purposes,
such as sizing, monitoring, or troubleshooting. Provides data for Top N analysis, lifetime counters, and historical trends.
• Distributed Firewall for Bare Metal Workloads
• Out-of-band NDR sensor for threat visibility beyond VCF workloads
• AI Assistant for VMware® vDefend™ covering both Distributed Firewall and Threat Defense.

Security Services Platform for VCF Model
This section covers the design details and decisions for implementing the Security Services Platform for VMware Cloud
Foundation.
vDefend Security Services Platform
The Security Services Platform for VMware vDefend employs an appliance-based deployment model. It is delivered
through the Security Services Platform Installer (SSPI). The Security Services Platform Installer also serves various
critical functions in managing the operational integrity of the Security Services Platform , providing upgrades, scale-out,
backup and restore capabilities, password management, and platform diagnostic functionalities. Furthermore, the Security
Services Platform Installer hosts the packages that are needed to deploy, operate, and upgrade the Security Services
Platform.
A single Security Services Platform Installer can deploy and manage up to five independent Security Services Platform
instances
• Security Services Platform Deployment Model
• Security Services Platform Sizing
• Security Services Platform Networking
Security Services Platform Deployment Model
Security Services Platform is deployed to support the design objectives for solution component availability and the number
of workloads that the solution must support.
Deployment Models
Even though a single Security Services Platform Installer can deploy and manage up to five Security Services Platform
instance, each of thoseSecurity Services Platform instances can only onboard a single NSX Manager cluster. This results
in a M:1:1 mapping for deployment model alignment.
In VMware Cloud Foundation, you can have one or more NSX Manager clusters (single NSX Managers in a Simple NSX
Manager Model deployment):
• One for the management domain.
• One for the first workload domain.
• Additional workload domains may share an existing workload domain NSX Manager cluster or have dedicated NSX
Manager clusters.
Broadcom 1663

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Depending on the number of NSX Manager clusters, one or multiple Security Services Platform instances may be
required. The Security Services Platform instance is not bound to a workload domain, but to an NSX Manager cluster.
Workload domains, which share a single NSX Manager also share the Security Services Platform instance.
vSphere High Availability protects the platform by restarting the Security Services Platform Installer and Security Services
Platform instance virtual machines on an alternate ESX host in the vSphere cluster, if affected by an ESX host failure.
The Security Services Platform, Kubernetes-based architecture, and declarative operational model ensure high availability
for the services running upon it.

Deployment for Multiple Availability Zones
In an environment with multiple availability zones, the Security Services Platform instance/s runs in the first availability
zone. If a failure occurs in the first availability zone, the Security Services Platform nodes are failed over to the second
availability zone. The "Machine Health Check" feature must be disabled on the Security Services Platform instance.

Security Services Platform Sizing
Platform Sizing & Scaling for the Security Services Platform requires some careful planning since this requirement involve
features activated, configuration inventory and the flows collected by the platform. For example, lowering the number of
features frees up resources for additional flows and configuration inventory limits, and vice-versa. Utilizing the collected
data for trending, the platform also makes recommendations based on various metrics and published configuration
maximums.
Sizing Compute and Storage Resources
Summary steps for sizing can be summarized into the following 3 broad recommendations:
1- Choose Form Factor(FF) based on NSX configuration inventory limits: Select from medium, large, or extra-large(XL)
Security Services Platform FF based on the VM counts, Groups, & Security Policies + Rules. Note that during the
onboarding pre-checks, Security Services Platform will give a warning if NSX inventory scale exceeds 80% of limits and
error if NSX inventory scale exceeds 90% for Medium/Large FF or 99% for XL FF. After Onboarding, Security Services
Platform generates an alarm if NSX inventory exceeds the supported limits of the deployed instance.
2 - Choose the initial number of Worker Nodes based on the required features: Note that advanced security capabilities
demand higher node counts and that the order of feature activation could impact resource utilization since some features
use more resources than the others
3 - Scale the number of Worker Nodes based on Flows: The platform administrator can utilize both the flow
capacity dashboard (requires a minimum of 3-days of Metrics collection) along with system alarms to aid in scaling
recommendations.
For a production deployment with the following core security features: Security Intelligence, Rule Analysis, and Metrics,
the Security Services Platform has the following minimum CPU, memory, and storage resources requirements.

Security Services Platform Networking
Network Connectivity
IP reachability is required among the Security Services Platform Installer, Security Services Platform, the NSX Manager
cluster, and NSX Transport Nodes (ESX hosts and NSX Edge Nodes). Furthermore, the Security Services Platform
requires Layer 2 (L2) connection for their inter-node (controller and worker) communications.
This validated solution outlines a deployment model for SSP using vSphere Distributed Port Group (DVPG). However,
deployment model using either types of NSX segments - Overlay or VLAN, as well as the NSX Virtual Private Cloud
(VPC) subnets are supported. Public VPC subnets are recommended since it does not require NAT when allowing SSP to
ingest data from components such as ESX and NSX Edge transport nodes, and NSX Managers.
Requirement Description
Management network Used to connect the Security Services Platform Installer. The existing VMware Cloud
Foundation VM Management DVPG can be used.
Security Services Platform instance Used to connect the SSP instance nodes.
network
Network Design for deployment in the Management domain
This design option places the appliances within the management domain of the VMware Cloud Foundation instance. It
ensures connectivity and close proximity to vCenter and NSX Manager. The Security Services Platform Installer appliance
is connected to the VCF VM management network. The Security Services Platform nodes are placed on a dedicated
network.
Note:
The Security Services Platform can be deployed on the VM Management network if sufficient IP address space is
available.
Broadcom 1674

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 223: Security Services Platform deployment in the Management domain
Broadcom 1675

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
NSX segments (Overlay or VLAN) or VPC public subnets are also supported. Bidirectional communication with
the VCF physical networks (ESX Management and VM Management) has to be allowed.
Network Design for deployment in the Workload domain
This design option solution places the Security Services Platform Installer appliance in the management domain and
the SSP instances in their respective workload domain of the VMware Cloud Foundation instance. This design solves
potential management domain resource constraints. The SSPI appliance is connected to the VCF VM management
network; whereas the SSP nodes are placed on a dedicated network (DVPG, NSX segment, or VPC subnet) in the
workload domain. Note that when using a VPC, the subnet type of the VPC must be public to avoid complex DNAT
configuration for SSP ingestion traffic.
Note:
1. The Security Services Platform network needs routed connectivity with the VCF VM Management network.
2. If traffic between the Security Services Platform network and the VCF VM management network passes
through a firewall, make sure that the required ports are opened as posted here: https://ports.broadcom.com/.

b. Requires 1 IP address.

b. Security Services Platform services (messaging).
c. With the Security Services Platform v5.1 onwards:
a. You can append a new IP pool for extra resources but you can't edit or remove an existing IP pool
b. The addresses within each IP pools must be contiguous..

Management Domain Security
The Management Domain Security blueprint covers the design details and decisions, planning and preparation, and
implementation steps for securing the VCF management plane.
Architecture Overview
The management domain of the first VMware Cloud Foundation instance of a VCF fleet hosts the management
components of the VCF Instance and the management components of the Fleet itself.
The VCF instance management components: VCF Operations, VCF Automation, VCF Management Services,
vCenter Servers, NSX Managers, vDefend Security Services Platform(s), and other appliances that are deployed in the
management domain are secured via the vDefend DFW, configured from the management domain NSX Manager. The
Management Domain Model also supports running customer business workloads, with management components and
workloads secured by a single vDefend Firewall instance.

Segmentation Planning
VCF Management segmentation planning design details, covering VMware Cloud Foundation management component
definitions in various security environments (zones).
The primary strategy for developing a segmentation model is alignment with the inherent boundaries of the data center's
virtual infrastructure. Segmentation by environment (or zone) is an efficient way to implement traffic controls, mitigate
lateral movement between zones, and restrict access to critical data. Using this security architectural technique, you
partition the VMware Cloud Foundation management domain components into distinct, logical groups with similar security
requirements.

Infrastructure Services Protection
In this stage, you design a vDefend DFW policy to protect communication between the VCF Management components
and common (shared) services, such as: DNS, NTP, DHCP, etc.
Infrastructure Services Distributed Firewall Policy Design
Protecting shared infrastructure services, such as DNS, NTP, DHCP, Active Directory (AD), and centralized logging
systems is critically important because they are the foundational trust boundary on which VMware Cloud Foundation
private cloud operations, security, and visibility depend. Compromising just one of these services can lead to total network
control loss, widespread service outages, or complete security blind spots.
The Infrastructure service protection is structured in a single DFW policy that grants access strictly based on a destination
server and a service port requirement. A unique allow rule is configured for each service, assuming each service runs on
an individual server.
The last policy rule is a lockdown that prevents potential traffic from reaching destinations other than enterprise-allowed
ones. Enable logging on the lockdown rule to monitor for potential policy misconfiguration and avoid service disruption.
The following table provides an example of the VMware Cloud Foundation management domain vDefend DFW policy and
rules for infrastructure services protection - based on the designed segmentation model.
Infrastructure Services Policy (DFW Infrastructure Category)

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Environment Level Protection
In this stage, you design a vDefend DFW policy to protect communication between VCF Management domain
Environments (zones).
Environments (Zones) Distributed Firewall Policy Design
Securing traffic between different Environments (often referred to as zone-to-zone security or macro-segmentation) is one
of the most critical and foundational elements of a robust VCF private cloud security strategy.
With respect to the VCF management domain, this control point is important because it enforces a trust boundary
between components with different management and operational functions, and security requirements, e.g., VCF Fleet-
level access needs, VCF Instance-level access needs, VCF management, and/or workload domain-level access needs.
The VCF management domain Environments DFW design is based on configuring a separate policy for each zone (see
Management Domain Segmentation Planning for the zones definition). The policies are organized by zone-level access
permissions, with the VCF Fleet external communications policy processed before the VCF Fleet management policy, and
the VCF management and workload domain policies processed after.
Each policy, aside from the VCF Fleet and external components communication that does not have a "lockdown" rule,
follows a unified structure:
• The policy is applied to the group representing the environment (policy-level Applied To).
• First rule for controlling intra-zone traffic. This rule has a specific action: "Jump to Application", which creates a
dynamic policy chain, allowing for the delegation of traffic inspection and enforcement. So the traffic that matches this
rule in the Environment category policy will continue to be inspected by the Application category policies and rules.
• Rules for required inter-zone communications with application-level granularity.
• Inter-zone communication rules are duplicated in individual policies to ensure policies remain order-independent.
• Environment rule(s) with unknown source and/or destination (Any) have an action: Jump to Application, for more
granular inspection.
• The last rule of each policy is a "lockdown" rule designed to prevent any other inbound/outbound zone communication.
This approach offers a flexible DFW design that begins with segmentation at the Environment level and allows for
the configuration of more specific Application category rules at a later stage, without necessitating modifications to
the Environment policies. Also, it enhances troubleshooting capabilities by pinpointing which specific policy may be
obstructing traffic that should otherwise be permitted.
Note:
1. Although the VCF management domain design is prescriptive and the management component
communication requirements are known, variations may exist across customer environments.
2. An initial action of "Allow and Log" within a lockdown rule should be followed by a transition to "Drop and Log"
or "Drop" based on the level of confidence in the policy.
3. This policy design offers flexibility and is effective in prescriptive environments such as the VCF management
domain. However, it may not be appropriate for large workload domain environments, where the outbound and
inbound communication patterns of various applications can differ significantly. Therefore, safeguarding this
traffic at the environment level may prove to be impractical.
The following table provides an example of the VMware Cloud Foundation management domain vDefend DFW policy and
rules for environments protection - based on the designed segmentation model.

Workload Domain Security
The Workload Domain Security blueprint covers the design details and decisions, planning and preparation, and
implementation steps for securing customer workloads using the vDefend DFW-1-2-3-4 staged prescriptive workflow.
Broadcom 1709

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Architecture Overview
Attribute Value
Security Assessment Before implementing VCF workload domain security, it is recommended to conduct a
security segmentation assessment to understand the current workload risk posture. Security
Intelligence evaluates the current ruleset and traffic flows to assign points to various security
areas. These areas include the status of the Distributed Firewall, the status of Malicious IP
protection, the percentage of infrastructure traffic protected, the percentage of protected
environment pairs, the application protection status, and the percentage of workloads using
obsolete operating systems or risky protocols. All these factors are used to calculate a
vDefend Security Segmentation Score.
A Security Segmentation Report can also be generated, including detailed information about
the risk posture and actionable recommendations to improve it.
Secure Infrastructure Involves creating policy to allow only necessary network connectivity from servers and
endpoints to critical common services in the VI workload domain. These shared services will
most likely be services like Active Directory, DNS, patching, logging, and more. The idea is
to limit connectivity to known enterprise workloads and prevent unauthorized connectivity
from external IPs or untrusted endpoints. Older operating systems are at greater risk and
should be protected with more fine-grained security policy instead of broad-based. Insecure
protocols like Telnet, SMBv1, LLMNR, FTP, and any other unencrypted ports and protocols
should also be denied with security policy.
Secure Environment Applications in the network are separated into multiple environments or zones such as
production, user acceptance testing, quality assurance, or development. These zones can
be utilized to create zone-based policy. Production servers should be protected from the
other zones, and only necessary network connectivity should be allowed between them. If
a workload in one of these zones is compromised, the inter-zone policy will protect lateral
movement and potential data exfiltration.
Secure Application Applications can require both inter-app policy and micro-segmentation policy.
• Inter-app Policy:
An application can be made up of one or more workloads. Security policy is created to
limit what ports and protocols other applications or workloads are allowed to access within
the application. Application policy can be created with no dependency on the network
architecture. The workloads within or between applications can be separated at a Layer
3 boundary or even live within the same Layer 2 broadcast domain. Policy between
applications should be created based on the documentation provided by the vendor
or application owners. Only necessary services should be allowed while all others are
denied. Inter-app policy can be created at a macro-level (App 1 to App 2 on port 80) or
to a specific tier ( Web, App, DB, etc) within the application depending on your security
policy requirements.
• Micro-segmentation Policy:
Network connectivity, external or internal, in the datacenter should be inherently
untrusted. Security policy is created to limit connectivity even between workloads grouped
within a single application. Traditionally, application communication was limited between
logical tiers like web, application, and database. Workloads within a tier would have free
access between each other and are susceptible to potential malicious lateral movement.
In a micro-segmentation framework, even workloads within the same tier are subjected
to security policy. Workload policy within an application should only allow necessary
ports and protocols based on the documentation and block all other services to prevent
potential lateral movement.

Workload Domain Security Model
This section covers the security design details and decisions for securing the workload domain for VMware Cloud
Foundation.
• vDefend DFW Stage Prescriptive Segmentation Design
• vDefend Grouping and Tagging Design
• vDefend DFW Policy Design
vDefend DFW Stage Prescriptive Segmentation Design
vDefend DFW 1-2-3-4 provides a 4-stage prescriptive deployment process that follows lateral traffic patterns to quickly
secure VCF workloads, with built-in guidance that mirrors lateral traffic components and policy categories within vDefend
DFW.
Stage 1: Security Segmentation Assessment
The initial phase involves assessing the current state of the environment to determine existing protection levels. This
foundational step helps establish a baseline and a measurable security score. The assessment tracks progress as new
rules are defined and enforced, providing a starting point for the entire segmentation initiative.
The score is structured using multiple factors, with a maximum of 95 points, all based on the latest 30 days of traffic.
Score Category Points Description
Distributed Firewall in Operation 5 Points are awarded for having the Distributed Firewall activated
along with Malicious IP Protection
Infrastructure Protection 5 Percentage of critical infrastructure traffic (14 predefined services)
that is protected by an explicit rule in the Infrastructure category.
Environment Protection 5 Percentage of environment pairs (e.g., Prod to Dev) that have
a default rule action set to Drop or Reject, and the coverage of
workloads by at least one environment rule.
Application Protection 70 Largest component, weighted by the percentage of application
workload and traffic coverage, as well as the presence of application
or datacenter lockdown rules.
Workloads without Obsolete OS & Risky 10 Percentage of workloads that are not running an obsolete operating
Protocols system or allowing connections using risky protocols.
The assessment serves as a benchmark and a continuous progress tracker. By following the prescriptive workflows in
Stage 2 (Secure Infrastructure), Stage 3 (Secure Environments), and Stage 4 (Secure Applications), you will be
implementing new policies and lockdown rules. As you complete these stages and your security coverage increases, you
can periodically rerun the score calculation to observe your progress. The score will steadily increase, validating your
progress toward a mature Zero Trust segmentation architecture.
The detailed report will also provide specific projects and recommendations to help you further improve your score.
Broadcom 1712

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stage 2: Infrastructure Services Protection (Secure Infrastructure)
This stage focuses on identifying and protecting critical, shared infrastructure services within the workload domain, such
as Active Directory, DNS, patching, and logging.
• Policy Creation: The primary goal is creating a policy to allow only necessary network connectivity from servers and
endpoints to these core services.
• Boundary Control: Connectivity must be limited to known enterprise workloads, preventing unauthorized access from
external IPs or untrusted endpoints.
• Risk Mitigation: Older operating systems, which are at greater risk, should be protected with more fine-grained
security policies.
• Insecure Protocol Denial: Insecure protocols like Telnet, SMBv1, LLMNR, FTP, and any other unencrypted ports and
protocols should be explicitly denied with security policy.
Broadcom 1713

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stage 3: Environment Segmentation (Secure Environment)
This stage involves dividing the data center or network into broader security zones or environments.
• Zone Definition: Applications are separated into logical environments such as production, user acceptance testing
(UAT), quality assurance (QA), or development.
• Zone-Based Policy: These zones are utilized to create zone-based policy, ensuring production servers are protected
from the other zones.
• Inter-Zone Control: Only necessary network connectivity should be allowed between environments. If a workload in
one zone is compromised, the inter-zone policy will prevent lateral movement and potential data exfiltration to more
sensitive areas.
Broadcom 1714

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Broadcom 1715

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stage 4: Application Segmentation (Secure Application)
This final stage implements the most granular security policies, which can be further refined into inter-application and
intra-application controls.
1. Inter-application Policy (App-to-App or Ring Fencing): An application may be composed of one or more workloads.
This policy focuses on controlling access between different applications.
– Access Limitation: Security policy is created to limit which ports and protocols other applications or workloads are
allowed to access the application.
– Network Agnostic: Application policy can be created with no dependency on the underlying network architecture,
even if workloads are separated at a Layer 3 boundary or live within the same Layer 2 domain.
– Documentation-Based: Policy between applications should be based on documentation provided by the vendor,
application owners, or Security Intelligence, allowing only necessary services and denying all others. Policy can be
created at a macro-level (e.g., App 1 to App 2 on port 80).
Figure 233: Policy Example 1
Example of using Application Ring Fencing policy
2. Intra-application policy (Micro-Segmentation or Zero Trust) : This is the most fine-grained level, operating on the
principle that all network connectivity, internal or external, should be inherently untrusted.
– Intra-Tier Control: Security policy is created to limit connectivity even between workloads grouped within a single
application tier (e.g., between two web servers).
Broadcom 1716

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– Inter-Tier Control: Security policy is created to limit connectivity between workload tiers within a single application
tier (e.g., between Web, App, DB tiers).
– Lateral Movement Prevention: Traditionally, workloads within a tier had free access to each other, making them
susceptible to malicious lateral movement. In a micro-segmentation framework, all workloads are subjected to
security policy.
– Rule Set: Workload policy within an application should only allow necessary ports and protocols based on
documentation or Security Intelligence and block all other services to prevent potential lateral movement.
Figure 234: Policy Example 2
Example of using both Inter-App and Application Ring Fencing policy
vDefend Grouping and Tagging Design
Before designing a security policy to secure workloads within a workload domain, it is important to identify and organize
the VM inventory within the workload domains of a VCF Fleet. This is achieved by leveraging various object grouping
techniques to simplify the design of the security policy finally implemented.
Groups
A group is a logical construct that allows grouping of workloads into a common collection based on static (IP Address/NSX
objects like segments) and/or dynamic (VM names/VM tags) membership criteria.

Tags
A tag is a user-defined label that can be associated with a virtual machine or group of virtual machines or NSX objects like
segments, segment ports etc.
Each tag has the following two attributes:
• Tag (refers to the tag name. It is required and must be unique and case-sensitive)
• Scope (optional)
Scope is analogous to a key and tag name is analogous to a value. For example, if all virtual machines are to be tagged
based on their operating system (Windows, Mac, Linux). You can create three tags, such as Windows, Linux, and Mac,
and set the scope of each tag to OS. Tags are used to group workloads logically, which can be helpful when defining
Broadcom 1719

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
security policies. They can be used to simplify and automate firewall rules and apply different security settings specific to
the workloads they are being applied to.
Naming Conventions and Tags
1. Use a descriptive name: Give your group a name that describes what it protects. Example: All workloads belonging to
"PROD" can be a part of group "SG_PROD".
2. If the number of tag and group requirements are within the supported scale limit then keep it simple, have multiple
individual tags, do not have a combined tag.
3. If the number of tag and group requirements are beyond the supported scale limit (ref. VMware Configuration
Maximums):
4. Combine scope and tag names to reduce the number of tags required.
5. Modify the name of the tag to accommodate for the description of multiple layers it can help protect (combined tag)
Example: For a workload that belongs to the zone: PROD, Application: APP1 and Tier: Web create a single tag:
PROD_APP1_Web instead of associating three separate tags with the workload.

vDefend DFW Policy Design
This section outlines the strategic framework for architecting a Zero Trust security posture for VCF workloads by
leveraging hierarchical use of DFW Policy Categories (Infrastructure, Environment, and Application) and the critical
importance of scoping rules in the "Applied To" field to minimize resource overhead.
Policy Design
Policy is a collection of one or more rules. Rules are a set of instructions that determine whether a packet should be
allowed or blocked. Rules in a policy are evaluated from top to bottom, and a match stops further processing when the
action is set to "Allow", "Drop", or "Reject". In the Environment category, a fourth action called "Jump to Application" will
stop rule evaluation in the Environment category and proceed to the Application category for further rule evaluation.
The vDefend Distributed Firewall has several categories where you can place rules. Policies and rules are assessed and
enforced starting with the Ethernet category. After rules are assessed from top to bottom, the flow is compared to policies
and rules in the Emergency category, followed by Infrastructure, Environment, and finally Application. Once a flow has
matched a rule with a allow/drop or reject action, it's not matched against any further rules.
Broadcom 1722

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 235: vDefend Distributed Firewall Policy Design for VMware Cloud Foundation
Ethernet
The ethernet category is for Layer 2 policy only. These policies have source and destination groups that only have MAC
addresses as members.
Emergency
The emergency category should be used for temporary rules only. These rules are created to block connectivity during
a security incident or allow connectivity to and from an application if there are connectivity issues. These rules are
eventually moved to the infrastructure, environment, or application sections that are explained below
Infrastructure
The infrastructure category is where all common services rules are placed. These rules should be created to protect
critical infrastructure services like Active Directory, DNS, patching, logging, and more. Broad rules to protect common
services from insecure protocols like Telnet, SMBv1, LLMNR, FTP, and any other unencrypted ports and protocols should
be placed here as well.

vDefend Distributed Firewall "Applied To"
Policy can be assigned groups in the "Applied To" field. This determines whether rules will be applied to all DFW protected
vNICs or to specific vNICs defined in one or many groups. Broad-based policies for infrastructure and environment
categories should set the "Applied To" field to groups identifying different workloads environments or left to the default
value - DFW.
Rules should utilize the "Applied To" field to ensure efficient rule enforcement on the VMs that the rules pertain to. This
also enables the ability to use a scoped deny ANY/ANY/ANY rule that enforces principle of least priviledge for targeted
application workloads defined using the "Applied To" field without affecting any other application.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

part of the application or specify the "Applied To" field for each rule individually.

Important:
For the most optimized rule enforcement, the "Applied To" field on the rule should be set to one or more groups.
This ensures only the required rules are enforced on the VM vNIC and rules that do not pertain to the workload
will not be installed or evaluated. The "Applied To" field at the policy level will need to include all groups that all the
rules use to ensure policy is installed correctly for all workloads. The result of using "Applied To" at the policy level
is rules that might not pertain to a workload will be installed on the VM’s vNIC resulting is evaluation of rules that
will never match and suboptimal rule installation.
Layer 7 Policy Considerations
A Layer 7 rule context profile should be coupled with the correlating service (port/protocol). An example being if you
configure a rule to inspect traffic to confirm the payload is actually HTTP traffic, the service should also be set to HTTP
(TCP/80) or whatever port you expect the HTTP traffic to utilize in the workload. L7 rules with multiple protocols (ie DNS,
SSH, etc) should be avoided. Create separate rules for each protocol and correlating context profile. While setting a
service to any and defining a context profile is allowed, it should be avoided to prevent large amounts of unnecessary
packets being sent to the deep packet inspection engine. Some examples are below:
Source Destination Service Context-Profile Action
RFC1918 Web-Server HTTP (TCP/80) HTTP Allow
App1 DB-Server MYSQL (TCP/3306) MYSQL Allow

Planning and Preparation for Workload Domain Security
Security Intelligence
Security intelligence provides a graphical user interface to visualize the security posture and network traffic flows that
occur in your environment.
A Security Services Platform, and therefore Security Intelligence is linked to an NSX manager cluster. Depending on your
private cloud needs, you may have multiple Security Services Platform instances and multiple Security Intelligence within
a single VMware Cloud Foundation instance.
Enabling Security Intelligence is a mandatory step for the Security Segmentation Journey.
Segmentation Planning
The metadata in CSV files is used to tag VMs and create groups, which are foundational for defining security policies in
the subsequent stages. The CSV file doesn’t have to contain ALL assets, and multiple iterative imports are possible. The
CSV can be exported from a CMDB that maintains datacenter assets metadata.
The CSV file must contain at least 1 column that will be used by the Security Services Platform to find the corresponding
asset from the NSX inventory. Commonly used fields are VM names, IP addresses or UUIDs. Multiple columns can also
be used as identifiers – this is useful when some identifiers might be duplicated: for example, if multiple VMs have the
same IP address, the VM name or the UUID can be used as a differentiator.
The fields in the CSV file define a hierarchy for your datacenter assets, which directly correlates to the segmentation
levels used in the Security Journey.

Distributed Virtual Patching
The Distributed Virtual Patching blueprint covers design details and decisions, planning and preparation, and
implementation details to deploy vDefend Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS) to protect unpatched
workloads in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF).
Architecture Overview
The mandate for the use of a compensating control, such as Distributed Virtual Patching, is intensified by the rapid
identification of novel vulnerabilities via Frontier AI Models. Consequently, these controls must be deployed in a highly
efficient and targeted manner. Incorporating these Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS) rules into the
Emergency policy section enables the architecture to evaluate highly specific traffic at the inception of the ruleset. This
ensures that subsequent standard threat rules are processed with minimal redundancy. This strategic placement is
paramount; the virtual patch control must be configured strictly to detect and prevent potential vulnerability exploitation
effectively while simultaneously minimizing the incidence of false positives.
To achieve this objective, the meticulous selection and targeted evaluation of IDPS signatures remain imperative.
Identifying only the most pertinent signatures is critical to preventing the inadvertent blocking of legitimate network traffic.
Furthermore, optimization of the Source and Destination fields within the IDPS rule should be pursued whenever feasible.
Broadcom 1734

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Additionally, utilization of the Services field is recommended to isolate the specific ports and protocols associated with the
exploit mechanism.
By deploying these rules within the hypervisor-embedded layer at the virtual network interface card (vNIC) of each
respective workload, vDefend effectively isolates threats prior to their propagation across the physical infrastructure
or penetration into the unpatched operating system kernel. This network-layer defense mitigates high-risk vulnerability
exposure, granting enterprise operations teams the requisite latency to systematically validate, schedule, and execute
permanent software remedies without inducing disruptive, emergency application downtime.
Broadcom 1735

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 239: Distributed Virtual Patching Architecture
Broadcom 1736

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design Profile
The VMware vDefend Distributed IDS/IPS represents a fundamental shift in how network intrusion detection and
prevention are architected within virtualized and private cloud environments. Instead of traditional models that treat
security as a perimeter-based or discrete hardware function, vDefend builds intelligence directly into the fabric of the
virtual infrastructure.
At its core, the vDefend Distributed IDS architecture eliminates the concepts of centralized inspection chokepoints and
network "hairpinning." It achieves this by moving the threat inspection engine directly into the ESXi hypervisor kernel,
attaching a purpose-built, software-defined IDS/IPS sensor to the virtual network interface card (vNIC) of every single
workload. Whether a workload is a virtual machine or a container running on VKS, it receives an individualized security
perimeter that travels with it dynamically.
Attribute Value
Hypervisor-Embedded Native Architecture Traditional network security forces internal "East-West" traffic out
of the virtual layer and onto physical appliances to be inspected,
halving link capacity and demanding complex VLAN/network
re-architecting. vDefend re-engineers this paradigm via kernel-
level sensors: the inspection engine runs natively within the
ESXi hypervisor layer, turning every host into an independent,
high-performance security sensor. The result is Zero Network
Disruption — the control sits directly inside the data path of the
hypervisor, inspecting 100% of packets passing through the vNIC
without requiring network taps, span ports, or modifications to
physical switches and routing topologies.
Context-Aware Curated Signature Distribution One of the most critical flaws of legacy IDS/IPS systems is
performance degradation caused by evaluating thousands of
irrelevant signatures against every packet. vDefend allows you to
target the most potent and relevant signatures against the most
appropriate workloads, reducing the active signature checklist
from tens of thousands down to a highly optimized, single-digit
fraction while maintaining high efficiency and security.
Security Services Platform compute, memory, storage, and
reservations requirements details.
Linear Elastic Scalability Centralized hardware appliances scale vertically — organizations
must over-provision expensive hardware to handle peak data
center volumes, creating inescapable bottlenecks. vDefend utilizes
the distributed, idle CPU capacity across all existing ESXi hosts
in the cluster. As the private cloud environment grows and more
compute nodes are added, threat inspection capacity scales out
linearly alongside it.
Complete East-West Visibility While perimeter firewalls successfully defend the boundaries
("North-South" traffic), they remain completely blind to malicious
lateral movements once an attacker establishes initial access.
vDefend provides absolute visibility inside the data center corridor,
capturing and neutralizing tactics and techniques like lateral
discovery, Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) abuse, and internal
data exfiltration.

Virtual Patching Prescriptive Workflow
The blueprint follows a 4-stage prescriptive workflow that takes an organization from risk identification through to control
retirement.
Stage 1: Identify Vulnerabilities. Use vulnerability scanners or Vulnerability Assessment Solutions to flag missing
patches. You will utilize this information to pinpoint the exact IDS signature to apply as the compensating control. These
scanning solutions should be run against the entirety of the workloads in the data center to ensure that as little time
passes between the discovery or disclosure of a vulnerability and the application of the Distributed Virtual Patch.
Stage 2: Identify the Compensating Control. Use the vTIS portal for IDPS Signature research. The output from the
scanners is likely one or more CVE numbers. A CVE number is a unique ID for a computer security flaw. It stands for
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. It acts like a standard dictionary name so people worldwide know they are
talking about the exact same software vulnerability.
Ensure that all relevant threats details are considered for inclusion into the overall IDPS rule. This may include one or
more IDPS signatures and will most often focus on one network port. Once the relevant IDPS Signatures are identified,
they will become the integral part of an IDPS Profile. This profile is simply a collection of one or more IDPS Signatures
that will be used to prevent any exploitation of the unpatched vulnerability against the workload.
While there are multiple methods that can be used to create this IDPS Profile, the recommended method is to use the
CVE itself. This will allow for a dynamic Profile of all of the relevant IDPS signatures that may be released or updated for
the protection against the exploitation of vulnerability. Choosing the signatures manually within this IDPS profile is possible
but does not allow for any automatic updates to be provided automatically as threat research evolves over time.
Stage 3: Create and Enforce the Virtual Patching Ruleset. Within the NSX Manager, build a granular IDPS profile
and emergency-section rule with the action set to Detect and Prevent. Ensure the use of NSX Groups made with Tags
(Dynamic Groups) and utilize the ApplyTo Field to tightly control where this control is applied.
Service or ports and protocols are critical here to ensure that the Ruleset is as tightly focused as possible. This will allow
for as little as possible overlap between the Distributed Virtual Patching Rule and all other IDPS Rules. This is due to the
way in which the IDPS Ruleset is evaluated. The processing of this rulebase is done Emergency first and then the Threat
Rules immediately after. Like all Firewall Rules, the processing of the traffic will stop on the first match. This means that
the more focused the Distributed Virtual Patching Rule is the less chance of overlapping a more broadly created rule. It
is important to set the Distributed Virtual Patching Rule to Detect and Prevent (IPS) to ensure the potential exploit of the
vulnerability is stopped automatically. Most often, the IDPS rules within the Threat Rules Section are set to Detect (IDS)
only.
Stage 4: Monitor, Integrate, and Decommission. Forward events to a SIEM (Security Information and Event
Management) program that are enriched by the NDR. It is critical to be alerted to the Distributed Virtual Patching Rule
Broadcom 1738

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
firing as it can mean that someone is actively trying to exploit the vulnerability. Optionally, there may be a process to
remove the virtual patch once the actual OS or Application patch is aplies. This will become part of the organization's
change control process and remove the virtual patch once the real software patch is applied.

Virtual Patching Events Correlation
This chapter details the requirement of IDPS logging and alerting and Security Information and Event Management
(SIEM) integration.
Logging, Alerting, and SIEM Integration
The solution must generate an event every time a rule fires and blocks an attack. Keeping these events isolated within
the NSX Manager is insufficient, as it requires manual log-ins to discover them. These events are vital for troubleshooting
false positives and hold significant value outside the vDefend system.
A SIEM is a centralized software platform that aggregates, normalizes, and analyzes log data and security events from
across an entire IT ecosystem. In a typical enterprise, thousands of independent systems — firewalls, servers, endpoints,
cloud services, and applications — generate massive volumes of telemetry daily. A SIEM acts as a single pane of glass,
ingesting this disparate data to look for patterns, detect potential cyberattacks, and help security teams manage incidents.

Virtual Patching Lifecycle Management
Effective lifecycle management of virtual patches requires systematically decommissioning rules via change control once
official software patches are applied.
Lifecycle Management and Operations
Once the compensating control is live and events are being monitored, you must manage the lifecycle of these rules.
After the actual software patch is tested and successfully applied to the host OS or application, plan for the removal of the
corresponding Distributed Virtual Patch.
Broadcom 1740

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Maintaining overlapping controls serves no long-term structural purpose. Ensure that your change control process
includes a post-patch task to decommission the IDPS rule when it is no longer needed.
As these Distributed Virtual Patching rules are very targeted at removing the risk from new and unpatched vulnerabilities
in the environment, it is crucial not to omit the remainder of the potential IDPS Controls. Having IDPS inspect traffic across
the associated Risk Profile is crucial to reducing overall risk in the environment. The Distributed Virtual Patching rules
are written in a manner to ensure that as little as possible overlap in rules or traffic occurs so as to not reduce the overall
effectiveness.

Planning and Preparation for Distributed Virtual Patching
The Mechanics of Virtual Patching
Because vDefend operates at the vNIC layer, it enables a highly effective defensive strategy called Distributed Virtual
Patching. When a high-severity vulnerability is disclosed (e.g., Log4j or an enterprise-wide OS flaw), the window between
discovery and manual patching is historically when organizations are most vulnerable. vDefend mitigates this risk
immediately.
By applying a network-level signature tailored to detect and block the specific exploit mechanism at the vNIC boundary,
the threat is neutralized at the earliest possible stage. Even if the application running inside the VM remains unpatched
and vulnerable, the exploit packet is detected and dropped before it can ever reach the OS kernel or application. This
allows the infrastructure teams the required weeks or months to schedule safe, orderly application maintenance windows.
The goal of a Distributed Virtual Patching rule is to reduce risk within the organization. The reduction of Risk can be
measured in terms or Exposure time as well as the risk of having unprotected and vulnerable workloads within the data
center.
IDPS Performance
Before implementing Distributed Virtual Patching, it is important to understand the overall health and remaining capacity
of the IDPS Engine. There are several methods that can be used to determine the overall performance and health of
the IDPS. Starting in SSP 5.2, there are built in dashboards that offer at a glance health and capacity graphs that will
help ensure that the engine is operating normally and has available capacity. However, if these dashboards are showing
that the engine is running at or near capacity, it may be prudent to review the existing rules to ensure that they are all
configured correctly according to the best practices.
Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS) resource utilization refers to the consumption of system assets -
specifically CPU and memory - required to perform deep packet inspection and signature matching.
Security Services Platform (SSP) monitors resource utilization through an asynchronous collection framework to help
identify whether performance bottlenecks originate from general infrastructure overhead or high volumes of inspected
traffic. Metrics are collected from the host transport nodes and are categorized to provide visibility into the security service
(L7/IDPS) footprint. The IDPS service operates as a specialized pipeline within the host capacity and may impact overall
host health even if other background processes remain low.
Broadcom 1741

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Security Services Platform evaluates historical utilization against defined thresholds to assign health status based on two
statistical percentiles over a 7-day window: P95 (representing worst-case peak hours) and P80 (representing typical high-
load periods).
Status Green Yellow Red
Notes The service has significant The service is approaching The service is oversubscribed,
headroom and can handle traffic its allocated resource which may lead to data path
spikes. threshold and monitoring is disruptions that affect the overall
recommended. performance.
The status transitions as follows:
• Normal (green): The service has significant headroom and can handle traffic spikes. The P95 metric is well below the
maximum threshold limit.
• High (yellow): The service is approaching its allocated resource threshold and monitoring is recommended. The P95
metric exceeds or equals the threshold, but the P80 metric remains safely below the threshold (occasional traffic
spikes).
• Critical (red): The service is oversubscribed, which may lead to data path disruptions that affect the overall
performance. The P95 metric exceeds or equals the threshold.
Host Capacity Usage represents how much host capacity is actively in use, allowing administrators to assess resource
pressure and plan capacity accordingly.
Key Components
• Host CPU/Memory Utilization: The total resource consumption of the physical transport node, including hypervisor
overhead and all running virtual machines.
• Security Service (L7/IDPS) CPU Utilization (Turbo mode): The specific percentage of CPU cycles dedicated to the
security pipeline for inspecting Layer 7 traffic and executing IDPS signature matching.
• Security Service (L7/IDPS) Memory Utilization (Turbo mode): The dedicated memory footprint used by the security
engine to maintain session states and signature databases.
If you see hosts that have Critical (Red) or High (Yellow) Alerts, then it is recommended not to enable additional Security
controls without considering a rebalance of the Virtual machines across the cluster. Enabling the Detailed Host Metrics
for those hosts will show where each individual Virtual Machine is running at from a performance perspective. You can
choose to vMotion any VM that is towards the higher end of the performance to a host that is less used. This should free
up the resources needed for implementation of the IDPS Control.
NSX Manager also has a number of Alarms that will signal if the IDPS engine is having any issues at or near capacity
in terms of resources. It is important to acknowledge open alerts within the Distributed IDPS area. Use these alarms to
consider the Security Dashboard within the SSP to evaluate the root cause of the capacity issue. Further troubleshooting
steps can also be taken from these alarms such as in the case of an IDPS engine failure or similar.
Many customers may also use VCF Operations for the active monitoring of the IDPS solution. There is also a community
provided IDPS Dashboard that will highlight any potential issues with the overall health and capacity of the engine.
Before adding any additional rules, it is important to review the current operational state of the IDPS engine using any of
these monitoring solutions.
Assessing and Defining IT Security Risk
A fundamental task in IT security is identifying and defining the areas within an organization's infrastructure that carry
some level of unmanaged risk. The primary goal of this step is to comprehensively understand and quantify this risk in
relation to the specific assets within the customer's environment, so that the organization can properly identify which
compensating controls are necessary to implement.
To accurately define the scope of a risk, security teams should begin by asking several foundational questions:
• What is the specific problem that needs to be addressed?
• What is the scope of the risk?
• What existing architecture and security controls are currently in place?
Broadcom 1742

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• How would the implementation of a new control effectively reduce this risk?
• What is the prioritization level of the issue?
• Who are the key stakeholders, and who will be consuming the resulting data or security events?
To fully qualify the risk, teams must also evaluate the broader context of the environment: the potential impact of
unauthorized access, existing vulnerabilities (OS or application flaws) alongside current mitigation strategies such
as patching procedures, user roles and access permissions, network restrictions already in place to prevent lateral
movement, and existing outbound access control and filtering policies.
Information Gathering
Organizations can utilize a variety of specialized tools and reports to help identify vulnerabilities and risks across their
infrastructure:
• SSP with Security Intelligence
• Security Segmentation Journey Reports
• Vulnerability Scanners
• Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) Tools
Reducing Risk by Mapping to Security Controls
Once risks are clearly defined and quantified, the next step is applying appropriate controls to reduce the risk surface by
directly mapping specific threat vectors to the controls designed to neutralize them.
Threat Vector Mitigating Control
Lateral Movement Distributed Firewall (DFW) configurations (1-2-3-4)
Unauthenticated Access Identity Firewall (IDFW)
Network-Based Exploits Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS)
Malicious Files or Scripts Malware Prevention and Detection
LOLbins (Living Off the Land Binaries) Network Traffic Analysis (NTA) alongside Behavioral IDPS
Aligning Controls with Security Personas
Risk reduction strategies must align with the specific operational goals of different security personas within the
organization.
Persona Primary Focus Relevant Controls
NetSec (Network Security) Teams High-fidelity detection and prevention; DFW, IDPS, NTA, Malware Prevention
blocking malicious activity and keeping bad
actors out of the network.
SOC (Security Operations Center) Teams Investigating end-to-end attacks and NDR for enhanced logging, event
maintaining deep visibility through security enrichment, and correlation
signals; forensic investigations.
Ultimately, establishing risk definitions and deploying controls is an ongoing journey rather than a final destination.
Organizations should start by assessing the risk associated with a specific service or area of interest, and then decide
whether broad or deep coverage is required based on their unique, customer-dependent needs.
Finding Vulnerabilities
One way to identify missing patches is through the use of a vulnerability scanner, such as those commercially available
from Tenable and Qualys. These tools reach out over the network and scan workloads for missing patches, flagging when
a specific VM is vulnerable to a known exploit. The detailed output of a scan will highlight missing patches and pinpoint
the exact IDS signature to apply as the compensating control.
Users with a Broadcom support account can log into the vTIS Portal to search for specific vulnerabilities and view
available IDPS signatures for protection.
Broadcom 1743

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Parallel Operation with Traditional Patching
Typically, identification of a missing patch kicks off a lengthy process of testing and negotiating for an outage window,
which historically takes several days or even weeks. As a parallel effort, a compensating control like Distributed Virtual
Patching allows the Distributed IDS to protect against the exploit immediately — without touching or modifying the running
virtual machine or its operating system.

Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
The Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats blueprint outlines how to secure your VCF private cloud across
different risk areas to defend against AI-driven threats.
Frontier AI Threat Overview
Frontier AI models accelerate innovation, software development, and operational efficiency, but they also allow attackers
to take advantage of vulnerabilities almost instantly.
Modern frontier AI models have a deep understanding of software systems, networking protocols, and cryptographic
constructs. They can identify known vulnerabilities across vast codebases, chaining disparate flaws together and
discovering complex Day-0 vulnerabilities in legacy systems without human instruction.
Securing VCF requires a secure-by-design, resilient platform baseline that systematically minimizes the exposed attack
surface.
Consider the implementing the following end-to-end security measures:
• Enforcing robust user and identity security controls, such as centralized single sign-on, federated multi-factor
authentication, and dynamic least-privilege role management
• Restricting lateral threat movement
• Ensuring rapid, uncorrupted recovery when incidents occur
Frontier AI Impact on the Threat Landscape
The integration of frontier AI into the threat landscape has fundamentally changed the economics and dynamics of
cyberattacks in terms of pace, ease, and the overall scale of cyber incidents.
Pace Reduces vulnerability-to-exploitation timelines from weeks to minutes. AI automates code audits,
vulnerability discovery, and payload creation, making manual patch cycles obsolete.
Human security teams no longer have enough time to manually review security advisories, test patches,
and schedule maintenance windows. Defense mechanisms must now operate continuously and
autonomously to keep pace.
Ease Lowers technical barriers. Entry-level attackers can launch high-sophistication cyberattacks which
previously required elite nation-state offensive teams.
AI transforms the entire kill chain into a unified, automated workflow with the following advantages:
• Reconnaissance and social engineering: Frontier AI models perform automated reconnaissance
in seconds by ingesting leaked databases and public profiles to build detailed target maps, while
crafting context-aware, hyper-personalized spear-phishing lures that perfectly mimic internal executive
communications.
• Chaining vulnerabilities: Frontier AI models combine vulnerabilities in the following way:
– Chain together vulnerabilities in creative ways to run complex attacks.
– Dynamically rewrite malware payloads on the fly, rendering traditional, signature-based antivirus
scanners, and perimeter defenses obsolete.
• Autonomous: Frontier AI agents can work with other malicious agents to carry out automated attacks
without human control.
• Lateral movement: Once inside a boundary, AI agents map internal infrastructure locally, moving
horizontally across virtual networks and escalating privileges. These agents do not need to rely on slow
command-and-control communication channels back to a human operator.
Cyber Incidents AI-assisted cyber threats represent systemic risks to organizations and financial infrastructure. Threat
actors who use automated AI can find vulnerabilities, bypass legacy controls, and access sensitive
enterprise data before detection teams can analyze the incoming alert.
Risk-Based Security Posture Assessment
The desired security posture of a VCF environment depends on the risk profile of your organization, workload placement,
and the workload itself. Consider the following items:
Broadcom 1745

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Likelihood of Initial Also known as the "front door" risk. Determining the right security baseline begins with analyzing the
Exploit Execution probability of initial exploitation. This dimension assesses exposure to threat actors, attack surface,
and the accessibility of management and workload boundaries. Environments that host public-facing
endpoints, demilitarized zones (DMZs), or Internet-accessible container services have a higher risk of initial
compromise compared to isolated corporate networks. Mitigating exploitation risk requires preventative
controls across the user security and platform security pillars. Organizations must reduce the exposed
attack surface through the following measures:
• Strict identity federation
• Mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA)
• Timely patching cycles
• Continuous configuration drift monitoring to ensure that vulnerabilities are fixed before threat actors can
exploit them
The Blast Radius of an Also known as the "impact" risk. You must determine the potential extent of operational, financial, and
Exploit reputational damage if an exploit breaches the perimeter. If an attacker can move laterally across the
infrastructure or access sensitive data, a single compromised entry point can result in catastrophic failure
even in low-risk environments. Addressing blast radius risk requires defense-in-depth mechanisms that
consider lateral security and application security.
Organizations must also consider the effort that is required to recover from a potential incident.
Organizations can contain threat actors to a single isolated segment and prevent lateral movement by
implementing micro-segmentation, zero-trust network boundaries, and strict multi-tenant isolation policies.
Organizations can recover quickly from cyber incidents by implementing immutable recovery cleanrooms.
Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Exploits
You can transition from reactive patch management to an automated, continuous security posture that handles the speed
and scale of frontier AI-era threats. Organizations must consider a risk-based security posture assessment across the
following five critical areas:
• People and Process for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
• User Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
• Platform Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
• Lateral Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
• Application Security and Recovery for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
People and Process for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
Establish operational rigor, rapid incident response, and predictable lifecycle governance in your VCF private cloud.
The strength of any technical architecture is related to the operational practices of the team managing it. This pillar
evaluates organizational readiness, patch cadence, and lifecycle strategies. A high-maturity posture requires moving away
from reactive "don't fix unless broken" mentalities toward standardized Service Level Agreements (SLAs), particularly
for VMware Security Advisories (VMSAs). Establishing dedicated rapid response teams, formal incident protocols, and
continuous vulnerability assessment schedules ensures that modern security baselines are maintained and operational
drift is caught early.

User Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
Enforce zero-trust identity controls, strict perimeter isolation, and immutable auditability in your VCF private cloud.
User security protects the VCF management plane by restricting administrative privileges across the fabric. It removes
identity fragmentation through centralized authentication with federated enterprise identity providers. Access is strictly
controlled by using mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) and granular role-based access controls (RBAC). Also,
it manages SSL/TLS certificate lifecycles and uses dynamic privileged access management (PAM) vaulting for service
accounts. Centralized, encrypted audit logs ensure complete traceability for all administrative actions across the cloud
environment.

Platform Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
Harden core infrastructure, enforce cryptographic standards, and eliminate configuration drift in your VCF private cloud.
Platform security forms the baseline defense for physical hosts, hypervisors, and storage fabrics. Automated alignment
with VMware Security Configuration Guides (SCG) and compliance frameworks, such as PCI-DSS, FIPS, and DISA
STIG, provides secure operations. Data security is provided both in transit (mandatory vMotion and cluster replication
encryption) and at rest (AES storage encryption with automated key rotation). Hardware-rooted trust, such as Trusted
Platform Module (TPM) 2.0 remote attestation and UEFI Secure Boot and using non-disruptive ESX live patching enables
continuously hardened infrastructure without sacrificing availability.

Lateral Security for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
Contain lateral threat movement using deep East-West network visibility and micro-segmentation in your VCF private
cloud.
Traditional perimeter firewalls are insufficient once a breach occurs within internal network boundaries. Lateral Security
mitigates the blast radius by enforcing distributed, zero-trust network policies down to the individual Virtual Machine or
container pod. Using deep East-West traffic inspection, Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS), and Network
Detection and Response (NDR), this pillar restricts unauthorized communication between workloads and sensitive shared

Application Security and Recovery for Securing VCF Against Frontier AI Era Threats
Safeguard containerized and virtualized workloads while ensuring automated ransomware resilience in your VCF private
cloud.
Application security and recovery is the final line of defense focuses on workload-level hardening and rapid operational
restoration following a cyber incident. This pillar handles continuous CVE vulnerability management across guest OS
and container runtimes, which is coupled with desired-state compliance enforcement. Automation provides an isolated
cleanroom recovery orchestration in case of a destructive attack or ransomware incident. Immutable snapshots, Next-
Gen antivirus (NGAV) fileless malware validation in isolated environments, and unified recovery workflows, enable
organizations to minimize Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and restore as trusted state with confidence.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Automation enables the modern private cloud. Playing a crucial role in both single-tenancy and multi-tenancy
scenarios by providing a unified platform for designing a modern private cloud platform with VMware Cloud Foundation.
Modern private cloud platform from the service provider perspective:
• Single tenancy: service providers offer dedicated private cloud environments to customers who require strong isolation,
compliance, or specific performance guarantees.
• Multi-tenancy: service providers use multi-tenancy to deliver cost-effective, shared cloud services to a broader
customer base.
Modern private cloud platform from the Enterprise perspective:
• Single tenancy: an enterprise using a single organization to isolate sensitive workloads, critical applications, or different
business units with specific requirements.
• Multi-tenancy: an enterprise using multiple organizations to completely segregate internal IT infrastructure to improve
efficiency, maintain strict security, and simplify management of less critical applications.
This design section is intended to guide both enterprise and service providers in designing and deploying a modern
private cloud with VCF Automation tailored to their organizational needs.
• Simple VCF Automation Model
• High Availability VCF Automation Model
Simple VCF Automation Model
The Simple VCF Automation Model consists of a single node that is deployed in a vSphere cluster. Availability is provided
by the native vSphere HA functionality within the vSphere cluster.

High Availability VCF Automation Model
The High Availability VCF Automation Model consists of a three-node deployment. This model provides resiliency at both
the application level through the clustered deployment and at the vSphere cluster level through vSphere HA and vSphere
DRS functionality.
The high availability discussion in this section focuses on the VCF Automation appliance level. For discussions on high
availability design for components supporting VCF Automation, see the following:
• vSphere Clusters - See vSphere Cluster Detailed Design for more details.
• vSphere Supervisor deployments - See vSphere Supervisor Detailed Design for more details.
• NSX Edges - See NSX Edge Cluster Detailed Design for more details.

VCF Automation Deployment Patterns
This section explains different deployment patterns of VCF Automation within VMware Cloud Foundation single and multi-
domain architectures.
• Deployment Pattern 1: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with Single Domain and Multiple Clusters
• Deployment Pattern 2: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with Multiple Domains
• Deployment Pattern 3: External-Facing Deployment of VCF Automation
Deployment Pattern 1: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with Single Domain and Multiple Clusters
VCF Automation is deployed in a management domain and organization workloads are placed in a different vSphere
cluster of the same management domain.
This deployment pattern separates the management and compute resources into two vSphere clusters in a single domain.
The management domain hosts the core management components of VCF. In this deployment pattern, different subnets
are used for various traffic types, ensuring security and performance. A transit gateway is used to connect upstream
network and it serves as a high-level network routing hub, linking multiple subnets, and networks across the architecture.
The vSphere cluster that hosts the organization workloads has NSX VPC configured and vSphere Supervisor enabled to
consume a modern private cloud with VCF Automation.
This deployment pattern:
• Enables high availability through the deployment of multiple instances of components to provide redundancy and
ensure reliability.
• Supports the use of either centralized gateway (CTGW) or decentralized gateway (DTGW) architectures.
Benefits Drawbacks
• Fast deployment. • Limited scalability compared to a multiple domain architecture.
• Simplified integrated management. • Management Overhead to manage each VCF Instance for a
• Dedicated VCF Instance for a tenant or a line of business. dedicated tenant.
• Near-edge deployments smaller environments and no plan of • VCF Automation HA deployment consumes more
growth. infrastructure resources.
• Smaller hardware footprint.
• VCF Automation HA is an option.

Deployment Pattern 3: External-Facing Deployment of VCF Automation
External-Facing Deployment of VCF Automation refers to implementing VCF Automation to seamlessly interact with
external networks or services in a secure manner.
This deployment pattern helps to minimize the attack surface, contain potential security breaches, and provides the
necessary controls for meeting various security and compliance standards for VCF Automation.
Broadcom 1765

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The DMZ VPC accommodates external facing services (like load balancers) and serves as a security barrier between the
Internet and the internal application network. To provide an additional layer of network isolation, this deployment pattern
also uses a second VPC for the VCF Automation instances. The Transit Gateway routes traffic between the two VPCs and
to the upstream network, enabling safe channels of communication.
The Tier-0 Gateway provides north and south routing as well as stateful firewall features. This offers a reliable and secure
design for hosting VCF Automation that is accessible over the Internet. Provider Admin can apply east/west firewall on the
Mgmt App VPC to protect access to VCF Automation appliances and limit lateral movement.
Drawbacks
Benefits
• Easier to manage and update one set of VCF Automation • Needs robust security (e.g., firewalls, WAF, and API security in
appliances. Reduces operational overhead. place).
• Limits lateral movement and isolates external-facing services • Load balancer misconfigurations could cause downtime or
from core management and workloads. abnormal traffic routing.
• Micro-segmentation approach securely exposes services • Adds network complexity; managing routing, firewall rules,
through DMZ network and Load Balancer for strong protection and subnet allocations needs careful planning for each
• Distributes traffic efficiently across multiple automation organization or tenants.
appliance instances for scale and availability.

Network Design Options for VCF Automation Instance Deployment
VMware Cloud Foundation provides flexibility in network segment design for a VCF private cloud. VCF Automation
supports two basic network designs.
Network Design Options for VCF Automation
VCF Automation supports two network design models:
1. Shared Subnet Model - VCF Automation resides on the same subnet as the other VCF fleet components.
2. Dedicated Subnet Model - VCF Automation resides on a dedicated subnet separate from the other VCF fleet
components.
Shared Subnet Design
The Shared Subnet Model focuses on VCF Automation residing on the same subnet as the other VCF fleet components.
For this model, refer to the VCF Management Network Detailed Design section of this guide.
This model applies to:
•
Deployment Pattern 1: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with Single Domain and Multiple Clusters
• Deployment Pattern 2: VCF Automation in a VCF Instance with Multiple Domains
Dedicated Subnet Design
The Dedicated Subnet Model is used where there is a requirement to place VCF Automation on a dedicated subnet in
parallel to the subnet for the other VCF fleet components. Most commonly this design is used where VCF Automation
must be placed in a DMZ (demilitarized zone).
This model applies to Deployment Pattern 3: External-Facing Deployment of VCF Automation.

Tenancy Deployment Models
This section describes how different tenancy models relate to the VCF fleet and VCF domain concepts, which impacts
how tenants are provisioned and managed within a private cloud environment. Businesses can select a deployment model
(or models) based on operational flexibility, compliance needs, and scalability requirements.
• Tenancy Deployment Model 1: Consolidated Management and Organization Workloads in a VCF Instance
• Tenancy Deployment Model 2: Shared Workload Domain for Multiple Organizations in a VCF Instance
• Tenancy Deployment Model 3: Centralized Management with Dedicated Workload Domains per Organization in a VCF
Instance
• Tenancy Deployment Model 4: Centralized VCF Automation Managing Dedicated VCF Instances per Organization
• Tenancy Deployment Model 5: Dedicated VCF Fleet with Independent VCF Automation Supporting Single or Multiple
Domains per Tenant
Tenancy Deployment Model 1: Consolidated Management and Organization Workloads in a VCF
Instance
This tenancy deployment model consists of one VCF domain that hosts the management components and organization
workloads.
Management components and workloads can share one vSphere cluster, or can be deployed on different vSphere
clusters.
When adopting this model, carefully evaluate the potential implications, including resource contention, performance
impact, security risks, and reduced availability that may arise from hosting organization workloads within the same cluster
as management components.

This section focuses the organizational (tenant) layer within VCF Automation. How resources are consumed by
administrators and end users through an organization.
