Understanding VCF Automation All Apps Organization Multi Tenancy Model
The All Apps Organizations are the primary multi-tenancy model within VCF Automation. All Apps Organizations uses
vSphere Namespaces within vSphere Supervisor (Supervisors) to abstract tenant users and groups from the underlying
vSphere and NSX infrastructure.
This Supervisor-based model:
• Completely isolates resources between All Apps Organizations.
• Within an All Apps Organization, allows for further isolation at the Project and vSphere Namespace levels.
• Controls user access to the resources.
The resulting Supervisor-based command and control model
• Completely removes the need for direct infrastructure access via individual tenant or service accounts.
• Removes potential security concerns that are created by the service account access models.
Remember:
The resources defined by a vSphere Namespace include: compute, memory, storage, and network resources
(network defined through VPCs).
The new structure guarantees tenant visibility to assigned infrastructure (vSphere Namespace) while protecting tenant
A from impacting tenant B. Total isolation is assured by the vSphere Namespace boundary between tenants working in
concert with the NSX Project boundary (for networking). Thus providing a modern, true cloud experience with secure
multi-tenancy for VCF Automation customers.
Broadcom 1776

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Implementing the All Apps Organization model within VCF Automation requires a few underlying components:
VCF Automation Structure Details
Organization • A top-level entity that is used to group and manage resources, users, policies, IaaS services,
and catalog entities, while maintaining a secure boundary from other organizations.
• Can be defined as a department or a line of business within an enterprise or a tenant or
customer for a service provider
• Offers a centralized structure for billing, access control, and resource sharing, facilitating
collaboration and governance across teams, departments.
• Maps to one or more Supervisor Clusters through Region Quota to provide the resources
(compute, memory, storage, and networking) available for assignment within vSphere
Namespaces.
vSphere Supervisor • A Supervisor is a capability that turns vSphere into a platform that can host multiple IaaS
services.
• Supervisor defines the scope of vSphere IaaS control plane on vCenter.
• A supervisor is a collection of one or more clusters on a vCenter instance and can span across
multiple zones for fault tolerance.vSphere Supervisor is a management plane for Infrastructure-
as-a-Service.
• Provides compute, memory, and storage resources to an Organization.
• Provides the structure on which vSphere Namespaces are deployed.
• A single Supervisor Cluster can be mapped to multiple organizations through a Region Quota
Region • A region consists of one or more Supervisor-enabled Clusters.
• A region is a collection of compute, memory, storage, and networking resources that can span
across vCenter instances.
Region Quota • A Region Quota is a subset, or allocation, of resources from a region.
• Defines the amount of capacity and the number of availability zones that are made available
from a region to an organization.
• On a per vSphere Zone basis, defines
– CPU limit/reservation
– Memory limit/reservation
– Available VM classes
– Available Storage Classes (also defines storage limits
Project • Resides within an organization
• There can be many projects within a single organization
• Manage users & resources at scale using projects
– Add users or groups to projects to give them access to IaaS services,
– Add catalog items to be shared with the project.
• Provide approvals and automate resource reclamation using project policies.
• Govern total allocated resources and access to VM and storage classes using vSphere
Namespaces in projects.
vSphere Namespace • Resides within a Project.
• There can be many vSphere Namespaces within a single Project.
• Defines resource limits for CPU, memory, and storage for workloads.
• Assigns available networks to workloads.
• vSphere Namespaces are bound to the scope of the project with which they are associated.
vSphere Namespace Class • Reusable templates for defining guardrails on parameters that are used during vSphere
Namespace creation.
• Defines at the vSphere Namespace level
– CPU limit/reservation
– Memory limit/reservation
– Available Storage Classes (also defines storage limits)
– VM classes available
– Content Libraries
VPC • A set of networking resources that provide a public-cloud experience to VCF customers.
• Can be assigned to one or many vSphere Namespaces within an Organization.
Broadcom 1777

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Automation Structure Details
Workload • Virtual machine or containers that are deployed within a vSphere Namespace.
• The number of workloads that are deployed in an organization is constrained by
– The overall amount of resources assigned via Region Quota
– The amount of resources that are then allocated to a particular vSphere Namespace
During All Apps Organization creation,
• All Apps Organizations are mapped to one or more vSphere Supervisors through Regions.
• Each organization then holds one or more projects.
• Each project then holds one or more vSphere Namespaces.
• vSphere Namespaces are instantiated within vSphere Supervisors that are mapped to the Organization.
Traditional virtual machine or VMware Kubernetes Service-based container workloads are then deployed utilizing the
Supervisor Cluster resources defined within vSphere Namespaces.
Broadcom 1778

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Provider Consumption Organization
The Provider Consumption Organization (PCO) is a special purpose All Apps Organization that is used by the provider
persona (the Provider or Enterprise-level admin)
Provider Consumption Organization allows you to:
• Consume their own resources
• Publish blueprints and catalog items to other Organizations
• Run published workflows from the embedded VCF Operations Orchestrator
Important:
The PCO is largely identical to all other All Apps Organizations. The primary difference is a special privilege
allowing the PCO to publish catalog items to other Organizations.
The publishing permissions do not change the management structure of the other Organization. This means that the PCO
cannot perform any resource management for other Organizations.

separately from the system level

Provider Admin vs Organization Admin
Broadcom 1779

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Providers vs Organization
VCF Automation introduces a multi-tenancy model that is based on a vSphere Supervisor running as a management
plane for all IaaS services including both VMs and containers.
• Controls access via vSphere Namespaces within the Supervisor Cluster
• Completely removes the need for direct infrastructure access by tenants
• Provides complete isolation between tenants and limits each tenant to only view their own environment
The organizational model is separated into two primary levels - Provider and Organization or Tenant. An additional
layer of separation exists within a tenant: Projects (which are covered in the Understanding VCF Automation All Apps
Organization Multi Tenancy Model section).
• Provider Administrators are responsible for
– The underlying infrastructure
– Allocating and assigning infrastructure resources to tenants.
• Organization Administrators
– Consume from their assigned resources and allocate them to different projects within their organization through
vSphere Namespaces
– Control over cross-project networking by managing Transit Gateways that can interconnect multiple VPCs, and their
upstream connectivity
– Also manages identity and access within the tenant
Figure 252: VCF Automation Organizational model
A graphical representation of the Provider and Tenant capabilities

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Understanding Supervisors, Regions, vSphere Zones, vSphere Namespaces, & Classes
The Supervisor is the component that owns the physical infrastructure and runs the organization workloads on those
resources. A region is a collection of one or more Supervisors that share a common NSX Local Manager. A vSphere
Zone is how the Supervisor maps to resources within a vSphere cluster. A supervisor can have multiple vSphere Zones.
Supervisors and vSphere Zones are defined in vCenter.
Supervisors and their vSphere Zones are assigned into Regions by the Provider. vSphere Namespaces are created within
a Project by the organization administrator using the resources that are allocated to the organization through Region
Quotas. vSphere Namespaces are defined using a vSphere Namespace class. vSphere Namespace classes define the
CPU, memory, and storage resource limits and reservations and Content Library assignments for a vSphere Namespace.
Each organization includes three default vSphere Namespace classes (small, medium, and large). Organization
administrators can customize the default vSphere Namespace classes or can define new ones as necessary.

Understanding Content Libraries
Content libraries are centralized repositories of VM images, like OVA, OVF, and ISO images, and scripts that are used to

management.

Understanding Organizations and Projects
Organization and projects are the top-level objects that are used to define isolated sets of users and resources. An
organization is fully isolated from other organizations, with separation at the resource, network, and identity layers.
One organization has no knowledge of any other organizations. Typically used when multiple separate entities share a
common infrastructure either with:
• A services provider model.
or
• A centralized corporate IT department providing resources with self-service workload deployment and billing to
different business units within the broader organization.
Within an organization, there is further grouping possible.
• Projects are the structures wherein vSphere Namespaces are created and access control to the resources within the
vSphere Namespaces is defined.
• Compute, storage, and network resources are defined independently for each vSphere Namespace.
• VPCs can be shared or dedicated as needed between any projects and/or vSphere Namespace within the
organization.
These separations help reduce the need for requests to central infrastructure teams (Provider and Infrastructure
Managers) and moving the operations closer to the consumers of the service.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Each Organization has a dedicated NSX project that is created when the provider creates the Region Network
Configuration. Providing each Organization their own Transit Gateway and IP block allocation which they can carve up
into VPCs and subnets to deploy different workloads.

Understanding Workload Networking within VCF Automation
VCF Automation uses the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Network Virtualization Model for workload networking. Specifically,
either the:
• Centralized Connectivity Model
or
• Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model
For detailed information on both, refer to the Workload Networking Detailed Designs section of this document.
Important:
When using VCF Automation Organizations for All Apps, administrators perform all workload network
configuration with the VCF Automation Provider or Organization Portals.
Do not configure any workload networks (VPCs) targeted for VCF Automation consumption outside of VCF
Automation.
VCF Automation defines workload networks at two levels:
Provider-level Networking Components
• Pertains to the functions managed within the Provider Portal
• Defines external connectivity - External IP Blocks, External Connections, VLAN-backed subnets
• Assigns external connectivity to organizations
Broadcom 1786

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Defined default private TGW and private VPC ip blocks assigned to organizations
Provider Level Networking
Definition
Component
External IP Blocks • Previously called IP Spaces, used to centrally manage IP addressing for organizations.
• External IP blocks are associated with external connections. Subject to quotas,
organizations can allocate individual IPs (for NAT and load-balancing use-cases).
• Organizations can also create subnets from these blocks for direct workload connectivity
without NAT
External Connections • External Connections define how organizations' NSX Transit Gateways (TGW) can be
connected to outside networks.
• Either centralized or distributed VLAN connections.
• An External Connection also associates provider-managed External IP Block with
organizations.
Centralized Connections • A type of External Connection.
• Define external network connectivity via NSX Tier-0 or Tier-0 VRF.
• Provides connectivity to designated Remote Networks and facilitates the advertisement of
Subnets and IPs originating from IP Blocks associated with this connection.
• Can connect to the default gateway if 0.0.0.0/0 is used rather than a specific Remote
Network.
• Enables a full set of stateful networking services within organizations, such as NAT, Load-
balancing, IPsec VPN and Gateway Firewall.
Distributed VLAN Connections • A type of External Connection.
• Define external network connectivity through a VLAN on the physical networking
infrastructure.
• Offer a simplified way to connect organizations' Transit Gateways (TGW) to outside
networks without using an NSX Tier-0 gateway.
Edge Clusters • A logical grouping of transport nodes providing stateful services for VPCs.
• Used with Centralized Connections.
VNA Clusters • A logical grouping of transport nodes providing stateful services for VPCs.
• Used with Distributed VLAN Connections.
Subnets • Create and manage subnets that are extended to a VLAN on a physical networking
infrastructure. Once subnets are shared with an organization, workloads there can be
directly connected to these subnets.
• Ensure the VLAN is available on all network switch ports that connect to hosts within the
region quotas shared with the organization.
Default Private IP Blocks • When an organization is created a default VPC is instantiated to include
– Default Private TGW IP Block
– Default Private VPC IP Block
• Upon installation of VCF Automation, there are initial settings for these IP blocks.
• Are inherited by every organization
• Can be customized for each organization during Regional Network Configuration for an
organization
Organization-level Networking Components
• Pertains to the functions managed within the Organization Portal
• Inherits default network configuration set during organization creation in the Provider Portal
• Define new VPC that is created and managed at the organization level
– Any VPC created at the organzation-level will use the external IP block (or blocks) assigned to the organization
– Will allow the use of an existing connectivity profle and transit gatewat or the create new ones

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Organization-level subnets to be shard with one or more namespaces.

one or more isolated domains of compute resources (vSphere namespace).

• Can be shared with one or more Namespaces.

or spanning multiple Namespaces

Understanding VCF Automation Blueprints and Catalog
Blueprints
Blueprints offer a declarative, YAML-based Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) methodology to facilitate the automated
provisioning of cloud services. The IaC methodology provides significant flexibility in both blueprint definition and how one
creates a blueprint.
Blueprints define the configuration of networks, virtual machines, container architectures, applications, and services
deployed through VCF Automation into a vSphere Namespace. They are used to enforce standards and governance by
using constructs such as vm and storage classes to define cpu, memory, and storage configurations. Blueprint can vary
in complexity. They can be as simple as a single virtual machine or as complex as a design with multiple VMs, networks,
services, and other components.
Attention:
You can capture the contents of an existing VCF Automation deployed vSphere Namespace as a reusable
blueprint. The resulting blueprint captures the entire configuration of the vSphere Namespace.
Organization administrators or project administrators have a few methods of blueprint creation:
Broadcom 1790

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Blueprint Creation Method Use Cases/Caveats
Organization Portal Blueprint Design • Manual blueprint creation.
Page • Editing existing blueprints.
Capture a vSphere Namespace as a • Without the need to manually, define or export infrastructure details, can be used to
blueprint enable
– Rapid environment cloning
– Migration
– Recovery
• An alternative to traditional, manually authored VCF Automation blueprints and provide a
way to create reusable deployments directly from existing workloads.
• Used to deploy identical or differentiated environments from the same blueprint.
• Suitable for use in:
– Hands-on labs
– Training environment
– Similar scenarios where reusable, preconfigured environments are required.
• After creation, can be edited using the Blueprint Design page.
Important:
To use a blueprint, it must be associated with one or more projects and published to the VCF Automation Catalog.
VCF Automation Catalog
The VCF Automation catalog is the streamlined user interface that you use to request and deploy infrastructure on a self-
service basis. Catalog items include VCF Automation blueprints, VM images, storage, networks, and so on, that you can
request for deployment. The items that are available to you depend on your project membership. At request time, the
information that you must provide depends on how the item was configured by your administrator. When you deploy an
item, it is provisioned based on the infrastructure available to the selected project. Projects also determine your options at
deployment time.
Multi-Tenancy Consumption Patterns
This section describes the Multi-Tenancy Consumption Patterns aligned with the Tenancy Deployment Model described
in the Tenancy Deployment Model section. It explains the different ways multiple organizations or tenants can consume
shared compute, memory, storage, and networking resources, depending on the chosen Tenancy Deployment Model.
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 1: Resource Isolation with Single VPC for Multiple Businesses in One Supervisor
Zone
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 2: Resource Isolation with Multiple VPCs for Multiple Lines of Business in One
Supervisor Zone
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 3: Resource Isolation with Single VPC for Multiple Lines of Business in Three
Supervisor Zones
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 4: Resource Isolation for Multiple Organizations with dedicated VRFs or Transit
Gateways (TGW)
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 5: Multi-Region, Multi-Tenant Resource Isolation with Dedicated and Shared
Gateways
• Multi-Tenancy Consumption Pattern 6: Multi-Organization resource isolation with shared NSX across workload
domains
• Bimodal Consumption Design for VM Apps and All Apps Workloads

This consumption pattern prioritizes cost optimization and simplified management over strict tenant isolation.

Bimodal Consumption Design for VM Apps and All Apps Workloads
VCF Automation with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 introduces a key capability that enables a bimodal consumption
model for VM App and All App organizations. This enhancement allows both organizations to share a common vCenter
Server and NSX instance, improving resource utilization and reducing operational overhead for selected deployment
topologies.
Important:
Design Recommendation: Although this capability enables shared consumption between VM App and All App
organizations within a common VMware vCenter and NSX environment, the primary intent of this enhancement is
to provide an easier transition path for existing VMware Aria Automation customers moving to VCF Automation.
This allows organizations to continue supporting traditional VM-based consumption models while progressively
adopting the modern All App consumption model side by side. For net-new greenfield environments without
existing Aria Automation operational dependencies, the recommended approach is to adopt the VCF Automation
All App consumption model from the start to align with the long-term cloud operating model and platform
architecture direction.
In this model, an Organization for All Apps and an Organization for VM Apps operate on shared infrastructure while
remaining logically isolated through policy, networking, and access controls. This enables traditional VM-based workloads
and modern application platforms to coexist efficiently within the same environment.
Prior to VCF 9.1, each organization typically required a dedicated workload domain, including its own vCenter and
NSX instances, leading to higher infrastructure footprint. VCF Automation 9.1 addresses this by enabling a shared
infrastructure approach, which is activated through the feature flag configuration setting: “Mixed Tenancy Mode”
This capability provides greater flexibility in how infrastructure is consumed, supporting both consolidated (shared) and
isolated (dedicated) deployment models based on workload and organizational requirements.
1. Shared Cluster Deployment: Both All App and VM App organizations can deploy their respective workloads and
services onto the same vSphere Cluster that is managed by the single vCenter.
2. Isolated Cluster Deployment: Alternatively, the organizations can deploy to different vSphere clusters (e.g., Cluster A
for VM App, Cluster B for All App) that are still managed by the same shared vCenter.
3. VM App workload deployment across VCF Fleets - VM App-based workloads can be deployed and managed
across multiple VCF Fleet or workload domains, enabling centralized governance with distributed execution for scale
and locality.
The unified management plane allows the organizations to effectively utilize shared physical and virtual resources (e.g.,
compute, storage, networking) while streamlining operational tasks such as monitoring and patching that need only be
performed on the single shared vCenter and NSX Local Manager pair.
A shared deployment serves as an ideal bridge for organizations looking to strategically transition from an existing Aria
Automation environment to the modern, expanded capabilities of VCF Automation Organization for All Apps. Rather than
executing immediate migration, the organization can:
• Co-exist: Run existing workloads and consumption models in the VCF VM Apps organization.
• Pilot: Gradually introduce new services, modern application development teams, or specific workloads into the VCF
Automation All Apps organization.
• Migrate: Systematically move eligible workloads and users from the Organization for VM Apps to the Organization
for All Apps over time, ensuring business continuity and allowing teams to adjust to the new platform capabilities at a
manageable pace.
This phased approach minimizes risk, maximizes return on existing investments, and ensures a smoother, more controlled
adoption of the full VCF Automation with VMware Cloud Foundation.
Attention:
Whenever the Organization types share a vCenter and NSX Local Manager pair, the Organization for VM
Apps must be created before the Organization for All Apps. The Organization for VM Apps must be configured
(including mapping the vCenter and NSX Manager cloud accounts) before a VCF Automation Region is
configured using the same vCenter and NSX Manager).
Broadcom 1809

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
During the upgrade from a legacy Aria Automation to VCF Automation, the legacy environment is converted to an
Organization for VM Apps. The converted Organization for VM Apps will be the first Organization deployed in the
new VCF Automation instance.

VM App and All App Deployments on a Single Cluster Within a Shared vCenter
Broadcom 1810

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This design enables both VM-based workloads (VM App) and modern platform services (All App) to be deployed on
a shared vSphere cluster managed by a single vCenter, optimizing resource utilization and simplifying infrastructure
operations. By consolidating workloads onto a common cluster, organizations benefit from reduced management
overhead, consistent policy enforcement, and improved capacity efficiency. This model is well suited for environments
prioritizing operational simplicity and cost efficiency, while still supporting a diverse mix of traditional and cloud-native
workloads.
Figure 264: Design #2 VM App and All App Deployments on Separate Clusters Within a Shared vCenter
VM App and All App Deployments on Separate Clusters Within a Shared vCenter.
This design separates VM-based applications (VM App) and modern platform services (All App) into dedicated vSphere
clusters while still operating under a single shared vCenter. By isolating workloads at the cluster level, organizations
gain stronger performance boundaries, improved resource predictability, and clearer operational ownership for different
workload types. This approach is particularly valuable for environments with differing SLAs, security requirements,
or lifecycle needs between traditional and cloud-native applications. At the same time, the shared vCenter maintains
centralized management, consistent governance, and simplified operations across clusters, enabling a balance between
isolation and operational efficiency.
Figure 265: Design #3 VM App Workload Deployment Across Multi-Fleet VCF Environments
VM App Workload Deployment Across Multi-Fleet VCF Environments
Broadcom 1811

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This design enables VM-based applications (VM Apps) to be deployed and managed across multiple VCF Fleet or
workload domains (in a multi fleet environment), providing flexibility to scale workloads beyond a single environment.
It supports centralized governance and consistent policy enforcement while allowing workloads to run closer to users,
data sources, or specific regions. This approach is well suited for organizations operating in multi-region or distributed
environments, where workload portability, resiliency, and geographic alignment are critical.
Important:
The multi-fleet workload design only supports the Organization for VM Apps consumption model. It does not
work with the Organization for All Apps model.

Design Context
This architecture illustrates a transitional adoption model for organizations migrating from existing VMware Aria
Automation environments to VMware Cloud Foundation with VCF Automation while preserving existing workload
operations and enabling gradual adoption of modern application consumption models.
In these scenarios, organizations may already operate existing Aria Automation environments using either:
• traditional VLAN-backed networking through a VDS-based architecture
• or existing NSX-backed networking and segment-based workload connectivity models
Following the transition to VCF Automation:
• existing workloads continue operating on their current networking and infrastructure constructs
• existing VLAN-backed or NSX-backed networking configurations remain unchanged
• existing workloads continue to be consumed through the VM App organization model
• operational disruption to existing workloads, routing models, firewall policies, and application connectivity is minimized
This design enables organizations to preserve existing operational and networking models while incrementally introducing
modern platform consumption capabilities through the VCF Automation All App model.
Transitional Bimodal Consumption Model
This architecture demonstrates how organizations can operate both:
Broadcom 1814

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• traditional VM-centric consumption models
• modern application-centric consumption models
Using the VCF Automation bimodal consumption model, organizations can simultaneously support:
Consumption Model Purpose
Supports traditional VM-based workloads operating on existing
VM App Organization
VLAN-backed or NSX-backed networking models
Supports modern platform consumption models for services such
as VM Service, VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, Database
All App Organization
Services Manager (DSM), and modern application workloads
using VPC-based networking
This allows organizations to modernize incrementally without requiring immediate migration of existing workloads into new
networking or operational constructs.
Network Architecture Transition Model
A key focus of this architecture is demonstrating how networking evolves during the transition from traditional
infrastructure consumption models toward modern VPC-based application consumption models.
Existing VM App Workloads
Existing workloads continue operating on:
• existing VDS-backed VLAN networking architectures
• or existing NSX segment-based networking architectures
• existing Layer 2 and Layer 3 routing constructs
• existing workload IP addressing and operational models
This allows organizations to preserve:
• existing firewall and security policies
• routing dependencies
• VLAN or NSX segment operational models
• existing operational tooling and processes
New All App Workloads
Modern workloads introduced through the All App consumption model operate using:
• VPC-based networking
• Supervisor-enabled infrastructure
• modern application platform constructs
• tenant-aware networking and workload isolation models
This requires enabling a vSphere Supervisor cluster either:
• on the existing cluster (if sufficient capacity exists)
• or on a newly deployed cluster operating alongside existing workloads within the same vCenter environment
The architecture also demonstrates how modern VPC-based networking environments can coexist alongside existing
VLAN-backed or NSX-backed networking environments during the transition period.
Shared Infrastructure Model
Using the VCF Automation bimodal architecture introduced in VCF 9.1, both VM App and All App consumption models
can share:
• the same VMware vCenter
• the same NSX environment
This enables organizations to modernize application consumption models without requiring completely separate workload
domains for traditional and modern workloads.

VCF Automation Identity and Access Management Design
As part of the VCF Automation, you configure authentication to grant user access and provide granular control of
resources.
VCF Automation contains two persona levels. The provider persona manages the core infrastructure and the tenant / line-
of-business (LOB) persona manages the individual tenants within that infrastructure. Each of these personas has different
authentication options.
VCF Automation Personas Capabilities
Provider • Installs and manages core VCF Automation infrastructure.
• Provider / Enterprise-level administrative functions.
• Manages shared content libraries published to organizations.
• Creates organizations, assigns resource quotas, regional networking, and first tenant
user.
Tenant / Line of Business • Manages organizations.
• Creates and manages projects.
• Creates and manages vSphere Namespaces.
• Configures Content Hub.
• Creates blueprints.
• Provides organization-level user management.

VCF Automation Role Base Access Control
Managing multi-tenant cloud environments demands a clearly established role-based access control (RBAC) strategy to
guarantee restricted access, tenant separation, and secure operations.
Table 537: Best Practices for Efficient Role-Based Access Control
Best Practice Recommendation
Principle of Least Privilege Ensure users are granted only the permissions absolutely
necessary for their specific roles, minimizing security risks.
Regular Review & Updates Continuously review and update RBAC assignments to ensure
they align with any changes in user roles and responsibilities.
Logging & Auditing Implement logging and auditing to track user access and actions,
providing transparency and accountability.
User Education Provide ongoing training on the importance of role-based access
and secure credential handling to prevent security breaches.
Integrate Third-Party Solutions for RBAC Optimization Consider using external tools for more streamlined RBAC
management, detailed reporting, and enhanced control.
VCF provides a platform to create and manage secure and multi-tenant environments. Implementing role-based access
control for the management components offers the following benefits.
Broadcom 1822

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 538: Role-Based Access Control Design for Service Providers
Attribute Detail
Separate Administrator roles Establish distinct roles for service provider admins, such as managing
infrastructure, provisioning resources, and troubleshooting tenant issues.
Provider Admin levels To control access to sensitive areas, differentiate roles for basic resource
management, advanced configuration, and network administration.
Multi-Factor Authentication for all privileged accounts Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all privileged accounts,
including both tenant and service provider administrators.
Table 539: Role-Based Access Control Design for Tenants
Attribute Detail
Predefined Tenant Roles Create predefined roles such as tenant user, tenant operator, and tenant
administrator with permissions based on specific needs.
Custom Roles for Granularity Implement custom roles for specific workflows, such as a deployment
engineer, with permissions to deploy templates without managing
infrastructure.
Least Privilege Apply the principle of least privilege to grant only the minimum permissions
needed for each role to perform their tasks effectively.

VCF Operations Orchestrator Design
VCF Operations orchestrator is a workflow automation solution that is designed to simplify the automation of complex IT
tasks.
VCF Operations orchestrator helps improve service delivery efficiency, operational management, and IT agility. VCF
Operations orchestrator is built with an open and flexible architecture that system administrators and IT operations staff
can use to streamline tasks and integrate functions with third-party software through workflows.
Broadcom 1825

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

deployment. Organization

administrator rights) to create workflows that
can be published to Organizations

and publish their own workflows.

and provides access to the external

This design outlines a robust and scalable architecture for deploying VCF Operation orchestrator in a multi-tenant
environment, catering to the distinct needs of multiple organizations in a Cloud Service Provider environment.
VCF Operation Orchestrator Deployment for Multiple Organizations with CTGW Model
Figure 270: VCF Operation Orchestrator Deployment for Multiple Organizations with CTGW Model
VCF Operation Orchestrator Deployment for Multiple Organizations with DTGW Model
Broadcom 1826

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 271: VCF Operation Orchestrator Deployment for Multiple Organizations with DTGW Model
The architecture introduces separate, isolated VCF Operations orchestrator instances for every organization in a CSP
environment (e.g., "Orchestrator for Org-A", "Orchestrator for Org-B"). These organizational VCF Operations orchestrator
instances are each hosted in a logically distinct network segment or a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). These dedicated VCF
Operations orchestrator instances ensure controlled and safe communication by establishing a secure connection to the
centralized VCF management components. Thus enabling any organization to take advantage of the economies of scale
provided by the shared underlying VCF infrastructure. Simultaneously the pattern allows for the use of unique automation
workflows and operational tasks with logical separation and autonomy.
Design Attributes Details
VCF Operations orchestrator Model A dedicated VCF Operations orchestrator instance is deployed for each organization (e.g.,
"Orchestrator for Org-A," "Orchestrator for Org-B").
Network Isolation and Segmentation • Each organization's VCF Operations orchestrator instance resides within its own distinct
Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), providing inherent network isolation (e.g., "Org-A VPC," "Org-
B VPC").
• Specific subnets are allocated within each organizational VPC for the VCF Operations
orchestrator instances (e.g., "Subnet-1" for Org-A, "Subnet-2" for Org-B).
Firewall and Security Enforcement Add-on services such as vDefend can be used to create east-west and north-south firewall
policies to further protect traffic patterns. These policies will control and secure traffic flow
to and from each organization's Orchestrator and its associated workloads, ensuring proper
access control and segmentation.
Provider Admin can apply DFW policies on the NSX Project level in the case of individual
NSX Projects.
Broadcom 1827

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations Orchestrator Rights Bundle within VCF Automation
VCF Automation maintains a specific rights bundle for VCF Operations orchestrator that are known as the "Orchestrator
Rights Bundle." After the VCF Operations orchestrator is deployed and integrated with the target VCF Automation
Organization, the rights needs configuration:
1. From the Provider Portal, publish the Orchestrator Rights Bundle to the target Organization
2. From the Organization Portal, assign the rights to target users and groups
For detailed instructions, refer to the Managing VMware Cloud Foundation Operations Orchestratordocumentation.
VCF Operations Orchestrator for the Provider Consumption Organization
The VCF Automation deployment includes the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator by default.
After the provider admin creates a workflow in the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator, the workflow can be published
to the catalog, either:
• As a catalog item for sole use by the provider admin
• As as catalog item that is available to all Organizations
Any workflow that is built in the PCO then published to all Organizations runs on the embedded VCF Operations
orchestrator, even when run by a user in a non-PCO Organization.
If an Organization wishes to create and publish their own workflows within their Organization, they cannot use of the PCO
embedded VCF Operations orchestrator. The Organization must use an external, dedicated VCF Operations orchestrator
instance.
Chargeback and Billing with VCF Automation
Chargeback is a cost management solution that is designed to help service providers accurately track and distribute
expenses within a private cloud environment. Enabling both providers and tenants to gain insights into resource usage
and ensures fair cost allocation-based on consumption. As a plug-in for tenants, Chargeback provides a metering and
billing interface that simplifies usage tracking, measurement, and invoicing for services delivered through VCF Automation
and VCF Operation.
Chargeback is an essential component of cloud services, particularly for service providers using VMware Cloud
Foundation. Involving assigning the costs of cloud resources and services to the users or departments that actually use
them. This practice is critical for both service providers and tenants, as it creates a transparent and clear method for billing
and payment.
In older versions of VCF, service providers used VMware Cloud Director (VCD) to handle things like pricing, billing, and
dashboards. Starting with VCF 9.x, however, these tasks are managed directly through VCF Automation. This change
likely aims to streamline operations, reduce dependencies on external systems, and provide a more integrated experience
for providers within the VCF platform.
The following figure describes a high-level overview of how Chargeback and Billing are integrated part of VCF Operation.
VCF Operations acts as the central management hub and the starting point for data collection and integration.
Management Packs (MPs):
VCF Operations utilizes Management Packs (MPs) to collect data from specific components. These MPs are like
plugins or modules that enable integration. Management packs shown are the VCF Automation MP and VMware Cloud
Foundation MP (collects vCenter, NSX, and vSAN data). This suggests a direct integration between each MP and its
respective data sources.
Broadcom 1828

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 272: Chargeback Integration with VCF Operations
Key Use Cases:
Flexible Pricing (Rate Cards):
• Service providers need the ability to set their own prices for different resources (like storage, compute, network) based on regions
or quotas. Allowing them to offer tailored pricing plans to their customers.
Accurate Billing (Bills):
• Providers must be able to generate and provide detailed bills to their customers, showing usage and charges for organizations or
specific resource allocations (quotas) in different regions.
Usage Monitoring (Dashboards):
• Providers need ready-to-use dashboards that give them a clear view of how their resources are being used by customers.
Customized Provider Interface (Control Panel and Launchpad):
• Providers need a customized interface (control panel and launchpad) that allows them to manage and configure their services and
Broadcom 1829
resources in a way that suits their specific needs.
High-level Steps to Initiate Billing
1. VCF Fleet is deployed - VCF Operations and VCF Automation are integrated by default
• Both VCF Operations and VCF Automation are deployed as part of the VCF Fleet
• VCF Automation has a one-to-one integration with VCF Operations, meaning that you can only connect one VCF Automation
instance to one VCF Operations instance
• VCF Operations automatically collects data from VCF Automation as well as being able to manage functions such as billing
(this can be verified in VCF Operations under Administrator > Integrations, then confirm that the VCF Automation for All Apps
Organization is collecting data
2. Create and configure an All Apps Organization
• Complete initial Organization creation in the VCF Automation Provider Administrator Portal
• Complete customization of the Organization and deploy any VM or container resources in the VCF Automation Organization
Administrator Portal
3. Create Organization Bill in VCF Operations
• In the VCF Operations UI, navigate to Manage > Cost > Bills
• In the Bills screen,
– Generate a one-time bill
– Schedule a recurring bill
– Note: The bill can be tied to either the Organization or a Region Quota
4. View Organization Bill in VCF Automation
• Log in to the VCF Automation Organization Administrator Portal with Organization Admin or Organization Auditor rights, then
navigate to Administer > Bills to view any bills associate with the Organization
• Note: Organization Users do not have access to billing

A VCF domain can include one or more of the supported vSphere Supervisor Models. The following sections details the
design of each deployment model types for vSphere Supervisor.

Simplified vSphere Supervisor Model
VMware Cloud Foundation allows you to create a Simplified vSphere Supervisor Model requiring fewer resources
and configuration steps than a typical deployment. This simplified deployment allows access to a limited subset of
vSphere Supervisor capabilities. You can then expand the deployment over time to build out to full vSphere Supervisor
functionality.
For information on how to deploy or scale the Simplified vSphere Supervisor Model, refer to Deploying Supervisor with a
Simplified Deployment Flow.
Important:
The Simplified vSphere Supervisor Model is not supported for use by VCF Automation.

vSphere Supervisor Zone Models
vSphere Supervisor management workloads can be deployed to one or three management zones. Workloads in vSphere
namespaces can be deployed to the same or separate dedicated zones to isolate them from management workloads.
This section details the different deployment models to choose from.
• Single Management Zone with Combined Workload Zones Model
• Single Management Zone with Isolated Workload Zones Model
• Three Management Zones with Combined Workload Zones Model
• Three Management Zones with Isolated Workload Zones Model

A Single Management Zone with Combined Workload Zones Model utilizes resources from a single vSphere Zone for
management and workloads. Availability protection is provided using vSphere HA.

VMware Data Services Manager Detailed Design
This section describes the options, requirements, and recommendations to deploy and configure VMware Data Services
Manager.
Architecture
VMware Data Services Manager (DSM) is designed to provide a "Database-as-a-Service" (DBaaS) solution for private
cloud. DSM is delivered as an Advanced Service for VMware Cloud Foundation. DSM simplifies and automates database
lifecycle management for database engines that are deployed in VCF environments: PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Microsoft
SQL Server.
The architecture is built on a central control plane that manages the lifecycle of these data services. DSM provides
centralized provisioning, backup, cloning, patching, scaling, and clustering for database environments. The DSM Virtual
Appliance (or DSM Provider) is deployed as a virtual appliance (OVA). DSM serves as the management control plane
providing an API Gateway & UI interfaces for self service.
VMware Data Services Manager integrates with VMware Cloud Foundation Automation to include databases as part of
a larger application blueprint. VMware Data Services Manager also supports GenAI and RAG applications by applying
PostgreSQL with pgvector for advanced vector search capabilities.

VMware Data Services Attributes
Attribute Detail
Data Services Provider Virtual Deployed as a photon virtual appliance (OVA), it serves as the control plane that coordinates
Appliance the deployment, scaling, and lifecycle of all database instances
Infrastructure Policy Allows vSphere administrators to define and set limits to specific compute, storage, and
network resources that VMware Data Services Manager database workloads can use.
For example, a VCF-A Organization admin creates a "Project" where they attach an
Infrastructure Policy to that project. Developers assigned to that project only see the database
options and resource limits that are defined by that specific policy
Data Services Manager (DSM) Is a software component deployed on VMware Supervisor Cluster, where customers with
Consumption Operator VCF Automation can integrate with DSM APIs
Infrastructure Policy Defines the compute, storage, and networking resources for the database to be deployed,
which the infrastructure administrator defines
Data Service Policy Data Service Polices combines with infrastructure policies to define settings for database
engines such as allowed versions, maintenance, and backup policy. Data Service policies
also offer multi-tenancy by which users/organizations can provision specific database types
and versions.
Database VM A virtual machine that hosts a data service which is requested by the VMware Data Services
Manager user. The Database VM is a Kubernetes node which runs the data service modules.
The Kubernetes nodes are of dual purpose. A single Database VM acts as the control plane
Kubernetes node and a Kubernetes worker node.
Database Topology and Resiliency VMware Data Services Manager supports one Kubernetes node for standalone Database
VMs and three nodes for replicated databases.
• Single-Server Database topology
Infrastructure resiliency is provided vSphere High Availability and underlying storage
redundancy
• Three-Node Database topology and Single vSphere Cluster
This topology includes one primary database, one database-level synchronous replica
and one monitor node. All database nodes share a vSphere Cluster and underlying
shared storage
• Three-Node Database topology and three vSphere Clusters.
This topology includes one primary database, one database-level synchronous replica
and one monitor node. The nodes are distributed in three vSphere clusters, providing
enhanced data durability and availability
Important:
In a three vSphere cluster topology, all vSphere clusters must share a distributed
vSphere switch
Data Services Manager Roles Three personas interact with DSM, each with distinct responsibilities.
• DSM Admin - manages the DSM platform, integrates with vCenter, defines infrastructure
policies, and configures the resource supply.
• Tenant Admin - focuses on VCF Automation, managing resources at that layer.
• Tenant User - application developers or DBAs provision databases through the DSM
portal or API, consuming resources within the guardrails established by the DSM Admin.
Data Services Namespaces Maps users to the infrastructure policies that they can consume.
Broadcom 1854

VMware Data Services Deployment Options
Design Area Options
Appliance Form Factor Data services VM deployment appliance is offered as a single OVA form factor, comprising of:
• 8 vCPUs
• 16-GB memory
• 595-GB virtual disk storage
Appliance Shared Datastore Options Can be deployed on any shared storage that supports vSphere features such as vSphere HA
and vSphere DRS.
Appliance Virtual Disk Formats Options are
• Thin-provisioned
• Thin-provisioned lazy-zeroed
• Thin-provisioned eager-zeroed
The capabilities of the underlying storage determine the virtual disk format.
Appliance Virtual Networking • A Provider VM's Management network can connect to a Standard or vSphere Distributed
Switch port group.
• Database VM workload network can connect to vSphere Distributed Switch port group or
can be assigning to an NSX VPC subnet.
• NSX VPC can be centralized or distributed.
Appliance Subnet Reservation DSM uses two internal networks, Docker networks and Workload cluster networks.
These networks can be customized from defaults and overridden:
• The docker network can be overridden during ovf deploy.
• The workload cluster networks can be overridden by updating the Data Services system
using the API or the DSM console.
VMware Data Services Design Objectives
Design Objective Description
Main Objectives • Provide a self-service platform for database as service in a VCF private cloud
architecture.
• Standardized life-cycle management applied to database workloads,
including.provisioning, backup, cloning, scaling, patching, and upgrades.
VCF Architecture Integration Single VCF instance architecture
• Management domain for control plane component (DSM appliance). See Management
Domain Model
• Workload domain for workload consumption (Database workloads). See Workload
Domain Model
VCF Automation Integration • Enable service catalog blueprints for self-service provisioning.
• Allow for tenant uses to create and consume databases under a Supervisor namespace
using VMware Cloud Foundation Automation.
See VCF Automation Models
Private AI Database support Enable Data service to allow provisioning of PostgreSQL databases to facilitate vector
database integration for generative AI applications. See Private AI Platform Detailed Design
Directory Authentication Authentication support for role-based access control
Backup and Recovery Control Plane and Database to Create multiple database backup locations to segregate
control plane data
• Provider VM backup and recovery with S3-compatible storage
• Database workload backup and recovery with S3 compatible storage
Certificate Management Using and managing trusted Certificates in VMware Data Services Manager
VCF Operations Integration Database Metrics forwarding to VCF Operations, see VCF Operations Detailed Design
Log Management Integration Configure log forwarding to Log management, see High Availability Log Management Model

Workload Connectivity Detailed Design
The workload connectivity models present different tradeoffs between simplicity, performance, service availability, and
scalability. The corresponding design library elements explain the architecture overview, key benefits, limitations, and
specific deployment considerations for each model.
Broadcom 1860

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Workload Connectivity Models
The following workload connectivity models are supported:
• Centralized Connectivity Model - Supports VCF Automation All Apps Orgs, vSphere Supervisor, and all VPC network
and stateful services.
• Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model - Supports VCF Automation All Apps Orgs, vSphere Supervisor, and most VPC
network and stateful services.
• Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 - Supports EVPN-VXLAN fabric integration.
• Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1- Supports EVPN-VXLAN fabric integration and VCF
Automation All Apps Orgs, vSphere Supervisor, and most VPC network and stateful services.
• NSX Segment Connectivity Model - Supports NSX Federation with VM mobility across VCF Instances.
• VLAN Networking Connectivity Model- Legacy connectivity model without the benefits of private cloud network
virtualization.
Centralized Connectivity Model
The Centralized Connectivity Model uses an NSX Edge cluster with Tier-0 gateway to provide VPC-compatible workload
domain with network connectivity established via a Centralized Transit Gateway.
Centralized Connectivity Model Overview
The model uses a primary (Tier-0) gateway configured in Active/Active or Active/Standby model. The Tier-0 gateway HA
mode is independent of the Transit Gateway HA mode, this allows the Tier-0 gateway to have an Active/Active mode
while a Transit Gateway can use Active/Standby. Individual tenants can connect to the Tier-0 gateway through their
own Centralized Transit Gateways (CTGWs). This workload networking model is the base building block to support all
the VCF Automation tenancy models that are described in VCF Automation Provider Tenant Models and Multi-Tenancy
Consumption Patterns. It can also be used in single tenant deployments without the integration with VCF Automation or
for vSphere Supervisor deployments without VCF Automation.
Centralized Connectivity Model Attributes
A Centralized Connectivity Model has the following attributes.

Centralized Connectivity Model with VRF Integration
When tenants need dedicated external network access but dedicated NSX Edge nodes are impractical, NSX VRFs
(Virtual Routing and Forwarding) offer a solution:
• VRFs provide similar capabilities to dedicated Tier-0 Gateways
• Multiple VRFs can share a single edge node with their parent Tier-0 Gateway
• A Centralized Transit Gateway can also have multiple gateway connections, either VRF or Tier-0.
– This can provide different communication paths through different external connections, e.g. Datacenter and Internet.
– Outbound route adveristment of the External IP block and filtering of inbound routes can be used to achieve path
selection for traffic to and from the Transit Gaetway.
• VRF limitations in this topology
Broadcom 1878

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– Gateway firewall and VPN services are restricted to uplink interfaces
VRF Gateways can be shared by multiple tenants. This variation may be desirable when multiple tenants, but not all, need
access to the same set of upstream resources, such as VPNs, private WAN circuits, or VRFs in the physical network.
When all tenants need access to the same upstream resources, a shared Tier-0 gateway is the most appropriate choice.

Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model
The Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model enables easy adoption of VPC network virtualization without requiring NSX
Edge deployment. It uses a Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) that connects via external VLANs in the physical
network fabric, utilizing a distributed forwarding model at the ESX host level.
Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model Overview
This model allows customers to adopt VPC network virtualization with minimal changes to the physical network fabric,
requiring only the addition of at least a single external VLAN. The external VLAN is defined in the physical network
infrastructure through the Distributed External Connection, which also specifies a default gateway for each subnet on that
external VLAN. East-west traffic between workloads is handled by GENEVE-based virtual networking. The Distributed
Transit Gateway is instantiated on each ESX host without requiring NSX Edge nodes, enabling near line rate physical
NIC performance for traffic that does not require stateful network services. vSphere Supervisor, VKS workloads and VCF
Automation All Apps Orgs require load balancing capabilities, this is achieved using either VNA load balancer or AVI Load
Balancer.
Note:
The Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model supports Avi Load Balancer. When only Avi Load Balancer is used, with
no other stateful network services such as Default Outbound NAT (Auto-SNAT) or custom NAT, a VNA cluster
does not need to be deployed, nor do N-S Services need to be enabled. More details, please refer to section Avi
Load Balancer Model.
Note:
Ensure the external VLAN is available on the VDS and pNICs where the host TEPs are connected.

VLAN Backed VPC Connectivity Model
The VLAN Backed VPC Connectivity Model introduced in version 9.1.1 enables easy adoption of VPC network
virtualization without requiring NSX host TEPs. It uses a Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) that connects via external
VLANs in the physical network fabric, utilizing a distributed forwarding model at the ESX host level.
VLAN Backed VPC Connectivity Model Overview
This model allows customers to adopt VPC network virtualization with the least number of changes to the physical
network fabric, requiring one or more external VLAN. The external VLAN is defined in the physical network infrastructure
through the Distributed External Connection, which also specifies a default gateway for each subnet on that external
VLAN. East-west traffic between workloads running on different ESX hosts is handled by the fabric in the VLAN physical
networking. The Distributed Transit Gateway is instantiated on each ESX host without requiring NSX Edge nodes,
enabling near line rate physical NIC performance for traffic that does not require stateful network services. vSphere
Supervisor, VKS workloads and VCF Automation All Apps Orgs require load balancing capabilities, this is achieved using
either VNA Load Balancer or Avi Load Balancer.

Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 integrates NSX with the physical EVPN-VXLAN network
fabric, unifying virtual workloads, and physical endpoints into a single routing domain.
Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 Overview
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 leverages a decoupled Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN control
plane and VXLAN data plane to connect Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) to the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric, with
Distributed Transit Gateways providing connectivity to tenant Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances within the
physical network fabric.
Ethernet VPN (EVPN) is a widely adopted data center technology that serves as the distributed control plane for
the physical network fabric, using BGP to advertise both Layer 2 MAC (not supported in the current EVPN-VXLAN
integration with NSX) and Layer 3 IP reachability across the network. VXLAN acts as the corresponding data plane
encapsulation protocol, the counterpart to the GENEVE protocol used for encapsulation and tunneling within the NSX
overlay environment.
With the Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0, the NSX control plane managed by the NSX Manager
appliances continues to use GENEVE for east-west traffic between ESX hosts, while leveraging VXLAN for north-south
routing with the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric to reach physical endpoints.
Note:
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0, unlike the Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model,
does not require an external VLAN spanning across the Distributed Transit Gateways. Connectivity between each
ESX host and the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric is established through the ESX host VTEP interface.
This Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 supports, for example, Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere
Cluster Model for workloads without compromising rack isolation through a Layer 3 boundary. However, it should
be noted that in VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.0, Active/Standby is the only supported mode for EVPN Route
Controller nodes, requiring Layer 2 adjacency on the Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN interface.
Note:
The ESX VMkernel Tunnel Endpoint (TEP) interface can handle both GENEVE and VXLAN traffic simultaneously.
In this document, TEP (GENEVE) and VTEP (VXLAN) are used interchangeably when referring to ESX hosts.
Egress data plane traffic sourced from a VM connected to a VPC subnet and hosted on an ESX host is forwarded by
the Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) via the ESX TEP interface to the EVPN gateway in the physical EVPN-VXLAN
Broadcom 1897

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
network fabric. The EVPN gateway role is configured either on all spine switches or on a subset of VXLAN leaf switches.
Configuring the EVPN gateway role on all spine switches achieves optimal traffic patterns. The EVPN gateway, often
referred to as the border gateway, must advertise its VTEP IP address as the next-hop to the EVPN Route Controller via
EVPN Route Type 5. This information is then propagated to each individual ESX host, ensuring every ESX host knows the
path to physical endpoints outside the VCF infrastructure by installing one or more default routes pointing to the VTEP IP
address on the EVPN gateway.
Ingress data plane traffic sourced from physical endpoints connected to a VXLAN leaf switch is initially forwarded to
the VTEP of the EVPN gateway using VXLAN encapsulation mapped to the configured Layer 3 VNI. Upon arrival at the
EVPN gateway, full topology visibility is provided by the /32 prefix list for each VM behind each ESX host VTEP, learned
via the EVPN Route Controller through EVPN Route Type 5. The EVPN gateway then forwards the traffic using VXLAN
encapsulation mapped to the same Layer 3 VNI to the ESX host VTEP where the destination VM is located.
Note:
To align Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) in NSX with the VRF tenants in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network
fabric, the Distributed Transit Gateway is mapped through the External Distributed VXLAN Connection to a
corresponding Layer 3 VNI in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric.
The EVPN Route Controller unifies both environments, establishing a common control plane across the virtual and
physical network fabric by peering directly with EVPN gateways using Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN. More details, please refer
to section Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 EVPN Route Controller Overview

Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0 EVPN Route Controller Overview
The EVPN Route Controller establishes a common control plane across the virtual and physical network fabric by peering
directly with EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric using Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN.
Although the EVPN Route Controller is not involved in data plane forwarding, its role is crucial and requires careful
consideration regarding High Availability, including for example, rack fault tolerance with independent storage per node. It
is therefore strongly recommended to deploy the EVPN Route Controller as a two-node Active/Standby cluster, where one
node is active while the other remains on standby. Only the active EVPN Route Controller establishes Multiprotocol BGP-
EVPN sessions with the EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric, while the standby node remains
in cold standby without an established Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN session. The standby node retains all configuration and
BGP routes in its local RIB, but the BGP connection to the EVPN gateway is not established until a failover occurs.
A single EVPN Route Controller cluster is sufficient to support multiple VRFs/tenants, each identified by the Layer 3 VNI
configured in the External Connection. Each External Connection supports only a single Layer 3 VNI, with a strict 1:1
mapping between the External Connection and the Distributed Transit Gateway.
The active EVPN Route Controller advertises a /32 host route for each workload VM, including the VTEP of the ESX
host where the VM is running, to the EVPN gateway in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric via Multiprotocol BGP-
EVPN. These /32 host routes, which represent either public IPs or External IPs (stateless 1:1 NAT), along with the VTEP
information, are carried as EVPN Route Type 5 together with the Layer 3 VNI and Router MAC (RMAC), to identify the
VRF/tenant represented by the Layer 3 VNI configured in the External Connection. The EVPN Route Controller learns this
information about each workload VM, represented as a /32 host route and VTEP, via the regular Central Control Plane
(CCP) channel from the individual ESX hosts through the NSX Manager.
The EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric advertise prefixes from physical endpoints, networks
or a default route to the EVPN Route Controller, including the next-hop information configured on each EVPN gateway.
To minimize the forwarding table on each ESX host where a Distributed Transit Gateway is instantiated, the EVPN Route
Controller advertises only the default route and the EVPN gateway next-hop to each ESX host via NSX Manager through
the Central Control Plane (CCP) channel.
Broadcom 1902

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
Centralized password management via VCF Operations is the only supported option; local credentials cannot
be configured during the EVPN Route Controller node deployment. VCF Operations supports the password
management task 'update', which requires the current password before a new one can be configured. A fresh
EVPN Route Controller node deployment generates randomized passwords, which can be, for example, retrieved
via the SDDC Manager API (GET /v1/credentials) and subsequently used to update the passwords using VCF
Operations.
Note:
The EVPN Route Controller is built on top of the Virtual Network Appliance, and this section applies exclusively
to its use as an EVPN Route Controller. Throughout this section, the term EVPN Route Controller refers to the
EVPN Route Controller function inclusive of the underlying Virtual Network Appliance nodes. For Virtual Network
Appliance nodes deployed for stateful network services such as NAT, refer to the Virtual Network Appliance
Cluster Detailed Design section.
Note:
Each EVPN Route Controller node exposes up to three configurable interfaces, each connected to a dedicated
distributed Virtual Port Group: a management interface and one or two interfaces for Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN
peering. An additional internal interface, not user-configurable, handles notification messages during vMotion
events.

Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 Overview
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 leverages a decoupled Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN control
plane and VXLAN data plane to connect Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) to the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric, with
Distributed Transit Gateways providing connectivity to tenant Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances within the
physical network fabric.
Ethernet VPN (EVPN) is a widely adopted data center technology that serves as the distributed control plane for
the physical network fabric, using BGP to advertise both Layer 2 MAC (not supported in the current EVPN-VXLAN
integration with NSX) and Layer 3 IP reachability across the network. VXLAN acts as the corresponding data plane
encapsulation protocol, the counterpart to the GENEVE protocol used for encapsulation and tunneling within the NSX
overlay environment.
With the Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1, the NSX control plane managed by the NSX Manager
appliances continues to use GENEVE for east-west traffic between ESX hosts, while leveraging VXLAN for routing with
the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric to reach physical endpoints attached to the physical EVPN-VXLAN network
fabric or external network.
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports multiple VRFs/tenants. Each VRF/tenant is
identified by a Layer 3 VNI configured in the External Connection, which maps 1:1 to a Distributed Transit Gateway.
Note:
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1, unlike the Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model,
does not require an external VLAN spanning across the Distributed Transit Gateways. Connectivity between each
ESX host and the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric is established through the ESX host VTEP interface.
This Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports, for example, Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere
Cluster Model for workloads without compromising rack isolation through a Layer 3 boundary.
Note:
The ESX VMkernel Tunnel Endpoint (TEP) interface can handle both GENEVE and VXLAN traffic simultaneously.
In this document, TEP (GENEVE) and VTEP (VXLAN) are used interchangeably when referring to ESX hosts.
The EVPN gateway in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric plays a crucial role in the Distributed VXLAN
Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 as it can be considered the central hub for both the data plane, handling VXLAN
tunnels, and the control plane BGP-EVPN session with the EVPN Route Controller. The EVPN gateway is configured
either on all spine switches or on a subset of VXLAN leaf switches in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric. The
EVPN gateway, often referred to as the border gateway, advertises its VTEP IP address to the EVPN Route Controller.
This VTEP IP, along with the default route advertised by the EVPN gateway, is then installed on each ESX host, with the
EVPN gateway as next-hop. This enables traffic to reach destinations outside of NSX and physical endpoints that are
connected to VXLAN leaf switches via the default route.
Note:
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 requires that the EVPN gateway advertise the
default route to the EVPN Route Controller, regardless of whether EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing is enabled
or disabled. The default route can either originate on the EVPN gateway itself or be advertised from any other
physical network device, such as a firewall.
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing. This feature
optimizes the traffic forwarding path and reduces packet processing overhead on the EVPN gateway. When EVPN-
VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing is disabled, which is the default setting, egress traffic from a VM connected to a VPC subnet
is forwarded by the Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) through the ESX VTEP to the EVPN gateway VTEP leverage
VXLAN encapsulation. At the EVPN gateway, the VXLAN tunnel is decapsulated for a route lookup to identify the physical
endpoint destination. The lookup is based on the prefix learned via EVPN Route Type 5 from the VXLAN leaf switch
where the physical endpoint is connected, or from outside the EVPN-VXLAN fabric via the routing protocol in use. The
traffic is then either re-encapsulated into a new VXLAN tunnel to reach that physical endpoint within the EVPN-VXLAN
network fabric, or forwarded without further VXLAN encapsulation to another physical endpoint outside the EVPN-VXLAN
network fabric.
Ingress data plane traffic from a physical endpoint connected to a VXLAN leaf switch towards a VM connected to a VPC
subnet is initially forwarded again to the EVPN gateway VTEP using VXLAN encapsulation. At the EVPN gateway, the
Broadcom 1911

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VXLAN tunnel is decapsulated for a route lookup to identify the destination VM on a VPC subnet. The route lookup is
based on the /32 host prefix learned via the EVPN Route Controller using EVPN Route Type 5. The traffic is then re-
encapsulated into another VXLAN tunnel toward the ESX VTEP hosting that VM. Regardless of traffic direction, when
EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing is disabled, and whether it originates from the ESX host or the VXLAN leaf switch,
VXLAN encapsulation is always removed and re-added on the physical switch acting as an EVPN gateway.
When EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing is enabled, a VXLAN tunnel is established directly between the ESX VTEP
and the VXLAN leaf switch VTEP to reach the physical endpoint. This feature can be enabled per External Connection
on the Distributed VXLAN Connection as an add-on to the default forwarding behavior. In this mode, selected traffic flows
use EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing, optional with enabled filters configured on the EVPN gateways and VXLAN leaf
switches, bypassing the EVPN gateway without its VXLAN decapsulation and encapsulation. Other traffic flows continue
using the path through the EVPN gateway with the additional VXLAN encapsulation. This feature should only be enabled
when an optimized datapath is required for latency-sensitive traffic flows, such as storage protocols like NFS and S3/
object storage.
Note:
When EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing is enabled, the EVPN Route Controller receives either EVPN Route
Type 5 or Route Type 2 to resolve routes to /32 host prefix destinations, depending on the physical network fabric
vendor and their recommendation. Regardless of the received Route Type, the EVPN Route Controller always
advertises only EVPN Route Type 5 toward the EVPN gateways.
Note:
EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing requires IP connectivity for VXLAN encapsulated traffic between each ESX
VTEP and the VTEPs of all EVPN gateways and VXLAN leaf switches. This is typically achieved either through
VRF leaking or by connecting the ESX VTEP interfaces to the global routing table where the physical switch
VTEPs reside. Without EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing, IP connectivity for VXLAN encapuslated is only
required between each ESX VTEP and the VTEPs of all EVPN gateways.
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports stateful network services such as Default Outbound
NAT (Auto-SNAT), custom NAT, DHCP relay for external DHCP servers, and load balancing. These stateful network
services require a Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster. vSphere Supervisor, VKS workloads and VCF Automation All
Apps Orgs require load balancing capabilities, this is achieved using either VNA load balancer or AVI Load Balancer.
The VNA nodes used for stateful network services are distinct from the VNA used for the EVPN Route Controller. When
stateful network services are required in the Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 the deployment
results in two separate VNA clusters at least one for the EVPN Route Controller and at least one for stateful network
services. For VNA nodes deployed for stateful network services such as NAT, refer to the Virtual Network Appliance
Cluster Detailed Design section.
Note:
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports Avi Load Balancer. When only Avi Load
Balancer is used, with no other stateful network services such as Default Outbound NAT (Auto-SNAT) or custom
NAT, a VNA cluster does not need to be deployed, nor do N-S Services need to be enabled. More details, please
refer to section Avi Load Balancer Model. More details, please refer to section Avi Load Balancer Model.
The EVPN Route Controller unifies both environments, establishing a common control plane across the virtual and
physical network fabric by peering directly with EVPN gateways using Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN. More details, please refer
to section Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 EVPN Route Controller Overview.

Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 EVPN Route Controller Overview
The EVPN Route Controller establishes a common control plane across the virtual and physical network fabric. The EVPN
Route Controller achieves this by peering directly with EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric using
Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN.
Although the EVPN Route Controller is not involved in data plane forwarding, its role is crucial. Careful High Availability
consideration is required, including rack fault tolerance with independent storage per node. Deploying it as a minimum
two-node cluster is recommended.
Broadcom 1922

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 supports EVPN Route Controller in Active/Active cluster
mode alongside the previously introduced Active/Standby mode. Active/Active supports up to eight nodes; more than
two nodes are useful, for example, when there is a need to spread them across multiple zones or failure domains.
Active/Active is the only mode allowing a Layer 3 boundary between the EVPN Route Controller nodes on all interfaces,
including the Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN interface. Active/Standby, by contrast, requires Layer 2 adjacency on the
Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN interface to establish the Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN session from the VIP source interface.
In Active/Active mode, each EVPN Route Controller maintains an active and independent Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN
interfaces and establishes sessions with all EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN network fabric. This
substantially reduces the data plane impact of EVPN Route Controller or Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN session failures. In
Active/Standby mode, only the active EVPN Route Controller node establishes Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN sessions with
the EVPN gateways. The standby node remains in cold standby, retaining its configuration but without an established
Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN session. Its Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN connection is established only after a failover, resulting in
some minimal data plane impact.
