A single EVPN Route Controller cluster is sufficient to support multiple VRFs/tenants, each VRFs/tenants identified by the
Layer 3 VNI configured in the External Connection. Each External Connection supports only a single Layer 3 VNI, with a
strict 1:1 mapping between the External Connection and the Distributed Transit Gateway.
Each active EVPN Route Controller advertises a /32 host routes to the EVPN gateways in the physical EVPN-VXLAN
network fabric via Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN. These /32 host routes are carried as EVPN Route Type 5, together with
the Layer 3 VNI and Router MAC (RMAC) to identify the VRF/tenant of the External Connection. These /32 host routes
represent one of the following address types:
• public IPs of workload VMs
• External IPs used for stateless 1:1 NAT
• Stateful network service IPs, such as the Default Outbound NAT (Auto-SNAT) translated IP or load balancer VIP
• DHCP relay on VPC public subnets to support external DHCP server connectivity. The VPC public subnet gateway
IP is advertised alongside the workload VM /32 host routes from the EVPN Route Controller to the EVPN gateway,
enabling reachability to the external DHCP server
Each /32 host route also includes VTEP information to identify the ESX host where the workload VM, or the Virtual
Network Appliance (VNA) with its IP for stateful network services, resides.
Broadcom 1923

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The EVPN Route Controller learns /32 host route and VTEP information for workload VMs through the Central Control
Plane (CCP) channel from individual ESX hosts through NSX Manager. IP addresses used by the Virtual Network
Appliance (VNA) for stateful network services are learned through a separate internal notification channel.
Note:
Each EVPN Route Controller node exposes up to three configurable interfaces, each connected to a dedicated
distributed Virtual Port Group: a management interface and one or two interfaces for Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN
peering (EVPN Route Controller in Active/Active mode supports only one Multiprotocol BGP-EVPN interface).
An additional internal interface, not user-configurable, handles notification messages during vMotion events and
advertises Service IP addresses used for stateful network services from the Virtual Network Appliance.
Without EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing, each EVPN gateway advertises prefixes representing physical endpoints
attached to the VXLAN leaf switches, or prefixes belonging to networks outside the EVPN-VXLAN network fabric. The
EVPN gateway must also advertise a default route configured by the network fabric administrator in the physical network.
The default route can either originate on the EVPN gateway itself or be advertised from any other physical network device,
such as a firewall.
Each EVPN gateway uses its VTEP as the next-hop toward the EVPN Route Controller, advertised via EVPN Route Type
5. To minimize the forwarding table on each ESX host where a Distributed Transit Gateway is instantiated, the EVPN
Route Controller installs only the default route (ECMP) and the corresponding EVPN gateway next-hop.
When the EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing feature is enabled, it requires additional Route Targets (RT) to be
configured on both the physical network fabric and the EVPN Route Controller. Once configured, each physical endpoint
within the EVPN-VXLAN network fabric is advertised either as a Route Type 5 with /32 prefix or as a Route Type 2 host
route (MAC/IP), including the VTEP of its attached VXLAN leaf switch. With EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing enabled,
more granular filtering of specific physical endpoints is recommended. Additional filters can be applied to these Route
Targets (RTs).
These advertised /32 host routes, representing the selected physical endpoints, are installed on each ESX host through
the Central Control Plane (CCP) channel. They are added alongside the routes already installed and received from the
EVPN gateway. These /32 prefix entries use the physical VXLAN leaf switch VTEP as next-hop. This finally enables a
direct VXLAN tunnel between the ESX host and the physical VXLAN leaf switch, bypassing the EVPN gateway and its
VXLAN encapsulation overhead for latency-sensitive traffic.
Important:
When enabled, EVPN-VXLAN Direct Prefix Routing increases the forwarding table size on each ESX host and the
number of VXLAN tunnels from each physical VXLAN leaf switch toward ESX hosts. Network administrators must
ensure that supported scale limits are not exceeded.
Important:
Centralized password management via VCF Operations is the only supported option; local credentials cannot
be configured during the EVPN Route Controller node deployment. VCF Operations supports the password
management task 'update', which requires the current password before a new one can be configured. A fresh
EVPN Route Controller node deployment generates randomized passwords, which can be, for example retrieved
via the SDDC Manager API (GET /v1/credentials) and subsequently used to update the passwords using VCF
Operations.
Note:
The EVPN Route Controller is built on top of the Virtual Network Appliance, and this section applies exclusively
to its use as an EVPN Route Controller. Throughout this section, the term EVPN Route Controller refers to the
EVPN Route Controller function inclusive of the underlying Virtual Network Appliance nodes. For Virtual Network
Appliance nodes deployed for stateful network services such as NAT, refer to the Virtual Network Appliance
Cluster Detailed Design section.
Broadcom 1924

NSX Segment Connectivity Model
This model employs a Tier-0 gateway, where Tier-1 gateways are directly connected to it rather than using a Centralized
Transit Gateway (CTGW) with VPCs. It leverages virtual networking based on GENEVE segments for workload
connectivity including full support of NSX Federation and centralized advanced security features, but lacks the simplified
consumption model of a VPC-based topology.
NSX Segment Connectivity Model Overview
This model offers strong north-south throughput scalability, with a single Tier-0 gateway supporting multiple workload
environments, each mapped to individual Tier-1 gateways. VRF support can be incorporated into this model when tenants
require dedicated external network access or when the VRF separation of the physical network fabric must be extended
into the virtual network. Best performance is achieved by deploying a stateless Active/Active Tier-0 gateway combined
with Tier-1 gateways running in DR-only mode, maximizing distributed routing benefits.
Broadcom 1944

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This model lacks the simplified consumption model of a VPC-based topology and does not support certain network
services required for specific use cases, such as VCFA All Apps Orgs.
Enabling centralized network services on specific Tier-1 gateways by associating them with an NSX Edge cluster is
supported, but should be limited to cases where those services are explicitly required. Such services include stateful
NAT, centralized NSX Edge node-based firewall requirements at Layer 4 or Layer 7, and advanced NSX Edge node
security services such as Identity Firewall, URL Filtering, FQDN Analysis, IDS/IPS, Malware Detection, and TLS
Inspection. VPN support is available on Tier-1 gateways, though it is not supported when running in DR -only mode.
Mixing Tier-1 gateways with and without centralized network services enabled is supported. This model supports VRF can
be incorporated into the topology when tenants need dedicated external network access or when the VRF separation of
the physical fabric must be extended into the virtual network.
Note:
Enabling centralized network services affects communication between workloads connected to different Tier-1
gateways by routing all traffic through the NSX Edge node. It also limits the north-south throughput of all the
workloads connected to the Tier-1 gateway to the capacity of a single NSX Edge node.

NSX Segment Connectivity Model with NSX Federation
NSX Federation provides a single point of management for workload networking and security across NSX instances,
regardless if those NSX instances are associated to workload domains, within, or across VMware Cloud Foundation
instances. The NSX Federation capabilities are:
• Centrally manages security policy and groups across NSX instances
• Layer 2 and Layer 3 network topology extension across NSX instances
NSX Federation allows you to extend the NSX Segment Connectivity Model across VCF workload domains, part of the
same or different VCF instances. Each workload domain assigned to a dedicated NSX instance maintains independent
control plane availability, making NSX Federation the preferred solution for disaster recovery use cases, while also
supporting an independent software lifecycle. Cross NSX instance traffic traverses the NSX Edge nodes and supports any
MTU above 1280 bytes (preferred is at least 1700 bytes for workload VMs using MTU 1500 bytes to avoid fragmentation,
or 9000 bytes for workload VM above 1500 bytes) via TCP automatic MSS adjustment. For non-TCP traffic such as UDP,
no MSS mechanism is available and fragmentation occurs. NSX Federation support local egress.
Note:
When extending the network topology across workload domains via NSX Federation, it's not possible to leverage
the NSX multi-tenancy framework, so all configurations must be performed centrally by the provider admin in the
NSX default Project.
Note:
See an NSX Segment Connectivity Model with NSX Federation use case in the VCF management domain here
VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Stretched Overlay Segment Network Model.
NSX Federation uses an Active/Standby model for NSX Global Managers, where Active and Standby NSX Global
Manager clusters can be deployed in the same or different VCF instances. Only Layer 3 connectivity is required between
the Active and StandbyNSX Global Manager clusters, with no Layer 2 connectivity required. Please refer to specific NSX
Global Managers content in NSX Manager and Control Plane Models for more details.

Tenant (NSX Project) administrators, and VPC administrators do not have the ability to configure global groups
and security policies spanning multiple NSX instances, nor managing local groups and security policies for
multiple NSX instances via the NSX Global Manager.

VLAN Networking Connectivity Model
The VLAN Networking Connectivity Model uses traditional VLANs with vSphere Distributed Switch port groups or NSX
VLAN segments as the method of connecting workloads to the network.
VLAN Networking Model Overview
In this model, the only VMware Cloud Foundation component participating in the networking functionalities is the vSphere
Distributed Switch, responsible for switching the traffic between the VMs running in the hypervisor and the physical
uplinks. Once the packets are delivered to the upstream physical switch, it is the responsibility of the physical network
fabric to deliver them to the appropriate destination. VMs are connected to vSphere Distributed Port Groups or NSX VLAN
segments.
This model lacks the benefits that are provided by the NSX network virtualization (VPCs or NSX overlay segments) which
decouples the physical network from the topology requirements of the applications and services that run on top of it. With
NSX network virtualization, the physical network fabric can be designed and operated based on a simpler and more stable
model that does not require following the application's lifecycle. The role of adapting to the ever-changing application
requirements is offloaded to the NSX network virtualization layer while the physical network fabric design can be centered
around maximizing throughput and high availability, minimizing latency, and optimizing operational efficiency.
The VLAN Networking Connectivity Modelis supported in VMware Cloud Foundation and may be appropriate for
specific use cases, but it is not recommended for the majority of scenarios as it lacks the benefits provided by network
virtualization.

Note:
In VCF 9.1.0 from a consumption perspective, using NSX VLAN Segments are better suited for environments
with a high number of vSphere Distributed Switches, vCenters, and vSphere Distributed Port Groups. When
creating a VLAN Segment in NSX, a corresponding vSphere Distributed Port Group is automatically created on
any vSphere Distributed Switch part of the corresponding NSX, VLAN Transport Zone. This provides simpler
lifecycle management of VLAN networks via NSX Manager in environments with numerous vSphere Distributed
Switches, across single or multiple vCenters. This consideration is relevant for VMware Cloud Foundation where
each vSphere cluster has a dedicated vSphere Distributed Switch, increasing the number of vSphere Distributed
Port Groups to be managed.

Load Balancer Detailed Design
A VCF Instance can include one or more supported Load Balancer Models. This section describes the options,
requirements, and recommendations for each model Load Balancer Model.
• Avi Load Balancer Model
• Virtual Network Appliance Load Balancer Model
• NSX Edge VPC Load Balancer Model
• NSX Edge Tier-1 Load Balancer Model
• Foundation Load Balancer Model
Avi Load Balancer Model
The Avi Load Balancer Model provides load balancing for vSphere Supervisor and VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
(VKS) workloads, it can also be used for NSX segment and traditional VLAN-based networking.
The Avi Load Balancer provides load-balancing capabilities for virtualized workloads including Kubernetes (VKS)
workloads, it provides web application security and automatic scale. It fully integrates with VCF Automation and enables
automated application deployment with Avi Load Balancer. The Avi controllers are deployed and life cycled using VCF
Operations, this provides an integrated experience for management of service accounts, password rotation, and certificate
management. A single Avi Load Balancer controller cluster can be deployed with NSX deployed in : many configuration
where one NSX instance is shared with multiple workload domains. Alternatively, if NSX is deployed 1:1 with one
workload domain per NSX instance, then a dedicated Avi Controller cluster can be deployed per NSX Instance. Service
Engines can be deployed to any workload domain cluster.

Avi Load Balancer integration with VPC
The Avi Load Balancer can be fully integrated with VPC to provide load balancing for Supervisor and VKS-based
workloads that can be deployed using VCF Automation. This can be achieved by setting VPC mode in the NSX Cloud
account on the Avi Controller cluster. Communication between the VPC and the Avi Service Engines happens over the
VPC Services subnet which allows VIP traffic to the service engines. When the Avi controller cluster is deployed using
VCF Operations, this setting is configured by default.
Note:
The Avi Load Balancer also supports traditional VMs connected to VPC subnets without vSphere Supervisor.
Avi Load Balancer with Centralized Transit Gateway for vSphere Supervisor
The Avi Load Balancer can be fully integrated with a Centralized Transit Gateway that is used for VPC connectivity for
vSphere Supervisor. This requires an NSX edge cluster and a Tier-0 gateway for external connectivity. A Tier-1 gateway
can provide management connectivity between the Avi Controllers and the Avi Service Engines via an NSX segment.
Alternatively, an NSX VLAN segment could be used for the Avi Service Engine management connectivity.

segment rather than an NSX overlay segment.

Foundation Load Balancer Model
The Foundation Load Balancer is a basic load balancer that can be used to provide load balancing for vSphere Supervisor
with VLAN networking. The Foundation Load Balancer requires vSphere Distributed port groups, it does not support VPC
Networking or NSX Segment networking.
You can deploy a Foundation Load Balancer during Supervisor activation in vCenter. It can be deployed as a single
appliance or in high availability mode using two appliances in active/standby mode. The Foundation Load Balancer
can be deployed in a one-arm or two-arm mode. In one-arm mode the Virtual Server Network is used both for incoming
application traffic and outgoing forwarded application traffic to the Workload Networks. In two-arm mode, these networks
are separated and the appliance uses a separate network adapter for each traffic type.

VCF Management Services Component Detailed Design
The components deployed as part of VCF management services differs depending on whether the VCF Instance being
deployed is the first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet or an additional VCF Instance.
• VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance Model
• VCF Management Services in an Additional VCF Instance Model
VCF Management Services in the First VCF Instance Model
The first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet runs a VCF management services cluster with a combination of fleet level and
instance level components for managing all VCF Instances in the fleet.
VCF management services provides a common framework for running VCF management components. Individual VCF
management components are deployed at either fleet level or at instance level.
• Fleet level components exist in one VCF Instance and are used to manage multiple VCF Instances.
• Instance level components exist in each VCF Instance and are used to manage that instance only.

Multi Availability Zone Network Configuration • VCF management network must be stretched in the Physical Network fabric
between availability zones.
• Provides automatic network connectivity at secondary availability zone if a failure
occurs at the primary availability zone.
Multi Region Network Configuration There are two options:
1. Option 1: Create a separate VCF management networkin the second region to
deploy the new VCF Automation and VCF management services instances that
are used for restore purposes.
– The VCF management network in the second region needs to be routable to
the first region VCF management network.
– The VCF management network in the first region must be available at second
region in the case of Fleet disaster recovery to provide IP mobility for VCF
Operations and optionally VCF Operations for Networks.
– During the restore proces the VIP DNS entries for VCF Automation and VCF
management services need to be updated to point to the new network.
2. Option 2: Use a single VCF management network and stretch the network
between regions.

VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Overlay Segment Network Model
In the VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Overlay Segment Network Model, the VCF management components
are deployed to two separate networks, VLAN and NSX overlay segment.
The VCF management services are deployed to a VLAN during initial deployment using VCF Installer. Additional
components VCF Operations and VCF Automation are deployed to an NSX overlay segment. This is done as a day 2
operation after VCF Installer has deployed the management domain. An NSX edge cluster with a Tier-0 gateway, Tier-1
gateway, and overlay segment must be created manually in NSX before you deploy the additional VCF management
components. Additionally VCF Operations for networks can be deployed to the NSX overlay segment. As the License
Server is deployed along with VCF Operations using VCF Installer it will also get deployed to the NSX overlay segment.
Note:
The cloud proxy is a VCF Instance level management component and is always deployed to the VM
management network when using VCF Installer UI. If cloud proxy must be deployed to another network this can
be achieved day2 using VCF Installer API.

VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Stretched Overlay Segment Network Model
In the VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Strethced Overlay Segment Network Model, the VCF management
components are deployed to two separate networks, a VLAN and an NSX overlay stretched segment between two regions
to provide fleet disaster recovery.
The VCF management services are deployed to a VLAN during initial deployment using VCF Installer. Additional
components VCF Operations and VCF Automation are deployed to an NSX overlay segment and the segment is then
stretched between sites using NSX Federation. This is done as a day 2 operation after VCF Installer has deployed the
management domain. An NSX edge cluster with a Tier-0 gateway, Tier-1 gateway, and overlay segment must be created
manually in NSX before you deploy the VCF management components. The NSX stretched overlay segment will provide
IP mobility for VCF Operations in the case of a failover from one region to another. Additionally VCF Operations for
networks can be deployed to the NSX stretched overlay segment as it also requires IP mobility.
Note:
VCF Automation does not require IP mobility when restored to a second region. But as part of the restore
procedure if the same NSX stretched overlay segment is used, no DNS repointing is needed for the VIPs during
the restore process.
Note:
The cloud proxy is a VCF Instance level management component and is always deployed to the VM
management network when using VCF Installer UI. If cloud proxy must be deployed to another network this can
be achieved day2 using VCF Installer API.

VCF Operations Detailed Design
VCF Operations is a mandatory component for each VCF fleet and is the central console for operating your VCF fleet,
providing dashboards for monitoring, log analysis, reporting, and licensing. With VCF Operations offers fleet management
capabilities such as lifecycle management, certificate, and password management. This section describes the options,
requirements, and recommendations for each VCF Operations Model.
The initial management domain hosts essential components, including SDDC Manager, vCenter, NSX Manager, VCF
Operations, and VCF Automation. These components work together to ensure smooth operations and orchestration
across the VCF fleet.
This streamlined and scalable approach provides centralized management, allowing a unified framework to oversee VCF
Instances through a single VCF Operations instance delivering a strong foundation to expand to multiple VCF Instances
while maintaining centralized operations and automation.
To enable more capabilities, VCF Operations can be further extended through the deployment of log management, real-
time metrics, andVMware Cloud Foundation Operations for networks. These components support their own deployment
models, this section describes the options, requirements, and recommendations for each.
• Simple VCF Operations Model
• High Availability VCF Operations Model
• Continuous Availability VCF Operations Model
Broadcom 2001

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations Placement
VCF Operations placement for an entire VCF fleet plays a critical role in monitoring, analyzing, licensing, life-cycle
management, optimizing the performance, and capacity of the VMware Cloud Foundation platform. Proper placement of
the VCF Operations components is essential to ensure high availability, scalability, and efficient resource utilization.
| Attribute | Details |     |     |
| --------- | ------- | --- | --- |
Resource Allocation Ensure that sufficient compute, memory, and storage resources are allocated to the VCF
Operations appliances to handle the expected workload. This is particularly important in
environments with large-scale deployments or high data ingestion rates.
Network Connectivity VCF Operations should be placed in a network segment with low latency and high bandwidth
to ensure efficient communication with vCenter, NSX, and other monitored components.
Scalability Plan for future growth by deploying VCF Operations in a manner that allows for easy scaling
as the VCF environment expands. This includes considering the placement of additional
nodes if required. By carefully planning the placement of VCF Operations, organizations can
ensure optimal performance, reliability, and scalability of their VCF environment while gaining
actionable insights to improve operations.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration Drift
Using a desired state approach, fleet management can be managed through a configuration drift capability for vCenter
and vSphere Clusters. This approach is based on a template style management. A single template can be applied against
each component, or multiple templates without overlapping configuration values can be applied to each component.
Due to the range of possible configuration drift values and their impact on security, operations should invite security and
compliance teams to participate in the process. Balancing the need to manage operations with the need for appropriate
security can alter the approach taken.

End to end configuration drift components assembled to support fleet management.

best approach to fleet management.

Availability Relies on vSphere HA to restart the nodes in the event of an ESX host failure.

High Availability VCF Operations Model
The High Availability VCF Operations Model deploys a three node cluster for the analytic engine, and single node cloud
proxy appliance. Fleet lifecycle is deployed as a single instance component in the VCF management services. To achieve
high availability after the initial deployment, additional cloud proxy nodes can be deployed and then combined in collector
groups.

Continuous Availability VCF Operations Model
The Continuous Availability VCF Operations Model separates the VCF Operations cluster into two fault domains,
stretching across two vSphere instances in two separate availability zones, and protects the analytics cluster against the
loss of an entire fault domain.

VCF Operations uses a robust architecture to ensure data availability and fault tolerance across analytics nodes.
Data is stored in pairs of analytics nodes, distributed across two fault domains, ensuring continuous availability and
synchronization. Each object is stored in two nodes (primary and replica) across fault domains, providing redundancy and
resilience in case of failures.
A fault domain consists of one or more analytics nodes, grouped according to their physical location in the data center.
The two fault domains enable VCF Operations to tolerate failure of an entire physical location and failures from resources
dedicated to a single fault domain. This design requires a VCF Operations witness in a third site.
Broadcom 2022

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To deploy the VCF Operations with continuous availability, you first deploy the initial VCF Operations instance by using the
Simple VCF Operations Model or the High Availability VCF Operations Model. You then create a second VCF Instance in
a separate site/availability zone where you deploy the VCF Operations witness.
Continuous Availability VCF Operations Model Attributes
A Continuous Availability VCF Operations Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Availability Implements design with two VCF instances, across two availability zones to protect data from
an availability zone failure.
Inside the availability zone, relies on vSphere HA to restart the nodes in the event of an ESX
host failure.
Scalability Supports scale-up and scale out.
Note:
Scale-out is supported for the VCF Operations data nodes and VCF Operations
collector nodes.
Recovery Redeploy of a component in one of the availability zones in case of availability zone failure.
Restore through a backup for the whole deployment, in case of both availability zones failure.
Load balancing Optional external load balancer for the VCF Operations cluster UI.

Log Management Detailed Design
A VCF fleet can include one of the supported Log Management Models. This section describes the options, requirements,
and recommendations for each Log Management Model.
• Simple Log Management Model
• High Availability Log Management Model
• Multi-Instance Log Management Model
Broadcom 2030

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Log Management Deployment Models
Table 675: Common Log Management Deployment Model Design Attributes
Attribute
Details
Centralized log management Provides a centralized log management solution for vCenter, ESX, VCF Automation, NSX,
and components running on VCF management services (e.g. log management, identity
broker).
The use cases that are listed are an example, but they are not limited to this subset, for a
high availability / cluster log management instance to manage:
• Fleet level deployments.
• Default deployment model for all management and workload environments.
• High availability environments.
The use cases listed are an example, but they are not limited to this subset, for a Simple /
Standard log management instance to manage:
• Test/Dev environments only.
The use cases that are listed are an example, but they are not limited to this subset, for a
multi instance log management model to manage:
• Environments that exceed the scale limits of a single log management instance.
• Environments that cannot send full logging traffic between locations/regions.
Centralized log source management Log sources for the VCF fleet can be managed in a single location under VCF Operations.
By default, all components in the VCF management services that support log collection are
enabled for logging to the VCF log management instance for the Fleet. Other components
require activation of log collection on the VCF Operations Integrations page.
When activating the log collection, there is the option to:
• Send logs directly to the log management instance.
• Send logs to the local cloud proxy or proxy group for optimization/aggregation before
sending to log management.
Once activated, configuration is performed on the Log Collection page under Configurations,
including setting custom FQDN/VIP, and managing the types of logs that are collected.
Important:
When log collection for a source uses the cloud proxy, logs are balanced across
all available VIPs in a round-robin manner. If a specific VIP is selected under Log
Collection configuration, the collection reverts to the direct path.
Initial deployment Deployed after initial deployment of infrastructure and operations, from the Build section of
VCF Operations.
Architecture flexibility Can be deployed in a Simple or Highly Available Cluster deployment.
The recommended deployment model is an HA Cluster deployment.
Simple deployment is recommended for test/dev environments and not recommended for
production use cases.
A deployment can be scaled up (increase replica size), scaled out (add replicas) or can
increase storage (add storage to every replica) up to the scale limits. There is no provision for
scaling back in once a scale-up or scale-out is performed.
Security & Compliance FIPS mode is enabled by default:
• Only FIPS-approved providers, keystores, ciphers, and algorithms are used.
• Non-FIPS algorithms are disabled.
• Certificates and keystores are in BCFKS format.
• End-to-end TLS communication uses supported ciphers only.
• Supports hosts with hardware acceleration for FIPS ciphers.
Broadcom 2031

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Attribute
Details
VCF management services Log management is deployed to the VCF services runtime, in the VCF fleet’s first instance.
dependency Therefore the cluster where VCF management services for the fleet is deployed must
be provisioned with sufficient resources to support the anticipated compute and storage
requirements of log management.
VCF management services automatically scales out additional management services nodes
when required by log management, but if nodes require scaling up (increase in size) that
change should be scheduled in a maintenance window as it can impact other services
running on VCF management services.
Log Management Sizing Considerations
There are three main considerations for log management sizing:
• Events per second (EPS)
• Connections (http & tcp)
• Storage capacity
The number of EPS can be approximated by the number of ESX hosts in the fleet multiplied by 250. Certain
configurations may require adjustment, for example, logging of firewall rules can generate a significant volume of EPS
that must be taken into account. Connections are generally related to the number of hosts and endpoints (more hosts and
endpoints require more connections and generate more logs). Storage capacity is a factor of the retention period and the
number of log messages received.
Log management relies on an integrated load balancer that receives and forwards messages to one of the log processing
and data replicas. There is one load balancer per VIP/FQDN, and the size of the load balancer is based on the log
management instance size profile (small & medium share the same size load balancer). Using an external load balancer
is not recommended as it would introduce an additional hop between the log source and log management, since the
integrated load balancer is still a required part of the traffic path.
Additional VIPs/FQDNs must be manually created on the integrated load balancer when the number of EPS or
connections will exceed the capacity of a single gateway. Log sources must be configured to send to different FQDNs to
keep the load on any individual FQDN within the limits shown in the table below.
The number of replicas (which process and store the log messages) can be scaled out independently of the instance's
size profile, up to a defined limit. The total capacity for log processing, storage, and queries of the instance is determined
by the number of replicas and the size of the instance shown in the table below.
Important:
To support a given EPS load, both the number of VIPs/FQDNs and the number and size of replicas must both be
sufficient to handle the total load. While load is automatically distributed by the load balancer across deployed
replicas, the traffic sent to each FQDN must be managed by the customer unless the cloud proxy is being used.
Log events sent through the cloud proxy will be balanced across all available VIPs using round-robin distribution.
In order for multiple VIPs to provide additional capacity, the VCF management services must be deployed with the
HA deployment model.
Capacity utilization and performance of the log management instance is best observed on the Log Management
Health Overview dashboard in VCF Operations.
Each replica has a minimum of 500 GB of disk, which can be scaled up to 9 TB per replica. All nodes scale to the same
size.
Once log management is scaled up to a number of replicas, it cannot be scaled back down to fewer replicas even if the
size profile is increased. Likewise the size profile cannot be reduced once scaled up. For this reason, we recommend
scaling up the size to medium once you exceed 5-6 small replicas, or large once you get to 6-8 medium replicas. If you
deploy a large number of replicas in a smaller size profile, future scaling up to a larger size profile will result in a large
jump in resources and capacity (e.g. 12 small to 12 medium replicas).
To provide a higher level of resilience, plan for an extra replica or two (N+1 or N+2) to provide sufficient log processing
capacity in case a replica (or the host it is running on) fails. Also consider whether you want to provision for peak loads,
Broadcom 2032

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
or support an average load with the understanding that some logs may be lost during peak rates if the load exceeds the
cluster's capacity.
Log Management does not consume resources directly from the management cluster hosts, but runs on VCF
management services worker nodes. VCF management services must have sufficient IP addresses in its pool to support
the number of worker nodes required for log management. Allow for 6 IPs for an initial log management installation plus 1
IP for every small or medium replica and 2 IPs for every large replica. The cluster VCF management services is running
on requires sufficient CPU and memory capacity for these worker nodes. Each VCF management services worker node
consumes 12 vCPU / 24 GB memory for small size log management profile and 24 vCPU / 48 GB memory for medium
profile. The large size log management profile uses the same size worker nodes but requires 2 per replica.
The datastore used by the VCF management services will need to support all log management nodes' storage
requirements, and as all VCF management services nodes run in a common vSphere cluster on a common datastore, all
log management replicas will also run on that common cluster & datastore.
The resources (CPU and Memory) shown in the table below are consumed by log management from the VCF services
runtime worker nodes. Depending on how much capacity is available in the existing VCF services runtime footprint,
additional worker nodes may be deployed, or worker nodes may be scaled up as required for the log management profile
selected.
Notice:
The actual number and size of VCF management services worker nodes is determined by all the components that
are deployed and their sizing and availability settings. The VCF services runtime automatically scales the size and
number of worker nodes to accommodate the selected size and number of log management replicas and VIPs.
In addition to EPS and the storage/sharding requirements described, there are some other factors that can impact log
processing capacity and impact sizing decisions:
• A high complexity & quantity of log filtering rules can decrease log processing capacity
• Disabling event clustering (machine learning-based grouping) can increase log processing capacity
• Running many queries (using automation or multiple administrators accessing the system) decreases available log
processing capacity
• Hosts that do not support FIPS-compliant ciphers have reduced capacity; scale numbers are based on hardware-
accelerated hosts.

Log Management Virtual IPs and FQDNs
Log management starts with a default Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) & IP that is configured during initial
deployment. Multiple Virtual IPs (VIPs) can be configured post-deployment under the Integrated Load Balancer tab on the
Log Collection configuration panel. Some reasons for creating additional VIPs:
Attribute Description
Scale Each VIP has a separate Load Balancer with its own event-per-second (EPS) and
connections processing capacity. By adding VIPs you can increase the total EPS &
connections capacity of the log management instance, up to the limit of the total for all
replicas in the instance.
Separation Every VIP has its own FQDN and the ability to add a key/value pair to every log
message that it processes. This can be used to separate logs to a different partition or
for easy filtering when searching logs.
Restriction:
Fields can only be added to logs sent using the HTTP (API) protocol, and not
those sent by syslog. For example, ESX hosts send syslog data, which will not
have any fields added by the VIP.
Tip:
The SSL certificate used by log management must include all the FQDNs for VIPs for the VIP creation to proceed.
Using the Cloud Proxy with log management
VCF deploys a cloud proxy by default in every VCF instance. This proxy serves to collect metrics, forward logs, and run
the log assist agent. To achieve high-availability or greater scale at a site, multiple cloud proxies can be deployed and
added to a collector group.
It provides three primary benefits for log collection:
• Optimizes network traffic to improve stability and efficiency of transmission over high latency connections.
• Buffers logs for a period of time in case of an unreliable network connection, to help minimize the loss of log
messages.
• Centralizes all log traffic to a single source/destination pair, making it easier to manage firewall rules.
Tip:
Log message buffering to disk is enabled by default, and is not dependent on the "Data Persistence" setting being
enabled. Once the buffer fills up, the oldest logs start to be removed to make room for new logs. The buffer holds
about 20GB of logs.
When using the cloud proxy in multi-VIP environments, all logs sent through the cloud proxy are always sent in round-
robin rotation to all VIPs configured in log management. When fields are added to log messages processed by a VIP, logs
must be sent directly to the VIP rather than the cloud proxy so only the desired logs are processed.
The cloud proxy is available in two sizes: Standard supports 500K EPS and 600 connections. Small size supports about
half the throughput and connections of the standard proxy. Both sizes can tolerate up to 300ms network latency to the log
Broadcom 2034

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
management instance. As latency increases, throughput will also decrease, so expect lower maximum EPS rates for sites
with high latency.
Log Retention and Archive Design for log management
Your organization might require specific retention periods for logs due to compliance, auditing, or for troubleshooting
purposes. You must factor in the quantity of storage that is required to retain logs in the active index, and the operational
impact and space requirements for archived logs. Archived logs are not directly searchable but can be imported to an
archive partition for searching and analysis.
By default, logs are split into two different partitions: Audit & Logs. Up to 9 additional partitions can be created to store
specific log messages. Each partition can have a custom retention period defined, as well as a different archive location.
Table 677: Log Archiving Attributes
Attribute Description
Retention period Logs are stored in a searchable index in the partition for the length of the retention
period. Each partition has its own index, and within that index, the logs are divided into
shards. A shard corresponds to one day of one replica's portion of the index. Each day
of retention therefore consumes one shard per index on each replica.
Because the number of shards per replica is fixed (700, 800 and 900 for small,
medium, and large size profiles respectively), the retention period has an upper limit.
As an example, a medium size profile with 8 partitions would have capacity for at most
100 days of retention. If your retention requirement is longer, you must adjust the size
or number of replicas, and/or the number of partitions to accommodate it.
Once the retention period for a log message is exceeded, it will be removed from the
index and discarded during the next log index cycle. If there is insufficient disk space
or insufficient shard capacity to honor the full retention period, logs may be discarded
earlier. The status can be monitored on the Log Management Health Dashboard.
If no retention period is specified, the system will manage it to maintain disk space and
shard capacity at an acceptable level.
Log indexes are rotated at least every 24 hours, which also runs the archival process.
This rotation can occur more frequently if the log index size, or the total size of log
messages exceeds a system-defined threshold. Each partition runs on an independent
indexing cycle.
Archive location The archive location must be on an NFS version 3 (NFSv3) shared storage, or an
S3-compatible endpoint. The archive location must provide write access, always be
available, and have enough capacity to accommodate the archives. Pruning or rotation
of archive files is not within the scope of log management, and must be handled by an
external solution if required.
S3 endpoints must support chunked transfer encoding, and the bucket must be in an
AWS-equivalent region (e.g. US_EAST_1).
NFS paths should be entered in all lower-case when adding external storage to Log
Management.
Logs are sent to the archive on the first index refresh cycle, meaning that log
messages will reach the archive in at most 24 hours (but possibly less). If using the
archive as a recovery solution, this defines the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for the
log data.
Important:
The storage connection will be initiated from the VCF management services
node's IPs. When configuring firewall rules or ACLs on storage devices, the
entire IP range allocated to the VCF management services should be allowed
access to the S3 or NFS endpoint(s).
Broadcom 2035

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Attribute Description
Partition A partition represents a distinct index for storing log messages. Incoming logs are
directed using filters applied to the partition, and the order of processing (logs will
go into the first partition they match). Audit is always the first partition processed on
ingestion, and default is always the last, and acts as a catch-all for logs that don't
match any filters. Any new partitions created can be re-ordered between the two
system-defined partitions.
When searching logs, queries can also be restricted to specific partitions.

Simple Log Management Model
A basic log management deployment in the VCF fleet's primary VCF Instance management domain. Availability is
provided by the VCF management services whose nodes are in turn protected by vSphere HA within a single vSphere
cluster. The goal of the simple model is to consume minimal resources and require minimal configuration.

High Availability Log Management Model
The High Availability Log Management Model consists of a three-node deployment behind an internal load balancer. This
model provides resiliency at both the application level through the multi-replica deployment, VCF management services to
restart replicas, and vSphere HA to restart nodes in the event of an ESX host or log management component failure.

Multi-Instance Log Management Model
The Multi-Instance Log Management Model consists of a single, VCF Operations integrated log management instance,
and multiple non-integrated, Aria Operations for Logs 8.18 instances. These non-integrated instances are deployed in
separate VCF Instances within the fleet, and logs from components in that instance are manually configured to go to this
non-integrated instance. This model provides increased scale and log segregation at the expense of higher management
overhead. Where connectivity, policy and scale permit, a subset of logs can be forwarded to the integrated instance for a
centralized view.

VCF Operations for Networks Detailed Design
A VCF fleet can include one of the supported VCF Operations for Networks Models. This section describes the options,
requirements and recommendations for each VCF Operations for Networks Model.
• Simple VCF Operations for Networks Model
• High Availability VCF Operations for Networks Model
VCF Operations for Networks - Logical Design
VCF Operations for networks can be deployed as a cluster or a single node. This cluster processes the collected data
and presents it using a dashboard. VCF Operations for Networks also uses collector nodes to collect data from the data
sources, such as vCenter server and NSX Manager which then sends the data to the platform cluster for processing.
The platform cluster capacity is based on the deployment size of each node and the number of nodes composing the
cluster. For more information about how to decide the platform brick (node) size and number of platform bricks (nodes),
see the VCF Operations for Networks documentation.
The collector capacity is based on the deployment size. The number of data sources that you can add to a specific
collector is based on the documented capacity of the collector size (accounting for the number of VMs and the number of
flows).
Important:
VCF Operations for networks is fully integrated with VCF Operations UI for viewing and analyzing flows, and with
VCF Operations Lifecycle for deployment and management of the installation. VCF Operations for Networks is
always deployed in a 1:1 ratio with VCF Operations, i.e. one VCF Operations for networks instance per VCF fleet.
VCF Operations for Networks - Scaling
VCF Operations for networks scales in two dimensions: the platform and the collectors. The platform can only be
clustered if using appliances of at least a large size. Medium deployments cannot be scaled into a cluster without first
scaling up to large.
The scaling of a platform to a cluster model does not provide additional availability to the platform. Scaling must be used
when maximums for a single node exceed.
The overall dimensioning for collector scaling is based on various factors including:
Broadcom 2046

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Number of vCenter instances

• Flow Planning
• Number of Edges
To understand how to properly size the environment see the Capacity for Non-Cluster and Clustered environments below.

License Server Detailed Design
License server appliances serve as a repository to store VCF component licenses.
License server does not always need to be online or connected to VCF Operations. It is required for the following license
operations:
• Licensing new ESX hosts or vCenters (they remain in evaluation mode (90 days) until expiration or the license server
can be replaced).
• Generate updated usage files.
• Import new license files.
A VMware Cloud Foundation platform can include one of the two supported License Server Models. This section
describes the design requirements, recommendations, and choices for each model.
• Single License Server Model
• Multiple License Server Model
Single License Server Model
The Single License Server Model is the default configuration for VMware Cloud Foundation platform, which is designed
to provide centralized license management for the entire fleet. It's suitable for most typical deployments where reduced
operational overhead is prioritized.
Broadcom 2054

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 692: Single License Server Model Attributes
Attribute
Detail
Use Cases This is the typical license server deployment model for VMware Cloud Foundation and is
suitable for most VCF deployments.
Deployment mechanism One license server per VCF fleet. A license server is automatically deployed as part of the
installation or upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.
Backup and restore Backup is not required. If the original license server becomes unavailable, deploy a new
license server instance and migrate the licenses within 90 days.
Lifecycle The upgrade and patch management of the license server is managed through VCF
Operations.
High Availability High availability is provided by vSphere HA.
License Scope A single license server provides licensing management for the whole VCF fleet.

Multiple License Server Model

Backup and restore Backup is not required. Deploy a new license server and migrate the licenses, or migrate
the licenses to an existing license server in VCF Business Services console within 90 days.
When licenses migrate between license server, license reassignment is not required.
High Availability High availability is provided by vSphere HA.
License Scope Each license server manages the licensing for one or multiple workload and management
VCF domains.

VCF Single Sign-On Detailed Design
VMware Cloud Foundation supports for multiple VCF Single Sign-on Models. This section describes the options,
requirements, and recommendations for each VCF Single Sign-on Models. For each of these VCF Single Sign-on Models,
both Identity Broker Models are supported (embedded and instance), however it is recommended to use the Instance
Identity Broker Model for multi-VCF Instance Single Sign-On deployments due to availability and scale.
Broadcom 2060

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
SSO Realm
Each Identity broker operates within its own SSO realm in a strict 1:1 mapping. This SSO realm defines the logical
boundary within which user authentication, identity tokens, and single sign-on sessions are shared and trusted.
An SSO realm can span across multiple VCF instances. However, all components belonging to a single VCF instance
must belong to the same SSO realm:
• Workload Domain Components (e.g., vCenter , NSX Manager): Must connect to the same Identity broker instance
within their VCF instance. Split-SSO configurations—where different components within the same VCF instance point
to separate identity brokers for SSO—are not supported.
• Fleet Management Components (e.g., VCF Operations, VCF Automation): Can connect to any Identity broker
instance within the fleet. However, connecting to the Identity broker running on their local VCF instance is strongly
recommended.
Instance Identity Broker Failure Recovery Considerations
When planning for VCF SSO failure and disaster recovery (DR), options for recovery and supportability depend on the
specific failure scenario and SSO realm boundaries.
Failure Scenario 1: VCF management services Cluster Failure
If a VCF management services cluster failure causes the identity broker to stop functioning while the underlying VCF
instance remains operational, you can perform an in-place restoration of the identity broker onto the restored VCF
management services cluster using the latest Identity broker configuration backup.
Failure Scenario 2: VCF Instance Failure
When a VCF instance hosting an Identity broker experiences a failure, recovery depends on whether the VCF instance
itself is being restored:
• Restoration option 2a: VCF Instance Restoration Required
When VCF Instance restoration is required, the impacted Identity broker can be restored as part of the VCF instance
restoration workflow using the latest Identity broker configuration backups.
• Restoration option 2b: VCF Instance Restoration Not Required
When VCF instance restoration is not required, the impacted Identity broker can be restored to another existing VCF
instance within the same SSO realm, or to a non-SSO enabled VCF instance, using the latest Identity broker configuration
backup. Please note that restoring an identity broker to a VCF instance in a different SSO realm is not supported.
Failure Scenario 3: VCF Fleet Failure
When a VCF fleet experiences a widespread failure, any impacted Identity broker can be restored as a part of the overall
VCF Fleet restoration process using the Identity broker configuration backups.
During all failure scenarios, local accounts and VCF SSO emergency access client (for API access) remain functional.
Supported Single Sign-On Model
• VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model
• Cross VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model
• Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model
VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model
With the VCF Fleet-Wide Single Sign-On Model each VCF fleet contains a single identity broker deployment. A user can
log in once and gain VCF Single Sign-On capabilities for all components across all VCF Instances in the same VCF fleet.
For each of these VCF Single Sign-On Models, both Identity Broker Models are supported (embedded and appliance),
however it is recommended to use the Instance Instance Identity Broker Model for multi-VCF Instance Single Sign-On
deployments due to availability and scale.

Cross VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model
The Cross VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model includes multiple identity broker instances. Each identity broker instance
serves a defined set of VCF instances in the same VCF fleet. VCF management components, such as VCF Operations
and VCF Automation, can connect to only one of identity broker instances for Single Sign-On.

Cross VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model Attributes
The Cross VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Scale Balanced Scale - A single identity broker services a set of VCF Instances in your VCF fleet.
Resources requirements Balanced Resource Footprint - Additional identity broker deployments will require additional
compute / memory / storage.
Operational Overhead Balanced Operational Overhead - Additional identity broker will need to managed
separately for operational tasks such as backup and restore.
Availability Balanced Availability per Private Cloud - A single identity broker servicing a set of VCF
Instances in the VCF fleet.
Blast Radius Balanced Blast Radius - An outage of your identity broker deployment will impact
authentication across a set of VCF Instances connected to that identity broker.
Single Sign-On Realm Balanced SSO Realm - With one identity broker deployment for a set of VCF Instances,
users authentication will carry across instances in the same fleet requiring no additional re-
authentication.
Disaster Recovery Supported DR scenarios:
• Failure Scenario 1
• Failure Scenario 2 (Restoration Option 2a and Option 2b): Restoring to another VCF
instance in the same SSO realm is supported
• Failure Scenario 3

Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model
With the Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model each VCF Instance will utilize its own dedicated identity broker. The
VCF Single Sign-On realm will be limited to the VCF Instance. VCF management components, such as VCF Operations
and VCF Automation, can connect to only one of identity broker instances for Single Sign-On.

Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model Attributes
The Single VCF Instance Single Sign-On Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Scale High Scale - A single identity broker service for each VCF Instance.
Resources requirements Large Resource Footprint - Each identity broker deployment will require additional
compute / memory / storage resources.
Operational Overhead High Operational Overhead - Each identity broker will need to be managed separately for
operational tasks such as backup and restore.
Availability High Availability per Private Cloud - A single identity broker servicing each VCF Instance.
Blast Radius Small Blast Radius - An outage of one identity broker instance will only impact logins for the
VCF Instance associated with it.
Single Sign-On Realm Small SSO Realm - For each identity broker deployment users will have an additional Single
Sign-On realm. Moving across instances will require re-entering credentials.
Disaster Recovery Supported DR scenarios:
• Failure Scenario 1
• Failure Scenario 2 (Restoration Option 2a only): Option 2b is not a viable option because
restoring across different SSO realms is not supported.
• Failure Scenario 3
Note: local accounts and VCF SSO emergency access client (for API access) continue to
work during outages.

Certificate Management Design
You design certificate management for VMware Cloud Foundation according to industry standards and the requirements
of your organization.
Access to all management component interfaces must be over a Transport Layer Security (TLS) connection. During
deployment, each component is assigned a certificate from a default signing CA. Replace the default certificate with a
trusted enterprise CA-signed certificate to provide secure access to each component.

The management domain in a VCF fleet hosts the management components of the VCF Instance where it is deployed
and the management components of the fleet.

Attribute Details
Resource Allocation • VCF fleet management components.
• VCF Instance management components.

Management Domain in the First VCF • The management domain in the first VCF Instance contains the following management

– SDDC Manager
Management Domains in Additional • Management domains in additional VCF Instances contain the following instance-level

– vCenter
– NSX Manager

vSphere Detailed Design
A VCF Instance includes vCenter and ESX, this section describes the options, requirements, and recommendations for
each both.
• vCenter Model
• ESX Model
vCenter Model
The vCenter design considers the location, size, high availability, and identity domain isolation of the vCenter instances for
the VCF domains in a VCF fleet.
vCenter Model Attributes
A vCenter Model has the following attributes.
Design Area Attributes
vCenter Deployment Type • One vCenter instance for the management domain that manages the management
components of the VCF Instance.
• Optionally, additional vCenter instances for workload domains to support workloads.
• vSphere HA protecting all vCenter appliances.
vCenter Single Sign-On • Each vCenter has a distinct vCenter Single Sign-On domain.
Methods for Protecting vCenter
VMware Cloud Foundation supports multi-rack management vSphere clusters, vSAN stretched clusters, or 3rd party
synchronous replication solutions such as metro clusters that are designed to provide disaster recovery and/or high
availability for the entire management stack (vCenter, NSX Manager, etc.) as opposed to a single vCenter.
Table 709: Methods for Protecting vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation
High Availability Method Supported in VMware Cloud Considerations
Foundation
vSphere High Availability Yes You must ensure sufficient resources in the cluster to
allow virtual machines to restart on another ESX host
in the event of an ESX host failure.
vCenter High Availability (vCenter HA) No • vCenter services must fail over to the passive node
so there is no continuous availability.
• Recovery time can be up to 15 mins.
• You must meet additional networking requirements
for the private network.
• vCenter HA requires additional resources for the
passive and witness nodes.
• Lifecycle management is complicated because you
must manually delete and recreate the standby
virtual machines during a lifecycle management
operation.
vSphere Fault Tolerance (vSphere FT) No • The vCPU limit of vSphere FT vCPU would limit
vCenter appliance size to medium.
• You must provide a dedicated network.

ESX Model
In the design of the ESX host configuration for your VMware Cloud Foundation platform, consider the resources,
networking, and security policies that are required to support the virtual machines in each VCF domain vSphere cluster.
ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
For more information on host sizing, refer to the VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook.
Broadcom 2082

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 712: ESX Hardware and Sizing Considerations
Hardware Element Considerations
BIOS/Firmware Ensure the ESX host hardware is on the Hardware Compatability List (HCL) and that you are
running the latest supported BIOS and firmware.
CPU • Total CPU requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• Host failure and maintenance scenarios.
• CPU over-commitment ratio guidelines
– Management Domain
• To ensure optimal performance and maintain resilience during host failures or
maintenance, keep the management domain vCPU-to-pCPU over-commitment
ratio at or below 2:1.
Note:
While higher ratios such as 3:1 or 4:1 are supported, you must closely monitor CPU
ready times to ensure that the management cluster has enough capacity to run the
workloads.
– Workload domains
• CPU over-commitment ratios for workload domains should be calculated on a case
by case basis depending on the CPU intensity of the workloads. You must closely
monitor CPU ready times to ensure optimal performance.
• Number of physical cores, not logical cores.
– Simultaneous multi-threading (SMT) in CPUs improve CPU performance however the
performance enhancement will not be equivalent to 100% more CPU power.
Memory • Total memory requirements for the workloads that are running in the cluster.
• When sizing memory for the ESX hosts in a cluster, to reserve the resources of one host
for failover or maintenance, set the admission control setting to N+1, which reserves the
resources of one host for failover or maintenance.
• vSAN OSA (Original Storage Architecture).
– To support the maximum number of disk groups, you must provide 32 GB of RAM.
• vSAN ESA (Express Storage Architecture).
– You must provide a minimum of 128GB of RAM.
Storage • Use high-endurance devices such as a hard drive or SSD for boot device.
• Use a 128GB or greater boot device to maximize the space available for ESX-OS Data.
• Use hosts with homogeneous configuration.
Network • Use multiple physical NICs connected to multiple ToR switches to ensure redundancy.
• 25GbE is recommended
• Use physical NICs of the same speed, vendor, and model across all host within a cluster.
Power • Use redundant power supplies, preferably connected to separate circuits to ensure
availability.
• Consider the impact of enabling Power Management on your ESX hosts. In order to allow
ESX to control CPU power-saving features you need to set power management in the
BIOS to OS Controlled Mode.

Multi-Rack vSphere Cluster Detailed Design
A VCF Instance can support one or more supported Multi-Rack vSphere Cluster Models. This section describes the
options, requirements, and recommendations for each Multi-Rack vSphere Cluster Model.
• Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model
• Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model
Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model
The Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model allows you to protect workloads on vSphere clusters in your environment
against a failure of a single fault domain. You implement vSphere cluster across multiple fault domains within a single
availability zone. The networks are stretched across racks using a single broadcast domain for each network.
The Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model incorporates multiple fault domains in the design can help reduce the
blast radius of a failure which can increase application availability. In this design the infrastructure networks are stretched
across racks, this reduces the number of VLANs and subnets needed for the multi-rack deployment but also uses a single
broadcast domain for each network.

Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model
The Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model allows you to protect workloads on vSphere clusters in your environment
against a failure of a single fault domain by implementing your vSphere cluster across multiple fault domains within a
single availability zone. The networks are isolated to a rack using a separate broadcast domain for each network per rack.
The Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model incorporates multiple fault domains in the design that can help reduce
the blast radius of a failure which can increase application availability. In this design the VCF infrastructure networks are
not stretched across racks, instead each rack has a separate VLAN and subnet. The network traffic is routed between
the racks, this increases the number of VLANs and subnets needed for the layer 3 multi-rack deployment but also uses a
single broadcast domain for each network thus reducing the impact of a layer 2 network issue across racks.

vSphere Stretched Cluster Model
The Stretched Cluster Model allows you to protect workloads on vSphere clusters in your environment against a failure of
a single fault domain by implementing a stretched cluster across multiple availability zones.
Incorporating multiple availability zones in your design can help reduce the blast radius of a failure and can increase
application availability.
Figure 332: Stretched Cluster Model
VCF Instance
Availability Zone 1 Availability Zone 2
Rack Rack
Workload Domain 1
Stretched Cluster
Broadcom 2101

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stretched Cluster Model Attributes
A Stretched Cluster Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Datacenters Multiple datacenters
Cluster rack mapping • Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, each zone in a single rack.
• Workload domain cluster with multiple availability zones, with Layer 2 multi-rack clusters
in each zone.
Resilience • vSphere HA protects workloads against host failures.
• Multiple availability zones protect against availability zone failures.
Bandwidth • When using VMware vSAN™ stretched clusters, the bandwidth between the zones must
be at least 10 Gbps and the round-trip latency must be less than 5 ms.
• When using storage array based stretched clusters, you must work with your storage
vendor to define the bandwidth and latency requirements.
Management Domain Requirements Having the management domain on a stretched cluster is a prerequisite to configure and
implement stretched cluster in a workload domain. In this way, the critical management
components managing the workload domains are still available if an availability zone failure
occurs.
Availability Zones • You can have up to two availability zones associated with a given stretched cluster.
– In the case of vSAN stretched clusters, a third, independent fault domain is required to
host the vSAN witness appliance.
Stretched Cluster Model VLANs and Subnets
Function VLANs and Subnets
VM management Shared across availability zones
ESX management Unique per availability zone
vSphere vMotion Unique per availability zone

Distributed Switch Detailed Design
A VCF Instance can support one or more supported Distributed Switch Models. This section describes the options,
requirements, and recommendations for each Distributed Switch Model.
• Single Distributed Switch Model
• Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model
• vSAN Storage Cluster Separation Distributed Switch Model
Single Distributed Switch Model
A Single Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation provides a minimal deployment of networking using a
single vSphere distributed switch for all network services such as management, vSphere vMotion, IP-based storage and,
NSX.
A Single Distributed Switch Model provides connectivity using the lowest number of physical NICs for each ESX host in
the vSphere cluster while still providing availability from a single physical NIC failure, the network services running on the
vSphere cluster will share the bandwidth provided by two physical NICs.
Broadcom 2108

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Single Distributed Switch Model can be suited to vSphere clusters where the number of physical NICs must be
reduced and the overall bandwidth requirements does not exceed that provided by two physical NICs. The bandwidth of
the ESX host physical NICs will determine the network performance that can be achieved for the vSphere cluster.

A Single Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) • Use a single 2-port NIC (no NLR).
• Use two separate 2-port NICs.
– Each traffic type is spread across two separate NIC to avoid single point of failure.
– Results in unused ports on NIC.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order.
• Route based on IP hash.

Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation provides separation of storage traffic from all
other network services running on the vSphere cluster.
A Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model requires two vSphere Distributed Switches to achieve this level of traffic
separation where one vSphere Distributed Switch will be dedicated for storage traffic and the other will be used for all
other network services, e.g. management, workload, vSphere vMotion, etc. Each vSphere Distributed Switch has two
uplinks requiring four physical NICs on the ESX hosts.
The Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model can be suited to clusters where dedicated network bandwidth is
required for storage traffic or if this traffic needs to be isolated to its own network fabric. This can be especially suited to
vSphere clusters where dedicated bandwidth with no contention is required for storage traffic.
Broadcom 2113

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
A Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation provides a separation of workload traffic
running on NSX segments from all other network services running on the vSphere cluster.
A Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model requires two vSphere Distributed Switches to achieve this level of traffic
separation where one vSphere Distributed Switch will be dedicated for workload traffic and the other will be used for all
other network services, e.g management, vSphere vMotion, etc. Each vSphere Distributed Switch has two uplinks so a
minimum of four physical NICs is needed on the ESX hosts.
The Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model model can be suited to clusters where dedicated network bandwidth
is required for workloads that cant be achieved with a shared network design using just two physical NICs. It also provides
the option to isolate workload traffic to a separate network fabric if this is a requirement for the design.

Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
The Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation provides for full separation
of storage and workload traffic from all other network traffic.
The Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model requires three vSphere Distributed Switches to achieve
this level of traffic separation where both storage and workload have dedicated vSphere Distributed Switches and a
third vSphere Distributed Switch will be used for all other network services, e.g. management, vSphere vMotion, etc.
Each vSphere Distributed Switch has two uplinks requiring six physical NICs on the ESX hosts in the vSphere cluster
connecting to each vSphere Distributed Switch. This basically combines the previous two network models providing
isolation and high performance for storage and production workloads running on NSX segments or VPCs.

Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model
A Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation provides the
network design for the deployment of NSX Edge nodes to the vSphere cluster. This vSphere cluster is dedicated to
running only NSX Edge to provide for a large-scale, high-performance NSX Edge cluster deployment. To see more details
please refer to NSX Edge Cluster Detailed Design.
The Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model uses two vSphere Distributed Switches with
two uplinks to provide the connectivity for two NSX Edge nodes to run on each ESX host in the vSphere cluster.

Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model Attributes
A Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Number of vSphere Distributed Switches Two (2)
Number of Physical NICs per ESX Host Four (4)
Bandwidth • Each NSX Edge node has dedicated Uplink/TEP traffic per ESX host pNIC.
• No vSphere vMotion traffic as each NSX Edge node is pinned to an ESX host as
per the design.
• vSAN traffic should be minimal as only two NSX Edge nodes deployed per ESX
host.
• Host TEP traffic should be minimal as recommended to have no workload virtual
machinces deployed using NSX overlay.
Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model Options
A Dedicated vSphere Cluster for NSX Edge Node Distributed Switch Model can leverage options from the design areas
listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Network Fabric Single (all traffic on same fabric).
Physical NIC Level Redundancy (NLR) No NLR:
• Don't spread network traffic types across separate network cards.
NLR:
• Use two or more network cards.
• Each traffic type is spread across separate network cards to avoid single point of failure.
Load Balancing Option • Route based on physical NIC load.
• Route based on the originating virtual port.
• Use explicit failover order. (only option for NSX Edge node uplinks).
• Route based on IP hash.
Data Path Mode • Standard.
• Enhanced Datapath Standard (default).
• Enhanced Datapath Dedicated.

vSAN Storage Cluster Separation Distributed Switch Model
A vSAN Storage Cluster Separation Distributed Switch Model in VMware Cloud Foundation is used for storage clusters
where the vSAN storage traffic is separated from all other traffic on the vSphere cluster.
A vSAN Storage Cluster Separation Distributed Switch Model requires two vSphere Distributed Switches to achieve a
design where vSAN storage traffic requires its own dedicated physical NICs for guaranteed bandwidth and optional vSAN
storage traffic isolation through a separate storage fabric within a rack.

vSphere vMotion, vSphere HA, vSAN, and NSX Host TEPs.

Network I/O Control Detailed Design
vSphere Network I/O Control version 3 is enabled by default on the vSphere Distributed Switches created in VMware
Cloud Foundation and provides a mechanism to reserve bandwidth for system traffic based on the capacity of the physical
adapters on an ESX host. This can be particularly useful when different traffic types share the same physical adapters on
the hosts.
vSphere Distributed Switch Network I/O Control Options
Network I/O Control supports different mechanisms for resource management of system traffic related to infrastructure
services, such vSAN, vMotion, etc and VM traffic. For system traffic shares are used to ensure a dedicated percentage of
the bandwidth at a time when there is contention on the physical adapter. Network I/O Control provisions bandwidth to the
network adapters of virtual machines by using constructs of shares, reservation, and limit. In VMware Cloud Foundation
the default shares are applied to the system traffic, the table below shows the default values.
| Traffic Type                           | Shares |     | Shares Value |
| -------------------------------------- | ------ | --- | ------------ |
| Management Traffic                     | Normal |     | 50           |
| Fault Tolerance (FT) Traffic           | Low    |     | 25           |
| vMotion Traffic                        | Low    |     | 25           |
| VM Traffic                             | High   |     | 100          |
| iSCSI Traffic                          | Low    |     | 25           |
| NFS Traffic                            | Low*   |     | 25           |
| vSphere Replication (VR) Traffic       | Low    |     | 25           |
| vSAN Traffic                           | High** |     | 100          |
| vSphere Data Protection Backup Traffic | Low    |     | 25           |
| vSphere Backup NFC Traffic             | Normal |     | 50           |
| NVMe over TCP                          | Normal |     | 50           |
| Provisioning Traffic                   | Normal |     | 50           |
Depending on the vSphere Distributed Switch configuration and the type of system traffic on the vSphere Distributed
Switch these value can be modified post deployment to meet the requirements of the environment.
Note:
* High if NFS storage is used as principal storage for the vSphere cluster.
** Low if vSAN is not used as principal storage for the vSphere cluster.
Note:
In some cases vSphere Network I/O Control needs to be disabled, for vSphere cluster hosting edge clusters, it is
recommended to disable the feature.

Single-Rack vSAN Storage Models
A Single-Rack vSAN Storage Model refers to a vSAN cluster deployed within a single physical rack or rack enclosure.
This approach uses the local vSAN compatible storage devices within the ESX hosts housed in that rack to create a
shared, distributed datastore accessible to all ESX hosts in a vSphere cluster. The following sections describe Single-
Rack vSAN Storage Models. A Single-Rack vSAN Storage Model can either be based on a vSAN ESA or vSAN OSA
architecture, and can be deployed as a vSAN Storage Cluster or a vSAN Compute Cluster.
• Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model
• Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model
• Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model
• Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model
vSAN ESA uses a single-tier architecture that uses high-performance flash storage devices. vSAN ESA supports only
NVMe high-performance storage devices.
