Virtual Machine Storage policies vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN 9.1 automatically configures vSAN Auto-RAID policy on new vSAN ESA clusters.
vSAN Auto-RAID policy manages the resilience for data residing in a cluster, regardless of
the size or topology of the vSAN cluster. vSAN Auto-RAID creates a single policy within the
vCenter server,

Data at Rest encryption Data at Rest Encryption is supported as a day 2 operation.

Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model
vSAN OSA uses a two-tier storage architecture that utilizes distinct cache and capacity tier storage devices within a disk
group construct. vSAN OSA can support a combination of flash and magnetic disks that can be a combination of SATA,
SAS, and NVMe storage devices.

Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model Attributes
A Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Two Tier vSAN OSA architecture consists of two tiers: a cache tier for the purpose of write cache, and
a capacity tier for persistent storage.
vSAN Storage Devices vSAN OSA can support of flash and magnetic disks that can be a combination of SATA, SAS,
and NVMe storage devices.
Data Services • Deduplication and compression at cluster / disk group level.
• Encryption.
• Integrated file services.
• vSAN iSCSI target service.
• Stretched cluster.
• Fault domains.
• Kubernetes persistent storage services (block and file).
Virutal Machine Storage polices vSAN storage policies (also known as Virtual Machine Storage Policies or VM Storage
Policies) are rules defining virtual machine (VM) storage requirements that vSAN
automatically enforces across a cluster.
vSAN OSA will use a vSAN Default Storage policy with Raid-1 protection if a VM Storage
Policy policy is not specified
Broadcom 2158

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model Options
A Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
Deduplication and Compression vSAN OSA can be deployed with duplication and compression either enabled or disabled at a
vSAN cluster level.
Note:
Enabling compression only data service is not allowed during VCF cluster
deployment.
Data In Transit Encryption Data In Transit is supported to be enabled as day 0 or day 2 operation.
Data at Rest encryption Data at Rest Encryption is supported as a day 2 operation.
vSAN Networking vSAN OSA can utilize 10GbE , 25GbE or higher. See Table 764: vSAN Host Network Model
Options.

Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model
VMware vSAN storage clusters (previously known as vSAN Max™) is a dis-aggregated storage solution for vSphere
clusters. A vSAN Storage cluster provides storage resources to one or more vSAN Compute clusters. vSAN Storage
Clusters are based on vSAN ESA architecture. vSAN Storage Clusters implements a de-converged network approach. A
"de-converged storage network" (or non-converged storage network) refers to a network architecture where vSAN storage
traffic is separated from vSAN compute client traffic. This facilitates using dedicated storage network adapters or physical
ports, rather than sharing the same infrastructure.
Figure 343: Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
This image depicts a vSAN Storage Cluster with multiple vSAN Client Clusters (vSphere Clusters) consuming storage
resources on a vSAN Storage Cluster.

Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model Attributes
A Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attributes Detail
vSAN Storage Cluster Architecture vSAN Storage Clusters are based on Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model architecture
vSAN Compute Cluster A vSAN Compute Cluster (vSphere cluster) that can consume vSAN Storage Cluster capacity
vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic • vSAN Storage Clusters introduce a new vSAN networking traffic type to enable a de-
converged storage network.
• This allows internal vSAN traffic, such as data replication, resync and rebalance to be
logically separated from vSAN client cluster traffic.
• vSAN client cluster traffic is used for vSAN compute client traffic and can be described as
a second vSAN network type configured on a vSAN Storage Cluster.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model Options
A Single-Rack vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below,
depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
vSAN Storage Cluster • Dis-aggregated vSAN Storage traffic
vSAN Storage traffic and vSAN VM IO traffic will be separated. If selected a new traffic type
called vSAN Storage Cluster Client traffic. This will require an additional VMkernel interface
and a separate network pool with an allocated IPv4 IP subnet and VLAN.
• Converged vSAN Storage Traffic
If selected vSAN traffic and vSAN VM IO traffic share the same physical resources.
• A vSAN Storage Cluster can be stretched or non stretched.
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Storage Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
MTU 1500 - 9000
vSAN Networking • vSAN Storage clusters can use minimum 25GbE or higher for vSAN Storage traffic
• With dis-aggregated vSAN traffic, vSAN Storage client traffic can use minimum 10GbE or higher
See Table 764: vSAN Host Network Model Options.

Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
A Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model is a cluster of ESX hosts configured to mount a remote vSAN
datastore provided by a vSAN Storage Cluster in the same VCF domain.
Figure 344: Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
A vSAN Compute Cluster is a vSphere Cluster with VMkernel interface tagged with vSAN traffic type to communicate to
an existing vSAN Storage Cluster in order to mount a vSAN remote datastore.

Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model Attributes
A Single-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Datacenters Single datacenter
Cluster Rack Mapping Hosts are deployed within a single physical rack or rack enclosure.
Resilience • vSphere HA protects workloads against host failures.
Availability Zones • Single availability zone only.
Networking • Layer 2 networking
vSAN Compute Cluster • A vSAN Compute cluster is a vSphere Cluster Models with a #unique_611/
unique_611_Connect_42_id-6b5ac9d1-3397-4f8c-b56e-4453c86757bb defined
• The primary function of a vSAN Compute cluster is to provide compute resources (CPU,
memory) for running virtual machines, vSAN Compute clusters do not contribute to
storage.
• A vSAN Compute cluster can act as a client to a vSAN Storage cluster.
• A vSAN Compute cluster does not have to be a certified vSAN Ready node, thus does not
require certified vSAN local storage devices for vSAN use.

Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Models
Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Models is a configuration of vSAN where the ESX hosts contributing storage to the vSAN
cluster are physically located in different racks. This design is primarily used for rack awareness and to provide resilience
against the failure of an entire rack. By spreading data across multiple racks, the architecture can tolerate the failure of an
entire rack, as workloads can automatically restart affected virtual machines on ESX hosts in other racks. The following
sections describe Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Models. A Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model can either be based on a vSAN
ESA or vSAN OSA architecture, or a vSAN Compute cluster.
• Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model
• Multi-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model
The Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model is based on vSAN fault domains and either the Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster
Model or Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model. This offers rack-level protection for workloads. This design protects
virtual machines and vSAN objects against rack level failures.
Figure 345: Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
This figure depicts a vSAN cluster that is distributed across four (4) racks. Each rack can be logically associated to a
vSAN fault domain.

Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model Attributes
A Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
vSAN HCI Cluster A cluster that provides both compute and storage to virtual machines.
vSAN Fault Domain A logical grouping of hosts based on their physical location such as a rack that allows vSAN
to protect against failures of an entire physical location.
vSAN Datastore A distributed datastore that supports features that require shared storage.
vSAN Physical Networking Host network interfaces can be dedicated or can be shared with other traffic types.
vSAN Availability Workloads are protected by synchronously replicating objects in a vSAN cluster.
Data Services • Deduplication and/or compression.
• Encryption.
• Integrated file services.
• vSAN iSCSI Target Service.
• Kubernetes persistent storage. services (block and file).
A Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model shares many of the same attributes as a Multi-Rack vSphere Cluster Detailed Design.
One of the key choices is the network topology that a multi-rack deployment consumes.
Broadcom 2178

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Multi-Rack vSAN Storage Model Options
A Multi-Rack Cluster Model can be deployed using the following networking types.
| Multi-Rack Cluster Type | Description |     |
| ----------------------- | ----------- | --- |
Layer 2 • Hosts are installed horizontally across different physical racks.
• Each physical rack shares the same set of Layer 2 broadcast domains for each VLAN.
Layer 3 • Hosts are installed horizontally across different physical racks.
• Each physical rack has a unique set of Layer 2 broadcast domains for each VLAN.

Multi-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
A Multi-Rack vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model consumes storage from a vSAN Storage cluster deployed in
the same VCF domain. A vSAN Compute cluster can be spread over multiple racks routed via Layer 3 networking.
Similar to the Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model this allows protection of workloads on vSphere clusters in your
environment against a failure of a single fault domain by implementing a vSAN Compute cluster across multiple fault
domains within a single availability zone. The networks are isolated to a rack using a separate broadcast domain for each
network per rack.

Resilience • vSphere HA protects workloads against host failures.
• Multiple fault domains protect workloads in the event of a failure of one or more fault
domains/racks.
Availability Zones Single availability zone only.
Networking Layer 3 routed networks with isolated broadcast domains per rack.
vSAN Compute Cluster • A vSAN Compute cluster is a vSphere Cluster Models with a #unique_611/
unique_611_Connect_42_id-6b5ac9d1-3397-4f8c-b56e-4453c86757bb defined
• The primary function of a vSAN Compute cluster is to provide compute resources (CPU,
memory) for running virtual machines, not storage.
• A vSAN Compute-only cluster can act as a client to a vSAN Storage cluster.
• A vSAN Compute cluster does not have to be a certified vSAN Ready node, thus does not
require certified vSAN local storage devices for vSAN use.
vSAN Network Traffic • vSAN client clusters have dedicated VMkernel interfaces tagged with standard vSAN
traffic type.
• The vSAN Compute cluster nodes can optionally communicate with the vSAN Storage
cluster client traffic type that is defined on the storage cluster. (if configured)
• On the vSAN Storage cluster, vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic can be tagged on
a dedicated VMkernel interface on the vSAN Storage cluster to have a disaggregated
network design to separate vSAN compute traffic from vSAN storage traffic.
vSAN Remote Datastore vSAN Compute cluster mount as a remote datastore from vSAN Storage cluster.

Stretched vSAN Storage Models
Stretched vSAN Storage Models provide a highly resilient and available storage architecture by distributing data and
services across multiple locations, leveraging synchronous replication over a low-latency inter-site link. Stretched vSAN
Storage Models span two distinct physical locations, acting as active-active sites for data storage. This means that data
is synchronously replicated between the sites, providing redundancy in case of a site failure. The following vSAN cluster
models can be deployed in a stretched cluster configuration, vSAN HCI Cluster (vSAN ESA or vSAN OSA architectures),
a vSAN Storage cluster, or vSAN Compute cluster.
• Stretched vSAN Storage Model
• Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model
• Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
Sample VLAN and IP Subnet Requirements for Stretched vSAN Cluster in a VCF Environment
In an environment stretched across multiple availability zones, Layer 2 networks must be stretched between the
availability zones by the physical infrastructure. You must also provide a Layer 3 gateway that is highly available between
availability zones. The method for stretching these Layer 2 networks and providing a highly available Layer 3 gateway is
vendor-specific.
This section displays a sample configuration for an environment with a stretched vSAN cluster across two (2) availability
zones.
For NSX Edge designs that have a requirement to be stretched, refer to NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability
Zones.

Stretched vSAN Storage Model
A Stretched vSAN Storage Model is a cluster configuration where the ESX hosts, that comprise a single vSAN cluster,
reside in two availability zones.

Stretched vSAN Storage Model Attributes
A Stretched vSAN Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Fault Domain / Avilability zone • Stretched vSAN clusters comprise of three (3) Fault domains. A fault domain comprises of
one or more vSAN nodes.
• A fault domain or availability zone can represent a physical location. Fault domains /
availability zones can either be two distinct data centers in a metro distance, or two safety
or fire sectors (data halls) in the same large-scale datacenter.
vSAN Traffic Type • Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Traffic type for data traffic.
• Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Witness Traffic type for vSAN meta-data traffic.
Note:
Stretched vSAN Storage clusters (ESA) can be configured to use vSAN Storage
Cluster Client traffic for vSAN compute client clusters. See Stretched vSAN Storage
Cluster Storage Model.
vSAN Witness Appliance A witness node is a pre-configured appliance that runs ESX and is distributed as an OVA file.
Stretched vSAN Storage Model Options
A Stretched vSAN Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Storage Models • Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model
• Single-Rack vSAN OSA Storage Model
Witness Traffic Separation • Witness traffic separation allows you to use a distinct VMkernel adapter for vSAN witness
traffic communication with the vSAN witness appliance.
• There are two choices when stretching a vSAN clusters.
– When enabled, the ESX management network is used to communicate with the vSAN

Broadcom 2203

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model Attributes
A Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Fault Domain / Avilability zone • Stretched vSAN clusters comprise of three (3) Fault domains. A fault domain comprises of
one or more vSAN nodes.
• A fault domain or availability zone can represent a physical location. Fault domains /
availability zones can either be two distinct data centers in a metro distance, or two safety
or fire sectors (data halls) in the same large-scale datacenter.
vSAN Traffic Type • Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Traffic type for data traffic.
• Stretched vSAN clusters utilize vSAN Witness Traffic type for vSAN meta-data traffic.
Note:
Stretched vSAN Storage clusters (ESA) can be configured to use vSAN Storage
Cluster Client traffic for vSAN compute client clusters. See Stretched vSAN Storage
Cluster Storage Model.
vSAN Witness Appliance A witness node is a pre-configured appliance that runs ESX and is distributed as an OVA file.
Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model Options
A Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below,
depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Witness Traffic Separation • Witness traffic separation allows you to use a VMkernel adapter for vSAN witness traffic
that is different from the adapter for vSAN data traffic.
• There are two choices when stretching a vSAN clusters.
– When enabled, the ESX management network is used to communicate with the vSAN
witness node.
– When disabled, The vSAN data traffic network is used to communicate with the vSAN
witness traffic.
vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic • Dis-aggregated vSAN Storage traffic - vSAN storage traffic and vSAN VM IO traffic will
be separated. If selected a new traffic type called vSAN Storage Cluster Client traffic can
be selected. This will require an additional VMkernel interface and a separate network
pool with an allocated IPv4 Segment.
• Converged vSAN Storage Traffic - If selected vSAN traffic and vSAN VM IO traffic share
the same physical resources.
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• vSAN Storage Cluster Separation Distributed Switch Model
MTU 1500 - 9000

Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model
Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model is a cluster of ESX hosts deployed over multiple availability zones,
configured to mount a remote vSAN datastore provided by Stretched vSAN Storage Clusters in the same VCF domain.
Figure 349: Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
A Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster is a vSphere Cluster, deployed over multiple availability zones. Each VMkernel
interface tagged with vSAN traffic type which communicates to an existing Stretched vSAN Storage Cluster to mount a
vSAN remote datastore.
Broadcom 2213

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Instance
Workload Domain
Availability Zone 1 Availability Zone 2
Rack Rack
vSAN Stretched
Compute Cluster
Note:
Stretched vSAN Compute Clusters are essentially vSAN Compute Clusters that's stretched over two availability
zones and inherit the same attributes. Additional attributes are outlined below.
Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model Attributes
A Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attributes Details
Fault Domain / Availability Zone • Stretched vSAN Compute Clusters comprise of two (2) fault domains.
• A fault domain or availability zone can represent a physical location. Fault domains /
availability zones can either be two distinct data centers within a metro distance, or two
safety or fire sectors (data halls) in the same large-scale datacenter.
vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic must be tagged on a VMkernel interface on the storage
cluster.
When enabled, the vSAN compute cluster nodes will use the vSAN client traffic (on the
storage cluster) to communicate with storage cluster nodes for VM IO traffic.
vSAN Remote Datastore This is a datastore shared from a vSAN storage cluster.
Broadcom 2214

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
vSAN Storage Cluster Client VMkernel 1500 - 9000
MTU Size
vSAN Compute Site Coupling vSAN Compute Site Coupling
This is the concept of configuring and establishing site affinity to the vSAN objects when
mounting a vSAN client cluster to a stretched cluster to take advantage of the most optimal
path to the data.
Compute Cluster Site Coupling can be configured to either availability zone, depending on the
characteristics of the network fabric.
This addresses scenarios where networking between availability zones has significant
differences, This is defined this as asymmetrical and symmetrical network connectivity.
Asymmetrical network connectivity would describe a topology where the network
capabilities (latency & bandwidth) between availability zones could be less than the network
capabilities between a local vSAN Compute Cluster and vSAN Storage Cluster fault domain
within the same physical location
E.g. A stretched cluster spanning across two physical sites with site local compute clusters
mounting the shared datastore.
Symmetrical network connectivity would describe a topology where the network
capabilities connecting the availability zones would be the same as the network capabilities
between the client cluster and server cluster within each availability zones. Connectivity
across each availability zone is equal across all connectivity possibilities.
Eg. A stretched cluster spanning across multiple rooms within a physical data-center.
vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic • When disabled vSAN client cluster will share the same network with vSAN Storage
Cluster traffic
• When enabled, the vSAN compute cluster client nodes will communicate via the vSAN
client traffic on the storage cluster nodes for vSAN client cluster traffic

Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model
The Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model allows multiple independent vSAN HCI Clusters to consume storage of
adjacent vSAN storage resources within the same VCF domain. Also known as “cross-cluster capacity sharing” this
represents the highly flexible cross-cluster capacity sharing capabilities between vSAN clusters. This feature was formerly
referred to as “HCI Mesh.”
Figure 350: Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
The diagram depicts mounting remote vSAN datastores on vSAN clusters or vSAN Compute clusters and vSAN datastore
sharing.

Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model Attributes
A Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Modelhas the following attributes.
Attributes Detail
vSAN Cluster Allows multiple independent vSAN clusters to consume storage of adjacent vSAN storage
resources within the same workload domain.
• vSAN cluster can be either a client cluster or a server cluster.
• vSAN clusters are based on Single-Rack vSAN ESA Storage Model or Single-Rack vSAN
OSA Storage Model.
vSAN Remote Datastore vSAN storage that is shared to a client cluster, such as another vSAN HCI Cluster or a vSAN
Compute cluster.
vSAN Compute Cluster A vSAN Compute cluster that can consume vSAN Storage cluster capacity.
Broadcom 2218

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Attributes Detail
Storage Models • Principle Storage:
– vSAN clusters can consume a remote datastore as principle storage.
• Supplemental Storage:
– vSAN storage can be shared to adjacent clusters within the same VCF domain as
supplemental storage using VCF native workflows.
– VCF 9.1 supports consuming vSAN storage resources residing in one workload
domain by clusters in other workload domains (where they use different vCenter
servers).
–
vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic • vSAN Storage clusters introduce a new vSAN networking traffic type to enable a de-
converged storage network.
• It allows internal vSAN traffic, such as data replication, resync, and rebalance to be
logically and physically separated from virtual machine / vSAN Storage Cluster Client
traffic.
• vSAN Cluster Client Traffic is used for vSAN client cluster traffic and can be described as
a second vSAN network type on a vSAN Storage cluster.
Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model Options
A Datastore Sharing vSAN Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on
objectives.
Design Area Options
vSAN Host Networking • Share vSAN traffic with vSAN Client cluster traffic.
• Use vSAN Storage Cluster Client Traffic, use dedicated client traffic for VM IO traffic.

NFS Storage Model
VMware Cloud Foundation can use NFSv3 Storage as the principal storage or supplemental storage for both the
management domain and workload domains. NFSv4.1 is only supported as a supplemental storage option. The size of
the compute and storage resources for the type of VCF domain will determine the NFS architecture, topology, and how
NFS storage is consumed.
NFS Storage Model Attributes
An NFS Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Storage Model Principal (NFSv3 only), Supplemental (NFSv3 or NFSv4.1)
Data Services Supports underlying data services that are provided by the storage array.
Distributed File System Uses a network protocol to manage data access between the storage server and ESX host.
Broadcom 2226

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
NFS Storage Model Options
An NFS Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
• Storage and Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
Cluster Models • Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model
• Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model
• Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model
Note:
Multi-rack NFS storage design will be dependant on the Storage vendor design.
Number of Connections to NFS • Single NFS VMkernel port (default)
Datastore(s) • Additional NFS VMkernel ports
• nConnect
Using multiple connections to NFS datastores can offer increased bandwidth, redundancy,
and traffic isolation
Note:
Configuring additional VMkernel ports or nConnect requires manual configuration.
Datastore Clusters • Enable
• Disable
Note:
vSphere Storage DRS is used to manage datastore clusters: A collection of
datastores with a shared storage type and a shared management interface.

Fibre Channel Storage Model
VMware Cloud Foundation supports Fibre Channel Storage as principal or supplemental storage for the management
domain and workload domains. Review the choices and requirements and follow the recommendations.
Fibre Channel Storage Model Attributes
A Fibre Channel Storage Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Detail
Storage models Principal, Supplemental
Data Services Supports underlying data services that are provided by the storage array.
SCSI interface protocol Uses a fibre channel protocol to manage data access between the storage fabric and ESX
host.
Fibre Channel Storage Model Options
A Fibre Channel Storage Model can apply options from the design areas that are listed below, depending on objectives.
Design Area Options
Distributed Switch Models • Single Distributed Switch Model
• Workload Separation Distributed Switch Model
Note:
Fibre Channel does not use the physical network. As a result not all network models
are available.
Cluster Models • Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model
• Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Model
• Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster Model
SAN Fabric • HBAs
– Single
– Multiple
• Switches
– Single
– Multiple
• Zoning
– Single-initiator
– Multi-initiator
Note:
Follow Storage Vendor best practices for configuration of the SAN Fabric.
Storage Array • Storage Provisioning
• Host Registration
• LUN Masking
Note:
Follow Storage Vendor best practices for configuration of the storage array.
Path Selection Policy • Round Robin (VMW_PSP_RR)
• Fixed
• Most Recently Used (MRU)
Note:
Follow Storage Vendor best practices for configuration of the storage array.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design Area Options
Datastore Clusters • Enable
• Disable
Note:
vSphere Storage DRS is used to manage Datastore clusters: A collection of
datastores with a shared storage type and a shared management interface.
Raw Device Mapping (RDM) • Physical Compatibility Mode
• Virtual Compatibility Mode
Note:
RDM is supported. Customers must make sure to maintain consistent LUN IDs
across all hosts in the vSphere Cluster.

NSX Manager and Control Plane Detailed Design
Apply these design and component principles to size, deploy, and configure NSX Manager as part of your VMware Cloud
Foundation platform.
NSX Manager Model
When you deploy NSX Manager appliances, either with a local or global scope, you deploy the appliance with a size and
availability suitable for your environment's scale and availability requirements.
• Simple NSX Manager Model
• High Availability NSX Manager Model
• High Availability NSX Manager With External Load Balancer Model
NSX Global Manager Model
For an environment with multiple VCF Instances, you can use NSX Federation, which requires the manual deployment of
NSX Global Manager nodes. Consider the placement requirements for using NSX Global Manager in VCF, and the best
practices for having an NSX Global Manager cluster operate in an optimal way, such as the number and size of the nodes
and high availability on a standard or stretched management cluster.
• High Availability NSX Global Manager Model
• High Availability with Standby NSX Global Manager Model
Simple NSX Manager Model
The Simple NSX Manager Model addresses use cases requiring a minimal infrastructure footprint with lower scale and
lower availability requirements.

NSX Edge Cluster Detailed Design
This section outlines various NSX Edge Cluster Models for virtualized data center environments, including the physical
rack placement of NSX Edge nodes. Each design is tailored to address specific requirements for high availability,
scalability, capabilities, and infrastructure footprint.
NSX Edge Cluster Models for Single Availability Zone
• Host Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model
• Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multiple Single-Rack vSphere Clusters
• Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster
• Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster
NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability Zones
• Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model
• Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge vSphere HA Recovery Model
NSX Edge Cluster Models for Single Availability Zone
NSX Edge cluster designs deployed in a single availability zone have their infrastructure components typically installed
in close proximity to each other. For example, when using multiple racks, they are placed in the same room or adjacent
rooms in the same building. Asymmetric traffic is not a concern in such single availability zone designs.
Consider the main design attributes of the available models.

resources requires additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain maximum packet
forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node. A ratio of two physical NICs for each

Note:
A Layer 2 vSphere cluster refers to a vSphere cluster implementation where the host relevant host networks,
including vMotion, ESX management, and storage traffic, reside within a single Layer 2 broadcast domain.
Note:
A Layer 3 vSphere cluster refers to a vSphere cluster implementation where for each individual ESX host or a
sub-set of ESX hosts from a vSphere cluster, the relevant host networks, including vMotion, ESX management,
and storage traffic, are assigned to individual Layer 2 broadcast domain, separated through Layer 3 boundaries.

Using two or more instances of the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model to host NSX Edge nodes from the same NSX

• This design ensures continuous service availability for north-south communication and
centralized network services during a complete rack failure.

• Mobility is not required when a compute policy type Best Effort Restart (BER) is

BGP Peering Establish BGP peering solely with the local ToR switches located within the same rack that

Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster
A single horizontally deployed vSphere cluster for hosting NSX Edge nodes provides host-level and rack-level availability
but without providing independent storage for each rack. The vSphere cluster is deployed with one or more hosts per
rack across two or more racks, unlike the other designs with separated vertical vSphere clusters where each vSphere
cluster is contained within a single rack. This design distributes ESX hosts from the same vSphere cluster within the same
Layer 2 domain between racks rather than across Layer 3 boundaries. The physical network fabric must support Layer 2
adjacencies (e.g., through VXLAN encapsulation) to enable connectivity between ESX hosts across different racks.
Broadcom 2265

Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster Attributes
The Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster has the following attributes.
Attribute Details
Availability Model • Host and rack-level redundancy.
• Single shared storage.
• This design ensures continuous service availability for north-south communication and
centralized network services during a complete rack failure, similar to the multiple vertical
vSphere cluster design.
NSX Edge Node Mobility Mobility is not required when a compute policy type Best Effort Restart (BER) is configured.
Optional during host maintenance by temporarily disabling the VM/host rule across racks, but
not recommended in order to maintain BGP peering local to each rack.
BGP Peering Because BGP peering over extended networks may be problematic in some physical network
fabrics, it's recommended to establish BGP peering only with local ToR switches to eliminate
this dependency, even when Layer 2 adjacency is available across racks.
NSX Edge Node and Link Failover • Fast NSX Edge node High Availability detection for NSX Edge node failures.
mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for BGP.
North-South Bandwidth Growth • Add hosts to existing racks or extend the vSphere cluster to span additional racks, with
NSX Edge nodes distributed evenly across the racks.
• When deploying more NSX Edge nodes on existing ESX hosts, ensure each ESX host
has sufficient CPU, memory, and importantly, additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain
maximum packet forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node.

Rack Fault Tolerant NSX Edge Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster
A single horizontally deployed vSphere cluster for hosting NSX Edge nodes provides host-level and rack-level availability
but without providing independent storage for each rack. The vSphere cluster is deployed with one or more hosts per rack
across two or more racks, unlike other designs with separated vertical vSphere clusters where each vSphere cluster was
contained within a single rack. This design distributes ESX hosts from the same vSphere cluster across multiple racks,
with Layer 3 network boundaries providing separation between each rack. This design has no dependencies on specific
Layer 2 capabilities (such as VXLAN) of the physical network fabric and works with a simple Layer 3 physical network
fabric.

Attribute Properties
Availability Model • Host and rack-level redundancy.

vSphere cluster design.
NSX Edge Node Mobility • Mobility is not supported across racks.
• Mobility within the same rack is not required and the configuration of a compute policy

same rack when multiple ESX hosts are available, by temporarily disabling the VM/host
rule.
BGP Peering Establish BGP peering solely with the local ToR switches located within the same rack that
hosts the NSX Edge node.
NSX Edge Node and Link Failover • Fast NSX Edge node High Availability detection for NSX Edge node failures.
Mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for BGP.
North-South Bandwidth Growth • Add hosts to existing racks or extend the vSphere cluster to span additional racks, with
NSX Edge nodes distributed evenly across the racks.
• When deploying more NSX Edge nodes on existing ESX hosts, ensure each ESX host
has sufficient CPU, memory, and importantly, additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain
maximum packet forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node.

NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability Zones
NSX Edge deployments across two availability zones require careful consideration of network characteristics, even though
these zones are located in close proximity to each other. The latency (RTT) requirements vary based on the underlying
vSphere cluster topology: a maximum of 5ms latency (RTT) is required when deploying on stretched vSAN clusters, while
up to 10ms latency (RTT) is acceptable when running on independent vSphere clusters in each availability zone. When
designing for these deployments, organizations must make a binary decision regarding asymmetric traffic flows between
availability zones—they are either acceptable or not acceptable, usually based on the presence of a stateful device
in the path or not. This decision, along with considerations about network failover speed and north-south throughput
requirements, will determine the appropriate design model to implement.

Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model
NSX Edge nodes can be hosted in two ways: either using multiple instances of the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model,
or using a single vSphere Stretched Cluster Model across two availability zones with half of the NSX Edge nodes from
the NSX Edge cluster restricted to the primary availability zone and the other half to the secondary availability zone. Note
that NSX Edge nodes cannot move between availability zones in these two design options. Each availability zone can
use separate VLANs for NSX Edge node uplink traffic (BGP sessions, north-south traffic, NSX Edge node TEP traffic,
and NSX Edge node management interface), improving failure isolation. These two designs supports adaptable Tier-0
gateway routing configurations that prevent asymmetric traffic issues.

Dual Availability Zone Design Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model Attributes
The Dual Availability Zone Design Based on NSX Edge Node HA Model has the following attributes.
Attribute Details
Availability Model • Host and availability zone redundancy.
• Independent shared storage per vSphere cluster when using vSAN or single shared
storage.
• This design ensures continuous north-south communication and centralized network
services even if one availability zone completely fails.
NSX Edge Node Mobility • Mobility is not supported across racks/availabilty zones when using multiple instances of
the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model.
Mobility is not supported across availability zones when using the vSphere Stretched
Cluster Model.
• Mobility is not required within a single availability zone when a compute policy type Best
Effort Restart (BER) is configured. Optional during ESX host maintenance by disabling the
VM/host rule.
BGP Peering Establish BGP peering solely with the local ToR switches located within the same availability
zones that hosts the NSX Edge node.
NSX Edge Node and Link Failover • Fast NSX Edge node High Availability detection for NSX Edge node failures.
Mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for BGP.
North-South Bandwidth Growth • Add more hosts to both vSphere clusters simultaneously or scale out the stretched
vSphere cluster with additional hosts in each availability zone.
• When deploying more NSX Edge nodes on existing ESX hosts, ensure each ESX host
has sufficient CPU, memory, and importantly, additional physical NICs (pNICs) to maintain
maximum packet forwarding rates (PPS) for each NSX Edge node.

Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge vSphere HA Recovery Model
NSX Edge nodes are hosted using a stretched vSAN cluster across two availability zones and support NSX Edge node
mobility between zones (unlike the previous design where mobility was not supported). The NSX Edge node uplink VLANs
(carrying BGP sessions and north-south traffic) and NSX Edge node management VLAN must be stretched across both
availability zones, which provides only limited fault isolation between zones. This approach is different from the previous
dual availability zone design where separate VLANs improved isolation. The design supports Tier-0 gateway configuration
in active/active mode with symmetric flows and availability zone awareness based on NSX Edge node location. This
approach is different from the previous adaptable Tier-0 gateway routing design.

Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Detailed Design
This section outlines various Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models for virtualized data center environments, including
the physical rack placement of Virtual Network Appliance nodes. Each design is tailored to address specific requirements
for high availability, scalability, capabilities, and infrastructure footprint.
Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models for Single Availability Zone
• Host Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model
• Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multiple Single-Rack vSphere Clusters
• Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster
• Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster (only support
with Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1)
Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models for Dual Availability Zones
• Dual Availability Zone Based on Virtual Network Appliance Node HA Model
• Dual Availability Zone Based on Virtual Network Appliance vSphere HA Recovery Model
Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models for Single Availability Zone
Virtual Network Appliance cluster designs deployed in a single availability zone have their infrastructure components
typically installed in close proximity to each other. For example, when using multiple racks, they are placed in the same
room or adjacent rooms in the same building.
Consider the main design attributes of the available models.

A Layer 2 vSphere cluster refers to a vSphere cluster implementation where the host relevant host networks,
including vMotion, ESX management, and storage traffic, reside within a single Layer 2 broadcast domain.
Broadcom 2300

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
A Layer 3 vSphere cluster refers to a vSphere cluster implementation where for each individual ESX host or a
sub-set of ESX hosts from a vSphere cluster, the relevant host networks, including vMotion, ESX management,
and storage traffic, are assigned to individual Layer 2 broadcast domain, separated through Layer 3 boundaries.

Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multiple Single-Rack vSphere
Clusters
Using two or more instances of the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model to host Virtual Network Appliance nodes from the
same Virtual Network Appliance cluster provides both host-level and rack-level availability, with each rack maintaining
independent storage when using vSAN. Each vSphere cluster's infrastructure is contained entirely within a single rack,
with one exception: When using the Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model, the required external VLAN for the Distributed
Transit Gateway (DTGW) must be stretched across the two or more instances of the Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model,
where the Virtual Network Appliance nodes from the same Virtual Network Appliance cluster are running.

Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 2 vSphere Cluster
A single horizontally deployed vSphere cluster for hosting Virtual Network Appliance nodes provides host-level and rack-
level availability but without providing independent storage for each rack. The vSphere cluster is deployed with one or
more hosts per rack across two or more racks, unlike the other designs with separated vertical vSphere clusters where
each vSphere cluster was contained within a single rack. This design distributes ESX hosts from the same vSphere
cluster within the same Layer 2 domain between racks rather than across Layer 3 boundaries. The physical network
fabric must support Layer 2 adjacencies (e.g., through VXLAN encapsulation in the physical network fabric) to enable
connectivity between ESX hosts across different racks. Virtual Network Appliance nodes mobility across racks is not
required when a compute policy type Best Effort Restart (BER) is configured.

Availability Model • Host and rack-level redundancy.
• Single shared storage.
• This design ensures continuous stateful network service availability for redirected traffic
from the distributed VPC gateway to the VNA cluster during a complete rack failure.
VNA Node Mobility • For versions before 9.1.1: Mobility is supported and required during ESX host
maintenance within the same rack and across racks.
• Starting with version 9.1.1: Mobility is not required within the same rack and across racks,
when a compute policy type Best Effort Restart (BER) is configured. Optional during ESX
host maintenance by disabling the VM/host rule.
VNA Node and Link Failover • Fast VNA node High Availability detection for VNA node failures.
Mechanisms • Fast link failure detection with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for data plane
failures.
Supported Distributed Connectivity • Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model
Models • Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1

Rack Fault Tolerant Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Model using Multi-Rack Layer 3 vSphere Cluster
A single horizontally deployed vSphere cluster for hosting Virtual Network Appliance nodes provides host-level and rack-
level availability but without providing independent storage for each rack. The vSphere cluster is deployed with one or
more hosts per rack across two or more racks, unlike the other designs with separated vertical vSphere clusters where
each vSphere cluster was contained within a single rack. This design distributes ESX hosts from the same vSphere
cluster across multiple racks, with Layer 3 network boundaries providing separation between each rack. This design has
no dependencies on specific Layer 2 capabilities (such as VXLAN) of the physical network fabric and works with a simple
Layer 3 physical network fabric. The Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.1 is the only supported model.

Virtual Network Appliance Cluster Models for Dual Availability Zones
Virtual Network Appliance deployments across two availability zones require careful consideration of network
characteristics, even though these zones are located in close proximity to each other. The latency (RTT) requirements
vary based on the underlying vSphere cluster topology: a maximum of 5ms latency (RTT) is required when deploying on
vSAN stretched clusters, while up to 10ms latency (RTT) is acceptable when running on independent vSphere clusters in
each availability zone.

Dual Availability Zone Based on Virtual Network Appliance Node HA Model
Virtual Network Appliance  nodes can be hosted in two ways: either using multiple instances of the Single-Rack vSphere
Cluster Model, or using a single vSphere Stretched Cluster Model across two availability zones with half of the Virtual
Network Appliance nodes from the same Virtual Network Appliance cluster restricted to the primary availability zone and
the other half to the secondary availability zone. Each availability zone can use a separate VLAN for Virtual Network
Appliance management interface, improving failure isolation. When using the Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model, the
required external VLAN for the Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) must be stretched across multiple instances of the
Single-Rack vSphere Cluster Model, or across the two availability zones spanning the vSphere Stretched Cluster Model,

Dual Availability Zone Based on Virtual Network Appliance vSphere HA Recovery Model
Virtual Network Appliance  nodes are hosted using a stretched vSAN cluster across two availability zones and support
Virtual Network Appliance node mobility between zones. The Virtual Network Appliance node management VLAN must
be stretched across both availability zones, which provides only limited fault isolation between zones. This approach is
different from the previous dual availability zone design where separate VLANs improved isolation.

Data Center Network Requirements
This section describes the options, requirements, and recommendations for the data center network requirements.
Due to the large number of hardware specifics between data centers, no one-size-fits-all approach to data center network
design exists. The specifics of bandwidth requirements depend heavily on the dynamism of the workloads. Environments
with high virtual machine churn, high virtual machine storage I/O, or high inter-virtual machine communication need more
network resources than computationally intensive workloads. Moreover, latency-sensitive applications require special
consideration even at low bandwidth.
Broadcom 2334

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
The terms "performant" and "adequate" describe a network that is sized and configured to meet the requirements
for VCF components, considering the expected workloads and traffic flows in the production environment.
Network paths must be reliable and stable, as even low levels of packet loss and retransmits result in a
substantial decrease in performance and throughput.
Sites, Availability Zones, and Rack Fault Tolerance
Underneath the virtual infrastructure is the physical infrastructure. Servers, storage, and network switches are all physical
objects which reside in physical locations. VMware Cloud Foundation uses compute, storage, and network virtualization to
abstract consumption from the physical underpinnings.
A key design aspect of a highly available deployment is to ensure that components are distributed into different physical
locations to avoid faults from a common source. It is up to each customer to evaluate their own risk tolerance and fault
isolation requirements.
The following areas are typical levels of physical fault tolerance that is found within an enterprise.
Sites: A separate site is typically a considerable geographic distance apart. In some instances, connectivity between
this site may have higher latency (over 10ms RTT) or lower bandwidth, so synchronous data replication technologies are
impractical.
Availability Zones: Availability zones are separate sites that are geographically close with low latency (under 5ms
RTT) and high-bandwidth connectivity. They may be physically separate buildings or parts of an existing data center that
meet the goals for physical fault tolerance. There may be a common or separate network fabric between the availability
zones. However the network must be able to provide a stretch Layer 2 network between these sites to support mobility of
management appliances. Availability zones should have independent network paths such that the failure of one availability
zone does not impact another.
Note:
With some fabrics, the network vendor may not support BGP peering over the Layer 2 networks that are stretched
between sites.
Witness Site: Clustered technologies, such as vSAN, require a third tie-breaker site to enable automated fast recovery.
These witness sites may be a separate availability zone or separate site. Network paths to other sites should be
independent of each other. Inter-site connections may have higher latency and lower bandwidth connections.
Racks: A rack is a physical location within a site or availability zone that contains physical servers or storage components.
Each rack typically has dedicated network switches to which all rack components connect. Typically, connectivity within
a rack provides the best network performance to other components within the rack with minimal or no over-subscription.
For this design, all servers that are connected to the same physical network switch are considered part of the same rack
regardless of where they are physically located within the data center.
Physical Data Center Network Design
This section describes the requirements and recommendations that are related to the physical characteristics of the data
center network.

Host to Host Bandwidth
Ensure adequate bandwidth between all ESX host NICs within a cluster. Two ESX hosts that are connected to the same
switch typically, will not have any fabric-induced bottleneck. However, ESX hosts that are connected to different switches
within the same rack or in different racks may have limited bandwidth due to the over-subscription of links between
switches or through the core/spine of the fabric. Considering the actual traffic flows when determining the required
bandwidth at each point in the fabric.
For example, a high over-subscription ratio between leaf and spine switches can degrade performance for data-intensive
operations, such as vSAN resynchronization or vMotion. Minimize traffic across highly oversubscribed links by properly
sizing switch-to-switch interconnects and localizing related traffic types to the same physical switch.
Network Link Aggregation
Link Aggregation within Fabric
Link aggregation within the fabric - between fabric switches, i.e., leaf and spine switches, or ISL between top of rack
switches - is supported. Ensure that the fabric vendor supports peering of BGP across link aggregation paths from non-
fabric endpoints - such as NSX Edge Node.
Link Aggregation to Host
Link aggregation to the host is supported but not recommended - the default switch independent load-based teaming
(LBT) provides benefits similar to those of LACP without added configuration complexity.
The use of LACP-based dynamic link aggregation between the ESX host and the Top of Rack is supported, provided that:
1. The switch port for the first pNIC in each host is configured to enable a link and traffic to flow before receiving LACP
PDU - i.e., LACP Failback mode.
2. Ensure that the fabric vendor supports peering of BGP across link aggregation paths from non-fabric endpoints - such
as NSX Edge Node.
The use of other link aggregation technologies - static, EtherChannel, etc. - is not supported.
When using link aggregation, ensure the host VMkernels are correctly configured to utilize a single VMkernel per traffic
type. NSX Edge nodes should utilize a single uplink design.

Number of Connected Top of Rack Switches per Host
Each physical NIC from the ESX host may be connected to the same or different switches. In a properly configured fabric,
connecting multiple switches provides connectivity continuity during a switch outage due to failure or maintenance.
Physical NICs from an ESX host may connect to multiple switches provided that:
1. All physical NICs associated with a single vSphere Distributed Switch are connected to the same fabric, with identical
access to all pertinent VLANs and gateways.
2. Ensure that the failure of a physical switch does not result in the loss of next-hop gateway availability. The use of
VRRP or similar technology is recommended.

Network Fabric Detailed Design
The data center network fabric supports the VCF private cloud in achieving the desired availability goals. The exact model
that is chosen should align with the customer availability and resilience goals.
Network Fabric Models
Three Network Fabric Models exist which a vSphere cluster is built upon:
•
Single-Rack Network Fabric Model
• Multi-Rack Network Fabric Model
• Multi Availability Zone Network Fabric Model

First Hop Gateway
A first hop gateway refers to the first router a network packet encounters as it leaves a VLAN segment enroute to another
network in the data center.
The data center fabric may provide resilience to the first hop gateway via VRRP or other method. Depending upon the
Availability model chosen, and the scope/span of the VLAN segment it is associated with, the gateway will need to tolerate
the failure of an individual switch, rack, or entire availability zone.
Table 920: First Hop Gateway Choices
First Hop Gateway Availability Highly Available - Between AZs The First Hop Gateway must be provided
by a single highly available IP which can
fail-over (Active/Standby) between AZs,
or be present in each AZ simultaneously
(Active/Active).
Highly Available - Within a Rack The First Hop Gateway must be provided
by a single highly available IP that can fail
over (Active/Standby) between the top-of-
rack switches or be present in each top of
rack simultaneously (Active/Active).

Infrastructure VLANs
Note:
Infrastructure networks are used to provide management, control, overlay, and IP Storage communications within
a VCF Instance. Workload networks are used to provide IP connectivity to non-management workloads.
The required span of a Layer 2 segment depends on the type of traffic and the design of the vSphere Cluster Models
chosen. Using a separate 802.1q-based VLAN for each type of infrastructure network traffic within each cluster is
advisable.
VMkernel Segments: Each cluster's network function should be separated into its own VMkernel and Layer 2 domain.
For clusters that span multiple racks or availability zones, different VLAN IDs and Layer 2 domains may be utilized for
each VMkernel traffic type in each rack.
Broadcom 2353

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VM Segments: Any infrastructure VLAN that supports management or workload VMs must be equally accessible to all
ESX hosts within the vSphere cluster to support workload mobility via vSphere HA or vMotion. Additionally, the VLAN
must be reachable across all racks or availability zones associated with the vSphere Cluster. The VLAN ID must be
consistent across all hosts/racks/AZ.
The gateway for these VLANs should also be resilient enough to handle the failure of a single switch, rack, or availability
zone. The use of a First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP) is recommended.
Note:
For cluster-level VLAN scope, each ESX host must have the same VLAN ID and VLAN segment presented,
including vSphere clusters that span racks or availability zones. The first hop gateway must also be highly
available across racks or availability zones.
Requirement Option Description
Required VLAN Scope Global across availability zones For this traffic type, a single VLAN segment with the same
VLAN ID is presented to all ESX hosts in both availability
zones.
Availability Zone Local A single VLAN segment with the same VLAN ID is
presented to all ESX hosts in individual availability zones.
ESX hosts in the second availability zone may have
different VLAN segments/VLAN IDs for this traffic type.
Rack Local A single VLAN segment with the same VLAN ID is
presented to the pNICs for an ESX host. Individual ESX
hosts may have different VLAN segments/VLAN IDs for
this traffic type.

Multi Availability Zone Network Fabric Model
This section describes the VLAN and gateway requirements to support a vSphere cluster within multiple availability zones.
This design requires stretching a minimum number of VLAN segments between each availability zone. The physical
network fabric stretches these segments to provide a single Layer 2 domain across zones, enabling virtual machine
mobility during an availability zone outage. For these fabric-stretched VLAN segments, the first-hop gateway must remain
highly available across both availability zones. You must give special consideration to VLAN segments for NSX Edge
uplinks when using the Dual Availability Zone Based on NSX Edge vSphere HA Recovery Model, as BGP peering from
the NSX Edge node to the fabric occurs over these networks.
Note:
VLAN IDs are switch-level numerical labels identifying a Layer 2 domain. In some fabric configurations, the same
VLAN ID may identify different domains, or different VLAN IDs may identify the same domain. A distributed port
group can be associated with a single VLAN ID. Any distributed port groups supporting virtual machines must
have the same VLAN ID and Layer 2 domain mapping across the entire vSphere cluster. You may use different
VLAN IDs for separate vSphere clusters that do not share a common vSphere Distributed Switch.

IP Connectivity and Symmetry
Traffic must be routed between availability zones for all VLAN segments that require cross-site communication. For
example, vSAN networks in each availability zone must have a route to each other to support synchronous data
replication.
For VLAN segments that stretch between availability zones, the physical network fabric determines the ingress and
egress paths. In most cases, to simplify troubleshooting, symmetrical routing is recommended.
For workloads, the ingress and egress path depends upon the Network Consumption Models chosen. For the Centralized
Connectivity Modelingress and egress paths depend on the specific NSX Edge Cluster Models for Dual Availability
Zonesand routing model:
• Static Routing: The physical network fabric determines the ingress and egress paths.
• eBGP: A combination of the physical fabric and the NSX Edge gateway determines the ingress and egress paths.
For all stretched VLAN network segments (infrastructure networks, VLAN Networking Connectivity Model or Distributed
VLAN Connectivity Model), or Distributed VXLAN Connectivity Model for Version 9.1.0, the physical network fabric must
provide a highly available Layer 3 gateway at the first hop. This ensures that virtual machines maintain connectivity on the
same IP address when moving between availability zones.
Witness Location
For vSAN stretched cluster, an independent witness site is required. This requires independent network paths from each
availability zone to the witness site, such that the failure of an individual availability zone does not impact the traffic path
from the other availability zones to the witness site.
When configured with vSAN Witness Traffic Separation (WTS), the vSAN witness traffic flows between the ESX
management VMkernels and the vSAN Witness node. This traffic uses the MTU of the ESX management VMkernels.
Availability Zone Data Center Interconnect
The data center inter-connect between the availability zones must be appropriately sized to handle all infrastructure,
workload, and storage replication traffic. The interconnect is important to the operations of the vSAN Cluster. It should
have the appropriate level of resilience to achieve business objectives.

Dual Stack IP Addressing Model
The dual-stack model enables the deployment of VCF components to minimize the consumption of IPv4 address and
optimize the usage of IPv6 addresses.
Guideline for Dual-Stack IPv4/IPv6 Infrastructure IP Addressing
Supported IP address families are unique to each component. Each component within the VCF solution has its own IP
address support where components may support single-stack IPv4, single-stack IPv6, or dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6).
VMware Cloud Foundation applies dual-stack networking as a domain-wide configuration for the management domain
or workload domain, rather than as a component-level choice. Dual-stack deployment of a new domain configures all
dual-stack capable management components with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, while it provisions single-stack capable
components with IPv4 only. Also, you may select either IPv4 or IPv6 for vMotion and storage (VSAN/NFS) interfaces to
best fit your specific storage and mobility requirements.
Note:
Dual-stack networking is applied as a domain-wide configuration rather than a component-level choice.
Note:
This model does not eliminate the need for IPv4 addressing.

Dual-Stack Physical Network Design Considerations
Implementing a dual-stack IP addressing model requires ensuring the underlying physical network fabric is explicitly
configured to support both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic concurrently. This configuration extends beyond basic IP allocation to
include considerations for Layer 2 multicast handling, routing advertisements, and security policy enforcement.
Furthermore, you must determine the appropriate method for assigning IPv6 addresses to management and infrastructure
components. VMware Cloud Foundation supports multiple assignment methods, including Stateless Address
Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) and Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6). Selecting the correct method
depends on your organizational requirements for address control, visibility, and automation.

Workload IP Addressing Detailed Design
Guideline for Workload IP Addressing
Workload networks—whether VLAN or NSX Overlay—can utilize either IPv4 or IPv6 addressing to meet specific
application requirements. The sizing and configuration of these segments are determined by organizational needs and the
chosen networking model. While these methods offer broad protocol flexibility, note that the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
network virtualization model currently provides a prescriptive design optimized for the IPv4 address family.
To optimize IP route management and ensure scalability, all overlay workload segments should originate from one
or larger super-net blocks. These blocks are delegated to the NSX software-defined network (SDN) through BGP or
static routing. This approach centralizes route propagation and reduces the complexity of managing individual workload
segments within the data center fabric. Refer to the Networking Consumption Models section for further details on
workload addressing

Design Options Without VCF Full Stack
VCF Edge offers flexibility in management of different VCF components in edge deployments.
Customers also have the flexibility to deploy a reduced infrastructure footprint without implementing the complete VMware
Cloud Foundation stack. In smaller environments or edge deployments, customers may choose to manually deploy only
selected core components such as:
• VMware vCenter
• VCF Operations components
• VMware License Server
These environments can still be licensed under a VCF Edge model for lightweight or resource-constrained deployments
where the full private cloud platform capabilities of VCF are not required.
This approach can reduce:
• Infrastructure footprint
• Hardware requirements
• Deployment complexity
• Operational cost for small-scale environments
However, this simplified deployment model introduces important tradeoffs compared to a full VCF deployment.
Tradeoffs and Considerations
By not deploying the full VCF stack, customers may lose several integrated platform capabilities that enable a consistent
private cloud operating model across data center and edge environments.

Design Consideration
While this approach simplifies a single deployment and reduces initial infrastructure overhead, it comes at the cost of
managing every site differently. Customers must evaluate whether this isolated simplicity outweighs the loss of centralized
governance, as this fragmented approach becomes impossible to manage when scaling to thousands of locations without
a complete VCF deployment.
In environments expected to scale over time, operational fragmentation, and manual lifecycle management overhead may
increase significantly without the centralized automation and governance capabilities of the full VCF platform.
The following design patterns support VCF Edge deployments without requiring the full VMware Cloud Foundation stack.

Design Decision – Option 1b: Centralized Operations Extension for Distributed Edge
Option 1b extends the architecture that is introduced in Option 1a by adding centralized operational services for
distributed edge environments, including centralized logging, password management, and certificate management
capabilities.
In this model, VCF management, operations, licensing, and operational governance services remain centrally
managed across all edge locations, while individual edge sites continue to follow the same hybrid deployment approach
defined in Option 1a. This enables organizations to maintain localized edge operations while benefiting from centralized
operational visibility, security management, and administrative consistency across distributed environments.
The primary enhancement that is introduced in this design is the addition of centralized operational management services
that provide:
• centralized log aggregation and observability
• centralized password and credential management
• centralized certificate lifecycle management
• consolidated operational monitoring and troubleshooting
• unified operational governance across edge environments
When to Choose Option 1b
Option 1b is recommended when organizations require:
• centralized logging and observability across edge sites
• centralized password and credential governance
• centralized certificate lifecycle and trust management
• consolidated operational monitoring and troubleshooting
• centralized security auditing and compliance visibility
• unified operational management for distributed edge environments
This model is particularly beneficial for organizations operating multiple edge sites that require stronger operational
governance, centralized security controls, and standardized operational management practices across environments.

As a result, this deployment model should not be implemented using the standalone manual deployment

Design Options With Full VCF Stack
Customers requiring a fully integrated private cloud operating model across both core data center and edge environments
can deploy the complete VMware Cloud Foundation stack. This approach provides a unified operational framework that
integrates compute, storage, networking, security, automation, and lifecycle management into a consistent cloud platform
architecture.
Importantly, deploying the full VCF stack does not require large-scale infrastructure footprints at every location. Customers
still have the flexibility to deploy smaller edge environments using compact configurations such as single-host or two-host
edge deployments while continuing to benefit from the broader capabilities of the full VCF platform.
This allows organizations to extend the same operational model, governance framework, and lifecycle management
capabilities from centralized data centers to lightweight edge locations without sacrificing consistency or platform
functionality.

Design Consideration
By deploying the full VCF stack, customers gain the flexibility to standardize operations across environments regardless
of deployment size. Even in smaller edge deployments with minimal infrastructure footprints, customers can still leverage
the broader value of VCF, including centralized governance, lifecycle management, automation, security integration, and
unified operations.
This approach enables organizations to maintain a consistent cloud operating model from the core data center to the far
edge while adapting infrastructure sizing to the requirements of each location.

Best Fit Scenarios:
• Remote Industrial Sites (Oil Rigs, Mines, Offshore Platforms): These locations often have limited or intermittent connectivity, and
local processing is crucial for real-time monitoring, control, and safety systems. Each VCF fleet can act as a self contained edge.
• Military and Defense: Secure and often disconnected environments with strict security protocols and the need for independent
operation.
• Specific Healthcare Applications: Operating rooms or intensive care units where real-time data processing from local sensors and
devices is critical for immediate patient care and cannot rely on external network stability.
•
Autonomous Vehicles and Robotics in Isolated Areas: Self-driving vehicles or robots operating in environments without consistent
network coverage must process sensor data and must make decisions locally.
• Smart Agriculture in Remote Farms: Farms in rural areas with poor connectivity can benefit from local data processing for
environmental monitoring, automated irrigation, and drone-based analytics.
• Decentralized Research or Field Science Stations: Remote research outposts that require local data acquisition, processing, and
storage without constant reliance on a central lab.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

| Design Attributes |     |     |     |     | Justification |     |     |     |     |     |     |      |
Multi-Region Deployment Addresses the need for global reach, localized services, data sovereignty requirements, and
improved latency for users in different regions.
Centralized Management (Per Region) Each major region (West US, East US, Europe) has its own independent VCF Instance
(Instance 1, Instance 2, Instance 3) with its own Management Domain.
It offers localized control and management within each region, enhancing resilience
against inter-region network disruptions and ensuring compliance with regional regulations.
Meanwhile, centralized monitoring, licensing, and lifecycle management for each VCF
instance are maintained from a central data center via VCF Operation.
VCF Fleet employs a dual-level management approach, combining centralized control with
regional administration to optimize efficiency and scalability. This involves a division of
responsibilities between Central IT and Regional IT teams:
• Central IT Responsibilities: Central IT provides overarching governance and
standardization for the entire VCF Fleet. This includes:
Lifecycle Management: Centralized planning, coordination, and execution of upgrades and
updates for all VCF instances across regions. This ensures consistency and reduces the risk
of compatibility issues.
Certificate Management: Centralized management of certificates for all VCF components
(vCenter, ESX, NSX). This simplifies certificate renewals, improves the security posture, and
ensures compliance with organizational security policies.
Password Management: Defining and enforcing password policies across the VCF Fleet,
including password complexity, rotation, and storage. Central IT may also manage the
storage of highly privileged passwords.
Architecture and Standards: Defining the overall VCF architecture, including workload
domain design, network segmentation, and storage configurations. This ensures consistency
and best practices are followed across all regions.
Policy Enforcement: Defining and enforcing global policies related to security, compliance,
and resource management.
• Regional IT Responsibilities: Regional IT teams are responsible for the day-to-day
operations and management of the VCF instances within their specific region. This
includes:
Day N Operations: Performing routine tasks such as monitoring, troubleshooting, and
maintaining the health of the local VCF instances.
Resource Management: Managing local compute, storage, and network resources, including
provisioning, allocation, and optimization.
User Management: Managing local user accounts, permissions, and access control within
the region, in accordance with central policies.
Application Support: Supporting the deployment and operation of applications running on
the local VCF infrastructure.
Local Compliance: Ensuring adherence to any region-specific regulatory or compliance
requirements, in addition to central policies.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design Attributes Justification
Distributed Edge Sites Extends compute and application capabilities closer to users and data sources in
geographically dispersed locations.
VCF Operations Collector (Regional) Enables localized monitoring and data collection within each region, potentially for
performance optimization and troubleshooting, especially given the WAN latency.
Best Fit Scenarios
• Organizations with geographically dispersed users or data sources: This is a fundamental requirement. If your users or data are
spread across multiple cities, regions, or countries, VCF Fleet can help you bring applications and services closer to them.
• Edge workloads with strict latency requirements: If your applications must respond quickly, VCF Fleet's distributed edge
architecture can help minimize latency by deploying workloads closer to the source of the data or the end user.
• Requirements for high availability and disaster recovery: VCF Fleet's multi-region capabilities enable you to deploy applications
across multiple locations, ensuring that they remain available even if one location experiences an outage.
• Need for centralized management and consistent operations at scale: If you have a large number of vSphere deployments
to manage, VCF Fleet simplifies management by providing a single point of control and enabling you to enforce consistent
configurations and policies across all locations.

Isolated VCF Instance The "Dark Site" has its own independent VCF Instance, separate from the primary VCF fleet.
A dark site has limited or no external network connectivity. An independent VCF Instance
ensures full functionality and management within the isolated environment without relying on
external services.
Local Management Domain VCF Instance 2 includes its own Management Domain components (VCF Operation VCF
Management Services, Collector, SDDC Manager vCenter, and NSX).
Essential for the local management of the compute, network, and storage resources within
the dark site's VCF Instance. It provides the necessary control plane for the dark site's
infrastructure.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design Attributes Details
Local Compute Clusters VCF Instance 2 manages its own compute clusters.
These clusters provide the necessary compute resources to run workloads within the isolated
dark site.
VCF Instance 3 with own VCF fleet, dedicate to the site and manages its own compute
clusters.
VCF Operations Collector In the case of Dark Site 1, Data collected locally during offline mode and synchronized
with VCF Operations, when connectivity is established with the central site. here might be
periodically exported or analyzed locally.
In the case of Dark Site 2, Enables monitoring and potentially local operational insights
within the dark site, even without direct connection to an outside world. Data collected here
monitored and analyzed locally with a dedicated VCF Operation.
VCF Offline Depot A local VCF Offline Depot is deployed within the dark site.
In the absence of direct Internet connectivity, the Offline Depot serves as a local repository for
software bundles, patches, and upgrades required for the VCF Instance and its components.
This ensures the lifecycle management of the dark site's VCF environment.
Harbor Bootstrap Registry For Dark Sites that require vSphere Kubernetes Service, a bootstrap container registry to
stage the initial components is deployed. Those components are then used to spin up a
production-grade Harbor registry operating as a native Supervisor Service. Bootstrap harbor
deployments steps can be based on upstream Harbor or Bitnami Virtual Harbor Appliance.
Load Carvel Packages and Push the Harbor Carvel packages and their dependencies into
the bootstrap container registry.
License Check-in VCF Operation mandates a periodic license check-in (e.g., every 180 days, even for
dark sites via their limited connectivity or alternative methods) to ensure the entire VCF
environment, including isolated edge locations, remains compliant with licensing terms and to
prevent operational disruptions.
Note:
If you are entitled for VCF Edge, you have the option to deploy a dark site edge using a combination of VCF
Operations and vCenter only. Refer to the other flexible design options available and select the one that best fits
your requirements.
Best Fit Scenarios
• Strict Isolation and Security Requirements
• Unreliable or Intermittent Network Connectivity
• Autonomous Operations Requirement - Situations where the edge location must function independently for extended periods
without external dependencies, including management, monitoring, and software updates.

Supervisor Cluster Supervisor is enabled in the vSphere environment at each edge site. Enables the deployment
