directly at the edge, supporting modern, containerized applications.
Zonal Separation Each edge site is further divided into Control Plane Zone and Workload Zone. Provides

The Supervisor's Control Plane VMs reside within the dedicated "Control Plane Zone" at each

nodes reside within the dedicated "Worker Zone" at each site.
2 Host Cluster with External Storage Both Control Plane and Worker Zones at each site running on a separate 2-host cluster with
external storage.
Best Fit Scenarios
Organizations Requiring Strong Local Control and Security: Environments where strict local control over the infrastructure and
data is paramount, and minimizing external dependencies is a key requirement.
Important:
This design can be implemented with a VCF Instance with a single workload domain or multiple domain and
clusters inside the workload domain as described in Pattern 6 above.

This design pattern focuses on deploying a highly efficient and compact vSphere Supervisor footprint at remote or edge
locations. A single host leverages vSphere Supervisor to bring Kubernetes capabilities directly to resource-constrained
environments, while maintaining centralized management from a core VCF instance.
Important:
Based on this design, to deploy and onboard single-host edge sites, including vSphere Supervisor and ArgoCD,
customers can use the VCF Edge at Scale automation script to simplify and streamline edge deployments.
Design Attributes Details
Single ESX Host per Site Each edge location is built upon a single physical ESX server. Emphasizing a minimal
hardware footprint.
vSphere Supervisor vSphere Supervisor is enabled on the host which enables the deployment and management
of Kubernetes workloads directly on the ESX host. This includes the deployment of a "Control
Plane VM" for the Supervisor functionality.
Centralized VCF Management A VCF Fleet (comprising License Server, VCF Operation, VCF Automation, vCenter, and
NSX) resides at a central data center or management location. Central vCenter instance
manages the distributed edge sites.
Single Cluster Host Deployment It is a manual process within the vCenter to create a cluster and add the host.
vSphere Supervisor Network vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS) is used for vSphere Supervisor management and workload
network
HA Admission control vSphere HA is enabled on the cluster however, to make vSphere Supervisor to work, we have
disabled HA Admission control in the cluster level in vCenter.
Storage Options Only shared storage or local storage supported.
Network Connectivity • Bandwidth: Aim for 1 Gbps or higher for efficient VM or container image transfer.
A minimum of 10 Mbps might be acceptable for smaller images or less frequent
deployments, but it is slow.
• Latency: Keep latency below 300 ms for a smooth management experience. While
deployments might complete with higher latency, the user experience degrades.
Broadcom 2402

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
To support single node vSphere Supervisor deployment, you must disable HA Admission Control on the vSphere
Cluster in vCenter.
Best Fit Scenarios
• Numerous Far Edge Locations: Such as retail stores, bank branches, quick-service restaurants, remote industrial sites, or cellular
towers, where space and IT staff are limited.
• Resource-Constrained Environments: Locations where deploying multiple servers or complex networking is not feasible due to
physical limitations or cost.
• Applications Requiring Ultra-Low Latency: Workloads like IoT data ingestion and real-time analytics, AI/ML inference at the edge,
or local POS systems that demand immediate responses.
• High Volume of Small Workloads: Deployments where many small, independent applications must run close to the data source or
end user.
• Simplified Operations for Distributed Deployments: Organizations looking to standardize and automate the deployment and
ongoing management of a large fleet of edge sites from a central location.

No vMotion for Local HA: With only one host, vMotion cannot be

Important:
For multi-node VKS clusters deployed at the edge, the resilience of even localized workloads depends on central
vCenter management. Should a Kubernetes pod crashes or its VKS worker node fails, the Kubernetes controller
automatically attempts to restart the pod. However, if a pod utilizes a persistent volume and needs to be restarted
on an alternative VKS worker node, the underlying vSphere Supervisor must establish communication with
vCenter Server to facilitate the necessary volume detach and attach operations between the nodes. Therefore,
maintaining dedicated and stable connectivity to vCenter Server is paramount. Without this vital connection,
the vSphere Supervisor is unable to coordinate with vCenter to provision resources or orchestrate the recovery of
the pod, ultimately preventing the affected pod service from coming back online.

VCF Edge Pattern 10: Colocated vCenter with ESX Host at the Edge
The standard VMware Cloud Foundation deployment model places the Management Domain along with the Workload
Domain vCenter and NSX components in a centralized data center, while edge-site ESX hosts are managed remotely
from that central location. This model is well suited for environments where latency between the management plane and
managed infrastructure remains within supported operational limits and where edge locations do not require independent
operational control.
This design addresses deployment scenarios where edge environments require greater operational locality or autonomy.
Typical use cases include:
• regional hub architectures where a locally colocated vCenter manages nearby edge sites within supported latency
boundaries, while the central data center may reside at higher WAN latency
• environments with data residency, sovereignty, or security requirements requiring localized management control
• intermittently connected or disconnected edge environments requiring local operational continuity during WAN outages
• existing independently managed edge vCenter environments that need to be brought under centralized VCF
governance
In these scenarios, a locally colocated workload domain vCenter can be deployed at the edge or regional site and
imported into VCF as a workload domain. This approach does not eliminate overall VCF latency and support requirements
between platform components; rather, it localizes operational control and management functions closer to the managed
infrastructure and applications.
This pattern supports two implementation approaches:
• Option A: deploy a new vCenter locally at the edge or regional site before performing a brownfield import into VCF
• Option B: import an existing locally managed vCenter already operating the edge ESXi hosts
Both approaches result in a VCF-governed workload domain with a locally colocated vCenter. The design also preserves
flexibility in networking architecture, allowing customers to either deploy NSX locally at the edge site or continue using
centralized NSX management services depending on operational and connectivity requirements.
Broadcom 2405

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 385: Colocated vCenter with ESX Host at the Edge
Design Attributes Details
Centralized Management Domain A central data center hosts the management components, including vCenter, NSX Manager,
VCF Operation Manager, and SDDC Manager. This suggests centralized control and
administration of the entire environment.
Workload Domains vCenter at the • Local control plane: each edge site that requires colocated management deploys a
Edge separate vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) on-site, colocated with the edge ESX cluster.
This eliminates WAN dependency for all vSphere control plane operations at that site.
• Workload Domain scope: the edge vCenter manages only the ESX hosts at its local
edge site or nearby edge sites where latency is not a concern.
Network Connectivity Typical latency between SDDC manager and vCener must be less than 100ms. Refer to
Latency Details for each component.
Deployment Path Options
Option A — New vCenter (Greenfield) Option B — Existing vCenter (Brownfield)
• No prior vCenter at the edge site • Existing vCenter already manages edge ESX hosts
• Deploy a fresh vCenter colocated with edge ESX hosts independently of VCF
• Perform brownfield import of the new vCenter into VCF • Import the existing vCenter into VCF 9 as a Workload Domain
• Add edge ESX hosts to vCenter
• Recommended for: new edge deployments • No vCenter redeployment - existing vCenter is retained in
place
• Existing VM workloads preserved - no maintenance window
required for VMs
• Recommended for: edge sites with existing production
workloads and an independently managed vCenter

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Private AI Platform Detailed Design
Selecting the right AI infrastructure deployment model for VMware Private AI Foundation begins with understanding the
specific use case requirements. The decision tree starts with what type of AI workload is your organization planning to run.
If the use case falls squarely within the realm of large language models, such as building conversational AI applications,
implementing retrieval-augmented generation systems, creating data indexing and retrieval solutions, developing MCP
servers, or generating content, then Private AI Services is the optimal choice.
Architectural Options
Private AI Services is purpose-built for LLM applications and provides a fully managed platform where application
developers can work through an intuitive UI to build knowledge bases, and AI agents leveraging model endpoints made
available by the cloud administrator without needing any knowledge of Kubernetes or virtual machine management.
The platform abstracts away the complexity of infrastructure management and delivers an end-to-end workflow that
spans from model selection through knowledge base integration to agent deployment, while providing production-ready
monitoring and governance. However, it's critical to understand that Private AI Services is specialized for LLM and RAG
use cases and cannot support workloads like computer vision, time-series analysis, optimization problems, or audio
processing models.
For organizations whose AI workloads extend beyond LLMs or require the flexibility to support diverse model types,
the choice narrows to either VKS Clusters or Deep Learning VMs. VKS Clusters are Kubernetes-based environments
designed for scalable AI and ML workloads where multiple data scientists or ML engineers need to share GPU resources,
run distributed training across multiple physical hosts, or deploy production inference services that require high availability
and scalability. These clusters support any type of AI workload, from computer vision and time-series forecasting to LLM
fine-tuning and audio processing, making them the most versatile option. The trade-off for this versatility is complexity,
users need at least a basic understanding of Kubernetes concepts, and while the VCF Automation catalog can simplify
deployment by pre-installing the NVIDIA GPU operator and providing form-based configuration, the underlying platform
still requires more technical sophistication than other options. VKS Clusters are particularly well suited for ML engineers
and platform teams building production-grade AI services, especially when workloads need to scale horizontally or when
distributed inference and training capabilities are required.
In contrast, Deep Learning VMs are designed for individual data scientists who need a personal GPU-accelerated
workstation for exploratory work, model development, and prototyping. These VMs provide the fastest path to productivity
because they come with a pre-built Ubuntu image that includes all the essential components, Docker, ML package
managers, popular frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and monitoring tools like
DCGM. The vGPU driver installation and the vGPU licensing happen automatically and matches the host driver version,
eliminating a common source of configuration errors. While DLVMs can be deployed through multiple methods, including
the VCF Automation catalog, vSphere Client from OVA or content library, or kubectl, the catalog deployment provides
the simplest experience, where data scientists simply select their desired software bundle and get a fully configured
workstation within minutes. For the vast majority of data science work involving model experimentation, fine-tuning, and
development, DLVMs provide the ideal balance of capability and simplicity. It is possible to validate ML models on DLVMs
against the security, privacy, and technical requirements of your organization, then upload the models to a dedicated
model gallery for use by AI application developers or MLOps engineers for automated CI/CD-based deployment of model
runtimes.
Private AI Services Model
VMware Private AI Services provide an end-to-end platform for deploying generative AI applications within the VMware
Private AI Foundation environment.
The architecture consists of four core modules: Model Gallery, Model Runtime, Data Indexing and Retrieval, and Agent
Builder.
The Model Gallery utilizes the Harbor container registry as the central repository for AI model artifacts. Models stored
in Harbor are consumed by the Model Runtime module, which executes both completion models and embedding
models through inference engines such as vLLM, llama.cpp, and Infinity. Model endpoints expose these models via
OpenAI-compatible APIs, with completion models generating text responses and embedding models producing vector
representations for semantic search operations.
Broadcom 2407

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Data Indexing and Retrieval module connects to an external PostgreSQL database with the pgvector extension,
to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This component indexes data from multiple sources including Google Drive,
Confluence, and SharePoint, and S3 splitting documents into configurable text chunks using configurable splitting
strategies. The embedding model transforms these chunks into vectors that are stored in the external PostgreSQL
database, enabling similarity search with configurable top-k retrieval and similarity thresholds. The Agent Builder
orchestrates interactions between completion models, knowledge bases, and indexes. Agents can be configured with
system instructions, session management policies, and context retrieval parameters, exposing chat completion endpoints
that inject relevant document chunks as context for the completion model's responses.

Design Options - Consumption Patterns
VMware Private AI Services offers two distinct consumption patterns for accessing AI models: Direct Model Endpoints
and Agents. Direct Model Endpoints provide a stateless, OpenAI-compatible API for maximum flexibility, requiring
developers to manage conversation state and implement RAG workflows themselves. In contrast, Agents offer a
Broadcom 2408

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
stateful, opinionated approach with built-in session management, automated knowledge base integration, and persistent
conversation tracking. The choice between these patterns depends on your application's complexity, control requirements,
and whether you prefer managing state client-side or server-side. The two approaches can coexist in the same Private AI
Services Deployment and share the same Model Endpoints.
The consumption pattern also determines how much of the platform has to be deployed. Starting in Private AI Services
version 3.0, the Agent Builder and the Data Indexing and Retrieval modules are optional and can each be disabled in the
paisconfiguration custom resource, allowing the footprint and the prerequisites of a Private AI Services instance to be
aligned to the intended use case. This results in three deployment profiles driven by the desired consumption pattern:
• Model Endpoints only. Both Agent Builder and Data Indexing and Retrieval are disabled. In this simplified
deployment, no external PostgreSQL database with pgvector is required, removing the dependency on VMware Data
Services Manager (or on any other externally provided compatible database) and the associated sizing, and lifecycle
work. The result is the fastest path to a governed, OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint, with conversation state and
any retrieval logic implemented by the consuming application.
• Agent Builder without Data Indexing and Retrieval. Agent Builder is enabled and Data Indexing and Retrieval
is disabled. An external PostgreSQL database is still required, because Agent Builder persists agent definitions,
sessions, and conversation history server-side. This middle ground delivers an OpenAI Assistants-style capability:
pre-configured system instructions, server-side session management with TTL and summarization, and MCP tool
integration that lets an agent call external APIs, query databases, and act on live systems — all without knowledge
bases, indexes, or data source connectors. Because no embeddings or text chunks are stored, the pgvector extension
is not exercised and database sizing is driven only by agent metadata and session data, so it is significantly smaller
than a RAG-enabled deployment. This profile fits action-oriented agents, where the value comes from tool invocation
against current system state rather than from retrieval over an indexed corpus.
• Agent Builder with Data Indexing and Retrieval. Both modules are enabled, adding knowledge bases, data source
ingestion, embedding generation, and automated context injection on top of the agent capabilities.

Design Options - Authentication Methods
Private AI Services validates every API and UI request against a configured authorization provider. Providers are declared
in the paisconfiguration custom resource, more than one may be configured on the same instance, and when several
are present the UI offers a provider picker at login. Because all three options are OIDC-based, an instance can be brought
up with one provider and moved to another with a configuration change rather than a redesign.
Direct OIDC points Private AI Services at the identity provider the organization already operates, authorizing users
from the claims in the resulting token. It requires nothing beyond the existing identity infrastructure and is suitable for
production. Identity is wired up per deployment and per service, and serving several organizations from one instance
requires them to share a single identity provider.
Broadcom 2410

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCFA OIDC places VCF Automation between Private AI Services and the organization's identity solution, federating each
tenant's identity provider upstream and issuing the tokens PAIS trusts. One integration covers any upstream identity stack.
Tenant entitlement is explicit and delegated to tenant administrators, and long-lived VCFA API tokens work directly as
bearer credentials for scripted access. It is production-suitable but requires VCF Auitomation All Apps Orgs to be part of
the architecture.
Local Authentication removes the external dependency altogether, running an embedded OIDC issuer with users held in
a Kubernetes Secret. It exists so evaluation can proceed where no identity provider is reachable, and it offers self-service
tokens for non-interactive clients. It is explicitly not intended for production.

Design Options - Model Endpoint Locations
Beyond how models are consumed, a Private AI Services deployment must decide where the models it exposes actually
run. Private AI Services presents every model through the same inference gateway and the same OpenAI-compatible
API. This holds regardless of whether the model is deployed and managed by Private AI Services itself, served by a
self-managed inference stack, hosted by another Private AI Services instance, or provided by a public cloud service.
Consumers of the data plane (external clients, Agents, and Data Indexing and Retrieval) see a single model catalog, and
are unaware of the underlying hosting location.
This abstraction turns model hosting into an infrastructure decision rather than an application one. The choice is made per
model, not per deployment: a single Private AI Services instance can expose a locally managed model, a self-managed
endpoint, a model borrowed from another instance, and a public cloud model side by side in the same catalog. A model
can also be relocated later without any change to the applications consuming it. Where an instance manages none
of its own models, the result is Private AI Services acting purely as an AI gateway. It provides authentication, tenancy
integration, Agents, and Data Indexing and Retrieval over models that all run elsewhere.
Private AI Services managed model endpoints are the default and the starting point for most deployments. The model
is deployed as a ModelEndpoint custom resource in the same namespace as the Private AI Services instance, with its
artifacts sourced from the Harbor Model Gallery. Inference is served on the Private AI Services managed VKS cluster.
Deployment, scaling, upgrade, and deletion are driven from the Private AI Services UI and API, and the corresponding
inference gateway routes are created automatically. Because everything sits inside one namespace, inference traffic
introduces no external network dependency, and GPU and inference telemetry are collected natively. High availability is
handled through model endpoint replicas, and no credentials have to be exchanged between components. The tradeoff
is resource locality. GPU capacity is dedicated to that namespace, so making the same model available to several teams
means deploying it several times. The supply of GPUs becomes the practical limit on how many Private AI Services
instances an organization can operate.
A self-managed VKS cluster is the right choice when the constraint is the serving architecture rather than the model
itself. The customer deploys and operates the inference stack directly, and exposes it through a customer-managed
ingress using an OpenAI-compatible API. It is then registered with Private AI Services as an InferenceGatewayRoute.
This opens up capabilities that sit above the inference engine, such as KV-cache-aware and prefix-aware routing across
replicas, and disaggregated inference. Model weights can be held on ReadWriteMany volumes, so that replicas start
without pulling multi-gigabyte artifacts. Multi-node inference becomes possible for models too large for a single node,
along with the freedom to adopt newer engines on the customer's own cadence. The model still appears in the Private
AI Services catalog and is consumed identically by Agents, knowledge bases, and the data plane API. So applications
are unaffected by the choice, and remain unaffected if the model is later migrated to a managed endpoint. In exchange,
the customer takes back responsibility for lifecycle, scaling, high availability, and telemetry, and governs model artifacts
outside Harbor. They gain no resource sharing benefit, since the GPU capacity is still consumed in the same namespace.
Consuming a model from a different Private AI Services instance addresses the duplication inherent in the first option.
One instance hosts GPU-backed model endpoints on behalf of others, which register those models as remote routes and
require no GPU capacity of their own. The serving instance may sit in another namespace on the same Supervisor, on a
different Supervisor, or in an entirely different VCF instance. The significant consequence is that isolation no longer has
to be traded for utilization. Each team or tenant runs a dedicated Private AI Services instance with its own authentication
and application data, while drawing on a shared pool of GPU-backed models. Onboarding an additional team no longer
requires an additional GPU allocation. The considerations are those of any shared service. The serving instance must be
sized and made highly available for aggregate demand, and its administrator owns model lifecycle exclusively.
A public cloud model is hosted entirely by an external provider and consumed through its OpenAI-compatible API, with
no compute footprint on premises at all. Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) and Google
Gemini are also supported. This is the fastest route to proprietary and frontier models that cannot be deployed locally. It
requires no capacity planning, and provides elastic headroom that a fixed on-premises GPU pool cannot. Because cloud
and private models share the same catalog and the same authentication, applications treat them identically. This makes it
Broadcom 2412

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a practical starting point for teams building against a model today and moving it on premises as GPU capacity arrives. The
defining consideration is that prompt and completion data leaves the environment.

Design options - Private AI Services Enablement and Lifecycle
Private AI Services is enabled in a vSphere Supervisor namespace in either design. The difference is how that
namespace is created and consumed.
In the first option, the namespace belongs to a VCF Automation All-Apps organization and project, and Private AI Services
is enabled through the guided workflow in the Build & Deploy tab. Organizations are the tenancy boundary, so a single
instance can be consumed by one organization or by several, and VCFA OIDC becomes available as an authorization
provider, allowing each organization to keep its own identity provider federated upstream.
In the second option, the namespace is created in the vCenter UI or on the Supervisor through the CLI. The service is
enabled with kubectl or through the Local Consumption Interface. There is no VCF Automation dependency, and any
Broadcom 2415

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Supervisor networking option can be used. But tenancy is expressed through namespace segmentation rather than an
organization construct, which suits a single operational organization or a centralized infrastructure team.

platform for running AI/ML workloads.

Design Options
When deploying VKS clusters for AI and ML workloads in VMware Private AI Foundation, organizations have two primary
deployment approaches that differ significantly in complexity and control. The choice between deploying through the
VCF Automation catalog versus manual kubectl-based deployment depends on your team's Kubernetes expertise, need
for customization, and infrastructure-as-code requirements. Understanding these differences helps determine which
approach aligns best with your operational model and technical capabilities.
The VCF Automation catalog approach provides a self-service deployment experience that reduces the complexity of
standing up GPU-accelerated Kubernetes clusters. When using the catalog, users interact with a form-based interface
where they select VM classes, specify node counts, and configure GPU sharing parameters without needing to write any
YAML or understand the intricacies of Kubernetes cluster provisioning. The catalog item automates the installation of the
NVIDIA GPU operator at deployment time, which eliminates the need to manually download Helm charts from the NVIDIA
NGC catalog, install the NGC CLI, or manage GPU operator installation scripts. This approach abstracts away a large part
Broadcom 2423

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
of the manual steps required for cluster deployment, making it accessible to ML engineers and data scientists who may
have only basic Kubernetes knowledge.
Manual VKS cluster deployment via kubectl offers complete control over every aspect of cluster configuration at the cost
of increased complexity. This approach requires administrators to create detailed YAML specifications that define the
cluster control plane and worker nodes, and manually install the NVIDIA GPU operator using Helm charts downloaded
from the NGC catalog. The manual deployment process involves many discrete steps spanning cluster provisioning,
GPU operator installation, NIM deployment, and application configuration. However, this investment in complexity
yields substantial benefits for organizations with advanced requirements. Manual deployment supports both vGPU
and DirectPath I/O GPUs, providing flexibility to choose the GPU virtualization model that best fits specific workload
performance characteristics. It also enables the optional installation of the NVIDIA Network Operator, which is essential
for distributed inference and training scenarios that require high-performance networking across multiple ESX hosts.
Manual deployment provides a true infrastructure-as-code capability where every configuration decision is captured in
version-controlled YAML files, enabling GitOps workflows, automated testing, and consistent deployments across multiple
environments.
Starting with VCF 9.1, both approaches support both vGPU and DirectPath I/O GPUs, enabling optimal GPU virtualization
choices for specific performance requirements.

AI and ML Platform Based on Deep Learning Virtual Machines Model
This model provides pre-configured Deep Learning Virtual Machines that deliver immediate GPU-accelerated compute
environments for machine learning workloads, complete with popular AI/ML frameworks and tools from NVIDIA NGC.

Design Options
When deploying Deep Learning Virtual Machines in VMware Private AI Foundation, organizations can choose from three
distinct approaches based on user roles, technical expertise, and infrastructure requirements.
The VCF Automation catalog approach targets data scientists and ML engineers who need rapid access to GPU-
accelerated development environments without infrastructure expertise. Users interact with a form-based interface to
customize machine parameters, select AI/ML frameworks, and specify NGC packages. This self-service model abstracts
away all YAML and OVF configuration complexity, but requires a fully configured VCF Automation infrastructure, an All
Apps organization, and Supervisor-enabled clusters.
The kubectl deployment method serves DevOps engineers with Kubernetes knowledge who need granular control over
VM specifications. Administrators create YAML manifests defining all configuration parameters, including networking,
storage, and GPU assignments, while managing cloud-init files for workload automation. It requires Kubernetes
competency and comfort with kubectl operations, but eliminates dependency on VCF Automation, needing only an
enabled Supervisor vSphere cluster. In this case, the supervisor manages the lifecycle of the virtual machine. Interacting
with the supervisor is possible via kubectl or by installing the local consumption interface supervisor service, which
provides a graphical user interface. Leveraging the standard vSphere Client UI workflows is not supported for supervisor
managed virtual machines.
Direct deployment through the vSphere Client suits VI administrators preferring traditional virtualization workflows with
complete independence from both VCF Automation and Supervisor infrastructure. Administrators deploy from content
libraries directly onto vSphere clusters, manually configuring OVF properties through the deployment wizard. This method
provides full configuration control, but demands a detailed understanding of OVF properties and manual cloud-init file
management, including base64 encoding.
Starting with VCF 9.1, all approaches support both vGPU and DirectPath I/O GPUs, enabling optimal GPU virtualization
choices for specific performance requirements.

Private AI Compute Detailed Design
VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) offers three distinct compute models to support AI applications.
Overview
vGPU enables multiple virtual machines to share a single physical GPU through either time-sliced execution or hardware-
isolated partitions (MIG). It also enables pooling multiple GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX platform. This model balances
performance with operational flexibility, supporting live migration and efficient resource pooling, though it requires NVIDIA
licensing and introduces an additional software layer.
DirectPath (Passthrough) dedicates one or more entire physical GPUs to a single virtual machine, providing bare-metal
performance with minimal overhead. This approach offers the highest performance for GPU-intensive workloads but
sacrifices flexibility. VMs cannot be live migrated and each GPU serves only one VM at a time. Pooling multiple GPUs on
the NVIDIA HGX platform requires additional software components on the workloads VMs.
CPU-only inference eliminates GPU hardware entirely by running AI workloads on standard CPU cores using optimized
runtimes like llama.cpp. While offering complete operational flexibility and zero specialized hardware costs, this approach
delivers lower throughput and is best suited for smaller models and less demanding inference tasks.
Accelerator Design Based on AI/ML Workloads Requirements
Foundational Concepts for GPU Sizing
For practical sizing examples, please refer to this blog.
Model Parameters and Memory Format
Large Language Models consist of billions of parameters (weights) that define the model's behavior. These parameters
are typically stored in FP16 (16-bit floating point) format, requiring 2 bytes per parameter. An 8 billion parameter model,
therefore, requires 16 GB of memory just to store the weights (8B × 2 bytes), while a 70 billion parameter model requires
140 GB. This memory footprint is fixed and must be loaded into GPU memory before the model can perform inference.
The Two Phases of LLM Inference
Broadcom 2427

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
LLM inference occurs in two distinct phases. The prefill phase processes the user's input prompt, computing attention
for all prompt tokens simultaneously in parallel. The generation phase then produces the response one token at a time
sequentially, with each new token depending on all previous tokens. This fundamental difference, parallel vs sequential
processing, determines which hardware resources bottleneck each phase.
KV Cache
The KV (Key-Value) cache stores intermediate attention results from previously processed tokens, enabling the model to
avoid recomputing attention for the entire conversation history when generating each new token. Each user conversation
maintains its own separate KV cache containing its unique context, while all users share the same read-only model
weights. The KV cache size per token is determined by the model architecture using the formula: 2 matrices × 2 bytes
× n_layers × n_kv_heads × d_head. For example, an 8B model with 32 layers and 8 KV heads has a KV cache size
of 0.000122 GiB per token. As conversations grow longer or more users connect concurrently, KV cache memory
consumption increases proportionally.
Attention Heads
Attention heads are parallel attention mechanisms within each transformer layer that allow the model to focus on different
aspects of the input simultaneously. Each attention head learns to attend to different patterns or relationships in the
data, for example, one head might focus on syntactic relationships while another captures semantic meaning. In the
attention mechanism, the input is projected into Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices, and each head performs
these projections independently with its own learned weights. The number of attention heads varies by model architecture:
smaller models might have 32 heads while larger models can have 64 or more. The dimension per head (d_head) is
calculated by dividing the model's hidden dimension by the number of heads. For memory efficiency, many modern LLMs
use Grouped Query Attention (GQA), where multiple query heads share the same key-value head, significantly reducing
KV cache memory requirements. The n_kv_heads parameter in the KV cache formula refers to these shared key-value
heads rather than the total number of query heads.
Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bound Operations
Prefill is compute-bound because it processes many tokens in parallel, reusing the same loaded weights across all
tokens, in this case the GPU's computational cores become the bottleneck.
Generation is memory-bound because the GPU must load the entire model (16 GB for an 8B model) from High Bandwidth
Memory (HBM) to cache for each token generated. The GPU spends most of its time waiting for this data transfer rather
than computing. The time to generate a token is determined primarily by how fast weights can be loaded: generation_time
= model_bytes ÷ memory_bandwidth.
GPU Memory Hierarchy
GPUs have a memory hierarchy with vastly different speeds and capacities. HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is the main
GPU memory—large (48-141 GB) but relatively slow (864-3,350 GB/s). L1/L2 cache is on-chip memory—extremely fast
(10,000+ GB/s) but tiny (~40-50 MB). Model weights are stored in HBM, but computation happens in GPU cores that
access data through cache. Since a 16 GB model cannot fit in 40 MB of cache, weights must be continuously streamed
from HBM through cache during inference, with different weight segments constantly loaded and evicted. This streaming
from HBM to cache is what creates the memory bandwidth bottleneck during token generation.
Context Window
Context window refers to the total number of tokens stored in the KV cache for a single user's conversation, calculated as
prompt_length + generated_response_length. This differs from a model's maximum context capacity—the architectural
limit it supports (e.g., 8K, 128K tokens). While a model may support 128K tokens maximum, real applications typically use
much shorter contexts (2-6K tokens). Context window directly impacts both memory consumption (longer contexts require
more KV cache memory) and latency (longer contexts take longer to process during prefill).
Batching
Batching refers to processing multiple user requests simultaneously on the same GPU. The model weights are loaded
once from HBM into the cache and then reused to generate tokens for all users in the batch, while each user maintains
their own separate KV cache containing their unique conversation. This amortizes the expensive weight-loading operation
across many users. For an 8 billions parameters model, instead of loading 16 GB for each user sequentially, the GPU
loads 16 GB once and serves all users. Batching dramatically increases total system throughput (tokens/second across all
users) while maintaining similar per-user latency, but is limited by available memory for storing multiple users' KV caches.
Broadcom 2428

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Data Parallelism vs Tensor Parallelism
Data parallelism deploys independent, complete copies of the model across multiple GPUs, with a load balancer
distributing user requests among replicas. Each GPU operates independently without inter-GPU communication.
Tensor parallelism splits a single model across multiple GPUs, with each GPU holding a fraction of the model's weights
and layers. During inference, GPUs must communicate during every forward pass to exchange intermediate results.
Data parallelism is simpler and achieves near-linear scaling but multiplies memory requirements (N replicas need N× the
model weight memory). Tensor parallelism is more memory-efficient and necessary when models exceed single-GPU
capacity, but it introduces communication overhead that degrades performance and requires high-speed interconnects like
NVLink.

vGPU Compute Model Attributes
| Attribute | Detail |     |     |

Platform type Flexible GPU allocation, from fractional sharing to multiple dedicated physical GPUs per VM
Resource sharing GPU sharing is enabled via Time-sliced mode (multiple VMs share GPU resources serially) or
MIG mode (hardware-isolated GPU partitions). Dedicating a full GPU or multiple GPUs to a
workload is also supported.
•
Performance Near bare-metal performance for dedicated full GPU profiles.

• MIG: consistent performance with hardware isolation and QoS guarantees
Live Migration Support Fully supported unless UVM is enabled for the VM (UVM is required for multi-GPU profiles)
High Availability • Full DRS integration for intelligent initial placement and load balancing

Supports fully automated cluster operations like maintenance mode (UVM VMs must be

Figure 390: Direct Path GPUs Compute Model in VMware Cloud Foundation
Direct Path GPUs Compute Model Attributes
Attribute Detail
Platform type Dedicated GPU assignment: one or multiple physical GPUs exclusively allocated to one VM
Resource sharing No sharing: GPU dedicated to a single VM
Performance Bare-metal equivalent performance with direct hardware access. Predictable and consistent,
no co-tenant impact
Live Migration Support Not supported: VM cannot be live migrated (vMotion unavailable)
High Availability • DRS can place a VM on any compatible host at power-on
• HA can restart the VM on alternate hosts.
GPU Pooling • To leverage NVLink/NVSwitch functionality, all GPUs and NVSwitches must be configured
as passthrough devices and assigned to the workload
• Multi-GPU configurations may communicate via the PCIe bus without proper placement
and Guest Driver configuration based on GPU topology
• NVIDIA GPU fabric manager software must be installed on a workload VM
Licensing Requirements No additional GPU software licensing required
Operational complexity Simpler software stack, standard workload GPU drivers only. No hypervisor GPU manager
layer.
Use Cases • Environments where workload requirements are clear, and the infrastructure can be
designed accordingly.
• Tight collaboration between the infrastructure team and the ML/AI platform team.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Planning and Preparation
As a VI administrator, size your environment and create a specification of the software, tools, and external services that
are required to build a VCF private cloud.
VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook
The workbook is a Microsoft Excel file that helps you gather the inputs that are required for deploying a VCF fleet
including workload domains, identity broker, vSphere Supervisor, and VCF Automation. You use the VCF 9.1.0 Planning
and Preparation Workbook or VCF 9.1.1 Planning and Preparation Workbook for understanding the prerequisites for
deploying the VCF fleet and VCF Instances, sizing your environment, as a dynamic VCF environment specification, for
updating requirements according to your design, and more.
VCF Planning Tools
You can use the VMware Configurations Maximums and VMware Ports and Protocols tools to plan the VCF setup that can
run your end user workloads according to the requirements of your organization.
Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes. For information about how to get onboarded to VCF, see Overview of VCF Deploy, Converge, and Upgrade.
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.

VCF Components FQDNs and IP addresses
Before you deploy VMware Cloud Foundation or vSphere Foundation, you must plan and allocate fully qualified domain
names (FQDNs) and IP addresses for all VCF components. Proper DNS and IP planning ensures successful deployment
and prevents address conflicts with existing infrastructure.
FQDN and IP address requirements vary depending on your deployment scenario.
• First VCF Instance FQDNs and IP addresses. The FQDNs and IP address requirements for the first VCF Instance in
a VCF fleet, including IP address ranges and sizing guidance for the VCF management network.
• Additional VCF Instance FQDNs and IP addresses. The incremental FQDN and IP address requirements when
deploying a subsequent VCF Instance in a VCF fleet.
• vSphere Foundation FQDNs and IP Addresses. The FQDN and IP address requirements specific to a vSphere
Foundation platform deployment.
Dual Stack Supported VCF Components
VCF 9.1 and later supports IPv4 only and dual stack (IPv4 and IPv6) networking, but not every VCF component supports
both stack configurations. VCF applies dual stack as a domain-wide setting, not a per-component choice. When you
enable dual stack, all dual stack-capable components receive both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Components that support
only IPv4 are provisioned with IPv4 addresses only.
A dual stack component supports either IPv4 only or both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. In a dual stack deployment,
communication uses IPv6 when both endpoints support it. Otherwise, IPv4 only.
Note:
For components that support dual stack networking, the FQDNs you configure must resolve to both IPv4 and IPv6
addresses.
For more information about dual stack networking and which VCF components support each IP family, see Dual Stack IP
Addressing Model.
First VCF Instance FQDNs and IP addresses
VCF requires unique fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) and static IP addresses for all VCF components, along with
properly configured forward (A) and reverse (PTR) DNS resolution for each. The top-level domain (TLD) label in the
FQDN must contain ASCII letters only.
Each FQDN must resolve to a unique, currently unassigned IP address, and those IP addresses must not overlap with
any IP ranges already reserved for VCF services runtime nodes or VCF Automation nodes. Unlike VCF Installer, which
requires a strict, predefined number of FQDNs and IP addresses, Day-N components have variable requirements that
depend on future deployment plans and scaling objectives.

vSphere Supervisor, do not support  .local  domains. Traditional virtual appliances, such as vCenter, ESX hosts,

Additional VCF Instance FQDNs and IP addresses
Additional VCF instances require unique FQDNs and static IP addresses for all VCF components, along with properly
configured forward (A) and reverse (PTR) DNS resolution for each. The top-level domain (TLD) label in the FQDN must
contain ASCII letters only.
Each FQDN must resolve to a unique, currently unassigned IP address, and those IP addresses must not overlap with
any IP ranges already reserved for VCF services runtime nodes or VCF Automation nodes. Unlike VCF Installer, which
requires a strict, predefined number of FQDNs and IP addresses, Day-N components have variable requirements that
depend on future deployment plans and scaling objectives.
Note:
Containerized services, such as VCF management services, VCF Automation, VCF Identity Broker, and VMware
vSphere Supervisor, do not support  .local  domains. Traditional virtual appliances, such as vCenter, ESX hosts,

Network Deployment Options for VCF Components
VCF supports flexible network placement for its components, providing control over traffic isolation, security boundaries,
and alignment with your existing infrastructure.
VM Management Network and VCF Management Network Options
Before you deploy VCF, you must determine how the VCF components are distributed across your network.
• VM management network carries traffic for core VCF management components, such as vCenter, NSX, SDDC
Manager, and cloud proxy. By default, this traffic runs on the ESX management network. If simplicity is a priority,
placing all VCF management components on the ESX management network is a supported option.
• With VCF 9.1 and later, VCF management network carries traffic for VCF management services, VCF Operations,
license server, and VCF Automation. You can place these components on the ESX management network, on the VM
Management Network, or on a dedicated network. By default, VCF management services share the VM management
network. If your environment requires strict network segmentation or must meet regulatory requirements, use a
dedicated VCF management network instead. See VCF Management Network Models.
• A dedicated network reduces the network incidents impact and simplifies firewall policy management and traffic
monitoring. If your organization requires separation between ESX host management traffic and the management
components, for example, for security, compliance, or operational clarity, direct this traffic to a dedicated network
segment.

Deployment, Convergence, and Upgrade
Get to VMware Cloud Foundation or VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x. Use VCF Installer and VCF Operations for
automated deployment workflows and manually deploy the final components to complete your platform.
You can deploy a new VCF or vSphere Foundation platform on pre-installed ESX hosts by using VCF Installer.
You can also use your existing virtual infrastructure, in multiple scenarios, as building blocks and converge it to a VCF or
vSphere Foundation platform.
You can upgrade your existing VCF 5.2.x or 9.0.x VCF environment to VCF 9.1.x.
You can only upgrade your VCF environment to a version that is released after the release date of your current VCF
version. See VMware Interoperability Matrix.
In This Chapter
• Paths to Building 9.1.x Environments
• Components in VCF and vSphere Foundation
• Deploying a New VCF or vSphere Foundation Platform
• Converging Existing Virtual Infrastructure to a VCF or a vSphere Foundation Platform
• Upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Upgrading to vSphere Foundation 9.1.x
• Upgrading vSphere 8 and Optionally vSAN and Aria Operations 8 to 9.1.x
VCF Upgrade Planner
You can now use the new VCF Upgrade Planning Tool to navigate you during the process of upgrading or converging
your existing infrastructure to vSphere Foundation and VCF 9.1.x. Different tailored scenarios exist for starting from just
vSphere or different other combinations that include NSX, Aria components and so on.
Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes.
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.
Paths to Building 9.1.x Environments
Multiple paths exist to get to VCF and vSphere Foundation 9.1. Depending on your starting state, you follow one of the
paths.
Depending on the starting state of your environment, you have three paths to VCF or vSphere Foundation environments:
• Deploy a VCF Instance in a new or existing VCF fleet, or deploy new vSphere Foundation instance.
• Use existing virtual infrastructure as building blocks to converge to a new VCF fleet, a VCF Instance in an existing
fleet, or vSphere Foundation .
• Upgrade your existing VCF Instances to a 9.1.x VCF fleet or upgrade your vSphere Foundation to 9.1.x.
The scope of the deploy, converge, and upgrade guidance for VCF is management domain-only as this is the minimum
logical block to form the first VCF Instance in a VCF fleet. The version of the management domain also defines the VCF
Instance version.
Broadcom 2459

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Deploying New VCF or vSphere Foundation 9.1.x
To deploy a new VCF fleet, VCF Instance, or vSphere Foundation, see Deploying a New VCF or vSphere Foundation
Platform.
Starting with version 9, the deployment process changes and you now install most of the components by using VCF
Installer and VCF Operations workflows. Deployment of standalone components by deploying an OVA is typically not
supported, apart from specific scenarios where you are explicitly instructed to do so.
• For information about the components installed by VCF Installer, see VCF Installer Overview.
• For information about the components you install after the VCF Installer workflow, see Completing the Deployment of
Your Platform.
By following the deployment guidance, you can directly deploy VCF 9.1.1 without first deploying 9.1.0 and then patching to
9.1.1.
Converging to VCF 9.1.x
To converge your vSphere 8 and Aria 8 components to a VCF fleet or VCF Instance, you follow a specific convergence
order. Depending on your existing components, proceed with one of the convergence scenarios:
• Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, and Optionally vSAN and NSX
• Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, VMware Aria Operations, and Optionally vSAN and NSX
• Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, VMware Aria Operations, and Optionally vSAN and NSX
• Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, VMware Aria Automation, and Optionally vSAN and NSX
• Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, VMware Aria Operations, and VMware Aria Automation, and Optionally
vSAN and NSX
For supported and unsupported configurations to converge to VCF, see Supported and Not Supported Configurations to
Converge to VCF.
Note:
Convergence of vSphere Foundation 9.1 with deployed VCF management services to VCF 9.1 is not supported.
Converging to vSphere Foundation 9.1.x
To converge your vSphere 8 components to vSphere Foundation 9.1, you follow a specific convergence order. See
Converge a vCenter Instance and ESX Hosts to vSphere Foundation.
Upgrading Existing VCF Instance or Fleet to 9.1.x
If you have an existing VCF 5.2.x or 9.0.x environment, see Upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x.
Upgrading Existing vSphere Foundation to 9.1.x
If you have an existing vSphere Foundation 5.2.x or 9.0.x environment, see Upgrading to vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.
Upgrading vSphere 8 and Optionally Aria Operations 8 to 9.1.x
If you have an existing vSphere 8 environment that can also have Aria Operations 8 and you want to upgrade to 9.1

VCF Management Services
VCF 9.1 introduces VCF management services to provide a unified architecture for centralized lifecycle and operational
functionalities. The VCF services runtime instance of the first VCF Instance hosts the fleet-level VCF management
services components that perform global operations and the instance-level components for that VCF Instance. Every VCF
Instance has a VCF services runtime instance that hosts the instance-level VCF management services. This foundation
allows for a unified architecture, simplified lifecycle management, and streamlined backup and recovery of all hosted
components.
For vSphere Foundation, VCF management services are optional. For vSphere Foundation environments with VCF
management services, every component gets deployed on the vCenter instance.
The following components are part of VCF management services. Certain components are deployed as part of the initial
deployment or upgrade to 9.1 and you deploy other components as a Day-N operation.

Preparing to Deploy a VCF or vSphere Foundation Platform
Before you can use the VCF Installer to deploy a new VMware Cloud Foundation or VMware vSphere Foundation
platform, you must prepare your environment.
Before you start deploying a new platform, you must deploy and configure the necessary infrastructure. You use
the planning section of VCF Installer to gather the information you require to deploy VCF or vSphere Foundation.
Alternatively, you can use the Planning and Preparation Workbook. See Planning and Preparation. You can also refer to
the VMware Cloud Foundation Design for specific requirements and recommendations for the design of each component.
Before you deploy a new platform, you must:
• Review the prerequisites page in VCF Installer.
–
Alternatively, review the prerequisite checklist in the Planning and Preparation Workbook. See Planning and
Preparation.
• Image your ESX hosts. See Preparing ESX Hosts for VCF or vSphere Foundation.
• Download the VCF Installer appliance from the Broadcom Support portal.
Broadcom 2467

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• If the VCF Installer appliance does not have direct access to the Internet, to download VCF installation binaries from
the Broadcom online depot (dl.broadcom.com), you download the VCF download tool from the Broadcom Support
portal (support.broadcom.com). Then, you create an offline depot and download the VCF binaries to the offline depot
or download and transfer the installation binaries manually to VCF Installer.
Preparing ESX Hosts for VCF or vSphere Foundation
Before you deploy a new VMware Cloud Foundation or VMware vSphere Foundation platform, you must prepare the ESX
hosts.
Note:
The number of required hosts depends on the type of storage and the deployment model that you plan to use.
You use the planning section of VCF Installer to determine the minimum number of ESX hosts required for your
environment. Alternatively, you can use the Planning and Preparation Workbook. See Planning and Preparation.
Preparing the ESX hosts involves installing the correct version of ESX and performing some basic configuration tasks. For
the supported ESX version, see the VMware Cloud Foundation Release Notes.
Note:
• VMware Cloud Foundation does not support stateless ESX hosts.
• VMware Cloud Foundation does not support heterogeneous cluster configurations during initial management
domain deployment. During this phase, vCenter is not yet available to manage cluster composition, requiring
all hosts in the initial cluster to share a uniform hardware profile.
• All VMware ESX hosts within the management domain must originate from a single hardware vendor. Cross-
vendor hardware configurations in the management domain are not supported.
With VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0.1 and later, you can use non-certified ESA disks during vSAN ESA cluster
configuration for proof-of-concept purposes only. For more information, see Broadcom knowledge base article 408300.
Custom ISO Image for ESX Hosts
If your environment requires a custom ISO file for ESX, you can create one using VCF PowerCLI or vSphere Lifecycle.
See Creating a Custom ESX ISO Image Using VCF PowerCLI and Creating a Custom ESX ISO Image Using vSphere
Lifecycle Manager.
You must create a custom ISO image for ESX in the following situations.
• The ESX version specified in the VMware Cloud Foundation Release Notes does not have an associated ISO file on
the Broadcom Support Portal. This can be the case for ESX patch releases.
• You need an async patch version of ESX.
• You need a vendor-specific (OEM) ISO file.
Install ESX on Hosts Using an ISO Image
Install ESX on all hosts you plan to use in your VMware Cloud Foundation or VMware vSphere Foundation platform.
Download the ESX ISO from the Broadcom Support Portal. For the supported ESX versions, see the VMware Cloud
Foundation Release Notes. If the required version of ESX does not have an ISO available on the Broadcom Support
Portal, you can create one. See Creating a Custom ESX ISO Image Using VCF PowerCLI or Creating a Custom ESX ISO
Image Using vSphere Lifecycle Manager.
Broadcom 2468

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Mount the ESX ISO on the host and restart the machine.
2. Set the BIOS or UEFI to boot from the mounted ISO.
3. On the welcome screen, press Enter to continue.
4. Accept the End User License Agreement by pressing Enter.
5. On the Select a Disk to Install or Upgrade screen, select the drive on which to install ESX on and press Enter.
6. Select the keyboard type for the host.
You can change the keyboard type after installation in the direct console.
7. Enter the root password for the host.
8. In the Confirm Install screen, press F11 to confirm the start of the installation.
9. On the Installation Complete screen, press Enter to reboot the host.
10.Set the first boot device to be the drive on which you installed ESX.
11.Repeat this procedure for all remaining hosts.
Configure the Network on the ESX Hosts
Use the ESX Direct Console User Interface (DCUI) for host network configuration and administrative access.
Perform the following tasks to configure the host network settings:
• Configure the network adapter (vmk0) and VLAN ID for the Management Network.
• Configure the IP address, subnet mask, gateway, DNS server, and FQDN for the ESX host.
Repeat this procedure for all hosts that you are adding to your VCF or VMware vSphere Foundation platform. If you
completed the Planning and Preparation Workbook, refer to it for the required values.
Before the VCF deployment begins, network adapter (vmk0) must be connected to a single management NIC on a
vSphere Standard Switch, for example, vmnic0. During the deployment process, VCF Installer migrates the ESX host to a
vSphere Distributed Switch and adds the required uplinks.
1. Open the DCUI of the ESX host.
a) Open a console window to the host.
b) Press F2 to enter the DCUI.
c) Log in using the .
esx_root_user_password
2. Configure the network.
a) Select Configure Management Network and press Enter.
b) Select VLAN (Optional) and press Enter.
c) Enter the VLAN ID for the ESX Management Network and press Enter.
d) Select IPv4 Configuration and press Enter.
e) Select Set static IPv4 address and network configuration and press the Space bar.
f) Enter the IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask, Default gateway, and press Enter.
g) If you plan to use dual-stack networking, configure an IPv6 address.
1. Select IPv6 Configuration and press Enter.
2. Select Set static IPv6 address and network configuration and press the Space bar.
3. Enter the IPv6 Address, CIDR, Default gateway, and press Enter.
Broadcom 2469

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
h) Select DNS Configuration and press Enter.
i) Select Use the following DNS Server address and hostname and press the Space bar.
j) Enter the Primary DNS Server, Alternate DNS Server and Hostname (FQDN) and press Enter.
k) Select Custom DNS Suffixes and press Enter.
l) Ensure that no suffixes are listed and press Enter.
3. Press Escape to exit and press Y to confirm the changes.
4. Repeat this procedure for all remaining hosts.
Configure NTP on the ESX Hosts
After you have configured the Virtual Machine Network port group, configure the NTP service to avoid time
synchronization issues.
Repeat this procedure for all ESX hosts you are adding. If you completed the Planning and Preparation Workbook, refer to
it for the required values.
1. In a web browser, log in to the ESX host using the VMware Host Client.
2. Configure and start the NTP service.
a) In the navigation pane, click Host > Configure > Time Configuration.
b) In the Network Time Protocol section, click EDIT.
The Edit Network Time Protocol dialog box appears.
c) Select the Enable check box.
d) Enter the NTP Server FQDN or IP Address and click OK.
3. Optional: Verify that the service is running.
4. Repeat this procedure for all remaining hosts.
Regenerate the Self-Signed Certificate on the ESX Hosts
After you have configured the NTP, you must regenerate the self-signed certificate to ensure that the correct common
name is defined in the certificate.
During the installation of ESX, the installer generates a self-signed certificate for each ESX host, but the process is
performed prior to the ESX hostname being configured. This means that all ESX hosts have a common name in their
self-signed certificate of . All communication between the VCF Installer and the ESX hosts
localhost.localdomain
is performed securely over HTTPS and as a result it validates the identity when making a connection by comparing the
common name of the certificate against the FQDN provided within the VCF Installer deployment wizard.
To ensure that the connection attempts and validation do not fail, you must manually regenerate the self-signed certificate
after the hostname has been configured.
Note:
If corporate policy requires that you use external CA-signed certificates instead of VMCA-signed certificates for
ESX hosts, you can add external certificates to the hosts using the SDDC Manager API.
1. In a web browser, log in to the ESX host using the VMware Host Client.
2. In the Actions menu, click Services > Enable Secure Shell (SSH).
3. Log in to the ESX host using an SSH client such as Putty.
4. Validate the ESX hostname and Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN).
esxcli system hostname get
If the FQDN is not configured correctly, you can edit it by running the
esxcli system hostname set --
NEW_FQDN command.
fqdn=
5. Regenerate the self-signed certificate by executing the following command:
/sbin/generate-certificates
Broadcom 2470

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. Reboot the ESX host.
7. Log back in to the VMware Host Client and click Services > Disable Secure Shell (SSH) from the Actions menu.
8. Repeat this procedure for all remaining hosts.
Configure ESX Hosts with Signed Certificates
If corporate policy requires that you use external CA-signed certificates instead of VMCA-signed certificates for ESX
hosts, you can manually add external certificates to the hosts.
External CA-signed certificate and key are available.
When you install ESX software on a server to create an ESX host, the host initially has an autogenerated certificate.
By default, when the ESX host is added to a vSphere cluster during deployment of the management domain or
other operations involving ESX hosts (for example, host commissioning, workload domain creation, and so on), the
autogenerated certificate is replaced with a certificate that is signed by the VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA).
When you use external certificates during deployment, they are not replaced by VMCA-signed certificates. After you
perform deployment with external certificates for ESX hosts, all future ESX hosts added to VCF must also use external
certificates.
To deploy the management domain using external certificates, you must use a JSON specification file with the VCF
Installer. You cannot use the VCF Installer deployment wizard. In the JSON specification file, use the
SecuritySpec
section in the to specify a value of for . For example:
SddcSpec Custom esxiCertsMode

Creating a Custom ESX ISO Image Using VCF PowerCLI
You can use VCF PowerCLI to create a custom ISO for installing ESX.
• Verify that your VCF PowerCLI version is 9.1 or later.
• Verify that you downloaded the following files.
ZIP
– ESX patch for the ESX version specified in the VMware Cloud Foundation Release Notes or in the list of supported
async patches in Broadcom knowledge base article 88287. You can download patches from the Broadcom Support
Portal.
– OEM add-on for ESX from the Broadcom Support Portal. If the ESX version specified in the BOM is not available,
contact your vendor to determine which OEM add-on version to use.
1. Gather the required information for the software spec that is used to create the custom ISO.
a) In VCF PowerCLI, use the cmdlet to get the base image version from the zip file for the
Get-DepotBaseImages
ESX patch that you downloaded from the patches portal.
For example:
Get-DepotBaseImages “c:\temp\VMware-ESX-9.1.x-xxxxxxx-depot.zip”
b) Use the cmdlet to get the add-on name and version from the zip file for the OEM add-on for
Get-DepotAddons
ESX that you downloaded from the Broadcom Support Portal. (if applicable)
For example:
Get-DepotAddons “c:\temp\HPE-9.1.x.x.x-xxx-Synergy-Addon-depot.zip”
2. Create the software spec using the information you gathered in step 1.
The software spec is a JSON file that contains information about the ESX version and vendor add-on (if applicable).
For example:
{
"add_on": {
"name": "HPE-Custom-Syn-AddOn",
"version": "9.1.x.x.x.x-xx"
},
"base_image": {
"version": "9.1.x-x.xx.xxxxxxxx"
},
"components": null,
"hardware_support": null,
"solutions": null
}
3. In VCF PowerCLI, use the cmdlet to generate a custom ISO.
New-IsoImage
For example:
New-IsoImage -SoftwareSpec “c:\temp\HPE-70U1d-custom.JSON” -Depots “c:\temp\VMware-ESX-9.0-17551050-
depot.zip” , “c:\temp\HPE-9.1.x.xx.x.x.xx-xxxxxxx-Synergy-Addon-depot.zip” -Destination “c:\temp\HPE-9.1-
custom.iso”
Provide the path to the software spec you created in step 2.
The depot(s) include the path to the zip files for the supported ESX version and vendor add-on.
Broadcom 2472

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The destination includes the path and file name for the custom ISO file.
For more information about the cmdlet, see New-IsoImage.
New-IsoImage

Deploy the VCF Installer appliance on a network that can access the ESX hosts and VM management network that you
plan to use for the deployment. The appliance must be able to access all required external services, such as DNS and

Where you deploy the VCF Installer appliance impacts how it can be used. You can deploy the appliance:
• Outside of the management infrastructure on any machine with connectivity to the management infrastructure. In this
case, you can use the appliance to deploy multiple VCF or vSphere Foundation platforms. You can deploy the VCF
Installer appliance on a vCenter instance or on a laptop running VMware Workstation or VMware Fusion.
• On one of the ESX hosts that will form the management domain. In this case, you can only use the appliance to deploy
a single VCF platform. Then the appliance switches to SDDC Manager mode, can no longer be used in installer mode,
and you use the VCF Installer FQDN for SDDC Manager.

Downloading Binaries to VCF Installer
Before you can deploy VMware vSphere Foundation or VMware Cloud Foundation, you must download the required
binaries to the VCF Installer appliance.
Table 959: VCF Installer Depot Connection Modes
You can configure the VCF Installer depot in the following connection modes.
Connection Mode Description
Online Depot If the VCF Installer appliance can connect to the Internet (either directly or through a proxy server), you
can connect it to the Broadcom depot and download the binaries by using your VMware Cloud Foundation
Business Services console account. For more information, see Connect VCF Installer to Broadcom or an
Offline Depot and Download Binaries.
Offline Depot If the VCF Installer appliance cannot connect to the Internet, you can connect it to an offline depot and use
the VCF download tool to download the required binaries to the offline depot. For more information, see
Connect VCF Installer to Broadcom or an Offline Depot and Download Binaries and Download Installation
Binaries to an Offline Depot.
Manual Transfer If the VCF Installer appliance cannot connect to an online or offline depot, you can use the VCF download
tool to download binaries to a computer with access to the Internet and then upload them to the VCF
Installer appliance. For more information, see Manually Transfer Binaries to VCF Installer.
Broadcom 2477

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Connect VCF Installer to Broadcom or an Offline Depot and Download Binaries
If VCF Installer can connect to the Internet, either directly or through a proxy server, you register it with Broadcom by
using your VMware Cloud Foundation Business Services console account. If VCF Installer cannot connect to the Internet,
you can connect it to an offline depot. After VCF Installer is connected, you can download the installation binaries from the
configured source.
• If you configure an online depot, for information about the URLs that must be accessible to download bundles, see
Broadcom knowledge base article 327186.
• If you configure an offline depot, verify that you deployed and configured an offline depot web server, and downloaded
required component binaries to the offline depot. See Set Up an Offline Depot and Download Installation Binaries to an
Offline Depot.
• Verify that your VCF Business Services console role has sufficient permissions. See Access Management.
You can only connect the VCF Installer appliance to one type of depot. If VCF Installer is connected to an online depot
and you configure a connection to an offline depot, the online depot connection is deactivated and the configuration is
deleted.
Note:
In environments where SSL/TLS interception is enabled, VCF Installer might not establish a trusted connection to
the Broadcom authorization server. For more information on adding your proxy's CA certificate to the truststore of
software depot, see Broadcom knowledge base article 442978.

Download Installation Binaries to an Offline Depot
If you are connecting the VCF Installer to an offline depot, you must download the install binaries to the offline depot
before you can use them to deploy VMware vSphere Foundation or VMware Cloud Foundation.
• Verify that you deployed and configured an offline depot web server. See Set Up an Offline Depot.
• The offline depot must have:
– The latest version of the VCF Download Tool. You can download it from the Broadcom Support portal.
– Internet connectivity (either directly or through a proxy) for downloading the bundles and other required files.
– Configure TCP keepalive in your SSH client to prevent socket connection timeouts when using the VCF Download
Tool for long-running operations.
• Connect the VCF Installer to the offline depot. See Connect VCF Installer to Broadcom or an Offline Depot and
Download Binaries.
• Verify that your VCF Business Services console role has sufficient permissions. See Access Management.
You can use the VCF Download Tool to download install bundles to the offline depot.
Note:
The VCF Download Tool is the only supported method for downloading binaries for VCF 9.1 in environments
without access to the Internet. Do not use third-party tools or other methods to download binaries.
In the steps below, where applicable, replace the following values.
Value Description
vcf-source-version Your current VCF version. For example, 9.1.1.0.
/path/to/binaries The download location for the binaries. For example, /var/www.
/path/to/activation-c Path to a text file that contains a single line with your activation code from the VCF Business
ode.txt Services Console.
Broadcom 2480

If the computer hosting the offline depot can only access the Internet using a proxy server, use the following options when
downloading binaries.
Option Description
--proxy-server, -s Provide the proxy server FQDN and port of the proxy server that the VCF Download Tool
uses for Internet access. The required format is <FQDN:Port>. The proxy server must be
reachable from the machine where the tool is running.
For example: --proxyServer proxy.example.com:3128.
--proxy-https Specifies whether the proxy server is configured to be used with HTTPS connections. To
use this option, the proxy certificate must be added to the JRE default trust store of VCF
Download Tool. The exact path to the /cacerts folder depends on the directory where the
VCF Download Tool tar file is extracted.
For example:
• Unix
/opt/obtu/jre/lin64/bin/keytool -importcert -file ca-bundle.crt -
keystore <tool root>/jre/lin64/lib/security/cacerts
• Windows
/opt/obtu/jre/lin64/bin/keytool -importcert -file ca-bundle.crt -
keystore <tool root>/jre/win32/lib/security/cacerts
--proxy-user, -r If the proxy server enforces authentication, this parameter allows you to provide the
necessary username required to authenticate to the proxy server.
For example, --proxy-user username.
--proxy-user-password-file Path to a text file path/to/password.txt containing the password for the provided --
proxy-user. The file should contain the password on a single line.
For example, --proxyPasswordFile path/to/password.txt.
Note:
VMware Cloud Foundation does not support proxy servers with Kerberos or NTLMv2 authentication.

proxy.example.com username path/to/password.txt

Manually Transfer Binaries to VCF Installer
If you cannot connect the VCF Installer appliance to an online or offline depot, use the VCF download tool to download
binaries to a computer with access to the Internet and then upload them to the VCF Installer appliance.
• A Windows or Linux computer with Internet connectivity (either directly or through a proxy) for downloading the binaries
and other required files.
Broadcom 2482

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Configure TCP keepalive in your SSH client to prevent socket connection timeouts when using the VCF download tool
for long-running operations.
• Obtain an activation code from the VCF Business Services Console.
• Create a text file on the VCF Installer appliance that contains the admin@local password.
• Verify that your VCF Business Services console role has sufficient permissions. See Access Management.
Note:
The VCF Download Tool is the only supported method for downloading binaries for VCF 9.1 in environments
without access to the Internet. Do not use third-party tools or other methods to download binaries.
Using the VCF download tool to download binaries involves the following steps:
• Download the latest version of the VCF download tool from the Broadcom Support Portal.
• On a computer with access to the Internet, use the VCF download tool to download the binaries and metadata for
VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF.
• Copy the binaries and metadata to the VCF Installer appliance.
• On the VCF Installer appliance, use the VCF download tool to upload the binaries and metadata to the internal
repository.
In the steps below, where applicable, replace the following values.
Value Description
vcf-source-version Your current VCF version. For example, 9.1.1.0.
/path/to/binaries The download location for the binaries. For example, /var/www.
/path/to/activation-c Path to a text file that contains a single line with your activation code from the VCF Business
ode.txt Services Console.
If the computer with Internet access can only access the Internet using a proxy server, use the following options when
downloading binaries.
Option Description
--proxy-server, -s Provide the proxy server FQDN and port of the proxy server that the VCF Download Tool
uses for Internet access. The required format is <FQDN:Port>. The proxy server must be
reachable from the machine where the tool is running.
For example: --proxyServer proxy.example.com:3128.
--proxy-https Specifies whether the proxy server is configured to be used with HTTPS connections. To
use this option, the proxy certificate must be added to the JRE default trust store of VCF
Download Tool. The exact path to the /cacerts folder depends on the directory where the
VCF Download Tool tar file is extracted.
For example:
• Unix
/opt/obtu/jre/lin64/bin/keytool -importcert -file ca-bundle.crt -
keystore <tool root>/jre/lin64/lib/security/cacerts
• Windows
/opt/obtu/jre/lin64/bin/keytool -importcert -file ca-bundle.crt -
keystore <tool root>/jre/win32/lib/security/cacerts
--proxy-user, -r If the proxy server enforces authentication, this parameter allows you to provide the
necessary username required to authenticate to the proxy server.
For example, --proxy-user username.
--proxy-user-password-file Path to a text file path/to/password.txt containing the password for the provided --
proxy-user. The file should contain the password on a single line.
For example, --proxyPasswordFile path/to/password.txt.
Broadcom 2483

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
VMware Cloud Foundation does not support proxy servers with Kerberos or NTLMv2 authentication.
