VCF Operations Analytics Node Data Storage and Fault Domain Behavior
VCF Operations uses a robust architecture to ensure data availability and fault tolerance across analytics nodes.
Data is stored in pairs of analytics nodes distributed across two fault domains, ensuring continuous availability and
synchronization. Each object is stored in two nodes (primary and replica) across fault domains, providing redundancy and
resilience in case of failures.
Table 972: Key Concepts of Data Storage and Fault Domain Behavior
Key Concept Details
Data Storage and Synchronization When an object is discovered, VCF Operations determines the
primary node to store the data and automatically replicates it to its
paired node in the other fault domain.
Synchronization between the primary and replica nodes ensures
data consistency across fault domains
Fault Domain Resilience Each fault domain contains half of the analytics nodes, and each
node has a paired replica in the other fault domain.
The cluster continues to function without data loss as long as one
node from each pair is available.
Continuous Availability The cluster can tolerate the loss of one fault domain or individual
nodes without data loss, but the system will operate in a degraded
state until the issue is resolved.
Latency and Network Requirements Latency between fault domains must be <10 ms, with peaks up
to 20 ms during 20-second intervals. High latency can impact
synchronization but does not stop the process.
Witness Node Role The witness node ensures cluster health and determines which
fault domain remains online during communication failures.
Broadcom 2549

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 973: Key Scenario and Behavior
Scenario Behavior
Data Storage Data is stored in a primary node and replicated to its paired node
in the other fault domain.
Loss of One Fault Domain The cluster operates in a degraded state but continues without
data loss. The fault domain must be repaired or replaced to
restore full functionality.
Loss of Two Nodes in One Fault Domain The cluster continues to operate as long as one node from each
pair is available.
Loss of Connectivity Between Fault Domains One fault domain will go offline automatically. After connectivity
is restored, the admin must manually bring the fault domain back
online to synchronize data.
Witness Node Unavailability If both fault domains are healthy, the witness node’s unavailability
has no impact. If communication issues occur, the witness
determines which fault domain remains online.
Node Replacement Use the "Replace nodes of cluster" functionality in the admin
UI. Sync time depends on object count, historical data, network
bandwidth, and cluster load.
Latency Exceeds 20 ms Synchronization continues but might be delayed. Latency must
return to <10 ms for optimal performance.
Primary Node Failover If the primary node becomes unavailable, the primary replica node
is promoted. The original primary node becomes the replica when
it returns online.
Entire Fault Domain Replacement If a fault domain is unrecoverable, it can be replaced with
newly deployed nodes. The admin UI allows replacing the
primary replica node.
Load Balancer Support Load balancers are supported for continuous availability.
Node Reboot or Offline Nodes automatically resume operation after reboot or being
brought offline/online. No additional steps are required.

Converging Existing Virtual Infrastructure to a VCF or a vSphere
Foundation Platform
When you converge your existing virtual infrastructure by using VCF Installer, the existing components become part
of the management domain of a new VCF Instance in a new or an existing VCF fleet. The process for converging
includes complying with the general requirements and scenario-specific prerequisites, manual upgrades of your existing
components, and deployments and configurations performed by VCF Installer.
Broadcom 2551

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The following configurations, requirements, and converge scenarios are applicable for your management domain only.
You import and upgrade workload domains in VCF Operations, after you deployed the management domain.
The versions of the converged VCF components determine which VCF features are available in your environment and
the component with the earliest version defines the effective VCF version for the entire instance. VCF features that are
introduced in later versions are available only after all VCF components reach the target version. To access the full feature
set of VCF 9.1.x, upgrade all components to version 9.1.x.
VCF Upgrade Planner
You can now use the new VCF Upgrade Planning Tool to navigate you during the process of converging your existing
infrastructure to vSphere Foundation and VCF 9.1.x. Different tailored scenarios exist for starting from just vSphere or
different other combinations that include NSX, Aria components, and so on.
Upgrading Converged Components
VCF enforces strict upgrade path validation. You can only upgrade your VCF components to a target version that is
released after the release date of your current version. The target version can be a major, minor, or a maintenance
release. In general, you can upgrade directly to a patch release only if you can also upgrade to its parent maintenance
release. For example:
• Supported: VCF 5.2.0 (25 JUN 2024) to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026).
• Not supported: VCF 5.2.4 (27 MAY 2026) to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026).
• Supported: VCF 5.2.4 (27 MAY 2026) to VCF 9.1.1 (03 SEP 2026).
This is valid for all components in a VCF source BoM. For example:
• Supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3a (18 JUN 2024) and ESX 8.0 Update 3 (25
JUN 2024), which are part of VCF 5.2.0 BoM.
• Not supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX 8.0 Update 3j (27
MAY 2026), which are part of VCF 5.2.4 BoM.
• Supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.1 (03 SEP 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX 8.0 Update 3j (27
MAY 2026), which are part of VCF 5.2.4 BoM.
VCF components might have further limitations, see VMware Interoperability Matrix.
Supported and Not Supported Configurations to Converge to VCF
Before you proceed with a supported scenario, verify that your existing configuration is supported.
vCenter and NSX Considerations
• For vCenter instances with existing NSX registration, the convergence procedure brings your vCenter environment
with an existing NSX deployment under SDDC Manager as the management domain. SDDC Manager imports NSX
Manager credentials, registers them in inventory, and explicitly trusts node certificates. vSphere clusters not prepared
for NSX remain unconfigured for NSX.
• For vCenter instances without existing NSX registration, SDDC Manager deploys NSX Manager VMs, configures the
NSX cluster, and registers vCenter as a Compute Manager in NSX. All eligible vSphere clusters in the domain are
prepared for NSX.
Convergence of vCenter instances with existing NSX registrations and without Enhanced Linked Mode (ELM) is
supported. Alternatively, you can deploy a new NSX 9.1.x instance during the convergence operation by using VCF
Installer. The version of the deployed NSX is the latest compatible NSX version for the related vCenter instance. To
change the NSX version, see Broadcom knowledge base article 429205.
• When deploying a new NSX Manager, you can choose between an HA deployment model with a cluster of 3 NSX
Manager nodes or a simple deployment model with 1 NSX Manager.
• You can choose to configure overlay traffic on a management VMkernel or on a VLAN-backed segment.
Broadcom 2552

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
After the convergence, you can only upgrade your VCF environment to a version that is released after the release
date of the earliest version of the existing VCF components, that you selected for convergence. If the NSX version
is released after a specific VCF minor or maintenance release, you cannot upgrade the management domain to
that specific VCF minor or maintenance version. See VMware Interoperability Matrix.
If you are converging an NSX Federation configuration, only the Local Manager is converted. To upgrade such an
environment, see Upgrading NSX Global Manager Nodes in a Federated Environment.
When you converge your existing infrastructure into a management domain, the associated NSX Manager can be shared
with workload domains in the VCF Instance.
Note:
During convergence, VCF Installer treats the network on which the existing vCenter instance resides as the
management network. All VCF management components deployed by VCF Installer, including SDDC Manager,
NSX Manager, VCF Operations, and VCF Automation, must reside on the same subnet as the existing vCenter
instance. For information about network deployment options, see Network Deployment Options for VCF
Components.

After you select a convergence path, depending on the version of your standalone components, you might need to

or VCF deployment. For either path, first verify that you meet the minimum version requirements and supported
configurations.
Converge a vCenter Instance, ESX Hosts, and Optionally vSAN and NSX
To converge your existing vCenter instance and ESX hosts to a management domain, ensure that you comply with the
prerequisites, follow the procedure, and perform the next steps. This scenario supports existing environments with and
without NSX.
Broadcom 2556

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Verify that your existing configuration is supported. See Supported and Not Supported Configurations to Converge to
VCF.
• Verify that your environment satisfies the minimum component versions.
Item VCF 9.1.x Requirements
Minimum component versions • VMware vCenter 8.0 Update 3a
• VMware ESX 8.0 Update 3
• (Optional) vSAN 8.0 Update 3
• (Optional) VMware NSX 4.2.1
To ensure a successful convergence process, you must follow this high-level convergence procedure in the provided
order. Each step includes a dedicated and detailed procedure, that you must complete, before proceeding with the next
one.
1. Deploy the VCF Installer appliance.
See Deploy VCF Installer.
2. Download the binaries for the components that VCF Installer deploys.
See Downloading Binaries to VCF Installer.
3. Ensure that your vCenter instance runs a supported version for your convergence scenario.
• If your vCenter instance is without an existing NSX registration, upgrade your vCenter instance to version 9.1.x.
See Upgrading the vCenter Appliance.
• If your vCenter instance is version 8.0 Update 3a or later and has an existing NSX registration with version 4.2.1 or
later, proceed without upgrading.
4. Converge your existing environment to a VCF platform by using VCF Installer.
VCF Installer validates and uses your existing components, deploys required new components, and configures the
platform. See Deploy Components by Using VCF Installer to Complete the Converging to VCF Process.
5. If VCF Installer deploys a new NSX instance, in VCF Operations, synchronize the inventory of the management
domain.
See Remediate VCF Domain Configuration Drift.

order. Each step includes a dedicated and detailed procedure, that you must complete, before proceeding with the next
one.

A VCF fleet is managed by a single VCF Operations instance. Only the instance you converge during
this procedure to the VCF fleet performs fleet, lifecycle, certificate, and license management of your VCF
environment.
If your existing environment has additional VMware Aria Operations instances, the instances operate in a
monitoring-only capacity only. You can manually upgrade an additional instance to VCF Operations 9.x or if you

Automation Orchestrator.

See Upgrading to VCF Operations 9.1
4. Ensure that your vCenter instance runs a supported version for your convergence scenario.
• If your vCenter instance is without an existing NSX registration, upgrade your vCenter instance to version 9.1.x.
See Upgrading the vCenter Appliance.
• If your vCenter instance is version 8.0 Update 3a or later and has an existing NSX registration with version 4.2.1 or
later, proceed without upgrading.
5. Converge your existing environment to a VCF platform by using VCF Installer.
VCF Installer validates and uses your existing components, deploys required new components, and configures the
platform. See Deploy Components by Using VCF Installer to Complete the Converging to VCF Process.

domain.
See Remediate VCF Domain Configuration Drift.

See Upgrading to VCF Operations 9.1.

Deploy Components by Using VCF Installer to Complete the Converging to VCF
Process
By using VCF Installer, you use your existing vSphere and Aria infrastructure to converge it to a new VCF fleet or a new
VCF Instance in an existing VCF fleet. During the process, VCF Installer deploys all required components that you do not
have in your existing environment and uses your vCenter instance and ESX hosts to create the management domain for
the new instance.
• Download the required binaries for VCF. See Downloading Binaries to VCF Installer.
• Verify that you deployed VCF Installer version 9.1.1 or later. See Deploy VCF Installer.
• Verify that you configured the required FQDNs and IP addresses for deployment. See VCF Components FQDNs and
IP addresses.
• Verify that you meet the requirements and have completed the pre-requisite tasks based on your convergence
scenario. See Supported Components and Scenarios to Converge to VCF.
• If you plan to use a load balancer in your VCF environment, verify it is deployed and configured.
A VCF fleet refers to an environment consisting of one or more VCF Instances and standalone vCenter instances that
are managed by the same VCF Operations instance. If you have a VCF fleet, you can converge your infrastructure to a
new VCF Instance within the fleet by connecting to your existing VCF Operations instance or you can deploy a new VCF
Operations instance to create a new VCF fleet. If you have an existing VCF Operations instance, you can also use it to
create a new VCF fleet.
During the procedure, you plan and gather all the information required for deployment. By specifying the scale of the
deployment and network types, you define the required resources for your deployment. You use the VCF Installer
deployment workflows to specify deployment information specific for your existing environment and other information. As a
result, the VMware Cloud Foundation platform is automatically deployed and configured using the information provided.
You can use the VCF Installer deployment wizard or a custom specification file. For more information, see Use a
JSON
JSON Specification File to Deploy VMware Cloud Foundation or vSphere Foundation.
VCF Installer allows you to skip VCF Automation during the initial deployment and deploy it as a Day-N operation. See
Deploying VCF Automation as a Day-N Operation.
1. In a web browser, log in to the VCF Installer appliance at .
https://installer_appliance_FQDN
Enter the user and password that you provided when you deployed the appliance and click Log In.
admin@local
Broadcom 2562

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. Under Deploy, select Deployment Wizard > VMware Cloud Foundation .
3. Review the introductory information and click Next.
4. Select Deploy a new VCF fleet or Deploy a VCF Instance in an existing VCF fleet.
5. On the Existing Components page, select your existing infrastructure components.
When you connect to your existing components, VCF Installer validates them to ensure compatibility.
When you select an existing VMware vCenter infrastructure, the Storage, Hosts, and Distributed Switch pages of
the wizard are not available.
You can also select the I have an existing VCF Automation instance or I will deploy later check box to deploy
VCF Automation as Day-N operation, instead of using the VCF Installer deployment workflows. See Deploying VCF
Automation as a Day-N Operation.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, it is mandatory that VCF Operations is always deployed in the management domain of the first
VCF Instance in the VCF fleet. If you selected the I have an existing VCF Operations 9.1 instance option, the I have
an existing VMware vCenter option is also always selected.
6. Select a deployment model and the scale for your VCF Instance.
Deployment model You can choose the deployment model for new appliances that
get deployed. High Availability is recommended for production
environments.
Note:
The deployment model that you select does not impact
existing appliances that you are using in your VCF fleet or
VCF Instance.
See the VMware Cloud Foundation Design documentation for
more information.
Note:
New appliances that get deployed are automatically
configured to comply with Federal Information Processing
Standards (FIPS).
Size You can choose the scale of the components in your VCF
Instance.
• Small
– In VCF 9.1, this is the only available option for the simple
deployment model.
– In VCF 9.1.1 and later, this is the default option for the
simple and HA deployment models.
• Medium
– In VCF 9.1, this is the default option for the HA deployment
model.
– In VCF 9.1.1 and later, this is an option for the HA
deployment model.
• Large
– In VCF 9.1 and later, this is an option for the HA
deployment model.
For more information about deployment sizes, see VCF Fleet
Sizing Models.
7. Select your network configuration.
Note:
VCF Installer supports only vCenter instances with IPv4 network configuration and deploys the remaining
components with IPv4 only. If your vCenter instance uses dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) networking, perform your
deployment by using a JSON spec, where all remaining components get deployed in the same configuration.
Broadcom 2563

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To use dual-stack networking, the VCF Installer virtual machine and VCF Installer must have IPv4 and IPv6
configured.
Management network configuration • VM management network: For core VCF components, such as
vCenter, ESX, and NSX. You can share this network with the
ESX management network or use a dedicated network.
• VCF management network: For broader VCF management
and automation components, such as VCF Operations and
VCF Automation. You can share this network with the VM
management network or use a dedicated network.
You can use one of the networks to segment management traffic
for security and compliance requirements. For more information,
see Network Deployment Options for VCF Components.
If you are deploying a new VCF fleet, you can select Deploy VCF Operations and VCF Automation to a specific
vSphere distributed switch or NSX segment. When you select this option, VCF Installer skips the deployment
of VCF Operations, cloud proxy, license server, and VCF Automation. For more information about deploying these
deferred components later, see Deploying Deferred Components on Custom Networking.
Note:
This option is not available when deploying a VCF Instance in an existing VCF fleet or when using an existing
VCF Operations instance.
When selecting this option, some of the pages in the VCF Installer wizard are not available.
8. Review the prerequisites for your deployment.
Depending on your selections in the wizard, the prerequisites for the deployment are listed.
You can click PRE-FILL GENERATED FQDNs IN WIZARD and specify the required FQDNs for the deployment.
You can use the provided template or specify custom FQDNs. These values are later populated in the VCF Installer
deployment workflows.
You can download a JSON template that is based on your choices in the VCF Installer so far. You can populate it
and deploy VCF by using a JSON specification file. See Use a JSON Specification File to Deploy VMware Cloud
Foundation or vSphere Foundation for more information.
9. On the General information page, enter the configuration details for your deployment.

Upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
As a mandatory part of the upgrade to version 9.1.x, you must upgrade your components that run on the fleet level and
the management domain to version 9.1.x. Before you upgrade, it is important to understand how VCF 9 is different from
earlier versions. Upgrading your workload domains is not a mandatory part of the upgrade and can be performed later as
a Day-N procedure.
By following the upgrade guidance, you can directly upgrade to VCF 9.1.1 without first upgrading to 9.1.0 and then
patching to 9.1.1.
Forward-Only Upgrade Requirement
VCF enforces strict upgrade path validation. You can only upgrade your VCF components to a target version that is
released after the release date of your current version. The target version can be a major, minor, or a maintenance
release. In general, you can upgrade directly to a patch release only if you can also upgrade to its parent maintenance
release. For example:
• Supported: VCF 5.2.0 (25 JUN 2024) to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026).
• Not supported: VCF 5.2.4 (27 MAY 2026) to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026).
• Supported: VCF 5.2.4 (27 MAY 2026) to VCF 9.1.1 (03 SEP 2026).
This is valid for all components in a VCF source BoM. For example:
• Supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3a (18 JUN 2024) and ESX 8.0 Update 3 (25
JUN 2024), which are part of VCF 5.2.0 BoM.
• Not supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX 8.0 Update 3j (27
MAY 2026), which are part of VCF 5.2.4 BoM.
• Supported upgrade to VCF 9.1.1 (03 SEP 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX 8.0 Update 3j (27
MAY 2026), which are part of VCF 5.2.4 BoM.
Broadcom 2572

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF components might have further limitations, see VMware Interoperability Matrix.
VCF Components
Before version 9, VCF always included the following core components:
• SDDC Manager
• NSX Manager
• vCenter
• ESX
Starting with VCF 9, the management components are part of the VCF fleet.
• VCF Operations (previously Aria Operations)
• Cloud proxy (previously Aria Operations Cloud Proxy)
• VCF Automation (previously Aria Automation, can be deployed as a Day-N operation after the upgrade)
• VCF management services (introduced in 9.1)
• License server (introduced in 9.1)
You begin the upgrade process of your SDDC with the VCF Instance that hosts the VCF Operations instance dedicated to
managing your VCF fleet.
Note:
The SDDC Manager UI is being deprecated and will be removed in a future release. After your upgrade to VCF
9.1 completes, use VCF Operations to perform lifecycle management activities.
High-Level Upgrade Order For a VCF 9 Fleet
1. Upgrade the management components and the management domain of the VCF Instance where the management
components are deployed by strictly following the upgrade order.
2. Upgrade the management domains of the remaining VCF instances in the fleet by upgrading any instance-level
components that are available for upgrade.
Upgrading the workload domains for VCF instances is optional and can be performed at any time after the management
domain of the respective instance is already upgraded. For information on how to upgrade your workload domains, see
Upgrading VMware Cloud Foundation Workload Domains to 9.1.x.
VCF Upgrade Planner
You can now use the new VCF Upgrade Planning Tool to navigate you during the process of upgrading or converging your
existing infrastructure to VCF 9.1. Different tailored scenarios exist for starting from different VCF versions.
Upgrading a VCF Instance from version 9.0.x to version 9.1.x
VCF 9.1 transitions the lifecycle management of VCF Operations, VCF Operations for logs, VCF Operations for networks,
VCF Automation, and VCF Identity Broker to the new fleet lifecycle and SDDC lifecycle components. The transition occurs
during the VCF Operations upgrade to 9.1.x. The upgrade process validates credentials, migrates critical data, including
component inventory, certificates, and service accounts, and automatically decommissions the VCF Operations fleet
management appliance.

procedures. See Upgrading to vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.
Redeploy VCF Identity Broker 9.0.x to a Supported Network and Datastore for
Upgrade to 9.1
Before you upgrade VCF Operations to 9.1, you must perform this procedure if your VCF Identity Broker 9.0.x is deployed
on an NSX overlay segment or on a network or datastore that are different than the ones where you plan to deploy the
VCF management services.
Important:
If VCF Operations is already on version 9.1.x, do not perform this procedure. To remediate the upgrade to identity
broker 9.1, follow the guidance in Broadcom knowledge base article 444734.
• Redeployment of VCF Identity Broker involves the back-up of the current configuration and importing the configuration
in the new cluster. This requires the newly deployed cluster to have the same build number as the existing cluster
(the same maintenance and patch version). Download and stage the necessary VCF Identity Broker binaries to your
software depot.
With VCF 9.1, VCF Identity Broker transitions to being part of VCF management services. To successfully upgrade to
identity broker 9.1, VCF Identity Broker 9.0.x and VCF management services must be deployed on the same network and
on the same datastore. For available VCF management services networking models, see VCF Management Services
Models.
You perform this procedure if:
• VCF Identity Broker in appliance mode is deployed on an NSX overlay segment. You cannot deploy VCF management
services on an NSX overlay segment.
• VCF Identity Broker in appliance mode is deployed on a different network than VCF management services.
• VCF Identity Broker in appliance mode is deployed on a different datastore than VCF management services.
You deploy a new VCF Identity Broker and reuse the existing certificate and FQDN. You reconfigure your DNS to repoint
the new IP address of the cluster to the existing FQDN. You then import the original configuration in the new VCF Identity
Broker to restore full functionality. Configured permissions are not affected. This process is a service-disruptive change
and requires a maintenance window.
1. Back up VCF Identity Broker. See On-Demand Backup of a VCF Identity Broker Appliance Cluster.
2. Power off the VCF Identity Broker virtual machines by using the vSphere Client.
3. Delete the VCF Identity Broker component in VCF Operations. See Delete VCF Identity Broker.
The first initiation of the delete workflow fails. You must retry the workflow with the property set to True.
Skip task
Broadcom 2576

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Allow for a VCF Identity Broker redeployment in VCF Operations. See Enable VCF Identity Broker Redeployment.
5. Reconfigure your DNS to repoint the VCF Identity Broker FQDN to the new IP address that you use during deployment
of the new VCF Identity Broker instance. This step is only required if you are changing the deployment network of the
new cluster.
6. Deploy a new VCF Identity Broker in appliance mode by using VCF Operations. See Deploying VCF Identity Broker.
• Reuse the same FQDN and certificate (stored in the VCF Operations fleet management locker) from the old VCF
Identity Broker cluster. Ensure that the certificate you use during deployment of the new cluster does not include
an IP address in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN). Provide only the VCF Identity Broker FQDN in the Subject
Alternative Name of the certificate.
• Deploy the new cluster on the VCF management network or on a custom VLAN-backed network, where you plan to
deploy VCF management services.
• Deploy the new cluster on the datastore where you plan to deploy VCF management services.
• Deploy the new cluster to the same maintenance and patch version as the old cluster.
7. Restore the VCF Identity Broker configuration from the backup by using VCF Operations. See Restore a VCF Identity
Broker Appliance Cluster.
After you validate that VCF Identity Broker is operational, proceed with the VCF Operations upgrade. See Upgrading to
VCF Operations 9.1.
Upgrading to VCF Operations 9.1
You begin a VCF fleet upgrade to 9.1 by upgrading the VCF Operations instance in the first VCF Instance.
Upgrading from 5.2.x
If your environment has VMware Aria Operations 8.x, you upgrade your Aria Operations instance by uploading the
VCF Operations 9.1 PAK file directly in the Aria Operations administration interface. For instances that are managed by
VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x, after you upgrade to VCF Operations 9.1, VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x can continue
to manage VMware Identity Manager. Do not delete VMware Identity Manager as it can still be an authentication source
for a VCF Automation instance. Preserve the VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x instance to perform all Day-N operations for
VMware Identity Manager 3.3.x.
After you complete the upgrade of VMware Aria Operations 8.x to VCF Operations 9.1, you must remove VCF Operations
from the VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x environment without deleting the associated VM from vCenter. See Delete a
Product from an Environment.
If your environment does not have VMware Aria Operations 8.x, you must deploy a new VCF Operations instance on the
management domain vCenter that hosts the core components. See Deploy VCF Operations for the 9.1 Upgrade.
Upgrading from 9.0.x
Before you begin the overall upgrade to 9.1.x, ensure your existing 9.0.x VCF Automation is deployed in the management
domain and not in a workload domain. If your environment has VCF Operations 9.0.x, you upgrade your VCF Operations
instance by uploading the VCF Operations 9.1 PAK file directly in the VCF Operations administration interface.
The upgrade process manages the transition of lifecycle orchestration from VCF Operations fleet management to VCF
management services. During upgrade, VCF Operations connects to the VCF Operations fleet management appliance
and collects inventory data, such as component inventory, service registry, user imported certificates, certificate signing
requests, content management endpoints, marketplace configuration, and service accounts. After the data is transferred,
the VCF Operations fleet management appliance is automatically decommissioned and shut down. The data is later
transferred to the new for VCF 9.1 fleet lifecycle and SDDC lifecycle components. Before VCF management services are
deployed and the data is transferred, you cannot perform certificate, password, and lifecycle operations by using VCF
Operations.
Certificates and Password Management for Management Components During an Upgrade from 9.0.x
When you are upgrading from 9.0.x, after you upgrade VCF Operations to 9.1, you cannot manage certificates and
passwords for your management components from the VCF Operations UI. VCF Automation, VCF Identity Broker,
Broadcom 2577

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations for logs, and VCF Operations for networks in version 9.0.x are managed by VCF Operations fleet
management, that is powered off after the VCF Operations upgrade to 9.1. Management from the VCF Operations UI is
not possible until you upgrade these components to version 9.1.
Internal certificates are renewed when you upgrade VCF Operations. Automatic root-CA certificate renewal occurs when
the cloud proxy component is upgraded. After each upgrade, the cluster receives a new root-CA certificate with a five-year
validity period.
Note:
Automatic certificate renewal does not affect custom certificates.
Certificate Subject Alternative Names
VCF 9.1 transitions lifecycle management of components to the new fleet lifecycle and SDDC lifecycle components
and enforces stricter certificate validation for management services. During the VCF Operations upgrade, the process
validates credentials, migrates component inventory and service accounts, and migrates certificates. Certificates with
incomplete Subject Alternative Names (SANs) are no longer supported. See Subject Alternative Name Requirements.
Before you begin the upgrade, verify the certificate Subject Alternative Names for the following components:
• VCF Operations
• VCF Automation
• VCF Operations for networks
Upgrading Cloud Proxies
A cloud proxy in the VCF Instance is required for the deployment of VCF Management services and the integration
between VCF Operations, SDDC Manager, and VCF Management services.
To upgrade the primary VCF Instance that hosts VCF Operations, the instance must have a cloud proxy. If a cloud proxy
is not present, upgrade VCF Operations, deploy a new cloud proxy, and then complete the VCF Instance upgrade. See
Deploy Cloud Proxy for the VCF 9.1 Upgrade.
If your environment has cloud proxies, they are upgraded automatically during the VCF Operations upgrade. Cloud
proxies do not collect any data during this period. Data collection resumes after the upgrade completes. The upgrade
process runs concurrently for up to 10 cloud proxy instances. If you have more than 10 cloud proxy instances, the
upgrade process runs sequentially and the next cloud proxy upgrade starts after any one of the 10 running upgrades
completes or fails. In case the automatic upgrade fails, upgrade your cloud proxy manually by using the CLI. See Using
the Cloud Proxy Command-Line Interface.
Unsupported Upgrade Scenario for Aria Operations Cloud Proxy 8.18.x with Log Forwarding
If your Aria Operations Cloud Proxy 8.18.x has all four of the following settings, it is not supported after upgrade to version
9.1:
• The Aria Operations Cloud Proxy is on version 8.18.x.
• The cloud proxy is not deployed in the first VCF Instance, where VCF Operations is deployed.
• The cloud proxy has an active integration with VMware Aria Operations for Logs.
• The cloud proxy has log collection configured during initial deployment with a one-time key.
If even one of the conditions is not met, the Cloud Proxy configuration is supported for upgrade to 9.1.
If your Aria Operations Cloud Proxy 8.18.x configuration meets all of these conditions, the Aria Operations Cloud Proxy
is upgraded, but it is not supported in VCF 9.1. An unsupported cloud proxy is shut down after the upgrade. You can view
the status of the cloud proxy in the VCF Operations UI.
You must deploy a new cloud proxy in the first VCF Instance, where VCF Operations is deployed. You deploy the new
cloud proxy instance after you complete the upgrade of VCF Operations. After you deploy the new cloud proxy, you must
configure the cloud proxy to collect data and metrics from SDDC Manager. See Deploy Cloud Proxy for the VCF 9.1
Upgrade.

Create Snapshots of the VCF Operations Nodes Before You Upgrade
Create a snapshot of each node before you upgrade the VCF Operations cluster. After the upgrade completes, delete the
snapshots to avoid performance degradation.
For more information about snapshots, see the vSphere Virtual Machine Administration documentation.
1. Log in to the VCF Operations Administrator interface at
https://<primary-node-FQDN-or-IP-address>/
.
admin
2. On the System status page, in the Cluster status section, click Take Cluster Offline.
3. In the Take Cluster Offline dialog box, enter a reason and click OK.
When you take the cluster offline, VCF Operations services are stopped, but the VCF Operations virtual machines are
not shut down.
4. When all nodes are offline, log in to the vSphere Client where VCF Operations is deployed.
5. Right-click a VCF Operations node and select Snapshots > Take Snapshot.
a) Enter the name for the snapshot.
b) Deselect the Include virtual machine's memory check box.
c) Deselect the Quiesce guest file system(requires VM tools) check box.
d) Click Create.
6. Repeat the previous step for each node in the cluster.
After you create snapshots of the VCF Operations cluster, bring back the cluster to status before you can
Online
proceed with the upgrade.
Back up Customized Content in VCF Operations Before an Upgrade
When you upgrade VCF Operations, the upgrade process overwrites out-of-the-box content and resets it to the latest
default versions. Out-of-the-box content includes alert definitions, symptom definitions, recommendations, dashboards,
views, reports, and widgets. If you modified any out-of-the-box content directly, those customizations are lost during the
upgrade. This behavior is by design: the upgrade does not preserve manual edits made to the original content.
To preserve your customizations through an upgrade, follow the best practice of cloning out-of-the-box content before you
customize it. The upgrade does not overwrite user-created cloned objects, so customizations applied to clones persist
after the upgrade.
If you must customize any of the existing out-of-the-box-content that is provided with VCF Operations, clone the content
and then customize the cloned content.
After you have cloned and customized your content, create a backup before you begin the upgrade. The backup ensures
that you can recover your customizations if they are lost during or after the upgrade.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. In the left pane, navigate to Infrastructure Operations.
3. Clone out-of-the-box-content and customize the cloned content.

Upgrade VCF Operations to 9.1
You upgrade VCF Operations 9.0.x and Aria Operations 8.18.x to version 9.1 by using a PAK file in the VCF Operations
administration interface. For maintenance upgrades, the PAK upgrade method is not recommended and the user interface
suggests you use alternatives. For upgrades from versions 8.x and 9.0.x, PAK upgrade is the only method.
• The upgrades to VCF Operations 9.1.0.x or VCF Operations 9.1.1.x have specific source version requirements:
– If you are upgrading to VCF Operations 9.1.0.x, verify that your Aria Operations version is 8.18 or later.
– If you are upgrading to VCF Operations 9.1.1.x, verify that your Aria Operations version is 8.18.6 or later.
See Broadcom Interoperability Matrix.
• If you upgrade from VCF 9.0.x, verify that all certificates for VCF Operations for networks 9.0.x meet the SAN attribute
requirements. The VCF Operations for networks certificates must have FQDNs and IPs for all platform and collector
nodes in the certificate SAN attributes. To replace non-compliant certificates, see Replace a Certificate with a CA-
Signed Certificate.
• Verify that the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field of the VCF Operations certificate contains the FQDNs of all VCF
Operations nodes and the FQDN of the Load Balancer / VIP. To replace non-compliant certificates:
– For VCF Operations, see Replace a Certificate with a Configured CA-Signed Certificate.
– For Aria Operations, see Replace VMware Aria Automation Certificate.
Broadcom 2581

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• The vCenter field in all vCenter integrations must not contain a URL or an IP address, or an FQDN that includes
slashes or sub-paths.
• Ensure that you have the VCF Operations fleet management appliance root user password to facilitate the inventory
transfer.
• If your environment has additional management components and your VCF Operations has a configured proxy server
with SSL termination, you must remove the proxy server configuration before you upgrade VCF Operations.
• If you have VCF Automation 9.0.x in your environment, ensure it is deployed in the management domain and not in a
workload domain.
The process first upgrades the VCF Operations nodes in the cluster and then automatically upgrades the cloud proxy for
the VCF Operations instance.
If you are upgrading from VCF Operations 9.0.x, the inventory of the VCF Operations fleet management appliance
is transferred to the VCF Operations instance. When the transfer completes, the fleet management appliance is
decommissioned. VCF Operations temporarily keeps the inventory until you deploy the VCF management services that
substitute the fleet management appliance functionalities.

Deploy VCF Operations for the 9.1 Upgrade
VCF Operations is a required component in VCF 9 and later. If you do not have an existing deployment of VMware Aria
Operations 8.18.x, you must deploy VCF Operations before you can proceed with the VCF 9.1 upgrade. You deploy the
VCF Operations nodes from the vSphere Client by using an OVA file.
After you deploy the VCF Operations nodes, you connect your instance to SDDC Manager to activate the fleet
management capabilities in VCF Operations.

Deploy Cloud Proxy for the VCF 9.1 Upgrade
You need cloud proxies to collect data from physical data centers. For high availability or load balancing, you deploy
two or more cloud proxies to create a cloud proxy group. A cloud proxy collects data from the end-point environment
and uploads it to VCF Operations. Cloud proxies can support multiple vCenter instances. For more information on cloud
proxies, see the Cloud Proxy FAQ.
• Verify that you have an IP address and a DNS configuration for the cloud proxy.
• Verify that you have proper permissions to deploy OVF templates in vSphere. For more information, see Deploy and
Export OVF and OVA Templates.
• Allow outgoing HTTPS traffic for cloud proxy over port 443.
• Allow incoming traffic to cloud proxy over ports 443, 4505, and 4506 for Telegraf based application monitoring.
Note:
For Telegraf based application monitoring in VCF 9.1 and later versions.
Port 8443 will reach end of support after a few releases. It is recommended that you use port 443 so that the end
point VM/physical server has access to port 443 of an individual cloud proxy or cloud proxies that are a part of a
cloud proxy group.
• As a new user, enable port 443 instead of port 8443 so that the end point VM/physical server has access to
port 443 instead of port 8443 of an individual cloud proxy or cloud proxies that are a part of a cloud proxy
group.
• For existing users who upgrade to VCF 9.1, it is recommended that you reconfigure your open source and
product managed Telegraf workloads to use port 443 instead of ports 8443 within the next few releases.
• Allow incoming traffic to cloud proxy over port 443 for push model adapters or Suite-API on cloud proxy.
• Verify that the user has the required cloud proxy roles to access configuration templates. For more information, see the
Access Control: Roles Tab.
Broadcom 2585

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Add a vCenter cloud account and provide an account with the following read and write privileges:
– vCenter IP address or FQDN.
– Permissions required to install a cloud proxy on the vCenter Server.
For more information on privileges, see Privileges Required for Configuring a vCenter Account.
• Cloud proxies must have a proper DNS resolution to the VCF Operations nodes when using short/long FQDN names.
Note:
Using a firewall to restrict traffic by IP is not recommended since IPs can change without notice. Restricting traffic
must be performed via FQDNs only.
Refer to the cloud proxy sizing requirements before configuring a cloud proxy. For more information, see
Collecting Data with Cloud Proxy in VCF Operations.

Proxy.
10.Optional: (Optional) Enter an IP in CIDR format for Docker Subnet.
The Docker Subnet value in CIDR format must be /27 or larger (for example, /27, /26, /25, /24 etc). If a custom
value is not provided, the Docker's default value gets assigned automatically (for example, /16 subnets starting from
172.17.0.0). For more information on docker subnet allocation, see Automatic subnet allocation.
Note:
The Docker Subnet creates a network subnet for the Docker containers running inside this cloud proxy, to prevent
any network overlap. For information related to connectivity issues between cloud proxy and connected nodes
due to network overlap, see Broadcom knowledge base article 392302.
11.Optional: (Optional) Select Prefer IPv6 to use IPv6 for internal communications.
12.Optional: (Optional) Set up a proxy server in the Customize template screen.
a) Enter details in the Network Proxy IP Address and Network Proxy Password properties.
Note:
If you use a network proxy for log forwarding, port 9543 must be open.
b) To activate SSL, select the Use SSL connection to proxy check box.
c) If you are using SSL, you can verify the certificate of the proxy server. Public certificate authorities are used to
verify the proxy server certificate. To activate this, select the Verify proxy's SSL cert check box in the Verify SSL
cert property.
d) You can specify the IP/FQDN URL that is used to access the system when a load balancer is used.
e) If you have a custom certificate authority, paste the root certificate authority in the Custom CA property to verify
the certificate of the proxy server. Include the following lines when you copy the root certificate authority:
"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----"
"-----END CERTIFICATE-----"
13.(Optional) Starting with version 9.1.1, you can set up Outbound Network Proxy Settings to route Broadcom Portal
traffic through a dedicated proxy. Expand Outbound Network Proxy Settings and enter the proxy IP address, port,
credentials, SSL, and custom certificate authority options. For more information, see Configuring Outbound Network
Proxy Settings on an Upgraded Cloud Proxy.
14.Click Finish.
The deployment takes a few minutes to finish.
15.Locate the cloud proxy you installed, select the VCF Operations Cloud Proxy, and click Power on.
Note:
Power on the cloud proxy within 24 hours of registration. After 24 hours, the Unique Registration Key expires. If
the key expires, delete the proxy and deploy a new one.
16.Return to the Cloud Proxy page in VCF Operations to view the status of the cloud proxy you installed. For more
information, see Monitoring the Health of Cloud Proxies.
17.After you deploy and configure the cloud proxy, assign the new cloud proxy to a new or existing VMware Cloud
Foundation (VCF) instance and its associated workload domains. For the existing domains of the same VCF Instance,
update the integrations for all vCenter instances to use the new Cloud proxy/ group. For more information, see
Configuring a Standalone VCF Account in VCF Operations.
Important:
VCF 8.18.x did not include unified cloud proxies. When you upgrade your VCF instance from 8.18.x to 9.1, you
must assign any newly deployed cloud proxy to your VCF instance. After installation, navigate to Operate >
Administration > Integrations and edit the VCF instance settings and replace the default cloud proxy with the
new cloud proxy.
Broadcom 2587

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
18.To view the accounts that are using this connection, click the Cloud Proxy.
19.Optional: To delete a cloud proxy, click the vertical ellipsis and then click Delete. For more information, see Deleting
Cloud Proxies .
Upgrade SDDC Manager to 9.1
After you complete the upgrade of VCF Operations, you continue by upgrading SDDC Manager in the first VCF Instance.
• If you have an AVI Load Balancer in your environment, verify that the version is compatible with the target version for
SDDC Manager. See the Product Interoperability Matrix.
• Download the SDDC Manager upgrade binary for your target release.
– If you are upgrading from SDDC Manager 5.2.x, see Download VMware Cloud Foundation Upgrade Bundles.
– If you are upgrading from SDDC Manager 9.0.x, see Download VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 Upgrade Bundles
Using an Online or Offline Depot.
– If your SDDC Manager does not have access to the Internet, you can download the upgrade binary by using the
VCF Download Tool to an offline depot or to the SDDC Manager. See Download Binaries to an Offline Depot by
Using the VCF Download Tool or Download VMware Cloud Foundation Upgrade Bundles Without an Online or
Offline Depot. You can also download the required binaries to deploy VCF management services and license
server, which are required in the subsequent procedure. See Deploy VCF Management Services and License
Server for the VCF Upgrade.
• Ensure that you have a recent successful backup of SDDC Manager using an external SFTP server.
• Ensure that you have taken a snapshot of the SDDC Manager appliance.
• Ensure that you have recent successful backups of the components that are managed by SDDC Manager.
• Perform upgrade prechecks in SDDC Manager and resolve any issues.
Upgrade from 9.0.x to 1. Log in to VCF Operations.
9.1 2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Build.
3. In the left pane, click Lifecycle.
4. Expand VCF Instances, select the respective VCF Instance that hosts the SDDC Manager to upgrade.
5. On the SDDC Manager Updates tab, click the Available updates, and click Update Now.
6. Click Finish.
Upgrade from 5.2.x to 1. Log in to SDDC Manager at https:// <sddc_manager_fqdn> with a user assigned the ADMIN
9.1 role.
2. On the Workload Domains page, click the management domain and then click the Updates tab.
3. In the Available Updates section, click Plan Upgrade.
4. On the Plan Upgrade page, select the target major version, and click Next.
5. On the Change Summary page, select the specific version and click Confirm.
6. On the Plan Upgrade page, click Done.
7. Click Update Now or Schedule Update next to the VMware Cloud Foundation upgrade bundle.
8. If you selected Schedule Update, select the date and time for the bundle to be applied and click
Schedule.
9. Click Finish.
After upgrading SDDC Manager to version 9.1, log in to your SDDC Manager instance, navigate to Administration >
Depot Settings, and reconfigure an online depot to use an activation code from the VCF Business Services console for
authentication, instead of a download token. See Configure a Software Depot Connection Mode.
Deploy VCF Management Services and License Server for the VCF Upgrade
After your VCF Operations and SDDC Manager instances are at version 9.1, to continue with the upgrade, you deploy
VCF management services. You can perform this procedure by using the VCF Operations UI or the SDDC Manager API
that provides more options to customize the configuration for the deployment.
Before you can deploy the VCF management services and license server components, ensure that the following
prerequisites are met.
• Verify that all required ports are open. See VMware Ports and Protocols.
Broadcom 2588

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Verify that you configured the required FQDNs and IP addresses for deployment. See VCF Components FQDNs and
IP addresses.
• Verify that VCF Operations and SDDC Manager are at version 9.1.x.
• Download the required install binaries in the software depot for the components that you install during the upgrade of
the first VCF instance that hosts VCF Operations.
Within a VCF fleet, as the required fleet level components are already deployed, during upgrades of additional VCF
instances, only VCF services runtime, Salt master, SDDC lifecycle, and telemetry are deployed.
For environments, where a license server already exists, this workflow does not deploy a second license server.
Table 978: Required Install Binaries for Fleet Upgrade
Component Binary Required for First Instance Binary Required for Additional Instances
VCF services runtime Yes Yes
SDDC lifecycle Yes Yes
Salt master Yes Yes
Telemetry Yes Yes
Software depot Yes No*
Salt RaaS Yes No
Fleet lifecycle Yes No
Identity broker Yes No*
License server Yes No*
* As part of the upgrade process, software depot, identity broker, and license server are deployed only in the first VCF
instance. You can later deploy them in any of the additional VCF instances per the requirements of your environment.
See Adding or Removing VCF Components Post Deployment.
If your SDDC Manager does not have access to the Internet, you can download the binaries for the following
components by using the VCF Download Tool to an offline depot or to SDDC Manager. See Download Binaries to an
Offline Depot by Using the VCF Download Toolor Download VMware Cloud Foundation Upgrade Bundles Without an
Online or Offline Depot.
• The VCF management services FQDNs are checked for validity, the FQDN validation relies on RFC1034 and
RFC1123, and only top level domains of the internet are validated. The domain is not supported as it does not
.local
fall into the list of top-level domains in the Domain Name System (DNS) of the Internet.
• Obtain administrative credentials for the VCF Operations instance to register the components with.
• If your environment does not have a cloud proxy for the VCF instance that hosts VCF Operations, you must deploy and
configure a new cloud proxy instance. See Deploy Cloud Proxy for the VCF 9.1 Upgrade.
• If your environment has additional management components and your VCF Operations has a configured proxy server
with SSL termination, you must remove the proxy server configuration before you deploy VCF management services.
Within a VCF fleet, as the required fleet level components are already deployed, during upgrades of additional VCF
instances, only VCF services runtime, Salt master, SDDC lifecycle, and telemetry are deployed.
CAUTION:
After deployment, do not move the VCF management services VMs to a different resource pool or VM folder.
If you move the VMs to a new resource pool or VM folder, subsequent patching, deployment, or scale out
operations fail.
Storage DRS (SDRS) is disabled by default during VCF management services deployment starting with VCF 9.1
EP2 (see VCF Services Runtime 9.1.0.0200 Release Notes). Do not manually use storage vMotion to migrate the
VCF management services virtual machines to a different datastore. Storage vMotion of the VCF management
services nodes is not supported and can cause subsequent patching, deployment, or scale-out operations to fail.
You can perform this procedure by using the VCF Operations UI or the SDDC Manager API. When using the SDDC
Manager API, you use the JSON file to configure the VCF management services
VcfManagementComponentsSpec
Broadcom 2589

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
and license server deployment parameters. See Deploy VCF Management Components. Each method has specific
requirements and advantages. For additional information, see the following table.
Deployment Configuration Description
Network placement • For target versions 9.1.0.x, with the UI, you deploy VCF management services and license
server on the VCF management network. If your environment does not have a dedicated VCF
management network, you can deploy the components to the VM management network. See
Network Deployment Options for VCF Components.
• For target versions 9.1.1 and later, with the UI, you can select the network where VCF
management services and license server are deployed to.
• With the API, you can deploy VCF management services and license server on the VCF
management network or on a VLAN-backed network by using the xRegionNetwork
parameter in the VcfManagementComponentsSpec JSON file. This option allows you to
avoid IP exhaustion on the VCF management network.
Dual-stack networking For dual-stack networking and VCF components that support the dual-stack model, the FQDNs must
resolve to IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. See Dual Stack IP Addressing Model.
• With the UI, you can provide FQDNs that resolve to and IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
• With the API, the necessary IPv6 parameters in the VcfManagementComponentsSp
ec JSON file are included but commented out. To configure dual-stack networking for VCF
management services, you must uncomment and provide values for the respective IPv6
parameters.
VCF Identity Broker If you have VCF Identity Broker 9.0.x in appliance mode, identity broker 9.1 deployment is skipped
and you can later upgrade, see Upgrade Identity Broker to 9.1.
If you have embedded VCF Identity Broker 9.0.x, it is upgraded to 9.1 during the vCenter instance
upgrade but an identity broker 9.1 instance is also deployed as part of this procedure. You can later
transition your 9.1 embedded instance to the highly available 9.1 instance. See Migration of Identity
Broker Embedded to Identity Broker Instance.
• With the API, the sample VcfManagementComponentsSpec JSON file contains
specification for deploying the identity broker component. If you have an existing VCF Identity
Broker in appliance mode, you must remove the vidbSpec specification or the deployment
validation fails.
• If you have an existing VCF Identity Broker for the primary VCF instance, when deploying a
subsequent VCF Instance, vidbSpec can be excluded from the JSON file.
With VCF 9.1, VCF Identity Broker transitions from being hosted by a dedicated VCF services
runtime to being hosted by the shared VCF services runtime, which hosts all VCF management
services. To successfully upgrade to the 9.1 identity broker component, both VCF management
services and VCF Identity Broker must reside on the same network.
• With the API, you can specify a custom network where you deploy VCF management services
by using the xRegionNetwork parameter. You can deploy VCF management services on the
same VLAN-backed network as VCF Identity Broker.
IP addresses for VCF services A minimum of 12 IP addresses are required for deployment (/28 CIDR block).
runtime A recommended number of 30 IP addresses in total can be added. The additional IP addresses are
reserved for new VCF management services components or scaling out existing components (/27
CIDR block).
• With the UI, for target versions 9.1.0.0 through 9.1.0.300, you allocate a /28 or a /27 CIDR block.
• With the UI, for target versions 9.1.0.400 and later:
– You can now exclude IP addresses from the provided CIDR block (comma-separated list).
Excluded IP addresses cannot be used for deploying additional VCF components.
– You can now provide a comma-separated list of IP addresses. The IP addresses can be
contiguous or non-contiguous.
• With the API, you can use CIDR, an IP range, or a list of IP addresses (can be non-contiguous).
If your VCF management network does not have sufficient IP addresses, you can use the API to
deploy to a custom VLAN-backed network.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Deployment Configuration Description
VCF services runtime internal VCF services runtime uses an internal CIDR block of 198.18.0.0/15. If this subnet is in use on your
network network, you must change the internal CIDR block for VCF management services to 240.0.0.0/15 or
250.0.0.0/15.
Different VCF services runtime instances on the same network can work with the same internal
network. For example, you can have the two instances of VCF services runtime for your VCF
management services and VCF Automation using the same internal network.
• With the VCF 9.1.0.x UI, you cannot change the default internal network. With VCF 9.1.1 and
later, you can change the default internal network. Select a CIDR block that does not overlap
with any of your infrastructure networks, including management, VM, and IP pool networks. An
overlap causes routing conflicts and breaks connectivity to or from the VCF services runtime
cluster.
• With the API, you can specify the internal CIDR block by using the internalClusterCidrI
pv4 or internalClusterCidrIpv6 JSON keys.
FQDNs for VCF management You must provide three FQDNs for the VCF services runtime, the fleet component, and the instance
services component. In the context of deploying VCF management services, the required FQDN for the fleet
component includes the fleet lifecycle, Salt RaaS, and software depot components. The FQDN
for the instance component includes the SDDC lifecycle, Salt master, real-time metrics, real-time
metrics store, and telemetry components. These FQDNs must resolve to unique and unused IP
addresses outside of the IP range provided for VCF services runtime, but still on the network that
hosts the VCF services runtime component.
FQDNs for identity broker and You must provide one FQDN for identity broker and one FQDN for license server. These FQDNs
license server must resolve to unique IP addresses outside of the IP range provided for the VCF services runtime,
but still on the network that hosts the VCF services runtime component.
You can deploy license server as IPv4 only. In VCF 9.1.1 and later, after the new deployment, you
can change the networking configuration to IPv6. If you upgrade a license server from version 9.1.0
to version 9.1.1, you cannot configure IPv6 on that license server instance. See Configure IPv6 on a
License Server.

Transfer Licenses After a VCF Operations Upgrade from Version 9.0.x
Starting with version 9.1, the license server component contains your VCF and vSphere Foundation licenses. After the
deployment of the license server as part of a VCF or vSphere Foundation upgrade from 9.0.x, if your VCF Operations
instance is in disconnected mode, you must transfer your licenses from the VCF Operations instance to the license server.
If your VCF Operations instance is in connected mode, the license server is automatically registered and licenses are
automatically transferred to the license server.
After the deployment of the license server, in VCF Operations, you might see duplicate licenses while the licenses are
transferred. The duplicate licenses disappear when the transfer completes. During that period, avoid assigning licenses to
assets as license assignments might fail.
If your VCF Operations instance is in disconnected mode, you must register the license server with the VCF Business
Services console. Licenses are then automatically transferred from VCF Operations to the license server. You must
generate a new license file from the VCF Business Services console, and import it in VCF Operations.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Licensing > Licenses &
Registration.
3. In the Register & License VCF Operations pane, click Continue.
The Register and License VCF Operations workflow appears.
The pre-registration steps of the procedure are complete because a license server is deployed during the upgrade of
the VCF Operations to version 9.1, and the connection mode remains unchanged.
Broadcom 2596

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Download the registration file.
a) In the Registration section, in the Download Registration File card, click Download.
b) Save the registration file.
5. Use a computer with Internet connection and log in to the VCF Business Services console with your Broadcom
Support Portal credentials.
a) In the VCF Operations instance, in the Import Registration File to the VCF Business Services console card,
click Start.

in the VCF Business Services console. The FQDN is only saved if you do not enter another display name. If you

Upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1
You use VCF Operations to manage the lifecycle of VCF Automation. Depending on your environment, you can import an
existing VMware Aria Automation 8.x instance and upgrade it to VCF Automation 9.1, or directly upgrade VCF Automation
from 9.0.x to 9.1.
The upgrade uses a blue-green deployment to provision a new VCF Automation instance while the existing instance
remains active during the upgrade. The upgrade deploys a dedicated VCF services runtime instance that hosts the VCF
Automation 9.1 nodes. During the upgrade, the system migrates data and configurations to the new environment before
switching network traffic to the 9.1 instance. After the upgrade completes, the source Automation nodes are shut down
automatically.
Networking Details
To allow for reduced risk and downtime during the upgrade process, you must provide additional IP addresses and an
FQDN for the VCF Automation 9.1 instance. You reuse the existing FQDN that you use to access the Automation UI.
You deploy the new VCF Automation 9.1 nodes on the same network as your existing Automation nodes. The network
requirements differ based on your Automation source and target version.
• For target versions 9.1.0.0 through 9.1.0.300, you must provide a unique network CIDR block that contains 8
sequential IP addresses.
– The required block is a /29 subnet mask representing 8 sequential IP addresses.
– All 8 IP addresses must reside on the same network where your current Automation nodes are deployed.
• 3 of the IP addresses are assigned to the VCF Automation 9.1 nodes
• 2 of the IP addresses are a buffer for automatic redeployment of failed nodes or for rolling updates in the future.
• 3 of the IP addresses are not used.
• For target versions 9.1.0.400 and later, you can now also provide 5 unique IP addresses that reside on the same
network where your current Automation nodes are deployed. The IP addresses can be contiguous or non-contiguous.
– 3 of the IP addresses are assigned to the VCF Automation 9.1 nodes
– 2 of the IP addresses are a buffer for automatic redeployment of failed nodes or for rolling updates in the future.
• 1 New FQDN with a unique corresponding IP for the VCF services runtime instance that hosts the 9.1 VCF Automation
nodes. The corresponding IP must be outside of the CIDR that you already dedicated. This FQDN is used only
internally between VCF components and is not user-facing.
• The FQDN from the existing Automation instance is automatically transferred as the VCF Automation FQDN of the 9.1
instance.
• If your existing Automation instance uses an external load balancer, no changes in its configuration are required.
• If you upgrade from Aria Automation 8.18.x, the IP addresses of the existing nodes are automatically assigned as VIPs
for the 9.1 instance.
• If you upgrade from VCF Automation 9.0.x, the IP addresses of the existing nodes are freed after the upgrade.
Account Details for the New 9.1 Instance
The upgrade wizard prompts for a single password that is assigned for both the vmware-system-user and
admin@vsp.local accounts for the newly deployed VCF Automation 9.1 instance.
Broadcom 2598

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Before starting the import and upgrade:

• Verify that you have configured a software depot. See Configure a Software Depot Connection Mode.
• Verify that you have downloaded the upgrade binaries for VCF Automation. See Download Binaries to Software Depot.

Upgrade VCF Automation to 9.1
You use VCF Operations to upgrade VCF Automation. Before you proceed, ensure that you are familiar with the
networking and account details for the new VCF Automation 9.1 instance. See Upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1.
• If you are upgrading from VCF 5.2.x, verify that you imported and integrated the VMware Aria Automation instance
version 8.18.1 and later to VCF Operations. See Import an Existing VMware Aria Automation Instance in VCF
Operations.
• If your VMware Aria Automation 8.18 has a vSphere or an NSX-T endpoint with a certificate signed by the same CA
as the Aria Automation certificate or by a well-known external CA, Aria Automation automatically trusts the connection
because the CA is already present in the truststore. During the upgrade to VCF Automation 9.1, the truststore is not
migrated and these endpoints become untrusted, causing TLS failures. Before you upgrade, follow the guidance in
Broadcom 2599

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Broadcom knowledge base article 425489. If the issue is not resolved, follow the guidance in Broadcom knowledge
base article 447667.
• VCF Automation 9.x enforces FIPS 140-2 compliance for all external integration endpoints. The pre-upgrade check
validates that every integration communicates over a secure, certificate-backed channel. The upgrade might be
blocked for environments with any of the following configurations:
– An IPAM integration endpoint configured with skip certificate check flag set to .
ON
– A VMware Aria Operations integration endpoint.
– An LDAP directory integration configured using plain LDAP.
See Broadcom knowledge base article 447667.
• Verify that you have an FQDN for the VCF services runtime that hosts VCF Automation in version 9.1. The FQDN must
resolve to an IP address that is not part of the IP addresses dedicated for the VCF services runtime to host the VCF
Automation nodes.
• For target versions 9.1.0.0 through 9.1.0.300, verify that you have a dedicated CIDR for use by the VCF services
runtime instance that hosts the VCF Automation nodes. For example, a /29 subnet mask as VCF Automation requires
5 IP addresses.
• For target versions 9.1.0.400 and later, verify that you have dedicated 5 unique IP addresses for use by the VCF
services runtime instance that hosts the VCF Automation nodes. The IP addresses can be contiguous or non-
contiguous.
• Verify that you have configured a software depot. See Configure a Software Depot Connection Mode.
• Verify that you have the necessary install and upgrade binaries. See Download Binaries to Software Depot.
– For 9.0.x to 9.1.x upgrade, verify that you have the 9.1.x upgrade binary for VCF Automation and the 9.1.x install
binary for the migration service engine component.
– For 8.18.x to 9.1.x upgrade, verify that you have the 9.1.x install binary for VCF Automation and the 9.1.x install
binary for the migration service engine component.
• Verify that the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field of the VCF Automation certificate contains the FQDNs and IP
addresses of all VCF Automation nodes and the FQDN and IP address of the Load Balancer / VIP.
– To replace non-compliant certificates for VCF Automation, see Replace a Certificate with a Configured CA-Signed
Certificate.
– To replace non-compliant certificates for Aria Automation, see Replace VMware Aria Automation Certificates.
• Verify that in VCF Operations, the cloud accounts for the integration of VCF Automation are working properly by
explicitly clicking the Validate Connection button.
• If you have a Data Services Manager instance integrated with VCF Automation, before you upgrade VCF Automation
to 9.1.x, see Upgrading your Data Services Manager in a VCF Environment.
• If your 8.18.x or 9.x Automation instance is not deployed on the primary datastore of your VCF Instance, you
can upgrade to VCF Automation 9.1.1.0200 and later if your fleet lifecycle, SDDC lifecycle, and SDDC Manager
components are on version 9.1.1.0200 or later.
• If your Aria Automation 8.18.x instance is a single-node deployment of extra-large size, scale it out to a 3-node cluster
before you start the upgrade.
Upgrading to VCF Automation starts with creating an upgrade plan to ensure the correct binary is mapped to the upgrade.
After you create the plan, you start the upgrade process.
During the upgrade from Aria Automation 8.18 to VCF Automation 9.1.x, VCF Automation retains and reuses the
certificate of the Aria Automation 8.18 instance.
If your existing Automation instance uses an external load balancer, no changes in its configuration are required.

After you upgrade VMware Aria Automation 8.x to VCF Automation 9.1, VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x
stops managing VCF Automation 9.1. Preserve the VMware Aria Suite Lifecycle 8.x instance to perform all

authentication source for VCF Automation 9.1.
VCF services runtime uses an internal CIDR block of 198.18.0.0/15. If this subnet is in use on your network, you must

can have the two instances of VCF services runtime for your VCF management services and VCF Automation using the

Migrate VCF Automation Authentication from VMware Identity Manager to VCF Identity Broker
VCF Automation 9.1 uses identity broker and VCF SSO to manage authentication, replacing the legacy VMware Identity
Manager (vIDM) model in Aria Automation. Complete the procedures in this section to migrate authentication for both the
Provider Management and the Organization Portal after upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1.
Aria Automation uses VMware Identity Manager to manage authentication. When you upgrade Aria Automation to VCF
Automation 9.1, the VMware Identity Manager configuration is preserved for backward compatibility. VCF Automation
9.1 introduces a different authentication model that uses VCF SSO and the identity broker component. Complete the
migration to replace the legacy vIDM configuration with the VCF Automation 9.1 recommended authentication model.
VCF Automation 9.1 introduces two distinct portals, each with a separate authentication model:
• The VCF Automation Provider Management authenticates users by using identity provider and VCF SSO. The
Provider Management UI must be configured after upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1.
• VCF Automation Provider Management uses a separate identity provider configuration from the VCF Automation
organization UI. After upgrade, configure an identity provider in VCF Automation Provider Management. Including VCF
Automation Provider Management in the fleet-wide VCF SSO is highly recommended.
• The VCF Automation organization UI authenticates end users through a direct connection (such as OIDC, LDAP, or
SAML) to an external identity provider or identity broker. Before the migration, the Organization for VM Apps, created
from the existing Aria Automation configuration during the upgrade, uses the legacy VMware Identity Manager OIDC
connection for authentication.
After you complete all procedures in this section, the legacy Aria Suite Lifecycle and VMware Identity Manager
deployments are no longer required for the operation of VCF Automation.
Configure Authentication for VCF Automation Provider Management
Configure authentication for the VCF Automation Provider Management by verifying that the identity broker is set as the
identity provider, then add the users and groups that require Provider Management access.
• Aria Automation is upgraded to VCF Automation 9.1, and the existing configuration is converted to an Organization for
VM Apps.
• VCF Single Sign-On is configured. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On.
• If you are migrating groups or users with administrative rights, VMware Identity Manager and identity broker must be
configured to use the same identity provider.
The Provider Management UI is the VCF Automation 9.1 interface through which provider administrators manage
organizations, identity providers, and tenants. The Provider Management UI does not exist in Aria Automation, there is
no configuration for identity providers and access control after upgrade to VCF Automation 9.1. Authentication for VCF
Automation Provider Management must be configured before provider administrators can access it.
Follow the guidance in the table to configure the authentication for VCF Automation Provider Management.
Step Description
1. Configure the VCF Automation integration with identity broker Configure VCF Single Sign-On for VCF Operations and VCF
and VCF SSO. Automation Provider
2. Import users to the System organization. Import Provider Users to Your VCF Automation
3. Import groups to the System organization. Import a Provider Group to Your VCF Automation
Broadcom 2602

Configure Authentication for the VCF Automation Organization Portal
After you upgrade Aria Automation to VCF Automation 9.1, the Organization for VM Apps continues to use the legacy
VMware Identity Manager OIDC connection for authentication. Complete the procedures in this section to replace VMware
Identity Manager-based authentication with a direct identity provider connection in the VCF Automation Organization
Portal.
• Aria Automation is upgraded to VCF Automation 9.1, and the existing configuration is converted to an Organization for
VM Apps.
• VMware Identity Manager and identity broker must be configured to use the same identity provider.
The Organization Portal is the VCF Automation interface through which users access and manage their assigned
organizations. When Aria Automation is upgraded to VCF Automation 9.1, the Organization for VM Apps retains the
VMware Identity Manager authentication configuration from the source environment. This configuration uses an OIDC
connection to VMware Identity Manager as the authentication source.
VCF Automation 9.1 supports direct integration between the Organization Portal and an external identity provider.
Migrating from VMware Identity Manager-based authentication to direct identity provider integration allows the
Organization Portal to authenticate users through a standard LDAP or SAML connection that is managed by the identity
broker component.
Although VCF Automation 9.1 continues to support VMware Identity Manager-based authentication for the Organization
for VM Apps after an upgrade, direct identity provider integration is the recommended authentication model for VCF
Automation 9.1 and later.
Configure the First User Account for the Organization for VM Apps
The first user account is a local account that provides access to the Organization for VM Apps during the transition from
VMware Identity Manager-based authentication to direct identity provider integration. Create this account before you
configure the identity broker component as the identity provider for VCF Automation.
The first user account is a local application account with full administrative access to the Organization for VM Apps in VCF
Automation. This account does not depend on an external identity provider and retains access to the Organization for VM
Apps when you disconnect VMware Identity Manager authentication and configure the direct identity provider integration.
You must assign all four administrator and owner roles to the first user account. If you do not assign all four roles, you lose
administrative access to the organization during the identity provider migration.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI using as the organization name.
System
2. In the left pane, click Organizations.
3. Click the Organization for VM Apps (the default organization name is <vidm_hostname> Classic Tenant).
4. On the organization page, in the left pane, click First User.
5. Click Add First User.
6. In the Create User, configure the user name and password, configure the following roles, and click Save.
Setting Description
Role • Assembler Administrator
• Orchestrator Administrator
• Organization Owner
• Service Broker Administrator
The first user account is created with full administrative access to the Organization for VM Apps. You can now use this
account to access the organization if your VMware Identity Manager-based accounts become unavailable during the
identity provider migration.

configuration. Configure a new LDAP or SAML connection as the identity provider in the Organization portal to replace

This topic covers the integration with an external LDAP identity provider. You can also configure an integration with a

rector,DC=example,DC=com.

connection by using the vCloud API.

with domain admin rights. VCF Automation uses this account to
