Migrate User Groups to the New Identity Provider for the Organization for VM Apps
After you configure a new LDAP identity provider for the Organization for VM Apps, import the corresponding groups by
using the Organization Portal to replace the existing VMware Identity Manager-based groups.
• Every VMware Identity Manager-based group in the Organization for VM Apps has a corresponding group configured
in the new identity provider.
• Each imported group must have at least the Organization Member role assigned.
After you configure the new external identity provider for the Organization for VM Apps, the groups in the Organization for
VM Apps still point to the VMware Identity Manager OIDC identity provider and are not automatically migrated to the new
identity provider connection. You must create new corresponding groups in the new identity provider for every existing
VMware Identity Manager-based group in the OIDC identity provider. You then import the newly created groups and
assign the corresponding roles in the Organization for VM Apps.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Organization Portal with the first user and as the organization
vidm Classic Tenant
name.
2. On the main navigation bar, click Administer.
3. In the left pane, click Access Control.
4. Click the Groups tab and click Import Groups.
5. In the Import Groups dialog box, configure the settings and click Save.
Setting Description
Source Select the LDAP identity provider configured in the prerequisite
task.
Search Enter the name of the group you are importing and select it from
the results.
Assign Role Select the organization role or roles to assign. Assign the same
roles that the corresponding vIDM-based group holds.
Broadcom 2605

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. Repeat the steps for each remaining vIDM-based group.
Existing VMware Identity Manager-based groups are not automatically removed when you import their new identity
provider equivalents. After you verify that all groups are successfully migrated and users can authenticate through the new
identity provider, remove the VMware Identity Manager-based groups from the Organization for VM Apps.
Migrate User Accounts to the New Identity Provider and Import them in the Organization for VM Apps
After you import groups from the new identity provider, update the existing user accounts in the Organization for VM
Apps to point to the new identity provider instead of the VMware Identity Manager OIDC connection. Use the bulk update
feature to migrate all identity provider-backed user accounts in a single operation.
When Aria Automation is upgraded to VCF Automation 9.1, user accounts in the Organization for VM Apps authenticate
through the VMware Identity Manager OIDC connection. After you configure a new identity provider, existing user
accounts do not automatically switch to the new connection. You must update each user account to point to the new
identity provider.
Two categories of user accounts exist in the Organization for VM Apps after an upgrade:
• Identity-provider-backed user accounts authenticate through VMware Identity Manager by using the OIDC connection.
These accounts are updated in the VCF Automation Organization UI to point to the new identity provider by using the
bulk update feature.
• Local VMware Identity Manager user accounts are created directly in VMware Identity Manager and have no
corresponding accounts in the new external identity provider. These accounts cannot be migrated using the bulk
update feature. They must be recreated as identity-provider-backed accounts.
Reconfigure Identity Provider Backed User Accounts to Point to the New Identity Provider for the Organization for VM Apps
By using the bulk update feature in the VCF Automation Organization UI, you reconfigure the existing identity-provider-
backed accounts from VMware Identity Manager to point to the new identity provider for the Organization for VM Apps
authentication.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Organization UI with the first user and as the organization
vidm Classic Tenant
name.
2. On the main navigation bar, click Administer.

Remove the VMware Identity Manager Configuration for Organization for VM Apps
After you verify that all users and groups authenticate successfully through the new identity provider, remove the legacy
VMware Identity Manager configuration from the Organization for VM Apps.
The legacy VMware Identity Manager configuration in the Organization for VM Apps consists of three components:
• The VMware Identity Manage-based group entries that reference the OIDC connection.
• The VMware Identity Manage-based user accounts registered in projects.
• The OIDC connection itself through which VMware Identity Manager provides authentication.
The three components must be removed in sequence. The OIDC connection cannot be removed while VMware Identity
Manage-based groups or user accounts still reference it.
Do not start any procedure in this section until you verify that all users and groups authenticate successfully through the
new LDAP identity provider. If you remove the OIDC connection before authentication is verified, users whose accounts
were not migrated correctly lose access to the organization and cannot log in.
After completing all procedures in this section, the Organization for VM Apps uses only the new identity provider for
authentication.

Upgrade Failure Notification During VMware Aria Automation Orchestrator Upgrade
The upgrade log indicates that the upgrade process has failed, but the individual nodes of the deployment are upgraded.
After the upgrade script finishes running, you receive the following message in your Automation Orchestrator Appliance
indicating that the upgrade has failed:
Upgrade failed and left the system in non-working state. Check the error report below
to correct the problem. Once addressed, you can continue the upgrade by running 'vracli
upgrade exec --resume'
However, the upgrade log lists that the nodes of your Automation Orchestrator deployment are upgraded.
Hostname: <your_orchestrator_node_FQDN>
Status: Upgraded
Cluster Member: Yes
Version Before: <build_before_upgrade>
Version After: <build_after_upgrade>
Description: The node is upgraded successfully.
To resolve this problem, verify that the nodes are running, and resume the upgrade.
1. Verify that your Automation Orchestrator nodes are running.
kubectl get all pods
2. If your Automation Orchestrator nodes are running, resume the upgrade process.
vracli upgrade exec --resume
Upgrading NSX Global Manager Nodes in a Federated Environment
Before you can upgrade any VCF instances and NSX Local Managers, you must upgrade standby and active NSX Global
Managers in the NSX Federation.
If NSX Federation is configured between two VCF Instances, VCF does not manage the lifecycle of the NSX Global
Manager nodes. For each VCF instance, you upgrade the Upgrade Coordinator for NSX Federation, before you upgrade
the standby and active NSX Global Manager nodes. To upgrade the NSX Global Managers, you must manually download
the NSX upgrade precheck and upgrade bundles.
The NSX Upgrade Coordinator is a self-contained web application that runs in NSX Manager. It orchestrates the upgrade
of the Upgrade Coordinator itself and NSX Global Manager nodes in the cluster. The Upgrade Coordinator provides a
centralized interface that enables administrators to track and manage the upgrade process end to end.
Broadcom 2615

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Attention:
In a federated environment, you must upgrade the standby Global Manager nodes first, before you proceed with
the active Global Manager nodes upgrade.

Cloud Foundation 9.
b) Click your VCF version and on the VMware NSX row, click View Group.
c) Locate the NSX version Upgrade Bundle and NSX version Precheck Bundle.
The upgrade precheck and upgrade bundles have the following format:
• versionnumber.buildnumber
VMware-NSX-upgrade-bundle- .mub
• versionnumber.buildnumber
VMware-NSX-upgrade-bundle- -pre-check.pub
d) Agree to the Terms and Conditions and Compliance Reporting Terms and Conditions.
e) Click the download icons to download the upgrade precheck and upgrade bundles to the system where you access
the NSX Global Manager UI.

3. From the navigation panel, select System > Upgrade.
4. Under Global Manager, click Upgrade.

Upload.
Alternatively, paste the URL where the file is located.
.pub

Plan a Domain Upgrade to 9.1
To upgrade the core components in your domain, plan a domain upgrade by setting a target VCF version and VCF
component versions, and defining the upgrade sequence for domain components.
Starting with VCF 9.1, vCenter and NSX Manager are upgraded in a common step in the upgrade plan. You can select
between the following upgrade scenarios.
• Optimized maintenance window upgrade
– Reduces the required time for the maintenance window for the upgrade. The vCenter reduced downtime upgrade
preparation stage is performed first and does not require downtime. After this stage is completed, within the same
maintenance window, the NSX Manager nodes are upgraded followed by the vCenter instance switchover stage.
• Sequential upgrade
– Upgrade operations for each component are performed in separate stages in different maintenance windows. The
upgrade starts with the NSX Manager nodes upgrade followed by the vCenter instance upgrade. You can select
between a vCenter in place upgrade or vCenter reduced downtime upgrade.
Note:
If you are upgrading from version 9.0 or later, both upgrade options are available. If you are upgrading from
version 5.2.x, the only available option is vCenter reduced downtime upgrade.
Broadcom 2617

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Depending on your choice, you upgrade the core components in your plan in one of the following sequences.
Optimized Maintenance Window Upgrade to 9.1 Sequential Upgrade to 9.1
1. Prepare the vCenter instance for upgrade 1. Upgrade the NSX Manager
2. Upgrade the NSX Manager 2. Upgrade the vCenter instance
3. Switchover of the vCenter instance – Option 1: vCenter in place upgrade
4. Upgrade the ESX hosts – Option 2: Preparation and switchover
5. Upgrade the NSX Edge Cluster and finalize NSX Upgrade 3. Upgrade the ESX hosts
4. Upgrade the NSX Edge Cluster and finalize NSX Upgrade
In both upgrade scenarios, you must complete the upgrade plan steps in a sequential order.

To create an optimized maintenance window upgrade, your vCenter target version and SDDC Manager current

Perform Upgrade Prechecks
To ensure that your environment is ready for an upgrade, before applying an upgrade, you can perform prechecks in VCF
Operations.
You can choose which pre-checks to run and either plan pre-check for all components or choose one or more
components. You can run general prechecks or prechecks against a specific VCF target version. Alternatively, after you
configure a component for upgrade, you can run a component precheck from the dedicated component card.
• After you start a precheck of a component, you cannot cancel the precheck and it is not recommended to start or
schedule an upgrade.
• After a precheck completes, only the latest results are saved. Previous results are not visible.
• Even when one or more precheck fails, you can attempt to upgrade the component. The recommendation is to review
the errors and warnings, before attempting the upgrade of the component.
If you silence a vSAN Skyline Health alert in the vSphere Client, SDDC Manager skips the related precheck and indicates
which precheck it skipped. Click RESTORE PRECHECK to include the silenced precheck. Silenced prechecks do not
send warnings or block upgrades.

Upgrading vCenter and NSX Manager
Starting with VCF 9.1, you upgrade your NSX Manager cluster and NSX Edge clusters separately. Depending on the
upgrade option you select in the domain upgrade plan, you proceed with updating your vCenter instance and NSX
Manager instances in one of the following ways: Upgrade vCenter and NSX Manager with an Optimized Maintenance
Window or Upgrade vCenter and NSX Manager Sequentially. The NSX Upgrade Coordinator is upgraded as part of these
workflows.
Checklist for an NSX Upgrade by Using VCF Operations
Use the following checklist to track your work through the automated upgrade process.
Automated Upgrade Task Instructions
Evaluate the operational impact of the upgrade. See Operational Impact of the NSX Upgrade.
Complete the pre-upgrade tasks. See Pre-Upgrade Tasks for Upgrading NSX.
Verify that the NSX environment is in a healthy state. See Verify the Current State of NSX.
Make the required changes in your system configuration if your See Manage Unsupported Features.
deployment contains features that are not supported in the target
release.
NSX Instances Shared by VCF Domains
For NSX instances that are shared across multiple domains, you must upgrade the NSX, vCenter, and ESX components
on all domains, where the NSX instance is shared. It is not recommended to cancel the automatically created upgrade
plan on a dependent domain, as this action cancels the upgrade plan on all domains that share the NSX instance. If the
upgrade plan is cancelled, you must create a new upgrade plan.
For example, if you create a domain upgrade plan or shared NSX component upgrade plan for domain A, you must add
and upgrade the vCenter instance and all ESX hosts on this domain. Before you can finalize the upgrade, you must visit
domain B, add the vCenter and ESX components to the component upgrade plan, and upgrade all three components.
After you upgrade the vCenter, ESX, and NSX components on domain B and all other dependent domains, you can
finalize the upgrade on domain A and the dependent domains.
If an NSX instance is shared between a management domain and workload domain(s), when all other components are
upgraded, you must start the VMware NSX Edge Clusters Upgrade and NSX Upgrade Finalize upgrade step from the
management domain only.
Note:
When you select the Optimized Upgrade sequence, the NSX Manager upgrade cannot proceed until every
domain that shares the NSX instance completes the vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade (RDU) switchover.

After the embedded identity broker is at version 9.1, it can be migrated to an instance that is part of VCF management
services for high availability. See Migration of Identity Broker Embedded to Identity Broker Instance.

In-Place Upgrades
In-place upgrades are integrated with the live patch process in VMware Cloud Foundation lifecycle management. When
upgrading to an NSX hot patch or express patch, VMware Cloud Foundation initiates a live patch when possible, and
initiates the in-place upgrade.
In-place upgrades are not supported in the following scenarios:
• More than 1000 vNICs are configured on the ESX host and the vNICs on the VMs connect to a single VDS. If the host
has multiple VDS for NSX, this vNIC limit is per VDS.
• Layer 7 firewall rules or Identity Firewall rules are enabled.
• A VProbe-based packet capture is in progress.
• The service is not running on the host.
nsx-cfgagent
• IDS/IPS or distributed malware prevention is enabled for your NSX environment.
Pre-Upgrade Tasks for Upgrading NSX
Before you upgrade NSX, perform the pre-upgrade tasks to ensure that the upgrade is successful.
Broadcom 2622

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Ensure that your transport node profiles include the appropriate transport zones. Otherwise, NSX Manager might not
display the list of transport node profiles.
2. Run the Certificate Analyzer, Results and Recovery (CARR) script. The goal of running the CARR script is to ensure
that NSX certificates, such as transport node (TN) certificates, do not expire within 90 days. For more information, see
Broadcom knowledge base article 369034.
3. Ensure that you back up the NSX Manager before you start the upgrade process. See Backing Up and Restoring NSX
Manager or Global Manager.
4. Ensure that your host OS is supported for NSX Manager. For more information, see the Broadcom Compatibility
Guide.
5. Turn off automatic backups before you start the upgrade process. For more information, see Configure Backups.
6. Terminate any active SSH sessions or local shell scripts that you might have invoked on the NSX Manager or the NSX
edge nodes, before you begin the upgrade process.
7. Ensure that the appropriate communication ports are open from the host transport nodes and edge nodes to the NSX
Manager nodes. For more information on ports, see VMware Ports and Protocols.
8. Delete all expired user accounts before you begin the upgrade. Upgrade for NSX on vSphere fails when your
exception list for vSphere lockdown mode includes expired user accounts. For more information on accounts with
access privileges in lockdown mode, see Specify Lockdown Mode Exception Users in the VMware Host Client in the
vSphere documentation.
9. VCF 9.x does not support the multi NSX feature. Ensure that you switch off the multi NSX features for all the compute
managers that are registered with NSX Manager. Alternatively, you can map the NSX Manager instances to individual
vCenter instances before upgrading.
10.Starting with VCF 9.0, a service account is created on vCenter for NSX to communicate with a registered compute
manager. If you are upgrading to VCF 9.0 and any registered compute manager lacks a service account, a pre-check
error is raised. To proceed with the upgrade, you must enable the Create Service Account setting on each registered
compute manager.
Verify the Current State of NSX
Before you begin the upgrade process, it is important to test the NSX working state. Otherwise, you cannot determine if
the upgrade caused post-upgrade problems or if the problem existed before the upgrade.
Note:
Do not assume that everything is working before you start to upgrade the NSX infrastructure.
1. Identify and record the administrative user IDs and passwords.
2. Verify that you can log in to the NSX Manager web user interface.
3. Inspect the Dashboard, system overview, host transport nodes, edge transport nodes, NSX edge cluster, HA status of
the edge, and all logical entities. Ensure that all status indicators are green, deployed, and do not show any warnings.
4. Validate North-South connectivity by pinging out from a VM.
5. Validate that there is an East-West connectivity between any two VMs in your environment.
6. Record BGP states on the edge devices.
•
get logical-routers
•
vrf <vrf>
•
get bgp
•
get bgp neighbor
Manage Unsupported Features
Certain features in the source version of NSX might not be supported in the target version. If your deployment contains an
unsupported feature, make the required changes to your system configuration before starting the upgrade. The upgrade
precheck step of the upgrade process returns an error when it detects an unsupported feature.
Broadcom 2623

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Multi-NSX
Starting with VCF 9.0, the multi-NSX feature is not supported. Before the upgrade, turn off the multi-NSX feature for all
registered compute managers, else the upgrade precheck step returns an error.
Alternatively, you can map the NSX Manager instances to individual vCenter instances before upgrading.
Compute Managers Without Service Accounts
Starting with VCF 9.0, a service account is created on vCenter for NSX to communicate with a registered compute
manager. If you are upgrading to VCF 9.0 or later and a registered compute manager lacks an enabled service account, a
pre-check error is thrown.
To proceed with the upgrade, you must enable the service account for those compute managers. Note that for compute
managers that already have a service account feature enabled, the same service account is used post upgrade for those
compute managers. The old privileges are deleted for such a service account and the predefined privileges are added.
Manager API
Starting with VCF 9.0, the Manager APIs for logical networking and security are removed. Before the upgrade, use the
Policy promotion tool in the source NSX deployment to migrate any Manager objects in your environment to the equivalent
Policy objects.
In addition, perform the following steps for specific use cases.
Retrieve Manager IDs of logical objects
After the upgrade, Manager IDs will no longer be available. To ensure the operation of any API that requires the Manager
ID of a logical object as an input, perform these steps before starting the upgrade:
1. Create the object using the equivalent Policy API.
2. Retrieve the Unique ID value of the Policy object. The Unique ID is equivalent to the Manager ID of the logical object.
3. Use the retrieved Unique ID as input to the API requiring the Manager ID.
For example, the API for transport node profile creation takes the Manager IDs of IP pool and logical switch objects as
inputs. After creating the IP pool and segment objects using Policy APIs, you can input the Unique ID values of these
objects to the API for transport node profile creation.
Perform intermediate upgrade for mixed-mode configurations
A configuration that contains a combination of policy and manager objects is known as a mixed-mode configuration. Some
examples of mixed-mode configurations are:
• NAT rules created through Manager APIs attached to routers created through Policy APIs
• Groups created through Policy APIs used in DFW rules created through Manager APIs
If your source deployment uses mixed-mode configurations, you must use the following workflow to upgrade to VCF 9.0 or
later.
1. Upgrade the deployment to NSX 4.2.1 or later.
2. In NSX 4.2.1 or later, use the Promotion feature to promote the mixed-mode objects to policy objects.
3. Upgrade to VCF 9.0 or later.
Convert mixed-mode IP allocations
The upgrade precheck process in the NSX Manager upgrade coordinator does not detect mixed-mode IP allocations or
warn you of the presence of this unsupported condition.
Before the upgrade, verify whether mixed-mode IP allocations exist in your environment. If present, use the Promotion
feature in the source NSX deployment to migrate the mixed-mode IP allocations to Policy equivalents.
Replace member types related to grouping
Broadcom 2624

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Certain member types are deprecated or no longer supported. If your source deployment uses any of these member
types, replace them with their supported equivalents which are functionally the same.
Deprecated or Unsupported Member Type Supported Equivalent
IPSET (deprecated) Group
Logical Switch (not supported) Segment
Logical Port (not supported) Segment Port
Remove any remaining Manager objects after the upgrade
After the upgrade, NSX Manager will raise an alarm if it detects any pure Manager logical objects that have not been
migrated to Policy equivalents.
Configure NSX Edge Failover Pre-checks
NSX Edge failover pre-checks ensure that routing services can continue without downtime across clusters during an
upgrade. As each edge node prepares to shut down for the upgrade, pre-checks validate the availability of peer nodes in
that edge cluster and alert the user if a peer is not ready for failover.
By default, edge failover pre-checks are activated during host and NSX Edge upgrades. You can deactivate them using
the NSX API. You can also selectively deactivate failover pre-check warnings for specific edges, edge clusters, and hosts
due to known issues in your environment.
In addition, you can use the API to run failover pre-checks before an upgrade, as part of your pre-upgrade planning
process.
Running Failover Pre-checks Before an Upgrade
To plan for an upgrade and identify areas of failover readiness that require attention, you can run the failover pre-checks
on demand. Use the following API call and request payload.
POST https://<nsx-manager>/api/v1/upgrade/pre-upgrade-checks/host/planned-maintenance
{
"vcenter-uuid": "<compute manager UUID>",
"entity-id": "<host moref ID>"
}
The pre-checks report any failover readiness issues in the response body.
Failover Pre-check Workflows During an Upgrade
The failover pre-checks run during both the host upgrade and edge upgrade steps of the upgrade process.
• When the host upgrade step begins, the pre-checks consider all the peers of edges on the candidate host to be
upgraded. If a peer is found not ready for failover, the upgrade pauses on the candidate host until the user makes the
peer edge available for failover. After this host completes its upgrade, the failover pre-checks run sequentially on the
next candidate host.
• When the edge upgrade step begins, the pre-checks validate the peers of each candidate node to be upgraded. If
a peer itself has recently been upgraded and is still starting up, the upgrade process implicitly waits for the peer to
become available before retrying the pre-check.
Deactivate Edge Failover Pre-checks
To deactivate some or all edge failover pre-checks, use the API call
PATCH https://<NSX Manager>/policy/api/
with a request payload consisting of key/value pairs as described in the following table.
v1/system-config
Broadcom 2625

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
By default, the key is set to , which activates all edge failover
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreChecks false
pre-checks.
Key Value Description
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreChecks true Deactivates all edge failover pre-checks.
false (default) Activates all edge failover pre-checks, with
the option to selectively turn off certain pre-
checks.
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreChecks false (default) Activates failover pre-checks for all edges
ForVmotionableEdges on a given host, including edges eligible for
vMotion migration.
true Deactivates failover pre-checks for edges
eligible for vMotion migration.
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreCheck Comma-separated list of edge cluster Deactivates failover pre-checks for the
ForEdgeClusterID UUIDs specified edge clusters.
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreCheck Comma-separated list of edge node UUIDs Deactivates failover pre-checks for the
ForEdgeNodeID specified edge nodes.
EdgeFailoverReadiness_DisablePreCheck Comma-separated list of hosts, represented Deactivates failover pre-checks for the
ForHostNodeID in either of these formats: specified hosts.
• Host UUID
• Compute manager UUID : Host MO-

Upgrade vCenter and NSX Manager with an Optimized Maintenance Window
If you choose the optimized option in the upgrade plan, you must upgrade NSX Manager and vCenter in the following
order: prepare the vCenter instance for migration, upgrade NSX, and switchover to the new vCenter instance.
• Verify that you planned a domain upgrade and selected the optimized maintenance window upgrade option. See Plan
a Domain Upgrade to 9.1.
• Verify that you upgraded SDDC Manager. See Upgrade SDDC Manager to 9.1.
• Verify that you downloaded the required upgrade binaries. See Download Binaries to Software Depot.
• Verify that you performed all upgrade prechecks. See Perform Upgrade Prechecks.
• If your workload domain contains vSphere Supervisor clusters, the supported target release depends on the version
of Kubernetes (K8s) currently running in the cluster. Older versions of K8s might require a specific upgrade sequence.
For the supported upgrade sequence for Supervisor clusters running older Kubernetes versions, see Broadcom
knowledge base article 92227.
• Pre-version 9 licenses for NSX security features are no longer supported. To avoid service interruption after the
upgrade, assign a valid vDefend license or your NSX security features enter evaluation mode for 90 days.
The optimized upgrade workflow reduces the maintenance window by moving vCenter instance upgrade preparation
outside the scheduled downtime and before the NSX Manager upgrade, consolidates the NSX and vCenter upgrades into
a single maintenance window, and ensures that the vCenter instance switchover occurs after the NSX Manager upgrade
is complete.
Note:
You can upgrade NSX in workload domains before or after upgrading NSX in the management domain.
After a new vCenter instance preparation stage completes and the NSX Manager nodes are upgraded, you complete the
upgrade and perform the vCenter switchover stage, where the current vCenter data and configuration is copied to the new
instance.
Note:
You must complete the upgrade tasks in a sequential order.
Optimized upgrade of vCenter and NSX Manager is not available for straddle states. For example, if SDDC Manager is at
version 9.1, while vCenter target version is below 9.1.
1. Log in to VCF Operations at <vcf_operations_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. Select Build > Lifecycle, expand VCF Instances, and select your domain.
3. On the Upgrades tab, under VMware vCenter Preparation Stage, click Configure.
4. Configure the preparation stage.
a) Review the upgrade mechanism information and click Next.
A vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade (RDU) uses a migration-based approach. In this approach, a new vCenter
appliance is deployed and the current vCenter data and configuration is copied to it.
During the preparation phase of a reduced downtime upgrade, the source vCenter instance and all resources
remain online. The only downtime occurs when the source vCenter instance is stopped, the configuration is
switched over to the target vCenter , and the services are started. The downtime is expected to take approximately
5 minutes under ideal network, CPU, memory, and storage provisioning.
Once the target vCenter instance is operational, SDDC Manager deletes the source vCenter appliance as part of
the upgrade. If the upgrade fails before the switchover completes, vCenter RDU performs an automatic rollback
and the configuration reverts to the source vCenter instance. You can take a file-based backup before starting the
upgrade so that you can restore it if the automatic rollback fails.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The RDU behavior in VCF is different than the behavior in vSphere Foundation, see Prepare Upgrade and Switch
Over to the Target vCenter appliance.
b) Select a backup option and click Next.
Before starting the upgrade, best practice is to have a file-based backup of the vCenter appliance. See On-
Demand Backup of vCenter. After taking a backup, do not make any changes to the vCenter inventory or settings
until the upgrade completes successfully.
c) Provide a temporary network to be used only during the upgrade and click Next.
Setting Value

the vCenter RDU process, which generates a temporary link-
local address for the parallel appliance. No DHCP or available IP
addresses on the existing subnet are required.
Static Enter an IP address, subnet mask, and gateway. The IP address
must be in the management subnet.
d) Select a deployment size and storage size.
Based on your selection, the resources that are required for the vCenter deployment change.
e) Review the upgrade configuration and click Finish.
If you are upgrading a management domain, after you confirm the domain configuration, the management domain
upgrade is scheduled or in progress. Therefore, upgrade operations for workload domains are unavailable.
5. Optional: Under VMware vCenter Preparation Stage, click Run Prechecks to run the upgrade prechecks.
You can click on View Details to monitor the progress of the preheck. You can review the report and evaluate all
errors and warnings.
6. Under VMware vCenter Preparation Stage, click Schedule and select scheduling options for the preparation and
switchover stages of the vCenter upgrade.
a) Schedule an option for the preparation stage.
You can start the vCenter preparation stage immediately or specify another time.
b) Schedule an option for the switchover stage.
Specify the switchover behavior after the target instance is created with the selected configuration and after NSX
Manager is upgraded.
• Automatic: Proceed with an automatic switchover after the preparation stage is complete.
• Manual: You must manually click Switchover Now to start the switchover.
c) Click Schedule.
Your new vCenter instance is deployed (preparation stage) and the current vCenter data and configuration is
copied to it
7. Under VMware NSX Manager Nodes Upgrade, click Configure.

After you upgrade the vCenter, ESX, and NSX Manager components, you can finalize the upgrade.

The NSX precheck runs on all workload domains in your environment that share the NSX Manager cluster.
9. Under VMware NSX Manager Nodes Upgrade, click Upgrade Now.

When all NSX Manager nodes are upgraded successfully, a message with a green background and check mark is

11.Under VMware vCenter Switchover Stage, click Switchover Now.
The migration to the new vCenter instance starts and you can monitor the progress. See Monitoring VMware Cloud
Foundation Upgrades. If you cancel the switchover, the configuration reverts to the source vCenter instance.
• Allow some time (approximately 15 minutes) for post-upgrade auto-reconciliation of configuration drift fixes before
scheduling another upgrade. If you schedule a second upgrade to run before the remediation task completes, the
upgrade might be cancelled or auto-reconciliation might fail.
• Use the vSphere Client to change the vSphere DRS Automation Level setting back to the original value (before you
took a file-based backup) for each vSphere cluster that is managed by the vCenter. See Broadcom knowledge base
article 87631 for information about using VMware PowerCLI to change the vSphere DRS Automation Level.
• Transition any clusters that use vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines to use vSphere Lifecycle Manager images
before upgrading ESX hosts. See Transitioning from vSphere Lifecycle Manager Baselines to vSphere Lifecycle

Upgrade vCenter and NSX Manager Sequentially
If you choose the sequential option during the domain upgrade plan, you must first upgrade NSX Manager followed by a
vCenter upgrade.
• Verify that you planned a domain upgrade and selected the sequential upgrade option. See Plan a Domain Upgrade to
9.1.
• Verify that you upgraded SDDC Manager. See Upgrade SDDC Manager to 9.1.
• Verify that you downloaded the required upgrade binaries. See Download Binaries to Software Depot.
• Verify that you performed all upgrade prechecks. See Perform Upgrade Prechecks.
• If your workload domain contains vSphere Supervisor clusters, the supported target release depends on the version
of Kubernetes (K8s) currently running in the cluster. Older versions of K8s might require a specific upgrade sequence.
See Broadcom knowledge base article 92227.
• Pre-version 9 licenses for NSX security features are no longer supported. To avoid service interruption after the
upgrade, assign a valid vDefend license or your NSX security features enter evaluation mode for 90 days.
The sequential upgrade workflow allows upgrade operations for each component to be performed in separate stages in
different maintenance windows. The upgrade starts with the NSX Manager nodes upgrade and is followed by the vCenter
instance upgrade. You can select between a vCenter In Place Upgrade or vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade. If you
choose the latter mechanism, you can schedule a time for the vCenter preparation and switchover stages. By decoupling
the preparation stage from the final switchover, the workflow allows for shorter maintenance windows.
Note:
The upgrade binary for vCenter is used to upgrade the vCenter instances managed by SDDC Manager. Upgrade
vCenter in the management domain before upgrading vCenter instances in workload domains. You can upgrade
NSX in workload domains before or after upgrading NSX in the management domain.
Note:
You must complete the upgrade tasks in a sequential order.
1. Log in to VCF Operations at <vcf_operations_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. Select Build > Lifecycle, expand VCF Instances, and select your domain.
3. Optional: On the Upgrades tab, under VMware NSX Manager Nodes Upgrade, click Run Prechecks to run the
upgrade prechecks.
The NSX precheck runs on all workload domains in your environment that share the NSX Manager cluster.
Broadcom 2629

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Under VMware NSX Manager Nodes Upgrade, click Upgrade Now or click Schedule to upgrade later.
To complete the upgrade of an NSX instance, you must upgrade the vCenter and ESX components of this domain.
After you upgrade the vCenter, ESX, and NSX Manager components, you can finalize the upgrade.
Note:
NSX 9.x features are not available until all ESX hosts in all vSphere clusters that share an NSX Manager are
upgraded to 9.x and the NSX finalize procedure completes.
5. Under VMware vCenter Upgrade, click Configure.
Note:
If you are upgrading from version 9.0 or later, both upgrade options are available. If you are upgrading from
version VCF 5.2.x or vSphere 8.x, the only available option is vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade.
vCenter Reduced A vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade (RDU) uses a migration-based approach. In this approach,
Downtime Upgrade a new vCenter appliance is deployed and the current vCenter data and configuration is copied to it.
During the preparation phase of a reduced downtime upgrade, the source vCenter instance and all
resources remain online. The only downtime occurs when the source vCenter instance is stopped, the
configuration is switched over to the target vCenter, and the services are started.
1. Select the vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade mechanism and click Next.
2. Select a backup option and click Next.
Best practice is to have a file-based backup of the vCenter appliance. See On-Demand Backup of
vCenter. After taking a backup, do not change the vCenter inventory or settings until the upgrade
completes successfully.

• Allow some time (approximately 15 minutes) for post-upgrade auto-reconciliation of configuration drift fixes before
scheduling another upgrade. If you schedule a second upgrade to run before the remediation task completes, the
upgrade might be cancelled or auto-reconciliation might fail.
• Use the vSphere Client to change the vSphere DRS Automation Level setting back to the original value (before you
took a file-based backup) for each vSphere cluster that is managed by the vCenter.See Broadcom knowledge base
article 87631 for information about using VMware PowerCLI to change the vSphere DRS Automation Level.
• Transition any clusters that use vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines to use vSphere Lifecycle Manager images
before upgrading ESX. SeeTransitioning from vSphere Lifecycle Manager Baselines to vSphere Lifecycle Manager
Images.
Transitioning from vSphere Lifecycle Manager Baselines to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images
vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines are not supported with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and later. Before you can
upgrade, you must transition any clusters that use vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines to use vSphere Lifecycle
Manager images.
You can transition to vSphere Lifecycle Manager images by using one of the following methods.
• A PowerShell script
– Menu-driven interface
– Command-line interface
• The SDDC Manager API
After you upgrade SDDC Manager, you transition all clusters in the management domain and in all workload domains. If
the transition is not possible or you have vSphere Supervisor (Workload Management) enabled, transition any remaining
vSphere Lifecycle Manager baseline clusters after upgrading vCenter and before upgrading ESX.
Learn about the planning considerations, prerequisites, and tasks for transitioning ESX clusters and standalone hosts
from vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines to vSphere Lifecycle Manager images. This process is for transitioning ESX
clusters and standalone hosts that are already managed by SDDC Manager. For ESX clusters and standalone hosts that
are not managed by SDDC Manager, you can transition to vSphere Lifecycle Manager images using the vSphere Client.
See Convert a Cluster or a Host That Uses Baselines Into a Cluster or a Host That Uses vSphere Lifecycle Manager
Images.
Warning:
For clusters and standalone hosts that are managed by SDDC Manager, the transition must be performed by
SDDC Manager supported mechanisms only.

The processes for transitioning to vSphere Lifecycle Manager images support the following topologies.
VMware Cloud Foundation Architecture Support
Topology vSAN Ready Nodes Minimum Workload Domain Version
Standard architecture Cluster 5.0
Standalone host 5.0 *
Consolidated architecture Cluster 5.1
vSAN Stretched Cluster 5.1
DR Protected Cluster 5.1
vSphere Supervisor (Workload Management) enabled Cluster Split BOM 9.0 **
Heterogeneous Hardware Cluster 9.0 ***
* Standalone host transition support is only possible in combination with SDDC Manager 9.1 or later.
** The workload domain vCenter must first be upgraded to vCenter 9.0 or later, while ESX must remain on version 8.0
Update 1a or later.
*** Clusters with heterogeneous hardware cannot transition to vSphere Lifecycle Manager images until all hosts are
running ESX 9.0 or later. Before you start this procedure on a heterogeneous hardware cluster, upgrade it to ESX 9.0 or
later. See Broadcom knowledge base article 424294.
Important Considerations
• You cannot combine the process of transitioning to vSphere Lifecycle manager images with the process of upgrading
ESX.
• vSphere clusters that use vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines must be transitioned to use images before they can be
upgraded to ESX 9.0 or later.
• During the transition process, you cannot perform any other operations on the cluster or their underlying hosts until the
transition is complete. This restriction includes, but is not limited to ESX password rotation.
• You must disable the Enforce Live Patch option in the vSphere Lifecycle Manager image-specific remediation
settings . If the Enforce Live Patch option is enabled, image compliance checks fail. For more information, see
Broadcom knowedge base article 447752.
Maximum Compliance Checks and Transitions for Clusters
• A maximum of 25 simultaneous cluster compliance checks might be run per SDDC Manager. Extra compliance checks
are discarded.
• A maximum of 25 simultaneous cluster transitions might be run per SDDC Manager. Extra transition requests are
discarded.
Maximum Compliance Checks and Transitions for Standalone Hosts
• A maximum of 25 simultaneous standalone host compliance checks might be run per Workload Domain. Extra
compliance checks are discarded.
• A maximum of 25 simultaneous standalone host transitions might be run per Workload Domain. Extra transition
requests are discarded.
Broadcom 2633

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Image Seeding Support for vLCM Image Auto-Generation
• A minimum workload domain version of 5.2.1 is required to activate the option of image seeding (to complement the
option of constructing and applying your own vLCM image).
Using Image Seeding
Baseline-managed standalone hosts or clusters with compatible ESX and vCenter sBOM support allow for image
seeding. This process auto-generates a vLCM image-based on a single host (standalone or cluster member). In a cluster
environment, the created image must be uniform across all hosts, with matching VIBs. Upon completion, the image is
stored in the vCenter depot.
Transitioning vSphere Lifecycle Manager Baseline Clusters to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Image
Clusters Using PowerShell
You can use the PowerShell script through a menu-driven interface or a command-line interface (CLI). The menu-driven
interface provides a guided transition process and is best suited for smaller environments. The command-line interface is
useful for larger environments and can be used to operate against a single cluster at a time or, at scale, using JSON files.
Attention:
After you start a task with PowerShell, entering or exiting PowerShell will not halt many tasks (for
Ctrl-C
example, image import, compliance checks, or transition tasks). Those tasks continue to run in the background in
SDDC Manager or vCenter.
Notice:
If the script execution system does not trust the certificate of the SDDC Manager, execute the following lines
before running the script:
Set-PowerCLIConfiguration -InvalidCertificateAction Ignore -Scope User
$Env:SkipCertificateCheck="enabled"
Logging
The script records all actions to time-stamped files in a sub-directory that is created under the directory containing
logs
the script. This functionality facilitates troubleshooting.
If you run the script and this directory does not exist, it is automatically created.
PS C:\Users\Admin> .\VcfBaselineClusterTransition.ps1 -Connect
LogFolder not found, creating C:\Users\Admin\logs
Transition to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images Using the PowerShell Script Menu-Driven Interface
The menu-driven interface provides a guided experience for the vLCM baseline to vLCM image management transition
process.
The PowerShell script imports vSphere Lifecycle Manager images from the vCenter Image Catalog in vCenter 9.0 or later
and from vSphere clusters and standalone-hosts in vCenter 8.0.3 and earlier.
Notice:
If the vLCM image is vSphere cluster-based and contains no hosts, the script will delete the vSphere cluster after
completing the import and safety checks.
Attention:
SDDC Manager enforces image uniqueness based on two criteria: name and manifest.
First, image names must be unique across all vCenters; for example, importing esx-803b from one vCenter
blocks a later import of the same name from another. Second, image manifests (metadata) must be unique.
Broadcom 2634

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
If two differently named images—such as esx-803-m01 and esx-803-w01—share identical components (e.g.,
base image ESX 8.0.3a and Vendor A Version 1.2.3), SDDC Manager rejects the second image. This manifest
validation occurs during the final stage, after the full image has been uploaded.
1. Launch the script.
.\VcfBaselineClusterTransition.ps1
2. Connect to SDDC Manager and select a vCenter that manages the vSphere clusters you want to transition.

Manager referenced in the file.
b) Select the vCenter(s) to which you want to connect.
You can connect to all vCenters, a single vCenter, or a comma-delimited list of multiple vCenters.

4. Check vSphere Lifecycle Manager baseline clusters or standalone hosts for compliance with a vSphere Lifecycle

Be mindful of the executing logic:
The menu-driven interface always processes clusters sequentially. Each compliance check of a cluster must finish
before the next one begins. Parallel checks are only possible using the command-line interface with the
-Parallel
option.
Standalone hosts, however, are processed in parallel, so long as the following conditions are met:
• Each batch does not exceed 25 standalone hosts
• Each batch contains identical images or uses image seeding
• Each batch uses the same workload domain vCenter.
Attention:
The compliance check mis-identifies certain non-user managed VIBs and components as non-compliant and in
need of removal.
The underlying files are not missing, but rather the metadata describing the entities is not yet installed. The
metadata installation occurs automatically post-vLCM image transition.
If the compliance check identifies the removal of these entities as the exclusive trigger for maintenance
mode, the hosts will not transition into maintenance mode during the operation, The transition instead can be
performed live.

Transition to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images Using the SDDC Manager API
If you do not want to use the PowerShell script to transition vSphere clusters to vSphere Lifecycle manager images, you
can use the SDDC Manager API instead.
The following procedure guides you how to use the SDDC Manager Developer Center to transition a single vSphere
cluster or a set of standalone hosts to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images.
CAUTION:
The API workflow does not contain the same guardrails and error handling as the PowerShell script. Use the
SDDC Manager API only if the PowerShell script does not meet your business requirements.

Upgrade ESX to 9.1
VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and later supports only vSphere Lifecycle Manager image clusters.
• Verify that all vSphere clusters in a domain are managed by vSphere Lifecycle Manager images. If any clusters are
still using legacy vSphere Lifecycle Manager baselines, transition them to use vSphere Lifecycle Manager images.
See Transitioning from vSphere Lifecycle Manager Baselines to vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images. For upgrade of
heterogeneous ESX clusters, see Broadcom knowledge base article 424294.
• Verify that the domain has no ESX hosts or vSphere clusters in an error state. It is recommended that all hosts are
connected and no health issues are present. You can resolve the error states or remove the ESX hosts and vSphere
clusters with errors.
• Verify that you upgraded NSX Manager and vCenter before you can upgrade ESX hosts with a vSphere Lifecycle
Manager image.
• Verify that you created a vSphere Lifecycle Manager image using the vSphere Client. See Working with Image Library.
– Verify that the ESX version used is specified in the VCF BOM.
– You can create a composite image for a cluster that has hosts from different vendors or from the same vendor but
different generations, family, or model. A composite image contains one default image and one or more alternative
images. All images in a composite image contain the same base image and solutions, but might include different
vendor or firmware and driver add-ons. When you create alternate images, you also specify the rules that are used
to filter the hosts to which the alternative image is assigned. See Edit a vSphere Lifecycle Manager Image on a
Cluster or Host Level.
– If you plan to use the Import from a file option to import a vSphere Lifecycle Manager image, you must first export
the files from the vSphere Client.
Before VCF 9.0, the NSX VIBs on ESX hosts were upgraded as part of the NSX Manager upgrade. In VCF 9,NSX VIBs
and ESX host clusters are upgraded as part of the VMware ESX Upgrade step. As a result of this change, ESX hosts no
longer go into maintenance mode during an NSX Manager upgrade.
If you are using external (non-vSAN) storage, the following procedure upgrades the ESX hosts attached to the external
storage. However, updating and patching the storage software and drivers is a manual task and falls outside of SDDC
Manager lifecycle management. To ensure supportability after an ESX upgrade, consult the vSphere HCL and your
storage vendor.
You can configure multiple cluster upgrade tasks with different schedules without having to wait for the first cluster
upgrade to complete. For example, you could schedule an upgrade for and to run immediately
cluster-1 cluster-2
and then configure another upgrade task for and schedule it to run overnight.
cluster-3
Note:
• If you are upgrading a stretched cluster with a physical vSAN Witness Host, upgrade the witness host
manually, before upgrading the ESX hosts in the stretched cluster.
• Virtual vSAN Witness Hosts are upgraded as part of the cluster upgrade workflow.
Broadcom 2656

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to VCF Operations at <vcf_operations_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. Select Build > Lifecycle, expand VCF Instances, and select your VCF Instance.
3. Import a vSphere Lifecycle Manager image.
a) Select Image Management.
b) Click Import Image.
c) Select the import method, provide the required information, and click Import.
Option Description
Import from a vCenter Select the vCenter where you created the image from the drop-
down menu.
Select the upgrade image.
Import from a file Enter a name for the image and then click Select File to import
each of the required files.
Select the JSON, ZIP, and ISO files from your local computer. The
ISO file is optional.
You can view status in the Tasks panel.
4. Expand VCF Instances and select your domain.
5. On the Upgrades tab, under VMware ESX Upgrade, click Configure to specify the ESX cluster upgrade.
a) Read the introductory information and click Next.
b) Select the clusters to upgrade and click Next.
• To upgrade specific clusters, select Custom Selection and select the clusters to upgrade.
– The default setting is to upgrade all clusters, including single host clusters.
• To select or deselect specific hosts in a cluster, select Custom Selection, select a cluster from the list, and click
Customize. In the Select Hosts dialog box, select Custom Selection, select the hosts to upgrade, and click
Select.
– The default setting is to upgrade all hosts in the selected cluster. You can skip one or more hosts for an
upgrade, for example, if there are issues or errors with the hosts.
c) Assign an image to upgrade the selected hosts in the selected clusters.
Depending on your configuration, you can upgrade ESX clusters in batches. For example, if you use different
vSphere Lifecycle Manager images for your hosts, you can upgrade all ESX hosts using the same image in batch
1, then the hosts using a different image in batch 2 and so on.
1. Select clusters from the list.
2. Click Assign Image.
3. Select an imported image to assign to the selected clusters, and click Assign Image.
4. Click Next.
d) Select the upgrade options and click Next.
• Select Enable sequential cluster upgrade to upgrade the clusters in a subsequent order. If you do not select
the check box, by default, the clusters are upgraded in parallel to reduce upgrade time. If you selected more
than ten clusters to be upgraded, the first ten are upgraded in parallel and the remaining clusters are upgraded
sequentially.
• Select Enable Quick Boot to reduce the upgrade time by skipping the physical reboot of the host.
• Under VM power state, select the desired virtual machine behavior during the host upgrade.
• Select Migrate Powered Off and Suspended VMs to migrate the suspended and powered off virtual machines
from the hosts that must enter maintenance mode to other hosts in the cluster.
• Select Retry policy to retry the host upgrade. Specify a desired delay time between the host upgrade attempts
and a number of allowed upgrade attempts.
• Select Enable Live Patch when the cluster image includes a Live Patch.
– With the Auto option, hosts in the cluster are upgraded using Live Patch when possible. If Live Patch is not
available, ESX hosts in the cluster are placed into maintenance mode and are rebooted.
Broadcom 2657

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– With the Enforce option, only Live Patch is used for remediation without maintenance mode. ESX hosts are
not rebooted and there is no need to migrate the virtual machines running on the hosts in the cluster. If a
host in the cluster requires Maintenance Mode or Reboot, remediation is blocked.
Note:
Live Patch is not applicable for major upgrades. For major upgrades, for example, when upgrading your ESX
hosts from version 9.0 to 9.1, either select the Auto option or deselect the Enable Live Patch check box.
e) Select standalone hosts to upgrade and click Next.
By default, all standalone hosts are selected for upgrade. To upgrade specific standalone host, click Custom
Selection and select hosts from the list.
f) If you selected standalone hosts for upgrade, assign an image to the selected hosts.
1. Select hosts from the list.
2. Click Assign Image.
3. Select an imported image to assign to the selected hosts, and click Assign Image.
4. Click Next.
g) If you selected standalone hosts for upgrade, select host upgrade options.
• Select Enable Quick Boot to reduce the upgrade time by skipping the physical reboot of the host.
• Under VM power state, select the desired virtual machine behavior during the host upgrade.
• Select Retry policy to retry the host upgrade. Specify a desired delay time between the host upgrade attempts
and a maximum number of allowed upgrade attempts.
h) Review the upgrade configuration, and click Finish.
You can click Export to download the cluster upgrade information in a file format. Standalone hosts are not
CSV
included in the configuration export.
6. If you did not select all available ESX hosts for upgrade, click Configure New Batch and perform the previous step
again to specify the upgrade options for the new batch.
7. Optional: Under VMware ESX Upgrade, click Run Prechecks to run the upgrade prechecks.
You can click View Details to monitor the progress of the precheck. You can also review the report to evaluate all
errors and warnings.
8. Click Upgrade Now.
Perform this step on all ESX host batches that are configured for upgrade.
Alternatively, you can click Schedule and specify another time for the upgrade.
The upgrade of the ESX hosts starts. If you are upgrading multiple clusters or standalone hosts in parallel and one or
more of the cluster or standalone host upgrades fails, the upgrade continues on the remaining hosts. In addition, you can
configure a new upgrade batch for one or more failed clusters or standalone hosts without having to wait for the original
upgrade batch to finish.
• You can monitor the progress. See Monitoring VMware Cloud Foundation Upgrades.
After the upgrade is complete, allow some time (approximately 15 minutes) for post-upgrade auto-reconciliation
of configuration drift fixes before scheduling another upgrade. If you schedule a second upgrade to run before the
remediation task completes, the upgrade might be canceled or auto-reconciliation might fail.

Apply VCF Configuration Upgrades
VCF configuration upgrades identify and resolve any discrepancies between the intended/prescribed configuration and
the actual configuration, ensuring that the deployment aligns with the recommended configuration. This process includes
reconciling the configuration for 2nd party software components that are listed in the VCF Bill of Materials (BOM).
Configuration upgrades might be required after you apply software upgrades. After a configuration upgrade becomes
available, you can apply it immediately or can wait until after you have applied all software upgrades. Configuration
Upgrades must be performed during a maintenance window.
Configuration Upgrades can be applied to multiple domains in parallel. However, if a Configuration Upgrade is in progress,
another configuration upgrade on the same domain should not be attempted.
1. Log in to VCF Operations at <vcf_operations_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. Select Build > Lifecycle, expand VCF Instances, and select your domain.
3. On your domain page, click the Upgrades tab.
4. Optional: Under Prechecks, click Run Prechecks.
Resolve any issues before proceeding with the upgrade.
5. Under Configuration Upgrades, click Apply All.
• FEATURE: Configuration change required for a new feature.
• FIX: Configuration change associated with a fix for a defect.
Note:
Pending Configuration Upgrades do not block future BOM upgrades.
6. Optional: Check the progress of a configuration upgrade by clicking the task in the Tasks panel.
After the configuration upgrades are successfully applied, they will no longer appear in the table.

Upgrading to vSphere Foundation 9.1.x
To upgrade your vSphere Foundation 5.2 or 9.0.x environment to version 9.1.x, you must upgrade your components in a
specific subsequent order.
Forward-Only Upgrade Requirement
vSphere Foundation enforces strict upgrade path validation. You can only upgrade your vSphere Foundation environment
to a target version that is released after the release date of your current version. The target version can be a major, minor,
or a maintenance release. In general, you can upgrade directly to a patch release only if you can also upgrade to its
parent maintenance release. For example:
• Supported upgrade to vSphere Foundation 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3a (18 JUN 2024) and ESX 8.0
Update 3 (25 JUN 2024).
• Not supported upgrade to vSphere Foundation 9.1.0 (11 MAY 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX
8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026).
• Supported upgrade to vSphere Foundation 9.1.1 (03 SEP 2026): vCenter 8.0 Update 3j (27 MAY 2026) and ESX 8.0
Update 3j (27 MAY 2026).
VCF components might have further limitations, see VMware Interoperability Matrix.
VCF Upgrade Planner
You can now use the new VCF Upgrade Planning Tool to navigate you during the process of upgrading your existing
infrastructure to vSphere Foundation 9.1.
Environments Without Aria Operations for Logs 8.x or VCF Operations for Logs 9.0.x
For environments that do not have Aria Operations for Logs or VCF Operations for Logs and are not subject to upgrade
to log management 9.1.x, you can also follow Upgrading vSphere 8 and Optionally vSAN and Aria Operations 8 to 9.1.x.
In this scenario, you do not deploy VCF management services as part of the upgrade to 9.1.x. You can deploy them later
as a Day-N operation as they are required to deploy log management 9.1.x. You cannot use the capabilities of the 9.1.x
components that are not yet deployed. For more information on the 9.1 components and capabilities, see Components in
VCF and vSphere Foundation.

Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes.
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.
Licensing Overview
You license your VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) fleet or VMware vSphere Foundation (vSphere Foundation)
environment by using theVCF Operations instance that manages them and the VMware Cloud Foundation Business
Services console (vcf.broadcom.com).
What's New in 9.1
• Before you can license your assets, you must register VCF Operations and a license server with the VCF Business
Services console, and you must add licenses to the license server. For more information, see Registering VCF
Operations and a License Server with the VCF Business Services Console.
• You can assign a license directly to specific assets other than vCenter instances, such as ESX hosts, and vSAN
clusters. The licenses that you assign directly to these assets override the vCenter license that is assigned
automatically to them. For more information, see What is an Override License.
Broadcom 2668

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Overview of Core Procedures and Concepts in 9.1
Subscriptions To license your environment, you purchase a term-based subscription for a product with a specified
capacity. For more details, see Licensing Model.
Licenses A license is an object that entitles you to use the products that you purchased subscriptions for. A license
can span multiple subscriptions or, when you split the default license, a license can be a portion of a
subscription.
Licenses and product VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation include different sets of product components.
components interaction You purchase a subscription for a specific product. With the provided license, you license all product
components by using a registered VCF Operations instance.
• With your subscription for a product, you receive both a version 9+ default license, and license keys for
version 8.x of the product. You can decide which version of the product to deploy and license. Your total
used capacity must not exceed your purchased capacity.
• After you assign a license to a vCenter instances, the other product components added to the licensed
vCenter instances are automatically licensed. For more information, see Assign a Primary License to a
vCenter Instance.
• One VCF Operations instance can manage a mix of different license types and licenses for different
products. For example, you can manage both VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation primary licenses
in the same VCF Operations instance, and add-on licenses for different product components.
Default licenses The initial license that is automatically created in VCF Business Services console after you purchase a
subscription is called a default license. The default license is a pool of capacity from all active subscriptions
for the same product in the same Site ID. Available capacity is displayed in the unit of measure for the
specific product.
For example, if you purchase a VCF subscription for 500 cores, you receive a default license for 500 cores
of VCF and you also receive a default license of 500 TiBs of vSAN, that are added in a separate license. If,
on top of that, you purchase a vSAN add-on subscription for 200 TiBs, the new number of TiBs is added to
your default vSAN license, and its capacity becomes 700 TiBs.
Note:
For more information about using your Broadcom Site ID, see Broadcom knowledge base article
142873.
Types of licenses There are two types of licenses - primary licenses, such as VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware
vSphere Foundation licenses, and add-on licenses, such as vSAN add-on capacity or VMware Private AI
Foundation with NVIDIA licenses. You have a single license capacity provided per product.
For example, for VMware Cloud Foundation, the single license capacity provided for that product is
VMware Cloud Foundation (cores). This is a primary license and you must assign it to your environment
before you can assign an add-on license. Components are licensed automatically after you assign the
primary license to a vCenter instance. With VCF and vSphere Foundation, you also receive VMware vSAN
(TiB)capacity. You also receive VMware vSAN (TiB) capacity when you purchase vSAN as an add-on. The
vSAN TiB license is called an add-on license.
For more information about types of licenses, see Licensing Model.
Supported add-on In 9.1, the two supported add-on licenses that you can manage in the VCF Business Services console are
licenses VMware vSAN (TiB) and VMware Private AI Foundation with NVIDIA (cores).
You can purchase subscriptions for add-ons which are compatible with your products. For information about
available add-ons for each product, contact your sales team. Add-ons might not follow the same licensing
model as VCF and vSphere Foundation. You can find information about how to license specific add-ons
within their respective documentation.
VCF Operations You can register VCF Operations in the VCF Business Services console either in connected or in
registration modes disconnected mode. Connected mode is recommended because it simplifies license management.
License usage reports License usage reports are required at least once every 180 days to maintain your licenses. You must
update your licenses to confirm that the license usage report was submitted.
• If VCF Operations is registered in connected mode, license usage data is sent to the VCF Business
Services console automatically, and licenses can be updated either automatically or with a click of a
button. See Updating Licenses and Viewing the License Usage File.
Broadcom 2669

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• If VCF Operations is registered in disconnected mode, to report license usage, you must generate
a usage file and upload it in the VCF Business Services console (vcf.broadcom.com). See Updating
Licenses and Viewing the License Usage File.
Subscription expiration The total capacity of a license at any point in time equals the sum of the license capacity from all
contributing subscriptions that are active. When a subscription expires, its contribution to each license
is removed. If other subscriptions still contribute capacity, the license remains active but with reduced
capacity. When the last contributing subscription expires the license expires.
License expiration License expiration applies when the last contributing subscription expires or if usage is not reported and the
license is not refreshed.
• Notifications are displayed before the license expiration.
• After the license expires, you have 90 days to update your license. License assignments are impacted
during this 90 day period and notifications appear in most components, including VCF Operations and
vCenter.
• 90 days after the expiration, your environment is impacted in several ways, including:
– Management operations of various components might be prevented;
– ESX hosts disconnect from vCenter, most host management operations are prevented;
– You cannot start workloads.
Note:
Existing workloads are not proactively stopped.
• You can recover expired environments by downloading an updated license file.
Usage analytics You can check your license consumption analytics in your VCF Operations instance, and the VCF Business
Services console. For more information about usage analytics, see License Usage Analytics.

Licensing Model
The licensing model is the same for VCF and vSphere Foundation. You assign licenses to vCenter instances. The other
product components that are connected to the licensed vCenter instances, are automatically licensed. Starting with
version 9.1, you can also assign a license directly to assets that use license capacity, for example, ESX hosts, and vSAN
clusters. The licenses that you assign directly to assets override the license that is automatically assigned.
How Capacity Pooling Works
When you purchase multiple subscriptions for the same product, capacity is pooled together in one default license per
product. For example, if you purchase a subscription for 200 cores for VCF, and then you purchase another subscription
for 300 cores, you have one default primary license for the product with 500 cores total capacity, instead of two licenses
with 200 and 300 cores capacity. If the different subscriptions have different end dates, the number of cores is reduced on
the end date of each subscription, but you can use the capacity for which you have an active subscription.
vSAN capacity, when purchased through VCF, vSphere Foundation, or a vSAN add-on, also pools together in one default
add-on license. For example, when you purchase a subscription for 300 cores for VCF, and 50 TiBs as a vSAN add-on,
you have one default vSAN license with 350 TiBs total capacity.
To pool together into the same default license, subscriptions must meet the following requirements:
• Must be for the same product, for example, VCF, or vSphere Foundation.
• Must have the same unit of measure, for example, cores or TiBs.
• Must have the same license (Site ID).
• Must not support overage billing. VMware Cloud Services Provider (VCSP) partner subscriptions are not eligible for
pooling.
Note:
For some products, you receive multiple default licenses. For example, with a VCF subscription you receive both
a default VMware Cloud Foundation license and a default vSAN Enterprise license.
What Are Primary Licenses?
Primary licenses are the licenses for VCF and vSphere Foundation. They are based on a core license unit. The only
assets in your environment which use the capacity of your primary licenses are ESX hosts. To calculate the capacity you
need for your environment, you need the total number of the physical CPU cores for each physical CPU on all ESX hosts
in your environment. Most products have a minimum consumption rule of 16 cores per physical CPU. CPUs that have
fewer than 16 cores use 16 cores. For example, if you have 1 ESX host in your inventory, with 1 CPU, and 8 CPU cores
per CPU, this ESX host uses 16 cores of your license total capacity because it is the minimum license capacity.
Number of ESX Hosts Number of CPUs per Host Cores per CPU Required License Capacity
1 1 8 16
2 2 8 64
2 2 16 64
2 2 24 96
For more information about calculating the license capacity you need for your environment, see Broadcom knowledge
base article 95927.
Broadcom 2673

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You assign primary licenses to your vCenter instances and optionally as overrides to individual hosts. When a primary
license is assigned to a vCenter instance, the other components of the product are licensed automatically with the license
you assign to the vCenter instance.
To assign licenses to your vCenter instances, you use a VCF Operations instance. For more information about the
licensing workflow, see High-Level Licensing Workflow .
Note:
The difference in the licensing model for VCF Edge and VMware Cloud Foundation is that VCF Edge has an 8
CPU cores per physical CPU minimum. For more information about VCF Edge license terms, see the Specific
Program Documentation for VCF Edge.
Evaluation Mode
After you install a product or component, it operates in evaluation mode for up to 90 days. During that period, you must
license your environment.
Evaluation mode applies to new deployments and upgrades from version 8.x to version 9.1. Examples of when evaluation
mode applies:
1. Deployment of ESX 9.1 or upgrade from ESXi 8.x to ESX 9.1. The ESX host is in evaluation mode for up to 90 days
from first boot.
2. Deployment of vCenter 9.1 or upgrade from vCenter 8.x to vCenter 9.1. The vCenter instance is in evaluation mode for
up to 90 days.
3. Deployment of VCF Operations 9.1 or upgrade from Aria Operations 8.x to VCF Operations 9.1. The VCF Operations
instance is in evaluation mode for up to 90 days.
4. When you add an ESX host to a licensed vCenter instance but there is no available license capacity to license the
host, the ESX host remains in evaluation mode for up to 90 days. The evaluation period starts when ESX is installed,
not when it is added to the vCenter instance.
Note:
ESX hosts that you provision as stateless hosts by using Auto Deploy have no evaluation period in version 9.0
and 9.1.
Evaluation mode ends when a license is assigned, or at the end of the 90 days. If a valid license is not assigned within the
90-day evaluation period, your environment is impacted in several ways, including:
1. Management operations of components are prevented.
2. ESX hosts disconnect from vCenter.
a. If the 90-day evaluation period of a vCenter instance expires, all hosts added to the vCenter instance are
disconnected from it.
b. If the 90-day evaluation period of an ESX host expires, but the vCenter instance is licensed, only the ESX host with
an expired evaluation period is disconnected from the vCenter.
3. You start workloads.
Note:
Existing workloads are not proactively stopped.
If the evaluation period expires, you can recover the operations in your environment by assigning a valid license.
1. If the 90-day evaluation period of a VCF Operations instance has expired, you must register the instance and add a
valid license to it.
2. If the 90-day evaluation period of a vCenter instance has expired, you must assign a valid license to it from VCF
Operations.
3. If the 90-day evaluation period of an ESX host has expired, you must add the host to a vCenter instance that has a
valid license with enough available capacity assigned to it.
Broadcom 2674

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
After you install VMware Cloud Foundation, it runs in evaluation mode for up to 90 days. If you fail to license your
VCF fleet before the evaluation period expires, you must reinstall the software because you cannot license a fleet
with an expired evaluation period.
Subscriptions and License Expiration
Multiple subscriptions for the same product can contribute capacity to a single default or split license, and a single
subscription can contribute capacity to multiple split licenses.
The total capacity of a default or a split license equals the sum of the license capacity units from all contributing
subscriptions that are active. When a subscription expires, its contribution to each license is removed. If other
subscriptions contribute capacity to the license, the license remains active but with reduced capacity. When the last
contributing subscription expires, the license capacity reaches zero, and the license expires.
VCF subscriptions with different expiration dates.
Name License Capacity Start Date Expiration Date
A 100 cores July 1, 2027 June 30, 2028
B 25 cores July 1, 2027 December 31, 2028
You use the license capacity from the two subscriptions to create two split licenses.
• License 1. 75 cores sourced entirely from subscription A. This license expires on June 30, 2028, when
Subscription A expires.
• License 2. 50 cores where 25 cores are sourced from subscription A, and 25 cores are sourced from
subscription B. Capacity changes over time based on the subscription terms:
– From July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2028: 50 cores (25 cores from subscription A and 25 cores from
subscription B).
– From July 1, 2028 through December 31, 2028: 25 cores (from subscription B only, subscription A
expires).
License 2 expires on December 31, 2028, when subscription B expires.
For more information about the impact of license expiration on your environment, see Licensing Overview.

Mixed-Version Environments
If you have pre-version 9.0 product components, for example, vCenter instances, ESX hosts, NSX, you can continue to
use license keys to license capabilities of those components without any changes. If you use a VCF Operations instance
for license management, you must update the instance to manage version 9+ licenses.
You can add ESXi 8.x hosts that are licensed with license keys to your vCenter instances of version 9.1. Those ESXi
hosts must be licensed with a pre-version 9 license key, and they also use license capacity from your version 9+ license
from your VCF or vSphere Foundation subscription. The used license capacity displayed in VCF Operations for this
vCenter instance of version 9.1 includes the license capacity used by the licensed ESX hosts of versions 9.0, 9.1, and 8.x
that are added to this vCenter instance. Used capacity for the license displayed in the VCF Operations instance and the
VCF Business Services console also reflects this. Version 8.x licenses cannot be assigned as override licenses. If you
want to upgrade an ESX host of version 9.0 to version 9.1, the host should either have remaining evaluation period, or it
must be added to a vCenter instance of version 9.1 that is connected to a license server.
Note:
In a VMware Cloud Foundation Instance, the management domain of version 9.1 can manage workload domains
of version 5.x, 9.0, and 9.1.
License usage data is collected for version 9+ licenses, and for licenses of earlier versions connected to VCF Operations.
You can view both your version 9+ and pre-version 9 license usage data by using the usage analytics available in VCF
Operations and the VCF Business Services console.
When you upgrade your vCenter instances to version 9.1, they operate in evaluation mode for up to 90 days. During that
period, you must license the vCenter instances with a primary license with sufficient capacity. The license must be for the
product you want to use.
Add-on Licenses Included in Your VCF Subscription
To be able to use an add-on license, you must first assign a primary license to your vCenter instances. Add-on licenses
are available for VCF and vSphere Foundation products.

When you purchase VCF, in addition to your VMware Cloud Foundation (cores) license you receive a vSAN tebibytes
(TiBs) license. Starting November 3, 2025, based on your VCF subscription, you might also receive a license for VMware

For information about available add-ons for each product that are not included in your subscription, contact your sales
