Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes.
Deploying or Converging to VCF
For information about deploying or converging to a VCF fleet or VCF Instance, see Deployment, Convergence, and
Upgrade.
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.
Managing ESX Hosts in VMware Cloud Foundation
Managing ESX hosts in VMware Cloud Foundation involves commissioning hosts into the global inventory, assigning them
to workload domains, and decommissioning them when they are no longer needed.
To add ESX hosts to the global inventory, you must first create a network pool or expand the default network pool created
during deployment. After you have a suitable network pool, you can commission ESX hosts for use in a VCF domain.
The ESX host lifecycle in VMware Cloud Foundation consists of the following stages:
Broadcom 2716

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Create or expand a network pool. A network pool provides the IP addressing and Layer 2 network specifications for
VMkernel adapters on ESX hosts. See Network Pool Management.
2. Commission ESX hosts. Commissioning associates ESX hosts with a network pool and adds them to the global
inventory. Newly commissioned ESX hosts appear in the global inventory with a host state of UNASSIGNED. The global
inventory is the central repository of all ESX hosts that are available to VMware Cloud Foundation, regardless of
whether they are assigned to a VCF domain. See Commission ESX Hosts.
3. Assign hosts to a VCF domain. When an ESX host is added to a workload domain, an IP address from the network
pool IP range is assigned to it. See View ESX Host Inventory.
4. Decommission ESX hosts. Decommissioning removes ESX hosts from the global inventory. If you want to reuse a host
in a different VCF domain, you must decommission, re-image, and commission the host before adding it to the VCF
domain. See Decommission ESX Hosts.
See VMware Configuration Maximums for information about ESX host maximums.
Note:
VCF does not support stateless ESX hosts. All ESX hosts must have a local installation of the ESX operating
system that persists across reboots.
Network Pool Management
Network pools in VCF manage the IP addressing and Layer 2 network specifications for VMkernel adapters on ESX hosts.
Use the following guidance to create, size, and manage network pools for vSAN, Network File System (NFS), Internet
Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI), and vMotion traffic.
When you create a workload domain or add an ESX host or vSphere cluster to an existing VCF domain, you only need to
enter an IP address manually for the vmk0 management interface. Network pools automatically assign static IP addresses
to vSAN, NFS, iSCSI, and vMotion VMkernel ports.
Overview
A network pool in VCF is a logical container that manages the IP addressing and Layer 2 network specifications, including
virtual local area network (VLAN) and maximum transmission unit (MTU), for the VMkernel adapters on ESX hosts.
Depending on the storage option, a network pool includes information about subnets reserved for the vMotion and vSAN,
vSAN Storage Client, NFS, or iSCSI networks that are required for adding a host to the global inventory.
Table 983: Information Required for a Network Pool
Storage Being Used Required Networks in Network Pool
vSAN vMotion and vSAN
vSAN compute vMotion and vSAN
vSAN storage (formerly known as vSAN Max) vMotion, vSAN, vSAN Storage Client
NFS vMotion and NFS
vSAN and NFS vMotion, vSAN, and NFS
VMFS on FC vMotion only or vMotion and NFS
vVols on FC* vMotion only or vMotion and NFS
vVols on iSCSI* vMotion and iSCSI
vVols on NFS* vMotion and NFS
* Starting with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and vSphere Foundation 9.0, the vSphere Virtual Volumes capability,
also known as vVols, is deprecated and will be removed in a future release of VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere
Foundation. Support for vSphere Virtual Volumes will continue for critical bug fixes only for versions of vSphere 8.x,
VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 5.x, and other supported versions until end-of-support for the
respective release.
Broadcom 2717

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The network pool contains a range of IP addresses for each network. IP addresses from the ranges are assigned to the
VMkernel ports on the ESX host. The use of IP ranges allows you to limit the IP addresses that are consumed from a
given subnet. You can add more IP ranges to expand the use of the provided subnet.
A default network pool is created when you deploy VMware Cloud Foundation. This network pool is automatically
associated with the management domain.
To create a workload domain with hosts in a different layer-2 network than the management domain, you must create a
new network pool. Also, if you want to use external NFS or VMFS on FC storage, you must create a new network pool. A
network pool can contain both vSAN and NFS networks.
When you create a workload domain with multiple vSphere clusters, those vSphere clusters can share a network pool or
each cluster can have its own network pool.
Dual-Stack Configuration
In VCF 9.1, network pools are expanded to support IPv6-only configuration for vmkernel adapters for storage and vMotion
traffic, allowing for greater scalability and flexibility in how storage and vMotion traffic is routed.
Traffic Type Supported IP Version IP Address Assignment Mode Description
Storage IPv4 or IPv6 IPv6 - Static, DHCP, SLAAC Must be dedicated to a single
IPv4 - Static protocol family per cluster (all
hosts use IPv6 for vSAN).
vMotion IPv4 or IPv6 IPv6 - Static, DHCP, SLAAC Allows offloading bulk mobility
IPv4 - Static traffic to IPv6 networks.
NSX Overlay (TEP) IPv4 Only Static, DHCP VCF 9.1 does not support IPv6
for Tunnel Endpoints (TEPs).
Management IPv4 or Dual-Stack Static Management interfaces support
static IP assignment.
You cannot mix IP versions for the same traffic type within a cluster. For example, if you assign an IPv6 vSAN network
pool to a cluster, all hosts in that cluster must use IPv6 for vSAN.
For Dual-Stack management pools, you must ensure that your DNS servers have both Forward (A/AAAA) and Reverse
(PTR) records configured for the components before deployment.
While the Management network can be Dual-Stack (carrying both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic), vSAN and vMotion networks are
typically configured as IPv6-Only or IPv4-Only to optimize performance and simplify routing.
Size a Network Pool
Properly sizing a network pool is critical to prevent future issues in the environment due to insufficient IP addresses. Care
must be taken when defining the subnets for a network pool as the subnet cannot be changed after it is deployed. The
scope of IP addresses used from the defined subnet can be limited by the definition of one or more inclusion ranges.
Thus, it is recommended that you begin with defining a larger subnet than what is initially required and utilize the inclusion
ranges to limit use. This will provide you the capability to grow with demand as needed.
You begin sizing a network pool by determining the number of ESX hosts that you will have in each vSphere cluster.
The minimum number of ESX hosts varies based on the storage type and deployment model. A vSphere cluster can be
expanded to the supported maximum number of ESX hosts.
Allocate a minimum of one IP address per ESX host plus enough additional IP addresses to account for growth and
expansion of the environment. Ensure that the subnet defined provides enough unused IP addresses and that appropriate
inclusion ranges are defined. Note that some of the IP addresses within the subnet will be used for other purposes, such
as defining the gateway address, firewalls, or other entities. Use care not to conflict with these addresses.
Here are some important considerations for determining the size of your network pool:
• Type of network architecture.
• Number of hosts that can be placed in each rack or layer-2 network domain.
• Number of hosts required in a vSphere cluster.
Broadcom 2718

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Number of workload domains and cluster you plan on creating.
View Network Pool Details
You can view the network details for a network pool as well as the total number of used and available (if IPv4) IP
addresses.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts > Network Pools.
2. Click the arrow to the left of the pool name.
A summary view of the network pools details is displayed.
3. Click the name of a network pool.
A detailed view of the network pool details is displayed, including network types and included IP ranges.
Create a Network Pool
A network pool must include the vMotion network information. Depending on the type of storage you are using, you must
provide network information for vSAN, NFS, and iSCSI.
Within a VCF instance, a given subnet must be defined in only one network pool per network type. Defining the same
subnet in two network pools is not supported, even if the included IP ranges do not overlap.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
Important:
Starting with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and vSphere Foundation 9.0, the vSphere Virtual Volumes capability,
also known as vVols, is deprecated and will be removed in a future release of VMware Cloud Foundation and
vSphere Foundation. Support for vSphere Virtual Volumes will continue for critical bug fixes only for versions of
vSphere 8.x, VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 5.x, and other supported versions until end-of-
support for the respective release.
Broadcom 2719

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts > Network Pools.
2. Click Create Network Pool.
3. Enter a name for the network pool.
4. Select the network type(s).
• For vSAN ESA/OSA and NFS, you can include both vSAN and NFS network information in the same network pool
or create separate network pools for vSAN and NFS.
• For vSAN storage, select vSAN, vSAN Storage Client, and vMotion.
• For vSAN compute, select vSAN and vMotion.
• For VMFS on FC, select vMotion only.
• For vVols on FC, select vMotion only or vMotion and NFS.
• For vVols on iSCSI, select iSCSI.
• For vVols on NFS, select vMotion and NFS.
5. Provide the following network information for the selected network type(s).
Option Description
IP Scheme IPv4 or IPv6
VLAN ID Enter a VLAN ID between 1 and 4094.
MTU Enter an MTU between 1500 and 9000.
(IPv6 Only) IP Assignment Method Select between static, DHCP, or SLAAC.
Default Gateway For IPv6 networking, this options is only available if you select static address assignment.
Enter the default gateway (CIDR notation).
Included IP Ranges For IPv6 networking, this options is only available if you select static address assignment.
Enter an IP address range from which an IP address can be assigned to hosts that are
associated with this network pool. The IP address range must be from within the specified
subnet. You cannot include the IP address of the default gateway in the IP address range.
You can enter multiple IP address ranges.
Note:
Ensure that you have entered the correct IP address range. IP ranges cannot be
edited after the network pool is created.
6. Click Save.
Add a Network Pool IP Address Range
You can edit a network pool to add a new IP address range.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts > Network Pools.
2. Click the vertical ellipsis (three dots) in the network pool row you want to edit and then click Add additional Network
Pool IP Range.
3. Enter the start and end IP addresses and click Add.
For IPv6, this option is available only when address assignment is set to static.
Rename a Network Pool
You can rename an existing network pool.
Broadcom 2720

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).

2. Click the vertical ellipsis (three dots) in the network pool row you want to edit and then click Rename Network Pool.

Delete a Network Pool
You can delete a network pool if none of the ESX hosts with an IP address from the pool belong to a workload domain.
The default pool created during deployment cannot be deleted.
Ensure that the ESX hosts in the network pool are not assigned to a workload domain. To verify this, view the network
pool details and confirm that the Used IPs for the network pool is 0.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts > Network Pools.
2. Click the vertical ellipsis (three dots) in the network pool row you want to edit and then click Delete.
3. Click Delete.
View ESX Host Inventory
The Hosts page in the vSphere Client displays details about all the ESX hosts in the global inventory, including CPU
utilization and memory usage across all hosts, as well as the total number of hosts used and unallocated.
For each ESX host, the Hosts page displays details, including name, status, vSphere cluster, and CPU and memory
usage.
The Hosts page also provides controls for commissioning hosts.
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts.
2. Click Assigned Hosts to see a list of ESX hosts that are assigned to a workload domain.
You can view details about each ESX host, including name, vSphere cluster, and CPU and memory usage. Click the
host name to view more details about the host in the vSphere inventory. Click the vSphere cluster name to view more
details about the cluster in the vSphere inventory.
3. Click Unassigned Hosts to see a list of commissioned ESX hosts that are available to create a new workload domain
or add to an existing workload domain.
You can view details about commissioned ESX hosts and also commission and decommission ESX hosts from the
Unassigned Hosts tab.
Commission ESX Hosts
Adding ESX hosts to the global inventory is called commissioning. You must commission ESX hosts before you can use
them to create a new workload domain or add them to an existing VCF domain.
Prepare your hosts. See Preparing ESX Hosts for VCF or vSphere Foundation.
Ensure that each ESX host you commission meets the following criteria:
• Hosts for vSAN-based workload domains are vSAN-compliant and certified on the VMware Hardware Compatibility
Guide.
Broadcom 2721

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Hosts for NFS-based workload domains are certified on the VMware Hardware Compatibility Guide.
• Hosts for VMFS on FC-based workload domains are certified on the VMware Compatibility Guide. In addition, the
hosts must have supported FC cards (Host Bus Adapters) and drivers installed and configured. For compatible FC
cards, see the VMware Compatibility Guide.
Important:
The VMFS datastore must be mounted on all the hosts before commissioning.
• Hosts for vVols-based workload domains are certified on the VMware Hardware Compatibility Guide.
– For vVols on FC-based workload domains, ensure that all ESX hosts have access to the FC array before launching
the workflow.
– For vVols on NFS-based workload domains, ensure that all ESX hosts must be able to reach the NFS server from
the NFS network assigned in the IP pool.
– For vVols on iSCSI-based workload domains, ensure that the iSCSI software initiator must be enabled on each
ESXi host and the VASA provider URL must be listed as the dynamic target.
Important:
Starting with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and vSphere Foundation 9.0, the vSphere Virtual Volumes capability,
also known as vVols, is deprecated and will be removed in a future release of VMware Cloud Foundation and
vSphere Foundation. Support for vSphere Virtual Volumes will continue for critical bug fixes only for versions of
vSphere 8.x, VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 5.x, and other supported versions until end-of-
support for the respective release.
• Each host must have the correct number of physical NICs for the desired network configuration for the host. Hosts can
have a single physical NIC or multiple physical NICs. For hosts with multiple physical NICs, only one can be connected
to a standard switch, and the NIC must support all management traffic.
• Management IP address is configured on a VMkernel interface connected to the Management Network on the
standard switch.
• Host has the drivers and firmware versions specified in the VMware Hardware Compatibility Guide.
• A supported version of ESX is installed on the host. See the VMware Cloud Foundation Release Notes for information
about supported versions.
• Has both forward and reverse lookup entries (FQDN) configured on the DNS server.
• Host name must be same as the FQDN.
• Self-signed certificate regenerated based on FQDN of host. See Regenerate the Self-Signed Certificate on the ESX
Hosts.
• Hardware health status is healthy without any errors.
• All disk partitions on HDD and SSD are deleted.
• A network pool must be created and available before host commissioning.
• The network pool must support the storage type you select for a host (vSAN, vSAN ESA, vSAN Storage Client, NFS,
VMFS on FC, vVols). See Network Pool Management.
• Host is configured with an appropriate gateway. The gateway must be part of the management subnet.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
You can add ESX hosts individually or use a JSON template to commission multiple hosts at once. You can also run
multiple commission hosts tasks at the same time.
After you specify host details and select the network pool to associate the hosts with, the platform validates and
commissions each host. Each host is added to the free pool and is available for VCF domains and vSphere clusters.
• Hosts that use vSAN storage can only be used with vSAN-based clusters.
– Hosts that are commissioned for vSAN HCI with ESA enabled can only be used for vSAN ESA clusters.
– Hosts that are commissioned for vSAN HCI without ESA enabled can only be used for vSAN OSA clusters.
– Hosts that are commissioned for vSAN Storage (formerly vSAN Max) can only be used for vSAN storage clusters (a
subset of vSAN ESA).
– Hosts that are commissioned for vSAN Compute Cluster can only be used for vSAN compute clusters.
Broadcom 2722

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Hosts that use NFS storage can only be used with NFS-based clusters.
• Hosts that use VMFS on FC storage can only be used with VMFS on FC-based clusters.
• Hosts that use vVols storage can only be used with vVols-based clusters.
See VMware Configuration Maximums for information about the maximum number of hosts you can commission at one
time and the maximum number of commission hosts tasks that you can run in parallel.
If you used ESX hosts with certificates generated by an external CA for deployment, hosts used for expanding VCF
domains or for creating workload domains must also use certificates generated by an external CA. See Configure ESX
Hosts with Signed Certificates.
Note:
When you add a host during host commissioning, the platform temporarily activates SSH on the host in order to
retrieve the host key. After it retrieves the host key, the platform deactivates SSH on the host.
With VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0.1 and later, you can use non-certified ESA disks during vSAN ESA cluster
configuration for proof-of-concept purposes only. For more information, see kB 408300.

Decommission ESX Hosts
Removing ESX hosts from the global inventory is called decommissioning. If you want to re-use a host in a different VCF
domain, you must decommission, re-image, and commission the host before adding it to the VCF domain.
The hosts that you want to decommission must not be assigned to a VCF domain. If a host is assigned to a VCF domain,
you must remove it from the VCF domain before you can decommission it.
To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
See VMware Configuration Maximums for information about the maximum number of hosts you can decommission at one
time and the maximum number of decommission hosts tasks that you can run in parallel.
1. In the vSphere Client, click Global Inventory Lists > Hosts > Unassigned Hosts.
2. Select one or more hosts and click Decommission Selected Hosts.
3. Activate or deactivate Skip failed hosts during decommissioning.
This setting is enabled by default. When enabled, hosts that fail are skipped and decommissioning continues on the
remaining hosts.
4. Click Confirm.
If the decommissioned host was previously part of a VCF domain, you must re-image it before commissioning it again
and adding it to a VCF domain. If the decommissioned host was not part of a VCF domain, you do not have to re-image it
before commissioning it again.
Managing VCF Domains in VMware Cloud Foundation
A VCF domain represents a logical unit of application-ready infrastructure that groups ESX hosts managed by a vCenter
instance with specific characteristics according to VMware recommended practices. VCF supports two types of VCF
domains; the management domain and workload domains.
The management domain is created during the deployment or convergence process by VCF Installer and contains the
management components for a VCF instance, including SDDC Manager, vCenter, NSX Manager, and ESX hosts. After
the management domain is created, you can deploy or import workload domains to run customer workloads. Workload
Broadcom 2724

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
domains include a vCenter and NSX Manager (which can be shared with other workload domains), as well as one or more
vSphere clusters with ESX hosts.
For more information about VCF domains, see the VMware Cloud Foundation Overview and Design Guide.
After creating or importing a workload domain in VCF Operations, you can add or remove vSphere clusters and ESX
hosts using the vSphere Client to support the resource and availability needs of your organization.
Certain operations related to VCF domains, such as expanding or reducing workload domains, stretching or unstretching
a cluster, changing the primary storage, creating or deleting datastores, can be performed outside of the VCF Operations
UI, which can create a configuration drift in VCF Operations and SDDC Manager. VCF 9.1 introduces specific guardrails
which allow making such out-of-band changes without affecting the configuration state of the environment in VCF
Operations.
Sharing a vSphere Distributed Switch Across Clusters in a VCF Domain
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, multiple vSphere clusters within a VCF domain can share a single vSphere Distributed Switch
(VDS) instead of maintaining a dedicated VDS for each cluster. This capability centralizes network management,
optimizes network deployment, and ensures uniform policy application across clusters.
Supported configurations for sharing a VDS between clusters:
• Layer 2 (L2) clusters
• Clusters in the management domain or workload domains.
• Clusters in the same datacenter and the same network pool.
• For full VDS reuse, clusters in the same network pool. For policy reuse and hybrid, clusters can be in different network
pools.
Unsupported configurations for sharing a VDS between clusters:
• Layer 3 (L3) clusters
• vSAN stretched clusters, including both the new cluster and the source cluster.
• Partial reuse of port groups. All port groups within a VDS must either be shared or distinct.
Create a New Workload Domain
Creating a new workload domain adds a logical pool of compute, network, and storage infrastructure to a VCF instance.
Requirements for a workload domain with a vSphere cluster (full deployment with cluster):
• Hosts must be commissioned with the target principal storage type. See Managing ESX Hosts in VMware Cloud
Foundation.
• If the hosts in the management domain have an express patch applied, the hosts for the new workload domain must
be imaged with the same express patch.
• If you are using vVols principal storage type, add a VASA provider to the inventory. See Add a VASA Provider for vVols
Storage in Workload Domains.
Important:
Starting with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and vSphere Foundation 9.0, the vSphere Virtual Volumes capability,
also known as vVols, is deprecated and will be removed in a future release of VMware Cloud Foundation and
vSphere Foundation. Support for vSphere Virtual Volumes will continue for critical bug fixes only for versions of
vSphere 8.x, VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 5.x, and other supported versions until end-of-
support for the respective release.
• If you are using vSAN principal storage type, SSD disks or NVMe disks without pre-existing disk partitions must be
available with each host.
• If you are using vSAN as the principal storage type, a vSphere Lifecycle Manager image must exist in the VCF image
library before you create the workload domain. See Managing vSphere Lifecycle Manager Images for VMware Cloud
Foundation.
• A static IP pool or a DHCP server configured and advertising IP addresses on the workload domain's NSX host overlay
(HOST TEP) VLAN.
Broadcom 2725

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, this is not required for VLAN backed VPC workload domains.
• Each host must have at least one physical NIC, connected to a standard switch.
• A network pool with free IP addresses must be available.
• The IP addresses and Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) for the vCenter and NSX Manager instances must be
resolvable over DNS.
• At least one IP address and a Fully Qualified Domain Names for the Virtual Network Appliance. If you are deploying
a cluster of Virtual Network Appliances, you need two IP addresses and FQDNs. Required only when you select
Full Stack VPC with Distributed Connectivity on the Networking page. See Create a Virtual Networking Appliance
Cluster.
• Starting with VCF 9.1.1 and later, the first vSphere cluster in a workload domain cannot share a vSphere Distributed
Switch (VDS) because no existing VDS is available to reuse. Subsequent clusters that you add to the workload domain
can share a VDS with the first cluster.
Requirements for a workload domain without a vSphere cluster (domain infrastructure only):
• A static IP pool or a DHCP server configured and advertising IP addresses on the workload domain's NSX host overlay
(Host TEP) VLAN.
Note:
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, this requirement does not apply when you deploy a TEP-less workload domain. In TEP-
less mode, you realize subnets with layer 2 support using a VLAN-backed VPC, and the Host TEP infrastructure
is not required.
• The IP addresses and Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) for the vCenter and NSX Manager instances must be
resolvable over DNS.
Requirements for a dual-stack workload domain:
• To deploy a workload domain with dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) networking, SDDC Manager must be configured in dual-
stack mode. If SDDC Manager is IPv4-only, the option to create a dual-stack workload domain is not available.
• All ESX hosts for the new workload domain cluster must use the same IP version configuration.
• You can configure vSAN and vMotion to run strictly on IPv6.
• The NSX Overlay network does not support IPv6 or dual-stack networking. It requires a dedicated IPv4 range in your
network pool.
For newly-deployed workload domains, NSX Manager and vCenter are deployed on the management domain primary
cluster.

Option Description
Distributed Switch name Enter a name for the distributed switch.
MTU Determines the largest size of a data packet that can pass through
the distributed switch.
Uplinks / LAG configuration
VDS Uplinks VDS Uplinks represent the individual physical network adapter
(VNICs) on an ESXi host connecting to the physical switch. In
this mode, the VDS manages load balancing and failover using
software-based algorithms like Route Based on Physical NIC Load
(LBT) or Route Based on Originating Virtual Port ID. The physical
switch ports do not need to be configured in a bond or channel;
they operate as independent links.
Number of uplinks The number of uplinks dedicated to this distributed switch.
Map uplinks to physical NICs on host Connects your logical virtual network to your physical network
hardware. This mapping pairs a logical uplink (a software object
on the distributed switch), with a physical adapter (hardware on
the ESXi host).
VDS Lag VDS LAG bundles multiple physical uplinks into a single logical
channel using the Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP). This
requires a corresponding LACP configuration on the physical ToR
(Top-of-Rack) switches. The physical switch and VDS negotiate
traffic hashing.
LAG Name The logical name that is assigned to this group of ports.
Broadcom 2733

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
LACP Mode • Active:
The VDS actively sends LACP packets to negotiate the link
with the physical switch. This is the recommended setting.
• Passive:
The VDS waits for the physical switch to initiate the LACP
negotiation.
LAG Load Balancing Defines the hashing algorithm used to distribute traffic across the
physical links.
LACP Time Out Determines how often LACP heartbeats (PDUs) are sent:
• Slow: 30 seconds
• Fast: 1 second
Number of ports Defines how many physical network adapters (VMNICs) will be
bundled into this single logical LAG per host.
Map ports to physical network adaptors on host Maps the logical ports of the LAG to the actual physical hardware
on the ESX hosts.
Traffic types for the distributed switch • ESX Management
• VM Management

c) To configure the traffic types for the distributed switch, turn on the toggle for each traffic type and configure the
settings.
Option Description
Distributed portgroup name Name of the distributed portgroup for this traffic type.
MTU Determines the largest size of a data packet that can pass through
the distributed switch for this traffic type.
Load balancing Route Based on Originating Virtual Port
(Default): the distributed switch maps port IDs to specific
uplinks based on the load balancing source of the NSX uplink
profile.
Route Based on Physical NIC Load (LBT): the
distributed switch monitors the saturation of the physical
uplinks. If the primary uplinks exceeds a set amout of utilization
(75% default) for 30 seconds, the distributed switch moves
some VM traffic to another active uplink. This is default load
balancing method for vSAN, vMotion, ESX management, and VM
management.
Route Based on Source MAC Hash: the distributed switch
uses the VM's MAC address and hashes it to an uplink, which
creates even distribution for VMs that might change port IDs but
keep MAC addresses.
Route Based on IP Hash: the distributed switch uses the
source and destination IP address of every packet to decide which
uplink to use. This allows a single VM to use multiple uplinks
simultaneously.
Note:
You must configure LACP (Link Aggregation Control
Protocol) or static EtherChannel on the physical Top-of-
Rack switches.
Use Explicit Failover Order: you define the order in
which uplinks are used in case of failure.
Broadcom 2734

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
Uplink Active: This traffic type uses the uplink immediately during
normal operation. In case of multiple active uplinks, traffic of this
type is distributed across all active uplinks simultaneously.
Standby: A standby uplink is connected, but no traffic is sent
through it as long as at least one "Active" uplink is healthy. If all
active uplinks fail, the distributed switch moves the standby uplink
to active status.
Unused: Traffic of this type never uses this uplink, regardless of
the status of the remaining uplinks.

Create a New Workload Domain without a vSphere Cluster
Create a workload domain without a vSphere cluster. The workflow deploys and configures a vCenter instance and
deploys and configures a new or joins an existing NSX Manager instance. The new vCenter and NSX Manager instances
are deployed in the management domain. No unassigned ESX hosts are required for creating this workload domain.
The IP addresses and Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) for the vCenter and NSX Manager instances must be
resolvable over DNS.
A workload domain without a vSphere cluster has the following limitations:
• A workload domain without a vSphere cluster cannot be a management domain.
• You cannot enable vSphere Supervisor for a workload domain without a vSphere cluster.
• You cannot patch or upgrade the components in the workload domain before adding a vSphere cluster. All workload
domains that share an NSX Manager with a workload domain without a vSphere cluster cannot be patched or
upgraded.
Requirements for a dual-stack workload domain:
• To deploy a workload domain with dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) networking, SDDC Manager must be configured in dual-
stack mode. If SDDC Manager is IPv4-only, the option to create a dual-stack workload domain is not available.
• The NSX Overlay network does not support IPv6 or dual-stack networking. It requires a dedicated IPv4 range in your
network pool.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the VCF Operations top navigation bar, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, select Overview >
Inventory.
3. Expand VCF Instances and select the VCF instance where you are creating a new workload domain.
4. From the Add workload domain drop-down menu, select Create new.
5. Review the prerequisites, click Select All, and click Proceed.
The Workload Domain wizard opens.

since resource object names (such as vSphere Distributed Switch

Deploy infrastructure only This option creates a workload domain without an ESX cluster.
The domain is deployed with vCenter and NSX Manager instances
only.

dual-stack networking.

Import an Existing vCenter to Create a Workload Domain
If you have an existing vCenter instance, with or without NSX Manager, you can use VCF Operations to import it to a VCF
Instance as a workload domain.
• Verify that your existing vSphere infrastructure satisfies the requirements and supported configurations that are listed
below.
• Verify that SSH is enabled on the existing vCenter instance.
• Verify that all ESX hosts use FQDNs instead of short names in your vSphere inventory. See Broadcom knowledge
base article 425102.
• Verify that SDDC Manager has access to all NSX Manager nodes on port 443.
• Verify that your NSX certificate contains the FQDNs of all NSX nodes and the NSX cluster VIP in the SAN field.
• If you are importing a vCenter without NSX, verify that you have available the NSX install bundle that corresponds to
the version of the vCenter.
• If you plan to use an existing shared NSX Manager instance, verify that the version meets one of the following
conditions.
– If no workload domains currently share the instance, the version must be the same or later than the version of the
management domain.
– If one or more workload domains share the instance, the version must be the same or later than the version of all
domains that share the instance.
Version Requirements
When you import existing virtual infrastructure, that infrastructure becomes a new workload domain in an existing VCF
Instance. All vSphere clusters in the existing vCenter are imported as part of this process. You cannot select a subset of
the clusters.
The versions of the imported VCF components determine which VCF features are available for that workload domain. The
component with the earliest version defines the effective VCF version for the workload domain. VCF features introduced
in later versions are available only after all components in the workload domain reach the target version. To access the full
feature set of VCF 9.1, upgrade all components to version 9.1.
The versions of the components you import must be compatible with the version of the VCF instance where you are
importing. Verify that all components meet the minimum version requirements:
Broadcom 2739

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 986: Minimum Component Version Requirements
Component Version
VCF (instance in which you are importing) 9.0
VMware vCenter 8.0 Update 3a
VMware ESX 8.0 Update 3
(Optional) NSX Manager 4.2.1
Forward-Only Upgrade Requirement for Imported Components
VCF enforces strict upgrade path validation. You can only upgrade your VCF components to a target version that is
released after the release date of your current version. The target version can be a major, minor, or a maintenance
release. In general, you can upgrade directly to a patch release only if you can also upgrade to its parent maintenance
release.
After the import, you can only upgrade your workload domain to a version that is released after the release date of the
earliest version of the imported VCF components. If the imported NSX version is released after a specific VCF minor or
maintenance release, this workload domain cannot be upgraded to that specific VCF minor or maintenance version.
Before you import, verify your target VCF upgrade paths in the VMware Interoperability Matrix to avoid deploying an
NSX version newer than your target VCF release. VCF components might have further limitations, see Broadcom
Interoperability Matrix.
NSX Considerations
• If your vCenter instance is earlier than version 9.0 and has no existing NSX registration, during the import procedure,
you deploy a new three-node NSX Manager cluster. If your vCenter instance is version 9.0 or later and has no existing
NSX registration, during the import procedure, you can choose to deploy a new single-node or three-node NSX
Manager cluster. The vCenter instance is registered as Compute Manager in NSX and all eligible vSphere clusters
in the domain are prepared for NSX. The version of the deployed NSX is the latest NSX version compatible with the
vCenter version, see Broadcom Interoperability Matrix. To change the NSX version, see Broadcom knowledge base
article 429205.
– If the imported vCenter is hosted on the management domain vCenter, the NSX Manager appliances are deployed
on the management vCenter.
– If the imported vCenter is co-located on its own cluster, the NSX Manager appliances are deployed on the vCenter
being imported.
• NSX 9.1 does not support vCenter 8.0 Update 3a or later. If your vCenter instance is without an existing NSX
registration and you plan to use a shared NSX 9.1 instance or deploy a 9.1 NSX instance during the import procedure,
first upgrade your vCenter instance to version 9.1.
• If your vCenter instance has an existing NSX registration, vSphere clusters that are not prepared for NSX are not
reconfigured.
• NSX on Distributed Virtual Port Groups (DVPGs) during import:
– With VCF 9.1.1 and later, the import worklflow no longer activates NSX on Distributed Virtual Port Groups (DVPGs).
– For VCF 9.1.0.x, the import workflow automatically activates NSX on Distributed Virtual Port Groups (DVPGs). This
action automatically activates the Distributed Firewall (DFW) on all DVPGs in the imported cluster, applying firewall
rules to existing workloads. The default DFW rules allow all Layer 2 and Layer 3 traffic. After the import completes,
you can deactivate NSX on DVPGs by using the NSX UI or the Transport Node Collection API.
• If you are importing an NSX Federation configuration, only the Local Manager is imported. To upgrade such an
environment, see Upgrading NSX Global Manager Nodes in a Federated Environment.
• For VCF 9.1 and earlier, if you are importing a vCenter without NSX and do not have TEP traffic configured on your
ESX hosts, you do not need to change the default MTU size of 1500.

– Add new clusters by using the SDDC Manager workflow or directly in vCenter.
– Add NSX Edge nodes or Edge clusters in vCenter or NSX Manager.

Create and Configure a Workload Domain with a Layer 3 Multi-Rack vSAN HCI
Cluster
A workload domain with a layer 3 multi-rack vSAN HCI cluster provides scalability, resilience, and optimal resource usage
for workloads.
The clusters in such workload domains have the following configuration:
• Layer 3 network fabric between the racks.
• A dedicated NSX host sub-transport node profile for each rack.
• Each rack can be configured as a vSAN fault domain
Deploy the L3 multi-rack vSAN workload domain so ESX hosts in different racks communicate over the L3 network and
vSAN spans those racks. You then disable the vSAN automatic policy management, set and assign a default vSAN
storage policy to match availability targets, and create vSAN fault domains to map racks and protect against rack-level
failure.
For more information on the layer 3 multi-rack cluster design, see the VMware Cloud Foundation Design Guide.
Deactivate Auto Policy Management for vSAN ESA Cluster
You cannot use auto policy management in a multi-rack cluster when using vSAN fault domains. This must be disabled if
vSAN fault domains are configured for each rack.
Broadcom 2746

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In a Web browser, log in to the workload domain vCenter at as
https://<vcenter_server_fqdn>/ui
administrator@vsphere.local.
2. In the Hosts and clusters inventory, navigate to the multi-rack vSAN cluster.
3. On the Configure tab for the cluster, select vSAN > Services.
4. In the vSAN ESA pane, click Edit.
5. Toggle Auto-policy Management off and click Apply.
Create and Assign a New Default Storage Policy for vSAN ESA Cluster
By default, the vSAN ESA default storage policy is based on the number of hosts in the cluster during creation. To
provide for fault domains that allow rack resiliency in a multi-rack cluster, you must create a default storage policy that is
compatible with the number of racks.
1. In the vSphere Client for the workload domain vCenter, from the vSphere Client menu, select Policies and Profiles.
2. On the VM Storage Policies page, click Create.
3. On the Name and description page, select the vCenter instance that manages the multi-rack cluster.
4. Type a name and a description for the storage policy and click Next.
5. On the Policy structure page, select Enable rules for "vSAN" storage, and click Next.
6. On the Availability tab of the vSAN page, set Failures to tolerate according to the configuration of your environment.
You use RAID 5 or RAID 6 (erasure coding) for vSAN ESA.
7. On the Storage Rules tab, select All flash and click Next.
8. On the Storage compatibility page, verify that the datastore is compatible and click Next.
9. On the Review and finish page, review the policy settings and click Finish.
10.In the Storage inventory of the vSphere Client, navigate to the vSAN datastore.
11.On the Configure tab, click General and next to the Default Storage Policy pane, click Edit.
12.Select the storage policy that you want to assign as default to the vSAN datastore and click OK.
Create vSAN Fault Domains
For vSAN multi-rack clusters with more than one ESX node per rack create a vSAN fault domain for each rack for rack
resilience.
1. In the vSphere Client for the workload domain vCenter, in the Hosts and clusters inventory, navigate to the multi-rack
cluster.
2. On the Configure tab, select vSAN > Fault Domains.
3. Click the plus icon.
4. In the New Fault Domain dialog box, enter the fault domain name, and select the hosts for the fault domain.
5. Click Create.
6. Repeat these steps for the other racks.
During a future cluster expansion, add hosts manually to their respective fault domains.
Delete a Workload Domain
You can delete a workload domain in VCF Operations.
• If remote vSAN datastores are mounted on a cluster in the workload domain, then the workload domain cannot be
deleted. To delete such workload domains, you must first migrate any virtual machines from the remote datastore to
the local datastore and then unmount the remote vSAN datastores from vCenter.
Broadcom 2747

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• If you require access after deleting a workload domain, back up the data. The datastores on the workload domain are
destroyed when it is deleted.
• Migrate the virtual machines that you want to keep to another workload domain using vMotion.
• Delete any NSX Edge clusters hosted on the workload domain.
When you delete a workload domain, the clusters within that workload domain are deleted and the hosts are returned to
the free pool with a host state.
need cleanup
Deleting a workload domain also removes the components associated with the workload domain from the management
domain. This includes the vCenter instance and the NSX Manager cluster instances.
Note:
If the NSX Manager cluster is shared with any other workload domains, it will not be deleted.
Note:
If the workload domain shares an NSX Manager cluster and VCF Operations for networks latency collection is
enabled for the NSX Manager cluster, NSX objects from the domain may be referenced and stop the workload
domain deletion. Disable the latency collection and delete the workload domain.
The network pools used by the workload domain are not deleted as part of the workload domain deletion process and
must be deleted separately.
CAUTION:
Deleting a workload domain is an irreversible operation. All clusters and virtual machines within the workload
domain are deleted and the underlying datastores are destroyed.
It can take up to 20 minutes for a workload domain to be deleted. During this process, you cannot perform any operations
on workload domains.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the VCF Operations top navigation bar, click Operate.
3. In the left pane, select Inventory > Detailed View.
4. Expand VCF Instances and select the VCF Instance that hosts the workload domain you are deleting.
5. Select the workload domain you want to delete and, from the Actions drop-down menu, select Delete domain.
6. On the dialog box, click Delete Workload Domain.
Decommission the hosts that were part of the workload domain, then re-image with ESX and commission them again. See
Managing ESX Hosts in VMware Cloud Foundation.
Expand a VCF Domain
You can expand the management domain or a workload domain to add resources to support additional workloads or
availability.
To expand a VCF domain, you can:
• Add an ESX host from the global inventory to an SDDC cluster.
By adding an individual host to an existing VCF domain, you can expand the amount of resources contained within an
existing SDDC cluster up to the supported vSphere maximums.
• Add a new SDDC cluster to a VCF domain.
VCF domains support multiple SDDC clusters. You can add an additional SDDC cluster to an existing VCF domain to
provide for increased capacity.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1 and later, when you add a new SDDC cluster to a VCF domain, the cluster can share a VDS
with an existing cluster in the same workload domain.
Broadcom 2748

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Post Upgrade Steps for NFS-Based VI Workload Domains
After upgrading VI workload domains that use NFS storage, you must add a static route for hosts to access NFS storage
over the NFS gateway. This process must be completed before adding a cluster to the workload domain or adding a host
to a cluster in the workload domain.
1. Identify the IP address of the NFS server for the VI workload domain.
2. Identify the network pool associated with the hosts in the cluster and the NFS gateway for the network pool.
a) Log in to SDDC Manager.
b) Click Inventory > Workload Domains and then click the VI workload domain.
c) Click the Clusters tab and then click an NFS-based cluster.
d) Click the Hosts tab and note down the network pool for the hosts.
e) Click the Info icon next to the network pool name and note down the NFS gateway.
3. Ensure that the NFS server is reachable from the NFS gateway. If a gateway does not exist, create it.
4. Identify the vmknic on each host in the cluster that is configured for NFS traffic.
5. Configure a static route on each host to reach the NFS server from the NFS gateway.
NFS-gateway-IP NFS-gateway
esxcli network ip route ipv4 add -g -n
6. Verify that the new route is added to the host using the NFS vmknic.
esxcli network ip route ipv4 list
7. Ensure that the hosts in the NFS cluster can reach the NFS gateway through the NFS vmkernel.
For example:
vmkping -4 -I vmk2 -s 1470 -d -W 5 10.0.22.250
8. Repeat steps 2 through 7 for each cluster using NFS storage.
Add an ESX Host to an SDDC Cluster in a VCF Domain
You can add an ESX host to an SDDC cluster using the vSphere Client. Adding an ESX host to an SDDC cluster in a VCF
domain increases the available resources. You can add multiple hosts at the same time.
• Verify that one or more unassigned hosts are available in the Hosts inventory. See View ESX Host Inventory.
• For information on commissioning hosts, see Commission ESX Hosts.
• Verify that the ESX hosts you want to add is in an active state.
• Verify that the ESX host to be added matches the configuration of the ESX hosts already in the SDDC cluster. This
allows the SDDC cluster configuration to remain balanced. If the host to be added does not match the pre-existing
hosts in the SDDC cluster, the cluster will be unbalanced and a warning is displayed. The warning does not prevent the
expansion and can be dismissed if needed.
• Verify that the ESX host you are adding has the same type of principal storage as the existing ESX hosts in the SDDC
cluster. A host using NFS for principal storage will automatically use the same NFS configuration as the other hosts
in the SDDC cluster. For a host using VMFS on FC, you must configure zoning, mount the associated volumes, and
create the datastore on the host before adding the host to a SDDC cluster. A host using vVols for principal storage will
automatically use the same vVols configuration as the other hosts in the SDDC cluster.
• If the SDDC cluster to which you are adding hosts uses a static IP pool for the NSX Host Overlay Network TEPs, that
pool must include enough IP addresses for the hosts you are adding.
• Different NIC enumeration is allowed.
• To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI
(https://<sddc-manager-fqdn>).
• If your environment is on version 9.1.1 or later, and the cluster uses a shared VDS, verify the following:
– The ESX host you are adding does not exceed the maximum of 16 vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) memberships
per ESX host. An ESX host that is already connected to 16 VDS instances cannot be added to a cluster that uses
an additional shared VDS.
Broadcom 2749

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– The cluster is not configured as a vSAN stretched cluster. vSAN stretched clusters do not support shared VDS. If
the cluster is a vSAN stretched cluster, the host is added to the cluster but does not use a shared VDS.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, you can add ESX hosts to a cluster that shares a VDS with another cluster.
When you use the vSphere Client to add an ESX host to an SDDC cluster, it uses the cluster's existing VDS for
management, vMotion, vSAN, and host overlay traffic. If the cluster shares a VDS with another cluster in the workload
domain, the added host connects to the shared VDS. The host uses the same uplinks and port groups that are configured
on the shared VDS.
When you add a host to an SDDC cluster managed with a vSphere Lifecycle Manager (vLCM) image, remediation is
scoped to only the newly added hosts. Existing, non-compliant hosts in the cluster are not remediated.
You can add hosts to or remove hosts from multiple different SDDC clusters in parallel. For example, you add three hosts
to Cluster A, and while that task is running, you can start a separate task to add (or remove) four hosts to Cluster B. See
VMware Configuration Maximums for information about the maximum number of add/remove hosts tasks that you can run
in parallel.
1. In the vSphere Client, browse to the vSphere cluster in the inventory.
2. Select the vSphere cluster and click Actions > Add Hosts > Add Unassigned Hosts.
3. Select the host to add to the vSphere cluster and click Next.
You can view both VDS and NSX networking configuration on the cluster. Each VDS has two uplinks in it, and you
can assign any free VMNICs on the host to the existing uplinks on the VDS. If the cluster uses a shared VDS, the
host connects to the shared VDS uplinks. The uplink assignments on the shared VDS are the same as the uplinks
configured for the existing hosts in the cluster.
4. Click Next.
5. Review the host, switch configuration, and license details and click Finish.
If the cluster uses a shared VDS and you made out-of-band changes to the VDS configuration, run the domain
synchronization workflow to reconcile the changes. See Remediate VCF Domain Configuration Drift.
Add an SDDC Cluster to a VCF Domain
If you want to add capacity to a VCF domain, you can use the vSphere Client to add an SDDC cluster to a VCF domain.
• Verify that there are unassigned hosts available in the Hosts inventory. See View ESX Host Inventory.
• For information on commissioning hosts, see Commission ESX Hosts.
• Ensure that the hosts you want to add to the SDDC cluster are in an active state.
• If you are using DHCP for the NSX Host Overlay Network, a DHCP server must be configured and advertising IP
addresses on the NSX Host Overlay VLAN of the VCF domain. When NSX creates TEPs for the VCF domain, they are
assigned IP addresses from the DHCP server.
• To perform this task in the vSphere Client, you must have access to the management domain vCenter, or your VCF
Instance must be configured with VCF SSO and vCenter linking. See Configuring VCF Single Sign-On and Linking
vCenter instances in VCF Operations. As an alternative, you can perform this task using the SDDC Manager UI.
• If your environment is on version 9.1.1 and later and you plan to reuse an existing VDS from another cluster:
– For full VDS reuse, verify that the source cluster and the new cluster are in the same network pool.
– Verify that the source cluster and the new cluster are in the same data center.
– Verify that the source cluster and the new cluster are not configured as a vSAN stretched cluster.
– Verify that the total number of VDS in the vCenter Server does not exceed the vSphere maximum of 128 VDS per
vCenter Server.
– Verify that the ESX hosts you select for the new cluster do not exceed the vSphere maximum of 16 VDS
memberships per ESX host.
Starting with version 9.1.1, you can create an SDDC cluster that shares a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) with an
existing cluster in the same workload domain. Sharing a VDS across clusters eliminates the need to create a dedicated
VDS for each cluster and ensures uniform network policy application through a centralized switch configuration. See
Sharing a VDS across clusters in a VCF domain.

Shrink a Workload Domain
You can reduce the management domain or a workload domain by removing a host from a vSphere cluster in the
workload domain or by deleting a vSphere cluster.
Remove a Host from a vSphere Cluster in a Workload Domain
You can remove a host from a vSphere cluster in the management domain or a workload domain through the Workload
Domains page in SDDC Manager UI.
• Delete any workload virtual machines created outside VMware Cloud Foundation or move them to another host.
• You cannot remove a host from a vSphere cluster if that host is hosting an NSX Edge node.
– Move the NSX Edge node to another host in the same vSphere cluster. You cannot move an NSX Edge node to a
host that already hosts another NSX Edge node.
Broadcom 2759

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– If you cannot move the NSX Edge node, delete the NSX Edge node on the host. You cannot delete NSX Edge
nodes if doing so would result in an NSX Edge cluster with fewer than two NSX Edge nodes.
• You cannot remove a host from a vSphere cluster if that vSphere cluster was selected for NSX Edge node placement
and the NSX Edge node deployment is still in pending state.
Before you remove a host from a vSphere cluster, ensure that you have enough hosts remaining to facilitate the
configured vSAN availability. Failure to do so might result in the datastore being marked as read only or in data loss.
Note:
You can add hosts to or remove hosts from multiple different vSphere clusters in parallel. For example, you
remove three hosts from Cluster A, and while that task is running, you can start a separate task to remove (or
add) four hosts to Cluster B. See VMware Configuration Maximums for information about the maximum number of
add/remove hosts tasks that you can run in parallel.
Starting with version 9.1.1, you can remove a host from a cluster that shares a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) with
another cluster in the workload domain. The shared VDS is not deleted when a host is removed. The host is disconnected
from the shared VDS uplinks, but the VDS and its port groups remain available for the remaining clusters.
1. In the navigation pane, click Inventory > Workload Domains.
2. In the workload domains table, click the name of the workload domain that you want to modify.
3. Click the Clusters tab.
4. Click the name of the cluster from which you want to remove a host.
5. Click the Hosts tab.
6. Select the host to remove and click Remove Selected Hosts.
An alert appears, asking you to confirm or cancel the action. If the removal results in the number of hosts in the
vSphere cluster being less than the minimum number of required hosts, you must click Force Remove to remove the
host.
7. Click Remove to confirm the action.
The details page for the cluster appears with a message indicating that the host is being removed. When the removal
process is complete, the host is removed from the hosts table.
Decommission the host. See Decommission ESX Hosts. After you decommission a host, you must re-image it and
commission it before you can use it again.
Delete a vSphere Cluster from a Workload Domain
You can delete a vSphere cluster from the management domain or from a workload domain. vSAN datastores on the ESXi
hosts in the deleted cluster are destroyed, while other types of storage are unmounted.
• If remote vSAN datastores are mounted on the cluster, the cluster cannot be deleted. To delete such clusters, you must
first migrate any VMs from the remote datastore to the local datastore and then unmount the vSAN remote datastores
from vCenter.
• Migrate or back up the VMs and data on the datastore associated with the cluster to another location if you want the
ability to restore them later.
• Delete the NSX Edge clusters hosted on the vSphere cluster or shrink the NSX Edge cluster by deleting NSX Edge
nodes hosted on the vSphere cluster. You cannot delete NSX Edge nodes if doing so would result in an NSX Edge
cluster with fewer than two NSX Edge nodes. For information about deleting an NSX Edge cluster, see KB 78635.
You cannot delete the last cluster in a workload domain. Instead, delete the workload domain.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, if the cluster you are deleting shares a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) with another cluster
in the workload domain, the SDDC Manager does not delete the shared VDS. The delete operation removes only the
configurations specific to the target cluster, such as port groups and host memberships, while preserving the shared
switch infrastructure for the remaining clusters. The VDS is deleted only when the last cluster sharing the VDS is
removed.
Broadcom 2760

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to SDDC Manager at <sddc_manager_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. In the navigation pane, click Inventory > Workload Domains.
3. Click the name of the workload domain that contains the vSphere cluster you want to delete.
4. Click the Clusters tab.
5. Click the vertical ellipsis (three dots) next to the cluster name and click Delete Cluster.
6. Click Delete Cluster to confirm that you want to delete the cluster.
You cannot perform additional workload domain tasks until the Delete Cluster workflow has completed.
Configuration Drift and Out-of-Band Operations in VMware Cloud Foundation
Configuration drift occurs when changes made directly in vCenter or NSX cause the SDDC Manager inventory to become
out of sync with the actual environment state. VCF 9.1 provides both a general synchronization workflow for broad
inventory reconciliation and targeted out-of-band storage workflow for specific storage changes.
Configuration Drift in VCF
A VCF domain represents a logical unit of application-ready infrastructure that groups ESX hosts managed by a vCenter
instance. SDDC Manager maintains an inventory of these domains, including hosts, clusters, distributed switches, network
pools, datastores, and NSX configurations.
Configuration drift occurs when the inventory state in SDDC Manager becomes out of sync with the actual state in vCenter
and NSX Manager. This happens when administrators make changes directly in vCenter or NSX Manager without using
SDDC Manager workflows. These direct changes are called out-of-band (OOB) operations.
When configuration drift occurs, day-N operations such as host add, host remove, stretch, unstretch, and cluster
expansion may fail or behave incorrectly because SDDC Manager is working with outdated data.
OOB changes are the primary cause of configuration drift. VCF 9.1 allows administrators to perform the following tasks in
vCenter without impacting SDDC Manager:
• Changes to vSphere Distributed Switch (add, remove, teaming policy, MTU, PNICs)
• Change primary datastore
• Changes to datastore
• Manual upgrade in vCenter
The following objects can be modified in NSX:
• Transport Node Profiles
• Uplink Profiles
Additional operations that can cause configuration drift include expanding or reducing workload domains, stretching or
unstretching a cluster, and creating or deleting datastores.
How VCF Handles Out-of-Band Changes
VCF 9.1 introduces guardrails that allow certain OOB changes without affecting the configuration state of the environment
in VCF Operations. VCF 9.1 resolves configuration drift through two complementary approaches:
• General drift remediation: a synchronization workflow that reconciles the entire VCF domain inventory after OOB
changes from vCenter or NSX Manager. This workflow rediscovers NSX Manager nodes, prepares eligible clusters for
NSX, and synchronizes hosts, clusters, distributed switches, port groups, network pools, Edge clusters, credentials,
and certificates.
Broadcom 2761

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Targeted out-of-band storage operations: a datastore specific workflow for storage changes that the general
synchronization workflow does not handle. This workflow addresses the primary datastore reference, OOB stretch and
unstretch detection, and vVol to vSAN migration.
Out-of-Band Storage Operations
An OOB storage operation is any storage configuration change that is made directly in vCenter. OOB storage operations
include changing the primary datastore, renaming or decommissioning a datastore, and stretching or unstretching a
cluster.
When you perform an OOB storage operation, SDDC Manager holds a stale reference to the previous configuration. This
creates a split-brain scenario in which the SDDC Manager inventory becomes out of sync with the actual vCenter state.
As a result, day-N operations such as add host, remove host, stretch cluster, unstretch cluster, and expand cluster might
fail.
VCF 9.1 gathers live data from vCenter and vSAN instead of relying on persisted copies. VCF 9.1 provides tools to
manually reconcile the SDDC Manager inventory with the actual state of the environment, where automatic detection is
not possible.
VCF 9.1 supports the following OOB storage workflows:
1. Update primary datastore: A new workflow allows administrators to update the primary datastore of a cluster when the
original datastore has been changed, renamed, or decommissioned directly in vCenter.
2. OOB stretch and unstretch cluster support: if a cluster is stretched or unstretched directly in vCenter, VCF 9.1 detects
the current stretch state and allows subsequent day-N operations from SDDC Manager without requiring manual
inventory updates.
3. vVol to vSAN primary datastore migration: due to vVol deprecation in VCF 9.1, you can change the primary datastore
type from vVol to any vSAN storage type. This is the only supported cross-type datastore change. This workflow is
performed using the Update Primary Datastore workflow.
The following primary datastore changes are not supported in VCF 9.1:
• Cross-type changes other than vVol to vSAN, such as NFS to VMFS or vSAN to NFS.
• vVol to vVol changes.
• vVol to NFS or VMFS changes.
Out-of-Band storage operations are supported even if SDDC Manager is in a straddle state, where SDDC Manager is
upgraded to 9.1 but vCenter instances remain on older versions, such as 8.0U3.
The following limitations apply to all OOB storage workflows in VCF 9.1:
• All OOB storage features apply only to clusters created in SDDC Manager. For imported or converted clusters, use the
sync operation in VCF Operations.
• VCF 9.1 does not orchestrate workload migration during primary datastore updates. You must migrate workloads to the
target datastore before initiating the change.
• Network pool IP changes made OOB on storage VMkernel adapters are not synchronized back to the SDDC Manager
network pool.
• Add and remove host operations on clusters with OOB changes must be performed through VCF Operations or SDDC
Manager, not directly in vCenter.
Remediate VCF Domain Configuration Drift
If you make out-of-band changes from vCenter or NSX Manager, you can use VCF Operations to sync the SDDC
Manager and vCenter inventories.
If the SDDC Manager and vCenter inventories are not synchronized, some workflows may be blocked. You can use this
procedure to unblock these tasks.
The synchronization workflow requires you to select a VCF domain. If you must sync multiple workload domains, you run
the synchronization workflow multiple times.
Broadcom 2762

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

changes that are made directly in vCenter or NSX Manager and preserves the rest of the domain's existing inventory
records. Synchronization covers the following inventory items.

Select the Primary Datastore of a Cluster in SDDC Manager
You can select a new primary datastore for a cluster in SDDC Manager after the original datastore has been changed or
decommissioned directly in vCenter. Supported scenarios include changing from a vVol datastore to a vSAN datastore,
and selecting a different datastore of the same type, such as when moving to a datastore with larger capacity or
recovering from the loss of the original datastore. Without this update workflow, SDDC Manager holds a stale reference,
which causes day-N workflows such as adding a workload domain to fail.
• Verify that the cluster is created in SDD Manager. For imported or converted clusters, use the sync operation.
• Verify that the target datastore is a shared datastore available on the cluster in vCenter.
• If you are changing from a vVol datastore, verify that the target vSAN datastore is already configured on the cluster in
vCenter.
• If you are changing from a vVol datastore, migrate all workloads to the target datastore before initiating this change.
VCF 9.1 does not perform workload migration.
Due to vVol deprecation in VCF 9.1, you can change the primary datastore type from vVol to any vSAN storage type,
including vSAN OSA, vSAN ESA, vSAN Remote, and vSAN Storage. This is the only supported cross-type datastore
change. SDDC Manager handles the associated network pool reconfiguration automatically.
For the vVol-to-vSAN datastore change, the following apply:
• Network pool IP changes made OOB on storage VMkernel adapters are not synchronized back to the SDDC Manager
network pool.
• The original network pool is not removed even if it becomes empty. This behavior is by design to prevent unintended
side effects.
• VCF does not orchestrate workload migration. You must migrate workloads to the target datastore before initiating the
change.
1. Log in to SDDC Manager with a user assigned the Administrator role.
2. In the left pane, navigate to Inventory > Workload Domains.
3. Click the VCF domain.
4. On the VCF domain page, click the Clusters tab.
5. Click the ellipsis drop-down menu next to the cluster with the updated datastore and select Update Primary
Datastore.
The Update Primary Datastore wizard opens.
6. On the Datastore Selection page, select the datastore you want to configure as the primary and click Next.
7. On the Validation page, wait for the validation to complete and click Finish.

Stretching vSAN Clusters in VMware Cloud Foundation
You can stretch a vSAN cluster in a workload domain across two availability zones within a region. Both availability zones
must contain an equal number of hosts to ensure failover in case any of the availability zones goes down.
VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 supports stretching the following types of vSAN clusters using the SDDC Manager API:
• vSAN ESA/OSA
• vSAN compute
• vSAN storage (formerly known as vSAN Max)
In addition to stretching existing clusters, you can use the SDDC Manager API to create a stretched vSAN compute
cluster. The following procedures provide the prerequisites and steps for stretching existing clusters, as well as creating
a stretched vSAN compute cluster. You can use the examples as the basis for performing these tasks in your own
environment. For more information about all the available parameters see the SDDC Manager API Reference Guide.
vSAN Compute Only clusters support a two-node configuration (one host per availability zone). A witness host is not
required for this specific topology.
The default management domain vSphere cluster must be stretched before a workload domain cluster can be stretched.
This ensures that the NSX control plane and management VMs (vCenter, NSX management cluster, and SDDC Manager)
remain accessible if the stretched cluster in the primary availability zone goes down.
VM-Host affinity rules for availability zone placement that you create manually in vCenter do not apply to VCF
management services VMs. VCF management services use Kubernetes Cluster API Provider vSphere (CAPV) node anti-
affinity for host placement. vSphere Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) rules are not required and are not honored for
these VMs.
With VCF 9.1 introduces support for the following remote datastore architectures in a mixed mode:
Cluster Type vSAN OSA Remote Datastore vSAN ESA Remote Datastore vSAN Storage Remote
Datastore
vSAN OSA Client Not Applicapble Supported Supported
vSAN ESA Client Supported Not Applicable Supported
vSAN Compute Only Supported Supported Supported
Note:
You cannot stretch a cluster in the following conditions:
• The cluster shares a vSAN Storage Policy with any other clusters.
• The cluster includes DPU-backed hosts.
• The cluster includes hosts from different subnets or networks (L3) within an individual availability zone.
Broadcom 2766

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• You cannot stretch a vSAN ESA or vSAN Max cluster if Global Deduplication is enabled.
Some use cases for stretching a cluster are described below.
• Planned maintenance
You can perform a planned maintenance on an availability zone without any downtime and then migrate the
applications after the maintenance is completed.
• Automated recovery
Stretching a cluster automatically initiates VM restart and recovery, and has a low recovery time for the majority of
unplanned failures.
• Disaster avoidance
With a stretched cluster, you can prevent service outages before an impending disaster.
For design details about stretched clusters, see vSphere Stretched Cluster Model.
Deploy and Configure vSAN Witness Host
vSAN HCI and vSAN storage stretched clusters require a witness host deployed in a vSAN witness zone, which must be
different from the location of both availability zones. vSAN compute stretched cluster do not require a witness host.
You deploy the vSAN witness host using an appliance instead of using a dedicated physical ESX host as a witness host.
The witness host does not run virtual machines and must run the same version of ESX as the ESX hosts in the stretched
cluster. It must also meet latency and Round Trip Time (RTT) requirements.
There are separate vSAN witness appliances for vSAN OSA and vSAN ESA. You must deploy the witness appliance that
matches the cluster type that you are stretching.
Cluster Type vSAN Witness Appliance
vSAN ESA vSAN ESA appliance
vSAN OSA vSAN OSA appliance
vSAN storage vSAN ESA appliance
vSAN compute n/a
Deploy vSAN Witness Host
You deploy the vSAN witness host for a stretched cluster at a site which is isolated from the existing availability zones to
prevent propagation of failure or outage in the data center.
Download the VMware vSAN Witness Appliance file from the Broadcom Support Portal.
.ova
• For stretching a vSAN OSA cluster, download the appliance for vSAN OSA.
• For stretching a vSAN ESA cluster, download the appliance for vSAN ESA.
• For stretching a vSAN storage cluster, download the appliance for vSAN ESA.
• For stretching a vSAN compute cluster or creating a vSAN compute stretch cluster, no vSAN witness appliance is
required.
Broadcom 2767

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

https:// /ui
2. Select Menu > Hosts and Clusters.
3. In the inventory panel, expand vCenter > Datacenter.
4. Right-click the cluster and select Deploy OVF template.

witness host file, and click Next.
