Register vSAN Witness Host
Before you can configure the vSAN witness host, you must register it with vCenter.
1. Use the vSphere Client to log in to the vCenter containing the cluster that you want to stretch.
2. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the datacenter.
3. Right-click the datacenter and select Add Host.
Important:
You must add the vSAN witness host to the datacenter. Do not add it to a folder or cluster..
4. On the Name and location page, enter the Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) of the vSAN witness host and click
Next.
Note:
Do not use the IP address.
5. On the Connection settings page, enter the root credentials for the witness host and click Next.
6. On the Host summary page, review the summary of the host details and click Next.
7. On the Host lifecycle page, select an option and specify a vSphere Lifecycle Manager image.
8. On the Assign license page, click Next.
9. Review the summary and click Finish.
Configure NTP on the Witness Host
To prevent time synchronization issues, configure the NTP service on the vSAN witness host.
Broadcom 2768

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the inventory panel of the vSphere Client, select vCenter > Datacenter.
2. Select the vSAN witness host and click the Configure tab.
3. Configure the NTP client on the vSAN witness host.
a) In the System section, click Time configuration and click the Add Service button.
b) Select Use Network Time Protocol (enable NTP client).
c) Configure the following settings and click OK.
Setting Value
NTP Servers NTP server address
Start NTP Service Selected
NTP Service Startup Policy Start and stop with host
Configure the VMkernel Adapters on the vSAN Witness Host
To enable vSAN data network communication between the availability zones, configure the witness network on the vSAN
witness host.
1. In the inventory panel of the vSphere Client, select vCenter > Datacenter.
2. Select the vSAN witness host and click the Configure tab.
3. Remove the dedicated witness traffic VMkernel adapter on the vSAN Witness host.
a) In the Networking section, click VMkernel adapters.
b) Select the kernel adapter vmk1 with as Network label and click Remove.
secondaryPg
c) On the Remove VMkernel adapter dialog box, click Remove
4. Remove the secondary switch from the vSAN witness host.
a) In the left pane, select Networking > Virtual switches.
b) Expand the Standard switch: secondary switch section.
c) Click the vertical ellipsis and from the drop-down menu, select Remove.
d) On the Remove standard switch dialog box, click Yes.
5. Remove the virtual machine network port group on the vSAN witness host.
a) Expand the Standard switch: vSwitch0 section.
b) In the VM Network pane, click the vertical ellipsis and from the drop-down menu, select Remove.
c) On the Remove port group dialog box, click Yes.
6. Enable witness traffic on the VMkernel adapter for the management network of the vSAN witness host.
a) On the VMkernel adapters page, select the vmk0 adapter and click Edit.
b) In the vmk0 - edit settings dialog box, click Port properties, select the vSAN check box, and click OK.
Stretch a vSAN ESA or OSA Cluster Using the SDDC Manager API
You can stretch a vSAN cluster (ESA or OSA) in the management domain or workload domain using a JSON specification
and the SDDC Manager API.
• See Stretched vSAN Storage Model for design requirements and recommendations.
• Verify that vCenter is operational.
• Verify that you have completed the Planning and Preparation Workbook with the management domain or workload
domain deployment option included. See Planning and Preparation.
• Verify that your environment meets the requirements listed in the Prerequisite Checklist sheet in the Planning and
Preparation Workbook. See Planning and Preparation.
• Create a network pool for availability zone 2.
• Commission vSAN ESA or OSA hosts for availability zone 2. See Commission ESX Hosts.
• Ensure that you have enough hosts such that there is an equal number of hosts on each availability zone. This is to
ensure that there are sufficient resources in case an availability zone goes down completely.
Broadcom 2769

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Deploy and configure a vSAN witness host. See Deploy and Configure vSAN Witness Host.
• If you are stretching a cluster in a workload domain, the default management vSphere cluster must already be
stretched.
Note:
You cannot stretch a cluster in the following cases:
• The cluster shares a vSAN Storage Policy with any other clusters.
• The cluster includes DPU-backed hosts.
• The cluster includes hosts within an availability zone that have different subnets or networks (L3).
• The cluster has vSphere Supervisor enabled.
When you stretch a cluster, SDDC Manager modifies the site disaster tolerance setting for storage policy associated with
datastore of that cluster from None - standard cluster to Site mirroring - stretched cluster. This affects all VMs using
default datastore policy in that cluster. If you do not want to change the site disaster tolerance setting for specific VMs,
apply a different storage policy to those VMs before stretching the cluster.

mapping as the existing hosts in availability zone 1.

Create a vSAN Compute Stretch Cluster Using the SDDC Manager API
You can create a vSAN compute stretch cluster using the POST /v1/clusters API.
• See Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model for design requirements and recommendations.
• A minimum of four ESX hosts commissioned with the vSAN type vSAN Compute Cluster. See Commission ESX Hosts.
• ESX, vCenter, and SDDC Manager must all be version 9.0 or later.
• An existing remote datastore. It can be a vSAN ESA, vSAN OSA, or vSAN storage datastore.
• The server cluster providing the remote datastore must be stretched. See Stretch a vSAN Storage Cluster Using the
SDDC Manager API.
No vSAN witness host is required for a stretched vSAN compute cluster.
If you want to stretch a vSAN compute cluster that you already created, see Stretch a vSAN Compute Cluster Using the
SDDC Manager API.
Broadcom 2782

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This procedure provides two different sample JSON specification files for the different topologies:
Topology Description
Symmetric This reflects a topology that has multiple routes to and from the
server cluster, with all routes having the same bandwidth and
latency characteristics. This is not typical in stretched cluster
deployments but may arise if the vSAN compute cluster is
deployed at different sites unrelated to where the stretched vSAN
storage cluster resides.
Asymmetric This typically reflects a topology that has multiple routes to and
from the server cluster, with one route having optimal bandwidth
and latency characteristics. This is typical in stretched cluster
deployments where a client stretched cluster needs to access
storage on a server stretched cluster would ideally access the
object data in the same site, known as inter-site-connectivity.
In this case you specify the site affinity between server and client
sites in the JSON specification file.
For example, if your environment looks like this:
• AZ1 (Server): East Coast
• AZ2 (Server): West Coast
• AZ1 (Client): East Coast
• AZ2 (Client): West Coast
Then you would use an asymmetric topology with the following
site affinity:
• AZ1 (Client) → AZ1 (Server)
• AZ2 (Client) → AZ2 (Server)

6. Retrieve the unique IDs for each ESX host that will be part of the stretched cluster and add the IDs to the JSON

a) Navigate to Hosts > GET /v1/hosts.
| b) In the Status text box, enter  |     |  and click Execute. |

UNASSIGNED_USEABLE

the JSON specification file.
| ESX Host   |     | Value         |
| ---------- | --- | ------------- |
| ESX Host 1 |     | ESX host 1 ID |
| ESX Host 2 |     | ESX host 2 ID |

7. Retrieve the ID of the workload domain in which you want to create the cluster and add the ID to the JSON
specification file.
a) Navigate to Domains > GET /v1/domains.
b) Click Execute.
c) In the Response section, click the domain name, copy the element, and replace the <domain ID> value in the
id
JSON specification file.
8. Retrieve the vSphere Lifecycle Manager image ID to use for the cluster and add the ID to the JSON specification file.
a) Navigate to Personalities > GET /v1/personalities.
b) Click Execute.
c) In the Response section, click the personality representing the image you want to use, copy the
personalityId
element, and replace the <personality ID> value in the JSON specification file.
9. Retrieve the datastore Uuid for the server cluster providing the remote datastore and add it to the JSON specification
file.
a) Navigate to Clusters > GET /v1/clusters.
b) Click Execute.
c) In the Response section, click PageOfCluster, and copy the element of the server cluster providing the remote
id
datastore.
d) Navigate to Clusters > GET /v1/clusters{id}/datastores.
e) In the Value text box, enter the unique ID for the server cluster and click Execute.
f) In the Response section, click the datastore, copy the element, and replace the <datastore ID> value in the
id
JSON specification file.
10.Navigate to Clusters > POST /v1/clusters.

Stretch a vSAN Compute Cluster Using the SDDC Manager API
You can stretch an existing vSAN compute cluster using the PATCH /v1/clusters/{id} API.
• See Stretched vSAN Compute Cluster Storage Model for design requirements and recommendations.
• A minimum of three ESX hosts commissioned with the vSAN type vSAN Compute Cluster. See Commission ESX
Hosts.
• An existing vSAN compute cluster with at least three ESX hosts.
• ESX, vCenter, and SDDC Manager must all be version 9.0 or later.
• The server cluster providing the remote datastore must be stretched. See Stretch a vSAN Storage Cluster Using the
SDDC Manager API.
• Unmount all datastores from the vSAN compute cluster, except for the primary datastore.
• Unregister all VMs running on the primary datastore.
No vSAN witness host is required for a stretched vSAN compute cluster.
If you want to create a new stretched vSAN compute cluster, see Create a vSAN Compute Stretch Cluster Using the
SDDC Manager API.
1. Create a JSON specification file in a text editor.
{
"clusterStretchSpec": {
"deployWithoutLicenseKeys": true,

You can expand a stretched cluster by adding ESX hosts. It is recommended that you add the same number of hosts to
both availability zones for symmetry and cluster balance.

Unstretch a Cluster in VMware Cloud Foundation
This procedure describes how to unstretch a vSAN cluster in VMware Cloud Foundation.
• Consolidate or delete all virtual machine snapshots on the vSAN cluster before unstretching the cluster.
• If you are unstretching a vSAN storage cluster (formerly known as vSAN Max), unmount any stretched vSAN compute
clusters to which the vSAN storage cluster is providing a remote datastore.
1. Get the ID of the cluster you are unstretching.
a) In the VCF Operations console, clickDeveloper Center > APIs & SDKs.
b) Click the API Explorer link for the SDDC Manager API.
c) In the API Explorer, navigate to APIs for managing clusters and click .
GET /v1/clusters
d) Click Execute.
e) Click Download to download the JSON file.
f) Open the JSON file and copy the cluster ID for .
SDDC-Cluster1
2. Prepare the JSON request body.
a) Click Patch /v1/clusters/id.
b) Under ClusterUpdateSpec field, click Cluster Update Data ClusterUpdateSpec{ ... }.
c) Click Download to download the JSON file.
d) Edit the downloaded JSON file so that it contains only the unstretch information similar to the example below.
Note:
The azToRemove variable is required for compute only clusters which are stretched through SDDC Manager
version 9.1 or higher.
availability_zone
{ "clusterUnstretchSpec": {"azToRemove": < >} }
3. Run the unstretch cluster API.
a) For the ClusterUpdateSpec field, update the cluster UID (you retrieved this in step 1) and unstretch JSON file with
the payload you prepared in step 2.
b) Click Execute.
The unstretch cluster task is displayed in the SDDC Manager task panel.
c) Monitor the unstretch cluster task till it is completed.
All hosts from AZ2 are removed from the unstretched cluster and the cluster is converted to standard vSAN cluster.

You can replace or change the vSAN witness host for a stretched cluster using the vSphere Client without affecting
lifecycle operations.
Verify that the vSAN witness host is not in use by another cluster, has a VMkernel configured for vSAN traffic, and has no
vSAN partitions on its disks.

https:// /ui

4. Select the stretched cluster and click Configure.
5. Under vSAN, click Fault Domains.
6. Click the Change button.
7. Select a new host to use as the vSAN witness host and click Next.
8. Claim disks on the new witness host and click Next.
9. Review the configuration and click Finish.
Configuring NSX Federation for the VCF Management Components in
VCF
With NSX Federation, you can federate the management domain NSX or a workload domain NSX across VCF instances.
You configure NSX Federation for the VCF management components that connect to an NSX overlay in the management
domain between two regions. The steps to configure NSX Federation can apply to a workload domain as well.
For information about the maximum number of federated NSX Managers and other NSX federation maximums, see
VMware Configuration Maximums.
Note:
Workload domains that share an NSX Manager are considered a single location.
You perform some of the tasks on the first NSX instance while others you perform on the second federated NSX instance.
NSX Instance Tasks to be Performed
First Instance 1. Create the NSX Global Manager Clusters for NSX Federation
2. Prepare the First Instance NSX Local Manager for NSX
Federation
3. Enable NSX Federation in the First VCF Instance
Enable high availability for NSX Federation Control Plane in an 1. Create the NSX Global Manager Clusters for NSX Federation
additional instance 2. Set the Standby NSX Global Manager
Additional Instance 1. Deploy NSX Edge Cluster to Additional Instance
2. Add an Additional Instance Location to NSX Global Manager
3. Stretching Fleet level management network between VMware
Cloud Foundation Instances:
a. Connect the Additional VCF Instance to the Cross-
Instance Tier-0 Gateway
b. Add the Additional VCF Instance as a Location to the
Cross-Instance Tier-1 Gateway

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Create the NSX Global Manager Clusters for NSX Federation
An NSX Federation environment contains an active and a standby NSX Global Manager and one or more NSX Local
Manager instance or NSX Local Manager clusters. The standby NSX Global Manager appliance provides high availability
and disaster recovery.
You perform the following tasks to create the NSX Global Manager cluster at each location.
• Set the Active NSX Global Manager in the Management Domain
• Set the Standby NSX Global Manager
Deploy the first NSX Global Manager Appliance
You deploy three NSX Global Manager nodes in the management domain.
1. Download the NSX OVF file from the Broadcom Support Portal.
2. In a web browser, log in to the vSphere Client at vcenter_fqdn .
https:// /ui
3. Right-click the default cluster in the management domain and select Deploy OVF template.
4. Select Local file, click Upload files, and navigate to the OVA file.
5. Click Next.
6. Enter a name and a location for the NSX Manager VM, and click Next.
The name you enter appears in the vSphere and vCenter inventory.
7. Select the compute resource on which to deploy the NSX Manager appliance page and click Next.
8. Review the OVF template details and click Next.
9. Accept the license agreement and click Next.
10.Specify the deployment configuration size and click Next.
You can refer to VMware Configuration Maximums to ensure that you choose the correct size for the scale or your
environment.
11.Specify storage for the configuration and disk files.
• Select the virtual disk format.
• Select the VM storage policy.
• Specify the datastore to store the NSX Manager appliance files.
• Click Next.
Note:
The virtual disk format is determined by the selected VM storage policy when using a vSAN datastore.
12.Select the management network as the destination network and click Next.
13.In the Application section, enter the system root, CLI admin, and audit passwords for the NSX Manager.
Your passwords must comply with the password strength restrictions.
• At least 12 characters
• At least one lower-case letter
• At least one upper-case letter
• At least one digit
• At least one special character
• At least five different characters
Broadcom 2807

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
14.In the Optional parameters section, leave the password fields blank.
15.In the Network Properties section, enter the hostname of the NSX Manager.
16.For Rolename, select the NSX Global Manager role.
17.Enter the default gateway, management network IPv4, and management network netmask.
18.In the DNS section, enter the DNS Server list and Domain Search list.
19.In the Services Configuration section, enter the NTP Server list and enable SSH.
20.Verify that all your custom OVF template specification is accurate and click Finish to initiate the deployment.
21.After the deployment is complete, power on the NSX Global Manager node.
Right-click the NSX Global Manager VM and, from the Actions menu, select Power > Power on.
22.In a web browser, log in to NSX Global Manager at gm_node1_fqdn .
https:// /
23.Accept the end-user license agreement and click Continue.
24.Join the VMware Customer Experience Program and click Save.
25.Repeat steps 4 to 22 to deploy two additional NSX Global Manager nodes.
Cluster the NSX Global Manager Appliances
Form a cluster from the three NSX Global Manager nodes you deployed in the management domain.
1. Log in to the first NSX Global Manager appliance by using an Secure Shell client as the account.
admin
2. Run the following command to retrieve the NSX Global Manager cluster ID.
get cluster config | find Id:
3. Run the following command to retrieve the thumbprint of the NSX Global Manager API certificate.
get certificate api thumbprint
4. Log in to the second NSX Global Manager appliance by using an Secure Shell client as the account.
admin
5. Add the second appliance to the cluster.
first_node_IP cluster_ID nsx_admin_password
join cluster-id username admin password
api_thumbprint
thumbprint
6. After the warning message that data will be lost on the appliance, enter .
Yes
The cluster creation and stabilization process might take up to 15 minutes.

Stretch the VCF Fleet Management Segment Between VCF Instances
You prepare the environment and stretch the network between both locations.
The management domain NSX Manager instance has a Tier-0 gateway, Tier-1 gateway, and one segment created during
the deployment of the VCF fleet level components. When the NSX Manager instance is federated, the Tier-1 gateway and
the Tier-0 gateways are imported to become global objects managed by the NSX Global Manager for cross-instance use.
See VCF Management Dedicated VLAN and NSX Stretched Overlay Segment Network Model.
Both gateways are configured to have locations for both instances. You can manage the ingress and egress routing for
the cross-instance segment when you move them between VMware Cloud Foundation instances.
Note:
Cross-instance segments cannot have overlapping IP addresses/ranges.

Managing Network Connectivity in vCenter
Starting with VCF 9.0, a simplified workflow is introduced to set up network connectivity and perform network
configuration.
The new NSX-based workflow for network connectivity is available both in vCenter and NSX for you to have a uniform
experience of performing network configurations from either of the components. The new workflow applies many default
settings that are recommended by Broadcom for simplifying the deployment process. The workflow covers various
scenarios that are related to deployment parameters, transport zones, and uplink profile. They help reduce the number
of user inputs that are required to perform network configuration. The workflow also provides a topology visualization to
correlate your inputs in the user interface. Contextual visualization helps you get a view of the setup before completing the
tasks in the workflow.
Based on the kind of network connectivity you have selected, you can create an edge cluster with a centralized gateway
or a distributed gateway with VLAN. For more information, see Workload Networking Detailed Designs and NSX Edge
Cluster Detailed Design. To configure a distributed Virtual Extensible Local Area Network (VXLAN) connection, use NSX
UI. For more information, see Add a Distributed VXLAN Connection.
Configure Centralized Network Connectivity with Edge Clusters
Create this connection if you have an environment that requires static or dynamic routing with physical fabric. A
centralized connection is the one where the traffic is routed through a NSX gateway on an edge node. You can use this
task to configure a centralized connectivity with edge cluster deployment from vCenter. For more information on network
connectivity using NSX, see Setting up Centralized Connectivity with Edge Clusters.
If you want to deploy edges on a vSphere cluster, ensure that the following requirements are met. VCF Installer and VCF
Operations fulfill various prerequisites by default.
• The vSphere cluster must have ESX hosts with vSphere Distributed Switch uplinks that are configured.
• If you are using DHCP to allocate MGMT or TEP IP addresses, then create and configure a DHCP scope accordingly.
• The Compute Manager must be registered with NSX Manager.
• Plan for Edge TEP VLAN. The same VLAN as the Host TEP can be reused. For more information on creating TEPs,
see Create an IP Pool for Host Tunnel Endpoint IP Addresses.
• Edges can be deployed on a host-group within a vSphere cluster or on a vSphere cluster. All hosts in the host-group
or the vSphere cluster must have identical access to management network, gateway uplinks, host, and Edge TEP
networks.
• The vSphere cluster must have a Transport Node Profile (TNP) attached to it. For more information on applying a TNP,
see Prepare Cluster Hosts as Transport Nodes by Using TNP.
• Activate NSX on DVPG option must be turned on for the host cluster on which the edge has to be deployed to use the
same VLAN for edge and host overlay. To turn it on, go to System > Fabric > Hosts page for cluster in NSX Manager.
• Edge node reserves 100% CPU shares and memory. vSphere cluster and resource pool must have enough resources
to deploy at least two edge nodes.
Broadcom 2817

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• NSX Edge VM Resource Requirements:
– Small: 4-GB memory, 2 vCPU, 200-GB disk space. The NSX Edge Small VM appliance size is suitable for lab and
proof-of-concept deployments.
– Medium: 8-GB memory, 4 vCPU, 200-GB disk space. The NSX Edge Medium appliance size is suitable for
production environments with load balancing.
– Large: 32-GB memory, 8 vCPU, 200-GB disk space. The NSX Edge Large appliance size is suitable for production
environments with load balancing.
– XLarge: 64-GB memory, 16 vCPU, 200-GB disk space. The NSX Edge Extra Large appliance size is suitable for
production environments with load balancing.
• Management network for NSX Edge must have connectivity to NSX Manager.
• DNS entries for NSX Edge components should be populated in your managed DNS server.
• If dynamic routing is desired, set up 2 BGP Peers on a ToR switch with an interface IP, local ASN, and BGP password.
For more information about configuring BGP, see Configure BGP.
• If you are using Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), reserve a local ASN to use for the NSX Edge cluster’s Tier-0
Interfaces.
• If static routing is desired, you can configure HA VIP for active/standby Tier-0 Gateway and can use VIP as the Next
Hop IP on Top-of-Rack (ToR) switch.
• When setting up the centralized connectivity by using the simplified workflow in vCenter, you must add a minimum
of two NSX Edge nodes to a NSX Edge cluster. You can add up to 10 edges to an edge cluster. Once a NSX Edge
cluster is successfully created, you see the NSX Edge cluster list on subsequent visits to the Network Connectivity
page.
• For more information on planning resources, see Planning and Preparation.
If you have upgraded to VCF 9.0, you can use this workflow to manage edge clusters created in the previous version.
Also, you can also use this workflow to set up a Tier-0 gateway for an edge cluster, add or delete an edge, and reset
passwords. Based on these configurations, you can start creating centralized gateway connectivity with edge cluster
deployment.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the vCenter for the Workload Domain and select Networks > Transit
Gateways.
2. Click Setup Network Connectivity.
3. In the Gateway Type page, select Centralized Connection.
4. Click Next.
5. Review and complete the Networking Prerequisites.
6. Click Continue.
7. Configure an Edge Cluster.
a) Enter a name for the edge cluster.
b) Enter the value for Tunnel Endpoint MTU. The maximum packet size that is allowed over a tunnel is already
selected from the Global Fabric Settings.
Note:
The Edge TEP MTU is the same across the host MTU within the same overlay Transport Zone, so you must set
the Global Fabric MTU accordingly.
8. Define the settings for edge nodes.
a) Select an appropriate size for edge cluster in Edge Form Factor.
b) A minimum of two Edge Nodes are required to deploy an Edge Cluster. Once you have added a node, you can add
another edge node by cloning the previously added edge node. Cloning is recommended only when the cloned

Edge nodes. If the Manage Edge Password with VCF is turned off, then you can manually set the password.
b) Enter the CLI and Root Administrator passwords to manage the Edge Nodes.

Add an NSX Edge Cluster
Learn how to add an edge cluster. Having a multi-node cluster of NSX Edges helps ensure here is at least one NSX Edge
is always available.
• Ensure that there is at least one NSX Edge node which is ready and it must not be part of any existing cluster.
• Optionally, create an NSX Edge cluster profile for high availability (HA). You can also use the default NSX Edge cluster
profile.
To create a tier-0 logical router or a tier-1 router, with stateful services such as NAT and load balancer, you must associate
it with an NSX Edge cluster.
Therefore, even if you have only one NSX Edge, it must belong to an NSX Edge cluster to be useful. An NSX Edge
transport node can be added to only one NSX Edge cluster. An NSX Edge cluster can be used to back multiple logical
routers.
After you have created the NSX Edge cluster, you can edit it to add more NSX Edges.
You can also configure failure domains for NSX edge nodes. A failure domain is a logical grouping of NSX Edge nodes
within an NSX Edge Cluster. If there is a failure affecting multiple NSX Edge node, failure domains compliment the auto
placement algorithm and guarantee service availability. For more information about configuring a failure domain, see
Configure Failure Domains.

Configure Distributed Network Connectivity
Distributed connection allows a lightweight distributed connection to the data-center fabric without the need to deploy
Edge nodes or configure dynamic routing. In addition to on-demand networking and distributed routing, it provides
distributed services—specifically External IPs (1:1 NAT) and distributed DHCP. It can be complemented by the Virtual
Network Appliance Cluster which offers extended NAT support and Load Balancer hence allowing to deploy the
Supervisor Cluster.
• Dedicated VLANs and subnets must be available for the Distributed Transit Gateway connection to the ToR. The same
VLAN must be configured on all the ToR switches where the ESX hosts are connected which offers VPCs. All the hosts
running VPC workloads must have access to these VLANs. The Transit Gateway can be scoped to specific vSphere
clusters by defining and associating a specific Network Span.
• Reserve external IP blocks for VPC connectivity. External IP blocks must be the same as or a subset of dedicated
VLAN subnets. For more information, see Create a Virtual Private Cloud in vCenter.
A distributed connection is the one where a Transit Gateway connects to a VLAN provisioned in the fabric. This happens
directly on the host which implies the VLAN must be available on the ESX hosts (on physical uplinks that are used by the
NSX VMkernel). The workflow is available in both NSX and vCenter. This section describes how to use the workflow from
vCenter to configure a distributed connectivity. To set up a distributed gateway connectivity for the first time from vCenter,
perform the following steps:
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the vCenter for the Workload Domain and select Networks > Network
Connectivity.
2. Click Setup Network Connectivity.
3. In the Transit Gateway page, select Distributed Connectivity.
Select gateway connectivity for the created VPCs that align with the infrastructure requirements and networking
preferences.
4. Complete the Networking prerequisites. Click Continue.
5. Enter the information on External Network Connectivity Details page.
Option Description

Gateway CIDR IPv4 Address Enter the gateway address through which the traffic should be
routed to the external network.

Private - TGW IPv4 Blocks Enter IP blocks for Private - TGW IPv4.

Managing Virtual Private Clouds in vCenter
Learn how to manage Virtual Private Clouds (VPC) in vCenter.
Broadcom 2829

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A virtual private cloud (VPC) is a pool of shared network resources that are allocated within a cloud environment,
providing isolation between the different organizations using the resources. A subnet is a network with an IP CIDR in VPC
and a workload is connected to a subnet.
A hierarchical folder-based approach is used to represent NSX projects and VPC in the vSphere Client that facilitates
separate management by its various users under the Virtual Managed Folder. With this framework, NSX DVPGs were
systematically organized in their respective folders. This streamlined the structural hierarchy between NSX and the
vCenter inventory.
VPCs, subnets, and various VPC services were configured only from NSX. To connect the workloads, administrators had
to navigate to vCenter. VCF offers a simplified networking solution. VPCs and Subnets are primarily NSX objects that
are integrated in vCenter. The administrator manages the VPC and subnet in vCenter. This implementation allows the
VC admin to create, read, update, and delete the NSX VPC from the vSphere Client. You can also navigate from and to
NSX objects within the vCenter. For more information on VPCs in NSX, see Virtual Private Cloud in NSX.
VCF provides a consistent networking consumption model that is based on Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) and Transit
Gateways (TGW). This model is natively multi-tenant and can be used not only from NSX, but also from VCF (vCenter,
VCF Automation, and monitored from VCF Operations). It aims to provide a standardized, simple, and powerful Cloud
networking experience to the network administrators and cloud users from VCF. This cloud networking consumption is
built using the following objects:
• External Connections: Defines outside connectivity for a Transit Gateway to the datacenter. An external connection
can be of the following types:
– Centralized
– Distributed
• Transit Gateway (TGW): Gateway inter-connecting VPCs and connecting to an external datacenter through external
connections.
• Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): On-demand logical networks connected together that can be either advertised (public
subnets) or exposed through networking services like External IPs or NAT. For simplicity, VPCs in VCF use these
profiles:
– VPC Connectivity Profile: Defines outside connectivity configuration for VPCs such as the Transit Gateway they are
connected to, the IP Blocks available for consumption, and if a default outbound NAT is configured
– VPC Service Profile: Defines the common configurations for services available in the VPC such as DHCP, DHCP
Relay, or different subnet profiles.
External Connections
External Connection defines how the Transit Gateway (TGW) interconnects the VPCs to the network outside NSX and
defines the services that are available on it. Those connections are created from Default (/infra) and define the connection
to the external environment.
The following types of External Connections are configurable from the vCenter server for different requirements. The
workflow is also available in VMware NSX. For more information about setting the connectivity through VMware NSX., see
Setting up Network Connectivity in the NSX section. This section describes how to use the workflow from vCenter.
You can select one based on the features you require for your network.
• Centralized connection: Connects the transit gateway through a Tier-0 gateway provisioned from NSX. The Tier-0
gateway is deployed on NSX Edge nodes and provides interconnection to the physical fabric. This connection type
requires you to deploy NSX Edge nodes and manage their lifecycle.
Centralized connections allow stateful services and dynamic routing with the physical fabric (BGP) at Tier-0 level. They
also allow NAT configuration at the transit gateway level. Create a centralized connection if you have an environment
that requires full-scale NSX networking and security services (such as DHCP, NAT, and gateway firewall for VPC and
transit gateway) and other stateful centralized network services.
• Distributed VLAN connection: Connects the transit gateway directly to VLANs provisioned in the fabric. The
connection happens directly on the ESX hosts, which mandates the availability of VLANs on the ESX.
A distributed VLAN connection allows lightweight connectivity to the data-center fabric without needing to deploy
NSX Edge nodes or configure dynamic routing. Stateful services are supported with this connection type using Virtual
Network Appliances (VNAs).
Broadcom 2830

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A Transit Gateway can be created with a centralized connectivity or it can be created with a distributed connectivity. A
TGW can also have multiple external connections to support complex routing, such as separating Internet and Intranet
paths. All external connections for a TGW must be of the same type, that is, either all centralized or all distributed. A TGW
cannot have a mixed type of connections. Note that a VPC in a project can connect to only one TGW.
In both cases, creating an external connection requires certain pre-requisites to be fulfilled. For a Centralized connection,
it requires a Tier-0 gateway deployed with NSX Edge nodes and external routing properly configured. For a Distributed
connection, it implies that the VLANs used for outside connections are available on ESX hosts on the same uplinks
(physical NICs) as NSX overlay VMkernel adapter.
Add a Centralized Connection
You can add a centralized connection to connect the transit gateway through a Tier-0 Gateway.
Tier-0 must be deployed with Edge nodes and external routing should be properly configured.
1. In the vSphere Client home page, select the Networking tab and click Configure.
2. On the Configure tab, expand Networking and select External Connection.
Figure 396: External Connection
3. Add External Connection. Enter the information.
Option Description
Name Enter a name for the external connection.
Type Click to select the type of connection you want to create. The
centralized connection is selected by default.
Tier-0 Gateway Select the Tier-0 or Tier-0 VRF gateway through which you want
to route the traffic to external networks.
Advanced Settings
Remote Networks Remote networks to be reachable through this connection for the
VPCs. The default gateway is 0.0.0.0/0.
If you do not specify this field, then only routes of specific
networks are programmed else the default route will be
programmed on the transit gateway to route traffic to the
connection.
Broadcom 2831

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
External IP Blocks Select the external IP blocks from the drop-down list. IP subnets
from the selected external IP blocks are advertised as static routes
to the tier-0 or tier-0 VRF gateway. If you do not specify this field,
IP subnets from all the external IP blocks are advertised.
Private - Transit Gateway IP Blocks If you turn on this toggle, then the private transit gateway IP
blocks are advertised through the external connection. The default
behavior is to advertise only external IP blocks (all external IP
blocks unless you mention the specific ones to be advertised in
the External IP Blocks field).
If you turn on this toggle, you must also add the transit gateway
route advertisement rule, "TGW_PRIVATE", to the transit gateway
attachment to get the private transit gateway IP blocks advertised.
Provider Outbound SNAT If this toggle is on, SNAT is enabled for all the outbound traffic
irrespective of the subnet type. Source IP that does not belong
to the selected External IP Blocks are NATed at the source. a
provider can control the outgoing traffic irrespective of the subnet
type. Any other NAT rule that is created on a transit gateway
uplink has a higher priority than the provider outbound SNAT rule.

Transit Gateways
When a new tenant (NSX Project) is created, a default Transit Gateway is created automatically in vCenter, for the
Project.
A Transit Gateway (TGW) provides both inter-VPC communication and connection to the outside network through
External Connections. This model keeps an inter-VPC communication inside a tenant. With a Transit Gateway, there is no
need for sharing a Tier-0 directly with an NSX Project. Instead, an External Connection is shared to the project, to which
the TGW is connected. A tenant admin can connect a TGW to one or more external External Connections. For more
information about connection types, see External Connections.
A TGW is a transit hub that interconnects tenant's virtual private clouds (VPCs), external connections, and tenant's remote
networks. It enables inter-VPC connectivity between external / project-scoped subnets of connected VPCs. It reduces
operational complexity and provides a more intuitive, centralized interface for managing network resources. Also, this
integration lays the foundation for the TGW span in VCF 9.1, offering a complete user experience.
A Transit Gateway can be created with a centralized connectivity or it can be created with a distributed connectivity. A
default TGW for every tenant, including Default is created automatically. Based on your network requirements, you can
also create more TGWs (both CTGWs and DTGW) for a project. With multiple TGWs in a project, a VPC can be re-
attached or made to point to another TGW as and when required. You can move a VPC to another TGW by changing the
VPC connectivity profile. When you move a VPC to another TGW, the system runs validation checks at different levels,
such as IPAM validation and VPC span validation. When you move a VPC to another TGW, ensure that the requirements
for dependent configurations are met.
A TGW can also have multiple External Connections to support complex routing, such as separating Internet and Intranet
paths. All external connections for a TGW must be of the same type, that is, either all centralized or all distributed. A TGW
cannot have a mixed type of connections.
Centralized Transit Gateway
A centralized transit gateway (CTGW) is created by attaching a TGW with a centralized external connection. Previously,
a CTGW shared a similar High Availability (HA) mode and placement on the Edge cluster as the Tier-0/VRF gateway to
which it connected. In this case, if the Tier-0/VRF had an active-active HA, CTGW VRF was not able to support stateful
services (auto SNAT).
Now, a CTGW can be deployed on an Edge cluster which can be different from the Edge cluster of the Tier-0/VRF
gateway to which it connects. Also, the CTGW can now have an independent HA mode that supports configuring multiple
topologies and assigning different HA modes per tenant. Note that CTGW sharing its HA mode with the Tier-0 gateway to
which it connects is deprecated now and post upgrade any new CTGW that you create will have indepedent an HA mode.
A CTGW can have the following HA modes:
• Active active - If you need a better traffic throughput, define the HA mode as active-active.
• Active standby - If you require services such as NAT, define the HA mode as active-standby. If there are multiple
CTGWs in a project, they can have different HA modes. The following image shows multiple centralized transit
gateways in a project.
Distributed Transit Gateway
A distributed transit gateway (DTGW) is created by attaching a TGW with a distributed external connection. If there are
multiple DTGWs in a project, each DTGW can use the same or a different VLAN but subnets must not overlap within
different DTGWs.
Broadcom 2834

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VPCs can be migrated between DTGWs by changing the connectivity profile of VPCs. Validations are triggered at the
policy layer when a VPC is moved across DTGWs. Ensure that the prerequisites are met before moving a VPC across
DTGWs. You can also move a VPC with a VLAN extendable subnet to a different DTGW.

This task helps you configure an external connection for a Transit Gateway. For a Centralized connection, the Transit
Gateway has its own HA Mode (Active/Standby or Active/Active). In Active-Active mode, it does not support NAT including

You can configure a static route on the tier-0 gateway to external networks. After you configure a static route, there is no
need to advertise the route from tier-0 to tier-1. The tier-1 gateways have a static default route to their connected tier-0
gateway.

Option Description
Name Enter a name for your NAT Rule.
Action Select an action. The following actions are available:
• SNAT
• DNAT
• Reflexive
• NO SNAT
• NO DNAT
Match Source IP Enter the source network address.
Specify an IP address, or an IP address range in CIDR format. For
SNAT, NO_SNAT and Reflexive rules, this is a required field and
represents the source network of the packets leaving the network.
For DNAT and NO_DNAT rules, optionally it can contain a
source network of incoming packets. For a NULL value, this field
represents any network.

Enabled Turn on the toggle to enable the rule.
Logging Turn on the toggle to enable logging.

SNAT or No DNAT rule should have a higher priority than other

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
Firewall The available settings are:
• Match External Address - The firewall is applied to the external
address of a NAT rule.
– For SNAT, the external address is the translated source
address after NAT is done.
– For DNAT, the external address is the original destination
address before NAT is done.
– For REFLEXIVE, to egress traffic, the firewall is applied
to the translated source address after NAT is done.
For ingress traffic, the firewall is applied to the original
destination address before NAT is done.
• Match Internal Address - is applied to the internal address of a
NAT rule.
– For SNAT, the internal address is the original source
address before NAT is done.
– For DNAT, the internal address is the translated destination
address after NAT is done.
– For REFLEXIVE, for egress traffic, the firewall is applied to
the original source address before NAT is done. For ingress
traffic, the firewall is applied to the translated destination
address after NAT is done.
• Bypass - The packet bypasses firewall rules.

Create a Virtual Private Cloud in vCenter
Learn how to create a VPC in vCenter.
A VPC connects to a Transit Gateway (recommended) and can have the following types of subnets:
• Private - VPC: A subnet scoped to the VPC and routed with other subnets inside the same VPC, but not to the outside
network. NAT is needed if outside communication is required.
• Private - Transit Gateway: Subnets allowing inter-VPC connectivity below the Transit Gateway without NAT. It
requires IP translation if workloads must be reachable to an outside network.
• Public: A subnet that is accessible from outside the environment, from other VPCs but also from customers and
workload above the Transit Gateway.
In case you have to grant access to specific workloads on private networks from the outside environment, you can use
External IPs.
External IPs: IPs that allow external connectivity for a VM on a private network by performing IP translation. It is
implemented with 1:1 NAT on the workload picking an IP from the External IP block and assigning it to the VM.
In addition to External IPs, it is also possible to configure Static Routes and Groups in a VPC.
Regardless of External Connection type (Centralized or Distributed), it is possible to configure Static Routes, Groups, and
DHCP Server in a VPC.
1. From your browser, log in to the vSphere Client.
2. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Virtual Private Clouds folder in the vCenter Networking inventory. From the
Actions drop-down menu, select New VPC.
3. On the Basic Info page, enter the following information.
Option Description
Name Enter a name for the VPC.
Description Enter a description for the VPC.
Private- VPC IP CIDRs Enter a block of IP CIDRs that can be assigned to private subnets
of this VPC. These CIDRs are local to VPCs and can overlap
between the VPCs.

about the VPC Connectivity Profile, see Add a VPC Connectivity
Profile.
The connectivity profile is used to connect VPCs through a transit
gateway and does not require you to share a Tier-0 gateway with
the project.
If your connectivity profile has some missing configurations, you
can configure them from the links in the warning that is displayed
in the topology.

gateway, connection type, and span information.
For example:
Transit Gateway: Default Transit Gateway | Centralized | Span:
Default Span
To create a connectivity policy, enter a name for the policy and
select the type of policy.
• Isolated: VPCs that have the isolated policy do not
communicate with each or outside the group span within
a VPC. However, it can communicate with VPCs with
promiscuous policy.
• Community: VPCs that have the community policy can
communicate to the VPCs in the same community or VPCs
with a promiscuous policy. These VPCs do not communicate
with other communities or isolated VPCs.
• Promiscuous: VPCs with promiscuous policy can communicate
with one another and all the other VPCs that are connected.

Policy

Add a NAT Rule for VPC
You can add a NAT rule for a VPC for external IP binding for mapping between internal and external networks.
For creating a NAT rule for CTGW, consider the following conditions.
• DNAT rule should be configured at the nearest point to the translated IP, that is, the VPC.
• SNAT rule should be configured at the furthest point till the Match IP is visible - VPC for Private IP and CTGW for
Project IP.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Virtual Private Clouds folder in your datacenter.
2. Select a VPC from the list of VPCs are under Virtual Private Clouds folder.
3. Select Configure > Services > NAT > Add NAT Rule.
Option Description
Name Enter a NAT name.
Action Select an action. The following actions are available:
• SNAT
• DNAT
• Reflexive
• NO SNAT
• NO DNAT
Source IP | Port Enter the source network address and source port. Specify
an IP address, or an IP address range in CIDR format. For
SNAT, NO_SNAT and Reflexive rules, this is a required field
and represents the source network of the packets leaving the
network. For DNAT and NO_DNAT rules, optionally it can contain
a source network of incoming packets. For a NULL value, this field
represents any network.
Destination IP | Port Enter a destination IP address or an IP address range in CIDR
format and destination port.
For DNAT and NO_DNAT rules, this is a required field and
represents the source network of the packets leaving the network.
This field is not applicable for Reflexive.
Select Protocol Select the required protocol.
Translated IP | Port Enter a value for translated IP. Specify an IPv4 address, or an IP
address range in CIDR format. If the translated IP is less than the
match IP for SNAT, it works as PAT.
Enabled Turn on the toggle to enable the rule.
Logging Turn on the toggle to enable logging.
Priority A lower value means a higher priority. The default is 0. A No
SNAT or No DNAT rule should have a higher priority than other
rules.
Broadcom 2849

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
Firewall The available settings are:
• Match External Address - The firewall is applied to the external
address of a NAT rule.
– For SNAT, the external address is the translated source
address after NAT is done.
– For DNAT, the external address is the original destination
address before NAT is done.
– For REFLEXIVE, to egress traffic, the firewall is applied
to the translated source address after NAT is done.
For ingress traffic, the firewall is applied to the original
destination address before NAT is done.
• Match Internal Address - Indicates that the firewall is applied to
the internal address of a NAT rule.
– For SNAT, the internal address is the original source
address before NAT is done.
– For DNAT, the internal address is the translated destination
address after NAT is done.
– For REFLEXIVE, for egress traffic, the firewall is applied to
the original source address before NAT is done. For ingress
traffic, the firewall is applied to the translated destination
address after NAT is done.
• Bypass - The packet bypasses firewall rules.
Description Enter a description for NAT.
Tag Enter the tag and scope for NAT.

Configure Network Spans
Network Span provides the ability for the administrative user to limit the availability of VPC networks on a specific set of
vSphere clusters. An enterprise administrator can configure the layout of the span that is based on the vSphere clusters.
A span is applied to a TGW which makes VPC subnets that are connected to that TGW available across the clusters
associated with that span
Cluster-based span is a collection of vSphere clusters. This span is applied at the transit gateway. When a gateway is
created, by default the TGW is associated with the default span.
• Exclusive Span: By default vCenter clusters can be shared across multiple spans. Span allows overlapping of
vSphere Clusters. You can apply an exclusive span when you want to specify a set of vCenter clusters for a dedicated
workload. Clusters that are part of an exclusive span configuration are not shared or overlapped with other span
configuration including default span.
• Default Span: Default Span includes all the VTEP vCenter clusters and standalone hosts in the environment excluding
the clusters that are part of exclusive span.
1. In the vSphere Client home page, select the Networking tab and click Configure.
2. On the Configure tab, expand Networking and select Network Spans.
3. Alternatively, in the vSphere Client, navigate to Virtual Private Clouds folder in your datacenter and select
Configure > Settings > Network Spans.
4. Click .
Add Network Span
5. Enter a name for the new network span.
6. Toggle Yes or No for Exclusive Span.
7. Select the clusters to be added to the span.
8. Click Ok.
For a global span view in vCenter, select the Networking tab, and click Configure. On the Configure tab, expand
Networking, and select Network Spans. This view provides information on spans across different clusters, datacenters,
and other objects. You can also view the clusters that are outside the selected vCenter.
Configure a Connectivity Policy
VPC connectivity policy simplifies VPC-to-VPC connectivity management for users with limited networking experience.
Administrators can configure VPC-centric policies with a few simple steps and the system translates these policies into
forwarding rules that are based on the current VPC state. You can define how VPCs communicate with each other by
applying a specific traffic pattern to a VPC. You can define how your VPCs communicate with each other based on
workload connectivity requirements.
1. In the vSphere Client, select the Networking tab and navigate to the Virtual Private Clouds folder in your
datacenter.
2. Select a transit gateway from the list under the Virtual Private Clouds folder.
3. Go to Configure > Routing and Forward > Connectivity Policies.
4. Click Add Policy.
For each policy, they belong to a group that is assigned internally. You can add only VPC members to a group. To see
the VPCs added to the group, click the number count under VPC Members.
Broadcom 2851

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. Enter a name for the policy. You can reuse the templated policy and can apply it to multiple VPCs.
6. Select the type of policy from the available options.
• Isolated: VPCs with the isolated policy cannot communicate with each or outside the group span within the same
VPC. However, they can communicate with VPCs that have a promiscuous policy.
• Community: VPCs that have the community policy can communicate to the VPCs in the same community or VPCs
with a promiscuous policy. These VPCs do not communicate with other communities or isolated VPCs.
• Promiscuous: VPCs with promiscuous policy can communicate with one another and all the other VPCs that are
connected.
7. Select one or more VPCs to the group to apply the connectivity policy.
8. Select View the Ungrouped VPCs to view the VPCs, that are not added to any connectivity policy. These VPCs can
connect with each other and can connect to Promiscuous VPCs.
9. Click Save.
Manage Groups
Groups that are used in different connectivity policies are displayed. Using vSphere client, you cannot edit any groups.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Virtual Private Clouds folder in your datacenter.
2. Select Configure > Settings > Groups.
You can view the groups that are used in connectivity policies. If a group is also used by other NSX services, you can
navigate to the NSX UI to view more information about the usage of the group.

Configure Overlay VMKernel Adapter
In VCF 9.1, overlay Tunnel EndPoint (TEP) can now be configured directly from vCenter like other VMkernel NICs. This
provides a central place to configure all the services running on ESX hosts. The overlay configuration was supported in
NSX and SDDC Manager to provide a configuration for VMK interface like vSAN or vMotion which is configured in vCenter
. VI Admin can now configure VMkernel setting in vCenter which will be used by NSX.
1. To create a VMkernel Network Adapter,
2. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the host and click Add Networking.
3. On the Select connection type page, select VMkernel Network Adapter and click Next.
4. From the Select an existing network option, select a distributed port group and click Next.
5. On the Port properties page, configure the settings for the VMkernel adapter.
Option Description
Network label The network label is inherited from the label of the distributed port
group.
IP settings Select IPv4, IPv6, or both.
Note:
The IPv6 option does not appear on hosts that do not
have IPv6 enabled.
MTU Choose whether to get MTU for the network adapter from the
switch or to set a custom size. You cannot set the MTU size to a
value greater than 9000 bytes.
TCP/IP stack Select an TCP/IP stack from the list. Once you set an TCP/IP
stack for the VMkernel adapter, you cannot change it later.
If you select the vMotion or the Provisioning TCP/IP stack, you are
able to use only these stacks to handle vMotion or Provisioning
traffic on the host.
All VMkernel adapters for vMotion on the default TCP/IP stack are
deactivated for future vMotion sessions.
If you set the Provisioning TCP/IP stack, VMkernel adapters
on the default TCP/IP stack are deactivated for operations that
include Provisioning traffic, such as virtual machine cold migration,
cloning, and snapshot migration.
If you select the vNetworking stack, no other service can run on
the same VMkernel adapter and a dedicated VMkernel adapter for
TEP Traffic is available.

Select from the available services:

another host as the network connection where vMotion traffic
is sent. The migration with vMotion to the selected host is not
possible if the vMotion service is not enabled for any VMkernel
adapter on the default TCP/IP stack, or there are no adapters
using the vMotion TCP/IP stack.
• Provisioning. Handles the data that is transferred for virtual
machine cold migration, cloning, and snapshot migration.
• Fault Tolerance logging. Enables Fault Tolerance logging on
the host. You can use only one VMkernel adapter for FT traffic

• Management. Enables the management traffic for the host
and vCenter. Typically, hosts have such a VMkernel adapter
that is created when the ESX software is installed. You can
create another VMkernel adapter for management traffic on

• vSphere Replication. Handles the outgoing replication
data that is sent from the source ESX host to the vSphere
Replication server.
• vSphere Replication NFC. Handles the incoming replication
data on the target replication site.
• vSAN. Enables the vSAN traffic on the host. Every host that is
part of a vSAN cluster must have such a VMkernel adapter.
• vSphere Backup NFC. VMkernel port setting for dedicated
backup NFC traffic. NFC traffic goes through the VMkernel
Adapter when vSphereBackup NFC service is enabled.

over TCP storage traffic. NVMe over TCP storage traffic goes
through the VMkernel Adapter when NVMe over TCP adapter

NVMe over RDMA storage traffic. NVMe over RDMA storage
traffic goes through the VMkernel Adapter when NVMe over
RDMA adapter is enabled. For more information, see vSphere
Storage Guide.
• vNetworking. To integrate NSX with other VCF components
in vCenter, a VMkernel setting for dedicated vNetworking is
added to support the overlay configuration in vCenter.

Configure vSphere Clusters with Overlay configuration
To integrate NSX closely with other VCF components, VCF 9.1 introduces overlay VMkernel (VTEP) lifecycle
management in vCenter. A new VMkernel NIC vNetworking is introduced for NSX overlay VTEPs. NSX applies
vNetworking enabled VMkernel (vcenterVtep) when preparing a cluster for overlay networking. Overlay Tunnel EndPoint
(TEP) can now be configured directly from vCenter like other VMkernel NICs.
If clusters are imported, upgraded, or if they are non-VCP clusters without an overlay configuration, then they are not VPC
ready clusters. You can prepare vSphere clusters with an overlay configuration to support the cases.
• For a vSphere cluster not prepared for NSX, and for a vSphere cluster with VLAN backed NSX configuration, configure
the cluster with an overlay on management interface and dedicated overlay TEP.
• For a vSphere Cluster with Overlay on Management Interface enabled, prepare a cluster with a dedicated overlay.
1. In the vSphere Client inventory, navigate to the cluster.
2. From the Actions drop-down menu, select vNetworking > Overlay and Network Configuration.
Alternatively, you can navigate to the cluster and click Configure > vNetworking > Overlay and Network
Configuration.
3. Click Configure to specify the overlay network settings to prepare this cluster for NSX.
If Configure is disabled, see NSX UI for advanced configurations.
4. Select the vSphere Distributed Switch from the drop-down menu.
The distributed switches that are configured with overlay transport zones are available in the drop-down menu.
5. Select the IPv4 Assignment from the drop-down menu.
Select IPv4 assignment as M to configure this cluster with overlay on management
anagement Kernel Adapter
interface and select DHCP or IP Pool for dedicated overlay TEP.
DHCP: DHCP Server provides IP addresses to the hosts. The external DHCP server allocates the TEP IP.
IP Pool: Transport Nodes are configured with tunnel endpoint (TEP pool) IP addresses.
Management VMkernel Adapter: Configure this cluster with an overlay on management interface
6. Select an IP Pool from the drop-down menu if IPv4 Assignment is set to IP Pool.

Traceflow
Traceflow allows you to inject a packet into the network and monitor its flow across the network. This flow allows you to
monitor your network and identify disruptions.
Traceflow allows you to identify the path (or paths) a packet takes to reach its destination or, conversely, where a packet is
dropped along the way. Each entity reports the packet handling on input and output, so you can determine whether issues
occur when receiving a packet or when forwarding the packet. The vCenter graphically displays the trace route, which
is based on the parameters that you set (IP address type, traffic type, source, and destination). This display page also
enables you to edit the parameters, retrace the trace flow, or create a one.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the vCenter for the Workload Domain and select Monitor > Troubleshooting >
Traceflow
2. Select an IPv4 or IPv6 address type.
3. Select a traffic type.
For IPv4 addresses the traffic type choices are Unicast, Multicast, and Broadcast. For IPv6 address the traffic type
choices are Unicast or Multicast.

b) Select a virtual interface.
c) The IP address and MAC address are displayed if VMtools is installed in the VM, or if the VM is deployed using
OpenStack plug-in (address bindings will be used in this case). If the VM has more than one IP address, select one
from the drop-down list.
d) If the IP address and MAC address are not displayed, enter the IP address and MAC address in the text boxes.
e) For a logical port, Select an attachment type: VIF, DHCP, Edge Uplink, or Edge Centralized Service.
f) Select a port.
6. If Traffic Type is set to Unicast under Destination, select a VM or a logical port. For a VM,
a) Select a VM from the drop-down list.
b) Select a virtual interface.
c) The IP address and MAC address are displayed if VMtools is installed in the VM or if the VM is deployed using
OpenStack plug-in (address bindings will be used in this case). If the VM has more than one IP address, select one
from the drop-down list.
d) If the IP address and MAC address are not displayed, enter the IP address and MAC address in the text boxes.
e) For a logical port, Select an attachment type: VIF, DHCP, Edge Uplink, or Edge Centralized Service.
f) Select a port.
g) For IP-MAC, select the trace type (layer 2 or layer 3). For layer 2, enter an IP address and a MAC address. For
layer 3, enter an IP address.

vSphere
Use vSphere as a VI administrator to virtualize physical infrastructure into managed CPU, storage, and networking
resources.
The two core components of VMware vSphere are ESX and vCenter. ESX is the virtualization platform where you create
and run virtual machines and virtual appliances, Kubernetes workloads, and AI/ML workloads. vCenter is the service
through which you manage multiple hosts connected in a network and pool host resources.
vSphere manages large collections of infrastructure, such as CPUs, storage, networking, GPUs, and DPUs as a seamless
and dynamic operating environment, and also manages the complexity of a data center.
vSphere Functional Area Capabilities
Lifecycle management of vSphere • Lifecycle management via pre-staging ESX images, remediating hosts in parallel,
and by applying updates in parallel across clusters.
• vSphere can manage infrastructure images to patch, update, or upgrade clusters
using a desired state model.
• vSphere can reduce maintenance windows via reduced downtime upgrades
for vCenter as well as live patching for ESX for near zero downtime for security
patches.
Workload performance • With its GPU support, vSphere improves workload performance for modern AI
workloads
• vSphere on DPUs (VMware vSphere® Distributed Services EngineTM) helps
accelerate infrastructure network functions on the Data Processing Unit (DPU) by
utilizing available CPU cycles achieve higher workload consolidation per host.
• Distributed Resource Scheduler (vSphere DRS) enables automatic load balancing
of resources allocated to workloads in a vSphere cluster. Storage DRS optimizes
VM data placement as the VM is created and used over time.
Business continuity • High Availability with vSphere automatically restarts your VMs following physical
machine failure.
• Fault Tolerance provides continuous availability of any application in the event of a
hardware failure with no data loss or downtime.
• vMotion enables live migration of virtual machines with no disruption to users or
loss of service, eliminating the need to schedule application downtime for planned
server maintenance. Storage vMotion avoids downtime for planned storage
maintenance.
Built-in security • Identity federation with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), ADFS and Okta:
Secure access and account management.
• Virtual Machine Encryption: Data-at-rest encryption for virtual machine data and
disks.
• vSphere Trust Authority: Remote attestation for sensitive workloads.
vSphere Documentation
For information about the built-in vSphere capabilities, see the vSphere documentation.

SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration

Designing vSAN Network
The Designing vSAN Network guide describes network requirements, network design, and configuration practices for
deploying a highly available and scalable VMware® vSAN™ cluster.
vSAN is a distributed storage solution. As with any distributed solution, the network is an important component of the
design. For best results, you must adhere to the guidance provided in this document as improper networking hardware
and designs can lead to unfavorable results.
At VMware, we value inclusion. To foster this principle within our customer, partner, and internal community, we create
content using inclusive language.
Intended Audience
This guide is intended for anyone who is designing, deploying, and managing a vSAN cluster. The information in this
guide is written for experienced network administrators who are familiar with network design and configuration, virtual
machine management, and virtual data center operations. This guide also assumes familiarity with VMware vSphere,
including VMware ESX, vCenter, and the vSphere Client.
• For more information about creating vSAN clusters, see the Planning and Configuring vSAN guide.
• For more information about vSAN features and how to configure a vSAN cluster, see the Administering VMware vSAN
guide.
• For more information about monitoring a vSAN cluster and fixing problems, see the Monitoring and Troubleshooting
vSAN guide.
What is vSAN Network Design
You can use vSAN to provision shared storage within vSphere. vSAN aggregates local or direct-attached storage devices
of a host cluster and creates a single storage pool shared across all hosts in the vSAN cluster.
vSAN is a distributed and shared storage solution that depends on a highly available, properly configured network
for vSAN storage traffic. A fast and resilient network is crucial to a successful vSAN deployment. This guide provides
recommendations on how to design and configure a vSAN network.
vSAN has a distributed architecture that relies on a fast, scalable, and resilient network. All host nodes within a vSAN
cluster communicate over the IP network. All hosts in the cluster must maintain IP unicast connectivity, so they can
Broadcom 2865

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
communicate over a Layer 2 or Layer 3 network. For more information on the unicast communication, see Using Unicast
in vSAN Network.
vSAN Networking Terms and Definitions
vSAN introduces specific terms and definitions that are important to understand. Before you get start designing your vSAN
network, review the key vSAN networking terms and definitions.
Terms Definitions
CMMDS The Cluster Monitoring, Membership, and Directory Service
(CMMDS) is responsible for the recovery and maintenance of a
cluster of networked node members. It manages the inventory of
items such as host nodes, devices, and networks. It also stores
metadata information, such as policies and RAID configuration for
vSAN objects.
DOM The Distributed Object Manager (DOM) is responsible for creating
the components and distributing them across the cluster. After a
DOM object is created, one of the nodes (host) is nominated as
the DOM owner for that object. This host handles all IOPS to that
DOM object by locating the respective child components across
the cluster and redirecting the I/O to respective components
over the vSAN network. DOM objects include vdisk, snapshot,
vmnamespace, vmswap, vmem, and so on.
NIC Teaming Network Interface Card (NIC) teaming can be defined as two or
more network adapters (NICs) that are set up as a "team" for high
availability and load balancing.
NIOC Network I/O Control (NIOC) determines the bandwidth that
different network traffic types are given on a vSphere distributed
switch. The bandwidth distribution is a user configurable
parameter. When NIOC is enabled, distributed switch traffic is
divided into predefined network resource pools: Fault Tolerance
traffic, iSCSI traffic, vMotion traffic, management traffic, vSphere
Replication traffic, NFS traffic, and virtual machine traffic.
Objects and Components Each object is composed of a set of components, determined by
capabilities that are in use in the VM Storage Policy.
A vSAN datastore contains several object types:
• VM Home Namespace - The VM Home Namespace is a
virtual machine home directory where all virtual machine
configuration files are stored. This includes files such as .vmx,
log files, vmdks, and snapshot delta description files.
• VMDK - VMDK is a virtual machine disk or .vmdk file that
stores the contents of the virtual machine's hard disk drive.
• VM Swap Object - VM Swap Objects are created when a
virtual machine is powered on.
• Snapshot Delta VMDKs - Snapshot Delta VMDKs are created
when virtual machine snapshots are taken. This is applicable
only for vSAN OSA cluster.
• Memory Object - Memory Objects are created when the
snapshot memory option is selected when creating or
suspending a virtual machine.
RDT The Reliable Data Transport (RDT) protocol is used for
communication between hosts over the vSAN VMkernel ports. It
uses TCP at the transport layer and is responsible to create and
destroy TCP connections (sockets) on demand. It is optimized to
send large files.
Broadcom 2866

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Terms Definitions
SPBM Storage Policy-Based Management (SPBM) provides a storage
policy framework that serves as a single unified control panel
across a broad range of data services and storage solutions. This
framework helps you to align storage with application demands of
your VMs.
VLAN A VLAN enables a single physical LAN segment to be further
segmented so that groups of ports are isolated from one another
as if they were on physically different segments.
Witness Component A witness is a component that contains only metadata and does
not contain any actual application data. It serves as a tiebreaker
when a decision must be made regarding the availability of the
surviving datastore components, after a potential failure.
Understanding vSAN Networking
A vSAN network facilitates the communication between cluster hosts, and must be fast, resilient, and scalable.
vSAN uses the network to communicate between the ESX hosts and for virtual machine disk I/O.
Virtual machines (VMs) on vSAN datastores are made up of a set of objects, and each object can be made up of one or
more components. These components are distributed across multiple hosts for resilience to drive and host failures. vSAN
maintains and updates these components using the vSAN network.
The following diagram provides a high-level overview of the vSAN network:
vSphere and vSAN
Distributed vSwitch
Uplink 1 Uplink 2
Broadcom 2867

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSAN Network Characteristics
vSAN is network-dependent. Understanding and configuring the right vSAN network settings is critical to avoiding
performance and stability issues.
A reliable and robust vSAN network has the following characteristics:
vSAN Network Traffic
vSAN network traffic is primarily made up of cluster, metadata, and storage replication traffic. A VM can access its storage
resources from any host within a vSAN cluster. It is not necessary for that data to be locally available, thus allowing a VM
to access its data on another node.
Unicast
vSAN uses unicast for communication. Unicast traffic is a one-to-one transmission of IP packets from one point in the
network to another point. Unicast transmits the heartbeat sent from the primary host to all other hosts each second. This
ensures that the hosts are active and indicates the participation of hosts in the vSAN cluster. You can design a simple
unicast network for vSAN. For more information on the unicast communication, see Using Unicast in vSAN Network.
Note:
If possible, always use the latest version of vSAN.
Layer 2 and Layer 3 Network
All hosts in the vSAN cluster must be connected through a Layer 2 (L2) or Layer 3 (L3) network.
VMkernel Network
Each ESX host in a vSAN cluster must have a network adapter for vSAN communication. All the intra cluster
communication happens through the vSAN VMkernel port.
VMkernel Interface
Each ESX host in a vSAN cluster must have a VMkernel interface used for vSAN traffic to handle data replication, I/O
traffic, and cluster health monitoring.
Virtual Switch
vSAN supports the following types of virtual switches:
• The Standard Virtual Switch provides connectivity from VMs and VMkernel ports to external networks. This switch is
local to each ESX host.
• A vSphere Distributed Switch provides central control of the virtual switch administration across multiple ESX hosts. A
distributed switch also provides networking features such as Network I/O Control (NIOC) that can help you set Quality
of Service (QoS) levels on vSphere or virtual network. vSAN includes vSphere Distributed Switch irrespective of the
vCenter version.
Network Interfaces
vSAN can have dedicated physical network interfaces to secure vSAN storage traffic and to provide bandwidth and
resources. vSAN traffic can share physical network adapters with other system traffic types, such as vSphere vMotion
traffic, vSphere HA traffic, and virtual machine traffic. To guarantee the amount of bandwidth required for vSAN, configure
Network I/O control on the distributed switch.
Bandwidth
In vSAN environments that share physical resources with other traffic, use Network I/O Control to allocate bandwidth
among traffic types. Assigning shares to vSAN traffic ensures that it receives sufficient bandwidth during network
contention. This prioritizes vSAN traffic and prevents other traffic types from affecting its performance when the physical
NIC is saturated.
Avoid using reservations or limits in vSAN environments. Reservations can leave unused bandwidth inaccessible to VMs,
while limits restrict traffic even when additional bandwidth is available.
vSAN recommends the usage of shares to allocate bandwidth for vSAN traffic. This offers the most balanced and efficient
use of shared physical NICs.
Broadcom 2868

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For information about using Network I/O Control to configure bandwidth allocation for vSAN traffic, see the vSphere
Networking guide.
Using Unicast in vSAN Network
Unicast traffic refers to a one-to-one transmission from one point in the network to another. vSAN uses unicast to simplify
network design and deployment.
All ESX hosts use the unicast traffic, and the vCenter becomes the source for the cluster membership. The vSAN nodes
are automatically updated with the latest host membership list that vCenter provides. vSAN communicates using unicast
for CMMDS updates. For more information on CMMDS updates, see Broadcom knowledge base article 385769.
DHCP Support on Unicast Network
vCenter deployed on a vSAN cluster can use IP addresses from Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) without
reservations.
You can use DHCP without reservations as the assigned IP addresses are tied to the MAC addresses of VMkernel ports.
IPv6 Support on Unicast Network
vSAN supports IPv6 with unicast communications.
With IPv6, the link-local address is automatically configured on any interface using the link-local prefix. By default, vSAN
does not add the link local address of a node to other neighboring cluster nodes. As a result, vSAN does not support IPv6
link local addresses for unicast communications.
Query Unicast with ESXCLI
You can run ESXCLI commands to determine the unicast configuration.
View the Communication Modes
Using command, you can view the CMMDS mode of the vSAN cluster node.
esxcli vsan cluster get

Intra-Cluster Traffic
In unicast mode, the primary node addresses all the cluster nodes as it sends the same message to all the vSAN nodes in
a cluster.
For example, if N is the number of vSAN nodes, then the primary node sends the messages N number of times. This
results in a slight increase of vSAN CMMDS traffic. You might not notice this slight increase of traffic during normal,
steady-state operations.
Intra-Cluster Traffic in a Single Rack
If all the nodes in a vSAN cluster are connected to the same top of the rack (TOR) switch, then the total increase in traffic
is only between the primary node and the switch.
If a vSAN cluster spans more than one TOR switch, you need to monitor the network traffic bandwidth and network
latency to ensure adequate resources are available to satisfy vSAN requirements. If a cluster spans many racks, multiple
TORs may be involved. A single L2 can span multiple racks or L3 can be used across multiple TORs. vSAN Fault
Domains could be considered with L3 to have a logical and physical fault domain at a rack boundary.
Broadcom 2871

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Intra-Cluster Traffic in a vSAN Stretched Cluster
In a vSAN stretched cluster, the primary node is located at the preferred site.
In a vSAN stretched cluster configuration, vSAN data is synchronously replicated bidirectionally between the preferred
site and the secondary site. vSAN read I/O is local to each site. As a result write I/O bandwidth between the sites depend
on many factors such as number of vSAN nodes on each site, the aggregate physical NIC bandwidth of the combined
hosts between each site, and the number of vSAN objects that are using site to site replication. To calculate bandwidth
requirements for vSAN OSA and vSAN ESA, see VMware vSAN Design and Sizing Guide.
Broadcom 2872

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
With the unicast traffic, there is no change in the witness site traffic requirements.

These network traffic types are not applicable to vSAN storage clusters if the VMs are not deployed on the cluster.

stack to facilitate the host connectivity and management. It can also handle the system traffic
such as vMotion, iSCSI, Network File System (NFS), Fiber Channel over Ethernet (FCoE),
and fault tolerance.
Virtual Machine network With virtual networking, you can network VMs and build complex networks within a single
ESX host or across multiple ESX hosts.
vMotion network Traffic type that facilitates migration of VM from one host to another. Migration with vMotion
requires correctly configured network interfaces on source and target hosts. Ensure that the
vMotion network is distinct from the vSAN network.
vSAN network A vSAN cluster requires the VMkernel network for the exchange of data. Each ESX host
in the vSAN cluster must have a VMkernel network adapter for the vSAN traffic. For more
