BGP Down Events
If a BGP Down or Dynamic BGP Down event occurs, an alarm is raised. For details about the alarm, see the Routing
Events table in the NSX Event Catalog. In this release, additional information is provided regarding the reason for state
changes of the BGP peer.
You can also use either the PUT or PATCH method with the following APIs to disable a specific BGP peer. This will
prevent alarms from being generated when that peer does not come up.
/policy/api/v1/infra/tier-0s/{tier-0-id}/locale-services/{locale-service-id}/bgp/neighbors/{neighbor-id}
/policy/api/v1/global-infra/tier-0s/{tier-0-id}/locale-services/{locale-service-id}/bgp/neighbors/{neighbor-
id}
To disable a BGP peer, set the parameter to . For example:
enabled false
PATCH https://<nsx-mgr>/policy/api/v1/infra/tier-0s/T0-1/locale-services/default/bgp/neighbors/peer-1
{
"enabled": "false"
}
You can also use the GET method to view the value of the and other parameters.
enabled
Note:
If the tier-0 gateway firewall is configured with a default or rule, you must manually add an
Drop Reject Allow
rule for BGP and for BFD if it is configured.
CAUTION:
Note the following scenarios when there are connection failures involving BGP or BFD:
• With only BGP configured, if all BGP neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With only BFD configured, if all BFD neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With BGP and BFD configured, if all BGP and BFD neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With BGP and static routes configured, if all BGP neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With only static routes configured, the service router's state will always be up unless the node is experiencing
a failure or in a maintenance mode.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateways.
3. To edit a tier-0 gateway, click the menu icon (three dots) and select Edit.
4. Click BGP.
a) Enter the local AS number (ASN).
In active-active mode, the default ASN value, 65000, is already filled in. In active-standby mode, there is no default
ASN value.
b) Click the BGP toggle to activate or deactivate BGP.
In active-active mode, BGP is activated by default. In active-standby mode, BGP is deactivated by default.
c) If this tier-0 gateway is in active-active mode, click the Inter SR iBGP toggle to activate or deactivate Inter-SR
iBGP. This feature is activated by default.
If the tier-0 gateway is in active-standby mode, this feature is not available.
Broadcom 3135

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
d) Click the ECMP toggle to activate or deactivate Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP), which allows load sharing across
equal-cost paths.
The implementation of ECMP is based on the 5-tuple of the protocol number, source and destination address, and
source and destination port.
e) Click the Multipath Relax toggle to activate or deactivate load sharing across multiple paths that differ only in AS-
path attribute values but have the same AS-path length.
Note:
ECMP must be enabled for Multipath Relax to work.
f) Specify the tier-0 gateway Graceful Restart option for BGP. You can choose from Deactivate, Helper Only, and
Graceful Restart and Helper.
You can optionally change the Graceful Restart Timer and Graceful Restart Stale Timer.
By default, the BGP Graceful Restart mode is set to Helper Only. Helper mode is useful for eliminating and/or
reducing the disruption of traffic associated with routes learned from a neighbor capable of Graceful Restart. The
neighbor must be able to preserve its forwarding table while it undergoes a restart.
For EVPN on a tier-0 gateway, the Graceful Restart and Helper mode is not supported.
BGP Graceful Restart is not recommended for an active/active tier-0 gateway configuration in which all NSX
Edge nodes actively process traffic. Enabling BGP Graceful Restart can delay convergence since it instructs BGP
neighbors to retain stale routes even after BFD has detected a failure, preventing the immediate redirection of
traffic to remaining healthy NSX Edge nodes.
Note:
Unless overridden by neighbor-specific configuration, the tier-0 gateway configuration applies to all BGP
neighbors.
BGP Graceful restart is not supported when a tier-0 gateway has only one BGP peer configured on a specific
NSX Edge node, because the NSX Edge node will go down by design when that single BGP peer goes down. If
you specify a BGP Graceful Restart mode for a configuration that has only one BGP neighbor, the BGP Graceful
Restart mode will not take effect.
5. Configure Route Aggregation by adding IP address prefixes.
a) Click Set for Route Aggregation.
b) Click Add Prefix.
c) Enter an IP address prefix in CIDR format.
d) For the option Summary - Only, select Yes or No.
6. Click Apply.
You must save the global BGP configuration before you can configure BGP neighbors.
7. Configure BGP Neighbors.
a) Click Set for BGP Neighbors.
b) Click Add BGP Neighbor.
c) Specify the IP address(es) of the neighbor. Use a single IP address to add a single static BGP neighbor, or use
CIDR notation to dynamically discover BGP neighbors within the specified IP range.
d) Enable or disable BFD.
e) Enter a value for Remote AS number.
For iBGP, enter the same AS number as the one in step 4a. For eBGP, enter the AS number of the remote BGP
peer.
f) Under Route Filter, click Set to add one or more route filters.
For IP Address Family, you can select IPv4, IPv6, or L2VPN EVPN (for static BGP neighbors only). The following
combinations are supported:
• IPv4 and IPv6
• IPv4 and L2VPN EVPN
Broadcom 3136

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The combination of IPv6 and L2VPN EVPN is not supported.
For the RFC 5549 feature, ensure that you provide an IPv4 address family along with the IPv6 address family for
the IPv6 BGP peer IP address.
For Out Filter and In Filter, click Configure and select filters, then click Save.
For Maximum Routes, you can specify a value between and . When the number of BGP routes
1 1,000,000
received from the peer reaches 75% of the configured limit, or when it exceeds the configured limit for the first
time, an alarm is raised. In addition, the output of NSX CLI command shows if the number of
get bgp neighbor
prefixes received exceeds the configured limit. Note that the tier-0 gateway will continue to accept routes from the
BGP neighbor even after the Maximum Routes limit is reached.
Note:
If you configure a BGP neighbor with one address family, for example, L2VPN EVPN, and then later add a second
address family, the established BGP connection will be reset.
g) Activate or deactivate the Allow as-in feature. This feature is deactivated by default.
The allow as-in feature enables a router to accept BGP updates containing its own Autonomous System number
(ASN) in the AS_PATH attribute, bypassing the default loop-prevention mechanism of BGP. This feature applies to
all the address families and cannot be applied to specific address families.
h) In the Source Addresses field, you can select a source address to establish a peering session with a neighbor
using this specific source address from a specific NSX Edge node. If you do not select any, the gateway will
automatically set up a BGP peering session with all the BGP neighbors on each NSX Edge node If an NSX Edge
node does not have an interface in the subnet of the neighbor, the BGP session configured on this NSX Edge node
will remain down.
i) Enter a value for Max Hop Limit. The default value is 1. You must configure this setting, along with configuring
static routing or an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP), to enable multi-hop BGP.
j) Optionally configure the BGP neighbor-specific Graceful Restart mode. By default, the tier-0 gateway's Graceful
Restart mode is selected. If you configure a different mode, that mode takes precedence over the mode set for
tier-0 gateway.
Option Description
Deactivate Graceful Restart is deactivated for this neighbor.
Helper Only Graceful Restart is configured as Helper Only for this neighbor.
Graceful Restart and Helper Graceful Restart is configured as Graceful Restart and Helper
for this neighbor.
Note:
Graceful Restart and Helper is not supported as a
neighbor-specific mode for dynamic neighbor ranges or
for EVPN.
Graceful Restart is not supported when a tier-0 gateway has only one BGP peer since the tier-0 service router
will go down by design when that single BGP peer goes down. If you specify a Graceful Restart mode for a
configuration that has only one BGP neighbor, the Graceful Restart mode will not take effect.
k) Enable Configure Neighbor Local AS if required.
• Choose 'Yes' if you want to override the Local AS for this neighbor
• Choose 'No' if you do not want to override the Local AS for this neighbor
Note:
Neighbor Local AS and AS Path Modifier fields appear after you enable Configure Neighbor Local AS.
Broadcom 3137

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
l) Enter the replaced local AS number, (ASN) which you want to override the Local ASN for this neighbor, in
Neighbor Local AS.
m) Choose the AS path option in AS Path Modifier:
• Default: BGP prepends neighbor's local ASN to the AS path for both outgoing and incoming route
advertisements from the peer neighbor. You can modify the default prepend action on the AS path in both
inbound and outbound direction.
• No Prepend: The local router does not prepend the incoming advertisement from the peer with neighbor's local
ASN. The advertised AS path only prepends the BGP local ASN of the router.
• No Prepend Replace AS: The local routes are advertised with the neighbor's local ASN instead of the BGP's
local ASN to peer router.
n) Click Timers & Password.
o) Enter a value in milliseconds for BFD Interval.
For an NSX Edge node deployed in VM form factor, the minimum interval value is 500. For a bare-metal NSX Edge
node, the minimum interval value is 50. The default value is 500.
p) Enter a value for BFD Multiplier. The default value is 3.
q) Enter a value, in seconds, for Hold Down Time and Keep Alive Time.
The Keep Alive Time specifies how frequently KEEPALIVE messages will be sent. The value can be between 0
and 65535. Zero means no KEEPALIVE messages will be sent.
The Hold Down Time specifies how long the tier-0 gateway will wait for a KEEPALIVE message from a neighbor
before considering the neighbor dead. The value can be 0 or between 3 and 65535. Zero means no KEEPALIVE
messages are sent between the BGP neighbors and the neighbor will never be considered unreachable.
Hold Down Time must be at least three times the value of the Keep Alive Time.
r) Enter a password.
A password is required when you configure MD5 authentication between BGP peers. Blank space characters are
not allowed in BGP passwords.
8. Click Save.
9. After a CIDR range for BGP neighbors is added, you can monitor the status of discovered neighbors.
a) Click the number from the BGP Neighbors field.
b) Expand the BGP neighbor, and click View Discovered Neighbors. From the dynamic list that appears, you can
view the status details of discovered neighbors. You can also use the options menu for a neighbor to download its
advertised and learned routes.
10.Optional: After a BGP neighbor is added, you can download its advertised and learned routes.
a) Click the number from the BGP Neighbors field.
b) From the Set BGP Neighbors dialog box, click the options menu (three dots) of a BGP neighbor and select
Download Advertised Routes or Download Learned Routes.
c) If you have configured a dynamic range of BGP neighbors, select a discovered neighbor from the drop-down menu
to download its advertised or learned routes.
11.To edit the CIDR value of a dynamic BGP neighbor or to change an existing static BGP neighbor to a dynamic
neighbor, you must first deactivate the existing neighbor and save the deactivated configuration.
a) Enter edit mode for the existing neighbor configuration. Deselect the Enable Neighbor toggle and click Save.
b) Reenter edit mode and specify the new CIDR value. Select the Enable Neighbor toggle and click Save.
BGP Autonomous System Number (ASN) per Tier-0 VRF Gateway and per BGP Neighbor
You can configure a different BGP ASN per Tier-0 VRF gateway and per BGP neighbor.
Broadcom 3138

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
BGP Autonomous System Number (ASN) per Tier-0 VRF Gateway
Tier-0 VRF gateways can have a different ASN other than the default/parent tier-0 gateway local Autonomous System
(AS). A separate ASN is important for service providers and multi-tenant topologies where end-customers provide their
own BGP ASN.
When a tier-0 VRF gateway is created and configured for BGP, you can define an ASN within the VRF in the Local AS
field. Else, you can leave the field blank to inherit the ASN from the parent tier-0 gateway. To learn more, see Deploy an
NSX VRF-Lite with BGP and Configure BGP.
Note:
BGP ASN per tier-0 VRF gateway supports active-active and active-standby NSX Edge node HA modes. EVPN is
currently not supported.
Changes in BGP ASN will cause the already established BGP connections to flap in the following situations until the
session is re-established:
• When the parent tier-0 gateway ASN changes, all child tier-0 VRF gateways that inherit the ASN from the parent will
change, causing all neighbors to flap.
• When the child tier-0 VRF gateway has its own ASN different from the parent tier-0 gateway:
– If the parent tier-0 gateway ASN is changed, the ASN of the child tier-0 VRF gateway will not change, and no flap
should occur.
– If the child tier-0 VRF gateway ASN is changed, all neighbors of that VRF will flap regardless of whether the
neighbor has a local AS set. The parent tier-0 gateway connections in other VRFs will not flap.
• Any change to the ASN for the neighbor local AS option causes that connection to flap. No other neighbors should be
affected.
BGP Per Neighbor ASN Override on Outgoing BGP Updates
NSX provides BGP mechanisms for seamless ASN migration.
When an ISP acquires a network that belongs to a different autonomous system (AS), its BGP peers must be moved to
the acquiring ISP's AS. This can be complicated and time-consuming. With the BGP mechanisms, you can configure
BGP neighbors in Tier-0 gateways and Tier-0 VRF gateways with a different local ASN than the gateway's ASN. Using a
neighbor's local ASN permits the routing devices in an acquired network to appear to belong to the former AS (Local AS).
BGP neighbors can be configured to have their ASN replaced in outgoing updates. Outgoing BGP updates use AS Path
prepending. It can be used to influence the best path algorithm by making it longer or shorter, as well as to enable routers
to migrate to new ASNs without having to upgrade all the peers simultaneously.
For more information, see RFC7795.
Note:
This is an eBGP feature. A neighbor's local AS must be different from the tier-0 gateway's local AS. Changes in
BGP local AS value will cause the already established neighbor BGP connections to flap until the session is re-
established.
Let’s take an example based on merging two ISPs to one ASN of ISP A:
Broadcom 3139

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
There are three AS path modifier options. Default Prepend is the default when Neighbor Local AS is enabled and
defined.
• Default Prepend: By default, AS Path prepends all received BGP updates with the old ASN while advertising it to
other BGP speakers (A').
A route received on CE-A from CE-B will have an AS PATH 64500 64510 64496.
• No Prepend: The local router will not prepend the old ASN to the incoming advertisement from that peer. AS Path will
be prepended only with router's local AS.
Broadcom 3140

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A route received on CE-A from CE-B will have an AS PATH 64500 64496.
• No Prepend Replace AS: Local routes will be advertised with the old ASN instead of the router's local AS, and they
will appear to be running with the old ASN.
A route received on CE-B from CE-A will have an AS PATH 64510 64499.
Tier-0 VRF Gateways
Virtual routing and forwarding (VRF) makes it possible to instantiate isolated routing and forwarding tables within a router.
VRFs are supported by deploying tier-0 VRF gateways. A tier-0 VRF gateway must be linked to a parent tier-0 gateway
and inherits some of the tier-0 gateway settings, such as HA mode, NSX Edge cluster, internal transit subnet, T0-T1
transit subnets, and BGP routing configuration.
Multiple tier-0 VRF gateway instances can be created under the same parent tier-0 gateway, which allows the separation
of segments and tier-1 gateways into multiple isolated tenants. With tier-0 VRF gateways, tenants can use overlapping IP
addresses without any interference or communication with each other.
Tier-0 VRF gateways can be used to connect tenant networks to external routers using static routes or BGP [RFC4364].
This is also known as VRF-Lite.
Broadcom 3141

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Tier-0 VRF gateways can also be deployed with EVPN. For more information, see Ethernet VPN (EVPN).
Note:
EVPN Inline and Route Server modes are not supported with the Multi-VRF Inter SR feature.
NSX Federation Support
• You can configure a tier-0 VRF gateway on a Global Manager in an NSX Federation. The Global VRF can have its own
locale operation mode and fallback preference and uses the same HA mode as tier-0 gateway.
• You can also stretch a tier-0 VRF gateways to multiple sites and enable inter-SR routing for an active-active tier-0
gateway.
Inter-SR routing is also supported on VRF gateways within a single site. You can also stretch a VRF gateway to multiple
sites in an NSX Federation setup and enable Inter-SR routing on them. To enable this feature, you must first turn on
the Multi-VRF Inter SR toggle under the Additional Settings section while configuring a tier-0 gateway. Turning on this
toggle runs MP-BGP between NSX Edge nodes, which is required for inter-node route sync to handle asymmetric VRF
connectivity and inter-site connectivity for stretched VRFs. If the Multi-VRF Inter SR toggle is off, inter-SR routing cannot
be enabled for a VRF gateway on this tier-0 gateway and the tier-0 VRF gateway cannot be stretched to multiple sites.
Note that in an NSX Federation setup, the Multi-VRF Inter SR toggle can be turned on the NSX Global Manager only

Note that even though a tier-0 VRF gateway has an HA mode, it does not have a mechanism to respond to a
communication failure that is independent of the parent tier-0 gateway's mechanism. If a tier-0 VRF gateway loses
connectivity to a BGP neighbor but the criteria for the parent tier-0 gateway to fail over is not met, the individual tier-0
VRF gateway will not fail over. The only time a tier-0 VRF gateway will fail over is when the parent tier-0 gateway does a
failover.
Deploy an NSX VRF-Lite with BGP
• The parent tier-0 gateway must be created before the tier-0 VRF gateway instance.
• The parent tier-0 gateway must have an external interface before you create an external interface on the tier-0 VRF
gateway.
• VLAN tagging (802.1q) is used to differentiate traffic among VRFs. The external interface on the tier-0 VRF gateway
must be connected to a trunk segment with the corresponding access VLAN ID defined in the segment VLAN range.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Configure the VLAN trunk segment.
a) Select Networking > Segments.
b) Click Add Segments.
c) Enter a name for the segment.
d) In Connected Gateway, set the type of connectivity for the segment as None.
e) Select a VLAN transport zone.
f) Expand the Additional Settings category.
g) In VLAN, enter a list or range of VLAN IDs allowed in the trunk segment.
h) Click Save.
3. Create the parent tier-0 gateway.
The parent tier-0 gateway must be created before the tier-0 VRF gateway instance. For more information about
configuring a tier-0 gateway, see Add an NSX Tier-0 Gateway.
Broadcom 3143

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Create the tier-0 VRF gateway.
a) Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateway.
b) Click Add Gateway > VRF.
c) Enter a name for the gateway.
d) Select a tier-0 gateway in Connect to Tier-0 Gateway.
Note:
Some advanced configurations are inherited from the parent tier-0, such as HA mode, edge cluster, internal transit
subnet, T0-T1 transit subnets.
e) If you are creating a VRF gateway on a Global Manager, In the Location field, select the location for which you
want the VRF gateway.
f) If you are configuring a VRF gateway on a Global Manager, you can click Add Location to add sites for VRF
stretching. Locations are a subset of the parent tier-0 gateway. Note that this button is available only if you had
turned on the Multi-VRF Inter SR toggle on for the tier-0 that this VRF will connect to.
Note:
Note that you can select the primary/secondary roles for a VRF independent of tier-0 primary/secondary mode.
g) Click VRF Settings.
Note:
The VRF settings are optional for regular VRF-Lite deployments, but are mandatory for EVPN use cases. For
EVPN use cases, see Ethernet VPN (EVPN).
h) Under L3 VRF Settings, specify a Route Distinguisher.
If the connected tier-0 gateway has RD Admin Address configured, the Route Distinguisher is automatically
populated. Enter a new value if you want to override the assigned Route Distinguisher.
i) Click Save and then Yes to continue configuring the VRF gateway.
5. Configure the external interfaces on the VRF gateway.
a) Expand the Interfaces and GRE Tunnels category.
b) In External and Service Interfaces, click Set or the hyperlinked number.
c) Click Add Interface.
d) Enter a name for the interface.
e) Enter the IP address and mask for the external interface.
f) In Type, select External.
g) In Connected To(Segment), select the trunk segment created from Step 2.
h) Select an edge node.
i) Enter the Access VLAN ID from the list as configured for the segment.
j) Click Save and then Close.
6. Configure BGP neighbor for VRF-Lite.
a) Click BGP.
b) Click the BGP toggle to enable BGP.
c) Turn on the Inter SR iBGP toggle to enable inter SR routing. Note that this toggle can be enabled only for an
active-active VRF gateway and if you had turned on the Multi-VRF Inter SR toggle on for the tier-0 that this VRF
connects to.
d) Enter Local AS number.
Note:
Leave this field blank to inherit the Local AS number from the parent tier-0 gateway.
You can configure the other advanced BGP settings such as ECMP.
Broadcom 3144

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
e) In the BGP Neighbors field, click Set > Add BGP Neighbor.
f) Enter the neighbor IP address.
g) Enable BFD if required.
h) Enter the Remote AS number of the neighbor.
i) Enter the source IP address.
There should be one or more addresses of created external interfaces or loopback.
j) Under Route Filter, click Set > Add Route Filter to enable IP Address Family, filters based on prefix lists, and
maximum routes received from the BGP neighbor.
k) Enable or disable the Allow as-in feature.
This is disabled by default. With this feature enabled, BGP neighbors can receive routes with the same AS, for
example, when you have two locations interconnected using the same service provider. This feature applies to all
the address families and cannot be applied to specific address families.
l) In the Source Addresses field, you can select a source address to establish a peering session with a neighbor
using this specific source address. If you do not select any, the gateway will automatically choose one.
m) Enter a value for Max Hop Limit.
n) In the Graceful Restart field, you can optionally select Disable, Helper Only, or Graceful Restart and Helper.
Note:
For EVPN, only the Helper Only mode is supported.
o) Enable Configure Neighbor Local AS if required.
• Choose 'Yes' if you want to override the Local AS for this neighbor
• Choose 'No' if you do not want to override the Local AS for this neighbor
Note:
Neighbor Local AS and AS Path Modifier fields appear after you enable Configure Neighbor Local AS.
p) Enter the replaced local AS number, (ASN) which you want to override the Local ASN for this neighbor, in
Neighbor Local AS.
q) Choose the AS path option in AS Path Modifier:
• Default: BGP prepends neighbor's local ASN to the AS path for both outgoing and incoming route
advertisements from the peer neighbor. You can modify the default prepend action on the AS path in both
inbound and outbound direction.
• No Prepend: The local router does not prepend the incoming advertisement from the peer with neighbor's local
ASN. The advertised AS path only prepends the BGP local ASN of the router.
• No Prepend Replace AS: The local routes are advertised with the neighbor's local ASN instead of the BGP's
local ASN to peer router.
r) Click Add and then Apply.
s) Click Save and then Close.
7. Re-distribute the routes in the VRF gateway and announce to the BGP neighbors.
a) Click Route Re-distribution.
b) In the Route Re-distribution field, click Set > Add Route Re-distribution.
c) Enter a name for the redistribution policy.
d) Click Set to select available sources, such as tier-0 connected interfaces and segments and then click Apply.
e) Click Add and then click Apply.
8. Make sure that your segments or tier-1 gateways are connected to the tier-0 VRF gateway.
VRF Route Leaking
By default, the data plane traffic between VRF instances is isolated in NSX. By configuring VRF route leaking, traffic can
be exchanged between VRF instances. Static routes must be configured on the tier-0 VRF instances to allow traffic to be
exchanged.
Two topology options are supported in NSX:
Broadcom 3145

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Local VRF-to-VRF route leaking
• Northbound VRF leaking
Multi-tier routing architecture is required for traffic to be exchanged in a VRF leaking topology since static routes pointing
to tier-1 distributed router (DR) uplinks are required.
Local VRF-to-VRF Route Leaking
Tier-1 DR IP addresses can be checked by using both the Edge node CLI or Network Topology in NSX Manager.
The diagram depicts a sample topology for the local VRF-to-VRF route leaking option.
Broadcom 3146

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The configuration workflow for the sample topology is as follows:
Tier-0 VRF A Configuration Workflow
1. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateway.
2. For tier-0 VRF A, click the menu icon (three dots) and select Edit.
3. Click Routing.
4. In the Static Routes field, click Set > Add Static Route and configure the static route:
a. Enter a name for the static route.
b. In the Network field, enter a prefix.
For example, 172.16.20.0/24
5. In the Next Hops column, click Set > Set Next Hops and define the next hops for the static route:
a. Enter the IP address of the tier-1 DR uplink in VRF B.
For example, 100.64.90.1
Note:
Tier-1 DR IP addresses can be checked by using both the Edge node CLI or Network Topology in NSX Manager.
b. Enter the Admin Distance of 1.
c. Enter the scope.
For example, VRF-B
Tier-0 VRF B Configuration Workflow
1. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateway.
2. For tier-0 VRF B, click the menu icon (three dots) and select Edit.
3. Click Routing.
4. In the Static Routes field, click Set > Add Static Route and configure the static route:
a. Enter a name for the static route.
b. In the Network field, enter a prefix.
For example, 172.16.10.0/24
5. In the Next Hops column, click Set > Set Next Hops and define the next hops for the static route:
a. Enter the IP address of the tier-1 DR uplink in VRF A.
For example, 100.64.80.1
Note:
Tier-1 DR IP addresses can be checked by using both the Edge node CLI or Network Topology in NSX Manager.
b. Enter the Admin Distance of 1.
c. Enter the scope.
For example, VRF-A
Northbound VRF Route Leaking
For this topology option, the northbound static route should have a next hop as an external IP address reachable in the
destination VRF routing table. It is not recommended to point static routes directly to connected IP address uplinks as the
static route would fail if an outage occurs on that link or neighbor. A loopback or virtual IP address host route (/32) can
be advertised in the network in the destination VRF. Since the host route is advertised by both top of rack switches, two
ECMP routes are installed in the tier-0 VRF. A return static route should be created in the destination VRF pointing to the
tier-1 DR uplink IP address as the next hop.

Inter-VRF Routing
The Inter-VRF Routing feature allows you to import and export routes between VRFs.
You can import and export routes between VRF gateways defined on the tier-0 gateway using the following methods:
1. Inter-VRF import and export policies:
– Inter-VRF Route Advertisement and In-Prefix Filter - Advertise routes that are not BGP, such as Static, Connected,
NAT, and all other sources that are available as inter-VRFstatic routes on connected gateway.
– Inter-VRF BGP Route Leaking - Enable BGP route leak for IPv4/IPv6 or both address families.
2. Manual Inter-VRF static route pointing to target VRF.
Inter-VRF routing can be configured:
• From Default/Parent tier-0 gateway to tier-0 VRF gateway
• From tier-0 VRF gateway to Default/Parent tier-0 gateway
• From tier-0 VRF gateway to another tier-0 VRF gateway
Configure an Inter-VRF Route Advertisement and In-Prefix Filter
With an inter-VRF route advertisement and in-prefix filter, you can configure advertisement rules to advertise routes on
the source and filter on prefixes on target connected gateway to create inter-VRF routing between two VRFs or between a
tier-0 gateway and tier-0 VRF gateway.
Broadcom 3149

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Ensure that the IP prefix list is created, see Create an IP Prefix List.
Inter-VRF forwarding is enabled when Inter-VRF routing is configured on either end between two tier-0 VRF gateways or
between a tier-0 VRF gateway and its parent Tier-0 gateway.
Configuration workflow example:
You can enable inter-VRF routing by configuring:
• Connected Gateway - To attach the Target VRF to the source parent tier-0 gateway or tier-0 VRF gatway.
• Set Advertisement Out Rules - To advertise the connected subnets of the source to the target VRF. You can allow or
deny the subnets that you want to advertise to the target VRF i.e., you want the target VRF to learn.
• Set In Filter Prefix Lists - To select prefixes that you want to accept or deny from the target VRF.
Note:
NSX assigns an IPv4 and IPv6 address to each interface. IPv4 subnet is configured in the Inter VRF Transit
Subnet field of the default tier-0 gateway. For assigning IPv6 addresses to inter-VRF interfaces, NSX allocates
one IPv6 subnet. A /64 IPv6 subnet is allocated from the tier-1-tier-0 transit subnets configured on the default
tier-0 gateway.
Broadcom 3150

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Connect the tier-0 gateway:
a) Select Networking.
b) Select either the default/parent Tier-0 gateway or the Tier-0 VRF gateway, which you would like to configure.
c) Click on the ellipsis button (three dots) and select Edit.
d) Click Routing.
e) Click Set next to Inter VRF Routing.
f) Click Add Inter VRF Routing.
g) In Connected Gateway, select the target VRF from the drop-down menu.
h) Click Save.
Note:
Wait for the Status to change to ‘Success’.
3. Set Advertisement Out Rules:
a) Click on the ellipsis button (three dots) and select Edit.
b) Click Set below Advertisement Out Rules.
c) Click Add Advertisement Out Rules.
• Enter Name - Requires validation for Name.
• Enter Subnets - Specify subnets that are used to assign addresses to logical links connecting parent tier-0
gatewayand child tier-0 VRF gateway.
Note:
Leave the Subnet field blank to set it as 'any'. If subnet is 'any', Route Advertisement Type filters must be applied.
• Apply filter – Click on the (i) icon for more information about it. Toggle to 'Yes' if you would like to apply the
filters.
Note:
Disable the filters to advertise the configured aggregate prefix subnets.
• Advertisement Action - Action to advertise filtered routes to the connected Tier0 gateway.
– Allow: Enables the advertisement
– Deny: Disables the advertisement
• Prefix Operator - Prefix operator to filter subnets.
– GE prefix operator: Filters all the routes with prefix length greater than or equal to the subnets configured.
– EQ prefix operator: Filters all the routes with prefix length equal to the subnets configured.
Note:
Prefix operation is ignored if no route advertisement type is specified.
• Select route advertisement types to be filtered.
d) Click Save.

Wait for the Status to change to ‘Success.’

Configure Inter-VRF BGP Route Leaking
With inter-VRF BGP route leaking, you can enable BGP route leaking for IPv4/IPv6 or both address families.
• Enable BGP and provide local AS on both source and target VRF.
• On source VRF, configure redistribution rules or learn external routes through BGP neighbours (To add prefixes to
BGP table). See Configure BGP.
• Use route maps to import/export filter. See Create a Route Map.
Inter-VRF BGP route leaking uses BGP VPN to leak BGP routes. NSX internally configures route targets (RTs) for route
import and export.
Note:
Inter-VRF BGP Route Leaking is supported on both IPv4 and IPv6.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking.
3. Select either the default/parent Tier-0 Gateway or the Tier-0 VRF Gateway, which you would like to configure.
4. Click on the ellipsis button (three dots) and select Edit.
5. Click Routing.
6. Click Set next to Inter VRF Routing.
7. Click on the ellipsis button (three dots) and select Edit.
8. Click Set below BGP Route Leaking.
a) Click on the ellipsis button (three dots) and select Edit.
b) Toggle the BGP Route Leaking button to 'On' for IPv4 and/or IPv6.
c) Assign a route map in the In Filter field for IPv4 and IPv6. The 'In filter' is used to determine which network or a
range of networks are permitted or denied in the direction of In.
d) Assign a route map in the Out Filter field for IPv4 and IPv6. The 'Out filter' is used to determine which network or
a range of networks are permitted or denied in the direction of Out.
9. Click Save.
Note:
BGP route leaking reduces the number of routes supported for the NSX Edge, since the BGP VPN table has to
contain an additional copy of the route for import and export.
Create an Inter-VRF Static Route with Next Hop as the Destination VRF
You can create a manual inter-VRF static route with next hop as the destination VRF.
Inter-VRF routing must be configured on both VRFs: source and destination.
You can allow a datapath to route traffic to another VRF as the next hop scope using inter-vrf static routes. You can
configure destination VRF path, for example 'Tier-0 VRF', as scope for route next hop. This will relax validation to require
IP address, as internally it will translate the scope to the next hop IP.
Note:
The recommended way to configure inter-VRF routing is to set scope as destination VRF and keep the next hop
IP blank.
By default, static routes are tagged as 'INTER_VRF_STATIC', are not advertised to another VRF, and are not included in
the BGP table. Static route only works if you have configured inter-VRF-routing with the destination VRF. Else, system will
show an error.

Configure OSPF
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is an interior gateway protocol (IGP) that operates within a single autonomous system
(AS).
The OSPF feature has the following capabilities and restrictions:
• Only OSPFv2 is supported.
• The tier-0 gateway can be active-active or active-standby (preemptive and non-preemptive).
• Only the default VRF is supported.
• You can configure a single area on a tier-0 gateway with a maximum of two tier-0 uplinks per NSX Edge node.
• Backbone, normal area, and NSSA (not-so-stubby area) are supported.
• No redistribution is supported between BGP and OSPF.
• OSPF and BGP can be used together in the case of BGP multi-hop where the peer IP is learned through OSPF.
• The same redistribution features supported for BGP are supported for OSPF (tier-0 gateway uplinks, downlinks,
loopbacks, tier-1 gateway downlinks, etc.). Depending on the area type, redistribution for all these networks will result
in the NSX Edge node generating Type 5 external LSA (link-state advertisement) or Type 7 external LSA with Type 2
metric only (External Type 2 or NSSA External Type 2 routes). The NSX Edge node itself can learn any type of LSA.
• MD5 and plain password authentication are supported on the area configuration.
• NSX Federation is not supported.
• Route summarization for External Type 2 and NSSA External Type 2 routes is supported.
• The interface running OSPF can be broadcast or numbered point-to-point (/31).
• BFD for OSPF is supported.
• For OSPF graceful restart, only the helper mode is supported.
• Redistribution route maps are supported. Only the matching of prefix lists is applicable. No set actions.
• OSPF ECMP is supported up to maximum of 8 paths.
• Default Originate is supported.
• NAT with OSPF protocol stack is not supported.
• The VIP configured with the tier-0 gateway does not support OSPF.
OSPF router ID (RID) determination
Broadcom 3153

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The OSPF router ID (RID) is determined as follows:
• Loopback interface is present: OSPF uses the loopback interface IP as the RID. If the loopback interface has an
IPv6 address, OSPF does not use it as RID. It will take the highest IPv4 interface IP.
• Loopback interface is not present: OSPF uses the highest interface IP address as the RID.
– If RID is the highest interface IP and loopback interface is present, the RID can be changed to the loopback
interface IP address by:
• Redeploying or replacing the edge transport node
• Modifying or deleting the highest interface IP address
– If RID is the highest interface IP and loopback interface is present, the RID does not change when:
• Disabling and enabling OSPF
• Rebooting the edge node, enabling maintenance mode on the edge node, or restarting the routing process
The RID, whether it is a loopback interface IP or the highest interface IP address, will not change under the following
condtions:
• Clearing OSPF neighbors
• A soft restart or hard restart of OSPF adjacency from a remote site
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateway.
3. Click Edit from the three-dot menu of the tier-0 gateway on which you want to configure OSPF.
If you do not plan to use BGP, turn off the BGP toggle under the BGP section.
4. Expand the OSPF section and click the OSPF toggle to enable OSPF.
5. In the Area Definition field, click Set to add an area definition.
You can add only one area definition.
a) Click Add Area Definition.
b) Enter an area ID.
The value must be a number or 4 numbers in IPv4 format (for example, 1.2.3.4).
c) In the Type column, select Normal or NSSA.
An OSPF NSSA (not-so-stubby area) allows external routes to be redistributed into the area by a local ASBR and
flooded as Type 7 LSAs, while still blocking Type 5 external LSAs from other areas.
d) In the Authentication column, select None, Password, or MD5.
e) If Authentication is set to MD5, enter a key ID. The Key ID identifies which MD5 secret key is used for
authenticating OSPF packets within the area. It can be any value between 1 to 255.
f) In the Password column, enter a password if Authentication is set to Password or MD5.
The MD5 password can have a maximum of 16 characters, and the plain-text password a maximum of 8
characters.
g) Click Save.
6. In the Graceful Restart field, select either Deactivated or Helper Only.
7. Click the ECMP toggle to activate or deactivate Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP), which allows load sharing across
equal-cost paths. By default, the toggle is activated. The implementation of ECMP is based on the 5-tuple of the
protocol number, source and destination address, and source and destination port.
ECMP (equal-cost multi-path) routing allows packet forwarding to occur over multiple best paths. It can provide fault
tolerance for failed paths.
8. In the Route Summarization field, click Set to add a summary address.
Route summarization can reduce the number of LSAs that are flooded into an area. You can summarize one or more
ranges of IP addresses and send routing information about these addresses in a single LSA.
Broadcom 3154

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a) Click Add Prefix. Enter an IP address prefix in CIDR format.
b) In the Advertise column, select Yes or No to indicate whether to advertise the summary route.
The default is Yes.
c) Repeat the steps above to add more prefixes.
9. Click the Default Route Originate toggle to enable or disable default route originate.
Enable this to redistribute the default route in OSPF.
10.In the OSPF Configured Interfaces field, click Set to configure OSPF on existing external interfaces. Note that the
Set link is available only when the interfaces on the tier-0 have been configured previosuly.
a) Click Configure Interface.
b) In the Interface column, select an interface from the dropdown list.
c) In the Area ID column, select an area ID from the dropdown list.
d) In the Network Type column, select Broadcast or P2P.
e) In the OSPF column, set the toggle to Enabled (the default setting).
f) Click the BFD toggle to enable or deactivate BFD (default is deactivated).
g) If BFD is enabled, select a BFD profile.
h) To change the OSPF Hello Interval, enter a new value.
The default is 10 seconds. This parameter specifies the time between Hello messages.
i) To change the OSPF Dead Interval, enter a new value.
The default is 40 seconds. If a Hello message is not received within this time interval, the neighbor is considered
unavailable.
j) Click Save.
k) Repeat the steps above to configure more interfaces.
11.Click Save.
12.Click Route Re-distribution to expand the section.
13.Click Set in the Route Re-distribution field.
• Select one or more of the sources:
– Tier-0 subnets: Static Routes, NAT IP, IPsec Local IP, DNS Forwarder IP, Router Link, Connected Interfaces
& Segments. Under Connected Interfaces & Segments, you can select one or more of the following: Service
Interface Subnet, External Interface Subnet, Loopback Interface Subnet, Connected Segment.
– Tier-0 subnets: Static Routes, NAT IP, IPsec Local IP, DNS Forwarder IP, EVPN TEP IP, Connected Interfaces
& Segments. Under Connected Interfaces & Segments, you can select one or more of the following: Service
Interface Subnet, External Interface Subnet, Loopback Interface Subnet, Connected Segment.
– Advertised tier-1 subnets: DNS Forwarder IP, Static Routes, LB VIP, NAT IP, LB SNAT IP, IPsec Local Endpoint,
Connected Interfaces & Segments. Under Connected Interfaces & Segments, you can select Service Interface
Subnet and/or Connected Segment.
• Add OSPF to the Destination Protocol of any rule that will redistribute routes into OSPF
14.Turn on the Via OSPF toggle to enable OSPF.
If you do not plan to use BGP, do not turn the Via BGP toggle on. Also, turn off the BGP toggle under the BGP section.
After you configure OSPF, in the OSPF Neighbors field, you can click View to see information about OSPF neighbors.
The information displayed includes Neighbor IP Address, Interface, Source, Edge Node, Priority, and State.
Note: If a neighbor is not reachable, an alarm about the neighbor will be raised. If the neighbor is no longer in the network,
simply acknowledge the alarm but do not resolve it. If you resolve the alarm, it will be raised again.
Configure BFD
BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) is a protocol that can detect forwarding path failures.
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) works with BGP and OSPF to detect link or neighbor failures much faster than
either protocol can on its own. BGP and OSPF register each neighbor with BFD, which monitors the forwarding path with
Broadcom 3155

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
fast hello packets and immediately notifies the routing protocol when a failure is detected. The protocol can then tear
down the session without waiting for its own timers to expire. BFD can also be used with static routes to remove a route
from the forwarding table when its next hop becomes unreachable.
Note:
Both IPv4 and IPv6 are supported.
CAUTION:
Note the following scenarios when there are connection failures involving BGP or BFD:
• With only BGP configured, if all BGP neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With only BFD configured, if all BFD neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With BGP and BFD configured, if all BGP and BFD neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With BGP and static routes configured, if all BGP neighbors go down, the service router's state will be down.
• With only static routes configured, the service router's state will always be up unless the node is experiencing
a failure or in a maintenance mode.
For more information about BFD for BGP, see Configure BGP. For more information about BFD for OSPF, see Configure
OSPF.
For more information about static routes, see Configure a Static Route.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateways.
3. To edit a tier-0 gateway, click the menu icon (three dots) and select Edit.
4. Click Routing and Set for Static Route BFD Peer.
5. Click Add Static Route BFD Peer.
6. Select a BFD profile. If the system default BFD profile named is
<default-external-gw-bfd-profile>
selected, it has a default Interval value of 500 ms that cannot be changed. A customizable profile can also be added.
See Add an NSX BFD Profile.
7. Enter the peer IP address and optionally the source addresses.
8. Click Save.
Configure Multicast Routing on a Tier-0 Gateway
IP multicast routing enables a virtual machine (source) to send a single copy of data to a single multicast address. Data is
then distributed to a group of recipients using a special form of IP address called the IP multicast group address. You can
configure multicast routing on a tier-0 gateway for an IPv4 network to enable multicast routing.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateways.
3. To edit a tier-0 gateway, click the menu icon (three dots) and select Edit.
4. Click the Multicast toggle to enable multicast.
5. In the Replication Multicast Range field, enter an address range in CIDR format.
Replication Multicast Range is a range of multicast group addresses (GENEVE outer destination IP) that is used in the
underlay to replicate workload/tenant multicast group addresses. It is recommended that there is no overlap between
the Replication Multicast Range and workload/tenant multicast group addresses.
6. In the IGMP Profile drop-down list, select an IGMP profile.
7. In the PIM Profile drop-down list, select a PIM profile.

State Synchronization of Tier-0 Gateways
Connection information of the traffic running on a given tier-0 gateway SR (Service Router) is synchronized to its peer
tier-0 gateway SR in active-standby or stateful active-active HA modes.
The state synchronization between the Active SR and Standby SR is triggered whenever there is a change in the local
state of TCP SYN packet, after a certain interval, or if a local state is created or deleted. During state synchronization,
NSX Edge uses a proprietary protocol to replicate CCP packets between Active and Standby SRs on the tier-0 gateway.
Note the following points about state synchronization:
• State synchronization is supported for Gateway Firewall, Identity Firewall, NAT, IPSec VPN, and DHCP.
• If new sessions were going through a tier-0 gateway SR just before a failover, it might happen that those sessions
were not synchronized on the associated tier-0 gateway SR and potentially affect the traffic for those sessions.
• In active-standby mode, state synchronization is supported for Gateway Firewall, Identity Firewall, NAT, IPSec VPN,
and DHCP.
• In active-active mode, state synchronization is supported for Gateway Firewall, Identity Firewall, and NAT. IPSec VPN
is not supported.
• If new sessions were going through a tier-0 SR just before a failover, it might happen that those sessions were not
synchronized on the associated tier-0 SR and potentially affect the traffic for those sessions.
Changing the HA Mode of a Tier-0 Gateway
You can change the high-availability (HA) mode of a tier-0 gateway in certain circumstances.
Changing the HA mode is allowed only if there is no more than one service router running on the tier-0 gateway, that is,
uplinks on only one NSX Edge node configured. However, you can have more than one uplink on the same NSX Edge
node configured.
After you set the HA mode from active-active to active-standby, you can set the failover mode. The default is non-
preemptive.
HA mode change is not allowed if the following services or features are configured.
• DNS Forwarder
• IPSec VPN
• L2 VPN
• HA VIP
• Stateful Gateway Firewall
• SNAT, DNAT, NO_SNAT, or NO_DNAT
• Reflexive NAT applied on an interface
• Service Insertion
• VRF
• Service Interface

Stateful Services on Tier-0 and Tier-1 on NSX
To meet the demands of stateful services such as more bandwidth and throughput, you can configure Tier-0 and Tier-1
gateways in Active-Active (A-A) configuration. Stateful services are required for next generation firewall, Layer 7 rules,
URL filtering or TLS decryption.
You can scale-out or scale-in the number of service routers by adding NSX Edge nodes to the cluster.
CAUTION:
As you scale-in or scale-out NSX Edge nodes, you might see loss of traffic packets for existing flows.
The supported stateful gateway services are:
• Gateway Firewall L3-L4
• APP-ID (L7)
• User-ID
• URL Filtering
• TLS Inspection
• IDS/IPS
• Malware Detection and Sandboxing
• NAT
• DHCP Relay Server
• DHCP Server
The unsupported services are:
• FQDN Analysis
• L2VPN
• IPSecVPN
• Gateway Network Introspection
• Local DHCP Server
• Service Interface
In your existing topology, if Tier-1 gateway is in active-standby (A-S) mode, you cannot reconfigure it in A-A HA mode
and it cannot share the same NSX Edge cluster with A-A stateful Tier-0 gateways. As a workaround, deploy that Tier-1
Broadcom 3159

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
gateway in active-standby mode on a separate cluster. Then, deploy Tier-0 gateway on another NSX Edge cluster. If your
environment requires a Tier-1 gateway, configure it in A-A HA mode. See Supported Topologies.
Key Concepts of Stateful Services with Active-Active Gateways
Understand the key concepts required to configure stateful services with an active-active gateway.
Interface Groups
Use an interface group to group equivalent external (uplink) interfaces across service routers. Equivalent interfaces refer
to interfaces that have the same inbound policies such as firewall rules, NAT rules, and so on, and equivalent network
reachability. NSX only supports external interface. You must only create homogenous interface groups, such as an
interface group comprising of only external interfaces.
To define an interface group, meet the following conditions:
• Only one interface link from each service router of the NSX Edge cluster must participate in the interface group.
• Every interface link must be part of a single interface group.
• Every interface group must have the same number of interfaces from each service router.
Note:
An interface group is required to create a stateful active-active group. If these conditions are not met, NSX raises
a status alarm on the tier-0 gateway or the tier-1 gateway UI screen.
Interface groups allow traffic flows to continue without disruption even when the original uplink interface that supported
packet transmission fails because the peer uplink interface takes over its traffic. So, if Uplink 1 or NSX Edge 1 fails, then
Broadcom 3160

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
the interface group decides where the next packet must be punted to, which is the peer shadow port on the peer edge
node on the same sub-cluster.
You can have more than one interface groups, where every interface group is dedicated to a specific requirement of the
NSX Edge node. For example, one interface group can serve internet traffic while another group can serve the DMZ.
On tier-1 gateway, a default interface group is automatically created. On the tier-0 gateway, you must manually create an
interface group.
To create an interface group, go to the Interfaces and Interfaces groups section on your tier-0 gateway. Alternatively,
run the API
PUT /infra/tier-0s/<name>/locale-services/<location>/interface-groups/<group-name>
{
"resource_type": "Tier0InterfaceGroup",
"id": "uplinkgroup",
"display_name": "uplinkgroup",
"path": "/infra/tier-0s/Tier0Gateway1/locale-services/Tier0LocalServices-1/interface-groups/uplinkgroup",
"relative_path": "uplinkgroup",
"parent_path": "/infra/tier-0s/Tier0Gateway1/locale-services/Tier0LocalServices-1",
"unique_id": "c5b2a758-7040-410b-a35d-298a16b55df0",
"realization_id": "c5b2a758-7040-410b-a35d-298a16b55df0",
"marked_for_delete": false,
"overridden": false,
"members": [
{
"interface_path": "/infra/tier-0s/Tier0Gateway1/locale-services/Tier0LocalServices-1/interfaces/
tier0_interface1"
},
{
"interface_path": "/infra/tier-0s/Tier0Gateway1/locale-services/Tier0LocalServices-1/interfaces/
tier0_interface2"
}
],
}
External Interface
Interface connecting to the physical infrastructure. It supports static routing and BGP. In previous releases, this interface
was referred to as uplink interface. This interface can also be used to extend a VRF (Virtual routing and forwarding
instance) from the physical networking fabric into the NSX domain.
Sub-clusters
When you configure stateful services on NSX Edge nodes, NSX automatically creates sub-clusters on the given NSX
Edge cluster. So, NSX Edge a cluster of four NSX Edge nodes becomes two sub-clusters, where each sub-cluster is a
pair of NSX Edge nodes.
All service routers on NSX Edge nodes participating in an interface group are converted into pairs.
For example, in sub-cluster 1, if NSX Edge node 1 goes down, all ingress or egress traffic on NSX Edge node 1 is
switched to NSX Edge node 2. So, NSX Edge node 1 and NSX Edge node 2 function as the original NSX Edge node
and peer NSX Edge node respectively in the sub-cluster. During the failover process, NSX Edge node 2 takes over the
backplane IP address that NSX Edge node 1 was serving to ensure no traffic is lost and traffic flow is maintained. When
the failed NSX Edge node 1 comes back up, the initial state is restored, where all traffic is redirected back to NSX Edge
node 1.
Failure Domain Considerations in Stateful Active-Active Gateway Deployments
Configure failure domains to ensure that both NSX Edge nodes selected for a sub-cluster do not belong to the same
failure domain. For more information, see Configure Failure Domains.
Broadcom 3161

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To ensure failure domain functions as per design, meet these conditions:
• Configure each NSX Edge with a failure domain and deploy one NSX Edge node in each failure domain. Both NSX
Edge nodes of a sub-cluster must not belong to the same failure domain.
• Ensure that both NSX Edge nodes of a sub-cluster remain as part of the same sub-cluster. To ensure that these nodes
are automatically paired in the same sub-cluster, follow a specific sequence when referencing these nodes to failure
domains. For example, in a sub-cluster, first reference NSX Edge node 1 to a failure domain and then reference
NSX Edge node 2 to a different failure domain. So, when NSX Edge node 1 comes back up after a failure, the failure
domain where the node was referenced to allows it to rejoin the same sub-cluster.
Understanding Traffic Flows
Traffic flows on stateful tier-0 and tier-1 gateways configured in stateful active-active HA mode.
South-North Traffic Flow
1. Based on a deterministic hash, an incoming packet from a southbound VM is punted to the backplane of the Edge-2.
2. Edge-2 determines that Edge-4 is actively managing the traffic flows and forwards the flow out through the external
interfaces (which are part of the interface group).
3. An IP hash is performed, based on external server destination IP, and traffic is punted from Edge-2 to Edge-4. The
packet is further forwarded to tier-0 gateway service router (SR), where SNAT changes the source IP address to
translated IP address.
4. After the flow reaches Edge-4 tier-0 SR, the shadow port forwards the NAT traffic to the uplink interface and then sent
out to the physical router.
Broadcom 3162

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. If tier-0 SR on Edge-4 fails, NSX punts traffic to its backup node in the sub-cluster, Edge-3, where SNAT changes
the source IP address to translated IP address. The backup interface on Edge-1 takes over the backplane IP and the
uplink IP of tier-0 gateway before beginning to process traffic. The backup interface on Edge-3 is operationally and
Up
the shadow interface on Edge-4 is .
Down
6. All traffic flows processed by firewall and NAT rules are synchronized on the tier-0 SR on Edge-3.
7. When Edge-4 comes back up, the flow is resynchronized back to Edge-4. When the shadow port comes back up, NSX
punts traffic to it.
North-South Traffic Flow
1. A packet from a northbound VM is hashed by the physical router using its own hashing algorithm to send the packet to
Edge-3, based on an ECMP routing choice. The tier-0 gateway is running on Edge-3.
2. Edge-3 determines that Edge-4 is actively managing the traffic flow and forwards the flow to Edge-4. The flow is
managed by the shadow interface of Edge-4.
3. An IP hash is performed, based on external server source IP, traffic is punted from Edge-3 tier-0 SR to Edge-4 tier-0
SR, where NAT is enabled. The source IP is changed to the translated IP address.
4. The packet is sent from Edge-4 Tier-0 SR to Edge 4 tier-0 DR and then to tier-1 gateway, finally reaching the
destination VM.
5. If tier-0 service router on Edge-4 fails, NSX punts traffic to its peer node (sub-cluster 2), which is Edge-3. NAT enabled
on Edge-3 changes the source IP address to translated IP address.
6. Before beginning to process traffic, the backup shadow port on Edge-3 manages the traffic flow. Now, the backup
shadow port on Edge-3 is operationally and the shadow port on Edge-4 is .
Up Down
7. All traffic flows processed by firewall and NAT rules are synchronized on the tier-0 SR on Edge-3.
8. When Edge-4 comes back up, the flow is resynchronized back to it. The shadow port on Edge-4 comes back up and
manages the punted traffic.
Sub-cluster Failure
If both the NSX Edge nodes in a sub-cluster go down, the sub-cluster goes down.
• Existing flows are disrupted causing traffic loss.
• New flows are punted to the other sub-cluster.
• When the failed sub-cluster comes back up again, the flows return to the original sub-cluster.
If a sub-cluster goes down for any reason, then the other sub-cluster in the NSX Edge cluster takes over.
Single NSX Edge Node Failure
Upon failure of an NSX Edge node, the following events happen:
1. Interface links of the NSX Edge node fail.
2. The shadow port on the failed NSX Edge node is in state.
Down
3. The backup port of the peer node in the sub-cluster takes over.
4. The firewall and the NAT states are synchronized on the peer NSX Edge node.
5. The backup port on the peer node provides connectivity to new traffic flows.
6. When interface links of the failed node comes back up, the firewall and the NAT states are resynchronized with the
shadow port of the active NSX Edge node.
7. NSX punts back traffic flows to the original NSX Edge node.
Supported Topologies
These are the supported topologies for stateful services on a tier-0 gateway or tier-1 gateway in active-active HA mode.
Greenfield Deployment Considerations
In new deployments, note the following considerations when building one of the supported topologies for stateful services
on a NSX Edge cluster:
Broadcom 3163

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Tier-1 gateway in stateful active-active HA mode running stateful services must be connected to a tier-0 gateway in
stateful active-active HA mode and must be hosted on the same NSX Edge cluster.
• Tier-1 gateway in active-standby HA mode can be connected to a tier-0 gateway in stateful active-active HA mode, but
tier-1 gateways must be hosted on a different NSX Edge cluster.
Brownfield Deployment Considerations
In existing deployments, note the following considerations when building one of the supported topologies for stateful
services on a NSX Edge cluster:
• An existing tier-1 gateway in active-standby HA mode cannot be converted to a tier-1 gateway in active-active HA
mode. You must create a new tier-1 gateway in active-active HA mode.
• Tier-0 gateway in active-standby HA mode cannot be converted to a tier-0 gateway in active-active HA mode.
• Tier-1 gateway in Distributed Only mode can be converted to a tier-1 gateway in stateful active-active HA mode, as
long the tier-1 gateway is not attached to the tier-0 gateway.

Configure Failure Domains
A failure domain is a logical grouping of NSX Edge nodes within an NSX Edge cluster. Failure domains complement auto
placement algorithm and guarantee service availability in case of a failure affecting multiple NSX Edge nodes.
In a failure domain, active and standby instances of a tier-1 gateway service router or members of a sub-cluster always
run in different failure domains. Without a failure domain, a tier-1 gateway service router could be auto placed on NSX
Edge nodes that are in the same rack. So, if rack1 fails, both active and standby instance of this tier-1 SR fail as well.
Without failure domains configured:
Figure 400:
- In an NSX Edge cluster consisting of four NSX Edge nodes (EdgeNode1, EdgeNode2, EdgeNode3, EdgeNode4), any
new tier-1 gateways in active-standby HA mode are automatically placed in any two of those four NSX Edge nodes.
Broadcom 3167

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
- However, high availability cannot be achieved if Tier-1 A/S is deployed in Rack1 and Tier-2 A/S is deployed in Rack2. If
Rack1 fails, Tier-1 A/S on EdgeNode1 and EdgeNode2 are lost as they are in the same rack.
With failure domains configured:
Figure 401:
- EdgeNode1 and EdgeNode2 are configured to be a part of failure domain FD-1, while EdgeNode3 and EdgeNode4 are
in failure domain FD-2. When a new tier-1 gateway in active-standby HA mode is created and if the active service router
of that tier-1 gateway is hosted on EdgeNode1 for example, then the standby service router of the same tier-1 gateway
will be instantiated in failure domain FD-2, which includes EdgeNode3 or EdgeNode4.
- After configuring failure domains on an NSX Edge cluster, any new tier-1 gateway and its active and standby service
routers are correctly placed in different failure fomains to ensure high availabilty in case of a rack failure.

Configure Stateful Services on NSX Tier-0 and Tier-1 Gateways in Active-Active HA mode
Configure tier-0 and tier-1 gateways in active-active stateful high-availability (HA) mode on an NSX Edge cluster and
enable stateful services.
• If there are odd number of NSX Edge nodes in the NSX Edge cluster, it leads to the scenario where one sub-cluster
does not have a backup node. On failure of that single NSX Edge node, traffic is disrupted. NSX triggers an alarm that
you must resolve to correctly configure stateful services. Ensure an NSX Edge cluster consists of an even number of
NSX Edge nodes. For example, in an NSX Edge cluster of four nodes, NSX forms two sub-clusters, where each sub-
cluster contains two nodes. One node in each sub-cluster is the backup node of the active NSX Edge node.
• Ensure the NSX Edge nodes you will use as part of the NSX Edge cluster are referenced to different failure domains.
The topology considered for this procedure uses tier-0 gateways and tier-1 gateways both in active-active stateful HA
mode.
Broadcom 3169

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Go to Networking > Tier-0 Gateways.
3. From the Add Gateway drop-down menu, click Tier-0.
4. Enter the name of the tier-0 gateway.
5. In the HA Mode field, select Active Active and enable Stateful.
Note:
Once you enable the tier-0 gateway to be stateful, you cannot edit the HA mode.

An interface group allows multiple segments to be grouped into a single group which is connected to an NSX

Add a GRE Tunnel to a Tier-0 and Tier-0 VRF Gateway
You can add GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) tunnels for NSX tier-0 and tier-0 VRF gateways to connect on-
premises and cloud networks.
For the tier-0 or tier-0 VRF gateway, ensure that:
• Either external or loopback interfaces are configured as the GRE tunnel source IP address (local endpoint).
• Routing is configured for reachability between the GRE source and remote endpoints.
• For BGP over GRE configuration, ensure that proper filters are installed on the BGP neighbor over GRE. Remote GRE
endpoint network should not be learned over BGP. Otherwise, it results in a routing loop.
NSX supports the following GRE tunnel deployment options:
• Active-standby edge clusters
• Active-active stateless
• Static routes
• BGP
• BFD
• IPv4 and IPv6 workloads
There are some limitations for the GRE functionality in NSX:
• No support for stateful services over GRE (Layer 4/7).
• GRE is not supported on tier-0 gateways in stateful active-active HA mode.
• Multicast over GRE is not supported.
• NSX Federation is not supported.
• OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) over GRE is not supported.
• IPv6 addresses cannot be used for outer IP addresses of the GRE tunnel (source and destination IP addresses).
• PMTU discovery and MTU updates are not supported.
• TCP MSS clamping is not supported.
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Tier-0 Gateways.
3. Expand the Interfaces and GRE Tunnels category.
4. For GRE Tunnels, click Set and then Add GRE Tunnel.
5. Enter a name for the GRE tunnel.
6. Click Set for Tunnel Addresses and configure the tunnel addresses:
a) Click Add Tunnel Address.
b) Select an NSX Edge node.
c) Select the source IP address of the GRE tunnel. This address is either an existing external interface or a previously
configured loopback interface per NSX Edge node.
d) Enter the subnets.
e) Click Add and then Apply.
7. Enter the destination IP address for the GRE tunnel.
8. Optional: Configure the GRE keepalive settings:
a) Use the Keep Alive toggle to enable or deactivate GRE keepalive signals to be periodically sent to the remote
GRE endpoint.
GRE keepalive signals are used to check the health of the stateless tunnel between the GRE tunnel endpoints and
whether the GRE tunnel should remain up.
Broadcom 3172

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
b) Use the Keep Alive Ack toggle to enable or deactivate GRE keepalive packets to be sent back to their source
GRE endpoint.
After the decapsulation of incoming keepalive packets, the NSX Edge datapath sends back the keepalive packets
to the source GRE endpoint with an acknowledgment (ack) packet. This setting is enabled by default.
c) Use the Dead Multiplier field to specify the number of consecutive failures or times when the GRE keepalive is not
received before making the GRE tunnel to go down.
Note:
The minimum is 3 and the maximum is 5.
d) Use the Keep Alive Timer field to specify the number of seconds for the intervals at which GRE keepalive signals
are sent.
Note:
The minimum is 2 and the maximum is 120.
9. Click Save.
10.Optional: After the GRE tunnel is created, you can view statistics for the GRE tunnel:
a) Click Tunnel Statistics to view a summary of the received and transmitted traffic.
b) Click Keep Alive Statistics to view details of the GRE keepalive signals and GRE keepalive acknowledgment,
including timestamps.
c) Click Tunnel Connectivity Status to view the connectivity related information.
Note:
To display the Last Up Time and Last Down Time data, the Keep Alive and Keep Alive Ack toggles must be
enabled.
Tier-1 Gateway
A tier-1 gateway has downlink connections to segments and uplink connections to tier-0 gateways.
You can configure route advertisements and static routes on a tier-1 gateway. Recursive static routes are supported.
Add an NSX Tier-1 Gateway
A tier-1 gateway is typically connected to a tier-0 gateway in the northbound direction and to segments in the southbound
direction.
• If you are adding a tier-1 gateway from Global Manager in NSX Federation, refer to Add a Tier-1 Gateway from Global
Manager.
• If you plan to configure the gateway DHCP server, refer to Attach an NSX DHCP Profile to a Tier-0 or Tier-1 Gateway.
Tier-0 and tier-1 gateways support the following addressing configurations for all interfaces (external interfaces, service
interfaces and downlinks) in both single tier and multi-tiered topologies:
• IPv4 only
• IPv6 only
• Dual Stack - both IPv4 and IPv6
To use IPv6 or dual stack addressing, enable IPv4 and IPv6 as the L3 Forwarding Mode in Networking > Networking
Settings > Global Networking Config.
Broadcom 3173

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. With admin privileges, log in to NSX Manager.
2. Select Networking > Segment Connectivity > Tier-1 Gateways.
3. Click Add Tier-1 Gateway.
4. Enter a name for the gateway.
5. In the HA Mode field, select a high availability (HA) mode: You can select from the following options:
• Active Standby: In the active-standby mode, traffic is load balanced by an elected active member. If the active
member fails, a new member is elected as the active member. To use this HA mode, you must assign an NSX Edge
cluster to the tier-1 gateway.
• Distributed Only: Select this mode to configure a Distributed Router-only (DR) gateway. This HA mode does not
require the assignment of an NSX Edge cluster to the tier-1 gateway. This HA mode uses the fully distributed
routing architecture of NSX and is the recommended option unless you require stateful network services, such as
NAT, on the tier-1 gateway.
• Active Active: In the active-active stateful mode, traffic is load balanced across all members and includes support
of stateful services such as NAT. This HA mode is available only when the linked tier-0 gateway is configured in
stateful active-active mode. To use this HA mode, you must assign an NSX Edge cluster to the tier-1 gateway.
6. Select a tier-0 gateway to connect to this tier-1 gateway to create a multi-tier topology.
7. Assign an NSX Edge cluster to this tier-1 gateway if you want this gateway to host stateful networking services such
as NAT.
Note:
If you do not require stateful services, leave the tier-1 gateway without an assigned NSX Edge cluster, and select
the Distributed Only HA mode to use the fully distributed routing architecture of NSX.
If you assign an NSX Edge cluster to the tier-1 gateway, a service router will always be created (even if you do not
configure stateful services), affecting the north/south traffic pattern.
8. After you select an NSX Edge cluster, a toggle gives you the option to select NSX Edge nodes.
9. If you selected active-standby HA mode and and also selected an NSX Edge cluster, select a failover mode or accept
the default. Failover modes are only available when you have selected active-standby HA mode.
Option Description
If the preferred NSX Edge node fails and recovers, it will preempt its peer and become the active
node. The peer will change its state to standby.
Preemptive
This mode triggers the switchover of the NSX Edge VM running services, which can lead to a
secondary disruption that causes packet loss.
If the preferred NSX Edge node fails and recovers, it will check if its peer is the active node. If so,
Non-preemptive the preferred node will not preempt its peer and will be the standby node. This mode is the default.
This mode does not trigger a reconvergence that could lead to unnecessary packet loss.
