Create an NSX Edge Cluster and Add Edge Nodes
NSX Edge transport nodes are service appliances that run network and security services. The task of creating an NSX
Edge node is intended for administrators who have thorough knowledge of NSX networking concepts and configurations.
To create NSX Edge nodes, complete the following high-level tasks:
Broadcom 3314

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Add an NSX Edge cluster and configure the NSX Edge cluster settings.
2. Create an NSX Edge node and configure settings.
a. Configure node placement settings.
b. Configure management network settings for the NSX Edge node.
c. Configure the uplink mapping for datapath interfaces of the NSX Edge node.
d. (Optional) Configure advanced settings for the NSX Edge node.
3. Deploy the NSX Edge node and verify its status.
Each high-level task is described in more detail later on this page.
Essential Prerequisites
Before creating an NSX Edge node, you must meet these essential prerequisites.
1. Identify the vCenter instance where you plan to deploy the NSX Edge node.
2. Identify the vSphere cluster where you plan to deploy the NSX Edge node.
3. Identify the data store to be used for the NSX Edge node. Verify that the data store is accessible to all ESX hosts in
the designated vSphere cluster.
4. Prepare a static IP address and gateway for assignment to the NSX Edge management interface. Alternatively, you
can use DHCP assignment for the NSX Edge management interface.
5. Identify the distributed virtual port group (DVPG) to which you plan to connect the NSX Edge management interface.
Verify that the DVPG is of type VLAN in vCenter. You may already have a DVPG in the VCF management domain.
6. By default, the deployment workflow provides pre-configured uplink profiles (such as <nsx-edge-multiple-vteps-
uplink-profile>) for the NSX Edge datapath interfaces. If you want to use your own uplink profile instead, configure
that uplink profile.
7. Identify the transport VLAN to be used by NSX Edge tunnel endpoints (TEPs) for overlay traffic.
8. Identify the overlay transport zone of the vSphere cluster where you plan to deploy the NSX Edge node. You will apply
this overlay transport zone to the NSX Edge node.
9. Prepare the static IP addresses and gateway for assignment to the NSX Edge TEPs. Alternatively, you can use DHCP
or IP pool assignment for the TEPs.
10.Identify the active and standby physical network interfaces (pNICs) that you plan to use for the uplink mapping of
the NSX Edge datapath interfaces. NSX automatically creates a trunk DVPG in vCenter for the uplink mapping.
Alternatively, you can use an existing DVPG as described in the next section, "Optional Prerequisites."
Optional Prerequisites
To use optional features of NSX Edge nodes, prepare the relevant requirements.
• To use NSX Edge nodes in UPT mode, meet the following conditions:
– Verify that the physical NIC of each ESX host is running on a UPT-compatible driver and firmware.
– Configure a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) to support network offloads, add ESX hosts with compatible physical
NICs to that VDS, and enable Advanced NIC Passthrough in the host switch configuration for the transport node
profile. For more information, see Enhanced Network Offloads and Advanced NIC Passthrough.
– Set the memory reservation to 100% on the NSX Edge node.
– Verify that all NSX Edge datapath interfaces are connected to the VDS that has network offloads (UPT) enabled.
– Ensure that all NSX Edge nodes in the NSX Edge cluster have homogeneous capabilities to provide equivalent
performance in cases of failover.
• To use a resource pool for the NSX Edge node VMs, reserve that resource pool.
• To support the host group affinity feature which uses the best effort restart (BER) policy, ensure that you have created
the host group in vCenter according to the network and/or failure boundaries and homogeneity.
• To have the NSX Edge deployment workflow automatically fetch the host overlay network configuration from a vSphere
cluster, verify that the vSphere cluster is properly prepared for NSX and enable the NSX on DVPGs setting on that
vSphere cluster.
• To use existing uplinks for the uplink mapping of the NSX Edge datapath interfaces, you must first prepare these
uplinks.
Broadcom 3315

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– To connect NSX Edge datapath interfaces to an existing trunk DVPG in vCenter, create the trunk DVPG in vCenter
for NSX Edge TEP and uplink traffic. For more information, see the vSphere Networking guide.
– To connect NSX Edge datapath interfaces to NSX VLAN segments, create VLAN trunk segments in NSX.
About NSX Edge Nodes
NSX Edge nodes can host tier-0, tier-1, VPC, and centralized transit gateways. They can be instantiated in virtual
machine form factor or as bare metal edges. They are grouped in one or several NSX Edge clusters. Each NSX Edge
cluster represents a pool of capacity for networking services.
Note:
The deployment workflow described on this page applies only to NSX Edge nodes in virtual machine form factor.
For information about deploying a bare metal edge, see Join NSX Edge with the Management Plane.
An NSX Edge node can belong to only one overlay transport zone, but it can belong to one or more VLAN transport zones
depending on your design.
About NSX Edge Clusters
Having an NSX Edge cluster of at least two NSX Edge nodes helps to ensure the availability of nodes. To create a tier-0
gateway or a tier-1 gateway with stateful services (such as NAT and load balancer), you must associate it with an NSX
Edge cluster. To associate a tier-0 or tier-1 gateway with a single NSX Edge node, create an NSX Edge cluster that
contains the single node.
Each NSX Edge node can belong to only one NSX Edge cluster. An NSX Edge node can be used to back multiple tier-1
gateways in active-standby mode, and multiple VPC and centralized transit gateways. However, there can be only one
tier-0 gateway per NSX Edge node.
You can edit an existing NSX Edge cluster to add more nodes to it.
Note:
Multiple NSX Edge clusters can be deployed within a single NSX Manager, allowing for the creation of pools of
capacity that can be dedicated to specific services: for example, NAT at tier-0 gateways or networking services
(NAT, DHCP, VPN, DNS) at tier-1 gateways. Within a given NSX Edge cluster, all NSX Edge nodes must be the
same type – either physical servers (bare metal) or VMs. When you deploy an NSX Edge cluster of node VMs
using the deployment workflow described on this page, all nodes in the NSX Edge cluster must have the same
form factor, or size.
You can also configure a failure domain, which consists of a logical grouping of NSX Edge nodes within an NSX Edge
cluster. Failure domains complement auto-placement algorithms and guarantee service availability during a failure
affecting multiple NSX Edge nodes. For more information, see Configure Failure Domains.
Broadcom 3316

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Add an NSX Edge Cluster
Broadcom 3317

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Select System > Fabric > Edges > Edge Clusters.
2. Select Add Cluster. The NSX Edge cluster configuration page appears.
3. Enter a unique Cluster Name.
4. Select or create a High Availability Profile. For more information, see Add a High Availability Profile.
5. For Edge Form Factor, designate the size of the NSX Edge nodes to be added to the NSX Edge cluster. All nodes in
the NSX Edge cluster must have the same form factor.
Ensure that you have met the resource requirements on the vSphere cluster where you plan to deploy the NSX Edge
nodes, as described in NSX Edge VM System Requirements.
6. Specify how you want to manage password credentials for the nodes in the NSX Edge cluster.
– To automatically generate passwords for the NSX Edge nodes and have these passwords managed by SDDC
Manager, select the toggle.
– To manually configure passwords for the NSX Edge nodes, deselect the toggle. Configure the CLI administrator
and root administrator credentials, in compliance with the password strength restrictions provided by the wizard.
Specify whether to allow root SSH logins to the NSX Edge nodes.
Note:
Use the following methods to manage NSX Edge passwords:
• In the case where you have deployed NSX using SDDC Manager and auto-generated the passwords, use
SDDC Manager to retrieve and manage the passwords. Once you have retrieved the passwords, you can also
manage them using VCF Operations.
• In all cases, you can run the Reset Password action on the deployed NSX Edge node to manually configure
new passwords.
7. (Optional) Under Advanced Resource Reservations, select Configure to adjust the resource reservation settings for
nodes in the NSX Edge cluster.
For example, the following screenshot shows the settings available in version 9.1.1 and later for nodes with Extra
Large form factor.
a. Select an option for CPU Shares.
CAUTION:
Configuring CPU shares does not guarantee that CPU cycles will be reserved for the NSX Edge VM. For optimal
performance, specify CPU reservations using the CPU Reservation (MHz) setting instead.
Broadcom 3318

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The NSX Edge form factor determines the options that you can select from this menu, as summarized in the
following table.
NSX Edge Form Factor Options for CPU Shares
Small • Low | 1000 Shares
• Normal | 2000 Shares
• High | 4000 Shares (default)
• Extra High | 6000 Shares
Medium • Low | 2000 Shares
• Normal | 4000 Shares
• High | 8000 Shares (default)
• Extra High | 10000 Shares
Large • Low | 4000 Shares
• Normal | 8000 Shares
• High | 16000 Shares (default)
• Extra High | 18000 Shares
Extra Large • Low | 8000 Shares
• Normal | 16000 Shares
• High | 32000 Shares (default)
• Extra High | 34000 Shares
b. For Memory Reservation (%), specify the percentage of memory to be allocated to an NSX Edge VM relative to
other VMs that are contending for shared memory. The default value is 100%.
CAUTION:
For maximum performance, NSX Edge nodes must be assigned 100% of the available resources. If you do
customize resource reservations, restore the reservation to 100% later to get maximum performance.
Reservation percentage is relative to the pre-defined value in the form factor. 100 indicates 100% of memory is
reserved for the NSX Edge VM. If you enter 50, it indicates that 50% of the allocated memory is reserved for the
NSX Edge node.
Note:
If you plan to enable Uniform Passthrough (UPT) mode, reserve 100% of the allocated memory for the NSX Edge
node.
c. Enter a value for CPU Reservation (MHz). This field is empty by default.
The maximum CPU reservation must not exceed the maximum CPU allocation for the NSX Edge VM, or the
number of vCPUs multiplied by the physical CPU speed. If the CPU reservation exceeds that value, the NSX Edge
VM might fail to start even though the allocation was accepted.
For example, consider a NSX Edge VM with four vCPUs backed by a physical multi-core CPU running at 2.20
GHz base frequency. The maximum CPU allocation for that VM is 4 x 2200 MHz = 8800 MHz. If you set the
CPU reservation to 10000 MHz, the ESX host fails to power on the VM because it cannot fulfill the 10000 MHz
reservation. If you reconfigure the NSX Edge VM with eight vCPUs, the maximum CPU allocation changes to 8 x
2200 MHz = 17600 MHz. In this case, the 10000 MHz reservation is fulfilled and the VM powers on.
d. In version 9.1.1 and later, for Core Allocation Profile, select a profile to configure how NSX Edge allocates
available cores between the datapath (fast-path), services, and Linux processes. The menu of available profiles is
based on the node form factor specified for the cluster.
If you leave the profile menu unselected or clear the existing selection, NSX Edge uses the default core allocation:
50% for datapath, 25% for services, 25% for Linux.
Broadcom 3319

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
After the NSX Edge cluster is created, you can change the core allocation profile if needed by editing the cluster.
You must then power off and power on all the NSX Edge nodes in that cluster to make the new profile take effect.
For more information, see Broadcom knowledge base article 441953.
Core Allocation Profile Description Supported Node Form Factors

forwarding performance of datapath:
• 75% for datapath
• 0% for services
• 25% for Linux
SECURITY Allocates more service and Linux cores to • Extra Large Edge VM
support advanced security workloads: • Bare metal
• 25% for datapath
• 25% for services
• 50% for Linux
e. For UPT Mode, select the toggle to enable Uniform Passthrough (UPT) mode on NSX Edge datapath interfaces.
In UPT mode, NSX Edge nodes can use Uniform Passthrough technology to offload intensive network datapath
tasks from the ESX host CPU to supported hardware NICs, accelerating networking performance.
CAUTION:
To make UPT settings effective on NSX Edge VM virtual network adapters, NSX Manager puts the NSX Edge VM
into maintenance mode, powers it off and powers it back on again.
8. (Optional) Enter a Description and specify Tags for the NSX Edge cluster.
9. In the Add Cluster page, select Add to start the workflow for adding an NSX Edge node. Proceed to the next section
for detailed instructions.
2a. Start the NSX Edge Node Workflow and Configure Node Placement Settings
The Add Node page contains configurable settings for the new NSX Edge node. As you adjust settings, the preview on
the right side of the page updates to reflect the resulting network topology.
Broadcom 3320

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. For Node Name (FQDN), enter a unique FQDN for the NSX Edge node, using the format subdomain.example.com.
2. For Compute Manager, select the registered vCenter instance where you want to deploy the NSX Edge node.
3. For vSphere Cluster, designate the vSphere cluster where you want to deploy the NSX Edge node.
4. (Optional) For Resource Pool, assign a resource pool that has been preconfigured for the NSX Edge node.
5. Select a Data Store for the NSX Edge node files from the drop-down menu.
6. For Host Group Affinity, select Yes if you want the NSX Edge node to be pinned to a host or a host group and want
to assign a Best Effort Restart (BER) policy to the NSX Edge node. Ensure that you have created the host group in
vCenter according to the network and/or failure boundaries and homogeneity. The following considerations apply to
this feature.
– If you deploy an NSX Edge node in a non-homogeneous network, you cannot use vMotion during a host
remediation. An example of a non-homogeneous network is a multi-rack horizontal vSphere cluster with a single
host per rack and L3 boundaries between the racks. vMotion is not allowed in such cases because migration of the
NSX Edge node to another host in another rack will cause connectivity loss with top-of-rack switches.
Broadcom 3321

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– When you pin an NSX Edge node to a host group, the node is associated with a host or a host group using an
affinity rule.
– During a host upgrade or remediation workflow when the current NSX Edge node has active contexts, NSX also
runs prechecks to find if any peer NSX Edge node is healthy and ready for failover before the host automatically
enters maintenance mode.
Note:
Failover prechecks do not apply when you manually put a host into maintenance mode. For more information, see
Broadcom knowledge base article 395307.
If a healthy peer NSX Edge node is available, a graceful failover is made to this peer node and then the first NSX
Edge node is put into maintenance mode and powered off.
If the precheck detects that no healthy peer NSX Edge node is available for graceful failover, the host upgrade or
remediation pauses until you manually resolve the precheck errors.
– If you have enabled DRS for the vSphere cluster, a Best Effort Restart (BER) policy is also applied to the NSX Edge
node. The BER policy waits for the guest VM to shut down and ensures that the node gracefully shuts down when
its host enters maintenance mode.
• If the host group contains a single host, the NSX Edge node stays powered off during the host maintenance
mode. The node is powered on again when the host exits the maintenance mode. If the NSX Edge node has
active contexts and a healthy peer NSX Edge node is available, the peer node takes over the services. Once the
host exits maintenance mode, the first NSX Edge node is powered on upon the same host.
• If the host group contains multiple hosts, a healthy peer NSX Edge node takes over the services of the NSX
Edge node that has shut down. Also, that node is powered on upon a compatible host if available. If no
compatible host is available due to affinity or availability constraints, the node stays powered off during the host
maintenance mode. Once the host exits maintenance mode, the NSX Edge node is powered on again on the
same host.
7. If you have set Host Group Affinity to Yes, select the Host Group to which you want to pin the NSX Edge node.
Note:
To change the pinned host group after the NSX Edge node is deployed, run the Edit action on that node. Once
the new host group passes vMotion compatibility checks, the NSX Edge node will undergo vMotion migration to
that new host group.
8. Proceed to the next section to configure the NSX Edge management network.
2b. Configure NSX Edge Management Network Settings
These settings specify the IP version and assignment type for the IP address of the NSX Edge node management
interface. This IP address is required to communicate with NSX Manager.
The NSX Edge management interface is connected to distributed virtual port groups (DVPGs).
Broadcom 3322

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the Add Node page, scroll to the Management Network Settings section.
2. For IP Assignment, specify the IP version of the assignment. You can select from the following options:
– IPv4 Only
– IPv4 & IPv6
– IPv6 Only
3. If you selected IPv4 Only, specify whether to use DHCP or Static assignment type.
Note:
If you select DHCP, the IP address of the edge management interface might change upon lease expiration.
4. If you selected static IPv4 Only, IPv4 & IPv6, or IPv6 Only, specify the following:
– Management CIDR: Enter the IP address of the edge node in CIDR notation.
– Default Gateway: Enter the gateway IP address of the NSX Edge node.
5. For Port Group, select the distributed virtual port group (DVPG) used to connect to the NSX Edge management
interface. This interface must be reachable from NSX Manager.
The NSX Edge management interface establishes communication with the NSX Manager management interface.
6. Proceed to the next section to configure the uplink mapping for edge datapath interfaces.
2c. Configure the Uplink Mapping for NSX Edge Datapath Interfaces
By default, NSX Manager fetches the host TEP configuration from the properly prepared vSphere cluster and uses it for
the NSX Edge node uplink mapping. You can accept the fetched configuration, or you can fine-tune datapath settings for
the NSX Edge node.
The NSX Edge datapath interfaces are connected to a distributed virtual port group (DVPG). You can either create the
DVPG automatically or select an existing DVPG, as described in step 9 of the following procedure.
1. In the Add Node page, scroll to the Uplinks section.
2. If desired, select the option to use the host overlay configuration from the selected vSphere cluster. The deployment
workflow fetches the existing host overlay configuration and applies it to the NSX Edge node TEP VLAN and TEP IP
Assignment.
Note:
To use this option, you must first prepare the vSphere cluster as described under "Optional Prerequisites" earlier
on this documentation page.
3. For Edge Node Uplink Mapping, click Configure. The NSX Edge node uplink mapping settings are displayed. The
selected uplink profile will determine the number of uplinks for the node.
Broadcom 3323

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Broadcom 3324

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. For Uplink Profile, select the uplink profile from the drop-down menu. Both default and custom uplink profiles are
available for selection. The available number of uplinks depends on the configuration in the selected uplink profile.
Note:
NSX Edge nodes support uplink profiles with Failover teaming policy (with a single active uplink) and
Loadbalancer Source teaming policy (with multiple active uplinks) only.
5. For Transport Zone, select the transport zones that this NSX Edge node belongs to.
– When assigned to a tier-0 gateway, an NSX Edge node belongs to at least two transport zones, an overlay for NSX
connectivity and a VLAN for uplink connectivity.
– When assigned to a tier-1 gateway, VPC, or centralized transit gateway, an NSX Edge node belongs to an overlay
transport zone.
Note:
NSX Edge nodes support multiple tunnel endpoints (TEPs) when the following prerequisites are met:
• TEP configuration must be done on one NSX Edge virtual switch only.
• All TEPs must use the same transport VLAN for overlay traffic.
• All TEPs must reside in the same subnet.
• All TEPs must use the same default gateway.
6. For TEP VLAN, specify the unique VLAN ID that identifies the VLAN used for overlay tunnels.
a. If specified, this value overrides the transport VLAN configured in the selected uplink profile.
b. If you leave this value unspecified, overlay tunnels use the transport VLAN configured in the selected uplink profile.
7. For TEP IP Address Type, select the IP version to be used for the tunnel endpoint (TEP). The options are IPv4 and
IPv6.
Important:
Ensure that the transport node forwarding mode and TEP IP address type are the same. For example, if the
transport node forwarding mode is set to IPv6, set the TEP IP address type to IPv6. If they are different, a loss of
traffic may result.
8. For IP Allocation (TEP), choose how IP addresses are assigned to the NSX Edge virtual switch that is configured.
The switch is used as the tunnel endpoint of the NSX Edge node. The options are:
• IP Pool: Select the IP pool. See Create an IP Pool for Tunnel Endpoint IP Addresses.
• Static IP List: Specify the following fields:
– Static List: Enter a list of comma-separated IP addresses to be used by the NSX Edge node.
– Static Gateway: Enter the default gateway of the TEP, which is used to route packets to and from another TEP
in another network. For example, if ESX TEP is in 20.20.20.0/24 and NSX Edge TEPs are in 10.10.10.0/24, then
we use the default gateway to route packets between these networks.
– (For IPv4) IP Subnet Mask: Enter the subnet mask of the TEP network used on the NSX Edge node.
– (For IPv6) Prefix Length: Enter the prefix length to use for IPv6 assignments.
• DHCP: Select to enable DHCP. If you are using IPv6, the underlay network must have an IPv6 router to advertise
the default gateway through Router Advertisement (RA).
9. In the mapping table, map each available uplink to a datapath interface, and map the datapath interface to active
and standby physical network interfaces (pNICs). For example, for an uplink profile with four uplinks, the datapath
interfaces are named fastpath interfaces fp-eth0, fp-eth1, fp-eth2, and fp-eth3.
You can configure a maximum of four unique datapath interfaces as uplinks on an NSX Edge VM. However, the
mapping table only displays the number of interfaces matching the number of uplinks in the uplink profile. For
example, it displays two datapath interfaces when the uplink profile has two uplinks.
• To have the edge deployment workflow automatically create a trunk DVPG on the selected VDS, turn off the Use
Existing DVPG/Segment toggle.
• To use an existing DVPG, turn on the Use Existing DVPG/Segment toggle. Select the DVPG to use, and click
Apply.
A deployment mode with a single NSX Edge virtual switch is recommended for both bare metal edges and NSX Edge
VMs. See Configure NSX Edge DPDK Interfaces.
Broadcom 3325

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
If the uplink profile applied to the NSX Edge node uses a Named Teaming policy, ensure the following condition:
Map all uplinks in the Default Teaming policy to the corresponding physical network interfaces on the NSX
Edge VM. This mapping enables traffic to flow through a segment that uses the Named Teaming policies. See
Configure Named Teaming Policy.
10.To validate the NSX Edge TEP transport VLAN and MTU configurations, click Run Check.
You can review the results of the health check for any detected configuration issues, such as an MTU mismatch or
untrunked VLAN. For more information, see Run a VLAN MTU Check.
11.If needed, use the Add VLAN Switch action to add more NSX Edge virtual switches to the configuration.
12.Click Apply to save the uplink mapping to the NSX Edge node and return to the Add Node page.
13.Optionally configure advanced settings for the NSX Edge node. For more information, see "2d. Advanced
Configuration (Optional)."
14.On the Add Node page, click Apply to save your configurations to the NSX Edge node.
2d. Advanced Configuration (Optional)
You can configure the following advanced settings for an NSX Edge node:
• NTP server
• Search domain
• DNS server
• Syslog server
Note:
Advanced Configuration settings apply specifically to the selected NSX Edge node. As a best practice, configure

Broadcom 3326

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the Add Node page, for Advanced Configuration (Optional), select Configure.
2. For NTP Servers, enter the IP address or FQDN of the NTP server.

4. For DNS Servers, enter the IP address of the DNS server.
5. For Syslog Servers, specify a server for storing the system logs.
6. Click Apply to save your configurations to the selected NSX Edge node.

1. To add more nodes to the NSX Edge cluster, repeat the steps beginning from "2a. Start the NSX Edge Node Workflow

Alternatively, you can reuse an existing node's configuration for a new node by selecting Clone from the existing

2. In the Edge Cluster Configuration page, click Next to review the NSX Edge cluster configuration.
3. Click Deploy to deploy the NSX Edge nodes in the cluster.
4. View the node deployment status on the Edges page.

Configure NSX Edge DPDK Interfaces
Configure an NSX Edge VM with a node switch to carry both overlay and external traffic.
In this topology, NSX Edge VM is configured with a node switch to carry overlay and external traffic.
Broadcom 3328

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In this topology, the uplink profile attached is configured to use Multi-TEP to provide load balancing for overlay traffic by
selecting default teaming to be Load Balancing Source teaming policy with active 'uplink1' and 'uplink2' on transport VLAN
200.

To create the topology, follow these steps.
1. Uplink Profile creation with named-teaming policy for VLAN networks and default teaming for overlay networks. If
named-teaming does not exist in uplink profile then default teaming is used for all networks.
2. VLAN Transport Zone is created or modified to use named teaming policy VLAN300-Policy and VLAN400-Policy (if
using named-teaming policy).

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. In the NSX Edge configuration, “Uplink1” (fp-eth0) is vNIC2 on Edge VM and is mapped to use VLAN 300 Trunk PG
and “Uplink2”(fp-eth1) is vNIC3 on Edge VM and is mapped to use VLAN 400 Trunk portgroup.
4. NSX Edge VM interfaces can connect to VDS Portgroups in vCenter or NSX VLAN Segments.
Note:
If Edge interfaces will be connecting to NSX VLAN Segments, ESX Hosts (hosting the Edge VMs) should be
configured as Host Transport Nodes and member of VLAN transport zone.
An example of connecting VM interfaces to NSX VLAN segments.
An example of an NSX Edge VM with interfaces on vCenter VDS Edge Trunk Portgroups
a) If VM interfaces connect to NSX VLAN segments, named-teaming is enabled on the segments. The diagram
shows that External VLAN segment 300 is configured to use a named teaming policy “Vlan300-Policy” that sends
traffic from this VLAN on “Uplink1” (vNIC2 of Edge VM). "External VLAN segment 400" is configured to use a
named teaming policy “Vlan400-Policy” that sends traffic from this VLAN on “Uplink2” (vNIC3 of Edge VM).
b) If VM interfaces connect to VDS Portgroups in vCenter, then “Trunk1 PG” is configured to use active uplink as
“VDS-Uplink1” and standby uplink as “VDS-Uplink2”. “Trunk2 PG” is configured to use active uplink as “VDS-
Uplink2” and standby uplink as “VDS-Uplink1”. This configuration ensures that the traffic sent on “External VLAN
Broadcom 3330

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Segment 300”uses vNIC2 of Edge VM to exit the Edge VM and then “VDS-Uplink1” and is sent to the left TOR
switch. Similarly, traffic sent on VLAN 400 uses “VDS-Uplink2” and is sent to the TOR switch on the right.
Important:
• ESX TEP and Edge TEP share the same VLAN: Use this configuration only if NSX Edge Trunk 1 portgroup
and NSX Edge Trunk 2 portgroup are created from NSX as VLAN segments. Because any traffic between the
Edge TEP to its own hypervisor’s TEP does not need to exit the hypervisor.
• ESX TEP and Edge TEP use different VLANs: Use this configuration if NSX EdgeTrunk1 portgroup and NSX
EdgeTrunk2 portgroup are created as VDS portgroups from vCenter. Any traffic between the NSX Edge TEP
and its hypervisor TEP must exit the ESX. The top of rack switch must then route it back toward the ESX.
Run a VLAN MTU Check
The VLAN MTU Check validates the configuration of tunnel endpoint (TEP) transport VLANs and maximum transmission
unit (MTU) settings during the creation of an edge node. Detecting and correcting VLAN and MTU misconfigurations at
this stage helps to ensure that the edge node is deployed successfully without network connectivity problems.
Running the VLAN MTU Check During Edge Creation
You can run the VLAN MTU Check during the uplinks configuration step of the edge creation workflow.
1. In NSX Manager, start the edge creation workflow.
2. On the Edge Node Uplink Mapping page, click Run Check.
The VLAN MTU Check performs the validation and generates a report showing the number of supported and
unsupported uplinks per ESX host in the specified host cluster.
3. Click the report link next to the Run Check button to view the report details.
Broadcom 3331

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To view report details for a specific uplink, click the number in that uplink column.
Broadcom 3332

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 412: Example Report for Matched MTU and Trunked VLAN
Figure 413: Example Report for Untrunked VLAN
Broadcom 3333

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 414: Example Report for Mismatched MTU
An unsupported uplink indicates that a problem exists with the VLAN or MTU configuration for that uplink. For more
information, see "Troubleshooting VLAN and MTU Misconfigurations" later on this page.
Running the VLAN MTU Check Using the NSX API
You can also create and run a manual health check of the VLAN and MTU configuration using the following API calls. For
detailed information, see the NSX API Guide.
• To create a manual health check:
POST https://<nsx-mgr>/policy/api/v1/infra/manual-health-checks/<manual-check-id>
Example payload:
{
"cluster_scope_filter": {
"cluster_external_id": "cfb040ff-71c6-4e7a-abd8-cae2a972742f:domain-c20",
"host_switch_id": "50 33 53 f4 e7 b7 ab f4-f0 6a 37 20 40 16 1a 8a",
"host_group_name": "test"
},
"vlans":{
"vlan_ranges":[{
"start": 0,
"end": 10
},{
"start": 20,
"end": 30
}]
}
}
• To fetch the results of a manual health check:
GET https://<nsx-mgr>/policy/api/v1/infra/manual-health-checks/<manual-check-id>/result

Because VLAN MTU Check relies on bidirectional active probing between two uplinks, ensure that you have
configured at least two uplinks to test in a cluster. You can configure these uplinks as either two uplinks in a single
host or at least two hosts in the cluster with a single uplink.

trunked to the same top-of-rack (ToR) interfaces that the ESX hosts connect to.
physical switch. 2. If the TEP transport VLANs are missing, add the
VLANs to the ToR interface configurations.

switch) does not match MTU of the ToR on the ToR physical switch.
physical switch. 2. Adjust the settings so that the MTU of the host
switch matches the MTU of the physical switch.
For optimal performance, set both MTUs to the
higher of the mismatched values.
Manually Deploying NSX Edge Node Outside of NSX Manager
In addition to deploying and configuring NSX Edge from the NSX Manager, you can manually deploy NSX Edge either as
a VM in vCenter or a Bare Metal server.
Install an NSX Edge on ESX Using the vSphere GUI
You can use the vSphere Web Client or vSphere Client to interactively install an NSX Edge on ESX. You can also use
the new Edge deployment workflow to install an Edge. For more information about using the workflow, see Setting up
Network Connectivity. The same workflow is also available in vCenter. For more information, see Building Your Cloud
Infrastructure. Although you can manually deploy an edge using the following procedure, Broadcom recommends the
deployment of Edge through NSX Manager.
See NSX Edge network requirements in Installation Requirements.
1. Locate the NSX Edge node appliance OVA file on the Broadcom Support portal.
Either copy the download URL or download the OVA file onto your computer.
2. In the vSphere Client, select the host on which to install NSX Edge node appliance.
3. Right-click and select Deploy OVF template to start the installation wizard.
4. Enter the download OVA URL or navigate to the saved OVA file, and click Next.
5. Enter a name and location for the NSX Edge node , and click Next.
The name you type appears in the vCenter and vSphere inventory.
6. Select a compute resource for the NSX Edge node appliance, and click Next.
7. For optimal performance, reserve memory for the NSX Edge node.
Set the reservation to ensure that the NSX Edge node has sufficient memory to run efficiently. See NSX Edge VM
System Requirements.
8. Power on the appliance. Open the console of the NSX Edge node to track the boot process.
If the console window does not open, make sure that pop-ups are allowed.
Broadcom 3335

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
9. After the NSX Edge node starts, log in to the CLI with admin credentials.
Note:
After NSX Edge node starts, if you do not log in with admin credentials for the first time, the data plane service
does not automatically start on the NSX Edge node.
10.Run the (without VLAN) to verify that the IP address was applied as expected.
get interface eth0
nsx-edge-1> get interface eth0

Address: 192.168.110.37/24

...

1600 (instead of 1500) on the physical host switch for the data NIC.
11.Run the command to verify that the NSX Edge node is registered.
get managers
- 10.173.161.17 Connected (NSX-RPC)

- 10.173.160.204 Connected (NSX-RPC)*
The NSX Manager with * next to it is the active manager for the NSX Edge transport node VM.
If an NSX Edge node is not registered with the management plane, see Join NSX Edge with the Management Plane.
12.Verify that the NSX Edge node has the required connectivity.
If you enabled SSH, make sure that you can SSH to your NSX Edge node and verify the following:
• You can ping your NSX Edge node management interface.
• From the NSX Edge node, you can ping the node's default gateway.
• From the NSX Edge node, you can ping the hypervisor hosts that are either in the same network or a network
reachable through routing.
• From the NSX Edge node, you can ping the DNS server and NTP Server.
13.Troubleshoot connectivity problems.
Note:
If connectivity is not established, make sure the VM network adapter is in the proper network or VLAN.
By default, the NSX Edge node datapath claims all virtual machine NICs except the management NIC (the one that
has an IP address and a default route). If you incorrectly assigned a NIC as the management interface, follow these
steps to assign management IP address to the correct NIC.
a) Log in to the NSX Edge CLI and type the command.
stop service dataplane
b) (Static IP) Run the
set interface <interface-name> ip <x.x.x.x/24> gateway <x.x.x.x> plane mgmt
command.
c) (DHCP) Run the command.
set interface interface-name dhcp plane mgmt
d) Type the command.
start service dataplane
The datapath fp-ethX ports used for the VLAN uplink and the tunnel overlay are shown in the get interfaces and
get physical-port commands on the NSX Edge node.
Configure NSX Edge as a transport node. See Edit Transport Node Configuration.

Install NSX Edge on Bare Metal
Use PXE server to automate installation of NSX Edge on a bare metal server or use ISO file to install NSX Edge on a bare
metal server.
• Disable sub-NUMA clustering by editing the BIOS settings. NSX does not support sub-NUMA clustering. For more
details, see Knowledge Base article 320664: Enabling sub-NUMA clustering on a Bare Metal Edge may result in a
shortage of heap memory.
• Starting with NSX v3.1.3, on Bare Metal NSX Edge nodes, you do not need to disable hyperthreading. Hyperthreading
is automatically disabled.
The NSX Edge bare metal node is a dedicated physical server that runs a special version NSX Edge software. The bare
metal NSX Edge node requires a NIC supporting the Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK). VMware maintains a list of the
compatibility with various vendor NICs. See NSX Edge Bare Metal Requirements.
Broadcom 3340

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The NSX Edge nodes in the diagram are illustrated with a single N-VDS switch, configured with two datapath interfaces
and two dedicated NICs for high availability of management plane.
Bare Metal NSX Edge nodes can be configured with more than 2 datapath interfaces depending on the number of
NICs available on the server. Bare Metal NSX Edge nodes use pNICs as uplinks that directly connect to the top of rack
switches. To provide high availability for bare metal edge management, configure two pNICs on the server as an active/
standby Linux bond.
The CPUs on the edge are assigned as either datapath (DP) CPUs that provide routing and stateful services or services
CPUs that provide load balancing and VPN services.
When a bare metal Edge node is installed, a dedicated interface is retained for management. This configuration is called
out-of-band management. If redundancy is desired, two NICs can be used for management plane high availability. Bare
metal Edge also supports in-band management where management traffic can leverage an interface being used for
overlay or external (N-S) traffic as in the diagram.
For bare metal edge nodes, all the cores from the first node of a multi-NUMA node server will be assigned to NSX
datapath. If the bare metal has only one NUMA node, then 50% of the cores will be assigned for the NSX datapath.
Bare Metal NSX Edge nodes support a maximum of two NUMA nodes.
Broadcom 3341

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
VMware does not support the sub-NUMA clustering, which is a server hardware feature, on a Bare Metal NSX
Edge is not supported as it may result in a shortage of heap memory.
The sub-NUMA clustering functionality changes the socket of heap memory from two NUMA domains to four NUMA
domains. This change limits the size of heap memory allocated to each socket and causes a shortage of heap memory for
socket 0 that the datapath requires. You must disable the sub-NUMA functionality in the BIOS. Any changes made to the
BIOS will require a reboot.
To check if the sub-NUMA functionality is enabled, log in to the bare metal NSX Edge as root and run . The output is
lscpu
also captured in the support bundle. If there are more than two NUMA nodes, it implies that the sub-NUMA functionality is
enabled and it must be disabled and must be disabled via the BIOS.
Note:
1. When configuring LACP LAG bonds on Bare Metal NSX Edge nodes, datapath cores (backing NICs) should
belong to same NUMA node for load balancing to occur on both devices. If devices forming the bond span
multipe NUMA nodes, then bond only uses network device CPU that is local NUMA node (0) to transmit
packets. So, not all devices do not get used for balancing traffic that is sent out of the bond device.
In this case, failover still works as failover is exclusive of load balancing. If the Ethernet device attached to the
local NUMA node is down, then the bond sends traffic to the other device even though it is not NUMA local.
The load-balancing optimization does not impact failover functionality.
Run command to view the NUMA node associated with each datapath interface. To move nics
get dataplane
associated with datapath to single NUMA node, physical reconfiguration of the server is required via the BIOS.
Prepare a PXE Server for Bare Metal NSX Edge Installation
PXE is made up of several components: DHCP, HTTP, and TFTP. This procedure demonstrates how to set up a PXE
server on Ubuntu.
• A PXE server must be available in your deployment environment. The PXE server can be set up on any Linux
distribution.
• Verify that the preseeded configuration file has the parameters net.ifnames=0 and biosdevname=0 set after to
--
persist after reboot.
• See NSX Edge Bare Metal Requirements.
• See NSX Edge network requirements in NSX Edge Installation Requirements.
DHCP dynamically distributes IP settings to NSX components, such as NSX Edge. In a PXE environment, the DHCP
server allows NSX Edge to request and receive an IP address automatically.
TFTP is a file-transfer protocol. The TFTP server is always listening for PXE clients on the network. When it detects
any network PXE client asking for PXE services, it provides the NSX component ISO file and the installation settings
contained in a preseed file.
1. Optional: Use a kickstart file to set up a new TFTP or DHCP services on an Ubuntu server.
A kickstart file is a text file that contains CLI commands that you run on the appliance after the first boot.
Name the kickstart file based on the PXE server it is pointing to. For example:
nsxcli.install
The file must be copied to your Web server, for example at .
/var/www/html/nsx-edge/nsxcli.install
In the kickstart file, you can add CLI commands. For example, to configure the IP address of the management
interface:
stop service dataplane
set interface eth0 <ip-cidr-format> plane mgmt
start service dataplane
To change the admin user password:
set user admin password <new_password> old-password <old-password>
Broadcom 3342

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
If you specify a password in the preseed.cfg file, use the same password in the kickstart file. Otherwise, use the
default password, which is "default".
To join the NSX Edge with the management plane:
join management-plane <manager-ip> thumbprint <manager-thumbprint> username <manager-username> password
<manager password>
2. Create two interfaces, one for management and another for DHCP and TFTP services.
Make sure that the DHCP/TFTP interface is in the same subnet that the NSX Edge resides in.
For example, if the NSX Edge management interfaces are going to be in the 192.168.210.0/24 subnet, place eth1 in
that same subnet.
# The loopback network interface
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback
# PXE server's management interface
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
address 192.168.110.81
gateway 192.168.110.1
netmask 255.255.255.0
dns-nameservers 192.168.110.10
# PXE server's DHCP/TFTP interface
auto eth1
iface eth1 inet static
address 192.168.210.82
gateway 192.168.210.1
netmask 255.255.255.0
dns-nameservers 192.168.110.10
3. Install DHCP server software and configure required settings to set up the PXE server. For more details, see Linux
documentation.
4. Install the Apache server and TFTP and other components required to configure the PXE server.
5. Copy or download the NSX Edge installer ISO file to a temporary folder.
6. Mount the ISO file and copy the install components to the TFTP server and the Apache server.
sudo mount -o loop ~/nsx-edge.<build>.iso /mnt
cd /mnt

Install NSX Edge on bare metal using an ISO file. See Install Bare Metal NSX Edge Automatically Using ISO File.
Install Bare Metal NSX Edge Automatically Using ISO File
Use the automated installation of NSX Edge on the bare metal servers because it automatically configures the NSX Edge
node according to the hardware configuration and the most frequently used NSX Edge configuration. After the installation
is complete, configure the management interface of the nodes as out-of-band or as in-band and provide the final IP
configuration of the management interface statically or over DHCP.
• Both BIOS and UEFI boot modes are supported.
• See NSX Edge Bare Metal Requirements.
• If the bare metal servers for NSX Edge nodes have integrated SD card devices, disable those SD cards. For more
information, see Knowledge Base article 321176: Booting a Bare Metal server with an NSX Edge ISO fails with the
error: "Incorrect CD-ROM detected".
• To prepare a bare metal server as an NSX Edge node, ensure there is a minimum of 200 GB disk space.
For more details about the supported NICs, see Broadcom Compatibility Guide.
Broadcom 3344

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Locate and download the ISO file for NSX Edge for Bare Metal on the Broadcom Support portal.
2. Log in to the Integrated Lights-Out (ILO) interface of the bare metal server.
3. Click Launch in the virtual console preview.
4. Select Virtual Media > Connect Virtual Media.
Wait a few seconds for the virtual media to connect.
5. Select Virtual Media > Map CD/DVD and browse to the ISO file.
6. Select Next Boot > Virtual CD/DVD/ISO.
7. Select Power > Reset System (warm boot).
The installation duration depends on the bare metal environment.
8. Choose Automated installation.
There might be a pause of 10 seconds after you press Enter.
9. Select the applicable primary network interface. This is for the management network interface.
During power-on, the installer requests a network configuration. Select static IP settings. If the static IP is not available,
use DHCP.
By default, the root login password is vmware, and the admin login password is default.
Note:
During deployment, the installer automatically selects the largest disk to install NSX on the NSX Edge node.
10.There are three ways to configure a management interface.
• Untagged interface. This interface type creates an out-of-band management interface.
(Static)
set interface eth0 ip <CIDR> gateway <gateway-ip> plane mgmt
(DHCP)
set interface eth0 dhcp plane mgmt
• Tagged interface.
set interface eth0 vlan <vlan_ID> plane mgmt
(Static)
set interface eth0.<vlan_ID> ip <CIDR> gateway <gateway-ip> plane mgmt
(DHCP)
set interface eth0.<vlan_ID> dhcp plane mgmt
• In-band interface.
set interface mac <mac_address> vlan <vlan_ID> in-band plane mgmt
(Static)
set interface eth0.<vlan_ID> ip <CIDR> gateway <gateway-ip> plane mgmt
(DHCP)
set interface eth0.<vlan_ID> dhcp plane mgmt
• Tagged interface and In-band interface.
Any existing VLAN management interface must be cleared before creating a new one.
clear interface eth0.<vlan_ID>
• (Optional) Create a interface for management HA interface with multiple interfaces.
bond0

Intel QAT Support for IPSec VPN Bulk Cryptography
Beginning with the NSX 3.0 release, support for the Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) is provided on bare metal servers.
Intel QAT provides the hardware acceleration for various cryptography operations.
The QAT feature is enabled by default if the NSX Edge is deployed on a bare metal server with an Intel QuickAssist PCIe
card that is based on the installed C62x chipset (Intel QuickAssist Adapter 8960 or 8970). The single root I/O virtualization
(SR-IOV) interface must be enabled in the BIOS firmware.
To check the status of the QAT feature, enter the following command on the NSX Edge bare metal server CLI.
get dataplane qat
The possible responses you might receive are listed in the following table.
Status of QAT Feature Definition
QAT present, enabled, running The QAT feature is enabled and running.
QAT present, enabled, not running The QAT feature has been enabled, but the dataplane service
must be restarted for the status change to take effect.
QAT present, disabled, not running The QAT feature is disabled.
QAT present, disabled, running The QAT feature has been disabled, but the dataplane service
must be restarted for the status change to take effect.
QAT not present The bare metal server on which you ran the CLI command does
not have a QAT device installed.
QAT not supported in VM You ran the CLI command on a VM edge.
To disable or enable the use of an installed QAT device, use the following CLI commands. The expected responses are
also shown.
set dataplane qat disabled
QAT disabled. Please restart service dataplane to take effect.
set dataplane qat enabled
QAT enabled. Please restart service dataplane to take effect.
Important:
You must enter the command at the CLI prompt for the QAT feature status change
restart service dataplane
to take effect.

Remove NSX Edge Nodes from an Edge Cluster
Remove NSX Edge nodes with Tier-1 Gateways or Tier-0 Gateway configured with service router (SR), DHCP and
metadata proxy.
Before you remove NSX Edge nodes, relocate the gateway configurations to a new standby node:
• To remove Tier-0 gateway configurations on an NSX Edge node, you must manually relocate Tier-0 configurations
such as Tier-0 SR, DHCP and metadata proxy configurations to a standby NSX Edge node.
• To remove Tier-1 gateway configurations on an NSX Edge node, do the following in these scenarios:
– If Tier-1 SR, DHCP and metadata proxy configurations are auto allocated to the NSX Edge node, you can enable
the standby relocation functionality to relocate Tier-1 configurations to a new standby NSX Edge node. The
procedure describes how to use the standby relocation functionality to relocate the configurations to a new standby
node.
– If Tier-1 SR, DHCP and metadata proxy configurations are manually allocated to the NSX Edge node, you need to
manually relocate Tier-1 configurations to a new standby NSX Edge node.
1. From a browser, log in with admin privileges to an NSX Manager at https://<nsx-manager-ip-address> or https://<nsx-
manager-fqdn>.
2. On NSX Edge nodes configured with Tier-0 configurations, manually move configurations to some other NSX
Edgenode.
Note:
The standby relocation functionality does not relocate Tier-0 configurations such as Tier-0 SRs, DHCP and
metadata proxy configurations to a standby NSX Edge node.
a) Select NetworkingTier-0 Gateways.
b) To edit a Tier-0 Gateway, select the gateway, click vertical ellipses and click Edit.
c) Navigate to Interfaces section and click the External and Service Interfaces.
d) In the Set Interfaces window, edit the interface configured for NSX Edge node.
e) Remove the existing NSX Edge node associated with the interface and select a new NSX Edge node that is
configured with the same VLAN connectivity required for the interface and click Save.
The above procedure deletes Tier-0 SRs, DHCP and metadata proxy on Tier-0 Gateways of the existing NSX Edge
and moves them to the new NSX Edge node.
Broadcom 3349

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
f) Delete the NSX Edge node from the edge cluster.
3. On NSX Edge nodes that are auto allocated with Tier-1 SR, DHCP and metadata proxy configurations, follow these
steps to trigger the standby relocation functionality to relocate those configurations and remove the NSX Edge node
from the NSX Edge cluster:
a) (Optional) For faster failover, change the BFD timers for NSX Edge cluster by setting it to ms.
500
b) Apply the new NSX Edge cluster profile to the transport node profile. It ensures faster failover when the NSX Edge
node is powered off.
c) Select Networking > Tier1 Gateways.
d) To edit a Tier-1 Gateway, select the gateway, click vertical ellipses and click Edit.
e) In the Edit view, select the NSX Edge cluster and enable the Enable Standby Relocation field.
Important:
For standby relocation to function successfully, there must be an additional healthy NSX Edge node in the edge
cluster. During the process of removing an NSX Edge node, Tier-1, DHCP or metadata proxy configurations are
relocated from an existing NSX Edge to a new standby node.
f) Select System > Fabric > Profiles > Edge Cluster Profiles.
g) Select the edge cluster profile and click Edit.
h) Set Standby Relocation Threshold (mins) that is applied to the edge cluster. The default recommended value is
30 mins and the minimum value is 10 mins.
Note:
Only auto allocated Tier-1 SR, DHCP and metadata proxy configurations are relocated to a standby NSX Edge.
If the NSX Edge node to be removed contains any manually allocated configurations, such configurations will not
be relocated out from existing NSX Edge node to a stanby node. You need to manually change the allocation for
those Tier-1 configurations.
i) Power off the NSX Edge without taking down the node into maintenance mode. If the NSX Edge is running any
active service, then all such active service configurations will failover to another NSX Edge because of the HA
failover trigger when the node is powered off.
j) Wait for the duration of standby relocation threshold timeout. After the threshold limit is reached, all Tier-1 service
configurations that have standby relocation enabled will be removed from the edge node being powered-off and
relocated to some other NSX Edge in the cluster. There can be minor delays in standby relocation to perform the
relocation task.
k) After Tier-1 configurations are relocated to a standby node, remove the NSX Edge that was powered off from the
cluster. Select the Edge Cluster, click Edit and remove the NSX Edge node from the cluster anc click Save.
Relocate and Remove an NSX Edge Node from an NSX Edge Cluster
You can use the NSX relocate and remove API to relocate the service configurations of an NSX Edge node to another
standby NSX Edge node in the same NSX Edge cluster and then remove the Edge node from the Edge cluster.
To relocate and remove an Edge node from an Edge cluster, the following conditions are required:
• The Edge node must not have any manually allocated service configurations. Only auto allocated service
configurations can be relocated.
• To be available for relocation, standby Edge nodes must not be configured with Layer 2 bridging.
• The Edge cluster must have at least two healthy Edge nodes where the auto allocated service configurations can be
relocated to.
• For HA (high availability), the Edge cluster must have more than two Edge nodes that are possible for relocation.
The relocate and remove API relocates the following service configurations:
• Logical routers
• DHCP server
• Metadata proxy
• L2 forwarder

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Run the API command to get the value of the Edge node that you want to relocate and remove from
member_index
an Edge cluster:
GET https://<nsx-manager-IP>/policy/api/v1/edge-clusters/<edge-cluster-id>

"deployment_type": "VIRTUAL_MACHINE",
"members": [
{
"member_index": 11,
"transport_node_id": "21a19cbf-eaba-4a59-b18d-ff71fe5d76aa",
"display_name": "edgeVm1New"
},
{
"member_index": 13,

"display_name": "edgeVm2New"
},

}
],
The value is used to specify the Edge node to relocate and remove. Assume that you want to relocate
member_index
the service configurations for the Edge node named , then its value is .
edgeVm1New member_index 11
2. Enter the relocate and remove API command and the value of the Edge node to relocate and remove:
member_value
POST https://<nsx-manager-IP>/api/v1/edge-clusters/<edge-cluster-id>?action=relocate_and_remove
{
"member_index": 11
}
3. Run the API command.
The Edge node enters maintenance mode and its service configurations are transferred to one of the standby Edge
nodes in the cluster. After the service configurations are transferred, the Edge node is removed from the Edge cluster
and exits maintenance mode.
Note:
The API command will not work if:
• The Edge node has any manually allocated service configurations.
• The Edge cluster does not have at least two healthy standby Edge nodes.
CAUTION:
It is possible for the API command to give a success response, but in the background, the relocation operation
fails. If this scenario occurs, then an alarm with the Event Type of
Edge Cluster Member Relocate
is raised.
Failure
The recommended action for this scenario is to review the available capacity of the Edge cluster. If more capacity
is required, scale your Edge cluster and then retry the API command.
Enable or Disable AutoRefresh on Edge Nodes
Enable or Disable AutoRefresh on Edge nodes.
Starting with 3.2.4, NSX introduces an AutoRefresh flag that will override any mismatch between the state you desire
for an NSX Edge node and the state NSX realizes for that NSX Edge server. NSX will not generate mismatch alarms
Broadcom 3351

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
if desired state and realized state is different. Before NSX 3.2.4, NSX generated mismatch alarms when there was a
mismatch between desired and realized state.
If you are upgrading to NSX 3.2.4 or installing NSX 3.2.4, the AutoRefresh feature will be enabled by default.
To modify the AutoRefresh feature, run the following API.
PATCH https://{mp}/policy/api/v1/system-config
Sample Payload:
{
"keyValuePairs": [
{
"key": "auto_refresh_edge_transport_nodes",
"value": "true/false"
}
]
}
If you set the value to false, NSX will continue to generate mismatch alarms.
Note:
(NSX Edge nodes deployed from NSX Manager) If you change vSphere parameters from the vSphere Client UI,
the desired state will be overriden with the realized state after the next Periodic Refresh task.
If you edit an NSX Edge node from the NSX Edge UI page, mismatch alarm will be generated if there is a
mismatch between desired and realized state.
Setting up Network Connectivity
NSX provides a simplified workflow to set up network connectivity and perform network configuration. The workflow
improves the operational efficiency of VPC environments by providing a simple way to establish external connectivity and
installing Edge nodes and Edge clusters. This simplified workflow for setting up network connectivity is available in both
NSX and in vCenter and thus users have a uniform experience of performing network configurations from either of the
components.
To simplify the deployment process, the new workflow leverages many defaults settings that are recommended by
Broadcom, such as transport zones and uplink profile, that reduces the number of user inputs required to perform network
configuration. The workflow also provides a topology visualization that includes user inputs. Contextual visualization helps
users to understand the topology better through which they can avoid misconfiguration as they get a view of the entire set
up.
If you are using the workflow in a fresh installation, you will need to start with setting up a network connectivity,
Centralized or Distributed. You can choose based on the following information.
• Centralized Connectivity: Create a Centralized connection if you have an environment that requires full-scale NSX
networking services, such as DHCP, NAT, and Layer 3 services. It connects the Transit Gateway through a Tier-0
router which is provisioned from NSX. The Tier-0 is deployed on NSX Edge nodes and provides the interconnection
to the physical fabric. For more information about adding a Transit Gateway with centralized connection, see Add a
Transit Gateway with a Centralized Connection.
Centralized connectivity supports stateful services either at Tier-0 level or at the Transit Gateway level (NAT) and
supports dynamic routing, BGP/OSPF, with the physical fabric. The Centralized connectivity requires the setting up of
Edge nodes.
• Distributed Connectivity: Distributed Connection allows a distributed connection to the data-center fabric that requires a
minimal physical fabric configuration (only VLAN/IP) and without the need to deploy Edge nodes or configure dynamic
routing. The Distributed connectivity connects the Transit Gateway directly to a VLAN provisioned in the fabric. This
happens directly on the host, which implies that the VLAN must be available on the ESX (on physical uplinks used by
NSX vmkernel). For more information about adding a Transit Gateway with distributed connection, see Add a Transit
Gateway with a Distributed VLAN Connection.
Broadcom 3352

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In addition to on-demand networking and distributed routing, other services available when using distributed
connections are 1:1 NAT and distributed DHCP. Stateful services, such as NAT and load balancing, can be provisioned
to VPCs using a distributed connectivity by deploying a Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster. For more information
about creating a VNA, see Create a Virtual Network Appliance Cluster.
To use this connectivity setup workflow, you must ensure that the ESX cluster must have the ESX host with VDS uplinks
configured.
If you have upgraded to VCF 9.0, you can use this workflow to add or delete an edge from edge clusters created in the
previous version. Note that the delete option is available only when the Edge does not have any dependent objects.
Additionally, you can also use this workflow to set up a Tier-0 gateway for an edge cluster, reset edge passwords, and
set VPC external IP blocks. Note that to edit an Edge node, you will have to go to NSX Manager. Navigate to System >
Fabric > Edges.
Set up Centralized Connectivity with NSX Edge Clusters
VCF provides a simplified workflow to set up network configuration. The workflow is available in both vCenter and
NSX. For more information about setting the connectivity through vCenter, see Building Your Cloud Infrastructure. This
section describes how to use the workflow from NSX to configure a centralized connectivity along with NSX Edge cluster
deployment.
To use the workflow you must have a role of NSX administrator. Also, before you start using the workflow ensure that the
following requirements are met:
• Plan for NSX Edge TEP VLAN and IP allocation for TEPs. The same VLAN as the Host TEP can be reused. For more
information on creating IP pools for TEPs, see Create an IP Pool for Tunnel Endpoint IP Addresses.
• NSX Edges can be deployed on a host-group within a vSphere cluster or on a vSphere cluster. All hosts in the host-
group or the vSphere cluster must have identical access to management network, gateway uplinks, host and Edge
TEP networks. If you want to deploy edges on a prepared vSphere cluster, ensure that the following requirements are
met:
– The ESX cluster must have a Transport Node Profile (TNP) attached to it. For more information on applying a TNP,
see Prepare Cluster Hosts as Transport Nodes by Using TNP.
– The IP Address Type field should not be set to IPv6 in the Transport Node Profile that is applied to the cluster. Also
for IPv4 address type, IPv4 Assignment Type should not be set to Use VMKernel Adapter. You can check it from
System > Fabric > Hosts > Transport Node Profile in NSX Manager.
• If you plan to use the NSX Edge Host Affinity feature, ensure that you configure a host group to include a host where
the NSX Edge node should be pinned. Select the "Host Group Affinity" option for the host group to enable the NSX
Edge Host Affinity feature. The NSX Edge Host Affinity feature automatically enables the Best Effort Restart compute
policy for the assigned NSX Edge node. For more information about host pinning, see the KB article Failover pre-
checks are not performed when ESX is put into maintenance mode manually.
• NSX Edge node will make a 100% memory reservation. vSphere cluster/resource pool must have enough resources to
deploy at least two edge nodes.
• Management network for NSX Edge must have connectivity to NSX Manager.
• If you want to configure dynamic routing with BGP, ensure that you set up two BGP peers per NSX Edge node on ToR
switch with an interface IP, local ASN, and optional BGP password. For more information about configuring BGP, see
Configure an BGP Neighbors for a Tier-0 Gateway.
• Reserve a local ASN to use for the Tier-0 gateway. For more information about ASN, see BGP Autonomous System
Number (ASN) per Tier-0 VRF Gateway and per BGP Neighbor.
• If static routing is desired, it is recommended to configure HA VIP for active/standby Tier-O Gateway and use VIP as
the Next Hop IP on ToR switch. You can configure static routing after completing the network connectivity workflow.
• Configure DVPGs for the NSX Edge management. It is recommended that these DVPGs should be different from
DVPGs configured for the ESX management.
• Reserve external IP blocks for VPC connectivity. External IP blocks should not overlap with any other used CIDR
addresses.
• (Optional) Populate your managed DNS server with DNS entries for NSX Edge components.

Add an Edge Node to a Cluster
This section covers the details about adding an NSX Edge node when you are setting up centralized network connectivity
from Networking > VPC Connectivity > Transit Gateway in the NSX Manager. You can also use this information when
you are adding an NSX Edge node by clicking Add Edge in the Action column of an existing NSX Edge cluster displayed
on the Setup Network Connectivity page once the initial connectivity is set up.
Note that at the time of initial connectivity set up, you will need to add a minimum of two NSX Edge nodes. You can add
up to 10 NSX Edges to an NSX Edge cluster. While adding an NSX Edge, you also have the option to clone a previously
created NSX Edge and add it to the NSX Edge cluster. Cloning is recommended only when the cloned NSX Edge is part
of the same vSphere cluster with identical networks (edge management, pNIC mapping, VLAN for Edge TEP, host group
affinity).
The Add Edge button for an NSX Edge cluster is enabled only if the NSX Edge cluster is homogenous in terms of
configuration, which implies that all member NSX Edge nodes:
• Should have the same form factor
• Should be part of a common Overlay Transport Zone
• Should have the deployment type as Virtual Machine
• Should have a single edge switch
• Should have "nsx-edge-multiple-vteps-uplink-profile" uplink profile
Note that the simplified workflow uses many recommended default settings for edge creation, such as the system-defined
multi-TEP uplink profile.
To add an NSX Edge node, perform the following steps:
1. Click Add when you are adding an edge node from the Edge Cluster page in the Setup Network Connectivity
workflow or click Add Edge in the Action column of the cluster when you are adding the edge from the Edge Cluster
list.
Field Name Description
Edge Node Name (FQDN) Enter the name of the NSX Edge node.
Compute Manager Select the compute manager for the Edge node.
vSphere Cluster Select the vSphere cluster where the Edge is to be deployed.
Resource Pool Select the resource pool for the Edge node.
Broadcom 3355

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Field Name Description
Host Group Affinity If an NSX Edge is deployed in a non-homogeneous network, for example a multi-rack horizontal
vSphere cluster with L3 boundaries between the racks, vMotion cannot be used during the host
remediation as vMotion of the NSX Edge to another host in another rack can cause connectivity loss
with the top-of-rack switches.
By selecting the Host Group Affinity option, you can pin an NSX Edge to a host/host group and
prevent its vMotion when the host of this NSX Edge goes into the maintenance mode.
To pin an NSX Edge with a host, the NSX Edge is associated with a host or a host group using an
affinity rule and a Best Effort Restart (BER) policy is applied to the NSX Edge.
The BER policy runs validations and ensures that the NSX Edge powers off when its host enters
a maintenance mode. While shutting down an NSX Edge, a check is also made to find if any peer
NSX Edge is ready for a failover. If a peer Edge is available, a graceful failover is made to this peer
Edge and then the edge is powered off. Note that during the precheck if a peer Edge is not available
for a graceful failover, host upgrade will not proceed until precheck errors are resolved manually.
In case of a single host in a host group, the Edge stays powered off during the host's maintenance
mode and is powered on again when the host exits the maintenance mode. If a peer Edge is
available, it takes over the services. Once the host exits the maintenance mode, the Edge is
powered on upon the same host.
In case of multiple hosts in a group, after shutting down the Edge if a peer Edge is available it
takes over the services and if a compatible host is available the Edge is powered on upon it. If
due to affinity or availability constraints there's no other compatible host that can host the Edge,
the Edge will continue to stay powered off during host maintenance mode. Once the host exits the
maintenance mode, the Edge is powered on again on the same host.
For more information on host groups, see Failover pre-checks are not performed when ESX is put
into maintenance mode manually.
Host Group If you have selected the Host Group Affinity as Yes, then select a host group to which the Edge
needs to be pinned.
For more information about host groups, see the prerequisite section about host pinning.
Data Store Select a data store where the Edge node files are to be saved.

Set up Distributed Network Connectivity
NSX provides a simplified workflow to set up network connectivity and perform network configuration. This section
describes how to use the workflow from NSX to configure a distributed connectivity. The workflow is available in both NSX
and vCenter.
You must have a role of NSX administrator to use the workflow. Also, before you start using the workflow ensure that the
following requirements are met.
• Dedicated VLANs and subnets must be available for Distributed Transit Gateway connection to Top of Rack (ToR). The
same VLAN must be configured on all the ToR switches where the ESX hosts are connected which offers VPCs. All
the hosts running VPC workloads must have access to these VLANs.

• Reserve external IP blocks for VPC connectivity. External IP blocks must be the same as or a subset of dedicated
VLAN subnets.

Create a Virtual Network Appliance Cluster
A distributed connectivity allows you to set up a VPC network without edge nodes. However, it lacks the support for
stateful services such as NAT and load balancer that are available to VPCs using a centralized connectivity. To provision
NAT and load balancer services to VPCs using a distributed connectivity, you can deploy a Virtual Network Appliance
(VNA) cluster A VNA cluster is a group of Virtual Network Appliances (VNA), which are virtual machines, working
collaboratively to provide these stateful networking services.
You can create a VNA cluster by navigating to System > Fabric > VNA Clusters and clicking Add Cluster. A minimum of
one VNA is required to deploy a VNA cluster, but two VNAs are recommended for high-availability. Once you have created
a VNA cluster, you can specify it in a project to provision VPC services for a distributed connectivity.
You can also create a VNA cluster at the time of setting up a distributed network connectivity on Day 0 when no other
connectivity is set up by navigating to Networking > VPC Connectivity > Transit Gateways. Click Setup Network
Connectivity and choose Distributed VLAN Connection. Provide the required configuration. On the VPC Services
page, you can provide the VNA cluster details. For more information about setting up distributed connectivity, see Set up
Distributed Network Connectivity.
Note that with each VNA cluster that you create, the system creates an overlay segment with the default transport zone
to which the VNAs in the cluster get connected with. Use the API if you want to specify a different overlay transport zone
where the segment is to be created.

Virtual Private Cloud in NSX
VCF 9.0 and later provides a consistent networking consumption model that is based on Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs)
and Transit Gateways (TGW). This model is natively multi-tenant and can be used not only from NSX, but also from VCF
(from vCenter, VCF Automation, and monitored from VCF Operations). It aims to provide a standardized, simple, and
powerful Cloud networking experience not only to the network administrators but to all cloud users from VCF.
This cloud networking consumption is built using the following objects:
• External Connections: Defines outside connectivity for a Transit Gateway to the datacenter. An external connection
can be of the following types:
– Centralized
– Distributed
– Distributed VXLAN
• Transit Gateway (TGW): Gateway interconnecting VPCs and connecting to outside datacenter through external
connections.
• Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): On-demand logical networks connected together that can be either advertised (public
subnets) or exposed through networking services like External IPs or NAT. For simplicity, VPCs in VCF leverage three
profiles:
– VPC Connectivity Profile: Defines outside connectivity configuration for VPCs such as the Transit Gateway they are
connected to, the IP Blocks available for consumption, and if a default outbound NAT is configured
– VPC Service Profile: Defines the common configurations for services available in the VPC such as DHCP, DHCP
Relay, or different subnet profiles.
– VPC Security Profile: VPC Security profiles, which is the default only, activates on a Gateway Firewall for all VPCs
in the project. (Stateless Gateway Firewall is part of VCF entitlement. For Stateful Gateway Firewall, you require a
vDefend license.)
The following image provides an overview of the new simplified model.
Figure 415: Simplified VPC model
Broadcom 3360

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
Note: In addition to the recommended method to create VPCs leveraging the VPC Connectivity Profile, VPC
Service Profile and the connection through the Transit Gateways it is supported to have VPCs directly connected
to the Tier-0 in user-defined Projects. Those VPCs won’t benefit from multiple enhancements provided in VCF 9.0
and later, such as the ability to create Private - Transit Gateway networks for cross- VPC connections, and cannot
be configured from vCenter or from VCF Automation.
Overview of VPCs in the Default Project
VPCs are available by default in NSX within the Default project without the need to create tenants (NSX Project). This
provision allows administrators to benefit from VPC independently with VPCs in the default context being configurable
from vCenter as well.
Figure 416: VPCs in the Default project
Use a multi-tenant platform with the ability to partition networking and security configurations of a single NSX deployment
in multiple tenants (NSX Project). Those tenants allow multiple users to configure networking and security and configure
Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs). For more information about multi-tenancy, see NSX Projects.
To offer simple on-boarding, a system is created with a Transit Gateway, a default Connectivity Profile, and a default
Service Profile in the Default Project. These objects can be configured as part of the workload domain setup deployment
and allow consumption of VPCs from NSX or vCenter.
• VPCs created in the Default Project will use the system default overlay transport zone.
• VPCs created in the Default Project will connect to the default Transit Gateway. It is not possible to have VPCs directly
connected to Tier-0 in the Default Project.
• VPCs created from vCenter will leverage the default Connectivity and Service profiles but other profiles can be created
and used from NSX.
The Default project is the default context for the administrator and as such is not made for multi-tenancy like a user-
defined project. You cannot assign a user to the Default project (it is possible to assign a user to a specific set of VPCs
only). Additionally, the Default project can access resources such as external connections, external IP blocks, and Edge
nodes without having the need to define them as shared resources, which is unlike a user-defined project where you have
to define resources that can be shared.
Broadcom 3361

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VPC Consumption from vCenter
As mentioned earlier, in VCF 9.0 and later, VPC offers a VCF-wide consumption framework for networking that is simple
and also standardized. VPCs are now available in vCenter for consumption so that a vCenter administrator can have a
control over compute, networking, and storage from one interface and at the same time also have the visibility so that the
objects are consistent between users and interfaces.
In VCF 9.0 and later, VPCs are visible in the vCenter network inventory and the vCenter administrator can also consume
the VPCs, subnets, and external IPs for VPCs of the Default project from there. You can also allow or restrict VPC
management in vCenter by configuring the required setting in NSX by navigating to System > Fabric > Compute
Manager. For more information about VPC access, see Add a Compute Manager.
Figure 417: VPC Access Setting
External Connections
An external connection defines how a transit gateway (TGW) connects to networks outside of NSX and which services it
supports. Those connections are created from Default (/infra) and define the connection to the outside environment.
Select the connection type that supports the features you require for your network environment.
• Centralized connection: Connects the transit gateway through a tier-0 gateway provisioned from NSX. The tier-0
gateway is deployed on NSX Edge nodes and provides interconnection to the physical fabric. This connection type
requires you to deploy NSX Edge nodes and manage their lifecycle.
Centralized connections allow stateful services and dynamic routing with the physical fabric (BGP) at tier-0 level. They
also allow NAT configuration at the transit gateway level.
• Distributed VLAN connection: Connects the transit gateway directly to VLANs provisioned in the fabric. The
connection happens directly on the ESX hosts, which mandates the availability of VLANs on the ESX.
A distributed VLAN connection allows lightweight connectivity to the data-center fabric without needing to deploy
NSX Edge nodes or configure dynamic routing. Stateful services are supported with this connection type using Virtual
Network Appliances (VNAs).
• Distributed VXLAN connection: Connects the transit gateway directly to the EVPN-VXLAN network fabric to create
a unified network fabric that delivers consistent connectivity across virtual and physical domains. Virtual private clouds
(VPCs) can establish connectivity to tenant Virtual Routing and Forwarding instances (VRFs) within the EVPN-VXLAN
network fabric.
In version 9.1.1 and later, this connection type supports advanced networking services using Virtual Network
Appliances (VNAs).

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

or VXLAN)

In all cases, an external connection requires that you properly configure the objects to be connected to the transit
gateway. For a centralized connection, you must deploy a tier-0 gateway with NSX Edge nodes and properly configure
external routing. For dynamic routing such as BGP, select the Transit Gateway Static option in the route redistribution
settings to enable proper VPC subnet advertisement by upstream tier-0 BGP peers.
For a distributed VLAN connection, ensure that the VLANs used for outside connections are available to ESX hosts on the
same uplinks (physical NICs) as the NSX overlay vmkernel adapter. For a distributed VXLAN connection, ensure that the
ESX host (NSX overlay vmkernel adapter) has reachability to the TEP addresses of the EVPN gateway.
You can share an external connection with a custom project and attach it to a transit gateway.
