Managing API Clients and Tokens
VCF single sign-on API tokens can be generated either by a single sign-on user or under an API client, with lifespans
ranging from 30 to 180 days.
Within a VCF fleet, these two token types serve distinct purposes:
• API client tokens: Highly recommended and utilized for system-to-system integrations (such as automation pipelines,
backups, or monitoring setups). VCF single sign-on provides a token regeneration API to automate the lifecycle of API
client tokens, ensuring uninterrupted system integration and preventing production downtime.
• Single sign-on user tokens: Linked directly to individual single sign-on user accounts for manual, on-demand
operations. Since these tokens are not used for automated system integrations, their expiration does not affect
background infrastructure operations. When a token expires, single sign-on users can generate a new token through
the VCF component user interface.
API Client Tokens
As a VCF Operations admin user, you can create an API client and can generate an API token to make API calls on
behalf of an authenticated user without requiring repeated interactive login. You can also view and manage the token
lifecycle and security.
• To create an API client and generate an API token, see Create an API Client and Generate an API Token.
• To edit, delete, and regenerate an API token, see Edit, Delete, and Regenerate an API Token.
• To create an emergency API client, see Create an Emergency Access Client.
• To view and manage the token lifecycle and security, see Identity and Access Management Settings.
Single sign-on User Tokens
• To generate a single sign-on user token, see Generate a Single Sign-On User Token.
Create an API Client and Generate an API Token
Starting with VCF 9.1, you can log in to VCF Operations and create an API client and generate an API token.
Create an API Client and Assign User Roles
Procedure
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Identity & Access.
2. In the Identity & Access pane, click VCF SSO Overview.
3. In the VCF SSO Overview page, in the section that is called VCF SSO, click the identity broker that you have
configured for VCF Single Sign-On.
4. Click the API Access tab and then click the API Clients tab.
5. In the API Clients tab, click Create.
6. Enter a name for the client. The client ID is autopopulated.
7. Optionally enter a description for the API client.
8. Click Create API Client.
Broadcom 4159

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
9. In the Roles section, scope the role by selecting one of the options as the Scope, select a role from the drop-down
options, and enter the validity of the role.
10.Click Save.
Note:
Use the drop-down options from the vertical ellipsis to edit and delete API clients.
Generate an API Token
Procedure
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Identity & Access.
2. In the Identity & Access pane, click VCF SSO Overview and then from the page on the right, click the API Access
tab.
3. In the API Clients tab, against the API client for which you want to generate an API token, click the vertical ellipsis >
Generate API Token.
4. In the Generate API Token page, add the following information:
Option Description
API Token Name Enter a name for the token.
API Token TTL Select a valid time-to-live period for the API token.
API Token TTL refers to the duration for which an API token remains valid and usable before
it expires.
The default is 30 days.
Note:
The maximum value is limited by the value that you set as the API Token Expiry
under Fleet Settings > IAM Setting. For more information, see Identity and Access
Management Settings.
Access Token TTL Select a valid time-to-live for the access token.
Access Token TTL is the maximum period for which the token is valid, after which it expires
and can no longer be used to authenticate or authorize requests.
The default acess token TTL is 30 mins.
Note:
The maximum value is limited by the value that you set as the Access Token Expiry
under Fleet Settings > IAM Setting. For more information, see Identity and Access
Management Settings.
Description Enter a meaningful description.
5. Click Generate API Token. The new API token is generated.
6. Click Copy against the token and then click Continue.
Note:
If you are not going to use the API token immediately, store the API token. After you click Continue, you cannot
retrieve the API token that was generated.
Note:
Use the API client to automate API token generation instead of generating it manually.
If an API token is generated by a human user, there is a possibility that the API token might remain valid after the
JIT user is deleted from the identity provider, remaining valid until the API tokens time-to-live (TTL) expires. As a
VCF Operations admin, you can manage the API tokens of JIT users by navigating to the API Access tab, and
then selecting API Tokens. You can then filter the list by setting Token Type as User and Principal status as
INACTIVE.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For more information about setting the retention period for an expired API token and to view and manage API and
access token lifecycle and security, see Identity and Access Management Settings.

Create an Emergency Access Client
You can create emergency API clients for break-glass scenarios that provide high-privilege and long-lived access tokens
to critical systems when standard methods fail.
Procedure
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Identity & Access.
2. In the Identity & Access pane, click VCF SSO Overview.
3. In the VCF SSO Overview page, in the section that is called VCF SSO, click the identity broker that you have
configured for VCF Single Sign-On.
4. Click the API Access tab.
5. Click the Emergency Access tab, click Create.
6. Enter a name for the client. The client ID is autopopulated.
7. Optionally enter a description for the API client.
8. Click Create Emergency Client. The Emergency Access Token is created.
Note:
Emergency access clients are assigned the highest role with the largest scope. The role cannot be edited.
9. Click Copy against the token and then click Continue.
Note:
• The default TTL for an emergency access token is 180 days.
• You can create only one emergency access token at a time.
• Use the drop-down options from the vertical ellipsis to regenerate and delete the emergency access token.

Migrating VMware Identity Manager to Identity Broker
In VCF 9.1, you can migrate from VMware Identity Manager to identity broker. Read and understand the scope,
prerequisites, limitations, and steps before you attempt migration.
Scope of Migration
Broadcom 4163

• Users and Groups Sync Settings: The sync settings for existing identity providers in VMware Identity Manager and
identity broker are compared and displayed, but not migrated. You can view the comparison and can make changes to
the sync settings in the identity broker if necessary.
• Component Updates: If VCF Operations, VCF Automation Provider, or NSX currently use VMware Identity Manager
for single sign-on, their identity source type is updated to point to the new identity broker. The identity broker must be
fully set up before this update. The migration script will not remove the VMware Identity Manager identity provider from
the components.

• Validation: Comprehensive data integrity and compatibility checks are carried out.

Migration Limitations
Before you proceed with migration, review these critical limitations to ensure that migration aligns with your environment
and requirements.
1. If you have a single VMware Identity Manager instance connected to multiple components, such as, VCF Operations,
VCF Automation, or NSX , all the components will point to the new identity broker after migration if you carry out
component migration.
2. Identity provider configurations in VMware Identity Manager are not migrated automatically by the script and must be
configured manually in identity broker.
3. OAuth clients are not migrated automatically. You must manually regenerate the client and secret using identity broker
and configure accordingly.
4. VMware Identity Manager local accounts and local accounts with multifactor authentication are not supported in
identity broker.
5. Multifactor authentication with Active Directory is not supported in identity broker.
6. This script only exports single tenant data from VMware Identity Manager. If you have multiple tenants, each tenant
should be exported separately.
7. If you have multiple VMware Identity Manager instances under the same domain, for example, one VMware Identity
Manager instance with VCF Operations and another VMware Identity Manager instance with NSX, you must run the
export script twice and subsequently import it into the same identity broker instance.
8. Supported Components:
– VCF Operations. Migrates identity source types from VMware Identity Manager to identity broker for all configured
domains. The migration is asynchronous and processes all users/groups that match between VMware Identity
Manager and identity broker.
– NSX: Updates NSX user/groups type from VMware Identity Manager to identity broker identity source (OIDC).
The migration filters users/groups based on the domains configured by the identity broker (if VCF Operations
credentials are provided), or migrates all VMware Identity Manager users/groups (with user confirmation if
VCF_OPS credentials are not provided).
Note:
Migration is not supported for Global Manager NSX.
– VCF Automation: Imports all identity broker users and groups to VCF Automation. Each imported user/group is
assigned the role (mandatory in VCF Automation). You can optionally choose to
Defer to Identity Provider
also assign the role to all imported users/groups during the migration process. Previous

roles will not be migrated.

Migration is supported exclusively for the VCF Automation Provider Organization. VCF Automation tenant
organizations are not supported.

Managing Certificates in VMware Cloud Foundation
Manage certificates for VCF components according to industry standards and the requirements of your organization. You
use VCF Operations to view and manage the certificates for all components.
For additional information on certificate management design, see Certificate Management.
Access to all management component interfaces must be carried over a Secure Socket Layer (SSL) connection. During
deployment, each component is assigned a certificate from a default signing Certificate Authority (VMware Certificate
Authority CA).
Certificate Categories in VCF
In a VCF environment, certificates fall into three categories based on how they are managed. The categories determine
whether VCF Operations provides full lifecycle management, monitoring and alerting, or no management or monitoring
capabilities.
Certificate Category Description
User-managed User-managed certificates are certificates that users can fully
manage through VCF Operations. VCF Operations provides
full lifecycle management for these certificates. Users can view,
monitor, generate certificate signing requests (CSRs), import,
replace, and enable automatic renewal for these certificates.
Externally managed Externally managed certificates are certificates that VCF
Operations can view and monitor but cannot manage. The
individual components own the management of these certificates.
Users must replace or renew these certificates through the
component's own UI, API, or CLI. VCF Operations provides
visibility into the certificate state and sends expiry alerts so that
users can take action before the certificate expires. Certificate
status for these certificates is available through the VCF
Operations API.
Broadcom 4167

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Certificate Category Description
System-managed System-managed certificates are internal component certificates
that are automatically managed by the individual components.
The components auto-renew these certificates during routine
operations such as upgrades. VCF Operations does not provide
a view or monitoring interface for these certificates, and certificate
status is not available through the VCF Operations API. When
unrecoverable issues occur, the component triggers alerts directly
in VCF Operations with a link to a Knowledge Base (KB) article for
remediation guidance.
VCF Operations provides different levels of management and monitoring depending on the certificate category.
Certificate Category View Monitor Manage
User-managed Yes Yes Yes, full lifecycle
Externally managed Yes Yes, expiry alerts No
No, alerts for unrecoverable
System-managed No No
issues only
Certificate Management Capabilities in VCF Operations
Use VCF Operations to:
• View certificates and certificate alerts.
• Enable automatic renewal of certificates.
• Configure a certificate authority (Microsoft CA and OpenSSL CA).
• Generate certificate signing requests (CSRs).
• Import certificates.
• Replace certificates with a configured CA-signed certificate, an external CA-signed certificate, or a VMCA-signed
certificate.
• Monitor certificate expiry for system-managed certificates.
Starting with VCF Operations 9.1, you can generate certificate signing requests, renew, import, and replace multiple
certificates simultaneously.
User-managed certificates are certificates that a user can replace with third-party CA-signed certificates or customize with
VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA). Users are expected to manage the lifecycle of these certificates, including renewal,
import, and replacement. VCF Operations cannot auto-renew user-managed certificates that are signed by a third-party
CA.
System-managed certificates are certificates that are managed by the component or system. Usually, no API, CLI, or UI is
available for customers to manage these certificates directly. The auto-renewal of system-managed certificates is handled
by the individual components. VCF Operations monitors these certificates for expiry and raises alerts when auto-renewal
fails.
Certificate Operations by Certificate Authority Type
The certificate operations available in VCF Operations depend on whether the certificate is signed by a configured CA or
an external CA.
A configured CA is a certificate authority that you configure in VCF Operations. VCF Operations supports the following
configured CA types:
• VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA)
• Microsoft Certificate Authority (MSCA)
• OpenSSL Certificate Authority
Before you can replace a certificate with a CA-signed certificate or activate auto-renewal for Microsoft Certificate Authority
or OpenSSL certificates, you must configure a Certificate Authority (CA). VCF supports automatic renewal for all VCF

Operations managed TLS certificates that are signed by VMware Certificate Authority CA, Microsoft CA, or OpenSSL CA
and support non-disruptive certificate updates.
Self-signed certificates and certificates signed by an external CA cannot be renewed from VCF Operations. You perform a
3-step manual replace (generate CSR, import the signed certificate, and replace).
Starting with VCF Operations 9.1.1, VCF Operations detects and displays component self-signed CAs and self-signed
CA certificates as self-signed in the VCF Operations UI. In VCF Operations 9.1, these certificates are categorized as
external CA certificates. Self-signed certificates do not support manual renew or automatic renew from VCF Operations.
Component certificates managed by VCF Operations cannot be self-signed. If existing component certificates are self-
signed or issued by a private internal CA, replace them through VCF Operations using VMCA, Microsoft CA, OpenSSL
CA, or an external CA.

Certificate Signing Requirements
VCF Operations supports the following certificate signing algorithms and key sizes:
• RSA with 2048, 3072, and 4096-bit key sizes.
Component certificates that are managed by VCF Operations must be signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) and
cannot be self-signed. If existing component certificates are self-signed or issued by a private internal CA, replace them
through VCF Operations using VMCA (default), Microsoft CA, OpenSSL CA, or a third-party CA.
Subject Alternative Name Requirements
VCF 9.1 enforces strict certificate validation and requires an FQDN for the VCF component in the Subject Alternative
Name (SAN) field. If a certificate does not include the FQDN in the SAN field, the automated inventory migration and
registration into VCF management services fails during the VCF 9.1 upgrade process. Optionallty, the SAN field can also
contain the IP of the component.
When you generate a certificate signing request (CSR) or import a certificate through VCF Operations, the SAN field must
contain the FQDN of the component. Optionally, the SAN field can also contain the IP of the component.
VCF Operations performs TLS hostname verification, as defined in RFC 6125, when it connects to a component over
HTTPS. The hostname verification matches the component FQDN against the DNS SAN entries in the certificate. If
the certificate does not include the FQDN as a DNS SAN entry, the hostname match fails and VCF Operations cannot
establish a connection to the component. A certificate that contains only an IP address in the SAN field does not satisfy
the hostname verification requirement.
VCF Operations supports the following SAN entry types:
• FQDNs — fully qualified, dotted domain names ( )
fqdn.domain.org
• IP addresses
Dot-less shortnames in the SAN field are not supported. A dot-less shortname is a bare hostname label without a domain
suffix. The SAN validation requires at least one dot in each SAN entry. If a dot-less shortname is included alongside an
FQDN or an IP address, the entire CSR generation fails.
Some VCF components, such as vSphere Supervisor, can be deployed using only an IP address and might not have an
FQDN assigned. You can use one of the following in the Subject Alternative Name field:
• A domain-structured FQDN string, for example, or
supervisor.local component.internal
• A Punycode-encoded label
• The string
localhost
Use a value that your issuing Certificate Authority (CA) accepts.
Configure a Certificate Authority for VMware Cloud Foundation
Before you can replace a certificate with a CA-configured certificate or activate auto-renewal for Microsoft Certificate
Authority or OpenSSL certificates, you must configure a Certificate Authority (CA).
For configuring a Microsoft CA:
• Prepare the Microsoft Certificate Authority. See Prepare Your Microsoft Certificate Authority to Allow VMware Cloud
Foundation to Manage Certificates.
• Verify connectivity between VCF Operations and the Microsoft Certificate Authority Server. See VMware Ports and
Protocols.
VCF Operations supports the following configured CA types:
• VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA)
• Microsoft Certificate Authority (MSCA)
• OpenSSL Certificate Authority
Broadcom 4170

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF supports automatic renewal of Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates for components with certificates that are
signed by VMware Certificate Authority CA, Microsoft CA, or Open SSL CA and support non-disruptive certificate updates.
If existing component certificates are self-signed or issued by a private internal CA, replace them through VCF Operations
using VMCA, Microsoft CA, OpenSSL CA, or a third-party CA. Certificates signed by an external CA and self-signed
certificates cannot be renewed from VCF Operations. For these certificates, you perform a 3-step manual replace:
generate a certificate signing request (CSR), import the signed certificate, and replace.
VMCA is the default signing CA for VCF. During deployment, each component receives a VMCA-signed certificate. You
can replace the default VMCA-signed certificates with certificates signed by Microsoft CA or OpenSSL CA.
Microsoft Certificate Authority
Microsoft Certificate Authority (MSCA) is an enterprise CA that runs on Windows Server with Active Directory Certificate
Services. VCF Operations connects to MSCA through a web enrollment interface to request and sign certificates
automatically. MSCA is suitable for enterprise environments with existing Microsoft PKI infrastructure.
Before configuring MSCA in VCF Operations, you must prepare the Microsoft Certificate Authority server by installing the
required roles, configuring basic authentication, creating a certificate template, and assigning certificate management
privileges to a service account. For more information, see Prepare Your Microsoft Certificate Authority to Allow VMware
Cloud Foundation to Manage Certificates.
With VCF Operations 9.1 and later, VCF Operations can request and sign certificates automatically if the Certificate
Authority role and the Certificate Authority Web Enrollment role are installed on different machines. In earlier versions,
both roles must be installed on the same server.
OpenSSL Certificate Authority
OpenSSL Certificate Authority is a certificate service hosted within VCF Operations. VCF Operations generates and
manages the OpenSSL CA root certificate internally, so unlike Microsoft CA, OpenSSL CA does not require external
infrastructure or preparation steps. OpenSSL CA is suitable for testing or development environments where an external
PKI infrastructure is not available.
OpenSSL CA functions independently and cannot be chained into an existing external CA hierarchy. To integrate with an
enterprise PKI infrastructure, use Microsoft CA or a third-party CA instead.
When you configure OpenSSL CA, VCF Operations generates a self-signed root CA certificate using the organization
details you provide.

Set Up Automatic Renewal of Certificates in VMware Cloud Foundation
You can activate automatic renewal of certificates for VCF management components or a VCF instance. Automatic
renewal uses the configured Certificate Authority to renew the certificate for each component.
• If you are using Microsoft CA or OpenSSL root certificates for auto-renewal, configure a Certificate Authority before
activating auto-renewal. See Configure a Certificate Authority for VMware Cloud Foundation .
• Verify that the certificates you want to auto-renew are signed by VMCA, Microsoft CA, or OpenSSL CA. VCF
Operations cannot auto-renew certificates signed by an external CA.
• Verify that the certificates are not root or intermediate certificates. You cannot auto-renew root or intermediate
certificates.
VCF supports automatic renewal of Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates for components with certificates that are
signed by VMware Certificate Authority, Microsoft CA, or Open SSL CA and support non-disruptive certificate updates.
You configure automatic renewal separately for VCF management components and VCF Instance components.
Automatic renewal happens 60 days before a certificate expires.
You must manually renew a certificate before turning on auto-renewal if that certificate is due to expire in 60 days or less.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet management > Certificates.
4. On the Certificates page, select VCF Management or expand VCF Instances, and select a VCF Instance.
You can enable or disable automatic renewal of certificates for VCF management components, VCF Instances, VCF
domains, and standalone vCenter instances.
5. Click the Activate Auto-renewal toggle to turn on automatic renewal of certificates.
6. In the Activate Auto-renewal dialog box, review the information and click Confirm.
Manually Renew Certificates in VMware Cloud Foundation
You can manually renew Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates for components that have certificates signed by
VMware Certificate Authority CA, Microsoft CA, or Open SSL CA.
• If you are using Microsoft CA or OpenSSL certificates to manually renew certificates, configure a Certificate Authority.
See Configure a Certificate Authority for VMware Cloud Foundation .
• You can renew multiple certificates simultaneously.
• You cannot renew root or intermediate certificates.
• You cannot renew self-signed certificates.

Tool. See Broadcom knowledge base article 445742.

You can manually renew certificates for VCF management components, VCF Instances, VCF domains, and
standalone vCenter instances.

Generate Certificate Signing Requests in VMware Cloud Foundation
Use VCF Operations UI to generate a certificate signing request (CSR) for a VCF component to replace the TLS
certificate with a CA-signed certificate.
You can generate certificate signing requests for a single or multiple VCF components in VCF Operations simultaneously.
When generating a CSR, the public key and Subject Alternative Names (SANs) are embedded in the CSR, while the
corresponding private key is retained in the VCF Operations keystore. When the CA-signed certificate is imported in VCF
Operations, the certificate is validated with the stored private key.

Reestablish Endpoint Connectivity in VCF Operations
When a VCF Operations adapter instance stops collecting data, resulting in blank reports and empty dashboard widgets,
this indicates a loss of connectivity between the configured endpoint and VCF Operations. To reestablish connectivity,
check the validity of the trusted certificate for the adapter and renew the certificate.
An endpoint certificate can become invalid due to:
• Trusted certificate expiration. See Managing VCF Operations Certificates for vSphere Foundation.
• Misconfigured account credentials. See Configuring Credentials in Integrations.
To correct the problem, perform the following steps to renew the endpoint certificate and delete the invalid certificate.
1. Check for trusted certificates that have expired.
a) Log in to the VCF Operations interface at as a user assigned the
https://<vcf_operations_fqdn>
Administrator role.
b) Under Operate > Administration > Control Panel, click Trusted Certificates.
c) In the table that appears, click to sort on the Expires column and identify the certificates that have expired.
For any certificate that has expired, hover over entries in the row and record the following information for that
certificate:
• Name of the certificate thumbprint.
Broadcom 4181

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Endpoint Issued to.
• Expiration date.
• Certificate type: ADAPTER_INSTANCE
2. To renew and delete an expired certificate, click the vertical ellipsis ( ) menu for the certificate and select Delete.
If a confirmation window appears with multiple objects that trust the certificate listed, that indicates that multiple
adapter instances are using the same certificate. Deleting the certificate can cause the other instances to lose their
connections, so click No. Then validate credentials on the adapter instances to import a new certificate before deleting
the expired certificate.
• For an ADAPTER_INSTANCE certificate type:
1. Navigate to Operate > Administration > Integrations.
2. For each Account instance that is correlated to the information collected for the expired certificate, click the
vertical ellipsis menu and select Edit.
3. On the Account Information page that appears, click Validate Connection to validate credentials.
4. If prompted to import a new certificate, click OK and Save.
5. Return to Operate > Administration > Control Panel, click Trusted Certificates, and then delete the
certificate.
Custom VCF Operations Certificates
For secure VCF Operations operation, you might need to perform maintenance on authentication certificates.
Authentication certificates are for a secure machine-to-machine communication within VCF Operations itself or between
VCF Operations and other systems.
By default, VCF Operations includes its own authentication certificates. The default certificates cause the browser to
display a warning when you connect to the VCF Operations user interface.
Your site security policies might require that you use another certificate, or you might want to avoid the warnings caused
by the default certificates. In either case, VCF Operations supports the use of your own custom certificate. You can upload
your custom certificate during the initial primary node configuration or later.
Custom VCF Operations Web Certificate Requirements
A certificate used with VCF Operations must conform to certain requirements. Using a custom certificate is optional and
does not affect VCF Operations features.
Requirements for Custom Certificates
Custom VCF Operations certificates must meet the following requirements.
• The certificate file must include the terminal (leaf) server certificate, a private key, and all issuing certificates if the
certificate is signed by a chain of other certificates.
• In the file, the leaf certificate must be first in the order of certificates. After the leaf certificate, the order does not matter.
• In the file, all certificates and the private key must be in PEM format. VCF Operations does not support certificates in
PFX, PKCS12, PKCS7, or other formats.
• In the file, all certificates and the private key must be PEM-encoded. VCF Operations does not support DER-encoded
certificates or private keys.
PEM-encoding is base-64 ASCII and contains legible BEGIN and END markers, while DER is a binary format. Also,
file extension might not match encoding. For example, a generic extension might be used with PEM or DER. To
.cer
verify encoding format, examine a certificate file using a text editor.
• The file extension must be .
.pem
• The private key must be generated by the RSA or DSA algorithm.
• The private key can be encrypted by a pass phrase. The generated certificate can be uploaded using the primary node
configuration wizard or the administration interface.
• The REST API in this VCF Operations release supports private keys that are encrypted by a pass phrase.
Broadcom 4182

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• The VCF Operations certificate must have IPs and Hostnames (wildcard certificates are supported) in the Subject
Alternative Name (SAN) extension.
For example, Subject Alternative Name comprises of the DNS Name: localhost and the IP Address: 127.0.0.1.
• The VCF Operations Web server on all nodes have the same certificate file, so it must be valid for all nodes. One way
to make the certificate valid for multiple addresses is with multiple Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries.
• SHA1 certificates create browser compatibility issues. Therefore, ensure that all certificates that are created and being
uploaded to VCF Operations are signed using SHA2 or newer.
• The VCF Operations supports custom security certificates with key length up to 8192 bits. An error is displayed when
you try to upload a security certificate generated with a stronger key length beyond 8192 bits.
Note:
Fill the certificate extension fields using the UTF-8 encoding.
If VCF Operations fails to accept and apply Custom CA Certificate. For more information, see the following KB article
2046591.
Configure a Custom Web Certificate
You can use OpenSSL to configure an authentication certificate for use with VCF Operations. You must first generate a
Certificate PEM for VCF Operations, then install the Certificate PEM in VCF Operations. The certificates applied through
the VCF Operations Admin UI will be used only for securely connecting and serving the user interfaces to (external)
clients. We do not update the SSL certificates used for establishing a secure connection from VCF Operations to other
services like VMware Identity Manager, vCenter, and Log management.
Take your cluster offline before uploading the custom web certificate.
Note:
If you are using VCF Operations 9.0 or later, update your certificates from the Fleet Management > Certificates
page.
1. Generate a Certificate PEM file for use with VCF Operations.
1. Generate a key pair by running this command:
openssl genrsa -out key_filename.key 2048
2. Use the key to generate a certificate signing request by running this command:
openssl req -new -key key_filename.key -out certificate_request.csr
3. Submit the CSR file to your Certificate Authority (CA) to obtain a signed certificate.
4. From your Certificate Authority, download the certificate and the complete issuing chain (one or more certificates).
Download them in Base64 format.
5. Enter the command to create a single PEM file containing all certificates and the private key. In this step, the
example certificate is server_cert.cer and the issuing chain is cacerts.cer.
Note:
The order of CA's certs in the .PEM file: Cert, Private Key, Intermediate Cert and then Root Cert.
cat server_cert.cer key_filename.key cacerts.cer > multi_part.pem
In Windows replace cat with type.
The finished PEM file should look similar to the following example, where the number of CERTIFICATE sections
depends on the length of the issuing chain:
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
(Your Primary SSL certificate: your_domain_name.crt)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
(Your Private Key: your_domain_name.key)
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
(Your Intermediate certificate: DigiCertCA.crt)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
Broadcom 4183

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
(Your Root certificate: TrustedRoot.crt)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
2. Install a PEM in VCF Operations.
1. In a Web browser, navigate to the VCF Operations administration interface.
https://vrops-node-FQDN-or-ip-address/admin
2. Log in with the admin user name and password.
3. At the upper right, click the yellow SSL Certificate icon.
4. In the SSL Certificate window, click Install New Certificate.
5. Click Browse for certificate.
6. Locate the certificate .pem file, and click Open to load the file in the Certificate Information text box. The
certificate file must contain a valid private key and a valid certificate chain.
7. Click Install.

Private keys can appear in different formats but are enclosed with clear BEGIN and END markers.
Valid PEM sections begin with one of the following markers.
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
Encrypted private keys begin with the following marker.
-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----

Add a Custom Web Certificate to VCF Operations
If you did not add your own SSL/TLS certificate when configuring the VCF Operations primary node, you can still add a
certificate after VCF Operations is installed.
• Create and configure the primary node.
• Verify that your certificate file meets the requirements for VCF Operations .
1. In a Web browser, navigate to the VCF Operations administration interface at https://node-FQDN-or-ip-address/
admin.
2. Log in with the admin user name and password.
3. At the upper right, click the SSL certificate icon.
4. In the certificate window, click Install New Certificate.
5. Click Browse for certificate.
6. Locate the certificate file, and click Open to load the file in the Certificate Information text box.
.pem
7. Click Install.
Managing Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
Manage passwords in your VCF fleet according to industry standards and the requirements of your organization. You can
use VCF Operations to manage the passwords for VCF components, view password alerts for managed accounts, create,
apply, and detach password policies to a VCF fleet or VCF instances.
Managing Passwords
VCF Operations does not store a copy of an account password in a local vault. This offers a robust approach to managing
passwords - changing an account password where the account resides does not affect the ability of VCF Operations to
update that password (on both where the account resides and where the account is used). Using VCF Operations to
Broadcom 4186

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
update passwords is the recommended way to manage passwords in your environment. Use the VCF Operations UI and
API to:
• Update passwords.
• Create, assign, and detach password policies.
• View password alerts and information about the components whose passwords are managed by VMware Cloud
Foundation.
• View the last password update date for managed accounts.
With VCF Operations 9.1, you can manage passwords for the VCF components for VCF version 5.2 and later. You can
also manage passwords for standalone vCenter instances and managed ESX hosts with version 8.0 Update 3 and later.
For additional information on account and password management, see Account Management Design.
You can also manage passwords by using SDDC Manager. VCF Operations is the preferred method for managing
password in VCF. Use SDDC Manager to manage local or application account passwords in case your environment
requires it. See Using SDDC Manager to Manage Passwords.
Password Policies
Starting with VCF 9.1, you can manage account passwords settings across VCF components by using password policies.
A password policy defines password length, password complexity, password expiration, account lockout, password
change interval, and password history.
You create password policies in VCF Operations. You can then assign the password policy to the entire VCF fleet, the
VCF management components, or separate VCF Instances. Every VCF fleet object can have only one active password
policy that applies. An instance-level password or management component level policy takes precedence over a fleet-
level policy when both are assigned.
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, if you remove an instance-level policy, the instance falls back to the fleet policy if one is
configured.
VCF Operations periodically checks (every 6 hours) if VCF components are compliant with their assigned password
policy. If components are not compliant (i.e. the password settings differ from the assigned password policy), you can use
VCF Operations to remediate the password settings of the respective component to the assigned password policy.
Password expiration and account lockout attributes are applied immediately when the password policy is applied to a VCF
component. The password expiration is calculated based on the last password update. If your password policy specifies
an N-day password expiration interval, if the password update occurred N+1 or more days ago, the password expires
when the policy is applied. To avoid password expiries and account lockouts, when applying a password policy, ensure
that all passwords have their last update within the new password policy expiration interval.
By default, password policy attributes (such as password expiration and account lockout) are not
enforced for the vCenter account. You can use the vCenter API
administrator@vsphere.local
to enable password policy for the
com.vmware.identity.admin.administrator.PasswordPolicy
account.
administrator@vsphere.local
Note:
Password policy tasks use the Salt master and Salt RaaS components. Password policy operations might fail if
they are started right after VCF management services deployment completes. After deployment, the Salt RaaS
component requires approximately 30 minutes to establish connections to all managed nodes.
Accounts in VMware Cloud Foundation
VMware Cloud Foundation comprises a number of local (OS), application, and service accounts.
Broadcom 4187

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Account Types in VCF
Account Type Intended Use
Local (OS) accounts Local or OS accounts are provisioned directly in the operating
system of the virtual appliance and are primarily intended to
facilitate secure shell (SSH) access to that appliance.
Application accounts Application accounts are provisioned for interactive logins and
have access to the application's UI and API.
Some VCF components use application accounts (for example,
the vCenter Single Sign-On account administrator@vsphe
re.local) for inter-component communication by default.
Service accounts Service accounts are system-managed and provisioned for inter-
component communication and use automated methods for
password management.

Service Accounts in VCF
Service accounts are used for inter-component communication and are managed according to the specific methods
outlined in the table.
Service accounts generated and utilized internally by VCF components must not be rotated, changed, or managed by
external Privileged Access Management (PAM) tools. Modifying or forcing password rotation on these internal service
accounts outside of VCF Operations or SDDC Manager workflows might break critical internal product dependencies,
resulting in loss of inter-component communications, loss of lifecycle management capabilities, and potential environment
Broadcom 4192

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
outages. Password rotation for supported components must always be orchestrated natively through VCF Operations or
SDDC Manager.

Password Policies in VMware Cloud Foundation

application and local (OS) accounts for VCF components.

Non-expiring Accounts
Password expiration and account lockout policies are not enforced on non-expiring accounts by default. This ensures that
upgrade or patching to VCF 9.1.1 does not distrupt the oerations of your SDDC. Of you require strict compliance, you can
enforce password expiration and account lockout policies on specific non-expiring account by using the VCF Operations
API in 9.1.1.
Account Lockout Behavior
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, when an account is locked due to a number of failed login attempts, the following behavior
applies:
Broadcom 4196

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• An alert is generated in VCF Operations.
• You can update the password for a locked account from VCF Operations.
• Password update does not unlock the account. The account follows the lockout duration before unlocking, irrespective
of the success of the password update operation.
• An expired account supports the update password operation from VCF Operations.
Create a Password Policy for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
Use VCF Operations to create a password policy that defines password complexity, history, expiration, and lockout
requirements for managed accounts.
• VCF Operations is version 9.1 or later.
• VCF management domain components are at version 9.1 or later.
• VCF services runtime is deployed in the management domain.
9.1 Procedure 1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the top navigation bar, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet management > Fleet settings.
4. On the Fleet settings page, click Password policy.
5. On the Password policy page, click Create pocliy.
6. On the Create new policy page, configure the password policy settings and click Save.
9.1.1 Procedure 1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the top navigation, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, click Passwords.
4. On the Overview page, click thePassword Policy tab.
5. Click Create Policy.
6. On the Create New Policy page, configure the password settings and click Create.
The password policy is created and appears in the password policy list. You can now apply the policy to the VCF fleet,
VCF management components, or individual VCF Instances.
Apply a Password Policy for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
You can assign a password policy to the entire VCF fleet, the VCF management components, or separate VCF Instances.
Every VCF fleet object can have one active password policy applied. You can assign a password policy on an instance
level even if a fleet policy is already assigned. The instance-level policy takes precedence over the fleet-levet policy.
• VCF Operations is version 9.1 or later.
• VCF management domain components are at version 9.1 or later.
• VCF services runtime is deployed in the management domain.
Password expiration and account lockout attributes are applied immediately when the password policy is applied to a VCF
component. The password expiration is calculated based on the last password update. If your password policy specifies
an N-day password expiration interval and the last password update occurred N+1 or more days ago, the password
expires when the policy is applied. To avoid password expiries and account lockouts, when applying a password policy,
ensure that all passwords have their last update within the new password policy expiration interval.
In VCF 9.1, VCF Automation does not support password policies. With VCF 9.1.1 and later, VCF Automation supports
password policies.
9.1 Procedure In VCF 9.1, assigning a policy to a VCF component does not change passwords or password settings
configured in that component. After you assign the password policy, you run a compliance check and if the
VCF component is not compliant (the password settings on the component differ from the assigned policy),
you can apply the password policy to that VCF component by running the remediation workflow.
The compliance check runs automatically every six hours. You can run the compliance check manually.
It might take up to 30 minutes for the check to complete, avoid running multiple compliance checks
simultaneously.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
Broadcom 4197

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. On the top navigation bar, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet management > Fleet settings.
4. On the Fleet settings page, click Password policy.
5. Assign a password policy to your VCF fleet.
a. In the Password Policies section, select the password policy to assign.
b. From the ellipsis drop-down menu, select Assign Policy to Fleet.
c. On the Assign Policy to Fleet dialog box, click Proceed.
6. Assign a password policy to a VCF Instance or your management components.
a. In the Password Policies section, select the password policy to assign.
b. From the ellipsis drop-down menu, select Assign Policy to Components.
c. In the Assign Policy to Components dialog box, select VCF Management or a VCF Instance and
click Assign.
You can assign a policy to VCF management components and single or multiple VCF Instances.
7. Apply a password policy.
a. In the Compliance status section, from the ellipsis drop-down menu, select Run compliance
check.
You can select VCF Management and one or multiple VCF Instances. If you do not select any VCF
Management or VCF Instances, the compliance check runs for the entire environment.
b. From the ellipsis drop-down menu, select Assign Policy to Components.
c. In the Assign Policy to Components dialog box, select VCF Management or a VCF Instance and
click Assign.
Ensure that all passwords have their last update within the new password policy expiration interval.
After remediation, the password policy is applied to VCF Management and the VCF Instances.
9.1.1 Procedure 1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the top navigation, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, click Passwords.
4. On the Overview page, click thePassword Policy tab.
5. Apply a password policy to a VCF fleet.
a. Click the ellipsis drop-down menu next to the password policy you want to apply and select Apply
Policy to Fleet.
b. Wait for the process to complete.
6. Apply a password policy to a VCF Instance or your management components.
a. Click the ellipsis drop-down menu next to the password policy you want to apply and select Apply
Policy to Component Groups.
b. In the Apply Policy to Component Groups dialog box, select the VCF instances and VCF
Management to apply the policy to and click Apply.
Detach a Password Policy from VMware Cloud Foundation Components
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, you can detach a password policy from a VCF fleet, VCF Instance, or the VCF management
components. Detaching a password policy stops VCF Operations from enforcing the policy, detecting drift, and
remediating the VCF components.
When you detach an instance-level policy from a component group, if a fleet-level policy is applied, the component group
falls back to the fleet-level policy. If no fleet-level policy is applied, the detached component group falls back to its local
component password policies.
Broadcom 4198

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. On the top navigation bar, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, click Passwords.
4. On the Overview page, click thePassword Policy tab.
5. Detach a fleet-level policy.
a) Click the ellipsis drop-down menu next to the password policy you want to detach and select Detach Fleet Policy.
b) Wait for the process to complete.
6. Detach a policy from a component group.
a) Click the ellipsis drop-down menu next to the password policy you want to detach and select Detach Policy from
Component Groups.
b) In the Detach Policy from Component Groups dialog box, select the VCF instances and VCF Management to
detach the policy from and click Detach.
Update Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
For security reasons, you can change passwords for the accounts that are used by VMware Cloud Foundation
components. Changing these passwords periodically or when certain events occur, such as an administrator leaving your
organization, reduces the likelihood of security vulnerabilities.
• Verify that there are no failed workflows. To check for failed workflows, in VCF Operations., click Fleet Management >
Tasks.
• Verify that no active workflows are running or are scheduled to run during the password update.
• Verify that the VCF Operations user has the following permissions:
– : :
Fleet Management PasswordsManage
– : :
Fleet Management PasswordsView
Using the VCF Operations UI to update a VCF component password is the preferred method for changing a password. If
the VCF component has a password policy applied, VCF Operations automatically validates the new password against
the password policy settings. In addition, this method does not create a configuration drift between VCF Operations and
the environment state.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet Management > Passwords.
4. Click VCF Management or click VCF Instances and click a VCF Instance or a VCF domain name.
5. Select a component and click Update password.
6. In the Update Password dialog box, enter the current password, enter and confirm the new password.
7. Click Update password.
Reset Local Account Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
You can reset a forgotten or an expired local account password for some VCF components.
Use the following table to reset a forgotten or an expired local or application account password.
VCF Component Account Expired Password Forgotten Password

Using SDDC Manager to Manage Passwords
VCF Operations is the preferred method for managing password in VCF. SDDC Manager will be deprecated in a future
VCF release. Use SDDC Manager to manage local or application account passwords in case your environment requires it.
Broadcom 4200

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In the context of password management actions, server refers to the component where the account resides, and client
refers to the component where the account is used. SDDC Manager offers the following password management actions:
Action Description
Remediate You use the Remediate action to provide the new password on
the client after the password is changed on the server.
Note:
Only available in SDDC Manager. Use VCF Operations to
manage passwords for your environment.
Rotate You use the Rotate action to change the password with an auto-
generated password on the server and on the client.
Note:
Only available in SDDC Manager. Use VCF Operations to
manage passwords for your environment.
SDDC Manager stores a copy of an account password in a local, internal vault. Changing an account password on
the VCF component itself causes a mismatch between SDDC Manager's vault and the new password, and requires
a remediation step, before the inter-component communication can be restored. Using SDDC Manager to manage
passwords is not advised. Use SDDC Manager UI to:
• Rotate multiple passwords simultaneously.
• Remediate passwords for VCF core components.
• Schedule automatic password rotation.
You can also use the SDDC Manager API to look up and manage credentials.
Rotate Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
You can rotate passwords for the core components in your VCF Instance by using the SDDC Manager UI. The process of
password rotation generates randomized passwords for the selected accounts. You can rotate passwords manually or can
set up automatic rotation for accounts that are managed by SDDC Manager.
• Verify that there are no failed workflows in SDDC Manager. To check for failed workflows, click Dashboard in the
navigation pane and expand the Tasks pane at the bottom of the page.
• Verify that no active workflows are running or are scheduled to run during the time period that the password rotation
process runs. It is recommended that you schedule password rotation for a time when you expect to have no running
workflows.
You can rotate passwords for the following VCF core components.
• ESX
Note:
Auto-rotate is not supported for ESX.
• vCenter Server
Note:
Auto-rotate is automatically activated for vCenter service accounts. It might take up to 24 hours to configure the
service account auto-rotate policy for a newly deployed vCenter.
• NSX
When rotating a password, SDDC Manager generates the new password that complies with the passwords settings or
password policy of the component.
Broadcom 4201

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to SDDC Manager with a user assigned the Administrator role.
2. In the navigation pane, click Security > Password Management.
3. Select one or more accounts and click one of the following operations.
Action Description
Rotate Generates randomized passwords for the selected accounts.
Schedule rotation You can set the password rotation interval to 30, 60, or 90 days.
You can also deactivate the automatic rotation. You can use the
SDDC Manager API to create a custom rotation interval.
The automated rotation runs at midnight on the scheduled date. If
auto-rotate could not start due to any technical issue, an auto-retry
occurs every hour until the start of the next day. In case schedule
rotation is missed due to technical issues, the UI shows a global
notification with failed task status. The status of the schedule
rotation can also be checked on the Tasks panel.
Rotate all Generates randomized passwords for the all accounts.
A message appears at the top of the page showing the progress of the operation. The tasks panel also shows detailed
status for the password rotation operation. To view sub-tasks, click the task name. As each of these tasks is run, the
status is updated. If the task fails, you can click Retry.
Password rotation completes when all sub-tasks complete successfully.
Remediate Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
To resolve any errors that might occur during password changes, you use password remediation. Password remediation
synchronizes the password of the account that is stored in the SDDC Manager with the updated password in the
component. After you reset the password in a component, you must remediate the password in VCF Operations.
Note:
You can remediate the password for only one account at a time.
For information on updating passwords manually, see Update Passwords for VMware Cloud Foundation Components .
Broadcom 4202

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

2. In the left pane, navigate to Security > Password Management
3. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage.
4. Select a component and, from the ellipsis drop-down menu, select Remediate Password.
5. Enter and confirm the password that was set manually on the component.
6. Click Remediate Password.

application/json' -d '{ "account_name": "sddc_m_to_vcenter_service_ac

Tags and Categories Overview
You can create, manage, and assign tag categories and tags in your VCF Operations instance and use them to organize
and manage your inventory objects at scale.
What Are Tags and Categories
A tag consists of a name and description that you specify. To group related tags together and manage inventory objects at
scale, you create categories and tags inside the categories. When you create a category, you can specify the object types
for its tags, and whether more than one tag in the category can be applied to an object. After you create the category and
tags, you can apply the tags to objects in your vSphere Client inventory or in your VCF Operations inventory to organize
and manage the objects more easily, and to tag specific inventory objects when you configure different vSphere policies.
For example, if you want to tag inventory objects with memory over-commitment, you can create a category named
Compute Memory, specify that the category applies to just ESX hosts as an object type, and then add a tag named
Memory Over-Commitment. After you create the category and tag, you can assign the tag to the specific hosts from your
inventory.
VCF Operations Tags and Categories
By using VCF Operations, you can manage tags from a central place for all VCF Instances that are managed by the VCF
Operations instance. You can create tags and categories, assign tags to objects in the VCF Operations inventory, import
existing tags and categories from vCenter instances. You can assign tags from VCF Operations to inventory objects that
are managed by vCenter instances. For more information, see Assign a Tag to an Object in VCF Operations.
Broadcom 4208

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
After you create or import categories and tags in VCF Operations, you can push them to selected vCenter instances. You
can then use the tags and categories in existing automation scripts or to tag objects in the vSphere Client. This ensures
scalability and prevents loss of tags and their associations to objects during vMotion. For more information, see How Do
You Assign or Remove a vSphere Tag.
For more information on how to select a tag management approach and define the provisioning scope, see VCF Tag
Management for vSphere.
Create a Tag Category in VCF Operations
When you create a tag category, you must also create at least one tag in that category. After you create the category, you
can create and add as many tags in it as you need.
• Verify that you have Tags > Manage permissions in VCF Operations.
You cannot create an empty category, you must create at least one tag in the category. For each category that you create,
you must specify whether a single or multiple tags are allowed per object, and which object types can be associated with
this category. After you create the category, you can edit the tags added to the category. You can add more tags, delete
some of the existing tags, or edit them.
Note:
You can also import existing tags and categories from vCenter instances. For more information, see Import Tags
and Categories to VCF Operations from a vCenter Instance.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, select Fleet Management > Tags .
3. Click Create.
The Create Category dialog box appears.
4. Enter a name for the category. The name can consist of up to 128 characters.
Once you create the category, you cannot change its name.
5. Optional: Enter a description for the category. The description can consist of up to 1024 characters.
6. Optional: To edit the tags per object and the object types that can be associated with the category, click Advanced
Settings.
a) Select the number of tags that can be assigned per associated object.
CAUTION:
If you select Multiple, after you create the category, you cannot change the value to Single.
a) Select to which objects types the tags from the category can be assigned to.
CAUTION:
After you create the category, you can only add more object types to be associated with the category, you cannot
remove the object types that you selected when creating the category. If you select All object types, after you
create the category, you cannot change the value.
7. Create a tag to add to the category:
a) Enter a name for the tag.
After you create the tag, you cannot change its name.
a) Enter a description for the tag.
8. Optional: To create more tags and add them to the category, click Add Tag, and enter a unique name and description
for each tag.
9. Click Create.
The category appears in the table with available categories for this VCF Operations instance.
Broadcom 4209

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You can edit, delete, or push the newly created category to vCenter instances or custom groups. When you delete a
category, you also delete all tags added to it. For backup purposes, you can also export all tag categories and tags
available in the VCF Operations instance in JSON file format.
Create a Tag in VCF Operations
In VCF Operations, you can create tags only inside an existing tag category or at the time when you create a category.
• Verify that you have Tags > Manage permissions in VCF Operations.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, select Fleet Management > Tags.
3. Click the arrow icon next to the category in which you want to create a tag.
A table with all tags added to this category appears.
4. Click Create.
The Create Tag dialog box appears.
5. Enter a unique name for the tag.
The name can consist of up to 128 characters.
6. Optional: Enter a description for the tag.
The description can consist of up to 1024 characters.
7. Optional: To create more tags and add them to the category, click Add Tag, and enter a name and description for each
tag.
8. Click Create.
The tag appears in the table with the available tags for the category.
You can edit the tag description or can delete the tag. You can also export all definitions for tag categories and tags
available in the VCF Operations instance in JSON file format.
Note:
When an export is in progress, initiated by you or another user, you cannot initiate the export again before the first
export completes.
You can assign tags to specific inventory objects in VCF Operations. For more information, see Assign a Tag to an Object
in VCF Operations.
Import Tags and Categories to VCF Operations from a vCenter Instance
You can import existing tags and tag categories from your VCF domain vCenter instances or standalone vCenter
instances to VCF Operations. Importing tags into VCF Operations enables you to manage tags and categories for more
than one vCenter instance from a single place.
• Verify that the vCenter instance from which you want to import tags and tag categories is of version 9.0 or later.
• Verify that the vCenter instance from which you want to import tags has a valid VCF 9.0 or later license.
• Verify that the vCenter instance from which you want to import tags and tag categories is integrated with this VCF
Operations instance.
• Verify that you have Tags > Manage permissions in VCF Operations.
After you import tags and categories to your VCF Operations instance, you can push them to other vCenter instances to
have consistent tagging across your VCF fleet.
Important:
If you cannot see the conflict details, verify that you have the REST API read privileges assigned.
When a task is in progress, you cannot initiate the same task again. For example, if another user or you initiate an import,
you cannot initiate import again before the first task completes.
Broadcom 4210

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, select Fleet Management > Tags.
3. In the Tags page, at the top-right corner, click Import.
The Import Categories dialog box appears, and you can see a list of all VCF domains that are integrated with your
VCF Operations instance.
4. Select a VCF domain from which you want to import tags and tag categories, and click Import.
You cannot initiate an import task if another import task is in progress. You must wait for the task to complete before
you can initiate it again.
If another user initiated an import task and it is in progress, a warning appears.
The tags and categories are imported from the vCenter instance.
If some of the categories cannot be imported, click View Conflict Details or View Import Details in the banner to view a
list with the import conflict or error reasons and possible resolutions. After you dismiss the banner notification, you cannot
view it again.
You cannot see banner notifications for tasks that are performed by another user.
Assign a Tag to an Object in VCF Operations
You can assign tags to objects connected to vCenter instances that are added to your VCF Operations instance.
• Verify that you have Tags > Attach/Detach permissions in VCF Operations.
• Verify that the VCF Operations instance is of version 9.1.
If you want to assign a tag to more than one object, the objects that you select must all meet the criteria for the tag
assignment. For example, if you want to assign the tag GOLD from a tag category with associable object type cluster, the
objects you select before you assign the tag must all be clusters. If you select both hosts and clusters, the tag GOLD does

Managing the Configuration of your Environment
You can use VCF Operations configuration management feature to monitor and view the configuration settings of vCenter
instances and vSphere clusters that have drifted from the desired configurations, without the need to manually track each
change.
Configuration management shows the changes in product configurations at a point in time and allows you to compare the
changes to the assigned desired values. It provides a proactive method to monitor configuration changes.
Why use Configuration Management
Configuration management offers several benefits, including:
1. Consistency: Ensures that vCenter instances and vSphere clusters are configured consistently. This helps reduce
potential issues from drifts.
2. Compliance: Helps ensure that vCenter instances and vSphere clusters are configured to meet organizational policies
and regulations.
3. Scalability: Allows for infrastructure configuration at scale.
For more information, see Recommendations for VCF Configuration Management.
Broadcom 4217

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Managing Configuration Templates in VCF Operations
You can define a configuration state based on your current environment using configuration templates. You can create,
edit, or delete configuration templates for vCenter instances and for vSphere clusters in VCF Operations .
A configuration template is a collection of product configuration settings representing desired values that you are
monitoring. A configuration template enables an administrator to define and monitor the configurations. For more
information, see Template Management and Versioning.
The Configuration Templates tab provides an overview of all configuration templates, including the object type (vCenter
or cluster) assigned to each template. It also includes the description, number of policies assigned to each template,
template author, and template creation date.
Optionally, you can manage configuration templates using a supported source control solution. For more information, refer
to Managing Configuration Templates with Source Control.
Creating Configuration Templates for vCenter Instances
You can create configuration templates for vCenter instances and assign policies. You can then use these templates to
detect drift for vCenter instances.
• If the target vCenter is not deployed as a part of the same VCF instance as the VCF Operations console, ensure that
the user is added to the vCenter Administrators group and that the account used to add vCenter to VCF Operations
has administrator privileges.
Note:
This applies only if you select user credentials when integrating a vCenter cloud account in VCF Operations. For
more information, see Configuring a vCenter Account in VCF Operations.
• Verify that the user has the required Configuration Management roles to access templates. For more information,
see the Access Control: Roles Tab.
– Manage Privilege: For creating templates, assigning them to policy, and running drift check.
– View Privilege: For viewing template content and viewing existing drifts.
• Verify that your cloud account is registered to a cloud proxy or a cloud proxy group.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management, and then click Configuration Management.
The vCenter Instances tile is selected by default.
2. Click Create Configuration Template.
3. On the Template Setup tab, enter a name and description for the template and ensure that the Object Type is set to
vCenter.
4. Select a Configuration Source vCenter from which you want to extract the configuration settings and click Next.
Note:
The Configuration Source vCenter must meet the following criteria:
• vCenter 9.0 or later.
• Possess a VCF Configuration Management license.
• vCenter must be registered to a cloud proxy or a cloud proxy group.
VCF automatically applies the required license and cloud proxy configuration to newly deployed vCenter
instances (version 9.0 and later). For vCenter instances (version 9.0 and later) that are imported into VCF , you
must manually apply the license and configure the cloud proxy. For more information, see Assign a Primary
