Managing Configuration Templates with Source Control
Integrating the VCF Operations configuration templates with a source control repository allows you to control versioning,
auditing, and the management of your configuration templates.
Broadcom 4220

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Integrating with Source Control
Integrating with a source control repository enables you to manage configuration templates under source control.
This functionality also facilitates accurate configuration updates, supports change control with reviews, and integrates
continuous integration and continuous development for automated testing and validation.
GitLab and GitHub are supported source control repositories.
The source control repository system must support the following Console requirements:
• Reachable by FQDN
• Access Token can be generated by the source control and used by the Console
• Accepts a Branch input field
• Accepts a Repository input field
This integration has been tested with the following Git-based source control solutions:
• GitLab: Version 15.x, 16.x, 17-17.6, and 18.8.1.
• GitHub: Version 3.13.13.
Generating Access Tokens in GitLab (Example)
The following is a generic workflow for generating an access token in GitLab. Your experience may vary based on your
environment.
1. Log in to your GitLab account.
2. Click the Profile icon and click Edit profile.
3. Click Access Tokens.
4. Enter the Token name and select the Expiration date.
5. Select the following scopes. Scopes set the permission levels granted to the token.
a. api
b. read_api
c. read_repository
d. write_repository
6. Click Create personal access token.
Generating Access Tokens in GitHub (Example)
The following is a generic workflow for generating an access token in GitHub. Your experience may vary based on your
environment.
1. Log in to your GitHub account.
2. Click the Profile icon and click Settings.
3. Click Developer settings.
4. Expand Personal Access Tokens and then select Tokens (classic).
5. Click Generate new token and then click Generate new token (classic).
6. Enter the Name and select the Expiration date.
7. Select the following scopes. Scopes define the access for personal tokens.
a. repo
b. Admin:repo_hook
c. project
8. Click Generate token.
Configuring Source Control in VCF Operations
You can configure source control settings in VCF Operations to synchronize configuration templates to and from a
repository.
Broadcom 4221

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Verify that your VCF Operations fleet management can establish a connection to the appropriate the source control
solution.
• Ensure bi-directional HTTPS connectivity between the VCF Operations management appliance and the Git repository.
• Verify that you are using a supported source control solution.
• Generate access tokens to authenticate and authorize a secure connection to the repositories.
– GitLab: Generate an access token for your repository following the documentation from GitLab.
Note:
The access token must have the Maintainer or Owner role. Ensure the access token has an expiration date and
the following scopes:
• Read access to the repository. ( in GitLab)
read_repository
• Write access to the repository. ( in GitLab)
write_repository
• Read access to the project. ( in GitLab)
read_api
• Read and write access to the project. ( in Gitlab)
api
– GitHub: Generate an access token for your repository following the documentation from GitHub.
After you configure a source control solution, it becomes the primary record holder for the configuration templates.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administration >
Control Panel, and then click Source Control.
2. For Source Control Type, select a source control solution.
3. Enter the Source Control Server address where the configuration templates will be stored.
4. Enter the access token from your source control type in the Access Key.
5. Specify the Branch for storing or reading content.
6. Provide the Repository path for storing or retrieving contents.
7. By default, Code Review is enabled by default. The code review process creates a merge request for any operation
on a configuration template. The content syncs to the repository after the merge request is approved.
Note:
To disable the code review process, uncheck the Code Review checkbox.
8. Click Test Connection to verify if the integration is successful. If the Connection Result is successful, click Save to
complete the integration.
After the setup is complete, you can manage the configuration templates from your source control solution.
Note:
If your VCF Operations instance uses a self-signed certificate, disable the SSL verification setting of the webhook
for the Git repository.
Template Organization and Repository Structure: Configuration templates are automatically created and organized in
a defined folder structure: . Each template must be
Operations-ConfigTemplate/config-templates/vCenter
stored in a unique folder in the source control repository.
Template Name and Storage: Each configuration template must have a unique name to avoid duplication.
Template Content and File Structure: For each configuration template, three files are automatically created in the
repository:
1. : Contains the desired state of the template.
<templatename>-desiredState.json
2. : Contains metadata information like template name, version, and selected
<templatename>-metaData.json
configuration.
3. : Used to manage and maintain the template's structure and metadata.
<templatename>-manifest.json
Broadcom 4222

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Syncing Configuration Templates with Source Control
After you configure the source control solution in VCF Operations, sync the configuration templates with the source control
repository. This topic outlines the different workflows that you can follow to manage the configuration templates and
integrate them with the repository.
Review, Sync, and Merge Templates from VCF Operations
Review Process Enabled
When you create, edit, or delete a template in VCF Operations, a merge request is created in source control and is
visible in the configuration template list view. You must review and approve the request in your source control solution.
After the request is approved, the template status changes to OUT_OF_SYNC. Sync the template using the Sync option
in VCF Operations. The template status changes to IN_SYNC after the sync is complete.
Note:
The edited or deleted content is reflected only after the merge request is approved and the content is synced.
Review Process Disabled
When you edit a template, the template is directly edited in the source control repository without a request. If you delete
a template from VCF Operations, the template is marked OUT_OF_SYNC and is directly deleted from the source control
during the next sync.
Sync Existing Templates in VCF Operations
Code Review Process Enabled
When source control integration is enabled, merge requests are created for syncing all existing templates from
VCF Operations to the source control repository. After the request is approved, the template status changes to
OUT_OF_SYNC. Use the Pull from GitHub option to sync content from the repository. The status of the template
changes to IN_SYNC after the sync is successful.
Code Review Process Disabled
The status of all existing templates reflects as OUT_OF_SYNC: No request is raised. You must use the Sync option to
sync content from source control. The status changes to IN_SYNC after the sync is complete.
Sync Remote Templates to VCF Operations
If you edit or delete existing templates in the source control repository, the status of the corresponding templates reflects
as OUT_OF_SYNC in VCF Operations.
When you edit a template in the source control repository, you must Pull from GitHub, and after the sync is successful,
the updated template content gets reflected in VCF Operations and the status changes to IN_SYNC.
When you delete a template in the source control repository, the template is removed from VCF Operations.
When you configure a source control in VCF Operations, existing templates without any content in the source control
repository are created in VCF Operations as placeholders and reflect the OUT_OF_SYNC status. You must sync the
content to populate the templates. The status changes to IN_SYNC after the sync is complete.
Additional Information
Merge Request Discarded
A merge request can be discarded if the changes proposed in the merge request are no longer valid or required. If a
merge request is discarded or closed by the user, a warning message is displayed informing the user that the changes
made to the corresponding template in VCF Operations are not merged and the current template might not reflect the
desired state in source control
You can edit the template to make the necessary updates and address the issues that caused the merge request to
be discarded. After you make the update, a new request is raised. This ensures that the latest template changes are
submitted for review.
Broadcom 4223

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Drift Detection
Drift detection is skipped if the template does not exist in the source control repository. This might occur in scenarios
where the template has not been synced with the source control.
Updating Source Control Configurations
Editing or Updating Branch or Repositories
You can update the branch or repository or switch to a new branch or repository. Once done, the templates from the
previous source control repository displays the OUT_OF_SYNC status. The existing templates in VCF Operations will
sync to the new branch or repository. For more information, see Sync Existing Templates in VCF Operations section.
If you delete a source control configuration, the templates stored locally in VCF Operations remain unchanged, however
the status changes to OUT_OF_SYNC.
Note:
If you want to update your source control type, you must first delete the existing configuration.
Using the Configuration Management Overview Page
The configuration management overview dashboard allows you to view and monitor vCenter and vSphere cluster drift
statuses.
You can view and compare drifts and identify settings that have changed.
A drift notifies you of any deviation from the assigned template values. Use the Configuration Management Enabled
Objects Summary bar to view the total number of objects and their enabled statues. Enabled objects are composed of all
the vCenter and vSphere clusters that have a configuration template attached to them.
The vCenter Instances Drift Status and Cluster Drift Status charts represent the state of the enabled vCenter
instances and vSphere clusters at a given point in time. All the potential drift statuses and their definitions are listed after
this:
• In Progress: This state shows that active drift detection is currently executing for vCenter instances or vSphere
clusters.
• Not Drifted: This state shows vCenter instances and vSphere clusters with no drifts from the configuration state.
• Drift Detected: This state shows when vCenter instances or vSphere clusters have deviated from their desired
template configuration.
• Drift Check Failed: This state occurs under the following scenario's
– vCenter instances or vSphere clusters are unavailable.
– The drift has not been computed against that specific resource.
– An internal error has occurred.
• Unavailable: This state shows a list of vCenter instances and vSphere clusters that are either
– Below version 9.0
– Not registered with the cloud proxy.
Additionally, you can click the Objects tab to view the objects assigned to your vCenter instances and clusters and view
all Objects.
Scheduling Drift Detection
You can automate the drift detection process and schedule drift detection in VCF Operations.
Scheduling drift detection enables you to run automatic drift checks on your vCenter instances or clusters at an interval of
your choice.
Broadcom 4224

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Configuration Management, and then click Schedule Drift Detection.
2. For step 1 of scheduling drift detection, enter the Configuration Drift Check Information.
a) Provide a name for the job. This information is displayed in the calendar in the Automation Central page.
b) Provide a description for the job.
c) Select the Adapter Type.
The vCenter adapter type is the only available adapter type for both vCenter and cluster templates.
d) Select the Object Type.
You can schedule drift detection for the vCenter or the Cluster Compute Resource object type.
e) Click Next.
3. For step 2, Select an object. Select Scope of the object which contains the vCenter on which VCF Operations must
run the automation jobs.
For example, if you click and drag a VCF instance from the right hand Scope box to the left hand Scope selection box,
it will include all vCenter instances or clusters, depending on your template, into the Scope Selection. You can filter
out objects in the next step if needed.
a) Drag and drop the object type to the left pane.
b) To delete members, click the X icon.
c) Click Next.
4. Optional: For step 3, you can Filter Criteria, and add multiple criteria for the vCenter object type.
5. Optional: Click Preview Scope at the bottom-right corner to see on which vCenter instances the jobs are executed.
6. Optional: Close the Preview Scope and click Next.
7. Set the Schedule and click Create.

Detecting Drifts and Downloading Drift Reports for vCenter Instances
You can detect drifts for each configuration template you have created for a specific vCenter.
To view vCenter configuration setting values and detect drifts, you must:
• Ensure that you have created at least one configuration template for your vCenter.
• Ensure that the user is configured with the Administrator role in VCF Operations. For more information, see Privileges
Required for Configuring a vCenter Account in VCF Operations.
• Verify that you have Configuration Management privileges to access configuration templates. For more information,
see Managing Users and Access Control.
– Manage Privilege: For creating templates, assigning them to an operations policy, and running drift check.
– View Privilege: For viewing template content and viewing existing drift.
• Verify that your vCenter instance is configured, registered with the cloud proxy, and has one or more operations policy
assigned to the configuration template.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Configuration Management, and then click the Drifts tab.
On the Drifts Details page, you can view the number of enabled vCenter instances on the vCenter Instances tile.
You can also view the number of vSphere Configuration Profiles enabled clusters on the Clusters tile. For more
information, see Detecting Drifts and Downloading Drift Reports for Clusters.
By default, the vCenter instances tile is selected.
2. Select one or more vCenter instances.
3. Click Detect Drift to detect configuration drift.
This detects drifts across all the configuration templates and displays the result in the Drifts table.
4. To view the drift for each vCenter, click the vCenter instance.
5. Select a Configuration Template to view the drift details.
If a drift is detected, the right pane displays the drifts between the Current vCenter Value and the Configuration
Template Value. If no drift is detected for the selected template, the message No drift found for this configuration
template since last configuration drift check status is displayed.
• Detect Drift: To further detect drift for a particular template in a vCenter instance.
• View Template: To view the template.
Broadcom 4226

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. Navigate to the Drifts Details page, select one or more vCenter instances, and click Download Drift Status Report
to download the historical drift detection reports PDF or XLS format.
The drift report displays the date, resource, template, and drift status for each vCenter instance. By default the report
shows data for the last seven days. You can update the duration to up to 30 days from the Global Settings page. For
more information, see List of Global Settings.
Detecting Drifts and Downloading Drift Reports for Clusters
You can detect drifts for each configuration template you have created for specific clusters in VCF Operations. The drift
status is visible only for vSphere clusters that have vSphere Configuration Profiles enabled.
• Verify that the target clusters are being managed by vCenter version 9.0 or later.
• Verify that vCenter managing your target clusters is registered with a cloud proxy.
• Target clusters are managed with vSphere Configuration Profiles. Ensure that vSphere Configuration Profiles are
enabled for all target clusters in vSphere. For more information, see vSphere Configuration Profiles.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Configuration Management, and then click the Drifts tab.
2. Click the Clusters tile.
The drift status of all vSphere Configuration Profiles enabled clusters that are associated with the VCF Instance is
displayed. You can also view the number of clusters that are managed by configuration templates.
3. Select one or more clusters and then click Detect Drift to detect configuration drift.
This detects drifts across all the cluster configuration templates and displays the result in the Drifts table.
4. Click Download Drift Status Report to download the historical drift data.
The drift report displays the date, resource, template, and drift status for each cluster. By default the report shows
data for the last seven days. You can update the duration to up to 30 days from the Global Settings page. For more
information, see List of Global Settings.
5. To view the Effective Cluster Configuration for individual clusters, click the number that is displayed in the Templates
(Including Inhertited) column.
6. To view the drift for each cluster, click a cluster.
The Drifts Details page opens and lists the total number of Hosts and the number of drifted Host in the cluster.
7. Switch between Hosts to view the associated cluster configuration templates, the drift status, and the drifted values.
8. Click Download Drift Status Report to download cluster drift report for individual hosts.
You can download the drift status report as a pdf or .xls file format.
Viewing Drifts and Manual Remediation Steps for Clusters
You can view the drift status and manually remediate a cluster that has drifted from the configuration template and its
expected configuration values.
• Ensure that you have created a configuration template for the cluster and assigned it to a policy. For more information,
see Creating Configuration Templates for Clusters.
• Ensure that you have run drift detection for the cluster. For more information, see Detecting Drifts and Downloading
Drift Reports for Clusters.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Fleet
Management > Configuration Management, and then click the Drifts tab.
2. Click the Clusters tile.
The drift status of all vSphere Configuration Profiles enabled clusters that are associated with the VCF Instance is
displayed. You can also view the number of clusters that are managed by configuration templates.
Broadcom 4227

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. View the Drift Status in Drifts table.
• Not Drifted: The cluster has not drifted from the configuration template.
• Drift Detected: The cluster has drifted from the configuration template and requires remediation.
4. Click a cluster that displays the Drift Detected status to open the Drifts Details page.
5. Click Download Remediation JSON to download the remediation draft for the cluster.
This JSON file contains the configuration template JSON file that can be applied to each cluster manually using the
vCenter vSphere Configuration Profiles API.
6. The following outlines the high-level steps to use the downloaded JSON file to manually apply to a cluster through the
vSphere Client UI. Navigate to the destination vSphere Client and create a draft using the downloaded json file. For
more information, see Create a Draft Configuration in vSphere Client.
7. Run the remediation for the drifted cluster. For more information, see Remediate a Cluster Against the Desired or Draft
Configuration.
8. Once done, log in to VCF Operations to the Clusters tile in Configuration Management.
9. Select the cluster, and click Detect Drift to detect configuration drift.
The drift status changes to Not Detected for the cluster.
Configuration Management FAQ
This topic covers some frequently asked questions about configuration management in VCF Operations.
• What are the prerequisites for setting up a configuration template?
– To view the prerequisites for setting up configuration template, see Creating Configuration Templates for vCenter
Instances.
• When does a configuration template creation fail?
– Configuration template creation can fail, if the template size exceeds 9 MB. You can copy the configuration template
contents to a file to check the file size and ensure it is under 9 MB.
– vCenter configuration template creation can fail, if a connection issues occurs between vCenter and the
configuration adapter. You can check the connection status of vCenter and the configuration adapter to ensure
that a proper connection exists between the two. To troubleshoot, see Cloud Proxy Troubleshooting and vSphere
Management Pack Issues.
• What should I do if there is an error while displaying drift details?
– If you encounter an error while attempting to view drift details, it may be due to connectivity issues between vCenter
and the configuration adapter. To troubleshoot, see Cloud Proxy Troubleshooting and vSphere Management Pack
Issues.
• Why is the drift report PDF generated with "No drift details available for the selected resource/resources" message?
– This message may appear if the Detect Drift operation has never been triggered for the selected resources. To
resolve this issue, run the Detect Drift process on the relevant resources first, and then try downloading the report
again.
• How can I remediate a vCenter if I receive a notification indicating that it has drifted from a configuration template?
– Remediation cannot be done at the VCF Operations console at this time. You must log in to the vCenter and
manually revert the drifted configurations to their original values as defined in the template to make the vCenter
compliant again.
– If you want the drifted values to be the configuration template values, edit the template under configuration
management to match the current configuration of the vCenter.
• How do I troubleshoot if a vCenter Drift status is in an Error state?
– Check the connection between VCF Operations and vCenter to ensure that vCenter is in a Collecting state within
VCF Operations. If it is not collecting, start or resume the data collection for vCenter. This will restore proper drift
detection and clear the error. To troubleshoot, see vSphere Management Pack Issues.
• How can I debug when the configuration template sync fails to and from a remote repository?
– In the VCF Operations navigate to Administration > Control Panel > Source Control and click Test Connection
to verify if connection with the Git Repository is successful or not. Ensure that the connection is successful before
Broadcom 4228

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
performing any action related to configuration drifts using Git. If the test fails, check the repository URL, credentials,
and network connectivity.
• Starting with version 9.1, why does the cluster show an old or incorrect drift status (like "Drifted" or "Not Drifted")
immediately after I assign a new template?
– The drift status of the cluster is not reset to "Unavailable" when previous templates are deleted. The system retains
those historical drift records and accordingly shows that old drift status for the cluster.
To clear this stale data and view the accurate status, manually trigger a new drift analysis:
a. Navigate to the affected cluster object.
b. Select Run Drift Detection.
c. Allow the analysis to complete to see the current, accurate drift state.
Managing Infrastructure Services for VMware Cloud Foundation
Name resolution and time synchronization are critical services on which your environment relies for connectivity,
authentication, certificate management, logging, and so on. You use VCF Operations to update the DNS and NTP
configuration for multiple VCF or VVF components.
Update the DNS Server Configuration for VCF Components
VCF Operations uses DNS servers to provide name resolution for the VCF components. You can update the DNS server
information that you provided during VMware Cloud Foundation deployment. You can update the DNS server information
for single or multiple VCF Instances in a single operation.
• Verify that both forward and reverse DNS resolution is functional for each component using the updated DNS server
information.
• Verify that the new DNS server is reachable from each of the VMware Cloud Foundation components.
• Verify that SDDC Manager can reach all VMware Cloud Foundation components over SSH.
• Verify that all VMware Cloud Foundation components are in an active state.
When you update the DNS server configuration, VCF Operations performs DNS configuration updates for the following
components:
• SDDC Manager
• vCenter
• ESX
• NSX
• VCF management services
• VCF Automation
If the update fails, VCF Operations rolls back the DNS settings for the failed component. Fix the underlying issue and retry
the operation.
Updating the DNS server configuration can take some time to complete, depending on the size of your environment.
Schedule DNS updates at a time that minimizes the impact to the system users.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet management > Fleet settings.
4. On the Fleet settings page, click the DNS settings card.
5. To create a DNS configuration that can be applied to VCF Instances, on the DNS settings page, click Create setting.
6. On the Create DNS setting page, configure the name of the setting, the description, provide a DNS server, and click
Create.
For multiple DNS servers, use a comma-separated list.
Broadcom 4229

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
7. On the DNS settings page, in the Instances section, select the VCF Instance to update and click Apply.
8. On the Apply setting to instance page, select the DNS configuration to be assigned to the VCF Instance and click
Assign.
Update the NTP Server Configuration for VCF Components
VCF Operations uses NTP servers to synchronize time between the VCF core components. You can update the NTP
server information that you provided during VMware Cloud Foundation deployment.
• Verify the new NTP server is reachable from all components.
• Time skew between new NTP servers is less than 5 minutes.
• Verify that SDDC Manager can reach all VMware Cloud Foundation components over SSH.
You must have at least one NTP server. When you update the NTP server configuration, SDDC Manager performs NTP
configuration updates for the following components:
• SDDC Manager
• vCenter
• ESX
• NSX
• VCF Operations
• VCF Automation
• VCF management services
• VCF Operations for networks
If the update fails, VCF Operations rolls back the NTP settings for the failed component. Fix the underlying issue and retry
the operation.
Updating the NTP server configuration can take some time to complete, depending on the size of your environment.
Schedule NTP updates at a time that minimizes the impact to the system users.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. From the navigation bar at the top, click Manage.
3. In the left pane, navigate to Fleet management > Fleet settings.
4. On the Fleet settings page, click the NTP settings card.
5. To create an NTP configuration that can be applied to VCF Instances, on the NTP settings page, click Create setting.
6. On the Create NTP setting page, configure the name of the setting, the description, provide an NTP server, and click
Create.
When using multiple NTP servers, use a comma-separated list.
7. On the NTP settings page, in the Instances section, select the VCF Instance to update and click Apply.
8. On the Apply setting to instance page, select the NTP configuration to be assigned to the VCF Instance and click
Assign.
Configuring the NTP Settings for VMware vSphere Foundation Components
To configure the NTP configuration for your VMware vSphere Foundation component, you can use the VCF Operations
administration UI.
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) setting is used to synchronize the time of your VCF Operations cluster nodes.
Configure the NTP setting in VCF Operations to ensure that all the cluster nodes follow the same time protocol. Following
the same time protocol allows your cluster's services to run smoothly. The primary node serves as the NTP server by
default and the time of all nodes are synchronized to the primary node. You can continue using the primary node as the
NTP server and add another NTP server to serve as a failover if the primary node fails. In case you do not want to use the
primary node, you can add the NTP server you wish to use.
Broadcom 4230

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the VCF Operations administration interface at https://primary-node-name-or-ip-address/admin.
2. Click the NTP Settings icon.
The Global Network Time Protocol settings wizard opens. The primary node is listed as the existing NTP server.
Note:
You must configure at least two NTP servers to have a back-up if one server fails.
3. Add a secondary NTP server. Enter the IP of FDQN of the NTP server you wish to use in NTP Server Address field.
4. Click Add.
The new NTP server is displayed along with the primary node.
5. Ensure that the status of the NTP server is green which means its reachable and working.
Configure Dual-Stack Networking for SDDC Manager
Starting with VCF 9.1, SDDC Manager supports dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) networking. You configure dual-stack
networking on SDDC Manager to deploy and manage VCF components with dual-stack networking (wherever supported).
• The VCF components in your management domain for this VCF Instance must be on version 9.1 or later.
• IPv6 must be enabled for all ESX hosts in the management domain for this VCF instance.
• SDDC Manager supports static, DHCP, or SLAAC IPv6 address assignment for storage and vMotion vmkernel
adapters.
• The FQDN for the SDDC Manager instance must resolve to an IPv6 address.
Native support for IPv6 networking resolves the IPv4 address exhaustion issue. With IPv6 you can avoid stop-gap
measures such as Network Address Translation (NAT) and extensive use of private RFC1918 address space.
After you convert to dual-stack networking, SDDC Manager retains backwards compatibility to manage IPv4-only
workload domains. However, IPv4-only SDDC Manager cannot manage dual-stack workload domains.
1. Log in to VCF Operations.
2. In the left pane, navigate to Administration > SDDC Manager.
3. Click VCF Management or click VCF Instances and click a VCF Instance.
4. On the Network settings tab, click Dual stack networking and click Enable dual stack.
The Enable dual stack wizard opens.
5. On the Introduction page, click Next.
6. On the IPv6 configuration page, enter the IPv6 address of the management network gateway.
7. On the Validate page, remediate any issues and click Next.
8. On the Enable dual stack page, click Finish.
During the configuration process, SDDC Manager becomes unavailable.

After the automated deployment of components for your VMware Cloud Foundation platform, you can manually add VCF
Automation, Identity broker, or a secondary software depot to a VCF instance.
Removing VCF Components Post Deployment
If the manual deployment of a component fails and the component appears listed in the UI, there is no option to delete the
listing. To remove the component from the UI, see Broadcom knowledge base article 441333.

Deploy Identity Broker as a Day-N Operation
When you run VCF Installer on Day-0, the identity broker component is automatically installed on your first VCF Instance
along with other management components such as Fleet lifecycle and SDDC Manager. However, if you want to install
identity broker on a subsequent VCF Instance or after an SDDC Manager upgrade, you must deploy it manually because
Fleet lifecycle will not deploy an additional identity broker if it detects that identity broker is already present in the
environment.
To manually deploy identity broker , perform the following steps.
1. Log in to the VCF Operations interface at as a user assigned the Administrator
https://<vcf_operations_fqdn>
role.
2. Navigate to Build > Lifecycle > VCF Management > Add Components.
3. On the Components tab, select VCF Identity Broker.
a) Provide the information required for deployment.
• Version: Select the version of the identity broker component.
• Size: Small, Medium, Large.
• VCF Instance: Select the VCF Instance where you want to have identity broker deployed.
• FQDN: Enter the Fully Qualified Domain Name of the identity broker component. The new FQDN must point to
a unique IP that is not assigned to VCF services runtime.
Note:
Do not use capital letters in the FQDN.
• Display Name: Provide a user-friendly name for the identity broker deployment on the VCF instance.
b) Click Next to proceed to the Summary step for final review before deployment.
c) Click to Install or Cancel the identity broker component deployment.
Deploy a Secondary Software Depot Instance
During the deployment and upgrade procedures of your management domain, software depot (part of VCF management
services) is deployed on the first VCF Instance as a fleet-level component. You can also deploy other software depot
instances as instance-level components. For example, when your environment requires a software depot instance in the
same region as your other VCF Instances or the primary software depot instance experiences bandwidth issues.
• Verify that the VCF services runtime component is deployed and running.
By default, a VCF fleet is operated by using a centralized software depot that is located in the first VCF Instance and
your VCF Instances within the same VCF fleet access installation, upgrade, and patch binaries from this source. While a
single software depot centralizes management, network latency between geographically distant instances can impact the
performance of downloads and lifecycle management operations.
To ensure optimal performance and reliability during lifecycle management operations for multi-region deployments, if the
network latency between the software depot of the first VCF Instance and another VCF Instance exceeds 150 ms, you
Broadcom 4233

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
can deploy a secondary local software depot within the other VCF Instance. After the deployment completes, this software
depot is automatically assigned to the VCF Instance on which it is deployed.
For more information, see Binary Management for VMware Cloud Foundation.
1. Log in to VCF Operations at <vcf_operations_fqdn> with a user assigned the Administrator role.
https://
2. Select Build > Lifecycle > VCF Management.
3. On the Components tab, select Add Component > Software depot.
4. Deploy the component to a VCF Instance.
a) Select a version.
b) Select a VCF Instance to deploy the component to.
c) Click Deploy.
The secondary software depot instance is deployed and assigned to the VCF Instance on which it is deployed.
To assign the new software depot instance to other VCF Instances, for example, in the same region, see Assign a
Software Depot to VCF Instances.
Deploy a License Server Version 9.1.0
A license server is deployed as part of a new deployment or upgrade of VCF or vSphere Foundation. You need at least
one license server and a VCF Operations instance to license your environment. If you need another license server, you
can download and install a license server manually.
• Verify that you have administrator privileges in the VCF Operations instance that you use for license management.
• Verify that you have administrator privileges in the vCenter instance that you use to deploy the license server.
• Verify that you have a Broadcom Support Portal role with sufficient privileges to download the license server binaries.
• Define a unique Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) for the license server and add an A record and PTR record to
your DNS server.
• Download the license server binaries from the Broadcom Support Portal.
Important:
For version 9.1.1, see Deploy a License Server Version 9.1.1.
You must deploy a license server by using an OVA file in the following cases:
• You do not use the VCF Operations UI/SDDC Manager API to upgrade VCF, or VCF Installer UI/ VCF Installer API to
upgrade vSphere Foundation.
• You need an additional license server for your environment.
• You need to replace a license server.
You must add at least one license server to each VCF Operations instance that you use for license management. One
license server can be used to license many VCF instances and vCenter instances in the same VCF fleet.
Note:
You cannot deploy a license server on a standalone ESX host. You must deploy the license server in a vCenter
instance as an OVF template.
The license server does not support IPv6.

The VCF Operations Registration page appears, and the License Servers tab is selected.

Linking vCenter instances in VCF Operations
vCenter linking in VCF Operations provides you with a single pane of glass view of all the linked vCenter instances from a
single vSphere Client.
• Verify that you have vCenter version 9.0 or later.
• Ensure that there is functioning forward and reverse DNS resolution between all vCenter instances in a vCenter linking
group.
• Ensure that the user used to register the vCenter account in VCF Operations has Administrator privileges.
Broadcom 4239

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
The Administrator privileges apply only when you manually configure the vCenter cloud account with user
credentials. When you use system managed credentials, these requirements are handled automatically. For more
information, see Configuring a vCenter Account in VCF Operations.
• Verify that the user has the required vCenter Linking role assigned to access the vCenter instances. For more
information, see the Access Control: Roles Tab.
– Manage: To add, edit, or delete the vCenter linking group.
– View Privilege: To view the vCenter linking group and its members.
• Ensure that common Identity Providers (IDP) is configured on all vCenter systems. For more information, see Identity
Providers and Protocols Supported for VCF Single Sign-On.
• Ensure that the IDP user has the required permission for each vCenter system.
Note:
IDP user permissions are not shared between vCenter systems and must configured on each vCenter individually.
• Verify that the vCenter systems are not part of an Enhanced Link Mode group.
Note:
From VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 onward, its recommended to use vCenter linking for vSphere Client single
pane of glass functionality instead of Enhanced Linked Mode (ELM). If a vCenter system is part of ELM, it cannot
be added to a vCenter linking group. You must deactivate ELM before proceeding. To deactivate ELM, see
Deactivate Enhanced Link Mode for Standalone vCenter Instances Using the cmsso-util break-elm Utililty.
Functionalities previously provided by Enhanced Linked Mode in vCenter like synchronization of roles, tags,
global permissions across the linked vCenter instances are not available in VCF Operations based vCenter
linking.
• To configure SSO for VCF components, see Configuring VCF Single Sign-On.
• To manage tags for a fleet of vCenter instances, see Tags and Categories Overview.
You can link a minimum of two and a maximum of 15 vCenter instances in a group. All the vCenter instances in a linked
group must be configured with common IDP users. Once linked, you can log into any one of the linked vCenter instances
using the vSphere Client, and monitor and manage the inventories of all the linked vCenter instances.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administration >
Configurations.
2. Under Logical Groupings, click the vCenter Linking tile.
3. Click Create Group.
4. Enter the Group Name and Description, and then click Next.
5. Select the compatible vCenter instances that you want to add to the group and then click Next.
Note:
You can view the list of compatible and incompatible vCenter systems.
• Compatible: vCenter instances that meet the version prerequisite and are not part of any other vCenter linking
group.
• Incompatible: vCenter instances that do not meet the version prerequisite or belong to another vCenter linking
group.
6. Review your selection and click Finish.
The vCenter linking group is created.
7. If the status of any of the vCenter instances shows an error, fix the cause, and then click Reset Linking to
troubleshoot.
Note:
Some of the common errors you might face and fix before you click Reset Linking as as follows:
Broadcom 4240

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• vCenter is not reachable from VCF Operations: You must fix the connection between VCF Operations and
vCenter.
• vCenter is part of Enhanced Linked Mode (ELM): You must deactivate ELM.
8. After the group is created, you can add or remove members from a group and you can also edit the group details or
delete the group.
You can log in to any vSphere Client for any one of the linked vCenter instances using the IDP user that has the required
permissions for all vCenter instances and view the inventory of all the vCenter instances in the group.
Collecting Data with Cloud Proxy in VCF Operations
Cloud proxies are used to collect and monitor data from your on-premises data centers across various geographical
locations within a VCF environment. They act as data collection points, ensuring continuous monitoring and operational
visibility.
Cloud proxies provide high availability within your VCF Operations environment, you can group two or more cloud proxies
to form a collector group. The cloud proxy collector group ensures that there is no single point of failure in your cloud
environment. If one of the cloud proxies experiences a network interruption or becomes unavailable, the other cloud proxy
from the collector group takes charge and ensures that there is no downtime. All other user-initiated manual operations
on the collector, such as to stop or restart the collector manually, do not result in automated re-balancing. For more
information, see Configuring Cloud Proxies in VCF Operations.
To configure cloud proxy using VCF Operations Fleet Management, see Add Nodes to VCF Operations.
Note:
When a node within the collector group goes down, high availability failover occurs, so that data collection is not
impacted. However some data loss is expected before the failover is complete.
You can also use cloud proxies to re-balance the resources in your collector group. The re-balance option is available as
part of the Edit menu in the Collector Groups page.
Note:
You can use the re-balance option before vCenter initiates data collection. After the data collection starts, the re-
balance option is disabled.
FIPS mode is supported in a cloud proxy. To leverage this functionality, make sure your cluster is in FIPS mode.
You can upgrade your cloud proxy. For more information, see Upgrading.
You can deploy a cloud proxy based on your sizing requirements. For more information, see KB article 324340.
Table 1144: Cloud Proxy Types
Cloud Proxy Type VM Scale Requirements CPU Requirements Memory Requirements
Classic Small Cloud Proxy Up to 16,000 VMs 2 vCPUs 8GB
Classic Standard Cloud Proxy Between 16,000 to 80,000 VMs 4 vCPUs 32GB
Unified Small Cloud Proxy Up to 16,000 VMs 4 vCPUs 16GB
Unified Standard Cloud Proxy Between 16,000 to 80,000 VMs 8 vCPUs 48 GB
Use a classic cloud proxy in VCF Operations, to collect and monitor data from your remote data centers. In addition to
data collection, you can use your cloud proxy to collect logs into the Log Cluster and to collect and upload support bundles
to the Broadcom support portal site. Use unified cloud proxy for log collection or log assist. For more information on log
assist, see Log Assist. For more information on log collection, see Configuring and Analyzing Logs.

Activating Data Persistence in Cloud Proxy
Use data persistence, to avoid data gaps if there are temporary connectivity issues. You can activate data persistence
to allow the cloud proxy to store data that is sent to VCF Operations, if the connection fails between the cloud proxy
and VCF Operations. The cloud proxy stores all the persisted data that includes metrics and properties, along with time
stamps.
Cloud proxy can store data for a maximum duration of one hour. If storage is full or a connection failure exceeds one hour,
the cloud proxy rotates data by replacing the oldest records with the most recent collections. If there is lack of space, you
can add additional storage, for more information, see Broadcom knowledge base article 318768.
After the connection is restored, the cloud proxy sends the stored data to VCF Operations before the real-time data. Data
appears in chronological order, with stored data displayed before real-time data. If the connection loss was more than one
hour, there can also be a gap in the displayed data.
You can activate data persistence after you deploy a new cloud proxy. For more information, see Add a Cloud Proxy. You
can also activate data persistence in an existing cloud proxy. For more information, see Monitoring the Health of Cloud
Proxies.

Deleting Cloud Proxies
You can delete a cloud proxy if there are issues with your cloud proxy. For example, you can delete the cloud proxy if it
was deployed incorrectly, needs to be redeployed to another cluster, or is no longer required. After you delete a cloud
proxy, data collection stops.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administration >
Cloud Proxies.
2. Click the vertical ellipsis in front of the cloud proxy you want to delete and then click Delete.
The confirmation wizard appears.

Configuring Outbound Network Proxy Settings on an Upgraded Cloud Proxy
After upgrading the unified cloud proxy to version 9.1.1, you can manually configure the outbound network proxy OVF
properties. Since these are not exposed in vCenter vApp Options, create them only if your deployment requires a
dedicated proxy to route Log Assist traffic to the Broadcom Portal.
• Verify that the unified cloud proxy is upgraded to version 9.1.1.
• Verify that you have access to the vCenter instance that manages the cloud proxy.
• Verify that you have the outbound network proxy values (IP address, port, user name, password, SSL, and SSL
verification) available from your network administrator.
Starting with version 9.1.1, you can optionally set up Outbound Network Proxy Settings to route Log Assist traffic to the
Broadcom Portal through a dedicated proxy.
When you upgrade a cloud proxy from any lower version to version 9.1.1, any existing network proxy values are
automatically applied to the outbound network proxy properties, but you cannot view or modify them in the user interface.
If the outbound network proxy requires different values from the existing network proxy, you must manually create the
outbound network proxy properties and set their values so that the outbound network proxy feature functions correctly.
1. Log in to the vCenter instance that manages the cloud proxy.
2. In the Inventory, locate and select the cloud proxy virtual machine.
3. Power off the cloud proxy virtual machine.
You must power off the virtual machine before you can add new OVF properties.
4. Click the Configure tab, and under Settings, select vApp Options.
5. Click ADD to add each property listed in the Outbound network proxy properties table. You must enter the Key, Label,
Category, and Type values exactly as shown, and click OK.
Key Label Category Type
outbound_network_proxy_ip Outbound Network Proxy IP Outbound Network Proxy string

rt Settings

6. Select each property you created, click SET VALUE, enter the appropriate value for your environment, and click OK.
7. Power on the cloud proxy virtual machine.
8. To verify that the outbound network proxy properties are applied, use SSH to connect to the cloud proxy and run the
following command:
ovfenv
The command output lists all OVF environment properties. Confirm that the newly added properties display the values
you configuredfor the following:
• outbound_network_proxy_ip
• outbound_network_proxy_port
• outbound_network_proxy_username
• outbound_network_proxy_password
• outbound_network_proxy_ssl
• outbound_network_proxy_ssl_verification
The outbound network proxy properties are created and configured on the cloud proxy. When you power on the cloud
proxy, it reads the property values from the OVF environment and applies the outbound network proxy settings.
Verify that the outbound network proxy settings are applied correctly by confirming that the cloud proxy communicates
through the configured outbound network proxy.
Using the Cloud Proxy Command-Line Interface
Use the cloud proxy command-line interface to upgrade your cloud proxy, generate support bundles, and view the cloud
proxy health status.
You can use SSH to access the cloud proxy instance and use its command-line Interface to run the following actions:
• Manually upgrade your cloud proxy in case the automatic download of the latest binary fails. When the automatic
download fails, you see a notification on the VCF Operations user interface. To manually upgrade your cloud proxy
instance to the latest version, see the following Broadcom knowledge base article 344168.
• Generate the support bundle.
• Gather the status of the cloud proxy's health and connectivity details.

Using VCF Operations APIs with Cloud Proxy
You can use a browser or an HTTP client program to send requests and receive responses.
REST Client Programs
Any client application that can send HTTPS requests is an appropriate tool for developing REST applications with the
VCF Operations API. REST client plug-ins are available for most browsers and many IDEs. The following open-source
programs are commonly used:
• cURL. http://curl.haxx.se
• Postman application. http://www.getpostman.com
In addition, VMware provides language-specific client bindings for the VCF Operations API.
About the Schema Reference
The VCF Operations REST API documentation includes reference material for all elements, types, queries, and
operations in the VCF Operations API. It also includes the schema definition files.
Swagger-based API documentation is available with the product, with the capability of making REST API calls right from
the landing page.
To access the API documentation, use the URL of your VCF Operations cloud proxy. For example, if the URL of your
cloud proxy is https://cloudproxy.vmware.com, the API reference is available from: https://cloudproxy.vmware.com/suite-
api/doc/swagger-ui.html
Note:
You must use your cloud proxy IP or FDQN in the url to access the API documentation.
Language-specific client bindings are available from:
https://<your-cloud-proxy-fqdn>/suite-api/
Authorize VCF Operations API
To perform API calls, you must authorize your VCF Operations cloud proxy. You can perform basic authorization and
enter the Username, Password, and the Auth Source, or perform token based authorization and enter the Ops Token
(apikey) value, and then click Authorize.
About the VCF Operations API Examples
You can view the VCF Operations API from Developer Center > APIs & SDKs > Operations API and then click API
Documentation. Browse the VCF Operations API and try the different API calls to automate available features. For
example to get all the Collectors registered with the VCF Operations system, use the following API:
GET/api/collectors/{id}/adapters
All examples include HTTP requests and responses. These examples show the workflow and content associated with
operations such as creating and querying for information about objects in your monitored environment.
Broadcom 4248

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Example request bodies are in JSON. Request headers required by the VCF Operations API are included in example
requests that are not fragments of a larger example.
Most example responses show only those elements and attributes that are relevant to the operation being discussed.
Ellipses (...) indicate omitted content within response bodies.
Cloud Proxy FAQ
This topic covers some frequently asked questions about VCF Operations cloud proxy.
Configuration
1. What are the prerequisites for setting up a cloud proxy account?
Prerequisites are given in the topic, Add a Cloud Proxy.
2. What does one-way connection mean?
Outbound connections are initiated from cloud proxy to VCF Operations, over . Cloud proxy can also
https/443
facilitate vCenter actions.
3. Which ports should be opened?
The most up-to-date technical information about ports can be found on Ports and Protocols.
4. Which ports should be allowed for incoming traffic to cloud proxy?
Allow port 443 https protocol for push model adapters like application monitoring or Suite-API on cloud proxy. Allow
ports 4505 and 4506 via TCP protocol for application monitoring. Allow the VRRP protocol for intercommunication
between cloud proxies in a application monitoring high availability activated cloud proxy group.
5. How do I edit environment settings for cloud proxy?
You can edit vApp options. For more information, see Edit OVF Details for a Virtual Machine.
6. How are trusted certificates managed?
Certificates are managed by cloud proxies. But for any additional proxy servers with SSL communication, you need to
provide certificate(s) in the cloud proxy vApp options.
7. What credential is used to login to cloud proxy?
You can login as the “root” user. You are expected to set a new password on the first login to cloud proxy VM.
SSH access is disabled by default, so the first login must be done via the vCenter console. You can run the following
command to start SSH service:
systemctl start sshd
systemctl enable sshd
To reset password, see the Broadcom knowledge base article 325005.
8. Will I be notified if the connection between cloud proxy and VCF Operations breaks down?
You can configure alerts/notifications on the VCF Operations cloud proxy object. For more information, see Monitoring
the Health of Cloud Proxies.
VCF Operations automatically generates notifications for the following scenarios:
• Cloud proxy is not reachable.
• Cloud proxy is nearing sizing limits.
9. How do I change account for cloud proxy?
You can edit vApp options. For more information, see Edit OVF Details for a Virtual Machine.
10.How can I check the status of cloud proxy?
For more information, see Monitoring the Health of Cloud Proxies.
11.Should I use Remote Collector or cloud proxy for monitoring?
VMware recommends that you use cloud proxy to take advantage of the latest enhancements. Also, application
monitoring, HA of cloud proxy groups, and data persistence are only supported through cloud proxy.
Sizing
1. How should I size the cloud proxy?
For information on sizing, see the Broadcom knowledge base article 318402.
Broadcom 4249

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Upgrade
1. How do I upgrade cloud proxy?
Cloud proxy is upgraded as part of VCF Operations upgrade. In case the upgrade fails, see the Broadcom knowledge
base article 344168.
High Availability
1. Is high availability supported?
Cloud proxy supports high availability. You can add multiple cloud proxies to a cloud proxy group. If the collecting cloud
proxy fails or gets disconnected, collection can be picked up by another proxy in the group.
Note:
Since the failover is initiated after a period of 10 minutes, few collection cycles are lost.
To troubleshoot cloud proxy issues, see Cloud Proxy Troubleshooting.

Configuring Collector Groups
VCF Operations uses collectors like cloud proxies to manage cloud account processes such as gathering metrics from
objects. You can select a single cloud proxy or a cloud proxy group when configuring a cloud account.
If there are cloud proxies in your environment, you can create a collector group, and add the cloud proxies to the group.
When you assign an account to a collector group, that account can use any collector in the group. Use collector groups to
achieve resiliency in cases where the collector experiences network interruption or becomes unavailable. If this occurs,
and the collector is part of a group, the total workload is redistributed among all the collectors in the group, reducing the
workload on each collector. For more information, see Configuring Cloud Proxies in VCF Operations.
You can add, edit, or remove collector groups in VCF Operations, and re-balance your cloud accounts.
Re-balancing a Cloud Account
Re-balancing of your cloud accounts is not intended to provide equally distributed cloud accounts across each collector
in the collector group. The re-balancing action considers the number of resources that each cloud account collects to
determine the re-balancing placement. The re-balancing happens at the cloud account, which can result in several small
cloud accounts on a single collector, and a single huge cloud account on another collector, in your VCF Operations
instance.
Re-balancing your collector groups can add a significant load on the entire cluster. Moving cloud accounts from one
collector to another collector requires that VCF Operations stops the cloud account and all its resources on the source
collector, then starts them on the target collector.
If a collector fails to respond or loses connectivity to the cluster, VCF Operations starts automated re-balancing in the
collector group. All other user-initiated manual operations on the collector, such as stopping or restarting the collector
manually, do not result in automated re-balancing.
If one of the collectors fails to respond, or if it loses network connectivity, VCF Operations performs automated re-
balancing. In cases of automated re-balancing, to properly re-balance the collector group, you must have spare capacity
on the collectors in the collector group.
Where You Manage Collector Groups
In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Home and in the left navigation pane, click Administration > Cloud
Proxies, and then click the Collector Groups tab.

Shutdown and Startup of VMware Cloud Foundation
Shutting down VMware Cloud Foundation, for example, during hardware or power maintenance, and then starting it up
must be done in a way that prevents data loss or appliance malfunction, and supports collection of troubleshooting data.
You follow a strict order and steps for shutdown and startup of the VMware Cloud Foundation management components.
Shutting Down VMware Cloud Foundation
To avoid data loss and maintain the SDDC components operational, you follow a specific order when shutting down the
management virtual machines in VCF.
• Verify that you have complete backups of all management components. See Component Backup and Restore of
VMware Cloud Foundation.
• Verify that the management virtual machines are not running on snapshots.
• If a vSphere Storage APIs for Data Protection (VADP) based backup solution is running on the management clusters,
verify that the solution is properly shut down by following the vendor guidance.
• To reduce the startup time before you shut down the management virtual machines, migrate the vCenter instance for
the management domain to the first VMware ESX host in the default management cluster in the management domain.
You shut down the customer workloads and the management components for the workload domains before you shut
down the components for the management domain. If you have multiple VCF Instances, you start with the instances that
do not run VCF Operations and VCF Automation. The VCF Instance that is running VCF Operations must be the last
instance to shut down.
If the NSX Manager cluster and NSX Edge cluster are shared with other workload domains, shut down the NSX Manager
and NSX Edge clusters as part of the shutdown of the first workload domain.
In this chapter:
• Shut Down a Workload Domain
• Shut Down the Management Domain
Shut Down a Workload Domain
You shut down the components of a workload domain that runs virtualized workloads in VCF in a specific order to keep
components operational by maintaining the necessary infrastructure, networking, and management services as long as
possible before shutdown.
You shut down the management components for the workload domains before you shut down the components for the
management domain.
If the NSX Manager cluster and NSX Edge or Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster are shared with other workload
domains, follow this general order:
1. Shut down the consumer workloads in all workload domains that share the NSX Manager instance. Otherwise, all NSX
networking services in the consumer workloads will be interrupted when you shut down NSX Manager.
2. Shut down the workload domain that runs the shared NSX Edge nodes.
3. Shut down the other workload domains.
Broadcom 4259

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Shutdown Order for a Workload Domain
Table 1154: Shutdown Order for a Workload Domain
Shutdown Order SDDC Component
1 Virtualized customer workloads
2 Protection and recovery for the workload domain *
4 If deployed in the workload domain, NSX Edge or VNA nodes
5 NSX Manager nodes for the workload domain
7 ESX hosts in the workload domain
8 vCenter for the workload domain
* The information on the shutdown steps is available in another documentation.
Shut Down the NSX Edge or VNA Nodes in the Workload Domain
You begin shutting down the NSX infrastructure in a workload domain in VCF by shutting down the NSX Edge nodes that
provide north-south traffic connectivity between the physical data center networks and the NSX SDN networks
1. Identify the vCenter instance that runs NSX Edge or VNA nodes.
2. Log in to vCenter for the workload domain at as a user with the Administrator role.
https://<vcenter_fqdn>/ui
3. In the VMs and Templates inventory, locate the NSX Edge or VNA appliance.
4. Right-click the NSX Edge or VNA appliance and select Power > Shut down Guest OS.
5. Repeat the steps for the remaining NSX Edge or VNA appliances in the VCF domain.
Shut Down the NSX Manager Nodes in a Workload Domain
You continue shutting down the NSX infrastructure for the workload domain by shutting down the NSX Manager VM or
cluster by using the vSphere Client.
1. Log in to the management domain vCenter at as administrator@vsphere.local.
https://<vcenter_fqdn>/ui
2. In the VMs and Templates inventory, locate an NSX Manager appliance.
3. Right-click the NSX Manager appliance and select Power > Shut down Guest OS.
4. In the confirmation dialog box, click Yes.
This operation takes several minutes to complete.
5. Repeat the steps for the remaining NSX Manager appliances.
Shut Down the ESX Hosts in a Workload Domain
You follow specific steps according to the principal storage of the clusters in the workload domain.
Save the Credentials for the ESX Hosts and vCenter for the Workload Domain
Before you shut down the workload domain, get the credentials for the workload domain hosts and vCenter and save
them. You might need these credentials to shut down the ESX hosts and then to start them and vCenter back up.
Shut Down vSAN and the ESX Hosts in a Workload Domain
You use the vSAN shutdown cluster wizard in the vSphere Client to shut down gracefully the vSAN clusters in a workload
domain. The wizard shuts down the vSAN storage and the ESX hosts added to the cluster.
You perform this operation on all vSAN clusters in all workload domains.
Broadcom 4260

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Identify the vCenter instance that runs the vCenter VM for this workload domain.
CAUTION:
If the vCenter VM is running on the infrastructure that it manages, note down the cluster in which it is running.
This cluster must be stopped last.
2. Log in to vCenter for the workload domain at as a user with the Administrator role.
https://<vcenter_fqdn>/ui
3. For a vSAN cluster, verify the vSAN health and resynchronization status.
a) Select the cluster and click the Monitor tab.
b) In the left pane, navigate to vSAN > Skyline health and verify the status of each vSAN health check category.
c) In the left pane, under vSAN > Resyncing objects, verify that all synchronization tasks are complete.
4. If any member host is in lockdown mode, add the host's root account to the Exception Users list.
a) Select the host in the inventory and click the Configure tab.
b) In the left pane, select System > Security Profile.
c) In the Lockdown Mode pane, click the Edit button.
d) On the Exception Users page, enter and click Add User.
root
e) Click OK.
5. Shut down the vSAN cluster.
a) In the inventory, right-click the vSAN cluster and select vSAN > Shutdown cluster.
b) In the Shutdown Cluster wizard, verify that all pre-checks are green and click Next.
c) Review the vCenter Server notice and click Next.
d) If vCenter is running on the selected cluster, note the orchestration host details.
Connection to vCenter is lost because the vSAN shutdown cluster wizard shuts it down. The shutdown operation is
complete after all ESXi hosts are stopped.
e) Enter a reason for performing the shutdown, and click Shutdown.
6. Repeat Step 3 to Step 5 for other vSAN clusters in the domain.
Shut Down ESX Hosts with NFS or Fibre Channel Storage in a Workload Domain
You use the vSphere Client to shut down gracefully the clusters with non-vSAN in a workload domain.
1. Identify the vCenter instance that runs the vCenter appliance for this workload domain.
CAUTION:
This cluster must be shut down last.

https://<vcenter_fqdn>/ui
3. In the Hosts and Clusters inventory, for a cluster that is not running the vCenter appliance for the workload domain,
put all hosts in the cluster in maintenance mode.
These operations take several minutes to complete.
4. If a cluster is running the vCenter appliance, note down the host on which it is running and put all hosts in the cluster
but this one in maintenance mode.
You need the details about this host during the startup process too.
5. Shut down the hosts in maintenance mode
a) Select the cluster and click the Hosts tab.
b) Select all hosts that are in maintenance mode, right-click Power > Shut Down.
This operation takes several minutes to complete

6. Repeat Step 3 to Step 4 for all clusters with non-vSAN storage in the domain.

a) Log in to the ESX host at as a user with the Administrator role.
https://<esx_fqdn>
b) In the left plane, click Virtual Machines.
c) Locate the vCenter appliance for the workload domain.
d) Right-click the appliance and select Power > Shut down Guest OS.
e) In the confirmation dialog box, click Yes.

f) In the left plane, right-click on Host > Shut down.
g) Read the warning and click Shut down.
You lose connectivity to the ESX host. The shut down operation takes several minutes to complete.

Follow vendor 's documentation to check if there are active clients and how to shut it down in a safe manner.
Shut Down the vCenter Appliance for a Workload Domain
If the vCenter appliance is running on a different infrastructure than the one it manages, to shut down the vCenter
appliance for a workload domain in VCF, you use the vSphere Client.
Verify that all ESX hosts in all clusters are stopped and are disconnected.
If the vCenter appliance is running on the infrastructure that it manages, you stop it as part of the shutdown operation for
ESX hosts.
1. Identify the vCenter instance that runs the vCenter appliance for this workload domain.
2. Log in to vCenter for the management or workload domain at as a user with the
https://<vcenter_fqdn>/ui
Administrator role.
3. Shut down vCenter Server.
a) Locate the vCenter virtual machine for the workload domain.
b) Right-click the virtual machine and select Power > Shut down Guest OS.
c) In the confirmation dialog box, click Yes.

Shut Down the Management Domain
You shut down the components of the management domain in VCF in a specific order to keep components operational by
maintaining the necessary infrastructure, networking, and management services as long as possible before shutdown.
After you shut down the components in all workload domains, you begin shutting down the management domain.
Shutdown Order for the Management Domain
Note:
If your VCF Instance is deployed without workload domains, shut down any customer workloads or additional
virtual machines in the management domain before you proceed with the shutdown order of the management
components.
You shut down VMware Live Site Recovery after you shut down the management components that can be failed over
between the VCF Instances. You also shut VMware Live Site Recovery down as late as possible to have the management
virtual machines that are protected as long as possible if a disaster event occurs. The virtual machines in the paired VCF
Instance become unprotected after you shut downVMware Live Site Recovery in the current VCF Instance.
Broadcom 4262

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
CAUTION:
If you plan to shut down all VCF Instances in a VCF fleet, you must shut down the first VCF Instance, which is
hosting VCF Operations, last.

2 VCF Operations for networks
3 Cloud proxy
4 License server
5 VCF management services
6 VCF Operations
7 Protection and recovery for the management domain *
8 If deployed in the management domain, NSX Edge or VNA nodes
9 NSX Manager
10 SDDC Manager

• Shut Down ESX Hosts with NFS or Fibre Channel Storage in the Management Domain

Starting Up VMware Cloud Foundation
To maintain the components integration and avoid operation faults, you follow a specified order to start up the
management virtual machines in VMware Cloud Foundation.
• Verify that external services such as Storage, Active Directory, DNS, NTP, SMTP, and FTP or SFTP are available.
• If a vSphere Storage APIs for Data Protection (VADP) based backup solution is deployed on the default management
cluster, verify that the solution is properly started and operational according to the vendor guidance.
You start the management components for the management domain first. Then, you start the management components
for the workload domains and the customer workloads.
If the NSX Manager cluster and NSX Edge cluster are shared with other workload domains, start the other workload
domains first. Start up NSX Manager and NSX Edge nodes as part of the startup of the last workload domain.
In this chapter:
• Start the Management Domain
• Start a Workload Domain
Start the Management Domain
You start the management components for the management domain in a specific order to provide the necessary
infrastructure, networking, and management services before powering on the components for cloud management.
You start the management components for the management domain first. Then, you start the management components
for the workload domains and the customer workloads.
CAUTION:
If you have shut down all VCF Instances in a VCF fleet, you must first start the VCF Instance, which is running
VCF Operations.
Startup Order for the Management Domain
You start the virtual infrastructure of the management domain that hosts VCF Operations and VCF Automation first.
Broadcom 4268

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Table 1156: Startup Order for the Management Domain
Startup Order SDDC Component
1 • Start vSAN and the ESX Hosts in the Management Domain
• Start ESX Hosts with NFS or Fibre Channel Storage in the
Management Domain
2 SDDC Manager
3 NSX Manager
4 If deployed in the management domain, NSX Edge or VNA nodes
5 Protection and recovery
6 VCF Operations
7 VCF management services
8 License server
9 Cloud proxy
10 VCF Operations for networks
11 VCF Automation
Start the ESX Hosts and vCenter in the Management Domain
You start the ESX hosts using an out-of-band management interface, such as, ILO or iDRAC to connect to the hosts and
power them on.
Important:
You perform this operation on all clusters in the management domain. Start the cluster where the management
vCenter must be running first.

Start a Workload Domain
You start the management components for a workload domain in a specific order to provide the necessary infrastructure,
networking, and management services.
You start the management components for the management domain first. Then, you start the management components
for the workload domains and the customer workloads.
If the NSX Manager cluster and NSX Edge or Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster are shared across workload
domains, follow this general order:
1. Start the other workload domains.
2. Start the workload domain that runs the shared NSX Edge nodes.
3. Start the customer workloads that rely on NSX services.

9 Virtualized customer workloads
* The information on the startup steps is available in another documentation.

Component Backup and Restore of VMware Cloud Foundation
Regularly backing up the management components of a VMware Cloud Foundation platform is essential to ensure
the resilience and continuity of your VCF private cloud. In the event of data loss or system failure, having up-to-date
backups allows for efficient restoration of critical services, minimizing downtime and maintaining operational integrity.
Implementing a consistent backup strategy safeguards your infrastructure against unforeseen disruptions and supports
effective disaster.
You implement scheduled backups to prepare for:
• A critical failure of a management component.
• An upgrade of a management component.
• A certificate update of a management component.
In addition, as a best practice, you can take on-demand manual backups in the following use cases:
• After a successful recovery operation.
• After resolving asynchronously reported errors in SDDC components.
• After resolving an incomplete workflow in SDDC Manager.
• After noting the failure of a scheduled backup of an SDDC component.
• Immediately before performing a system upgrade.
It is recommended that you configure an external SFTP server as a backup location for the following reasons:
• An external SFTP server is a prerequisite for restoring SDDC Manager file-based backups.
• Using an external SFTP server provides better protection against failures because it decouples NSX backups from
SDDC Manager.
Prerequisites
Before performing backup and restore operations in your VMware Cloud Foundation platform, ensure the following
requirements are met:
General Requirements:
• Administrator permissions to VMware Cloud Foundation platform components.
• A stable network connection between the management domain and backup storage.
• Sufficient storage capacity to accommodate backup data.
• A defined backup and retention policy aligned with best practices or organizational requirements.
• Access to an image-level backup solution for required components.
• Sufficient time allowed between backup operations so that a new backup request is not submitted when another
backup of the same environment is in progress.
Backup-Specific Requirements:
• Configure and validate an external backup target based on individual management component requirements.
• Ensure all management components, including SDDC Manager, vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations, and VCF
Automation, are configured with a regular backup schedule and retention policy.
Restore-Specific Requirements:
• Access to the most recent backup files.
Broadcom 4277

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
•
In place infrastructure for restoring.
• Proper sequencing and verification of component restoration to maintain dependencies and system integrity.

Configure an External SFTP Server for VCF Management Services and VCF Automation
Backups
To allow for backup and restore of VCF management services and VCF Automation, you configure an SFTP target in
VCF Operations. This designated backup location is also used for automatic backups that are generated during patching
and upgrade procedures. This configuration is a prerequisite for patching or upgrading VCF management services
components, and for scheduled backups.
Verify that no post-deployment actions are in progress for VCF Automation or any of the following VCF management
services:
• Log management
• Identity broker
• Software depot
• Fleet lifecycle
• SDDC lifecycle
• Real-time metrics
• Salt RaaS
Running tasks in parallel can cause the SFTP configuration to fail.
• Host Key algorithms: At least one of the following
– ssh-ed25519
– rsa-sha2-512
– rsa-sha2-256
1. Log in to the VCF Operations interface at as a user assigned the Administrator
https://<vcf_operations_fqdn>
role.
2. Navigate to Build > Lifecycle.
3. In the Lifecycle navigation, select VCF Management.
4. On the VCF Management page, select the Backup & Restore tab.
5. Click Add Backup Location.
6. Enter the following information, click Add to fetch the fingerprint, then click Confirm Fingerprint, and click Add to
save the configuration.
Table 1158: SFTP Configuration
Configuration Value
VCF Instance Select the target VCF Instance.
SFTP Host FQDN or IP Address The FQDN or IP Address of the SFTP server.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration Value
Port 22
Note:
With VCF 9.1.1 and later, you can configure a custom SFTP port.
Username A service account with privileges to the SFTP server.
For example: svc-vcf-bck.
Password The password for the username provided.
Backup directory The directory on the SFTP server where backups are saved.
For example: /backups/.
Important:
The SFTP user must have read access to all sub-directories of the backup directory
path.
Encryption passphrase The encryption passphrase used to encrypt the backup data.
Important:
The encryption passphrase should be stored safely as it is required during the
restore process.
Note:
Before saving, ensure that the SFTP host, port, username, and password are correct and validated. Any incorrect
information that you enter propagates to all VCF management services components and causes the SFTP
configuration to fail.
The SFTP server configuration is automatically pushed to the VCF management services and VCF Automation instances.
Note:
If there is a failure, an option to Retry appears. Click Refresh to fetch the status of the SFTP configuration and
display it in the UI.
Configure an External SFTP Server for SDDC Manager and NSX Manager Backups
By default, SDDC Manager and NSX Manager backups are stored on the SDDC Manager appliance. Change the
destination of the backups to an external SFTP server.
• The external SFTP server must support a 256-bit length ECDSA SSH public key.
• The external SFTP server must support a 2048-bit length RSA SSH public key
• You will need the SHA256 fingerprint of RSA key of the SFTP server.
• Host Key algorithms: At least one of rsa-sha2-512 or rsa-sha2-256 and one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-
nistp384, or ecdsa-sha2-nistp521.
• On servers running openSSH 9.8 or later, the server should exclude the SDDC Manager and NSX Manager IPs from
this list. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
– PerSourcePenaltyExemptList <SDDC Manager IP> <NSX Manager IP>
