Managing Custom Object Groups in VCF Operations
A custom object group is a container that includes one or more objects. VCF Operations uses custom groups to collect
data from the objects in the group, and report on the data collected.
Why Use Custom Object Groups?
You use groups to categorize your objects and have the system collect data from the groups of objects and display the
results in dashboards and views according to the way you define the data to appear.
You can create static groups of objects, or dynamic groups with criteria that determine group membership as VCF
Operations discovers and collects data from new objects added to the environment.
VCF Operations provides commonly used object group types, such as World, Environment, and Licensing. The system
uses the object group types to categorize groups of objects. You assign a group type to each group so that you can
categorize and organize the groups of objects that you create.
Types of Custom Object Groups
When you create custom groups, you can use rules to apply dynamic membership of objects to the group, or you can
manually add the objects to the group. When you add an adapter, the groups associated with the adapter become
available in VCF Operations.
• Dynamic group membership. To dynamically update the membership of objects in a group, define rules when you
create a group. VCF Operations adds objects to the group based on the criteria that you define.
• Mixed membership, which includes dynamic and manual.
• Manual group membership. From the inventory of objects, you select objects to add as members to the group.
• Groups associated with adapters. Each adapter manages the membership of the group. For example, the vCenter
Server adapter adds groups such as datastore, host, and network, for the container objects in the vSphere inventory.
To modify these groups, you must do so in the adapter.
Administrators of VCF Operations can set advanced permissions on custom groups. Users who have privileges to create
groups can create custom groups of objects and have VCF Operations apply a policy to each group to collect data from
the objects and report the results in dashboards and views.
When you create a custom group, and assign a policy to the group, the system uses the criteria defined in the applied
policy to collect data from and analyze the objects in the group. VCF Operations reports on the status, problems, and
recommendations for those objects based on the settings in the policy.
Note:
Only custom groups defined explicitly by users can be exported from or imported to VCF Operations. Users are
able to export or import multiple custom groups. Once an import function has been executed, the user must check
to determine if a policy or policies should be associated with the imported group. Export-import operations are
available for user defined (created explicitly by user) custom groups only.
How Policies Help VCF Operations Report On Object Groups
When you apply a policy to an object group, VCF Operations uses threshold settings, metrics, super metrics, attributes,
properties, alert definitions, and symptom definitions that you activated in the policy to collect data from the objects in the
group, and report the results in dashboards and views.
When you create a new object group, you have the option to apply a policy to the group.
• To associate a policy with the custom object group, select the policy in the group creation wizard.
• To not associate a specific policy with the object group, leave the policy selection blank. The custom object group will
be associated with the default policy. If the default policy changes, this object group will be associated with the new
default policy.
VCF Operations applies policies in priority order, as they appear on the Active Policies tab. When you establish the priority
for your policies, VCF Operations applies the configured settings in the policies according to the policy rank order to
analyze and report on your objects. To change the priority of a policy, you click and drag a policy row. The default policy
Broadcom 4742

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
is always kept at the bottom of the priority list, and the remaining list of active policies starts at priority 1, which indicates
the highest priority policy. When you assign an object to be a member of multiple object groups, and you assign a different
policy to each object group, VCF Operations associates the highest ranking policy with that object.
Object Group Types in VCF Operations
An object group type is an identifier that you apply to a specific group of objects in your environment to categorize them.
You can add new group types, and apply them to groups of objects so that VCF Operations can collect data from the
object group and display the results in the dashboards and views.
How the Group Types Work
Use group types to categorize your objects so that the system can apply policies to them to track, and display specific
status, such as alerts, workload, faults, risk, and so on.
When you create a new group type, VCF Operations adds it to the existing list of group types, and creates a new folder
with the name of your group type in the Environment Custom Groups list.
When you create a new group of objects, you assign a group type to that group of objects. You add objects from the
inventory trees to your custom group, then create your dashboard, add widgets to the dashboard, and configure the
widgets to display the data collected from the objects in the group. You can then monitor and manage the objects.
You can apply a group type to a group of objects that you create manually, or to object groups that you cannot modify,
such those added by adapters. Each adapter that you add to VCF Operations adds one or more static groups of objects to
group the data received from the adapter sources.
The list of group types appears in the Content area under Group Types. The custom object groups appear in the
Environment area under Custom Groups.
Where You Create and Modify a Group Type
In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Inventory and then
click Custom Group and Datacenters. Click Group Types next to custom groups. You can add, edit, delete, and select
groups from the group types page.
Group Type Options
You can add, edit, or delete group types. You cannot edit group types that are created by adapters.
Groups Tab on the Environment Overview Pane
Groups are containers that can contain any number and type of objects in your environment. VCF Operations collects
data from the objects in the group and displays the results in dashboards and views that you define.
How Groups Work
Groups are installed with VCF Operations, created by an adapter, or created by a user. Based on the group criteria, you
can use groups to organize your environment and monitor all objects in the group together. You can also assign policies to
groups and make group membership dynamic.
For example, if you have a set of vSphere hosts and you do not want to generate alerts when the host goes into
maintenance mode, you can put the vSphere hosts in a group and assign a policy that includes a maintenance schedule
setting. During the maintenance period, VCF Operations ignores any metrics for those objects and does not generate any
alerts. After the maintenance period ends, VCF Operations returns to monitoring the objects and generates alerts if an
outage occurs.
Where You Find Custom Groups
In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administration >
Configurations, and then click the Custom Groups tile.

Custom Object Groups Workspace
You can create and edit custom groups of objects to have VCF Operations collect data from the objects and display the
results in the dashboards and views so that you can monitor your objects and take action on them when problems occur.
How the Custom Groups Workspace Works
When you create a new object group, you define a meaningful group name, and select the group type. To associate the
custom object group with a policy for analysis, you select the policy in the group creation wizard. You can leave the policy
selection blank to not associate a policy with the object group. When the policy selection is blank, the custom object group
is associated with the policy that is designated as the default policy.
You select the object types, and determine whether membership in the object group is static, dynamic, or a combination of
static and dynamic membership.
• To create a static object group, you add objects to the group. You do not include criteria for object membership.
• To create a dynamic object group that VCF Operations updates based on specific criteria, you select the object type
and define membership criteria for the group based on metrics, relationships, and properties.
When you add objects to a custom object group, a new folder appears in the Custom Groups navigation pane on the left,
and includes the member objects.
Where You Create and Modify Object Groups
To create or modify static or dynamic object groups, or object groups that have a combination of static and dynamic
membership, in the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Broadcom 4744

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Administration > Configurations, and then click the Custom Groups tile. The Custom Groups page displays a list of
custom object groups, and the object groups for adapters added to VCF Operations.
To edit existing groups, select a group, and then click the vertical ellipsis and select Edit.
Custom Object Groups Workspace to Create a New Group
You can create a new object group, define custom properties, assign a group type and objects to the group. When you
create the group, you can assign a policy, or leave the policy selection blank to apply the default policy. VCF Operations
collects data from the objects in the group based on the settings in the policy that is associated with the group. The results
appear in the dashboards and views.
Where You Assign Custom Group Type, Policy, and Membership
To assign the group type, policy, and membership, in the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in
the left navigation pane, click Administration > Configurations, and then click the Custom Groups tile. Click Add to
add a new group. In the New Group workspace, you can define the membership criteria, and select the objects to include
or exclude.
To associate a policy with the custom object group, select the policy in the group creation wizard. To not associate a
specific policy with the object group, leave the policy selection blank. The custom object group will be associated with the
default policy. If the default policy changes, this object group will be associated with the new default policy.

Inventory Details and Tabs
The organization of the tabs and options in VCF Operations provides a built-in workflow that you can use when you work
with objects in your environment.
The tabs, Summary, Metrics, Alerts, Topology, Capacity, and so on, provide progressive levels of detail about the
selected object. As you work through the tabs, starting with the high level Summary and Alerts tabs, you see the general
state of an object. The Environment tab provides you with specific data about the object.

list of the inventory in your VCF Operations environment where the objects are grouped logically. When you select an
object from the detailed view, you see information such as summary information, metrics, alerts, capacity, and other
details specific to the selected object.

Inventory Detailed View
The Inventory detailed view is a panel that displays logical grouping/hierarchies for the vCenter and and VCF Instances
that are configured in the VCF Operations environment. You can view either a tree or list view and then select the object
to view object related information.
To access the Inventory Detailed View, in the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left
navigation pane click Inventory, and then click on a vCenter instance from the data grid or click Detailed View from the
top. You will see the Inventory panel with the Inventory detailed view.

Evaluating Object Information Using Badge Alerts and the Summary Tab
The Summary tab that is associated with the other object tabs summarizes Heath, Risk, and Efficiency badge alerts for
the selected object and displays the top alerts that lead to the current state.
Use this tab as an overview of alerts for an object, object group, or application - to evaluate the effect that alerts are
having on an object and to begin troubleshooting problems. For more detail on the badge Alerts, click Badge Alerts,
further to the right on the tool bar.
Badge Alert Types
The Health, Risk, and Efficiency badge states are based on the impact of the generated alerts for the selected object.
• Health alerts indicate problems that affect the health of your environment.
• Risk alerts indicate problems that are not immediate threats.
• Efficiency alerts tell you where you can improve performance or reclaim resources.
Alerts for an Object or an Object Group
For a single object, the Top alerts are the alerts generated for the object. The Top Alerts for Children are the alerts
generated for any child or other descendant objects in the currently selected navigation hierarchy. For example, if you are
working with a host object in the vSphere Host and Clusters navigation hierarchy, children can include virtual machines
and datastores.
Object groups can include one object type, such as hosts, or multiple objects types, such as hosts, virtual machines, and
datastores. When you are working with object groups, all the group member objects are children of the group container.
The most critical generated alerts for the member objects appear as Top Alerts for Children.
For an object group, the only Top Alerts that might be generated are the predefined group population alerts. If the average
health is above the Warning, Immediate, or Critical threshold, a group population alert considers the health of all group
Broadcom 4749

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
members and is triggered. If a group population alert is generated, the alert affects the badge score and color. If a group
population alert is not generated, then the badges are green. This behavior is because an object group is a container for
other objects.
Summary Tab and Related Hierarchies
The alerts that appear on the Summary tab for an object can vary depending on the currently selected hierarchy in the
Related Hierarchies in the left pane.
Depending on the selected hierarchy, you see different alerts and relationships on the Summary tab for an object. The
current focus object name is on the center pane title bar, but the children alerts depend on the relationships that the
highlighted hierarchy defined in the Related Hierarchies list in the upper left pane. For example, if you are working with
a host object relative to virtual machines in the Hosts and Clusters hierarchy, then children commonly include virtual
machines and datastores. But if you are working with the same host as a member of an object group, then any alerts
on virtual machines that are also members of the group do not appear. The alerts do not appear because the host and
the virtual machines are considered children of the group and peers among each other. In this example, the focus of the
Summary tab is the host in the context of the group, not the Hosts and Clusters hierarchy.
Summary Tab Evaluation Techniques
You can evaluate the state of objects, starting with the Summary tab, by selecting an object or object group, click the
alerts on the Summary tab, and resolve the problems that the alert indicates.

the impact that alerts are having on the object and use the information to begin troubleshooting problems.

Evaluating Metric Information
The Metrics tab provides a relationship map and user-defined metric charts. The topological map helps you evaluate
objects in the context of their place in your environment topology. The metric charts are based on the metrics for the
selected object that you think helps identify the possible cause of a problem in your environment.
Although you might be investigating problems with a single object, for example, a host system, the relationship map allows
you to see the host in the context of parent and child objects. It also works as a hierarchical navigation system. If you
double-click an object in the map, that object becomes the focus of the map. The available metrics for the object become
active in the lower-left pane.
Note:
The yellow diamond icon next to the metric indicates dynamic threshold breach, the blue diamond icon next to the
metric indicates the metric value is within threshold.
You can also build your own set of metric charts. You select the objects and metrics that provide you with a detailed view
of changes to different metrics for a single object, or for related objects over time.
Where available, the Metrics tab provides pre-defined sets of metrics to help you when looking at a specific aspect of an
object. For example, if you have a problem with a host, access the most relevant information about the host by looking
at the metrics displayed in the pre-defined lists. You can edit these groups of metrics, and create additional groups, by
dragging and dropping metrics and properties from the All Metrics and All Properties lists.
Broadcom 4772

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Where You Find the Metrics Tab
• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Inventory and then
select a group, custom data center, application, or inventory object.
Create Metric Charts When You Troubleshoot a Virtual Machine Problem
You create a custom group of metric charts when you troubleshoot a problem with a virtual machine so that you can
compare different metrics. The level of detail that you can create using the Metrics tab, can contribute significantly to
your effort to find the root cause of a problem.
As an administrator investigating a performance problem with a virtual machine, you determined that you must see
detailed charts about the following reported symptoms.
• Guest file system overall disk space usage reaching critical limit
• Guest partition disk space usage
The following method of evaluating problems using the Metrics tab is provided as an example for using VCF Operations
and is not definitive. Your troubleshooting skills and your knowledge of the particulars of your environment determine
which methods work for you.
1. Enter the name of the virtual machine in the Search text box on the menu bar.
In this example, the virtual machine name is .
sales-10-dk
2. Click the Metrics tab.
3. In the relationship topology map, click the virtual machine, dk-new-10.
The metrics list, located in the left of the center pane, displays virtual machine metrics.
4. On the chart toolbar, click Date Control and select a time that is on or before the symptoms were triggered.
5. Add metric charts to the display area for the virtual machine.
a) In the metric list, select Guest Files System Stats > Total Guest File System Free (GB) and double-click the
metric name.
b) To add the guest partition, for example, C:\, select Guest Files System Stats > C:\ > Guest File System Free
(GB) and double-click the metric name.
c) To add disk space for comparison, select Disk Space > Capacity Remaining (%) and double-click the metric
name.
6. Compare the charts.
You can see a decrease in the file system free space, and that the virtual machine disk space capacity remaining is
decreasing at a steady rate. You determine that you must add disk space to the virtual machine. However, you do not
know if the datastore can support the change to the virtual machine.
7. Add the datastore capacity chart to the charts.
a) In the topology map, double-click the host.
The topology map refreshes with the host as the focus object.
b) Click the datastore.
c) In the metric list, which is updated to display datastore metrics, select Capacity > Available Space (GB) and
double-click the metric name.
8. To determine if sufficient capacity is available on the datastore to support increasing the disk space on the virtual
machine, review the datastore capacity chart.
You know that you must increase the size of the virtual disk on the virtual machine.
Expand the virtual disk on the virtual machine and assign it to stressed partitions. Click Actions, on the object title bar,
and view the virtual machine in the vSphere Web Client.
Broadcom 4773

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Troubleshooting with the Metrics Tab
The Metrics tab provides a relationship graph and metric charts. The relationship graph helps you evaluate objects in the
context of their place in your environment topology. Metric charts are based on the metrics for the active map object that
you think can help you identify the cause of a problem.
How the Metrics Tab Works
You can double-click any object in the graph and view the specific parent-child objects for the focus object. If you point
to an object icon, you can see the health, risk, and efficiency details. You can also click the Alerts link for the number of
generated alerts. Click the purple icon to view the child relationships of the object. If you double-click an object icon, the
selected object becomes the focus of the map. The graph is updated for the selected object, and the metrics list shows
only the metrics for the selected object.
Using the metrics list, you create charts based on metrics that you think can help you investigate problems. You customize
the charts to evaluate the data in detail. To save the configured charts, you create a dashboard using the toolbar option.
Where available, the metrics list also displays pre-defined groups of metrics that contain the most relevant metrics for the
selected object. You can edit these groups, and create your own customized groups of metrics by dragging and dropping
metrics and properties from the All Metrics and All Properties lists.
Where You Find the Metrics Tab
• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Inventory and then
select a group, custom data center, application, or inventory object.
• Alternatively, in the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Inventory and then use the hierarchies in the left pane to locate the objects that you want.
Edit Metric State
The edit metric state option allows you activate, deactivate, or inherit metric state, DT state and KPI state. You can use the
All Filter option to search and edit the metrics based on the following criteria.
• Name
• State
• Instanced State
• DT State
• KPI State
• Show Only Supermetrics
• Local Changes
• Unsaved Changes

Table 1278: Metric Chart Toolbar
Option Description
Split Charts Displays each metric in a separate chart.

for seeing how the total or sum of the metric values vary
over time. To view the stacked chart, ensure that the split
chart option is turned off.
Y Axis Shows or hides the Y-axis scale.
Metric Chart Shows or hides the line that connects the data points on
the chart.
Trend Line Shows or hides the line and data points that represents the
metric trend. The trend line filters out metric noise along the
timeline by plotting each data point relative to the average
of its adjoining data points.
Dynamic Thresholds Shows or hides the calculated dynamic threshold values for
a 24-hour period.
Show Entire Period Dynamic Thresholds Shows or hides dynamic thresholds for the entire time
period of the graph.
Anomalies Shows or hides anomalies. Time periods when the metric
violates a threshold are shaded. Anomalies are generated
when a metric crosses a dynamic or static threshold, either

Investigating Object Alerts
The Alerts tab provides a list of generated alerts for the currently selected object. When you are working with objects,
reviewing and responding to generated alerts on the Alert tab helps you manage problems in your environment.
The alerts notify you when a problem occurs in your environment based on configured alert definitions. Object alerts are
useful to you as an investigative tool in two ways. They can provide you with early notification about problems in your
environment before a user calls you to report a problem. As well, object alerts can provide information about the object
that you can use when troubleshooting general or reported problems.
As you review the Alerts tab, you can add ancestors and descendants to the list to broaden your view of the alerts. You
can see if alerts on the current object affect other objects. Conversely, you can examine how problems reflected in alerts
on other objects affect the current object.
Depending on the practices and workflows of your infrastructure operations team, you can use the object Alerts tab to
manage generated alerts on individual objects.
• Take ownership of alerts so that your team knows that you are working to resolve the problem.
• Suspend an alert so that is temporarily excluded from affecting the Health, Risk, or Efficiency state of the object while
you investigate the problem.
• Cancel alerts that you know are a result of a deliberate action. For example, a network card is removed from a host
for replacement. Also cancel alerts that are known issues that you cannot resolve currently because of resource
constraints. Canceling an alert that is generated because of only message event or metric event symptoms cancels
the alert permanently. If the underlying metric or property condition remains true, canceling an alert that is generated
because of metric, super metric, or property symptoms can result in the alert being regenerated . It is only effective to
cancel alerts generated because of message event or metric event symptoms.
Investigating and resolving alerts helps you provide the best possible environment to your customers.
Broadcom 4778

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Alerts Tab
The Alerts tab is a list of all the alerts generated for the selected object, group, or application. Use the alerts list to
evaluate the number of generated alerts for the object so that you can begin resolving them.
How the Alerts Tab Works
All the active alerts for the selected object appear in the list. By default, the system groups the alerts by Definition. You
can select multiple rows in the list using Shift+click, Control+click. Modify the filter if you want to see inactive alerts.
Manage the alerts in the list using the toolbar options. Click the alert name to see the alert details for the affected object.
The alert details appear on the right, including the symptoms triggered with the alert. The system offers recommendations
for addressing the alert and links to additional information. A Run Action button might appear in the details. Point to the
button to learn what recommendation is performed if you click the button. To return to the list view, click the X at the top
right of the alert details.
To see the object details, click the Summary Tab.
Where You Find the Alerts Tab
• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Inventory, and
then select a group, custom data center, application, or inventory object. Click the Alerts tab.

The alert options include toolbar and data grid options. Use the toolbar options to sort the alert list and to cancel, suspend,
or manage ownership. Additional toolbar options enable you to review parent and child alerts related to the alert you are
reviewing. Use the data grid to view the alerts and alert details.

The Related Scope displayed on the right, shows the objects that are one level above and one level below the object on

• If the same alert was triggered on the object in the past 30 days. This helps you understand if this is a recurring
problem or something new.

peer analysis to understand if others are impacted with the same problem.

downstream in the environment which are impacting the health of the object.

See the Potential Evidence tab for potential evidences around the problem, and to arrive at the root cause. This tab

scope are fixed. To modify the scope or the time range and investigate further, click Launch Workbench. This runs the
troubleshooting workbench.
The time range that is displayed in the potential evidence tab is two hours and thirty minutes before the alert was
triggered. VCF Operations looks for potential evidences in this time range.

Events Display
An event is any change to an object defined by a change in the metrics for that object. You can compare changes to an
object with symptoms and other data to identify a possible cause for a generated alert.
How the Events Display Works
The Events tab is a list of all the events generated for the selected object, group, or application based on messages send
by either external sources or by internal self troubleshooting system.
The following vCenter activities are some of the activities that generate VCF Operations events:
• Powering a virtual machine on or off
• Creating a virtual machine
• Installing VMware Tools on the guest OS of a virtual machine
• Adding a newly configured ESX system to a vCenter system
Depending on alert definitions, these events might generate alerts.
You might monitor the same virtual machines with other applications that provide information to VCF Operations, with
the adapters for those applications configured to provide change events. In this instance, the Events tab includes certain
change events that occur on the monitored objects. These change events might provide further insight into the cause of
problems that you are investigating.

Timeline Display
The generated alerts, triggered symptoms, and change events for the current object over time appear on the Timeline
display. You use the timeline to identify common trends over time that are contributing to the status of objects in your
environment.
How the Timeline Display Works
The Timeline works by combining the data for alerts, symptoms and events and displaying it in a unified view. By default
only active items are shown, however you can customize the data for each independently tab by using the filters to the
top right and from the INCLUDE menu, which allows you to use parent, child and peer options to examine the object in a
broader environmental context, as it is not always effective to investigate a problem on an individual object by looking only
at the object. This context often reveals unexpected influences or consequences for the problem.
The timeline is a tool that provides you a graphical view of patterns. If the system triggers a symptom and then cancels it
at various intervals over time, you can compare the event to other changes to the object or to the related objects. These
changes might be the root cause of the problem.
The view is limited to 700 alerts, symptoms, and events accordingly. If your timeline includes more than this number,
you can use the filters in each tab to remove data from the timeline until it contains data that you find useful for your
investigation.

• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, select Search and locate the object of interest. Click the Alert tab,
then to display the object's Summary subtab. Click the SHOW TIMELINE button in the Alerts tab

Configuring Automation Jobs
You can automate jobs to perform certain actions as per a schedule. You can create and manage automation jobs from
the Automation Central page. Scheduling of jobs allows you to perform actions without manual supervision. For example,
you can automate jobs to run during a maintenance window, which could be outside of working hours.
Automation Central
Automation Central is where you can create jobs to automate optimization actions which reclaim or rightsize VMs. You
can also schedule additional actions such as powering on, powering off, and rebooting VMs and instances. Once you set
up recurring jobs, you can track and obtain reports on them. You can customize jobs so that they only run based certain
on parameters. For example, if you choose to delete a snapshot as an action, you can specify how old the snapshot must
be before it is deleted. You can also schedule jobs from the Reclaim and Rightsizing pages, where you configure the job
in the context of a recommendation provided by VCF Operations.
Actions that you can Automate
You can automate the following actions using Automation Central:
Reclaim • Delete old snapshots. You can include idle and powered off VMs for reclamation.
• Delete idle VMs
• Poweroff Idle VMs
• Delete powered off VMs
Rightsize • Downsize oversized VMs. You can include idle VMs when resizing.
• Scale-up undersized VMs.
Other Schedule additional actions such as powering on, powering off, and rebooting VMs and instances. The
additional actions are based on the public cloud (GCP, AWS, Microsoft Azure) or vCenter adapter.
Where you find Automation Central
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Automation Central.
How Automation Central Works
In the Automation Central page you see a list of upcoming jobs and a calendar under the Schedule tab. The calendar
displays all the jobs that are scheduled for the current month. You can move between months to see future or past
scheduled jobs.
View the Summary of When you click on a date in the calendar, you see a summary of the job. The summary displays the
Scheduled Jobs frequency of the job, the type of job, and if the job is activated or deactivated. You can click Preview to see
more details about the job, or click Deactivate All Recurrences to deactivate the job. To edit the job, click
the Edit link.
View a Report of Jobs View reclamation and rightsizing reports. The reclamation report displays graphical and numerical data on

Configuring and Analyzing Logs
VCF Operations provides capabilities to collect, parse, modify, process, and analyze logs collected from various VCF
components. The prerequisite is the deployment of the log management component. VCF provides an integrated user
experience for log analysis. You can view and analyze logs from the VCF Operations console.
Broadcom 4794

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Overview of Log Management
Log Management has evolved from Aria Operations for Logs. Log Management is now integrated with VCF Operations.
Log Management component architecture has evolved significantly across recent releases to deliver tighter integration,
higher performance, and simplified operations.
• Aria Operations for Logs (Version 8.x): The legacy, standalone appliance-based solution originally deployed as part of
the Aria Suite.
• VCF Operations 9.0: Logs experience was converged into VCF Operations while the logs platform remained separate.
This release rebranded the standalone solution and introduced native integration with VMware Cloud Foundation,
delivering drastically improved scale and performance.
• VCF Operations 9.1: The latest architecture that comes with fully integrated Logs platform. Log Management is now
a built-in, containerized core service running natively within the VCF Management Services Platform. The entire
logging user experience, including deployment lifecycles, centralized configuration, access control, and alerting, is fully
consolidated into VCF Operations.
Log Collection Architecture
The centralized log collection architecture offers benefits such as granular configuration and cross-data center collection
across various VCF components. To enable this capability, the Log Management component should be installed.
Installaing the Log Management component is a Day-N operation, done via the lifecycle process, which automatically
integrates it with VCF Operations. VCF Operations provides centralized management for log collection and supports
diagnostic features that rely on these logs.
Overview of Log Management Architecture
Log Management replaces Aria Operations for Logs, providing a comparable set of features and capabilities to what was
previously offered. Log Management offers greater scalability than Aria Operations for Logs.
Log Management adopts OpenSearch and focuses on enhanced built-in security, better handling of resiliency during
failures, and the ability to scale to much larger cluster sizes than was possible with Aria Operations for Logs.
Log Management runs within VCF management services. There is no longer a separate user interface for Log
Management. All the functionality is available within VCF Operations. Content packs have been eliminated and replaced
by content integrated into management packs. All lifecycle functions for Log Management, such as deployment, patching,
upgrading, and resizing persistent volumes, are standardized based on VCF management services workflows. A break-
glass UI provides access to the stand-alone interface, for emergency scenarios when VCF Operations is not accessible.
The deployment architecture of Log Management consists of three main service types within a VCF management services
cluster: the gateway pod (Envoy), the log processor service, and the log store. The Envoy pod acts as the gateway,
responsible for accepting all traffic from various log sources and communicating with external services. The log processor
service is the basic engine of the platform, interacting with the log store (OpenSearch) and handling ingestion, querying,
and all log management activities. The log store uses OpenSearch to index and persist all log data, including configuration
data.
The Envoy pod acts as the gateway, responsible for accepting all traffic from various log sources and communicating with
external services. In HA mode, the gateway is deployed with a single instance per VIP/FQDN. In non-HA mode, a single
gateway handles all VIPs. Traffic ingestion flows from the gateway to the log processor and finally to the log store. The log
processor implements rules for masking, forwarding, filtering, and creating with partitions, while the log store handles the
indexing of log messages, persisting data, and implementing alerts and queries.
Centralized Configuration Management
The log collection configuration is stored in the Log Management cluster, but updates are always initiated through
VCF Operations. If you have remote VCF instances and need to send log data to the main, central Log Management
deployment, you can deploy a Unified Cloud Proxy. The Unified Cloud Proxy acts as a secure log forwarder that
aggregates and routes data from your remote environments to the primary cluster.
Broadcom 4795

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Irrespective of whether logs are forwarded via the Unified Cloud Proxy, or sent directly to the Log Management cluster,
the interface for providing centralized log collection is through VCF Operations for the components which follow the log
standard introduced in 9.0.
Unified Cloud Proxy
Unified Cloud Proxy plays a key role in collecting logs from multiple data centers. It works as follows:
1. VCF Operations requests credentials.
a. VCF Operations requests credentials from Log Management for the log forwarder.
b. This request includes the Cloud Proxy ID.
2. Credential transmission.
a. The credentials and Log Management FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name) are sent to the Cloud Proxy.
b. This data is encrypted.
3. Log forwarder setup.
a. The log forwarder decrypts the payload and establishes a connection with Log Management.
4. Configuration updates.
a. Any future configuration updates are sent via this established connection.
For more information about the types of Cloud Proxy deployment, see the topic, Collecting Data with Cloud Proxy in VCF
Operations.
Getting Started with Log Management
Log Management (formerly VCF Operations for Logs, and before that, VMware Aria Operations for Logs) collects,
analyzes, and visualizes logs across your VMware Cloud Foundation fleet.
As of VCF 9.1, Log Management is a built-in, containerized core service that runs natively within the VCF Management
Services Platform and is fully integrated into VCF Operations. There is no longer a separate logs UI for normal use.
What Log Management Provides
• A centralized log collection framework for vCenter, ESX, NSX, VCF Automation, VCF Operations, VCF Operations
HCX, VCF Operations for networks, Identity Broker, SDDC Manager, and other VCF management services
components.
• An architecture built on OpenSearch, giving greater scale and resiliency than the legacy Aria Operations for Logs
appliance.
• Log search, filtering, saved queries, charts, log comparison, and log-based alerts.
• Log processing controls - masking, filtering, forwarding, and partitioning with configurable retention.
• Agents for Linux (filelog, journald) and Windows (via Fluent Bit) log collection, plus native syslog and CFAPI ingestion.
• Role-based access control down to which logs a user can see (data sets/scopes).
• A Log Management Health Overview dashboard, plus a drill-down dashboard for advanced troubleshooting.
• Log Assist, for generating and uploading support bundles to Broadcom Support.
• A standalone “break-glass” UI for emergency access if the VCF Operations console itself is unreachable.
Choose a Deployment Model
Log Management is added to your VCF fleet as a Day-2 operation, and at deployment time you choose one of three
models.
Model Best for Key attributes
Simple Test/dev environments Single replica; smallest footprint; relies on
VCF management services and vSphere
HA to restart on failure; no application-level
HA
Broadcom 4796

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Model Best for Key attributes
High Availability Default for production/fleet deployments 3–19 replica cluster behind an integrated
load balancer; full-to-partial service
maintained on node failure
Multi-Instance Large-scale or bandwidth-limited/ One VCF Operations–integrated instance
segregated environments plus additional independently managed
instances (each Simple or HA); non-
integrated instances run standalone on Aria
Operations for Logs 8.18
All three are deployed in the same way (through VCF Operations), and all can scale up (bigger nodes) or out (more
replicas) later, but never back down.
Before You Deploy Log Management
Timing Log Management is not part of the day-zero install. Deploy it after your initial VCF/vSphere Foundation
provisioning is complete.
Networking Decide your FQDN(s) and IP address(es) up front. At least one Virtual IP (VIP) + FQDN is required at
deployment; more can be added later, but your SSL certificate must include every VIP’s FQDN in the SAN
field before you can create additional VIPs.
Capacity Log Management runs on the VCF management services runtime cluster in your fleet’s first VCF Instance,
so that cluster needs spare CPU/memory/IP-pool capacity.
VCF management services auto-scales out to accommodate Log Management, but scaling up (bigger node
size) should be scheduled in a maintenance window.
Storage Log data is stored on persistent volumes in the management services runtime cluster's default datastore.
Plan datastore capacity and IOPS for your ingestion rate and retention. To use other datastores, migrate log
store volumes with vSphere CNS. See Migrating Log Management log store container volumes in vSphere.
Sizing Estimate Events Per Second (EPS) as roughly 250 × number of ESX hosts (adjust for high-volume sources
like firewall logging), plus expected connections and retention needs. This drives your size/replica choice.
Use the VCF Operations Sizing Estimator for sizing requirements.
Retention/archive Decide whether you need long-term archiving. If so, you need an NFSv3 share or S3-compatible endpoint
planning (up to 5 external storage locations).
Backups Configure an SFTP location so Log Management’s configuration is backed up automatically as part of VCF
management services.
Security FIPS mode is on by default. Hosts with CPUs that don't support FIPS cipher acceleration may see reduced
ingestion capacity.
Deploy Log Management
For more information, see the topic, Deploy Log Management.
Connect Your Log Sources
• Log collection is on automatically for components that are hosted on VCF management services (VCF Automation,
Identity Broker, Log Management itself) and cannot be disabled.
• For the following components, you must explicitly activate log collection on that component’s adapter
(Administration > Integrations ).
– vCenter
– NSX
– VCF Operations HCX
– VCF Operations for networks
• Choose whether each source sends logs directly to the Log Management VIP or via a Cloud Proxy (recommended for
remote sites as it buffers and optimizes traffic, but always round-robins across all VIPs).
Broadcom 4797

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Version notes: vCenter 9.1.x uses the new Logs Agent (supports custom filtering/fields). Earlier vCenter versions fall
back to rsyslog without that support. Windows hosts need Fluent Bit, configured to forward to the Log Management
VIP on port 9543.
For more information, see Configuring Log Sources for Log Management.
Configure Core Log Processing Settings
All under Operate > Administration > Configurations
Log Partitions Segment logs by filter criteria with per-partition retention (2 days to limitations of the storage) and archive
configuration. Audit and Default partitions always exist; up to 9 custom ones can be added. For more
information, see Configuring Log Partitions.
Log Masking Redact sensitive fields/text matching a filter. For more information, see Log Masking.
Log Filtering Drop unwanted logs before indexing (useful when a source cannot filter itself, for example, syslog). For
more information, see Log Filtering.
Log Forwarding Relay filtered/tagged logs to up to 10 external syslog/log-management destinations. For more information,
see Log Forwarding.
External Storage Register NFS or S3 targets used for archiving, import, and export. For more information, see Configuring
External Storage.
Integrated Load Manage VIPs/FQDNs; add more when you need extra ingest capacity or want to tag logs by source. For
Balancer more information, see Integrated Load Balancer.
Agents and Agent Manage Linux/Windows collector agents, authentication secrets, and grouped configuration pushes. For
Groups more information, see Overview of Log Management Agents.
Analyze and Troubleshoot with Logs
• The Logs page (Operate > Logs) is where you search, filter, build fields, save queries, and chart results.
• Compare Logs lets you line up results from up to four queries side by side.
• Logs also surface per-object in Inventory > Logsand in the Workbench, so you can correlate log entries with metrics
during an investigation.
• You can define log-based alerts from saved queries, and combine log symptoms with metric symptoms in the same
alert definition.
• Several core components (vCenter, ESX, NSX, HCX, Operations for Networks, VCF Operations, Identity Broker,
VCF Automation) now emit a standardized, structured log format, which simplifies both manual troubleshooting and
automated parsing.
Control Access to Logs
Log access control is unified into standard VCF Operations RBAC:
1. Define a Data Set (Access Control > Scopes ) — a set of log filters (for example, “hostname contains x”).
2. Check role permissions (Access Control > Roles) — make sure that the assigned role has permissions that you need
(Log Processing, Log Forwarding, Log Collection, and so on).
3. Assign the Scope and Role to a user or group.
A Scope can independently carry an Object Scope (which infrastructure objects are visible) and a Log Data Set (which
log data is visible). Assigning one does not automatically restrict the other.
Monitor the Health of Log Management
Use the Log Management Health Overview dashboard (Operate > Dashboards > All) as your first stop for both active
alerts and general health checks. It is organized into four areas:
• Ingestion,
• Retention
• Availability
• Operation
Broadcom 4798

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Each of these dashboards has guided remediation steps. A disabled-by-default drill-down dashboard exposes per-
component (gateway/processor/store) metrics for deeper troubleshooting, and a companion VCF management services
cluster health dashboard helps you rule out resource contention on the underlying platform.
Get Support When You Need It
• If the VCF Operations console itself is down, use the standalone break-glass U at the Log Management FQDN to
search logs directly.
• From that same standalone UI, you can generate a cluster-wide support bundle.
• For day-to-day support cases, use Log Assist (requires Connected Mode licensing and a Cloud Proxy with outbound
access to ) to auto-generate and upload log bundles plus diagnostic findings straight to a
eapi.broadcom.com
Broadcom support case.
If You are Upgrading from an Older Logs Product
Log Management is never an in-place upgrade. It is always a fresh 9.1 deployment plus a configuration import:
• From an existing 9.0 VCF Operations for Logs instance: credentials are auto-detected and imported.
• From Aria Operations for Logs 8.18.x: you enter the FQDN/credentials manually.
• After import, you get a 90-day query federation window against the old cluster, an on-demand Data Migration Utility,
and a separate Log Data Transfer tool for historical data.
• Custom content (dashboards, alerts, queries) does not migrate automatically. Export it as a Content Pack and run it
through the CLI conversion utility to produce a Management Pack.
What's New in Log Management
Log Management brings several enhancements to how you can handle logs from different VCF components.
• Monitoring
– Detection and surfacing of issues based on logs, alerts, and notifications.
– Visual analytics provided through dashboards and reports.
• Troubleshooting
– Log pattern detection and pattern trends.
– Log compare.
– Capabilities to detect outliers or the absence of logs.
• Security Operations (Log Administration):
– Data set definition scope.
– Merging the data set within the VCF Operations scope, which aligns with user role, group creation, and user role
assignment.
Access control, which allows for data set restrictions based on a log scope to define what you can or cannot access.
Roles have also been enhanced to include log pages and other related aspects.
– Role-based access control (RBAC).
– Log segregation and retention.
• Log Processing Rules
– Log Masking: Masking critical fields or text for security sensitivity. This requires providing the field or text to mask,
the pattern on which to apply the masking (for example, the entire field or a portion), the mask value, and the filter
criteria.
– Log Forwarding: Forwarding a select set of logs or security audit logs based on filter criteria to a central security
product or third-party endpoint. This can also forward tags.
– Log Filtering: Logs are filtered out or dropped based on a filter criteria from the source. This is useful when the
sender cannot filter the logs themselves, for example, with syslogs.
– Log Archival: Archiving logs for compliance and regulatory needs and primary storage offloading. S3 Endpoint
support for archive destinations is a new capability.
– Log Partition: Logical segregation of logs based on various criteria such as retention, routing, or filtering. You can
define the retention period (from 2 days to forever) for any specific partition.
– Audit Record partition for audit logs.
Broadcom 4799

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Logs Page. Workflow-related changes and fine-tuning were brought in to make the page more usable and easier to
consume.
– Saved queries, direct text search, and additional filters, including partition selection and a time range.
– A quick link to Log Compare is available.
– An export function allows exporting query results in JSON format to external storage (NFS) or local storage (if the
log size is 20,000 or fewer logs) for consumption or analysis.
– You can view the distribution of data for any field (for example, app name) within the selected time range.
– A fields library allows you to view all existing fields, including system-defined indexed fields and discovered non-
indexed fields, which customers can choose to index for performance reasons. You can also rediscover fields to get
rid of old ones.
– Logs migrated from a previous version are detected, and a time window for accessing those logs is retained in the
current release, accessible under a legacy log integrated partition. You are encouraged to reconfigure log sources
through the VCF adapter and vCenter integrations.
• Global Settings Updates
– New settings in the Global Settings page for agent authentication and for event cluster management. As part of
security hardening settings, by default, SSL ingestions are enabled for CFAPI and Syslog.
Deploy and Upgrade Log Management
Log Management is not an in-place upgrade from Aria Operations for Logs. The process starts with a new installation of
the Log Management component via the VCF Operations console. The Log Management component is not part of the
day-zero installation flow, so you must deploy it after the initial VCF provisioning and installing day-zero components.
During the installation wizard, you must provide at least one FQDN and corresponding IP address. The wizard also
presents an option to import settings from Aria Operations for Logs and while importing settings from VCF Operations for
logs.
Configuration and Settings Migration
A key part of the upgrade is migrating configurations from the Aria Operations for Logs 8.18.x and VCF Operations for
Logs to the new Log Management installation.
• From 9.0: If you are upgrading from VCF 9.0 with an existing integrated VCF Operations for Logs instance, the system
automatically detects the old credentials via the service registry. These settings are then automatically imported to the
new Log Management, eliminating the need for manual input of the address and credentials
• From 8.18.x: If you are upgrading from Aria Operations for Logs 8.18.x, then you must manually enter the FQDN and
admin credentials of the old Aria Operations for Logs instance in the import flow.
• Configurations Migrated: During this import flow, the system pulls specific configurations from the Aria Operations
for Logs and adds them to Log Management, including log filters, log masking, and log forwarder rules. Existing log
collection configurations are also integrated into Log Management.
• Report Generation: After the installation and configuration import are complete, a PDF report is generated. This report
lists all the configurations that were successfully pulled from the legacy Aria Operations for Logs and added to Log
Management. It also includes a list of configurations that cannot be migrated automatically (for example, Datasets) with
instruction on how to move those over post-import.
Data Access and Migration
The upgrade process focuses on configuration migration but provides a mechanism to access old data:
Query Federation After installation, Log Management creates an integration with Aria Operations for Logs. This integration is
used to provide federation of queries for a period of time, specifically 90 days after the Log Management
installation. During this window, you can query your Aria Operations for Logs data from the Logs page in
VCF Operations. If you select a legacy Aria Operations for Logs partition, Log Management forwards the
query to the legacy instance and fetches the data.
Data Migration Utility There is an on-demand data migration utility that you can use anytime you want to migrate log data from
Aria Operations for Logs to Log Management. This is a long-running process due to the potential volume of
log data.
Broadcom 4800

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Post-Upgrade Behavior
Following the VCF provisioning, when you navigate to any log capability page in VCF Operations before Log Management
is installed, you see a notice prompting you to install the Log Management component.
For upgrade scenarios, specifically from 9.0, where partial integration existed, the day-zero pages are shown to enforce
the installation of Log Management. Until the installation is complete, no log data is available in VCF Operations, and
accessing log capabilities will redirect you to the installation flow. After the Log Management component is successfully
installed, it will appear in the component list, and the option to deploy it will no longer be available, as there is one-to-one
mapping between VCF Operations and Log Management.
As part of Day-N operations, you can scale up (vertical, increasing size) and scale out (horizontal, increasing replicas) the
cluster. Scale-down operations (decreasing size or number of replicas) are not possible using the VCF Operations UI. You
can also scale up the log store storage size as a Day N operation.
How to Deploy or Upgrade
• For information on how to deploy Log Management, see Deploy Log Management.
• For information on how to upgrade to Log Management, see Upgrading to Log Management 9.1.
• To copy historical logs from VMware Aria Operations for Logs 9.0, integrated VCF Operations for Logs 9.0 to Log
Management, see Log Data Transfer.
• To configure log forwarding from standalone single/multiple Aria Operations for Logs 8.18.x instances to Log
Management, see Configuring Log Forwarding.
Log Data Transfer
You can transfer log data for up to 90 days from Aria Operations for Logs 8.x and VCF Operations for Logs 9.0 and to
VCF 9.1. The migrated logs are stored in the Log Management cluster. You must deploy Log Management before you can
proceed.
Why Transfer Log Data
VCF does not permit integration of VCF Operations with Aria Operations for Logs. If you had previously integrated Aria
Operations for Logs and Aria Operations, and you have upgraded to VCF, then you must use the Log Data Transfer
feature to transfer ingested logs to Log Management.
When you set up operations-logs as a log forwarding destination in Aria Operations for Logs, logs which are already
ingested by Aria Operations for Logs are not forwarded to VCF Operations. To forward already ingested logs, use the Log
Data transfer functionality in VCF Operations.
How to Transfer Log Data
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Administration > Control Panel. Under Content and Support section, click Logs Data Transfer. If you have not set
up any transfer, click the INITIATE TRANSFER button and configure the authentication details about the VMware Aria
Operations for logs 8.x or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x appliance. You can select the duration of logs to transfer from the
drop-down. Transfer logs from the last 10 days to start with.
After you initiate the task, you can check the status of the transfer from the Logs Data Transfer card at any time.
Note:
• Not all data buckets may be copied unless Log Management has enough free disk space. It is recommended
to run this check manually prior to starting the migration to guarantee that all logs from the VMware Aria
Operations for logs 8.x or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x instance are migrated to VCF Operations. Before
starting the migration, know the location of the live storage in VCF Operations, and the volume of logs stored
in the live storage of the old instance.
• Data for any selected interval is fully re-imported. Check the audit record to avoid redundant transfers.
• All source nodes of the Aria Operations for Logs instance must have the same SSH credentials as each other,
and be reachable via port 22 from the Log Management nodes, otherwise the migration is unsuccessful.
Broadcom 4801

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Log Partitions and Searching Older Partitions
Log Management provides with you with options to create partitions and query them. You can create multiple custom
partitions using specific filtering criteria to segregate log data and perform targeted queries against individual partitions.
For upgrade scenarios where a legacy cluster FQDN is specified, the system supports querying from legacy partitions for
up to 90 days. Finally, you can query re-imported archive data. To query archived logs, the data must first be re-imported
into the platform using the archive import workflow, which creates a searchable archive partition available for selection.
Querying is performed on one partition at a time.
Aria Operations for Logs or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x Logs Partitions
In a brownfield deployment, you upgrade from an existing Aria Operations for Logs or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x
instance. You can connect the newly installed Log Management instance with a VMware Aria Operations for logs 8.x or
VCF Operations for Logs 9.x instance to the new Log cluster instance as part of the upgrade workflow, and not later on.
After this configuration is complete, the Logs page in VCF Operations displays a banner which serves as a notification
that the connection with the VMware Aria Operations for Logs 8.x or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x instance will expire in
90 days.
You must complete all data and settings, such as datasets, before 90 days. After 90 days, VCF Operations will not be able
to query data from older versions.
The connection with Aria Operations for Logs makes it possible to search for logs in legacy partitions directly from the
Logs page in VCF Operations. This connection with VMware Aria Operations for Logs 8.x or VCF Operations for Logs 9.x
instance will automatically be deleted after 90 days, at which point the banner will be hidden, and these legacy partitions
will no longer be available for searching. For more information, see Configuring Log Partitions.
Archive Locations
You can import logs from from archives in a configured external stroage location (S3 or NFS), and search against these
locations. This can be found in the Log Partition tab under Administration > Configurations > Log Processing. To
query these archived logs, you must use the archive import workflow to re-import the data into the platform. Once re-
imported, the data resides in a searchable archive partition that can be selected for querying. Note that only one imported
log archive can be active for querying at a time. To search a different archive, you must purge the current one and repeat
the import process.
You can restore the archived information back to Log Management. VCF Operations allows for restoring archived
logs not only from Log Management archive locations but also from Aria Operations for Logs archived locations. It is
recommended to import the logs with a small time range because if the import logs fill the storage more than 80%, the
task fails. When importing from Aria Operations for Logs archives, only NFS storage is supported. You must provide the
mounted path and specify the time range of the archived data that you wish to import.
Initiating an import generates a task that can be monitored under Log Tasks which can be found under Administration >
Control Panel > Log Import/Export Tasks. Once the logs have been successfully imported, you can search against this
archived data from the Logs page using the Import Partition drop-down menu. By applying the archived logs option in
this section, you can view all the logs that were imported from the specified time range. For more information, see Archive
Log Import.
Configuring Log Partitions
Log partitions enable the segmentation of log data through defined filter criteria and support specific retention and archival
policies. This segmentation facilitates efficient log management by allowing for different retention periods and ingestion
orders across multiple custom partitions. Separate partitions can be configured to archive to specific NFS or S3 locations.
Archiving lets you shorten retention in the log store, which reduces storage use and improves query performance, while
the older data stays available in the archive. Each partition's retention policy ensures that logs are either kept until storage
reaches the 80% threshold and then are automatically purged. From the Log Partitions page, you can create partitions,
edit, clone, activate, deactive, and delete partitions.
The order of evaluation for these rules is top-to-bottom. Partitions are processed based on an ingestion order, which you
can modify. Since the first matching partition rule takes precedence, you can change the order to ensure logs flow to the

records partition is always the first filter covered and the default partition the last.

Migrating Log Management Log Store Container Volumes in vSphere
You can migrate Log Management log store persistent container volumes from one datastore to another using the
vSphere Cloud Native Storage (CNS) migration feature. In VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) and VMware vSphere
Foundation (VVF) environments, runtime services cluster VMs are placed on a single datastore. If you face capacity
limitations, like max node size, you can migrate the log volumes using the workaround that is provided here. You
should note the limitations and reapply the workaround in case of scale and DR actions. Relocating these volumes
across multiple target datastores balances IOPS while maintaining continuous log ingestion, data integrity, and platform
functionality.
Before migrating log store volumes, ensure the following conditions are met:
• Environment: A VCF Operations 9.1 environment with Log Management deployed on a VCF Management Services
(VCFMS) cluster is active and healthy.
• Storage Accessibility: At least two datastores (the source datastore and one or more target datastores) must be fully
accessible from all ESX hosts underlying the VCF Management services.
• Capacity: Target datastores must have sufficient free capacity to accommodate the migrated persistent volumes.
• Permissions: Your vSphere Client user account must possess administrative permissions to view and migrate
container volumes.
• Establish Baselines:
– Record the baseline mapping of your current datastore layout and identify the specific volume IDs and sizes
backing your log store.
– Execute a baseline query in the the Logs page. Document the sample entries and total result counts for
comparison.
– Ensure active log ingestion streams (via agents and syslog) are operating smoothly.
Limitations and Constraints:
• Only single block volumes can be migrated.
Broadcom 4804

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• PMEM (Persistent Memory) datastores are not supported as migration targets.
• The VCF Management services worker node hosting the persistent volume will be locked during the CNS relocation
process, meaning no other infrastructure control operations can be performed on it until the move completes.
1. Log in to the vSphere Client.
2. Navigate to the datacenter, cluster, or source datastore hosting your infrastructure.
3. Select the Monitor tab and click Cloud Native Storage > Container Volumes.
4. To easily isolate the log management volumes, click Add Filter and filter by the Kubernetes component label:
Label: app.kubernetes.io/component:log-store
5. Select the specific log store persistent volume (PV) you intend to move and click Migrate.
6. In the Migrate Volume dialog box, select your preferred target datastore.
7. Review and acknowledge any compatibility warnings (such as storage policy mismatches or datastore inaccessibility),
then click Migrate.
8. Monitor the migration progress under the Recent Tasks pane in the vSphere Client until the task completes
successfully.
Once the vSphere migration task finishes, verify data integrity and workload continuity:
• In the Container Volumes view, confirm that the volume's location has updated to the target datastore and its Health
Status returns to Accessible or normal.
• Browse the target datastore files to ensure the virtual disk backing the volume exists within the proper First Class Disk
(FCD) directory or VM folder.
• Verify that the matching Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) status remains Bound and shows no active pod
scheduling errors.
• In the Logs page, re-run your baseline search query to verify that no log data was lost or corrupted during the
migration window.
Important Operational Considerations
• Scale-Out Operations: During any post-migration cluster scale-out operations, newly added log-store node volumes
will automatically attach to the default platform-managed services Datastore. Administrators must manually repeat this
migration procedure if they choose to redistribute new volumes to preferred datastores.
• Disaster Recovery (DR): If a DR event occurs and the Log Management component is restored from a backup into a
fresh VCF Management Services cluster environment, all custom disk placements are reset to the default single VCF
Management Services Datastore configuration. You must execute this volume relocation procedure again after the DR
environment is online to clear potential storage hotspots.

You enable Log analysis for vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations HCX, VCF Operations for networks, VCF Operations when
you configure the adapter, and for Identity Broker, and VCF Automation when you deploy the component.
Log Collection for VMware Cloud Foundation Components
When you activate log collection on the vCenter Server Cloud Account or VMware Cloud Foundation pages, Log
Management automatically begins collecting vCenter events, tasks, and alarms, alongside VMware ESX and vSphere
Supervisor logs.
To collect logs for the vCenter instance, you must explicitly activate vCenter log collection on the Log Sources page.
The method used to collect vCenter logs depends on the version you are running:
• vCenter 9.1 and later: Log collection is performed using the Logs Agent, which supports advanced log processing.
• Earlier versions of vCenter: Log collection relies on rsyslog. When using rsyslog, custom filtering and extracted fields
are not applied to the collected logs.

Overview of Log Standardization
By introducing a unified log standard, VCF enhances log usability, simplifies troubleshooting, and improves automation
capabilities. The adoption of industry standards and structured logging ensures that logs are more consistent, easy to
interpret, and valuable for your organization, your support teams, and your automation processes. The log standard
introduced in VCF is a significant step toward greater observability, system efficiency, and proactive problem resolution.
Broadcom 4809

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Why a New Log Standard?
Logging serves as a key source of information for system management, troubleshooting, and automation. Global support
teams rely on log statements to diagnose issues, optimize performance, and enhance automation processes. In previous
versions, VMware products such as vCenter, vSphere, Aria Operations for Networks, have followed their own logging
standards, often based on the RFC 5424 Syslog Protocol. Though functional, this approach introduced inconsistencies in
log formats and patterns, making interpretation more complex and reducing the efficiency of automated log analysis.
To address these challenges, VCF introduces a standardized log format. This new format aligns with industry best
practices, including OpenTelemetry principles. It is designed to improve log consistency across components, simplify
troubleshooting, and facilitate automation-driven log consumption. In VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, three components
follow a unified format, offering greater interoperability. In future versions, more components will adopt the standardized
log format. This reduces the complexity of integrating new tools or migrating to new VCF versions since updates will follow
this standardized approach.
Objectives of Log Standardization
VCF benefits from standardizing logs because of the following reasons:
• Unified Logging Standard: Establishing a single log statement standard across the VMware Cloud Foundation platform
while incorporating industry standards.
• Enhanced Automation and Parsing: Enabling automated log parsing and interpretation to improve operational
efficiency.
• Ease of Configuration: There is now a single place to enable or disable log collection as well as configure its
granularity. The approach is applicable for cross-datacenter VCF platforms by utilizing log forwarder capability within
the cloud proxy.
Impact of Log Standardization on Existing Workflows and Automation
• Automation Adjustments: If you use automated workflows that are tied to logging data, then you may need to adjust
your processes for the components using the new log standard. Since the standardized format introduces specific
fields (for example, timestamps, user actions, and component details), any custom scripts or automation routines
relying on previous formats will require updating to the new structure.
• Dashboard and Alert Configuration: If you have dashboards or alert definitions that are connected to log data, initial
reconfiguration is necessary. You can combine log based symptoms with metric based symptoms, ensuring that crucial
insights are not missed due to format discrepancies. You can build log based widgets with the existing VCF Operations
dashboards. This functionality is new in VCF 9.0.
Scope of Log Standardization
Logs Within Scope The standardization effort covers log statements that are generated by VCF components that document
system operations. This includes:
• Application Logs: These logs capture events, user interactions, errors, and warnings generated by VCF
applications. An example is the vCenter logs stored at .
/var/log/vmware
• System Syslog Transmissions: Standardized messages from network devices, servers, and
applications, adhering to the syslog protocol. For instance,VCF Operations for networks logs syslog
messages when a PAM session closes.
• Syslog Transmission of Audit Records: Many organizations collect and retain audit records for
compliance and security. The new standard applies to transmitting these records via syslog but does
not mandate or modify how VCF components store them internally.
Logs Out of Scope Certain types of logs are excluded from standardization due to their unique characteristics and existing
industry adherence:
• Transaction/Database Logs: These logs track changes within a database, such as SQL transactions,
and are essential for data integrity and disaster recovery.
• Third-Party Logs: Logs generated by external software like Kafka, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, and
Kubernetes, which already conform to independent standards.
• Network Logs: While network logs provide critical information about IP traffic, they are categorized
under system logs and remain outside the current standardization effort.
Broadcom 4810

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Using the Chart to Analyze Logs
The chart in the Logs page lets you visualize the results of your query.
The chart summarizes the events that your query returns, so you can identify patterns without reading individual log
entries. The chart updates when you change the query. You can also change what the chart calculates, how it groups the
results, how it looks, and how finely it divides time.
By default, the chart shows the COUNT OF EVENTS over time as a column chart.
Where You Find the Chart
Click Operate in the top navigation bar, and in the left navigation pane, click Logs. On the ANALYZE LOGS tab, run a
query. The chart appears below the query bar.
Chart Toolbar
