Viewing Logs, Queries and Fields
In the Logs page of VCF Operations, you can search and filter log events, view the logs for an object, create queries,
view charts of the query results, and extract fields from log messages. For more information, see Log Fields.
The Logs Page
After you log in to VCF Operations, click Operate in the top navigation bar, and in the left navigation pane, click Logs. The
Logs page opens on the ANALYZE LOGS tab. On this tab, you can view logs, create queries, and extract fields from log
messages. You can search and filter log events, and create queries to extract events based on timestamp, text, source,
and fields in log events. Besides presenting the log stream, VCF Operations presents charts of the query results. You can
save these charts to look them up later in the Dashboards page. You can access the Logs page if your user account is
associated with a role that has the appropriate permission. You can view or edit settings in the Logs page, depending on
the sub-categories and corresponding access levels selected for the permission.
Viewing the Logs for an Object
You can view the logs for a selected supported object from the Logs tab in the inventory. You can troubleshoot a problem
in your environment by correlating the information in the logs with the metrics.
Where You Find the Logs Tab
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Inventory. Click the Logs tab. The Logs tab is available after you have configured Log Management in VCF Operations.
Log Queries
Queries in VCF Operations can retrieve and summarize events. Once created, you can compare queries.
You can create and save queries from the Logs page. To see saved queries click Operate in the top navigation bar,
and in the left navigation pane, Administration > Configurations. Then, click the Saved Queries card. You can export
query results, share your queries with other users, and can save, delete, rename, and load existing queries. You can take
snapshots of queries and can save them to dashboards.
A query consists of one or more of the following:
Keywords Complete, or full-text, alphanumeric, hyphenated, and/or underscore matches.
Globs Complete, or full-text, alphanumeric, hyphenated, and/or underscore matches.
Regular expressions Sophisticated string pattern matching based on Java regular expressions.
Field operations Keyword, regular expression, and pattern matches applied to extracted fields.
Aggregations Functions that are applied to one or more subgroups of the results.
VCF Operations supports the following types of queries:
• Message. A query made up of keywords, regular expressions and/or field operations.
• Regular expression or field. A query made up of keywords and/or regular expressions.
• Aggregation. A query made up of a function, one or more groupings, and any number of fields.
Broadcom 4814

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You can define custom alerts in VCF Operations and trigger them from scheduled queries of any type.
Note:
Some saved queries may contain expressions that cannot be converted into the VCF Operations UI‑supported
format. Attempting to interpret or partially render these queries may lead to incorrect behavior or confusion.
Some complex saved queries and l og‑based alert definitions may not appear in the UI due to parsing limitations.
These items are skipped when their expressions cannot be converted into the VCF Operations UI‑supported
format. Saved queries do not save the aggregated query (chart view).
Best Practices for Creating Search Queries
You can enter queries by using the search bar, or by entering filters.
Use the search bar to refine the results for events. While you can use a filter instead of the search bar, it is often easier to
understand a query that uses the search bar over an equivalent filter. The best practice is to use the search bar instead of
an equivalent filter when possible.
A filter allows you to create queries by using a regular expression, a field, Logical OR and AND operations, or a
combination of search bar and filter queries.
When you create queries by using the search bar and filters, the following best practices apply:
• Ensure queries are not environment specific.
• When you construct a query, use the simplest query type that returns the results you need. Keyword queries use the
fewest resources. Glob queries use more. Regular expression queries use the most.
– A keyword query matches exact words, for example error.
– A glob query matches a pattern that contains wildcard characters, such as * (any number of characters) and ? (a
single character), for example err*.
– A regular expression query matches a pattern that is written in regular expression syntax.
• Provide as many keywords as possible when using regular expressions or fields. If a regular expression includes
a logical OR, for example this|that, do not include keywords. VCF Operations is optimized to perform keyword
queries prior to regular expressions to minimize regular expression overhead.
Log Fields
Fields are a powerful way to add structure to unstructured events and allow the manipulation of both the textual and
visual representation of data. You can view the distribution of data for a specific field and access the fields library to view
indexed and non-indexed fields. You can choose to index non-indexed fields for performance reasons.
Saved fields are available in the Fields Library card. To see the Fields Library card, click Operate in the top navigation
bar, and in the left navigation pane, Administration > Configurations. You can export or import extracted fields from one
VCF Operations instance to another.
Using Fields in the Logs Page
Click Operate in the top navigation bar, and in the left navigation pane, click Logs. The Logs page displays a stream of
log messages. You can extract any part of a log message that might be applicable to a query or aggregation by selecting
the part of the message and clicking Extract Field. Fields are a type of regular expression query and are useful for
complex pattern matching so you do not need to know, remember, or learn complicated regular expressions.
You can use Fields in different ways including aggregations and filters. Aggregations allow you to apply functions and
groupings to fields. Filters allow you to perform operations over fields.

and then select Extract Field, you see the Create Field flyout section on the right side. Enter the values and click SAVE
to create a Field.

Extracted Fields and Regular Expression Handling
To ensure optimal performance and stability, the logs platform enforces strict handling of extracted fields. If an extracted
field contains a complex or malformed regular expression (Regex) pattern, VCF Operations cannot process it. Instead,
VCF Operations automatically drops the invalid field.
This strict validation applies to all extracted fields in your environment, including:
• Custom extracted fields that you create.
• Out-of-the-box extracted fields that are defined within installed Management Packs.
If you notice that specific extracted fields are missing from your log search results, or certain alerts that rely on extracted
fields are failing to trigger, then VCF Operations may have dropped the extracted fields during processing because their
underlying Regex patterns were too complex or malformed.
To verify if the logs platform dropped your extracted fields, review the system logs for specific warning messages. Look for
log entries marked with a WARNING severity level that match the following format:
Unable to extract fields:["<field_name_1>", "<field_name_2>"]
Field Governance in the Fields Library
Fields can be manually added from the endpoints sending the logs, such as a FluentD agent. When a log is ingested, Log
Management discovers the field, but does not index it by default. Indexing a field makes it quickly searchable in the Logs
page. Searching by a non-indexed field takes a long time, though it is still searchable. The rediscover option removes a
field from the database. This is an option when you want to remove the indexing manually. You can decide which fields
Broadcom 4816

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
are indexed, thus saving storage and index bloat. This helps maintain capacity limits to prevent performance degradation.
If the field continuously appears in subsequent logs, it is discovered again as a non-indexed field.
A Field can be:
• Indexed or Non-Indexed
• System Defined or Discovered
System Defined and • These are well-known fields that come when the Log Management component is installed, and is
Indexed Fields required for proper functioning. This includes Fields for diagnostics, findings, and audit trails.
• The system marks these Fields as indexed by default.
• Approximately 77 indexed Fields are included by default.
• System-defined Fields cannot be rediscovered.
Discovered and Non- • When a Field which is not predefined in the system is ingested from an agent, it is marked as non-
Indexed Fields indexed and discovered.
You can manage Fields by clicking the vertical ellipsis next to a field in the Fields Library. To see the Fields Library card,
click Operate in the top navigation bar, and in the left navigation pane, Administration > Configurations.
• Indexing a Discovered Field: You can choose to index a discovered field by clicking Index Field. You see a
confirmation message stating that indexing a field can reduce storage size and affect performance.
• Rediscovering a Field: For discovered fields, you can choose to rediscover a field by clicking Rediscover. This action
removes the field from the index. If the same field continues to be ingested, it will be rediscovered but will remain non-
indexed. You can then choose whether to index it again.
Best Practices for Fields
In addition to the various components that make up a field, several best practices apply.
• Only create fields for regular expression patterns. If a field can be queried using keyword queries, or will only ever
return a single value, then use keyword queries instead of a pre-defined field. If a field will only return two values then
consider constructing individual queries instead of extracting a field. Fields are meant to add structure to unstructured
data as well as provide a way to query over specific parts of an event.
• Only create fields for regular expression patterns that return a fraction of the total events. Fields that will match
most events and/or return a very large number of results are not a good candidate for field extraction. The regular
expression will need to be applied to a large quantity of events resulting in a resource intensive operation. If possible
add additional keywords to reduce the number of results returned and optimize the query.
• If a field contains keywords within regular expression syntax, then add such keywords as a filter without regular
expression syntax. For example, if the value or the context of a field contains keywords within regular expression
syntax such as this|that, then add the keywords as a text filter to optimize the query like
text contains this,
.
that
• Use of the additional context with one or more keywords is recommended over complex regular expressions in the
before or after context.
• Add additional context to all extracted fields in order to optimize query performance.
• Extracted fields must be specific because the extraction is executed only on the target logs. You must use ASCII
characters in the name of extracted field.

Performing a Search
To find only events that contain the specified keywords, enter any complete keywords, globs, or phrases in the search text
box.
You can search for log events that match certain values of specific fields. Using quoted text in the main search field
matches exact phrases. Entering a space in the main search field is a logical AND operator. Search uses only full tokens.
A token is a continuous string of letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores. Whitespace and other characters, such as a
period or a slash, separate tokens. For example, searching for "err" does not find "error" as a match.
Note:
The field name for an ingested event must begin only with a letter or an underscore character and contain only
letters, digits, or the underscore character.
Note:
If you search for esx within a larger string, format the query according to the position of esx in the token:
• If esx is a complete token, for example in , enter .
esx.example.com esx
• If esx is at the beginning of a longer token, for example in , enter .
esx01 esx*
You cannot find esx at the end or in the middle of a token by placing a wildcard before it. Queries such as
*esx
and do not work.
*esx*
Within a single-row filter, add multiple search queries by typing each query and hitting the Enter key. This behaves like OR
filters. For example, select hostnamecontains and type hit enter and then type and hit enter
127.0.0.1 127.0.0.2
again. The search returns events with the host name 127.0.0.1 or 127.0.0.2.
Note:
The text contains filter treats each word or phrase that you type before hitting enter as a complete keyword.
Queries with fields using the internal query language syntax names, for example, or , are not able to be
from in
processed and should not be used.
You can combine multiple field filters by creating a filter row for each field. You can toggle the operator that is applied to
multiple-row filters.
• To apply the AND operator, select All.
• To apply the OR operator, select Any.
Note:
Regardless of the toggle value, the operator for comma-separated values within a single filter row is OR.
You can use globs in search terms. A glob is a search term that contains wildcard characters. For example, or
vm* vmw?
.
re
• To match zero or more characters, use .
*
• To match exactly one character, use .
?
A wildcard matches characters only within a single token. It does not match across token separators such as a period.
Note:
A glob can begin with a wildcard only when the wildcard stands alone as a complete token, followed by a
separator. For example, matches and , because the wildcard
*.10.11.12 192.10.11.12 10.10.11.12
matches the first token. However, returns no results, because a wildcard cannot be attached to the
*10.11.12
front of the characters in a token.
You can save the current query to load it at a later stage.

• Do either of the following:

– Enter a query and in the upper-right corner of the page, click the pin icon. Pin multiple queries to the
pinboard and then click Compare Logs.
2. In the COMPARE LOGS tab, enter details for the first query.
• Enter a name for the query.
• Select the indexed partition on which you want to run the query and click Apply. If you do not select an indexed
partition, VCF Operations searches for logs in all the indexed partitions.
• Enter a start date and time for querying the logs. VCF Operations uses the start date and time and the duration in
the upper-right corner of the page to calculate the time range for the query. When the query runs, it searches for
logs within the time range.
• Add one or more filters for more specific query results.
3. Click Add Query to add another query and enter the details described in step 2. You can compare logs for up to four
queries.
Tip:
You can copy an existing query by clicking the copy icon next to the query name.
4. In the bottom-right of the query section, enter the common duration for the added queries. VCF Operations uses the
start date and time in a query and the common duration to calculate the time range for the query. When a query runs, it
searches for logs within the time range.
Note:
You can enter a maximum duration of 29 days, 23 hours, and 59 minutes.
5. Click Compare.
The log comparison is displayed as a stacked line chart and the log results appear side by side in query tabs under the
chart. You can select a query tab on the left side and a query tab on the right side to compare the log results.
By default, the chart is based on the logs corresponding to the selected query tabs. However, to view the chart for all the
queries, in the upper-right corner of the chart, click Show All.
The chart is plotted based on the common time range for the queries. To view the specific time at which a log was
ingested, you can hover over the data point in the chart.
Information in Log Events
VCF Operations collects and analyzes all types of machine-generated log data, including application logs, configuration
files, messages, performance data, and system state dumps.
You can connect VCF Operations to everything in your environment, including operating systems, applications, storage,
firewalls, network devices for enterprise-wide visibility using log analytics.
When VCF Operations is configured and ready to collect logs, there are several ways you can ingest log data including:
• vSphere Integration — VCF Operations can integrate with vSphere components to automatically collect events, tasks
and alarms from vCenter and logs from ESX hosts.
• Agents — VCF Operations has collection agents available to send filelog, windows events and journald generated logs
to VCF Operations.
• Syslog — VCF Operations can ingest data from any source via syslog. Just set the VCF Operations server as your
syslog destination.
• CFAPI — Events are sent in their original format to VCF Operations using cfapi. Events sent over cfapi do not have to
follow the guidelines of a syslog event and are not modified to comply with the syslog RFC.
Each event contains the following information.
Broadcom 4822

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Type Description
Timestamp The time when the event occurred
Source Where the event originated. This could be the originator of the
syslog messages such as an ESX host or a forwarder such as a
syslog aggregation.
Text The raw text of the event.
Fields A name-value pair extracted from the event. Fields are delivered
to the server as static fields only when an agent uses the CFAPI
protocol.
Note:
VCF Operations is not responsible for the content of the log messages from the individual component. If you have
a question about the log contents, contact the team that generated the log message.
Event Types Grouping
VCF Operations summarizes a large number of individual events into a smaller number of broad event types. VCF
Operations uses machine learning to group similar events together, with each group showing the approximate number
of events in the group. Grouping events helps identify the most communicative events and the most quiet ones, both of
which are critical for troubleshooting.
The Event Types tab in the Analyze page, under the search bar, provides an aggregated view of the events for the given
time range of the query. An event in a group is selected as the representative event. You can click the Expand link under
each representative event to view the events in the group.As a result of grouping events, an Event Type is assigned to
each event. An appropriate event_type field is created, which you can further use in regular queries. VCF Operations
does not document the exact mechanism for grouping events. It tries to automatically detect groups of similar events
based on the number of common parts that the events have. For example, let us consider the following events:
•
[2019-05-20 06:41:24.291+0000] ["SearchWorker-thread-12999"/10.113.164.150 INFO]
[com.company.product.analytics.distributed.LogSearchWorkerService] [Worker fully
completed query (token=5f6e5e1faf93e4ce) in 11 msec]
•
[2019-05-20 06:41:24.284+0000] ["SearchWorker-thread-11961"/10.113.164.167 INFO]
[com.company.product.analytics.distributed.SearchWorkerService] [Worker fully completed
query (token=3b247b2ba6057c47) in 24 msec]
These events have eight common parts - timestamp, thread name, host IP, logging level, class name, message text, token
number, and duration. Now, let us consider the following events:
•
[2019-05-20 06:41:24.291+0000] ["LogSearchWorker-thread-12999"/10.113.164.150 INFO]
[com.vmware.loginsight.analytics.distributed.LogSearchWorkerService] [Worker finished
search (wait=59500 token=5f6e5e1faf93e4ce) in 12 msec]
•
[2019-05-20 06:41:20.136+0000] ["AliasStudentStudyPool-thread-1"/192.168.110.24 INFO]
[com.vmware.loginsight.analytics.alias.AliasStudent] [looking for alias due to rule
DatastoreFromVmFileSystem]
These events only have three common parts - timestamp, host IP, and logging level. In addition to grouping events
together VCF Operations identifies useful fields in each event of the group, known as smart fields. Each smart field
appears within the representative event as a hyperlink with a drop-down menu icon next to it. You can click the icon to
view a histogram for the values of the field or to define an extracted field based on the smart field.
Analyze Event Trends
You can analyze log events for trends and anomalies.

click Logs.
2. Construct and run your query by using the search text box and applying filters.
3. Click the Event Trends tab.
VCF Operations compares your query to the same time period immediately before and displays the results.

Configuring Log Filtering
Filtering log events allows you to control which log messages are dropped based on defined criteria. This capability
enables focused logging, improves performance by reducing noise, and enhances security by excluding irrelevant or
sensitive logs. This is useful when endpoints are unable to filter logs, allowing for the removal of unwanted data before
indexing. Filtering at this stage still consumes resources from the log management Virtual IP (VIP), and this processing
overhead should be factored into overall scale and performance considerations.

Configuring External Storage
Configure NFS or S3 external storage locations for exporting logs, archiving logs, and importing archives. You must define
a location before you can perform any of these operations. In the External Storage page, you can add, edit, and delete
locations and view their settings. Click the chevron against an entry to see more details. Click the vertical ellipsis to edit or
delete an entry, or to import an external archive.
• Before you configure an NFS location as external storage, ensure that an NFS export is already set up and reachable
from your VCF Operations deployment:
– If you are using vSAN as the backing storage for your NFS export, see Enable vSAN File Service and Create a
vSAN File Share to create an NFSv3 or NFSv4.1 export.
– If you are using a third-party NAS or NFS server, set up the export according to your vendor's documentation.
• Before configuring an NFS share for import, export, or archive operations, ensure the target directory has the correct
ownership and permissions and the path specified is relative to the mount point, and does not start with a leading "/".
• Before adding an NFS share or S3 location, ensure that all IPs in the VCF Management services Node pool are
allowed by the NFS server or S3 endpoint, and by any firewalls between them, because log management traffic can
originate from any of those IPs.
• To allow the system to write data successfully, the mounted NFS directory and its subdirectories require specific
permissions. If the directory does not have the correct permissions, the log management service fails to start.
– Ownership: The directory must be created by the root user.
– Minimum Permission Level: 447 — read-only for Owner and Group, and read/write/execute for Others. This is the
minimum permission level that VCF Operations requires to write log data successfully. You can also use a more
permissive setting such as 777, but 447 is the minimum.
If your NFS directory does not meet these requirements, update them using the following commands on your NFS
server:
sudo -i
chmod -R 447 /path/to/your/directory
• Ensure that adequate free disk space is available in the external storage.
Note:
S3 is preferred to NFS for archive locations. Unlike S3, if an NFS filesystem is unavailable when the log
management service is starting, the service will fail to start.
1. After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane,
click Administration > Configurations. Click the External Storage card.
2. Click Add New Storage. You can add up to 5 external storage locations.
3. Under Storage Type, select either NFS or S3 from the drop-down list.
4. For S3, enter the following details:

select the location from drop-down lists in Log Management.

uses to connect to the S3 bucket.
SecretKey The secret access key that goes with the access key ID.
Bucket Name The name of the S3 bucket where the log data is stored. The
bucket must already exist.
Endpoint The URL of the S3 endpoint. The endpoint must use a certificate
issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. Self-signed certificates
are not supported.
Server Side Encryption Specifies whether the S3 service encrypts the archived data at
rest.

Log Import and Export
You can export logs to extract specific datasets resulting from an analysis or search query.
Why Export Logs
• Data Extraction: You can search for specific logs within the Logs page and export the results for external use.
• Reporting: You can export event results and chart data, which is useful for offline reporting or external auditing.
• External Storage Archival: Up to 20K chart data logs can be exported to the local machine for long-term retention or
backup. Event data can be exported to an external storage.
External Storage Requirement
You can export logs to a configured external storage location, such as NFS or S3. For more information, see Configuring
External Storage.
Note:
Imports operate at the index level, not at the individual log entry level. If an index's data range overlaps with
the requested import interval even partially, the entire bucket is imported. As a result, some logs outside the
requested interval may be included in the import.
Exporting Logs and Chart Data
You can export log search results and chart data from VCF Operations for offline analysis, auditing, or archival purposes.
You can initiate exports directly from the Analyze page and monitor the progress of these tasks from the Configurations
menu.
To export datasets containing more than 20,000 results, you must configure an external storage path. Direct downloads to
the local file system are limited to 20,000 results.

Configuring Log Forwarding
You can configure a log management to forward incoming log events to a remote syslog server. A maximum of 10
forwarding rules can be created.
Before You Begin
Note:
• Verify that the destination can handle the number of logs that are forwarded. If the destination cluster is much
smaller than the forwarding instance, some logs might be dropped.
• Use log forwarding to send filtered or tagged logs to one or more remote destinations such as another log
management instance in a different VCF Fleet, a syslog server, or both. Log forwarding can be used to support
existing logging tools such as SIEM and to centralize logging within a single site or geographic location.
• Log Forwarding adds additional load to the log management instance, so it should be sized accordingly to
avoid impacts to log ingestion or forwarding capacity.
• During the upgrade process, any existing log forwarder rules from the Aria Operations for Logs or VCF
Operations for Logs are are imported into log management.
• Forwarding to Aria Operations for Logs 8.1x is supported. Forwarding from Aria Ops for logs 8.18 to log
management is also supported.
Configure Log Forwarding

click Administration > Configurations. Then click the Log Forwarding card.

xample.com:514
CAUTION:
A forwarding loop is a configuration in which a Log
Management cluster forwards logs to itself, or to another
cluster, which then forwards the logs back to the original
cluster. Such a loop might create an infinite number of
copies of each forwarded log.
When creating forwarding destinations, take care not to
create indirect forwarding loops.
Protocol When logs are forwarded using Syslog, the log's original source is
lost and the receiver can record the message's source as the Log

When logs are forwarded using Raw, the behavior is similar to
syslog, but syslog RFC-compliance is not ensured. RAW forwards
a log exactly the way it is received, without a custom syslog
header added by Log Management. The RAW protocol is useful
for third-party destinations, because they expect syslog events in
their original form.

• The source field might have different values
depending on the protocol selected on the Log

a. For syslog and RAW, the source is the the IP
address of the VCF Management services node
the forwarding Log Management replica is running

To verify your configuration, click VALIDATE CONNECTION. This

incoming log messages with additional metadata for filtering and

Log Management Filters
The fields and operators that you can select when you add filters in the log processing pages are not the same as those
on the Logs page. However, you can select settings that produce similar results in both places.
This difference is important when you click PREVIEW after you add filters in the following log processing pages, and when
you click ADD FILTER on the ANALYZE LOGS tab of the Logs page:
• Log Masking
• Log Filtering
• Log Forwarding
• Log Partitions
Matching Logic Differences Between Log Filtering and Log Processing Filter Preview
When you compare log search using filters in the Logs page with filter preview in the log processing pages, you will
observe differences in how search strings are matched. This behavioral difference occurs because Logs page search
ues Query Domain Specific Language (DSL) which has a strict token-based matching, whereas log processing filters use
flexible full-text matching.
Token-Based Matching In Query DSL, most operators (with the exception of regular expressions) evaluate text at the token level.
(Query DSL) The system divides the log text into individual tokens separated by specific delimiters. The following
characters act as token separators: ~ ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) + = [ ] { } \ | ' : ; / ? , . < > " \t \n
Space
For a query to return a match in Query DSL, the search criteria must align perfectly with the defined token
boundaries.
Full-Text Matching (Log Unlike Query DSL, the DSL used in the log processing tabs (Log Masking, Log Filtering, Log Partition,
Processing) and Log Forwarding) evaluates the full text string as a single entity rather than breaking it into tokens. This
approach is more flexible and successfully matches partial words or substrings, even if they do not align
with token boundaries.
Matching Behavior Examples
The following examples illustrate how the different matching engines evaluate the same log text and query.
• Target Log Text:
Filter Logic In|VCFOps

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Generated Tokens: , , ,
Filter Logic In VCFOps
Query DSL Result (Logs page
UI Query Log Processing filter Reason
filter)
text contains Logic In Match Match The query phrase exactly
matches complete, individual
tokens (Logic and In), and
also exists as a substring in the
full text.
text contains Logic I No Match Match The letter I is a partial string
and does not match the full
token In. Therefore, Query
DSL rejects it. However, the

within the full text.
Because of this architectural difference, you might experience inconsistent behavior when testing preview in the log
processing pages, and when using the logs filter in the Logs page, particularly when your search criteria includes partial
words or substrings that do not align with standard token boundaries.
Overview of Log Management Agents
A Log Management agent collects logs from log files and forwards them to a Log Management server or any third-party
syslog destination.
Agents support syslog and the Log Management ingestion API (cfapi protocol) and can be used withLinux-based
Operating systems. For windows systems, see, Set up the Windows system to collect logs in VCF Operations. You
configure agents through their web interface, through the file on the server and client side, or as part of
liagent.ini
installation.
Agents include the following features:
• Single or group deployment
• Automatic upgrade
• Parsing that operates on log messages and extracts structured data. You can configure parsers for FileLog and
WinLog collectors or both.
• Support for multi-line messages
• Native support for several log rotation schemes
• An extensive ingestion API that includes client-side compression, encryption, and the ability to add metadata to logs
The Log Management server supports centralized configuration management and creation and management of groups of
agents.
The following figure shows the elements of an agent deployment configuration.
Broadcom 4833

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A Log Management log forwarder is a dedicated instance of a Log Management server whose primary job is to forward
logs to a remote destination. Normally, a server instance used as a forwarder is not used for query. The forwarder uses an
internal load balancer and is otherwise structured like a Log Management server.
Agents write their own operation logs. For Linux, the path for the operation log is
/var/log/loginsight-agent/
. Log files are rotated when an agent is restarted or when the file reaches a size of 10 MB. A combined
liagent_*.log
limit of 50 MB of files is kept in rotation. You cannot collect agent logs with the Log Management agent itself.
Agents are used for real-time log collection. Use the Log Management importer to import historic log collections, including
support bundles.
On Linux systems, the agent runs as a daemon and starts immediately after installation. The Log Management
Linux agent collects logs from log files on Linux machines and forwards them to Log Management servers or syslog
destinations. Debian, Red Hat, and Linux binary installation packages are available.
Use the following commands to install the Linux packages:
• For deb:
dpkg -i <deb_package>
• For RPM:
rpm -i <rpm_package>
In both cases, you must have appropriate permission to install the packages.
System and Operating System Requirements
Log Management Agents support installation on Linux operating systems that satisfy the following core system component
dependencies:
• OpenSSL: Version 3.0 or higher
• systemd: Version 235 or higher

Agent Authentication for Log Ingestion
Agent authentication secures the HTTP ingestion path for log data by introducing an optional authentication mechanism
using secrets and tokens. This feature supports both the Log Management agent and 3rd-party agents such as Fluentd or
FluentBit. By default, authentication is enabled but optional. The server accepts both authenticated and unauthenticated
logs. However, you can enforce authentication globally, rejecting any log ingestion requests that do not possess a valid
token.
Why Agent Authentication
Enhanced Security Prevents unauthorized log injection into the logging infrastructure.
Flexible Integration Works with native Log Management agents and standard 3rd-party log shippers.
Granular Control Secrets can be managed, revoked, and tracked individually.
Prerequisites & Limitations
Before configuring authentication, ensure the following requirements are met:
• Agent Version: Log Management agent version 9.1 or higher is required.
• Protocol: Authentication applies only to HTTP/HTTPS ingestion APIs. Legacy Syslog ingestion remains
unauthenticated.
Note:
Windows agents are not supported.
Managing Secrets
Secrets serve as the initial credentials used to authenticate an agent. You must generate a secret before configuring the
agent. You can generate a secret in VCF Operations, or using REST API. For large-scale or automated deployments, use
the REST API. For information on how to generate a secret using VCF Operations, see Configuring Agents.
Broadcom 4839

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuring the Native Log Management Agent
1. Locate the agent configuration file on the target machine.
liagent.ini
2. Open the file and locate the section.
[server]
3. Add the property with the secret value generated from the Agent configuration page:
secret
[server]
hostname=log-server-address
proto=cfapi
secret=<your_generated_secret>
4. Save the file.
The agent automatically exchanges this secret for a token and handle renewal when the token expires.
Configuring Third-party Agents
Third-party agents do not have a built-in mechanism to exchange secrets for tokens. This process must be performed
manually or using an external script. Refer to the FluentBit or FluentD documentation for more information.
Enforcing Authentication
By default, authentication is optional. Unauthenticated logs are accepted, but if an agent attempts to authenticate with an
invalid key, it is rejected.
To enforce strict authentication and reject all unauthenticated traffic, enable the setting in the Global Settings. Once
enabled, any ingestion request without a valid Bearer token is dropped. Ensure that all agents are correctly configured
before enabling this setting. For more information, see List of Global Settings.
Revoking the Secret
If a secret is compromised or an agent is decommissioned, you can revoke the secret to block access. Revoked secrets
are retained in the list for approximately 7 days for audit purposes before being permanently deleted. During this time, the
name cannot be reused.
Log Statement Standardization Format
VMware Cloud Foundation comprises various components each of which issue log messages.
In VCF , the following components use the standard format for their application log messages:
• vCenter
• ESX
• NSX
• VCF Operations HCX
• VCF Operations for networks
• VCF Operations
• Identity Broker
• VCF Automation
This standard addresses a long-standing problem of VCF components using component-specific formats, in some cases,
multiple formats for the same component. These different formats complicate troubleshooting due to such factors as using
different time stamp formats and recording information in different parts of the log message. The different formats also
make it more difficult to automatically parse log messages.
Standardizing the log message format addresses both problems. It will make it easier to manually troubleshoot problems
using the log statements and process the log statements programmatically. This standard is based on the ESX log formats
for application log files that was introduced in ESX 8.0. If automatic parsing of log messages was developed for the earlier
versions of the above noted components, this parsing logic may need to be updated to correctly parse the log statements
compliant with the standard.
Broadcom 4840

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Application log messages are written into files that are maintained by components on their local file systems. The log
statement standard applies to log statements issued by software modules authored by the VCF division and not to third-
party software modules such as Apache Tomcat. In 9.1, centralized log collection transmits only ESX logs via syslog and
these logs are already standardized
Log Statement Standard
The log statement standard is described below using Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation. The standard
describes the format of an application log message. This section summarizes the key elements.
In the standard, an application log message comprises three parts that are separated by spaces and terminated by a
newline. The line below lists the format.
HEADER <space> STRUCTURED-DATA <space> MSG
Note:
HEADER and STRUCTURED-DATA must be in every log statement while the MSG part may be omitted.
The following log message is an example of one that is compliant with the standard:
2025-06-05T05:21:29.840Z INFO api 25572 [ops@4413 threadId=”639”
threadName=”127.0.0.1-8010-exec-26”] Completed POST /diagnostics/findings
The list below maps this example back to the format of a log message:
• HEADER:
2025-06-05T05:21:29.840Z INFO api 25572
• STRUCTURED-DATA:
[ops@4413 threadId=”639” threadName=”127.0.0.1-8010-exec-26"]
• MSG:
Completed POST /diagnostics/findings
This example illustrates three key principles of the log message format.
First, the first two parts of the log message format (HEADER and STRUCTURED-DATA) contain sub-parts separated by
spaces. For example, the header includes four sub-parts (timestamp, severity, app-name (application name), and proc-
id (process ID). The meaning and format of the sub-parts are defined in the table below using Augmented Backus-Naur
Form (ABNF) notation.
Second, the timestamps comply to the format defined in the RFC 5424 standard and, in addition, always use UTC/
GMT. In earlier VCF versions, the lack of a uniform timestamp made it difficult to manually or programmatically order log
messages. The log standard addresses this problem by mandating that all timestamps be in this format.
Finally, every log message that is compliant with the standard includes the sub-part in the
<string>@4413
STRUCTURED-DATA part. In the above example, the string is . This string reports the component that issued the
ops
log statement. In the example above, the log message was issued by VCF Operations. It is abbreviated as . The
ops
formal name for this sub-part is SD-ID. Its format is defined in the table below. The standard requires all compliant log
messages to contain the SD-ID. This fact can be used in automatic parsing of log messages. Log messages that include
the SD-ID are compliant with the standard. Log messages that do not include SD-ID may be partially compliant or not at
all compliant. Parsing logic that is written for the standard will correctly parse compliant messages and may not parse non
compliant messages.
If automatic parsing of log messages was developed for the earlier versions of the above noted components, this parsing
logic may need to be updated to correctly parse the log statements compliant with the standard. Follow this guidance for
reviewing existing parsing logic:
• Review existing automation logic
• If the logic is parsing log statements from components other than the three listed in this section, no action is required.
• If the logic is parsing log statements from the components that are mentioned above, search the application log files
of the component for examples of the log messages of interest. Generally, the MSG part of the log message did not
change. So, start by searching for the message ignoring any timestamps or other parts of the original log line.
• Review the log message examples found in the previous step. If the message includes the SD-ID, review the parsing
logic for any changes.
To create a parser that can programmatically process the VCF application log message format, use the ABNF notation
given below. Parser generators can be used to generate a parser that understands the format. Finally, as already noted,
Broadcom 4841

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
the standard is based on the ESX 8.0 standard. There are a few differences between these standards, which can be
understood by comparing the VCF log ABNF to the ESX ABNF for log files that the service manages. An
vmsyslogd
existing parser that understands this ESX log format can be modified and applied for parsing log messages compliant to
the standard.
VCF Application Log Message Format
Application logs are written by a component to its local file system.
Parameter Value
SP ASCII space %x20
LOG-MSG HEADER SP STRUCTURED-DATA [SP MSG] %0A
HEADER TIMESTAMP SP SEVERITY SP APP-NAME SP PROC-
IDENTIFIER
APP-NAME 1*48PRINTUSASCII
PROC-IDENTIFIER NILVALUE / 1*DIGITS
TIMESTAMP FULL-DATE "T" UTC-TIME
Complies to RFC 5424 with the requirement for UTC/GMT
formatting.
FULL-DATE DATE-FULLYEAR "-" DATE-MONTH "-" DATE-MDAY
DATE-FULLYEAR 4DIGIT
DATE-MONTH 2DIGIT ; 01-12
DATE-MDAY 2DIGIT ; 01-28, 01-29, 01-30, 01-31 based on
month/year
UTC-TIME TIME-HOUR ":" TIME-MINUTE ":" TIME-SECOND
[TIME-SECFRAC] "Z"
TIME-HOUR 2DIGIT ; 00-23
TIME-MINUTE 2DIGIT ; 00-59
TIME-SECOND 2DIGIT ; 00-59
TIME-SECFRAC "." 3*6DIGIT
Providing fractional seconds is considered very important.
Millisecond resolution is the minimum allowed (3 digits) when they
are added.
SEVERITY [ LINE-MARKER ] SEVERITY-STRING
SEVERITY-STRING "EMERGENCY" / "ALERT" / "CRITICAL" /
"ERROR" / "WARNING" / "NOTICE" / "INFO" /
"DEBUG"
LINE-MARKER "-" | "+"
NILVALUE "-"
STRUCTURED-DATA 1*SD-ELEMENT
SD-ELEMENT "[" SD-ID [*(SP SD-PARAM)] "]"
SD-PARAM PARAM-NAME "=" %d34 PARAM-VALUE %d34
SD-ID SD-COMP-ID "@4413"
SD-COMP-ID 1*27PRINTUSASCII

']' MUST be escaped.

Log Based Alerts
You can create alerts in VCF Operations for events triggered by log symptoms. You can create a query directly in the
Log Symptom definition, or select a list of saved queries. Alerts are triggered when incoming logs match the defined alert
criteria and contain log entries corresponding to the alert's configured object type.
For more information, see Create a Log Based Alert Definition.
Integrated Load Balancer
Integrated Load Balancer allows you to manage the IP and DNS addresses of their log management deployment. You
can add multiple Virtual IP (VIP) addresses and corresponding FQDNs. You can also configure dual-stack (IPv4/IPv6)
deployments by including IPv6 addresses (AAAA records). You can attach up to 5 static fields to VIPs. Logs flowing or
ingested through that VIP will have those fields attached, making them searchable via those fields.
To ensure full functionality of Virtual IPs (VIPs), updating the certificate to include all VIP and FQDN entries is required,
before a VIP can be created. This is necessary not only to prevent SSL host verification issues but also to satisfy system
validation during the addition of new entries.

click Administration > Configurations. Then click the Log Collection tile.

4. To add a new virtual IP, click CREATE NEW VIRTUAL IP. Optionally, click the vertical ellipsis next to the existing
virtual IP and click Edit.
Note:
You cannot edit the default Virtual IP and FQDN. However, you can add field values to tag the default virtual IP.
5. Provide or edit the following information.
Note: While HTTP-based logs should use the FQDN, syslog messages can be sent directly to the Virtual IP address.
Option Description
Virtual IP Provide the virtual IP address that will be used by the load
balancer to accept log messages. This address must be on the
same network as the default virtual IP.
FQDN Provide the FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name). This name
must be included in the SAN field of the certificate used by
Log Management. The active certificate can be found under
Manage > Certificates > VCF Management.
Fields (Optional) Provide one more field names and values to tag logs received
by this VIP. For (TCP) syslog-based ingestion field tagging is not
supported.
6. Click CREATE.
Log Administration
Log Administration is facilitated by the data set capability, which defines restrictions on which logs a user can access. This
involves applying a scope, which can be restricted to specific log data sets (example, logs containing "application name
x"), to a user or user group. The roles include log pages and other aspects.
Defining a Data Set
You can define a data set to provide users access to specific content.

User Management and Role-Based Access Control
Role-based access control lets you manage users and the tasks that they can perform.
What are Roles
Roles are sets of permissions required to perform particular tasks. VCF Operations has a set of predefined roles.
Additionally, you can create custom roles as part of defining security policies, and grant the roles to users. To change the
permissions and tasks associated with a custom role, you can update the role settings. The updated settings take effect
for all users associated with the role.
• To allow a user to perform a task, you grant the role to the user.
• To prevent a user from performing a task, you revoke the role from the user.
Managing roles for each user is based on their user login account. You can assign multiple roles to a user, in which case
the role permissions are merged.
Users who cannot view or access certain objects or cannot perform certain operations were not assigned the roles with
the permissions to do so.
Role-Based Access Control
In VCF 9.1, the log management functionality has been converged into the VCF Operations role based access control
through VCF Operations user accounts. As part of this integration, the legacy log-specific access controls have been
migrated to the centralized VCF Operations roles.
This unification allows administrators to manage users, groups, roles, and scopes for both infrastructure monitoring and
log management from a single control panel.
For more information, see Access Control in VCF Operations.
Users You can control the access and actions of each user by granting or revoking roles to or from the login
account of the user.
Broadcom 4844

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Permissions Specific permissions control access to log features. If a user’s role lacks a specific permission, the
corresponding feature tile, APIs, or page in the UI will not be visible to them. For example, tiles such as Log
Processing, Log Forwarding, Log Collection, and External Storage are controlled by permissions.
You can manage permissions in the Access Control card by clicking Operate in the top navigation bar and
in the left navigation pane, clicking Administration > Control Panel. Go to the Roles tab and edit a role
to select or deselect the permissions appropriately. For more information, go to the topic, Add or Edit Roles
and Assign Permissions.
Data Sets Data sets consist of a set of filters. You can use data sets to provide users with access to specific content
by associating a data set with scopes. The logs that the user sees in the Logs page, log based widgets and
saved queries, is dependent on the data set assigned to them.
Roles Roles determine what a user can do within the platform. A role is a collection of specific permissions
(privileges).
• Built-in Roles: VCF Operations includes built-in roles, such as Administrator (full permissions) and
Read-only (limited permissions).
• Custom Roles: Administrators can create custom roles by selecting a specific subset of permissions to
tailor access for different user personas.
Scopes Scopes determine what data a user can see. In VCF Operations 9.1, a Scope is a container that can
include two distinct types of visibility configurations:
• Object Scope: Defines which infrastructure objects (example, Clusters, VMs) are visible to the user in
the inventory.
• Log Data Set: Defines filters for the raw log data available to the user (example, Text contains 'error').
In VCF Operations 9.1, Object Scopes and Log Data Sets are independent. Selecting a set of objects (example, Cluster
A) in the Object Scope does not automatically restrict log visibility to only logs coming from Cluster A.
• Log visibility is determined solely by the filters defined in the Assign Log Data Set section of the Scope.
• It is possible to assign a Log Data Set to a user without assigning an Object Scope. In this scenario, the user will see
the filtered logs but may not see the related infrastructure resources in the inventory.
Configuration Workflow
1. Define the Scope (Data Sets)
a. Navigate to Access Control > Scopes.
b. Create a new Scope or edit an existing one.
c. Define Log Filters: Under the Assign Log Data Set section, add specific filters to define which logs belong to this
scope.
d. (Optional) Define Object Scope: Select the infrastructure objects (Clusters, VMs) relevant to this scope.
For more information, see Defining a Data Set.
2. Define the Role (Permissions). Ensure the role assigned to the user has the necessary log-related privileges.
a. Navigate to Access Control > Roles
b. Select a built-in role or create a new custom role.
c. Verify Log Permissions: Ensure permissions such as Log Processing, Log Forwarding, or Log Collection are
checked if the user is required to manage those configurations.
For more information, see, Add or Edit Roles and Assign Permissions.
3. Assign to User or Group
a. Navigate to Access Control > User Accounts (or User Groups).
b. Create a new user or select an existing one.
c. Assign Role by selecting the role that you configured previously.
d. Assign Scope by selecting the scope that you configured previously.
When you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top and click Operate and in the left navigation
pane click Logs. You will only see logs that match the criteria defined in the assigned Log Data Set in the Logs page.
When you go to Administration > Configurations, or Control Panel, you will only see the tiles for which they have
been assigned permissions.

Converting Content Packs to Management Packs
The Log Content Pack to VCF Management Pack converter is a utility designed to address the change in content
packaging following the introduction of Log Management in VCF Operations. This tool allows you to convert any third-
party and custom content packs into Management Packs, ensuring they remain usable within VCF Operations, which only
supports Management Packs.
Purpose of the Tool
• Converting any third-party Content Pack into a VCF Operations compatible Management Pack.
• Converting any custom Content Pack created into a Management Pack.
How to use the Tool
Note:
Ensure that you have Java Runtime Environment (JRE) 17 or higher installed on the machine where you intend
to run the conversion tool. You can run the following command to verify the version of Jave that is installed on the
machine:
java -version
Converting the Content 1. Download the conversion utility, and the README file wich contains the instructions. The utility can be
Pack found in the Drivers and Tools tab here, after you log in to the support.broadcom.com portal.
2. Log in to the Aria Operations for Logs or VCF Operations for logs and export the content pack you
intend convert and install in VCF Operations.
3. Extract the downloaded utility zip file, which contains the JAR file and the README text file.
4. Go to the command line and execute the command provided in the README file to convert the
exported content pack into a management pack. A new folder containing the converted pack file is
created.
Post-Conversion 1. You must enable the setting. Unsigned Pack File Installation in VCF Operations. This
is to prevent the error message, No signature found on pack file which is displayed
during installation. Log in to the VMware Cloud Foundation Operations Administration UI and activate
the Allow Unsigned PAK Installation under Administrator Settings.
2. Log in to VCF Operations and in navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane,
click Administration > Integrations. Click the Repository tab.
3. Click ADD and then click BROWSE to add the newly created management pack file.
4. Install the pack file even if it is already installed and ignore signature checking.
5. Upload the PAK file.
6. Accept the EULA (End-User License Agreement).
7. Proceed with the installation, which will take some time to complete.
Post-Installation 1. Once the installation has completed, verify that the management pack is available under the
Repository tab.
2. The management pack will be a content-only management pack, meaning it will not have any metrics
and the source is content pack converter tool.
3. Under the content tab, you can see the dashboards, alerts, and symptom definitions that originated
from the original content pack.

You can export custom, user-defined alerts from Aria Operations for Logs 8.18, execute the command-line conversion
utility, and install the resulting Management Pack within VCF Operations 9.1. Executing this transition preserves legacy
monitoring intelligence. To prevent unauthorized modification of platform monitoring files, the custom management pack
installation requires administrative privileges and a temporary modification of the security posture of the VCF Operations
cluster.
Ensure that the following prerequisites are met before you begin.

Log Management Health Overview Dashboard
The Log Management Health Overview dashboard is available to assist you in determining the appropriate course of
action when a system alert is triggered. The Log Management Health Overview dashboard is used as a secondary
function to assess the overall operation of the system when no alarms are present. The primary intent for this dashboard
is to provide additional insights when an alert is raised, helping you understand the underlying condition that triggered the
alert.
Where You Find the Dashboard
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Dashboards > All and in the VCF Operations group, select the Log Management Health Overview dashboard.
Dashboard Structure
The dashboard is structured around four main categories that correspond to four alerts related to logs. The dashboard has
a separate section for each of these four key aspects of the system.
Ingestion This relates to the process of logs being published to the gateway, sent to the log processor, and then to
the log store.
Retention This covers the log store indexing the data and then storing it on a disk.
Availability This category covers any conditions that could cause the log service to become unavailable.
Operations This focuses on asynchronous operations, specifically archiving (writing logs to external storage) and
forwarding (configuring the system to send logs to another endpoint).
How to Use the Dashboard
The recommended flow for troubleshooting an alert is as follows:
1. Identify the Alert: The dashboard summarizes the number of critical and warning alerts and lists the triggered alerts.
2. Review Symptoms: Multiple conditions can be grouped under a single alert (for example, an ingestion problem). Click
on the alert to view the specific symptoms that have been triggered (for example, "ingest queue capacity is greater
than 10%" or "dropped events exceed 5%").
3. Find Remediation Steps: Return to the main dashboard and open the corresponding section (for example, the
"Ingestion" section for an ingestion alert). This section describes each condition and provides remediation steps for
diagnosis.
4. Review Data and Guidance: Within the relevant section, for each condition, data is presented to illustrate the current
and recent behavior.
a. Dial: Shows the current behavior.
b. Chart: Shows the historical behavior.
5. Read the guidance provided in the text and follow the suggested steps, which may include reviewing other alerts (for
example, checking the Availability alert if an ingestion queue capacity issue is observed).
6. Check Knowledge Base (KB): If the suggested remediation actions do not seem to apply, review the Knowledge Base
article that is linked or mentioned.
Broadcom 4848

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The dashboard can be used to assess the overall operation of the system even when no alarms are present. In a healthy
state, you would expect to see no red indicators. By reviewing the widgets, a user can gain comfort that the system is
operating as expected.
The dashboard provides information such as:
• The current ingestion rate.
• The response time of the network.
• The status of retention problems.
• Confirmation that services and pods are up and running, and the log store health is green.
Advanced Troubleshooting
For advanced troubleshooting, there is a drill down dashboard that can be activated. The drill down dashboard is disabled
by default. To activate it, go to Manage, search for log,and enable the disabled dashboard. This dashboard is laid out in
the same style as the Log Management Health Overview dashboard, but it allows access to metrics about each individual
component of the solution.
The log system architecture has three primary components: the gateway, the log processor, and the log store. The drill
down dashboard is structured around these components (referred to as ingestion and retention services). Users can click
on a component, see the listed instances, and then view the related metrics for a specific instance.
VCF management If troubleshooting based on the logs dashboard suggests the VCF management services VMs may be
services Cluster Health overloaded, you can review the separate companion dashboard for the VCF management services itself.
This page is an overview of the health of the VCF management services and the services running on it.
Information This dashboard presents utilization metrics and a table listing the availability and memory usage of all
services in the VCF management services cluster, including ops logs. It also details storage usage, backup,
gateway information, and node details.
You should start with the application health perspective (the logs dashboard) and then drill down to lower layers of
the system, such as the VCF management services health page, to investigate potential issues like overloaded VCF
management services VMs. For example, if CPU utilization is high but all applications are behaving well, it does not
necessarily indicate a problem.
Accessing Logs when the VCF Operations Console is Inaccessible
Log Management is integrated as a built-in, containerized core service running natively within the VCF Management
Services. The VCF Operations console serves as the primary administrative interface for searching logs, running queries,
analyzing trends, and configuring forwarding destinations. If the primary VCF Operations console is offline, unreachable,
or undergoing maintenance, you can access local logs directly using the standalone Log Management emergency UI.
• The standalone Log Management FQDN or IP address that is configured during deployment is known and reachable.
• The local system administrator password that is created during VCF Management services runtime deployment is
retrieved.
Note:
The standalone emergency interface uses the local admin@vsp.local system-level account. Bypassing the VCF
Operations identity broker must be restricted to emergency troubleshooting and avoided in standard production
workflows.

2. At the login screen loads, enter the following administrative credentials:
a) Username:
admin@vsp.local
b) Password: The password that is assigned to the vmware-system-user during VMSP platform deployment.
3. After you sign in, you can see the standalone interface, where you can click the Analyze Logs tab to perform direct
diagnostic searches and verify platform status.

About VCF Operations for networks
VCF Operations for networks delivers intelligent operations for software-defined networking and security. It helps
customers build an optimized, highly-available, and secure network infrastructure across multi-cloud environments.
VCF Operations for networks accelerates micro-segmentation planning and deployment, enables visibility across virtual
and physical networks, and provides operational views to manage and scale the VMware NSX deployments.

VCF Operations for networks Security Compliance
VCF Operations for networks is a pre-hardened and secured appliance. VCF Operations for networks is hardened against
well-established and industry-accepted security benchmarks, for example: CIS. Additionally, VMware security team has
put internal controls to minimize the security footprint.
VCF Operations for networks also follows all security and privacy best practices defined by VMware Security Engineering,
Communications, and Response (vSECR) team.
For any critical known vulnerabilities that require immediate action, VMware releases security advisories for those
vulnerabilities with step-by-step instructions on how to keep the appliance secure. In general, all known vulnerabilities are
fixed in every release. Use the latest version of the appliance to take advantage of these security fixes.
Working with Data Sources
VCF Operations for networks allows you to add various data sources to gather information about your data center.
Adding a Data Source in VCF Operations for networks
You must add data sources into VCF Operations for networks to gather data of your data center.
To add a data source, go to Settings > Accounts and Data Sources > Add Source.
After adding a data source, you see the Accounts and Data Sources page where data sources are categorized based
on the following options:
• All: Displays all the available data sources.
• With Problems: Displays the data sources where VCF Operations for networks has found one or more problems.
• With Recommendations: Displays auto generated recommendations from VCF Operations for networks for the data
sources that require additional information.
Each data source displays the following details
Properties Description
Type Displays the type of data source.
Name Displays the name of the data source.
Identifier Displays IP address or FQDN details of data source.
Last Metric Collection Displays the time stamp of the last metric data collection.
Last Configuration Collection Displays the time stamp of the last configuration data collection.
Local Tags Displays all the Working with Local Tags associated with the data source.
Polling Interval Displays the polling interval that is defined for the data source.
Discovered Entities Displays the number of VMs that are discovered for that data source.
Note:
The Discovered Entities column is populated only if the data source is VMware
vCenter or AWS.
Flows Displays the count of flows for the data source.
Data Collection Indicates if the date collection on the data source is enabled or not.

To edit or delete a data source, you can click the More Options icon next to the data source. For the data sources that
support customizable polling interval, you can also use the Collect Now option to run the configuration data collection

VCF Operations for networks provides the following functions to enable easy access to the information of data sources.

• You can sort information by clicking the sort icon on any column.

Supported VMware Managers
You can add VMware Managers into VCF Operations for networks and collect the details.
Note:
If a data source is deleted and then added again, allow for a five-hour buffer period.
Add VMware vCenter
You can add VMware vCenter servers as data source in VCF Operations for networks.
• Your predefined roles in the VMware vCenter must have the Global.Settings privilege assigned at the root level. Also,
you must propagate this privilege to the children roles.
Note:
When you add a role in the VMware vCenter, by default the role is created with three system-defined privileges:
System.Anonymous, System.Read, and System.View. These privileges are not visible in the vSphere
Client but are used to read certain properties of some managed objects. See the vSphere Web Services API
documentation for more information.
• To configure and use IPFIX, you must have following VMware vCenter privileges:
– Distributed switch: Modify, Port configuration operation and IPFIX Operation.
– dvPort group: Modify, Policy operation and IPFIX Operation.
Note:
IPFIX is supported on the following VMware ESX versions:
• 5.5 Update 2 (Build 2068190) and later.
• 6.0 Update 1b (Build 3380124) and later.
• VMware VDS 5.5 and later.
• To identify the VM to VM path, you must install VMware tools on all the VMs in the data center.
To know more about roles in VMware vCenter, see the vSphere Security guide.
Multiple VMware vCenter instances can be added to VCF Operations for networks to start monitoring data.
You can also add VMware vCenter data sources directly from VCF Operations by navigating to Administration >
Integrations. To activate data sync between the VMware vCenter data source and VCF Operations for networks, select
the data source, activate the Network and Flow option under Network Operations, and select a data collector. You can
also enable NetFlow collection with the Enable NetFlow (IPFIX) on this vCenter option.
Note:
To enable Antrea IPFIX for collection of Supervisor, namespace, and VKS cluster flows, select Enable Antrea
(IPFIX) on this vCenter.
Migration, editing, activating, deactivating data sources managed in VCF Operations is restricted.. If you are upgrading
to VCF 9 from a previous version, the data source sync from VCF Operations for networks to VCF Operations does not
happen automatically and must done explicitly by the user to see the data correctly on the Network Inventory dashboard.
1. From the left navigation pane, go to Settings > Accounts and Data Sources.
2. Click Add Source.
3. Under VMware Managers, select VMware vCenter.
4. Provide the following details:

collector.

Add VMware NSX Manager
NSX is designed to address the emerging application frameworks and architectures that have heterogeneous endpoints
and technology stacks. In addition to vSphere, these environments may also include other hypervisors, containers, bare
metal, and public clouds.
VCF Operations for networks supports NSX deployments where the VMs are managed by VMware vCenter.
Considerations
• VCF Operations for networks supports only the NSX setups in which VMware vCenter manages the ESX hosts.
• VCF Operations for networks supports NSGroups, NSX-T Firewall Rules, IPSets, NSX-T Logical Ports, NSX-T Logical
Switches, NSX-T distributed firewall IPFIX flows, Segment, Group, and Policy Based VPN.
• VCF Operations for networks supports only NSX-T deployments. Support for NSX-V is removed starting with 9.0. If
NSX-T is used instead of NSX, then only those entities are displayed. The same logic applies to the entities such as
firewall rules, IPSets, and logical switches.
• With NSX-T 2.4 release, VCF Operations for networks supports NSX Declarative Policy Management which simplifies
and automate network and security configurations through outcome-driven policy statements.
Note:
Micro-segmentation for Security Group is done based on NSX Policy data. But in case there is no corresponding
NSX Policy Group, the standalone NS Group is included in the Micro-segmentation analysis.
• Ensure to add only local users in an NSX-T Federation setup.
• Verify that the user has both Auditor and Network/Security Admin roles are added for use with the data source.
Prerequisites
Here are the prerequisites for adding an NSX-T Manager as a data source:
• You must have at least the Read only privilege.
• You must add all the VMware vCenter associated with the NSX-T Manager as data sources in VCF Operations for
networks.
Note:
If you add the NSX-T Manager before adding VMware vCenter, then VCF Operations for networks takes around
four hours to stabilize.
• Ensure that there are no logical switches in the exclusion list in the Distributed Firewall (DFW). If there are any logical
switches in this list, then the flows are not reported for any VMs attached to these logical switches.
Adding NSX-T Manager directly in VCF Operations

enable data sync between the NSX data source and VCF Operations for networks, select the data source, activate the

by enabling the Enable IPFIX and Enable latency metric collection options.

• To enable latency metric collection, you must have enterprise_admin permission.
• Ensure that the port 1991 is open on the collector to receive the latency data from the ESX node.

Security Planning for NSX-T
To plan security for the NSX-T network, you can select the scope as NSXT Layer2 Network and use the following query:
plan NSX-T Layer2 Network ‘<NAME_OF_NSX_T_LOGICAL_SEGMENT>’
You can also obtain the same result by performing the following steps:
1. Select Plan & Assess > Security Planning from the left navigation from.
2. Select either NSX-T L2 Network or NSX Policy Segment as the scope from the drop-down menu.
Note:
NSX related entities such as NSX-T L2 Network and NSX Policy Segment are available in the scope. You can
use these NSX related entities for security planning.
NSX Projects and VPCs
VCF Operations for networks provides Enterprise administrators with complete visibility to NSX Projects and VPCs
included in data sources.
What are NSX Projects and VPCs
An NSX Project enables multi-tenancy for NSX network and security objects where each project is analogous to a tenant.
A NSX VPC is an additional layer of tenancy that you can configure within an existing project. Both NSX Projects and
VPCs are primarily configured and managed in NSX Manager by an administrator. For more information on NSX Projects
and VPCs and how to add them in your NSX Manager environment, go to NSX Multi-tenancy.
Note:
VCF Operations for networks supports the discovery of Projects and VPCs created in NSX 9.0 and later
NSX Projects and VPCs in VCF Operations for networks
VCF Operations for networks can now identify and extract data associated with Projects and VPCs included in the NSX-T
Manager data source added to your environment. New entities, flow analytics, metrics, and network map topology options
are added to VCF Operations for networks and used in Project and VPC specific dashboards and updated data included
in existing NSX dashboards. You can receive a general overview of the Projects and VPCs from the NSX Managers
and VPCs widget on the Network Operations page in the VCF Operations Console. By selecting View Details and
expanding the entry for a given data source, you can view the Projects and VPCs associated with it. Clicking on the entry
for a Project or VPC opens the dashboard page for that resource.
Note:
You can also view these dashboards from VCF Operations for networks.
You can use the data provided from Projects and VPCs to perform more granular analysis and troubleshooting of your
NSX data sources. For example, you can use the uplink and downlink data on the VPC dashboard to troubleshooting
connectivity issues.
Current limitations and specifics for VCF Operations for networks VPC usage include:
Broadcom 4864

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Network map path search does not take into account the uplink named teaming policy associated with VLAN backed
segments.
• VPC external IP NAT metrics are not captured or displayed in VCF Operations for networks, as these metrics are not
exposed by NSX.
• In the Transit Gateway (TGW) dashboard, under router interface metrics, both TGW uplink and VPC uplink router
interfaces are displayed. The metrics for the VPC uplink router interface correspond to the TGW downlink metrics.
• Only one service interface to NAT rule association is utilized and displayed in VCF Operations for networks,.
Note:
For VCF Operations for networks 9.0. network map path search does not take into account the uplink named
teaming policy associated with VLAN backed segments.
Disk Requirement for Projects and VPCs in VCF Operations for networks
To support the efficient use of this feature, customers are recommended to increase the disk capacity of their VCF
Operations for networks appliance by at least 500 GB if they are running at full capacity.
