Clustering - General
Can a collector VM be clustered?
No. Clustering of collector VMs is not supported.
Does VCF Operations for networks need a load balancer like VCF Operations for logs?
VCF Operations for networks clustering functions as a scale-out mechanism rather than a high availability solution; a
failure of the primary node causes the entire service to become unavailable.
What happens if the connection between remote collector & platform goes down?
In case the connection between platform and collector VM is down, the collector VM stores data locally (depending on the
disk space) and sends it whenever it is connected again.
Can VCF Operations for logs be integrated with VCF Operations for networks?
Yes, VCF VCF Operations for logs can be integrated with VCF Operations for networks for direct log collection using the
VCF Operations UI.
Broadcom 5242

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
What happens when a node reboots?
If a collector node reboots, there is data loss during the downtime. For more information, see the Broadcom Knowledge
Base article 314428.

In a cluster, you can change the IP of any collector or platform node using the CLI commands.

How much disk space is needed on platform1?
Platform1 requires more disk space compared to other nodes in the cluster as some of the configuration data is stored on
Platform1 only.
What happens if any of the nodes ran out of disk space?
The UI starts showing error messages when disk space on any particular platform node reaches a certain threshold. Add
more disk space to the platform node by logging in to VMware vCenter. The platform/collector VM must be in powered-on
state while adding disk space. For more information, see Increase the Disk Size.
What is the replication factor of data in the platform cluster?
The replication factor is 2 for all persisted data in the platform cluster. There is no replication on the collector side.
How to change the hostname of a platform or a collector node?
You can update the hostname of a platform or a collector VM using the command. Updating
hostname update
the hostname helps you easily identify the collector VM or the platform VM in your data center and align the naming
convention of the VM with other VMs in your data center.
To change the hostname of platform VMs or collector VMs, perform these steps:
1. Log in to the respective VM console.
2. Switch to a Ubuntu user.
3. Run the command to view the present hostname of VCF Operations for networks collector or platform
hostname show
VMs.
hostname show
4. To view the supported options, run the following command:
hostname update --help
Broadcom 5245

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

You use the command to update the hostname.
hostname update
Option Description
--dryrun This option validates the new hostname without updating the
hostname in VCF Operations for networks.
--hosts This option updates the hostname of your VMs in VCF Operations
for networks.
5. Run the command to validate the new hostname.
hostname update --dryrun
Syntax:
– To validate the hostname of a platform or a collector VM in a single node VCF Operations for networks instance,
run the following command:
hostname update --dryrun --hosts <new_hostname>
– To validate hostnames of platform VMs in a cluster, run the following command:
hostname update --dryrun --hosts platform1:<new_hostname1> platform2:<new_hostname2>
platform3:<new_hostname3>
Note:
• Use the following guidelines for hostnames:
– Use only alphanumeric characters, period ("."), and hyphens("-") in the hostname.
– Use less than 64 characters.
– Do not start or end the hostname with a period or a hyphen.
6. Run the command to update the hostname.

Syntax:

To update the hostname of one or more platform VMs in a cluster, run the following command:

Note:
After changing the hostname, it takes up to an hour for the hostname to reflect on the VCF Operations for
networks UI.
Clustering - Installing and Configuring
Do all platform VMs have to be on the same L2/L3 segment?
No. However, it is best to keep all platform nodes on a common network with low latencies between nodes. This is
because many of the distributed components replicate data among the nodes and high latencies can cause system
performance and stability issues. For more information, see VCF Operations for Networks System Recommendations
and Requirements.
What happens if there is a failure during the cluster creation process?
• Cluster creation for single node: Before converting a single node to a multi-node cluster, take a cold snapshot of the
original platform, the new platform, and all deployed collectors. If a failure occurs, delete the secondary platform nodes
and recover the primary platform and collector virtual machines from the snapshot.
Broadcom 5246

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
What happens if there is a failure during the cluster expansion process?
Similar to the cluster creation scenario, take snapshots of the existing cluster and the newly deployed nodes (all platform
nodes and collectors) and perform the steps mention in the following Broadcom Knowledge Base article KB article
314428.
What happens to the existing data and configuration when I expand the single node deployment to a cluster?
All data and configuration is maintained without any change. The data will be accessible after cluster creation.
Can you have platform VM in different regions?
No, we require the Platform nodes to co-located be in the same site. The collector servers can be geo-distributed.
The collector communicates with vCenter over HTTPS to pull inventory, configuration, VM topology, and push that data to
the platform. You only need one collector for each vCenter instance. Collectors do not need to be assigned for each ESXi
host or cluster—even if that vCenter manages hundreds of remote sites.
IPFIX data is exported toward the collector over UDP port. Every exporter (ESXi host) must have a working network path
to the collector. If hosts are in remote sites with high latency or bandwidth constraints, sending flows across WAN links to
a central collector can be inefficient.
Can platform hosted on vSAN Stretch clusters (2 Data centers)?
Yes, vSAN clusters within the same or across data centers would still ensure certain IO performance like local storage.
For more information, see VCF Operations for Networks System Recommendations and Requirements.
Can we host cluster nodes on different vSAN Clusters?
Yes, Different nodes of a Platform cluster could be hosted on different underlying datastores.
Clustering - Scaling
Can I extend an already created cluster?
Yes, extending a cluster is supported up to 15 nodes.
What happens if a non-primary platform VM becomes unavailable?
Grid processing halts; however, UI and API access remain available through the primary node. The system retains
previously processed and stored data. Extended node unavailability can result in the permanent loss of incoming data.
Upon node restoration, the system processes only the most recent data.
What kind of load balancing is supported?
External load balancers are not supported. The system internally load balances API calls directed to the platform,
whether accessed directly or through the user interface. The collector manages load balancing for collector-to-platform
communication, routing traffic to the platform cluster using a round-robin method.
Will creating a platform cluster increase network bandwidth consumption between collector and platform?
Collector-to-platform traffic is distributed across the platform cluster. Aggregate bandwidth consumption from the collector
remains constant. However, as the cluster forms and processes additional data, bandwidth requirements increase
proportionally.
What is the frequency of data transmission between collector VM to platform VM?
The collector VM sends data to the platform VM continuously.
Broadcom 5247

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Does any optimization of data take place in the collector VM?
Various deduplications, compressions, reduction, or batching steps happen in the collector VM. When the connection
between the platform VM and the collector VM is down, the collector VM stores data locally (depending on the disk space)
and sends it whenever the connection is restored.
Is there any optimization done for network bandwidth?
Yes, various deduplication/ compressions/ reduction/ batching steps happen on the collector VM.
Is clustering possible on the collector?
No. Clustering is not possible on the collector.
How does vCenter send traffic to the collector?
vCenter instances do not send traffic to the collector. The collector connects to configured vCenter instances to fetch
inventory and metric data. VDS exports IPFIX NetFlow data to the collector via UDP.
Clustering - Deployment
What is Platform1 and why do I need to remember this node?
The system designates the node that is used to initiate the cluster creation process as Platform1. Perform all external
integrations and backend operations exclusively from Platform1. Platform1 also helps to change network across cluster
nodes from CLI.
How do I access the UI after scaling out the cluster?
The UI can be accessed from any platform node.
Can I use a platform node which is deployed in different data center for creating clusters?
Nodes within a cluster exchange data continuously. To prevent latency, a cluster must consist of platform nodes deployed
in the same data center.
What happens to data on existing platform when I scale out the platform node?
The data on an existing platform node is preserved and distributed across all nodes in a cluster.
Do the number of collector VMs and data sources, including physical devices, determine the required platform
cluster size?
The size of the platform cluster is determined by the number of VMs, number of flows, number of network rules, and
applications, etc. For more information, see VCF Operations for Networks System Recommendations and Requirements.
Does VCF Operations for networks support platform cluster distributed across 2 data centers for HA reasons?
No. The platform Cluster does not support splitting across data centers. All Platform Cluster VMs should be in the same
site. Platform Cluster does not support HA today.

Comprehending Metric Data
You can view your metric data at different levels of granularity, based on the time range. For example, you can choose a
one day view, which can be useful when troubleshooting. Or, choose a broader time range (for example, 30 days) so that
you can see trends over time.
When you view metric data for different time ranges, you see different values indicated in the metric chart. This difference
is because VCF Operations for networks displays different resolutions of data for different time ranges.
The default time range of any metric in VCF Operations for networks is 1 day and the resolution is 5 minutes. As the
metric resolution becomes coarser, the metric data is down-sampled. That is, the resolution of the data is reduced. This is
performed to create better metric graph visualizations by retaining only the important characteristics of the metric.

The retention interval you choose has a direct impact on disk space.
Reducing the log retention period deletes all logs older than the new retention period specified. For example,
changing the retention period of the entity metrics from 6 months to 1 month deletes all logs older than a month.
Therefore, consider backing up your log files before reducing the retention period.
Increasing the log retention period adds new logs to the collection. Therefore, check the available disk space and
consider upgrading your disk space when increasing the log retention period.
Entity Metrics
VCF Operations for networks collects entity metrics from data sources in your environment such as VMware vCenter,
NSX to display information such as resource utilization, and performance.
To learn about the retention period of entity metrics, see Metric Definitions.
Viewing Entity Metrics
To view the entity metrics on the user interface, do the following:
1. Enter the entity name on the search bar.
2. On the search result page, click Add More Filters under the Filters option.
3. Select Metrics. The entity related metrics are displayed to the right.
4. Select the metric you want to view.

information.

1. Enter on the search bar.
Flows

Health Metrics
VCF Operations for networks collects health metrics from the Collector, Platform, and system to diagnose and monitor
health problems related to the VCF Operations for networks instance.
Health metrics are of the following types:
• Node metrics
• Service metrics
• System metrics
Viewing Health Metrics
You can view the node and service metrics on VCF Operations for networksPlatform and Collector pages. Where as, you
can view the system metrics only on the System Dashboard page.
To view node and service metrics:
1. Enter or on the search bar.
Platform Collector
2. On the search results page, select a Platform or Collector to view the health metrics available for that entity.
To view the system metrics, Enter on the search bar.
System Dashboard

configured memory in the given node.

Service Metrics
Service metrics indicate if a service is running. In the metric API name, you must replace with your
<service_name>
service name (such as IpfixProcessor, ElasticSearch, Kafka) to view the state of the service.
Metric Name Metric API Name Description
Service Uptime CUSTOM_METRIC[service.name:<service_name>]vRNI.service.uptime.rate.average.number Binary indicator to check if the VCF Operations
for networks service is running and is healthy.
• 0 denotes that the service is running and is
healthy.
• 1 denotes that the service is running, and
is not healthy.
• 2 denotes that the service is not running.

Processing Lag grid.messageAge.absolute.latest.millisecond The lag time of the system's data processing
grid.
High processing lag may result in the system
showing stale data.
Grid Usage grid.busy.absolute.latest.percent The capacity utilization of VCF Operations for
networks's processing grid.
The utilization percentage is constantly high if
the processing load increases. This may result
in potential risk of developing high processing
lag.
Adding many data sources, frequent addition
and deletion of VMs, and increase in flow
count are few of the reasons for increase in
the processing load.

showing stale data.

To view the latency metrics on the user interface, do the following:

entity.

NSX managers as data sources in VCF Operations for networks.

User Account Locked After Failed Login Attempts
You are not able to log in to VCF Operations for networks.
After several failed login attempts your account is locked, and you are not able to log in VCF Operations for networks user
interface (UI).
After five consecutive failed login attempts, the system temporarily locks the account for 15 minutes. Each subsequent
failed login attempt adds an additional 15 minutes to the lockout duration. If you keep trying to log in after the initial
lockout, your account can get locked for a maximum of one day.
You can use the new password that you have received from the admin to log in to the VCF Operations for networks UI.

Create a Migration Plan and Export Migration Waves
You can use VCF Operations for networks to create a migration plan for your workloads. After creating your migration
plan, you export it as part of migration waves and perform the migration in VCF Operation HCX.
To enhance your search and filtering capabilities, you can include more VM attributes in a CSV file you upload in VCF
Operations for networks. In addition to the VM attributes you want to use, this file must contain the mandatory and
vc_ip
attributes. The attribute value is the IP address of the vCenter instance where the VM is hosted and the
vm_moref vc_ip
attribute is the ID of the VM in the vCenter instance. To retrieve these attributes:
vm_moref
1. From VCF Operations for networks, select your VMs and from the top-right menu click Export as CSV.
2. In the Selected properties (CSV columns) field, click Add properties.
3. Search for and add the and properties.
Vendor ID Manager
4. Click Export.
5. Open the exported CSV file. The column contains the value for the property and the
vCenter vc_ip Vendor ID
column contains the value for the property.
vm_moref
Use the comprehensive search, filtering, and flow analysis capabilities of VCF Operations for networks to identify and
select the VMs for your workload migration. The creation of the migration plan consists of:
• Creating the scope for your workload migration. Optionally, you can upload a CSV file with more VM attributes to
further enhance the scoping process.
• Adding the workload of your migration scope to migration waves.
• Organizing your migration waves into mobility groups.
After creating your migration plan in VCF Operations for networks, you export the migration waves by commiting them
which imports them toVCF Operation HCX where the actual workload migration is performed.
Note:
The following procedure outlines how you can create a migration plan in VCF Operations for networks, you export
the migration to VCF Operation HCX, You can also perform this action from VCF Operations by navigating to
Launchpad > Workload Mobility.
Broadcom 5322

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. From the left navigation panel, navigate to Plan and Access > Migration Planning and click Create Plan.
2. Add more VM attributes for your migration plan.
a) From the Migration Attributes widget, select Upload.
b) Select your CSV file.
c) Verify that you are familiar with the content rules and that your CSV file includes the mandatory and
vc_ip
attributes and click Upload and Proceed.
vm_moref
After uploading the CSV file, you can see a breakdown of the total number of identified VMs, how many of them
match the new attributes, and if there are any errors. The newly added attributes are available as filters in all views
for VMs and migration planning.
3. Enter a name for your migration plan and click Proceed.
4. Define the migration scope.
a) Filter the VMs you want to add to your migration plan by using the available attributes or add more attributes from
the Filters tab.
b) After selecting the VMs you want to add to the migration plan, click Add to Scope.
c) Optional: By selecting Review Network Dependency, you can view any out-of-scope VMs identified as
dependencies and can add them to the current migration scope.
5. Create migration waves.
Note:
The following procedure outlines the process of creating migration waves and groups manually. You can also
generate the waves and groups in your plan automatically by selecting Auto Generate Waves and Groups. You
can also start the process of automatic generation even if you have selected the manual generation process. After
automatic generation is complete, you are sent to the Summary page.
a) Select the VMs you want to add to a migration wave.
Note:
You can only add VMs belonging to the same vCenter instance in a specific migration wave. Parts of your
workload from different vCenter instances must be included in a separate migration wave.
b) Select Add to Migration Wave.
c) Enter a name for the migration wave, add the destination HCX manager, and click Proceed.
Note:
Selecting a destination HCX manager during this step is only available if you have added that HCX manager as a
data source in VCF Operations for networks.
6. Organize your migration waves into mobility groups.
a) Select the VMs from your migration wave that you want to add to a mobility group.
Note:
You can add the VMs from a single migration wave to multiple mobility groups.
b) Select Create Mobility Group.
c) Enter a name for the mobility group and click Proceed.
d) Repeat for all of your migration waves.
7. On the Summary page, you see an overview of your migration plan and the option to make edits to your waves and
groups before commiting the plan to VCF Operation HCX.
Note:
You can remove the automatically generated migration waves from your plan by selecting Remove Auto
Generated Waves and Groups. If you have munally updated the content of these waves, they will no
longer be considered automatically generated and the above option used to removed them will disappear.
Broadcom 5323

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
8. When you are ready to export a migration wave to VCF Operation HCX, navigate to the migration wave entry under
Migration Waves and click Commit.
The Commit option is only available if you have added a destination HCX manager. If you have not added an HCX
manager in the previous step, you can select the migration wave and add it now. Alternatively, you can manually
export the migration wave by clicking the vertical elipsis menu to the left of the migration wave and selecting
Download Wave.
After clicking Commit, the migration wave is sent to VCF Operation HCX. Depending on the validation results, the
wave status is marked as either Commited or Failed. Failed migration waves include an error message describing
the encountered issue and the option to re-commit the relevant wave. The status for migration waves for which the
workload migration in VCF Operation HCX is in progress is marked as Executing.
9. Repeat for all of your migration waves.
You have created a migration plan and exported your migration waves.
Perform the workload migration in VCF Operation HCX. For more information on VCF Operation HCX, go to the About
Migrating Mobility Groups from Migration Waves.

Compute Gateway Firewall Rule
When communicating with the VCF Operations for networks platform; the collector requires HTTPS port 443 to be open
for outgoing traffic.
Following VMware hosted URLs are accessed by the collector through the firewall:
• *.vmwareidentity.com
• gaz.csp-vidm-prod.com
• *.vmware.com
• *.ni-onsaas.com
Broadcom 5330

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Additionally, NTP and DNS traffic should be allowed for the correct functioning of the VCF Operations for networks or VCF
Operations for networks collector.
Create a firewall rule with the following details:
• Name: An appropriate descriptive name
• Source: The name of the VMware Cloud on AWS Group containing the collector IP address.
• Destination: Select ANY
• Services – Select HTTPS, DNS, DNS-UDP, NTP, ICMP
• Action – Allow
• Applied To – Internet Interface
• Logging – Enable logging, if required.
Using VCF Operations Diagnostics
Discover and remediate known issues, and monitor the operational state of the private cloud infrastructure in VCF
Operations.
• How Diagnostics Helps You Keep a Healthy VCF Software Stack
• See Known Issues in Your Environment and Apply Fixes with Findings
• Overwriting the Diagnostics Configuration
• Monitor Your Environment and Prevent Issues with VCF Health
• Use Log Assist to Accelerate Your Support Cases
How Diagnostics Helps You Keep a Healthy VCF Software Stack
With VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics, you can quickly diagnose and address issues to minimize their impact and
improve operational efficiency, security, and reliability of your VCF platform.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics facilitates your job as a VCF private cloud infrastructure administrator, providing
an in-product capability to discover, troubleshoot, and remediate known and potential issues. VCF Operations Health
and Diagnostics builds on diagnostic tools and operational data to address the top drivers of service support requests to
help you avoid or resolve such issues yourself. With health and diagnostics data, you can act immediately as it provides
recommendations on how to resolve known issues or narrow down and even isolate possible root causes for emerging
issues. If you cannot find sufficient information to resolve an issue, you can reach out to support. But you do so with
proper context and using automated log bundling with Log Assist. The complexity and size of some VCF infrastructure
might pose a challenge to collect and act on all operational data. VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics makes it easy
by uniting all metrics in a single pane of glass and at the same time providing means of self-support on known issues.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics solves the challenge in three ways:
• Findings, where you discover known issues and can apply fixes that are based on recommendations, such as best
practices, knowledge base articles (KBs), and VMware Security Advisory (VMSA) notifications. Starting with VCF
Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, you can also use a set of public APIs that allow you to consume findings in your
own tracking and monitoring systems.
• VCF Health, where you proactively monitor the operational state of all components of the VCF software stack. VCF
Health helps you prevent issues that are not related to product bugs, but are caused by factors such as:
– Availability/Performance: issues with physical devices: servers, storage, or network components.
– Misconfigurations: incorrect settings affecting functionality.
– Security
– Need for optimization
– Lack of immediate observability: issues such as expired certificates or NTP drifts leading to integration issues.
• Log Assist, where you automatically generate log bundles along with other relevant context and transfer to the
Broadcom support portal for a speedy resolution of issues.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics also helps you with identifying and resolving product bugs. With VCF Operations
health and diagnostics 9.1, you can:
• Self-diagnose connectivity, availability, and performance issues impacting ESX hosts.
Broadcom 5331

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Troubleshoot vSphere High Availability issues, such as failure to restart protected VMs.
• Avoid disk size breaches when VMs have a large number of snapshots.
• Track the CPU and Memory utilization on cluster level and CPU, Memory, and Disk utilization on node level for VCF
services runtime.
With Findings and VCF Health combined, you can detect and remediate issues, resulting in generating a lower number
of support tickets, avoiding downtime, and reducing the mean time to resolution.
For example, if you see slowness in migration tasks in your environment, you can troubleshoot vSphere vMotion
operations, looking at the precopy time, duration, and bandwidth. You can also check CPU usage, CPU contention, and
memory utilization, and see error logs in a single screen, without changing context and tools.
Note:
For a comprehensive experience with the diagnostics workflow, you must register your environment in Connected
Mode to use the Log Assist capability. You need an Internet connection on the client browser to access KB links,
troubleshooting guides, and documentation.
What are Findings in Diagnostics
Findings in VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics helps you find and resolve known issues in your VCF software stack
by using a list of log and property-based findings, also called diagnostic rules, or signatures.
Findings result from scanning your VCF software stack for known product bugs, security notifications from VMware
Security Advisory (VMSA), and actionable best practice recommendations.
Figure 448: Diagnostic Findings Summary View
You see what are the affected objects, details of the finding, the recommendation for resolution, and usually a link to a KB.
Broadcom 5332

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 449: Findings Details Grid
The Findings capability in health and diagnostics also integrates with Log management to provide more depth and
flexibility in troubleshooting. You review the available findings and decide on the appropriate next steps to keep your VCF
platform up-to-date and healthy.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics works with more than 900 property and log-based rules, which are updated by
the Diagnostics Content Management Pack. You can see a list of all signatures in the Findings Catalog.
For more information, read See Known Issues in Your Environment and Apply Fixes with Findings.
Findings Rules
Log-based rules detect an actual occurrence of a known issue in your environment. Property-based rules indicate that
the issue is present in the current build and could occur or have already occurred. All finding rules relate to specific build
numbers. Depending on the finding, you can decide what corrective actions are applicable to your environment and how
urgent it is to apply such actions. An example of corrective action is to apply a patch or upgrade.
For more information, read See Known Issues in Your Environment and Apply Fixes with Findings.
What is VCF Health in Diagnostics
VCF Health is a comprehensive, high-level overview of your VCF deployment, enabling you to proactively monitor,
diagnose, and remediate the operational state of your environment.
VCF Health is designed to reduce downtime, improve visibility, and increase operational resilience by offering actionable
insights into VCF software stack, affecting compute, networking, storage, and the management layer.
The structure of VCF Health allows a drill-down to the hierarchy from a VCF instance to its management and workload
domains, vCenter instances, NSX instances, vSAN, and ESX hosts. VCF Health only works on environments that are
installed by using the VCF Installer and provide the level of centralized data that health and diagnostics collects, such
as certificates and configurations. This data is not available if you manually add components. With VCF Health, you can
reduce downtime or the mean time to resolution by identifying failures of underlying infrastructure such as ESX hosts or
remediating emerging performance issues.
Broadcom 5333

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 450: VCF Health Summary View
For example, if you see expiring certificates or notice NTP drift or DNS sync, you can avoid networking and configuration
issues. Or if you see a trend of failing tasks with virtual machine snapshots or vSphere vMotion migrations: you can
handle the underlying cause for the emerging negative trend to prevent issues from occurring.
From the Component view, you see a holistic overview, summarizing the health of all objects within the environment.
Broadcom 5334

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 451: VCF Health Component View
How to Set up and Maintain Diagnostics
Complete VCF Operations health and diagnostics for your VCF software stack by installing and configuring Log
management and Real-time metrics, and setting up integration between components.
The Findings capability has no license dependency and works on both VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation. Anything
that applies to VCF applies to vSphere Foundation as well, within the scope of your environment. You can apply only
diagnostic capabilities relevant to your setup. For example, you must take care of the NSX integration only if you use NSX
in your environment. You also do not need to have an SDDC Manager in your environment for Findings to work.
Broadcom 5335

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The management pack for VCF Operations health and diagnostics is automatically installed and the integration does
not require manual configuration. Some VCF platform components need installation or integration by using adapters to
become active and start collecting diagnostics data.
Setup
• After the initial installation of VCF management services, make sure you install log management and real-time metrics.
See Deploy Log Management and Deploy Real-Time Metrics.
• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, select Administration >
Configurations > Log Management to configure log collection into log management from VCF inventory objects,
such as vCenter instances.
• When you install VCF by using the VCF Installer, you get by default one unified cloud proxy that facilitates log
collection and the Log Assist capability. You use a unified cloud proxy to collect logs into the log cluster and to collect,
and upload support bundles to the Broadcom Support Portal. For more information, see Set up Log Assist and
Collecting Data with Cloud Proxy in VCF Operations.
• Make sure that you have connectivity between components in your environment. The networking port that is required
between VCF Operations and endpoints in ESX , vCenter, NSX, and SDDC Manager, is SSL 443. For Log Assist, the
connection is between the cloud proxy and the respective component, not from the cluster node.
• For log management, the required port is 9543. The minimum bandwidth is 200 KB/s.
• Generation of diagnostic findings depends on the following adapters:
– VcfAdapter (VMware Cloud Foundation)
– VMWARE (vCenter Adapter)
– NSXTAdapter (NSX)
– CASAdapter (VCF Automation for VM Apps Organization, formerly vRealize Automation Adapter)
– VCF 9.1 adds an adapter for the VCF services runtime component. With the data that the adapter provides, you can
self-diagnose connectivity, availability, and performance issues impacting your VCF components that are part of the
VCF management services.
Note:
Diagnostic findings are produced for VCF components only if their adapters are in collecting state. You see
property and log-based findings only for inventory objects that have an active cloud proxy and are in green
Collection Status.
• For findings related to earlier versions of VCF Automation, you must:
– add and activate the VCF Automation for VM Apps Organization adapter from the Repository at Operate >
Administration > Integrations.
– Create an account.
– Add the account to a Default Cloud Proxy group.
Scalability
Each VCF instance that you deploy gets one cloud proxy by default, but adding more cloud proxies to segregate
workloads helps with accelerating computation times.
Performance
The Diagnostics rule engine depends on I/O and requires SSD type of storage, preferably sub-millisecond access times,
such as NVMe. Slower disks might lead to an increase of computation times linear to the performance of the disk.
Update Cadence
Update cadence depends on the urgency of hot fixes and the number of accrued signatures. Usually comes along with
a maintenance release of VCF Operations for which you see notifications in Build > Lifecycle. Starting from VCF 9.1,
updates of the Diagnostics Content Management Pack might be released between maintenance releases as well.
The other updates are security-related and come in the form of a VMware Security Advisory (VMSA).
Broadcom 5336

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Record-keeping
Log-based findings expire 36 hours after the issue was first detected in the logs. Property-based findings are removed
from the system when the issue is resolved. VCF platform private cloud infra admins can export findings in tabular format
from the Findings tab to share with the other teams or keep for auditing purposes.
Roles
You use Role-Based Access Control to manage access to health and diagnostics. Normally, VCF platform private cloud
infra admins manage health and diagnostics and reach out to respective teams, such as storage or networking, for further
investigations outside of the VMware software stack.
VCF Operations Health
Along with VCF Operations health and diagnostics , you can track the health and resiliency of your VCF Operations
environment in a dedicated dashboard.
VCF 9.1 adds the VCF Operations Health dashboard to provide visibility on the health and resiliency of your VCF
Operations platform, log management, and real-time metrics. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click
Operate, in the left navigation pane select Dashboards, and expand All to get to the VCF Operations Health, Log
Management Health Overview, and Real-time metrics Health dashboards.
In the VCF Operations Platform health section, you see the health of your VCF platform, including supporting services and
integrated components, such as:
1. VCF Operations cluster - a high-level summary on the state of the cluster: if vSphere High Availability is active, the
number of nodes, cloud proxies, and adapter instances in the cluster.
2. Nodes and cloud proxies - a list of all nodes and cloud proxies that are associated with the VCF Operations cluster.
Shows the high-level summary of availability, number of vCPUs associated with them, and the percentage of available
storage in databases and storage logs.
3. Structure - shows the interactive topology of cluster, nodes, cloud proxies, and their associated services.
4. Details of the selected object - shows detailed metrics that are associated with an object you select: either the cluster,
its nodes, a cloud proxy, or any of the services.
5. License server - shows a high-level summary of the license server availability along with percentage usage of CPU,
Disk, and Memory.
6. About and How To Use widgets to help with your onboarding.
7. Links to Log Management Health Overview and Real-time metrics Health dashboards for more information on the
VCF services runtime cluster.
The VCF Operations Health dashboard replaces the following self-help dashboards:
• Self Performance Details
• Self Services Communications
• Self Services Summary
• Self Cluster Statistics
• Self Health
• Self Troubleshooting
See Known Issues in Your Environment and Apply Fixes with Findings
Findings collect data from all VCF components to help you identify existing or potential issues in your environment.
Findings are derived from properties and product logs data from vCenter, ESX, NSX, SDDC Manager, VCF Operations,
vSAN, and VCF Automation. Findings help you identify potential problems or inform you about existing issues in your
environment, and provides steps to resolve them.
Broadcom 5337

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Active Findings
In the Findings screen, you see Active Findings that shows all the findings that are discovered within the last 24 hours.
Checks against property-based signatures run every four hours scanning vCenter, ESX, NSX, SDDC Manager, VCF
Operations, vSAN, and VCF Automation. Within 24 hours, whenever a condition in your setup matches a signature, you
see it in the Active Findings grid. When you expand a finding in the grid, you see:
• a summary and description of the identified issue
• the affected objects with links that take you to an object summary page
• recommendations on how to handle the issue, either specific steps or a KB
The severity of a finding is defined by the following criteria:
• Critical: Findings that can cause possible data corruption, environmental outage, significant performance impact, or a
moderate to important security vulnerability within your environment.
• Immediate: Findings impacting the functionality of your environment that requires immediate attention but are not
critical.
• Warning: Findings that are an advanced notice of a potential issue that might result in loss of data or an error state
within your environment.
In the four-hour window of checking against property-based signatures, if you see null results, then your environment is
healthy.
Figure 452: Architecture Diagram and Data Flow of Findings
Broadcom 5338

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In addition to the scheduled property-based scans, within the 24-hour window of Active Findings, you can run on-
demand log-based checks by using the Refresh Findings option. With that option, you can narrow down the scope of
your monitoring to a specific component, capability, or functionality. To run a log scan, you must have Log management
installed and integrated in your environment. For more information, see How to Set up and Maintain VCF Operations
Health and Diagnostics. VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics also provides configuration findings, but they are part of
the operational state workflow in VCF Health.
You can trigger Refresh Findings for one or more specific management appliances or ESX hosts. This capability is
important for three reasons:
Broadcom 5339

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Some log scans might time out, which can cause some hosts to be skipped from assessment in the final result. If you
troubleshoot a problem with such hosts or a cluster comprising such hosts, a refresh guarantees that the final result
includes all known issues in your system.
• Some troubleshooting flows include checks also implemented as findings, for example, known issues with vSphere
vMotion. With a refresh, you do not need to scan all inventory, but limit to specific objects.
• You can use Refresh Findings to troubleshoot upgrade failures.
In the Check Last Run column, you see the date and time when automated scans were completed or a manual scan for
log-based findings was triggered.
In the Last Observed column, you see when findings were observed or occurred. For more details, see KB 375104.
Note:
Diagnostic findings for all objects are displayed on the Findings page even if the object no longer exists in your
environment. This behavior is due to the global settings of VCF Operations that retain historical objects.
Log-based rules detect an actual occurrence of a known issue while property-based rules state that the issue is present
in the build or configuration and might occur, or has occurred. In previous releases, all signatures were related to specific
build numbers. With VCF 9.0 and later, property-based rules are derived from the configuration of objects such as the
installed network drivers and ESX host configuration, regardless of the specific version. Depending on the findings,
you can decide if corrective actions are applicable to your environment and how urgent it is to apply such actions.
Sometimes, the corrective action is to apply a patch or upgrade, which requires planning, and you cannot immediately
apply the recommendations. Findings are categorized by severity, component, type, and capability. In Findings, you
see the number of affected objects for each issue, which helps in assessing the impact of the findings, prioritizing their
remediation.
You can review and store the results in the Active Findings grid in tabular format by using the Export button.
The export function collects all available data, including automatic findings, such as the Active Findings,
and on-demand findings, such as logs when you use Refresh Findings or Historical Findings. In the file
that you get from the export package, you see the three
vcf_operations_diagnostic_findings_summary.csv
categories under the Refresh Type column with values , , and respectively.
Auto Manual Active Manual Historical
VMSA Findings
To facilitate safeguarding your infrastructure, starting with health and diagnostics 9.1.1, all security-related findings
for which Broadcom issues a VMware Security Advisory (VMSA), are collected in a separate tab. You can see the
VMSA-related findings in the Active Findings tab along with all other findings, but in the VMSA Findings tab these are
highlighted to facilitate immediate action. In the details grid, you see the same columns as in the Active Findings tab, but
when you expand a row, you can see a summary of the vulnerability, a list of links to the affected objects in the inventory,
and the recommendations you need to follow to resolve it.
Historical Findings
If you investigate an issue that has occurred beyond the 24-hour window of active findings, you can use the Historical
Findings option. By using this option, you can evaluate log-based findings for a specified time in the past and for the
relevant inventory. With Historical Findings, you can also check if an active finding that you have fixed based on the
recommendations has been fully addressed. You can also see what specific fix you used for a given issue.
Note:
Refresh Findings and Generate Findings are active only if you configure log management or if a log scan is
already in progress.
You can also export the Historical Findings report for auditing purposes or for sharing with other teams,
or subject matter experts. The Export button is on the Active Findings tab. The export operation captures
historical logs as well under the category in the Refresh Type column in the file
Manual Historical
that you get from the export package.
vcf_operations_diagnostic_findings_summary.csv

Note:
You can run only one Historical Findings query at a time. Current results overwrite previous reports. For new
installations or migrated systems, active and historical findings might not immediately show results.
Findings Catalog
Click the Findings Catalog tab to see the complete list of signatures that are being checked in your environment at any
given time.
Findings Catalog replaces KB 371661 as the central reference point for available signatures.
Log Assist
Starting with VCF Operations 9.0, Findings provide a shortcut to the Log Assist capability. Log Assist extends the log
exports functionality with the diagnostics capability. You can use Log Assist to automatically upload the support bundles
and diagnostic findings to your existing support ticket for troubleshooting by Broadcom Support.

such as risk management or ticketing. The VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics API allows you to centralize
