Overwriting the Diagnostics Configuration
By using a JSON solution configuration file, you can manage some parameters of VCF Operations health and diagnostics
. You can deactivate rules or set defaults for some tasks, depending on your environment.
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics, you can consider sizing limits for your environment. If you use the full
capabilities of a VCF platform, you aim to avoid excessive use of resources for the cloud proxies. Best practice is to
segregate workloads to optimize performance and computation time of health and diagnostics. This means dividing an
environment by some logical grouping, such as by geography or business function. You can manage the limit of the
number of objects that are part of such workloads and can set up a cloud proxy for each workload. You see an alert for
the threshold of the max object count that you must consider when segregating workloads. This alert gives you a decision
point whether to segregate workloads or increase the limit if it makes sense for your setup. For more information on how
to use the JSON solution configuration file, see KB 369791. For sizing considerations, see KB 397782.
Monitor Your Environment and Prevent Issues with VCF Health
With VCF Health, private cloud infrastructure administrators can monitor the entire VCF stack in depth and breadth that
goes beyond the capacity of any individual VCF component or capability.
VCF Health provides a suite of monitoring capabilities that help private cloud infrastructure administrators to ensure the
optimal performance, availability, and stability within private cloud environments, across all VCF instances. With VCF
Health, you gain immediate insights into the overall health and status of the private cloud infrastructure and you can
proactively identify and resolve issues.
VCF Health gives two starting points for monitoring:
• VCF View, which allows a drill-down in the inventory tree from a VCF instance to its management and workload
domains, vCenter instances, NSX instances, vSAN, and ESX hosts..
• Component View, which provides a holistic view summarizing all objects in your environment.
Based on data from support requests, VCF Health screens are structured to help you with the most critical steps in the
maintenance and management of the VCF platform. For example, tracking certificates, NTP sync, and DNS reverse
lookup from operational point of view or tracking the performance of vCenter instances from infrastructure point of view.
You can drill down to each tile that summarizes a VCF operational metric to an individual dashboard or panel in VCF
Operations by following the View Dashboard or View Details link.
Broadcom 5343

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 453: Links for Drill-down from the VCF Health Tiles
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, the list of tracked VCF components and capabilities extends to include
vSAN, NSX, ESX, VCF services runtime, and vSphere High Availability. VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1 adds
new metrics to the existing reporting for vSphere vMotion, VM Operations, vCenter, and Snapshots.
Note:
VCF Health provides data only on active inventory objects. If you delete a resource, all related events are deleted
immediately.
vCenter is the key object for monitoring and reporting as it is the key building block in a VCF platform. VCF Health also
covers the key support request-generating areas in a VCF environment: health of ESX hosts, workload operations, such
as deployments and updates of virtual machines, virtual machines snapshots, and vSphere vMotion tasks.
Certificates Health in Diagnostics
VCF 9.0 and later provides centralized certificate management to monitor and manage all certificates across all VCF
components.
Certificate issues are reported for objects that have a VCF 9.0 or later entitlement. A VCF domain is entitled if the vCenter
in the domain is of version 9.0 or later and has a non-expired 9.0 license.
Clicking View Details on the Certificates tile takes you to the VCF Management screen under Manage > Fleet
Management > Certificates, where you can take pending action on certificates as necessary: renew, import, or replace a
certificate, or activate auto-renewal.
Broadcom 5344

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 454: Certificates Tile in VCF Health
Note:
To see all certificates, data collection of each VCF Operations health and diagnostics integration must be in a
healthy state.
Click any of the certificates to open the certificate details pane to see the particulars for this certificate. Use certificate
management to monitor the status and expiration of the following certificate categories:
• Platform Certificate
• Root Certificate
• STS Certificate
• TLS Certificate
After you add a new certificate or update your certificate, it takes approximately 10 minutes for the certificate information
to be reflected on the certificates page.
For more information, see Managing Certificates in VMware Cloud Foundation.
NTP and DNS Health in Diagnostics
Monitor NTP and DNS health to avoid issues that NTP drift and DNS forward and reverse lookups might cause, such as
failing vSphere vMotion tasks.
You need to monitor NTP and DNS settings over time to avoid issues that NTP drift and DNS reverse lookup might cause,
such as failing vSphere vMotion tasks. For example, if you do not set up a DNS forward and reverse lookup, in some
environments you get some connections labeled as insecure. As a result, certain integrations might break with errors
Broadcom 5345

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
that no secure connection can be established. With VCF Operations health and diagnostics, you can see if NTP is not
configured or is out of sync, as well as the DNS lookup issues for each object in your environment.
Figure 455: NTP and DNS Tiles in VCF Health
NTP
On the NTP tile, you see if NTP is not configured on some components. You can use the dashboard that is linked to
the tile to check which NTP server you must use to configure NTP. You can verify that components within each VCF
deployment are configured with the correct NTP servers.
The count of configured components only includes components that are accessible. You also see the NTP server drift,
which is computed for each component as follows:
1. Fetching the current time from the component
2. Subtracting the current time of the Cloud Proxy performing this check
3. Adding the result to the difference already accrued in the Cloud Proxy time drift from its NTP server
For example, the current time from the component minus the current time of the cloud proxy equals 35 seconds. We add
35 seconds to the difference already accrued in the time drift of the cloud proxy, say another 35 seconds. The result is a
time drift larger than a minute and you see it on the tile. This calculation executes every 5 minutes for vCenter and every
six hours for ESX and NSX.
Note:
You might see some transient discrepancies between VCF Health and the VMware Infra Health Overview
dashboard that shows NTP configuration data. The Infra Health dashboard gets data from the SDDC Manager
every 24 hours, while Health and Diagnostics gets data from the individual components in maximum six hours.
Broadcom 5346

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
DNS
On the DNS tile, you see if DNS is not configured on some components. You can use the dashboard that is linked to
the tile to check which DNS server you must use to configure DNS. You can verify that components within each VCF
deployment are configured with the correct DNS servers.
The count of configured components only includes components that are accessible. You also see a count of failed forward
and reverse lookups, evaluated based on the DNS server with which the VCF Operations appliance is configured. The
DNS lookups report failure if the PTR or A record lookups do not return a value.
vCenter Health in Diagnostics
With VCF Health, you can track data for connectivity, utilization, and services in a vCenter system that you cannot derive
from any individual tool for vCenter monitoring.
vCenter is the key object for monitoring and reporting as it is the key building block in a VCF platform. VCF Health helps
you with that task and adds value by providing data for connectivity, utilization, and services that you cannot derive from
any individual tool.
Figure 456: vCenter Instances View in VCF Health
Given the complexity and size of VCF deployments, testing multiple vCenter instances for reachability might be
challenging. Especially if you want to confirm all aspects - networking, user interface, and API, since one does not
guarantee the rest. For example, API calls to a vCenter instance might be successful, but the vSphere Client might not be
reachable. Such cases might indicate issues with the vCenter services or the vCenter database.
Broadcom 5347

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 457: Individual vCenter Instance Level View
Connectivity
In the Connectivity screen, you see the connectivity trend over the last seven days. The data tracks the reachability of
vCenter instances by network, UI, and API.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 adds endpoint monitoring, replacing the ping reachable/unreachable check to
the vSphere Client and APIs. The SDK/API endpoint metrics track any internal or external integration of your environment
that uses API calls. The UI endpoint metrics track the vSphere Client endpoint availability, focused on vCenter. Availability
by ping and UI is scored from 0 to 100 points. The check includes the server error
HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
response, and the , when API session limits are reached.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
Broadcom 5348

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Pings to a vCenter instance check if the vCenter virtual machine is powered on and available online. Pings to a vCenter
instance also check if all vCenter services are active and if the vSphere Client is responsive. Since many of the VCF
integrations also occur by using APIs, VCF Health checks reachability by API.
You can drill down data for each reachability alternative and can investigate any unexpected sustained outages by
reviewing findings for known issues or can use recommendations for general troubleshooting.
Note:
Data on the List of failed API for SDK/UI endpoint availability table depends on the log management adapter.
Make sure that the adapter is in a connected and receiving state.
Utilization
In the Utilization screen, health and diagnostics measures thresholds for CPU, Memory, Disk, and Database space
usage, so you can easily identify issues that might result from a memory leak or a scalability issue, and to proactively
resolve issues before they occur.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 enhances the usability of the Utilization screen by providing details in
condensed charts that give all information in one layer. You no longer have to drill down to see details in multiple charts
and layers.
Note:
VCF Health supports the CPU, Memory, and Disk metrics on the Utilization dashboard under vCenter Health
only for environments that migrate from vCenter 8.0 Update 3 and later.
The panel of each metric gives you a seven-day overview of the utilization against a warning threshold of 75% and a
critical threshold of 85%. Charts are similar to this sample:
Broadcom 5349

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 458: CPU utilization panel
The utilization of the vCenter Database is presented in two charts: one for the overall utilization of the vCenter DB, DB
logs, and Stats, Events, Alarms, Tasks (SEAT), and another for SEAT alone, with a breakdown for each category.
The Disk chart is different from the other charts in the Utilization screen, because it provides a breakdown of the current
utilization of all virtual disks in the selected vCenter instance and prompts immediate action, unlike the other charts, where
you see historic results and act retroactively.
Click the Check Recommendations button in each metric panel to get guidance on remediation steps.
Broadcom 5350

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Services
In the Services screen, you see the health and run state of the critical vCenter services over a period of seven days,
which allows you to take immediate action on any currently unhealthy service or follow the health trend to monitor if
any service is repeatedly unhealthy, or unhealthy for a prolonged period. You can troubleshoot by using the KB article
available in this screen.
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, the list of services covers all 18 critical services for vCenter, including
some of its related capabilities such as the vSphere Supervisor. For more information, see KB 381709.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 provides data that allows you to investigate the warning and critical states.
For example, see a Memory utilization chart for the specific service that helps you realize that a certain memory limit is
reached. Each service has its own set of metrics.
Note:
For vCenter 9.1, a Critical status is reported when the vpxd service memory, connectivity, or thread utilization
exceeds 85%. Warning status is between 75% and 85%. Checks run on every 5 minutes. In earlier versions, the
health status of the vpxd service was collected periodically from the vCenter Appliance Management Interface.
Status of Healthy, Warning, and Critical is based on the memory and connection state of services. The health status of
vCenter services is calculated differently in VCF Operations for health and diagnostics, based on data from the Real-time
metrics adapter, than in vCenter. You might see different statuses when looking at an individual service in the vSphere
Client or the Virtual Appliance Management Interface.
You can drill down to see the health graph for each service.
Note:
The health charts depend on the Real-time metrics adapter. Make sure that the adapter is in a receiving and
connected state.
Capabilities
On the vCenter instance level, you can follow through with monitoring specific aspects of infrastructure and performance,
covering:
• Virtual machine (VM) operations
• vSphere vMotion
• Snapshots
• vSphere High Availability
In each tile, you see an overview with data for the past seven days. You also see a ranking in each capability for the
highest number of incidents, or most impactful issues, or objects with the highest number of failures.
Virtual Machine Operations Health in Diagnostics
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics, you can track data from all tasks to create, delete, power, and reconfigure
virtual machines in a vCenter instance.
VM Operations under Capabilities on vCenter instance level replaces the legacy Workload Operations tile in
Diagnostic Findings 5.2 and later. VM Operations covers the entire span of tasks to create, delete, power, and
reconfigure virtual machines in a vCenter instance.
Broadcom 5351

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 459: VM Operations Tile in VCF Health
The VM Operations data allows you to catch issues before they occur during large or automated deployments. Often
workload operational tasks are not run by a VCF admin, but from VCF Automation agents, or API tools, which create and
destroy VMs in large numbers.
For example, from VM Operations you can spot when a blueprint that an automation workflow uses is failing, which
might prevent production-down scenarios. With VM Operations, you see the balance between VM provisioning requests
that succeed and fail, which gives you a reliable means of identifying such potential issues. In addition, you can drill
down to see the distribution of failures by cause or type of initiator. You also get specific recommendations on the type of
operation, such as Reconfigure, which further helps you troubleshoot existing or to catch emerging issues.
VM Operations monitors vCenter tasks and reports such that fail with context details and the respective error message, so
you can proactively troubleshoot a potential issue before it occurs. To help you better understand of root cause of a failure,
every report includes a link to the vCenter API documentation for the API that was invoked.
You can also see the distribution of VM Operation failures for the last seven days, the main reasons for failures, and the
main initiators with failures.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 adds the VM Operations Task ID parameter that allows a drill-down to
particular task. Starting from VCF Diagnostics 9.1, you can also use the Error Stack panel to analyze the logs upon a VM
failure, in the same screen.
When you expand a row in the grid, you see specific recommendations and links to API docs and KBs that help you
identify errors:
Broadcom 5352

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 460: VM Operations Details Screen
VM Operations covers the following operations, as displayed in the vSphere Client:
Create Operations Failures:
• Apply DRS clone recommendation
• Create New Virtual Machine
• Clone vApp
• Clone Virtual Machine or Template
• Deploy OVF
• Mark a template as Virtual Machine
• Register Virtual Machine
Power Operation Failures:
• Apply DRS power on recommendation
• Power on, off, and suspend virtual machine
• Initiate guest OS shutdown
• Start, stop, and suspend vApp
• Initiate guest OS standby
• Hard stop virtual machine
• Reset Virtual Machine
• Reboot Guest
Broadcom 5353

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Delete Operation Failures:
• Delete Virtual Machine
• Unregister and Delete Virtual Machine
• Delete and unregister vApp
Reconfigure Operation Failures:
• Reconfigure Virtual Machine
• Attach or detach a virtual disk
• Update VM Hardware version
• Guest OS operations, such as VMware Tools and Guest OS Customization
vSphere vMotion Health in Diagnostics
With vMotion Health, you can directly see the root cause of vSphere vMotion failures instead of running multiple checks or
calling support.
In the vSphere vMotion tile under Capabilities on vCenter instance level, you see data from vCenter events and log
statements that are collected and analyzed to help you troubleshoot possible failures. The span of vCenter monitoring
under Tasks and Events is relatively short and vSphere vMotion failure events roll over quickly. You might not identify an
issue before you see an impact on the operations, such as applications slowing down or failing. vMotion Health provides
you with this capability at a glance, allowing you to see critical issues as they emerge.
Broadcom 5354

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 461: vSphere vMotion Tile in VCF Health
Critical issues indicate definite failure of vMotion tasks. If such an issue affects either the source or destination host, or
the connection between them, VM migrations fail. Warning issues indicate a possible failure, depending on the VMNICs,
configuration, and connectivity.
Note:
If you see no vMotion operations available on the screen, confirm that you have configured log management to
collect events from your vCenter instances.
If you see no time or bandwidth values available for successful vMotion operations, check if log management
receives events from vCenter instances.
In the vMotion screen, you not only get all data in real time, but also see breakdown by status, failed or success,
and by reason, such as Invalid state or Invalid Power state. You also see a description of the possible issue and
recommendations for resolution. In the success scenario, you see data for the pre-copy time, pre-copy bandwidth, and
switchover time. These metrics help you see how well your infrastructure is configured and provide insight into why a
vMotion could take longer than expected.
For example, an increase in the pre-copy time and switchover time compared to earlier vMotion tasks of the same VM
indicates a possible issue with your physical network and infrastructure: it might be a physical switch too busy or a NIC
driver dropping packets. Or, it could be that the vMotion task was run while the VM was issuing many writes or the source/
destination hosts were overloaded at the time.
Broadcom 5355

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For failure scenarios, you see the type of failure, such as timeout, and an explanation of this failure type. For failure types
that can result in a vMotion task timing out, VCF Health provides a troubleshooting flow.
From the cluster level in the details grid, you see the Configuration and Connection checks, which create an inventory
of issues on several categories. These checks evaluate both the source and destination host that is involved in the task,
including VMkernel port groups, network connectivity, and jumbo frames. You can expand each of the checks and can see
details. For example, you might see that the root cause for a failure are MTU of different sizes, 9000 and 1500.
Other important vMotion health checks are available in the Findings tab. If the troubleshooting flow reports no issue,
review the manual and auto-refreshed findings on vSphere vMotion. After the troubleshooting is complete, you can see
the details on recommended steps to fix the parameter after you click Check Results. You can export the results or can
rerun the troubleshooting.
Virtual Machine Snapshots Health in Diagnostics
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics, you can track long-running snapshot delete, create, and consolidation
operations, and details on failed snapshots, or disks in need of consolidation.
VCF Health monitors vCenter snapshot tasks of every virtual machine, VMs that need consolidation, and VMs with too
many or too large snapshots. Similar to vSphere vMotion tasks, you cannot consistently track snapshot operations in
the vCenter Tasks and Events because they are rolling over fast, and you come to know about an underlying issue
with snapshots too late. Snapshots in production environments are not best practice, but any VM backup software uses
snapshots and such use drives a serious number of support requests.
Broadcom 5356

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 462: Snapshots Tile in VCF Health
In the Overview panel of the Snapshots tile under Capabilities on vCenter level, you see a list of critical issues that are
related to snapshots and the following data for the last seven days:
• Ratio of failed snapshots
• VMs with most failed snapshots
• Top initiators of failed snapshots
• A chart for the deletion and consolidation time.
Broadcom 5357

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Snapshot Operations
In the Snapshot Operations screen, you see the status of ongoing snapshot delete, create, and consolidate operations,
and details on snapshots that have failed. You can filter out snapshot operations that run for 4 or more hours. Such
operations might be a business problem and might require to consider a cancellation of the operation. To see data latency
of the source data stores, click Check under the Check Latency column of the detail grid. You can see relevant data such
as the actual data store latency, I/Os for the VM, and the overall write I/O load for the data store. Assess if networking,
storage, or system contention are increasing the time to complete the operation. If networking or storage issues are
suspected, you might need to involve your infrastructure team or vendor.
For snapshot failures, you see the error that vCenter reports. You can expand each row in the data grid to see details
on the error and recommendations for troubleshooting. Recommendations include KBs and links to API documentation,
similar to the other detail grids in VCF Health.
Note:
The list of snapshot failures does not include snapshot delete operations that fail during the second step of a
delete operation. In the first step, snapshots are removed from the snapshot tree, and the second, snapshot data
is consolidated to the parent snapshot. If a snapshot delete fails in the second step, vCenter intentionally reports
the task as successful and issues events to warn about the failure. The Snapshot Operations screen does
not report this type of failure. When a failure occurs in this second step, such VMs show in the VMs that need
consolidation screen.
If the underlying datastore is using native snapshots, long-running snapshot delete and consolidate operations are
not expected. Native snapshots do not involve the movement of data when deleting snapshots.
For failed events, VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1 adds the task ID, which is linked to the respective vCenter
instance and provides all details on the failed task in the same screen. In addition, the details screen includes the Fault
stack trace section, where you directly see the error logs. This section saves you logging in to a shell of an ESX host and
using ESXCLI commands to get the logs, which requires training and experience. Even if you need to contact the support
team, you can do so with the logs and details ready.
VMs needing consolidation
In the VMs needing consolidation screen, you see the allocation of VMs on datastores and the free space so that you
can decide whether to run a consolidation.
Snapshot delete operations can fail if the space on a datastore is not sufficient to consolidate the disks. You can use the
VMs needing consolidation screen to determine the storage used by a VM on each of its datastores. Space can be
freed up on a datastore by consolidating VMs with smaller footprints first, deleting all snapshots, or moving the disks to
other datastores. Act before the free space falls below 200 MB.
When consolidation is initiated, the task might take long, depending on the size of the disk and the data store
performance. Consolidation tasks might also affect latency and some tasks that take seconds might turn into minutes. In
the VMs needing consolidation tab, you can see such conditions and can prevent them from aggravating. For example,
you can:
• Reduce the number of users accessing an application,
• Schedule a consolidation window and inform users not to access the app,
• Move to other VMs from the data store.
The view also adds the Max data to consolidate parameter for the running consolidation so that you make sure to
allocate the necessary space and avoid memory outages.
VMs with Snapshots
VMs with too many or too large snapshots can cause performance and storage issues.
You might not know that a VM runs on a snapshot: for example, when a backup software takes care of snapshots.
Snapshot files can also significantly increase in size with every snapshot taken and by the time of consolidation, the size
might become huge. The unhandled volume of such automatic snapshots can affect the performance of the VM and other
VMs in the same datastore. To provide visibility on such scenarios, VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1 adds
tracking of the number of snapshots per VM, the pace of growth in size, and the biggest VMs with snapshots.
Broadcom 5358

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In the Overview panel of the VMs with snapshots tab, you see VMs with fast-growing snapshot sizes, the biggest VMs
in terms of snapshot size, and VMs with more than three snapshots. These metrics help you prevent a situation when a
datastore goes out of space due to unattended snapshot issues.
In the details grid, you get all metrics that you need to decide how to handle VMs with large snapshots that might affect
your environment.
vSphere High Availability Health in Diagnostics
vSphere High Availability metrics help proactive identification of issues and preventive resolution from a view that lists all
high availability clusters with their operational state.
In the vSphere High Availability tile under Capabilities on vCenter instance level, you see all configuration issues and
High Availability agents with errors.
You can drill down to specific configuration issues or agent errors per cluster by expanding the details grid on the landing
page.
Broadcom 5359

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 463: vSphere High Availability Tile in VCF Health
In the detail view per cluster, under the Cluster Summary tab, you can see a summary of the cluster in terms of CPU and
Memory reservations, and policies.
Note:
The CPU and Memory chart data depends on the HA configuration policy. You can see the current policy in the
Admission Control Policy field on the cluster level in the vSphere Client, before you drill down to the details
view.
Broadcom 5360

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 464: Cluster Summary View
In the other tabs, Configuration Errors and Agent Status, you see cluster and host-specific configuration issues, and
agent status, along with recommendations for resolution.
Note:
Diagnostics track a curated list of critical HA configuration issues that require immediate attention. In the vSphere
Client, you might see more HA configuration errors but they might not be critical.
In both sections, you can use the REFRESH button to get the latest list of issues and respective recommendations, and
the DOWNLOAD OUTPUT button to export the list.
ESX Health in Diagnostics
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, you can monitor all ESX hosts in your environment in a single screen,
diagnose all aspects of operation and performance, and proactively resolve issues.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 adds a gateway to monitor the operational state of ESX hosts across your
environment. You can track the connectivity and availability of ESX hosts and the state of critical services in a single
screen.
Broadcom 5361

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 465: ESX Tile in VCF Health
ESX metrics are available in several layers of progressive disclosure. You start from a landing page with a summary of
the critical issues for the entire fleet. Next, you can see a breakdown by metric on the level of a VCF instance or domain.
Finally, you can get to detail on specific checks for capabilities and services for each ESX host.
The ESX Health tile on the VCF instance and domain levels summarizes the critical issues that impact availability and
connectivity of ESX hosts, which are grouped in the following categories:
• Reachability
• Connectivity
• Services
• Hardware (Memory and SSD)
• Purple Screen of Diagnostic Failures (PSOD)
• Utilization
For each category, you can drill down to see health details, investigate the root cause, and get guidance for resolving the
issues that you identify.
When you click View Details on the ESX tile on the Component View on a VCF instance level or on a domain-level
page, you end up on the ESX Hosts page. This page lists all hosts in the selected instance or domain, and summarizes
results from checks that run every 5 minutes for each ESX health category. You can see a summary of the critical issues,
but also a breakdown of the results from the checks for each host in the details grid below the Overview panel.
The Filters menu in the left-hand side of the details grid mirrors the columns in the grid to allow you quickly getting to
specific insights.
Broadcom 5362

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 466: ESX Details View
From the host-level page, you have three levels of drill-down:
• When you select an ESX host, you get a details page, where you see the breakdown of issues per category or service.
You also see an NSX-specific panel, and separate tabs for health-related, and network-related checks and statuses.
• You can drill down to health-related and network-related checks and statuses:
– From the Health tab, you see groups of ESX-related checks that return either a system status, such as
Expired
for certificates, or an operational status, such as for the hostd service, which indicates that the hostd
Critical
process is down on the given host.
The ESX-related checks are grouped as follows:
• Connectivity: Checks the connection state between ESX hosts and vCenter, VCF Operations, and NSX.
• Connectivity Health: Checks certificates, NTP, and DNS health to avoid issues that expired ceritifcates, NTP drift,
and DNS reverse lookup might cause, such as failing vSphere vMotion tasks.
• Services Status: Checks the three key daemons that work to manage compute and storage in your environment.
Note:
To get data for the Services Status section, you need to obtain an API session token by making a POST request
to the vCenter REST API endpoint . Using that token, you
https://<vcenter-ip-or-fqdn>/api/session
can connect to ESX hosts and get the health report for each host for each service. The report is generated on
each ESX host, and the API is exposed by the ESX hosts. These reports do not exist in vCenter and require a
separate connection to ESX hosts. You can use a Cloud Proxy to handle restrictions such as firewalls, but such
proxies also needs to first get a vCenter token to ensure connectivity.
• Hardware Status: Checks the memory, SSD storage, and hardware sensors health.
Broadcom 5363

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1 also tracks the most impactful operational state, which is the failure of
ESX hosts with a purple diagnostic screen. In the PSOD (Purple Screen of Diagnostic) Failure tile, you can see a
Warning flag for PSOD events in the last seven days or a Critical flag, which indicate three or more PSODs in the
last 15 days or invalid core dump target configuration. For the core dump target, either a file or partition is missing or
is set at less than the minimum size that you see in the tile.
Note:
Always set up a scratch partition when installing ESX. The scratch partition collects the core dumps on persistent
memory, as opposed to RAM, and allows better traceability of PSOD events.
If the core dump target configuration is not valid, you see the PSOD Status as Critical.
When you click on View Details under the PSOD (Purple Screen of Diagnostic) Failure tile, you can see the
PSOD stack trace and history. From the PSOD details tile, you can also navigate to Findings to check for an
underlying known issue.
– From the Network Stats, you see charts of the Host CPU and Datapath CPU usage over the past seven days with
a threshold of 85% utilization that triggers a Critical status.
• For operational issues, each section in the host-specific view provides either:
– A KB to troubleshoot or resolve an unhealthy or critical status;
– A link to a details page, where you see the current status, historic status, description of the status if unhealthy, and
recommendations for resolution.
ESX metrics also provide a series of data that is important from the perspective of NSX:
• The details grid on the ESX Hosts landing page adds the Tunnels column that tracks critical issues with NSX tunnels.
• In the Summary panel of the domain-level page, you see NSX-related data, such as running state of NSX tunnels,
PNIC/Bond, and TEP IP.
• The Network Utilization tab of the ESX landing page adds a section for PNIC Network Statistic, the physical network
tile of ESX hosts. This tab provides interface statistics, such as bits per second, packets per second, and dropped
packets percentage.
vSAN Health in Diagnostics
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 gives you a single pane of glass for any vSAN-related monitoring, issue
detection, and troubleshooting tasks.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 builds on the Storage Operations capability, which is a centralized
monitoring console that is configured to observe storage across VCF deployments. Storage Operations removed the
limitation that vSAN performance and health metrics were only available in vCenter instances. Collecting vSAN data
required logging in to each vCenter instance. Such a task was difficult, but also unreliable, because in this case you do not
find the most urgent issues first. VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 gives you all operational data and insights at
a glance. You can see the actual health status of all storage clusters across the fleet at any time, and can act on the most
urgent ones without a delay. And you can drill down from the high-level metrics to specific clusters and vCenter instances
from a single screen.
Broadcom 5364

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 467: vSAN Tile in VCF Health
In VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, Storage Operations is integrated with the VCF Health capability to add
value by combining health scores and metrics with the means of accessing vCenter instances from the same screen. With
the combined capability, you can spot a negative health condition in the vSAN Health screen, follow up on the root cause,
and take guided remediation steps in the vCenter instance.
In VCF 9.1, you have three entry points to vSAN storage metrics. Under VCF Health, you can get to the vSAN storage
metrics from either the VCF fleet level view or the vCenter level view. You can also get to the vSAN tile in VCF Health
from Storage Operations.
• From Operate > Overview > Storage, you see a summary of the critical and warning health issues, and the count of
important performance insights for vSAN clusters.
Broadcom 5365

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• From the VCF fleet level, under Operate > VCF Health > VCF Instances, you have two entry points: the VCF View
and Components View respectively:
– In the details grid of the VCF View, when you select an instance with issues that are highlighted in the vSAN
Cluster column, you get to the vSAN Storage view.
• The Health view lists all vSAN clusters for the given VCF instance and provides a details grid with row for each
error on each cluster. When you expand a row, you see details on the issue, description, risk if no action is taken,
and the impact that the issue has or might have on other issues in your environment.
Note:
In the Health tab, you can set the sequence and number of columns in the details grid by using the Manage
Columns button. For example, the Score Impact column is hidden by default, but you can make it available by
managing the columns.
You can click the Troubleshoot in vCenter button to get into the vSphere Client, where you can follow the
prescribed remediation directly in the vCenter instance managing the vSAN cluster.
Figure 468: Link for Troubleshooting in the vSphere Client
You can click the Troubleshoot in vCenter button to get into the vSphere Client, where you can follow
the prescribed remediation directly in the vCenter instance managing the vSAN cluster.
• The Performance Insights view, you can drill down the inventory to check for specific insights, severity, and
type over a given period. Similar to the Health tab, when you expand a row, you see details on the issue,
description, charts, and a link to the vCenter instance, where you can take corrective action.
– In the Component View, you see a summary of the availability, performance, capacity, and compliance issues
across your fleet. When you click View Details, you get to the vSAN Storage view and can follow up on the health
or performance issues respectively.
• When you drill down to the vCenter Health view from the VCF instance view, you see a summary of health and

For more information, see Monitoring Storage Operations, Configuring a vCenter Account in VCF Operations, and

NSX Health in Diagnostics
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 provides the key metrics for NSX building blocks that help you track points of
failure to prevent overutilization and optimize performance in your system.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 adds a tile with NSX metrics to answer the most important question in
infrastructure operations - what is wrong and how to fix it. NSX-related data covers all operational aspects of the
underlying infrastructure and appliances, and leads you to resolution such as balancing loads or moving around
workloads. NSX metrics in VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1 are helpful to both infrastructure admins and NSX
Broadcom 5366

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
experts. Infrastructure admins can holistically monitor the performance of the VCF environment, while NSX experts can
dig into data for troubleshooting and creating action plans based on the real-time metrics.
Figure 469: NSX Tile in VCF Health
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 replaces the use of different screens or tools just to get data and adds further
value by directly providing actionable insights. The NSX Instances tile in VCF Health gives you a summary of the critical
issues, which require immediate attention across NSX building blocks, and is an instant starting point for troubleshooting.
NSX data is available from two paths:
1. Operate > VCF Health > VCF Instances > Component Viewfor infrastructure admins, who need a high-level view of
NSX in parallel to other VCF components.
Broadcom 5367

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. Operate > Overview > Network, for networking admins who directly need access to NSX status.
You can drill down to all network-related operational and performance details on component and infrastructure level from
both starting points..
The NSX critical issues are split in four categories: NSX Manager, Edge/Virtual Network Assessment (VNA), ESX hosts
networking, and Capabilities.
You get to the NSX tile from theComponent Viewin either:
• VCF Instances, where you see the critical issues count for each category summarized across the entire fleet
• Individual VCF Instance views, where the summary is narrowed down to the specific deployment.
Clicking View Details on the NSX Instances tile takes you to the details page, listing NSX instances in scope. You see a
summary of the most urgent issues and their type, such as application or capability issues, or NSX Manager issues. A pie
chart for each of the metrics provides better visualization for the most urgent or wide-spread ones.
Figure 470: NSX Details View
Broadcom 5368

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
When you drill down to a specific NSX instance, you get to the VCF Networking Health screen, which tracks four areas
for the selected instance:
• VCF Networking Health
• Networking Utilization
• Network Capabilities
• Services Capabilities
Note:
An NSX instance might stretch across multiple workload domains and the same NSX instance tile appears in
each of the domains that use that NSX instance.
VCF Networking Health
VCF Networking Health provides you with data on the operational state, such as cluster and node status, and adds the
infrastructure aspect: you get data for underlying networking issues of ESX hosts.
View Details on the NSX Management Cluster tile under VCF Networking Health, takes you to a screen that gives the
following information for the management cluster:
• Overview: provides operational statuses for the management node and underlying ESX hosts
• Utilization: tracking CPU, Memory, Disk, and Current Usage Per Partition
• Services: operational and performance status for NSX-related services
• API Metrics, summarizing API requests and response statistics.
View Details on the NSX Edge or Virtual Network Appliance Clusters tile under VCF Networking Health, takes you to
a screen that gives operational and performance status for NSX Edge or VNA Cluster.
View Details on the ESX Host Networking tile under VCF Networking Health, takes you to the ESX Hosts detail view
under the ESX tile in VCF Health.
On ESX host level, compute and network details are combined in a single view. ESX and NSX track similar metrics, but
apart from the common issues, such as connectivity status, the ESX landing page also shows NSX-specific metrics such
as Tunnels and Utilization. The ESX landing page provides an NSX-specific summary of the NSX versions, tunnels,
PNICs, and Tunnel End Point (TEP) IPs in your environment.
If you want to drill down to utilization metrics, in the ESX Hosts landing page you get to the Network Utilization tab. This
tab gives you a visual representation of historic data on the key performance indicators per host. For example, when your
network is dropping packets, you can quickly check if the condition comes from a resource perspective due to a specific
utilization issue.
• In the Interface Stats tab, you also have the key metrics that are related to packet drops, such as packets per second,
bits per second, or dropped packets percentage. For each metric in the Statistics column, data is provided in five-
minute intervals and the View Details button provides time series data over a period of time.
• In the Resources tab, you can see if the cause for current networking issues is the CPU utilization of the ESX host.
Networking Utilization
If you want to focus on troubleshooting network-related utilization issues, the Networking Utilization section combines
the NSX Edge/ VNA Cluster Utilization and ESX Host Network Utilization views.
When you click View Details on the NSX Edge/ VNA Cluster Utilization tile, you can get to a specific NSX edge or VNA
cluster view. When you drill down to a particular cluster, you can see the specific status and configuration details, and the
underlying ESX host information.
The Network Utilization tab provides edge datapath and service metrics. The datapath metrics provide usage details
around datapath CPU, memory pools, interface statistics, and and insight to NSX Capabilities such as T0, T1, and VPCs
configured to use the edge node. Service metrics provide information about services CPU, memory, and associated Load
Balancer usage.

When you drill down into the edges, you can bridge the operational state with performance issues. If an edge is down, you
can see what is the cause. For example, you can see that an edge is down because of a connectivity issue or an issue
with the underlying ESX host. This association can be found on the overview tab for easy navigation.
Network Capabilities
In the Network Capabilities, you see details on:
• Tier-0 Gateway

VCF Management Services Health in Diagnostics
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, you can monitor the health of VCF management services, the group of
components that run on the VCF services runtime component.
With VCF 9.1, the following components are deployed as part of VCF management services:
• Real-time metrics, which provides real-time data analytics
• Log management, which is the VCF log analysis solution
• Salt master, which provides centralized management of configuration drift and compliance
• Real-time metrics store, which helps to store data at scale and short interval metrics.
• Software depot, the unified depot that consolidates all VCF component binaries and metadata
• Fleet lifecycle, which provides a centralized and automated management of multiple VCF instances
• Identity broker, the dedicated authentication solution for the VCF components
• SDDC lifecycle, which handles automated updates and essential maintenance tasks
• Telemetry, which collects configuration, performance, and feature usage data
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, you can self-diagnose scaling, performance, connectivity, and availability
issues impacting theReal-time metrics, Log management, Identity broker, Fleet lifecycle, and Salt master components that
run on VCF services runtime component.
Broadcom 5372

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
The term VCF management services refers to the group of management components deployed in each VCF
instance that runs on the VCF services runtime component, which provides a standard and common runtime.
Figure 471: Structure of the VCF management services metrics and health in VCF Operations health and
diagnostics
Structure of the VCF management services metrics and health in VCF Operations health and diagnostics
From the VCF View, you can see the summary of critical issues for either services that enable components running
on VCF services runtime or the respective components running on it. From theVCF View, you can drill down to VCF
instances, VCF domains, and vCenter instances.
In the Management tile of the Component View, you see the number of VCF instances with component availability
issues. From the Component View, click View Details to go to the VCF Management Services page.
Broadcom 5373

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 472: VCF Management Services Tile in VCF Health
The VCF Management Services dashboard provides health metrics for components including services runtime nodes
and services, focusing on essential issues such as utilization and availability.
In the Overview panel of the VCF Management Services page, you see the number of issues that need immediate
attention from either component or services runtime perspective. You drill down to specific metrics per component, node,
or service in the Components panel.
In the Management Services Utilization Overview panel under VCF Management Services, you can see the overall
CPU and memory utilization details focusing on scale and performance issues. The scale-related metrics are static and
you get recommendations on thresholds and actions by KBs.
Broadcom 5374

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
In the Components panel, you can track the availability and memory utilization for each component and the storage
utilization of storage volumes.
In the Backup Details panel, you see the status of backup jobs for the past 24 hours.
Note:
When you first run a backup of a VCF instance, you see the task as complete, but you do not immediately see
a record in the Backup Details panel. It takes two completed tasks to trigger the count of backup jobs in the
Backup Details panel.
In the Gateway Services panel, you can also track the utilization of the underlying services for the containerized
environment and see the health of each service, based on its specific performance parameters. For example, request
sizes, request/response sizes, and latency.
In the Nodes panel, you see the breakdown by CPU, memory, and disk utilization per node, and the health status.

Use Log Assist to Accelerate Your Support Cases
To accelerate resolution of support cases, you can use Log Assist to automatically generate log bundles and attach
diagnostic findings data.
Log Assist provides a streamlined mechanism for creating and securely transferring support bundles to Broadcom
Support, accelerating the resolution of technical issues related to VCF. Log Assist automates processes to eliminate the
manual effort that is usually required to collect and upload logs and diagnostic information. The automated gathering of
pertinent technical data allows Broadcom Technical Support to diagnose and resolve issues faster and more efficiently.
Sometimes, in Findings you might not see a known issue reflecting a problem in your environment. Or you cannot
proactively identify the issue by drilling down to the VCF infrastructure metrics that VCF Health provides. In such cases,
you can reach out to Broadcom support, but you do so with context and automatically generated log bundles by using Log
Assist.
Log Assist adds both property and log-based findings that are active at the time of downloading the diagnostic report to
your automatically generated log bundles. A link to Log Assist is available from Findings.
You can also add log-based findings that you generate by using the Refresh Findings workflow in Findings and the
Export functionality. Broadcom Support uses the diagnostic findings data to identify known issues that might contribute to
the issue in the support case. For more details, see KB 375820.
Note:
Log Assist does not perform cleanups. You can manually remove support bundles when no longer necessary.
After an upgrade to VCF Operations 9.1 or later, make sure Log management is also on the same version. Otherwise, you
do not see it in the Log Assist inventory and Log Assist cannot collect bundles from Log management.
Important:
To use the online functionalities of Log Assist and send log bundles, you must provide access from the could
proxy in your environment to the eapi.broadcom.com URL. For more information, see Public URLs Required for
Online Functionalities for VCF and vSphere Foundation.
Before generating a log bundle for the selected inventory object, Log Assist runs several connectivity checks:
1. Connectivity from your environment to the assigned cloud proxy.
2. Connectivity from the assigned cloud proxy to the selected component.
3. Connectivity of your environment to the Broadcom Support Portal to make sure that you can upload the log bundles.
Broadcom 5377

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Validates that the permissions of the integration are sufficient for downloading a log bundle.
Upon failure, you see error-specific messages and directions for resolution.

Note:
Each unified Cloud Proxy that you use with Log Assist supports up to five parallel support bundles at a time. If you
select more components, they are grouped in a queue. The speed of the support bundle upload depends on the
uplink bandwidth.
The upload of log bundles to Broadcom support servers does not require external FTP clients.
With VCF Operations health and diagnostics 9.1, Log Assist adds the following options:
• Generate bundles for selected VCF Operations nodes, not only the cluster-level bundle option.
• Transfer log bundles from Log management and Identity broker under VCF services runtime.
Note:
The support bundles for VCF services runtime cannot transfer when the management cluster is down.
Set up Log Assist
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, Log Assist is enabled by default and you do not need to activate it on the Cloud Proxies page.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, Log Assist is active by default on all cloud proxies in your environment.
Important:
You still need to assign objects from the Inventory for each cloud proxy, as described in step 4 in this procedure.
For VCF versions earlier than VCF 9.1.1, to start using Log Assist you must make sure that your environment is registered
in Connected Mode, activate Log Assist on a cloud proxy, and assign Inventory objects to the cloud proxy.
• In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, select Licenses >
Registration and make sure you register your licenses in Connected Mode.
Broadcom 5378

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• See the topic Collecting Data with Cloud Proxy in VCF Operations on how to add a unified cloud proxy to your
environment. The legacy cloud proxy capability, which in VCF 9.0 and later is defined as the Classic type, does not
work with Log Assist.
• Provide access from the could proxy in your environment to the URL. For more information,
eapi.broadcom.com
see Public URLs Required for Online Functionalities for VCF and vSphere Foundation.
• Verify the connectivity between the cloud proxy and objects from the VCF Inventory that you assign to Log Assist. The
required connection is between the cloud proxy and the respective component, not to the cluster node.
After you activate Log Assist on a cloud proxy, you can assign Inventory objects to Log Assist as described in Step 4. You
can map different Inventory objects to specific could proxies.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, select Operate > Administration > Cloud Proxies.
2. Select a cloud proxy. Click the ellipsis next to the check mark, and select Activate Log Assist.
The Log Assist adapter only runs in standalone mode, no groups are supported.
3. (Optional) If you want to activate Log Assist on all cloud proxies:
a) Select the checkbox on top.
b) Click the ellipsis next to the Add button.
c) Select Activate Log Assist.
4. Go to Operate > Administration > Configurations > Log Assist Assignments and assign objects from the
Inventory to the Log Assist-enabled cloud proxy by drag-and-drop.
Attach Logs and Diagnostic Findings to Support Tickets with Log Assist
You can generate a log bundle for any selected inventory object, link and upload it to your support case with Broadcom.
With Log Assist, you can:
• Generate a log bundle on demand
• Link the bundle to a support case
• Attach diagnostic findings to your support case
1. Log in to the Broadcom Support Portal with your credentials.
2. Select the component for which you file a support case and create the case.
With creating a case, you get a case number. Keep this number for further reference in your support workflow. If you
get support from a Broadcom partner, you should note the partner ID along with the case number.
3. Upload data to the case.
a) Log in to VCF Operations.
b) In the Control Panel, navigate to the Log Assist card.
c) Click Prepare a Transfer.
In the new screen, the Select an inventory object tab is automatically selected.
d) Select the affected object from the VCF inventory tree.
You can select objects from the VCF inventory tree up to the ESX host level. You cannot select an individual virtual
machine. Dimmed check boxes indicate that the object has no mapping to a unified collector. To configure the
mapping, go to Infrastructure Operations > Configurations > Log Assist Assignment and drag and drop the
required object. After assignment is complete, continue with your cloud transfer.
e) Click Next and wait for the connectivity validation.
The check might fail due to intermittent connectivity issues and you can click RE-VALIDATE to get the latest
connectivity status for your environment. If the check fails again, you must troubleshoot your network connectivity
and click RE-VALIDATE when you resolve the underlying issue.
The connectivity check might also fail due to missing required privileges for the object. To fix privileges and
connectivity, see KBs 375817 and 375818.
Broadcom 5379

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. On the Transfer to Support Portal tab, enter your case number in the Support case ID field.
5. Click Transfer.
If the transfer is successful, you return to the Operate page.
6. In case a transfer fails, you can see the errors for specific objects and can retry the task.
Log Assist is designed to handle intermittent network or infrastructure issues automatically before requiring user
intervention.
If a log bundle operation or transfer fails, Log Assist automatically retries the task up to three times. If the issue
persists, the task is marked as failed.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 adds the Retry button to facilitate manual retries of failed log bundle
operations.
a) In the Log Assist page, under Transfer History, expand the row for the current Support Case and look at the
Activity Feed, where you see a breakdown of the successfully completed and failed log bundle operations.
b) Click the Retry button to re-run only the failed tasks that you see in the Activity Feed.
VCF Operations Health and Diagnostics 9.1 simplifies the retry process by pre-populating the Support Case ID and
inventory selections from the original request, so you only re-run the failed tasks.
Troubleshooting with the Workbench
The Workbench is where teams can collaborate, build a knowledge base of issue investigations which can be saved for
future reference, and enhance troubleshooting by viewing real time data. You can view data with 20-second granularity
for real-time performance evaluation by default in the Real Time Analysis tab, selecting the Overview sub-tab. For Host
System and Virtual Machine object types, an additional ESX Top view is available that provides 2-second granularity data.
To enable this view, activate the ESX Top category under Real time metrics for ESX hosts being investigated, in the policy
settings.
What Does the Troubleshooting Workbench Do
The Workbench page is where you investigate your VCF stack comprising of the following components:
• vCenter
• ESX
• vSAN
• NSX
The new observability engine, introduced in VCF 9.1, collects metrics in real time, provides alerts and notifications,
analyzes and summarizes rich data, provides data enrichment, recommends actions and provides user-driven enrichment.
The real-time data component must be installed, and is not available by default.
The Workbench page provides:
• Unified visibility into all operational data
• Real-time data at 20-second, and 2-second granularity for mission-critical workloads, containers, and applications
hosted on ESX.
• Summary dashboard for selected objects
• Top N data for VM, Host, Cluster, Datacenter type of objects
• Quick access to metrics and alerts
• SSH access and Script execution
• Collaboration tools and note taking
• Log Analysis
• Network Flow Analysis
Where You Find the Troubleshooting Workbench Home Page
In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Workbench.
Broadcom 5380

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Workbench home page displays a search bar, a list of troubleshooting sessions, and recent searches. You can open
a session to find potential evidence for your problems.
How Workbench Home Page Works
All troubleshooting sessions that are active in the current login are displayed in the Workbench home page. The
Workbench now organizes investigations into two distinct sections:
Draft Sessions Your active investigations are automatically preserved as drafts. Any changes made to the scope, time
settings, and notes are retained upon logout. When you log back in, you can resume your work from the
Draft Sessions section, where your previous context is restored.
Saved Sessions Investigations that you explicitly save are stored in the Saved Sessions section. These sessions
permanently retain your specific scope, time parameters, and notes for future reference.
Starting the Troubleshooting Workbench
The Troubleshooting Workbench is where you perform advanced troubleshooting tasks on an alert that triggered on an
object. You can investigate both known and unknown issues in VCF Operations .
Where You Find the Troubleshooting Workbench
You can start the troubleshooting session with an alert in context from the alert information page, or you can search for an
object and start the troubleshooting session to investigate known or unknown issues related to the object.
• To start the Workbench with an alert in context, in the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in
the left navigation pane, click Alerts.
• To start the Workbench with an alert in context, but for a specific object, select a group, custom data center,
application, or inventory object from the Inventory. Click the object and then the Alerts tab. Click the
TROUBLESHOOT button on the top right.
• On the Workbench page to investigate known or unknown issues with an object in context, search for the object.
The Workbench navigation bar provides quick access to the following tabs for comprehensive investigation:
• Potential Evidence
• Real Time Analysis (containing Overview, Top N, and Custom Query)
• Logs
• Flows
• Metrics
• Alerts
• Tools
• Notes
Potential Evidence in Workbench
You look for potential evidences of a problem within a specific scope and time range in the Potential Evidence tab. The
Selected Scope control on the left of the Workbench page is where you vary the scope.
You can vary the scope in the following ways:
• You can select only the object that you are investigating, or include several upstream and downstream relationships
by increasing the scope. As you increase the scope, more objects are displayed in the inventory tree. The number of
objects in scope should not exceed 300.
• You can select a custom scope to include objects of your choice. Click Custom to open an interactive window where
you use the pointer to visually rearrange your objects, view relationships and add peers to modify the relationships. To
see details about the object, place the pointer for a few seconds above the object. You can reset a custom scope to
start all over again.
• You can use the drop-down menu to narrow down the type of objects displayed.
Broadcom 5381

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The default time range is two hours before and thirty minutes after the alert triggered when the context is alert based,
or when the context is object based, the default time range is last 6 hours. You can select a different time range, up to 7
days, using the date and time controls.
The time range selector offers a split view:
• Presets: Quickly select from Last hour, Last 6 hours, Last 12 hours, Last 24 hours, Last 7 days, Today, Last day, Last
week
• Custom Range: Manually define a specific Start date/time and End date/time for precise analysis. The custom
selection date range should not exceed 7 days.
The potential evidence is based on Events, Property Changes, and Anomalous Metrics which are displayed on the right of
the Workbench change in the Potential Evidence tab. Information in these sections is displayed as cards.
Events Displays events, based on a change in the metrics. Events for metrics that have breached the usual
behavior, and major events that have occurred within the selected scope and time are displayed. The cards
are based on dynamic thresholds for a metric, which is calculated based on historical and incoming data.
Property Changes Displays important configuration changes that occurred within the selected scope and time. Both single
and multiple property changes are displayed. For multiple property changes, you can view the latest and
previous changes.
Anomalous Metrics Metrics which have shown drastic changes within the selected scope and time. Ranks the results based on
the degree of change. The most recent anomalous metric based on a time-sliced comparison in the current
time range is given the highest weightage.
You can explore more details about any of the cards that are displayed in the Workbench by clicking the card pop-out
option. You can close a card and it is no longer displayed in the Workbench. To load the cards again, click Go in the Time
Range.
Real-time Data in the Workbench
The Real Time Analysis tab in the Workbench page helps you visualize near real-time data, offering live performance
data streaming at 20-second granularity. The Real Time Analysis is the central hub for performance analysis and is
divided into three sub-tabs, namely, OVERVIEW, TOP N, and CUSTOM QUERY. OVERVIEW and TOP N sub-tabs in the
Workbench page help you visualize near real-time data, offering performance data streaming at 20 seconds (or more)
and 2-second granularity and covering esxtop use cases. The Real-time functionality offers high-granularity metrics,
interactive charts, date range pickers, and the ability to add chart screenshots to notes. The Real-time metrics component
of VCF works on supported objects in the Inventory.
Real-time Troubleshooting
The OVERVIEW sub-tab under the Real Time Analysis tab provides instant visibility into system performance metrics
across ESX, virtual machines (VMs), NSX Transport nodes, Edge (for transport nodes object type objects), and other
vSphere components. It is designed to help you diagnose issues such as sudden performance drops, CPU spikes, or
memory overuse.
The tab applies the observability engine that streams real-time performance data at 20 seconds (or more) and 2-second
granularity for selected objects within a defined scope and category. You can view, filter, and interact with performance
data to isolate problems in real time.
The key features of the real-time troubleshooting in the OVERVIEW sub-tab are as follows:
• High-Granularity Data. The performance metrics refreshed every 20 seconds (or more) and 2 seconds for esxtop
subset of metrics in the OVERVIEW sub-tab. For more information how to change the metric collection to 2-second

Top N Troubleshooting
Located within the Real Time Analysis tab, the TOP N sub-tab, helps you identify and analyze the top resource
consumers for VM, Host, Cluster, Datacenter, NSX and vSAN type of objects, without using command-line tools. Top N
metrics now feature explicit labeling. This ensures that the most resource-intensive objects are easily identifiable within
the charts. The system displays child metrics, offering deeper visibility into the performance of underlying sub-components
and object hierarchies.
It presents the Top N descendant objects of the same type based on selected performance metrics, simplifying the
detection of resource bottlenecks and abnormal activity.
The key features of the Top N tab are as follows:
• Configurable Visualization: The Visualise Top N panel lets you drill down to different levels of the Inventory to see the
objects with the worst metrics or performance in the given hierarchy or object over the selected period. You can refine
your view as follows:
– Metric Selection: Choose the specific metric you wish to analyze (for example, CPU Contention).
– Visualise Limits: toggle between viewing the Top 5, Top 10, or All objects to focus on the most critical offenders.
– Multi-Metric Support: Click Add Another Metric to compare different performance indicators simultaneously.
• Interactive Charts:
– Zoom in or reset zoom for comparative views.
Broadcom 5383

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– Reload data to refresh metrics.
– Export charts as PDF, copy to clipboard, or add to notes.
• Custom Time and Value Ranges: Enables detailed comparisons of performance values over selected periods.
Note:
2-second interval metrics are not available in the TOP-N sub-tab.
2-Second Granularity
The Workbench page offers high-resolution (2-second) metrics in the OVERVIEW sub-view. Once the ESX Top policy is
activated for your Host Systems, the Troubleshooting Workbench provides access to 2-second granularity data. However,
the availability and behavior of this high-resolution data vary depending on the specific view you are using within the
OVERVIEW sub-tab.
In the OVERVIEW sub-tab, you can view 2-second data for specific objects.
• Supported Objects: High-resolution data is available when you select a Host System or a Virtual Machine from the
scope.
• Enabling the View: You must explicitly select the ESX Top view from the view dropdown menu to see 2-second
granularity.
• Time Range Constraint: High-resolution data is resource-intensive. If you select a time range greater than 6 hours
while in the ESX Top view, the system will display an error message rather than showing the data. You must reduce
the time range to 6 hours or less to view these metrics.
The Top N sub-tab behavior differs from the Overview. Data in the Top N view is always displayed at 20-second
granularity, regardless of whether the ESX Top policy is enabled or if the metric supports higher resolution. This design
choice prevents clutter and confusion by maintaining a consistent step window for ranked lists.
When using the Custom Query sub-tab to analyze metrics with enabled, you may encounter duplicate
esxtop: true
data lines if not filtered correctly.
By default, if you query a metric that has both standard and high-resolution data, the chart will display two concurrent
lines: one for 2-second data and one for 20-second data. This can make the chart difficult to read and may show
conflicting spikes due to aggregation differences.
To view only the 2-second granularity data, you must filter your PromQL query using the ESX_TOP feature flag.
When building your query, ensure you add a filter for (syntax: for example
Feature equal to ESX_TOP
mem.tier.consumed.MEMTYPE{feature='ESX_TOP'}) to exclude the standard 20-second data stream.
Custom Query
The Custom Query sub-tab, located within the Real Time Analysis tab, allows you to execute specific queries using
PromQL (Prometheus Query Language) to retrieve granular performance data that may not be covered by standard
dashboards. This tool is essential for deep-dive analysis where specific, custom metric correlations are required.
Use the Add Query input field to enter and run your PromQL query. To assist you in constructing valid queries without
autocomplete, the Query Builder Help section provides three tabbed resources below the input field.
Note:
This field does not provide autocomplete or suggestions. You must enter a complete PromQL query exactly as
you want it to run. Ensure you have the exact metric names and syntax ready before typing.
When you click Need help? Use the quick Query Builder, the query builder displays the following tabs.
Functions Lists all supported PromQL functions available for your queries.
• Usage: Browse this list to find mathematical or aggregation functions such as sum, min, max, avg,
and topk.
• Description: Each function includes a brief description of its logic (for example, sum calculates the Sum
of values across all time series).
• Copy: Click the copy icon next to a function name to paste it into your query string.
Broadcom 5384

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Metrics Provides a searchable catalog of all available performance metrics in the system.
• Search: Use the search bar to find specific metrics (for example, IOPS or Packet Drop).
• Reference: This is critical for finding the exact internal name of a metric (for example,
LWD_SNAP_SES_TOTAL_WRITE_TIME) since there is no autocomplete.
• Copy: Locate the metric you need and click the copy icon to add it to your query.
Sample Queries Offers pre-built templates to help you understand syntax and structure. These samples demonstrate how to
combine metrics and functions correctly. You can copy these samples and replace the metric names with
those relevant to your specific investigation.
• Sample query for host system cpu.ready.HOST
• Sample query for host system filtered for 2 sec granularity, after the 2 sec policy is configured for the
selected host: cpu.ready.HOST{feature='ESX_TOP'}
• Sample query for host system filtered for 20 sec granularity
cpu.ready.HOST{feature='TROUBLESHOOTING'}
Alerts and Metrics in the Workbench
When you pin a metric, it appears in the Metrics tab of the Workbench page. You can perform further investigation on
the metric in the Metrics tab. You can compare the pinned metrics with other metrics that are displayed in the tab. You can
close the pinned metrics and browse other metrics for specific objects. Similarly, the Alerts and Events tabs are where
you investigate the potential evidences further. You can filter and group alerts. If you want to focus on the alerts for a
specific object in your selected scope, you can clear all the alerts and then click the object in the scope.
Collaboration in the Workbench
You can add notes and save troubleshooting sessions for further investigation. Investigations can be marked as resolved,
shared with other users or teams, or deleted if no longer needed. You can add comments and screenshots. The
collaborative feature allows seamless handover of investigations between users.
Saving and Sharing Sessions
When an issue arises with the resource, administrators typically begin their investigation on the Workbench page by
adjusting the scope and time settings to help identify the root cause. However, investigations may be interrupted by
higher-priority tasks or require an extended period to complete, risking the loss of progress.
The Save and Share feature lets you preserve your current troubleshooting state and resume it later. Additionally, a
sharing feature enables you to invite colleagues into the same troubleshooting session, creating a shared space for joint
investigation.
Each troubleshooting session includes a status indicator that reflects its current progress through the investigation
workflow:
Status Description Behavior
Draft Unsaved session Changes made to the scope, time settings,
and notes do not persist after logout.
In-Progress Saved session with ongoing investigation The session is persisted and can be
accessed later. Investigation is actively
ongoing.
Resolved Issue identified and documented The session is marked as complete.
The investigation findings have been
documented, and the issue is considered
closed.
Other users that you collaborate with can view saved investigations with the following details:
• Troubleshooting Name
