Optimizing Capacity in VCF Operations
In VCF Operations, capacity optimization focuses on efficiently using and managing resources within a virtualized
infrastructure, such as a VMware vSphere environment. These features help organizations maximize the utilization of their
resources while ensuring that capacity remains within acceptable limits.
Capacity Optimization
This aspect of VCF Operations involves forecasting and planning for future resource needs based on historical data and
current usage patterns. The goal is to ensure that the virtual environment has the necessary resources to accommodate
workload growth. Capacity optimization involves activities like identifying underutilized or overprovisioned resources,
predicting when additional resources will be needed, and suggesting right-sizing of virtual machines and ESX hosts.
Capacity Optimization Concepts
Capacity optimization in VCF Operations involves various key concepts and practices to ensure optimal resource
utilization, plan for growth, and maintain performance within a virtualized environment.
How Does Capacity Optimization Work in VCF Operations
Capacity optimization in VCF Operations is achieved using powerful integrated functions - capacity overview, workload
balancing and optimization, repurposing of underutilized resources, and what-if predictive scenarios - to reach optimal
system performance.
Capacity planners must assess whether physical capacity is sufficient to meet current or forecasted demand. With robust
capacity planning and optimization, you can manage your production capacity effectively as your organization addresses
changing requirements. The objective of strategic capacity optimization is to reach an optimal level where production
capabilities meet ongoing demand.
VCF Operations analytics provide precise tracking, measuring and forecasting of data center capacity, usage, and trends
to help manage and optimize resource use, system tuning, and cost recovery. The system monitors stress thresholds and
alerts you before potential issues can affect performance. Multiple pre-set reports are available. You can plan capacity
based on historical usage, and run what-if scenarios as your requirements expand.
Capacity Optimization Using Overview, Reclaim, Workload Optimization and What-If
Capacity management is organized into three primary functions, Assess, Optimize, and Plan. Together, they provide a
comprehensive view of data center activity and resource trending.
Use the Assess page to conduct on-the-spot analysis of your environment's capacity health. This dashboard
highlights Time Remaining until resources (CPU, Memory, or Disk Space) run out and provides high-level Optimization
Recommendations to reduce waste. The Cluster Utilization graph shows the time remaining until CPU, Memory and Disk
Space run out based on demand and allocation models.
The Optimize page allows you to rebalance and tune compute resources through dedicated tabs - Reclaim, Rightsize,
Workload Placement, and Resource Efficiency. Specifically, the Reclaim tab identifies underutilized workloads and
calculates the potential cost savings and reclaimable capacity (CPU, Memory, Disk Space) available for redeployment.
Workload Placement provides for moving virtual workloads and their file systems dynamically across datastore clusters
within a data center or custom data center. From the Reclaim and Rightsize tabs, you can also schedule automation jobs
Broadcom 6468

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
that act on these recommendations, so reclaim and rightsize actions run on your own schedule and conditions instead of
requiring manual follow-up each time.
Plan enables forward-looking capacity planning through What-If Analysis and Committed Scenarios, allowing you to
interact with and manipulate data outcomes based on your future requirements. The What-If analysis function- can run
scenarios that help determine where additional system resources can be accommodated.
Note:
You may see a data center or cluster labeled as optimized when it has few or no days remaining before CPU,
memory, or storage is predicted to run out. That is because these are two different measures of data center
and cluster health. A data center can be running at optimum levels based on policy settings for balance and
consolidation, yet be almost out of resources. It is important to consider both measures when managing your
environment.
How Does VCF Operations Calculate and Forecast Capacity
Capacity analytics helps you assess the utilization and capacity remaining in objects across your environment. An
evaluation of the historical utilization of resources generates a projection of the future workload. You can plan for
infrastructure procurement or migrations based on the projection and avoid the risk of capacity shortage and high
infrastructure costs.
Capacity analytics uses the capacity engine to assess historical trends, including utilization peaks. The engine selects an
appropriate projection model to predict future workload. The amount of historical utilization data that the engine considers
depends on how much data has been collected..
Capacity Engine and Calculations
The capacity engine analyzes historical utilization and projects future workload by using real-time predictive capacity
analytics, which is based on an industry-standard statistical analysis model of demand behavior. The engine takes the
Demand and Usable Capacity metrics as input and generates the output metrics, which are Time Remaining, Capacity
Remaining, Recommended Size, and Recommended Total Capacity, as shown in the following figure.
The projection window for the capacity engine is 1 year into the future. The engine collects data points every five minutes
and processes them once in 24 hours to calculate output metrics. Any changes made to the policy applied to the objects
and object groups, or total capacity, will trigger an immediate recalculation.
The capacity engine projects the future workload in a projected utilization range. The range includes an upper bound
projection and a lower bound projection. Capacity calculations are based on the time remaining and risk level. The engine
considers the upper bound projection for a conservative risk level and the mean of the upper bound projection and lower
bound projection for an aggressive risk level. For more information about setting risk levels, see, Capacity Details.
The capacity engine calculates the Time Remaining, Capacity Remaining, Recommended Size, and Recommended Total
Capacity.
You can define custom metrics to compute capacity. The custom metric configuration is available in the policy settings.
The calculation algorithm itself does not change. The custom metrics that you configure in the policy is used by VCF
Operations in the capacity calculations. You can select the default metrics shipped with VCF Operations, or create super
Broadcom 6469

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
metrics and select them for custom capacity calculations. Changes that you make take effect after the next collection
cycle.
Note:
Enabling custom metrics in the capacity calculations is an advanced configuration. Custom metrics alter the way
VCF Operations calculates capacity across your enivronment. Use this setting only when needed.
For more details on how to enable custom metrics, see see, Capacity Details.
Time Remaining The number of days remaining till the projected utilization crosses the threshold for the usable capacity. The
usable capacity is the total capacity minus the resources that vSphere HA admission control reserves for
failover.
Capacity Remaining The largest difference between the usable capacity and the projected utilization between now and 3 days
into the future. If the projected utilization is above 100% of the usable capacity, the capacity remaining is 0.
Recommended Size The maximum projected utilization for the period from now to 30 days beyond the time remaining warning
threshold. The warning threshold is the period during which the time remaining is green. You set this value
in the Time Remaining policy element. See Policy Time Remaining Element.
For example, if the warning threshold for time remaining is 120 days, which is the default value, the
recommended size is the maximum projected utilization 150 days into the future.
The recommended size does not include the capacity that vSphere HA reserves for failover. To obtain your
actual sizing requirement, add your vSphere HA spare capacity requirement on top of the recommended
size.
VCF Operations caps the recommended size that is generated by the capacity engine to keep the
recommendations conservative.
• VCF Operations caps an oversized recommended size at 50% of the currently allocated resources.
For example: a virtual machine is configured with 8 vCPUs but has never used more than 10% of that.
Instead of recommending a reclaim of 7 vCPUs, the recommendation is capped to reclaiming 4 vCPUs.
• VCF Operations caps an undersized recommended size at 100% of the currently allocated resources.
For example: a virtual machine is configured with 4 vCPUs, and has been constantly running very
hot. Instead of recommending the addition of 8 vCPUs, the recommendation is capped at adding 4
additional vCPUs.
Recommended Total The maximum projected utilization for the projection period from the current time to 30 days after the
Capacity warning threshold value for time remaining. The recommended total capacity includes vSphere HA settings.
For example, if the warning threshold value for time remaining is 120 days, which is the default value, the
recommended size is the maximum projected utilization including vSphere HA values, 150 days into the
future.
Note:
Recommended total capacity is not available for objects.
The following figure shows the capacity calculations for a conservative risk level.
Broadcom 6470

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The following figure shows the capacity calculations for an aggressive risk level.
Note:
• If vSphere HA is not enabled in vCenter then Usable Capacity = Total Capacity. In this case, the Usable
Capacity value can be 0 only if there are no ESX hosts in the vSphere cluster.
• If vSphere HA is enabled, then Usable Capacity can be 0 in the following cases:
– There are no ESX hosts in the vSphere cluster.
– vSphere HA is configured incorrectly. For example: Admission Control is configured with a cluster resource
Percentage policy set to 100% of CPU or Memory. Please check the HA configuration in vCenter.
– vSphere HA Active host count is less than 2.
– The ESX host is not vSphere HA Active if:
• ESX host is in maintenance mode.
• ESX host is powered off.
• Value of “runtime.dasHostState” property is not equal to “connectedToMaster” or “master”. This can be
because of some network issues between the ESX hosts.
Broadcom 6471

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Utilization Peaks
The historical utilization of resources can have peaks, which are periods of maximum utilization. The projection of future
workload depends on the types of peaks. According to the frequency of peaks, they can be momentary, sustained, or
periodic.
Momentary Peaks Short-lived peaks that are a one-time occurrence. The peaks are not significant enough to require
additional capacity, so they do not impact capacity planning and projection.
Sustained Peaks Peaks that last for a longer time and impact projections. If a sustained peak is not periodic, the impact on
the projection lessens over time because of exponential decay.
Periodic Peaks Peaks that exhibit cyclical patterns or waves. The peaks can be hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, during the
last day of the month, and so on. The capacity engine also detects multiple overlapping cyclical patterns.
Because these peaks recur, their impact does not decay over time. The capacity engine projects the pattern
forward, so periodic peaks have the greatest influence on capacity planning and projection.
Projection Models
The capacity engine uses models to generate projections. The engine constantly modifies projections and chooses the
model that best fits the pattern of historical data. The projection range predicts the general usage pattern that covers 90%
of the future data points. Projection models can be linear or periodic.
Linear Models Models that have a steadily increasing or decreasing trend. Multiple linear models run in parallel and the
capacity engine chooses the best model.
Examples of linear models are linear regression and autoregressive moving average (ARMA).
Periodic Models Models that discover periodicity of various lengths, such as hours, days, weeks, months, or the last day
of the week or month. Periodic models detect square waves that represent batch jobs and handle data
streams that contain multiple overlapping periodic patterns. These models ignore random noise.
Examples of periodic models are Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs), pulses (edge detection), and wavelets.
Forecast In Trend Views
Forecasts are generated based on the time range specified in the view settings and are forecasted for the number of
days specified in the forecast setting. The forecast is generated based on 3 main algorithms - Change-point detection to
find sections of the history with significant changes, linear regression to find linear trends, and cyclical analysis to identify
periodic patterns.
Historical Data Window
The capacity engine captures historical data over a period of time depending on the historical data window. The historical
data window that the engine uses is an exponential decay window.
The exponential decay window is a window of unlimited size in which the capacity engine gives more importance to the
most recent data points. Beginning from the projection calculation start point, the engine consumes all the historical data
points and decreases the weight attributed to each one exponentially based on how far back in time they are.
Altering Capacity Calculation
Capacity calculations in VCF Operations can be managed by changing the date from when the historical utilization is
calculated or excluding up to 6 time periods from the capacity calculations. Storage considerations can also be excluded
from capacity calculations to exclude storage utilization from influencing the overall capacity calculation. This can be done
either by editing the policy settings (Capacity Details) or adjusting capacity configuration settings (Using the Capacity
Page to Asses and Optimize Capacity). These changes influence future trend calculations.
Allocation and Demand Model in Workload Optimization
VCF Operations uses the demand model and allocation model for Workload Optimization. By default, only the demand
model is used. You can turn the allocation model on in the active policy.
Broadcom 6472

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
What is Allocation Model?
The allocation model determines how much compute, memory, and storage resources are allocated to object types. You
define the allocation values by modifying the policy which is applied to the objects. The allocation values, also known as
overcommit ratios, affect performance and cost.
The allocation model works alongside the demand model. Unlike the demand model which always affects the capacity
calculations, the allocation model can be turned on or off in the policy setting. You can control the ratio by which VCF
Operations overcommits either the CPU, memory, or disk space. By specifying the allocation values in the policy, you
can choose whether you want to overcommit your resources or not. Overcommitting helps you measure utilization of
resources in a pay-as-you-go model. When you do not overcommit, the utilization of your cluster will never exceed 100%.
If your resource utilization is over the allocation ratio that you set, Capacity Remaining becomes zero.
What is Demand Model?
The demand model is a concept used to predict future resource requirements based on historical data and usage
patterns. The demand model is a key component of capacity planning and optimization, allowing administrators to
anticipate the growth of workloads and infrastructure resources needed to support those workloads over time.
The demand model takes into account various factors, such as historical resource consumption, trends, seasonality, and
potential changes in workloads. By analyzing this information, VCF Operations can provide insights into when additional
resources (such as CPU, memory, storage, and network capacity) will be needed to meet the expected growth in demand.
Difference between Allocation Model and Demand Model in Workload Optimization
When clusters in a data center are not optimized, VCF Operations uses the demand model by default to optimize the VMs
placed in the cluster. While VCF Operations moves VMs to optimize the cluster, it uses the capacity demand to calculate
the best way to optimize the cluster.
When you turn on the Allocation Model in the active policy, VCF Operations optimizes based on the Demand Model,
and takes into consideration the overcommit ratios defined by the Allocation Model. As the VCF Operations WLP engine
takes into the consideration the overcommit ratios based on the allocation model for CPU, memory, and disk space, these
resources will not be under stress after optimization due to the over allocation. In any optimization model which is based
on allocation the target is always to reduce the stress on all clusters and ensure that after the VM migration the target
clusters are not over-allocated.
How to Enable Allocation Model
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Administrations > Configurations. Click the Policy Definition tile. Select the active policy and click the Capacity card.
In the Capacity Setting section, click the lock icon next to the Allocation Model for your vCenter object type. The available
object types are:
• Cluster compute resource. Set the overcommit ratios for CPU, memory and disk space. You can also consider
powered off VMs by selecting the Activate checkbox.
• Datastore. Set the overcommit ratio for the vSAN datastore disk space.
• Datastore cluster. Set the overcommit ratio for cluster disk space.
After you have set the overcommit ratios, click Save. After setting the overcommit ratios for the Allocation Model in the
active policy, go to the Workload Placement page to see the Allocation Model displayed under the Are your clusters
meeting your utilization objective? section.
Policy Settings for Capacity
VCF Operations lets you define capacity and workload automation policies on objects and object groups. These policies
help you define custom metrics, and set symptom thresholds, alerts, and recommendations for capacity planning.
To set the capacity settings for your policy, from the left menu, after you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation
bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administrations > Configurations. Click the Policy
Definition tile. Click Add. Alternatively, click the Policy Definition , select a policy from the list, and click Edit from the
horizontal ellipsis.
Broadcom 6473

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For more information on policy settings for capacity, see the topics, Capacity Details and Workload Automation Details.
How to View and Assess Capacity
VCF Operations helps you assess capacity by predicting future resource needs based on historical data and usage
patterns. VCF Operations helps you analyze trends, forecast demand, and allocate resources accordingly to prevent
capacity shortages and overprovisioning. To view capacity, you can open the Assess page or view the Capacity tab for an
object in the Inventory page.
Assessing Capacity on the Assess Page
The Assess page in VCF Operations helps you assess workload status and how much capacity is remaining in data
centers across your environment.
Where You Find the Assess Page
On the Assess page, you see time remaining, optimization recommendations, and cluster utilization for the data center
that you select.
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Assess under Capacity.
Note:
Select a data center card to refresh the page with the time remaining, optimization recommendations, and cluster
utilization for that data center.
For more details on how to use the Assess and Optimize pages to assess and optimize capacity, see the topic, Using the
Capacity Pages to Assess and Optimize Capacity.
For more details on viewing capacity for an object on its Capacity tab, see the topic, Viewing Object Capacity in the
Capacity Tab.
Viewing Object Capacity in the Capacity Tab
The Capacity tab provides Time Remaining and Capacity Remaining data for the selected object. Virtual Machine
Remaining data is the sum of Virtual Machine remaining from each Cluster Compute Resource and is available for
datastores, datastore clusters, clusters, data centers, CDC, and VC based on the average profile, or when you activate
one or more custom profiles in the policy.
Where You Find the Capacity Tab at an Object Level
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Inventory. Then select a group, custom data center, application, or inventory object. Click the Capacity tab.
Understanding the Capacity Tab
For the selected object, the Capacity tab displays the Time Remaining, Capacity, and Virtual Machine Remaining
information. These panes display the value of the resources remaining till they run out.
Below the Time Remaining, Capacity and Virtual Machine Remaining panes, the time and capacity utilization
metric for CPU, memory, and disk space are displayed in three panes. By default, the most constrained resource is
selected. Click CPU, Memory, or Disk Space to change the views to these resources. These panes display the resource
information based on the Demand model (default) or Allocation model (if configured).
For datastores, if you have activated Allocation Model and Capacity buffer in the assigned profile, you see the Disk Space
information based on Allocation and Usage.
Time Remaining Pane When you select the Time Remaining pane and click one of the resource types, the utilization graph
displays the historical value of the utilization metric and its forecast plotted against time, projecting how
swiftly resource utilization is approaching the usable capacity.
Broadcom 6474

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For example, if the capacity calculation is using historical data based on the duration when you were
provisioning a large number of VMs, but in the recent past, there was no provisioning done. Then, VCF
Operations may not project a trend that is based on the recent data when there was no provisioning, but
still will consider historical data when there were a large number of VMs provisioned. This historical data
may show an increasing trend. In this case, you can change the capacity computation to start from a date
after the VM provisioning is complete.
Capacity Pane The Capacity Remaining pane indicates the unused capacity of your virtual environment to accommodate
new virtual machines. VCF Operations calculates the Capacity Remaining as a percentage of the remaining
capacity, compared to the total. Capacity Remaining is calculated as the utilization metric forecast 3 days
from now subtracted from the Usable Capacity.
VCF Operations calculates the average profile and always computes the virtual machine remaining number
based on the average profile. You can change the profile by clicking the Go to Custom Profiles link.
VCF Operations calculates virtual machine remaining numbers when you activate one or more custom
profiles from the policy. The overall virtual machine remaining is based on the most constrained profile. The
Average Profile size is derived by calculating the average utilization of consumers and overcommit ratios (if
enabled) against the usable capacity of this object.
When you select Capacity and click one of the resource types, a bar chart and a table of values based on
the Demand and Allocation model (if configured) appears. The bar chart displays total usable resource, the
percentage used, the percentage allocated for high availability and buffer, and the percentage remaining
based on the Demand and Allocation models (if configured).
The table displays the following information for each resource type:
• Total: The total usable capacity for each resource type based on the Demand model or Allocation
model (if configured). The difference in Total capacity and Usable capacity is set in the HA (admission
control) that is set in the clusters in vSphere.
• Usable: The total usable capacity for each resource type based on the Demand model or Allocation
model (if configured).
• Used: Approximate value how much utilization do you have now. Shows the forecast value of utilization
metric in 3 days from now.
• Recommended Size: The Total Capacity that must be available for a green level of Time Remaining.
The slider in the policy controls the Time Remaining green zone, and the default value is 150 days.
• Remaining: The Capacity Remaining metric value and also the percentage. The value of Capacity
Remaining metric is calculated by forecasting the utilization metric 3 days from now and subtracting it
from Usable capacity.
• Buffer: The percentage of the capacity buffer based on the buffer value that you set in the policy. The
Capacity Buffer element determines how much extra headroom you have and ensures that you have
extra space for growth inside the cluster when required.
• High Availability: The percentage of the high availability based on the high availability buffer.
Virtual Machine The virtual machine remaining number is based on the average profile. The virtual machine remaining
Remaining numbers are calculated when you activate one or more custom profiles from the policy. The overall virtual
machine remaining is based on the most constrained profile.
When you click on Virtual Machine Remaining, you see the number of virtual machines based on the
Average Profile. Select a different policy by clicking Policy from the drop-down list on the top right-hand
side of the page. To activate custom profiles in that policy, or other policies, click the Go to Custom
Profiles link.
Only vSAN datastore objects, and not other datastore objects, display disk space based on Buffer and HA.
Utilization graph Data shows current and trending resource usage and pinpoints when a given cluster is projected to run out
of CPU, memory, or disk space based on the allocation or demand model (default). VCF Operations takes
into account the business hours which you set in the current policy. View the legend of the colors in the
Utilization graph. Click on any one of the legends to toggle its display in the chart.
The Capacity tab is a subset of the Capacity optimization capability. For additional details, refer to Assessing Capacity on
the Assess Page.
Managing the Capacity Calculations
Click the RESET button on the top right of the page if you want to change the date from when the historical utilization is
calculated. By default, it is calculated from the object creation or VCF Operations installation date. The Utilization graph
displays the reset calculation start point. Click RESET if you want to change projected utilization, for example, drop the
Broadcom 6475

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
irrelevant historical data from the calculation. Using the reset button doesn't impact actual data, just the calculations being
shown on the page.
When you click the RESET button, you can also exclude up to 6 time periods from the capacity calculations. This is useful
if you want to exclude anomalous data patterns from impacting capacity projections. Click Advanced Settings to bring up
the option to exclude dates. For the time intervals you select, VCF Operations will consider linearly projected values of the
metrics. You can delete time intervals if you want to add more than six exclusions.
You can also exclude storage consideration from influencing the overall capacity calculation for a cluster compute
resource. This option will help you deliberately maximize your storage utilization. To exclude storage from influencing the
capacity calculations, use one of these methods:
• By editing the policy. Click Edit Capacity under the Policy drop-down list on the top right-hand side of the Capacity
Tab page. Click the lock icon and select the option, Exclude storage capacity. For more information on policy settings
for capacity, see, Capacity Details.
• By editing the capacity configuration settings. On the Assess page, click CAPACITY CONFIGURATION DETAILS.
In the Cluster Time Remaining Settings dialog box, click the lock icon next to Storage consideration for capacity
calculation and turn on Exclude storage capacity. For more details, see, Using the Capacity Pages to Assess and
Optimize Capacity.
These changes affect the capacity calculation for the future trend, which will impact Capacity Remaining, Time Remaining,
Recommended Size, and VM Remaining (if it is available for the particular resource, namely, Datastore, Cluster, Datastore
Cluster). It will also impact all the resource containers (CPU, Memory, Disk Space, etc.)
Note:
If you are unable to see the RESET button, make sure that you have the Manage Capacity Calculation
permission. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane,
click Administration > Control Panel > Access Control > Roles. Capacity permissions are available under
Manage > Capacity > Assess.
Capacity Shortfall
Capacity Shortfall is a metric that reports capacity overcommitment as a positive number. When an object is
overcommitted, Capacity Remaining cannot go below zero, so VCF Operations instead reports the size of the
overcommitment as Capacity Shortfall. In the Metrics tree, this appears as Capacity Shortfall (Profile), alongside
Capacity Remaining (Profile), under Capacity Analytics Generated.
Capacity Shortfall is available for Cluster, Datastore, and Datastore Cluster objects only. It appears in the Capacity
Summary pages next to VM Remaining, and only when VM Remaining is zero. It does not appear while VM Remaining is
still positive.
For all these objects you can create custom profiles directly from the Capacity tab. Click the Go to Custom Profiles link
under Virtual Machine remaining. From the Custom Profiles page, click Add to add a new profile. You can either add
new profile or import from existing object. You can modify the required metric value and click OK.
How Does Capacity Shortfall Work
When an object has more VMs than its capacity can support, Virtual Machine Remaining shows zero rather than a
negative number, and Capacity Shortfall reports how far over capacity the object is. VCF Operations evaluates every
profile configured on the object and bases Capacity Shortfall on the profile with the largest number of overcommitted VMs.
Whenever there is no capacity in that case, Capacity Shortfall detects the VM profiles in the setup and finds the profile for
which we have the maximum number of VMs that are overcommitted.
Capacity Shortfall Formula
It is possible that when one datastore is connected with multiple clusters, each cluster thinks that the whole diskspace
available in the datastore is for itself. We can calculate the Capacity Shortfall as:
Capacity Shortfall = (Used - Usable Capacity) / Profile Sizes
Broadcom 6476

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This calculation is done per profile because a datastore shared across multiple clusters can otherwise be overcounted.
Each cluster's Usable Capacity may include the full capacity of the shared datastore, as if it were the only consumer.
Calculating shortfall against a specific profile size avoids that overcounting.
Note:
In the above formula the Used Capacity represents the specific value that is displayed in the Capacity >
Capacity Remaining tab.
If you have two clusters, one cluster has 20 VMs remaining and the other cluster has shortfall of 20 VMs, then the number
of VMs remaining for the datacenter will be 20 VMs, however, if you have a shortfall of VMs in the datastore connected to
that cluster, then we will see on the datacenter the remaining VMs as zero.
Metrics
The Capacity Shortfall displays metrics under Capacity Analytics Generated and under Profiles. The metrics are:
• Capacity Remaining Profile (Average)
• Capacity Shortfall Profile (Average)
vSAN HCI Mesh
The vSAN HCI Mesh is applicable if you have a vSAN OSA HCI cluster. The vSAN HCI Mesh allows vSAN clusters to
remotely mount the datastore of another (remote) vSAN cluster, hence sharing the storage capacity and span its usage
to a wider pool of compute resources. HCI Mesh allows multiple vSAN clusters to share their datastores remotely. If the
vCenter version is 7.0U1 and greater you can share other cluster datastores and provision VMs to the remotely shared
data stores.
A new card is created under Capacity > Assess > vSAN HCI Mesh. The vSAN HCI Mesh card is displayed only when
there are eligible clusters which can be part of the vSAN HCI mesh. If the version of the vCenter is less than 7.0U1 for the
selected datacenter, this card is not displayed. If the mesh is not configured, click the link, which lets you configure the
clusters from vCenter.
The vSAN HCI Mesh displays the following information:
• Total Capacity - Displays the total capacity of all the vSAN datastores connected to the mesh.
• vSAN Mesh - Displays how the datastores are interconnected in the HCI mesh.
• Inner Circle - Represents the local datastore and displays capacity details like, free capacity, used capacity, and total
capacity.
• Outer Circle - Represents the remote datastore and displays capacity details like, total mounted capacity, free capacity,
and total capacity usage percentage.
• Arrow Heads - The arrow heads points to the clients connected to the server vSAN cluster.
Datastore View Displays the capacity consumption details for the selected datastore. You can also identify which are the
client and server clusters.
Cluster View Displays the capacity details of the remote datastores. You can also view the capacity details for the
mounted datastores. The Total Usage % displays the total capacity consumed by all the client clusters
connected to these mounted datastores including the selected cluster.
Health Alerts Related to Displays the health alerts related to the HCI Mesh. You can also view alerts for individual datastores, which
HCI Mesh is part of the HCI mesh.
vSAN Remote Datastores
The vSAN Remote Datastore card is displayed if you have a vSAN Max ESA cluster and a vSAN Compute cluster
mounting the vSAN Max cluster. The vSAN Compute cluster does not have any storage of its own and uses the storage
provided by the vSAN Max cluster. vSAN Max cluster allows vSAN compute to remotely mount it's datastore, hence
sharing the storage capacity and span its usage to a wider pool of compute resources. vSAN Max cluster allows multiple
vSAN Compute clusters to share their datastores remotely.
The vSAN Remote Datastores card displays the following information:
• Total number of clusters mounted: Displays the total number of the vSAN Compute clusters mounted on the vSAN Max
cluster.
Broadcom 6477

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Total Capacity: Displays the total capacity of the vSAN datastores connected to the vSAN Max cluster.
• Free Capacity: Displays the remaining capacity of the vSAN datastores connected to the vSAN Max cluster.
Click View Remote Datastores for a more detailed view of the
information.
The total capacity details of the remote datastore and the health alerts (if any) of the remote datastore are displayed along
with the relationship between the vSAN Compute clusters and the remote datastore they use.
You can view which vSAN Compute cluster is mounting the vSAN Max cluster and their usage trends. Hover over each
cluster type to view the details related to it. For example, if you hover over a vSAN Compute cluster, you can see the
number of datastore it is using along with the total amount of mounted and free capacity in gigabytes and the total usage
percentage of the cluster. If you hover over the vSAN Max cluster, you can view the total, free, and used capacity in
gigabytes, and the usage percentage of the datastore.
Custom Profiles in VCF Operations
A custom profile defines a hypothetical configuration of a virtual machine. Custom profiles help you determine how many
instances of that virtual machine can fit in your environment, depending on the capacity remaining and the configuration
of the parent object. You activate the custom profile in policies for specific object types. The custom profiles are used
to calculate VM remaining when the policy is selected for those object types in the Capacity tab of the VCF Operations
object browser.
Broadcom 6478

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
How Custom Profiles Work
As with default profiles, custom profiles are based on metric values for a virtual machine. You can add as many custom
profiles as you need for an object. For example, you might create one custom profile for a virtual machine that has a
memory demand model of 2 GB. You create another custom profile that has a memory demand model of 4 GB.
VCF Operations uses custom profiles to calculate the number of instances of those virtual machines that can fit in your
environment for specific objects. The number of virtual machines is based on the capacity allocation and demand defined
for the object.
After you define the metric values for a custom profile, you configure for which policies and object types the custom
profiles are activated.
How Custom Profiles are Related to Policies
After you create a custom profile, you activate it in a policy for one or more of the following object types:
• Datastores
• Datastore clusters
• Cluster compute resource
The custom profile is then available for all objects of that type in the Capacity tab of the VCF Operations inventory
browser.
To determine how many instances of the virtual machine with a specific configuration as defined by the custom profile you
can include in the parent object, go to the Capacity tab of the parent object. Select the Capacity Remaining | Virtual
Machine Remaining pane. Select the policy in which the custom profile is activated from the top right hand side drop-
down list. The custom profiles appear in the Virtual Machine remaining section and indicate how many instances of the
virtual machine can fit in your environment. The overall virtual machine remaining is based on the most constrained
profile.
Where You Find Custom Profiles
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Administrations > Configurations. Click the Custom Profiles tile under the Other section. A list of all the custom
profiles available in VCF Operations is displayed in a table. Click the name of a custom profile from the Name column to
view the metric values and policies of that custom profile on the right pane.

profile to perform the following actions:

• Clone. Clone selected profiles.
Sorting options Click the title of the table to sort the contents. You can sort by name, description, object type, or adapter type.

You can create a custom profile that models a virtual machine's resource requirements, then apply the profile to a cluster
compute resource, datastore cluster, or datastore to determine how many VMs of that profile can fit on the object. In the
Custom Profiles workspace, you define the metrics for the virtual machine and select the object types the profile applies
to.

Where you Import or Export Custom Profile

Predefined Dashboards for Capacity
VCF Operations provides predefined dashboards to help you monitor and manage your virtualized environments.
Capacity dashboards help you analyze the capacity of your environment by providing insights into resource consumption
trends, utilization patterns, and potential bottlenecks. They can help you plan for future growth and optimize resource
allocation.
For more information on the predefined dashboards available for capacity optimization in VCF Operations, see the topic,
Capacity Dashboards.
How to Optimize Capacity in VCF Operations
VCF Operations helps you optimize capacity by identifying and reclaiming unused or underutilized resources, such as
reclaiming idle CPU or memory from VMs. This practice can help free up resources for other workloads. Rightsizing
helps you adjust the resources allocated to virtual machines based on their actual usage. VCF Operations identifies
overprovisioned or underutilized VMs and provides recommendations to optimize their resource allocations.
Where You Find Optimize
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Capacity > Optimize. Select a data center card to see the recommendations for that data center. The Optimize page has
four tabs:
• Reclaim: Identify powered off VMs, idle VMs, VMs with snapshots, and orphaned disks, and reclaim their resources.
See Using Reclaim to Free Up Resources.
• Rightsize: Adjust the CPU and memory of oversized and undersized VMs. See Using Rightsize to Adjust Resource
Allocation.
• Workload Placement: Rebalance virtual machines and storage across clusters. See Using Workload Optimization.
• Resource Efficiency: Evaluate memory tiering to support more VMs on the same hardware. See Using Memory
Tiering for Resource Efficiency.
Settings That Control the Recommendations
Settings determine which VMs and disks the Reclaim and Rightsize tabs include. For example, you define how long a
VM must be powered off or idle before it is reclaimable, how old snapshots and orphaned disks must be, how much data
must be collected before a VM is rightsized, and whether Broadcom appliances are excluded. You can open the Settings
dialog box from the page heading of the Optimize page, or go to Administration > Global Settings > Capacity Optimization.
A banner in the Settings dialog box reminds you that changes apply to all data centers. For a description of each setting,
see Capacity Optimization Settings.
Broadcom 6481

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Excluding VMs from Reclaim and Rightsizing
In addition to the settings, you can exclude specific VMs from reclamation and right-sizing recommendations. Excluding
VMs gives you more control over resource optimization and ensures that essential system VMs, or VMs with expected
resource consumption patterns, are not subject to unexpected modifications or reclamation.
The following exclusion mechanisms are available:
• Manual exclusion - On the Reclaim or Rightsize tab, select VMs and click EXCLUDE VM(S). Click SHOW|HIDE
EXCLUDED VMS to see the excluded VMs, and select them and click INCLUDE VM(S) to return them to the list.
• Exclusion by tags - You can exclude VMs from optimization recommendations using tags created in the vCenter.
• Exclusion by age - You can exclude VMs based on how long they have been in a state, or on how long data has been
collected. For right-sizing, you set a minimum number of days of data collection before a VM can be considered. For
reclamation, you set how long a VM must be powered off or idle, how old snapshots and orphaned disks must be, and
how recently provisioned VMs are excluded from idle.
• Exclusion of Broadcom appliances - You can exclude Broadcom appliance VMs from optimization.
Considerations for exclusion based on tags:
Container-Level Setting Tag-based exclusion settings are applied at the level of a data center, custom data center, or cloud zone.
If a data center has multiple containers, the exclusion setting must be designed and applied separately for
each container.
Reclamation and Right- Tag-based exclusions can be applied to both reclaim and right-size recommendations.
Sizing
Intersection of If a VM belongs to multiple intersecting containers, for example, a VM is in both a Data Center and a
Containers Custom Data Center, an exclusion setting defined in one container's exclusion settings will apply and be
visible in all other intersecting containers to which the VM belongs.
Reversing Exclusion To reverse a tag exclusion, you must clean up the tag exclusion setting within the container configuration.
For right-sizing, exclusion by age allows you to set a minimum number of days of historical data collection required before
a VM is considered for right-sizing optimization. It helps you ensure that VCF Operations has collected enough historical
data to accurately determine if a VM is oversized or undersized based on its memory and CPU usage behavior. You turn
this on with Exclusion settings based on time, in the Settings dialog box or on the Global Settings page.
Considerations for exclusion by age:
Right-Sizing Only This exclusion setting is specifically for right-sizing optimization recommendations.
Disabling the Feature If this setting is disabled (the default state), VCF Operations uses all the lifetime data available. VMs
receive recommendations as soon as their capacity has been calculated, even if only a minimal number of
historical data points are available.
Capacity Calculation Only VMs that have the required minimum number of days of historical data will have their capacity
Requirement calculated and appear in the right-sizing list.
For reclamation, the duration thresholds are described in Capacity Optimization Settings.
When Exclude Broadcom appliances from Optimization is on (the default), appliance VMs are excluded from the Powered
Off VMs, Idle VMs, Oversized VMs, and Undersized VMs lists. They remain available in the list of VMs with snapshots.
Excluded appliance VMs appear on the Appliance VMs tab when you click SHOW|HIDE EXCLUDED VMS on the Reclaim
tab.
For more information, see Exclusion Settings in Using Reclaim to Free Up Resources and Using Rightsize to Adjust
Resource Allocation.
Using the Capacity Pages to Assess and Optimize Capacity
The capacity pages in VCF Operations offers a comprehensive view of resource utilization, allocation, trends, and
forecasts, allowing administrators to make informed decisions about resource provisioning, performance optimization, and
future growth.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Where you find Capacity
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Capacity.
• Click Assess to see time remaining, optimization recommendations, and cluster utilization for a data center.
• Click Optimize to act on those findings. Select a data center, then use the Reclaim, Rightsize, Workload Placement,
and Resource Efficiency tabs.

When you open the Assess and Optimize pages, graphical representations of all the data centers and custom data
centers in your environment appear.
By default, they are shown in order of time remaining, beginning from the upper left, where the most constrained data
centers appear. To review the status of a data center, click the graphic.

Note:
You might see that a data center or cluster is labeled optimized when it has few or no days remaining before
CPU, memory, or disk space is predicted to run out. The seemingly odd assessment is due to optimization and
time remaining being two different measures of data center and cluster health. A data center can be running at
optimum based on policy settings for balance and consolidation, yet be almost out of resources. It is important to
consider both measures when managing your environment.
Cluster Time Remaining Settings
Click CAPACITY CONFIGURATION DETAILS on the Assess page to open the Cluster Time Remaining Settings dialog
box. The dialog box shows the policy that your changes affect (Affected Policy). Each section has a lock icon. A locked
section shows the values the policy currently uses and cannot be edited; click the lock icon to unlock the section and
change its values. A warning in a section reminds you that applying the changes affects all clusters or objects that use the
policy. Click SAVE to apply your changes or CANCEL to close the dialog box.
Criticality Threshold Set the time remaining thresholds in days. Critical Threshold: a cluster is at the Critical level when its time
remaining falls below this number of days. Warning Threshold: a cluster is at the warning level when its
time remaining falls below this number of days. A bar from 0 days to 1 year shows the thresholds. Applying
these changes affects all clusters in the policy.
Risk Level Use the slider to choose how conservatively time remaining is calculated. The six positions run from
Aggressive to Conservative, and the selected level is shown above the preview graph, for example
Conservative Level 3. Conservative settings are usually chosen for critical workloads like production, where
performance is paramount. Time remaining is calculated from a higher projected capacity utilization, and all
peak values, regular or occasional, are considered. Aggressive settings can be used for workloads where
performance impact is minimal or irrelevant, such as development and test environments. Time remaining
is calculated from the actual projected capacity utilization, and occasional peak values are not considered.
Applying these changes affects all objects in the policy.
Storage consideration Turn on Exclude storage capacity to stop storage from influencing the overall capacity calculation for the
for capacity calculation cluster. Use this option to deliberately maximize your storage utilization.
Allocation Model Select CPU, Memory, and Disk Space and enter an overcommit ratio for each to turn on the Allocation
model. Time remaining is then also calculated against the overcommit ratios. Applying these changes
affects all clusters in the policy.
Capacity Buffer Set the percentage of capacity to hold back as headroom for CPU, memory, and disk space, separately
for the Demand and Allocation models. The buffer ensures that you have extra space for growth inside the
cluster when required. A diagram shows how the HA reservation and the buffer reduce the total capacity to
the usable capacity. Applying these changes affects all clusters in the policy.
Broadcom 6486

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

the start and end of business hours, for example 08:45 to 18:00. The forecast takes business hours into
account, and the graph legend distinguishes business-hours data from non-business-hours data.
Optimize Page
The Capacity Optimization and Reclaim features are tightly integrated functions that allows you to assess workload status
in data centers across your environment. You can determine time remaining until CPU, memory, or disk space resources
run out and realize cost savings when underutilized VMs can be reclaimed and deployed where needed.
On the Optimize page, the same data center cards appear above four tabs:
• Reclaim: For more information, see Using Reclaim to Free Up Resources.
• Rightsize: For more information, see Using Rightsize to Adjust Resource Allocation.
• Workload Placement: For more information, see Using Workload Optimization.
• Resource Efficiency: For more information, see Using Memory Tiering for Resource Efficiency.
To control which VMs and disks the Reclaim and Rightsize tabs include, open the Settings dialog box from the page
heading. Changes apply to all data centers. See How to Optimize Capacity in VCF Operations.
Using Reclaim to Free Up Resources
Use the Reclaim feature in VCF Operations to identify underutilized workloads and reclaim resources from across your
environment.
Where You Find Reclaim
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Capacity > Optimize. Select a data center card to display details about the data center on the page.
How Reclaim Works
The Capacity Optimization and Reclaim features are tightly integrated functions that allows you to assess workload status
and resource contention in data centers across your environment. You can determine time remaining until CPU, memory,
or storage resources run out, and realize cost savings when underutilized VMs can be reclaimed and deployed where
needed.
When you open the Reclaim page, graphical representations of all the data centers and custom data centers in your
environment appear. By default, they are shown in order of time remaining, beginning from the upper left, where the most
constrained data centers appear. To review the status of a data center, click the graphic. The area following refreshes
to display details about the selected data center. The How much you can potentially save pane reflects potential
capacity savings and indicates a possible cost savings once you have reclaimed underused or powered off VMs. The
Total Reclaimable Capacity pane gives details of the reclaimable percentages for CPU, memory, and disk space.
The table at the bottom of the page provides important information about the VMs that offer the most cost savings. The
VMs are listed by Powered Off VMs, Idle VMs, VMs with snapshot, and Orphaned Disks. The highest priority heading
is at the far left. You can specify what information is included in your reclaim action. For example, when you click a column
heading, the table lists, by data center and then by VM, the allocated and reclaimable CPUs and memory, respectively.
Then, for example, you can select the box next to one or more VM names and click the EXCLUDE VM(S) button to keep
those VMs from being included in any reclaim action. You can also select VMs to resize.
Note:
Ensure that you enable permissions for the users accessing the Reclaim page. In the VCF Operations navigation
bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click Administration > Control Panel, and then click
the Access Control tile. Edit or add a role with the following permissions enabled:
• To browse to the Orphaned Disks tab in Reclaim, you must select the checkbox next to the Reclaim
permission.
• To perform the Delete Orphaned Disks action, you must select the checkbox next to the Delete Orphaned
Disks permission.

You can use the search function in the Edit Role Information page to find and enable the above permissions. For
more information, see Add or Edit Roles and Assign Permissions.
VMs in the Snapshot List
In earlier versions, a VM that qualified for both snapshot reclamation and a higher-priority reclamation factor, such as idle
or power-off, would not appear in the snapshot list. VCF Operations recognized the higher priority of the power-off or idle
reclamation factor, resulting in the snapshot list being empty for such objects. In previous versions, you could only choose
to power off or delay an idle VM. Snapshot reclamation was not an option for idle VMs.
Starting in VCF 9.1, VCF Operations displays a VM qualifying for multiple factors such as snapshot reclamation and
power-off or idle reclamation, in all the respective sections, including the Snapshot list, the Idle section, and the Power
Off section. It offers visibility and control, allowing you to decide which type of reclamation to perform.
You can easily perform snapshot reclamation on an idle VM. Performing a snapshot reclamation will only delete the
snapshots. The VM itself will not be powered off or deleted as an idle VM. The VM will be kept as an idle VM and will
qualify for idle reclamation again. For more information on how to automate deleting idle and powered off VMs for
reclamation, see Automation Central.
Settings
Open the Settings dialog box from the page heading to customize the settings. This affects all data centers. Using the
settings, you can exclude, for example all snapshots from being included in the reclaim action - by deselecting the VMs
with snapshot check box. Similarly, you can include or exclude powered-off VMs, idle VMs, and orphaned disks. For more
information, see Capacity Optimization Settings.
Note:
To provide read-only access to the settings for a user, configure the user role in the Access Control page
(Roles tab). In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Administration > Control Panel > Access Control > Roles. After you click Add or after you edit an existing
role, select the Manage Global Settings permissions under Operate > Administration > Global Settings.

2. Click the name of a listed cluster to show its VM list.
3. Select each VM or snapshot you want to reclaim.
4. Click Delete VM(s) to reclaim their resources.

Capacity Optimization Settings
Use these settings to define which powered off VMs, idle VMs, snapshots, and orphaned disks are reclaimable, and which
VMs and appliances are excluded from Reclaim and Rightsize recommendations. This helps to identify the amount of
resources that can be reclaimed and provisioned to other objects in your environment or amount of potential savings that
can be done in each month.
Where You Find the Settings
You can set these options in two places:
• In the Settings dialog box on the Optimize page. After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top,
click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click Capacity > Optimize, and then open the Settings dialog box from
the page heading. A banner warns that any changes that you make apply to all data centers.
• On the Global Settings page. Click Operate in the top navigation bar, click Administration > Global Settings in the
left navigation pane, and then click Capacity Optimization.
The values in the Settings dialog box and on the Global Settings page are independent of each other. Show Cost Savings
is available only in the Settings dialog box, and Orphaned Disks Collection Time is available only on the Global Settings
page.
The types of VMs are ranked in the order of their importance in a reclamation action. A VM whose attributes match more
than one VM type is included with the higher-ranking VM type. Grouping the VMs this way eliminates duplicates during
calculations. As an example, powered-off VMs are ranked higher than snapshots, so that a powered-off VM that also has
a snapshot appears only in the powered-off VM group.
If you exclude a given type of VM, all VMs matching this type are included with the next lower-ranked group they match.
For example, to list all snapshots regardless of whether their corresponding VMs are powered-off or idle, deselect the
Powered-off VMs and Idle VMs check boxes.
Further, you can configure how long a given class of VMs must be in the designated state - powered-off, for example, or
idle - to be included in the reclamation exercise. You can also choose to hide the cost savings calculation.

Idle VM Calculation and Criteria
These capacity optimization settings are a global configuration that impacts the operation of the entire system. Use
these settings to configure idleness criteria and define reclaimable idle conditions for Virtual Machines (VMs). Through
these configurations, VCF Operations ensures that VM idleness and Reclaim status is accurately tracked and updated
according to real-time data and defined metrics.
Broadcom 6492

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VM Idleness Criteria The VM idleness criteria defines the specific threshold of CPU utilization that a VM must maintain within
and Analysis Period a day to be classified as idle. When a VM's CPU demand falls below the utilization percentage set in
the capacity optimization settings for the required portion of the day, VCF Operations, sets the idleness
indicator property to 1. Conversely, if the CPU demand exceeds this threshold, VCF Operations, sets the
property to 0. The default criteria for this assessment are set to a CPU demand of ≤100 MHz for 100% of
the time.
The identification process begins with a 24-hour analysis period for the idleness indicator. Upon the initial
installation of VCF Operations, it takes exactly 24 hours on the first day to perform the initial determination
of whether a VM qualifies as idle. Following this initial window, VCF Operations conducts hourly evaluations
based on the preceding 24 hours of data. It is possible for a VM to be excluded from the idle classification
after the first 24 hours but qualify later. For example, during a check three hours later, if its CPU demand
satisfies the idleness criteria for the entire preceding 24-hour period.
Reclaimable Idle Reclaimable idle status is determined by the number of consecutive days a VM must meet the idleness
Conditions criteria. If a VM consistently maintains an idleness criteria value of 1 for the specified number of
consecutive days, it is marked as reclaimable idle with a value of 1. This reclaimable idle metric is
published daily, with its value adjusting dynamically based on whether the condition remains satisfied.
Reset and Evaluation VCF Operations employs a multi-tiered evaluation logic involving hourly and daily checks:
Logic • Hourly Check: The idleness status is evaluated based on data values received within the last hour. If a
drop in idleness occurs during this window, the count resets to zero and the process begins again.
• Daily Evaluation: The system records the total number of non-idle periods over the last day. If these
non-idle periods exceed the set threshold, the property is set to 0; otherwise, it is maintained at 1. For
example, if a VM becomes non-idle for three periods within a single hour, it will not be considered idle.
• 24-Hour Reset: Every 24 hours, VCF Operations performs a reset of all records to re-evaluate the VM's
idleness based on the specific periods within that timeframe that fell below the set limit.
Impact of Modifying the When you make modifications to the idleness or reclaimable criteria, the following global changes occur:
Configuration • Less Strict Conditions: VMs previously classified as idle will retain their status. Within one day of the
change, VMs meeting the new condition will have their idleness property updated, though this update
can occur earlier within the same day if the condition is met.
• More Strict Conditions: Any VM that was considered idle but fails to meet a new, stricter condition will
have its idleness indicator changed to 0 within one hour of the system receiving a non-compliant data
point.
• Decreased Consecutive Days: Reducing the required number of days may lead to an increase in the
number of VMs identified as reclaimable.
• Increased Consecutive Days: The system evaluates the date when the idleness indicator last
transitioned to 1. If the new duration requirement is shorter than the time elapsed since the last
recorded idle state, the VM remains reclaimable idle. If the requirement is not met, the VM becomes
non-reclaimable until it satisfies the new requirement without violating any conditions.
Using Rightsize to Adjust Resource Allocation
Rightsizing in VCF Operations refers to the process of adjusting the resource allocations of virtual machines (VMs)
to match their actual workload requirements. It involves optimizing the allocation of CPU, memory, storage, and other
resources to ensure that VMs are neither overprovisioned (allocating more resources than necessary) nor underutilized
(allocating fewer resources than needed). The goal of rightsizing is to achieve efficient resource utilization, improve
performance, and potentially reduce costs. Use the Rightsize page to alter the number of CPUs and amount of memory in
oversized and undersized virtual machines.
Where You Find Rightsizing
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane,
click Capacity > Optimize. Select a data center, then click the Rightsize tab. The Optimize page also has the Reclaim,
Workload Placement, and Resource Efficiency tabs.
How Rightsizing Works
The Capacity Optimization, Reclaim, and Rightsizing features are tightly integrated functions that allows you to assess
workload status and resource usage in data centers across your environment. You can determine time remaining until
Broadcom 6493

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
CPU, memory, or storage resources run out, and realize cost savings when underutilized VMs can be reclaimed and
deployed where needed. With this function, you can change CPU size and memory values for oversized and undersized
virtual machines to achieve optimum system performance.
When you open the page, graphical representations of all the data centers and custom data centers in your environment
appear. By default, they are shown in order of time remaining, beginning from the upper left, where the most constrained
data centers appear. To identify possible oversized and undersized VMs in a data center, click its graphic. The area
following refreshes to display details about the selected data center.
The Summary section has two panels. The Oversized VMs panel shows the number of VMs to downsize. For CPU
and memory, it lists the Recommended Reduction and the % Reduction of total resources. The Undersized VMs panel
shows the number of VMs to upsize. For CPU and memory, it lists the Recommended Increase and the % Increase. Click
EXCLUSION SETTINGS below the panels to exclude VMs by tag.
The table at the bottom of the page provides important information about the VMs. Table headings are Oversized VMs
and Undersized VMs. VMs under each heading are grouped by cluster, and each cluster row shows the total vCPU and
memory change recommended for its VMs. Use Search VMs to find a VM by name. Click the chevron to the left of a
cluster name to list all the oversized or undersized VMs, respectively, in that cluster. You can check the box next to one or
more VM names and click the EXCLUDE VM(S) button to prevent those VMs from being included in a resizing action. You
can also select individual VMs to resize before clicking the RESIZE VM(S) button.

4. Click RESIZE VM(S). The Resize VM(S) workspace appears. The table displays suggested reductions for vCPU and
memory. Click the edit icons to accomplish to changes you wish.
Note:
Operational Actions must be activated in the vCenter cloud adapter instance.
Note:
To resize the VMs later, click SCHEDULE ACTION instead of RESIZE VM(S). Manage scheduled jobs in

to accommodate resizing, some work may be interrupted.
Run a Rightsize Action on Undersized VMs

3. Select the VMs you want to include in the resizing action, or click the checkbox next to VM Name to include all VMs.
4. Click RESIZE VM(S). The Resize VM(S) workspace appears. The table displays suggested increases for vCPU and

Using Workload Optimization
Workload Optimization in VCF Operations focuses on intelligently balancing and optimizing workloads across your
virtualized infrastructure. The goal is to ensure that resources are distributed efficiently to maintain optimal performance,
prevent resource contention, and make the best use of available hardware resources.
Using Workload Optimization, you can rebalance virtual machines and storage across clusters, relieving demand on
an overloaded individual cluster and maintaining or improving cluster performance. You can also set your automated
rebalancing policies to emphasize VM consolidation, which potentially frees up hosts and reduces resource demand.
Broadcom 6496

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Workload Optimization further allows you to potentially automate a significant portion of your data center compute and
storage optimization efforts. With properly defined policies determining the threshold at which resource contention
automatically runs an action, a data center performs at optimum.
Starting with version 9.1, VCF Operations, Workload Placement is available for both VCF Automation managed VMs and
non-VCF Automation managed VMs. Migration is supported across different physical network segments for VMs deployed
using VCF Automation. Traditionally Automation Cloud Zones were not aware of network segments but now that limitation
is not present.
VCF Automation Integration
When you add an instance to a VCF Automation adapter or solution pack as well as to a vCenter adapter instance that is
connected to the VCF Automation server, using VCF Automation-managed resources, VCF Operations automatically adds
a custom data center for the vCenter, using VCF Automation-managed resources.
On the VCF Operations side, to get the day2 chain configured, you must make the following initial configurations:
1. In vCenter, Administration -> Solutions and then add the VMware vSphere adapter instance for the vCenter that is
configured as an endpoint in VCF Automation Server.
2. In vCenter, Administration -> Solutions and then add the VCF Automation adapter instance for the server that will
appear in the VCF Operations and VCF Automation integration day2 chain.
VCF Operations can manage workload placement and optimization for the custom data centers that reside in VCF
Automation-managed clusters.
However, VCF Operations is not permitted to set tag policies for the custom data center. (At the Workload Optimization
screen, the Business Intent window is not operational for VCF Automation custom data centers.) When rebalancing a VCF
Automation custom data center, VCF Operations uses all applicable policies and placement principles from both systems:
VCF Automation and VCF Operations For complete information on creating and managing VCF Automation custom data
centers that are managed by VCF Operations see the VCF Automation documentation.
Configuring Workload Optimization
Workload Optimization offers you the potential to automate fully a significant portion of your cluster workload rebalancing
tasks. The tasks to accomplish workload automation are as follows:
1. Configure the Workload Automation Details. See Workload Automation Details.
2. If you do not use the AUTOMATE function on the Optimization Recommendation card on the Workload Placement tab,
configure the two Workload Optimization alerts to be triggered when cluster CPU/memory limits are breached, and
configure them as automated. When the alerts are automated, the actions calculated by Workload Optimization are
run automatically. See Configuring Workload Optimization Alerts
Prerequisites
Workload Optimization acts on objects associated with the VMware vSphere Solution that connects VCF Operations to
one or more vCenter instances. The virtual objects in this environment include a vCenter data centers and custom data
centers, cluster compute and storage resources, host systems, and virtual machines. Specific requirements:
• Workload Optimization is supported when the optimization candidate clusters are in the same network or port group.
• Optimization candidate clusters should have one of the following datastore configurations:
– Shared Datastore
– Datastore Cluster
– vSAN Datastore
• A vCenter Adapter configured with the actions activated for each vCenter instance.
• A vCenter instance with at least two datastore clusters. sDRS must be activated and fully automated for datastore
clusters configuration only.
• Any non-datastore clusters must have DRS activated and fully automated
• Storage vMotion must be set to ON at Workload Automation Details. The default is On.
• You must have permission to access all objects in the environment.
Broadcom 6497

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Design Considerations
The following rules constrain the possible computer and storage resource moves that can be performed.
Note:
When VCF Operations suggests that you optimize clusters in a data center, the system does not guarantee it can
run an optimization action. VCF Operations analytics can determine that optimization is desirable and can create
a rebalancing plan. However, the system cannot automatically identify all the architectural constraints that may be
present. Such constraints may prevent an optimization action, or cause an action in progress to fail.
• Moving compute and storage resources is allowed only within, not across data centers or custom data centers.
• Storage resources cannot be moved across non-datastore clusters.
• Compute-resource-only moves are permitted through shared storage.
• Virtual machines defined with affinity rules or anti-affinity rules are not to be moved.
• Virtual machines cannot be moved when residing on a local datastore, unless a storage swap exists on the local
datastore.
• Virtual machines cannot be moved if they have data residing across multiple datastore clusters. Compute-only moves
with similar shared storage are not permitted.
• A virtual machine cannot have data that resides across different storage types. For example, if a virtual machine has a
VM disk on a datastore and a second VM disk on a datastore cluster, the virtual machine does not move, even when
the datastore is shared with the destination or has swap on it.
• A virtual machine can use RDM so long as the destination datastore cluster can access the RDM LUN.
• A virtual machine can implement VM disks on multiple datastores inside a single datastore cluster.
• Workload Optimization may suggest moving virtual machines that are protected by vSphere Replication or Array
Based Replication. You must ensure that all the clusters within a selected data center or custom data center have
replication available. You can set up DRS affinity rules on virtual machines that you do not want moving across
clusters.
Workload Placement Page
Workload Placement lets you optimize virtual machines and storage across clusters to reduce resource contention and
maintain optimum system performance.
Where You Find Workload Placement
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Capacity > Optimize. Click on a data center and you see four tabs - Reclaim, Rightsize, Workload Placement and
Resource Efficiency.
Workload Placement Page Options
On the Workload Placement tab, a carousel of data center cards appears at the top of the page. Each card shows the
days remaining, the potential monthly cost savings, and the optimization status (Optimized or Not Optimized).
After you select a data center, you see the ALL DATACENTERS button on the upper right. Click ALL DATACENTERS
when you want to switch the view to a filtered list of all data centers. Click X to return to a carousel view of data centers.
Note:
The workload placement automation operates by checking the optimization status of workloads every 5 minutes.
When the system identifies a workload that is not optimized, it begins the optimization procedure. After this
process, the next optimization status verification is scheduled for 6 hours later. If workload placement automation
is disabled, manual optimization is accessible through the user interface at any time. While the workload
placement engine attempts to resolve tag violations, it is restricted from migrating tag violating VMs to clusters
that are incompatible or unable to support the current load.

Custom Datacenters in VCF Operations
A custom data center is a user-defined container for a group of objects that includes clusters, hosts, and virtual machines.
Custom data centers provide capacity analytics and capacity badge computations based on the objects it contains. You
can use custom data centers to forecast and analyze the capacity needs for your environment.
When you create a custom data center, you can include multiple cluster objects that span multiple vCenter instances. For
example, you might have a production environment that spans multiple clusters, and you must monitor and manage the
performance and capacity of the entire production environment.
After you create your custom datacenter, you can select it in the list of custom data centers to display a summary of its
health, risk, and efficiency. To access the list of custom data centers, click the Global Inventory in the left menu.
This view displays the top alerts for the data center. To examine the capacity remaining for the custom data center, click
the Capacity tab underDetails after you select an object.
How Custom Datacenters Work
In vSphere, a data center serves as a container for objects that a vCenter instance manages. A custom data center is a
container that can include objects from multiple vCenter instances.
Custom data centers can contain vCenter instances, data centers, clusters, hosts, virtual machines, and datastores. You
can add vSphere object types to a custom data center.
When you add an object, the hierarchical children of that object become part of the custom data center. An object can
belong to multiple custom data centers.
When you create custom data centers, the system runs capacity analytics on the objects in the custom data center, even
if those objects span multiple vCenter instances. For example, you might need to examine the capacity analytics data
across multiple clusters, and the multiple vCenter instances that manage those clusters. You do not have to analyze the
capacity of one cluster or one vCenter instance at a time. You can create a custom data center, add all the clusters to it,
and see the capacity analysis in a single location.
Custom Datacenters List
You can view the list of custom data centers that exist in your environment, and a summary view of its health, risk, and
efficiency. In this view, you can click a custom data center to display the top alerts that the objects in the custom data
center triggered.
Where You Find Custom Datacenters
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Operate and in the left navigation pane, click
Inventory. Select a vCenter and then select the Custom Group and Datacenters tab.

Business Intent Workspace
You can use vCenter tagging to tag VMs, hosts, and/or clusters with specific tags. VCF Operations can be configured to
leverage tags to define business-related placement constraints. Using tags, you can place VMs on hosts/clusters with
matching tags, or exclude VMs and clusters from participating in Workload Placement.
Where You Find Business Intent
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Manage and in the left navigation pane, click
Capacity > Optimize. Click on a data center and you will see four tabs - Reclaim, Rightsize, Workload Placement, and

and click Edit in the Business Intent window.
