Network Profile Configuration Examples
The following examples depict how the service mesh appliances might be wired up.
In fully private VCF Operations HCX deployments where the environments are inside of the same private network, it is
typical for the source HCX appliance and the destination HCX appliance network profiles to be structured identically.
It is possible (and common) for the network profile configurations to differ at the source and destination when they are
separated by the Internet. The reason for this is that the destination service mesh appliances must have an Uplink
network profile with Public IP assignments (this requirement is not true at the source, where internal addresses can use
Source NAT for Internet access).
HCX Network Configuration 1 - Shared Management, Replication and Uplink with Dedicated vMotion
• This configuration trades the benefits gained from separation of traffic to simplify deployments. The same network is
selected for Management, Uplink and Replication traffic.
• This configuration requires the management IP addresses assigned to HCX appliances at the destination to be fully
reachable from the source HCX appliances without NAT translation. Because of this requirement, this configuration is
most typical in HCX appliance deployments fully within a private network.
Broadcom 6555

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Network Configuration 2 - Dedicated Replication Network
• Configuration 2 adds a dedicated network for the Replication traffic (Bulk Migration).
• This configuration variation is only possible when the cluster hosts use a dedicated Replication VMkernel network.
• Separating the replication traffic is a recommended practice. This configuration is used when a dedicated replication
VMkernel interface is available.
•
Important:
In deployments where ESX hosts use a dedicated VMkernel configuration for vSphere Replication services,
the HCX Interconnect uses a Network Profile configuration dedicated to the vSphere Replication traffic. This
configuration does not include the vSphere Replication NFC traffic. The HCX appliance always uses its
Management interface for vSphere Replication NFC traffic.
Broadcom 6556

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Network Configuration 3 - Dedicated Uplink Network
• Configuration 3 adds a dedicated network for Uplink traffic (Service Mesh Transport traffic).
• This configuration trades simplicity of deployment (see configuration 1) for the benefits of separating the uplink and the
management traffic.
• A dedicated Uplink network is a good way to isolate the migration traffic for applying Quality of Service (QoS).
• A dedicated Uplink can be used to consume bandwidth/networks dedicated to the migration project.
• For deployments over the Internet:
– Public IP addresses are assigned at the destination using the Uplink network profile.
– The source HCX appliances can use traditional Internet SNAT to securely connect to the destination public IP
addresses using strong encryption.
– Providers leverage this configuration to make VCF Operations HCX services easy to deploy before dedicated
private circuits become available.
Broadcom 6557

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Network Configuration 4 - OS Assisted Migration Using Guest Network
This configuration shows OS Assisted Migration networking when using a dedicated Guest Network for migrations.
Broadcom 6558

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Network Configuration 5- OS Assisted Migration Using Management Network
Configuration shows OS Assisted Migration networking when using the Management Network for the Guest Network
function.
Compute Profile Considerations and Concepts
The compute profile is a sub-component of the service mesh. The compute profile describes which HCX services run, and
how they are deployed when the service meshh is created.
Introduction to Compute Profiles
A compute profile configuration is required for service mesh deployments. It defines deployment parameters and enables
services. For configuration procedures, see Create a Compute Profile. A compute profile is constructed of the following
elements:
Services The VCF Operations HCX services that are activated when a Service Mesh is created.
Service Clusters At the HCX appliance source, the service cluster hosts contains the virtual machines for migration. For
network extension, only distributed switches connected to selected service clusters are displayed. A
datacenter container can be used to automatically include clusters within the datacenter container. Clusters
are automatically adjusted in the compute profile when clusters are removed or added to the datacenter
container.
At the HCX appliance destination, the service clusters can be used as the target for migrations.
Deployment Clusters The cluster (or resource pool) and datastore that host the service mesh appliances.
For migrations to be successful, the deployment cluster must be connected such that the service clusters
vMotion and Management/Replication VMkernel networks are reachable to the HCX-IX appliance.
For network extension to be successful, the deployment cluster must be connected to a distributed switch
that has full access to the VM network broadcast domains.
Management Network The network profile that the HCX appliance uses for management connections.
Profile
Uplink Network Profile The network profile that the HCX appliance uses for HCX appliance to HCX appliance traffic.
vMotion Network Profile The network profile that the HCX appliance uses for vMotion-based connections with the ESX cluster.
Broadcom 6559

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Replication Network The network profile that the HCX appliance uses for Replication-based connections with the ESX cluster.
Profile
Distributed Switches for The distributed switches containing the virtual machine networks for extension.
Network Extension
Guest Network Profile The network profile that the HCX appliance uses to receive connections from the sentinel agents.
for OSAM
Characteristics of Compute Profiles
• An HCX appliance system must have one compute profile.
• The compute profile references clusters and inventory within the vCenter Server that is registered in the HCX
appliance.
• Creating a compute profile does not deploy the HCX appliances (compute profiles can be created and not used).
• Creating a service mesh deploys appliances using the settings defined in the source and the destination compute
profiles.
• A compute profile is "in use" when it is used in a service mesh configuration.
• Changes to a compute profile profile are not affected in the service mesh until a service mesh Re-Sync action is
triggered.
Compute Profiles and Service Appliances
The VCF Operations HCX Services defined in the compute profile identify the appliances that the HCX appliance deploys
when creating the service mesh. The compute profile configuration can include the following appliances:
• HCX appliance Interconnect (HCX-IX)
• Network Extension (HCX-NET-EXT)
• Sentinel Gateway (HCX-SGW)
• Sentinel Data Receiver (HCX-SDR)
• Sentinel Replication Gateway (HCX-SRG)
The following compute profile considerations apply to these appliances.
• For the dataplane appliances (HCX-IX, HCX-NET-EXT, HCX-SGW, HCX-SDR, HCX-SRG), it is recommended
to change the compute profile if a change in the appliance deployment containers (compute, storage or folder) is
required. In such a case, you must resync the service mesh to relocate the appliances.
• If you do not use the compute profile as described above, you can use vSphere vMotion to relocate dataplane
appliances to different containers with the following restrictions:
– The host/cluster must have a port group association with all networks defined under the network profile. For
example, this can includes the Uplink, Management, and vMotion networks.
Broadcom 6560

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– VCF Operations HCX redeploys appliances into same deployment cluster as configured under the compute profile
during Upgrade or Redeploy operations, and removes previously deployed appliances from other clusters.
– The appliances will be relocated/vMotion back to same deployment cluster as configured under compute profile
during a service mesh Resync operation. The HCX appliance relocates (vMotion) the appliances back to the same
deployment cluster configured in the compute profile.
Note:
For Storage vMotion requirements, the target datastore must have an association/reachability with all hosts/
clusters to which the appliances relocate.
When relocating Network Extension appliances, which are carrying data traffic over an extended datapath, the
relocation process might experience some packet drops. This applies during relocation (vMotion) to the same
cluster or a different cluster depending on the Compute Profile configuration.
Compute Profiles and Clusters
HCX appliance compute profiles provide flexibility when designing service mesh deployments. The following are examples
of different service mesh deployments.
Configuration 1 - Single Cluster Deployments
In the illustrated example, Cluster-1 is both the deployment cluster and service cluster.
• Single cluster deployments use a single compute profile.
• In the CP, one cluster is designated as a service cluster and as the deployment cluster.
Broadcom 6561

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration 2 - Multicluster
In the illustrated example, Cluster-1 is the deployment cluster. Both cluster-1 and cluster-2 are service clusters.
• In this compute profile configuration, one cluster is designated as the deployment cluster, and all clusters (including the
deployment cluster) are designated as service clusters.
• All the service clusters must be similarly connected (that is, same vMotion/Replication networks).
• When the service mesh is instantiated, one HCX-IX is deployed for all clusters.
• In larger deployments where clusters might change, a satacenter container can be used (instead of individual clusters)
so VCF Operations HCX automatically manages the service clusters.
Broadcom 6562

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration 3 - Multicluster (Dedicated Deployment Cluster)
In the illustrated example, cluster-1 is the deployment cluster and cluster-2 is the service cluster.
• In this compute profile configuration, one cluster is designated as the deployment cluster and is not a service cluster.
All other clusters are designated as service clusters:
– This compute profile configuration can be used to dedicate resources to the HCX appliance functions.
– This compute profile configuration can be used to control site-to-site migration egress traffic.
– This compute profile configuration can be used to provide a limited scope vSphere distributed switch in
environments that heavily leverage the vSphere Standard Switch.
• For VCF Operations HCX migrations, this compute profile configuration requires the service cluster VMkernel networks
to be reachable from the deployment cluster, where the HCX-IX is deployed.
• For network extension, this compute profile configuration requires the deployment cluster hosts to be within workload
networks' broadcast domain (service cluster workload networks must be available in the deployment cluster distributed
switch).
• When the service mesh is instantiated, one HCX-IX appliance is deployed for all clusters.
Broadcom 6563

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration 4 - Cluster Exclusions
In the illustrated example, cluster-2 is not included as a service cluster.
• In this compute profile configuration, one or more servers have been excluded from the service cluster configuration.
• This configuration can be used to prevent portions of infrastructure from being eligible for VCF Operations HCX
services. Virtual machines in clusters that are not designated as a service cluster cannot be migrated using VCF
Operations HCX(migrations will fail).
Note:
If vSphere hosts or virtual machines are in a folder outside of all clusters, those will be considered as excluded
from the service resources/clusters even if the compute profile allows you to select the entire data center and
select folders.
Broadcom 6564

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuration 5 - Multiple Compute Profiles (Optional, for Scale)
In the illustrated example, compute profile 1 has been created for cluster-1, and compute profile-2 has been created
for cluster-2, and the VMkernel networks are the same. Creating additional compute profiles is optional (for scaling
purposes).
• In this compute profile configuration, service clusters are separated into compute profiles.
• Every compute profile requires a deployment cluster, resulting in a dedicated service mesh configuration for each
compute profile.
• For clarity, if there were 5 clusters in a vCenter Server, you can have dervice clusters separated out in various ways,
such as the following:
– CP-1: 1 Service Cluster, CP-2: 4 Service Clusters
– CP-1: 2 Service Clusters, CP-2: 3 Service Clusters
– CP-1: 1 Service Cluster, CP-2: 2 Service Clusters, CP-3: 2 Service Clusters
– CP-1: 1 Service Cluster, CP-2: 1 Service Cluster, CP-3: 1 Service Cluster, CP-4: 1 Service Cluster, CP-5: 1 Service
Cluster
Broadcom 6565

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
Compute profile configurations can leverage the same network profiles for ease of configuration.
Configuration 6 - Multiple Compute Profiles (with Dedicated Network Profiles)
In the illustrated example, cluster-1 uses vMotion and Mgmt networks 1. cluster-2 uses vMotion and Mgmt networks 2.
The VMkernel networks are different, and isolated from each other. Creating dedicated network profiles and dedicated
compute profiles is required.
• In this compute profile configuration, the service clusters are separated into distinct compute profiles. The compute
profiles reference cluster-specific network profiles.
• When the service mesh HCX-IX appliance connects directly to the cluster's vMotion network, where the Replication
and vMotion are different, you must create cluster-specific network profiles and assign them to cluster-specific
compute profiles. These profiles will then be used to create a cluster-specific service mesh.
Broadcom 6566

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Appendix - Installation Summary Steps
This reference lists all the steps involved when deploying source and destination VCF Operations HCX appliances. The
steps are listed here as a quick reference. Requirements are not listed here. Use the checklists in this publication to
prepare for the installation.
Install (or Enable) VCF Operations HCX at the Destination
The following steps summarize the initial HCX appliance deployment and configuration in private data center destination
environment. For a detailed description, see VCF Operations HCX Licensing.
Note:
If you are using a Provider for the destination site, contact your Provider for enabling HCX.
1. Install the HCX appliance:
Broadcom 6567

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a. Use the VCF Operations HCX OVA from to deploy the HCX appliance in the vSphere
support.broadcom.com
Client. See Deploy the OVA in the vSphere Client.
b. Log in to the HCX Manger Appliance Management interface (:9443) .
c. Set the location and system name.
d. Register the vCenter Server and NSX Manager.
e. Restart the VCF Operations HCX services.
f. Define role mapping (this setting defines the groups that can perform mobility operations).
2. Create a network profile:
a. Browse to the VCF Operations HCX interface UI (:443) to create a network profile. The network profile is a compute
profile requirement for service mesh deployment.
3. Create a compute profile:
a. Browse to the VCF Operations HCX interface UI (:443) to create a compute profile. The compute profile defines how
service mesh appliances are deployed in the destination environment.
4. Configure inbound firewall rules for the destination HCX appliance:
a. Allow TCP-443 inbound from the source HCX appliance to the destination HCX appliance (this might be a NAT
Public IP if the environments are separated by Internet).
b. Allow UDP-4500 inbound from the source HCX-IX and HCX-NET-EXT appliances IP addresses (this might be a
NAT IP if the environments are separated by Internet).
5. Configure any site-specific firewalls for traffic between HCX service appliances. Reference ports.broadcom.com for the
complete list of HCX appliance network ports.
Next, install the HCX appliance at the source site.
Install VCF Operations HCX at the Source Site
The following steps summarize the initial HCX appliance deployment and configuration in the source environment. For a
detailed description, see VCF Operations HCX Licensing.
1. Use the HCX appliance OVA to deploy the HCX appliance system in the vSphere Client. See Deploy the OVA in the
vSphere Client.
After the OVA is deployed and the system is initialized:
a. Log in to the HCX Appliance Management interface (:9443), and authenticate with the Admin user credentials.
b. Set the location and system name.
c. Register the vCenter Server, SSO, and optionally the NSX Manager registered with that vCenter Server.
d. Restart the VCF Operations HCX services.
e. Configure Role Mapping (this defines the SSO user groups that can perform mobility operations).
2. Create a site pair:
a. The VCF Operations HCX interface (:443) registers the destination HCX appliance using the SSO group from the
destination environment.
3. Create a compute profile:
a. Log in to the VCF Operations HCX interface (:443) at the source, and authenticate with a user that is part of the
role-mapping group.
4. Create a service mesh:
a. The VCF Operations HCX interface (:443) uses the service mesh wizard to instantiate services.
a. In the service mesh interface, you select a compute profile for the HCX appliance source environment, and a
compute profile for the destination environments.
b. Service mesh creation deploys data plane appliances in parallel at the source and the destination
environments.
c. The source HCX appliance service mesh appliances are Initiators, and will automatically attempt to establish
tunneling connections to the destination side.
d. The destination appliance components are Receivers that will only accept tunneling requests from the Initiators.
Broadcom 6568

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Administering VCF Operations HCX
About Administering VMware® Cloud Foundation Operations HCX™
This information describes how to plan for, install, and operate VMware Cloud Foundation Operations HCX services in
a VMware Cloud Foundation platform. The information includes step-by-step configuration instructions and operational
procedures.
Intended Audience
This information is for anyone who wants to install or use VCF Operations HCX. The information is for virtual infrastructure
administrators and architects and who are familiar with virtual machine technology and data center operations.
Overview
VCF Operations HCX is a workload mobility platform that is designed for simplifying workload migration, and workload
rebalancing across data centers and clouds.
Use cases:
• Rehosting application workloads
You can schedule and migrate vSphere virtual machines within and across data centers without requiring a reboot.
Use cases include data center consolidation, moving workloads for efficient host resource utilization, moving workloads
from private to public cloud sites or from public to private cloud sites, and flexible migration options for managing large
or small migration waves with the least disruption and greatest efficiency.
• Upgrading and re-platforming applications and infrastructure
With VCF Operations HCX, you can migrate workloads from vSphere and non-vSphere (KVM and Hyper-V)
environments, within and across private or public clouds, to current vSphere versions without requiring an upgrade.
Use cases include moving applications to the latest VMware Cloud Foundation software and hardware platform, and
performing platform maintenance without impacting application workloads.
• Workload rebalancing
VCF Operations HCX provides a mobility platform across data centers and providers to allow customers to move
applications and workloads at any time to meet scale, cost management, compliance, and vendor neutrality goals. Use
cases include balancing application workloads across public and private clouds, moving workloads between providers,
and extending the networks serving those workloads between sites.
System Services
To build and maintain a secure optimized transport fabric between paired sites, and to provide feature rich functionality,
VCF Operations HCX managed sites run various connectivity and mobility services.
VCF Operations HCX delivers the connectivity and mobility services to enable hybrid interconnect and migration services.
These services provide additional functionality for scalability and performance when transforming large data centers or
moving large quantities of virtual machines.
The following services are available with VCF Operations HCX.
VCF Operations HCX Services Description
Interconnect This service creates and secures connections between VCF Operations HCX installations,
supporting management, migration, and replication operations. This service is deployed as a
virtual appliance.
WAN Optimization The WAN Optimization service works with the HCX Interconnect service to improve network
performance through a combination of deduplication and compression techniques. This
service is optionally deployed as part of the enhanced HCX-IX virtual appliance.
Network Extension This service extends the virtual machine networks from a VCF Operations HCX source site
to an VCF Operations HCX destination site. Virtual machines that are migrated or created on
the extended segment at the destination site are Layer 2 adjacent to virtual machines placed
on the origin network. This service is deployed as a virtual appliance.
Broadcom 6569

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations HCX Services Description
Network Extension High Availability Network extension High Availability protects extended networks from disruptions that are
associated with network extension appliance downtime. Network extension High Availability
creates a redundant pair, or group, of connections for network extension appliances. In
the event that a network extension appliance fails or is taken offline, the active connection
fails over to the standby connection, and the extended network operations continue without
interruption.
Bulk Migration This service uses vSphere Replication protocol to move virtual machines in parallel between
sites.
vMotion Migration This migration method uses the vSphere vMotion protocol to move a single virtual machine
between sites with no service interruption.
Mobility Optimized Networking (MON) MON is a capability of the network extension feature. MON enables optimized virtual machine
trafffic for virtual machines that span multiple segmented networks, that have multiple VLAN
dependencies, or have hybrid applications during the migration cycle. Migrated virtual
machines can be configured to access any destination through an optimized path.
OS Assisted Migration (OSAM) This migration service moves Linux or Windows-based non-vSphere guest virtual machines
from their host environment to a VMware Cloud Foundation platform.
The OSAM service operates in one of two modes: multi-site and single-site.
• Multi-site mode applies to site pairs where the source site runs both vSphere and
non-vSphere environments, and the destination site runs vSphere. In this mode, VCF
Operations HCX deploys the HCX-SGW (Sentinel Gateway) appliance at the source site
and the SDR (Sentinel Data Receiver) appliance at the destination site.
• Single-site mode means vSphere and all VCF Operations HCX services are deployed at
the destination site. In this mode, VCF Operations HCX deploys the HCX-SRG (Sentinel
Replication Gateway) appliance at the destination site where the non-vSphere workloads
will be migrated.
Regardless of the mode, every guest workload requires the installation of sentinel software.
Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV) This service uses both vSphere Replication and vSphere vMotion technologies for large-
scale, parallel migrations with no service interruption.
HCX Assisted vMotion (Direct) The HCX Assisted vMotion (HAV) service works in conjunction with native cross-vCenter
vMotion migration to orchestrate migrations between the ESX hosts associated with the
source and destination vCenter Servers.
Supervisor Onboarding VCF Operations HCX supports onboarding traditional virtual machines into specified
Supervisor clusters.
Broadcom 6570

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VCF Operations HCX Services Description
Traffic Engineering VCF Operations HCX provides settings for optimizing network traffic for HCX Interconnect
• Application Path Resiliency and network extension services.
• TCP MSS Clamping (TCP Flow • Application Path Resiliency is available for either Interconnect or network extension
Conditioning) services.
• Generic Receive Offload (GRO) This setting creates multiple tunnel flows for both Interconnect and network extension
• Tunnel Encryption (network traffic, which can follow multiple paths across the network infrastructure from the source
extension or migration services) to the destination data centers. The service then intelligently forwards traffic through the
tunnel over the optimal path and dynamically switches between tunnels depending on
traffic conditions.
Application Path Resiliency forwards traffic over one tunnel at a time and does not load
balance across multiple paths.
• TCP MSS Clamping is available for network extension service.
This setting adjusts the segment size during the TCP connection handshake between end
points across the network extension. This optimizes the average packet size to reduce
fragmentation and lower the overall packet rate.
• Generic Receive Offload is available for the network extension service.
VCF Operations HCX reassembles inbound packets into larger ones before delivery to the
workload applications, allowing for enhanced application performance.
• Tunnel encryption is available for either network extension or migration services.
By default, this setting uses transport encryption to protect network extension data and
migration traffic between site pairs. Deactivating encryption may increase performance for
migration or network extension connections.
Deactivating encryption is available only on Uplink networks that have been verified as
Secure in the network profile configuration.
System Components
VCF Operations HCX consists of a virtual appliance at the source and destination sites along with associated service
virtual appliances for each site.
In the VCF Operations HCX site-to-site architecture, there is a notion of a source and a destination environment with an
VCF Operations HCX appliance deployed at each site. In hosted environments, the provider may deploy VCF Operations
HCX at the destination. For specific VCF Operations HCX deployment details in a hosted environment, contact your
provider.
The source and destination sites are paired together to perform mobility and network extension operations.
In both the source and the destination environments, the VCF Operations HCX virtual appliance is deployed to the
same management zone as the site's vCenter Server, enabling deployment of the VCF Operations HCX service virtual
appliances across both the source and destination sites.
You initiate migration of virtual machines and establishing service mesh services from the VCF Operations HCX console.
During creation of the service mesh, the VCF Operations HCX virtual appliance deploys service virtual appliances
supporting mobility and network extension operations.
Interconnect Appliance
The Interconnect service (HCX-IX) appliance provides replication and vMotion-based migration capabilities over the
Internet and private lines to the destination site while providing strong encryption, traffic engineering, and virtual machine
mobility.
The Interconnect appliance includes deployment of the Mobility Agent service that appears as a host object in the
vCenter Server. Mobility Agent is the mechanism that VCF Operations HCX uses to perform vMotion, Cold migration, and
Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV) migration to a destination site.
The Interconnect appliance includes the WAN Optimization (WAN-OPT) service. This appliance improves the
performance characteristics of private lines or Internet paths by applying WAN optimization techniques like the data de-
duplication and compression techniques.
Broadcom 6571

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Network Extension Appliance
The network extension (HCX-NET-EXT) appliance provides layer 2 connectivity between sites. A network extension
provides the ability to keep the same IP and MAC addresses during virtual machine migrations. When the network
extension service is enabled, a pair of virtual appliances is deployed: one in the source and one in the destination site.
Sentinel Gateway Appliance
When using the OS Assisted Migration (OSAM) service in multi-site mode, you migrate guest (non-vSphere) virtual
machines between vSphere-based source and destination VCF Operations HCX sites. In multi-site mode, VCF
Operations HCX deploys the Sentinel Gateway (SGW) appliance at the source vSphere environment for connecting and
forwarding guest workloads.
Sentinel Data Receiver Appliance
When using the OS Assisted Migration (OSAM) service in multi-site mode, VCF Operations HCX deploys the Sentinel
Data Receiver (SDR) appliance at the destination vSphere environment for receiving, managing, and monitoring data
replication operations.
Sentinel Replication Gateway Appliance
When using the OS Assisted Migration (OSAM) service in single-site mode, you migrate guest (non-vSphere) virtual
machines between non-vSphere environments and vSphere-based VCF Operations HCX sites. In single-site mode, VCF
Operations HCX deploys the Sentinel Replication Gateway (SRG) appliance at the destination vSphere environment. The
SRG manages data replication operations from the non-vSphere environment.

requirements, like software versions and feature interoperability requirements.

Migration Host and Datastore Requirements
The requirements in this section apply to vSphere-to-vSphere migrations.
During a virtual machine migration operation, the destination compute and storage resources are selected. These

Destination Host/Datastore

Requirements
Host CPU and Memory Capacity The destination host must support the original vCPU and Memory configurations of the virtual

Host CPU and Memory Usage The destination host capacity must satisfy admission control requirements.
Host Compatibility with VMware Tools The destination hosts must support the VMware Tools version of the original virtual machine.
For more information, see the VMware Certified Compatibility Guides.

• Complete original virtual machine data (everything that makes up the virtual machine)

configuration
System Requirements for Scaling Out Deployments
Consider the following requirements when scaling out VCF Operations HCX deployments:
• When scaling VCF Operations HCX, the hardware requirements apply for each additional virtual appliance. For virtual
appliance limit information, refer to the VMware Configurations Maximums.
• The migration service, in its default configuration, encompasses all source and destination clusters in the service mesh
with a single Interconnect appliance. The migration service can be scaled out by deploying additional service meshes.
The additional meshes can be selected during migration operations.
• Multiple network extension appliances can be deployed per vSphere Distributed Virtual Switch (VDS) or NSX Transport
Zone.
• When using network extension High Availability (HA), at least two network extension appliances must be deployed
per VDS or NSX Transport Zone in order to form an HA group. In the HA group, one appliance is Active and one is
Standby.
Note:
HA Standby appliances must be considered when calculating the overall hardware resource requirements.

• You must configure the network extension appliance count in the service mesh to include all planned standalone, HA
Active, and HA Standby appliances.
Note:
For scale-out procedures, use KB article 93605.

Network Port and Protocol Requirements
VCF Operations HCX deployments require communication over various ports between all HCX appliances at each site
and between HCX sites.
You must allow the following connections in VCF Operations HCX deployments:
• The perimeter firewalls must allow VCF Operations HCX connections to vcsa.vmware.com. For systems not
participating in CEIP, this is not required.
• The source VCF Operations HCX site firewalls must be configured to allow outbound connections to the destination
VCF Operations HCX systems.
• The destination VCF Operations HCX site firewalls must be configured to allow inbound connections from the source
VCF Operations HCX system.
• All local connections (within a single VCF Operations HCX site deployment) at the source and destination environment.
These connections never traverse from source to destination or from destination to source.
• In environments that rely on a proxy server to centralize outbound HTTPS connnections, the proxy server must be
configured on the VCF Operations HCX . Refer to Configure a Proxy Server.
For a complete list of network port and protocol requirements, see VMware Ports and Protocols.
Network Underlay Minimum Requirements
The infrastructure providing network connectivity to a VCF Operations HCX deployment (the underlay) must meet the
minimum requirements. The underlay includes any intermediate system that is customer managed, provided by a third
party, or part of an Internet service provider network.
Broadcom 6574

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
What Is the Network Underlay
A network underlay provides the physical or logical connectivity on which the VCF Operations HCX transport packets
are tunneled, where a transport packet contains an overlay header. The underlay network does not need to know that
it is carrying HCX transport packets. This includes the physical routing infrastructure in the customer data center and (if
applicable) any hosted infrastructure, and any physical network services joining the connected locations.
A network underlay can vary from high-bandwidth low-latency private paths between server racks in a data center,
to lower-bandwidth higher-latency Internet based connectivity. We use the term "network underlay" to encompass all
elements that affect the performance characteristics of an underlay, including the servers and network devices and
connections between the vSphere environments. The network underlay requirements must be satisfied when considering
all elements of the underlay.
Virtual Private Networks Based Network Underlays
Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) are frequently used for creating secure network connections to private and public
vSphere clouds over the Internet. Software-Defined Wide Area Network (SD-WAN) and custom tunneling solutions
are used over the internet to improve data traffic transmissions. The SD-WAN, VPN, and other tunneling solutions are
collectively referred to as VPN in this document.
The network underlay includes connections with VPN configurations. The network underlay requirements must be
satisfied when considering all elements of the underlay.
General Network Underlay Requirements
HCX supports multiple uplinks and each uplink can be connected to a different network underlay. Examples of different
network underlays include private line, public Internet, and multi-homed connectivity.
Broadcom 6575

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The following table summarizes the requirements from the Network Underlay to use the VCF Operations HCX migration
and extension services:
• This table applies to migration and extension overlays (service mesh appliances).
• This table does not apply to HCX Manager or the management connections.

the HCX uplink IP at the source site and the destination site.

supported at the minimum performance level. The minimum requirement applies to all
network underlays and is provided in the next table.

Bandwidth distribution with VCF Operations HCX on a network underlay can be visualized as a set of nested pipes, where
the underlay network is the main channel. VCF Operations HCX and non-VCF Operations HCX traffic is carried through
main channel. Migration and network extension traffic can be thought of as separate pipelines through the site manager
channel. The network extension pipe provides the throughput for all the extended network traffic. The migration pipe
handles the vMotion, Bulk, and OS Assisted Migration service traffic.
Note:
The number of parallel migrations that are allowed depends on the bandwidth of the migration pipe.

VCF Operations HCX Licensing
VCF Operations HCX service licensing happens during installation when the system detects a VMware Cloud Foundation
(cores) license or the system enters evaluation mode.
About Licensing
VCF Operations HCX has a flexible licensing scheme that allows for multiple use cases and modes of operation. All VCF
Operations HCX services are enabled by default for all license types.
License types
VMware Cloud VMware vSphere environments that are licensed for VMware Cloud Foundation are entitled to all VCF
Foundation (cores) Operations HCX services.
VCF Operations HCX systems that register with vCenter version 9.0 and higher automatically discover and
inherit the VCF license. VCF Operations HCX systems that have registered with a non-VCF vCenter enter
evaluation mode.
VCF Operations HCX polls the vCenter Server periodically for VMware Cloud Foundation license
information. If a VMware Cloud Foundation site license is updated, or a vCenter Server becomes licensed
for VMware Cloud Foudation, VCF Operations HCX discovers and inherits that license information.
VCenter Entitlement VCF Operations HCX Managers that are registered with vCenter Servers running version 4.x and earlier
Server must retrieve the entitlements from a vCenter Server that runs VCF Operations HCX 9.0 or later.
Evaluation Mode If no license is discovered during installation, VCF Operations HCX enters Evaluation Mode. Evaluation
Mode provides temporary entitlement to all VCF Operations HCX services.
Evaluation Mode is limited to 90 days from the day of installation, with a maximum of 20 virtual machine
migrations per migration type. Evaluation mode ends after 90 days or when VCF Operations HCX detects a
VMware Cloud Foundation license through monitoring of the vCenter Server.
If VCF Operations HCX is deployed at VMware vSphere Foundation or non-VCF sites without a valid
license:
• The system enters into Evaluation Mode by default.
• VCF Operations HCX installations display a banner in the Appliance Management UI (:9443) to indicate
the system is running in evaluation mode, which is an expected notification.
• Systems in evaluation mode can get feature inheritance (not the license inheritance) from its paired
VCF Operations HCX .
• You can trigger all services from the source site appliance towards the paired destination site appliance
which has entitlement to use those services.
• The expiration of a site license generates a warning message letting you know that a site is no longer
active. This message can be ignored provided there is a valid license associated with the site pair that
continues service inheritance.
Broadcom 6582

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
When the license validity expires for an VCF Operations HCX site, or the Evaluation Mode period ends,
VCF Operations HCX feature inheritance continues to allow operations as long as one site in the site
pair has a valid license.
When Evaluation Mode ends, VCF Operations HCX enters Restricted Mode.
Grace Period When a VMware Cloud Foundation license expires, VCF Operations HCX enters a grace period. VCF
Operations HCX continues normal operation for the duration of this period. This length of this period varies
with each VMware Cloud Foundation license subscription. During this time, users can renew their VMware
Cloud Foundation license.
When the grace period expires, VCF Operations HCX enters Restricted Mode.
Restricted Mode In this state, the VMware Cloud Foundation license has expired and the grace period has ended. No
additional operations are allowed for VCF Operations HCX.
For a detailed description of VCF Operations HCX Services, see System Services.
Service Inheritance
VCF Operations HCX provides a notion of inheritance to provide the most flexibility for sites that do not have VMware
Cloud Foundation license entitlement or that are running in evaluation mode. With inheritance, VCF Operations HCX
considers the entitlements that are associated with each licensed site during site pairing. Inheritance logic looks at what
services have been enabled at each site and compares that with the entitlements associated with the site pair to generate
a service mesh supporting those services. See Understanding Service Inheritance.
Installing New Systems
Installation requirements refer to any information required to set up a newly deployed VCF Operations HCX system.
VCF Operations HCX Installation
After you have deployed the VCF Operations HCX OVA file through the vSphere Client, VCF Operations HCX requires
you to log in to the Appliance Management interface and perform the initial system configuration. For more information,
see Configuring VCF Operations HCX.
Note:
By default, VCF Operations HCX installations participate in the Customer Experience Improvement Program
(CEIP), which establishes a connection with Broadcom to collect site telemetry. See About the Customer
Experience Improvement Program.
About the Customer Experience Improvement Program
The Customer Experience Improvement Program (CEIP) helps to improve VCF Operations HCX products and services, to
identify and fix problems, and to develop best practices and procedures for deploying and using VCF Operations HCX.
Participation in the CEIP is provided by default. With CEIP, VCF Operations HCX periodically collects technical
information about your organization's use of VCF Operations HCX and its services and provides that information to
Broadcom. This information does not personally identify any individual.
For VCF Operations HCX sites participating in CEIP, perimeter firewalls must allow connections to .
vcsa.vmware.com
See Network Port and Protocol Requirements.
You can choose to leave the program at any time by selecting an option in VCF Operations HCX interface. For more
information, see Leave or Join the Customer Experience Improvement Program.
Air-Gap sites do not participate in CEIP. Air-gap sites never transmit information to Broadcom. For more information, see
Installing New Systems.
Leave or Join the Customer Experience Improvement Program
An VCF Operations HCX site can leave or join the Customer Experience Improvement Program (CEIP) at any time.
Broadcom 6583

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Obtain the user name and password of the administrator account.
• Sites participating in the CEIP make an Internet connection to vcsa.vmware.com. When leaving or joining CEIP,
remove or add firewall rules as necessary.
1. Log in to HCX Manager Appliance Management.
2. Navigate to the Configuration tab.
3. Select CEIP.
4. Click Leave CEIP or Join CEIP.
Understanding Service Inheritance
To provide the most flexibility for sites activated with different service entitlements, VCF Operations HCX provides a notion
of inheritance.
VCF Operations HCX services operate between paired sites. Before mobility operations can take place, the system
creates a service mesh between each site pair. The service mesh deploys the appliances and makes the service
connections necessary to allow mobility operations. To complete the service mesh, the required services must be enabled
in the compute profile at each site, and each site must have a license entitlement to use those services.
With inheritance, the logic to decide what a site can do is a function of the site pairing along with the entitlements granted
to each site during activation. When creating the service mesh, the inheritance logic compares the entitlements applied
at each site and then employs the broadest level of entitlement. After establishing the level of service entitlement for the
site pair, the inheritance logic looks at each site's compute profile configuration to determine whether the service mesh
supports the configured services.
Note:
Regardless of what services are configured in the compute profile, the service mesh for the site pair determines
the entitlement to those services. For example, for any VCF Operations HCX site, you can configure the compute
profile for all services, but if the service mesh for the site pair provides enablement of only some services, only
that subset of services is allowed between sites. For site pairs that have entitlement to all VCF Operations HCX
services, the compute profile provides a means to customize services between sites.
For a description of VCF Operations HCX Services, see System Services.
Refer to the following examples.
Example 1:
Site A is paired with Site B and Site C, creating a "V" topology. Site A was activated in Evaluation Mode, providing limited
access to all VCF Operations HCX Services. Site B was activated using VCF Solution Licensing, giving entitlement to
all VCF Operations HCX services. Site C was also activated in Evaluation Mode. In this example, Site A inherits the
entitlements of Site B, but Site A inherits no additional entitlements from Site C. Site pairs A and B will operate in VCF
mode. Site pairs A and C will operate in Evaluation Mode.
Example 2:
Sites B and D are paired. Site B was activated using VCF Solution Licensing, which provides entitlement to all VCF
Operations HCX services. Site D was activated in Evaluation Mode, which supports all VCF Operations HCX services but
with limitations. In this example, even though Site D is activated in Evaluation Mode with capacity limits on migrations,
it inherits all the VCF entitlements since it is paired with a site licensed with VCF Solution Licensing and can perform
mobility operations without any restrictions.
View Site License Information
You can view site licensing information and entitlement server information in HCX Manager Appliance Management.
Broadcom 6584

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the HCX Manager Appliance Management.
2. Select the Configuration tab.
3. Select Licensing.
The system displays the VCF Operations HCX license status based on the vCenter license, including the license
validity, or expiration date.
The License status can have the following values:
License Status Description
Active Indicates VCF Operations HCX has active license entitlement based on the VMware Cloud
Foundation license for the vCenter Server registered with VCF Operations HCX.
Evaluation Period Indicates VCF Operations HCX is registered with a vCenter Server that does not have a
VMware Cloud Foundation license, and VCF Operations HCX is running in Evaluation Mode.
Grace Period Indicates VCF Operations HCX has reached the validity date for an active license, and is
operating in the grace period.
Restricted Mode Indicates the VCF Operations HCX has reached the end of the grace period for an active
license or for the evaluation period, and no further mobility or network extension operations
are permitted.
Active license entitlements from a registered vCenter server configured with HCX are automatically displayed. If the
vCenter Server registered with VCF Operations HCX does not have valid VMware Cloud Foundation entitlements, an
alternate mechanism is to add a vCenter Entitlement Server that has active VMware Cloud Foundation entitlements.
Add a vCenter Entitlement Server
VCF Operations HCX provides an option to add a VCF 9.0 vCenter Server as a vCenter Entitlement Server in
environments where no registered vCenter Server has an active VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 license.
VCF Operations HCX automatically discovers the active VMware Cloud Foundation license entitlements from a registered
vCenter Server that is configured in VCF Operations HCX. If the registered vCenter Server does not have valid VMware
Cloud Foundation entitlements, VCF Operations HCX operates in Evaluation Mode with limited migration capability. In
some scenarios, such as evacuating a legacy data center, you might not want to update the vCenter license, but need the
extra migration capability provided by VCF Operations HCX with active VMware Cloud Foundation license entitlements.
In this case, you can associate VCF Operations HCX with a vCenter Server that has an active VMware Cloud Foundation
license.
VCF Operations HCX inherits the VMware Cloud Foundation license entitlements from the vCenter Entitlement Server,
enabling VCF Operations HCX with the full range of mobility features and services.
Note:
Adding a vCenter Entitlement Server provides license entitlement only. Inventory objects that are associated with
the vCenter Entitlement Server are not visible to VCF Operations HCX.
1. Log in to HCX Manager Appliance Management.
2. Navigate to the Configuration tab.
3. Select Licensing.
If the VCF Operations HCX license status is Evaluation Mode, the system provides the option to add a vCenter
Entitlement Server.
4. Click Add, and enter the vCenter Entitlement Server URL and credentials.
5. Click Save.
The license status is updated to Active, and VCF Operations HCX is updated for full mobility operations.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
NSX Requirements for VCF Operations HCX Deployments
In VCF Operations HCX installations connecting private environments, NSX must be installed and configured at the
destination before deploying VCF Operations HCX. This section details the requirements.
NSX Requirements for Deployments
For environments requiring NSX virtual networking, you must install and configure NSX, including integration with vCenter,
before deploying VCF Operations HCX.
• In the destination environment, the NSX Manager must be installed and integrated with vCenter. For a list of supported
NSX versions, see the VMware Product Interoperability Matrix.
• The NSX Manager must be registered during VCF Operations HCX installation with the admin user.
• If the NSX Manager IP or FQDN uses self-signed certificates, it might be necessary to trust the NSX system manually
using the Import Cert by URL interface in the HCX Appliance Management .
• VCF Operations HCX requires an NSX Manager registered with the same vCenter Server used to register with HCX
Manager.
• When NSX is registered, both Overlay and VLAN segments can be used during the network profile creation.
• Deployment of VCF Operations HCX in environments with multiple data centers that are prepared for NSX and a single
vCenter Server (sharing transport zones and datastores) is not supported.
Note:
The network extension service has additional NSX requirements. See Requirements for Network Extension.
NSX Requirements Source Site Installation
NSX is not required for VCF Operations HCX installation at the source site, but requirements apply if you are extending
NSX networks. When extending any source network, the destination site must be configured with NSX.
For more information, see NSX Requirements for Deployments.
Installing VCF Operations HCX
This section describes how to install and configure HCX Manager at the source or destination sites.
The source and destination sites work together to provide VCF Operations HCX services. VCF Operations HCX requires
installation of HCX Manager at both the source and destination sites.
Installation Workflow
A fully private VCF Operations HCX installation, where both the destination/modernized environment and the source/
existing environments must be considered involves the following steps.
1. Prepare for deployment as described in Preparing for General Installation
2. Download the VCF Operations HCX OVA. See Download the OVA.
3. Deploy VCF Operations HCX in both the source and destination environment using the VCF Operations HCX OVA.
See Deploy the OVA in the vSphere Client.
4. Configure firewall rules at source and destination sites to allow inbound and outbound connectivity based on the VCF
Operations HCX services or features used. See https://ports.broadcom.com/home/VMware-HCX.
5. Configure VCF Operations HCX at both the source and destination sites. See Configuring VCF Operations HCX
6. Pair source and destination sites. See Add a Site Pair.
7. Configure the network profile and compute profile for both the source and destination VCF Operations HCX
installations. See Configuring and Managing the Interconnect.
8. Configure VCF Operations HCX. See Configuring VCF Operations HCX.
9. Create the service mesh at the source site for the site pair. See Configuring and Managing the Interconnect.
Broadcom 6586

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
If you have VCF 9.0 and later installed and are deploying VMware Operations HCX using VCF Operations, see https://
techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/deployment/deploying-a-new-vmware-cloud-
foundation-or-vmware-vsphere-foundation-private-cloud-.html.
About OVAs
You use the same OVA file to deploy VCF Operations HCX at the source and destination sites.
For private cloud deployments, you download the OVAs from the Broadcom Support Portal. From the Downloads site, you
select the latest version of the VCF Operations HCX OVA.
In hosted environments, the provider may deploy and install VCF Operations HCX.
Download the OVA
The OVA file is used for deploying VCF Operations HCX.
Use the following procedure to download the VCF Operations HCX OVA.
1. Log in to .
https://support.broadcom.com
2. From the drop-down menu, select VMware Cloud Foundation.
3. In the navigation pane, select My Entitlements.
4. Expand your site and navigate to the VCF Operations HCX entitlement.
Under entitlement, the screen displays an option to download binaries.
5. Select a download option to display the list of bundles available for download.
6. Select a release, and download the OVA file.
Deploy the downloaded OVA in the vCenter instance.
Deploy the OVA in the vSphere Client
Use this procedure to deploy the downloaded VCF Operations HCX OVA using a standard OVA template installation
through the vSphere Client.
Use the downloaded OVA to install the latest version of VCF Operations HCX at the sites that will serve as the source and
destination of mobility operations.
Broadcom 6587

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the vSphere Client.
2. Right-click any inventory object that is a valid parent object of a virtual machine, such as a data center, folder, cluster,
resource pool, or host, and select Deploy OVF Template.
3. Enter a URL to download and install the OVF package from the Internet. Alternatively, browse to a location accessible
from your computer, such as a local hard drive or a network share for a local file, and click Next.
4. Enter a unique virtual machine name and the inventory location, and click Next.
5. Select a compute resource location, and click Next.
6. On the Review details page, verify the OVA template details, and click Next.
7. On the License agreements page, read and accept the VMware End User License Agreement, and click Next.
8. On the Select storage page, select the virtual disk format, storage policy, storage name, and then click Next.
9. On the Select networks page, select the destination network, and click Next.
10.On the Customize Template page, set the appropriate deployment properties:
• Passwords - Configure the CLI and Appliance Management admin password and the root user password.
• Network Properties - Enter the network properties such as IP address, netmask, and default gateway.
• Static Routes - Add a static route for a destination subnet or host.
• DNS
– DNS Server List - Enter the list of DNS servers for this virtual machine.
– Domain Search List - Domains that you enter are searched in the order you list them, and the search stops
when a valid name is found.
Note:
Add the .local subdomain in environments without multicast DNS correctly configured as in RFC-6762.
• Services Configuration
– NTP Server List - Enter the list of NTP servers and ensure that the NTP server can be reached from the virtual
machine. If the NTP time is out of sync, services fail to start.
Note:
During OVA deployment, use “space” or “comma” separation for multiple NTP/DNS/Domain Name servers.
11.Click Next.
12.Review the deployment settings and click Finish.
Allow up to 5 minutes for initialization, then log in to the Appliance Management for the initial configuration.
To complete the VCF Operations HCX installation, see Configuring VCF Operations HCX.
Support for NSX Federation
NSX Federation provides a centralized management plane that is known as an NSX Global Manager (GM) which provides
consistent networking across physical sites, and an NSX Local Manager (LM). The LM is a local NSX instance in each
data center that receives policies from the GM. This set-up is known as a federated NSX environment.
When you configure VCF Operations HCX, you register with an LM. Registration with a GM is not supported. However,
the NSX LM that you select during configuration can be registered to an NSX GM.
In federated NSX environments, the NSX GM populates the NSX LM with global network segments. In VCF Operations
HCX, these global segments have the following uses and restrictions:
• With network extension, such global networks cannot be extended.
• You can create network profiles using global segments. However, network profiles that are backed by global segments
can only be used in the compute profile for assignment as the Guest Network. They cannot be used to configure
Management, Uplink, vMotion, Replication Assisted vMotion services.
• You can perform a migration that uses global segments as the destination network.
Broadcom 6588

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
When the NSX LM is not registered to an NSX GM, Interconnect constructs such as network profiles, compute profiles,
and service meshes are created on local segments. If the NSX LM is registered at a later point with an NSX GM,
ownership of the segments transitions to the GM, effectively converting local segments to global segments. As a result:
• Backing for the network profile becomes inconsistent, affecting both the network profile and the compute profiles. This
inconsistency means that the only service mesh operation that can be performed on existing service meshes is service
mesh deletion.
• Established network extensions between sites continue to work, but you cannot extend a new network or cannot
enable/disable Mobility Optimized Networking (MON) for an already extended network. Also, the only operation that
you can perform on extended networks in a federated environment is Force Unextend.

After you have deployed the OVA file in the vSphere Client, perform the initial configuration immediately when you next
open HCX Manager Appliance Management.
• Deploy the OVA in the vSphere Client. Allow up to five minutes after the OVA deployment for the services to initialize.
• Configure firewall rules at source and destination sites to allow inbound and outbound connectivity based on the VCF
Operations HCX services or features used. See https://ports.broadcom.com/home/VMware-HCX.
During configuration, you register with NSX. You can only register an NSX Local Manager and not an NSX Global
Manager. You might find it useful to review how VCF Operations HCX supports NSX federation. See, Support for NSX
Federation
1. Log in to the Appliance Management using admin user credentials.
2. (Optional) If there is a proxy server in the environment in the path for outbound HTTPS connections, configure it now:
a) Select the Administration tab, and navigate to Network Settings > Proxy Configuration.
b) Click Edit.
c) Enter the proxy server information, including any exclusions.
Important:
Add the local vCenter, ESX, NSX, SSO, VCF SSO, and service mesh appliances as exceptions not to be sent to
the proxy server.
d) Make any required changes to the system settings specified when deploying VCF Operations HCX. These
changes can include NTP and DNS settings. For more information see, Deploy the OVA in the vSphere Client.
e) Select the Configuration tab to continue the activation procedure.
3. Enter the location where you are deploying the system.
Select the nearest major city to where the system is geographically located. VCF Operations HCX sites are
represented visually in the Dashboard.

5. Enter the system name, and click Continue.
6. Select the cloud instance to which to connect VCF Operations HCX . This is an extended network on the destination
site.
VCF Operations HCX can connect to only one cloud instance per deployment.
7. Click Continue, and enter the required information.

Configure VCF SSO
Configuring VCF Single Sign-on (SSO) provides login access to VCF Operations HCX using the VMware Identity Provider
credentials.
Prior to configuring VCF SSO, Admins must create an OAuth application in VCF Operations that specifies the Client ID
and Client Secret. To manage the identity source, go to the VMware Cloud Foundation Operations console. See, https://
techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-1/fleet-management/managing-identity-and-access-
using-vcf-single-sign-on/what-is/setting-up-sso/cofigure-vmware-cloud-foundation-identity-provider/configure-identity-
provider-for-okta/configure-the-identity-provider.html
VCF Operations HCX allows for two authentication methods: local and VCF SSO. By default, installing VCF Operations
HCX requires registration with vCenter. VCF Operations HCX uses vCenter for local authentication.
Optionally, you can configure VCF Operations HCX for login authentication using the VMware Identity Provider, which
provides single sign-on access for VCF Operations HCX and for other VCF components.
Note:
You can add or delete VCF SSO authentication at any time without affecting VCF Operations HCX or mobility
operations.
1. Log in to the Appliance Management.
2. Select the Configuration tab and navigate to VCF SSO.
3. Click Configure and enter the configuration details:
• Identity Broker Issuer (example):
https://<fqdn of VIDB>/acs/t/<tenant name>
• Client ID (fetched from VCF Operations Console)
• Client Secret (fetched from VCF Operations Console)
4. Click Test Connection to validate the inputs.
5. Click Save.
If prompted for the certificate, click Import Certificate.
6. To view the VCF SSO configuration, click the Dashboard tab and review the VCF SSO tile.
After configuring VCF SSO, you must assign or map Identity Provider User Groups to HCX Roles. To map these user
groups, see Configure HCX Role Mapping.
