Compliance Alerts
You use the compliance score card as an investigative tool when you evaluate the state of objects in your VCF platform,
or when you research the root cause of a problem. If the score card indicates a problem, you can view the alerts to see
details about the violation. Violated rules are based on the symptoms defined in the compliance alert.
Note:
Compliance Benchmarks are deprecated in VCF 9.1. Compliance is now managed by Security Posture
Management.
The compliance alerts, which have the subtype named Compliance, include one or more symptoms that represent the
compliance rules. Compliance alerts that are triggered appear in the Symptoms tab in an object when you navigate to
the Alerts tab in the Inventory section of VCF Operations. Compliance alerts appear as violations to the standard, and the
triggered symptoms appear as violated rules. The rules are the alert symptoms, and the symptom configuration identifies
the incorrect value or configuration. If a rule symptom is triggered for any of the alerts in the standard, the triggered rule
violates the standard and affects the score.
How To Configure Compliance Benchmarks
Configure VMware SDDC, VCF, Custom and Regulatory benchmarks from the Compliance page available when you
navigate to Protect > Compliance. Unlike previous releases, you can now enable alert definitions in one of the active
policies, from the Compliance page directly.
Note:
Compliance Benchmarks are deprecated in VCF 9.1 and is replaced by Security Posture Management.

included for assessment are ESX, SDDC Manager, vCenter, vSAN and NSX.

Security Posture Management
Security Posture Management is where you measure compliance of supported VCF components. It offers a centralized
portal for reviewing, investigating, and managing the compliance of supported VCF resources against established security
benchmarks. It automates benchmark assessments across multiple components and presents actionable data for
remediation.
Compliance Assessment and Reporting using Security Posture Management
Security Posture Management introduces a way to view, manage, and analyze compliance results of components in the
VCF platform within VCF Operations. A new unified data grid interface displays the benchmark details and compliance
score in a single view, so you do not have to navigate across multiple pages. You can now quickly locate non-compliant
controls, understand their context, and take corrective actions. The Security Posture Management functionality deprecates
the compliance functionality available in previous versions.
What Security Posture Management Offers
Viewing Results You can see the compliance results in a data grid. The data grid displays compliance and non-compliance
results together, enabling you to filter, sort, and search assessment data. The results are the outcome
of evaluating components against the benchmark, which is categorized as compliant, non-compliant, or
unknown.
For more information, see Compliance Assessment Results and Remeditation.
Rule Browsing and You can browse all benchmark rules that are associated with a compliance benchmark.
Management • You can add values to rules where site specific settings, such as DNS server, login banner, etc. can be
provided.
• You can preview each rule.
• You can tailor benchmark rules to align with specific organizational requirements.
For more information, see Working with Benchmark Rules.
Broadcom 6746

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Compliance The compliance dashboard displays compliance and non-compliance status at the granularity of the
assessment and Non- compliance control across all or a selected subset of the inventory, providing sufficient detail regarding the
compliant/non-compliant results. After running the assessement, you can view the compliance rules and
compliance remediation
compliance results for a designated compliance benchmark. You can run remediation on non-compliant
objects.
You can export assessment data and compliance results for external analysis and reporting purposes.
• Export assessment results in CSV format for further processing or archival.
• Generate compliance reports summarizing compliant and non-compliant items at the compliance control
level for all or selected inventory.
For more information, see Compliance Assessment Results and Remeditation.
What Security Posture Management Does
Compliance assessment is a core requirement for maintaining security, operational consistency, and regulatory adherence
in VCF environments. The automated controls that are introduced in this release provide automated assessments of the
native and custom benchmarks.
The main advantages are:
• Availability of out of the box benchmarks such as VMware Cloud Foundation Security Configuration and Hardening
Guide (SCG), PCI DSS v4.0.1 for VCF and VCF 9 General Controls.
• A complete view of compliant and non-compliant items at the control level as per the selected policy.
• Remediation of non-compliant objects for supported list of rules.
How Compliance Assessment using Security Posture Management Works
Security Posture Management covers the following components, reflecting their status per benchmark rules.
• SDDC Manager
• Virtual Machines
• VMware Avi Load Balancer
• VMware Cloud Foundation Automation
• VMware Cloud Foundation Managed Service
• VMware Cloud Foundation Operations
• VMware Cloud Foundation Operations for networks
• VMware Cloud Foundation Operations Orchestrator
• VMware Cloud Proxy
• VMware ESX
• VMware HCX
• VMware NSX
• VMware NSX Edge
• VMware vCenter Server
VCF Operations measures compliance in the following way:
1. You enable a compliance benchmark by selecting a relevant policy. The assessment will run against all supported VCF
objects associated with the policy linked to that benchmark. For more information on policies in see Policies.
2. VCF Operations assesses the environment against the controls that are defined in the selected benchmark.
3. You can see the following assessment results:
– Which rules are non-compliant and compliant. A third state called Unknown is for those objects whose compliance
cannot be acertained.
– The associated inventory objects for each rule.
– The current parameter values contributing to the assessment outcome.
4. You can filter or export the results.
You perform remediation by following these steps:
1. You run the assessment to measure compliance against a particular benchmark.
Broadcom 6747

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. You view the compliance results.
3. You select the rules for which remediation is available. You can perform bulk remediation across all non-compliant
rules or apply specific rules to a targeted selection of non-compliant objects.
4. You run the remediation.

options are available:

Compliance Assessment Schedule that you set in the Global Settings page. For more information, see List of Global
Settings.

Running an Assessment
Assessments are run as per the Compliance Assessment Schedule that you set in the Global Settings page. Or, you can
run an assessment on demand. Parallel assessments cannot be run on a same benchmarks. However, assessments can
be run across different benchmarks at the same time.
1. In the VCF Operations navigation bar at the top, click Protect and in the left navigation pane, click Security Posture
Management.
2. Click the vertical ellipses against a benchmark and select Run Assessment.
3. Alternatively, click the benchmark rule and go to the View Control Set tab in the rule page. Click RUN ASSESSMENT.
4. The results of the assessment are available in the View Result tab after the assessment is completed. You can view
the results by navigating to the compliance score link from the benchmark grid or navigating to the benchmark.
Compliance Assessment Results and Remeditation
The assessment results page includes the current parameter value for each control. This helps users understand exactly
which configuration values contributed to the result. Configuration value for compliant objects are displayed as N/A. You
can export the assessment results CSV and PDF formats for audit and reporting.

Audit Records and Audit Trail
The Audit Records page provides a centralized location where you can examine the diverse audit records that are
generated across the supported VCF components. Each audit record has information which helps you analyze the user
actions in your VCF environment.
Broadcom 6751

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Your organization may be required to provide audit data to support both internal and external audit reviews. Audit cycles
are shortened by audit records, because data is collected from various components, and presented in a unified interface.
For the supported audit records, see Audit Record Coverage.
Using Audit Trail, you can get complete traceability of the supported user actions in the VCF environment, so that any
suspicious or unauthorized activity can be dealt with in a timely manner.
Viewing Audit Records
Audit records help you track user actions and changes (including security and compliance related modifications) to ensure
operational robustness and traceability in your VCF environment. Use the Audit Records page in VCF Operations to
review, filter, and export logged actions that are performed by users on various VCF components. You can also establish
lateral movement from one VCF component to another. The page supports searching within a selected time range and
offers filtering capabilities by severity, result, component, object, and more.
Supported VCF Components for Audit Records
The following VCF components use standardized audit records:
• ESX
• NSX
• VMware Management Services Platform
• VCF Operations
• vCenter
• VCF Operations for networks
• Identity Broker
• VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service
• log management
Prerequisites for Viewing Audit Records
You must configure Log collection from the supported VCF components to see audit records. Audit records and audit trail
are only available to the user with certain roles. For more information, see Roles and Privileges in VCF Operations.
To configure the Log collection, see, Managing Collection from Log Sources. Click the Check Log Collection Status link
in the Audit Records page to check if the supported VCF components are configured for log collection.
The Audit Records Page
The Audit Records page in VCF Operations is where you review detailed audit records that are generated by supported
VCF components. Each record provides insights into user activities, helping you analyze actions that are performed within
your VCF environment.
Where You Find Audit Records
After you log in to VCF Operations, from the navigation bar at the top, click Protect and in the left navigation pane, click
Audit Records. A list of audit records is displayed in a table in the right pane on the page for a given time range. You can
change the time range and filter the audit records by using the filters on the left pane. Click a record entry in the right pane
to see more details.

vSphere Supervisor Concepts
Learn the key concepts and architecture of vSphere Supervisor.
vSphere Supervisor Concepts
vSphere Supervisor is a control plane that is built in vSphere that integrates desired state and a single consistent API
directly in the hypervisor. vSphere Supervisor enables native deployment and management of Kubernetes clusters,
declarative virtual machines, and vSphere Pods alongside traditional workloads in VCF. It transforms vSphere into an
extendable platform by providing a declarative API for self-service provisioning of modern infrastructure services in a
resource boundaries enabled by vSphere Namespaces.
What Is vSphere Supervisor?
You can use vSphere Supervisor to enable a consistent declarative API in VCF and a platform for building a modern
cloud experience with VCF Automation. vSphere Supervisor is a workload domain capability that you can activate during
the workload domain creation or separately through the vSphere Client. When activated on vSphere clusters, vSphere
Supervisor provides self-service cloud consumption capabilities for running and managing workloads, including upstream
Kubernetes clusters, virtual machines, and vSphere Pods . The resource boundaries where workloads run in a vSphere
Supervisor are called vSphere Namespaces.
Broadcom 6755

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Challenges of Today's Application Stack
Today's distributed systems are constructed of multiple microservices usually running a large number of Kubernetes
pods and virtual machines. A typical stack that is not based on vSphere Supervisor consists of an underlying virtual
environment, with Kubernetes infrastructure that is deployed inside VMs and Kubernetes pods also running in these VMs.
There are three separate operational roles to administer each part of the stack, application developers, Kubernetes cluster
administrators, and vSphere or Cloud administrators.
Figure 490: Today's Application Stack
The different roles do not have visibility or control over each other's environments:
• As an application developer, you can run Kubernetes pods, and deploy and manage Kubernetes based applications.
You do not have visibility over the entire stack that is running hundreds of applications.
• As a DevOps engineer or cluster admin, you only have control over the Kubernetes infrastructure, without the tools to
manage or monitor the virtual environment and resolve any resource-related and other problems.
• As a vSphere or Cloud administrator, you have full control over the underlying virtual environment, but you do not
have visibility over the Kubernetes infrastructure, the placement of the different Kubernetes objects in the virtual
environment, and how they consume resources.
Operations on the full stack can be challenging, because they require communication between all three roles. The lack
of integration between the different layers of the stack can also introduce challenges. For example, the Kubernetes
scheduler does not have visibility over the vCenter inventory and it cannot place pods intelligently.
How Does vSphere Supervisor Help?
vSphere Supervisor provides a declarative API and desired state by deploying a Kubernetes control plane directly on
vSphere clusters. As a VI administrator, you activate existing vSphere clusters for vSphere Supervisor, thus creating a
Kubernetes layer within the clusters.

Having a Kubernetes control plane on the vSphere clusters enables the following capabilities in vSphere:
• As a VI administrator, you can create namespaces on the Supervisor, called vSphere Namespaces, and configure
them with specified amount of memory, CPU, and storage. You create user assignments to vSphere Namespaces for
DevOps engineers.
• As a DevOps engineer, you can run workloads on the same platform with shared resource pools within a vSphere
Namespace. You can deploy and manage multiple upstream Kubernetes clusters created by using vSphere
Kubernetes Service. You can also deploy Kubernetes containers directly on the Supervisor inside a special type of VM
called vSphere Pod. You can also deploy regular VMs.
• As a DevOps engineer, you can use VCF Automation to deploy and manage workloads on the Supervisor, when it is
deployed with full on-premises cloud experience using the NSX VPC networking stack.
• As a VI administrator, you can manage and monitor vSphere Pods, VMs, and VKS clusters using the vSphere Client.
• As a Platform operator, you can leverage the capabilities in VCF Operations to monitor the workloads deployed in the
Supervisor instances in the VCF fleet.
• As a VI administrator, you have full visibility over vSphere Pods, VMs, and VKS clusters running within different
namespaces, their placement in the environment, and how they consume resources.
Having Kubernetes running on vSphere clusters also eases the collaboration between VI administrators and DevOps
teams, because both roles are working with the same objects.
What Is a Workload?
In vSphere Supervisor, workloads are applications that are deployed in one of the following ways:
• Applications that consist of containers running inside vSphere Pods.
• Virtual Machines provisioned through the VM service.
• Kubernetes clusters deployed by using vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS)
• Application pods that run inside VKS clusters.
What are vSphere Zones?
vSphere Zones protect against cluster-level failure by providing high-availability to workloads deployed on vSphere
Supervisor. As a VI administrator, you create vSphere Zones in the vSphere Client and then map vSphere clusters to
Broadcom 6757

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
zones. You can dynamically add and remove vSphere Clusters from vSphere Zones in case you must scale up or down
the resources in a zone.
You can use zones to provide isolation between the management plane and workloads in the Supervisor in the following
way:
• Deploy the Supervisor on one or three vSphere Zones, which you reserve for running the Supervisor control plane.
These zones are marked as management in the vSphere Client. Deploying the Supervisor on three vSphere Zones
spreads the control plane VMs across these three zones, which provide cluster-level high availability to the Supervisor
control plane. Deploying the Supervisor on a single vSphere Zone only provides host level high availability. For more
information, see Supervisor Architecture and Deployment Options.
• Assign vSphere Zones to vSphere Namespaces and use them for running workloads only. You can have multiple
vSphere Clusters assigned to a zone.
For more information about the Supervisor architectural options with vSphere Zones and different deployment designs in
VCF, see vSphere Supervisor Models and vSphere Supervisor Detailed Design.
What Is vSphere Kubernetes Service or VKS Cluster?
You can use the vSphere Kubernetes Service to deploy upstream Kubernetes clusters on vSphere Supervisor.
Kubernetes clusters deployed by the vSphere Supervisor service are also called VKS clusters. A VKS cluster is a full
distribution of Kubernetes that is built, signed, and supported by VMware by Broadcom.
A VKS cluster has the following characteristics:
Figure 492: VKS characteristics
A vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) cluster is:
Opinionated Well- Production - Fully-supported Managed by
integrated ready Kubernetes
• Opinionated installation of Kubernetes. vSphere Kubernetes Service provides well-thought-out defaults that are
optimized for vSphere to provision VKS clusters. By using vSphere Kubernetes Service, you can reduce the amount of
time and effort that you typically spend deploying and running an enterprise-grade Kubernetes cluster.
• Integrated with the VCF and vSphere Infrastructure. A VKS cluster is integrated with the VCF SDDC stack, including
storage, networking, and authentication. In addition, a VKS cluster is built on a Supervisor that maps to vSphere
clusters. Because of the tight integration, running a VKS cluster is a unified product experience.
• Production Ready. VKS provisions production-ready VKS clusters. You can run production workloads any additional
configuration. In addition, you can ensure availability and support rolling Kubernetes software upgrades and run
different versions of Kubernetes in separate clusters.
• High-availability for Kubernetes workloads. VKS clusters deployed on more than one vSphere Zones reserved for
workloads are protected against failure on vSphere cluster level. The workload and control plane nodes of VKS
Broadcom 6758

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
clusters are distributed across all vSphere Zones, which makes the Kubernetes workloads running inside them highly
available. VKS clusters running on one vSphere Zone are protected against failure at ESX host level, through vSphere
HA.
• Fully Supported by VMware by Broadcom. VKS clusters use open source based Linux., are deployed on VCF
infrastructure, and run on ESX hosts. If you experience problems with any layer of the stack, from the hypervisor to the
Kubernetes cluster, VMware is the only vendor you need to contact.
• Managed by Kubernetes. VKS clusters are built on top of the Supervisor, which itself is a Kubernetes cluster. A VKS
cluster is defined in the vSphere Namespace using a custom resource. You provision VKS clusters in a self-service
way using familiar kubectl commands and the VCF CLI. There is consistency across the toolchain, whether you are
provisioning a cluster or deploying workloads, you use the same commands, familiar YAML, and common workflows.
For more information see vSphere Kubernetes Service and Components.
What Is a vSphere Pod?
vSphere Supervisor introduces a construct that is called vSphere Pod, which is the equivalent of a Kubernetes pod. A
vSphere Pod is a VM with a small footprint that runs one or more Linux containers. Each vSphere Pod is sized precisely
for the workload that it accommodates and has explicit resource reservations for that workload. It allocates the exact
amount of storage, memory, and CPU resources required for the workload to run. vSphere Pods are only supported with
Supervisors that are configured with NSX as the networking stack.
Figure 493: vSphere Pods
ESX Host
vSphere Pod vSphere Pod
Container
Container
Container
Linux Kernel Linux Kernel
CPU Memory Storage CPU Memory Storage
vSphere Pods are objects in vCenter and enable the following capabilities for workloads:
• Strong isolation. A vSphere Pod is isolated in the same manner as a virtual machine. Each vSphere Pod has its own
unique Linux kernel that is based on the kernel used in Photon OS. Rather than many containers sharing a kernel, as
in a bare metal configuration, in a vSphere Pod, each container has a unique Linux kernel
• Resource Management. vSphere Distributed Resource Schedular (DRS) handles the placement of vSphere Pods on
the Supervisor.
• High performance. vSphere Pods get the same level of resource isolation as VMs, eliminating noisy neighbor problems
while maintaining the fast start-up time and low overhead of containers.
• Diagnostics. As a VI administrator you can use all the monitoring and introspection tools that are available with
vSphere on workloads.
vSphere Pods are Open Container Initiative (OCI) compatible and can run containers from any operating system as long
as these containers are also OCI compatible.
Broadcom 6759

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 494: vSphere Pod Networking and Storage
vSphere Pods use three types of storage depending on the objects that are stored, that are ephemeral VMDKs, persistent
volume VMDKs, and containers image VMDKs. As a VI administrator, you configure storage policies for placement of
container image cache and ephemeral VMDKs on the Supervisor level. On a vSphere Namespace level, you configure
storage policies for placement of persistent volumes. See Storage Policies for Supervisor and VKS Clusters for details
about the storage requirements and concepts with vSphere Supervisor.
For networking, vSphere Pods and the VMs of the VKS clusters use the topology provided by NSX. For details, see
Supervisor Networking.
Spherelet is an additional process that is created on each host. It is a kubelet that is ported natively to ESX and allows the
ESX host to become part of the Kubernetes cluster.
For information about using vSphere Pods on Supervisors, see Deploying Workloads to vSphere Pods.
Using Virtual Machines in vSphere Supervisor
vSphere Supervisor offers a VM Service functionality that enables DevOps engineers to deploy and run VMs in a
declarative manner, in addition to containers, in a common, shared Kubernetes environment. Both, containers and VMs,
share the same vSphere Namespace resources and can be managed through a single vSphere Supervisor interface.
The VM Service addresses the needs of DevOps teams that use Kubernetes, but have existing VM-based workloads that
cannot be easily containerized. It also helps users reduce the overhead of managing a non-Kubernetes platform alongside
a container platform. When running containers and VMs on a Kubernetes platform, DevOps teams can consolidate their
workload footprint to just one platform.
Note:
In addition to stand-alone VMs, the VM Service manages the VMs that make up VKS clusters.

Each VM deployed through the VM Service functions as a complete machine running all the components, including its
own operating system, on top of the vSphere Supervisor infrastructure. The VM has access to networking and storage
that a Supervisor provides, and is managed using the standard Kubernetes command. The VM runs as a fully
kubectl
isolated system that is immune to interference from other VMs or workloads in the Kubernetes environment.
When to Use Virtual Machines on a Kubernetes Platform?
Generally, a decision to run workloads in a container or in a VM depends on your business needs and goals. Among the
reasons to use VMs are the following:
• Your applications cannot be containerized.
• Applications are designed for a custom kernel or custom operating system.
• Applications are better suited to running in a VM.
• You want a consistent Kubernetes experience and avoid overhead. Rather than running separate sets of infrastructure
for your non-Kubernetes and container platforms, you can consolidate these stacks and manage them with a familiar
command.
kubectl
• Running VMs that are deployed and managed by VCF Automation within the All Applications Organization setup.
For information about deploying and managing stand-alone virtual machines in a Supervisor, see Deploying and
Managing Virtual Machines.
Supervisor Services in vSphere Supervisor
Supervisor Services are vSphere certified Kubernetes operators that deliver Infrastructure-as-a-Service components
and tightly-integrated Independent Software Vendor services to developers. You can install and manage Supervisor
Services on the vSphere Supervisor environment so that to make them available for use with Kubernetes workloads.
When Supervisor Services are installed on Supervisors, DevOps engineers can use the service APIs to create instances
on Supervisors in their user namespaces. These instances can then be consumed in vSphere Pods and VKS clusters.

Learn more about the supported Supervisor Services and how to download their service YAML files at http://vmware.com/
go/supervisor-service.
For information about how to use Supervisor Services, see Managing Supervisor Services.
What is a vSphere Namespace?
A vSphere Namespace sets the resource boundaries where vSphere Pods, VMs, and VKS clusters, and Supervisor
Services can run. As a VI administrator, you create and configure vSphere Namespaces through the vSphere Client. As
an Organization administrator, you createvSphere Namespaces through VCF Automation
When initially created, a vSphere Namespace has unlimited resources within the Supervisor. As a VI administrator,
you can set limits for CPU, memory, storage, and the number of Kubernetes objects that can run within the vSphere
Namespace. Storage limitations are represented as storage quotas in Kubernetes. A resource pool is created in vSphere
per each vSphere Namespace on the Supervisor
You can map up to three vSphere Zones to a vSphere Namespace for running workloads on them. If a vSphere Zone has
more than one vSphere cluster associated with it, the Supervisor selects a specific cluster in the vSphere Zone to run the
workloads that are associated with the vSphere Namespace:
• The Supervisor filters the vSphere clusters in the zones that are mapped to the vSphere Namespace based on their
resource availability and datastore assignments. The datastore connectedto the vSphere clusters must match the
storage policy assigned the vSphere Namespace.
• After the Supervisor filters the vSphere clusters in the vSphere Zones, it places the vSphere Namespace to the
clusters that meet the requirements for resources reservations and assigned datastores.
Note:
Only one cluster per vSphere Zone can host workloads of a vSphere Namespace that spans acrross several
zones.
The resources utilized in a vSphere Namespace are taken from all the underlying vSphere clusters where the vSphere
Namespace is placed with the vSphere Zone on equal parts. For example, if you dedicate 300 MHz of CPU, 100 MHz are
taken from each vSphere cluster.
To provide workload isolation, you should use vSphere Zones marked as management only for running the Supervisor
control plane on these zones.

To provide access to vSphere Namespaces to a DevOps engineer, as a VI administrator, you assign permissions to
users or user groups available within an identity source that is associated with vCenter Single Sign-On or from an OIDC
provider that is registered with the Supervisor. For more information, see Understanding Authentication and Authorization
in vSphere Supervisor.
After a vSphere Namespace is created and configured with resource and object limits as well as with permissions and
storage policies, as a DevOps engineer, you can access the vSphere Namespace to run workloads such as VKS clusters,
vSphere Pods ,and VMs created through the VM service.
Differences Between a vSphere Namespace and Kubernetes Namespace
Although in its core a vSphere Namespace serves the same function as a Kubernetes namespace, a vSphere
Namespace is specific to the vSphere Supervisor. You should not confuse a vSphere Namespace with a Kubernetes
namespace.
A vSphere Namespace is implemented as an extension to a vSphere resource pool and its function is to provide
resources to workloads running in the Supervisor. A vSphere Namespace has a direct mapping to a Kubernetes
namespace through which object and storage quotas are enforced upon workloads.
Another difference with a regular Kubernetes namespace is that the VI administrator manages the user access to vSphere
Namespaces, as mentioned from above. The VI administrator can also associate VM classes and Content Libraries
containing VM templates that DevOps engineers can use to self-service VMs. For more information, see Deploying and
Managing Virtual Machines in vSphere Supervisor.
vSphere Supervisor Inventory
The vSphere Supervisor inventory is a representation of the Supervisor folder and its associated resources.
vSphere configures separate Supervisor folders for each Supervisor and all the associated resources. The vSphere
Namespaces and control plane VMs are mapped under the respective Supervisor folder isolating them from the resources
of other Supervisors, even though names of namespaces must be unique within vCenter.
The vSphere Pods within each namespace are segregated into a folder called vSphere Pods. This ensures their isolation
from other VMs and VKS clusters that are in the same namespace and allows distinct and precise privilege allocation.

Starting with VCF 9.0, every newly deployed Supervisor is represented by a dedicated Supervisor folder under the
Folders tab. The Supervisor folders are created under the Namespaces folder which is the root folder for workload
management. This Namespaces folder represents the resource pool for CPU/memory allocation for the vSphere
Namespaces created under it. The control plane VMs for the cluster are placed within this folder as shown in the
screenshot below. User-created namespaces appear as child folders within the Supervisor folder. Each Namespace
folder includes all workload entities created under it, such as VMs deployed through VM Service and VKS clusters.
Additionally, each Namespace folder contains a subfolder named vSpherePods which contains all the vSphere Pods
associated with the Namespace. Since Pod VMs primarily serve infrastructure purposes, the vSpherePods folder is
configured with restrictive permissions to prevent users from performing any direct operations on the pods.
For environments upgrading to VCF 9.0 from earlier versions, the existing Supervisor folder structure remains
unchanged. The new folder hierarchy is applied only when the Supervisor is upgraded to version 9.0.

Understanding Authentication and Authorization in vSphere Supervisor
Authentication controls who can access to the vSphere environment and authorization controls what resources the users
can access.
Authentication and authorization govern access to your vSphere environment. vCenter Single Sign-On supports
authentication, which means it determines whether a user can log in to vSphere components at all. Each user must also
be authorized to view or manipulate vSphere objects.
vCenter allows fine-grained control over authorization with permissions and roles. When you grant a permission to an
object in the vCenter object hierarchy, you associate a role to a user or group on that object. To specify the privileges, you
use roles, which are sets of privileges.
Broadcom 6767

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For more information on authorization in vSphere, see https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=vsphclient_048&appid=vsphere-9-1&language=&format=rendered.
Authenticating to Supervisor using vCenter Single Sign-On or External Identity Provider
vCenter Single Sign-On is an authentication broker and security token exchange infrastructure. vCenter Single Sign-On
issues a token when a principal, such as a user, group, or service account, authenticates. The principal can use the token
to authenticate to vCenter services. The principal can then perform the actions that the principal has privileges for.
A user or group with the necessary privileges can be authenticated through vCenter Single Sign-On or an external identity
provider (IdP) integrated with the Supervisor, such as Okta or Azure AD and can access the vSphere Namespace using
VCF CLI. For information on how on register external IdP with Supervisor, see Register an External Identity Provider with
Supervisor.
When you log in to the Supervisor using VCF CLI, the authentication proxy forwards your request to vCenter Single
Sign-On if the Supervisor has not been configured with an external IdP. The VCF CLI then initiates a session with
vCenter, obtains an authentication token, and retrieves the list of vSphere Namespaces you have access to and updates
the kubeconfig accordingly. For more information, see https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=vks-2&appid=sv-async&language=&format=rendered.
If you use an external identity provider (IdP), the Pinniped Supervisor and Concierge components facilitate federated
authentication for users and groups. Any changes to your account permissions are reflected the next time you log in, and
the list of accessible vSphere Namespaces is refreshed.
The VCF CLI command for logging in to vSphere Namespace is below. After logging in, you can set context to the
vSphere Namespaces the user has privileges on and then run commands on the Supervisor.
kubectl
VCF CLI command
export SUPERVISOR_ENDPOINT=<supervisor cluster IP address or FQDN>
to connect with
Supervisor for SSO or
vcf context create <context_name> --endpoint=<SUPERVISOR_ENDPOINT> --type=k8s --
external IdP user
username=<user_name>

How Permissions Work in Supervisor
The permission model for Supervisor relies on assigning permissions to objects in the object hierarchy.
Users get permissions to Supervisor in the following ways.
• From a specific permission for the user or from the groups that the user is a member of.
• From a permission on the object.
Permissions give a specific role to a user or group, granting them corresponding privileges on selected inventory objects.
You can use the vSphere Client to add permissions. That role gives those users the corresponding privileges on the
objects in the vCenter inventory.
Object-Level Permission Model
The following define the permission model:
• Permissions - Each object in the vCenter object hierarchy has associated permissions. Each permission defines the
privileges that a specific group or user has on the object. Permissions can propagate to child objects.
• Users and Groups - On vCenter systems, you can assign privileges only to authenticated users or groups of
authenticated users. Users are authenticated through vCenter Single Sign-On. Users and groups must be defined in
the identity source that vCenter Single Sign-On uses to authenticate. Define users and groups using the tools in your
identity source, for example, Active Directory.
• Privileges - Privileges are fine-grained access controls. You can group those privileges into roles, which you can then
map to users or groups.
• Roles - Roles are sets of privileges. Roles allow you to assign permissions on an object based on a typical set of tasks
that users perform. System roles, such as Administrator, are predefined on vCenter and cannot be changed. vCenter
also provides some default sample roles, such as Resource Pool Administrator, that you can modify. You can create
custom roles either from scratch or by cloning and modifying sample roles. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/
gethidpage?ux-context-string=vsphclient_045&appid=vsphere-9-1&language=&format=rendered.
For more information, https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=vsphclient_046&appid=vsphere-9-1&language=&format=rendered.
vCenter Roles for the vSphere Namespaces
VCF 9.0 introduces a new role called Supervisor Administrator. The Supervisor Administrator role is granted by default to
members of the Administrators group on the vSphere Namespace resource pool and folder in newly deployed Supervisors
instead of the Read-only role in the prior versions.
Based on the vCenter role assigned within the Supervisor inventory, a user or group can be assigned one of the following
roles:
Administrator Role As a VI administrator, you can view and manage the vSphere infrastructure, including VKS clusters,
vSphere Pods, and VM service VMs.
The VI administrator has the membership of the "Administrators SSO Group".
This Administrators group is automatically assigned the Supervisor Administrator role on the Supervisor
hierarchy.
Supervisor A Supervisor Administrator role can only be assigned on the Supervisor folder.
Administrator Role
You will be able to view the namespaces inventory only after assigning it the Read-only role on the
Cluster.
When the Supervisor Administrator role is assigned on the Supervisor folder, a context is created that
gives access only to cluster level resources in the Supervisor and not the vSphere Namespace. That is,
you cannot list or view vSphere Namespaces. To be able to view vSphere Namespaces when you log in

How Does vSphere Supervisor Change the VCF Environment?
A Supervisor adds objects to the vCenter inventory, such as namespaces, vSphere Pods, and VKS clusters, and VMs.
Under each Supervisor, you can view:
Broadcom 6776

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• vSphere Namespaces that represent logical grouping of resources running in the Supervisor.
• Resource pools for each vSphere Namespace on the Supervisor. In a multi-zone deployment, a resource pool for each
vSphere Namespace is created on each vSphere compute cluster part of a vSphere Zone. When a vSphere Zone
has multiple compute clusters that are associated with it, a vSphere Namespace is placed on the clusters that best
fit the resource and datastore requirements of the nameapce. See What are vSphere Zones?For review regarding
VGL-43945 - Supervisor on wide range of topologies
Within every namespace, you can view:
• vSphere Pods.
• vSphere Pods of Supervisor Services and other objects that are brought by Supervisor Services.
• VKS clusters.
• Stand-alone VMs created by using the VM service.
• Supervisor control plane VMs found in the system namespace.
• User permissions for that namespace.
Licensing for vSphere Supervisor
Starting with vSphere 9, product components are licensed automatically after you license the vCenter instance connected
to the component. You no longer license vSphere Supervisor independently. For more information, see Licensing
Overview in the Licensing guide.
vSphere Supervisor Security
vSphere Supervisor leverages vSphere security features and provisions VKS clusters that are secure by default.
vSphere Supervisor is an extension to vSphere that is able to leverage the security features that are built into vCenter and
ESX. For more information, see the vSphere Security documentation.
The Supervisor encrypts all secrets stored in the database (etcd). The secrets are encrypted via a local encryption key
file, which is provided at boot by vCenter. The decryption key is stored in memory (tempfs) on the Supervisor nodes and
on disk in encrypted form within vCenter database. The key is available in clear text to the root users of each system.
Secrets held within the database of each workload cluster are stored in clear text. All etcd connections are authenticated
with certificates that are generated at installation and rotated during upgrades. The same encryption model applies to the
data in the database (etcd) that is installed on the control plane for each VKS cluster.
In Supervisor, you can run confidential vSphere Pods on compatible systems. You can create confidential vSphere Pods
by adding Secure Encrypted Virtualization-Encrypted State (SEV-ES) as a security enhancement. For more information,
see Deploy a Confidential vSphere Pod.
A VKS cluster is secure by default. Restrictive Pod Security Admission (PSA) and PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) are available
for VKS clusters. If developers need to run privileged pods or root containers, at a minimum a cluster administrator must
create a RoleBinding that grants user access to the default privileged PSP. For more information, see Security for VKS
Clusters.
A VKS cluster does not have infrastructure credentials. The credentials that are stored within a VKS cluster are only
sufficient to access the vSphere Namespace where the VKS cluster has tenancy. As a result, there is no privilege
escalation avenue for cluster operators or users.
The authentication token used to access a VKS cluster is scoped such that the token cannot be used to access the
Supervisor or other VKS clusters. This prevents cluster operators, or individuals who might try to compromise a cluster,
from using their root-level access to capture a VI administrator's token when they log in to a VKS cluster.
How Supervisor Artifacts are Delivered and Consumed in a VCF Environment
In VCF 9.1 online deployments, vSphere Supervisor and related components use a unified artifact delivery model. After
VCF is deployed, Supervisor artifacts are no longer pulled directly from public repositories. Instead, compatible artifacts
are downloaded automatically from the online VCF Unified Depots to a local Software Depot and consumed from there.
This model applies to all components related to Supervisor, including:
Broadcom 6777

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• vSphere Supervisor
• vSphere Kubernetes release (VKr)
• Supervisor Services
• vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS ) add-ons
• VCF CLI and CLI plugins
Note:
Offline deployments in VCF 9.1 continue to use existing workflows.
Artifact Delivery Overview
In VCF 9.1 online deployments, the Software Depot performs these actions:
• Acts as a proxy for artifact download requests to online depots.
• Handles authentication and authorization to the online depots.
• Might cache downloaded artifacts locally for a period of time.
No manual configuration of external repositories or registries is required.
Artifact Consumption by Component Type
• Non-OCI artifacts, for example, OVF templates used by Supervisor and VKr, are consumed through vCenter Content
Library by subscribing to the endpoint of the local Software Depot.
Another example is VCF CLI, which is downloaded by proxying through the local Software Depot on the Supervisor
landing page.
• OCI artifacts used by Supervisor Services, VKS add-ons, and CLI plugins are pulled from a regional Harbor registry.
The regional Harbor registry is configured as a proxy cache to the local Software Depot.
This model ensures consistent, validated, and protected access to artifacts across Supervisors and clusters.
Asynchronous Releases
Supervisor components can be released asynchronously, outside of the main VCF release cycle. When an installation
or upgrade workflow requires an asynchronous release artifact, the workflow can request the artifact through the local
Software Depot.
VMware vSphere Foundation Deployments
In VVF 9.1 deployments, refer to the Software Depot documentation for VVF deployments for details about required
configuration and workflow differences.
vSphere Supervisor Architecture and Components
vSphere Supervisor provides a platform for running workloads in a declarative fashion by enabling a Kubernetes control
plane in vSphere. You can deploy the Supervisor on one vSphere cluster mapped to a vSphere Zone, or three vSphere
Clusters mapped to vSphere Zones. You can also select to deploy one Supervisor control plane VM or three control plane
VMs for high availability.
Supervisor Architecture and Deployment Options
When you activate a Supervisor on vSphere Zones, a Kubernetes control plane is created. This control plane enables the
capability to run workloads in a declarative fashion on vSphere clusters.
Figure 504: Supervisor General Architecture
The diagram shows the vSphere Supervisor high-level architecture, with vSphere Kubernetes Service on top, the
Supervisor in the middle, then ESX hosts, networking, and storage at the bottom, and vCenter managing them.
Broadcom 6778

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSphere
vSphere Kubernetes Service
vSphere Supervisor vCenter
DevOps vSphere
Admin
Compute Networking Storage
A Supervisor runs on top of an SDDC layer that consists of ESX for compute, NSX or vSphere Distributed Switch
networking, and vSAN or another shared storage solution. Shared storage is used for persistent volumes for vSphere
Pods and VMs running inside the Supervisor, and pods in a VKS cluster. After a Supervisor is created, as a vSphere
administrator you can create vSphere Namespaces within the Supervisor. As a DevOps engineer, you can run workloads
consisting of containers running inside vSphere Pods, deploy VMs through the VM service, and create VKS clusters.
Supervisor Components
The Supervisor has the following components:
• Supervisor control plane VM. You can select to deploy the Supervisor with either one or three control plane VMs. For
control plane HA, three VMs are recommended. The three Supervisor control plane VMs are load balanced as each
one of them has its own IP address. Additionally, a floating IP address is assigned to one of the VMs and a 5th IP
address is reserved for patching purposes. vSphere DRS determines the exact placement of the control plane VMs on
the ESX hosts part of the Supervisor and migrates them when needed.
• VKS and Cluster API. Modules running on the Supervisor and enable the provisioning and management of VKS
clusters.
• Virtual Machine Service. A module that is responsible for deploying and running stand-alone VMs and VMs that make
up VKS clusters.
• Spherelet. An additional process called Spherelet is created on each host. It is a kubelet that is ported natively to ESX
and allows the ESX host to become part of the Kubernetes cluster.
• Container Runtime Executive (CRX) component. CRX is similar to a VM from the perspective of Hostd and vCenter.
CRX includes a paravirtualized Linux kernel that works together with the hypervisor. CRX uses the same hardware
virtualization techniques as VMs and it has a VM boundary around it. A direct boot technique is used, which allows the
Linux guest of CRX to initiate the main init process without passing through kernel initialization. This allows vSphere
Pods to boot nearly as fast as containers.
Workload and Management Isolation
You can deploy a Supervisor on three vSphere Zones, that become marked for management and host the Supervisor
control plane. In a three-zone deployment, all three vSphere clusters mapped to the vSphere Zones become one
Supervisor. A three-zone deployment provides cluster-level high-availability that protects the control plane VMs against
a single cluster-level failure. Each control pane VM is placed in a different vSphere Zone. A vSphere Zone maps to one
vSphere cluster that you can setup as an independent failure domain. The resources utilized to a vSphere Namespace on
a three-zone Supervisor are taken from all three underlying vSphere clusters on equal parts. For example, if you dedicate
300 MHz of CPU, 100 MHz are taken from each vSphere cluster.
To provide isolation between the management components and workloads running on the Supervisor, you can reserve
the vSphere Zones where the Supervisor control plane VMs are deployed as a management plane only. Respectively, you
can assign different vSphere Zones to vSphere Namespaces and use them for running workloads. A vSphere Namespace
requires at least one vSphere Zone, and you can configure up to three vSphere Zones to a vSphere Namespace.
On single-zone deployment, as Supervisor control plane VMs run on a single vSphere Cluster, providing cluster-level HA.

Supervisor Networking
A Supervisor can either use a vSphere networking stack or NSX to provide connectivity to Supervisor control plane VMs,
services, and workloads.
Depending on your requirements, you can configure a networking stack and load balancer to provide connectivity to
external services and DevOps users.
The table summarizes the different networking stacks and load balancers that you can configure for your Supervisor
environment.

Starting with VCF 9.1, it is recommended that you deploy Supervisors with VPC for greenfield deployments.
Brownfield deployments of Supervisors configured with NSX are supported. For NSX configuration through the
API, see vSphere Automation API.
Note:
When you plan your network infrastructure, make sure that downstream VKS clusters do not use overlapping IP
addresses. For the specific non-overlap requirements across different VCF versions, see the CIDR rules in the
v1beta1/v1beta2 Example: Default Cluster topic.
When a Supervisor is configured with the vSphere networking stack, all hosts from the Supervisor are connected to a VDS
that provides connectivity to workloads and Supervisor control plane VMs. A Supervisor that uses the vSphere networking
stack requires a load balancer on the vCenter management network to provide connectivity to DevOps users and external
services.
A Supervisor that is configured with NSX, uses virtualized networks of the solution and NSX Load Balancer, Virtual
Network Appliance Load Balancer, or the Avi Load Balancer to provide connectivity to external services and DevOps
users. You can configure the Avi Load Balancer on NSX if your environment meets the following conditions:
• NSX version is VCF 9.1.x.
• The Avi Load Balancer version is 32.1.1 or 32.1.3.
• The Avi Load Balancer Controller you plan to configure is registered on NSX.
• An NSX load balancer or a Virtual Network Appliance Load Balancer is not already configured on the Supervisor.
Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC
For networking and security of vSphere Supervisor, you can use Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). VPC is the recommended
workload network for deploying the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) stack as it is the supported network stack for
VCF Automation environments. The Supervisor can be activated as an optional configuration during workload domain
creation and by default, it uses VCF Networking with VPC. If you do not activate the Supervisor during the workload
domain creation, you can deploy the Supervisor later with VPC from vCenter to gain the full cloud experience with VCF
Automation.
For more information, see Deploying Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC.
For more information about the Virtual Network Appliance Load Balancer, see https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/
gethidpage?ux-context-string=design-library-002&appid=vcf-9-1&language=en&format=rendered.
Supervisor Networking with VDS
In a Supervisor that is backed by VDS as the networking stack, all hosts from the vSphere clusters backing the Supervisor
must be connected to the same VDS. The Supervisor uses distributed port groups as workload networks for workloads
and control plane traffic. You assign Workload Networks to vSphere Namespaces in the Supervisor.
Depending on the topology that you implement for the Supervisor, you can use one or more distributed port groups
as Workload Networks. The network that provides connectivity to the Supervisor control plane VMs is called Primary
Workload Network. You can assign this network to all the vSphere Namespaces on the Supervisor, or you can use
different networks for each namespace. VKS clusters connect to the Workload Network that is assigned to the namespace
where the clusters reside.
A Supervisor that is backed by a VDS uses a load balancer for providing connectivity to DevOps users and external
services. You can use Foundation Load Balancer or Avi Load Balancer.
In a single-cluster Supervisor setup, the Supervisor is backed by only one vSphere cluster. All hosts from the cluster must
be connected to the same VDS.
In a three-zone Supervisor, you deploy the Supervisor on three vSphere zones, each mapped to a vSphere cluster. All
hosts from these vSphere clusters must be connected to the same VDS. All physical servers must be connected to the
same physical network. Workload networks that you configure to a vSphere Namespace span across all three vSphere
zones.

• NSX Container Plugin (NCP) provides integration between NSX and Kubernetes. The main component of NCP runs
in a container and communicates with NSX Manager and with the Supervisor control plane. NCP monitors changes
to containers and other resources and manages networking resources such as logical ports, segments, routers, and
security groups for the containers by calling the NSX API.
The NCP creates one shared tier-0 gateway for system namespaces and a tier-1 gateway and load balancer for each
namespace, by default. The tier-1 gateway is connected to the tier-0 gateway and a default segment.
System namespaces are namespaces that are used by the core components that are integral to functioning of the
Supervisor and VKS clusters. The shared network resources that include the tier-1 gateway, load balancer, and SNAT
IP are grouped in a system namespace.

• NSX Edge provides connectivity from external networks to Supervisor objects. The NSX Edge cluster has a load

any application that must be published and be accessible from outside the Supervisor.
• A tier-0 gateway is associated with the NSX Edge cluster to provide routing to the external network. It can use dynamic
routing protocols such as BGP or static routing.
• Each vSphere Namespace has a separate network and set of networking resources shared by applications inside the
namespace such as, tier-1 gateway, load balancer service, and SNAT IP address.
• Workloads running in vSphere Pods, regular VMs, or VKS clusters, that are in the same namespace, share a same
SNAT IP for North-South connectivity.
• Workloads running in vSphere Pods or VKS clusters will have the same isolation rule that is implemented by the
default firewall.
• A separate SNAT IP is not required for each Kubernetes namespace. East west connectivity between namespaces will
not need SNAT.
• The segments for each namespace reside on the VDS functioning in Standard mode that is associated with the NSX
Edge cluster. The segment provides an overlay network to the Supervisor.
• Supervisors have separate segments within the shared tier-1 gateway. For each VKS cluster, segments are defined
within the tier-1 gateway of the namespace.
• The Spherelet processes on each ESX hosts communicate with vCenter through an interface on the Management
Network.
In a three-zone Supervisor configured with NSX as the networking stack, all hosts from all three vSphere clusters mapped
to the zones must use be connected to the same VDS and participate in the same NSX Overlay Transport Zone. All hosts
must be connected to the same L2 physical device.

Supervisor networking with NSX Segment Network and Avi Load Balancer
NSX provides network connectivity to the objects inside the Supervisor and external networks. A Supervisor that is
configured with NSX can use the NSX Load Balancer or the Avi Load Balancer.
The components of the Avi Load Balancer include the Avi Load Balancer Controller cluster, Service Engines (data plane)
VMs and the Avi Kubernetes Operator (AKO).
Broadcom 6786

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Avi Load Balancer Controller interacts with the vCenter to automate the load balancing for the VKS clusters. It is
responsible for provisioning service engines, coordinating resources across service engines, and aggregating service
engine metrics and logging. The Controller provides a Web interface, command-line interface, and API for user operation
and programmatic integration.After you deploy and configure the Controller VM, you can deploy a Controller Cluster to set
up the control plane cluster for HA.
The Service Engine, is the data plane virtual machine. A Service Engine runs one or more virtual services. A Service
Engine is managed by the Avi Load Balancer Controller. The Controller provisions Service Engines to host virtual
services.
The Service Engine has two types of network interfaces:
• The first network interface, of the VM, connects to the Management Network where it can connect to the Avi
vnic0
Load Balancer Controller.
• The remaining interfaces, , connect to the Data Network where virtual services run.
vnic1 - 8
The Service Engine interfaces automatically connect to correct distributed port groups. Each Service Engine can support
up to 1000 virtual services.
A virtual service provides layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing services for VKS cluster workloads. A virtual service is
configured with one virtual IP and multiple ports. When a virtual service is deployed, the Controller automatically selects
an ESX host, spins up a Service Engine, and connects it to the correct networks (port groups).
The first Service Engine is created only after the first virtual service is configured. Any subsequent virtual services that are
configured use the existing Service Engine.
Each virtual server exposes a layer 4 load balancer with a distinct IP address of type load balancer for a VKS cluster.
The IP address assigned to each virtual server is selected from the IP address block given to the Controller when you
configure it.
The Avi Kubernetes operator (AKO) watches Kubernetes resources and communicates with the Avi Load Balancer
Controller to request the corresponding load balancing resources. The Avi Kubernetes Operator is installed on the
Supervisors as part of the enablement process.
For more information, see the Avi documentation.

vSphere Kubernetes Service Architecture and Components
Checkout what is the architecture for VKS and how it integrates with the Supervisor and its components. Learn how
networking and storage work for VKS clusters as well what is high-availability for VKS and which Supervisor deployment
supports it.
VKS Architecture
The VKS provides self-service life cycle management of VKS clusters. You use the VKS to create and manage VKS
clusters in a declarative manner that is familiar to Kubernetes operators and developers.
VKS Components
The VKS exposes three layers of controllers to manage the lifecycle of a VKS cluster.
• The VKS provisions clusters that include the components necessary to integrate with the underlying vSphere
Namespace resources. These components include a Cloud Provider Plug-in that integrates with the Supervisor. In
addition, a VKS cluster passes requests for persistent volumes to the Supervisor, which is integrated with VMware
Cloud Native Storage (CNS). See Storage Policies for Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
• The Cluster API provides declarative, Kubernetes-style APIs for cluster creation, configuration, and management. The
inputs to Cluster API include a resource describing the cluster, a set of resources describing the virtual machines that
make up the cluster, and a set of resources describing cluster add-ons.
• The Virtual Machine Service provides a declarative, Kubernetes-style API for management of VMs and associated
vSphere resources. The Virtual Machine Service introduces the concept of a virtual machine class that represents an
abstract reusable hardware configuration. The functionality provided by the Virtual Machine Service is used to manage
the lifecycle of the control plane and worker node VMs hosting a VKS cluster.

VKS Cluster Components
The components that run in a VKS cluster span four areas: Authentication and authorization, storage integration, pod
networking, and load balancing.
• Authentication webhook: A webhook running as a pod inside the cluster to validate user authentication tokens.
• Container Storage Interface (CSI) Plug-in: A Paravirtual CSI plug-in that integrates with CNS through the Supervisor.
• Container Network Interface (CNI) Plug-in: A CNI plug-in that provides pod networking.
• Cloud Provider Implementation: Supports creating Kubernetes load balancer services.
VKS API
You use the VKS API to provision and manage VKS clusters. It is a declarative API that you invoke using kubectl and
YAML. You can download the VMware expanded kubectl executable from the Supervisor API endpoint IP.
With a declarative API, instead of making imperative commands to the system, you specify the desired state of the VKS
cluster: how many nodes, available storage, VM sizes, Kubernetes software version. The VKS does the work to provision
a cluster that matches the desired state.
To call the VKS API, you invoke kubectl using a YAML file, which in turn invokes the API. After the cluster is created, you
update the YAML to update the cluster.
Broadcom 6790

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VKS Cluster Networking
A VKS cluster provisioned by the VKS supports two CNI options: Antrea (default) and Calico. Both are open-source
software that provide networking for cluster pods, services, and ingress.
VKS clusters provisioned by the VKS support the following Container Network Interface (CNI) options:
• Antrea
• Calico
Antrea is the default CNI for new VKS clusters. If you are using Antrea, you do not have to specify it as the CNI during
cluster provisioning. To use Calico as the CNI you have two options:
• Specify the CNI directly in the cluster YAML. See v1alpha3 Example: VKS Cluster with Custom Network.
• Change the default CNI. See v1beta1 Example: VKS Cluster with Calico CNI.
Note:
The use of Antrea as the default CNI requires a minimum version of the OVA file for VKS clusters. See Updating
VKS Clusters on Supervisor.

High-Availability for VKS Clusters
You can provide high-availability to VKS clusters when they are deployed on vSphere Namespaces that have more than
one vSphere Zones configured for running workloads.
A vSphere Zone maps to one or more vSphere clusters. When you configure a vSphere Namespace with multiple
vSphere Zones (up to three), it utilizes the resources of the vSphere clusters that best fit the resource and datastore
requirements of the vSphere Namespace. This protects your workloads running inside VKS clusters against failure on
a vSphere cluster level. On a vSphere Namespace configured with only one vSphere Zone, high-availability for VKS
clusters is provided on an ESX host level by vSphere HA.
In a multi-zonal vSphere Namespace, control plane nodes of VKS clusters are automatically placed across the vSphere
Zones. However, you control how VKS cluster worker nodes are spread across zones. You must define a NodePool object
Broadcom 6791

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
for the worker nodes of VKS clusters and map each vSphere Zone to a FailureDomain within each NodePool. This way,
Cluster API takes care to spread the worker nodes across vSphere Zones accordingly.
VKS Authentication
As a DevOps engineer, you access Supervisor to provision VKS clusters. You only have access to the namespaces where
you have permissions set by the VI administrator.
For information on how to connect to VKS clusters, see Connecting to vSphere Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
Storage for Supervisor and VKS Clusters
The Supervisor and VKS clusters use vSphere storage to serve two distinct needs: infrastructure storage for internal
platform components, and persistent storage for workloads. Both depend on vSphere Storage Policy-Based Management
(SPBM) to control placement, protection, and access to storage resources across VMFS, NFS, and vSAN datastores.
Storage Topologies for vSphere Zones
When you deploy a Supervisor across vSphere Zones, each zone acts as an independent fault domain. A failure in one
zone does not affect the others. The Supervisor supports three types of datastore topologies for zonal deployments.
Zonal datastore A zonal datastore is local to a single vSphere Zone. It is attached to all the ESX hosts that are part of the
underlying cluster.
• It can replicate data to provide higher availability within the zone.
• Its availability depends on the zone. If the zone goes down, the zonal datastore also goes down.
• Examples of a zonal datatore include: non-stretched vSAN, non-stretched vSAN storage cluster, non-
stretched VMFS or NFS external storage. A stretched cluster can also have a single vSphere zone.
Cross-zone datastore A cross-zone datastore spans multiple vSphere Zones. It is attached to ESX hosts from all the zones it
covers.
• A cross-zone datastore uses a single logical storage pool, such as a vSAN stretched cluster, that is
accessible across all zones.
• It can be stretched storage, for example, stretched vSAN.
• It can be non-stretched storage that pools hosts from multiple zones, for example, non-stretched vSAN
storage cluster.
• It typically replicates data across zones.
• It stays available if one of the zones goes down.
• Examples of a cross-zonal datastore: stretched vSAN, stretched vSAN storage cluster, metro storage
cluster, non-stretched vSAN or vSAN storage cluster deployed from hosts across multiple zones.
Multi-zone datastore A multi-zone datastore uses independent storage instances, such as a vSAN storage cluster or HCI cluster,
across multiple vSphere Zones.
• Zones can be located in different racks, rooms, or buildings.
• Unlike the cross-zonal datastores, the storage layer does not provide replication or failover across
zones. Applications deployed in multi-zone topologies must have built-in, application-level high
availability (HA).
• It is ideal for modern, distributed applications like Cassandra, PostgreSQL, or MongoDB that manage
their own data replication.
• StatefulSet replicas are distributed across zones to ensure high availability at the application layer.
• Zone-aware storage policies ensure that pods and volumes stay co-located within the same zone.
• If a zone fails, the specific datastore in that zone becomes unavailable, but the application remains
available through replicas running in other zones.
When you work with zonal and cross-zonal datastores in Supervisor, avoid the following misconfigurations:
• A zonal datastore is attached to other zones.
Example: A zonal vSAN datastore in Zone 1 is attached to Zone 2 and Zone 3 using vSAN remote datastore.
• A zonal datastore is only partially attached to ESX hosts in the zone.
Broadcom 6792

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Example: A VI administrator accidentally unmounts a datastore from a host.
Example: A new host is added to the zone, but the administrator forgets to attach all zonal datastores to it.
• A cross-zonal datastore is only partially attached to ESX hosts in multiple zones.
Example: A datastore is accidentally unmounted from one of the hosts.
Example: A new host is added to a zone, but the administrator forgets to attach all cross-zonal datastores to it.
• Editing storage policies to switch between zonal and cross-zonal compatibility.
This action changes the storage class behavior and affects DevOps.
• Storage policies that match both zonal and cross-zonal datastores.
DevOps cannot tell whether the volume they are getting is zonal or cross-zonal.
• A multi-zone topology is used for an application without built-in replication.
If the zone fails, the data is lost because there is no infrastructure-level replication.
Storage Policies for vSphere Zones
When you configure storage policies for datastores to be used with zones, follow these best practices:
• Make sure that a storage policy matches either zonal datastores only or cross-zonal datastores only. Mixing both in a
single policy leads to unpredictable behavior.
• Use a policy with zonal constraints to target zonal datastores.
The system guarantees compatibility with zonal datastores and catches any misconfigurations during placement.
• If you create a policy without zonal constraints to use with zonal datastores, ensure it remains compatible with zonal
datastores only.
You must verify that no cross-zonal datastores match this policy.
• If you create a policy that matches cross-zonal datastores only, ensure it always remains compatible with cross-zonal
datastores.
Prevent any zonal datastore from matching this policy.
• If you use multi-zone datastores, ensure that datastores are attached to every host in every cluster within the zone.
Inconsistent attachment causes placement failures.
Storage Policies for Supervisor and VKS Clusters
Supervisor and VKS clusters use storage policies to integrate with storage available in your vSphere environment. The
policies represent datastores and manage storage placement of such components and objects as control plane VMs,
vSphere Pod ephemeral disks, and container images. You might also need policies for storage placement of persistent
volumes and VM content libraries. If you use VKS clusters, the storage policies also dictate how the VKS cluster nodes
are deployed.
Storage policies support any shared datastores in your environment, such as VMFS, NFS, vSAN, and vSAN ESA.
Depending on your vSphere storage environment and the needs of DevOps, you can create several storage policies for
different classes of storage. When you enable a Supervisor and set up vSphere Namespaces, you can assign different
storage policies to be used by various objects, components, and workloads.
For information about creating storage policies, see Create Storage Policies.
For general information about storage policies, see the Storage Policy Based Management chapter in the vSphere
Storage documentation.
Storage Policies for a Supervisor
A vSphere storage policy is a set of rules that specifies storage requirements, such as performance, protection, capacity,
and encryption, for virtual machines and Kubernetes persistent volumes. Storage policies let administrators automate
storage placement and ensure that VMs and virtual disks reside on datastores that meet their specific requirements.
The Supervisor uses storage policies to control placement of the following platform components.
Control Plane VMs The specialized VMs that run the Supervisor control plane.
Broadcom 6793

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Ephemeral Virtual Disks Temporary disks used by vSphere Pod during execution to store short-lived Kubernetes objects, such as
container logs. This storage persists across container restarts but is automatically destroyed when the pod
reaches the end of its lifecycle.
Image Virtual Disks Disks that store container images that are pulled from your container registry. The Image Service
transforms these images into virtual disks to be mounted by running pods, and caches them locally to
accelerate subsequent pod deployments.
VM Content Libraries Repositories used to store and distribute VM and container images.
Assign dedicated storage policies to each component type. Separating platform infrastructure storage from persistent
workload storage allows you to tune performance and availability settings independently.
To change storage settings, see Change Storage Settings on the Supervisor.
Storage Policies for Persistent Workload Storage
After you define a storage policy, you can assign it to one or more vSphere Namespace. The Supervisor converts each
assigned policy into a matching Kubernetes StorageClass that appears automatically in the namespace and propagates to
any VKS clusters deployed within it.
Each assigned storage policy determines which datastores the namespace can access for persistent volume provisioning.
Optionally, you can set a storage consumption limit per policy per namespace to prevent a single namespace from
exhausting shared datastore capacity.
Persistent storage is required by certain workloads to store data permanently. It can be used by vSphere Pods, VKS
clusters, VMs, and other workloads that run on the namespace.
To assign a storage policy to a namespace, see Create and Configure a vSphere Namespace on the Supervisor. To
change storage settings on the namespace, see Change Storage Settings on a vSphere Namespace.
Storage Policies for VKS Cluster
To provide persistent storage to the VKS clusters, an administrator configures storage policies that describe different
storage requirements. The administrator then adds the storage policies to the namespace where the VKS cluster is
deployed. Storage policies visible to the namespace determine which datastores the namespace can access and
use for persistent storage. They also control how the cluster nodes and workloads are placed in the vSphere storage
environment.
For specific details about storage policies for VKS clusters, see Create a vSphere Storage Policy for VKS Clusters.
Supervisor propagates each namespace storage policy to the VKS cluster as a Kubernetes StorageClass.
For more information about storage classes in VKS clusters, see Using Storage Classes for Persistent Volumes.
How Supervisor Integrates with vSphere Storage
Supervisor uses several components to integrate with vSphere storage.
Broadcom 6794

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Cloud Native Storage The CNS component resides in vCenter. It is an extension of vCenter management that implements
(CNS) on vCenter provisioning and lifecycle operations for persistent volumes.
When provisioning persistent volumes, the component interacts with the vSphere First Class Disk
functionality to create virtual disks that back the volumes. In addition, the CNS server component
communicates with the Storage Policy Based Management to guarantee a required level of service to the
disks.
The CNS also performs query operations that allow VI administrators to manage and monitor persistent
volumes and their backing storage objects through vCenter.
First Class Disk (FCD) Also called Improved Virtual Disk. These disks reside on datastores and back ReadWriteOnce persistent
volumes.
When you use FCDs, keep in mind the following:
• FCDs do not support NFS 4.x protocols. Instead, use NFS 3.
• vCenter does not serialize operations on the same FCD. As a result, applications cannot simultaneously
perform operations on the same FCD. Performing such operations as clone, relocate, delete, retrieve,
and so on simultaneously from different threads causes unpredictable results. To avoid problems,
applications must perform operations on the same FCD in a sequential order.
• FCD is not a managed object and does not support a global lock protecting multiple writes to a single
FCD. As a result, FCD doesn't support multiple vCenter instances managing the same FCD. If you need
to use multiple vCenter instances with FCDs, you have the following options:
– Multiple vCenter instances can manage different datastores.
– Multiple vCenter instances do not operate on the same FCD.
Broadcom 6795

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Storage Policy Based Storage Policy Based Management is a vCenter service that supports provisioning of persistent volumes
Management and their backing virtual disks according to storage requirements described in a storage policy. After
provisioning, the service monitors compliance of the volume with the storage policy characteristics.
For more information about Storage Policy Based Management, see the About Storage Policy Based
Management chapter in the vSphere Storage documentation.
vSphere CNS-CSI The vSphere CNS-CSI component conforms to the Container Storage Interface (CSI) specification, an
industry standard designed to provide an interface that container orchestrators like Kubernetes use to
provision persistent storage. The CNS-CSI driver runs in the Supervisor and connects vSphere storage
to Kubernetes environment on a namespace. The vSphere CNS-CSI communicates directly with the CNS
component for all storage provisioning requests that originate from the namespace.

Storage for VKS Clusters
VKS clusters, as some other components and workloads that run in vSphere Namespace require persistent storage. They
consume storage through the same Supervisor storage infrastructure but use a dedicated CSI driver called Paravirtual
CSI (pvCSI) that runs inside each VKS cluster.
How VKS Clusters Integrate with vSphere Storage
To integrate with the Supervisor and vSphere storage, VKS clusters use Paravirtual CSI (pvCSI).
The pvCSI is a version of the vSphere CNS-CSI driver modified for VKS clusters. The pvCSI runs inside the VKS cluster
and is responsible for all storage requests originating from the VKS cluster. The requests are delivered to the CNS-
CSI in the Supervisor, which then propagates them to CNS in vCenter. As a result, the pvCSI does not have direct
communication with the CNS component, but instead relies on the CNS-CSI for any storage provisioning operations.
Unlike the CNS-CSI, the pvCSI does not require infrastructure credentials. It authenticates with a service account in the
namespace.

Volume Snapshots Yes
For information, see Creating Snapshots in a VKS Cluster.
Full Clone from Volume Snapshot Yes
4kn Support Yes
Create Storage Policies for Supervisor
Before you deploy a Supervisor, create storage policies to be used in the Supervisor and namespaces. The policies
represent datastores and manage storage placement of such components and objects as Supervisor control plane VMs,
vSphere Pod ephemeral disks, and container images. You might also need policies for storage placement of persistent
volumes and VM content libraries. If you use VKS clusters, the storage policies also dictate how the VKS cluster nodes
are deployed.
• Be familiar with information about storage policies in vSphere Supervisor, see About Storage Policies.
• Make sure that the datastore you reference in the storage policy is shared between all ESX hosts in the cluster. Any
shared datastores in your environment are supported, including VMFS, NFS, or vSAN.
• For details about storage policies for VKS clusters, see Create a vSphere Storage Policy for VKS Clusters.
• For specific requirements in vSAN stretched cluster environments, see Configuring Storage Policy for vSphere
Supervisor on vSAN Stretched Cluster.
• Required privileges:VM storage policies > Update andVM storage policies > View.
Depending on your vSphere storage environment and the needs of DevOps, you can create several storage policies for
different classes of storage. For example, if your vSphere storage environment has three classes of datastores, Bronze,
Silver, and Gold, you can create storage policies for all datastore types.
When you enable a Supervisor and set up namespaces, you can assign different storage policies to be used by various
objects, components, and workloads.
Note:
Storage policies that you create for a Supervisor or for a namespace in a one-zone Supervisor do not need to be
topology aware. Do not enable consumption domain for those policies.
Storage policies that you create for a namespace in a three-zone Supervisor must be topology aware and have
the consumption domain enabled in Step 4b. The three-zone namespace prevents you from assigning storage
policies that are not topology aware.
