After creating storage policies, a VI administrator can perform the following tasks:
• Assign the storage policies to the Supervisor. The storage policies configured on the Supervisor ensure that the control
plane VMs, pod ephemeral disks, and container images are placed on the datastores that the policies represent.
• Assign the storage policies to the vSphere Namespace. Storage policies visible to the namespace determine which
datastores the namespace can access and use for persistent volumes. The storage policies appear as matching
Kubernetes storage classes in the namespace. They are also propagated to the VKS cluster on this namespace.
DevOps engineers can use the storage classes in their persistent volume claim specifications. See Create and
Configure a vSphere Namespace.
Best Practices for Storage Configuration and Policies in Supervisor and VKS Environments
Follow these best practices when you configure storage and create custom storage policies for your Supervisor and VKS
clusters.
General Storage Policy Best Practices
Name storage policies Use names that reflect the policy purpose and service level. For example, prod-gold-raid5 or dev-
clearly and use silver-noreplication. When a single vCenter manages multiple Supervisor clusters, include a
cluster identifier to distinguish policies across environments.
Kubernetes-compatible
names Storage policy names become Kubernetes StorageClass names directly. Names must follow RFC 1123
requirements:
• Lowercase alphanumeric characters and hyphens (-) only
• Maximum 80 characters
• No consecutive hyphens
• No leading or trailing hyphens
• Unique within vCenter Server
Create separate policies Define distinct policies per performance tier, availability level, redundancy requirement, encryption need,
for each workload class and replication tier. A single general-purpose policy cannot meet the differing SLA requirements of
production, development, and test workloads.
Match every policy Verify that the capabilities defined in a storage policy, such as performance tier, encryption, replication, exist
definition to actual on the target datastores. A policy referencing capabilities a datastore cannot satisfy causes provisioning
failures. For VMFS and NFS datastores, apply tags based on performance type or replication capability,
datastore capabilities
then build placement rules from those tags.
Add a zonal topology Set the Storage topology type to Zonal on every storage policy assigned to a zonal Supervisor or three-
attribute to all policies zone namespace. Zonal topology ensures the system schedules a pod’s persistent volume in the same
availability zone as the pod itself. Without this attribute, volume attachment fails when a pod lands in a
when vSphere Zones
different zone from its volume. Three-zone namespaces block assignment of any policy that is not topology-
are in use
aware.
Assign at least one Mark one storage policy per namespace as the default Kubernetes StorageClass. Any
policy as the default PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) submitted without a storageClassName automatically use this default. Select
a policy that reflects the preferred performance and availability requirements for that namespace.
StorageClass for each
namespace
Set a storage Apply a consumption limit to every storage policy assigned to a namespace. Without a limit, one
consumption limit per namespace can exhaust a shared datastore and degrade other workloads. Limits enforce predictable
capacity allocation and surface unexpected growth early.
policy per namespace
Run compliance checks After any infrastructure change, such as adding hosts, extending datastores, modifying policy definitions,
after every storage verify that persistent volumes and virtual disks still comply with their assigned policies. Non-compliant
objects mean the underlying storage no longer satisfies the policy. Reapply or update the policy to restore
infrastructure change
compliance.
Remove storage Before removing a storage policy from vCenter or from a namespace, confirm that no PVC in the
policies only after namespace uses the corresponding StorageClass. Removing a policy leaves the StorageClass in

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

reference them existing workloads can behave unpredictably.
Configure anti-affinity On vSAN datastores, storage policy FTT settings distribute control plane VM data across hosts
rules for control plane automatically. On VMFS or NFS datastores, no such placement control exists at the storage layer. Create
DRS VM-VM anti-affinity rules to ensure that Supervisor control plane VMs distribute across different hosts
VMs on non-vSAN
in the cluster. Without these rules, all control plane VMs can land on a single host, creating a single point of
datastores
failure for the entire Supervisor.
Note:
This step is not required for vSAN-backed Supervisor deployments.
Use late-binding If a namespace is configured across a multi-zone Supervisor, enforce the use of late-binding storage
storage classes in a classes for all stateful workloads, including VKS worker node pools, guest cluster applications, and VMs
deployed via the VM Service. Delaying disk provisioning ensures perfect data locality. It also prevents
namespace configured
cross-zone mounting failures where an immediate volume is accidentally provisioned in Zone A, but its
across a multi-zone

Supervisor
Using Storage Classes for Persistent Volumes.
vSAN-Specific Storage Policy Best Practices
vSAN Original Storage Architecture (OSA) uses a two-tier model with dedicated cache and capacity devices organized
into disk groups. This architecture is designed for environments with mixed flash and magnetic disk hardware. vSAN
Express Storage Architecture (ESA) uses a single-tier pool where all NVMe devices contribute to both capacity and
performance, delivering higher throughput and more efficient erasure coding.
Use RAID-1 mirroring vSAN Original Storage Architecture performs best with RAID-1 mirroring. Size the cluster to support
for vSAN OSA clusters automatic rebuild after a host failure:
• Minimum 4 hosts for automatic rebuild after 1 host failure
• Minimum 7 hosts for automatic rebuild after 2 simultaneous host failures
Use erasure coding for vSAN Express Storage Architecture is optimized for erasure coding. Enable Auto Policy Management
vSAN ESA clusters where available — it automatically adjusts protection as the cluster changes and removes the need for
manual policy tuning.
When Auto Policy Management is unavailable, choose the erasure coding level based on your failure
tolerance requirement:
• RAID-5: minimum 5 hosts for automatic rebuild after 1 failure
• RAID-6: minimum 8 hosts for automatic rebuild after 2 failures
Define a dedicated Assign a highly resilient storage policy to first class disk (FCD) home objects. The FCD home stores
storage policy for the metadata and configuration files for the independent virtual disks that back persistent volumes. Leaving
FCD home objects on the default VM storage policy can expose persistent volume metadata to data loss if
Improved Virtual Disk
a host or disk fails. In vSAN ESA environments with Auto Policy Management enabled, the recommended
(FCD) home
policy is applied automatically.
Enable Force On vSAN stretch cluster deployments, set Force Provisioning on all Supervisor storage policies. Force
Provisioning on stretch Provisioning ensures that volume creation succeeds during planned site maintenance or a partial site
outage. Without it, provisioning requests fail when the cluster cannot fully satisfy policy requirements due to
cluster policies
reduced site capacity.
For information about vSAN stretch cluster deployments, see Overview of Running vSphere Supervisor on
vSAN Stretched Cluster.
Managing Thin-Provisioned Storage and Space Reclamation
All virtual disks that back persistent volumes in a Supervisor or VKS cluster are thin-provisioned by default. Because thin-
provisioned disks grow without explicit allocation events, you should monitor datastore capacity regularly and configure
alarms to catch overprovisioning before it causes provisioning failures.
Maintain 25–30% free space on vSAN datastores to accommodate rebalancing, host rebuild operations, and storage
policy changes. For VMFS and NFS datastores, maintain at least 15–20% free space.
For space reclamation configuration, follow the guidance for your datastore type.
Broadcom 6801

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VMFS On VMFS datastores, deleted blocks are returned to the datastore through space reclamation. For
information, see Space Reclamation on vSphere VMFS Datastores.
NFS Space reclamation on NFS requires a VAAI-NAS plugin from the storage vendor that supports UNMAP.
Without it, deleted blocks are not reclaimed. For information, see vSphere Hardware Acceleration on NAS
Devices.
vSAN vSAN processes TRIM and UNMAP automatically. No additional configuration is required. Enable Reserved
Capacity on vSAN datastores to prevent out-of-space conditions during unexpected workload spikes. For
details, see About Reserved Capacity in vSAN Cluster.
Deploying Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC
For networking and security of vSphere Supervisor, you can use Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). VPC is the recommended
workload network for deploying the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) stack as it is the supported network stack for
VCF Automation environments. The Supervisor can be activated as an optional configuration during workload domain
creation and by default, it uses VCF Networking with VPC. If you do not activate the Supervisor during the workload
domain creation, you can deploy the Supervisor later with VPC from vCenter to gain the full cloud experience with VCF
Automation.
The VPC networking framework is natively multi-tenant and is used by VCF Automation where each tenant organization
can create a tenant (NSX Project) in NSX. You can deploy vSphere Namespaces in the NSX default space where the VI
administrator creates the VPCs, or in a specific tenant (NSX Project). You can associate workload namespaces with VPCs
in an NSX Project or in the NSX default space irrespective of where the vSphere Namespaces have been deployed.
For more information about VPC models, see Workload Networking Detailed Designs.
The NSX Container Plugin (NCP) automatically creates the following:
• A VPC for System Namespaces in the NSX System project.
• A Supervisor Service VPC for Supervisor Services
• An individual VPC per vSphere Namespaces that is separate from the above two if an existing VPC is not configured
during namespace creation.
The shared network resources that include the VPC, load balancer, and SNAT IP are grouped in a namespace.
VPCs have three subnet types for workloads:
• Private - VPC subnets: This subnet is strictly isolated to its specific VPC using local IP ranges that can overlap with
other VPCs. Workloads on these subnets can only communicate internally unless a NAT rule is explicitly configured for
external access.
• Private Transit Gateway subnets: This subnet allows communication between different VPCs connected to the same
Transit Gateway, but remains inaccessible from outside the physical network without a NAT rule. These subnets are
primarily used by vSphere Pods.
• Public subnets: These subnets are accessible from other VPCs and outside the VPC. Workloads that are connected
are assigned unique external IPs from a CIDR carved from an external IP block.
VPCs created for vSphere Namespaces are configured with default outbound NAT enabled allowing workloads on private
networks to establish connectivity to outside resources. For more information about VPC, see NSX Virtual Private Clouds.
When you create a VPC in VCF Automation, you can choose to not configure a load balancer. Also, when you create a
connectivity profile, you can deselect the default outbound SNAT. For more information see, Create a Virtual Private Cloud
in VCF Automation.
Users with the Namespaces role in the VPC can create subnet CRs or SubnetSet CRs. The NSX operator creates NSX
subnets in the backend for the two CRDs separately.
Default subnetSet custom resources are created automatically in the namespace which is used to connect the vSphere
Pods and VMs when no subnet or subnetSet is specified.
VM Services VMs can be placed on any of the subnet types. By default they are placed on the Private subnet. The default
VM SubnetSet and VM network interface cannot be changed. VPC and network constructs are exposed as Kubernetes
custom resource definitions in the Supervisor API.
Broadcom 6802

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
NSX Container Plugin (NCP) and the Avi Kubernetes Operator (AKO) provide networking for the vSphere Pods and VMs,
subnet provisioning, IPAM, and service types network policy, ClusterIP, LoadBalancer, and Ingress. For more information,
see NSX.
Supervisor Architecture with VCF Networking with VPC
VPCs are connected together by a Transit Gateway which provides connectivity to the datacenter through an external
connection.
You can deploy a Supervisor in an environment using one of the following connections:
• Distributed Connection. A distributed connection is a simple connection that directly connects to the VLAN of the
datacenter without requiring additional configuration on the physical environment. Distributed connections supporting a
Supervisor require a Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster.
• Centralized Connection. A centralized connection attaches the Transit Gateway to a Tier-0 Gateway for external
connection. The connection uses the Tier-0 networking capabilities and services like BGP and requires an Edge
Cluster.
A Transit Gateway can have multiple connections but all the connections must either be distributed connections or
centralized connections. A Transit Gateway is called as a Distributed Transit Gateway or a Centralized Transit gateway
depending on the type of connections that it uses.
For more information, see External Connections and Transit Gateways.
When you activate the Supervisor during workload domain creation, you can configure the Virtual Network Appliance
(VNA) cluster, network connectivity, external transit gateway, and VPC external IP blocks for the Distributed Transit
Gateway. For more information, see Create a New Workload Domain Using VCF Operations.
If you require to configure a Centralized Gateway, you must configure NSX Edge nodes.
Note:
The choice of Transit Gateway for the Supervisor does not limit VCF Automation connection options. Transit
Gateways are specific to tenant organizations and when you create an organization through VCF Automation, you
can select either centralized or distributed connections.
Supervisor networking with VPC with a Distributed Transit Gateway
A VPC with a Distributed Transit Gateway requires a VLAN available on all ESX hosts spanned by the Transit Gateway
and connected VPCs. This VLAN and its CIDR block are used directly for IPs allowing outside connectivity.
The Distributed Transit Gateway does not require Edge Nodes, dynamic routing, or any specific configuration on the
physical network. It allows a distributed model which scales out as you add hosts since traffic directly goes from the host
to the VLAN. Services like DHCP or the ability to expose a workload with an external IP (1:1 NAT) are also distributed.
For networking services like Load Balancer or outbound SNAT, the Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) is used. The VNA is
multi-tenant and the same VMs can be used for multiple namespaces and multiple VCF Automation Organizations. For
more information on VNA, see Transit Gateways.

VCF 9.1.1 introduces support for a VLAN-backed VPC or networking model without TEPs under the Distributed Transit
Gateway. In this model, all traffic flows directly on physical VLANs without overlay encapsulation. It does not support
Private networks as the IP scheme is limited to the CIDRs backed by physical VLANs.
The region to which the Supervisor belongs to must be homogenous. The network stack must be fully VLAN-backed
(model without TEPs). For more information see, Managing Regions in Your VCF Automation.
As an administrator, you can pre-create subnets and assign them to vSphere Namespaces for specific workload types.
Subnets are created within VPCs with CIDRs allocated from the VPC external IP blocks. SNAT is not supported in models
without TEPs. Because of this restriction, deselect the default outbound SNAT when creating a connectivity profile. For
more information about VPC and subnets, see NSX Virtual Private Clouds.
In namespaces with VLAN-backed VPC, the NSX operator does not automatically create a default network for pods or
VMs. You must specify a shared subnet explicitly.
In namespaces with the full-stack VPC, if a Private Transit Gateway IPBlock and private CIDR blocks are configured,
the NSX operator can automatically create default networks for pods and VMs. You need not set a shared subnet as the
default network.
Note:
In the VCF 9.1.1 release, the VLAN-backed VPC model supports only greenfield deployments of Supervisor and
VCF Automation.
Note:
vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7.1 and earlier releases do not support the VLAN-backed VPC model. If you
are using vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7.1 or earlier versions on a 9.1.1 Supervisor, you cannot configure the
VLAN-backed VPC for VKS workloads.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Supervisor networking with VPC with a Centralized Transit Gateway
A VPC with a Centralized Transit Gateway uses centralized connections where traffic is routed through a tier-0 gateway
on NSX Edge nodes. Centralized connections allow stateful services and dynamic routing with the physical fabric (BGP)
at Tier-0 level.
VCF 9.1 supports a tier-0 gateway in Active/Active configuration and a Centralized Transit Gateway in Active/Standby
configuration with the required stateful services such as NAT for the Supervisor.

Workflow to Activate Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC
At a high level, the workflow to deploy Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC is as follows:
1. Review the requirements for configuring a Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC. See Requirements for
Supervisor Deployment with VPC Networking.
2. The Supervisor is activated as an optional configuration during workload domain creation and it uses VCF Networking
with VPC by default. If you do not activate the Supervisor during the workload domain creation, you can deploy the
Supervisor later with VPC from vCenter to gain the full cloud experience with VCF Automation.
3. Configure the distributed port groups or VPC subnets for the Supervisor management network if you use the non-
default ESX management network. For more information about subnets see NSX Virtual Private Clouds.
4. Optionally configure a Transit gateway with outside connectivity. When you activate the Supervisor , you have
the option of configuring the external connection and gateway. You can select either a distributed connection or a
centralized connection.
a. For a Centralized Transit Gateway, verify that a tier-0 gateway with outside connectivity and an Edge cluster are
configured. See Configure the Centralized Transit Gateway.
b. For a Distributed Transit Gateway, verify that a VLAN-backed network with outside connectivity is available on the
required hosts and the Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) with NAT, load balancing is deployed.
5. Optionally, install and configure the Avi Load Balancer.
Broadcom 6806

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
See the Avi documentation.
6. Activate the Supervisor. See Deploy a Supervisor with VPC Networking.

Create vSphere Zones for a Multi Zone Deployment with VPC
To activate a Supervisor, you must create at least one vSphere Zone that will be designated for the management plane
of the Supervisor, where the control plane will be placed. To provide zone-level HA to the Supervisor control plane, you
deploy the Supervisor on three vSphere Zones designated for management. In Supervisor with three management
zones and HA for the control plane, meaning with three control plane VMs, each control plane VM is placed on a different
Management Zone.
• Create one or three vSphere clusters to add to the zones:
Broadcom 6810

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– 2 ESX hosts in each zone for NFS or FC storage. For HA, use 4 hosts
– For storage with vSAN, the cluster must have 3 hosts. For HA, use 4 hosts.
– For test of POC environments, each cluster must have at least 1 host, and 2 hosts when using vSAN.
Note:
Recommendation: Restrict direct access to the ESX host console. Without that restriction, an administrator could
override vSphere Zone assignments, undermining the intended isolation and policy enforcement.
• Configure storage with vSAN or other shared storage solution for each cluster.
• Enable vSphere HA and vSphere DRS on Fully Automate or Partially Automate mode.
• All clusters in a zone must be connected to the same vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS). Each zone can use its own
management network.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to vCenter.
2. Click Configure.
3. Select vSphere Zones.
4. Click Add New vSphere Zone.
5. Name the zone, for example and add an optional description.
zone1

7. Repeat the steps to create three vSphere Zones.

Deploying vSphere Supervisor with Foundation Load Balancer
Foundation Load Balancer provides basic load balancing to the Supervisor and supports layer 4 services. Foundation
Load Balancer is packed with vCenter and provides load balancing support to the Supervisor and the workloads running
on it. You can only use Foundation Load Balancer with a Supervisor with VDS networking.
You can deploy an instance of Foundation Load Balancer as part of the Supervisor activation, or add it as the load
balancing solution to an existing Simplified Supervisor instance.
Supervisor Architecture with Foundation Load Balancer
Learn what are the supported topologies for Foundation Load Balancer and, it's placement in vSphere Zones, and
availability modes.
Foundation Load Balancer Networking and Supported Topologies
Foundation Load Balancer handles the following types of network traffic.
• Virtual Server traffic. The incoming traffic from clients to Foundation Load Balancer Virtual IPs (VIPs).
• Traffic to the IP pool members. The outgoing traffic from Foundation Load Balancer that is forwarded to one of the
workload IP pool members and then to the Workload Networks.
• Management traffic. The traffic which is used for CRUD operations of Foundation Load Balancer .
Foundation Load Balancer supports three topologies.

The dataplane has a combined Virtual Server and Transit interface, in addition to a dedicated Management

In One-Arm configuration, the Virtual Server Network is used both for incoming application traffic and then
for forwarded application traffic to the Workload Networks.
One-arm one-nic The dataplane has a single network interface for all Virtual Server, Transit, and Management traffic. This
configuration Foundation Load Balancer topology is only supported in a Simplified Supervisor deployment.
Placement and Availability Modes
Foundation Load Balancer is placed on a Management Zone of the Supervisor instance. In a Supervisor deployed on
three Management Zones, one Management Zone is selected for the placement of the Foundation Load Balancer. The
Foundation Load Balancer VMs are located in the same folder ( ) and resource
Namespaces > <Supervisor Name>
pool ( ) as the Supervisor control plane VMs.
Namespaces
Foundation Load Balancer supports two availability modes:
• One VM. In this mode, DRS handles the host placement of the Foundation Load Balancer VMs within the vSphere
cluster.
• Two VMs. To ensure host-based high availability, the Foundation Load Balancer VMs have soft host anti-affinity rule
in the same cluster in the two VM (active-passive) configuration. The active node is determined by leader election
performed by both VMs . The elected leader is the active node that serves all of the client traffic coming at the server
endpoints. If the active node goes down, for example due to host or VM crash, the passive node takes over leadership
and become the new active node. The leader election and failover process is performed without vCenter involvement.
The VM disks of Foundation Load Balancer are place on the datastore determined by the storage policy configured to the
Supervisor control plane VMs.

Create vSphere Zones for a Multi-Zone Supervisor Deployment
To activate a Supervisor, you must create at least one vSphere Zone that will become the Management Zone of
the Supervisor. To provide cluster-level HA to the Supervisor control plane, you can deploy the Supervisor on three
Management Zones. In Supervisor with three Management Zones and HA for the control plane, meaning with three
control plane VMs, each control plane VM is placed on a different Management Zone.
• Create one or three vSphere clusters to add to the zones:
– 2 ESX hosts in each zone for NFS or FC storage. For HA, use 4 hosts
– For storage with vSAN, the cluster must have 3 hosts. For HA, use 4 hosts.
– For test of POC environments, each cluster must have at least 1 host, and 2 hosts when using vSAN.
Note:
Recommendation: Restrict direct access to the ESX host console. Without that restriction, an administrator could
override vSphere Zone assignments, undermining the intended isolation and policy enforcement.
• Configure storage with vSAN or other shared storage solution for each cluster.
• Enable vSphere HA and vSphere DRS on Fully Automate or Partially Automate mode.
• All clusters in a zone must be connected to the same vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS). Each zone can use its own
management network.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to vCenter.
2. Select vSphere Zones.
3. Click Add New vSphere Zone.
4. Name the zone, for example and add an optional description.
zone1
5. Select a vSphere clusters to add to the zone and click Finish.
6. Repeat the steps to create three vSphere Zones.

Maintaining Foundation Load Balancer
Learn what are the high availability options that are available for the Foundation Load Balancer , as well as monitoring and
observability, failover and recovere, backup and restore, and more.
High Availability and Failover Performance
In an event of a ESX host or VM crash affecting the health of the active Foundation Load Balancer VM, the recovery
time for the Foundation Load Balancer active VM is 5 seconds. During these 5 seconds, the standby Foundation Load
Balancer VM takes over as the new active VM. VIPs on the new Foundation Load Balancer active VM start working when
the standby VM takes over the active VM.
Broadcom 6828

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Impact on active TCP Connection states are not synchronized between the active and standby Foundation Load Balancer VMs.
sessions Existing active TCP connections will break during the 5 seconds downtime while the active Foundation
Load Balancer is being recovered. If a client or server application does not send any TCP packets during
the recovery of the active Foundation Load Balancer VM, they will not notice that the connection is broken.
When a client or server sends TCP packets after the recovery of the active Foundation Load Balancer VM:
• When a client sends TCP packets to the new active Foundation Load Balancer VM, the Foundation
Load Balancer VM does not have the connection information. The Foundation Load Balancer VM
responds to the client with a TCP RST (reset) packet.
• When a server sends TCP packets to the new active Foundation Load Balancer VM, the Foundation
Load Balancer VM responds to the server with a TCP RST (reset) packet. Depending on the
application, it might attempt to reestablish the TCP session.
Restoring Foundation Information about the Foundation Load Balancer is stored in the vCenter database. In case both the
Load Balancer when Foundation Load Balancer VMs are down, vCenter automatically restores the VMs.
both active and standby
Foundation Load
Balancer VMs are down
Redeployment of You can redeploy any of the Foundation Load Balancer VMs from the vSphere Client Administration >
the Foundation Load Solutions > Foundation Load Balancers view.
Balancer VMs • If you redeploy the standby Foundation Load Balancer VM, workloads are not impacted.
• If you redeploy the active Foundation Load Balancer VM, an automatic active-standby failover is
triggered before the redeployment takes place. The current active Foundation Load Balancer VM
becomes standby and the standby VM becomes the active one.
If you want to redeploy two Foundation Load Balancer VMs in a single Foundation Load Balancer instance,
you must wait for the first Foundation Load Balancer VM redeployment to complete before you start
redeploying the second VM

Collect the Foundation Load Balancer Support Bundle
To collect a support bundle for Foundation Load Balancer:
1. Establish an SSH session with either of the active or standby Foundation Load Balancer VMs.
2. Run the following command:
flbctl supportbundle
3. Collect the generated bundle file.
Monitoring and Observability
You can view and monitor all the Foundation Load Balancer instances available in vCenter from Administration >
Solutions > Foundation Load Blanacer. See Monitor Foundation Load Balancer for more information. VCF Operations
dashboards are not available for Foundation Load Balancer.
Foundation Load Balancer Health Errors
You view the errors that occur in Foundation Load Balancer instances from Administration > Solutions > Foundation
Load Blanacer option in the vSphere Client. See Foundation Load Balancer Heath Errors and Troubleshooting.
Backup and Restore
The backup of Foundation Load Balancer VIPs configurations and endpoints are included in the Supervisor control plane
backup. Once the Supervisor is restored from a backup, Foundation Load Balancer resynchronizes the load balancer
configuration with the restored Supervisor control plane. See Backup and Restore the Supervisor Control Plane for more
information.
In the case when the Foundation Load Balancer instance is still active, the restored state of the Supervisor includes
a reference to the existing Foundation Load Balancer instance. Supervisor reconnects the Foundation Load Balancer
service to vCenter to refresh the Foundation Load Balancer authentication tokens. This allows the Foundation Load
Balancer instance to re-establish connection with its XDS runtime control plane in the Supervisor and to obtain the up-to-
date load balancer virtual server configurations for the Supervisor.
See High Availability and Failover Performance for the cases when both Foundation Load Balancer VMs are down and
redeployed.
Health Checks and Statistics
To provide health checks on VIPs and endpoints of Foundation Load Balancer , you can configure liveness and readiness
probes on the Foundation Load Balancer endpoints. Foundation Load Balancer only consumes healthy endpoints from
Supervisor Kubernetes API.
You can get real-time statistics from Envoy. Establish an SSH session with the active Foundation Load Balancer VM and
use the following command:
curl http://<active FLB VM IP>:19000/stats
For information on the Envoy statistics, check the listener and server statistics in the Envoy documentation.
Get Foundation Load Balancer Logs
You can get the Foundation Load Balancer logs from the following locations in case the Supervisor Kubernetes Services
are not realized:
• Envoy logs in the active Foundation Load Balancer VM. Establish an SSH session with the active Foundation Load
Balancer VM and use the following command:
sudo journalctl -u envoy
• Logs generated by the component in the active Foundation Load Balancer VM. Establish an SSH session
flb-agent
with the active Foundation Load Balancer VM and find the logs in the following location:
flb-agent
/var/log/flb-agent/
Broadcom 6830

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Logs from the Foundation Load Balancer support bundle. Establish an SSH session with any of the Foundation Load
Balancer VMs and use the following command:
flbctl supportbundle
• Logs that are generated from the Foundation Load Balancer system pod, which is named, for example
flb-
and is located in the system namespace. You can check
controller-5689c6bf74-t5rk2 vmware-system-flb
the exact name of the pod from the Pods view on the Supervisor in the vSphere Client. Then log into the Supervisor as
an administrator by using VCF CLI and use the following command:
kubectl logs flb-controller-5689c6bf74-t5rk2 -n vmware-system-flb
• Perform a tcpdump on the active Foundation Load Balancer VM front-end interface and workload network interface.
This captures live client traffic and indentify potential issues on the physical network, and provide additional useful
information.

curl http://127.0.0.1:19000/config_dump?include_eds > config_dump.json
Troubleshooting VIP Traffic Connectivity Loss
In case the VIP traffic is down, perform the following actions:
• First, check the , , and Envoy logs like shown from above.
flb-controller flb-agent
• Establish an SSH session is the active Foundation Load Balancer VM and check the following VIP configurations:
–
/var/lib/flb-agent/listeners/
–
/var/lib/flb-agent/clusters/
–
/var/lib/flb-agent/endpoints
• Check if a VIP is configured to the active Foundation Load Balancer VM. Establish an SSH session with the
activeFoundation Load Balancer VM and use the following commands:
–
sudo ip a show vsphere-lb0
–
sudo ip route show table all
–
sudo ip rule show
–
sudo iptables-save
• Raise the Envoy log level and check the Envoy logs in the active Foundation Load Balancer VM.Establish an SSH
session with the activeFoundation Load Balancer VM and use the following command to raise the Envoy logs level:
–
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:19000/logging?level=trace
– Restore the log level to info:
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:19000/logging?level=info
Lastly, perform on Foundation Load Balancer VM front-end interface and workload network interface.
tcpdump

Deploying Supervisor with a Simplified Deployment Flow
VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 allows you to create a simplified Supervisor deployment requiring fewer resources and
configuration steps than a typical deployment.
This simplified deployment allows access to a limited subset of Supervisor capabilities. You can then expand the
deployment over time to build out to full Supervisor functionality.
The initial deployment consists of the following:
Broadcom 6837

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• A single control-plane VM.
• A single network used for both management and workload traffic.
• Support for the VM Service only. vSphere Pods and Supervisor Services are not supported with this configuration.
The next step in expanding this configuration is to add a load balancer. Currently Avi and Foundation load balancers are
supported. After the load balancer has been added, support for vSphere Pods and Supervisor Services is enabled.
After the load balancer is added, you have two additional options for modifying the topology of the Supervisor, which can
be done in any order:
• Scaling out control-plane VMs: Scaling from 1 control-plane VM to 3 control-plane VMs enables high-availability for the
Supervisor.
• Adding a NIC: Adding a NIC allows you to set a different network to be the primary workload network, that is, the
network that the control-plane VMs dedicate for their workload traffic.
Requirements for Simplified Supervisor Deployment
Ensure that you meet the following requirements for deploying Supervisor in a simplified deployment.
Network Routing Requirements
Ensure that network routing is configured between the following components.
Components Purpose
Supervisor Management Network and vCenter Management traffic between vCenter and Supervisor.
Supervisor Management Network and Spherelet vmkernel Needed for ESX hosts to be managed as Kubernetes worker
management NIC. nodes.
Workload Network and virtual IP (when adding a load balancer) Needed for load balancer DNS lookups.
Load balancer backend interface and control plane VM workload The workload network may either be the same as the
network management network (single homed) or not (dual homed). The
initial simplified deployment is single homed.
Requirement for Secure Access Using FQDN
Use of a fully-qualified domain name (FQDN is required for login to the Supervisor in order to prevent certificate issues.
Server Name Indication (SNI) is used to provide the VIP certificate to incoming requests when the request is made by
FQDN.
Configure the DNS record for the FQDN to point to whatever address is indicated for the control plane in the vCenter UI.
• If there is no load balancer, this is the floating IP address.
• If there is a load balancer, this is the virtual IP address for the service type load balancer fronting the Supervisor.
Limitations of Simplified Supervisor Configurations
Simplified Supervisor configurations have certain limitations when compared to a full Supervisor deployment.
Make sure you understand the limitations before deciding to use a particular type of configuration.
Limitations of Configurations Without a Load Balancer
Limitations of configurations without a load balancer are:
• vSphere Pods and Supervisor Services are not supported with this configuration. Only the VM Service is available.
• Simplified Supervisor does not support provisioning of persistent volumes.
• Kubernetes Service type load balancers do not receive an external IP address.
• Supervisor Control Plane scale out is not possible.
Add a load balancer to the simplified deployment to allow for scale out and additional workloads.
Broadcom 6838

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Limitations of a Single Control Plane VM
Limitations of a single control plane VM configuration are:
• The single control plane VM is a single point of failure. Any downtime of the control plane VM affects control plane
availability. Any form of data corruption might require a Supervisor restore operation to recover the system.
etcd
• A single control plane configuration experiences brief downtime during the following operations:
– Upgrade of Supervisor Services that run on the control plane
– Upgrade of the Supervisor itself.
• The single control plane VM configuration might result in memory and/or CPU contention among system controllers
due to the inability to distribute work across multiple control plane nodes. Control plane VMs run a number of
vSphere controllers to provide various services. A three control plane VM configuration runs two instances of most
of these controllers, allowing for another instance to take over if a single node goes down. On a single control plane
configuration, all controllers must run on a single node.
Limitations of a Single Network
Limitations of a single network are:
• Workload and management traffic travel on the same network, which might affect how you configure routing in your
environment.
• In a dual-homed (two network) configuration, management traffic such as that for vCenter, etcd, backup-restore, and
so on uses the management network (eth0), while intra-cluster traffic for operators and services uses the workload
network (eth1). Using a single network means potentially more contention and less isolation for management traffic at
the Linux VM level.
Activate Supervisor Using the Simplified Deployment Flow
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client and select the cluster where you want to activate the Supervisor.
2. Select Actions > Activate Supervisor.
3. Select a network mode to use for the management and workload network.
In the initial deployment, workloads run on the management network.
• DHCP - In this networking mode, all of the IP addresses and network settings for the management and workload
network are acquired through DHCP.

Supervisor. Namespaces that do not have a different port group

configuration. The DNS record for the FQDN should point to the

5. Click Activate.
Supervisor is activated in a simplified deployment with a single control-plane VM, a single NIC, and no load balancer.
Add a Load Balancer to a Simplified Supervisor Deployment
After the initial simplified Supervisor deployment, the next step you can take to scale out your deployment is to add a load
balancer.
Back up both the Supervisor and vCenter before making this or any other topology change to your simplified Supervisor
deployment. If you need to restore the Supervisor to the state it was in prior to the topology change, you must also restore
vCenter in order to ensure that vCenter recognizes the correct configuration of the Supervisor.
If you are using the Avi Load Balancer, deploy the load balancer before you begin this task as described in the Avi
documentation.
If you are using the Foundation Load Balancer, you do not need to deploy it in advance. It is deployed as part of this
workflow.
Adding a load balancer enables use of the vSphere Pods and Supervisor Services in addition to the VM Service.
Currently, the following load balancers are supported:

• Foundation Load Balancer
• Avi Load Balancer

1. From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
2. Select the Supervisors tab, and click the Supervisor you want to add the load balancer to.
3. Select Network and expand the Load Balancer section.
4. Select the load balancer to deploy and click Add Load Balancer.
• Avi Load Balancer
• Foundation Load Balancer

After you add the load balancer, reconfigure the DNS record for the Supervisor FQDN so that it points to the virtual IP
address for the service type load balancer fronting the Supervisor.
Add a Second NIC to a Simplified Supervisor Deployment
After you have added a load balancer to your simplified deployment, you can add a second NIC to allow for separating
Workload Network traffi from Management Network traffic.
• Ensure that you have added a load balancer to your simplified deployment.
• Review the network routing requirements listed in Requirements for Simplified Supervisor Deployment to ensure that
your new primary network meets these requirements.
Broadcom 6841

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Back up both the Supervisor and vCenter before making this or any other topology change to your simplified Supervisor
deployment. If you need to restore the Supervisor to the state it was in prior to the topology change, you must also restore
vCenter in order to ensure that vCenter recognizes the correct configuration of the Supervisor.
Adding a second NIC and adding additional control plane VMs can be done in either order. After you have added a
second NIC, you cannot revert to a single NIC configuration.
1. Add a workload network to the Supervisor by following the instructions in Add Workload Networks to a Configured with
VDS Networking.
Select primary as the port group and set the network name to .
primary
2. Set the new workload network to be the primary workload network.
a) In the vSphere Client, select Supervisor Management.
b) Under Supervisors, select the Supervisor, and select Configure.
c) Select Network and expand Workload Network.
d) Select the primary network, and click Set Primary.
e) Click OK to confirm that you want to set the new primary network.
Scale Out Control Plane VMs in a Simplified Supervisor Deployment
After you have added a load balancer, you can scale out the number of control plane VMs from 1 to 3 to allow for high-
availability.
Ensure that you have added a load balancer to your simplified deployment.
Back up both the Supervisor and vCenter before making this or any other topology change to your simplified Supervisor
deployment. If you need to restore the Supervisor to the state it was in prior to the topology change, you must also restore
vCenter in order to ensure that vCenter recognizes the correct configuration of the Supervisor.
Adding a second NIC and adding additional control plane VMs can be done in either order. After you have scaled out to 3
control plane VMs, this operation cannot be reversed.
1. From the vSphere Client home menu, select Management.
2. Under Supervisors, select the Supervisor, and select Configure.
3. Select General and expand the Control Planesection.
4. Next to the text Control Plane HA is not activated, click Activate.
5. Click Activate to confirm that you want to scale out the control plane VMs.
Additional control plane VMs are deployed. You can monitor the status of the reconfiguration on the Supervisors tab of
the Supervisor Management page.
Deploying vSphere Supervisor with NSX and Avi Load Balancer
A Supervisor that is configured with NSX networking uses the software-based networks of the solution and Avi Load
Balancer to provide connectivity to external services and DevOps users.
For information about how to deploy the Supervisor with NSX networking and Avi Load Balancer, see the Avi
documentation.
Deploying vSphere Supervisor with vDS and Avi Load Balancer
In a Supervisor environment that uses vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS) networking, you can use the Avi Load Balancer
for load balancing services.
For information about how to deploy the Supervisor with vDS and Avi Load Balancer, see the Avi documentation.
Deploying vSphere Supervisor from an Exported Configuration
Broadcom 6842

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Export a Supervisor Configuration
Checkout how to export the configuration of an existing Supervisor, which you can later import in the Supervisor activation
wizard to deploy a new Supervisor instance with a similar configuration. The Supervisor exports in a JSON configuration
file, which you can modify as needed and use to deploy a new Supervisor instance.
Deploy a Supervisor.
Exporting a Supervisor configuration allows you to:
• Persist Supervisor configurations. You can export all previous Supervisor configurations and reuse them when needed.
• More efficient troubleshooting. If a Supervisor activation fails, you can adjust the Supervisor configuration directly into
the JSON file and restart the process. This allows for quick troubleshooting, as you can modify the settings directly in
the JSON file before importing it.
• Streamlined administration. You can share the exported Supervisor configuration with other administrators, to setup
new Supervisors with similar settings.
• Consistent format. The exported Supervisor configurations adhere to a standardized format that is applicable to the
supported deployment types.
You can also export the Supervisor configuration during the Supervisor activation workflow.
1. Go to Supervisor Management > Supervisor > Supervisors.
2. Select a Supervisor and select Export Config.
The configuration is exported and saved in a ZIP file named that is stored locally in the browser’s
wcp-config.zip
default download folder. Within the file you can find:
wcp-config.zip
• A JSON file containing the Supervisor configuration named . Each configuration setting has a
wcp-config.jso
corresponding name and location in the JSON file. This JSON file adheres to a hierarchical data structure.
• A valid JSON schema file named . This file outlines all exportable settings for the
wcp-config-schema.json
Supervisor, encompassing their type, location within the JSON file, and whether they are required. You can use the
schema file to generating a sample configuration JSON file , which you can populate manually and import to a fresh

Edit the JSON configuration as needed and use it to deploy new Supervisors.
Deploy a Supervisor by Cloning an Existing Configuration
Learn how to deploy a Supervisor by cloning the configuration of an existing Supervisor instance. Clone a Supervisor in
case you want to deploy a new Supervisor instance with similar settings as an already deployed Supervisor.
• Complete the prerequisites for configuring vSphere clusters as a Supervisor. See the requirements for each
deployment type in the relevant chapters.
1. Go to Supervisor Management > Supervisor > Supervisors.
2. Select the Supervisor, which you want to clone and select Clone Config.
The Supervisor activation wizard opens with values pre-filled from the Supervisor that you selected.
3. Go through the wizard by modifying the values as needed.
Once you complete the wizard for enabling a Supervisor, you can track the activation process and observe potential
issues that require troubleshooting. In the Config Status column, click view next to the status of the Supervisor.
Broadcom 6843

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 515: Supervisor activation view
For the deployment process to complete, the Supervisor must reach the desired state, which means that all 16 conditions
are reached. When a Supervisor is successfully enabled, its status changes from Configuring to Running. While the
Supervisor is in Configuring state, reaching each of the 16 conditions is retried continuously. If a condition is not reached,
the operation is retried until success. Because of this reason, the number of conditions that are reached could change
back and forth, for example 10 out of 16 conditions reached and then 4 out of 16 conditions reached and so on. In very
rare cases the status could change to Error, if there are errors that prevent reaching the desired state.
For more information on the deployment errors and how to troubleshoot them, see Resolving Errors Health Statuses on
Supervisor Cluster During Initial Configuration Or Upgrade.
Deploy a Supervisor by Importing a JSON Configuration File
Checkout how to automatically populate all the configuration values in the Supervisor activation wizard by importing
a JSON configuration file that you have exported from previous Supervisor deployments. When troubleshooting an
unsuccessful Supervisor deployment or deploying a new Supervisor with a similar configuration, you can change the
configuration values directly in the JSON file before you import it in the wizard. This way you save time from filling in all
the values in the activation wizard manually and can just focus on the areas that need change.
Broadcom 6844

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Complete the prerequisites for configuring vSphere clusters as a Supervisor. See the requirements for deploying a
Supervisor int the relevant chapters.
• Verify that you have a JSON configuration file that you have exported from an existing Supervisor deployment. The
default name of the file is .
wcp-config.json
You can export the configuration of a Supervisor in two ways:
• During the Supervisor deployment on the Ready to complete page of the wizard.
• Export the configuration of an already deployed Supervisor.
1. Initiate a Supervisor deployment in one of the following ways:
• If you haven't successfully deployed Supervisor yet, click Get Started on the Supervisor Management page.
• If you want to deploy an additional Supervisor in your environment, select Supervisor Management >
Supervisor > Supervisors > Add Supervisor.
2. From the top right corner, select Import Config.
The vSphere Client verifies the values in the JSON file. Errors might be displayed if the uploaded file is invalid or
corrupted JSON. Similarly, errors will appear if the JSON file lacks the spec version or if the spec version exceeds
what is currently supported by the client. Therefore, you should only edit the setting that you needed before importing
the configuration file. If the file is corrupt, you can use the JSON schema to generate a an empty Supervisor
configuration, that you can fill in with the values that you need.
3. In the Upload Supervisor Configuration dialog, click Upload and select a JSON configuration file you have exported
previously.
4. Click Import.
The values recorded in the JSON configuration file are populated in the Supervisor activation wizard. You still might
need to enter certain settings manually, such as load balancer password.
5. Click Next through the wizard and fill in any values where required.
6. In the Review and Confirm page, scroll up and review all the settings that you configured thus far and make final
changes if needed.
7. Click Finish when ready with reviewing the settings.
The activation of the Supervisor initiates the creation and configuration of the control plane VMs and other
components.
Once you complete the wizard for enabling a Supervisor, you can track the activation process and observe potential
issues that require troubleshooting. In the Config Status column, click view next to the status of the Supervisor.

Figure 516: Supervisor activation view
For the deployment process to complete, the Supervisor must reach the desired state, which means that all conditions
are reached. When a Supervisor is successfully enabled, its status changes from Configuring to Running. While the
Supervisor is in Configuring state, reaching each of the conditions is retried continuously. If a condition is not reached, the
operation is retried until success. Because of this reason, the number of conditions that are reached could change back
and forth, for example 10 out of 16 conditions reached and then 4 out of 16 conditions reached and so on. In very rare
cases the status could change to Error, if there are errors that prevent reaching the desired state.
For more information on the deployment errors and how to troubleshoot them, see Resolving Errors Health Statuses on
Supervisor Cluster During Initial Configuration Or Upgrade.
Configuring and Managing vSphere Namespaces
vSphere Supervisor workloads, including vSphere Pods, VMs, and VKS clusters, are deployed to a vSphere Namespace.
A VI administrator defines the namespace on a Supervisor and configures it with resource quota and user permissions.
Depending on the needs of DevOps engineers and workloads they plan to run, the VI administrator might also assign
storage policies, VM classes, and content libraries for fetching VM images.
Broadcom 6846

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
When initially created, the namespace has unlimited resources within the Supervisor. As a VI administrator, you can set
limits for CPU, memory, storage, and the number of Kubernetes objects that can run within the namespace. Storage
limitations are represented as storage quotas in Kubernetes. A resource pool is created in vSphere per each namespace
on the Supervisor
In a Supervisor activated on vSphere Zones, a namespace resource pool is created on the vSphere clusters that are
mapped to the zones. For vSphere Zones that have more than one cluster associated with them, a resource pool for the
vSphere Namespace is create to only one of the clusteres that are part of the zone. The resources that are utilized to the
namespace that spread to more than one vSphere Zone are taken from all three underlying vSphere clusters where the
namespaces resouroce pool resides in equal parts. For example, if you dedicate 300 MHz of CPU, 100 MHz are taken
from each vSphere cluster.
To provide access to namespaces to DevOps engineer, a VI administrator assigns permission to users or user groups
available within an identity source that is associated with vCenter Single Sign-On or from an ODIC provider that is
registered with the Supervisor. For more information, see Understanding Authentication and Authorization in vSphere
Supervisor.
After a vSphere Namespace is created and configured with resource, object limits, permissions, and storage policies, as a
DevOps engineer, you can access the namespace to run the following workloads:
• For information about running Supervisor Services, see https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=svservices-1&appid=sv-async&language=&format=rendered.
• For information about running vSphere Pods, see https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=vsphere-pods-1&appid=vcf-9-1&language=&format=rendered.
• For information about deploying VMs, see Deploying and Managing Virtual Machines in vSphere Supervisor.
Create and Configure a vSphere Namespace on the Supervisor
Check out how to create and configure a vSphere Namespace on the Supervisor. As a vSphere administrator, after you
create a vSphere Namespace, you set resources limits to the namespace and permissions so that DevOps engineers can
access it. You provide the URL of the Kubernetes control plane to DevOps engineers where they can run workloads on
the namespaces for which they have permissions.
• Deploy a Supervisor.
• Create users and groups for DevOps engineers and developers, who need access to the vSphere Namespace. Create
the users or groups in identity sources that are connected to vCenter Single Sign-On or in an OIDC provider configured
with the Supervisor.
• Create storage policies for persistent storage. If the vSphere Namespace is in a multi-zone Supervisor, use topology
aware policies. You cannot assign storage policies that are not topology aware to the multi-zone vSphere Namespace .
• Create VM classes and content libraries for stand-alone VMs.
• Create a vSphere Zone to associate with the vSphere Namespace. For isolation of between the workload and
management plane, you can assign a vSphere Zone that is different from the zone where the Supervisor is running.
See Add a Cluster as a vSphere Zone to a Supervisor.
Broadcom 6847

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Required privileges: , , and . See How Permissions Work
Namespaces.view Namespace.edit Namespaces.owner
in Supervisorfor more information.
You can also set resources limits to the vSphere Namespace, assign permissions, and provision or activate the vSphere
Namespace service on a cluster as a template. As a result, DevOps engineers can create a vSphere Namespace in a
self-service manner and can deploy workloads within it. For more information, see Provision a Self-Service Namespace
Template in vSphere Supervisor.
If you use NSX for your Supervisors, you choose to override the networking settings on vSphere Namespace level. Have
in mind the following considerations if you select that option:
Table 1792: vSphere Namespace Network Planning Considerations
Consideration Description
NSX Installation To override Supervisor network settings for a particular vSphere Namespace, the NSX must
include an Edge Cluster dedicated for Tier-0 Gateways (routers) and another Edge Cluster
dedicated for Tier-1 Gateways. Refer to the NSX installation instructions provided in the guide
Installing and Configuring vSphere Supervisor.
IPAM Required If you override Supervisor network settings for a particular vSphere Namespace, the new
vSphere Namespace network must specify Ingress, Egress, and Namespace Network subnets
that are unique for the Supervisor and from any other vSphere Namespace network. You will
need to manage IP address allocation accordingly.
Supervisor Routing The Supervisor must be able to route directly to the VKS cluster nodes and ingress subnets.
When selecting a Tier-0 Gateway for the vSphere Namespace, you have two options for
configuring the required routing:
• Use a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) Gateway to inherit the configuration from the
Supervisor Tier-0 Gateway
• Use the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to configure routes between the Supervisor Tier-0

that is configured with the Supervisor.

policies. You cannot assign storage policies that are not topology aware to the three-zone namespace.

Create vSphere Namespaces on VPCs without SNAT and Load Balancer
As a VI administrator or Tenant administrator, you can create vSphere Namespaces on VPCs that have do not have the
SNAT and load balancer configured.
vSphere Namespaces usually require load balancing and SNAT as most workloads require ingress/egress. However,
internal-only services, batch processing jobs, development, test environments, and deployments where each VM sits on a
public Subnet do not require access to the external network. In such environments, you can create vSphere Namespaces
on VPCs without SNAT and Load Balancer.
If you provision VKS clusters on vSphere Namespaces without SNAT and load balancers, the clusters might not deploy.
To prevent deployments from failing, a validation webhook runs a check on the network information in the NetworkInfo
custom resource.
Keep the following considerations in mind when SNAT or load balancers are not enabled:
• VMs. If SNAT is not enabled, network paths might be affected if VMS use Private or Private Gateway access modes.
Different VPCs or project can have the same Private or PrivateTGW CIDRs.
• If the load balancer is not activated, then the LoadBalancer-type services, including
VirtualMachineService
resources, cannot be deployed. For more information on load balancers, see NSX Native Load Balancers.
Clusters are created only if the following requirements are met:
• If NAT is disabled, the VKS cluster can only be created with .
accessmode: public
• If load balancer is disabled, the VKS cluster can only be created with a Custom ClusterClass.
Broadcom 6852

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Change Storage Settings on a vSphere Namespace
Storage policies assigned to a namespace in a Supervisor make persistent storage available to the DevOps team. These
storage policies control how persistent volumes and VKS cluster nodes are placed within vSphere datastores. As a VI
administrator, you typically assign storage policies when configuring the namespace. If you need to make any changes in
the initial storage policy assignments, perform this task.
• Before deleting a storage policy from vCenter or a vSphere Namespace, or changing the storage policy assignment,
make sure that no persistent volume claim with the corresponding storage class runs in the namespace. Also, ensure
that no VKS cluster is using the storage class.
• If the namespace is in a three-zone Supervisor, use topology aware policies. You cannot assign storage policies that
are not topology aware to the three-zone namespace.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

b) Click the Namespaces tab and click the namespace.
2. Click the Storage tab and click Storage Policies.
3. Click the Edit icon to change storage policy assignments.
Remove a Workload Network from a Supervisor
You can remove a secondary workload network from the Namespaces on the Supervisor.
1. In the vSphere Client, select Supervisor Management.
2. Under Supervisors, select the Supervisor and select Configure.
3. Select General to see a list of configured networks.
4. Select the network that you want to remove and click REMOVE.
You cannot remove the default network. When you remove a network, it is marked for deletion. You cannot deploy
new workloads on the removed network. Workloads running on the removed network continue to use it until they are
migrated to a different network. Once the workloads are migrated, the network is automatically removed.
Remove a vSphere Namespace from Supervisor
You can remove a vSphere Namespace from Supervisor.
• Remove any deployed workloads, including VMs, vSphere Pods, and VKS clusters.
• Required privileges:
– Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
– Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
1. From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
2. Click the Namespaces tab.
3. From the list of namespaces available on the Supervisor, select the vSphere Namespace you want to remove.
4. Click Remove.
The system removes the vSphere Namespace. It might take time for the process to complete.

string=vks-16&appid=sv-async&language=&format=rendered.

As a VI administrator, you can create a vSphere Namespace, set CPU, memory, and storage limits to the namespace,
assign permissions, and activate the namespace service on a cluster as a template. As a result, DevOps engineers can
create a vSphere Namespace in a self-service manner and deploy workloads within it.
Self-Service Namespace Creation and Configuration Workflow
As a VI administrator, you can create a vSphere Namespace, set CPU, memory, and storage limits to the namespace,
assign permissions, and provision or activate the namespace service on a cluster as a template.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

As a DevOps engineer, you can create a vSphere Namespace in a self-service manner and deploy workloads within it.
You can share it with other DevOps engineers or delete it when it is no longer required. To share the namespace with
other DevOps engineers, contact the VI administrator.

Create and Configure a Self-Service Namespace Template
As a VI administrator, you can create and configure a Supervisor Namespace as a self-service namespace template.
DevOps engineers can then create and delete Supervisor Namespaces using the command line.
kubectl
Enable a Supervisor.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the Supervisor.
2. Click the Configure tab, and select General under Supervisor.
3. Select Namespace Service.
4. Toggle the Status switch to enable the feature.
The Create Namespace Template page appears.
5. In the Configuration pane, configure resources for the namespace.
Option Description
CPU The amount of CPU resources to reserve for the namespace.
Memory The amount of memory to reserve for the namespace.
Storage The total amount of storage space to reserve for the namespace.
Storage Policy Storage policies to use with workloads that require persistent
storage.
Network From the Network drop-down menu, select a network for the
namespace.
VM Classes VM classes to deploy stand-alone VMs.
Content Libraries Content libraries with VM images to use for VM deployments.
6. Click Next.
7. In the Permissions pane, add DevOps engineers and groups to empower them to use the template to create
namespaces.
Select an identity source and a user or a group and click Next.
8. In the Review and Confirm pane, the properties you configure are displayed.
Review the properties and click Done.
A namespace template is configured and is in Active state. As a VI administrator, you can edit the template. DevOps
engineers can use the template to create namespaces.
Deactivate a Self-Service Namespace
As a VI administrator, you can deactivate a self-service namespace on the cluster.
When you deactivate a self-service namespace template, DevOps engineers cannot use the template to create new
namespaces on the cluster. They can delete the namespaces that they have already created.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the Supervisor.
2. Click the Configure tab, and select General under Supervisor.
3. In the Namespace Service pane, toggle the Status switch to deactivate the template.
4. To activate the template again, toggle the Status switch.
You can either create another self-service namespace or use the existing one.
Broadcom 6859

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Create a Self-Service Namespace
As a DevOps Engineer, you can create a self-service namespace and run workloads within it. Once you create the
namespace, you can share it with other DevOps Engineers or delete it when it is no longer required.
• Verify that a VI administrator has created and activated a self-service namespace template on the cluster. See Create
and Configure a Self-Service Namespace Template .
• Verify that you are added to the permissions list in the self-service namespace template either individually or as a
member of a group .
• Get the IP address of the Supervisor control plane.
1. Using the VCF CLI, authenticate with the Supervisor. See Connect to the Supervisor as a vCenter Single Sign-On
User.
IP-ADDRESS USERNAME
kubectl vsphere login --server= --vsphere-username
2. Switch context to the Supervisor.
SUPERVISOR-CLUSTER-IP
kubectl config use-context
3. Create a self-service namespace on the cluster.
NAMESPACE NAME
kubectl create namespace
For example
kubectl create namespace test-ns
Note:
Owner permissions are available to DevOps Engineers after you enable the Supervisor and upgrade the cluster. If
you have only upgraded vCenter and not the cluster, the DevOps engineers will only have edit permissions on the
namespaces.
The namespace that you create appears in the cluster. To share the namespace with other DevOps engineers, contact
the VI administrator.
Create a Self-Service Namespace with Annotations and Labels
DevOps engineers can create self-service namespaces with annotations and labels using the kubectl command line.
DevOps engineers can use a YAML manifest with user-defined annotations and labels.
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
kubectl vsphere login --server IP-ADDRESS-SUPERVISOR-CLUSTER --vsphere-username VCENTER-SSO-
USERNAME
2. Create a namespace YAML manifest file with annotations and labels.
kubectl create -f ns-create.yaml
For example, create the following file:
ns-create.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
name: test-ns-yaml
labels:
my-label: "my-label-val-yaml"
annotations:
my-ann-yaml: "my-ann-val-yaml"
3. Apply the YAML manifest.
kubectl create -f ns-create.yaml
Or
kubectl apply -f ns-create.yaml
Broadcom 6860

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Describe the namespace that you created to see the changes.
root@localhost [ /tmp ]# kubectl describe ns test-ns-yaml
Name: test-ns-yaml
Labels: my-label=my-label-val-yaml
vSphereClusterID=domain-c50

User.

NAMESPACE NAME
kubectl delete namespace

kubectl delete namespace test-ns
Add Security Policies to an NSX vSphere Namespace
A Supervisor that uses NSX networking supports network security policies configured through a security policy CRD.
Create a Security Policy
As a DevOps, you can configure the security policy CRD to apply an NSX based security policy to a Supervisor
namespace. The security policy protects traffic for vSphere Pods and VMs. VMs include VKS cluster nodes and other
VMs deployed in the Supervisor.
Use NSX version 3.2 or later.
1. Create a security policy CRD.
For the fields to use and CRD examples, see NSX Operator Security Policy CRD documentation on GitHub.
2. Access your namespace in the Kubernetes environment.
See Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
3. Apply the security policy to the namespace.
policy-name.yaml
kubectl apply -f
4. View your security policy.
a) View details for the security policy.
policy-name
kubectl get securitypolicy
b) View a description of your security policy.
policy-name
kubectl describe securitypolicy
You can also use the NSX UI to view details of your policy. For information, see the VMware NSX Documentation page.
Configuring and Managing vSphere Zones
Check out how to manage vSphere Zones in vCenter. After the initial deployment, you can then add more vSphere Zones
to the Supervisor and assign them to vSphere Namespaces. You can also increase the capacity of a vSphere Zone by
adding new clusters to it. To provide separation between the workload and management planes in your environment, you
can dedicate the vSphere Zones where the Supervisor runs to the management plane only and assign different vSphere
Zones to vSphere Namespaces for workloads only. You can also remove vSphere Zones from vSphere Namespaces and
the Supervisor.
Broadcom 6864

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Add a Cluster as a vSphere Zone to a Supervisor
You can add a vSphere Cluster as a vSphere Zone to a Supervisor and assign it as a workload zone to vSphere
Namespaces.
• Configure vSphere DRS in fully-automated mode to the cluster.
• Configure vSphere HA to the cluster.
• Configure shared storage with vSAN to a different solution to the cluster.
• Add the cluster to the same VDS where the Supervisor is connected.
• Required privileges:
– Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
– Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
• In NSX-based setup, the cluster must have connectivity to the same NSX overlay network as the Supervisor.
• In a VDS networking setup, verify that the cluster is connected to distributed port group that is configured as Workload
Network to the Supervisor.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the cluster that you want to add as a vSphere Zone to a Supervisor.
2. Select Actions > Add as a Zone to a Supervisor
3. Select New Zone and click Next.
4. Enter a vSphere Zone name and click Next.
5. Select the Supervisor where you want to add the zone and click Next.
6. Review your settings and click Finish.
The new zone is added to the Supervisor and you can add to vSphere Namespaces.
Add a New Cluster to an Existing vSphere Zone
You can expand the capacity of the existing vSphere Zones by adding a new vSphere cluster to them. vSphere
Namespaces that are already associated with the vSphere Zone will not use the newly-added cluster. Only when
you associate new vSphere Namespaces with the vSphere Zone, they can use the newly-added cluster for resource
utilization.
• Configure vSphere DRS in fully automated mode to the cluster.
• Configure vSphere HA to the cluster.
• Configure shared storage with vSAN to a different solution to the cluster.
• Add the cluster to the same VDS where the Supervisor is connected.
• Required privileges:
– Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
– Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
• In NSX based setup, the cluster must have connectivity to the same NSX overlay network as the Supervisor.
• In a VDS networking setup, verify that the cluster is connected to distributed port group that is configured as workload
network to the Supervisor.
• If you add the cluster to a vSphere Zone that is used for workloads.
– The cluster must have access to at least 1 datastore that is compatible with the storage policy that is configured with
the vSphere Namespaces the vSphere Zone is associated with.
• If you want to add the cluster to a vSphere Zone used for management.
– The cluster must be configured with the Supervisor management network.
– The cluster must have acces to at least one datastore that is compatible with the storage policy used for the
Supervisor control plane.
Broadcom 6865

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the vCenter instance.
2. Select vSphere Zones.
3. Right-click the zone to which you want to add a new cluster and select Associate cluster.
4. Select from clusters that are not associated with any vSphere zone.
5. Click Run Compatibility Check to determine which clusters do not meet the compatibility requirements for that zone.
If a cluster is not connected to the workload or management networks that are associated with the zone, an error is
displayed.
6. Click Associate cluster.
Add a vSphere Zone to a vSphere Namespace
You can configure up to three vSphere Zones to a vSphere Namespace in a Supervisor to increase the capacity for
running workarounds on the vSphere Namespace.
• Add a vSphere cluster as a zone to the Supervisor.
• Required privileges:
– Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
– Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Select Namespaces, and select the vSphere Namespace where you want to add the zone.
3. Select Zones and select Add Zone.
4. Select a zone that you want to add as a vSphere Zone to the vSphere Namespace and click Add Zone.
Remove a vSphere Zone from a vSphere Namespace
Check out how to remove a vSphere Zone from a vSphere Namespace in case you want to move it another vSphere
Namespace or stop using the zone for running containerized workloads.
• Migrate all the workloads currently running on the zone to a different zone or vSphere Namespace.
• Verity that there's at least one vSphere Zone that is assigned to the vSphere Namespace. You cannot remove a Zone
if it's the only zone that is assigned to the vSphere Namespace.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Select Namespaces, and select the vSphere Namespace that is associated with the Workload Zone that you want to
remove.
3. Select Zones.
4. Select the vSphere Zone that you want to remove and click Mark for Removal.
The vSphere Zone is marked for removal and you are unable to run any new workloads on it. The zone will be
automatically removed once it's empty of workloads, or after a few seconds in case it's emptied of workloads already.
Remove a vSphere Zone from a Supervisor
Remove a vSphere Zone from the Supervisor and respectively from all the vSphere Namespaces that are part of the
Supervisor. You cannot remove the vSphere Zone marked as Management where the Supervisor is running.
• Migrate all the workloads currently running on the zone to a different zone.
Note:
Migration of Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) and Persistent Volumes (PVs) to a different zone is not supported.
If you remove a zone, the PVC or PV from the removed zone cannot be used by a pod in a different zone.
• Verify that all vSphere Namespaces with which the vSphere Zone is associated have at least one different zone
configured.
Broadcom 6866

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Select Supervisors, and select the Supervisor from which you want to remove the vSphere Zone.
3. Select Zones.
4. Select the vSphere Zone that you want to remove and click Mark for Removal.
The vSphere Zone is marked for removal, and you are unable to run new workloads on it. The zone will be automatically
removed once it is removed from any other vSphere Namespaces it is associated with, or after a few seconds if there are
no vSphere Namespaces using it.
Remove a vSphere Cluster from a vSphere Zone
Remove a cluster from a vSphere Zone when you want to decommission the zone or to use the cluster resources in a
different zone. A vSphere Zone must have at least one cluster that is associated with it. You cannot remove a cluster from
a vSphere Zone if the cluster is the last remaining in that zone.
Workloads that are running on the custer that you remove will be migrated to the remaining clusters in the vSphere Zone.
The vSphere Zone must have enough resources to accommodate the workloads running on the cluster that you want to
remove.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the vCenter instance.
2. Select vSphere Zones.
3. Select the zone from which you want to remove a cluster.
4. Select the cluster that you want to remove and click Remove Cluster.
Once all the workloads are migrated from the cluster to be removed to the remaining clusters in the vSphere Zone, the
cluster is removed from the zone.n
