Configure Secure Login for vSphere Supervisor.
Configure Secure Login for vSphere Supervisor
To log in securely to the Supervisor and VKS clusters, configure VCF CLI with the appropriate TLS certificate and ensure
that you are running the latest edition of VCF CLI .
Supervisor CA Certificate
vSphere Supervisor supports vCenter Single Sign-On for cluster access by using the VCF CLI command
vcf context
. To install and use this utility, see Download and Install the VCF CLI.
create…
The VCF CLI defaults to secure login and requires a trusted certificate, the default being the certificate signed by the
vCenter root CA. Although the CLI supports the flag, for security reasons this is not
--insecure-skip-tls-verify
recommended.
To securely log in to the Supervisor and VKS clusters by using the VCF CLI, you have two options:
Option Instructions
Download and install the vCenter root CA certificate on each client Refer to the Broadcom knowledge base article How to download
machine. and install vCenter root certificates.
Replace the VIP certificate used for the Supervisor with a See Replace the VIP Certificate to Securely Connect to the API
certificate signed by a CA each client machine trusts. Endpoint in the Supervisor documentation.
Note:
For additional information on vSphere authentication, including vCenter Single Sign-On, managing and rotating
vCenter certificates, and troubleshooting authentication, see the vSphere Authentication documentation. For more
information about vSphere Supervisor certificates, see Broadcom Knowledge Base article 323421.
VKS Cluster CA Certificate
To connect securely with the VKS cluster using the VCF CLI, you download the VKS cluster CA certificate. Although the
CLI supports the flag, for security reasons this is not recommended.
--insecure-skip-tls-verify
For details on connecting to the VKS cluster, see Connect to a VKS Cluster with VCF CLI.
Connect to the Supervisor as a vCenter Single Sign-On User
To provision vSphere Pods, VKS clusters, or VMs, you connect to the Supervisor using the VCF CLI and authenticate with
your vCenter Single Sign-On credentials.
• Get your vCenter Single Sign-On credentials from the VI administrator.
• Get the IP address of the Supervisor control plane from the VI administrator.
• To log in by using an FQDN instead of the control plane IP address, get an FQDN configured during the Supervisor
enablement.
• Get the name of the vSphere Namespace for which you have permissions.
• Get confirmation that you have Edit permissions on the vSphere Namespace to be able to perform such actions as
create resources in the namespace.
• Download and Install the VCF CLI.
Broadcom 6869

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Verify that the certificate served by the Supervisor is trusted on your system, either by having the signing CA installed
as a Trust Root or by adding the certificate as a Trust Root directly. See Configure Secure Login for Supervisor
Clusters.
After you log in to the Supervisor, the VCF CLI generates the context for the Supervisor. Configuration context contains a
Supervisor, a vSphere Namespace, and a user. You can view the cluster context in the file in the user's
.kube/config
home directory. This file is commonly called the file.
kubeconfig
Note:
If you have an existing file, it is appended with each Supervisor context. The VCF CLI respects the
kubeconfig
KUBECONFIG environment variable that kubectl itself uses. Although not required, it can be useful to set this
variable before running , so that the information is written to a new file, instead of
vcf context create...
being added to your current file.
kubeconfig
1. To view the command syntax and options for logging in, run the following command.
vcf context create --help
2. To connect to the Supervisor, run the following command, using the Supervisor IP address or FQDN as the endpoint.
vcf context create --endpoint <SUPERVISOR-ADDRESS> --username <VCENTER-SSO-USER> --ca-certificate <PATH-
TO-CERTIFICATE-FILE>
For example:
vcf context create --endpoint 10.92.42.13 --username administrator@example.com --ca-certificate ~/
ca_root.cert
vcf context create --endpoint wonderland.example.com --username administrator@example.com --ca-certificate
~/ca_root.cert
This action creates a configuration file with the JSON Web Token (JWT) to authenticate to the Kubernetes API.
3. To authenticate, enter the password for the user.
You can also set an environment variable with the password value.
VCF_CLI_VSPHERE_PASSWORD
After you connect to the Supervisor, you can view the configuration contexts that are accessible to you.
4. To view details of your configuration contexts, run the following command:
vcf context list
The CLI displays the details for each available context.
5. To switch between contexts, use the following command:
vcf context use <example-context-name>
You can now connect to a VKS cluster as a vCenter Single Sign-On user.

Connect to a VKS cluster using the VCF Consumption CLI.

• Get your vCenter Single Sign-On credentials.
• Get the IP address of the Supervisor control plane.
• Get the name of the vSphere Namespace.
• Download and Install the VCF Consumption CLI.
After you log in to the VKS cluster, the VCF CLI generates the context for the cluster. In Kubernetes, a configuration
context contains a cluster, a namespace, and a user. You can view the cluster context in the file . This file
.kube/config
is commonly called the file.
kubeconfig
Note:
If you have an existing file, it is appended with each cluster context. The VCF CLI respects the
kubeconfig
KUBECONFIG environment variable that kubectl itself uses. Although not required, it can be useful to set this
variable before running so that the information is written to a new file, instead of
vcf context create...
being added to your current file.
kubeconfig
Broadcom 6870

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Log in to a VKS Cluster Using vCenter Single Sign-On Credentials
Follow these steps to log in to the VKS cluster using vCenter Single Sign-On credentials and create CLI context. The
context allows you to use other VCF CLI commands to manage the cluster.
1. To view the command syntax and options for logging in, run the following command.
vcf context create --help
2. To connect to the VKS cluster, run the following command.
vcf context create --endpoint <SUPERVISOR-ADDRESS> --username <VCENTER-SSO-USER> --ca-certificate <PATH-
TO-CERTIFICATE-FILE> --workload-cluster-name <VKS-CLUSTER-NAME> --workload-cluster-namespace <VSPHERE-
NAMESPACE>
For example,
vcf context create --endpoint 10.92.42.137 --username operator@example.com --ca-certificate ~/ca_root.cert
--workload-cluster-name vks-cluster-01 --workload-cluster-namespace vks-cluster-ns
Or, if the Supervisor has been enabled with a fully qualified domain name (FQDN):
vcf context create --endpoint wonderland.example.com --username operator@example.com --ca-certificate ~/
ca_root.cert --workload-cluster-name vks-cluster-01 --workload-cluster-namespace vks-cluster-ns
This action creates a configuration file with the JSON Web Token (JWT) to authenticate to the Kubernetes API.
3. To authenticate, enter your vCenter Single Sign-On password.
You can also set an environment variable with the password value.
VCF_CLI_VSPHERE_PASSWORD
If the operation is successful, you see the message , and you can run kubectl
Logged in successfully
commands against the cluster. If the command returns , it usually means you
Error from server (Forbidden)
do not have the required permissions.
4. To get a list of contexts available to you, run the following command.
vcf context list
This command lists the configuration contexts you have access to. You see a configuration context for the target
cluster, such as .
vcf-cluster-01
5. To use the context for the target cluster, run the following command.
vcf context use <example-context-name>
Log in Using the VKS Cluster Plugin
Alternatively, you can log in using the cluster plugin of VCF CLI. This method works with the Identity Provider (IdP)
configured on the Supervisor cluster.
1. To view the command syntax and options for logging in, run the following command.
vcf context create --help
2. Connect to the Supervisor and activate the namespace context that has the VKS cluster.
For information, see Connect to the Supervisor as a vCenter Single Sign-On User.
3. Check if the cluster plugin is installed.
vcf plugin list
You see all plugins installed on your system. Look for the cluster plugin in the list.
4. If the cluster plugin is not installed, run the following command.
vcf plugin install cluster
5. Use the cluster plugin to create a kubecontext for the VKS cluster.
vcf cluster kubeconfig get <VKS-CLUSTER-NAME> --export-file <PATH-TO-VKS-KUBECONFIG-FILE>
Broadcom 6871

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For example,
vcf cluster kubeconfig get vks-cluster-01 --export-file ~/vks_kube_config
6. After successful context creation, to list cluster nodes, run the following command.
kubectl get nodes --kubeconfig <PATH-TO-VKS-KUBECONFIG-FILE>
You see the control plane and worker nodes in this cluster.
7. To list all the cluster pods, run the following command.
kubectl get pods -A --kubeconfig <PATH-TO-VKS-KUBECONFIG-FILE>
You see all the pods in this cluster across all Kubernetes namespaces that you have access to. If you have not
deployed any workloads, you do not see any pods in the default namespace.
Grant Developer Access to VKS Clusters
Developers are the target users of Kubernetes. Once a VKS cluster is provisioned, you can grant developer access using
vCenter Single Sign-On authentication.
Authentication for Developers
A cluster administrator can grant cluster access to other users, such as developers. Developers can deploy pods to
clusters directly using their user accounts, or indirectly using service accounts.
• For user account authentication, VKS clusters support vCenter Single Sign-On users and groups. The user or group
can be local to the vCenter, or synchronized from a supported directory server.
• For service account authentication, you can use service tokens. For more information, see the Kubernetes
documentation.
Adding Developer Users to a Cluster
To grant cluster access to developers:
1. Define a or for the user or group and apply it to the cluster. For more information, see the
Role ClusterRole
Kubernetes documentation at
Using RBAC Authorization.
2. Create a or for the user or group and apply it to the cluster. See the following
RoleBinding ClusterRoleBinding
example.
Example
RoleBinding
To grant access to a vCenter Single Sign-On user or group, the subject in the must contain either of the
RoleBinding
following values for the parameter.
name
Table 1793: Supported User and Group Fields
Field Description
sso: USER-NAME @ DOMAIN For example, a local user name, such as sso:joe@vsphere.
local.
sso: GROUP-NAME @ DOMAIN For example, a group name from a directory server integrated with
the vCenter, such as sso:devs@ldap.example.com.
The following example RoleBinding binds the vCenter Single Sign-On local user named Joe to the default ClusterRole
named . This role permits read/write access to most objects in a namespace, in this case the namespace.
edit default
kind: RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:

namespace: default

name: edit #Default ClusterRole

Configuring and Managing a Supervisor
As a VI administrator, you enable a vSphere cluster as a Supervisor. You can select between creating the Supervisor
with the vSphere networking stack or with VMware NSX (NSX) as the networking solution. A cluster configured with NSX
supports running a vSphere Pod and a VKS cluster created through the vSphere Kubernetes Service. A Supervisor that is
configured with the vSphere networking stack only supports VKS clusters.
After you enable the Supervisor, you can use the vSphere Client to manage and monitor the cluster.
Replace the VIP Certificate to Securely Connect to the Supervisor API Endpoint
As a VI administrator, you can replace the certificate for the virtual IP address (VIP) to securely connect to the Supervisor
API endpoint with a certificate signed by a CA that your hosts already trust. The certificate authenticates the Kubernetes
control plane to DevOps engineers, both during login and subsequent interactions with the Supervisor.
Verify that you have access to a CA that can sign CSRs. For DevOps engineers, the CA must be installed on their system
as a trusted root.
For more information about the Supervisor certificate, see Supervisor CA Certificate.

Figure 519: Replacing Supervisor default certificate
5. Provide the details for the certificate.
Note:
If you use an identity provider service, you must also include the entire certificate chain. The chain is not required
for standard HTTPS traffic, however.
6. Once the CSR is generated, click Copy.
7. Sign the certificate with a CA.
8. From the Workload Platform Management pane, select Actions > Replace Certificate.
9. Upload the signed certificate file and click Replace Certificate.

successfully by using the browser. On a Linux or Unix system you can also use
echo | openssl s_client -
.
connect <SUPERVISOR_VIP_IP>:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -text -noout

Configuring HTTP Proxy Settings in vSphere Supervisor
Checkout how to configure HTTP proxy settings to the Supervisor and VKS clusters and what is the workflow for
configuring a proxy when you register the Supervisor and VKS clusters with Tanzu Misson control.
You can configure a proxy to the Supervisor through the vSphere Client, the Cluster Management API, or DCLI
commands. You can use a proxy if you need to handle container traffic or image pulling from networks external to the
Supervisor. For on-premises Supervisors that you register as management clusters in Tanzu Mission Control, you use an
HTTP proxy for image pulling and container traffic .
Configuring Proxy Settings on Newly-Created vSphere 7.0 Update 3 and Later Supervisors
For newly-created Supervisors on a vSphere 7.0 Update 3 and later environment, HTTP proxy settings are inherited
from vCenter. No matter if you create the Supervisors before or after you configure HTTP proxy settings on vCenter, the
settings are inherited by the clusters.
See Configure the DNS, IP Address, and Proxy Settings in the vSphere documentation to learn how to configure the
HTTP proxy settings on vCenter.
You can also override the inherited HTTP proxy configuration on individual Supervisors through the vSphere Client,
Cluster Management API, or DCLI.
Since inheriting the vCenter proxy settings is the default configuration for newly-created vSphere 7.0.3 Supervisors, you
can also use the Cluster Management API or DCLI to not inherit any HTTP proxy settings in case the Supervisors don't
require a proxy, but vCenter still does.
Configuring Proxy Settings on Supervisors Upgraded to vSphere 7.0 Update 3 and Later
If you have upgraded your Supervisors to vSphere 7.0 Update 3 and later, the HTTP proxy settings of vCenter are not
automatically inherited. In that case, you configure proxy settings Supervisors by using the vSphere Client,
vcenter/
API, or DCLI command line.
namespace-management/clusters
Broadcom 6884

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configuring HTTP Proxy to VKS Clusters in vSphere Supervisor
Use one of the following methods to configure a proxy to your VKS clusters in vSphere Supervisor:
• Configure proxy settings to individual VKS clusters.
• Create a global proxy configuration that will be applied to all VKS clusters.
Note:
If you use Tanzu Mission Control to manage your VKS clusters, you do not have to configure proxy settings
through the cluster YAML file in vSphere Supervisor. You can configure proxy settings when you add the VKS
clusters as workload clusters to Tanzu Mission Control.
Configure HTTP Proxy Setting on the Supervisor by Using the vSphere Client
Checkout how to configure HTTP proxy settings to the Supervisor through the vSphere Client. You can override the proxy
settings inherited from vCenter on individual Supervisors or select not to use any proxy settings at all.
• Verify that you have the Modify cluster-wide configuration privilege on the cluster.

2. Under Supervisors, select the Supervisor, and select Configure.
3. Select Network, expand Proxy Configuration, and click Edit
4. Select Configure proxy settings on Supervisor and enter the proxy settings.
Option Description

certificates. Enter the bundle in plain text.

names that do not require the proxy server and can be accessed
directly.

5. Click OK.
The proxy settings you configured on this Supervisor override the settings inherited from vCenter.

Configuring HTTP Proxy Settings on the Supervisor and VKS Clusters for Tanzu Mission
Control
To configure an HTTP proxy on Supervisors that you want to register as management clusters with Tanzu Mission Control,
follow the steps:
1. In vSphere, configure HTTP proxy on Supervisors by either inheriting the HTTP proxy settings from vCenter, or
configuring proxy settings on individual Supervisors through the vSphere Client, Namespace Management Clusters
APIs, or DCLI command line.

Cluster. See Register a Management Cluster with Tanzu Mission Control and Complete the Registration of a
Supervisor Cluster in the in the VMware Tanzu Mission Control Product Documentation.
To configure an HTTP proxy to VKS clusters that you provision or add as workload clusters in Tanzu Mission Control:
1. Create a proxy configuration object with the proxy settings that you want to use
with VKS clusters. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/bin/gethidpage?ux-context-
string=vsphclient_001&appid=vsphere-9-1&language=&format=rendered.
2. Use that proxy configuration object when you provision or add VKS clusters as workload clusters. See Provision a
Cluster and Add a Workload Cluster into Tanzu Mission Control Management in the VMware Tanzu Mission Control
Product Documentation
Configure an External Identity Provider for VKS Clusters
You can configure Supervisor with any OIDC-compliant identity provider (IDP), such as Okta. To complete the integration,
you configure the IDP with the callback URL for Supervisor.
Supported External Identity Provider
You can configure Supervisor with any OIDC-compliant identity provider. The table lists common ones and includes links
for configuration instructions.
External IDP Configuration
Okta Configure Okta as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
Workspace ONE Configure Workspace ONE Access as an OIDC provider for
Pinniped
Dex Configure Dex as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
GitLab Configure GitLab as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
Google OAuth Using Google OAuth 2
Configuring the IDP with the Callback URL for Supervisor
Supervisor acts as an OAuth 2.0 client to the external identity provider. The Supervisor callback URL is the redirect URL
used to configure the external IDP. The callback URL takes the form https://SUPERVISOR-VIP/wcp/pinniped/callback.
If the IP portion of the callback URL is represented as a fully qualified domain name (FQDN), ensure that the DNS server
used by both the Supervisor and the VKS can resolve the FQDN to the correct virtual IP (VIP).
Note:
When performing the IDP registration, the callback URL might be called the "redirect URL" in the OIDC provider
you are configuring.
When configuring the external identity provider for use with VKS on Supervisor, you supply the external identity provider
with the Callback URL that is available in vCenter at Supervisor Management > Supervisors > Configure > Identity
Providers screen.

Register an External Identity Provider with Supervisor
To connect to VKS clusters on Supervisor using an external identity provider, register your identity provider with
Supervisor.
Prerequisites
Before you register an external identity provider with Supervisor, complete the following prerequisites:
• Enable Supervisor Management and deploy a Supervisor instance.
• Configure an external OpenID Connect identity provider with the Supervisor callback URL. See Configure an External
Identity Provider for VKS Clusters.
• Get the Client ID, Client Secret, and Issuer URL from the external IDP. See Configure an External Identity Provider for
VKS Clusters.
Register an External Identity Provider with Supervisor
Supervisor runs as pods the Pinniped Supervisor and the Pinniped Concierge components. VKS clusters run as pods the
Pinniped Concierge component only. For more information about these components and how they interact, refer to the
Pinniped authentication service documentation.
Once you register an external identity provider with Supervisor, the system updates the Pinniped Supervisor and Pinniped
Concierge pods on Supervisor and the Pinniped Concierge pods on VKS clusters. All VKS clusters running on that
Supervisor instance are automatically configured with that same external identity provider.
To register an external ODIC provider with Supervisor, complete the following procedure:
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client.
2. Select Supervisor Management > Supervisors > Configure > Identity Providers.
3. Click the plus sign to begin the registration process.
4. Configure the provider. See Identity Provider Configuration.
Figure 533: OIDC Provider Configuration
5. Configure OAuth 2.0 client details. See OAuth 2.0 Client Details.
Broadcom 6895

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 534: OAuth 2.0 Client Details
6. Configure additional settings. See Additional Settings.
7. Confirm provider settings.
Figure 535: Confirm Provider Settings
8. Click Finish to complete the OIDC provider registration.
Broadcom 6896

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Change Storage Settings on the Supervisor
Storage policies assigned to the Supervisor manage how such objects as a control plane VM, vSphere Pod ephemeral
disk, and container image cache are placed within datastores in the vSphere storage environment. As a VI administrator,
you typically configure storage policies when enabling the Supervisor. If you need to make any changes in the storage
policy assignments after initial Supervisor configuration, perform this task. You can also use this task to activate or
deactivate file volume support for ReadWriteMany persistent volumes in VKS clusters.
If you plan to activate file volume support on VKS clusters for persistent volumes in ReadWriteMany mode, make sure
to activate vSAN File Services must be enabled on the vSAN cluster. For additional information, follow the guidelines
in Using vSAN File Service to Create ReadWriteMany Volumes in Supervisor Environment in the vSphere Supervisor
Services and Workloads documentation.
Generally, the changes you make to the storage settings apply only to new objects in Supervisor. If you use this procedure
to activate file volume support in VKS clusters, you can do it for the existing clusters.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Click the Supervisors tab and select the Supervisor to edit from the list.
3. Click the Configure tab and click Storage.
Figure 536: Updating Supervisor storage settings
4. Change storage policy assignments for the control plane VMs.
If your environment supports a vSphere Pod, you can also change storage policies for an ephemeral virtual disk and
container image cache.
Option Description
Control Plane Node Select the storage policy for placement of the control plane VMs.
Pod Ephemeral Disks Select the storage policy for placement of the vSphere Pods.
Container Image Cache Select the storage policy for placement of the cache of container
images.
Broadcom 6898

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. Enable file volume support to deploy ReadWriteMany persistent volumes.
This option is available only if your environment has been configured with vSAN File Service. See Enable vSAN File
Service in the vSAN Administration guide.
Modify the List of Supervisor Control Plane DNS Names
Checkout how to modify the list of FQDNs for accessing the Supervisor control plane. You can provide a list of Supervisor
FQDNs during the Supervisor enablement and later update that list. You can also set a list Supervisor FQDNs if you did
not provide one during the Supervisor enablement.
Use the following DCLI command to update the list of FQDNs for the Supervisor control plane:
dcli com vmware vcenter namespacemanagement clusters update --cluster <cluster_ID> --master-dns-name <FQDN 1>
--master-dns-name <FQDN_2>
• To add a new FQDN to the list you pass the already existing names as arguments as well as add the new FQDN.
• To remove an FQDN from the list, you call the command by omitting the FQDN that you want to remove and
update
passing the rest of the FQDNs that you want to keep.
For a three-zone Supervisor you can pass the ID of any of the clusters that are part of the Supervisor.
In the following example, the Supervisor running on cluster is already configured with an FQDN
domain-c50
. You are adding a new FQDN to the list of DNS names for the
supervisor.acme.com supervisor.vmware.com
Supervisor:
dcli com vmware vcenter namespacemanagement clusters update --cluster domain-c50 --master-dns-name
supervisor.acme.com --master-dns-name supervisor.vmware.com
• The VIP certificate to securely connect to the Supervisor is not automatically updated with the new FQDNs. Therefore,
you need to do that manually, see Replace the VIP Certificate to Securely Connect to the Supervisor API Endpoint.
• Once you update the VIP certificate to connect to the Supervisor, log in to the Supervisor control plane by using the
newly-added FQDNs. See Connect to the Supervisor as a vCenter Single Sign-On User

You can change the default key size of the Supervisor internal certificates. The Supervisor generates certificates that
arae used for securing internal communication between its components. For example, ,
authproxy apiserver,
scheduler, , and others. All of these components use their own certificates with a default algorithm and key size
etcd
of RSA-2048, which you can change. The default certificate size is 3072 bits for a greenfield VCF deployment and

• Upgrade vCenter to VCF 9.1.

Configuring a Supervisor Management Proxy
The Supervisor Management Proxy allows workloads to access components that are exposed in the VCF management
domain. Currently, components in VCF that run workloads requiring access on the VCF management domain include the
software depot component, AVI controller, VCF Operations for Networks, and VCF Operations for gathering VKS cluster
metrics. Workloads that can require access to the Supervisor management network are VKS cluster nodes, vSphere
Pods, and VMs created by using the VM Service.
Components that run workloads requiring access to the VCF management domain are called management services.
Every management service has access grants assigned for the workloads it runs. An access grant is the combination from
the vSphere Namespace and workload types that are given access to the VCF management domain.
Create Management Services on the Supervisor
You create management services to provide access of workloads running on the Supervisor to the VCF management
domain.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Click the Supervisors tab and select the Supervisor to edit from the list.
3. Click the Configure tab select .
Network
4. Click Add Management Service.
5. Enter a name and a description for the management service.
6. Enter the IP address of the endpoint of the management service.
7. Configure ports and certificates for the management service.
8. Click Add.
Create access grants for the new management service.
Create Access Grants for Management Services on the Supervisor
You add access grants to management services to provide access to the VCF management domain to the workloads
running in the management service.
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor Management.
2. Click the Supervisors tab and select the Supervisor to edit from the list.
3. Click the Configure tab select .
Network
4. Select from the available network services and click Add Access Grant.
5. Select the vSphere Namespace to which you want to configure access grants to management services.
6. Select the scope for access grant.
You select virtual machine and vSphere Pods. Virtual machines include nodes of VKS clusters and VMs created by
using the VM Service.

Maintenance Mode for a Datastore Used by Supervisor
Starting with vSphere 9.0, you can decommission a datastore that is used for different Supervisor workloads. To do this,
you need to place the datastore in maintenance mode.
Requirements
• vSphere 9.0 or later.
• Supervisor is enabled.
• Storage DRS is enabled. It is enabled only to support the datastore decommissioning and maintenance mode
migration flow, and is not required for standard stable-state operations.
• The datastore is not part of a vSAN cluster or shared across multiple vCenter instances.
Prerequisites
Before putting the datastore in maintenance mode, make sure to follow these guidelines.
• Wait for ongoing operations on the datastore to complete, or cancel them manually.
• Do not create new content libraries on the datastore.
• Stop adding new items to any content library that resides on the datastore.
• Identify any applications that create First Class Disks (FCDs) independently, for example, OpenStack or direct API use.
Prepare to migrate, back up and restore, or delete these FCDs as needed.
• For vSphere Pods not managed by deployments or stateful sets, prepare to recreate them manually from spec or
pipeline.
• Unmount all ISO or shared images attached to VMs, VM Service VMs, vSphere Pods, and content libraries on the
datastore.
• For vSAN clusters, verify that sufficient capacity and the required number of vSAN nodes meet the storage policy in
use before initiating maintenance mode. Use the vSAN maintenance mode pre-check to confirm the cluster can satisfy
all existing storage policies after the host is removed.
Migrating Storage Components
A Supervisor or VKS deployment involves four distinct storage components. Before putting the datastore in maintenance
mode, account for each component and its migration method.
Broadcom 6902

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Before starting a migration, verify storage policy assignments, namespace configuration, and available capacity on the
destination datastore. See Migrate Persistent Volumes.
Note:
If only virtual disks backing persistent volumes reside on the datastore, but no VMs, the system does not warn
you before entering maintenance mode. Migrate those volumes before putting the datastore in maintenance mode
to avoid accidentally deleting a datastore that still contains active volumes.
Component Description Migration method
Virtual disks for the Supervisor control
Supervisor cluster VM VMDKs Automatic
plane VMs
PVCs used by Supervisor services,
Supervisor PVCs Manual, backup and restore
including vSphere Pod VMs
Virtual disks for VKS controller and worker
VKS cluster node VMDKs Automatic
node VMs
VKS cluster workload PVCs Application PVCs in VKS clusters Manual, backup and restore
For PVCs, use a backup and restore solution to migrate workloads to the destination datastore. For additional information,
see KB 319402.
Automatic Migrations
When the datastore enters maintenance mode, the system automatically migrates the following items. No administrator
actions are required.
• VMs with attached VMDKs.
• Supervisor VM Service VMs.
• VKS clusters.
Manual Migration
The following items require manual handling by an administrator. After the datastore enters the maintenance mode, you
must perform a number of tasks to migrate several of these items manually.
• Content library images.
• Standalone FCDs not attached to any VMs.
• vSphere Pods
• Orphaned or unused items in the datastore:
– Unregistered or orphaned VMs.
– Orphaned VMDKs.
– Stale VM snapshots.
– Orphaned Supervisor images and snapshots.
– Orphaned vSphere Pods image disks.
– ISO images.
Place a Datastore Used by Supervisor in Maintenance Mode
Begin the process by placing the Supervisor datastore into maintenance mode. This action triggers automatic migration
for supported workloads.
1. Browse to the datastore in the vSphere Client.
2. Right-click the datastore and select Maintenance Mode > Enter Maintenance Mode.
A list of recommendations appears for datastore maintenance mode migration.
Broadcom 6903

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. Optional: On the Recommendations tab, review the recommendations and deselect any recommendations you do
not want to apply.
Note:
The datastore cannot enter maintenance mode without evacuating all disks. If you deselect the recommendations,
you must manually move all disks before entering maintenance mode.
4. Check the Faults tab for any VM artifacts that cannot be migrated.
5. Click Continue to initiate migration using Storage vMotion.
After you place the datastore in maintenance mode, perform additional manual migration tasks.
Migrate vSphere Pods
Manually delete and prepare to recreate vSphere Pods that are not automatically handled during datastore maintenance.
1. Identify the datastore MoID.
2. Go to the following URL to list all vSphere Pods using the datastore.
https://<VC>/mob/?moid=<datastore-moid>
3. Use the command to remove the vSphere Pods.
kubectl delete
kubectl delete pods <pod-name> --namespace <namespace>
4. Delete dangling image disks after vSphere Pods deletion.
kubectl delete imagedisk <imagedisk>
vSphere Pods that are part of a deployment or stateful set will restart automatically. vSphere Pods that are deployed
outside of deployments or stateful sets are not recreated. You must manually recreate them.
Migrate Content Library Images
Move all content library data from the datastore and ensure no ISO images remain mounted to dependent VMs.
1. In the vSphere Client, select the datastore and click the Files tab.
2. Filter by folder name: .
contentlib-
3. Identify all content libraries present on the datastore.
4. For each library, perform the following steps.
Ensure the correct source and destination datastores are selected. Unmount any ISOs from VMs or VM Service VMs
before migration.
a) Click Actions > Migrate.
b) Ensure the correct source and destination datastores are selected.
c) Unmount any ISOs from VMs or VM Service VMs before migration.
Migrate Detached FCDs
Manually migrate First Class Disks (FCDs) that are not attached to VMs, using different methods depending on whether
they are managed by CNS or not.
To access and migrate CNS-managed FCDs, make sure that you have the ServiceProviderUsers role.
Note:
FCDs that are attached to VM Service VMs or vSphere Pods are migrated automatically with a corresponding VM
and placed in the VM folder.
1. Migrate FCDs managed by CNS.
For more information, see Monitoring and Migrating Persistent Volumes in Supervisor Environment.
Broadcom 6904

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a) In the vSphere Client, navigate to the datastore cluster, and click Monitor > Container Volumes.
b) Select the volumes and click Migrate.
c) Select the destination datastore, and confirm.
2. Migrate FCDs not managed by CNS.
a) Go to the following URL:
https://<VC>/mob/?moid=VStorageObjectManager
b) Use the method with the datastore MoID to get a list of FCD IDs.
ListVStorageObject
c) Use the method to move each FCD.
RelocateVStorageObject_Task
Enter the FCD ID, source, and destination datastore MoIDs.
Decommissioning a Supervisor Cluster
VCF does not support decommissioning a vSphere cluster while a Supervisor is active on the cluster or zone. You must
disable the Supervisor before decommissioning the cluster or zone.
Disable the Supervisor only after you have completed this workflow:
1. Delete all workloads running in VKS clusters in the affected zone.
For information about workloads, see Deploying Workloads on VKS Clusters.
2. Delete all VKS clusters in the affected namespaces.
See Delete a VKS Cluster Using Kubectl or Using VCF CLI.
3. Remove all Supervisor namespaces.
See Remove a vSphere Namespace from Supervisor.
4. Disable the Supervisor on the cluster or zone.
See Disable a Supervisor.

Monitoring and Migrating Persistent Volumes in Supervisor Environment
As a vSphere administrator, you can use the vSphere Client to view details and monitor key metrics related to persistent
volumes, such as PV health status, storage compliance status, and binding information. You can identify potential issues
like PV detachment or storage non-compliance and, if needed, remediate the issues by reapplying the storage policy or
migrating the volume to another datastore.
Monitor and Manage Persistent Volumes
Use the vSphere Client to display persistent volumes and review their details.
For information about using to identify orphaned volumes, see Identify and Remove Orphaned Volumes.
govc
To monitor datastores, see Monitor Datastore Capacity.

a) From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
b) Click the Namespaces tab, and select the namespace from the list.
2. Click the Storage tab and click Persistent Volume Claims.
The vSphere Client lists all persistent volume claim objects and corresponding volumes available in the namespace.
3. To view details of a selected persistent volume, click the name of the volume in the Name column.
The Container Volumes panel opens.
4. Click the Details icon, and switch between the tabs.
The tabs display the following information related to the Kubernetes persistent volume.
Item Description

Volume ID An ID of the volume.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Item Description
Volume Path Path to the virtual disk that backs the volume. The path includes the datastore
name, the folder on the datastore, and the name of the disk. For example,
[sharedVmfs-0] fcd/1b325557eb7f4a0991fb47ab1f32f74d.vmdk.
Pod or VM Name of the pod or VM that uses the volume.
You can click the link to display the item in the vSphere inventory.
Datastore Datastore where the virtual disk that backs the volume resides.
You can click the link to display the datasotre in the inventory. Use the datastore
browser to navigate to the virtual disk. See Using Datastore Browser in vSphere
Environment in vSphere Storage.
Storage Policy The storage policy that the volume uses.
Compliance Status The storage compliance status of the volume.
Health Status The health status of the volume.
Namespace The namespace where the volume resides.
Persistent Volume Claim Information related to the persistent volume claim bound to the volume.
Physical Placement The device information, such as name, identifier or UUID, number of devices used for
a persistent volume, and how it is mirrored across hosts.
Performance You can use vSAN performance service to monitor the performance of your vSAN
environment, and investigate potential problems. For more information, see the
Monitoring vSAN Performance documentation.
For more details, see https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article?legacyId=90607.
Check Health and Storage Compliance Status of a Persistent Volume
On the Basics tab, you can check the health status of the persistent volume. You can also check its storage compliance
status and reapply the storage policy if the status is out of date.
1. Click the Basics tab and verify the health status of the volume.
Health Status Description
Accessible The persistent volume is accessible and available for use.
Inaccessible The persistent volume is inaccessible and cannot be used. For example, the volume
becomes inaccessible if the datastore that stores the volume cannot be reached by the
hosts that connect to the datastore.
2. Verify the storage compliance status.
You can see one of the following statuses in the Compliance Status column.
Compliance Status Description
Compliant The datastore where the virtual disk backing the volume resides has the storage
capabilities that the policy requires.
Out of Date This status indicates that the policy has been edited, but the new storage requirements
have not been communicated to the datastore. To communicate the changes, reapply
the policy to the volume that is out of date.
Broadcom 6908

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Compliance Status Description
Noncompliant The datastore supports specified storage requirements, but cannot currently satisfy
the storage policy. For example, the status might become Noncompliant when
physical resources of the datastore are unavailable. You can bring the datastore into
compliance by making changes in the physical configuration of your host cluster, for
example by adding hosts or disks to the cluster. If additional resources satisfy the
storage policy, the status changes to Compliant.
If you cannot bring the datastore in the compliance, you can migrate the volume to a
compliant datastore.
Not Applicable The storage policy references datastore capabilities that are not supported by the
datastore.
3. If the compliance status is Out of Date, select the volume and click Reapply Policy.
The status changes to Compliant.
Migrate Persistent Volumes
In the Supervisor environment, you can use the vSphere Client to migrate persistent volumes to a different datastore.
For example, you might need to migrate a volume when its current datastore can no longer satisfy the volume storage
requirements.
• Make sure that the original and target datastore is accessible to all Supervisor nodes. This applies to one-zone and
three-zone deployments.
For example, in a single-zone deployment, the target datastore must be shared across the nodes. The system doesn't
prevent you from moving a volume from shared storage to non-shared storage, but the volume becomes inaccessible,
which can affect the apps that use the volume.
• Ensure that a storage policy covering the target datastore is assigned to the namespace. If the target datastore uses a
different storage policy than the source, assign both policies to the namespace before starting the migration.
• If a volume is attached to a VM, the VM remains locked during volume relocation. If the volume you relocate is
attached to a node VM, such as the VKS node, the system does not allow any other control operations on the VM. The
operations include attaching or detaching other volumes to the VM, migrating the VM to a different datastore, changing
any configuration of the VM, and so on.
• Because PMEM datastores are not supported, attempts to relocate a volume to a PMEM datastore fail.
• The target datastore must have sufficient free capacity to accommodate the migrated volume. If the free space of a
datastore is less than the volume size, you cannot select the datastore for migration.
• The system does not support storage policy changes during the migration operation. However, the system doesn’t
prevent you from selecting a target datastore that is not compatible with the volume policy.
For additional details and known issues, see the following Broadcom Knowledge Base articles:
• 313416
Broadcom 6909

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• 313308
• 319402
Note:
When VMs reside on a datastore, the system alerts you and prevents the task from completion if you attempt
to put the datastore into maintenance mode. However, if virtual disks backing persistent volumes are on the
datastore, it can enter maintenance mode without warning. This means no safeguards prevent you from deleting a
datastore in maintenance mode that still contains active volumes. To avoid accidentally deleting such a datastore,
consider migrating the volumes to a different datastore before putting the original datastore into maintenance.
1. In the Container Volumes panel, select the volume or several volumes and click the Migrate button.
2. In the Migrate volume dialog box, select the target datastore.
Make sure that the target datastore is compatible and accessible to the volume.
3. Acknowledge that you accept the potential consequences of the migration.
For example, the volume might become inaccessible or the target datastore might be incompatible with the storage
policy the volume uses.
4. Click Migrate.
Forwarding Supervisor Logs to External Monitoring Systems
Checkout how to configure forwarding of Supervisor control plane logs to external monitoring systems, such as Grafana
Loki, or Elastic Search, by using Fluent Bit.
Supervisor control plane logs are automatically forwarded to the syslog server configured to the vCenter appliance by
using Fluent Bit. Fluent Bit is an open-source lightweight logging and metrics processor and forwarder that provides
configurations to support various log data types, filtering and log tag enhancements.
During Supervisor activation or upgrade, bootstrap logs are still forwarded by rsyslog to the syslog servers that are
configured to the vCenter appliance. Once the Supervisor control plane VMs are up and running, Fluent Bit becomes the
default log forwarder for the Supervisor control plane logs.
As a VI administrator, you can use Fluent Bit to:
• Forward Supervisor control plane logs and system journal logs to major external log monitoring platforms such as Loki,
Elastic Search, Grafana, and other platforms that are supported by Fluent Bit.
• Update or reset the log forwarding configuration for the Supervisor control plane by using the k8s API.
Fluent Bit runs as a DeamonSet on Supervisor control plane nodes. It exposes the
fluentbit-config-custom
ConfigMap under the namespace that VI administrators can edit to configure log forwarding
vmware-system-logging
to external platforms by defining log servers.
inputs-custom.conf: |
[INPUT]
Name tail
Alias audit_apiserver_tail
Tag audit.apiserver.*
Path /var/log/vmware/audit/kube-apiserver.log
DB /var/log/vmware/fluentbit/flb_audit_apiserver.db
Buffer_Max_Size 12MBb
Mem_Buf_Limit 32MB
Skip_Long_Lines On
Refresh_Interval 10
filters-custom.conf: |
[FILTER]
Name record_modifier
Alias audit_apiserver_modifier
Match audit.apiserver.*
Record hostname ${NODE_NAME}
Record appname audit-kube-apiserver
Broadcom 6910

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Record filename kube-apiserver.log
outputs-custom.conf: |
[OUTPUT]
Name syslog
Alias audit_apiserver_output_syslog
Match audit.apiserver.*
Host <syslog-server-host>
Port <syslog-server-port>
Mode tcp
Syslog_Format rfc5424
Syslog_Message_key log
Syslog_Hostname_key hostname
Syslog_Appname_key appname
Syslog_Msgid_key filename
Customize Fluent Bit Log Forwarding
Follow the steps to customize the Fluent Bit log forwarding configuration:
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
For information, see Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
2. Update or add a syslog output in the section in the
outputs-custom.conf fluentbit-config-custom
ConfigMap, which will forward all control plane VM system logs to an external server.
[OUTPUT]
Name syslog
Alias syslog_system
Match system*
Host <syslog-server-host>
Port <syslog-server-port>
Mode tcp
Syslog_Format rfc5424
Syslog_Message_key log
Syslog_Hostname_key hostname
Syslog_Appname_key appname
Syslog_Msgid_key filename
# add the following if the mode is TLS
Tls on
Tls.verify off
Tls.ca_file /etc/ssl/certs/vmca.pem
3. Apply the changes to the ConfigMap.
fluentbit-config-custom
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging edit cm fluentbit-config-custom
# use the below command if the change is stored in outputs-custom.conf file
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging create configmap fluentbit-config-custom --from-file=filters-
custom.conf --from-file=inputs-custom.conf --from-file=outputs-custom.conf -o yaml --from-file=parsers-
custom.conf --dry-run | kubectl replace -f -
4. Monitor the Fluent Bit pod to apply the configuration changes automatically, and query Supervisor logs on the
syslog server. If the Fluentbit DaemonSet runs to an error after updated configuration isreloaded, repair or reset the
configuration in the ConfigMap to ensure that the Fluentbit DaemonSet healthy.
fluentbit-config-custom
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging get pod
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging logs <fluentbit-pod-name>
Forward Kubernetes API Server Audit Logs to a Grafana Loki Server
Follow the steps to configure log forwarding to an external Grafana Loki server:
Broadcom 6911

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
For information, see Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
2. Update or add a Loki output in the section in the ConfigMap,
outputs-custom.conf fluentbit-config-custom
which will forward all control plane VM system logs to the Loki log server.
[OUTPUT]
Name loki
Alias system_output_loki
Match system*
Host <loki-server-host>
Port <loki-server-port>
Labels $hostname,$appname,$filename,$procid,$labels
3. Apply the changes to the ConfigMap.
fluentbit-config-custom
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging edit cm fluentbit-config-custom
# use the below command if the change is stored in outputs-custom.conf file
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging create configmap fluentbit-config-custom --from-file=filters-
custom.conf --from-file=inputs-custom.conf --from-file=outputs-custom.conf -o yaml --from-file=parsers-
custom.conf --dry-run | kubectl replace -f -
4. Monitor the Fluent Bit pod to apply the configuration changes automatically, and query Supervisor logs on the
syslog server. If the Fluentbit DaemonSet runs to an error after updated configuration isreloaded, repair or reset the
configuration in the ConfigMap to ensure that the Fluentbit DaemonSet healthy.
fluentbit-config-custom
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging get pod
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging logs <fluentbit-pod-name>
Forward Logs to Elastic Search
Follow the steps to configure log forwarding to an external Elastic Search server:
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
For information, see Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
2. Update or add a Elastic Search output in the section in the
outputs-custom.conf fluentbit-config-custom
ConfigMap, which will forward all control plane VM system logs to the ES log server.
[OUTPUT]
Name es
Alias system_output_es
Match system*
Host <es-server-host>
Port <es-server-port>
Index supervisor
Type controlplanevm
3. Apply the changes to the ConfigMap.
fluentbit-config-custom
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging edit cm fluentbit-config-custom
# use the below command if the change is stored in outputs-custom.conf file
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging create configmap fluentbit-config-custom --from-file=filters-
custom.conf --from-file=inputs-custom.conf --from-file=outputs-custom.conf -o yaml --from-file=parsers-
custom.conf --dry-run | kubectl replace -f -
4. Monitor the Fluent Bit pod to apply the configuration changes automatically, and query Supervisor logs on the syslog
server.
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging get pod
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging logs <fluentbit-pod-name>

Forward Supervisor Auth Logs to a Syslog Server
Follow the steps to configure forwarding of Supervisor Auth logs to an external syslog server:
1. Add and input to ConfigMap:
kubectl-plugin-vsphere authproxy fluentbit-config-custom
[INPUT]
Name tail
Tag auth.kubectl-plugin.*
Path /var/log/containers/kubectl-plugin-vsphere*.log
DB /var/log/vmware/fluentbit/flb_auth_kubectl-plugin.db
Skip_Long_Lines Off
Refresh_Interval 10
[INPUT]
Name tail
Tag auth.authproxy.*
Path /var/log/containers/wcp-authproxy*.log
DB /var/log/vmware/fluentbit/flb_auth_authproxy.db
Skip_Long_Lines Off
Refresh_Interval 10
2. Add and filter to the ConfigMap:
kubectl-plugin-vsphere authproxy fluentbit-config-custom
[FILTER]om
Name kubernetes
Match auth.*
Kube_URL https://localhost:6443
Tls.verify Off
K8S-Logging.Parser On
K8S-Logging.Exclude On
[FILTER]
Name record_modifier
Match auth.*
Operation lift
Nested_under kubernetes
[FILTER]
Name modify
Match auth.*
Rename container_name appname
Rename host hostname
Rename pod_name procid
3. Add and output to syslog server to the
kubectl-plugin-vsphere authproxy fluentbit-config-custom
ConfigMap:
[OUTPUT]
Name syslog
Match auth.*
Host <syslog-server-host>
Port <syslog-server-port>
Mode tcp
Syslog_Format rfc5424
Syslog_Message_key log
Syslog_Hostname_key hostname
Syslog_Appname_key appname
Syslog_Msgid_key filename
4. Monitor the Fluent Bit pod to apply the configuration changes automatically, and query the Supervisor auth logs on the
syslog server.
Broadcom 6913

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging get pod
> kubectl -n vmware-system-logging logs <fluentbit-pod-name>
Streaming Supervisor Metrics to a Custom Observability Platform
Learn how to stream Supervisor metrics gathered by Telegraf to a custom observability platform. Telegraf is enabled
by default on the Supervisor and it collects metrics in Prometheus format from Supervisor components, such as the
Kubernetes API server, VM service, VKS, and others. As a VI administrator, you can configure an observability platform
such as VCF Operations, Grafana, and others to view and analyse the collected Supervisor metrics.
Telegraf is a server-based agent for collecting and sending metrics from different systems, data bases, and IoT. Each
Supervisor component exposes an endpoint where Telegraf connects. Telegraf then sends the collected metrics to
an observability platform of your choice. You can configure any of the output plug-ins that Telegraf supports as an
observability platform for aggregating and analyzing Supervisor metrics. See the Telegraf documentation for the supported
output plug-ins.
The following components expose endpoints where Telegraf connects and gathers metrics: Kubernetes API server, etcd,
kubelet, Kubernetes controller manager, Kubernetes scheduler, VKS, VM service, VM image service, NSX Container
Plug-in (NCP), Container Storage Interface (CSI), certificate manager, NSX, and various host metrics such as CPU,
memory, and storage.
View the Telegraf Pods and Configuration
Telegraf runs under the system namespace on the Supervisor. To view the Telegraf pods
vmware-system-monitoring
and ConfigMaps:
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
For information, see Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
2. Use the following command to view the Telegraf pods:
kubectl -n vmware-system-monitoring get pods
The resulting pods are the following:
telegraf-csqsl
telegraf-dkwtk
telegraf-l4nxk
3. Use the following command to view the Telegraf ConfigMaps:
kubectl -n vmware-system-monitoring get cm
The resulting ConfigMaps are as follows:
default-telegraf-config
kube-rbac-proxy-config
kube-root-ca.crt
telegraf-config
The ConfigMap holds the default Telegraf configuration and it is read-only. You can
default-telegraf-config
use it as fallback option to restore the configuration in in case the file is corrupt or you want to just
telegraf-config
restore to the defaults. The only ConfigMap that you can edit is , it defines which components are
telegraf-config
sending metrics to the Telegraf agents, and to which platforms.
4. View the ConfigMap:
telegraf-config
kubectl -n vmware-system-monitoring get cm telegraf-config -o yaml
The section of the ConfigMap defines all the endpoints of Supervisor components from
inputs telegraf-config
which Telegraf gathers metrics as well as the types of metrics themselves. For example the following input defines the
Kubernetes API server as an endpoint :
[[inputs.prometheus]]
# APIserver
## An array of urls to scrape metrics from.
alias = "kube_apiserver_metrics"
Broadcom 6914

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
urls = ["https://127.0.0.1:6443/metrics"]
bearer_token = "/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
# Dropping metrics as a part of short term solution to vStats integration 1MB metrics payload limit
# Dropped Metrics:
# apiserver_request_duration_seconds
namepass = ["apiserver_request_total", "apiserver_current_inflight_requests",
"apiserver_current_inqueue_requests", "etcd_object_counts",
"apiserver_admission_webhook_admission_duration_seconds", "etcd_request_duration_seconds"]
# "apiserver_request_duration_seconds" has _massive_ cardinality, temporarily turned off. If histogram,
maybe filter the highest ones?
# Similarly, maybe filters to _only_ allow error code related metrics through?
## Optional TLS Config
tls_ca = "/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt"
The property indicates the component from where metrics are gathered. The property specifies which
alias namepass
component metrics are exposed and respectively collected by the Telegraf agents.
Although the ConfigMap already contains a broad range of metrics, you can still define additional
telegraf-config
ones. See Metrics For Kubernetes System Components and Kubernetes Metrics Reference.
Configure Observability Platform to Telegraf
In the section of you configure where Telegraf streams the metrics that it gathers. Several
outps telegraf-config
options exist such as , , , and .
outputs.file outputs.wavefront outputs.prometheus_client outps-https
The section is where you can configure the observability platforms that you want to use for aggregation
outps-https
and monitoring of the Supervisor metrics. You can configure Telegraf to send metrics to more than one platform. To edit
the ConfigMap and configure an observability platform for viewing Supervisor metrics, follow the
telegraf-config
steps:
1. Log in to the Supervisor.
For information, see Connecting to Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
2. Save the ConfigMap to the local kubectl folder:
telegraf-config
kubectl get cm telegraf-config -n vmware-system-monitoring -o jsonpath="{.data['telegraf
\.conf']}">telegraf.conf
Make sure to store the ConfigMap in a version control system before you make any changes to
telegraf-config
it in case you want to restore to a previous version of the file. In case you want to restore to the default configuration,
you can use the values from the ConfigMap.
default-telegraf-config
3. Add sections with the connection settings of the observability platforms of your choice by using a text
outputs.http
editor, such as VIM:
vim telegraf.config
You can directly uncomment the following section and edit the values accordingly, or add a new
outputs.http
sections as needed.
#[[outputs.http]]
# alias = "prometheus_http_output"
# url = "<PROMETHEUS_ENDPOINT>"
# insecure_skip_verify = <PROMETHEUS_SKIP_INSECURE_VERIFY>
# data_format = "prometheusremotewrite"
# username = "<PROMETHEUS_USERNAME>"
# password = "<PROMETHEUS_PASSWORD>"
# <DEFAULT_HEADERS>
For example, here's how an configuration for Grafana looks like:
outputs.http
[[outputs.http]]
url = "http://<grafana-host>:<grafana-metrics-port>/<prom-metrics-push-path>"
data_format = "influx"
[outputs.http.headers]
Authorization = "Bearer <grafana-bearer-token>"
Broadcom 6915

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
See Stream metrics from Telegraf to Grafana for more information on configuring dashboards and consuming metrics
from Telegraf.
And here's an example with VMware Aria Operations for Applications (former Wavefront):
[[outputs.wavefront]]
url = "http://<wavefront-proxy-host>:<wavefront-proxy-port>"
The recommended way of ingesting metrics to Aria Operations for Applications is through a proxy. See Wavefront
Proxies for more information.
4. Replace the existing file on the Supervisor with the one that you edited on your local folder:
telegraf-config
kubectl create cm --from-file telegraf.conf -n vmware-system-monitoring telegraf-config --dry-run=client -
o yaml | kubectl replace -f -
5. Check if the new configuration is saved successfully:
– View the new ConfigMap:
telegraf-config

kubectl -n vmware-system-monitoring get pods

kubectl -n vmware-system-monitoring logs <telegraf-pod>
Migrate Telegraf Configuration after Upgrading to VCF 9
Learn how to migrate the Telegraf configuration values after upgrading your environment to VCF 9 so that you can keep
collecting metrics with the same configuration values prior the upgrade.
When you upgrade the Supervisor from version 8.x to 9.0, the configmap is created to
telegraf-user-config
maintain user managed configuration. The data from the configmap is automatically backed up
telegraf-config
to the configmap and you need to copy your configuration data from the backup to the
telegraf-config-backup
.
telegraf-user-config
1. Log in to the Supervisor as a vCenter Single Sign-On user.
vcf context create --endpoint <SUPERVISOR-ADDRESS> --username <VCENTER-SSO-USER> --ca-certificate <PATH-
TO-CERTIFICATE-FILE>
2. Switch to the context of the Supervisor.
kubectl config use-context <SUPERVISOR-ADDRESS>
3. Verify if your vCenter Single Sign-On user has edit permission on the configmap.
telegraf-user-config
kubectl auth can-i update cm/telegraf-user-config -n vmware-system-monitoring
The command returns if the role assigned to the user has privilege.
yes Namespaces.Observe
4. Copy the required configuration from the configmap.
telegraf-config-backup
kubectl get cm/telegraf-config-backup -n vmware-system-monitoring -o yaml
5. Update the configmap with the data copied from the
telegraf-user-config telegraf-config-backup
configmap.
kubectl edit cm/telegraf-user-config -n vmware-system-monitoring
You have to copy the information in an appropriate section in the
telegraf-config-backup telegraf-user-
configmap. Following are the different configuration sections that are available in the
config telegraf-user-
configmap that are mounted as separate files on the Telegraf pods.
config
• - The base configuration that is mounted on both deamonset and deployment instances. It
telegraf.conf
provides the common configurations to both the instances like agent config, output plug-ins, and others.
• - This configuration is mounted on the Telegraf deployment pods. It provides input
telegraf-deployment.conf
plug-in configuration for collecting metrics from IaaS controllers running in the Supervisor.
• - This configuration file is mounted on Telegraf daemonset instance pods. It
telegraf-daemonset.conf
provides input plug-in configuration for collecting metrics from kube-system and node metrics.

Updating vSphere Supervisor
Learn how to update the vSphere Supervisor environment, including the version of vSphere Supervisor instances and the
underlying infrastructure.
Updating the vSphere Supervisor Environment
You can update to the latest version of vSphere Supervisor, including the vSphere infrastructure supporting Supervisors,
VKS clusters, and the VCF Consumption CLI.
Important:
When upgrading vCenter from 8.0 Update 3 and later, 9.0.0, 9.0.1, or 9.0.2 to 9.1.0 or 9.1.1, Supervisor data
can potentially be lost if the vLCM database was previously reset. To avoid data loss, you must determine if your
environment if affected and take mitigation steps. See Broadcom KB article 455737 for more information.
Note:
Before you update vCenter, make sure that the Kubernetes version of all Supervisors is of the minimum
supported version, and that the vSphere Kubernetes release version of the VKS clusters is of the minimum
supported version. See the compatibility matrix for more information.
In VCF 9.1 online deployments, Supervisor artifacts required for upgrade are automatically synchronized to the local
Software Depot. No manual repository or registry configuration is required before initiating the upgrade.
How vSphere Supervisor Updates Work
Check out how to update the Supervisors and VKS clusters in your vSphere Supervisor environment. vSphere Supervisor
supports rolling updates for Supervisors and VKS clusters, and for the infrastructure supporting these clusters.
When you update your vSphere Supervisor environment, you update the Kubernetes version of your Supervisors and
VKS clusters along with the underlying infrastructure components and services. Therefore, the term update is used to
describe this process instead of the term upgrade, which is a limited form of update that increments the software version.
Supervisors and VKS clusters are built by using a common Kubernetes distribution core. Kubernetes versions for the
Supervisor and VKS clusters are delivered differently:
• Starting from VCF 9, some Supervisor Kubernetes releases, such as patches, can be delivered independently from
vCenter. For these releases, you can update the Supervisor version by deploying a Supervisor release version from
the Supervisor Content Library. For other Supervisor releases, in which more significant architecture changes are
involved, the Supervisor update is still delivered through vCenter, and requires a vCenter upgrade.
• VKS clusters are built by using vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKrs). A VKr provides upstream aligned Kubernetes
software distribution, signed, tested, and supported by VMware. VKrs are intended for VKS clusters. VKrs are released
independently from vCenter. A VKr is a combination of an operating system such as Photon or Ubuntu combined with
VKS core components necessary to provide pod functionality. A VKr includes components such as Antrea and Calico
that you can deploy in VKS clusters. For more information, see the VMware vSphere Kubernetes releases Release
Notes.
You can only update the Kubernetes version of Supervisors and VKS clusters sequentially due to the update policy of
upstream Kubernetes. You cannot skip a minor version. For example, if a Supervisor is running 1.28, you cannot update
straight to 1.30. The correct update path is, 1.28, 1.29, 1.30.
Broadcom 6917

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Support Policy for the Supervisor and VKS Cluster Kubernetes Versions
Both Supervisor Kubernetes versions and VKrs implement an N-2 support policy for Kubernetes releases, similarly to the
upstream Kubernetes support policy. This means that each Kubernetes release in vSphere Supervisor (Supervisor or VKr)
is supported for a minimum of 12 months from the time it is released.
Note however, that the Supervisor and VKS clusters must run compatible Kubernetes versions, see the Compatibility
Matrix for the compatible VKrs releases and Verify VKS Cluster Compatibiity for Updates.
Rolling Updates of Supervisors and VKS Clusters
vSphere Supervisor uses a rolling update model for Supervisors and VKS clusters. The rolling update model ensures
that there is minimal downtime for cluster workloads during the update process. Rolling updates include upgrading the
Kubernetes software versions and the infrastructure and services supporting the VKS clusters, such as virtual machine
configurations and resources, vSphere Namespaces, and custom resources. For more information, see Understanding
the Rolling Update Model for VKS Clusters for more details.
Important:
Upgrading to version 9.1 in environments with regional Harbor triggers an automatic rolling update of all VKS
clusters. The rolling update occurs so that nodes can adopt new certificates and DNS entries. To avoid an
unplanned rollout, before starting the upgrade, upgrade the VKS to 3.6.1 or later, retire legacy (v1alpha3) clusters,
and manually upgrade your VKS clusters to ClusterClass 3.6.0 or later.
For the update to succeed, your environment must meet several compatibility requirements. The system enforces
precheck conditions to ensure that clusters are ready for updates, and supports rollback if cluster upgrade is not
successful.
Updating the Supervisor
You can update the Kubernetes version of the Supervisor, and the infrastructure supporting the Supervisor and VKS
clusters. You might need to update the Supervisor Kubernetes versions 3 times per year to maintain pace with the
Kubernetes release cadence. The following is the Supervisor Kubernetes version update sequence that is still applicable
for VCF 9.
1. Create a Supervisor content library.
2. Update the Supervisor Kubernetes version and infrastructure components. See Update the Supervisor
When you initiate an update of the Supervisor Kubernetes version the update is performed in the following order of
operations:
1. The system creates a new control plane VM and joins it to the existing Supervisor control plane. During this phase
of the update, the vSphere inventory shows four control plane VMs as the system adds a new updated VM and then
removes the older out-of-date VM.
2. Objects are migrated from one of the old control plane VMs to the new one, and the old control plane VM is then
removed. This process repeats one-by-one until all control plane VMs are updated.
3. Once all the control plane VMs are updated, the worker nodes are updated in a similar rolling update fashion. The
worker nodes are the ESXi hosts, and each spherelet process on each ESXi host is updated one-by-one.
You can choose between the following updates:
• Update the Supervisor Kubernetes version only.
• Update everything, including VMware versions and Kubernetes versions.
Updating VKS Clusters
Updating your VKS clusters depends on the VKS service version that is running on the Supervisor as well as the VKr
versions the clusters are running. For more information, see Installing and Updating VKS and Updating VKS Clusters.
Broadcom 6918

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Configure a Subscribed Content Library for Supervisor Images
You can use a subscribed content library for Supervisor enablement and upgrade. Starting from VCF 9, the Supervisor
releases can be delivered separately from vCenter.
Ensure that the Software Depot is installed and configured in your environment and that you have the Software Depot
subscription endpoint URL for your environment.
To find your subscription URL, log in to the vCenter Developer Center, open the API Explorer, and execute a GET request
on the lcm/depot/services API. Use the returned and values to format
VcenterLcmDepotServicesAddress base_url
your URL as: https://{VcenterLcmDepotServicesAddress}{base_url}/PROD/COMP/SUPERVISOR/lib.json. See Configure
a Software Depot Connection Mode.
To enable or upgrade vSphere Supervisor, you can create a subscribed content library and synchronize the Supervisor
release images. Starting with VCF 9.1, you can create a content library that subscribes to Supervisor image publications
directly from the Software Depot.
The subscribed content library can be in immediate or on-demand synchronization mode. Immediate synchronization on
the public content delivery network might take more time and disk space.
Important:
Do not attempt to delete or edit the content library that is assigned with the Supervisor release images. You must
unassign the Supervisor release images before you attempt to delete or edit the content library. Use the following
DCLI command:
> dcli> com vmware vcenter namespacemanagement lifecycle content libraries unassign --library
libraryId
< >
1. Log in to the vCenter as a VI administrator.
2. Create the subscribed content library for Supervisor release images.
a) From the Home menu, select Content Libraries.
b) Click Create.
c) Name the content library, for example, Supervisor Releases Content Library, and click Next.
d) On the Configure content library page, select Subscribed Content Library.
e) Set the subscription URL to the Software Depot address you constructed in prerequisites.
f) In the Download content section, select the synchronization mode of the content library and click Next.
Option Description
Immediately The subscription process synchronizes both the library metadata
and images. If items are deleted from the published library, their
contents remain in the subscribed library storage and you have to
manually delete them.
When needed Use this option to save storage space.
The subscription process synchronizes only the library metadata.
The system downloads the images when published. If you no
longer need the item, you can delete the item contents to free
storage space.
g) When prompted, accept the SSL certificate thumbprint.
The SSL certificate thumbprint is stored on your system until you delete the subscribed content library from the
inventory.
Broadcom 6919

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
h) On the Add storage page, select a datastore as a storage location for the content library contents and click Next.
i) Review the details and click Finish.
3. Assign the content library to the vSphere Supervisor platform.
a) From the Home menu, select Supervisor Management.
b) Select Content Distribution.
c) On the Supervisor Images Library card, click Assign.
d) Select the Content Library that you created and click Assign.
The new content library starts synchronizing which might take some time. Once the synchronization completes, the new
Supervisor Kubernetes versions contained in the images appear in the available versions on the Updates tab.
Configuring a Subscribed Content Library for Supervisor Images in Air-Gapped Environment
Learn how to create a subscribed content library in an air-gapped environment. You can then use this subscribed content
library to enable and upgrade the Supervisor. Starting from VCF 9, the Supervisor Kubernetes releases can be delivered
separately from vCenter. To enable or upgrade the Supervisor in an air-gapped environment, you can create a subscribed
content library and synchronize vSphere Supervisor release images.
Broadcom publishes vSphere Supervisor images to a content delivery network. In an air-gapped environment, where
direct internet access is restricted, you must first download the vSphere Supervisor release artifacts on a separate host
that is connected to the internet.
Once the artifacts are downloaded, depending on the specific environment properties, you can apply the following
approaches to create a subscribed content library:
• For VCF 9.1.1 and later. Use the VCF Download Tool to download the Supervisor release images and upload them
to the Software Depot. Then create a subscribed content library subscribing to the Software Depot directly. For the
subscribed library creation steps, see Configure a Subscribed Content Library for Supervisor Images.
To download the Supervisor release images:
./bin/vcf-download-tool artifacts download \
--vcf-version=9.1 \
--component=SUPERVISOR \
--depot-download-activation-code-file=activation-code.txt
To upload the Supervisor release images to the Software Depot:
./bin/vcf-download-tool depot artifacts upload \
--vcf-version=9.1 \
--component=SUPERVISOR \
--depot-store=./depot-store \
--depot-fqdn=<DEPOT_FQDN> \
--ops-fqdn=<OPS_FQDN> \
--ops-user=admin \
--ops-user-password-file=vcfops.txt
• For VCF earlier than 9.1.1, or for environments that require legacy Supervisor versions or a customized publisher. Use
one of the following approaches to set up a local publisher, then create a subscribed content library that subscribes to
it:
– Remote content library publisher in your local environment.
– vCenter publisher.
Note:
New Supervisor release images might not be published to https://wp-content.broadcom.com/supervisor/v1/latest.
All new Supervisor release images are published to the Broadcom online depot and are accessible through the
Software Depot.
For all approaches, you can select between the immediate and on-demand synchronization modes. Immediate
synchronization can take substantial time and disk space.
Broadcom 6920

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
Do not attempt to delete or edit the content library that is assigned with the Supervisor release images. These
attempts might cause Supervisor node deployment failures.
You must unassign the Supervisor release images before you attempt to delete or edit the content library. Do not
unassign a content library if its Supervisor release images are actively used by running Supervisor.
To unassign, use the following DCLI command:
> dcli> com vmware vcenter namespacemanagement lifecycle content libraries unassign --library
libraryId
< >
Create a Remote Content Library Publisher for vSphere Supervisor Releases in an Air-Gapped
Environment
Learn how to create a subscribed content library for vSphere Supervisor release images by setting up a remote content
publisher in your local network. This approach is for pre-9.1.1 deployments, or for 9.1.1+ deployments where you need
legacy Supervisor versions or want a customized publisher.
Note:
For VCF 9.1.1 and later, the recommended approach is to create a subscribed content library subscribing to the
Software Depot directly. See Configure a Subscribed Content Library for Supervisor Images.
The following steps apply to pre-9.1.1 deployments, or to 9.1.1 and later deployments where you need legacy
Supervisor versions or want a customized publisher that includes both legacy and newer versions.
You set up a remote content publisher in your local network by using a staging host that downloads release artifacts and
acts as a publisher for internal consumption. You can then create a subscribed content library to update the Supervisor
releases in an air-gapped environment where internet access is prohibited.
1. Download the Supervisor release bundle.
The download method depends on the Supervisor version you need.
• For legacy Supervisor versions.
Using a machine with internet access, download the full release bundle including the lib.json file from https://wp-
content.broadcom.com/supervisor/v1/latest (version 9.0) or https://wp-content.broadcom.com/ (version 9.1).
• For newer Supervisor versions (9.1.1 and later).
Use the VCF Download Tool to download the Supervisor release images and upload them to the Software Depot:
./bin/vcf-download-tool artifacts download \
--vcf-version=9.1 \
--component=SUPERVISOR \
--depot-store=./depot-store \
--depot-download-activation-code-file=activation-code.txt
./bin/vcf-download-tool depot artifacts upload \
--vcf-version=9.1 \
--component=SUPERVISOR \

Create a vCenter publisher for vSphere Supervisor release artifacts by uploading downloaded artifacts to a local content
library on a vCenter system and enabling publishing. This approach is for pre-9.1.1 deployments, or for 9.1.1 and later
deployments where you need legacy Supervisor versions or want a customized publisher.
Note:
For VCF 9.1.1 and later, the recommended approach is to create a subscribed content library subscribing to the
Software Depot directly. See Configure a Subscribed Content Library for Supervisor Images.
The following steps apply to pre-9.1.1 deployments, or to 9.1.1 and later deployments where you need legacy
Supervisor versions or want a customized publisher that includes both legacy and newer versions.
You upload the downloaded vSphere Supervisor release artifacts to a local content library on a vCenter system. The
content library is marked as published, exposing a subscription URL for downstream consumption. The same or a
separate vCenter system can then host a subscribed content library that pulls content from the published library.
