Update the Supervisor
Learn how to update your Supervisors, including the Kubernetes version that the Supervisors are running. The
Supervisors in your environment must always run a supported Kubernetes version.
• Check the supported Kubernetes versions for the Supervisor in the vSphere Supervisor Release Notes.
• Create a content library for the Supervisor releases.
• Create a content library containing the most recent Supervisor build.
• For additional details and critical information regarding VKS rolling updates in version 9.1, see How vSphere
Supervisor Updates Work.
Note:
Updating a Supervisor can trigger a rolling update of the VKS clusters deployed there. See Understanding the
Rolling Udate Model for VKS Clusters.
There is a version entity for the Supervisor. The version entity is a semantic version string in the form
, where the prefix is the Kubernetes version ( ) and the suffix is
v1.30.10+vmware.1-fips-vsc9.0.0.0100 v1.30.10
the Supervisor Kubernetes release version release number ( ).
vsc9.0.0.0100
1. Log in to the vCenter as a VI administrator.
2. Select Menu > Supervisor Management.
3. Select the Namespaces > Updates tab.
4. Select the Available Version that you want to update to.
For example, select the version .
v1.30.10+vmware.1-fips-vsc9.0.0.0100
Note:
You must update incrementally. You cannot skip updates, such as from 1.28 to 1.30. The path should be 1.28,
1.29, 1.30.
5. Select a Supervisor to update.
6. Click Apply Updates.
The system runs a series of pre-checks to verify the compatibility of the different components against the Supervisor
Kubernetes version to which you want to update. When the pre-checks are completed successfully, you can update
the Supervisor.
What are Supervisor Update Pre-checks and How to Troubleshoot Them
Learn which are the pre-checks that are run before updating the Supervisor and how to troubleshoot in case of errors
resulting from failed pre-checks.
The Supervisor and the workloads that it runs interact with multiple vSphere resources (storage, memory, CPU, and
network) running on different layers of vSphere. As a VI administrator, when you initiate a Supervisor update, the system
runs pre-checks to verify that workload compatibility and resource requirements are met. These pre-checks include
health checks, resource checks, and dependency checks on different software components to ensure that a successful
Supervisor update is possible.

Update the VCF CLI
Once you have performed a vSphere Namespace update and upgraded the Supervisor, update the VCF CLI, if it is
recommended.
If a newer version of the VCF CLI is available, you will be prompted with the message in the terminal when you use the
VCF CLI.
To download and install the the VCF CLI, see Download and Install the VCF CLI.
Working with vSphere Lifecycle Manager
As a VI administrator, you can enable vSphere Supervisor on vSphere clusters that you manage with a single VMware
vSphere Lifecycle Manager image. You can then use the Supervisor while it is managed by vSphere Lifecycle Manager.
vSphere Lifecycle Manager allows you to manage the ESXi hosts and clusters in your environment. You can upgrade
a Supervisor to the latest version of vSphere Supervisor. You can also upgrade the ESXi version of the hosts in the
Supervisor.
vSphere Lifecycle Manager is a service that runs in vCenter. When you deploy vCenter, the vSphere Lifecycle Manager
user interface is enabled in the HML5-based vSphere Client.
For more information about the vSphere Lifecycle Manager, see the Managing Host and Cluster Lifecycle documentation.
Requirements
To configure vSphere Supervisor on a vSphere cluster that is managed by vSphere Lifecycle Manager, your environment
must meet specific requirements.
System Requirements
To enable vSphere Supervisor, verify that the components on the vSphere cluster meet the following requirements:
• Verify that vCenter and ESX are of version 7.0 Update 2 and later if you use NSX.
• Verify that vCenter and ESX are of at least version 7.0 Update 1 and later if you use vSphere Networking.
• Verify that HA and DRS are enabled on the vSphere cluster.
• Verify that vSphere Distributed Switch version 7.0 Update 2 and later is configured.
• Verify that vSphere Networking or NSX 3.1 or a later version is configured on the cluster. You cannot use vSphere
Lifecycle Manager image to manage a cluster that is configured with earlier versions of NSX.
Enable vSphere Supervisor on a Cluster Managed by vSphere Lifecycle Manager
To run Kubernetes workloads, you can enable vSphere Supervisor on a cluster that you manage with a single vSphere
Lifecycle Manager image. After it is enabled, you can manage the Supervisor using vSphere Lifecycle Manager.
When you enable the cluster with vSphere Supervisor that uses NSX, the vSphere Lifecycle Manager installs the
Spherelet vSphere Installation Bundle (VIB) on every ESX host in the cluster. Enabling the cluster assigns the version
of the Kubernetes version that ships with vCenter. After the installation is complete, the WCP service performs the post
installation tasks such as, starting and configuring the Spherelet.
For the steps to enable the cluster, see Deploying Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC.
Upgrade a Supervisor
You can update to the latest version of vSphere Supervisor, including the vSphere infrastructure supporting vSphere
Supervisor clusters, the Kubernetes versions, and the VCF CLI on clusters that use a single vSphere Lifecycle Manager
image.
You upgrade the ESX version of the hosts in the Supervisor. During the upgrade the Spherelet VIB on every ESX host is
upgraded.
Broadcom 6932

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSphere Lifecycle Manager uses DRS and puts the hosts in maintenance mode before remediation. DRS first attempts to
migrate the virtual machine running vCenter Server to another host, such as VMs that are affinitized to the host or running
on the local storage of the host, and workloads, including vSphere Pods to other hosts, so that the remediation succeeds.
Note:
You can use vSphere Lifecycle Manager to upgrade a Supervisor only on clusters that use a single vSphere
Lifecycle Manager image.
1. From the vSphere Client menu, select Workload Management.
2. Select the Updates tab.
3. Select the Available Version that you want to update to.
For example, select the version .
v1.17.4-vsc0.0.2-16293900
4. Select the Supervisor to apply the update to.
5. To initiate the update, click Apply Updates.
6. Use the Recent Tasks pane to monitor the status of the update.
Add Hosts to a Supervisor
As a VI administrator, you might need to scale out the Supervisor to run more workloads. To add capacity to a cluster, you
can add ESXi hosts to the cluster thats uses a single vSphere Lifecycle Manager image.
• Obtain the user name and password of the root user account for the host.
• Verify that hosts behind a firewall might communicate with the vCenter.
When you add a host to the Supervisor that is configured with NSX, vSphere Lifecycle Manager installs the Spherelet VIB
and the image on the host. After it is installed, vSphere Supervisor configures the Spherelet process on the newly added
host, which allows running containers natively on ESXi.
1. From the vSphere Client menu, select Workload Management.
2. Right-click the data center, cluster, or folder and select Add Host.
3. Enter the IP address or the name of the host and click Next.
4. Enter the administrator credentials and click Next.
5. Review the host summary and click Next.
6. Assign a license to the host and click Finish.
7. In the Add Host wizard, click Next.
8. Review the summary and click Finish.
Note:
If a host is part of the same data center, you can move it into the Supervisor. To move the host, put it in
maintenance mode and drag it into the cluster.
Remove Hosts from a Supervisor
As a VI administrator, you might need to scale in the Supervisor to save cost. To reduce the capacity of a Supervisor, you
can remove ESXi hosts from a cluster that uses a single vSphere Lifecycle Manager image.
Before you can remove a host from a cluster, you must power off all virtual machines that are running on the host or
migrate the virtual machines to a new host.
When you remove a host from the Supervisor that is configured with NSX, vSphere Supervisor clears the configuration of
the Spherelet and stops the Spherelet process on the ESXi host. vSphere Lifecycle Manager then uninstalls the Spherelet
VIB and image from the host and vSphere Supervisor removes the host metadata from the cluster control plane.
Broadcom 6933

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. In the vSphere Client, navigate to the cluster from which you want to remove the host.
2. Right-click the host and select Enter Maintenance Mode from the pop-up menu.
3. In the confirmation dialog box that appears, click Yes.
The confirmation dialog box also asks if you want to move virtual machines that are powered off to other hosts. Select
this option if you want those virtual machines to remain registered to a host within the cluster.
The host icon changes and the term “maintenance mode” is added to the name in parentheses.
4. Select the host icon from the inventory, and drag it to the new location.
The host can be moved to another cluster or another data center.
vCenter Server moves the host to the new location.
5. Right-click the host, and select Exit Maintenance Mode from the pop-up menu.
6. Optional: Restart any virtual machines, if needed.
Disable a Supervisor
You can disable vSphere Supervisor from a vSphere cluster that uses a single vSphere Lifecycle Manager image, to make
it available for traditional workloads.
When you disable a vSphere Supervisor on a cluster, vSphere Lifecycle Manager uninstalls the Spherelet VIB and image
from each ESXi host and the service stops and deletes all workloads from the cluster.
WCP
1. From the vSphere Client menu, select Workload Management.
2. Select the Clusters tab.
3. Select the cluster on which you want to disable vSphere Supervisor.
4. Click Disable.
The Disable Cluster dialog box appears with a message that all Kubernetes workloads and NSX configuration will be
disabled on the cluster.
5. Click Disable.

When to Back Up and Restore the vSphere Supervisor Control Plane
This topic outlines when it is safe to back up and restore the Supervisor. It also highlights scenarios where backups or
restores should not be performed.
CAUTION:
You must exercise caution when performing a Supervisor restore. Use the restore only for specific recovery
scenarios. You should not use it as a general solution for addressing issues that might occur during lifecycle
Broadcom 6935

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
operations, such as a Supervisor upgrade. Restoring might result in existing workloads to become orphaned or
the Supervisor control plane not fully return to a healthy running state.
When to Take a Supervisor Backup
This section lists scenarios in which it is recommended to take a backup of the Supervisor. It also identifies cases when
you should avoid taking a backup. Backing up the Supervisor in unsupported states might lead to inconsistent or unusable
backups and unpredictable behavior during restore.
vSphere Supervisor State Backup Recommended Details
Supervisor is enabled and status is Yes The Supervisor is in a stable state and
Running backup is safe.
Supervisor is upgraded and status is Yes The upgrade is complete and the Superviso
Running r is stable.
Supervisor is in an error state No The error state might be due to network
issues, pod failures, or etcd issues.
Backing up in this condition can result in an
unusable restore.
Supervisor is being upgraded No A backup taken during an upgrade might be
inconsistent and can cause problems when
restoring.
Supervisor upgrade failed No A failed upgrade leaves the cluster in an
unstable state. Backups taken in this state
can lead to inconsistent backup data and
cause restore issues.
Supervisor Service is being upgraded No Do not take a backup when a Supervisor
Service, such as VKS, is being upgraded.
Backups taken in this state might record
inconsistent data. For example, etcd and
Supervisor Service metadata might be out
of sync.
When Not to Perform a Supervisor Restore
Restoring the Supervisor is not supported in certain scenarios. Avoid restore operations in the following cases as they
might cause orphaned resources, version mismatches, an unstable cluster state, or other unpredictable behavior.
Restore Scenarios to Avoid Details
Supervisor Kubernetes Version Do not restore if the Supervisor Kubernetes version in the backup differs from the version in
Mismatch your current environment.
Example: You backed up Supervisor running Kubernetes 1.28.3 in a vCenter 8.x environment.
Later, you upgraded to vCenter 9.0, where the default Supervisor version is 1.28.14. If you
attempt a restore, the version mismatch blocks the operation.
Restoring vCenter After Upgrading If you restore vCenter from a backup taken before a Supervisor upgrade or restore, Supervisor
and Restoring the Supervisor might become out of sync with vCenter.
You can encounter several problems. For example, existing control plane VMs become
orphaned and are placed to the Discovered Virtual Machines folder. Or you might see duplicate
control plane VMs that cannot be powered on.
If those problems occur, and you want to recover the Supervisor, perform these steps:
1. Delete discovered and orphaned control plane VMs before you start the Supervisor
restore.
2. Restore the Supervisor using a backup taken when vCenter backup was taken.
Broadcom 6936

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Restore Scenarios to Avoid Details
Restoring Supervisor After New VKS Avoid restoring the Supervisor if either of these applies:
Cluster Creation or VKS Upgrade • You created new VKS clusters after the backup.
Any VMs from those clusters might become orphaned during the restore, even if the VKS
service was not upgraded. See Cleaning Up Orphaned Objects After Supervisor Restore
from a Backup.
• You upgraded the VKS after the backup.
Restoring at this point causes a service downgrade. The downgrade can make existing
clusters incompatible and unmanageable by VKS.
Restoring Supervisor After New Do not restore the Supervisor if you created new vSphere Pods after the backup was taken.
vSphere Pods Were Created If new vSphere Pods were created after the backup was taken, during restore, the system
might attempt to downgrade internal components on the ESX hosts to match the backup
version. The downgrade might fail or get blocked if ESX hosts fail to enter maintenance
mode, with an error such as Waiting for all VMs to be powered off or
suspended or migrated.
If this situation occurs and you want to recover the Supervisor, cleanup orphaned VMs
associated with vSphere Pod resources and wait for a couple of minutes for the restore
operation to succeed. See Cleaning Up Orphaned Objects After Supervisor Restore from a
Backup.
Backup and Restore the Supervisor Control Plane
You can include the option for recording the state of the Supervisors in vCenter as part of the vCenter file-based backups.
Later on you can restore the Supervisor control plane from the created backup files.
Back up the Supervisor State
Learn how to back up the state of the Supervisors in your environment. You can include the backup of the Supervisors
available in vCenter as part of the vCenter file-based backups.
• You must have an FTP, FTPS, HTTP, HTTPS, SFTP, NFS, or SMB server up and running with sufficient disk space to
store the backup.
• The lowest supported version for the Supervisor control plane backup is vSphere 8 Update 3. If the Supervisor control
plane is running a lower version, the backup is not included in the vCenter file-based backups.
The backup files for the Supervisor control plane capture the state of the following components:
• The etcd state.
• Container images that are used for infrastructure pods to ensure that control plane VMs can be restored post vCenter
upgrade.
• The Kubernetes CA certificate and key to ensure that all Kubernetes certificates can be regenerated after a restore
from the same CA. This ensures that vSphere Pods and the Spherelet do not have to be reconfigured after restore to
trust a new Kubernetes CA.
• All vSphere Namespaces and the state of all the Kubernetes resources that are associated with workloads, such as
deployments, pods, VMs, VKS resources, persistent volume claims, and others.
For more information on the vCenter file-based backup and restore, see File-Based Backup and Restore of vCenter
Server in vCenter Server Installation and Setup.
Certain Supervisor settings are stored in vCenter and hence are captured in the vCenter backup:
• Resource pools for vSphere Namespaces.
• General settings such as control plane VM settings, VKS service content libraries, and others.
• Network settings such as network configuration updates of CIDRs, DNS settings, and NTP settings.
• Storage settings such as storage policies.
• Certificates.
• Container registries.
• Identity providers.
• Default CNI.
Broadcom 6937

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Permissions
• vSphere Zones.
• PNID changes.
1. In a web browser, go to the vCenter Management Interface, .
https://appliance-IP-address-or-FQDN:5480
2. Log in as root.
3. In the vCenter Management Interface, click Backup.
4. Click Edit if a backup schedule already exists.
If a backup schedule does not exist, see Backing Up and Restoring NSX Manager in the NSX-T documentation for
information on how to create one.
5. In the Edit Backup Schedule pane, select Supervisors Control Plane.
The state of all Supervisors in vCenter is backed up as part of the vCenter backups.
Restore the Supervisor Control Plane
You can restore the Supervisors control pane in vCenter from the backup files of the vCenter system itself.
Broadcom 6938

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Configure recording the Supervisor state from the vCenter management interface file-based backups.
Note:
Restoring the Supervisors control plane in vCenter and restoring the state of vCenter are two different workflows.
Restoring vCenter does not lead to restoring the Supervisor control plane.
Supervisor settings that are managed by vCenter are captured in the vCenter backup. After the Supervisor backup is
created, restoring only the Supervisor state will not revert the settings that are managed by vCenter . To ensure that
these configurations are restored to their state at the time of the backup, perform a vCenter restore before restoring the
Supervisor state. If you only restore the Supervisor state, the configuration on the Supervisor is overwritten to match
the desired configuration on vCenter . When you restore both vCenter and Supervisor, you avoid discrepancies in the
Supervisor configuration.
• Resource pools for vSphere Namespaces.
• General settings such as control plane VM settings, VKS service content libraries, and others.
• Network settings such as network configuration updates of CIDRs, DNS settings, and NTP settings.
• Storage settings such as storage policies.
• Certificates.
• Container registries.
• Identity providers.
• Default CNI.
• Permissions
• vSphere Zones.
• PNID changes.
If a vSphere Namespace is deleted by using the vSphere Client, the vSphere Namespace is not created after restoring the
Supervisor. To restore the vSphere Namespace, you must restore the vCenter state.
To restore workloads running in vSphere Namespaces, use a backup tool such as Velero or Velero Plug-in for vSphere to
restore the workloads. See Considerations for Backing Up and Restoring vSphere Supervisor.
1. In the vSphere Client, go to Supervisor Management.
2. Select Supervisors and select Restore.
3. Enter the backup details.
Option Description
vCenter Select the vCenter system that manages the Supervisor.
Backup selection • Select Browse backup server folder to upload the files that are stored in the root
folder of the backup file server that is configured with this vCenter system.
• Select Single backup location to upload a particular backup file, then enter the URL
to that backup file.
• Select Use backup location and user name from vCenter backup schedule
to populate the root folder location and user name for the backup location that are
configured with vCenter.
Location Enter the location of the backup root folder.
Username Enter the user name to access the backups.
password Enter the password for that user name.
4. Click Next.
5. Select a backup file to restore from and click Next to start the download of the backup file.
6. Select the Supervisor to restore and click Next.
7. Review the settings and click Finish.
The Supervisor goes back to configuring state and all the control plane VMs are deleted and re-deployed with the data
from the backup file. You can monitor the process by clicking View in the Config Status column.

Installing and Configuring the Velero Plugin for vSphere on a Supervisor
The Velero Plugin for vSphere provides a solution for backing up and restoring workloads. Once you have the Velero
Plugin for vSphere installed and configured on a Supervisor, you can back up and restore VKS cluster workloads and
vSphere Pods. For persistent workloads, the Velero Plugin for vSphere lets you take snapshots of the persistent volumes.
Install and Configure the Velero Plugin Version 1.8.x for vSphere
Learn how to install and configure the Velero Plugin for vSphere to back up and restore workloads running on vSphere
Pods and VKS clusters.
Before You Begin
Be familiar with the following information and perform the required steps:
• These installation instructions apply only to Velero Plugin for vSphere version 1.8.0-embedded+24696422 or any
version with the 1.8 prefix. For information about installing version 1.7.x and earlier, see Install and Configure the
Velero Plugin Version 1.7.x in the vSphere Supervisor 8.0 documentaiton.
• Before installing the new Velero versions, uninstall the current Velero installation. Failing to do so might have
unintended consequences. Use the uninstall command that is described in Uninstall the Velero Plugin for vSphere.
• If you use an air-gapped environment, before following these installation instructions, perform the required steps in
Install the Velero Plugin for vSphere in an Air-Gapped Environment.
Supported Versions
Velero Plugin for vSphere Supervisor 8.x and Earlier vSphere Supervisor 9.0 and Later
1.8.0-embedded+24696422 or any version Yes Yes
with the 1.8 prefix With Supervisor version 8.0 Update 3g and
later
1.7.x and earlier Yes No
Using Velero Commands
Velero is installed in the Supervisor Service namespace. All Velero commands must specify the Velero Supervisor Service
namespace explicitly. For more details, see https://velero.io/docs/v1.16/namespace/.
If you use the following command, you can avoid specifying the namespace repeatedly.
velero client config set namespace=svc-velero-domain-c38
Where is the Velero Supervisor Service namespace.
svc-velero-domain-c38
Prerequisites
• Supervisor is activated.
• A vSphere Namespace is created and configured.
• You must be a member of the VI administrator role. See Using vCenter Roles to Assign Privileges.
• Create a Linux VM where you can run the Velero CLI. Or use an existing Linux jump host where you access
Supervisor.
• The Velero version numbers are presented as . Refer to the Velero Compatibility Matrix for the specific versions
X.Y.Z
to use, and substitute accordingly when running the commands.

Step 0 (Optional): Create a Dedicated Network for Backup and Restore Traffic
Although not required, it is recommended that for production environments you separate the backup and restore traffic
from the Supervisor control plane management network traffic.
There are two aspects to this:
• Tag the ESX hosts to support network file copy (NFC)
• Configure the backup and restore network using NSX.
To configure ESX hosts to support a dedicated network block device (NBD) transport, you add a VMkernel NIC on each
ESX host in the vSphere clusters where the Supervisor runs and set the on that NIC. When the
vSphereBackupNFC
tag is applied to the NIC type for a VMkernel adapter, backup and restore traffic goes through the
vSphereBackupNFC
selected virtual NIC.
To perform this configuration, you use the Virtual Disk Development Kit. See the Best Practices for NBD Transport in the
Virtual Disk Development Kit Programming Guide.
Note:
If the is not enabled on the VMkernel NIC, the backup and restore traffic will be not be sent
vSphereBackupNFC
on the backup and restore network, even if you configure one. If is not enabled, the traffic
vSphereBackupNFC
will travel on the vSphere management network.
Once the tag is enabled, configure the backup and restore network to use NSX by updating the
vSphereBackupNFC
existing vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS) for the cluster as follows.
1. In the vSphere Client, select Menu > Networking.
2. Select the existing VDS for the cluster.
3. Right-click the VDS and select Distributed Port Group > New Distributed Port Group.
4. Create a new Distributed Port Group named BackupRestoreNetwork.
5. Add a VMkernel adapter to the BackupRestoreNetwork Distributed Port Group.
6. Attach all the ESX hosts in the vCenter cluster where the Supervisor is enabled to the BackupRestoreNetwork
Distributed Port Group.
7. Enable the tag.
vSphereBackupNFC

Step 2: Install and Configure Data Manager
To facilitate backup and restore using the Velero Plugin for vSphere, you deploy one or more Data Manager VMs to move
persistent volume backup data in and out of S3-compatible object storage. Data Manager moves the volume snapshot
data from the vSphere volume to the remote durable S3-compatible storage on backup, and from remote S3-compatible
storage to a vSphere volume during restore.
Warning:
Data Manager is only functionally tested and it is not meant to work at scale and does not promise any
performance expectations. It is not meant to backup business critical applications in production.
In a Supervisor environment, install Data Manager as VM.

Step 4: Configure the Velero vSphere Operator Service on the Supervisor
vSphere Supervisor provides the Velero vSphere Operator as a Supervisor Service. The Velero vSphere Operator service
works with the Velero Plugin for vSphere to support backup and restore of Kubernetes workloads, including snapshotting
persistent volumes.
For more information about Supervisor Services, see Managing Supervisor Services.
The Velero vSphere Operator is a core Supervisor Service, which means that the service operator comes pre-registered
with vCenter.

Using the Velero Plugin with Third-Party Backup Solutions
Third-party backup solutions can use the Velero Plugin for vSphere to back up and restore VKS clusters.
The third-party solution uses the Velero Plugin to take VKS backups. But backup orchestration and workflows are handled
through the vendor’s own user interface. This approach allows third-party vendors to integrate with VKS while providing
their own backup and restore experience.
For vendor-specific implementation details, refer to the documentation provided by the third-party backup solution.
Backing Up and Restoring VKS Clusters and Workloads
Refer to this section to backup and restore VKS clusters and workloads.
Backing Up and Restoring VKS Cluster Node VMs
To backup and restore VKS cluster nodes, you backup the Supervisor state. Doing so lets you restore vSphere
Namespaces objects and VKS cluster node VMs.
You activate the Supervisor backup and restore by using the vCenter backup feature available through the vCenter
Management Interface. For details, see Back up the Supervisor State
Note:
You can use Supervisor backups only to restore VKS cluster node VMs. You cannot use Supervisor backups to
restore workloads deployed on VKS clusters. You must backup workloads separately, then restore them after the
VKS cluster nodes are restored.
Backing Up and Restoring Workloads Running on VKS Clusters
You can backup and restore workloads running on VKS clusters by using Velero. See Backing Up and Restoring VKS
Cluster Workloads.
Backing Up and Restoring VM Service VMs in vSphere Supervisor
As a VI administrator, you use backup partner solutions based on VMware vSphere Storage APIs – Data Protection
(VADP) to automatically perform a backup, full restore, and registration of a VM Service VM on a Supervisor. If the
automatic registration fails due to issues with the underlying infrastructure, you can correct the issues and then invoke the
API manually to re-register the VM.
registerVM
Backing Up a VM Service VM
You can perform automatic backups of VM Service VMs through a backup partner solution, such as Veeam, that uses
VMware vSphere Storage APIs – Data Protection.
Typically, the VI administrator uses the partner solution to perform the following tasks:
• Sets up backup infrastructure, including installing backup software and configuring backup storage and repositories.
• Creates a backup job targeting a VM or a group of VMs.
• Initiates backups by triggering the job.
When triggered, the partner software backs up the configuration, data, and Kubernetes state of the VM.
Typically, the backup includes the following items:
• VM's configuration stored in vCenter.
• VMX file.
• Contents of VM data disks that could be static or FCDs.
Broadcom 6949

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For VM Service VMs, the backup also includes VM's Kubernetes state and additional resources necessary to bootstrap
the virtual machine upon restore.
For more information about VMware vSphere Storage APIs – Data Protection and how to use the partner backup
solutions, see the Knowledge Base article 1021175 and your partner documentation.
Restoring a VM Service VM
When necessary, the VI administrator can use the backup to restore the VM. For example, you can restore a VM that fails.
vSphere Supervisor supports full VM restore, which restores an entire VM from a backup file to the latest state of the
original VM.
Starting with 9.0 release, Supervisor also supports partial restore, or restoring into an existing VM.
To perform full restore, make sure that the original VM does not exist on the Supervisor and vSphere. If it still exists, use
the command in the Supervisor before triggering the restore job.
kubectl delete vm
After you trigger the restore process from the backup software, the backup software recreates the VM in the resource pool
and folder specified during restore. The VM can be restored to the same or a different VM name.
If the process is successful, the system detects and automatically registers the restored VM on the Supervisor in the same
vSphere Namespace where it was originally created. During the restore process, a VirtualMachine resource is created on
the Supervisor. If applicable, any additional resources such as, a Secret to bootstrap the VM or PersistentVolumeClaims
for additional volumes used by the virtual machine, are also created.
For more information about Secrets, see Kubernetes documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/
secret/. For information about Persistent Volumes, see https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/.
Guidelines and Considerations
When restoring the VM, consider the following:
• Before starting the restore process, make sure to perform the following steps:
– Verify that the original VM has been removed from the Supervisor and vSphere. If it still exists, use the
kubectl
command in the Supervisor to delete it.
delete vm
– Verify that the underlying infrastructure has not changed between backup and restore. Make sure that all
appropriate resources that the original VM used, such as VM classes and storage policies, are intact on the target
vSphere Namespace .
Otherwise, the automatic registration of the VM fails with an error.
• The restored VM is registered on the same target vSphere Namespace where it was originally created.
• Target resource pool and folder name should be the same as those where the original VM existed.
• The name of the restored VM can be the same as the original VM name. You can also use a different VM name.
Manually Register a VM Service VM
If for any reason the automatic registration of the VM does not succeed, you get an error message that notifies you about
the exact issues causing the failure. After you correct the issues, you can invoke the API and use the VM's
registerVM
moID to manually register the VM.
The following example uses the Datacenter CLI (DCLI) commands to register the VM.
1. Obtain the moID of the VM to register.
# dcli com vmware vcenter vm list
The moID, also called MORef ID, is composed of the vm prefix, followed by a numerical ID, for example, vm-123456.
2. Manually register the VM.
my-namespace vm-123456
# dcli com vmware vcenter namespaces instances registervm --namespace --vm
my-username my-password
+username +password
The command returns a task that is similar to the following:
Broadcom 6950

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
task-637:6b051692-7aff-4d59-8a3f-699d114d37e3
3. Use the VAPI task service to get the status of the task.
my-username
# dcli com vmware cis tasks get --task task-637:6b051692-7aff-4d59-8a3f-699d114d37e3 +username
my-password
+password
The command returns the status of the task and any error messages if unsuccessful.
Backup and Restore vSphere Pods Using the Velero Plugin for vSphere
You can use the Velero Plugin for vSphere to backup and restore workloads running on vSphere Pods.
Overview
You can use the Velero Plugin for vSphere to backup and restore workloads running on vSphere Pods in the Supervisor.
You can back up and restore both stateless and stateful applications running on vSphere Pods. For stateful applications,
you use the Velero Plugin for vSphere to take snapshots of the persistent volumes (PVs).
Note:
You cannot use Velero standalone with Restic to backup and restore vSphere Pods. You must use the Velero
Plugin for vSphere installed on the Supervisor.
Prerequisites
Before you can back up and restore vSphere Pods, your VI administrator must install and configure the Velero Plugin for
vSphere. See Installing and Configuring the Velero Plug-in for vSphere on a Supervisor.
Note:
The Velero Plugin for vSphere is not backing up and restoring the state of the Supervisor.
Back Up a vSphere Pod
To backup a stateless vSphere Pod, run the following command:
velero backup create <backup name> --include-namespaces=my-namespace
The backup is marked after all local snapshots have been taken and Kubernetes metadata is uploaded
Completed
to the object store. However, the backup of volume snapshots occurs asynchronously and may still be occurring in the
background and take some time to complete.
You can check the status of volume snapshots by monitoring Snapshot and Upload custom resources.
Snapshot CRD
For each volume snapshot, a Snapshot custom resource is created in the same namespace as the PVC that is
snapshotted. You can get all Snapshots in PVC namespace by running the following command.
kubectl get -n <pvc namespace> snapshot
The Snapshot CRD has several phases for the field, including:
status.phase
State Description
New Not processed yet
Snapshotted Local snapshot was taken
SnapshotFailed Local snapshot failed
Uploading Snapshot is being uploaded
Uploaded Snapshot is uploaded
UploadFailed Snapshot failed to be uploaded
Canceling Upload of snapshot is being cancelled
Canceled Upload of snapshot is cancelled
CleanupAfterUploadFailed Cleanup of local snapshot after the upload of snapshot failed
Broadcom 6951

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Upload CRD
For each volume snapshot to be uploaded to object store, an Upload CR will be created in the same namespace as
Velero. You can get all Uploads in Velero namespace by running the following command.
kubectl get -n <velero namespace> upload
Upload CRD has several phases for the field, including:
status.phase
State Description
New Not processed yet
InProgress Upload in progress
UploadError Upload failed
CleanupFailed Delete local snapshot failed after the upload
Will be retried
Canceling Upload is being cancelled
Can occur if velero backup delete is called while
snapshot upload is in progress
Canceled Upload is cancelled
UploadError uploads will be periodically retried. At that point their phase will return to InProgress. After an upload has
been successfully completed, its record will remain for a period of time and eventually be removed.
Restore a vSphere Pod
To restore a vSphere Pod workload that has been backed up using the Velero Plugin for vSphere, complete the following
steps.
1. Create a vSphere Namespace for the workload you will restore.
2. Configure the storage policy for the namespace.
3. Run the following Velero command to restore the workload:
backup-name
velero restore create --from-backup
Velero restore will be marked as when volume snapshots and other Kubernetes metadata have been
Completed
successfully restored to the current cluster. At this point, all tasks of vSphere plugin related to this restore are completed
as well. There are no asynchronous data movement tasks behind the scene as that in the case of Velero backup.
Before Velero restore is , you can check the status of volume restore by monitoring CloneFromSnapshot/
Completed
Download CRs as below.
CloneFromSnapshots CRD
For restore from each volume snapshot, a CloneFromSnapshot CR will be created in the same namespace as the PVC
that is originally snapshotted. We can get all CloneFromSnapshots in PVC namespace by running the following command.
kubectl -n <pvc namespace> get clonefromsnapshot
CloneFromSnapshot CRD has several phases for the field, including:
status.phase
State Description
New Clone from snapshot is not completed
Completed Clone from snapshot is completed
Failed Clone from snapshot failed
Download CRD
From each restore of volume snapshot to be downloaded from object store, a Download CR will be created in the same
namespace as Velero. We can get all Downloads in Velero namespace by running the following command.
kubectl -n <velero namespace> get download
Broadcom 6952

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Download CRD has several phases for the field, including:
status.phase
Status Description
New Not processed yet
InProgress Download in progress
Completed Download is completed
Retry Download is retried.
When there is any failure during the download of backup data, the
download is retried
Failed Download is failed

Overview of Running vSphere Supervisor on vSAN Stretched Cluster
Learn what are the general topologies and guidelines for deploying a Supervisor on a stretched vSAN cluster. Stretched
vSAN cluster brings the capability to run VMs with high availability across a stretched data center environment. Starting
from the vSphere 8 Update 3 release, you can also run VKS workloads on a single vSAN stretched cluster that has equal
numbers of hosts that are geographically separated. This way, you provide distributed high availability for VKS workloads
across a stretched data center environment.
A vSAN stretched cluster is a vSAN cluster that spans across two data sites for faster level of availability and inter-site
load balancing. Both sites have equal number of ESX hosts and are part of the same vSphere cluster. Typically, sites part
of a vSAN stretched cluster are geographically separated locations and are referred to as vSAN fault domains. In most
cases, you deploy vSAN stretched clusters in environments where the distance between data centers is limited, such as
metropolitan or campus environments. In a stretched vSAN cluster configuration, both data sites are active sites. In case
of a site failure, workloads are restarted on the site that is still active. Each vSAN stretched cluster also has a witness
node that serves as a tiebreaker when a decision must be made regarding availability of datastore components when the
network connection between the two sites is lost.
For more information on vSAN stretched clusters, see the VMware vSAN Documentation and the vSAN Stretched Cluster
Guide.
You can deploy a Supervisor on an existing vSAN stretched cluster in active/active mode. When a Supervisor is deployed
on a vSAN stretched cluster and settings are applied to provide HA to the Supervisor workloads, this configuration is
referred to as a deployment-mode.
The supported Supervisor deployment on a vSAN stretched cluster is a single-zone Supervisor, where the underlying
vSphere cluster is a vSAN stretched cluster.
Note:
You can only use a greenfield deployment for a Supervisor running on a stretched vSAN cluster starting from the
vSphere 8 Update 3 release. A greenfield deployment in this case means a Supervisor that is freshly deployed on
a vSAN stretched cluster. If the Supervisor is already deployed on a different storage solution or a non-stretched
vSAN cluster, you cannot convert the Supervisor to run on a vSAN stretched cluster.
To deploy a vSAN stretched cluster, follow the recommendations and instructions provided in vSAN Stretched Cluster
Guide and the VMware vSAN Documentation.
Workflow for Activating and Configuring Supervisor on vSAN Stretched Cluster
Check out what is the workflow for activating a Supervisor on a vSAN stretched cluster and configuring HA for workloads
on VKS clusters.
For information on configuring networking for a Supervisor, see Supervisor Networking.

Configuring Storage Policy for vSphere Supervisor on vSAN Stretched Cluster
When you run vSphere Supervisor on a vSAN stretched cluster, you can use a default vSAN storage policy or create a
storage policy compliant with the requirements of the vSAN stretched cluster.
If you decide to create the vSAN stretched cluster storage policy, create it before deploying the Supervisor. During the
deployment, this policy is used for the storage placement of Supervisor control plane VMs and should protect the VMs
across locations.
After you create the vSAN stretched cluster policy, assign the policy to vSphere Namespaces. Use storage classes
associated with this vSAN stretched cluster policy to deploy VKS clusters, persistent volumes, and any other storage
objects in the vSphere Namespaces.
Create a vSAN Stretched Cluster Storage Policy for vSphere Supervisor
When you create the storage policy for vSphere Supervisor, make sure to specify the following settings that apply to the
vSAN stretched cluster.
1. On the Policy structure page, select Enable rules for vSAN storage.
Broadcom 6962

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. On the vSAN page, click Availability, and set the following parameters.
a) Specify Site disaster tolerance.
This setting defines the data redundancy method used by stretched clusters to handle a site failure.
The recommended option is Site mirroring - stretched cluster.
This option allows vSAN data to be mirrored, or replicated, across the two sites of the vSAN stretched cluster.
When you set this parameter, the vSAN stretched cluster can tolerate one site failure. The data remains accessible
even when the site fails.
b) Specify Failures to tolerate.
For the stretched cluster, this setting defines the number of disk or host failures a storage object can tolerate within
each site.
You can select a RAID configuration optimized for either performance (Mirroring) or capacity (Erasure Coding).
With vSAN ESA, it is recommended to use erasure code as it provides the same performance as RAID-1 mirroring.
Table 1804: RAID Configurations, FTT, and Host Requirements
RAID Configuration Failures to Tolerate (FTT) Minimum Hosts Required
| RAID-1 (Mirroring)      | 1   | 2   |
| ----------------------- | --- | --- |
| RAID-5 (Erasure Coding) | 1   | 4   |
| RAID-1 (Mirroring)      | 2   | 5   |
| RAID-6 (Erasure Coding) | 2   | 6   |
| RAID-1 (Mirroring)      | 3   | 7   |
Broadcom 6963

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. Click the Advanced Policy Rules tab, and enable Force provisioning.
If the option is enabled, the vSAN object is provisioned even if other rules defined by the storage policy, such as
site disaster tolerance, cannot be satisfied by the datastore. Use this parameter during an outage when standard
provisioning is no longer possible.
After you create the vSAN stretched cluster policy, assign the policy to vSphere Namespaces. Use storage classes
associated with this vSAN stretched cluster policy to deploy VKS clusters, persistent volumes, and any other storage
objects in the vSphere Namespaces.
Configure vSphere HA for Supervisor Running on vSAN Stretched Cluster
Learn how to configure vSphere HA for a Supervisor running on a vSAN stretched cluster so that to provide HA for
workloads.
• Enable and configure a vSAN stretched cluster.
• Activate a Supervisor on the vSphere cluster configured as a vSAN stretched cluster.
Broadcom 6964

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Locate the vSphere cluster where the Supervisor is deployed respectively on a vSAN stretched cluster.
2. Select Configure and select vSphere Availability.
3. Next to vSphere HA Turned On, click Edit.
4. Configure Failure and Responses settings.
Option Value Description
Host monitoring Turned on Uses network heartbeat to determine the
status of hosts participating in the cluster,
and whether a corrective action is required,
such as restarting a VM on a different host
from the cluster
Response for Host Isolation Power off restart VMs Determines what happens to the VMs
on an isolated host, that is a host that
cannot communicate to other hosts in the
cluster nor reach the isolation response
IP address. You configure this setting to
Power o? and restart, because a clean
shutdown is not possible on an isolated
host, and the access to the vSAN Datastore
and the ability to write to disks is lost.
5. Configure Admission Control.
The compute capacity in a vSAN stretched cluster is typically equally divided between the two sites in the cluster. You
need to ensure that all the VMs on site 1 can be restarted on site 2 when an entire site goes down. To achieve this,
you reserve 50% of the cluster's capacity for failover to allow restart of all the VMs during site failure.
a) Set Define host failover capacity by to Cluster resource Percentage.
b) Enable Override calculated failover capacity and set the CPU and memory reservations to 50% each.
With this setting, vSphere HA ensures that 50% of cluster's aggregate CPU and memory resources are reserved for
failover.
Broadcom 6965

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. Configure Datastore Heartbeating.
In addition to network heartbeating, vSphere HA provides datastore hearbeating for determining the state of the hosts
in the cluster. However, a vSAN datastore cannot be used for heartbeating and you must deactivate this function for
the vSAN datastore.
Note:
If any additional datastore (other than vSAN) is available and if it is accessible by an alternate network path,
independent of the vSAN network, then using heartbeat datastores is fully supported.
To not use datastore heartbeating for the vSAN datastore, select Use datastores only from the specified list and
make sure that the vSAN datastore is not selected. You will still see an alert that there are less than the required
heartbeat datastores, you can disable that alarm by configuring .
das.ignoreInsufficientHbDatastore = true
Broadcom 6966

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
7. Configure isolation response addresses.
When vSphere HA is enabled on a vSAN cluster, HA uses network heartbeat to validate the state of an ESX host.
In a vSAN environment, vSphere HA uses the vSAN traffic network for communication. This is different from traditional
vSphere environments where vSphere HA uses the management network for communication. However, even in
a vSAN environment, vSphere HA continues using the default gateway of the management network for isolation
detection responses. For this reason, you must configure isolation response IP addresses that reside on the vSAN
network to allow HA to react to a vSAN network failure and trigger host isolation response.
It is recommended that you specify two additional isolation response addresses, and each of these addresses should
be site-specific - one isolation address residing in site 1 and the other residing in site 2. This enables vSphere HA
to validate host isolation even in the case of network failure between sites. Use the following settings for additional
isolation response addresses:
• . Set the value to an IP address on the vSAN network which resides on site 1.
das.isolationaddress0
• . Set the value to an IP address on the vSAN network that resides on the site 2.
das.isolationaddress1
• . Set to .
das.usedefaultisolationaddress false
Broadcom 6967

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
8. Save the settings.
9. Configure HA restart priority for individual VMs.
In case of host or site failure, a possibility exists that the resources are insufficient to restart all the VMs in the vSAN
cluster. Therefore, you have to ensure that certain VMs that are of high importance, such as the Supervisor control
plane VMs, are restarted first. To do so, configure vSphere HA restart priority to individual VMs, as follows:
• - Supervisor control plan VMs, NSX Edge VMs, and Avi Load Balancer Service engine VMs.
Highest
• - all VKS cluster control plane VMs.
High
• - all VKS cluster worker VMs.
Medium
a) On the cluster where the Supervisor is enabled, go to Configure > VM Overrides.
b) Select VMs from the list, for example all the Supervisor control plane VMs, and click Next.
Broadcom 6968

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
c) Under vSphere HA, next to VM Restart Priority, select Override, and select a priority level, for example Highest.
d) Repeat the steps until you set restart priority to all the VMs described from above.

Troubleshooting vSphere Supervisor
Use the following troubleshooting techniques and best practices for your infrastructure in vSphere Supervisor. This
information explains how to approach solving problems by breaking down potential failures in the core Supervisor layers
such as storage, networking, identity, life cycle, and others.
How to Approach vSphere Supervisor Issues
Learn what are the practices that might be helpful when you are troubleshooting Supervisor issues.
• Narrow the scope. Determine whether the issue originates from the entire Supervisor, a vSphere Namespace, a
Supervisor Service, a VKS cluster, or a workload running in a VKS cluster. By narrowing the scope, you can determine
whether to start troubleshooting from the VCF storage, networking, or compute layers, or within the VKS layer. See
Troubleshooting VKS Clusters for more information.
• Identify your VCF stack for the Supervisor,.
– Networking - Possible solutions are NSX VPC, NSX Classic (NSX tier 1), or vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS).
– Storage - Might be configured with vSAN or other datastores, which are targeted using vSphere storage policies.
– Load Balancer - The available solutions are Foundation Load Balancer, NSX Load Balancer, Avi, or HA Proxy.
– Focus the debug on core component layers.
• Get evidence early. If you anticipate opening a Broadcom support case, collect critical diagnostic data immediately.
– Collect a Supervisor support bundle.
– Note exactly what changed in the environment, such as recent upgrades, configuration changes, or maintenance
windows.
– Record the exact error messages if possible.
Infrastructure Layer Functional Scope Who can debug?
Networking Connectivity, image pull failures, load Users with Namespaces.Manage
balancers, and firewall rules. permission for vCenter, and access to NSX
or Avi management interfaces.
Authentication and authorization Certificates, login, credentials, and user Users with Namespaces.Manage
permissions (RBAC). permission for system components. View
or Edit for namespace RBAC or login
issues.

or capacity issues. permission for vCenter, and storage policy
checks.

Note:
If the issue is related to a
VKS cluster lifecycle, follow
Troublshooring VKS Clusters
instead.
Important:
Some of the troubleshooting steps for the Supervisor require SSH access to the Supervisor control plane VMs.
Follow the instructions in Broadcom KB 90194.
Supervisor Access Issues
When you cannot reach the Supervisor API, execute kubectl commands, or log in to a Supervisor, the failure typically falls
into one of the following categories:
• API Server Down. The API server is unresponsive. Check the Troubleshooting Core Supervisor Issues section.
• Network Reachability. The Supervisor control-plane VIP or load balancer is not responding. Check the The
Troubleshooting Networking section.
• Authentication. Issues involving certificates, credentials, or kubeconfig tokens. Check the Troubleshooting Certificate
Issues and Troubleshooting Login Issues sections.
• Authorization. The user or service account exists but lacks the explicit RBAC permissions that are needed for the
targeted namespace or resource. Check the Troushleshooting Supervisor Login Issues section.
Enablement and Upgrade Issues
Troubleshooting the Supervisor lifecycle involves the initial enablement and configuration and ongoing upgrade and
maintenance operations.
• Initial Enablement. Focus on ensuring that the fundamental VCF and vSphere infrastructure, including networking,
storage, identity, and topology, is configured correctly as outlined in the core VCF and vSphere Supervisor
documentation.
• Upgrades. Pre-check failures require a methodical approach that is focused on verifying resource capacity, component
health, and compatibility matrixes before the upgrade workflow begins.
When facing issues with initial setup or upgrades, investigate these specific areas:
• Initial enablement or provisioning failures. Start by checking the Supervisor status and consult the documentation
for the Supervisor architecture, storage policies, and networking stacks (NSX, VDS, Avi, or HAProxy). Identity
configurations such as SSO or external IDPs to ensure that all prerequisite components are correctly deployed and
integrated.
• Troubleshooting upgrade precheck failures. Understand pre-check failures and how to remediate them.
• Troubleshooting certificate issues. Check the certificate validity of components in the system.
Networking Issues
Common issues include:
• Access issues to the Supervisor API endpoint.
• Service type objects in Kubernetes getting stuck in pending state.
loadbalancer
• Certificate errors.
• Communication errors between the Supervisor and vCenter or Supervisor and the NSX controller.
The following sections address troubleshooting networking issues:
Broadcom 6971

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Troubleshoot service type load balancer creation errors. If you are using Avi, follow Troubleshooting Avi Load
Balancer.
• Troubleshoot networking errors.
– When using the NSX Tiеr 1 or VPC networking type, the health of the Supervisor networking depends on the health
of the NSX fabric. Health issues in the NSX tunnel endpoint (TEP) on ESX hosts might cause disruptions to the
Supervisor networking. NSX distributed load balancer health issues might cause disruptions to the Kubernetes
ClusterIP Service functions in the Supervisor. If you observe node, pod, or ClusterIP Service networking failures
in NSX Tier 1 or VPC environments, validate the health status of the NSX fabric in the NSX Management Plane. If
health warnings or errors are present, check the NSX Troubleshooting Guide.
• Troubleshoot vSphere Pod or Supervisor Services image pull failures. When Supervisor Services deployment
or vSphere Pod initialization fails due to container image retrieval errors, consult the Troubleshooting Failures in
Supervisor Service Pod Image Pulls section.
Storage Issues
Key areas to investigate when troubleshooting storage issues in the Supervisor environment include the following:
• Storage policy verification.
Ensure the storage class that is configured to the Supervisor maps to a valid and available vSphere storage policy. A
common problem is a policy mismatch or a storage policy that no longer meets the requirements, such as datastores
tagged incorrectly or out of capacity. The vSphere storage policy dictates the capabilities and placement rules for the
resulting persistent volumes.
• Namespace configuration check.
Confirm that the vSphere Namespace has been correctly associated with the necessary storage policies through the
vSphere constructs, for example, a vSphere Namespace linked to appropriate storage policies. Incorrect or missing
associations prevent persistent volume claims (PVCs) within that namespace from being provisioned correctly.
• CNS (Cloud Native Storage) troubleshooting guide.
The CNS component is the critical bridge between Kubernetes and vSphere storage. You must check the CNS logs
and behavior to understand why a provisioning or de-provisioning operation has failed. Issues often stem from CNS
failing to register a newly-created vSphere volume as a first-class disk (FCD) or failing to clean up vSphere objects
after a PVC is deleted in Kubernetes.
To pinpoint the exact failure point in the storage provisioning workflow, start by reviewing the relevant vSphere and
Kubernetes events and logs, such as the logs on the Supervisor control plane VMs, and the vCenter
kube-apiserver
server logs.
Logs and Support Data
• Make sure that Supervisor logs are forwarded to an external location, such as VCF Operations or an external system.
See Forwarding Supervisor Logs to External Monitoring Systems.
• Collect a Supervisor support bundle from the vSphere client, which is helpful in troubleshoot Supervisor issues. You
can collect a support bundle even when the Supervisor is in an error or configuring state.
Troubleshooting Core Supervisor Issues
Learn how to troubleshoot core Supervisor issues such as the Supervisor status and API server.
Supervisor Status
The Supervisor activation process comprises multiple steps. They include the deployment and configuration of the
Supervisor control plane VMs, configuring ESX hosts as Kubernetes nodes, preparing a virtual IP on the load balancer for
the Supervisor API server, and deploying core Supervisor Services.
You can view the Supervisor activation status in the vSphere Client, Workload Management > Supervisor table view,
where the Supervisor activation status is displayed in the config status and host config status columns. Issues that are
encountered in the activation process appear in these columns. Based on the issue description, consult other sections of
this troubleshooting guide or Broadcom KBs.
Broadcom 6972

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Troubleshooting the Supervisor API Server
If the Supervisor API server is unresponsive or unreachable, remote diagnostics fail. In this scenario, bypass the API and
perform low-level node diagnostics directly through control plane SSH.
• Check and node health. When the Supervisor control plane components cannot communicate, check the
kubelet
local node agent status. Run to verify if the service is running, and inspect the journal
systemctl status kubelet
logs for system lifecycle errors, resource starvation, or crashes by using the following command.
journalctl -u kubelet -n 100 --no-pager
• Inspecting the container runtime ( ). If the infrastructure or pod scheduling is stalled, check the container
containerd
runtime engine to see if underlying pods such as the pod are failing to launch. Run the
kube-apiserver mirror
following command.
journalctl -u containerd -n 100
• Review the vCenter logs. To troubleshoot synchronization mismatches between vSphere constructs and the
Supervisor control plane, inspect the Workload Control Plane (WCP) management agent logs on vCenter. These logs
help identify why cluster enablement or configuration updates are failing to push downward. Inspect the active sync
states by running the following command, noting that you must SSH to vCenter if you are not streaming logs.
tail -n 200 /var/log/vmware/wcp/wcpsvc.log
Troubleshooting Supervisor Certificate Issues
Learn how to address certificate issues within the Supervisor environment.
Certificate Components
• Supervisor API server certificates. On port 443, these certificates serve the VIP certificate, and on port 6443 it serves
the Kubernetes certificate.
• Supervisor internal certificates. Kubernetes components use those certificates for internal communication through
TLS between themselves and the Supervisor, and the rest of the VCF stack, including vCenter, NSX Manager, Avi
controller, and others.
• VKS certificates. Generated by VKS and managed by individual VKS clusters automatically.
• NSX Load Balancer TLS certificate. Used to secure communication transiting or terminating at the NSX load balancer
layer. This certificate is only used in network topologies using NSX Tier1 or NSX VPC. The NSX load balancer serves
as the entry point provisioning layer 4 virtual servers (VS) to expose Kubernetes services. The associated TLS
certificates encrypt communications to these endpoints.
All internally managed certificates are rotated automatically, but if you have an older version and suspect a certificate
issue, follow these guidelines.
Check for Expired Certificates
1. First, check the Supervisor VIP certificates.
a. Navigate to Supervisor > Configure > Networking > Certificates to review the expiration dates.
b. Ensure that no certificates expire within the planned upgrade window.
2. Check internal Kubernetes certificates on the Supervisor.
a. Download the script hosted on the Supervisor Certificates KB to verify certificates on the Supervisor.
b. Unzip the script in vCenter, and run these commands to check the Supervisor certificates.
# Unzip the script
$ unzip wcp_cert_manager.zip
Archive: wcp_cert_manager.zip
inflating: certmgr
# Retrieve the ID of the Supervisor Cluster to check its certificates
$ ./certmgr supervisors
# Use certmgr to list the certificates for the Supervisor Cluster
$ ./certmgr certificates list -c <domain id for the supervisor cluster>
Broadcom 6973

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. Check for managed certificates. In VCF 9 and later, cert-manager manages system and VMware pod
cert-manager
certificates separately from the Kubernetes certificates. Therefore, the tool that is used from above does not
certmgr
cover the certificates that are managed by .
cert-manager
To debug certificate errors that are reported by the Supervisor system pods, SSH directly to one of the Supervisor
control plane VMs.
# Check cert-manager pod logs

kubectl logs -n <cert-manager-namespace> <cert-manager-pod>
# Restart cert-manager to force renewal
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n <cert-manager-namespace>
# Confirm certs renewed, then restart affected pods
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n <affected-namespace> <deployment>
Check the Certificate Trust Chain
In certain cases, you might identify a repeating error in multiple logs that is related to an x509 certificate that is signed by
an unknown authority. This error indicates for a missing certificate authority in the Supervisor trust store that prevents the
system from verifying the entire certificate chain.
The CA trust chain must be consistent across five distinct layers. A certificate that is accepted in one layer but missing
from another layer is the most common cause of image pull failures. Work through these layers top-down.
1. VCF Automation, if deployed.
2. vCenter.
3. Supervisor control plane.
4. , connected to the vCenter content libraries.
imageregistry
5. (VCF 9 and later) to pull images from the hosted VCF Automation registry.
mgmt-image-proxy
6. on the Supervisor control plane nodes.
containerd
7. to pull images for Supervisor Services from hosted or private container registries such as Harbor
kapp-controller
and others
8. Workloads running on the Supervisor, including load balancers, VKS clusters, and others.
9. VKS cluster nodes if VKS clusters experience image pull issues.
– on VKS cluster nodes.
containerd
– on VKS cluster nodes.
kapp-controller

Troubleshooting Supervisor Upgrade Pre-check Failures
The upgrade pre-check helps you identify and resolve issues before the Supervisor upgrade begins. If a pre-check fails, it
falls into one of five categories, specifically storage, running workloads, Supervisor Services, health, or certificates.
Error Category What to Check Resolution
Storage Datastore free space Add storage capacity or delete unused files.
VKS clusters VKS clusters versions Upgrade the VKS clusters first.
Update Supervisor Services to the required
Supervisor Services Supervisor Services versions
versions.
Resolve unhealthy status in the Supervisor
Health Etcd and control plane
nodes.
Certificates VIP certificates Renew any certificates expiring soon.
Resource and Storage Capacity
The upgrade process requires deploying a temporary or new control plane VM. If your environment lacks sufficient
resources, the pre-check blocks upgrade.
Check if there is enough free datastore space. If the error indicates insufficient storage space, verify that the physical
datastores that are assigned to the Supervisor storage policy have free space of at least 32 GB. Here are some of the
possible fixes is the datastores lack sufficient space:
• Reclaim space immediately by deleting unused snapshots or ISOs.
• Add storage capacity.
If you add storage capacity but the vSphere Client fails to reflect the recent additions, restart the service through the
vpxd
vCenter command line can force-refresh the capacity state.
Component Health and Connectivity
The Supervisor relies on a healthy internal state connectivity to external components such as NSX, if this is the
networking stack of choice.
• Etcd Health. If the Etcd cluster is reported as unhealthy, the internal database of your Kubernetes environment is out of
sync. Follow Troubleshooting ETCD Issues in vSphere Supervisor
• Network compatibility. Ensure that your NSX version is on the compatible list that is provided in the error message. An
incompatible version of NSX can prevent the new Supervisor version from communicating with the underlying network.
Broadcom 6978

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Version and Service Compatibility
The target Supervisor version to which you want to upgrade might be incompatible with the currently installed VKS or
Supervisor Services versions.
• VKS version. If a pre-check indicates , one or more VKS clusters are running a
VKS clusters Compatibility
VKS version that is incompatible with the target Supervisor version.
Resolution: Upgrade VKS to version that is compatible with the target Supervisor version and retry the Supervisor
upgrade. See Installing and Updating VKS.
• Supervisor Services versions. Supervisor Services such as Harbor or ArgoCD might be running versions that are not
supported with the target Supervisor version. The error message specifies which versions are required.
Resolution: Upgrade these services from the vSphere Client, see Upgrade a Supervisor Service to a Newer Version.
NSX Load Balancer Certificate Validity
NSX expired or near-expiry certificates might cause the upgrade to hang or networking to fail post-upgrade.
In the vSphere Client, navigate to Supervisor > Configure > Certificates to verify that all entries are valid and not set to
expire during the upgrade window.
Troubleshooting Failures in Supervisor Services Pod Image Pulls
Most of the Supervisor Services run as vSphere Pods and issues might accrue in pod image pulls.
Before a vSphere Pod is deployed, its container image must be:
1. Downloaded from its container image repository.
2. Stored on the ESX hostas an image disk.
A failure at either of these steps blocks the vSphere Pod deployment.
Quick Remediation Flow
When a vSphere Pod is stuck in or :
ErrImagePull ImagePullBackOff
1. Run and find the image that is in state.
kubectl get images -n <namespace> Failed
2. Run and check the .
kubectl get image <name> -n <namespace> -o yaml status.lastError
3. Classify the message in by using the table in Step 3:
lastError
– , indicates a DNS failure. Check if the CoreDNS is reachable.
dial tcp: lookup ...
– , indicates a network failure. Check the routes and firewall to the container
dial tcp <ip>:<port> ...
registry.
Step 0: Get Access to the Service Namespace
Request that your user account is assigned at least the permissions on the Supervisor Service namespace.
View
Creating a context for this namespace fails if you do not have access to that namespace.
Step 1: Check the vSphere Pods Status
1. Identify the failing pod and inspect its status:
kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
2. Map the pod status to a likely cause:
Pod Status Meaning
ErrImagePull The image download from the repository has failed.
ImagePullBackOff Repeated ErrImagePull; kubelet is preventing retries.
Possible root causes for image pull failures are the following:
• A DNS resolution failure, cannot reach the registry hostname.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• The image storage disk on the host has no sufficient free space.
• The registry is unreachable due to network or firewall restriction..
• The registry returned an error, such as image not found or manifest invalid.

An custom resource tracks each pod image. Inspect the custom resource to find the exact failure reason.
Image Image
1. List images in the Supervisor Service namespace:
kubectl get images -n <namespace>
2. Find the image that the failing pod is referencing. If its is , dump the full object:
STATE Failed
kubectl get image <image-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml

metadata:
name: ...
namespace: ...
...

...
status:
