Step 3: Classify the Failure from
lastError
Match the error text against the table from below to identify the problem.
Error pattern in status.lastError Classification Likely cause
dial tcp: lookup <host>: i/o DNS resolution failure The image fetcher cannot reach the DNS
timeout server (CoreDNS).
dial tcp <ip>:<port>: i/o Network reachability failure The registry IP is reachable from the host
timeout but the port is closed or the route missing.
or
connection refused
Step 4: DNS Resolution Failures
A error indicates that the image fetcher cannot reach the DNS server.
dial tcp: lookup ..
CoreDNS in the Supervisor is the DNS server that is used by image fetchers. If CoreDNS cannot recognize a DNS name,
CoreDNS acts as a DNS relay to the Workload DNS Server that is specified as part of the Supervisor configuration. How
image fetchers reach CoreDNS depends on the Supervisor network topology. If you observe a
dial tcp: lookup …
error, check the connectivity to CoreDNS.
i/o timeout
Topology How image fetchers reach CoreDNS
VPC CoreDNS is exposed through a load-balancer Virtual IP (VIP) that
is behind the kube-dns ClusterIP Service.
NSX Tier 1 CoreDNS is exposed through the kube-dns ClusterIP Service.
Broadcom 6980

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Topology How image fetchers reach CoreDNS
VDS CoreDNS is reached over the workload network through the
kube-dns ClusterIP Service.
Note:
Image fetchers and Supervisor control plane VMs use different network paths to reach CoreDNS and name
servers.
• Supervisor control plane VMs. Name lookups connect to CoreDNS directly through localhost.
• Image fetchers. These routing paths bypass and use a separate network route.
localhost
Because of this routing difference, a DNS lookup can succeed inside a control plane VM but still fail during an
image pull.
Storage Best Practices and Troubleshooting
You can use best practices and troubleshooting techniques for your storage environment in vSphere Supervisor.
Place Control Plane VMs on Separate Datastores
When you use datastores other than vSAN in your cluster with vSphere Supervisor, place the three control plane VMs
on separate datastores for availability reasons. Spreading control plane VMs across datastores ensures that a single
datastore failure does not affect more than one control plane VM.
Verify that at least three shared datastores are available and attached to all hosts in the Supervisor cluster.
On vSAN, the platform handles VM placement automatically. This procedure applies to VMFS and NFS datastores only.
1. In the vSphere Client, create a datastore cluster.
a) Navigate to data centers.
b) Right-click the data center object and select New Datastore Cluster.
c) Name your datastore cluster and make sure Turn ON Storage DRS is enabled.
d) Set the cluster automation level to No Automation (Manual Mode).
e) Leave the Storage DRS runtime settings as default.
f) Select the ESX cluster enabled with vSphere Supervisor.
g) Select all shared datastores to add to the datastore cluster.
h) Click Finish.
2. Define Storage DRS rules for control Plane VMs.
a) Navigate to the datastore cluster.
b) Click the Configure tab and click Rules under Configuration.
c) Click the Add icon and enter a name for the rule.
d) Make sure Enable rule is enabled.
e) Set Rule type to VM anti-affinity.
f) Click the Add icon and select the three supervisor control plane VMs.
g) Click OK to finish your configuration.
3. Create VM overrides.
a) Navigate to the datastore cluster.
b) Click the Configure tab and click VM Overrides under Configuration.
c) Click the Add icon and select the three control plane VMs.
d) To enable the Storage DRS automation level, select the Override check box and set the value to Fully
Automated.
e) Click Finish.
This task enables Storage DRS for the control plane VMs only and rebalances the VMs to be on different datastores.
Broadcom 6981

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Once the Storage vMotion takes place, you can remove the SDRS rules and overrides, disable Storage DRS, and remove
the datastore cluster.
Restore a Removed Storage Class
When you use the vSphere Client to remove the storage policy from vCenter or a namespace in the Supervisor, its
matching storage class remains in the Kubernetes environment, but cannot be used. Recreating the policy with the same
name restores the storage class and resolves the issue.
If you run the command, the output continues to list the storage class as available in the namespace.
kubectl get sc
However, the storage class cannot be used. For example, attempts of a DevOps engineer to use the storage class for a
new persistent volume claim fail.
If the storage class is already used by a Kubernetes deployment, the deployment might behave unpredictably.
1. To verify which storage classes exist in the namespace, run the
kubectl describe namespace
namespace_name command.
The output for this command does not list the storage class if its matching storage policy is removed.
2. If the storage class is already used by a deployment, restore the storage class.
a) Use the vSphere Client to create a new storage policy with the same name as the policy you removed.
For example, if you deleted the Gold policy, name the new policy Gold. See Create Storage Policies for
Supervisor.
b) Assign the policy to the namespace.
See Change Storage Settings on a vSphere Namespace.
After you assign the policy to the namespace, vSphere Supervisor deletes the old storage class and creates a
matching storage class with the same name. Existing PVCs in Pending state resume binding once the storage
class is available.
Use External Storage with vSAN Direct
When you use vSAN Direct in the vSphere Supervisor environment, you can use external shared storage to store
management internal VMs and other metadata.
When you deploy a homogeneous vSAN Direct cluster, you must create a replicated vSAN datastore on each ESX host in
the cluster to store Supervisor control plane VMs and other metadata. The vSAN datastore consumes space, requires an
additional I/O controller on each host, and limits hardware configuration on which vSAN Direct can be supported.
Instead of configuring the vSAN datastore, you can use external shared storage for storing management internal VMs and
other metadata.
1. If vSAN or vSAN Direct was deployed on the ESX hosts in the cluster, clear the hosts from any configuration.
a) Remove any disks assigned to vSAN or vSAN Direct. See Remove Disk Groups or Devices from vSAN in
Administering VMware vSAN.
b) Optional: Use the script to tag disks on the hosts for vSAN Direct. See Use Script to Tag Storage Devices for vSAN
Direct in vSphere Supervisor Services and Standalone Components documentation.
2. Use VMware Cloud Foundation to create a workload domain with external storage.
Make sure to select one of the storage options, such as NFS, vVols, or Fibre Channel. Only one of these options can
be selected.
For more information, see Managing VCF Domains in VMware Cloud Foundation.
This step deploys a workload domain with vCenter and specified ESX hosts. The external storage is mounted on all
hosts and added to the default cluster.
3. Enable vSAN.
Make sure that no disks are claimed for vSAN.
For more information, see Enable vSAN on an Existing Cluster in Administering VMware vSAN.
Broadcom 6982

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This step creates a zero byte vSAN datastore with vSAN network. No local disks are used for vSAN.
4. Claim local disks on the hosts for vSAN Direct.
For information, see Create a vSAN Direct Datastore in vSphere Supervisor Services and Standalone Components
documentation.
For each device you claim, vSAN Direct creates a separate datastore.
5. Create storage policies for vSAN Direct.
For information, see Create vSAN Direct Storage Policy in vSphere Supervisor Services and Standalone Components
documentation.
6. Enable the Supervisor.
For information, see the Installing and Configuring vSphere Supervisor documentation.
Identify and Remove Orphaned Volumes
Orphaned volumes are storage objects that remain on the datastore after their corresponding Kubernetes
PersistentVolume or first class disk (FCD) catalog entry is gone. You can use to investigate discrepancies between
govc
the Kubernetes volume inventory and the vSphere layer, and to identify and remove orphaned volumes.
Orphaned volumes consume datastore capacity and indicate a gap in the cleanup sequence. Common causes include:
• A VKS cluster deleted without first removing its PVCs.
• A StatefulSet deleted without explicitly deleting its PVCs.
• Finalizers manually removed from PVCs during troubleshooting, allowing Kubernetes objects to be cleaned up while
leaving the backing FCD on the datastore.
• vCenter or FCD operations returning errors while the virtual disk remains on the datastore.
not found
• A Supervisor restore from backup deleted Kubernetes resources created after the backup was taken, leaving their
associated virtual disks on the datastore.
For cleanup after a Supervisor restore from backup, see Cleaning Up Orphaned Objects After Supervisor Restore from
a Backup.
For more information about and for installation instructions, see https://github.com/vmware/govmomi/blob/main/
govc
govc/README.md
1. Identify orphaned volumes.
a) Run to list all volumes tracked by vCenter and cross-reference the output against the
govc volume.ls
Kubernetes PersistentVolume list.
govc volume.ls
kubectl get pv
Any FCD visible in the vCenter inventory that has no corresponding PersistentVolume is a candidate orphan.
b) To confirm, retrieve the disk metadata and check whether the
cns.k8s.pv[].referredEntity.pvc.name
field matches an active PVC.
govc disk.metadata.ls -json=true <fcd-id> | jq '.'
c) To verify that no active snapshot is bound to the volume before removing it, list snapshots at the vSphere layer and
cross-reference against .
kubectl get volumesnapshotcontent
govc volume.snapshot.ls <volume-id>
2. Remove orphaned volumes.
Before removing a volume, confirm it has no active PersistentVolume binding and no running workloads attached.
Then run the following command:
govc volume.rm <fcd-id>
Broadcom 6983

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
Never delete VMDKs directly from the datastore. Deleting a virtual disk outside the FCD API creates an
inconsistency in the vCenter inventory that the system cannot repair automatically. Always remove volumes
through the Kubernetes API or vCenter.
Reconcile the First Class Disk Catalog
The vSphere managed virtual disk inventory can become temporarily inconsistent with datastore backing metadata. This
issue occurs after transient conditions such as I/O errors or brief datastore unavailability. Or when virtual disks are created
or removed using tools other than the vSphere Client or vSphere API.
When the first class disk (FCD) inventory appears incorrect, for example, volumes visible on the datastore do not appear
in the vCenter volume list, invoke the FCD reconciliation task. Use the vSphere Web Services API. The reconciliation task
reviews the managed virtual disk inventory and attempts to correct any inconsistencies.
After reconciliation completes, verify the FCD and vCenter volume lists are consistent before resuming normal operations.
For details, see the Broadcom KB article 321994.
Monitor Datastore Capacity
Insufficient free space on a datastore causes volume provisioning failures and can affect running workloads that rely on
thin-provisioned disks or snapshots. Follow these guidelines to avoid problems.
For information about decommissioning a datastore, see Maintenance Mode for a Datastore Used by Supervisor.
For information about monitoring volumes on a datastore, see Monitoring and Migrating Persistent Volumes in Supervisor
Environment.
For VMFS and NFS Datastores
• Maintain 15–20% free space at all times.
• Do not allow utilization to exceed 90%.
Note:
Redo-log based snapshots can grow to the full size of the original virtual disk, increasing the risk of a datastore-
full condition.
• Enable datastore utilization alarms in vCenter to alert before thresholds are exceeded.
• Where the datastore supports it, enable Reserved Capacity to prevent thin-provisioned disks from exhausting all
available space without warning.
For vSAN Datastores
• Enable the following vSAN health alarms:
Storage space — alerts when vSAN datastore capacity or vSAN managed datastore usage exceeds configured
thresholds.
• Enable automatic rebalancing to redistribute data when the cluster becomes unbalanced after adding or removing
hosts or capacity devices.
By default, vSAN rebalancing is disabled. When enabled, vSAN moves components from over-utilized disks when
imbalance exceeds the configured threshold. Default is 30%.
Uneven data distribution across vSAN disk groups can cause provisioning latency for Supervisor control plane VMs
and VKS workload PVCs, even when overall datastore capacity appears sufficient. Review rebalancing status as part
of routine capacity checks, particularly after adding or removing hosts or changing storage policies.

Verify NSX Distributed Load Balancer Health
In a Supervisor that is configured with NSX VPC networking, the Supervisor Kubernetes ClusterIP Services are
implemented by using NSXDistributed LoadBalancer. The overall health of the NSX fabric and the health of the Distributed
Load Balancer determine the proper function of NSX VPC.

1. Log in to NSX Manager and search for .
Supervisor Instance ID
The search results might include multiple objects that are grouped by type.

3. Locate the NSX Distributed Load Balancer instance.
One NSX Distributed Load Balancer instance is available for per Supervisor.
4. Check the status of the load balancer.
Any status other than might indicate that the NSX Distributed Load Balancer is unhealthy or misconfigured.

For a Supervisor using the NSX Load Balancer, the health of the NSX Load Balancer instance serving the CoreDNS

attempting the image pulls.

Collect Support Bundles for Troubleshooting NSX
You can collect support bundles on registered cluster and fabric nodes for troubleshooting and download the bundles to

If you choose to download the bundles to your machine, you get a single archive file consisting of a manifest file and

Troubleshooting Network Topology Upgrade
When you install vSphere Supervisor version 7.0 Update 1c or upgrade the Supervisor from version 7.0 Update 1 to
version 7.0 Update 1c, the networking topology is upgraded from a single tier-1 gateway topology to a topology that has a
tier-1 gateway for each namespace within the Supervisor.
You can troubleshoot problems that you might encounter during the upgrade.
Upgrade Precheck Fails Due to Insufficient Edge Load Balancer Capacity
The upgrade precheck fails and the error message indicates insufficient load balancer capacity.
The upgrade precheck process fails with an error message that indicates that the load balancer capacity is less than the
capacity required by the Supervisor.
Perform one of the following steps to resolve the problem:
• Force the upgrade by clicking on the Force Upgrade button in the error message or use the vCenter Server command
line with the flag.
--ingnore-precheck-warnings true
Note:
This solution is recommended only if the Edge cluster can support the existing namespace workloads. Otherwise,
these workloads might be skipped during upgrade.
• Delete unused workloads.
• Add additional Edge nodes to the cluster.
Supervisor Workload Namespaces Skipped During Upgrade
During the Supervisor upgrade some namespace workloads are not upgraded.
The Supervisor upgrade succeeds but some namespace workloads are skipped during the upgrade. The Kubernetes
resources indicate insufficient resources and the newly created tier-1 gateway is in state.
ERROR
The load balancer capacity is insufficient to support the workloads.
Perform one of the following steps to resolve the problem:
• Delete unused workloads, restart NCP, and run the upgrade again.
• Add additional Edge nodes to the cluster and trigger a re-allocation to the tier-1 gateway. Restart NCP and run the
upgrade again.
Load Balancer Service Skipped During Upgrade
During the Supervisor upgrade some load balancer services are not upgraded.
The Supervisor upgrade suceeds but some Kubernetes load balancer services are skipped during the upgrade.
The number of Kubernetes load balancer type services in the Supervisor workloads and associated VKS cluster exceed
the NSX Edge virtual server limit.
Delete unused workloads, restart NCP, and run the upgrade again.
Shut Down and Start Up the vSphere Supervisor Workload Domain

must follow the specified order when shutting down or starting up the components.

Supervisor environment.

center (SDDC). As such, you must consider the entire vSphere infrastructure stack when performing a shutdown and

Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes.
Extending Your VCF Private Cloud with Services in VCF Automation and vSphere Supervisor
You can extend the capabilities of your VCF private cloud by installing services in VCF Automation or vSphere Supervisor.
For example, you can install a Harbor OCI registry for storing containers, Cavel packages, and other types of deployment
artifacts. For more information about installing services, see the VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and
Development documentation.
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.
Migration Tool
In VCF Automation 9.1, you can use the Migration Tool to perform an in-place migration from VMware Cloud Director to
VCF Automation. For more information, contact your Broadcom representative.
Overview of VCF Automation Provider Management
With VCF Automation, as a provider administrator, you can build secure, multi-tenant clouds by pooling virtual
infrastructure resources, which are an abstraction of their underlying vSphere and NSX resources, into regions and
exposing them to users through web-based portals and programmatic interfaces.
The VCF Automation Provider Management Guide provides information about adding resources to the system,
creating and provisioning organizations, and managing resources and organizations. This guide is intended for provider
administrators responsible for managing the overall infrastructure, services, and tenancy model across multiple
organizations or tenants. The provider administrator role can either be an Enterprise IT Administrator in an enterprise
environment or a Provider Administrator in a service provider context. Within this guide, provider administrator and system
administrator are used interchangeably.
The VCF Automation Provider Management Guide uses the following terms.
Broadcom 6990

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSphere and NSX Resources
VCF Automation relies on vSphere resources to provide CPU and memory, and on NSX to support the VCF Automation
networking capabilities. Adding storage is provided through vSphere, whether vSAN or external storage.
You can use the underlying vSphere and NSX resources to create cloud resources.
Infrastructure Resources
Infrastructure resources consist of Supervisors, regions, external connections, and region quotas. Infrastructure resources
provide an abstraction of the underlying vCenter and NSX resources that supply compute, storage, memory, and
networking to VCF Automation. Using the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you can view the connection status
of all vCenter and NSX instances that VCF Automation automatically discovers from VCF Operations. See Integrating
Data Sources with VCF Operations.
Supervisor
A VMware vSphere Supervisor is a collection of one or more clusters on a vCenter instance that provide and manage
Kubernetes resources. The Supervisor is the component that owns the physical infrastructure resources and runs
organization workloads on those resources. Each Supervisor can only be associated with one region.
VCF Automation deploys Supervisors deployed with NSX Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networking.
Supervisor VPC Network Stacks
Starting with version 9.1.1, VCF Automation supports two network stack types for Supervisor VPCs:
• Full-stack
Full-stack is the standard deployment model. VPCs rely on Tunnel Endpoints (TEPs) to create an overlay network.
Full-stack VPC networking supports both private and public subnets, NAT, and SNAT.
• VLAN-backed
Designed for environments where no NSX overlay is configured. All traffic runs directly over VLANs. VLAN-backed
VPC networking supports public subnets only.
For more information, see Managing Regions in Your VCF Automation and Deploying Supervisor with VCF Networking
with VPC.
Zone
Zones represent vSphere clusters that provide compute resources for Supervisors. A Supervisor can span across multiple
zones. Zones are created and managed in vCenter. See Configuring and Managing vSphere Zones. It is important to use
meaningful, user-friendly names because the names assigned to zones in vCenter are visible to end users.
A zone can consist of multiple vSphere clusters, but only one cluster binds to a specific vSphere Namespace in each
zone. When enabling a Supervisor, you must choose between two configuration types:
• HA mode: Controller nodes are distributed across three zones, offering high availability. This mode requires exactly
three zones.
• Default mode: All controller nodes are placed in the first zone. You can add additional zones to isolate workloads and
management functions. This mode provides flexibility for physical separation while maintaining simplicity.
To provide an optimal user experience, configure Supervisors and Namespaces with either one or three zones. You can
scale beyond three zones if requirements are driven by workload diversity rather than HA, such as creating dedicated
zones for Windows and Linux. Broadcom supports exceeding three zones per Supervisor and Namespace in these cases.
Region
In VCF Automation, a region combines compute, storage, memory, and networking resources from one or more
Supervisors across one or more vCenter instances that are managed by the same NSX Manager instance.
You can create regions for different geographies, business units, or performance needs, but all Supervisors within a region
must have homogeneous configurations:
Broadcom 6991

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Identical names and definitions for storage classes
• Matching Kubernetes versions
• A consistent set of IaaS services
VCF Automation does not support heterogeneous configurations within a region. Resources in a region can be dedicated
to a single organization or shared across multiple organizations.
If multiple Supervisors are part of the same region and have zones with identical names, such as Zone A, B, C, those
zones are combined and presented as a single set of zones to users. For example, if Supervisor 1 and 2 each have
Zone A, B, and C, the system presents three zones instead of six. To avoid merging, assign unique zone names across
Supervisors.
Important:
In VCF Automation 9.1.1, the region homogeneity requirement also pertains to the network stack type of the
zones within a region.
Region Quota of an Organization
A region quota defines the compute and storage resources allocated to an organization for a given region. The key
aspects of a region quota are:
• CPU and memory utilization limits which represent the upper bound of quota in a region
• CPU and memory reservations which represent the guaranteed capacity that is allocated in a region
• VM classes which represent the t-shirt-sized classes of compute that an organization has access to
• Storage classes which represent the storage classes and the quota assigned in a region
Key constraints for the region quota are:
• An organization can receive region quotas from multiple regions, but there can be only one quota per region.
• In multi-zone regions, you can assign quotas to all or a subset of the zones
When assigning a region quota:
• You can select to fully allocate the capacity or you can specify the CPU and memory capacity per zone.
• VM classes and storage classes are defined at the region quota level and apply to all zones in that quota.
VCF Automation Networking
To leverage the networking capabilities of VCF Automation for organizations for all applications, you can add and manage
your infrastructure and cloud networking resources through the Provider Management UI.
Before you define networking configurations for regions in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you must first
set up the connectivity to the physical network:
• Create a Tier-0 gateway or Tier-0 VRF in NSX Manager, see Add an NSX Tier-0 Gateway.
• Create a VLAN-backed segment and configure the uplink teaming policy in NSX Manager, see Create an NSX
Segment.
• Create IP allocations corresponding to the physical network.
Note:
VCF Automation 9.1.1 supports environments that use VLAN-backed Supervisor VPCs without an NSX overlay.
For such deployments, you must configure a distributed transit gateway connected to the target VLAN in your
physical infrastructure.
As a provider administrator, you then use the VCF Automation Provider Management UI to perform the following tasks for
each region:
1. Determine the set of IPs that organizations have access to and define IP blocks for these IPs. At least one IP block is
required per region.
The IP blocks are used to define the routing for an organization centralized or distributed gateway. You must define in
NSX the external IP ranges that are being routed.
2. Define external connections, centralized or distributed, that organizations can use for North-South connectivity.
Broadcom 6992

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– You create centralized connections by using your preexisting Tier-0 gateways in an or
Active-Active Active-
mode from NSX . For more information about Tier-0 gateways, see Tier-0 Gateways.
Standby
– You create distributed connections by using your existing VLAN or EVPN-VXLAN connection.
Important:
Organizations assigned to a region with VLAN-backed zones must use distributed external connections.
Centralized connections, which are Tier-0-based, are not available for such regions.
3. Depending on the type of connection that you want to create, verify that you have edge or VNA clusters available in
VCF Automation. Also, ensure that all edge clusters or VNA clusters are synchronized with NSX Manager.
4. Assign networking resources to organizations during organization creation or as a Day-2 operation of setting regional
networking for an existing organization.
Organizations
VCF Automation supports multi-tenancy by using organizations. An organization is a top level entity that represents a line
of business or a tenant. Each organization operates in a secure and isolated environment where users can access only
allocated services and resources. The default organization name to log into the Provider Management UI is .
System
You can create two types of organizations. The organizations for all applications are the primary multi-tenancy model
within VCF Automation. Organizations for All Apps use the underlying vSphere Supervisor infrastructure. From the VCF
Automation Provider Management UI, you can create a VM Apps organization using vSphere cluster capabilities which
do not require a Supervisor, shared infrastructure, or tenancy isolation. This option is most suitable for VMware Aria
Automation customers who want to continue leveraging the capabilities to provision VM-based applications without any
disruptions to your business operations.
Regardless of the type, each organization has its own organization portal where users log in to consume resources and
services. Every organization has its own identity source that they connect to and can import users from.
Content Libraries
A VCF Automation provider content library is an abstraction in VCF Automation that provides a single interface for
provider administrators to share content with organizations across regions and to manage their content across the
regions. Content libraries contain VM images hosted in vCenter that can be used in blueprints or IaaS services. The
provider content libraries are read-only to the users of the organizations.
Content libraries host VM images that application teams use when deploying resources. Organizations can either use
content libraries that are provided by the provider administrator or create their own organization-specific content libraries.
VCF Services and Partner Services
VCF services and partner services in VCF Automation are value-added solutions provided by Broadcom and third-
party vendors. The VCF Automation services enhance and extend the functionality of the VCF platform. These services
integrate natively with the VCF architecture enabling VCF Automation organizations to leverage tailored solutions for
automation, scalability, security, and application management. A service can encapsulate UI and API VCF Automation
extensions together with their backend services and lifecycle management. For more information, see the Managing
Services in Your VCF Automation Provider Management UI topic in the VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration
and Development 9.1 documentation.
Provider Administrator Workflow Example
As a Provider Administrator, you manage the overall infrastructure in VCF Automation. You must create one or more
organizations and assign resources to those organizations. You can use this sample workflow of your primary tasks as a
Provider Administrator.
1. Configure the Provider Management infrastructure
a. Configure an identity provider. See Managing Identity Providers in VCF Automation.
b. Configure the VCF Automation access control. See Configuring the VCF Automation Access Control.
c. Create a Region in Your VCF Automation.
d. Configure the networking resources. See Managing Networking Resources in VCF Automation.
Broadcom 6993

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
e. Upload a Partner Service to Your VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. Create and configure an organization
a. Create an organization for All Apps or VM Apps. See Create a VCF Automation Organization for All Applications,
or Create a VCF Automation Organization for VM Applications.
b. Configure the Regional Networking of a VCF Automation Organization.
c. Create a Region Quota for a VCF Automation Organization.
When you set up the necessary infrastructure, Organization Administrators can use the first user credentials, that you
configure during the organization creation, to log in to their respective organizations by using the Organization UI. See
Managing Organizations in VMware Cloud Foundation Automation and Managing Organizations for VM Apps in VMware
Cloud Foundation Automation.
Managing Identity Providers in VCF Automation
You can integrate your VCF Automation with one or more external identity providers (IdPs), and import users and groups
to your organizations. You can configure an LDAP server connection at the system or the organization level, a SAML
integration at the organization level, an OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration at the organization level, and a VCF Single
Sign-On (SSO) integration at the organization level.
Until you configure an identity provider and import users or groups, the only account that can access VCF Automation is
the default administrator account created during deployment. To enable access for additional users, you must configure an
identity provider and import the users or groups you want to grant access. See the relevant procedures in this section.
Broadcom recommends configuring VCF Single Sign-On (SSO) as the identity provider for VCF Automation. VCF SSO
uses the VCF Operations provider identity configuration, making the identity broker the identity provider. VCF SSO is an
automatically configured OIDC integration — the configuration is pushed from VCF Operations, so you do not need to
manually configure the integration in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. VCF SSO does not support multi-
tenancy. For the steps to enable VCF SSO, see Configure a New VCF Single Sign-On for a VCF Instance. If you are
upgrading from VMware Aria Automation 8 to VCF Automation 9.1 and later, both the Provider Administrator and the
Organization Administrator must complete the SSO migration from VMware Identity Manager to the identity broker. See
Migrate VCF Automation Single Sign-On Configuration from VMware Identity Manager to VCF Identity Broker.
Note:
Configuring VCF Automation for VCF SSO makes most of the steps in the rest of this section unnecessary. After
you configure VCF SSO, you can proceed directly to Configuring the VCF Automation Access Control. You must
still import the users and groups that you want to grant access to. For more information, see Import Provider
Users to Your VCF Automation and Import a Provider Group to Your VCF Automation.
Note:
To determine the correct values and settings and to ensure proper and accurate configuration, see also the
product documentation of those identity providers.
You can also use the VCF Operations provider identity configuration, making VIDB the identity provider. See Identity
Broker Models and Configuring VCF Single Sign-On. If you already have an OIDC connection for the provider
organization, you cannot connect to VCF Single Sign-On (SSO). You must remove the OIDC configuration to configure
VCF SSO. If you configure VCF SSO, a VCF SSO tab replaces the OIDC tab on the Identity Providers page.
An organization can define an identity provider that it shares with other applications. Users authenticate to the identity
provider to obtain a token that they can then use to log in to the organization. Such a strategy can enable an enterprise to
provide access to multiple, unrelated services, including VCF Automation, with a single set of credentials, an arrangement
often referred to as single sign-on.
When integrating your VCF Automation organizations with more than one identity provider, you must not have identical
user names across IdPs. You can have only one integration per IdP technology. VCF SSO and OIDC use the same
technology, so you can configure either VCF SSO or OIDC, but not both. For example, you can have one LDAP, one
SAML, and either one OIDC or one VCF SSO integration simultaneously. If you have configured VCF SSO, you can add
SAML or LDAP as additional identity providers. The login page displays all configured sign-in options and to make the
login more user friendly, you can customize the button labels from the IdP edit pages.
Broadcom 6994

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Managing LDAP Connections in Your VCF Automation
As a Provider administrator, you can configure your VCF Automation system organization and any other organizations
in the system to use an LDAP server as a source of users and groups. The organizations can use either the system LDAP
connection or a private LDAP connection.
Note:
You can use VCF Single Sign-On (SSO) instead of configuring your VCF Automation organizations to use an
LDAP server.
VCF Automation has a centralized, tenant-aware storage area for certificate management. This way, VCF Automation
centralizes all certificates in one place so thatsystem administrators andorganization administrators can view, audit,
and manage all certificates in use by various components in the system. You can use the VCF Automation API to add,
update, or remove certificates from the new tenant-aware storage area. See VCF Automation API Schema Reference.
When adding or editing a new LDAP server endpoint, you can use the VCF Automation UI to test a remote connection
to an endpoint and to establish a trust relationship. See Test the VCF Automation Connection to a Remote Server and
Establish a Trust Relationship Using the Provider Management UI. VCF Automation adds any certificate you decide to
trust to a centralized certificate storage area.
Note:
To determine the correct values and settings and to ensure proper and accurate configuration, see also the
product documentation of those identity providers.
Configure a System LDAP Connection in Your VCF Automation
To provide VCF Automation and its organizations with shared access to users and groups, you can configure an LDAP
connection at a system level.
Note:
You can use VCF Single Sign-On (SSO) instead of configuring your VCF Automation organizations to use an
LDAP server.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation pane, under Administration, click Identity Providers.
3. On the Identity Providers page, click the LDAP tab.
The current LDAP settings appear.
4. Click Configure.
5. In the Connection tab, enter the required information for the LDAP connection.
Required Information Description
Server The host name or IP address of the LDAP server.
Port The port number on which the LDAP server is listening.
For LDAP, the default port number is 389. For LDAPS, the default port number is 636.
Base distinguished name The base distinguished name (DN) is the location in the LDAP directory where VCF
Automation to connect.
To connect at root level, enter only the domain components, for example, DC=exampl
e,DC=com.
To connect to a node in the domain tree structure, enter the distinguished name for that
node, for example, OU=ServiceDirector,DC=example,DC=com.
Connecting to a node limits the scope of the directory available to VCF Automation.
Connector type The type of your LDAP server. Can be Active Directory or OpenLDAP.
Use SSL If your server is LDAPS, select this check box.
Broadcom 6995

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Required Information Description
Authentication method Simple authentication consists of sending the user's DN and password to the LDAP
server. If you are using LDAP, the LDAP password is sent over the network in plain text.
If you want to use Kerberos, you must configure the LDAP connection by using the
vCloud API.
User name Enter the full LDAP distinguished name (DN) of a service account with domain admin
rights. VCF Automation uses this account to query the LDAP directory and retrieve user
information.
If the anonymous read support is enabled on your LDAP server, you can leave these
text boxes blank.
Password The password for the service account that connects to the LDAP server.
If the anonymous read support is enabled on your LDAP server, you can leave these
text boxes blank.
6. Click the User Attributes tab, examine the default values for the user attributes, and, if your LDAP directory uses
different schema, modify the values.
7. Click the Group Attributes tab, examine the default values for the group attributes, and, if your LDAP directory uses
different schema, modify the values.
8. If you want to customize the Sign in with LDAP button label that appears on the VCF Automation login page, enter a
new custom button text.
You can enter up to 24 symbols. You can use special characters and accented letters. If you want to revert to the
default text, delete the custom label. The default button label is localized, and depending on your browser language
settings, the text might appear in a different language. Custom labels always appear as you enter them.
9. Click Save.
10.If you selected the Use SSL check box, and if the certificate of the LDAPS server is not yet trusted, on the Trust
Certificate window, confirm if you trust the certificate presented by the server endpoint.
11.To test the LDAP connection settings and the LDAP attribute mappings:
a) Click Test.
b) Enter the password of the LDAP server user that you configured and click Test.
If connected successfully, a green check mark is displayed.
The retrieved user and group attribute values are displayed in a table. The values that are successfully mapped to
LDAP attributes are marked with green check marks. The values that are not mapped LDAP attributes are blank
and marked with red exclamation marks.
c) To exit, click Cancel.
12.To synchronize VCF Automation with the configured LDAP server, click Sync.
VCF Automation synchronizes the user and group information with the LDAP server regularly depending on the
synchronization interval that you set in the general system settings.
Wait a few minutes for the synchronization to finish.
You can import users and groups from the newly configured LDAP server.

Configure Your VCF Automation System to Use a SAML Identity Provider
If you want to import users and groups from a SAML identity provider to your VCF Automation organization,
System
you must configure the organization with this SAML identity provider. Imported users can log in to the
System System
organization with the credentials established in the SAML identity provider.
• Verify that you have access to a SAML 2.0 compliant identity provider.
Broadcom 6998

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Obtain an XML file with the following metadata from your SAML identity provider.
– The location of the single sign-on service
– The location of the single logout service
– The location of the service's X.509 certificate
For information on configuring and acquiring metadata from a SAML provider, consult the documentation for your
SAML provider.
To configure VCF Automation with a SAML identity provider, you establish a mutual trust by exchanging SAML service
provider and identity provider metadata.
To determine the correct values and settings and to ensure proper and accurate configuration, see also the product
documentation of those identity providers.
When an imported user attempts to log in, the system extracts the following attributes from the SAML token, if available,
and use them for interpreting the corresponding pieces of information about the user.
•
email address = "EmailAddress"
•
user name = "UserName"
•
full name = "FullName"
•
user's groups = "Groups"
• (this attribute is configurable)
user's roles = "Roles"
Group information is used if the user is not directly imported but is expected to log in by virtue of membership in imported
groups. A user can belong to multiple groups, so can have multiple roles during a session.
If an imported user or group is assigned the Defer to Identity Provider role, the roles are assigned based on the
information gathered from the attribute in the token. If a different attribute is used, this attribute name can be
Roles
configured using API and only the attribute is configurable. If the Defer to Identity Provider role is used, but no
Roles
role information can be extracted, the user can log in but has no any rights to perform any activities.

Configure Your System to Use an OpenID Connect Identity Provider Using Your
VCF Automation Provider Management UI
If you want to import users and groups from an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider to your VCF Automation
System
organization, you must configure your organization with this OIDC identity provider. Imported users can log in to
System
the organization with the credentials established in the OIDC identity provider.
System
Note:
If VCF Single Sign-On (SSO) is configured, a VCF SSO tab replaces the OIDC tab on the Identity Providers
page.
OAuth is an open federation standard that delegates user access. OpenID Connect is an authentication layer on top of
the OAuth 2.0 protocol. By using OpenID Connect, clients can receive information about authenticated sessions and end-
users. The OAuth authentication endpoint must be reachable from the VCF Automation cells which makes it more suitable
when you use public identity providers or provider-managed ones.
Important:
Endpoint misconfigurations can lead to user inability to complete the SSO logout from VCF Automation. See
Broadcom knowledge base article 394731.
You can allow organizations to generate and issue API access tokens that applications can use on their behalf.
You can configure VCF Automation to automatically refresh your OIDC key configurations from the JWKS endpoint you
provide. You can configure the frequency of the key refresh process and the rotation strategy that determines whether
VCF Automation adds new keys, replaces the old keys with new, or the old keys expire after a certain period.
Note:
To determine the correct values and settings and to ensure proper and accurate configuration, see also the
product documentation of those identity providers.
VCF Automation generates audit events for both successful and failed key refreshes under the event topic
com/vmware/
. The audit events for failed key refreshes include additional information
vcloud/event/oidcSettings/keys/modify
about the failure.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation panel, click Administration.
3. In the left pane, under Identity Providers, click OIDC.
4. If you are configuring OIDC for the first time, copy the client configuration redirect URI and use it to create a client
application registration with an identity provider that complies with the OpenID Connect standard, for example,
VMware Cloud Foundation® Identity Broker.
You need this registration to obtain a client ID and a client secret that you must use during the OIDC identity provider
configuration.
Broadcom 7000

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. Click Configure.
6. Verify that OpenID Connect is active, and enter the client ID and client secret information from the OIDC server
registration.
7. Optional: To use the information from a well-known endpoint to automatically fill in the configuration information, turn
on the Configuration Discovery toggle and enter a URL at the site of the provider that VCF Automation can use to
sent authentication requests to.
8. Click Next.
9. If you did not use Configuration Discovery in Step 6, enter the information in the Endpoints section.
a) Enter the endpoint and issuer ID information.
b) If you are using VMware Cloud Foundation® Identity Broker as an identity provider, select SCIM as access type.
For other identity providers, you can leave the default User Info selection.
c) If you want to combine claims from the endpoint and the ID Token, turn on the Prefer ID Token toggle.
UserInfo
The identity providers do not provide all the required claims set in the endpoint. By turning on the
UserInfo
Prefer ID Token toggle, VCF Automation can fetch and consume claims from both sources.
d) Enter the maximum acceptable clock skew.
The maximum clock skew is the maximum allowable time difference between the client and server. This time
compensates for any small time differences in the time stamps when verifying tokens. The default value is 60
seconds.
e) Click Next.
10.If you did not use Configuration Discovery in Step 6, enter the scope information, and click Next.
VCF Automation uses the scopes to authorize access to user details. When a client requests an access token, the
scopes define the permissions that this token has to access user information.
11.If you are using User Info as an access type, map the claims and click Next.
You can use this section to map the information VCF Automation gets from the user info endpoint to specific claims.
The claims are strings for the field names in the VCF Automation response.
12.If you want VCF Automation to automatically refresh the OIDC key configurations, turn on the Automatic Key Refresh
toggle.
a) If you did not use Configuration Discovery in Step 6, enter the Key Refresh Endpoint.
The Key Refresh Endpoint is a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint and it is the endpoint from which VCF
Automation fetches the keys.
b) Select how often the key refresh occurs.
You can set the period in hourly increments from 1 hour up to 30 days.
c) Select a Key Refresh Strategy.
Option Description
Add Add the incoming set of keys to the existing set of keys. All keys in
the merged set are valid and usable.
For example, your existing set of keys includes keys A, B, and D.
Your incoming set of keys includes keys B, C, and D. When the
key refresh occurs, the new set includes keys A, B, C, and D.
Replace Replace the existing set of keys with the incoming set of keys.
For example, your existing set of keys includes keys A, B, and D.
Your incoming set of keys includes keys B, C, and D. When the
key refresh occurs, key C replaces key A. The incoming keys B,
C, and D become the new set of valid keys without any overlap
with the old set.
Broadcom 7001

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
Expire After You can configure an overlap period between the existing and
incoming sets of keys. You can configure the overlapping time
using the Expire Key After Period, which you can set in hourly
increments from 1 hour up to 1 day.
The key refresh runs start at the beginning of every hour. When
the key refresh occurs, VCF Automation tags as expiring the keys
in the existing set of keys that are not included in the incoming
set. At the next key refresh run, VCF Automation stops using the
expiring keys. Only keys included in the incoming set are valid and
usable.
For example, your existing set of keys includes keys A, B, and D.
The incoming set includes keys B, C, and D. If you configure the
existing keys to expire in 1 hour, there is 1 hour of overlap during
which both sets of keys are valid. VCF Automation marks key A
as expiring and until the next key refresh run, keys A, B, C, and
D are usable. At the next run, key A expires and only B, C, and D
continue working.
13.If you did not use Configuration Discovery in Step 6, upload the private key that the identity provider uses to sign its
tokens.
14.If you want to customize the Sign in with OIDC button label that appears on the VCF Automation login page, enter a
new custom button text.
You can enter up to 24 symbols. You can use special characters and accented letters. If you want to revert to the
default text, delete the custom label. The default button label is localized, and depending on your browser language
settings, the text might appear in a different language. Custom labels always appear as you enter them.
15.Click Save.
• Subscribe to the event topic.
com/vmware/vcloud/event/oidcSettings/keys/modify
• Verify that the Last Run and the Last Successful Run are identical. The runs start at the beginning of the hour. The
Last Run is the time stamp of the last key refresh attempt. The Last Successful Run is the time stamp of the last
successful key refresh. If the time stamps are different, the automatic key refresh is failing and you can diagnose the
problem by reviewing the audit events.
Enable PKCE in VCF Automation
VCF Automation supports Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).
Verify that you configured your system to use an OpenID Connect Identity Provider. See Configure Your System to Use an
OpenID Connect Identity Provider Using Your VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
PKCE is an extension to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow that is used to prevent CSRF and authorization code
injection attacks. For more information, see Proof Key for Code Exchange in the OAuth 2.0 documentation.
1. Run the request to retrieve your organization's settings.
organization_id
GET https://vcfa.example.com/api/admin/org/ /settings/oauth
The response contains the OAuth settings for your organization.
2. Under , make the following changes.
OrgOAuthSettings
a) Modify the element to .
usePkce true
b) Optional: If your identity provider requires that client credentials be sent as an authorization header when making
the API request to retrieve the access token, modify the
sendClientCredentialsAsAuthorizationHeader
element to .
true
The default behavior is for the client credentials to be sent in the body of the API request.
3. To update your OAuth settings with your modifications, run a PUT request.
PUT https://vcfa.example.com/api/admin/org/organization_id/settings/oauth
In the body of the request, include the modified elements of your OAuth settings.
Broadcom 7002

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Remapping VCF Automation Users Between Identity Providers
You can remap VCF Automation users between identity providers.
You can remap individual users from one identity provider (IDP) to another by using the VCF Automation API. You can use
the VCF Automation UI for bulk remapping of users between identity providers.
Remap Users Between Identity Providers Using Your VCF Automation Provider Management
UI
You can use the VCF Automation UI for bulk remapping of users between identity providers.
• Verify that the users you want to remap are imported into the organization. See Managing VCF Automation Provider
Users and Groups.
• Verify that your role includes theGroup / User: Manage right.
• Verify that the organization is configured with the identity provider types that you want to remap between.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. From the primary left navigation pane, click Access Control.
3. Click Users.
4. Click Bulk Update.
5. Click Export Users.
The users are exported into a CSV file.
6. In the CSV file with the users, change the value in the field to identify the new IdP for each user.
providerType
VCF Automation supports the , , and values. To remap a user to an OIDC identity provider, you must
SAML LDAP OAUTH
change the value in the field to .
providerType OAUTH
7. Optional: To match the user name in the IdP that each user is remapping to, modify the user name.
For VCF Automation to continue to associate the user's assets with the user when they log in through the new login
flow, the ID of the user must remain unchanged. Changes to all other fields are ignored.
8. Save your changes and close the CSV file.
9. In the Users Bulk Update wizard, click Next.
10.Click Select CSV File, browse for the file, and upload it.
11.Click Next.
12.Click Update.
When you start the update process, users are remapped one by one. Users for which no changes are detected are
skipped. If you close the VCF Automation UI tab while before the process is complete, the update stops.
Remap a User Between Identity Providers by Using the VCF Automation API
You can remap individual users from one identity provider (IdP) to another by using the VCF Automation API.
• Verify that the users you want to remap are imported into the organization. See Managing VCF Automation Provider
Users and Groups.
• Verify that your role includes theGroup / User: Manage right.

Using VCF Automation as an Identity Provider Proxy Server
You can take advantage of the OIDC Services to use VCF Automation as a tenant-aware identity provider proxy server.
When VCF Automation is configured as an identity provider proxy server by using the OAuth 2.0 OpenID Connect
standard, relying parties can use VCF Automation for tenant-aware authentication of users known to VCF Automation. For
detailed information on the OpenID Connect standard, see OpenID Connect Core 1.0.
As an identity provider proxy server, VCF Automation acts as intermediary between the client application (relying party)
and the identity provider, and delegates actual authentication to the respective authentication mechanism used by the
provider or tenants.
System administrators can configure relying parties that enable organizations to use VCF Automation as an identity
provider proxy. Starting with version 9.1.1, organization administrators can also configure tenant-specific relying parties
exclusively for their organization.
Important:
When making browser-based requests to the endpoints, the default behavior is for browser pages to be
/oidc
loaded from the VCF Automation host. To use OIDC, you can also configure a non-VCF Automation host into the
CORS filtering list.
Authentication Flow
Integration with VCF Automation is implemented through the OAuth 2.0 OIDC authorization code flow standard. For
detailed information, see Authentication using the Authorization Code Flow.
When a relying party redirects a user to VCF Automation without an existing client session, VCF Automation prompts
the user to log in by identifying the target organization or provider UI. The user authenticates through the configured
authentication mechanism, which might involve further redirections to external identity providers. If the browser of the
user detects an existing VCF Automation user session, the authentication flow provides an SSO experience and no user
interaction is necessary for reauthentication.
After successful authentication, VCF Automation returns an access token and an ID token. The authorization code is valid
for 5 minutes. The ID token is valid for one hour. Starting with version 9.1.1, the access token is also valid for one hour.
You cannot use the access token that VCF Automation returns upon successful authentication for accessing the UI portals
or for making regular VCF Automation API calls. Starting with version 9.1.1, you can use the token to make regular VCF
Automation API calls only if you specified the when creating the relying party.
vcfa_api scope
ID Token Details The ID token that VCF Automation returns contains the following OpenID standard claims and VCF
Automation specific claims.

VCF Automation

associate a client session with an ID token, and to

included in the relying party request.

token. The value is the client ID of requesting relying
party.

Provider and Tenant OIDC Relying Parties
Starting with version 9.1.1, provider and tenant organizations can create and manage OIDC relying parties (RPs) in VCF
Automation. Managing RPs at both levels provides granular control over authentication scopes and tenancy access.
The field on an RP controls the tenancy scope. You must set this field during creation.
isGlobal
The value determines how VCF Automation resolves the effective operating organization when issuing tokens:
isGlobal
• Global provider-org RP ( ): Standard tenancy resolution applies. The RP does not alter the operating
isGlobal: true
organization of the system user.
• Restricted provider-org RP ( ): When a system user requests a token for this RP, VCF Automation
isGlobal: false
sets their effective operating organization to the provider organization. The token does not include cross-tenant scope.
• Tenant-org RP: Always behaves as non-global. VCF Automation scopes the token to the tenant that owns the RP.
Broadcom 7009

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
You can set only during RP creation. You cannot change it afterward. If you attempt to modify the field
isGlobal
on an existing RP, the API returns an HTTP 400 error. To change the global or non-global designation, you must
delete the RP and recreate it with the required value.
Provider organization RPs
When you create an RP in the provider organization using API version 9.1.1 or later, set to control whether the
isGlobal
RP is available across all tenant organizations or restricted to the provider organization.
isGlobal value at creation Behavior
true The RP is global. System users can obtain tokens for this RP
regardless of their operating tenant organization.
false The RP is restricted to the provider organization. Tokens issued
for this RP apply exclusively to the provider organization.
Omitted or null Defaults to true.
Note:
In API version 9.1.0 and earlier, provider organization RPs are always global. If you set to false, the
isGlobal
API returns an HTTP 400 error. Omitting the field defaults to true. This behavior preserves compatibility for API
clients that omit the field.
Tenant organization RPs
Starting with version 9.1.1, tenant organizations can create organization-scoped RPs without provider organization
involvement. For tenant organization RPs, you must set to or omit the field.
isGlobal false
isGlobal value at creation Behavior
false or omitted The RP applies only to the tenant organization.
true The API returns an HTTP 400 error. Tenant organizations cannot
create global RPs.
Audience Validation Requirement for Tenanted Relying Parties
Starting with version 9.1.1, the VCF Automation tenanted OIDC service enforces tenancy boundaries through two
complementary requirements. VCF Automation never issues a token where the audience or the relying party and the
authenticated user belong to different tenant organizations. Relying parties must uphold the complementary requirement:
reject any token whose claim does not include the registered client ID of the relying party.
aud
Every relying party registered in VCF Automation is assigned a UUID that is globally unique across all tenant
organizations. This UUID is set as the (audience) claim in every token VCF Automation issues for that relying party.
aud
Because relying party IDs never collide across tenants, a valid match confirms that the token was issued for your
aud
application within your organization.
When a user authenticates through the VCF Automation tenanted OIDC service, VCF Automation verifies that the
target relying party exists within a tenant organization accessible to that user before issuing the token. The resulting
token carries an audience value that is bound to the tenancy context of the user. A token issued for a relying party in
Organization A never carries the audience value of a relying party registered in Organization B.
Relying parties integrating with the VCF Automation tenanted OIDC service must validate the claim as specified by:
aud
• For ID tokens - OpenID Connect Core 1.0 — ID Token Validation
• For access tokens - RFC 9068 §4 — JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens
Specifically, a relying party must:
1. Extract the claim from the received token.
aud
2. Verify that the claim contains the registered client ID of the relying party.
aud
Broadcom 7010

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
3. Reject any token where this check fails, regardless of whether the token is otherwise cryptographically valid.
Skipping or weakening this check breaks the tenancy boundary. A compliant OIDC or JWT library performs this validation
automatically when configured with the expected audience value — the client ID assigned at relying party registration in
VCF Automation.
Note:
VCF Automation provides no additional backstop beyond the claim. If you omit audience validation, your
aud
integration assumes full responsibility for any cross-tenant token acceptance.
Configure VCF Automation as an OpenID Provider Proxy Server
You can use VCF Automation as a tenant-aware OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider proxy server.
Verify that your role includes the OIDC Server: Manage right.
After you configure VCF Automation as an OIDC proxy server, when a user attempts to log in to the OIDC relying party
(OIDC client), they are redirected to VCF Automation and prompted to enter the name of their organization and their SSO
or local credentials. After providing the necessary credentials, the user is directed to the OIDC relying party.
VCF Automation delegates actual authentication to the authentication mechanism used by the provider or organization.
This can result in additional redirects to any external Identity Providers that perform authentication for those users.
Starting with version 9.1.1, to use the RP to call VCF Automation API endpoints outside the OIDC authorization flow, such
as , you must include in the scope array during creation through the VCF Automation API. If you
/cloudapi vcfa_api
omit this scope, VCF Automation rejects the RP tokens on non-OIDC endpoints. You cannot add the scope after creation.
For more information about scopes, see Using VCF Automation as an Identity Provider Proxy Server.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation pane, click OIDC Services.
3. Click Relying Parties and click New.
4. Enter a relying party name for the client application registration, and make a note of it.
5. Starting with version 9.1.1, if you want this relying party to be usable across all tenant organizations, select the Is
Global check box.
When Is Global is selected, system users can obtain tokens for this relying party regardless of which tenant
organization they operate in. When deselected, tokens are scoped to the provider organization only. You cannot
change this setting after the relying party is created. To change the designation, delete the relying party and recreate it.
6. Enter the URI to which to redirect users attempting to log in to the relying party.
7. Click Save.
8. Copy the relying party ID and secret, and make note of them.
9. Configure your OIDC relying party to use VCF Automation as an identity provider proxy server with the relying party ID
and secret.
Tip:
You can retrieve the provider configuration values, including the JWKS endpoint and information about other
endpoints and scopes necessary for the OIDC proxy configuration at the well-known configuration URL
hostname . See View and Edit the OIDC Proxy General
/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration
Settings in Your VCF Automation.
When a user attempts to log in to the OIDC relying party, the redirection behavior depends on the relying party
configuration.
• For a tenant organization relying party, VCF Automation automatically redirects the user to the login page of the

Managing OIDC Proxy Keys in Your VCF Automation
When you configure VCF Automation to function as an OIDC identity provider proxy, VCF Automation generates a pair of
OIDC keys with which it signs the JWT tokens that it issues.
Verify that your role includes the OIDC Server: Manage right.
When configured as an identity provider proxy server, VCF Automation automatically generates a single built-in 2048-bit
RSA signing key, which the system administrator can choose to use or to discard. Any new keys must comply with the
minimum key size and the other VCF Automation cryptographic requirements.
When rotating the signing key you must upload the new key, wait at least 24 hours before marking the new key as the
active signing key, and keep the previous signing key for a sufficient period before decommissioning it, in order to prevent
the invalidation of any tokens issued by the old key.
Tip:
To view the VCF Automation key requirements, in the left navigation bar, click SSL.
The relying parties that are using VCF Automation as an OIDC proxy server can retrieve the provider configuration values,
including the list of available public keys from the JWKS endpoint listed at
{{hostname}}/oidc/.well-known/
.
openid-configuration

Configuring the VCF Automation Access Control
By using the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you can import Provider Administrators to VCF Automation
individually, or as part of an IdP group. You can also create and modify global roles that determine what rights a user has
within their organization.
Managing VCF Automation Rights and Roles
A right is the fundamental unit of access control in VCF Automation. A role associates a role name with a set of rights.
Each organization can have different rights and roles.
VCF Automation uses roles and their associated rights to determine whether a user or group is authorized to perform
an operation. Many of the procedures documented in the VCF Automation guides include a prerequisite role. These
prerequisites assume that the named role is the unmodified predefined role or a role that includes an equivalent set of
rights.
SystemAdministratorscan use rights bundles and global roles to manage the rights and roles that are available to each
organization.
Broadcom 7014

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The is not published to any organization. The system also contains built-in global roles that
System Rights Bundle
are published to all organizations managed by the organization. For information about the predefined roles, see
system
Predefined VCF Automation Roles and Their Rights.
Rights Terminology
Right Each right provides view or manage access to a particular object type in VCF Automation. Rights
belong to different categories depending on the objects to which they relate, for example, Catalog,
Organization, and so on. The provider organization contains all rights available in the system. The
System Administrator defines the rights that are available to each organization. You cannot create or
modify the rights included in VCF Automation.
Rights Bundle
Note:
By default, VCF Automation shows the rights bundles in Simple Mode and you can only
view the built-in read-only rights bundles and publish the to
Orchestrator Rights Bundle
organizations in which you want to enable VCF Operations orchestrator.
If you enable the Advanced Rights Bundle Mode feature flag, you can use rights bundles to manage the
rights that are available to each organization. You can manage feature flags by navigating to the Feature
Flags page from the left navigation pane.
A rights bundle is a set of rights that you as a System Administrator can publish to one or more
organizations. You can create and publish rights bundles that correspond to tiers of service, separately
monetizable functionality, or any other arbitrary rights grouping. Only System Administratorscan view and
manage the rights bundles. You can publish multiple bundles to the same organization.
Organization Rights Organization rights are the full set of rights that are available to an organization. Organization rights can
comprise multiple rights bundles, but the organization administrators and users see a flat set of rights
that they can use to create and modify tenant-specific roles.
Roles Terminology
Role A role is a set of rights that is assignable to one or more users and groups. When you create or import a
user or group, you must assign it a role.
Provider Roles Provider roles are the set of roles that are available only to the provider organization. System
Administrators can assign provider roles only to provider users. System Administrators can create
custom provider roles.
Global Roles Global roles are the set of roles available to an organization.
System Administrators can create and edit global roles and publish them to one or more organizations.
Administrators can assign global roles to users in the organizations to which they are published.
Organization administrators cannot edit global roles.
Note:
Organization users can use only those rights from their roles that are published to their
organizations.
Organization-Specific Organization administrators can create and edit organization-specific roles, which are local to their
Roles organizations. Organization-specific roles can be assigned only to users in the organization to which they
belong. Organization-specific roles can contain a subset of the organization rights only.
Predefined VCF Automation Roles and Their Rights
Each VCF Automation predefined role contains a default set of rights required to perform operations included in common
workflows. By default, all predefined global roles are published to every organization in the system.
Predefined Provider Roles
By default, the provider roles that are local only to the provider organization are the System Administrator roles. System
administrators can create additional custom provider roles.
Broadcom 7015

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The System Administrator role exists only in the provider organization. The System Administrator role includes all
rights in the system. For a list of rights available only to the System administrator role, see System Administrator Rights
in VCF Automation. The System administrator credentials are established during installation and configuration. A
System Administrator can create other system administrator and user accounts in the provider organization.
Predefined Global Roles
By default, the predefined global roles and the rights they contain, are published to all organizations. System
Administrators can unpublish rights and global roles from individual organizations. System Administrators can edit or
delete predefined global roles. System administrators can create and publish other global roles.
Defer to Identity Rights associated with the predefined Defer to Identity Provider role are determined based on information
Provider received from the user's OAuth or SAML Identity Provider. To qualify for inclusion when a user or group is
assigned the Defer to Identity Provider role, a role or group name supplied by the Identity Provider must
be an exact, case-sensitive match for a role or group name defined in your organization.
• If an OAuth Identity Provider defines the user, the user is assigned the roles named in the roles array
of the user's OAuth token.
• If a SAML Identity Provider defines the user, the user is assigned the roles named in the
SAML attribute whose name appears in the RoleAttributeName element, which is in the
SamlAttributeMapping element in the organization's OrgFederationSettings.
If a user is assigned the Defer to Identity Provider role but no matching role or group name is available in
your organization, the user can log in to the organization but has no rights. If an Identity Provider associates
a user with a system-level role such as System Administrator, the user can log in to the organization but
has no rights. You must manually assign a role to such users.
Organization After creating an organization, a System Administrator can assign the role of Organization
Administrator Administrator to the first user of the organization. A user with the predefined Organization Administrator
role can manage users and groups in their organization and assign them roles, including the predefined
Organization Administrator role. Roles created or modified by an Organization Administrator are not
visible to other organizations.
Organization Auditor The Organization Auditor is a read-only role that can view anything that an Organization Administrator
can see, however, they cannot edit or manage users and groups in their organization.
Organization User A base-level role that allows users to log in and be added to projects.
Except the Defer to Identity Provider role, each predefined role includes a set of default rights. Only a System
Administrator can modify the rights in a predefined role. If a System Administrator modifies a predefined role, the
modifications propagate to all instances of the role in the system.
Rights in Predefined Global Roles
A System Administrator can use the Provider Management UI to view the list of rights included in a role.
1. From the primary left navigation pane, click Access Control.
2. Click the Global Roles tab.
3. Click the name of the role you want to view.
An Organization Administrator can log in to their organization to view the rights in a role or create roles local to the
organization.
Various rights are common to multiple predefined global roles. These rights are granted by default to all new
organizations, and are available for use in other roles created by the Organization Administrator. For a list of the rights
in predefined tenant roles, see VCF Automation Rights in Predefined Global Roles.
System Administrator Rights in VCF Automation
The System Administrator role exists only in the provider organization. By default, the System Administrator role has
all VCF Automation rights.
The System Administrator role has all VCF Automation rights. This list consists of the rights available only to System
Administrators. The System Administrator role has also the VCF Automation Rights in Predefined Global Roles.

Publish or Unpublish a Rights Bundle to VCF Automation
You can publish a rights bundle to one or more VCF Automation organizations in your system. After you publish a rights
bundle to an organization, the rights in this bundle become part of the organization set of rights.
Organization rights can comprise multiple rights bundles, but the organization administrators and users see a flat set of
rights that they can use to create and modify roles.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.

a) Turn on the Publish to Tenants toggle.
b) Select the organizations to which you want to publish the role.
• If you want to publish the bundle to all existing and newly created organizations in your system, select Publish
to All Tenants.
• If you want to publish the bundle to particular organizations in your system, select the organizations individually.

• To unpublish the bundle from all organizations in your system, deselect Publish to Tenants.
• To unpublish the bundle from particular organizations in your system, deselect Publish to All Tenants, and
deselect the organizations individually.
7. Click Save.
The rights in the published bundle are available in the selected organizations and can be used in the roles in these
organizations.
The rights in the unpublished bundle are removed from the selected organizations and cannot be used in the roles in
these organizations.
