Edit the Default QoS Configuration of an Edge Cluster
Using the VCF Automation Provider Management UI , you can set limits on the traffic rates for the organizations that use
a selected edge cluster. The Quality of Service (QoS) profile applies to the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) traffic in the VPCs
deployed on the selected edge cluster.
Because the default QoS profile is used by all organizations that are associated with the selected edge cluster, any
change to the values of the default profile might affect multiple organizations.
To set limitations, you can specify the permitted information rate and the burst size for both the ingress and egress traffic.
Any traffic that does not conform to the QoS policy, is dropped. QoS profiles can be set for all traffic types, for example,
unicast, BUM, IPv4.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the Infrastructure section of the left-hand navigation menu, select Networking > Edge/VNA Clusters.
3. Click the Edge Clusters tab.
4. Select a cluster from the list and click its name.
5. In the left-hand menu for the selected cluster, click General.
6. In the Default QoS Configuration section, click the Edit button and make the desired modifications in the dialog box
that opens.
a) Deselect the Unlimited check box for any of the fields whose value you want to modify.
The Unlimited check box is selected by default.
b) Enter the desired committed bandwidth limits for the ingress and egress traffic.
c) Enter the desired burst size for the ingress and egress traffic.
d) Click Save.
Managing VLAN Extension Subnets in VCF Automation
As a provider administrator, you can use the VCF Automation Provider Management UI to create a VLAN extension
subnet and share that subnet with different organizations in your environment.
When you create a subnet for the first time, the provider consumption organization, if not already enabled, is automatically
enabled and configured with networking. The provider consumption organization is a provider-managed organization that
is used for storing and managing provider resources that can be shared with all the organizations in your VCF Automation
instance. You can enable the feature flag to see the provider consumption organization
Provider Consumption Org
in the list of your organizations and use it for sharing content. If you do not enable the
Provider Consumption Org
feature flag, the provider consumption organization is enabled, but you cannot access it and cannot use it. For more
information about the provider consumption organization, see Create a Provider Consumption Organization in VCF
Automation.
Starting with version 9.1.1, VCF Automation supports VLAN-backed environments. In VLAN-backed environments, VLAN
extension subnets have an expanded role. Because private subnets are not available in VLAN-backed deployments,
VLAN extension subnets are the mechanism that gives Supervisor control-plane VMs and workloads direct Layer 2
Broadcom 7073

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
connectivity to the physical network. Organization administrators can use VLAN extension subnets as the default network
for PodVMs or VM Service VMs in a namespace, replacing the auto-created private subnet that is used in a full-stack
environment.
Create a VLAN Extension Subnet
You can create a VLAN extension subnet that you can share with the organizations in your environment.
When you create a subnet, a dedicated VLAN connection and a VPC are automatically created for the provider
consumption organization. The created subnet consumes the VLAN connection in that VPC.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the Infrastructure section of the left-hand navigation menu, select Networking > Subnets.
3. Click the New button.
The New Subnet wizard opens.
4. In the Configure General Settings tile, provide the general configuration for the new subnet.
a) Provide a name and, optionally, a description for the subnet
b) From the Region drop-down menu, select a region for the subnet.
c) Click Next.
5. In the VLAN Details tile, define the VLAN specifics.
a) Enter a VLAN ID.
b) Enter a Gateway CIDR for the VLAN.
c) Click Next.
6. In the Review and Complete tile, review the subnet settings and click Create.
The new subnet appears in the list of available subnets in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. Creating a
subnet automatically creates several other resources that you can see in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI:
• A distributed external connection with the name
shared-subnet-<subnet_name>
The distributed connection is dedicated to the subnet. You cannot directly delete the distributed connection.
• An external IP block with the name
shared-subnet-<subnet_name>
The external IP block is also fully dedicated to the newly created subnet. You cannot directly delete that external IP
block.
Share the VLAN subnet with an organization, see Share a Subnet With a VCF Automation Organization.

Managing VCF Automation Organizations
You can use the VCF Automation Provider Management UI to create, configure, and manage VCF Automation
organizations.
An organization is a top-level entity used to group and manage resources, users, policies, IaaS services, and catalog
entities, while maintaining a secure boundary from other organizations. It offers a centralized structure for billing, access
control, and resource sharing, facilitating collaboration and governance across teams and departments.
Use VCF Automation Provider Management UI to manage organizations, set quotas and VM and storage classes to
determine how users consume resources that are allocated to an organization.
Create a VCF Automation Organization for All Applications
From the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you can create an organization using the underlying vSphere
Supervisor infrastructure. The organizations for all applications are the primary multi-tenancy model within VCF
Automation.
• Verify that your vCenter instance has a Supervisor enabled.
• If you want to assign a custom role to the first user of the organization, create a custom role. See Create a Global Role
in Your VCF Automation.
• If you want to add infrastructure policies to the region quota when creating an organization, verify that you have at least
one infrastructure policy in your environment. See Create an Infrastructure Policy in VCF Automation.
• When organization types share a vCenter and NSX Local Manager pair between the two organization types, you must
create the organization for VM Apps before the organization for All Apps. You must also configure the organization for
VM Apps, including mapping the vCenter and NSX Manager cloud accounts, before you configure a VCF Automation
region that uses the same vCenter and NSX Manager.
During the upgrade from VMware Aria Automation to VCF Automation, the legacy environment becomes an
organization for VM Apps. This converted organization for VM Apps deploys as the first organization in the new VCF
Automation instance.
Organizations for all applications use vSphere Namespaces within vSphere Supervisor to abstract the users and groups
of the organizations from the underlying vSphere and NSX infrastructure. Within an Organization for All Apps, there is
further isolation at the project and namespace levels. You can use this organization to run a wide variety of applications,
including virtual machines (VMs), Kubernetes, data services, and so on. You can also create multiple tenants with secure
infrastructure isolation, quotas, and chargeback.
Note:
Using the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you can create only one organization for VM applications
in your VCF Automation. After one organization for VM applications is created, the Create Organization wizard
skips the step for selecting an organization type and continues with the wizard for the creation of an organization
for all applications.

Create a Provider Consumption Organization in VCF Automation
As a provider administrator, you can create a provider consumption organization that you can use for easy access to the
Organization UI for consuming your own infrastructure resources.
From the provider consumption organization, you can publish content to other organizations for all appliacations. For
example, you can use this organization to publish blueprints and catalogs to the other organizations. As a provider
administrator you can use the provider consumption organization to provision your own workloads.
The provider consumption organization does not have access to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI and
cannot manage regions, global roles, rights bundles, and so on. When creating the provider consumption organization,
VCF Automation configures it to use the same IdPs as the organization.

2. If the organization is configured to use any other IdP, the configuration is incomplete and you can update the
System
clients in their IdPs to also contain the redirect URI for the provider consumption organization.

Setting Up Regional Networking for an Organization in VCF Automation
As a provider administrator, you define the external connections for all organizations within your VCF Automation
instance. External connections link the organization's network to the external network. The transit gateways that are
associated with provider-created external connections can be centralized or distributed.
In a single region, an organization can have either centralized transit gateways or distributed transit gateways, but not
both types at the same time. An organization can use only one connection type per region — centralized, distributed
VLAN, or distributed VXLAN. Mixing connection types within a single region is not supported. For information about each
connection type, see Managing External Connections in VCF Automation.
Assigning Connections to One or Multiple Organizations
You can assign a single external connection to multiple organizations, or you can assign a connection to a single
organization only. The behavior of a connection that is assigned exclusively to a single organization depends on the
connection type.
• Centralized connections
You can create a centralized connection that permits an organization to advertise its private transit gateway IP
blocks externally through the connection. Such a centralized connection becomes dedicated to the organization that
advertises its private IP blocks and cannot be assigned to any other organizations. For more information, see Create a
New Centralized Connection.
• Distributed VLAN connections
You can create a distributed VLAN connection that is dedicated to a single organization. When you create a dedicated
VLAN connection and assign it to an organization, the organization administrator can create a VLAN extension subnet
within their respective organization. Afer you assign a dedicated VLAN connection to an organization, you cannot
afterwards reassign the connection to any other organization. For more information, see Create a New Distributed
VLAN Connection.
Connection to the Default Transit Gateway of an Organization
When you complete setting up the regional networking configuration for an organization, a default transit gateway is
automatically created in NSX. You can set up the networking configuration for the organization at the time of organization
creation, see Create a VCF Automation Organization for All Applications. Alternatively, you can add a default centralized
or distributed transit gateway to an organization as a Day-2 operation. At this stage, you also configure the remaining
network settings. For more information, see Configure the Regional Networking of a VCF Automation Organization.
In either case, the connection that you use to set up the regional networking configuration gets assigned to the
organization's default transit gateway. You can add an unlimited number of external connections to the organization
later. You can also remove external connections from the organization, except for the default connection, that is, the one
associated with the organization's default transit gateway. You cannot delete the default connection for an organization.
Important:
The default centralized connection for an organization must be associated with at least one IP block. You cannot
select a centralized connection that is enabled to advertise its private IPs as the default connection for an
organization.
Configure the Regional Networking of a VCF Automation Organization
You can use the Provider Management UI to set up the regional networking configurations of an organization.
• Verify that you have an organization for all applications, see Create a VCF Automation Organization for All
Applications.
• Verify that you have external connections created in your environment, see Managing External Connections in VCF
Automation.
• If you intend to use advanced networking services over a distributed VXLAN external connection, verify that a
distributed VXLAN external connection exists in your environment and that you have an external IP block covering the
ranges to be used for Load Balancer VIPs and NAT IPs.
Broadcom 7080

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Important:
Advanced networking services over a distributed VXLAN connections are available for VCF Automation 9.1.1 and
later.
To create VPCs and connect to the Internet, organizations need networking resources per region. You can use the
organization regional network configuration to assign these resources to an organization.
Each organization in VCF Automation ties to an NSX Project that represents the organization in NSX Manager. You can
configure regional networking for each organization per region.
Organizations can use the default VPC and default VPC connectivity profile to connect networking workloads using the
VCF Automation Organization UI. For more information about VPCs, see Virtual Private Cloud in NSX and Managing
Networking in VCF Automation Organizations.
If you have set up the regional networking for an organization at the time of organization creation, you can make additions
and modifications to the initial configuration, such as the following:
• Add a connection to the organization.
• View the external IP blocks that are associated with the organization.
• Change the edge cluster for your connection.
• Share one or multiple subnets with the organization.
• Override the default QoS settings in the VPC Connectivity Profile.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the Infrastructure section of the left-hand navigation menu, click Organizations.
3. Click the name of an organization for all applications.

VM Apps
organizations, see Organization Management.

a) In the Connection Type tile, select the type of connection for the organization and click Next.
The available connection options depend on the types of clusters, edge or VNA, that are configured for your region.
If you have only edge clusters in your region, the only type of external connection that you can configure for the
organization is centralized.
If you have only VNA clusters in your region, the only type of connection that you can configure for the organization
is distributed.
If you have both edge and VNA clusters in your region, you can choose what type of connection to configure for the
organization depending on your needs.
b) In the Connection tile, select an external connection from the list and click Next.
c) In the VPC Service Configuration tile, select the edge cluster or VNA cluster in which you want the VPC services
of this organization to run and click Next.
If the connection you create is centralized, you can use the default edge cluster of the Tier-0 centralized
connection. Alternatively, you can select a specific edge cluster from your environment that is suitable for running
VPC services.
If the connection you create is a distributed VLAN or a distributed VXLAN connection, you must select a VNA
cluster. For distributed VXLAN connections, the VNA cluster provides advanced networking services, such as NSX

Tier-0 gateway.

Networking of a VCF Automation Organization.
If an organization's regional networking configuration uses a centralized transit gateway, the additional connections
that you can add to the organization can only be centralized. If the regional networking configuration uses a distributed
gateway, the additional connections that you can add to the organization can only be distributed VLAN connections. You
cannot add both centralized and distributed connections in a single region in an organization.

You can add dedicated VLAN connections to organizations that are configured with either a distributed or a
centralized transit gateway.

Setting Up the Regional Avi Load Balancer for an Organization in VCF
Automation
VCF Automation discovers Avi controllers and their associations with vCenter and NSX Manager. As a provider
administrator, you can use the VCF Automation Provider Management UI to govern Avi resources by specifying quotas for
the organizations. You can also enable organization administrators to manage Service Engine Groups (SEGs) based on
specific application requirements within their respective organization.
To configure an organization to use Avi Load Balancer, all the underlying region Supervisors must be configured to use
Avi Load Balancer instead of the default NSX load balancer.
You manage the Avi resource quota for organizations per region. The quota configurations map directly to the
corresponding quota limits defined in the settings of the Avi controller.
While setting up the regional Avi Load Balancer for an organization, you specify if Avi runs in provider-managed mode or
organization-managed mode. When Avi Load Balancer is configured in provider-managed mode, you create and manage
SEGs and assign them to the organization. You configure SEGs in Avi by using the specific VCF Automation zones. If
Avi Load Balancer is configured in organization-managed mode, SEGs are created and managed by the organization
administrator of the respective organization.
You can use VCF Automation Provider Management UI to perform the following Avi-related actions.
• View and manage your Avi Load Balancer instance.
• Configure the regional Avi Load Balancer for an organization.
• Edit the Avi resources allocated to an organization.
• Add a SEG assignment to an organization, if Avi Load Balancer runs in provider-managed mode.
For detailed information about Avi Load Balancer and instructions on how to perform these actions, see Managing Load
Balancing for All Apps Organizations in VCF Automation.

Region Quota of a VCF Automation Organization
A region quota defines the compute and storage quota that an organization gets against a given region. Region quotas
are applicable only to organizations for all applications.
One organization can get a quota from more than one region. For a multi-zone region, you can give quotas to
organizations for all of the zones or a subset of the zones. When creating a region quota for an organization, you must
give a quota for at least one zone from the region. You can assign compute capacity and vGPU Reserved VM class
capacity only on a per zone basis. vGPU Reserved VM class capacity is optional and applicable only for environments
where vGPUs are present. Storage classes and VM classes are not given on a per-zone basis and apply to all the zones
that are part of the region quota.
If you want to add infrastructure policies to the region quota, verify that you have at least one infrastructure policy in your
environment. See Create an Infrastructure Policy in VCF Automation.
Note:
You cannot set a region quota for organizations, and you cannot set a region quota with unlimited
VM Apps
capacity.
Region quotas constrain the ability of organization users to consume storage and processing resources. One organization
cannot get more than one region quota from a given region. An organization can get many region quotas if each region
quota is coming from a different region.
Storage Use for Project Content Libraries
Because VCF Automation copies project content libraries across all Supervisors within the scope of a region quota, the
number of Supervisors directly impacts storage use. To determine the total storage consumption for a single content
library item, multiply the image size by the total number of Supervisors or data centers in the regions that include that
content library. For example, consider a project content library is available in Region A with two Supervisors and in Region
B with one Supervisor. If you upload a 10-GB image to this library, the image consumes a total of 30 GB of the region
quotas. Because consumes 10 GB per Supervisor, the upload uses 20 GB of the region quota in Region A and 10 GB of
the region quota in Region B.
Important:
You must ensure that the region quota has sufficient capacity to accommodate the multiplied storage
requirements of library items across all associated Supervisors.

libraries.

policy in your environment. See Create an Infrastructure Policy in VCF Automation.

Edit a Region Quota
After you create a region quota, you can use the VCF Automation Provider Management UI to change the settings and the
resource allocation through the region quota.
Broadcom 7088

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
If you want to add infrastructure policies to the region quota, verify that you have at least one compatible infrastructure
policy in your environment. See Create an Infrastructure Policy in VCF Automation.
When you edit the region quota, you can select between two allocation options:
• Full allocation - you share the entire capacity of the region with the organization. If a region quota has a partial
allocation and you change the allocation to sharе the entire capacity of the region, the CPU and memory limits can
increase but the pre-set reservations remain unchanged.
• Partial allocation - you control the resource distribution by sharing a portion of the capacity with the organization. You
can edit an existing full allocation region quota and convert it to a partial region quota. Such a quota retains the existing
quota values, but the quota no longer reflects the direct changes to the region.
Note:
Tenant content libraries are pinned to certain vCenter instances in certain regions. For this reason, if you add
or remove Supervisors from a region quota, the scope of the affected content libraries expands or shrinks
accordingly. VCF Automation copies project content libraries across all vCenter instances in the scope of the
region quota. You can remove any Supervisor, but the region quota defining the scope of the project content
library must have at least one Supervisor. Organization content libraries have one published or local copy and
multiple subscribed copies across vCenter instances.

Managing VCF Automation System Settings
A VCF Automation system administrator can control system-wide settings that are related to LDAP, email notification,
licensing, and general system preferences.
By default, VCF Automation uses FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules and runs in FIPS-compliant mode. In VCF
Automation, FIPS is deactivated only if you upgrade from a VMware Aria Automation installation with deactivated FIPS
mode. After installing or upgrading to VCF Automation 9.1, you cannot activate or deactivate FIPS mode.
The Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 140-3 is a U.S. and Canadian government standard that specifies
security requirements for cryptographic modules. The NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) validates
the cryptographic modules compliant with the FIPS 140-3 standards.
VCF Automation uses the BouncyCastle FIPS 2.0.0 cryptographic module compliant with FIPS 140-3 (Certificate #4743).

Configure Blocking Task Settings On Your VCF Automation
You can configure certain operations as blocking tasks. These operations are suspended until a system administrator
acts on them or a preconfigured timer expires. You can specify the timeout settings and default actions for blocking tasks.
The settings apply to all organizations in the installation.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation bar, click Events and Tasks, and click the Blocking tasks tab.
3. To edit the default extension timeout and default timeout action, click Configure.
a) Edit the Default blocking task timeout.
b) Edit the Default Action.
The Default Action is the action after a Default blocking task timeout expires.
c) Click Save.
4. To edit the list of operations, considered as blocking tasks, click the Edit button under the Operations section.
a) Select or deselect operations from the list of blocking tasks.
Blocking tasks can be pre-blocking and post-blocking and occur before and after activities like deployments,
system upgrades, and similar major changes.
Important:
If you deselect the organization-related post-blocking task or pre-blocking task,
orgCreate orgDeleteOrg
when you create a new organization, VCF Automation cannot create the default objects for the organization
and the default VMware Cloud Foundation® Operations orchestrator integration for the provider consumption
organization.
If you change the organization-related post-blocking task or pre-blocking task
orgCreate orgDeleteOrg
selections, the organization creation and deletion might get stuck.
b) Click Save.

expires.

As a provider administrator, you can use an MQTT client to subscribe to messages about Provider Management events
and tasks.
• Verify that you have an MQTT client that supports WebSocket.

MQTT is a lightweight, binary, messaging transport protocol. VCF Automation Provider Management UI uses MQTT to
publish information about events and tasks to which you can subscribe by using an MQTT client. MQTT messages pass
through an MQTT broker which can also store messages in case the clients are not online.
You can use an MQTT client to subscribe to metrics.
Organization administrators can use VCF Operations orchestrator workflows with event subscriptions. See Managing
Event Subscriptions in VCF Automation.

This request has the following form:
GET http://vcfa.example.com/api/versions
b) POST a request to the login URL to create a login session.
This request has the following form:
POST https://vcfa.example.com/cloudapi/1.0.0/sessions/provider

mqtt
the path, add an authorization header, and follow the standard MQTT connect flow.
/messaging/mqtt
You receive the JWT token from the standard login request to VCF Automation.
Enter your account name in the username field and the JWT token as the password in your MQTT client.

{JWT_token}
Authorization: Bearer

Changing the VCF Automation Portal Branding
To match your corporate branding standards and to create a fully custom cloud experience, you can customize the VCF
Automation portals. In addition, you can modify and add custom links to the login and logout pages.
The VCF Automation UI provides a live preview of all changes so that you can see the modifications instantly without the
need to save the theme.
Note:
By default, the individual organization branding is not shown outside of a logged-in session. The individual
organization branding does not appear on the login and logout pages, so that organizations cannot discover the
existence of other organizations. You can enable branding outside of logged in sessions by clicking Settings and
turning on the Enable Login and Logout Page Branding toggle.
Portal Branding
As part of the installation, VCF Automation contains two themes - light and dark. You can create, manage, and apply
custom themes. In addition, you can change the portal name, the logo, the image on the login screen, and the browser
icon. The browser title adopts the portal name that you set and the login background.
When you create a theme, you can assign it to one or more organizations. You can specify a theme to be the default
theme, applicable to all organizations apart from the ones with specifically assigned themes through the Assign option.
For a particular theme, you can selectively override any combination of the portal name, colors, logo, icon, custom links,
and the login background. Any color value that you do not set uses the corresponding theme base color.
Certain operations are not applicable to some of the theme types.

You can change the branding for the VCF Automation Provider Management UI .
When changing the theme, you can instantly see how the selection would change the appearance of the theme.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left pane, click Branding and click Create.
3. Enter a name for the theme.
4. Change the platform branding from the option in the Branding tab.
a) Enter a platform name.
The platform name replaces the VCF Automation name on the top navigation bar, the login page, and the browser
title.
b) Upload a platform logo.
The platform logo replaces the default logo on the top navigation bar and the login page. You can also select to
include an additional dark theme logo.
c) Upload a browser favicon.
The favicon, or browser tab icon, is the icon that appears next to the page title in a browser tab.
d) Upload a background image for the login page.
The layout adapts to screen sizes at 768 px and 544 px. The login background image might fill the full size of the
screen and part of it might be hidden below the login form. Depending on the browser window size and screen
resolution settings, some parts of the background image might not appear. Consider using a background with a
pattern or an image that looks complete even if parts of it do not appear.

Manage Your Customer Experience Improvement Program Participation in VCF
Automation Provider Management
By default, the Customer Experience Improvement Program (CEIP) is active in VCF Automation. You can activate or
deactivate your CEIP participation for a specific cluster in a workload domain by using the VCF Fleet LCM Service API.
• Identify the FQDN of your fleet lifecycle component.
• Verify that you have provider administrator credentials.
• If necessary, schedule a maintenance window. VCF Automation is temporarily unavailable while the pods restart during
the CEIP update.
For details regarding the data collected through CEIP, and the purposes for data collection, see the Customer Experience
Improvement Program page.
1. Generate a VCF services runtime access token by running the following command to request a token.
curl
To authenticate your requests to the VCF Fleet LCM Service API, you must obtain a Bearer token from the Identity
Service.
curl -ks --request POST \
<platform_fqdn>
--url https:// /api/v1/identity/token \
--header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data grant_type=password \
admin@vsp.local
--data 'username= ' \
<admin_password>
--data 'password= ' | jq -r '.access_token'
Broadcom 7100

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
Replace <platform_fqdn> with the FQDN of your management VCF services runtime.
2. Retrieve the component ID for the cluster.
a) Run a GET request to the components endpoint.
curl -ks -X GET \
<access_token>
-H "Authorization: Bearer " \
-H 'Accept: application/json' \
https://<fleet-fqdn>/fleet-lcm/v1/components | jq
b) Search the objects in the response to find the for your VCF Automation cluster.
VspCluster componentId
c) Make note of the .
componentId
3. Update the CEIP setting by running the following request to update the cluster configuration.
PATCH
curl -ks -X PATCH \
<access_token>
-H "Authorization: Bearer " \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data '{"type": "VspClusterConfigSpec", "ceip": true}' \
<fleet-fqdn> <componentId>
https:// /fleet-lcm/v1/components/ /config

Test the VCF Automation Connection to a Remote Server and Establish a Trust
Relationship Using the Provider Management UI
You can test the connection of VCF Automation to a remote server, and establish a trust relationship with it.
Verify that your role includes the SSL: Test Connection and the Truststore: Manage rights.
You can test and secure the connection of VCF Automation to a remote server by entering the server URL.
When you test a remote connection to a server, if the connection involves SSL communication and VCF Automation
has not already established a trust relationship with the server, you are prompted to review a certificate, or a chain of
certificates, and to make a trust choice.
If the certificate chain is not complete and there are additional certificates available, you can choose to retrieve them to
view more details before making a trust choice.
When testing remote connections, there is the potential to exploit the Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability.
An attacker can scan the common Kubernetes subnet ranges, such as or , and
10.244.0.0/16 100.96.0.0/16
so on, and then enumerate the services by scanning for open ports. To test connections to remote servers and to
verify the server identity as part of an SSL handshake, you can use the VCF Automation API. An attacker can scan
the common Kubernetes subnet ranges such as 10.244.0.0/16 or 100.96.0.0/16, and so on, and then, enumerate the
services by scanning for open ports. To protect the internal network in which a VCF Automation instance is deployed
from malicious attacks, you can configure a denylist of internal hosts that are unreachable to organizations. This way, if a
malicious attacker with organizational access attempts to use the connection testing API to map the network in which VCF
Automation is installed, they would not be able to connect to the internal hosts on the denylist. Managing this denylist is
possible through the API.
/cloudapi/1.0.0/testConnection/restrictions

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

6. Click Connect.

the server, review the certificate information and make a trust choice.

Import Certificates to the Certificates Library Using Your VCF Automation
Provider Management UI
In the VCF Automation certificates library, you can import certificates used when creating entities that you must secure,
such as servers, Edge gateways, and so on.
• Verify that your role includes the Certificate Library: Manage right.
• Verify that the private keys you want to use are in the PKCS#8 format. VCF Automation does not support private keys
generated with the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA).
The certificate library contains information about single certificates, certificate chains, private keys, certificate expiration
dates, the entities that the certificates secure, and so on.

Terraform Configuration in VCF Automation Provider Management
You can automate the deployment and configuration of VCF Automation infrastructure resources using Terraform.
Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool developed by HashiCorp. You can use the open-source tool to define and
provision your cloud infrastructure using the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). Terraform uses the configuration
files with the descriptions of the desired state of your infrastructure to create, manage, and delete the necessary
resources across various cloud providers and platforms. Terraform providers are plug-ins that Terraform uses to interact
with cloud providers, SaaS providers, third-party tools, and other APIs. Each provider defines its resources and data
sources that map directly to the functionalities of the specific service.
For end-to-end operation of Terraform in VCF Automation, you need three open-source Terraform providers.
• Terraform Provider for VCF Automation - You can use this provider to perform CRUD operations for the Provider
Management UI and a subset of the Organization UI resources that belong to organizations for All Apps, such as
Supervisor namespaces. This provider is available on GitHub and is distributed as part of the HashiCorp Terraform
registry. The greenfield folder contains examples of configuration files for fresh VCF Automation installations that show
how all resources interact with each other and provide guidance on how you can use the provider. The folder contains
two parts:
Broadcom 7103

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
•
Provider: Using this part, you can create the necessary organizations and configure the underlying infrastructure,
such as vCenter instances, NSX instances, provider gateways, roles, and so on.
• Tenant: This part includes tenant-side operations. You can use this part to configure the layout of the organization,
such as content libraries.
• Terraform Provider for Kubernetes - You can use the Kubernetes (K8S) provider to perform CRUD operations against
the VCF Automation Organization UI resources exposed through the VCF Automation Kubernetes API layer, such as
projects.
To see a usage example, navigate to  .
https://<FQDN>/automation/api-docs/#/terraform-provider
• Terraform Provider for VMware Aria Automation - You can use this provider to perform CRUD operations against
the VCF Automation Organization UI resources that belong to VM Apps organizations and for VCF Automation
Organization UI resources that belong to
organizations for All Apps but are not yet exposed through the VCF Automation Kubernetes API layers, such as
blueprints.

Managing Defined Entities in VCF Automation
To create extensions that provide additional VCF Automation capabilities to the organizations, provider administrators can
use the VCF Automation API.
Defined entities represent external resources that VCF Automation can manage. Extension and UI plug-in developers
can create runtime defined entities, enabling extensions and UI plug-ins to store and manipulate the extension-specific
information in VCF Automation. If you create an extension and it needs to store a state or references to external
resources, the extension can use runtime defined entities instead of a local database. For example, a Kubernetes
extension can store information about the Kubernetes clusters it manages in runtime defined entities. The extension can
then provide extension APIs for managing those clusters using the information from the runtime defined entities.
You can access runtime defined entities only through the VCF Automation API. Users with admin privileges can track and
observe the way extensions operate by verifying the state of the defined entities that the extensions create. The states of
the defined entities can also help you to troubleshoot problems with the extensions.
Defined Entity Type
You define at runtime the schema of the information that you can store by using defined entities. The schema is defined
in the entity type through a JSON document. When you create a defined entity type, you create a new custom VCF
Automation type which you can manage by extensions and behaviors.
Once you create an instance of a defined entity type, you cannot change the type, schema, and behaviors anymore.
To add new functionalities to the entity type, you must create a new version of the type. When a defined entity instance
is based on an earlier version of the entity type, you can upgrade the defined entity to use a later version of the type
by setting the type property of the entity to the ID of the new type. When you create a defined entity, in the API call, the
contents of the entity property must match the JSON schema specified in the entity type. You can grant access to an
entity type only to specific users and organizations. You can set different access restrictions to the different versions of an
entity type.

Access to Defined Entity Instances
Two complementary mechanisms control the access to runtime defined entities.
• Rights - When you create a runtime defined entity type, you create a rights bundle for the type. To provide access to
specific operations, you must assign rights from this bundle to other roles. Each bundle has five type-specific rights:
View: TYPE, Edit: TYPE, Full Control: TYPE, Administrator View: TYPE, and Administrator Full Control: TYPE.
The View: TYPE, Edit: TYPE, and Full Control: TYPE rights work only in combination with an ACL entry.
• Access Control List (ACL) - The ACL table contains entries defining the access users have to specific entities in the
system. It provides an extra level of control over the entities. For example, while an Edit: TYPE right specifies that a
user can modify entities to which they have access, the ACL table defines which entities the user has access to.
System administrators with the View General ACL right can view the ACLs assigned to a specific defined entity by
using the API.
accessControls
System administrators with the Manage General ACL right can create, modify, and remove specific ACLs by using
the API.
accessControls

Sharing Defined Entities in VCF Automation
You can grant access to Runtime Defined Entities (RDEs) by sharing them with other VCF Automation system
administrators or other organizations.
Sharing Defined Entities with Another User
1. If you want to grant access to defined entities to other organizations, publish the rights bundle of the defined entity
type to the organization of your choice. For example, for the creation and management of Kubernetes clusters, you
must publish the vmware:tkgcluster Entitlement rights bundle. See Publish or Unpublish a Rights Bundle to VCF
Automation.
If you want to share the defined entity with a system administrator, skip this step.
2. Assign the View: TYPE, Edit: TYPE, or Full Control: TYPE right from the bundle to the user roles you want to have
the specific level of access to the defined entity.
For example, if you want the users with the tkg_viewer role to view Kubernetes clusters within the organization, you
must add the View: Tanzu Kubernetes Guest Cluster right to the role. If you want the users with the tkg_author
role to create, view, and modify Kubernetes clusters within this organization, add the Edit: Tanzu Kubernetes Guest
Cluster to that role. If you want the users with the tkg_admin role to create, view, modify, and delete Kubernetes
clusters within this organization, add the Full Control: Tanzu Kubernetes Guest Cluster right to the role.
3. Grant the specific user an Access Control List (ACL) by making the following REST API call.
[address] [vendor] [type name] [version] [UUID]
POST https:// /cloudapi/1.0.0/entities/urn:vcloud:entity: : : : /
accessControls
{
"grantType" : "MembershipAccessControlGrant",
[Access_level]
"accessLevelId" : "urn:vcloud:accessLevel: ",
[User_ID]
"memberId" : "urn:vcloud:user: "
}
Access_level must be , , or . User_ID must be the ID of the user to which
ReadOnly ReadWrite FullControl
you want to grant the access to the defined entity.
Users with the tkg_viewer role, described in the example, cannot grant ACL access. Users with the tkg_author
or tkg_admin role can share access to a VMWARE:TKGCLUSTER entity with users who have the tkg_viewer,
tkg_author, or tkg_admin role by granting them ACL access using the API request.
You can also use REST API calls to revoke access or to view who has access to the entity. See the VCF Automation
REST API documentation.
Sharing Administrator Rights to Defined Entities
1. If you want to grant access to defined entities to organizations, publish the rights bundle of the defined entity type
to an organization. For example, for the creation and management of Kubernetes clusters, you must publish the
vmware:tkgcluster Entitlement rights bundle. See Publish or Unpublish a Rights Bundle to VCF Automation.
If you want to share the defined entity with a system administrator, skip this step.
2. Assign the Administrator View: TYPE or Administrator Full Control: TYPE right from the bundle to the user roles
you want to have the specific level of access to the defined entity.
For example, if you want the users with this role to view all Kubernetes clusters within the organization, you must add
the Administrator View: Tanzu Kubernetes Guest Cluster right to the role. If you want the users with this role to
create, view, modify, and delete Kubernetes clusters in all organizations, add the Administrator Full Control: Tanzu
Kubernetes Guest Cluster right to the user role.
Users with the Administrator Full Control: Tanzu Kubernetes Guest Cluster right can grant ACL access to any
VMWARE:TKGCLUSTER entity.
Changing the Owner of a Defined Entity
The owner of a defined entity or a user with the Administrator Full Control: TYPE right can transfer the ownership to
another user by updating the defined entity model and changing the owner field with the ID of the new owner.

VCF Automation Webhook Behaviors
To connect two different applications, you can use webhooks. By using webhooks, you can set up event notifications.
A webhook is an HTTP callback. When an event happens, a web application implementing webhooks broadcasts data
about that event and sends it to a webhook URL from the application that you want to receive the information. For more
information, see https://github.com/vmware/.
In the context of VCF Automation, you can configure webhooks by using webhook behaviors. Webhook behaviors send
out a POST request to a remote webhook server. The body of the request contains information about the behavior
invocation and the entity that the behavior was invoked on. You can also customize the body by using a template.
The webhook server response determines the result of the behavior invocation task. There are three different types of
responses that the server can return.
The remote webhook server can be any server that VCF Automation can reach. However, before creating a webhook
behavior, you must verify that the endpoint of the webhook is secure.
• Verify that the webhook endpoint is an HTTPS endpoint.
• Verify that the organization of the user invoking the behavior trusts the webhook server certificate. This means that
even if the certificate is present in a VCF Automation trust store, if the organization of the user, who invokes the
behavior does not trust the certificate, the webhook behavior will not run.
• You can add a certificate to the trust store by using the UI or the VCF Automation API. See Managing Certificates
Using Your VCF Automation.
Creating Webhook Behaviors
Request:
"POST https"://host/cloudapi/1.0.0/interfaces/<interface_id>/behaviors{
"name":"webhookBehavior",
"execution":{
"type":"WebHook",
"id":"testWebHook",
"href":"https://hooks.slack.com:443/services/T07UZFN0N/B01EW5NC42D/rfjhHCGIwzuzQFrpPZiuLkIX",
"key":"secretKey",
"execution_properties":{
"template":{
"content":"<template_content_string>"
},
"_secure_token":"secureToken",
"invocation_timeout":7
}
}
}

Automation.
_internal_key Required field for the shared secret used for signing the requests
sent to the webhook endpoint.

from the webhook server
template.content Optional field for customization of the payload sent to the webhook
server. You can provide a template as a string. You can add other
fields to execution_properties, accessible to the template.

Authentication of the Webhook Behavior Requests
Hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) authentication secures webhook behavior requests. HMAC is a
mechanism ensuring the authenticity and integrity of HTTP requests. To ensure the authenticity and integrity, HMAC
includes two custom headers to each HTTP request. The custom headers are a signature header and a digest. For VCF
Automation, the signature header is and the digest is .
x-vcloud-signature x-vcloud-digest
The signature header is a custom header sent with each webhook request. The signature header
x-vcloud-signature
consists of an HMACSHA512 algorithm, headers, and a VCF Automation generated signature. The headers show what is
in the base string which is signed to create the signature.
Table 1818: Header Fields
Field Description
host The webhook server host
date Date of the request
(request-target) Linked lowercase HTTP method, ASCII space, and request path
headers. For example, post /webhook.
digest SHA-512 digest of the request body
To generate the signature header, you need a shared secret. The shared secret is a string that only VCF Automation and
the webhook server know.
The digest header is a Base64-encoded SHA-512 digest of the request body.
x-vcloud-digest
Each webhook request from VCF Automation can be verified by generating the signature using the shared secret and
comparing it to the signature in the signature header from VCF Automation.

Organization Management
Use VCF Automation as a cloud administrator (or organization administrator) to set up projects for application teams,
allocate resources, and apply governance.
In VCF Automation, an organization is a top level entity that represents a line of business or a tenant. Each organization
operates in a secure and isolated environment where users can access only allocated services and resources.
Organizations consume resources and cloud services from a shared pool of resources. The resources allocated
to organizations can be further allocated to application teams which are modeled in VCF Automation as projects.
Organizations have users with varying levels of permissions depending on their role and duties.
Organizations in VCF Automation are created by the provider administrator in the VCF Automation Provider Management
UI. The provider administrator can create two types of organizations: an All Apps organization and a VM Apps
organization. VM Apps organizations can run VM-based applications, while All Apps organizations are enabled to run a
comprehensive set of built-in cloud services. For more information about creating VCF Automation organizations in the
VCF Automation Provider Management UI, see Managing Organizations.
Regardless of the type, each organization has its own organization UI where users log in to consume resources and
services. Every organization has its own identity source that they connect to and can import users from.
All Apps Organizations in VCF Automation
All Apps оrganizations offer application teams a comprehensive set of built-in cloud services to provision VMs,
Kubernetes, networking, volumes, Secret Store, databases, Harbor container registries, external DNS, certificates, and
AI workloads. These cloud services can be consumed on a self-service basis through a curated catalog or self-service
interfaces.
Organizations enable line-of-business or tenant organization administrators to further organize and govern resources that
are allocated to them among application teams through the following capabilities:
• Resource management for project teams.
• Centralized content management for the organization.
• Policy-based governance on usage of resources.
• Quota-based management of networking resources.
• Workflow orchestration and extensibility through event subscriptions.
• Integration with identity providers of their choice.
For information on working with All Apps organizations, see the Managing Organizations for All Apps in guide.
Provider Consumption Organizations in VCF Automation
A Provider Consumption organization (PCO) is a special type of All Apps organization in VCF Automation that the provider
administrator enables in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. The provider administrator can enable only one
Provider Consumption organization. For more information about PCOs, see Create a Provider Consumption Organization.
The PCO is intended for use when the provider wants to have their own consumption service for their users and/or they
want to share catalog items with other organizations under their management.
PCOs are administered in the same way as other All Apps organizations, but they offer some additional capabilities on top
of what a standard All Apps organization provides.
• PCOs come with a preconfigured VCF Operations orchestrator instance that is embedded in the organization UI, which
you access on the Orchestrate tab.
• As a PCO administrator, you can publish VCF Operations orchestrator objects as catalog items to other organizations
that use the same embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance.
• You can publish catalog items to other organizations that use VM images from a provider content library.
For more information about managing your VCF Operations orchestrator integration, see Managing VMware Cloud
Foundation Operations Orchestrator.
Broadcom 7117

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
VM Apps Organizations in VCF Automation
VM Apps organizations help existing VMware Aria Automation users transition to VCF Automation 9.0 without any impact
to infrastructure, automation, or end-user experience.
In VM Apps organizations, the allocation of resources, like cloud accounts, cloud zones, profiles, image mappings and
so on, is contained in the organization itself. The organization administrator defines and works with the infrastructure; the
provider administrator does not allocate resources to organization of this type.
Important:
If you upgrade an existing VMware Aria Automation 8.x deployment to VCF Automation 9, your organizations are
automatically mapped to VCF Automation for VM Apps organizations. You continue to use vIDB and VMware Aria
Suite Lifecycle to manage vIDM to maintain legacy authentication.
For information on working with VM Apps organizations, see the Managing Organizations in for VM Apps guide.
Best Practices for Organizations in VCF Automation
When to use All Apps vs VM Apps?
• All Apps organizations are used when organizations are ready to leverage the comprehensive set of built-in cloud
services to provision VMs, Kubernetes, and so on. The underlying infrastructure requires vSphere Supervisor clusters
and is managed in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. Talk to your provider administrator about how you
can leverage these capabilities.
• VM Apps organizations are intended for current users of VMware Aria Automation who want to continue their journey
with minimal disruptions. The VM Apps organization is fully self-contained with built-in infrastructure management and
consumption capabilities.
When to use blueprints vs the IaaS self-service console?
• Blueprints and the catalog offer a controlled manner to build and curate infrastructure. They are prescriptive in terms of
the provisioned resources and so are suitable to deploy applications in production. They are also suitable for end users
who do not want to concern themselves with details of the infrastructure.
• The IaaS self-service console offers more flexibility and is more suitable for development purposes.
Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release
Notes.
Consuming Administration Services in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can use functionality in the VCF Automation organization UI that is additionally
installed by your provider administrator.
• Managing VKS Clusters with VKS Cluster Management
• Using VMware Cloud Foundation Encryption Management in a VCF Automation organization
SDKs, APIs, and CLI for VCF Administration
You can build, operate, and manage your VCF private cloud by using the VCF SDK and APIs, and VCF PowerCLI. See
Administration SDKs, APIs, and CLI.
Managing Organizations in VMware Cloud Foundation Automation
With VMware Cloud Foundation Automation (VCF Automation), you, as an organization administrator, and your
application teams can view and consume infrastructure that the provider administrator made available to your
organization. As an organization administrator, you create projects, manage users, and define resource limits for running
workloads.
The underlying infrastructure in VCF Automation is based on VMware vSphere Supervisor, which serve as the
foundational structure for resource allocation. Supervisor-based infrastructure supports modern application use cases for
Broadcom 7118

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
provisioning containers and VMs. Provider administrators allocate infrastructure resources to organizations using regional
quotas, while organization administrators use namespaces to distribute the allocated infrastructure to different projects
within the organization.
Infrastructure Concepts
VCF Automation enables private cloud functionality by providing a multi-tenant management plane. Rather than
abstracting the underlying infrastructure, VCF Automation routes organizations to their specific resources and services
through a centralized interface.
Regions. A region acts as a unified networking and management boundary, comprising all supervisors linked to a
common NSX Manager. Regions enable cross-vCenter network, resource, and IaaS service management.
Zones. A zone represents one or multiple vSphere clusters that provide the compute, memory, and storage resources for
the organization.
Region Quota. A region quota defines the compute and storage resources that are allocated to an organization in a given
region. The organization can receive quotas from multiple regions. The provider administrator decides from which regions
to give a quota to an organization. The region quota can be split across more than one zone in a region. A region quota
includes the following:
• CPU and memory utilization limits which represent the upper bound of quota in a region.
• CPU and memory reservations which represent the guaranteed capacity that is allocated in a region.
• VM classes which represent the T-shirt-sized classes of compute that are available to the organization.
• Storage classes which represent the storage policies and the quota that is assigned in a region.
Resources for Application Teams
Resources allocated to the organization in the form of a region quota can be further subdivided and allocated to
application teams.
Project. Projects are logical representations of users and user groups and the resource pools that those users are entitled
to. The resource pools that projects use are called namespaces. Resources, like VMs and Kubernetes clusters, are
provisioned on namespaces.
Namespace. A vSphere Namespace is a resource pool that comprises CPU, memory, and storage resources that are
assigned to projects inVCF Automation. Namespaces derive their quota from the overall region quota of the organization
and come with controls such CPU, memory, and storage usage. Each namespace is bound to the scope of the project that
it is associated with. Each project can contain multiple namespaces. Because the region quota can be split across multiple
vSphere zones, the resource pool of a namespace can also be split across multiple vSphere zones. As an organization
administrator, you can configure which zones a namespace can derive its resource limits from.
Namespace Class. Namespace classes are templates for defining guardrails on parameters that are used to create
a namespace, like CPU limits, storage limits, permissible VM and storage classes, and content libraries. Namespace
classes are a prerequisite for creating namespaces. In the namespace class, you can set default values for CPU and
memory limits and reservations. If a namespace class has a zone defined, default values for namespace limits and
reservations are used from the zone section. As an organization administrator, you create namespace classes that fit your
project needs. You can create one or more namespaces using the default namespace classes that come preconfigured in
your organization. You can also override those defaults in a given project to suit specific configurations.
An example of an organization quota:
• Region region-one has three vSphere Zones - vs-zone-1, vs-zone-2, and vs-zone-3.
• Organization org-1 has a region quota of 25 GHz of CPU in vs-zone-1 and 50 GHz of CPU in vs-zone2 for a total
quota of 75 GHz of CPU in region-one.
Networking Concepts
VPC. Virtual private clouds (VPCs) are the foundational networking element used in VCF Automation to enable
applications to communicate with each other and the outside world. A VPC provides an isolated domain of networking
resources that can be associated with one or more namespaces. As an organization administrator or a project
Broadcom 7119

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
administrator, you create VPCs for your organization. In addition, organization administrators and advanced project users
can use the Networking Service in the IaaS Console to create, update, and manage resources within a given VPC.
Connectivity Profile. A connectivity profile is a template for VPC configuration. You can provide one or more external and
private Transit Gateway IP address blocks that are used by VPCs configured with a specific connectivity profile. When the
provider administrator allocates the regional networking configuration to the organization, а default connectivity profile is
created. As an organization administrator, you can create additional connectivity profiles to use in your organization.
Subnets. A subnet is a subdivision of a VPC that defines a range of IP addresses. Organization administrators can create
subnets for their organization. Using the Network service, advanced project users can create subnets in VPCs that are
associated with their namespaces.
Transit Gateways. A transit gateway provides both inter-VPC communication within the organization and connection to
the outside network through external connections. In addition to using the default transit gateways that the organization
comes with, organization administrators can create transit gateways for their organization.
Consumption Concepts
Application teams can provision resources on a self-service basis in VCF Automation using the catalog or the services.
Catalog items are generated from blueprints that are curated and maintained by the organization administrator, while
cloud services can be accessed directly without blueprints. Both methods of provisioning IT resources require content
libraries that host the VM images.
Blueprints and Catalog. Blueprints are infrastructure templates that define the resources and cloud services you want to
create to run an application. Organization administrators create the blueprints and publish them as catalog items for end
users. End users interact with form entries of catalog items to request resources. These forms can be customized to hide
unnecessary fields or to create dynamic entries.
Services. Users can provision cloud services directly on namespaces from the VCF Automation user interface, the VCF
Automation APIs, and CLIs without the need for blueprints and the catalog.
Content Library. Content libraries host VM images that application teams use when deploying resources. Organizations
can either use content libraries that are provided by the provider administrator or create their own organization-specific
content libraries.
Policies. Policies provide governance on resources like VMs and VKS clusters that are provisioned from cloud services.
Policies can be applied to the whole organization or to individual projects. VCF Automation supports two types of policies:
• Policies that are applied to resources provisioned from the catalog, such as Approval, Day 2, and Lease policies.
• Policies that are applied to resources provisioned through the self-service IaaS console.
Getting Started with Organizations in VCF Automation
As an administrator of a VCF Automation organization, you manage user access, network configurations, including VPCs
and subnets, and policies for your organization. You also create namespaces and manage provider-assigned quotas for
the resources associated with the namespaces in your organization.
Using the VCF Automation Organization User Interface
An overview of the VCF Automation organization user interface includes the following basic functions.
Note:
This overview covers what organization administrators with full access to the user interface see. Depending on
your user rights, you may not see and access all tabs.
• The Overview tab shows you important infrastructure and consumption metrics in your organization. It also provides
quick links to your IaaS services. VCF Automation 9.1.1 introduces the Get Started guided checklist on the Overview
tab.
Broadcom 7120

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• The Build & Deploy tab is your content hub and development home. Administrators can create blueprints and content
libraries, publish workflows to the catalog, and create extensibility events. Project users can deploy cloud services from
catalog items or can access the IaaS Services console.
• The Manage & Govern tab is where administrators manage the slices of infrastructure that the provider allocated to
the organization. That includes projects, namespaces, namespace classes, policies, and networking.
• The Orchestrate tab is where you access the VCF Operations orchestrator integration that your provider administrator
configured for the organization.
• The Administer tab is where you manage expenses, identity providers, users and user roles, integrations, certificates
and passwords, email notifications, and so on.
• The Inbox tab is where you can see and respond to policy-based approval requests and deployment requests that
require user input.
Review Assigned Resources
On the Manage & Govern tab, review the following pages to familiarize yourself with the interface and to review the
default objects created for your organization.
• Projects. All organizations are created with a default project. The default project is empty and does not have any
namespaces or users.
• Regions. The Regions page lists all the regions where the organization has a quota in. Organizations can have a
quota in one or many regions. Your provider administrator assigns the regional quota to your organization. Quota in a
region can come from one or many vSphere Zones within that region.
Click the double arrow next to a region name to review the region details. The details page contains information about
available CPU and memory from each zone in the region.
• Namespace Class. Namespace classes are templates for creating namespaces. These templates can be used
to standardize namespace attributes, like utilization limits, reservations, VM classes, storage classes, and content
libraries. Your organization comes preconfigured with three default namespace classes (small, medium, and large),
which serve as example templates. The only different attributes among these built-in templates are the CPU and
Memory limits. Organization administrators can use these templates as-is or can modify them to suit their needs.
Click the namespace class name to inspect the limits, VM class, and storage class presets.
• Networking. Review the default VPC (virtual private cloud). A VPC is an isolated domain of networking resources.
You can also review the Connectivity Profiles tab. A connectivity profile is a template for creating VPCs.
Using the VCF Automation API Help Center
The VCF Automation API Help Center is a built-in UI which documents the API interface for the organization. Users can
also execute and test APIs from the API Help Center.
You can access the API Help Center from the VCF Automation organization UI. Click your user profile in the upper right
corner and then click API Help Center.
VCF Automation API Help Center has the following components.
• Automation APIs. The Automation API section provides details about various automation-specific components that
are used to administer the organization, such as blueprints, catalog, instances, projects, custom forms, and so on. This
documentation includes OpenAPI specifications. Each section defines the available endpoints, required input/output
formats, and how to authenticate requests.
• The Admin APIs are used to create VCF Automation resources like projects and provision additional resources. It
brings automation-specific capabilities into the Kubernetes management framework.
• The Consumption APIs are used to create and manage infrastructure resources, like virtual machines, networks,
storage, and so on. This allows users to work with infrastructure using Kubernetes-native methods.
• Terraform Provider. The Terraform Provider section provides details about using Terraform provider to interact with
VCF Automation. For more information on the supported Terraform providers, see Terraform Configuration in VCF
Automation.
• SDK Generation & Usage. The VCF Automation SDK provides a standardized way to generate APIs for various
components. You can explore examples that demonstrate its usage for various use cases to get started with the SDK.
Broadcom 7121

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Set Up Your VCF Automation Organization
As the organization administrator, you set up your organization using the following procedure.
1. Log in to the organization UI.
When you log in to the organization for the first time, you must get the login credentials for the local account from your
provider administrator. After you configure identity providers, you can use those credentials to log in.
2. Add users to your organization.
You can onboard an identity provider and import users from there. VCF Automation supports LDAP, OIDC, and SAML-
compliant identity providers. As you add users to the organization, you assign roles to them.
a. Configure an identity provider. See Managing Identity Providers in VCF Automation Organizations.
b. Import users and user groups. See Add Users and Assign Roles in VCF Automation.
3. Set up networking.
VPCs are required networking constructs for namespaces. Connectivity profiles define and templatize common
configuration elements for VPCs. You can use the default connectivity profile and VPC or you can create new ones.
Note:
In VLAN-backed regions in VCF Automation 9.1.1, before you configure networking, verify the following with your
provider administrator:
• A Distributed VXLAN Connection is configured for your region.
• External IP address blocks is allocated to your organization.
a. Create a connectivity profile. See Create a Connectivity Profile in VCF Automation.
b. Create a VPC. See Create a Virtual Private Cloud in VCF Automation.
Note:
In VLAN-backed regions in VCF Automation 9.1.1, after VPC creation, verify that your VPC connectivity profile
does not include private TGW IP blocks. In VLAN-backedregions, these fields are not available and do not appear
in the UI. Default SNAT is not created automatically in VLAN-backed regions. SNAT is not supported in VLAN-
backed mode.
4. Set up a content library.
VCF Automation has two types of content libraries, provider content libraries and organization content libraries. You
can use the content library provided to you by your provider administrator or you can create your own.
a. Create a content library. See Managing Content Libraries in VCF Automation.
b. Upload VM images to the content library and publish them to the catalog. See Add a VM Image to a Content
Library in VCF Automation.
5. Create a namespace class.
To create namespaces, you need a namespace class. You can use the default namespace classes and override the
values in them at the time of creating a new namespace. You can edit any or all of the default namespace classes.
Alternatively, you can create your own namespace classes. See Create a Namespace Class in VCF Automation.
6. Configure a project.
You can use the default project and change the name and description or you can create your own projects.
a. Create the project. See Create a Project in VCF Automation.
b. Projects are created without namespaces. To create a namespace, see Create a Namespace in a VCF Automation
Project.
c. Add project users. See Assign Project Roles to Users and Groups in VCF Automation.
7. Create blueprints and publish them to the catalog for project users to request and consume. See Creating Blueprints in
VCF Automation.
8. Publish VCF Operations orchestrator workflows to the catalog. See Publish a VCF Operations orchestrator Workflow
to the Catalog in VCF Automation.
9. Set up event subscriptions. See Managing Event Subscriptions in VCF Automation.
10.Set up policies to apply governance to provisioned resources. See Managing Policies in VCF Automation.

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Using the Get Started Guided Checklist
VCF Automation 9.1.1 introduces a Get Started checklist for users who have not yet completed the required organization
setup. By following the steps in the Get Started checklist, users can provision their first workloads. The steps in the
checklist depend on the role of the user.
• For Organization Administrators, the steps include connecting an identity provider, viewing projects, defining
the resource library, provisioning workloads, adding users and assigning project roles, and enabling projects for
namespace creation.
• For Project Administrators, the steps include viewing projects, viewing namespaces for workload provisioning, creating
a vSphere namespace, and provisioning workloads.
• For Project Advanced Users, the steps include viewing projects, viewing namespaces for workload provisioning, and
provisioning workloads.
• For Project Users, the steps include viewing projects, viewing namespaces for workload provisioning, and launching
catalog items to deploy workloads.
Users can dismiss the checklist at any time during a session. After completion or dismissal, users can reopen the checklist
in a new browser session.
Managing Identity Providers in VCF Automation Organizations
As an organization administrator, you can use one or more external identity providers to import and manage users and
groups in your organization. You can configure an LDAP server connection, a SAML integration, and an OpenID Connect
(OIDC) integration.
VCF Automation supports user login with an identity provider directly. Any third-party provider with OIDC, SAML, AD/
LDAP protocols can be configured to use Single Sign-on to VCF Automation for identity and access management.
Configure Your VCF Automation Organization to Use a Custom LDAP
Connection
As an organization administrator, you can configure your VCF Automation organization to use an LDAP server as a
source of users and groups.
When adding or editing a new LDAP server endpoint, you can test a remote connection to an endpoint and to establish a
trust relationship. VCF Automation adds any certificate that you decide to trust to a centralized certificate storage area.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Administer > Identity Providers.
3. On the Identity Providers page, click the LDAP tab.
4. If you are configuring LDAP for the first time, click Configure and select a configuration option.
If you are reconfiguring an existing LDAP connection, click Edit and proceed to the next step.
Option Description
Do not use LDAP. Use this option if you want to add VCF Automation users who
are private to the organization. If you select this option, you
cannot create or import user groups.

administrator and the organization is a member of the cloud
provider company.
If you select this option, enter a distinguished name for the
organization and click Save.
Custom LDAP service Used when you want the organization to use its own directory
service. Before you can use this option, you must configure your
cloud system LDAP service to link to their LDAP service.
If you select this option, proceed to Step 5.

5. Click the Custom LDAP tab.
6. Click Edit and enter the required information for the LDAP connection.
Required Information Description
Server The host name or IP address of the LDAP server.
Port The port number on which the LDAP server is listening.
For LDAP, the default port number is 389. For LDAPS, the default port number is 636.
Base distinguished name The base distinguished name (DN) is the location in the LDAP directory where VCF
Automation to connect.
To connect at root level, enter only the domain components, for example, DC=exampl
e,DC=com.
To connect to a node in the domain tree structure, enter the distinguished name for that
node, for example, OU=ServiceDirector,DC=example,DC=com.
Connecting to a node limits the scope of the directory available to VCF Automation.
Connector type The type of your LDAP server. Can be Active Directory or OpenLDAP.
Use SSL If your server is LDAPS, select this check box.
Authentication method Simple authentication consists of sending the user's DN and password to the LDAP
server. If you are using LDAP, the LDAP password is sent over the network in plain text.
If you want to use Kerberos, you must configure the LDAP connection by using the
vCloud API.
User name Enter the full LDAP distinguished name (DN) of a service account with domain admin
rights. VCF Automation uses this account to query the LDAP directory and retrieve user
information.
If the anonymous read support is enabled on your LDAP server, you can leave these
text boxes blank.
Password The password for the service account that connects to the LDAP server.
If the anonymous read support is enabled on your LDAP server, you can leave these
text boxes blank.
7. Click the User Attributes tab, examine the default values for the user attributes, and, if your LDAP directory uses
different schema, modify the values.
8. Click the Group Attributes tab, examine the default values for the group attributes, and, if your LDAP directory uses
different schema, modify the values.
9. If you want to customize the Sign in with LDAP button label that appears on the VCF Automation login page, enter a
new custom button text.

b) Enter the password of the LDAP server user that you configured and click Test.
If connected successfully, a green check mark is displayed.
If a user name is entered for the test, the retrieved user and group attribute values are displayed in a table. The
values that are successfully mapped to LDAP attributes are marked with green check marks. The values that are
not mapped to LDAP attributes are blank and marked with red exclamation marks.

configure the organization with this SAML identity provider. Imported users can log in to the organization with the
credentials established in the SAML identity provider.
• Verify that you have access to a SAML 2.0 compliant identity provider.

file with the following metadata from your SAML identity provider in return.
– The location of the single sign-on service
– The location of the single logout service

For information on configuring and acquiring metadata from a SAML provider, consult the documentation for your

To configure VCF Automation with a SAML identity provider, you establish a mutual trust by exchanging SAML service
provider and identity provider metadata.
To determine the correct values and settings and to ensure proper and accurate configuration, see also the product
documentation of those identity providers.
When an imported user attempts to log in, the system extracts the following attributes from the SAML token, if available,
and use them for interpreting the corresponding pieces of information about the user.
•
email address = "EmailAddress"
•
user name = "UserName"
•
full name = "FullName"
•
user's groups = "Groups"
• (this attribute is configurable)
user's roles = "Roles"
Group information is used if the user is not directly imported but is expected to log in by virtue of membership in imported
groups. A user can belong to multiple groups, so can have multiple roles during a session.
If an imported user or group is assigned the Defer to Identity Provider role, the roles are assigned based on the
information gathered from the attribute in the token. If a different attribute is used, this attribute name can be

configured using API and only the attribute is configurable. If the Defer to Identity Provider role is used, but no

role information can be extracted, the user can log in but has no any rights to perform any activities.
