Edit Namespace Settings in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can edit the CPU, memory, and storage utilization limits and reservations for existing
namespaces to accommodate changing application team demands.
You can increase or decrease the resources that are available to a namespace at any time. You can add content libraries,
VM classes, and subnets, add storage classes and update storage class limits, and add and remove zones and change
limits and reservations for each zone.
Updating a namespace might take a long time to complete depending on the changes made and the state of the
underlying infrastructure. Some specific zone changes might be especially time-consuming, for example:
• If you decrease the CPU and memory limits of a namespace that has workloads running that exceed the updated
capacity, the update request is paused until the workloads are deleted and the target capacity becomes available.
• If you delete a zone that has workloads running, the request is paused until all workloads are deleted.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Navigate to the namespace you want to edit using one of the following paths.
• Select Manage & Govern > Namespaces. Click the namespace name to open the details page.
• Select Manage & Govern > Projects. Click the project that contains the namespace and then click the
Namespaces tab. Click the vertical ellipsis next to the namespace name and then click Edit.
3. Next to Annotations, click Edit to add metadata for the namespace.
For more information on metadata, see Working with Metadata for VCF Automation Resources.
4. Next to Subnets, click Edit to add or remove shared subnets.
You can add subnets that the provider administrator shared with you or subnets that you created for your
organizations. See Create a Subnet in a VCF Automation Organization.
5. In the Capacity section, edit zone limits.
a) Click Resource Limits.
b) Select capacity type.
• To edit resource limits across zones in bulk, select Apply the same limits and reservations across all zones and
enter the updated values.
• To edit resource limits for specific zones, select Apply different limits and reservations for each zone and enter
the updated values for the desired zones.
Broadcom 7166

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
6. In the VM Classes section, add or remove VM classes.
You cannot edit VM classes.
7. In the Storage Classes section, add, edit, or remove storage classes.
8. In the Infrastructure Policies section, add or remove infrastructure policies.
Infrastructure policies define constraints and requirements for resource placement and configuration across the
regions and zones that are allocated to your organization.
At least one compatible policy must be available to the namespace.
In the Services section, you can access all services that are enabled for the namespace, for example, VM Service,
Kubernetes Services, Volume Service, and so on. To access a service, click the respective tile.
Setting up the Content Hub in VCF Automation
The Content Hub houses blueprints, VM images and content libraries, VCF Operations orchestrator workflows, and other
objects that you manage and publish to the catalog where your application teams can request them for deployment. The
requirements and process for setting up your VCF Automation catalog depends on the content that you are providing to
your users.
Working with the Content Hub
The Content Hub contains the following sections.
Blueprint Design The Blueprint Design page is where you create VCF Automation blueprints. You can design blueprints
from scratch or you can import OVA and YAML files from VMware Cloud Director or other VCF Automation
organizations.
See Managing Blueprints in VCF Automation.
VM Images VM images and related binaries are stored in content libraries and can be reused in regions that are
mapped to one or multiple vCenter instances.
Content Libraries Content libraries are collections of VM images and other files, like OVA/OVF, ISO images, and scripts, that
you can reuse in different scenarios with allocation dependent on your business needs.
Workflows A workflow is a set of actions, decisions, and results that are run sequentially to perform a specific task,
such as provisioning VMs, backing up, managing infrastructure, and so on. Workflows can run according
to a predefined schedule or they can be triggered by certain events. Workflows can request input that is
provided by a user, by another workflow, or externally.
Publishing Content to the Catalog
The Content Hub is where you create and store your VCF Automation content. For users in your projects to be able to
access and deploy this content, you must publish it to the VCF Automation catalog.
Ensure that the content is working properly before you add it to the catalog.
See Publishing and Sharing Content in the VCF Automation Catalog.
Working with blueprints
As an administrator authoring blueprints, you can update the name, description, catalog icon of the blueprint, and you can
version the blueprint.
Blueprint-backed catalog items are available for all project members to request and deploy when a blueprint version is
published to the catalog. Any changes to the blueprint are reflected in the corresponding catalog item. The blueprints are
refreshed every six hours.
You can also edit the request form of the catalog item, in which case the changes are reflected in the blueprint.
Broadcom 7167

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Managing Content Libraries in VCF Automation
Content libraries are centralized repositories of VM images, like OVA/OVF, ISO images, and scripts, that are used
to deploy workloads. VCF Automation content libraries can be created by provider administrators and organization
administrators. Content libraries created by provider administrators are called provider content libraries. Organization
administrators can create two types of content libraries, organization content libraries and project content libraries.
Provider Content Libraries
Provider content libraries are configured by the provider administrator in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
Provider content libraries are available to all organizations on a read-only basis. Provider administrators can create one or
more content libraries, each serving a specific need.
Organization and Project Content Libraries
Organization administrators can create and manage their own content libraries that they scope to either the whole
organization or to individual projects. Content libraries created for the organization are not accessible to other
organizations managed by the same provider administrator.
To allow project teams to operate independently, like create and manage project- or application-specific images,
organization administrators can create a project content library for their project.
The following table provides a comparison between organization content libraries and project content libraries.
Organization Content Library Project Content Library
Scope Organization Single or multiple projects
Supported file types • OVA • OVA
• OVF • OVF
• ISO
Created and managed by • Organization administrator • Organization administrator
• Provider administrator when launching • Provider administrator when launching
the organization from the Provider the organization from the Provider
Management UI Management UI
Project permissions Read only. All projects in the organization • Read only. Associated projects with
can consume content from this library read permissions can consume content
from this library
• Read/write. Associated projects with
read/write permissions can consumer,
upload, and capture content from this
library
Subscribe to an external library Yes. Must be enabled by the provider Yes. Must be enabled by the provider
administrator administrator
Subscribe to a Canonical library Yes. Must be enabled by the provider Yes. Must be enabled by the provider
administrator administrator
Content Library Concepts
Regions
• Content libraries can be made available in one or more regions in VCF Automation.
• Provider content libraries are automatically available to all organizations that have quota in a region where the content
library is available.
• Organization content libraries and project content libraries are explicitly made available in every region where the
organization has quota in. For example, if the organization has quota in Region1 and Region2, a content library can be
available in Region1 only and so workloads that are provisioned in Region2 do not have access to the content library.
Storage
• Storage consumed by organization content libraries count towards the organization storage quota.
Broadcom 7168

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Organization content libraries subscribed to external sources use storage allocated to the organizational quota as the
remote images are downloaded and stored locally in VCF. This could also lead to increased storage utilization than
expected.
• Sometimes a region may be backed by more than a single vCenter. In such cases, content libraries created in such
regions may be replicated in each vCenter, leading to higher than expected storage utilization. Check with your
provider administrator to understand how this might affect your storage utilization.
Namespaces
• Organization content libraries are generally available to all namespaces created by all projects across all regions that
were selected when the content library was created. In some cases, organization administrators might want to create
content libraries specific only to a namespace. This is achieved by first turning off the toggle Assign to all current
and future namespaces when creating the organization content library. When a new namespace class is created, the
organization administrator can add a content library which makes it available only to namespaces created from that
namespace class.
• Project content libraries are available only to namespaces that belong to the same project.
Create an Organization Content Library in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can create a content library for your organization to which you can then upload VM
images.
Only ISO and OVA/OVF file types are supported as content library items.
You can also create an organization content library in VCF Automation by subscribing to an external publisher if your
provider administrator enabled those options for your organization. Subscribed content libraries are read-only. You cannot
upload new items to the library and you cannot delete items from it. You can, however, delete the whole library from VCF
Automation. You can subscribe to externally published VCSP-compliant content libraries.
When you create a subscribed library, VCF Automation checks the total size of the items in the library and library creation
fails if the items exceed the storage quota for your organization. Automatic or scheduled synchronization of subscribed
libraries is not supported.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Content Libraries, and click New.
3. Enter a name and description for the content library.
After you create the content library, you can update the name and description of the content library only through the
VCF Automation API.
4. Next to Type, select Organization Content Library.
Only organization administrators can add, edit, and delete images from this content library. All non-administrator users
have read permissions only.
5. If you want to assign the content library to all current and future namespaces, turn on the toggle.
You cannot change this setting later.
6. If you want to create a subscribed library, turn on the Subscribe to an external library toggle.
a) Click Next.
b) Enter the URL of the external content library.
c) If the content library is password-protected, enter the password for it.
7. Click Next.
8. Select one or more regions and a corresponding storage class for each region.
9. Click Next.
10.Review your settings and click Confirm.
You created an organization content library that is available in each selected region.
Broadcom 7169

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
To troubleshoot issues with content libraries in VCF Automation, you need VCF Automation Provider Management POD
logs. You can download the log bundles from the component-specific area on the Build > Lifecycle > VCF Management
page in VCF Operations. Debug logs are in the
/opt/vmware/vcloud-director/logs/vcloud-container-
file.
debug.log
Upload VM images to the content library. See Add a VM Image to a Content Library in VCF Automation.
Create a Project Content Library in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can create a content library that you can scope to individual projects for better
resource isolation and management.
Project content libraries allow you to make VM images available to specific users and resources within a project, as
opposed to organization or provider content libraries which are always available to all users within the organization that
the library is shared with. Project content libraries cannot be shared with other organizations.
When a content library is shared with a given project, all namespaces within that project can access the library. The
namespace association also means that the library can be accessed by the VM Service.
By default, each project can be associated with up to 100 project content libraries. Provider administrators can configure
this limit for the organization. See Create a Content Library.
Project content libraries can span multiple regions and multiple vCenter instances within a single region. In case a region
is backed by more than one vCenter, project content libraries created in such regions may be replicated in each vCenter,
leading to higher than expected storage utilization. Check with your provider administrator to understand how this might
affect your storage utilization.
After an image is uploaded to a project content library, it can be published to the catalog, referenced in a blueprint, or
directly deployed from the VM Service. The images are only available within the scope of the projects that the content
library is shared with. Project content libraries support OVA/OVF images. Images from project content libraries can also be
copied to a provider content library so that they become available to all organizations, if the provider administrator enabled
this option for the organization.
Important:
Project content libraries do not support ISO files, vApp OVA files, or multi-VM OVA files.
Because project content libraries are owned by the organization, storage cost is incurred by the organization as a whole.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Content Libraries, and click New.
3. Enter a name and description for the content library.
4. Next to Type, select Project Content Library.
5. If you want to create a subscribed library, turn on the Subscribe to an external library toggle.
6. Click Next.
7. Select the type of subscribed library you want to create.
a) Click Next.
b) Enter the URL of the external content library.
c) If the content library is password-protected, enter the password for it.
8. Click Next.
9. Configure project permissions.
The content library is accessible to all namespaces associated with each project that is part of the scope. You can
change the associated projects at any time.
You can configure read and/or write permissions for all current and future projects that you associate with the content
library or you can configure permissions for individual projects.
Broadcom 7170

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For subscribed content libraries, you can assign only read permissions to projects. Project users will not be able to
upload VM images to the content library.
10.Click Next.
11.Select one or more regions and a corresponding storage class for each region.
Note:
Changing the storage class used by any of the regions that the library is attached to will result in an error.
12.Click Next.
13.Review your settings and click Confirm.
• Upload VM images to the content library. See Add a VM Image to a Content Library in VCF Automation.
Subscribe to Ubuntu OS Images from a Canonical Content Library in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can create a content library that is subscribed to Ubuntu VM images from a
Canonical content library.
• The provider administrator must enable the option to subscribe to Canonical for your organization.
VCF Automation content libraries can subscribe to Canonical, integrated with VCF, to get pre-verified Canonical content
without the need for any additional configuration. Supported content includes Canonical Ubuntu Pro images which can be
used to provision licensed Ubuntu VMs using the VM Service.
You create a content library for Canonical Ubuntu VM images to automate the image procurement pipeline. VCF
Automation connects directly to the VCF Software Depot to synchronize validated images into local storage on a 90/60-
day schedule.
Canonical publishes updates every 15 days. To fetch the newest releases, you can manually sync your VCF Automation
project content library as needed.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Content Libraries, and click New.
3. Enter a name and description for the content library.
4. Next to Type, select Organization Content Library or Project Content Library.
5. For organization content libraries, if you want to assign the library to all current and future namespaces, turn on the
toggle.
6. Turn on the Subscribe to a library toggle.
7. Click Next.
8. Next to type, select Canonical.
9. Click Next.
10.Configure project permissions.
The content library is accessible to all namespaces associated with each project that is part of the scope. You can
change the associated projects at any time.
For Canonical libraries, you can assign only read permissions for all current and future projects that you associate with
the content library or you can configure permissions for individual projects. Project users in these projects will not be
able to upload VM images to the content library.

Add a VM Image to a Content Library in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you add a VM image to a content library. As a project administrator, you can add VM
images to project content libraries in your project. You can then publish the VM image to the catalog.
Every VM image you upload has a unique identifier (VMI) which you can use in blueprints or to provision VMs directly.
Before you begin, ensure that you have a VM image in a supported format, saved on your local machine.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > VM Images.
3. Click Upload.
4. Click the arrow next to Select Source and select a local file to upload.
Organization content libraries support OVA/OVF and ISO files. Project content libraries support OVA or OVF files.
Note:
While you can upload an ISO image to an organization content library, you cannot publish the image directly to
the catalog. You must create a blueprint containing the image first, deploy the blueprint, and then convert it to an
OVF blueprint.
5. Select a content library to which to upload the VM image.
6. Enter a name and, optionally, a description for the image.
7. Click Submit.
It can take a few minutes for the file to get uploaded. Once the upload is complete, verify that the image status is Ready.
Provider administrators can copy images from project content libraries to a provider content library so that the images
become available to all organizations.
Next, publish the VM image to the catalog for project users can request it. See Publish a VM Image to the VCF
Automation Catalog.
Users with the Project Administrator or Project Advanced User role can use the image to deploy a VM using the VM
Service.

As an organization administrator in VCF Automation, you can copy images from a project content library in your

• Verify that the provider administrator gave you the necessary permissions to copy VM images to provider content

Provider consumption organizations have the necessary permissions by default.
• Verify that you have a project content library that contains the VM image you want to copy to your provider library.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Navigate to the desired VM image using one of the following paths.
• Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > VM Images and locate the VM image.

VM image. Click the VM Images tab and locate the VM image.

Publishing and Sharing Content in the VCF Automation Catalog
As an organization administrator, you publish content to the VCF Automation catalog to make it available to project users.
Publish a Blueprint to the Catalog in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you publish blueprints to the VCF Automation catalog for project users to request them
and provision resources.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Blueprint Design > Blueprints.
3. Open the blueprint that you want to publish.
4. On the blueprint design canvas, click Version.
5. Rename the blueprint version as necessary.
6. Select the Publish this version to the catalog check box.
7. Click Create.
8. Close the blueprint.
Verify that the blueprint is available in the catalog. Catalog users can now request the blueprint for deployment.
By default, the blueprint becomes available to users that are members of the project that the blueprint is associated with.
You can share the catalog item with other projects within your organization or with other VCF Automation organizations.
See Share Blueprints with Other VCF Automation Projects and Organizations.
Share Blueprints with Other VCF Automation Projects and Organizations
As an organization administrator, you can share VCF Automation blueprints with other VCF Automation projects and

Enable Cross-Organization Content Sharing in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. If you do not have these

a) To create a blueprint, click New From > Black Canvas.
b) To edit an existing blueprint, click the blueprint name. In the blueprint design canvas, click All Actions > Settings.

Managing Blueprints in VCF Automation
A blueprint is a declarative template used to define and automate the deployment of infrastructure, applications, and
services. It allows users to model complex cloud resources, such as VMs, networks, storage, and software components.
Blueprints orchestrate the deployment of multiple resources in the VCF platform. They act as a reusable design for
deploying resources and services consistently.
Blueprint Features
• Blueprint designer. The Blueprint Designer offers a single interface to create blueprints for various resource types,
including single machines, multi-machine deployments, and multi-tiered applications.
• Declarative Infrastructure-as-Code. Blueprints define the desired state of the infrastructure using YAML or a visual
designer, rather than specifying step-by-step instructions.
• Reusability and versioning. Blueprints can be versioned, imported, exported (YAML format), and shared across
projects or organizations, promoting reusability and collaboration.
• Self-Service provisioning. VCF Automation provides self-service portals where users can deploy and manage
resources based on predefined blueprints.
• Inputs and Customization. Blueprint inputs enable customization during deployment, allowing users to select options
like machine size or image.
• Governance. To ensure consistency, reusability, and governance across environments.
• Day 2 operations. Blueprints support day 2 operations, allowing for updates, modifications, and management of
existing deployments.
Blueprint Concepts
• Versioning. Blueprints can be versioned. At deployment time, you can select any of your versions to deploy.
• Resource objects. Resource objects represent the infrastructure components and services that are provisioned and
managed in a blueprint.
• Dependencies between resources in blueprints. When you deploy a VCF Automation blueprint, one resource might
need another resource to be available first.
• Instances. Instances are created when blueprints are deployed from the catalog.
• Day 2 actions. Actions that can be performed on the provisioned resource objects.
Broadcom 7176

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Property groups. Instead of defining the same properties repeatedly across multiple blueprints, property groups
enable you to define them once and then link them to various resources. This promotes consistency and simplifies
management, as updates to a property group are automatically reflected in all linked templates.
• Property bindings. Sometimes, a resource property needs a value found in a property of another resource. For
example, a backup server might need the operating system image of the database server that is being backed up, so
the database server must exist first.
• Custom forms. Allows users to design and customize request forms for catalog items, providing a tailored user
experience for submitting requests. They can be designed with a drag-and-drop interface and configured with various
properties, including conditional logic and external data sources.
• Custom resources. VCF Automation supports the use of custom resources within blueprints to extend automation
capabilities beyond native resource types. These custom resources are built upon VCF Operations orchestrator
workflows and can represent a resource.
When to Use Blueprints
Blueprints allow you to streamline and automate the deployment process, ensuring consistency and reducing manual
effort.
With blueprints, you can model complex IT services by visually designing infrastructure components like VMs, networks,
and storage. You can use blueprints when you want to hide the complexities of the infrastructure provisioning from the end
user.
You can publish blueprints to the self-service VCF Automation catalog which allows users to request and deploy services
based on predefined templates.
Best Practices for Designing Blueprints
• Leverage input properties in blueprints to allow users to customize deployments while maintaining a degree of control.
Consider providing default values for required fields to improve user experience and prevent errors.
• Establish clear and consistent naming conventions for blueprints, catalog items, and other resources to improve
manageability and organization.
• Using an iterative method to build and version blueprints helps teams adopt Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) practices.
Start with a minimum viable blueprint (MVB) and add features iteratively. Additionally, use tools like Git for version
control.
Sharing Blueprints with Projects and Organizations
When you first create a blueprint, you associate it with a project so that when you publish the blueprint to the catalog,
users in the selected project can see request and deploy the blueprint. You have the option of making the published
blueprint available to other projects in the organization either when you create the blueprint or at a later time.
If you are managing a Provider Consumption organization, you can share blueprints with all other organizations under
the same provider administrator or you can select specific organizations. After the blueprint is shared, whenever PCO
administrator publishes a blueprint to the catalog, the catalog item is shared with the selected organizations. That means
one blueprint backs multiple catalog items, one in each organization.
When sharing blueprints with other organizations, consider the following limitations.
• Blueprints that contain any of the following resource types cannot be shared:
– property groups;
– custom resources;
– secrets;
– namespaces;
– VM images from provider content libraries.
• If a blueprint is shared with an organization, a blueprint version with restrictions cannot be published to the catalog.
• If a blueprint is not shared with any organizations yet, and it has versions that have restrictions and have been
published to the catalog, the blueprint cannot be updated and shared with any organization.
Broadcom 7177

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Creating Blueprints in VCF Automation
You use VCF Automation to create blueprints, which are the fundamental way to define and automate the deployment and
management of resources, such as virtual machines, networks, and volumes in a namespace.
Important:
Blueprints in VCF Automation organizations are specific to VMware Cloud Foundation elements. Public cloud
capabilities are supported in cloud templates in VCF Automation for VM Apps organizations. See Managing
Organizations in for VM Apps.
How blueprints work
VCF Automation blueprint creation is an infrastructure-as-code process. You start by adding resources in the design
canvas. Then, you complete the details using the YAML code editor. The code editor allows you to type code directly or
enter values in a form.
Designing blueprints
You use the Blueprint Design page to create and design VCF Automation blueprint specifications for the machines and
applications that you want to provision, including property groups, custom resources, and resource actions.
Working with the Blueprint Design Page
To create a blueprint from scratch, go to Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Blueprint Design. Then, click New from >
Blank canvas.
Note that other options allow you to create the blueprint from another, existing Automation blueprint to which you have
access.
Once you have created the blueprint, you can populate it by adding and configuring resources as shown below.
1. Locate resources.
2. Drag resources to the canvas.
3. Connect resources.
4. Configure resources by editing the blueprint code.
Selecting and adding resources to the design canvas
Resources appear at the left of the design page for selecting and dragging.
Connecting resources
Use the design canvas graphical controls to connect resources. Resources must be compatible for a connection.
To connect, hover over the edge of a resource to reveal the connection bubble. Then, click and drag the bubble to the
target resource and release.
If your resources have a context-driven relationship, you can drop them in a nested configuration with the following rules:
• Drop directly onto canvas.
CCI.Supervisor.Namespace
• Drop onto a resource or directly on canvas.
CCI.Supervisor.Resource CCI.Supervisor.Namespace
In the code editor, additional code for the source resource appears in the target resource code.
Editing blueprint code
The code editor allows you to type, cut, copy, and paste code directly. If you're uncomfortable editing code, you can click a
resource that's already in the design canvas, click the code editor Properties tab, and enter values there. Property values
that you enter appear in the code as if you had typed them directly.
Note that you can copy and paste code from one blueprint to another.
Broadcom 7178

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Code completion help
Adding resources to the blueprint and connecting those resources in the design canvas only creates starter code. To fully
configure your blueprint resources, edit the blueprint code.
The code editor allows you to type code directly or enter property values into a form. To help with direct code creation, the
editor includes syntax completion and error checking features.
Other ways to create blueprints
In addition to building a blueprint from a blank canvas, you can take advantage of existing code.
• Cloning
To clone a blueprint, go to Blueprint Design, select a source, and click Clone. You clone a blueprint to create a copy
based on the source, then assign the clone to a new project or use it as starter code for a new application.
• Uploading and downloading
You can upload, download, and share blueprint YAML code in any way that makes sense for your site. You can also
modify blueprint code by using external editors and development environments.
Note:
A good way to validate shared blueprint code is to inspect it in the code editor on the design page.
• Integrating VCF Automation with a repository
An integrated git source control repository can make blueprints available to qualified users as the basis for a new
deployment. See Integrate for All Apps with Git.
• You can also get code samples from the YAML that is generated when you create a new VM using the Virtual Machine
Service.
Creating bindings and dependencies between resources in blueprints in VCF
Automation
When you deploy a VCF Automation blueprint, one resource might need another resource to be available first.
Important:
Arrows only indicate a dependency, not a connection. To connect resources so that they communicate, see
Creating Blueprints in for All Apps.
Explicit dependencies
Sometimes, a resource needs another to be deployed first. For example, a database server might need to exist first,
before an application server can be created and configured to access it.
An explicit dependency sets the build order at deployment time, or for scale-in or scale-out actions. You can add an
explicit dependency using the graphical design canvas or the code editor.
• Design canvas option—draw a connection starting at the dependent resource and ending at the resource to be
deployed first.
• Code editor option—add a property to the dependent resource, and identify the resource to be deployed
dependsOn
first.
An explicit dependency creates a solid arrow in the canvas.
Property bindings
Sometimes, a resource property needs a value found in a property of another resource. For example, a backup server
might need the operating system image of the database server that is being backed up, so the database server must exist
first.
Also called an implicit dependency, a property binding controls build order by waiting until the needed property is available
before deploying the dependent resource. You add a property binding using the code editor.
• Edit the dependent resource, adding a property that identifies the resource and property that must exist first.
Broadcom 7179

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
A property binding creates a dashed arrow in the canvas.
Versioning Blueprints in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator creating blueprints, you can safely capture a snapshot of a working design before risking
further changes. At deployment time, you can select any of your versions to deploy.
Restoring an older version
From the design page, click Version History.
On the left, select an older version to inspect it in the canvas and code editor. When you find the version that you want,
click Restore. Restoring overwrites the current draft without removing any named versions.
Publishing a Blueprint Version to the Catalog
You can publish a blueprint version to the VCF Automation catalog using one of two ways.
• When you create a blueprint version, select Publlish to catalog.
• From the design page, click Version History. On the left, select a version and release it.
You can't release a Current Draft to the catalog until you version it.
Comparing Blueprint Versions
When changes and versions accumulate, you might want to identify differences among them.
From the Version History view, select a version, and click Diff. Then, from the Diff against drop-down, select another
version to compare to.
Note that you can toggle between reviewing code differences or visual topology differences.
Cloning a Blueprint
Although it's not the same as saving a version, from the design page, All Actions > Clone makes a copy of the current
blueprint for alternative development.
Specifying formatVersion in Blueprints in VCF Automation
After versioning your blueprint, you can change the value in your YAML to support additional
formatVersion
deployment features.
The appears at the top of your YAML and its value determines what you can specify in your blueprint.
formatVersion
• includes blueprint specifications for inputs and resources. It automatically applies to all basic
formatVersion: 1
blueprints.
• adds blueprint specifications for metadata, variables, and outputs. It automatically applies to the
formatVersion: 2
blueprints that are deployed using Private AI Automation Services, but supports any kind of deployment.
As an administrator, you can use the specifications included with to make deployments more
formatVersion: 2
accessible to your users. The following code samples show examples of how to use the blueprint
formatVersion: 2
specifications in your YAML.
Metadata blueprint specification
Use metadata to hide or unhide the day 2 operations that appear for your users.
metadata:
deploymentSettings:
disableUpdateDay2Action: true
hideDisabledDay2Actions: true
Broadcom 7180

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• When is true, users do not see the Update day 2 operation in the Actions menu. If the
disableUpdateDay2Action
user does not have permission to update, the option appears unavailable (dimmed).
• When is true, any day 2 operation that has been deactivated for the user will not
hideDisabledDay2Actions
appear in the Actions menu.
Variables blueprint specification
Use to specify values that are reused multiple times within a blueprint, such as in dynamic configurations. A
variables
variable definition can include plain strings, inputs, and refer to other variables. You reference the variables that you define
in the resources and outputs sections of the blueprint.
variables:
applications:
- name: App1
port: 3000
showAppInfo: true
- name: App2
port: 4000
showAppInfo: false
Outputs blueprint specification
Use to define the deployment information that you want to make available to your user. All outputs are displayed
outputs
on the deployment details page under User Events, except for values which appear under the
__deploymentOverview
deployment Overview.
The outputs example includes:
• defined in the variables blueprint specification
variables
• defined in a resources section and included in the following code sample
resources

Reusing a Group of Properties in VCF Automation
When you have VCF Automation properties that always appear together, you can assemble them into a property group.
You can quickly add a property group to different VCF Automation designs, which saves the time of adding the same
multiple properties one by one. In addition, you have a single place to maintain or modify the set of properties, which
ensures their consistent application.
Only users with the Organization Administrator role may create, update, or delete a property group. The administrator can
share a property group with an entire organization or limit its use to only within a project.
CAUTION:
A property group might be included in many blueprints, including ones that are already released to the catalog.
Changes to a property group can affect other users.
There are two types of property groups.
• Inputs
Input property groups gather and apply a consistent set of properties at user request time. Input property groups can
include entries for the user to add or select, or they might include read-only values that are needed by the design.
Properties for the user to edit or select can be readable or encrypted. Read-only properties appear on the request form
but can't be edited. If you want read-only values to remain totally hidden, use a constant property group instead.
• Constants
Constant property groups silently apply known properties. In effect, constant property groups are invisible metadata.
They provide values to your VCF Automation designs in a way that prevents a requesting user from reading those
values or even knowing that they're present. Examples might include license keys or domain account credentials.
The two property group types are handled very differently by VCF Automation. When you create a property group, you
must first select whether to create inputs or constants. You can't create a blended property group nor convert an existing
set of properties and their property group from one type to the other.
Modifying a Property Group
Changes to a property group affect every blueprint that uses it. When the changed version of the blueprint is released,
those changes also affect catalog users.
The property group editing pages show the number of blueprints that include the property group. To see which blueprint
would be affected by a change, click the number.
Before modifying a property group, make sure that the change is acceptable to everyone who is creating or updating
deployments based on the blueprints listed.
Deleting a Property Group
Deleting a property group causes errors in every blueprint that uses it. You cannot delete a property group before you
manually remove it from all of the blueprints in which it is included.
To remove a property group from a blueprint, open and edit the blueprint in the design canvas. Use the code editor to
delete the associated entry or entries in the section of the code.
propgroup resources
Note:
You cannot delete a property group if it is included in a versioned blueprint. Versioned blueprints are read-only.
Broadcom 7183

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Input Property Groups in VCF Automation
VCF Automation input property groups usually include related settings for the user to enter or select. They might also
include read-only values needed by the blueprint design.
Create an input property group
1. Go to Build & Deploy > Blueprint Design > Property Groups, and click New.
2. Select Input Values.
3. Name and describe the new property group.
Name Property group names must be unique within a given organization.
Only letters, numbers, and underscores are permitted.
Display Name Add a heading for the entire group of properties, which appears on
the request form.
Description Explain what this set of properties is for.
Scope Decide whether an administrator may share the property group
with the whole organization. Otherwise, only one project can
access the property group.
Although you can always add or modify properties in the group,
the scope is permanent and can't be changed later.
Project When the scope is project-only, this project can access the
property group.
4. To add a property to the group, click New Property.
The panel for adding a new property is very similar to the Inputs tab of the VCF Automation design page code editor.
Name Free-form name for the individual property. Only letters, numbers,
and underscores are permitted.
Display Name Add an individual property name to appear on the request form.
Type String, Integer, Number, Boolean (T/F), Object, or Array.
Default Value Preset value entry that appears in the request form.
The presence of default values affects whether input is optional or
required.
Encrypted When selected, obscures the value when entering it into the
request form and in the subsequent deployment. Encrypted
properties can't have a default value.
Read-only An uneditable but visible value in the request form. Requires a
default.
More Options Options that vary according to property type. Expand the drop-
down, add any additional settings, and click Create.
5. Add more properties to the group, and click Create when finished.
Adding the property group to blueprint inputs
Even for a long list of property inputs, you only need to add the property group to make them all part of the request form.
Enter the inputs code directly into the blueprint design page, and take advantage of the automatic prompting as you type
in the code editor. Your code might look similar to the following example.
$ref: /ref/p...
inputs:
pgmachine:
type: object
title: Machine Properties
$ref: /ref/property-groups/machine
pgrequester:
type: object
Broadcom 7184

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
title: Requester Details
$ref: /ref/property-groups/requesterDetails
Binding blueprint resources to the property group
To make use of property group input values, add bindings under the resource.
propgroup
Depending on what kind of values are in a property group, you might want to reference them individually. You can enter
them separately, by property group name and property name.
You can also quickly add an entire set of values to a resource by referencing an entire property group.
The following example shows how you reference an input property from a property group.
pve-vm:
type: CCI.Supervisor.Resource
properties:
context: ${resource.CCI_Supervisor_Namespace_1.id}
manifest:
apiVersion: vmoperator.vmware.com/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualMachine
metadata:
name: virtual-machine-1-${env.shortDeploymentId}
spec:
className: small
imageName: ${input.pgmachine.image}
Property groups in the custom form editor
Property groups are not editable like other fields in the custom form designer.
Constant Property Groups in VCF Automation
VCF Automation constants allow you to silently apply known key-value pairs to your designs.
How constants work
The key appears in the blueprint code, and the value becomes part of deployments that are based on that blueprint.
Constants require the binding under the resource.
propgroup
The binding is only used with constant property groups, not input property groups.
propgroup
Secret properties
If you expect to add a secret property to a property group, create the secret property before proceeding.
Create a constant property group
1. Go to Build & Deploy > Blueprint Design > Property Groups, and click New.
2. Select Constant Values.
3. Name and describe the new property group.
Name Property group names must be unique within a given organization.
Only letters, numbers, and underscores are permitted.
Display Name Leave blank. No heading appears on the request form.
Description Explain what this set of constants is for.
Broadcom 7185

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Scope Decide whether an administrator may share the property group
with the whole organization. Otherwise, only one project can
access the property group.
Although you can always add or modify properties in the group,
the scope is permanent and can't be changed later.
Secrets—If you expect to add a secret property to the property
group, you must use single project scope. Secret properties are
saved only at the project level.
Project When the scope is project-only, this project can access the
property group.
4. To add a constant property to the group, click New Property.
5. Enter a name that acts as the key, and a description.
6. Select a property type.
7. Enter the constant value that you want, and click Create.
• String, integer, and number types use direct entry.
• For a secret string value, select from the list of secret properties for the project.
• The boolean type uses a selection box to indicate true.
• For the object or array type, replace with the value that you want.
null
8. Add more constants to the group, and click Save when finished.
Binding blueprint resources to the property group
To make use of property group input values, add bindings under the resource.
propgroup
Depending on what kind of values are in a property group, you might want to reference them individually. You can enter
them separately, by property group name and property name.
You can also quickly add an entire set of values to a resource by referencing an entire property group.
The following example shows how you reference an input property from a property group.
pve-vm:
type: CCI.Supervisor.Resource
properties:
context: ${resource.CCI_Supervisor_Namespace_1.id}
manifest:

name: virtual-machine-1-${env.shortDeploymentId}

className: small
imageName: ${input.pgmachine.image}
Creating Custom Forms for Blueprints in VCF Automation
To create useful forms based on input parameters, you can design how the information appears at request time, how the
parameter values are populated, and add any specialized constraints.
Creating a Custom Request Form
Each blueprint version is coupled with a custom form. You use the Blueprint Design page to create and edit custom forms.
1. Go to Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Blueprint Design.
2. Open the blueprint for which you want to customize the request form.
3. On the blueprint canvas, click Create Custom Form.
4. Drag any custom elements onto the design canvas.
Broadcom 7186

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
5. Configure each element using the properties pane. For more about the fields properties, see Custom form designer
field properties in for All Apps.
Custom forms support data validation by adding constraints to a field.
6. Use the Actions menu options to import or export the form, or import or export a CSS file.
7. When you are ready, click Create.
To preview the request form, on the blueprint canvas, click Version History, select the blueprint version, and click the
View Form tab.
Importing and Exporting Custom Forms between Blueprints
You might find, after you develop a custom form, that you want to use part or all of it with another blueprint. You can
export a form from one blueprint and import it into another blueprint, and then continue customizing the form for the new
blueprint.
To share the custom forms, you can click Actions on the custom form designer and select one of the following options.
Action Menu Item Description
Import form Imports a JSON or YAML file.
Export form Exports your current custom form as a JSON file.
Export form as YAML Exports your current custom form as YAML.
Export the file as YAML when you want to move a custom
form from one instance to another. For example, from your test
environment to your production environment. If you prefer to edit
the form as YAML, you can export the form, edit it, and then import
it back into the blueprint.
Adding Your Own Style Sheet to a Custom Form
You can use a custom cascading style sheet to refine how the text appears on the screen. You must create the CSS file
outside of VCF Automation. You can export and import a CSS file from one blueprint to another.
Action Menu Item Description
Import CSS Imports a CSS file that enhances the catalog request form.
The file might be similar to the following example.
#input_<field_ID> {
font-size: 20px;
font-weight: bold;
color: red;
width: 600px;
}
#input_<field_ID> {
font-size: 20px;
font-weight: bold;
font-style: italic;
width: 600px;
}
In this example, replace <field_ID> with the actual field
IDs from the custom form. You can locate the values by
selecting the field in the form, and then you can see the
value in the properties pane, beneath the field name. For
example, Field ID: deploymentName or Field ID:
textField_fe7cf66a.
Export CSS Exports your customized CSS.
Remove CSS Discards your custom CSS.
The discarded CSS is not recoverable.
Broadcom 7187

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Adding External Validation to a Custom Form
You can also validate catalog request forms by adding an external validation. External validations are run once the user
submits a form request from the UI or the API. External validations use VCF Operations orchestrator action scripts that
return a string value when the input parameter value validation fails. The returned string value is displayed as an error
message in the catalog request form. If the input parameter value is valid, the external validation must return nothing.
You can add an external validation from the Validations tab in the form editor. You drag a VCF Operations orchestrator
validation element to the canvas and add a VCF Operations orchestrator action that you want to use for validation.
External validations can be related to more than one field at a time.
Custom Form Designer Field Properties in VCF Automation
The field properties in VCF Automation determine how the fields looks and what default values are presented to the user.
You can also use the properties to define rules that ensure that the users provide a valid entry when they request the item
in the catalog.
You configure each field individually. Select the field and edit the field properties.
Value source
For many of the properties, you can select from various value source options. Not all source options are available for all
field types or properties.
• Constant. The value does not change. Depending on the property, the value might be a string, an integer, a regular
expression, a complex value, for example, based on columns in a datagrid or another complex field, or selected from a
limited list, for example, Yes or No. For example, you can provide 1 as a default value integer, select No for the Read-
only property, or provide the regular expression to validate a field entry.
• Conditional value. The value is based on one or more conditions. The conditions are processed in the order listed. If
more than one condition is true, the last condition that is true determines the behavior of the field for that property. For
example, you can create a condition that determines if a field is visible based on the value in another field.
• External source. The value is based on the results of a VCF Operations orchestrator action. For example, calculate
cost based on a scripted VCF Operations orchestrator action.
• Bind field. The value is the same as the field to which it is bound. The available fields are limited to the same field
type. For example, you bind default value for an authentication needed check box field to another check box field.
When one target field check box is selected in the request form, the check box on the current field is selected.
• Computed value. The value is determined based on how the operator processes the selected fields and values. Text
fields use the concatenate operator. Integer fields use the selected add, subtract, multiply, or divide operations. For
example, you can configure an integer field to convert megabytes to gigabytes using the multiply operation.
Field appearance
You use the appearance properties to determine whether the field appears on the form and what label and custom help
you want to provide to your catalog users.

VCF Automation blueprint designs that prepare for day 2 changes
In addition to the day 2 actions already associated with VCF Automation resource types, you have design options that let
you prepare in advance for custom updates that users might need to make.
CAUTION:
To change a deployment, you can edit its blueprint and reapply it, or you can use day 2 actions. However, in most
cases you should avoid mixing the two approaches.
Lifecycle day 2 changes such as power on/off are usually safe, but others require caution, such as when adding
disks.
For example, if you add disks with a day 2 action, and then take a mixed approach by reapplying the blueprint, the
blueprint could overwrite the day 2 change, which might remove disks and cause data loss.
Day 2 preparation can involve either direct use of blueprint code, or the VCF Automation blueprint designer.
• You can use inputs in blueprint code so that, when you update the deployment or deployed resource, the interface
prompts for fresh values.
• You can use VCF Automation to design a custom action based on a VCF Operations orchestrator workflow. Running
the custom action results in the workflow or action making changes to the deployment or deployed resource.
For custom day 2 resource actions you can use the schema for deployment resource types to specify criteria for your
resource action. For example, you can use the deployment name property to define which deployments can use the
create resource action.
Important:
Bindings don't work for CCI.Supervisor.Resource objects. You can still create a day 2 operation, but the resource
should be selected again as in input.
Broadcom 7191

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

Capturing Namespaces as Blueprints in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator or a project administrator, you can capture the contents of an existing namespace and
create a reusable blueprint from it that you make available to your project users. The resulting blueprint captures multiple
resources in the namespace, including virtual machines, their hardware, Guest OS settings, networking (subnets, VPC
configurations), and storage (PVCs), secrets, and so on.
What Is a Capture
A capture is a generated blueprint that is used for defining and provisioning complete applications and environments.
Captures extract the live configuration, state, and dependency graph of all VMs within the environment, and convert
them into a deployable definition. The capture includes namespaces, VPCs, VMs and disks from content library images,
networking resources like subnets, shared subnets, and load balancers, and so on. Captured VMs are saved to a project
content library.
Broadcom 7197

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The resulting captured blueprint can be reused, enabling rapid environment cloning, migration, or recovery without the
need to manually define or export infrastructure details. Captures are an alternative to traditional, manually authored VCF
Automation blueprints and provide a way to create reusable deployments directly from existing workloads. You can reuse
these blueprints to deploy identical or differentiated environments from the same blueprint.
Captures are suitable for use in hands-on labs, training environments, and similar scenarios where reusable,
preconfigured environments are required.
How Do Captures Work
You publish blueprints to the VCF Automation catalog for entitled project users to request and deploy.
When a project administrator captures a namespace, VCF Automation generates a blueprint that represents the
discovered namespace settings and IaaS resource configurations, including:
• Namespace based on the namespace class and blueprint specification
• New project-scoped VPC or using existing bounded organization-scoped VPC
• Includes VM PVCs and content library VM images with specified VM class and disks
• VM customizations (Cloud-init, LinuxPrep, Sysprep)
• Network attachments (subnets) for VMs to VPC segments
• VM groups for VM boot order
• Networking resources
The project administrator publishes the blueprint to the catalog. The custom form for the blueprint can also be modified.
The blueprint can be exported, imported, and redeployed in different projects, enabling consistent replication of the
captured environment.
When a user requests the blueprint from the catalog, they provide parameters and customizations during request time.
Note:
Namespaces that contain VKS clusters, Avi load balancers, or vSphere pods cannot be captured.
Capture Types
You can capture the state of an existing namespace as a blueprint. You can capture namespaces as identical copies or
you can enable request-time VM customization.
• Identical Copy. You can capture a namespace keeping the exact settings of all VMs within the namespace, like Mac,
IpAddress, BIOS, and other settings. See Capture an Identical Copy of a Namespace in VCF Automation.
• Copy with customizations. See Capture a Namespace with Customizations in VCF Automation.
Managing Captures
• If you have a capture in progress, you cannot create a new capture out of the same namespace before the first one is
complete.
• You can delete namespace capture requests on the Recent Captures page.
• You can run day 2 operations on deployed instances of the captured blueprint. For a list of supported actions, see Day
2 Actions on Catalog-Provisioned Resources Provided with VCF Automation.
Capture an Identical Copy of a Namespace in VCF Automation
In VCF Automation, you can capture an identical copy of a namespace, where a blueprint is generated that recreates the
contents of a namespace. The blueprint includes a namespace with similar settings as the source, self-service VPC and
all of its associated resources, and virtual machine configurations including hardware, GuestOS, networking, and storage.
This mechanism ensures that every deployment is a fully independent, exact replica of the original source.
• Verify that you have an active namespace. The namespace can only be associated with a dedicated VPC and may
contain VPC private subnets.
Broadcom 7198

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Verify that the organization administrator configured self-service namespaces for the project. See Enable Namespace
Self-Service for Projects in Your VCF Automation Organization.
• All virtual machines within the namespace must be initialized and powered off.
• All virtual machines must belong to a single VM group. The namespace must contain only one VM group. See Create a
VM Group Using Self Service in VCF Automation.
• If you have any migrated VMs, these VMs do not have any VM classes associated with them so all VM classes must
be created before you start a capture. During capture, VCF Automation detects the right VM class based on the size of
each VM.
• Verify that the organization administrator configured at least one project content library associated with the
namespace. See Create a Project Content Library in VCF Automation.
When you capture an identical copy of a namespace, the resulting blueprint contains the following.
1. Identical namespace settings, including the region where the namespace is deployed, the namespace class used to
create the namespace, and subnets which are shared with the namespace.
2. Identical VPC settings and associated resources. Captured properties include the connectivity profile of the VPC and
private IP CIDRs.
3. VM hardware settings. Some of the captured hardware properties include:
a. the unique identifier for the VM instance within the namespace;
b. the VM class instance which specifies CPU, memory, and other core resources;
c. the virtual BIOS of the VM which represents the lowest-level hardware identifier that the guest operating system
typically sees;
d. IP and MAC of the VM NIC cards, which are present in the SubnetPort associated with the VM NIC card.
4. VM GuestOS settings. The bootstrap field in all VMs is cleared so that guest customizations do not rerun. Secret
resources that might be referenced in the GuestOS customization are not recreated.
5. Networking. Captured properties include network interfaces and subnets and subnet sets to which the VM NIC cards
are connected.
6. VM storage. Captured properties include storage class, volumes, disk capacity, and disk volume provisioning mode.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as a project administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy.
3. Under Services, select the namespace that you want to capture.
4. On the Overview page, click Capture as a Blueprint.
5. Configure the blueprint details.
a) Enter a name and description for the blueprint.
b) Select a content library where you want to save the captured images.
c) Select Capture as identical copy.
d) If you want to publish the capture to the catalog, select the checkbox.
You cannot publish the capture to the catalog if there are any issues with the capture.
e) Click Next.
6. Review your configuration and click Capture.
• View the generated blueprint and confirm that the blueprint includes all resources from the original namespace.
• Publish the blueprint to the catalog so that users in your project can request and deploy the namespace. See Publish a
Blueprint to the Catalog in VCF Automation.
Capture a Namespace with Customizations in VCF Automation
VCF Automation provides capabilities for customizing guest operating systems, including setting passwords, defining
hostnames, and executing scripts on both Windows and Linux hosts by leveraging various bootstrap types to handle guest
customization.
To enable individual VM customization within the blueprint, you select the option to capture the namespace with
customizations when requesting the capture.
Broadcom 7199

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Supported customizations include the following options:
• Hostname. Assign a unique hostname to each VM.
• Password. Set or auto-generate guest OS administrator or root passwords. For an example configuration, see Capture
a Namespace with an Auto-Generate Password Customization in VCF Automation.
• Scripts. Run pre- or post-customization scripts for Windows and Linux. Windows VMs can use GuiRunOnce
commands or custom PowerShell scripts via Sysprep. Linux VMs can execute shell scripts via LinuxPrep.
• Domain configuration. For Windows VMs, join an Active Directory domain. For an example configuration, see Capture
a Namespace with a Join Domain Customization in VCF Automation.

Importing or Exporting Blueprints in VCF Automation
In VCF Automation, you can export and import content to move artifacts from your development or staging environments
to a production environment or between different organizations or projects.
Importing Blueprints
You can import .OVA/.OVF or .YAML files as blueprints, for example, exported from another VCF Automation organization
or a VMware Cloud Director or a vCenter environment.
Note:
OVAs containing ISO media files are not supported during import.
By default, you can have a maximum of 5 concurrent import requests per organization. You can configure the import limit.
For more information, see the following topics:
• Import a Blueprint into VCF Automation
• Import a VMware Cloud Director OVA as a Blueprint in VCF Automation
Exporting Blueprints
You can export VCF Automation blueprints and associated VM images. you can create a single zip file containing the
blueprint content and the payloads for all the dependent resources used in the blueprint which can be re-imported into
another tenant to re-create the same blueprint with all of the associated resources.
Broadcom 7202

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Note:
When you export blueprints containing VM images that are ISO files, these images are skipped during export.
Only valid blueprints can be exported. You can select which blueprint version you want to export. By default, you can have
a maximum of five concurrent export requests per organization. You can configure the export limit.
For more information, see Export a Blueprint from VCF Automation.
Import a Blueprint into VCF Automation
In VCF Automation, you can import OVA/OVF and YAML files, for example, that you exported from another VCF
Automation organization.
• Verify that you have the Organization Administrator, Project Administrator, or Project Advanced User role.
• Verify that the organization administrator configured self-service namespaces for the project.
• Verify that you have the file you want to import saved on your local machine.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Build & Deploy > Content Hub > Blueprint Design > Blueprints.
3. On the Blueprints page, click New From > Import.
4. Enter a name and description for the blueprint and select a project where you want to import it.
5. Select the file to import. You can preview the contents of the file.
6. Optional: Upload a custom icon for the blueprint.
7. Click Next.
8. On the Image Settings page, select the content library where you want to upload the images.
Review the list of images identified from blueprint content. By default, images are included in the blueprint, unless you
disable this option.
9. Click Next.
10.On the Summary page, review your inputs and any potential warnings.
If any errors appear, you cannot continue the import. You must close the dialogue and restart with a valid OVA file.
11.Click Import to begin uploading the files and start the asynchronous import task.
You can monitor progress on the Imports tab.
Upon successful completion, the import request is linked to a blueprint. If the imported bundle contains a custom form, the
blueprint also has a custom form attached.

Managing Event Subscriptions in VCF Automation
You can extend your application lifecycles by using VCF Operations orchestrator workflows with event subscriptions.
When a triggering event occurs in your environment, the subscription is initiated and the specified workflow is run. You
can view system events on the event log. Subscriptions are project-specific, meaning they are linked to blueprints and
deployments through the specified project.
Provider administrators can use an MQTT client to subscribe to messages about Provider Management events and tasks.
See Subscribe to VCF Automation Provider Management Events, Tasks, and Metrics by Using an MQTT Client.
Blocking event topics
Some event topics support blocking events. The behavior of a subscription depends on whether the topic supports these
event types and how you configure the subscription.
Event subscriptions can use two broad types of event topics: non-blocking and blocking event topics. The event topic type
defines the behavior of the event subscription.
Non-blocking event Non-blocking event topics only allow you to create non-blocking subscriptions. Non-blocking subscriptions
topics are triggered asynchronously and you cannot rely on the order that the subscriptions are triggered in.
Blocking event topics Some event topics support blocking. If a subscription is marked as blocking, all messages that meet the set
conditions are not received by any other subscriptions with matching conditions until the runnable item of
the blocking subscription is run.
Blocking subscriptions run in priority order. The highest priority value is 0 (zero). If you have more than
one blocking subscription for the same event topic with the same priority level, the subscriptions run in
a reverse alphabetical order based on the name of the subscription. After all blocking subscriptions are
processed, the message is sent to all the non-blocking subscriptions at the same time. Because the
blocking subscriptions run synchronously, the changed event payload includes the updated event when the
subsequent subscriptions are notified.
You can use blocking event topics to manage multiple subscriptions that are dependent on each other.
For example, you can have two provisioning workflow subscriptions where the second subscription
depends on the results of the first subscription. The first subscription changes a property during
provisioning, and the second subscription records the new property, such as a machine name, in a file
system. The ChangeProperty subscription is prioritized as 0 and the RecordProperty is prioritized as 1
because the second subscription uses the results of the first subscription. When a machine is provisioned,
the ChangeProperty subscription begins running. Because the RecordProperty subscription conditions
are based on a post-provisioning condition, an event triggers the RecordProperty subscription. However,
because the ChangeProperty workflow is a blocking workflow, the event is not received until it is finished.
When the machine name is changed and the first workflow subscription is finished, the second workflow
subscription runs and records the machine name in the file system.
Broadcom 7205

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For blocking event topics, you can add a recovery runnable item to the subscription. The recovery runnable
item in a subscription runs if the primary runnable item fails. For example, you can create a workflow
subscription where the primary runnable item is a workflow that creates records in a CMDB system such as
ServiceNow. Even if the workflow subscription fails, some records might be created in the CMDB system. In
this scenario, a recovery runnable item can be used to clean up the records left in the CMDB system by the
failed runnable item.
For use cases that include multiple subscriptions that are dependent on each other, you can add a
ebs.recover.continuationproperty to the recovery runnable item. With this property, you can
direct if the system must continue with the next subscription in your chain, if the current subscription fails.
Event Log
The Event Log tab on the Event Subscriptions page displays a list of all events that have occurred within your
environment.
You can view the event logs on the Events tab. You can also filter the list of events by one or more properties. To view
additional details of an individual event, select the event ID.
Event Topics Provided with VCF Automation
VCF Automation includes predefined event topics.
You can see the list of all the events that get generated in the system and you can subscribe to those events. You can
trigger different workflows for different events. You can subscribe to VM Service events for operations on VMs. For

Operations orchestrator workflow that takes the VM and registers it in CMDB.

Create an Event Subscription to Manage Deployment Expiry in VCF Automation
You can manage expired deployments and their resources by using the action alongside existing event topics.
Expire
After a deployment lease in your environment expires, you can use event topics to perform tasks, such as stopping the
back up or monitoring of any deployment resources. To perform these day 2 operations, the VCF Automation API uses a
system-level action. This action is triggered automatically by the system whenever a deployment lease in your
Expire
organization expires. The action trigger precedes the power off event for any resources associated with that
Expire
deployment.
The Expire action is included in the payload of existing event topics, such as and
Deployment action requested
, and uses the parameter to perform pre-expiry and post-expiry
Deployment action completed deploymentid
tasks associated with the deployment resources.
Because Expire is a deployment-level action, you must subscribe to event topics related to deployment actions, like
or .
Deployment action requested Deployment action completed
The Expire action is triggered approximately 10 to 15 minutes after your deployment lease expires. The system does not
trigger lease expiry events prior to the actual lease expiry. The Expire action is a system-level action and users cannot
trigger the events associated with it manually.
For the current use case, you are using the event topic along with the Expire action
Deployment action requested
to back up a virtual machine in your deployment as a template. For this case, the back up is performed by using a VCF
Operations orchestrator workflow but the same task can also be performed by using an extensibility action as the runnable
item of the subscription.
1. Select Build & Deploy > Subscriptions > New.
2. Enter a name for the subscription.
3. Under Status, verify that the subscription is enabled.
4. Under Event Topic, select the Deployment action requested event topic.
5. Toggle on the Condition option and add a filter for the expiry action.
event.data.actionName == 'Expire'
Note:
The Deployment action requested event topic can be triggered by different deployment day 2 operations, such
as changing the deployment lease duration. Adding the lease expiry action filter guarantees that the subscription
is triggered only for expiry events.
6. Under Workflow, add the VCF Operations orchestrator workflow.
The schema of this sample workflow includes a scriptable task and a workflow element which includes the
Clone
workflow which comes preconfigured with VCF Operations orchestrator.
virtual machine, no customization
The scriptable task element includes the following sample script:
System.log("Lease expiry action triggered to clone a VM...")
System.log("Deployment Id is: " + inputProperties.deploymentId);
inputHeaders = new Properties();

deploymentId = inputProperties.deploymentId;
pathUriVariable = "/deployment/api/deployments/" +deploymentId +"/resources";

var keys = inputHeaders.keys;
for(var key in keys){
request.setHeader(keys[key], inputHeaders.get(keys[key]));
}
var response = restClient.execute(request);
System.log("Content as string: " + response.contentAsString);
var content = response.contentAsString;
var obj = JSON.parse(content);

System.log("Resource name is: " + resourceProperties.resourceName)
resourceName = resourceProperties.resourceName;

vcVM=vms[0];
System.log("VM input is: " + vcVM);
