name="test-vm-name"
7. Decide whether to set the subscription as blocking or non-blocking.
Note:
Making the subscription blocking means that the power off event for the deployment resources is triggered
only after the runnable item, in this case the lease expiry workflow, finishes its run successfully. Making the
subscription non-blocking means that power off event is triggered for the deployment resources regardless of the
status of the workflow run.
8. To finish editing the subscription, click Save.
After the subscription is triggered by the lease expiry event and the workflow run is successful, navigate to vSphere and
validate that your virtual machine is converted to a blueprint.
Subscribe to Events and Tasks in Your VCF Automation Organization Using an
MQTT Client
As an organization administrator or a project user, you can use an MQTT client to subscribe to messages about events
and tasks in your VCF Automation organization.
1. Log in to your VCF Automation organization by using the OpenAPI endpoint.
a) Make an API versions request to VCF Automation to obtain the VCF Automation API login URL.
GET http://vcfa.example.com/api/versions
b) POST a request to the login URL to create a login session.
POST https://vcfa.example.com/cloudapi/1.0.0/sessions/provider
Broadcom 7209

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. To establish a WebSocket connection, set the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol property to mqtt, set the client to connect to
the /messaging/mqtt path, add an authorization header, and follow the standard MQTT connect flow.
You receive the JWT token from the standard login request to VCF Automation. You can leave the user name and
password empty.
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: mqtt
Authorization: Bearer {JWT_token}
3. Once the connection is established successfully, subscribe to topics through the MQTT client.
publish/{user_org_id}/{user_id}
Example:
publish/debd63a0-6eae-11ea-8c7b-0050561776be/d19fd8ff-6eae-11ea-bb42-0050561776c8
You can use wildcards to access all organization topics.
publish/{user_org_id}/+
Managing Custom Resources in VCF Automation Blueprints
When you create a blueprint in VCF Automation, the resource type palette includes a number of default resource types.
You might have use cases where you want to create blueprints based on an expanded list of resource types. You can
create custom resource types, add them to the design canvas, and create blueprints that support your design and
deployment needs.
Important:
Before you begin, ensure that a VCF Operations orchestrator instance is associated with your organization.
As an organization administrator, you have two ways to create custom resources.
• VCF Operations orchestrator inventory type. You can create custom resources based on existing VCF Operations
orchestrator inventory objects, with or without leveraging the Dynamic Types plug-in for VCF Operations orchestrator.
Dynamic type is required if the desired resource does not exist out-of-the-box in VCF Operations orchestrator as a
SDK inventory object type. You can expose any VCF Operations orchestrator resource type, be it native, provided by a
plug-in in VCF Operations orchestrator, or created using the Dynamic Types plug-in.
• New schema. You can define custom resource types that are based on workflows with any kind of input and output.
Every input and output becomes part of the schema and its value is shown in the deployment. Because this custom
resource type is based on your own custom outputs instead of VCF Operations orchestrator inventory objects, you
must provide a READ workflow in addition to the Create and Delete workflows. You also define what inputs that
workflow has.
For the Read and Delete workflows, you can map the inputs and outputs to schema properties. This is necessary
because the schema property names might not match the input/outputs of the Read and Delete workflows.
Custom resource name and resource type
The custom resource name identifies your custom resource inside the blueprint resource type palette.
The resource type of a custom resource must begin with and each resource type must be unique. Although the
Custom.
inclusion of is not validated in the text box, the string is automatically added if you remove it.
Custom.
To add custom resources to blueprints, you must activate the custom resource. You can make the custom resource
available to blueprints associated with a single project or make it available to all projects.
Lifecycle actions for custom resources
You define the following lifecycle actions for your custom resources:
• Create: this action is called when a deployment is started.
• Read: this action is used to retrieve the latest state of the deployed resource. The READ workflow is run every few
minutes to get the latest status of every provisioned custom resource. You also define what inputs that workflow has,
Broadcom 7210

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
for example, you can just pass the resource ID as an input. The Read action is required only for new schema-based
custom resources.
• Destroy: this action is called when a deployment is deleted.
Note:
You can edit the VCF Operations orchestrator workflow associated with your lifecycle actions by clicking the
Change option for the action.
VCF Operations orchestrator custom resources
Each VCF Operations orchestrator custom resource is based on a SDK inventory type and is created by a VCF
Operations orchestrator workflow that has an output which is an instance of your desired SDK type. Primitive types, such
as , , , and are not supported for the creation of custom resource types.
Properties Date string number
Note:
SDK object types can be differentiated from other VCF Operations orchestrator property types by the colon (":")
used to separate the plug-in name and the type name.
You can use the built-in workflows in VCF Operations orchestrator, or you can create your own. You can create custom
resources by clicking on the Resource Definition option in the custom resource editor and selecting Orchestrator
inventory type.
VCF Operations orchestrator custom resource inventory type
The inventory type property defines the type of your custom resource.
When you define your custom resource types, you can define the scope of the availability of the selected external type.
The selected external type can be:
• Shared across projects.
• Available only for the selected project.
When you select a Create workflow in your custom resource type, the inventory type drop-down appears underneath it.
The drop-down includes inventory type properties, that are selected from the output parameters of the VCF Operations
orchestrator workflow. The selected workflow output properties included in the drop-down must be non-array SDK object
types such as .
VC:VirtualMachine
Note:
When creating custom workflows that use the dynamic type plug-in, verify that their variables are defined by using
the method.
DynamicTypesManager.getObject()
You can only have one custom resource type with a specific inventory type value per defined scope. For example, if
you create a custom resource in your project that uses as an inventory type, you cannot create
VC:VirtualMachine
another custom resource for the same project that uses the same inventory type. You also cannot create two shared
custom resources that use the same inventory type.
VCF Operations orchestrator lifecycle action validation
When you add Create, Destroy, and Read workflows as lifecycle actions to your custom resource, VCF Operations
orchestrator validates that the selected workflows have correct input and output property definitions.
• The workflow must have an output parameter that is an SDK object type, such as or
Create SSH:Host
. If the selected workflow does not pass the validation, you cannot add Read or Destroy workflows, or
SQL:Database

CR types(based on the Inventory), it is possible to create a deployment with CR by executing the create wf used in the
CR as a Catalog item
• The workflow must have an input parameter that is an SDK object type that matches the inventory type of
Destroy

Read

Custom resource property schema
You can edit and view the custom resource properties schema by selecting the Schema Properties tab. The schema
includes the name, data type, property type, and, if it is available, the description of a given property. The schema also
defines if a specific property is required or optional in the blueprint.
When you add VCF Operations orchestrator workflows to your custom resource, their input and output parameters are
added as properties.
From this tab, you can also modify and format the properties of your VCF Operations orchestrator-based custom
resources. For example, you can change the display name of a given property, add constraints, or make it read- or write-
only for the deployment.
Note:
When adding constraints to either the item section of array fields or properties section of objects fields in the
properties schema, verify that you have validated these constraints as incorrectly applied constraints can cause
issues with the custom resource. For example, when adding a maximum constraint to a numbers array, you must
verify that this constraint does not break the property's default value.
You can edit the property schema for custom resources by navigating to the Schema Properties tab and using either the
Code or Form tab.
• Code: Edit the property schema by using YAML content. When selecting this option, the property schema is defined by
using the JSON Schema.
• Form: Hide non-required and non-computed properties from the schema by clicking Remove Property.
Day 2 Operation Custom Request Forms
You can streamline the request form of the day 2 operations included in your custom resource by adding and modifying
different types of resource properties.
For example, you can bind the value of an input parameter in your request form to an external source, such as a VCF
Operations orchestrator action that retrieves a deployment name or project name. You can also bind the value of a
specific input parameter to the computed value of two other text boxes included in the same request form.
Note:
This functionality is available for both custom resources and resource actions. You can customize the value of
the input properties of your request form from the Values tab of the Request Parameters page of the custom
resource or resource action editor.
Day 2 Operation Request Form Validation
You can validate the request form of your day 2 operations by adding an external validation. By using an external
validation, you prevent the user from submitting the request form until the validation parameters are satisfied. You can add
external validation from the Validations tab of the Request Parameters page of the custom resource or resource action
editor. After selecting the tab, you can drag an Orchestrator validation element to the canvas and add a VCF Operations
orchestrator action that you want to use for validation.
For example, you can create a custom resource that includes a day 2 operation for changing a user password. For
such a use case, you can add a VCF Operations orchestrator action with and input
newPassword confirmPassword
parameters that use the type.
SecureString

This is a sample script for validating a user password. For your own use case, you can decide to use a different
script.
if (newPassword != confirmPassword) {
return 'passwords are different';
}
if (newPassword.lenght < 7) {

Managing Policies in VCF Automation
Governance is one of the key aspects of building a cloud-like experience for an organization. Application teams in a VCF
Automation organization can use the self-service catalog and the services console to provision resources depending
on their project needs and permissions. As an organization administrator, you can impose guardrails around those
provisioning requests. You use VCF Automation policies to enforce the governance through approval workflows and policy
templates. Each VCF Automation policy is a set of rules or parameters that are applied to VCF Automation projects to
govern deployment requests from application teams, freeing the organization administrator for other tasks.
Policy Types
You can create two general categories of policies in VCF Automation:
• Policies that apply to catalog requests.
– Approval Policy. An approval policy adds a layer of governance before the requested resources can be deployed.
Approval policies control who must approve resource deployment before the request is provisioned. If an approval
policy is configured, approvers can view the list under the Inbox section for pending requests for their approval. See
Configure Approval Policies in VCF Automation.
– Day 2 Action Policy. Day 2 action policies control what group of users can run the selected actions on deployed
resources. See Configure Day 2 Action Policies in VCF Automation.
– Lease Policy. Lease policies define the maximum amount of time a deployment can exist. When a deployment
expires, it is destroyed and its resources are reclaimed. A lease policy reduces the need for the organization
administrator to intervene manually to reclaim resources, allowing administrators to specify when they want
deployed resources to expire. See Configure Lease Policies in VCF Automation.
• Policies that apply to service requests.
– IaaS Resource Policy. Organization administrators can configure IaaS resource policies to govern requests by
application teams to provision services, like the Virtual Machine Service, and to apply granular control over the type
of provisioned resources and their configurations. IaaS resource policies offer a policy-as-code capability to enforce
custom constraints on IaaS resources, beyond the built-in policy templates. See Configure IaaS Resource Policies
in VCF Automation.
• Provider-managed policies.
– Infrastructure Policy. The provider administrator assigns infrastructure policies to your organization to define zone
placement criteria for workloads, such as namespaces and VMs. Some infrastructure policies might be mandatory
for your organization, which means they are always enforced when a new namespace is created. If the requested
infrastructure resources in the selected zones are not compatible with the policies, the namespace creation fails. If
a policy is not mandatory, when creating a namespace, you can choose whether you want to apply that policy to the
namespace.
Policy Scope and Criteria
VCF Automation policies can be scoped to the entire organization or a selection of projects in the organization.
Organization administrators can further refine the policy scope by defining policy criteria. For example, to apply a policy to
all the deployments except the deployments named pipeline test, add criteria and construct an expression similar to
name
. Policy criteria can be based on project name, namespace name, namespace class,
not equal to pipeline test
and so on. For details on constructing policy criteria, see Configure Deployment Criteria in Policies in VCF Automation.
Organization administrators can configure multiple policies for resources, projects, or namespaces. First, policies are
evaluated, ranked, and, where applicable, merged to produce an effective policy.
On the Policies page, organization administrators can create and delete policies, and view a list of defined policies, policy
assignments, and policy enforcements.
• Policy Definition. A list of all the policies defined for your organization. You can view policy details or delete a policy
which is no longer required. To create a policy, click New Policy and select one of the policy types.
Broadcom 7213

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Policy Assignments. On the Policy Assignment tab, you can view policies that are effectively applied to resources,
namespaces, and projects, based on the defined policy criteria.
• Policy Enforcement. Use the Policy Enforcement tab to audit when policies are applied. It lists the enforcement date,
policy name, and policy status.
• Infrastructure Policies. You can view the infrastructure policies that your provider administrator assigned to your
organization.
To get you started, use the full use cases that are provided for each policy type. The use cases guide you through the
process of creating more than one policy. The use case provides contextual explanations of the choices and the desired
behavior.
The use cases are followed by more in-depth information about how multiple policies are processed.
Configure Approval Policies in VCF Automation
Approval policies are a level of governance that you add to exercise control over deployment and day 2 action requests
before they are run. You define approval policies so that you, or others that you designate, review requests before
resources are consumed or destroyed. The approval policy use cases in this procedure are an introduction that you can
use as you explore your governance options.
If you have only a small team adding and deploying catalog items, then approval policies might be less useful. As you
make the catalog available to a larger group of developers and general consumers, you can use the approval policies
to ensure that someone reviews a request before the resources are consumed or changes are made to the provisioned
items.
For example, you have a catalog item that is important, but it consumes a significant amount of resources. You want
one of your IT administrators to review any deployment requests to ensure that the request is needed. Another example
applies to day 2 actions. Making changes to a deployment that is used by many might be devastating. You want the
project administrator who manages the deployment for that team to review all changes to the deployed catalog instance.
Who works with or is affected by approval policies
• Organization administrator. Configures the policies.
• Catalog consumers. Users who request catalog items or day 2 actions to which one or more policies apply.
• Users deploying blueprints in VCF Automation. Users who request blueprints or day 2 actions to which one or more
policies apply.
• Designated approvers. Users who must review and then approve or reject a request. You can grant approver rights to
selected users and user groups, or you can choose from the following approver roles.
– Project Administrators. Administrators of projects within the policy scope are automatically assigned as approvers. If
a project does not have a dedicated administrator, the approval policy is not applied to that project.
– Project Auditor. Members of projects within the policy scope who are assigned the Auditor role. Auditor access
rights are limited to approving and rejecting deployment requests for a project. If a project does not have a
dedicated auditor, the approval policy is not applied to that project.
What happens when approval policies are enforced
Multiple approval policies might be enforceable. The approval policies are evaluated, and an enforced policy is applied to
the request. When there are multiple valid policies, where the approvers are different people, all the approvers are added.
When you have multiple policies, it is important to understand this process. For more information, see Approval policy
goals and enforcement examples.
1. Approval policies are defined.
2. A user requests a catalog item or day 2 action. At request time, VCF Automation evaluates the catalog item to see if
any policies apply.
3. An approval policy is enforced.
a. The deploy card displays the status. For example, Create - Approval Pending.
b. An email notification is sent to the requester.
c. An email notification is sent to the approvers.
Broadcom 7214

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The deployment does not begin deploying and consuming infrastructure resources, or make changes to a
deployed system, until the request is approved. The requesting user is notified by email that the request is waiting
for approval.
d. The approvers respond to the request using the Approvals page.
4. The approval process is completed.
a. If the request is rejected, the requesting user is notified and the deployment request is canceled.
b. If the request is approved, the deployment proceeds.
c. It is possible that the enforced policy is configured to automatically approve or reject a request if the approver does
not take any action.
How can I use the deployment criteria
To limit what items or activities the policy applies to, you can define the deployment criteria. For more about the criteria,
see Configure deployment criteria in policies in for All Apps.
Prerequisites
• An approver who must have the Organization Administrator or Project Administrator role.
• Verify that the email notification server is defined. See Add an email server in for All Apps to send notifications.
Procedure
As you review the approval policies use case and create your own policy, consult the signpost help on the key text boxes
for more information.

Configure Day 2 Action Policies in VCF Automation
You define day 2 action policies so that you can control what changes your users can make to deployments and their
component resources. By creating a list of permitted actions that all or some users can run on deployments, you ensure
that the users cannot initiate any destructive or costly changes. The use cases related to day 2 actions policies are an
introduction to the procedure.
When you entitle users to run day 2 actions, you select the individual actions that they can run. You are creating an
inclusion list, not an exclusion list.
When does a day 2 actions policy go into effect
• If you do not have any Day 2 Action policies defined, then no governance is applied and all users have access to all
the actions. This initial lack of governance as you are starting out ensures that you and your users can exercise the
day two actions in VCF Automation without the need to understand day 2 policies.
• After you determine that you are ready to control who has access to what actions, you add governance in the form of a
single Day 2 Action policy. When the first policy goes into effect, the Day 2 Action policies are enforced for all users in
VCF Automation. As a result, only the users for whom the first policy is true can run the selected actions. All others are
excluded. They are excluded because the actions policies include the trusted users. By excluding all others, you are
able to craft the policies to match your governance goals.
• To entitle other users, you must create policies that entitle them to run the actions you select.
When are day 2 actions policies applied
To focus when the Day 2 Actions policies are applied, you can configure scope, role, and criteria. These configurations
control what deployments the policy is applied to and who can run the actions when the policy is enforced.
• What deployments the policy is applied to.
– Scope determines whether the policy is applied to deployments at the organization or project level.
– Criteria narrow the scope of the policy to particular aspects of deployments.
• Who can run what actions on those deployments.
– Role entitles the members of the selected role, within the selected scope and criteria, to run the selected actions.
The role can be project administrator, project advanced user, project user, or a named custom role.
Broadcom 7217

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Day 2 policies are enforced when a user tries to manage a deployment using the Actions menu on the deployment or on
the component resources.
Selecting day 2 actions
As you review the day 2 actions policies use case, you must also select the actions. You must select the actions that
support your deployments.
Prerequisites
• For a list of possible actions, see What actions can I run on deployments or IaaS resources in for All Apps.
• For more information about constructing deployment criteria, see Configure deployment criteria in policies in for All
Apps.
Procedure
1. Select Manage and Govern > Policies > Definitions > New Policy > Day 2 Actions Policy.
2. Configure Day 2 Policy 1.
As an administrator, you want to control storage costs by restricting the ability of users to request snapshots.
a. Define when the policy is valid.
Setting Sample Value
Scope Organization
This policy applied to all deployments in your organization.
Criteria None
Enforcement type Soft
This enforcement type allows you to create other policies related
to the snapshot actions that override this policy.
Soft policies are overridden by hard policies.

b. Select the actions that the users can run, but do not select any snapshot actions.
You explicitly entitle users to run actions. To exclude users from running snapshot actions, ensure that the actions
are not selected.
In this scenario, none of the project members in your organization are entitled to create snapshots. Nor can your
project administrators. Your next step is to create a policy that entitles the project administrators to create and manage
snapshots.

In this scenario, the project administrators are entitled to run the snapshot-related actions and all the actions that their

• For more examples of how the policies are processed and enforced, see How are policies processed in for All Apps.
• Configure policies that are relevant to your organizations and projects.

Configure Lease Policies in VCF Automation
By using policy-based leases, you reduce the need to intervene manually to reclaim resources. You define lease policies
so that you can control the amount of time that a deployment is available to your users. The lease policy use cases in this
procedure provide a beginning point for learning about and implementing policies for your organization.
If you do not have any lease policies defined, then the deployments never expire. To reclaim the resources, you must
manually destroy the deployments.
When does a lease policy go into effect
• If the policy scope is Organization, then all the deployments in your organization are managed based on the defined
policies.
• If the policy scope is a project, then the deployments that are associated with that project are managed based on the
defined lease. Other projects are not affected.
When are lease policies applied
Lease policies are applied when you:
• Create or update a lease policy. After lease policies are applied, they continuously evaluate the deployments in the
background to ensure that they are in compliance with the defined leases.
Broadcom 7221

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Request a catalog item. The maximum lease and maximum total lease values go into effect when the deployment is
created.
Lease-specific options
As you review the lease policies use case, you must also configure lease-specific options. The following descriptions
provide a brief summary. Consult the signpost help for more information.
• Maximum Lease (days). The number of days that the deployment resources are active without being renewed. If they
are not renewed, the lease expires and the deployment is destroyed. If a grace period is specified, the user can renew
the lease for up to the same number of days that the lease has been active.
• Maximum Total Lease (days). The combined total number of days that the deployment can be active, including lease
renewals. Each renewal cannot exceed the maximum lease, and the cumulative renewal value cannot exceed the
maximum total lease. After the total lease is reached, the deployment is destroyed and the resources within that
deployment are reclaimed.
• Grace period (days). The number of days the user has to renew an expired lease before the deployment is destroyed.
The grace period is not included in the total lease days. If you don't define a grace period, it defaults to 1 day.
What happens when I update an existing lease policy
You can increase the maximum lease, the maximum total lease, and the grace period of your lease policies. The updated
policy is applied to new deployments only.
Note that increasing the policy parameters does not extend the expiry date of existing deployments. Existing deployments
expire on the same date as originally scheduled.
If you decrease the lease values, however, the deployment expiry date is affected and existing deployments expire earlier
than originally scheduled.
What happens when a deployment expires
When a deployment is about to expire, the deploying user receives an email notification. If the user doesn't extend the
lease, the deployment expires and is scheduled for deletion. The deployment owner can see the scheduled deletion date
in the deployment details. If the deletion date is set to Soon, then the deployment is already queued for deletion.
Expired virtual machines are powered off within several minutes after expiry. Unless the lease is extended, a powered-
off machine can't be powered back on in VCF Automation. The machine can be powered back on manually in the original
environment, in which case VCF Automation registers the machine as powered on. Even though the deployment is
already expired, the machine is not automatically powered off for a second time until the grace period of the lease policy is
elapsed and the deployment is deleted.
Procedure
In this use case, there are three policy definitions that illustrate how you can construct policies and the results when they
are enforced. The last policy is not enforced, but the reasons are provided in the scenario results.
1. Select Manage & Govern > Policies > Definitions > New Policy > Lease Policy.
2. Configure Lease Policy 1.
As an administrator, you want to control costs by limiting the starting lease time for all deployments to 30 days, with the
option to renew the lease for a total of 90 days.
a. Define when the policy is valid.
Setting Sample Value
Scope Organization
This policy is applied to everyone in your organization.
Criteria None
Enforcement type Soft
This enforcement type allows you to create other policies related
to this lease that override this policy.
Broadcom 7222

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
b. Define the lease.
Setting Sample Value
Maximum lease (days) 30
Maximum total lease (days) 90
Grace period (days) 10
In this scenario, the deployment is shut down after 30 days and an email is sent to the user. During the grace period,
the user extends the lease by 30 days. After the lease expires again, the user renews it for another 30 days. At the
end of the third extension, the lease reaches the maximum total lease period of 90 active days and the user cannot
extend it anymore. The deployment is shut down and destroyed 10 days later.
3. Configure Lease Policy 2.
As an administrator, you want to control costs by limiting the lease time on an expensive blueprint to two weeks. For
this example, the blueprint name is .
Multi-tier 5 machine with LB
a. Define when the policy is valid.
Setting Sample Value
Scope Project MT5
This policy applied to deployments associated with this project.
Criteria
Blueprint equals Multi-tier 5 machine with LB
Based on this criteria expression, only deployments for the
referenced blueprint are considered for policy enforcement.
Enforcement type Soft
This soft enforcement still overrides the organization policy of 90
days in Policy 1 because the values are more meaningful at the
project level.
b. Define the lease policy.
Setting Sample Value
Maximum lease (days) 14
Maximum total lease (days) 28
Grace period (days) 3
In this scenario, both policies are applied, but Policy 2 takes precedence over Policy 1 because it is more specific.
When applied, the deployment is shut down after 14 days. If the user does not extend the lease, it is destroyed three
days later. If the user extends the lease for up to another 14 days, the deployment is shut down at the end of the
second extension and it is destroyed three days later.
4. Review the configuration of Lease Policy 3.
As a project manager, you realize that one of your developers is working on a complex application. The developer
requires the blueprint and another blueprint,
Multi-tier 5 Machines with LB Distributed Database
, but for a longer lease than defined in Policy 2.
Across Clouds
Unless you understand how the policies are processed based on how they are defined, you might encounter
unexpected results. Policy 3 is an example of how processing and precedence affect the result.
This policy, as provided, will not be enforced. This example provides an opportunity for you to see how leases are
applied and enforced when there is more than one that applies.
Broadcom 7223

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
a. Define when the policy is valid.
Setting Sample Value

This policy is applied to deployments in this project.
Criteria
(Blueprint equals Multi-tier five machine with LB
OR
Catalog Item equals Distributed Database Across
Clouds)
AND

You use Catalog Item because the item is not a blueprint.
Enforcement type Soft
This soft enforcement still overrides the organization policy of 90
days in policy 1 because the values are more meaningful at the
project level.
b. Define the lease policy.
Setting Sample Value
Maximum lease (days) 21
Maximum total lease (days) 50
Grace period (days) 3
In this scenario, Lease Policy 2 is applied, not Lease Policy 3.
• Lease 3 has a lease time that is less than or equal to 21 days, and the policy is applied. Lease 2 has a lease
time that is less than or equal to 14 days, and the policy is applied.
• Lease 2 is applicable and it does not violate the lease 3 policy. But, lease 2 is more restrictive, so it takes
precedence. Lease policy 2 is more restrictive because it is for a shorter period of time.
• When both lease definitions are true and applicable, the more restrictive policy is the one that is enforced.
5. To resolve the unexpected behavior in Lease Policy 3, you can implement one of the following solutions.
– To ensure that you can provide Jan with the needed policy, change the enforcement type to hard.
– Alternatively, you could create a new project with access to the same resources, and then create Lease Policy 3 for
that project. While this solution isolates the working policy, you must maintain a parallel project. The effort needed
to set up and maintain the content sources, content sharing, and so on, are time consuming and subject to error.
What to do next
• For more examples of how the lease policies are processed and enforced, see How are policies processed in for All
Apps.
• Configure policies that are relevant to your organizations and projects. If you are just getting started with lease policies,
begin with one lease policy at the organization level.
• To send an email to the deploying user, configure the email server for notifications. See Add an email server in for All
Apps to send notifications.
• If your organization is integrated with VCF Operations orchestrator, you can manage expired deployments and their
resources by using event subscriptions. See Create an Event Subscription to Manage Deployment Expiry in for All

Configure IaaS Resource Policies in VCF Automation
You define IaaS resource policies to validate and control what namespace resources deployments can consume when
users request catalog items or create resources using the services console in VCF Automation. The use cases in this
procedure are an introduction to configuring IaaS resource policies.
Broadcom 7224

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Before your users can generate workloads on namespaces, you must establish policies to ensure the conformity and
security of the workloads. An IaaS resource policy outlines a set of guidelines applicable to the objects on the namespace.
These objects can include built-in items like VMs, Kubernetes clusters, PodVMs, or new objects introduced through the
installation of additional services. As an organization administrator, you can configure and enforce these rules across
various namespaces.
When you create an IaaS resource policy, it is applied to both newly created and existing namespaces within a project or
the organization, based on namespace specifications.
What can I control with IaaS resource policies
As an organization administrator using IaaS resource policies, you control whether a user can create the following:
1. Resources for all services running in a namespace.
2. Resources for a sub-set of services, such as the VM Service only or the Kubernetes Service only. For example, you
can allow only specific VMs with a certain VM class.
3. Control the number of worker or control nodes for Kubernetes clusters. For example, you might want to enforce a limit
of three control nodes for a production cluster.
4. Enforce a minimum Kubernetes version for Kubernetes clusters.
What happens when IaaS resource policies are enforced
• When the policy is enforced, users can provision resources within the specified constraints.
• Multiple IaaS resource policies can be enforceable. VCF Automation does not merge overlapping IaaS policies. Both
policies are applied. As the organization administrator, you are responsible for defining policies that do not conflict with
each other. For example, if one policy states that all VM names must start with vm-1 and another policy states that all
VM names must start with vm-2, then both of these policies are applied. Because a VM name cannot start with both
vm-1 and vm-2, no VM is provisioned in the namespace.
• IaaS policies are not enforced on deployments that request no resources, such as a VCF Operations orchestrator
workflow deployment.
When are IaaS resource policies applied
• A user requests a catalog item.
• A user provisions resources using the IaaS services console.
How many IaaS policies can I create
• You can create up to 10 IaaS resource policies for your organization unless your provider administrator set a different
limit for your organization. Policies can be scoped to an entire organization or to a specific project. The limit of policies
per project is half of the organization limit.
• Up to 50 IaaS resource policies can be created per supervisor across all organizations that might share the supervisor.
When a new policy is created or when a new namespace is created that matches the criteria of an existing policy, a
per-supervisor limit is enforced.
See VMware Configuration Maximums for information about the maximum number of IaaS resource policies that can be
created per supervisor.
What IaaS policy templates are available
The following IaaS policy templates are available out of the box. In addition, you can define your own policies.
Broadcom 7225

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
IaaS policies are backed by Kubernetes validating admission policies. Modifying the policy templates requires use of
the Common Expression Language (CEL), which is used in the Kubernetes API. For more information about validating
admission policies, see the official Kubernetes documentation.
Policy template Description
Select Enforce single-control-node Kubernetes cluster Ensures a Kubernetes cluster has only 1 control node.
(development)
Enforce multi-control-node Kubernetes cluster (production) Ensures a Kubernetes cluster has a minimum of 3 control nodes.
Enforce minimum Kubernetes version for Kubernetes cluster Enforces a minimum version specified in a template.
Disallow Kubernetes cluster resource Does not allow provisioning of Kubernetes cluster resources.
Disallow VM resource Does not allow provisioning of VM resources.
Label enforcement Requires a specific label for a resource.
Kubernetes cluster restricted pod security level Requires cluster to have restricted pod security level
Kubernetes cluster baseline pod security level Requires Kubernetes cluster to have baseline pod security level
Using the Assignments tab
After you create an IaaS policy, you can use the Assignments tab to get an overview of all IaaS policies affecting a given
namespace, to track which policies were applied successfully, and to review any errors.

Order of operations for the expression
An expression is processed in the following order. Groups are illustrated as parentheses.
1. Expressions in groups
2. AND

Use the following examples to understand the order.
• X OR Y AND Z. In this example, Y AND Z is evaluated before X OR Y. Next, the X OR is evaluated against the results
of Y AND Z.
• (X OR Y) AND Z. In this example, X OR Y is evaluated before AND because the expression in the group is always
evaluated first. Next the AND Z is evaluated against the results of X OR Y.

How are Policies Processed in VCF Automation
Policies are processed based on the policy definition. In particular, the scope and the enforcement level determine which
policy is valid when you have multiple policies that might apply to a single deployment.
This article provides general information about policy processing, but it also includes more details for the different types of
policies.
How policies are ranked based on organization level and enforcement type
When a user, who is a member of a project, creates a deployment, there might be more than one policy that applies to
that deployment.
To evaluate the policies, the system first identifies and ranks
policies.
1. Are there any hard policies at either the organization and
project level. If there are hard and soft policies, then only the
hard policies are considered and ranked. If there are only soft
policies, then the soft policies are ranked.
2. The ranking of all hard or all soft policies is ordered by scope,
with organizational policies having a higher rank than project
policies.
3. The final discriminating characteristic is the creation date, with
older dates be ranked higher than newer dates.
How policies are processed based on organization level and enforcement type
The policies are evaluated, ranked, and, where applicable, merged to produce an effective policy. An effective policy
produces the intended results but is not always a specific named policy.
This section includes the following examples:
• Lease policies
• Day 2 actions policies
Broadcom 7231

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Review the following lease policy examples.
After identifying the policies to be considered and ranking them,
the policies are then evaluated to identify the merge order.
• The highest ranking policy becomes the baseline. The second-
level policy is applied on top of it, and so on.
• If a policy is incompatible with the preceding policies, then it
is discarded from consideration. For example, the values are
higher they the preceding policies.
• Any policy that is discarded is ignored. To see which policy is
applied, select Content and Policies > Policies > Enforceme
nt, locate the deployment, and review the decision notes.
Rather than applying one policy and excluding all the others
above, the policies are merged and might include values from
more than one individual policy.
In this example, the merging process excludes Policy 2 from
consideration because the values are higher than Policy 1.
Next, Policy 3 is evaluated against Policy 1. The Lease and Total
Lease values in Policy 3 are lower than Policy 1, so those values,
in addition to the Grace period, become part of the effective policy.
Review the following day 2 actions policy examples.
After identifying the policies to be considered and ranking them,
the policies are then evaluated to identify the merge order.
• The highest ranking policy becomes the baseline. The second-
level policy is applied on top of it, and so on.
• If a policy is enforced by preceding policies, for example,
policy 3, then it is discarded from consideration.
• Any policy that is discarded is ignored. To see which policy is
applied, select Manage & Govern > Policies > Enforcement,
locate the deployment, and review the decision notes.
Lease policy management goal considerations
Now that you know how lease policies are processed, identify your policy management goals. By understanding how the
policies are processed, you can meet your management goals without creating an excessive and unmanageable number

Approval policy goals and enforcement examples
The approval policy evaluation follows this process.
1. A request for a deployment or day 2 action is submitted.
2. The approval service queries for policies that apply to the project that is requesting a catalog item or changing a
deployed item.
3. All the applicable project- and organization-level scope policies are returned.
4. The approval policies are filtered based on the deployment criteria. Deployment criteria apply to deployments and day
2 actions.
5. If no matching policies are found, no approval is required and the deployment process proceeds.
6. If there are matching policies, for example, AP1, AP2, APn, then an approval item is created as:
– Enforced policies = AP1, AP2, APn.
– Approvers = A union of all the approvers in all the enforced policies.
– Auto expiry = Reject, if any policy has a reject value; otherwise, approve.
– Expiry = Minimum number of days of any of the enforced policies.
The following table provides a sample of multiple policies. The description of how they are processed is below the table.
Policy Configuration example
AP1 Scope = Organization
Auto expiry = Approve
Expiry = 7 days
AP2 Scope = Project 1
Auto expiry - Approve
Expiry = 3 days
AP3 Scope = Project 1
Auto expiry = Reject
Expiry = 4 days
AP4 Scope = Project 2
Auto expiry = Approve
Expiry = 5 days
Based on the policies and configuration examples above, the following information explains how a Project 1 request is
processed.
1. The scope evaluation returns AP1, AP2, and AP3. AP4 is not included because it is a Project 2 policy.
2. Assuming that AP1, AP2, and AP3 satisfy the deployment and action criteria, then the approval item includes the
following values:
– Approvers = Any or all the approvers from AP1, AP2, and AP3 are added as approvers.
– Auto expiry = Reject. AP3 provides the more restrictive behavior.
– Expiry = 3 days. AP2 provides the lowest value.
Broadcom 7234

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Provisioning Resources in VCF Automation
In VCF Automation, resources like VMs and VKS clusters are provisioned in namespaces either through blueprints or
through the IaaS Services console.
Provisioning Resources Using Blueprints
When using blueprints, namespaces and the desired resources are dragged and dropped on to the blueprint canvas. The
resulting blueprint is then published to the catalog where end users can request it for deployment.
Blueprints are recommended when the organization administrator needs better control over the exact resource that are
provisioned by end-users. Blueprints are also used when the process of provisioning resources needs to be repeatable.
Provisioning Resources Using the IaaS Services Console
When using the IaaS Services console, the desired namespace is selected from the Build & Deploy page. End users can
create the desired resources directly on the selected namespace.
The self-service IaaS Services console enables end users to provision resources without depending on blueprints. The
IaaS Services console is suitable for development needs when agility and flexibility of provisioning resources are more
important than repeatability.
Requesting an Item from the Catalog in VCF Automation
Catalog items are blueprints, VM images, and other infrastructure objects that project users can request for deployment.
At request time, the information that the requesting user must provide or configure depends on how the blueprint was
designed. When an item is deployed, it is provisioned based on the namespaces that are associated with the selected
project.
Who Works with the Catalog
As the organization administrator, you provide the catalog items. The items that are available to users depend on their
project membership.
• If a user is a member of one project, they can see only the catalog items for that project.
• If a user is a member of several projects, they can see the catalog items for those projects.
• If a project does not have any configured catalog items, the Catalog section does not appear for members of that
project.
Projects also determine user options at deployment time.
For more information on working with the catalog, see Request an Item from the Catalog in VCF Automation for All Apps
in the Consumer Interfaces in VMware Cloud Foundation guide.
Managing Deployed Instances in VCF Automation
Catalog consumers use the Instances page in VCF Automation to view and manage all of their provisioned resources
across their projects. Resources include deployed catalog items, virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, and other custom
resources.
For more information on working with instances, see Managing Deployed Instances in VCF Automation for All Apps in the
Consumer Interfaces in VMware Cloud Foundation guide.
Using the Self-Service IaaS Console in VCF Automation
VCF Automation provides application teams with access to modern services enabled by vSphere Supervisor and cloud
native applications. Users can consume necessary infrastructure by provisioning resources including VMs, Kubernetes,
volumes, load balancers and networking objects, storage, and others, in a public cloud-like fashion, without depending on
the organization administrator to create and distribute blueprints through the catalog.
Broadcom 7235

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Who Works with the IaaS Services Console
The IaaS Services console in the VCF Automation organization UI is available to users with the Project
Administrator or Project Advanced User role.
What IaaS Services Are Supported
Supported services include VM Service, VM Image Service, Kubernetes Service, Network Service, Volume Service,
Private AI Service, Avi Load Balancer, and extensible VCF services like Secrets, Key Management, and Data Service.
IaaS Services are scoped to a namespace. Users can use the namespace selector to switch between namespaces to
which they have access. What namespaces are available to users depends on their project membership.
For more information about using the self-service IaaS Console, see the following topics in the Building Your Applications
guide:
• Provision a VM Using the Self-Service in VCF Automation
• Provision a Kubernetes Cluster Using Self-Service in VCF Automation
Administering VCF Automation Organizations
As an administrator, you use the Administer tab in the organization UI to monitor and manage critical infrastructure and
user management aspects of a VCF Automation organization.
Integrating VCF Automation with Other Applications
Integrations enable you to add external systems to VCF Automation. Integrations include Git, Active Directory, and VCF
Operations orchestrator.
Integrate VCF Automation with Git
VCF Automation supports integration with various flavors of Git repositories so that you can manage blueprints and action
scripts under source control. This functionality facilitates auditing and accountability of processes around deployment.
VCF Automation supports different flavors of Git integration as described in the following list. Each of these options is a
separate integration.
• GitHub cloud
• GitLab cloud
• GitLab Enterprise
• GitHub cloud, GitHub Enterprise on-premises
• GitLab cloud GitLab Enterprise on-premises
• BitBucket on-premises
You must have an appropriate local Git repository configured with access for all designated users in order to set up
Git integration with VCF Automation. Also, you must save your blueprints in a specific structure in order for them to be
detected by Git. To create an integration with GitLab or GitHub, select Administer > Connections > Integrations and
then make the appropriate selection. You will need the URL and token for the target repository.
When Git integration is configured with an existing repository, all blueprints associated with selected projects become
available to qualified users. You can use these blueprints with an existing deployment or as the basis of a new
deployment. When you add a project, you must select some properties regarding where and how it is stored in Git.
You can save actions to a Git repository directly from VCF Automation. You can version action scripts either directly
to Git or you can create versions in VCF Automation. If you create a version of an action in VCF Automation, then it is
automatically saved to Git as a version. Blueprints are a bit more complicated, because you cannot directly add them to a
Git integration from VCF Automation. You must save them directly to a Git instance, and then you can retrieve them from
Git when working with the blueprint management page in VCF Automation.
Broadcom 7236

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Before you begin
You must create and save your blueprints in a specific structure in order for them to be detected by GitLab or GitHub.
• Configure and store blueprints to be integrated with GitLab correctly. Only valid blueprints are imported into GitLab.
• Create one or more designated folders for the blueprints.
• All blueprints must be stored within files.
blueprint.yaml
• Ensure that the top of your blueprints include the name: and version:properties.
• Extract an API key for the applicable repository. In your Git account, select your login in the upper right corner, and
click Developer Settings. Navigate to Personal Access Tokens, and then name your token and set an expiration
date. Then, select API and create the token. Copy the resulting value and save it.
The following guidelines must be observed for all blueprints used with Git integration.
• Each blueprint must reside in a separate folder.
• All blueprints must be named .
blueprint.yaml
• All blueprint YAML files must use name and version fields.
• Only valid blueprints are imported.
• If you update a draft blueprint imported from Git, and its content differs from that in the top version, the draft will not
be updated in subsequent syncs and a new version is created. If you want to update a blueprint and also allow further
sync's from Git, then you must create a new version after final changes.
Configure a GitLab Blueprint Integration in VCF Automation
This procedure demonstrates configuring GitLab integration in VCF Automation so that you can work with blueprints in the
repository and automatically download saved blueprints that are associated with designated projects. To use blueprints
with GitLab, you must create a connection to an appropriate GitLab instance, and then save the desired blueprints to that
instance.
• Extract an API key for the applicable repository. In your GitLab account, select your login in the upper right corner, and
navigate to the Settings menu. Select Access Tokens, then name your token, set an expiration date. Then, select API
and create the token. Copy the resulting value and save it.
You must have an appropriate local Git repository configured with access for all designated users in order to set up Git
integration with VCF Automation. Also, you must create and save your blueprints in a specific structure in order for them
to be detected by GitLab.
• Configure and store blueprints to be integrated with GitLab correctly. Only valid blueprints are imported into GitLab.
When GitLab integration is configured with an existing repository, all blueprints associated with selected projects
become available to qualified users. You can use these blueprints with an existing deployment or as the basis of a new
deployment. When you add a project, you must select some properties regarding where and how it is stored in GitLab.
Note:
You cannot push new or updated blueprints to the Git repository from VCF Automation. To add blueprints to a
repository, developers must use the Git interface.
If you update a draft blueprint imported from Git, and its content differs from that in the Git version, the draft will not be
updated in subsequent syncs and a new version is created. If you want to update a blueprint and also allow further sync's
from Git, then you must create a new version in Git after final changes.
After you set up your blueprints for use with GitLab and collect required information, you must set up integration with your
GitLab instance. Then, you can import the designated blueprints into GitLab.
Broadcom 7237

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Set up integration with your GitLab environment in VCF Automation.
a) Select Administer > Integrations.
b) Select GitLab.
c) Enter an appropriate name and description.
d) Enter the URL for your GitLab instance.
e) Enter the Token, also known as an API key, for the specified GitLab instance. See the prerequisites above for
information about extracting the token from your GitLab instance.
f) Click Validate to verify the connection.
g) Click Add.
2. Configure the GitLab connection to accept blueprints in an appropriate repository.
a) Select Administer > Integrations and choose the appropriate GitLab integration.
b) Select Projects.
c) Select New Project and create a name for the project.
d) Enter the Repository path within GitLab. Typically, this is the user name of the main account appended to the
repository name.
e) Enter the appropriate GitLab Branch that you want to use.
f) If applicable, enter a Folder name. If left blank, all folders are available.
g) Click Next to finish adding the repository.
When you click Next, an automated synchronization task is initiated that imports blueprints into the platform.
When the synchronization tasks are complete, a message indicates that the blueprints have been imported.
You can now retrieve blueprints from GitLab.
Configure a GitHub Integration in VCF Automation
You can integrate the GitHub cloud-based repository hosting service in VCF Automation.
• You must have access to GitHub.
• Configure and store blueprints to be integrated with GitHub correctly. Only valid blueprints are imported into GitHub.
You need a valid GitHub token to configure GitHub integration in VCF Automation.
See the GitHub documentation for information about creating and locating your token.
1. Select Administer > Integrations and click Add Integration.
2. Select GitHub.
3. Enter the required information on the GitHub configuration page.
4. Click Validate to verify the connection.
5. Click Add.
6. Configure the GitHub connection to accept blueprints in an appropriate repository.
a) Select Administer > Integrations and choose the appropriate GitHub integration.
b) Select Projects.
c) Select New Project and create a name for the project.
d) Enter the Repository path within GitHub. Typically, this is the user name of the main account appended to the
repository name.
e) Enter the appropriate GitHub Branch that you want to use.If applicable, enter a Folder name. If left blank, all
folders are available.
f) Click to finish adding the repository.
Next
An automated synchronization task is initiated that imports blueprints into the platform.
When the synchronization tasks are complete, a message indicates that the blueprints have been imported.
GitHub is available for use in VCF Automation blueprints. You can now retrieve blueprints from GitHub.

Configure a Bitbucket Integration in VCF Automation
VCF Automation supports integration with Bitbucket for use as a Git-based repository for blueprints.
• Set up an on premises Bitbucket Server deployment with one or more blueprint-based projects that you want to use
with your deployments. Bitbucket Cloud is not supported.
• Create or designate a VCF Automation project to associate your Bitbucket integration.
• Blueprint files to be synched to a Bitbucket integration must be named .
blueprint.yaml
In VCF Automation, you can work with blueprints (also called templates) using the Bitbucket integration. You must
synchronize projects that you want to work with before using a Bitbucket integration. You cannot write back blueprints
from the integration. If you want to create new versions of blueprint files, you must do so manually.
1. Select Administer > Integrations and click Add Integration.
2. Select Bitbucket.
3. Enter the server URL and Bitbucket credentials.
4. Click Validate to verify the connection.
5. Click Add.
6. Open the Bitbucket integration and select the Projects tab on the main page to associate a project with this Bitbucket
integration.
7. Select the project to associate with this Bitbucket integration.
8. Click Next to add a Repository to Bitbucket project and indicate the type of repository you are adding and then specify
the Repository name and Branch, as well as the Folder.
9. Click Add.
If you want to add one or more repositories to a project, click Add Repository.
The Bitbucket integration is configured with the specified repository configuration, and you can view and work with
blueprints contained in configured repositories. When you add a project to a Bitbucket integration, a synch operation runs
to pull the latest versions of blueprint files from the designated repository. The History tab on the Bitbucket integration
page shows records of all synch operations for the integration. By default, files are automatically synched every 15
minutes, but you can manually synch a file by selecting it and clicking SYNC at any time.
You can work with blueprints on the Blueprint Design page.
Integrate VCF Automation with VCF Operations orchestrator
As a provider administrator, you integrate a VCF Automation organization with VCF Operations orchestrator so that the
organization administrator and project users can use VCF Operations orchestrator workflows in VCF Automation.
Important:
Organization administrators cannot create an integration with VCF Operations orchestrator in the organization
that they manage. Organization administrators must request that the provider administrator creates the VCF
Operations orchestrator integration for the organization.
VCF Operations orchestrator embedded in Provider Consumption organizations in VCF Automation
A VCF Operations orchestrator instance is embedded and configured by default as part of the Provider Consumption
organization in VCF Automation. Only one VCF Operations orchestrator can be embedded in a Provider Consumption
organization. That instance can also be added as an integration in VCF Automation for VM Apps organizations. The
embedded instance is not supported in All Apps organizations.
An external VCF Operations orchestrator instance can be used as a replacement of the embedded VCF Operations
orchestrator instance in the Provider Consumption organization in scenarios where the resource load on VCF Automation
is very high.
Broadcom 7239

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You access the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance on the Orchestrate tab in the Provider Consumption
organization UI.
The service provider can publish workflows from the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance as catalog items to
VCF Automation for All Apps organizations.
Note:
Embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instances in VCF Automation are primarily used in the provider
consumption organization. It is recommended that you integrate your All Apps organizations with an external VCF
Operations orchestrator instances.

When you configure an authentication provider for VCF Operations orchestrator, that VCF Operations orchestrator
instance is restricted to the respective All Apps organization.

root

ALL_APPS_ORG_NAME
tenant
3. Redeploy the VCF Operations orchestrator pods.
/opt/scripts/deploy.sh
The VCF Operations orchestrator instance is configured and associated with the All Apps organization.
Create a VCF Operations orchestrator Integration in VCF Automation
You integrate VCF Operations orchestrator into your All Apps organization to use it for extensibility automation tasks.
Important:
Only one external VCF Operations orchestrator instance can be integrated with the organization. Provider
Consumption organizations have an embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance by default.
1. To log in to the VCF Automation organization with credentials, click Launch Organization
System Administrator
on the organization details page in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. Once you are logged in to the organization UI, select Administer > Connections > Integrations.
3. Select Orchestrator.
4. Enter a name and description for the VCF Operations orchestrator integration.
5. Under VCF Operations Orchestrator URL, enter the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of your external VCF
Operations orchestrator instance.
For example, .
https://my_Orchestrator_FQDN.com:443
Note:
If you have a clustered VCF Operations orchestrator environment, enter the URL of the load balancer.

Enable VCF Operations orchestrator for the VCF Automation Organization
To enable extensibility through VCF Operations orchestrator for the All Apps organization, you must publish the
Orchestrator rights bundle to that organization.
1. Log in to VCF Automation Provider Management with System Administrator credentials.
Broadcom 7240

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
2. Select Administer > Access Control > Rights Bundles.
3. Select the Orchestrator Right Bundle.
4. On the Orchestrator Rights Bundle page, click Publish.
5. Select the All Apps organization and click Save.
6. Verify that the organization is added to the Published To list.
Next, the organization administrator can manage extensibility with VCF Operations orchestrator-related authorizations for
users in that organization.
Data Collection for VCF Operations orchestrator Integrations
VCF Operations orchestrator performs periodic data collection for your VCF Operations orchestrator integration.
After you configure VCF Operations orchestrator for your VCF Automation organization, you must wait about 10 minutes
for data collection to sync. After that, data collection events for VCF Operations orchestrator integrations are triggered
every 10 minutes.
Important:
As you work on VCF Operations orchestrator workflows, verify that you version up the workflow when you are
finished editing it. Changes to non-versioned up workflows are not picked up by the data collector.
You can find information about the last data collection performed on a VCF Operations orchestrator integration by
navigating to Administer > Connections > Integrations and selecting the VCF Operations orchestrator integration. You
can also trigger a manual data collection event by clicking Start Data Collection.
Managing a VCF Operations orchestrator Integration in VCF Automation
Provider administrators manage the VCF Operations orchestrator integration in the VCF Automation organization.

Move from an Embedded to an External VCF Operations orchestrator Instance in a PCO
By default, an embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance is integrated in the Provider Consumption Organization
(PCO).
In cases where you use heavy automation, however, you might need to fine-tune resources available for VCF Operations
orchestrator when resources provided to the embedded instance are not enough in any resource profile.
1. Deploy an external VCF Operations orchestrator instance.
2. Export custom VCF Operations orchestrator content by using option 1 or option 2 from the Move Custom VCF
Operations orchestrator Content between VCF Automation Organizations section.
3. Configure the external VCF Operations orchestrator authentication for the PCO.
4. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI as a provider administrator.
5. In the side navigation panel, navigate to Infrastructure > Organizations.
6. Open the PCO and then click Launch Organization Portal.
7. In the PCO UI, click the Administer tab.
8. In the side navigation bar, click Integrations.
9. Open the VCF Operations orchestrator integration tile.
a. Change the name of integration to indicate that the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator is no longer used.
b. Select the newly deployed external VCF Operations orchestrator.
c. Enter external VCF Operations orchestrator FQDN.
d. Click Validate.
e. Click Save.
10.Wait for the data collection to start or start it manually. Data collection is run automatically every 10 minutes.
11.Validate that extensibility automation is working properly.
12.Click the Orchestrate tab. You can now import the custom content using one of the options from the Move Custom
VCF Operations orchestrator Content between VCF Automation Organizations section.
The embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance continues to run but is no longer used for workloads.
If there are VM Apps organizations that are using the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance, consider
replacing it with the same or another external VCF Operations orchestrator instance following the same procedure. VM
Apps organizations can continue to share the embedded VCF Operations orchestrator instance for their workloads.

organization, deselect it from the list.
5. Click Save.

Launch Organization Portal.

to Connections > Integrations.

it.
Integrate VCF Automation with Active Directory
VCF Automation supports integration with Active Directory servers to provide creation of computer accounts in a specified
Organizational Unit (OU) within an Active Directory server when provisioning a virtual machine. As an organization
administrator, you can add one or more Active Directory endpoints in VCF Automation to centralize authentication, user
management, and VM access and provisioning.
• Verify that you configured an LDAP connection to the Active Directory server.
• Verify that you created an organizational unit (OU) on your Active Directory.
• Verify that the Active Directory administrator user configured for the integration has the necessary permissions to
create/delete/search for computer objects in the configured OU.
After you register an Active Directory server in VCF Automation, you configure profiles for the integration. An Active
Directory profile defines the OU where all virtual machines deployed through the VCF Automation catalog or the VM
Service are registered. A profile can be applied to the entire organization or it can be associated with specific projects. If
an existing profile is changed, the updated profile is applied to new deployments while previously provisioned VMs remain
unaffected.
You can scope only one profile to the entire organization at a time, regardless of the number of Active Directory
integrations you have in your VCF Automation organization. The organization-scoped profile is used for all VMs
provisioned in the organization. You cannot create a new organization-scoped profile if another one already exists.
If you need more granularity, you can create a project-scoped profile. You can create multiple project-scoped profiles.
Each profile can be associated with multiple projects, but each project can be associated with only one profile at a time.
When a user deploys a VM in VCF Automation, the VM is registered in Active Directory OU based on the defined profile.
When a VM is deleted in VCF Automation, it is unregistered from Active Directory.
Broadcom 7244

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to the VCF Automation organization as an organization administrator.
2. Select Administer > Connections > Integrations and then click Add Integration.
3. Click Active Directory.
4. On the Summary tab, configure your integration.
a) Еnter a name and description for the integration.
b) In the Credentials and Configuration section, enter the appropriate LDAP host and port.
The specified LDAP host is used to call the Active Directory server to validate, register, and unregister computers.
c) Enter the user name and password for the LDAP server.
d) Enter the appropriate Base DN that specifies the root for the desired Active Directory resources, for example,
.
DC=org,DC=mycompany,DC=net
You can specify only one DN per Active Directory integration.
e) Click Validate.
f) When prompted, trust the Active Directory certificate.
The certificate is added to the trust store immediately. You can view it on the Certificate Management page.
g) Click Save.
The Active Directory integration is added.
5. Add an Active Directory profile.
The profile defines the OU where the virtual machines are registered.
a) Open the integration again and click the Profiles tab.
b) Click New.
c) Add a name for the Active Directory profile.
Enter a unique name.
d) Enter a relative DN, for example, .
OU=QA
The relative DN is the subdirectory (OU) that exists within the root domain that you specified in Step 4d.
e) (Optional) Select the Allow profile override check box.
• If the check box is not selected, the VM is automatically added to the group configured in the profile.
• If the check box is selected, users can specify a different Active Directory domain in the blueprint, which will
override the profile. Provisioned machines are added to the group specified in the blueprint.
Important:
Join domain is supported only for Windows machines.
f) Select the scope.
• Organization. All provisioned VMs use the domain of the organization.
• Project. Add projects to which you want to apply the profile. All VMs provisioned in the selected projects are
added to the specified OU.
VCF Automation checks whether there is an existing organization-scoped profile across all profiles defined for all
available Active Directory integrations.
g) Click Create.
The Active Directory profile is created.
Override an Active Directory profile in a blueprint
Active Directory profiles can be overridden through blueprints where the user can provide an alternative Active
Directory domain name and credentials directly in the blueprint.
• If Allow profile override is enabled in the profile, users have the following options:
Broadcom 7245

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– Provide an alternative domain name and credentials in the blueprint, which takes precedence over
the ones specified in the profile. See Capture a Namespace with a Join Domain Customization in VCF
Automation.
– Prevent a VM from joining any Active Directory domain by adding the following annotation to the YAML
of the VM.
<reason>
skip.config.service.vmware.com/ad:
• If Allow profile override is not enabled in the profile, but the user still provides an alternative domain
name and credentials in the blueprint, VM creation fails.
• If there is no Active Directory profile configured, the user can manually define a SysPrep in the blueprint
and specify a domain name and administrator credentials.
Terraform Configuration in VCF Automation
As an organization administrator, you can automate the deployment and configuration of VCF Automation infrastructure
resources using Terraform.
Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool developed by HashiCorp. You can use the open-source tool to define and
provision your cloud infrastructure using the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). Terraform uses the configuration
files with the descriptions of the desired state of your infrastructure to create, manage, and delete the necessary
resources across various cloud providers and platforms. Terraform providers are plug-ins that Terraform uses to interact
with cloud providers, SaaS providers, third-party tools, and other APIs. Each provider defines its resources and data
sources that map directly to the functionalities of the specific service.
For end-to-end operation of Terraform in VCF Automation, you can use three open-source Terraform providers.
• Terraform Provider for VCF Automation - You can use this provider to perform CRUD operations for a subset of the
VCF Automation resources that belong to organizations, such as namespaces. This provider is available on GitHub
and is distributed as part of the HashiCorp Terraform registry. The greenfield folder contains examples of configuration
files for fresh VCF Automation installations that show how all resources interact with each other and provide guidance
on how you can use the provider. The folder contains two parts. As an organization administrator, you can use the
tenant part to create content libraries and namespaces in your organization.
Note:
The provider part is available to provider administrators to create the necessary organizations and configure the
underlying infrastructure, such as vCenter instances, NSX instances, provider gateways, roles, and so on.
• Terraform Provider for Kubernetes - You can use the Kubernetes (K8S) provider to perform CRUD operations against
the VCF Automation resources exposed through the VCF Automation Kubernetes API layer, such as projects.
To see a usage example, navigate to .
https://<FQDN>/automation/api-docs/#/terraform-provider
• Terraform Provider for VMware Aria Automation - You can use this provider to perform CRUD operations for VCF
Automation resources that are not yet exposed through the VCF Automation Kubernetes API layers, such as
blueprints.

Managing Secrets in VCF Automation
A VCF Automation secret is a reusable, encrypted value that project users may add to their blueprint designs.
Secure access keys and credentials are typical examples of secret properties. Once created and saved, a secret's value
can never be unencrypted or read.
Create a secret
1. Log in to VCF Automation as a project administrator.
2. Go to Administer > Certificates > Secrets and click New.
3. Enter a unique property name for the secret, without spaces or special characters.
The name is the visible identifier for the secret.
4. Scope the secret to the entire organization or to specific projects.
To assign the secret to one or more projects, click Assign Projects, select your projects, and click Add.
You can't associate a secret with the same project twice. You also can't associate two secrets with the same name
with the entire organization.
5. Enter the secret value.
When typing, the value is obscured by default, which protects it if the screen is shared.
If needed, you can click the eye symbol to reveal and verify a value. After it is saved, a secret value becomes
encrypted in the database and can never be re-exposed.
6. Optionally, enter a longer description of the secret property.
7. Click .
Create
Adding a secret to a blueprint
You can add a secret property as a binding in blueprint code.
Note that starting to type reveals a selection list of secrets that have been created for the
'${secret.characters
project.
If two secrets with the same name but different values exist at the project level and at the organization level, the project
secret takes precedence. The organization secret is not available for selection in the blueprint.
properties:
name: ourvm
image: mint20
flavor: small
remoteAccess:
authentication: publicPrivateKey
sshKey: '${secret.ourPublicKey}'
