http-rest configuration
2. Locate the Add a REST operation workflow and click Run.
3. Select the parent host to which you want to add the operation.
4. In the Name text box, enter the name of the operation.
5. In the Template URL text box, enter only the operation part of the URL.
You can include placeholders for parameters that are provided when you run the operation.
The following is an example URL syntax.
/customer/{id}/orders?date={date}
6. Select the HTTP method that the operation uses.

Invoking a REST Operation
To make REST requests, you can either invoke a configured REST operation or invoke a REST operation dynamically by
using a configured REST operation as a template and replacing any of the parameters at runtime.
There are several ways to invoke a REST operation.
• Configure REST hosts and associate REST operations with them by running the Add a REST Host and Add a
REST Operation workflows. The registered REST hosts and REST operations are persistent and can be found in the
Inventory and Resources views.
• Invoke a REST operation without previously configuring REST hosts and adding REST operations by running the
Invoke a dynamic REST operation workflow from Library > Workflows. With this workflow, you can provide
REST host base URL and operation parameters. The data is not persistent and is not available in the Inventory and
Resources views.
• Configure REST hosts, associate REST operations with them, and use the configured REST hosts and REST
operations as templates for further use, by running the Invoke a REST host with dynamic params and Invoke
a REST operation with dynamic params workflows from Library > Workflows. You can replace some of the
parameters of already configured REST hosts and REST operations when you run the workflows. The original REST
hosts and REST operations are not affected.

Using proxy workflows
You can use proxy workflows to manage the interaction between the local VCF Operations orchestrator server and
workflows on a remote VCF Operations orchestrator server.
You can use the Multi-Node plug-in to generate local workflows which interact with remote workflows. These local
workflows are called proxy workflows. A proxy workflow takes the input parameters from the inventory of the Multi-Node
plug-in. When you run the proxy workflow, it converts the parameters to the types required by the remote workflow. When
the remote workflow finishes its run, the output parameters are converted back to the local representation on the primary
VCF Operations orchestrator server.
Broadcom 7797

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Synchronous proxy workflows
The synchronous type of proxy workflows preserve the API and the operation contract of the remote workflows.
The schema of all synchronous proxy workflows is the same, but contains different scripting.
The synchronous proxy workflow completes the run after the remote workflow completes and provides output parameters.
The local workflow consumes no server resources while waiting for the results of the remote workflow.
At the end of a successful run the output parameters of the proxy workflow contain a local representation of the remote
workflow token. The output parameters can be used directly by other workflows on the local VCF Operations orchestrator
server when they are of simple type, such as, boolean, number, string, and similar.
Asynchronous proxy workflows
You can use asynchronous proxy workflows to optimize the run of remote workflows.
The schema of all asynchronous proxy workflows is the same, but contains different scripting.
Broadcom 7798

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
An asynchronous proxy workflow returns immediately a result that is a local wrapper of the remote workflow token object.
The proxy workflow uses this token to check the state of the run and to retrieve the output parameters when the remote
workflow completes its run. The output parameters can be used directly by other workflows on the local VCF Operations
orchestrator server when they are of simple type, such as, boolean, number, string, and similar.

Using the Multi-Node plug-in inventory
The Multi-Node plug-in mirrors all inventories of the connected VCF Operations orchestrator servers in the Inventory
view.
The inventory for a single remote server consists of two major parts, system objects and plug-in objects. Both objects are
wrappers of the remote objects into locally usable types:
System object System objects are under a top-level group called System. They contain configurations, packages,
workflows, actions, and related folders. Remote system objects have individual wrapper types.
Plug-in objects Plug-in objects mirror the inventories of all plug-ins attached to the remote VCF Operations orchestrator
server. Remote plug-in objects are all wrapped into a single local type VCO:RemotePluginObject.

Using the Net Plug-In
You can use the Net plug-in to implement the Telnet, FTP, POP3, and IMAP protocols in workflows. The POP3 and IMAP
implementations allow downloading and reading email. In combination with the Mail plug-in, the Net plug-in provides full
email sending and receiving capabilities in workflows.
Using the PowerShell plug-in
The PowerShell plug-in allows interaction between VCF Operations orchestrator and Windows PowerShell. The
PowerShell plug-in workflow library contains workflows that allow you to manage PowerShell hosts and run custom
PowerShell operations.
You use the plug-in to call PowerShell scripts and cmdlets from VCF Operations orchestrator actions and workflows,
and to work with the result. In addition to the standard workflows that come with the plug-in, you can also create custom
workflows that implement the plug-in API.
You can use the Inventory view in the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to manage the available PowerShell resources.
You can use the scripting API of the plug-in to develop custom workflows.
PowerShell plug-in components
The PowerShell plug-in relies on a number of components to function properly.
VCF Operations orchestrator and Windows PowerShell provide the platform for the plug-in, and the plug-in provides
interaction between those products. The PowerShell plug-in can also interact with other components, such as vCenter and
vSphere PowerCLI.
Broadcom 7802

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The plug-in communicates with Windows PowerShell through the WinRM communication protocol. See Configuring
WinRM.
Optionally, you can integrate the PowerShell plug-in with vSphere PowerCLI and vCenter. See PowerCLI Integration with
the Plug-In.
You can install all components on a local host. The usage, functionality, and communication protocol requirements of the
PowerShell plug-in do not change if VCF Operations orchestrator and Windows PowerShell are installed on the same
machine.
Access the PowerShell plug-in API
To access the API Explorer from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, click API Explorer in the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client navigation pane.
To access the API Explorer from the Scripting tabs of the workflow, policy, and action editors, click Search API on the
left.
You can copy code from API elements and paste it into scripting boxes. For more information about API scripting, see
Developing with VCF Operations orchestrator.
Using the PowerShell plug-in inventory
The PowerShell plug-in exposes all objects in the connected PowerShell hosts in the Inventory view.
Within the inventory of the plug-in, you can monitor PowerShell hosts and their snap-ins and cmdlets. Each remote host
can contain snap-ins and each snap-in can contain cmdlets.

Configuring WinRM
To establish a connection between the PowerShell plug-in and Windows PowerShell, you must configure WinRM to use
one of the supported communication protocols.
The PowerShell plug-in supports Windows Remote Management (WinRM) 2.0 as a management protocol.
The following authentication methods are supported.
Authentication method Details
Basic Non-secure authentication mechanism that requires a user name
and a password.
Kerberos Secure authentication protocol that uses tickets to verify the
identity of the client and the server.
Note:
The PowerShell plug-in does not support delegation of user credentials in WinRM and CredSSP is not a
supported authentication method.
WinRM Through HTTP
The PowerShell plug-in supports communication with the WinRM host through the HTTP protocol. Although WinRM
authenticates the communication, the data transfer is not encrypted and is sent as plain text on the network. You should
use the HTTP protocol if IPSec is configured between the machines that communicate.
To use Basic authentication, you must set the property to in both the service and client
AllowUnencrypted true
WinRM configuration. For an example of HTTP configuration, see Configure WinRM to Use HTTP.
Broadcom 7804

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
WinRM Through HTTPS
The PowerShell plug-in supports communication with the WinRM host through the HTTPS protocol. You can use the
HTTPS protocol as a more secure communication method.
To use the HTTPS protocol, you must generate a certificate for server authentication and install the certificate on the
WinRM host. For an example of HTTPS configuration, see Configure WinRM to use HTTPS.
Kerberos authentication
You can use Kerberos authentication when you add and manage a PowerShell host. With Kerberos authentication,
domain users can run commands on remote PowerShell-enabled machines over WinRM.
To configure WinRM on the PowerShell host, run the following command.
winrm quickconfig
winrm set winrm/config/service/auth '@{Kerberos="true"}'
winrm set winrm/config/winrs @{MaxMemoryPerShellMB="2048"}
For more information, see Configure Kerberos Authentication for VCF Operations orchestrator Plug-Ins.
Configure WinRM to Use HTTP
You can configure the WinRM host to enable communication with the PowerShell plug-in through the HTTP protocol.
You must modify the WinRM configuration by running commands on the WinRM host machine. You can use the same
machine as both the WinRM service and WinRM client.
Important:
If you skip any of the steps when configuring WinRM to use HTTP, the host might not be added, and you might
get an error message in the logs such as:
Caused by: org.dom4j.DocumentException: Error on line -1 of document : Premature end of file.
Nested exception: Premature end of file.
at org.dom4j.io.SAXReader.read(SAXReader.java:482)
at org.dom4j.DocumentHelper.parseText(DocumentHelper.java:278)
at
com.xebialabs.overthere.cifs.winrm.connector.JdkHttpConnector.sendMessage(JdkHttpConnector.java:117)
1. Run the following command to set the default WinRM configuration values.
c:\> winrm quickconfig
2. Optional: Run the following command to check whether a listener is running, and verify the default ports.
c:\> winrm e winrm/config/listener
The default ports are 5985 for HTTP, and 5986 for HTTPS.
3. Enable basic authentication on the WinRM service.
a) Run the following command to check whether basic authentication is allowed.
c:\> winrm get winrm/config/service
b) Run the following command to enable basic authentication.
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/service/auth '@{Basic="true"}'
4. Run the following command to allow transfer of unencrypted data on the WinRM service.
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/service @{AllowUnencrypted="true"}
5. If the channel binding token hardening level of the WinRM service is set to , change its value to .
strict relaxed
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/service/auth @{CbtHardeningLevel="relaxed"}
6. Enable basic authentication on the WinRM client.
a) Run the following command to check whether basic authentication is allowed.
c:\> winrm get winrm/config/client
Broadcom 7805

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
b) Run the following command to enable basic authentication.
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/client/auth @{Basic="true"}
7. Run the following command to allow transfer of unencrypted data on the WinRM client.
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/client @{AllowUnencrypted="true"}
8. If the WinRM host machine is in an external domain, run the following command to specify the trusted hosts.
host1 host2 host3
c:\> winrm set winrm/config/client @{TrustedHosts=" , , "}
9. Run the following command to test the connection to the WinRM service.
winrm_server user_name password
c:\> winrm identify -r:http:// :5985 -auth:basic -u: -p: -
encoding:utf-8
Configure WinRM to use HTTPS
You can configure the WinRM host to enable communication with the PowerShell plug-in through the HTTPS protocol.
• Configure WinRM to use the HTTP protocol. For more information, see Configure WinRM to Use HTTP.
• Verify that you can access the Microsoft Management Console ( ) on the WinRM host.
mmc.exe
The WinRM host requires a certificate so that it can communicate through the HTTPS protocol. You can either obtain a
certificate or generate one.
1. Generate a self-signed certificate.
The following command line contains example syntax for creating a certificate on the WinRM host by using the
Powershell Cmdlet .
New-SelfSignedCertificate

Scripting examples for common PowerShell tasks
You can cut, paste, and edit the JavaScript examples to write scripts for common PowerShell tasks.
For more information about scripting, see the VCF Operations orchestrator Developer's Guide.
Run a PowerShell Script Through the API
You can use JavaScript to run a PowerShell script through the plug-in API.
This example script performs the following actions.
• Opens a session to a PowerShell host.
• Provides a script to run.
• Checks invocation results.
• Closes the session.
var sess;
try {
//Open session to PowerShell host
var sess = host.openSession()
//Set executed script
var result = sess.invokeScript('dir')
Broadcom 7811

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
//Check for errors
if (result.invocationState == 'Failed'){
throw "PowerShellInvocationError: Errors found while executing script \n" +
result.getErrors();
}
//Show result
System.log( result.getHostOutput() );
} catch (ex){
System.error (ex)
} finally {
if (sess) {
//Close session
host.closeSession( sess.getSessionId() );
}
}
Work with Result
You can use JavaScript to work with the result of a PowerShell script run.
This example script performs the following actions.
• Checks the invocation state.
• Extracts a value from the result.
• Checks the type.
RemotePSObject
var sess = host.openSession()
sess.addCommandFromString("dir " + directory)
var invResult = sess.invokePipeline();
//Show result
System.log( invResult.getHostOutput() );
//Check for errors
if (invResult.invocationState == 'Failed'){
System.error(invResult.getErrors());
} else {
//Get PowerShellRemotePSObject
var psObject = invResult.getResults();
var directories = psObject.getRootObject();
var isList = directories instanceof Array
if ( isList ){
for (idx in directories){
var item = directories[idx];
if ( item.instanceOf('System.IO.FileInfo') ){//Check type of object
System.log( item.getProperty('FullName') );//Extract value from result
}
}
} else {
System.log( directories.getProperty('FullName') );//Extract value from result
}
}
host.closeSession( sess.getSessionId());

Troubleshooting
If you encounter problems when using the PowerShell plug-in, you can refer to a troubleshooting topic to understand the
problem or solve it, if there is a workaround.
Activate Kerberos Event Logging
For troubleshooting purposes, you might want to activate Kerberos event logging on the Key Distribution Center (KDC)
machine.
Back up the Windows registry.
1. Log in to the domain controller that acts as a Key Distribution Center (KDC).
2. Run the registry editor as an administrator.
3. In the registry window, expand
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Kerberos
.
\Parameters
4. If a registry key value does not exist, right-click to create it.
LogLevel
a) Right-click Parameter, select New > DWORD (32-bit) Value, and enter .
LogLevel
b) Select Parameter and in the right pane, double-click and enter in the Value data: text box.
LogLevel 1
The new setting becomes effective without a reboot on Windows Server 2003 and later.
The Kerberos error event entries are recorded in the System Windows Event Log.
To deactivate Kerberos event logging, delete the registry key value or change its value data to .
LogLevel 0
Servers Not Found in Kerberos Database
After you add PowerShell servers with Kerberos authentication, the servers might not be found because they are not
added correctly.
When you try to connect to a server, the server is not found in Kerberos database.
No valid credentials provided (Mechanism level: No valid
credentials provided (Mechanism level: Server not found in Kerberos
database (7)))
This error might be caused by several misconfigurations.
• The PowerShell host is not part of a domain.
Broadcom 7813

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• The host to realm mapping is not correct.
• The Service Principal Name of the PowerShell host is not built correctly.
Note:
Kerberos authentication does not work when the destination is an IP address.
When you add a PowerShell host using the Kerberos authentication, enter a DNS or NetBIOS destination.
Unable to Obtain a Kerberos Ticket
When you provide wrong credentials, the plug-in fails to obtain a Kerberos ticket.
You are unable to add a host to the plug-in inventory and the result is the following error message.
Pre-authentication information was invalid (24)
You have provided wrong credentials.
Provide the correct credentials.
Kerberos Authentication Fails Due to Different Time Settings
Inconsistent time settings in the environment that uses Kerberos configuration might lead to authentication failure.
Attempts to use Kerberos for initial authentication of a host or for resource access fail, and the following error message
appears.
Clock Skew
If the system time on the computers in the environment differs with more than 5 minutes from the domain controller, or
from one another, the Kerberos authentication fails.
Synchronize the system times in the environment.
Kerberos Authentication Session Mode Fails
When you use Kerberos authentication with Shared Session or Session per User, adding the PowerShell host might fail.
When you attempt to add a PowerShell host to the plug-in inventory using Shared Session or Session per User, the
workflow fails with the following error.
Null realm name (601) - default realm not specified (Dynamic Script Module name :
addPowerShellHost#16)
The default realm is not specified in the Kerberos configuration file , neither is provided as a part of the user
krb5.conf
name.
Provide a default realm in your Kerberos configuration file or include the realm in your user name when authenticating with
Kerberos.
Unable to Reach a Key Distribution Center for a Realm
Any misspelling in the file might cause a failure when you add a host.
krb5.conf
When you are adding a host, the Kerberos authentication is unable to reach a Key Distribution Center (KDC) for
yourrealm.
YOURREALM.COM
Cannot get kdc for realm
The and sections in the file might be misspelled.
libdefaults realms krb5.conf
Verify that the and sections in your file are spelled correctly.
libdefaults realms krb5.conf
Unable to Locate the Default Realm
VCF Operations orchestrator workflows that require Kerberos authentication might fail if the Kerberos configuration file
does not have the correct format or encoding.
Kerberos authentication cannot identify the default realm.
Broadcom 7814

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Cannot locate default realm
The Kerberos configuration file that you upload to the VCF Operations orchestrator Appliance has been
krb5.conf
edited on a non-UNIX operating system. As a result, the format and the encoding might be incorrect.
In order for the VCF Operations orchestrator appliance to read the file, the format of the file must be UNIX
krb5.conf
and the character encoding must be ANSI as UTF-8.
Using the SNMP Plug-In
The SNMP plug-in allows VCF Operations orchestrator to connect and receive information from SNMP-enabled systems
and devices. You can define SNMP devices as inventory objects by running workflows, and perform SNMP operations on
the defined objects.
You can use the plug-in to connect to SNMP devices such as routers, switches, network printers, and UPS devices. The
plug-in can also receive events from vCenter over the SNMP protocol.
The SNMP plug-in provides two methods of communication with the SNMP devices.
• Queries for the values of specific SNMP variables.
• Listening for events (SNMP traps) that are generated from the devices and pushed to the registered SNMP managers.
The plug-in contains a set of standard workflows related to managing SNMP devices, queries, the trap host, and
performing SNMP operations. You can also create custom workflows to automate tasks in an SNMP environment.
Managing SNMP Devices
You can run workflows to register SNMP devices with , edit the settings for existing devices, and unregister devices.
SNMP Device Management Workflows
The Device Management workflow category contains workflows that allow you to manage SNMP devices.
To access these workflows in VCF Operations orchestrator, navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the and
snmp
tags in the workflow search box.
device_management

Edit an SNMP device Edits the configuration of a registered SNMP device.

Note:
To establish a more reliable connection, use an IP address.

If you leave the text box blank, the device address is used to generate a name automatically.
6. Optional: To configure the advanced connection parameters, select the check box, and navigate to the Advanced tab.
a) In the Port text box, specify the connection port.
The default port is 161.

b) From the Version drop-down menu, select the SNMP version that you want to use and provide the credentials.

the same as the MD5 password.
Note:

c) In the Community name text box, enter a name for the device. The default name is public.
7. Click Run.
After the workflow runs successfully, the SNMP device appears in the Inventory view.
You can add queries to the SNMP device and run workflows from the Inventory view.

Managing the SNMP Trap Host
VCF Operations orchestrator can act as an SNMP listener. You can start and stop the SNMP trap host, and change the
port on which VCF Operations orchestrator listens for SNMP traps.
The SNMP plug-in supports SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c traps.
Important:
When using a clustered VCF Operations orchestrator deployment, you must send the SNMP trap to all nodes in
the cluster.
Broadcom 7816

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Add a SNMP trap port to the VCF Operations orchestrator Appliance
Before running the Set the SNMP trap port workflow, you must add the port to the VCF Operations orchestrator
Appliance.
1. Log in to the VCF Operations orchestrator appliance command line as root.
2. Create a variable for the SNMP trap port.
SNMP_PORT=port_value
Note:
The ports open for SNMP traps are 81 to 32767.
3. Run the command.
vracli network ports expose
vracli network ports expose --proto udp --targetPort $SNMP_PORT $SNMP_PORT vco-app
Set the SNMP Trap Port
You can run a workflow to set the port on which VCF Operations orchestrator listens for SNMP traps.
• Prepare the VCF Operations orchestrator Appliance for the configuration of the SNMP trap port. See Add a SNMP trap
port to the VCF Operations orchestrator Appliance.
• In the VCF Operations orchestrator, select Administration > Inventory and verify that the SNMP device is connected.
The default port for SNMP traps is 162. On Linux systems, you can open ports below 1024 only with superuser privileges.
The ports open for SNMP traps are 81 to 32767.
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator as an administrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the and tags in the workflow search
snmp trap_host_management
box.
3. Run the Set the SNMP trap port workflow.
4. Enter the port number on which VCF Operations orchestrator listens for SNMP traps.
5. Click Run.
The workflow stops the trap host, sets the new port, and starts the trap host again.
Note:
If you upgrade your VCF Operations orchestrator environment, you must run the VCF Operations orchestrator
Appliance and the Set the SNMP trap port workflow again.
Receiving SNMP Traps
The SNMP plug-in can receive SNMP traps by running a workflow, which waits for a single trap message, or with a policy,
which can handle traps continuously. The plug-in supports SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c traps.

You can run a workflow that waits to receive an SNMP trap from a specified device.
• Verify that you are logged in to the VCF Operations orchestrator Client as an administrator.
• Verify that you have a connection to an SNMP device from the Inventory view.
This workflow features a trigger, which stops the run of the workflow and waits for an SNMP trap before continuing. When
a trap is received, the workflow run resumes. You can use the workflow as part of more complex workflows, or as a
sample that you can customize or extend for a specific need.

You can set a policy to continuously listen for traps from an SNMP device that is already registered in the plug-in

Configure an SNMP Trap Host Policy
With the SNMP Trap Host policy listens for SNMP traps from hosts that might not be added as registered SNMP devices.
• Verify that you are logged in to the VCF Operations orchestrator Client as an administrator.
• Verify that you have a connection to an SNMP device from the Inventory view.
1. In the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, navigate to Library > Policies.
2. Open the SNMP Trap Host policy template and click Run.
3. Enter a name for the policy that you want to create.
4. Optional: Enter a description for the policy.
5. Select from the inventory tree.
Trap Host (Online)
6. Click Run to create the policy.
The Orchestrator client switches to Run perspective.
Broadcom 7818

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
7. Right-click the policy and select Edit.
8. In the tab, expand host > OnTrapAll.
Scripting
a) Select a workflow or a script to associate with the policy.
9. Click Save and close to apply the edited settings.
10.On the Policies view, right-click the policy that you edited and select Start policy.
You can edit the SNMP Trap Host policy.
Edit a Trap Policy
You can edit a trap policy to customize it for a specific use case. When you edit a trap policy, you can change its priority
and startup settings, and customize the scripting and permissions associated with the policy.
• Verify that you are logged in to the VCF Operations orchestrator Client as an administrator.
• Verify that you have a connection to an SNMP device from the Inventory view.
1. In the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, navigate to Library > Policies.
2. If the policy that you want to edit is running, right-click the policy and select Stop policy.
3. Right-click the policy and select Edit.
4. From the General tab, edit the startup settings, priority, and description of the policy.
5. Optional: From the Scripting tab, you can associate a specific workflow or scripting code with the policy, for
integration in a more complex scenario.
You can set the policy to trigger a custom workflow when a trap is received.
6. Optional: From the Permissions tab, you can modify the access rights.
You can give permissions to a user or to a group to start the policy, without giving permissions to edit the policy.
7. Click Save and close to apply the edited settings.
8. On the Policies view, right-click the policy that you edited and select Start policy.
Using the SOAP plug-in
The SOAP plug-in allows you to manage SOAP Web services by providing interaction between VCF Operations
orchestrator and SOAP hosts. You can define SOAP services as inventory objects by running configuration workflows,
and perform SOAP operations on the defined objects.
The plug-in contains a set of standard workflows related to managing SOAP hosts and invoking SOAP operations. You
can also generate custom workflows to automate tasks in a SOAP environment.
Configuring the SOAP plug-in
You must use the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to configure the SOAP plug-in.
The Configuration workflow category contains workflows that allow you to manage SOAP hosts.
To access these workflows in the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the
and tags in the workflow search box.
soap configuration
Workflow Name Description
Add a SOAP host Adds a SOAP host to the plug-in inventory.
Reload plug-in configuration Refreshes the list of SOAP hosts in the plug-in inventory.
Remove a SOAP host Removes a SOAP host from the plug-in inventory.
CAUTION:
When you remove a host from the inventory, all workflows
generated from it stop working.
Update a SOAP host Updates a SOAP host in the plug-in inventory.
Broadcom 7819

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Workflow Name Description
Update a SOAP host with an endpoint URL Updates a SOAP host with a preferred endpoint address. The
new endpoint address is used for sending and receiving SOAP
messages, instead of the endpoint address defined within the
WSDL.
Add a SOAP Host
You can run a workflow to add a SOAP host and configure the host connection parameters.
1. Log in to the VCF Operations orchestrator Client as an administrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the and tags in the workflow search box.
soap configuration
3. Locate the Add a SOAP host workflow and click Run.
4. On the SOAP host tab, provide the properties to create a host.
a) In the Name text box, enter the name of the host.
b) Select whether to provide the WSDL content as text.
Option Action
Yes Copy the text in the WSDL content text box.
No Enter the correct path in the WSDL URI text box.
c) In the Connection timeout text box, enter the number of seconds within which VCF Operations orchestrator must
connect to the SOAP host, otherwise the connection times out.
d) In the Request timeout text box, enter the number of seconds within which a SOAP request must succeed before
it times out.
5. On the Proxy tab, select whether to use a proxy.
Option Action
Yes Provide the proxy address and proxy port.
No Continue to the next step.
6. On the Host authentication tab, select the authentication type.
Option Description
None No authentication is required.
Basic Provides basic access authentication.
On the User credentials tab, select the session mode.
• If you select Shared Session, provide credentials for the
shared session.
• If you select Per User Session, the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client retrieves credentials from the user who is
logged in.
Digest Provides digest access authentication that uses encryption.
On the User credentials tab, select the session mode.
• If you select Shared Session, provide credentials for the
shared session.
• If you select Per User Session, the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client retrieves credentials from the user who is
logged in.
NTLM Provides NT LAN Manager (NTLM) access authentication within
the Window Security Support Provider (SSPI) framework.
On the User credentials tab, select the session mode.
Broadcom 7820

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Option Description
• If you select Shared Session, provide credentials for the
shared session.
• If you select Per User Session, the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client retrieves credentials from the user who is
logged in.
On the NTLM settings tab, enter the NTLM domain and NTLM
workstation.
Negotiate Provides Kerberos access authentication.
On the User credentials tab, select the session mode.
• If you select Shared Session, provide credentials for the
shared session.
• If you select Per User Session, the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client retrieves credentials from the user who is
logged in.
On the Negotiate tab, provide the Kerberos service SPN.
7. Click Run.
After the workflow runs successfully, the SOAP host appears in the Inventory view.
You can explore the SOAP host objects and run workflows on them from the Inventory view.

Using the SQL Plug-In
You can use the API that the SQL plug-in provides to implement connectivity to SQL databases and other tabular data
sources, such as spreadsheets or flat files.
The SQL plug-in API, which is based on JDBC, provides a call-level API for SQL-based database access. The SQL plug-
in also provides sample workflows that demonstrate how to use the API in workflows.
Configuring the SQL plug-in
You can use the workflows included in the SQL plug-in and run them from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to
configure the SQL plug-in and to add, update, or remove a database.
The Configuration workflow category of the SQL plug-in contains workflows that allow you to manage databases and
database tables.
To access these workflows in the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the
sql
and tags in the workflow search box.
configuration
When configuring a JDBC connector, you must provide the Java version.
• VCF Operations orchestrator 9.1 uses Java 17.
• VCF Operations orchestrator 9.1.1 uses Java 25.
Workflow Name Description
Add a database Adds a database object to the SQL plug-in inventory.
Add tables to a database Adds database tables to a database in the SQL plug-in inventory.
Remove a database Removes a database object from the SQL plug-in inventory.
Remove a table from a database Removes a database table from a database in the SQL plug-in
inventory.
Update a database Updates the configuration of a database object in the SQL plug-in
inventory.
Validate a database Validates a database in the SQL plug-in inventory.

Running the SQL Sample Workflows
You can run the SQL plug-in workflows to perform JDBC operations such as generating a JDBC URL, testing a JDBC
connection, and managing rows in JDBC tables. You can also run the SQL plug-in workflows to manage databases and
database tables, and to run SQL operations.
Generate a JDBC URL
You can run a workflow from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to generate a JDBC connection URL.
Verify that the user account you are logged in with has the necessary permissions to run JDBC workflows.
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the tag in the workflow search box.
jdbc
3. Locate the JDBC URL generator workflow and click Run.
4. On the General tab, select the type of database for which to generate a URL.
Note:
If you use a Microsoft database, select the Microsoft tab and provide the database instance name and database
user domain name.
5. Provide the required information to generate a database URL.
a) Enter a database server name or IP address.
b) Enter a database name.
c) Optional: Enter a database port number.
If you do not specify a port number, the workflow uses a default port number.
d) Enter a user name to access the database.
e) Enter a password to access the database.
6. Click Run.
Test a JDBC connection
You can run a workflow from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to test the connection to a database.
Verify that the user account you are logged in with has the necessary permissions to run JDBC workflows.
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the tag in the workflow search box.
jdbc_examples
3. Locate the JDBC connection example workflow and click Run.
4. Provide the required information to test a database connection.
a) Enter a user name to access the database.
b) Enter the URL to test.
c) Enter a password to access the database.
5. Click Run.
Create a table by using JDBC
You can run a workflow from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to create a database.
Verify that the user account you are logged in with has the necessary permissions to run JDBC workflows.
Broadcom 7825

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the tag in the workflow search box.
jdbc_examples
3. Locate the JDBC create table example workflow and click Run.
4. Provide the required information, and click Next.
a) Type a password to access the database.
b) Type a database connection URL.
c) Type a user name to access the database.
5. Enter an SQL create statement.
Example syntax is:
CREATE TABLE "table_name"
("column1" "data_type_for_column1",
"column2" "data_type_for_column2")

jdbc_examples

jdbc_examples

Adding a JDBC connector for the VCF Operations orchestrator SQL plug-in
This example demonstrates how you can add a MySQL connector for the VCF Operations orchestrator SQL plug-in.
The VCF Operations orchestrator SQL plug-in supports only certain database types. Before adding a MySQL connector,
verify that you use one of the following database types:
• Oracle
• Microsoft SQL Server
• PostgreSQL
• MySQL
1. Add the MySQL connector.jar file to the VCF Operations orchestrator Appliance.
Note:
For clustered VCF Operations orchestrator deployments, perform this operation on the appliances of all the
nodes.
a) Log in to the VCF Operations orchestrator appliance command line over SSH as root.
b) Navigate to the directory.
/data/vco/var/run/vco
cd /data/vco/var/run/vco
c) Create a directory.
plugins/SQL/lib/
mkdir -p plugins/SQL/lib/
d) Copy your MySQL connector.jar file from your local machine to the
/data/vco/var/run/vco/plugins/SQL/
directory by running a secure copy (SCP) command.
lib/
scp ~/local_machine_dir/your_mysql_connector.jar root@orchestrator_FQDN_or_IP:/data/vco/var/run/vco/
plugins/SQL/lib/
Note:
You can also use alternative methods for copying your connector.jar file to the VCF Operations orchestrator
Appliance, such as PSCP.
2. Restart the VCF Operations orchestrator server.
Using the SSH Plug-In for VCF Operations Orchestrator
You can use the SSH plug-in workflows to run SSH commands on a remote host that supports SSH and transfer files
between a VCF Operations orchestrator server and a remote host through a secure connection.
Specify Ciphers Used by the SSH Plug-In
Ciphers and key exchange algorithms that are provided by the SSH plug-in depend on the release version of VCF
Operations orchestrator. You must configure the remote SSH host with FIPS-compatible algorithms. You specify ciphers
for the SSH plug-in by adding a system property in VCF Operations orchestrator.
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator and navigate to System Settings.
2. Click Configuration Properties.
3. Click Add Property.
4. Under Name, enter .
com.vmware.o11n.ssh.cipher
5. Under Value, enter a comma-separated list of ciphers, for example, .
aes256-ctr,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
Broadcom 7829

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The default list of available ciphers is
aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr,aes256-cbc,aes192-
.
cbc,aes128-cbc,3des-ctr,3des-cbc,arcfour256,arcfour128,arcfour,blowfish-cbc
6. Enter a description for the new system property.
7. Click Add.
8. To finish setting the configuration property, click Save.

Running the SSH Plug-In Sample Workflows in VCF Operations Orchestrator
You can run the SSH plug-in sample workflows from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to test the connection
between the VCF Operations orchestrator server and the SSH host.
Generate a Key Pair in VCF Operations Orchestrator
You can generate a key pair by running a workflow in the VCF Operations orchestrator Client. Alternatively, you can use a
key pair that you generate in third-party tools. You can use the key pair to connect to an SSH host without a password.
A key pair consists of a public key and a private key. VCF Operations orchestrator can use the private key to connect to
the public key on an SSH host.
Generate a Key Pair in VCF Operations Orchestrator
You can run a workflow from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client to generate a key pair.
Verify that the user account you are logged in with has the necessary permissions to run SSH workflows.
CAUTION:
All VCF Operations orchestrator users with the right set of privileges can read, use, and overwrite your private
key.
1. Log in to VCF Operations orchestrator.
2. Navigate to Library > Workflows and enter the tag in the workflow search box.
ssh
3. Locate the Generate key pair workflow and click Run.
4. Provide the required information.
a) Select the key type and the key size.
Depending on which key type you select during the key-pair generation, you might have to change the SSH service
endpoint configuration to enable the type of certificate generated.
Key Type Key Sizes
RSA • 1024
• 2048
• 3072
• 4096
• 8192
DSA • 1024
• 2048
• 3072
ECDSA • 256
• 384

Use an Externally Generated Key Pair
You can generate public or private key pairs using external tools such as OpenSSH or OpenSSL.
When generating RSA, DSA, and ECDSA private keys, the key must be in the PEM format.
Broadcom 7831

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
1. To generate key pairs with an external tool, you must pass specific parameters to the commands of each tool.
Tool Parameters
OpenSSH Use the -m pem parameter.
For example, you can run the following command:
ssh-keygen -m pem -t ecdsa -b {256, 384, 521} -f
vco_key
OpenSSL The default format is PEM, so no additional parameters are
needed.
For example, you can run the following command:
openssl ecparam -name {prime256v1, secp384r1,
secp521r1} -genkey -noout -out vco_key
Using OpenSSH, extract the corresponding public key from the
private key.
ssh-keygen -f vco_key -y > vco_key.pub

orchestrator.

Using the vCenter plug-in
You can use the vCenter plug-in to manage multiple vCenter instances. You can create workflows that use the vCenter
plug-in API to automate tasks in your vCenter environment.
vCenter Plug-In Scripting API
The vCenter plug-in maps the vCenter API to the JavaScript that you can use in workflows. The vCenter scripting
API contains classes, with their respective attributes, methods, and constructors that allow interaction between VCF
Operations orchestrator and vCenter.
The vCenter plug-in supports registering vCenter 6.5, 6.7, 7.0 instances as endpoints. Based on the vCenter version that
you register, the plug-in exposes vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 API as SDK, and vSphere 7.0 API as scripting SDK. For information
about vCenter scripting objects, navigate to the API Explorer in VCF Operations orchestrator.
The vCenter plug-in provides a library of standard workflows that automate vCenter operations. For example, you can run
workflows to create, clone, migrate, or delete virtual machines. The plug-in also provides actions that perform individual
vCenter tasks that you can include in workflows. You can use the API to develop custom workflows.
Most vCenter plug-in workflows communicate only with the vCenter. However, some guest operations workflows require
communication with the ESXi host managed by vCenter. Before you run these workflows, you must import the ESXi host
certificate by running one of the Import a certificate from URL workflows.
Broadcom 7834

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The vCenter plug-in includes the Policy-Based Management (PBM) and the Storage Monitoring Service (SMS) APIs as
scripting objects in the VCF Operations orchestrator scripting API. The Storage Policy-Based Management policies and
components appear in the Inventory page of the VCF Operations orchestrator.
Using the vCenter Plug-In Inventory
The vCenter plug-in exposes all objects of the connected vCenter instances in the Inventory view.
To display the workflows that are available for a vCenter inventory object, navigate to Administration > Inventory >
vSphere vCenter Plug-in in VCF Operations orchestrator.

Before you can manage the objects in your vSphere inventory and run workflows on those objects in VCF Operations
orchestrator, you must first connect VCF Operations orchestrator and the vCenter instances you want to orchestrate.
You configure the vCenter plug-in by running the vCenter configuration workflows from the VCF Operations orchestrator.

Performance Considerations for Querying
With the vCenter plug-in for VCF Operations orchestrator, you can query the vCenter inventory for specific objects.
Querying Methods
For querying, you can either use the managed object, or the object finder methods that are included
vCSearchIndex
in the plug-in inventory, such as , , , and
getAllDatastores() getAllVirtualMachines() findAllForType()
others.
Performance
By default, both methods return the queried objects without including any of their properties, unless you specify a set of
properties as an argument for the method parameters in the search query.
Note:
You must always use query expressions with the and finder objects to prevent
getAll...() findAll...()
the VCF Operations orchestrator Client from filtering large sets of returned objects, which might affect the overall
performance of the VCF Operations orchestrator server.
Broadcom 7836

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You can use two types of expressions for querying the vCenter inventory.
Type of Expression Description
Name expressions You can specify a name as an argument for a query parameter.
Note:
The objects are filtered by the specified name argument
according to the name of the plug-in object as it is
appears in the vCenter plug-in inventory.
XPath expressions You can use expressions based on the XPath query language. For
more information, see Using XPath Expressions with the Plug-In.
When you invoke a vCenter inventory object with custom properties, each reference to this object, in a workflow or an
action, sends a query to vCenter, which generates a noticeable performance overhead. To optimize performance and
avoid serializing and deserializing the object multiple times within a workflow run, it is best to use a shared resource to
store the object, instead of storing it as a workflow attribute, an input, or an output parameter. Such shared resource can
be a configuration element or a resource element.
Using XPath Expressions with the vCenter Plug-In
You can use the finder methods in the vCenter plug-in to query for vCenter inventory objects. You can use XPath
expressions to define search parameters.
The vCenter plug-in includes a set of object finder methods such as ,
getAllDatastores()
, . You can use these methods to access the inventories of the vCenter
getAllResourcePools() findAllForType()
instances that are connected to your VCF Operations orchestrator server and search for objects by ID, name, or other
properties.
For performance reasons, the finder methods do not return any properties for the queried objects, unless you specify a set
of properties in the search query.
For example XPath queries, see XPath Syntax.
Important:
The queries based on XPath expressions might impact the VCF Operations orchestrator performance because
the finder method returns all objects of a given type on the vCenter side and the query filters are applied on the
vCenter plug-in side.
Using the VCF Operations orchestrator Plug-In for vSphere Web Client
You can use the VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client to perform operations on certain VCF
Operations orchestrator content from your vSphere Client.
The content that the plug-in exposes in the vSphere Client includes workflows, workflow runs, scheduled workflows, and
workflows waiting for input. In the vSphere Client, users can see workflow details, run or schedule workflows, and manage
workflow runs.
Context Actions
You can add VCF Operations orchestrator workflows as context actions in the vSphere Web Client. With context actions,
you can map a particular workflow to a specific vSphere item and run or schedule the workflow directly from the vSphere
inventory.
When you use the VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client for the first time, a configuration element
is created in VCF Operations orchestrator. You must not change or edit the location and any configuration items in that
location because they are managed by the VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client service.
Broadcom 7837

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Group Assignments
Administrators can use group assignments to assign context actions to specific VCF Operations orchestrator groups.
Users in these groups can then use context actions in vSphere. Users can run only the workflows that are assigned to
their group.
When a user logs into the vSphere Client, they have the same views and/or permissions in the VCF Operations
orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client as in VCF Operations orchestrator. For example, if a user has the Viewer role
in VCF Operations orchestrator, they can't run workflows in the vSphere Client.
To use group assignments, you must have at least one group defined in VCF Operations orchestrator.
When you assign context actions to a group, all of the mapped workflows are added as group items in the assigned group,
along with the configuration item.
Functional Requirements for the Plug-In
The VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client supports the following:
• Standalone VCF Operations orchestrator environments only. The plug-in is not supported for instances of VCF
Operations orchestrator that are embedded in VCF Automation.
• The VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client plug-in is available only with VCF Operations
orchestrator. To upgrade the plug-in, you must upgrade VCF Operations orchestrator.
• vSphere 8.0 U3 and later.
• Maximum one VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client can be registered per vCenter Server.
• In vSphere deployments with multiple vCenter instances (in Enhanced Linked Mode), you can register a single plug-
in with multiple vCenter instances (maximum one plug-in installation per vCenter), or you can register multiple plug-ins
with multiple vCenter servers.
• Before you can use the plug-in, you must configure the plug-in by enabling the service on the VCF Operations
orchestrator appliance. See Configuring the.
Configure the VMware Cloud Foundation Operations orchestrator Plug-in for vSphere Web
Client
As an administrator, you configure the VCF Operations orchestrator plug-in for vSphere Web Client.
• Verify that your VCF Operations orchestrator instance authenticates with vSphere. The authentication provider must
use the vCenter FQDN as the target vCenter instance FQDN. For more information on configuring the authentication

documentation.

Using the vCloud Suite API (vAPI) Plug-In
The vCloud Suite API plug-in provides the ability to consume API exposed by any vCloud Suite API provider. The vCloud
Suite API provides a service-oriented architecture for accessing resources in the virtual environment by issuing requests
to vCenter, through the vCloud Suite Endpoint.
The plug-in contains a set of standard workflows and example workflows. You can also create custom workflows that
implement the plug-in to automate tasks in your virtual environment. For information about vCloud Suite API, see VMware
vCloud Suite SDKs Programming Guide.
Access the vCloud Suite API Plug-In API
VCF Operations orchestrator provides an API Explorer to allow you to search the vCloud Suite API plug-in API and see
the documentation for JavaScript objects that you can use in scripted elements.
To access the API Explorer from the VCF Operations orchestrator Client, click API Explorer in the VCF Operations
orchestrator Client navigation pane.
To access the API Explorer from the Scripting tabs of the workflow, policy, and action editors, click Search API on the
left.
You can copy code from API elements and paste it into scripting boxes. For more information about API scripting, see
Developing with VCF Operations orchestrator.

You don't need to import separate metamodels for each endpoint. One metamodel per vCenter is enough for all endpoints

Using the VCF Operations orchestrator Plug-In for VCF Automation for VM Apps
The VMware Cloud Foundation Operations orchestrator™ Plug-in for VMware Cloud Foundation Automation™ for VM
Apps integrates VCF Operations orchestrator with VCF Automation. With the plug-in, you can run VCF Operations
orchestrator workflows from your VCF Automation instance. You can use the workflows that are provided with the plug-in
to deploy and manage VCF Automation resources in VM Apps organizations.
Important:
The VMware Cloud Foundation Operations orchestrator™ Plug-in for VMware Cloud Foundation Automation™
for VM Apps is not supported in VCF Automation for All Apps organizations. In All Apps organizations, use the
VMware Cloud Foundation Operations orchestrator™ Plug-in for VMware Cloud Foundation Automation™ for All
Apps instead. For more information, see Using the VCF Operations orchestrator Plug-In for VCF Automation for
All Apps.

VCF Operations orchestrator powers the Automation plug-in for VM Apps. You use VCF Operations orchestrator to run
and create workflows and access the Automation plug-in API.

Multi-Tenancy Support
You can configure the Automation plug-in to work with your multi-tenant environment. You must add a dedicated VCF
Automation host for each tenant (organization), using the tenant FQDN as the host name. For each VM Apps organization
that is not the default organization, configure CNAME records so that the organization identifier is included in the
hostname as a subdomain. For example, for a organization named org1, the hostname is org1.vcfa-fqdn. For the
default organization, the hostname is vcfa-fqdn.
If you use the plug-in with a VCF Operations orchestrator instance that is embedded in VCF Automation, the default
connection does not use an organization-specific URL. Instead, it uses the default VCF Automation host name.
Broadcom 7843

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Token Expiry Behavior
When a host is created with an API token, note the token expiry time in the workflow output. When the API token expires,
you must update the host.

Placement policy Placement policy drives host selection for deployments within

Apply one of the following placement strategies:
• DEFAULT. Places compute resources on random hosts.
• BINPACK. Places compute resources on the most loaded
host that has enough resources to run the given compute.

level, to the cluster or host with the least number of virtual

Using the XML Plug-In
You can use the XML plug-in to run workflows that create and modify XML documents.
The XML plug-in adds an implementation of a Document Object Model (DOM) XML parser to the VCF Operations
orchestrator JavaScript API. The XML plug-in also provides some sample workflows to demonstrate how you can create
and modify XML documents from workflows.
Alternatively, you can use the ECMAScript for XML (E4X) implementation in the VCF Operations orchestrator JavaScript
API to process XML documents directly in JavaScript. For an E4X scripting example, see Developing Workflows with VCF
Operations orchestrator.
For information about E4X, go to the website of the organization that maintains the ECMA-357 standard.

documents for testing purposes.
The workflows can create, read, or modify files, so you must have sufficient access rights to the working directory.

orchestrator

system. If you use the Orchestrator Appliance, the folder is named and is located at .
vco /var/run/vco

JavaScript. See Installing and Configuring VCF Operations orchestrator, Setting Server File System Access from

Getting to Know VCF
To apply this documentation, you must be acquainted with the VCF Product Overview, VCF Design, and VCF Release

VMware Cloud Foundation APIs and SDKs
VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) is a comprehensive solution for building software-defined data centers with compute,
storage, networking, devops, and hybrid cloud management. VMware offers various APIs to help manage your
virtualization infrastructure, VCF, or vSphere Foundation.
VMware developed vCenter in the early 2000s to help customers manage large data centers with many ESX hosts. After
several products that are intended to simplify multi-site management, VMware Cloud Foundation appeared about 20
years later, with SDDC Manager to organize multiple vCenters. Built on top of vCenter, SDDC Manager offers an intuitive
interface to convert, import, and synchronize existing vSphere data centers into an easy-to-manage software-defined data
center (SDDC). In addition, a VCF installer tool is available to help unify and build multi-function vSphere data centers.
VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) provides a unified platform for traditional enterprise and modern applications. Based
on a comprehensive software stack, VCF provides a set of services for compute, storage, network, container, and cloud
management. VCF is a proven infrastructure package that offers efficient operations for private and hybrid clouds.
VMware vSphere Foundation (vSphere Foundation) is an alternative for customers with smaller data centers. It provides
vCenter to manage ESX hosts, but no cloud management features. vSphere Foundation can create an aggregated
infrastructure including compute, storage, and networking, and can manage the infrastructure as a unified operating
environment.
VMware offers various APIs and SDKs to help manage your virtualization infrastructure, some for VCF only, others
for vSphere Foundation as well. APIs help manage components of a data center, such as vCenter, ESX hosts, virtual
machines, aggregated storage, NSX networking, Kubernetes containers, fleet management operations, and VCF
Automation. This publication introduces APIs in VCF release 9.0 and later.

OAuth Token Support for API and CLI Access
As of VCF 9.1, VMware provides unified API and CLI access across most VCF components with OAuth standards-based
token authentication, based on VCF Identity Broker (VIDB). Sample code for vSphere often demonstrates user-password
authentication, however token authentication is more suitable for customers developing automation applications with an
emphasis on security.
Broadcom 7859

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Administrators start in the VCF Operations console with Fleet Management Identity & Access, where they create API
clients and generate API refresh tokens. Then a bearer access token, which is derived from the API refresh token and
transmitted as JSON, can authenticate across all components in a VCF single sign-on (SSO) domain. The previous user-
password authentication method remains available locally.
For VCF Operations, Orchestrator, HCX, and NSX, the flow is as follows. Other VCF components take slightly different
approaches.
1. POST https://{vidb.host}/acs/t/{role}/token
Body: grant_type=...&api_token={vidb_token}
Response: {"access_token": "{bearer_token}"}
2. In API calls, include
Header: Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token}
Some advantages of OAuth:
• Enhanced security by using tokens with limited lifespan instead of passwords.
• Password-less authentication helps customers integrate their tools with VCF.
• Automation scripts can obtain access without being tied to a user.
• Access is delegated and role-limited to prevent accidental or malicious use.
• Token distribution is scalable and efficient.
• Multiple sign-ons are possible with unlimited authentication across datacenters.
OAuth establishes a durable API refresh token which usually lasts for months, though it can be revoked. API clients then
generate a bearer access token, which usually lasts for only minutes. An API client is associated with VCF role(s), but not
with a user, so password sign-in is avoided. Roles can be limited in scope to promote security. VCF components include
vCenter, NSX, VCF Operations, (for logs, for networks, Orchestrator), VCF Operations HCX, and VCF Automation.
VCF Identity Broker (VIDB) can be federated with external identity providers such as Okta and Entra ID. These identity
providers can issue an OAuth bearer access token for federated SSO users. External identity providers exchange their
own ID provider tokens for a VIDB issued bearer access token, and in specific cases, can generate durable API refresh
tokens through a component user interface. For details, see topic "Deployment Modes of the Identity Broker" under VCF
Fleet Management.
Eventually in VCF, every API and CLI should accept OAuth standard VIDB bearer access tokens to authenticate against
VCF components. API clients can be created and audited with specific roles for API and CLI access. As stated before,
traditional login-password methods continue to work, but security conscious customers need not deploy them.
Prerequisites:
• VCF SSO must be enabled in the Fleet for one or more VIDB instances.
• VCF role assignment to VIDB principals: federated users/groups, and VIDB owned API clients.
Implementation of OAuth in VCF
For programmatic access, VCF administrators create and manage API clients, separate from regular users and groups.
Clients acquire an API refresh token and exchange it for a bearer access token, which authorizes actions of client
applications and scripts.
In the VCF Operations user interface under Fleet Management, visit Identity & Access > Manage > VCF SSO Overview >
API Clients. After an API Client is created, click # (three vertical dots) and select Generate API Token. This produces an
API refresh token, which you should retain (copy and paste it into a file) so that the API client can continue exchanging it
for a bearer access token.
For steps to create an API client and generate API refresh tokens using VCF Operations, see "Managing API Clients and
Tokens" in VCF documentation under Fleet Management > Managing Identity. A screenshot of the generate step follows.

Token Exchange Architecture
After creating an API client, the administrator hands off the API refresh token to a client. The API client exchanges it for a
short-duration bearer access token, which then authorizes the actions of client applications and scripts.
Not all VCF components employ identical token authentication methods, but many of them start with VCF Operations and
VCF Identity Broker (VIDB). The following figure shows the architecture of OAuth implementation in VCF.
Broadcom 7862

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Figure 545: Steps for clients to acquire bearer access token from API refresh token
Steps to acquire a bearer access token for authentication:
1. Administrator creates API clients with credentials that are recorded in VIDB.
2. Administrator requests a long-lived API refresh token from the VCF Operations UI.
3. Automation script passes the API refresh token to VIDB and gets a bearer access token in return.
Broadcom 7863

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
4. Automation script uses the bearer access token to authenticate with VCF components.

Tokens for API Clients and SSO Users
In addition to API clients, programmatic access can be arranged for SSO users, as needed for on-demand automation
tasks. For SSO users, tokens fail after a personal account is discontinued. Whereas API clients persist until removed.
The least privilege principle recommends creating separate clients for distinct functions, such as one for Backup and
another for Monitoring. Token permissions are inherited from the access levels assigned to the associated principal (API
client or SSO user) at the VCF level. Administrator privilege for vCenter does not grant administrator privilege at the fleet
level.
Various built-in roles are available for vCenter, VCF Operations, NSX, and VCF Automation. You can also create custom
roles such as vcf-fleet-admin, which enable fleet management operations for API tokens assigned to that role. Built-in and
custom roles may be assigned to an API client. Tokens subsequently generated for an API client inherit the privileges of
those roles. Built-in roles include:
• Identity Management
– identity.management.manage
– identity. management.view
• Certificate Management
– vcf_certificates.manage
– vcf_certificates.view
• Password Management
– vcf_password.manage
Broadcom 7864

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– vcf_password.view
• Fleet Settings (password, NTP, DNS)
– administration.fleetSettings.manage
– administration.fleetSettings.view
• Config Management
– configuration_drifts.manage
– configuration_drifts.view
• Tag Management
– tag_management.assignments
– tag_management.manage
– tag_management.view
• Task Tracking
– ops.administration.management_tasks.manage
– ops.administration.management_tasks.view
– administration.api.read_access
After defining a client, you can generate one or more API refresh tokens for it. When the client makes a call, its API
refresh token goes to VMware Identity Broker (VIDB), which authenticates the client and issues a bearer access token for
making API calls. Here is a token exchange request to the VIDB access control service (ACS):
curl --request POST \
--url https://{vidb-fqdn}/acs/t/{client}/token \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data grant_type=urn:custom:vcf:params:oauth:grant-type:api-token \
--data api_token=vidb_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Obtaining an API Token as an SSO User
Procedure: SSO users log into a VCF Components UI (such as VCF Operations, vCenter, NSX, or VCF Automation) to
generate an API token. The initial API refresh token is exchanged via Identity Broker for a short-lived bearer access token
used for fleet-wide operations. API refresh tokens inherit permissions assigned only at the VCF Fleet level. For example, if
a "vCenter Admin" is only a "VCF Viewer" at the fleet level, the exchanged token grants only Viewer permissions.
VCF SSO API tokens can be generated by an SSO user or under an API client. These tokens have a lifespan ranging
from 30 through 180 days.
SSO User Tokens: Tied directly to personal human accounts and restricted to manually triggered, on-demand activities.
Because these tokens are not used for automated system integrations, their expiration has no impact on background
infrastructure operations. SSO users can simply log into the VCF user interface and manually generate a new one.
API Client Tokens: Highly recommended for use in system-to-system integrations (such as automation pipelines, backups,
or component monitoring). To maintain continuous, uninterrupted system integrations and prevent production connection
failures, VCF SSO provides a dedicated token regeneration API to programmatically cycle these secrets.
By determining the SSO realm ID, creating an API client, assigning to it a role, generating an initial API refresh tokan for
the client, determining its expiration date, and regenerating the token when near expiration, organizations can achieve
password-less continuous system integrations across all VCF components.
Different Patterns for Token Exchange
This topic shows examples of token exchanges with various VCF components.
Most components authenticate directly with VIDB, using the standard header, and return ready-to-use
Authorization
tokens in the response body. However vCenter uses a custom header name, session ID value, and requires client-side
token compression. VCF Automation returns tokens in the response header, and uses HTTP header instead of JSON
parsing.
VCF Operations for networks and VCF Operations for logs cannot exchange tokens with VIDB. They use VCF Operations
as a proxy.
Broadcom 7865

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
It is the responsibility of the VCF administrator to create API clients, assign permissions and roles to clients, and generate
the initial API refresh token for each API client. For procedures to create an API client and generate API refresh tokens
using VCF Operations, see section "Managing API Clients and Tokens" under Fleet Management in VCF documentation.
To generate the API refresh token, VCF Operations has a drop-down menu under the API client name. Other user
interfaces may have a Generate button to click. VCF Automation has a link to generate the API refresh token on the user's
MyAccount page.
For specific instructions, go to one of these topics:
• Token Exchange for VCF Operations
• Token Exchange for vCenter
• Token Exchange for VCF Automation
• Token Exchange for NSX
• Token Exchange VCF Orchestrator for networks
• Token Exchange VCF Orchestrator for logs
Token Exchange for VCF Operations
Many VCF components perform token exchange using VCF Operations communicating with VIDB, or follow a similar
workflow.
VCF Operations, VCF Operations Orchestrator, VCF Operations HCX, and NSX networking use a flow that exchanges an
API refresh token directly for a bearer access token:
1. POST /acs/t/CUSTOMER/token
Body: grant_type=...&api_token={vidb_token}
Response: {"access_token": "{bearer_token}"}
2. in API Calls
Header: Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token}
Here is an example showing the API to exchange the VIDB Token for an API access token.
curl --request POST \
--url https://{vidb-fqdn}/acs/t/{client-name}/token \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data grant_type=urn:custom:vcf:params:oauth:grant-type:api-token \
--data 'api_token={apiToken}'
For detailed procedures to create API clients and generate API refresh tokens, among other tasks, see Managing API
Clients and Tokens in the Fleet Management section of the VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 guide for VCF Operations.
Token Exchange for vCenter
With vCenter, the client must perform base64 decode, compression, and base64 encode.
gzip
# Input: SAML token (base64 string)
saml_token="PD94bWwgdmVyc2lvbj0iMS4wIiBlbmNvZGluZz0iVVRGLTgiPz4..."
# Required processing:
compressed_token=$(echo "$saml_token" | base64 -d | gzip | base64 -w0)
# Output: Compressed token ready for session creation
Flow for vCenter with multi-step exchange and compression:
1. POST /acs/t/CUSTOMER/token → Bearer Access Token (response body)
2. POST /api/vcenter/authentication/token → SAML Token (response body)
3. Client processing: base64 decode → gzip compress → base64 encode
4. POST /api/session → Session ID (response body)
5. API Calls with header: vmware-api-session-id: {session_id}
Broadcom 7866

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Token Exchange for VCF Automation
With VCF Automation token exchange, the token must be extracted from the response header, not the response body.
Request and response:
POST /cloudapi/1.0.0/sessions/provider
Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token};org=system
Accept: application/json;version=9.1.0
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-VMWARE-VCLOUD-ACCESS-TOKEN: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
Content-Type: application/json
{
"user": "administrator@system",
"org": "System"
}
Flow for VCF Automation with multi-step exchange and token in response header:
1. POST /acs/t/CUSTOMER/token → Bearer Access Token (response body)
2. POST /cloudapi/1.0.0/sessions/provider → Session Token (response header)
Header: Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token};org=system
Response Header: X-VMWARE-VCLOUD-ACCESS-TOKEN: {session_token}
3. API Calls with header: Authorization: Bearer {session_token}

If you are a federated SSO user and granted NSX access, you can generate an API refresh token and exchange it for a

2. On the NSX Home page, click Generate API Tokens from the drop-down menu under the profile name.
3. On the VCF Identity Broker page, click Generate to create an API refresh token.
4. After obtaining an API refresh token, exchange it with a bearer access token for API calls.
1. POST /acs/t/CUSTOMER/token
Body: grant_type=...&api_token={vidb_token}
Response: {"access_token": "{bearer_token}"}
2. in API Calls
Header: Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token}
Token Exchange for HCX
If you are a federated SSO user, you can generate an API refresh token and exchange it for a bearer access token to
authenticate public APIs in VCF Operations HCX.
1. Log in to VCF Operations as an administrator, providing a username and password.
2. On the API Access page, click Generate API Tokens from the drop-down menu under the profile name.
3. On the VCF Identity Broker page, click Generate to create an API refresh token.
4. After obtaining an API refresh token, exchange it with a bearer access token for API calls.
1. POST /acs/t/CUSTOMER/token
Body: grant_type=...&api_token={vidb_token}
Response: {"access_token": "{bearer_token}"}
2. in API Calls
Header: Authorization: Bearer {bearer_token}
Broadcom 7867

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Token Exchange VCF Operations for networks
VCF Operations for networks and VCF Operations for logs follow the same steps as VCF Operations, except they also
exchange a JWT token from VCF Operations.
1. Get a bearer access token by generating it from VIDB.
curl --request POST \
--url https://acs/t/CUSTOMER/token \
--header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data grant_type=urn:custom:vcf:params:oauth:grant-type:api-token \
--data api_token={API_REFRESH_TOKEN
The bearer access token appears in the response body, along with .
serviceKeys
Body: {"serviceKeys": ["ops-ni"]}
2. Exchange the bearer access token for a JWT token (for logs, use ).
ops-li
curl --request POST \
'{vcfops_url}/suite-api/api/auth/token/exchange?includeServiceDetails=false' \
-H 'accept: application/json' \
-H 'Authorization: VIDBToken {ACCESS_TOKEN_FROM_STEP_1}' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{ "serviceKeys": [ "ops-ni" ] }'
3. Use that JWT token to call the public API (for logs, the bearer label changes).
curl --request GET \
--url '{ops4netwk_url}/api/v2/fields' \
--header 'Bearer: {JWT_FROM_STEP_2}'
Token Exchange VCF Operations for logs
Token exchange in VCF Operations for logs follows the same steps as VCF Operations for networks, except for minor
differences summarized here.
1. Get a bearer access token by generating a token from VIDB, as above.
2. In step 2, substitute "li" (log insight) for "ni" (network insight)
-d '{ "serviceKeys": [ "ops-li" ] }'
3. Exchange the bearer access token for a JWT token, as above. But in step 3, advertise JWT instead of Bearer token.
curl --request GET \
--url '{ops2logs_url}/api/v2/fields' \
--header 'X-JWT-TOKEN: {JWT_FROM_STEP_2}'

Core vSphere APIs
The user interface enables administrators to manage vSphere by calling various vSphere APIs to perform backend
operations. Two main sets of APIs provide core vSphere management capabilities: VIM and vAPI.
The vAPI (vSphere Automation API) uses REST principles with JSON-based protocols, providing a simpler interface
for automation. The VIM API, on the other hand, follows RPC principles and uses a SOAP protocol, offering broader
functionality and compatibility with previous vSphere versions.
More recently, VI/JSON enables VIM-like operations over a JSON transport.
The core functional areas can be viewed as configuration and management of hosts, virtual machines, and networks, as
well as storage at an abstract level. The two core APIs that address these functional areas complement each other both
in function and in design principles. As the code samples under Tagging Examples Using vSphere APIs demonstrate, you
can use the two APIs together to achieve complete functionality.
vSphere Automation API
The VMware vSphere Automation SDK is optimized for developing applications that use major vSphere features such as
virtual machine management, content libraries, resource deployment, tagging, and managing security certificates.
The vSphere Automation API follows a resource-based REST architecture with native JSON requests and responses.
Clients can use the following technologies to send requests to vSphere Automation endpoints:
• Java SDK
• Python SDK
• REST
• PowerCLI™
Additional language bindings are available through open-source projects on GitHub.
The vSphere Automation API currently provides core features including:
• Federated authentication with support for AD FS and Okta.
• VMware vSphere Lifecycle Manager supports desired-state management of hosts in a cluster.
• The content library feature manages templating, storage, and deployment of virtual machines and vApps.
• Metadata tagging of vSphere objects facilitates filtering and sorting of objects when managing large data centers.
• Management of security certificates issued by the VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) or third-party and custom-
made certificates in your environment.
Most major new vSphere features are introduced through the Automation API.
Broadcom 7870

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Automation API supports two protocols: JSON-RPC, used by the Automation SDKs, and a simplified JSON protocol
for REST clients. The SDKs are available for download from Broadcom.
The Automation API service endpoint is
https://{domain}/api/{service}
where is the server's IP address or fully qualified domain name, and is the name of a specific
{domain} {service}
interface.
For example, you can reach the Session service through the following URL:
https://<vCenter_IPaddr_or_FQDN>/api/session
