vSphere Web Services API
The vSphere Web Services API (VIM API) provides programmatic access to essential resources for building robust,
fault-tolerant virtualized applications across compute, networking, and storage. It supports resource types such as virtual
machines, ESX hosts, clusters, datastores, networks, and system abstractions including events, alarms, authorization,
and plug-in extensions.
The vSphere Web Services API is a mature, comprehensive management interface that operates with both ESX and
vCenter. It provides access to a hierarchy of managed objects used to configure, monitor, and manage data center
resources. Formerly called VIM API, a name that started with for version 2.5 and still exists in the SDK source tree.
vim25
Developers have several options for accessing the VIM API:
• vSphere Management SDK (Java): Provides Java bindings and samples that use SOAP.
• pyvmomi SDK (Python): An SDK that provides bindings and utilities for Python developers interacting with the VIM
API.
• The open source govmomi SDK is a comprehensive set of bindings, utilities, examples, and a CLI for Go developers.
• WSDL Code Generation (Language-neutral): The vSphere Management SDK supplies language-neutral WSDL files
for the SOAP protocol, enabling you to generate client bindings in your preferred language.
• OpenAPI Specification (Language-neutral): The vSphere Management SDK includes a language-neutral OpenAPI
specification, allowing you to generate code for a REST-like JSON protocol in your chosen language.
The vSphere Web Services API includes the following core features:
• Data center inventory management, using a hierarchy of folders and resource objects
• A powerful server-side data retrieval feature, the Property Collector
• Host system configuration and management
• Datastore configuration and management
• Network configuration and management
• Virtual machine configuration and management, including guest OS operations
• Virtual machine encryption
• Cluster and resource pool configuration and management
• Management of events and alarms
The vSphere Web Services API is included in the vSphere Management SDK. Both support either a SOAP-XML RPC
protocol or a JSON-based protocol. The Management SDK provides RPC stubs for clients with Java language bindings.
The vSphere Web Services API endpoint is
https://{domain}/sdk
The VI/JSON protocol service endpoint is
Broadcom 7871

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
http://{domain}/sdk/vim25/8.0.1.0
For more information, see the following documentation.
• vSphere Web Services SDK Developer Setup Guide
• vSphere Web Services SDK Programming Guide
Python with pyvmomi
For Python programmers, offers an open-source Python binding for vSphere Management and Automation
pyvmomi
APIs.
The package provides a convenience layer on top of the core VIM API and the following related extension APIs
pyvmomi
that use the SOAP/XML protocol:
• ESX Agent Manager (EAM)
• Storage Based Policy Management (SPBM)
• Storage Monitoring Service (SMS)
• Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management (VSLM)
The package is notable for:
pyvmomi
• Simplified approach to connection, authentication, and retrieval of the ServiceContent object
• Module to handle client-server synchronization and asynchronous task tracking
• Convenient retrieval of managed object properties
• Facility to interface with vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO)
For more information about using the , see documentation in the VCF SDK.
pyvmomi
Supplementary vSphere APIs
Supplementary vSphere APIs enhance the core APIs with several extensions that provide specialized capabilities for
managing specific areas of your cloud infrastructure.
The vSAN API
The vSAN management API is a Web service (like VIM) that runs on both vCenter and ESX systems. The API provides
access to methods that you can use to configure and manage vSAN storage. VMware vSAN is a distributed software layer
that aggregates local storage devices to create a shared storage pool across hosts in a cluster.
The vSAN API centers around a small set of managed objects, around 30. Methods associated with these managed
objects allow developers to set up and configure all aspects of vSAN, query runtime state, and check storage health.
The vSAN API can be used for solution integration, allowing you to configure and monitor vSAN disk clusters and related
services on ESX hosts and vCenter instances. It also manages virtual disk functions such as mounting, partitioning,
secure erasing, and snapshots.
Functional features of the vSAN API include:
• Cluster configuration and query methods.
• Stretched cluster configuration and query methods.
• Performance, health, and diagnostics.
• Virtual disk formatting and space usage queries.
• Software upgrade handling.
• Cloud Native Storage (CNS): a Tanzu feature that helps Kubernetes provision storage on-demand, and provides
visibility into container volumes through the vSphere Client UI.
• VMware Live Site (and Cyber) Recovery are optional data backup products offering self-service data protection and
fast recovery of business-critical data by saving virtual machines to a remote cloud location.
Broadcom 7872

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The vSAN API uses a SOAP-XML RPC protocol, modeled after the vSphere Web Services (VIM) API, and is included as
part of the vSphere Management SDK.
The vSAN API service endpoints for ESX and vCenter are:
https://{domain}/vsan
https://{domain}/vsanHealth
For more information, see the following documentation.
• vSAN SDKs Programming Guide: mostly Python code examples
• vSAN Data Protection SDK for Python
• vSAN Data Protection SDK for Java
• REST API for vSAN Snapshot Service
Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management API
The Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management (VSLM) API is a Web service integrated into vCenter, operating as part of the
Storage Policy Services (SPS). This API allows you to connect to the VSLM endpoint to access information about First
Class Disks (FCDs). In addition to VSLM, SPS also encompasses Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM) and the
Storage Management Service (SMS).
First class disks, also called improved virtual disks (IVD), are disks not associated with a virtual machine. FCD simplifies
management of stand-alone virtual disks, avoiding creation of a dummy VM with one or a few attached disks. Snapshots
worked on a per-VM basis, and to snapshot a single virtual disk formerly required configuration overhead. VSLM allows
snapshot of just an FCD.
FCD offers full lifecycle management of virtual storage objects, independent of any VM. VSLM APIs are able to create,
delete, snapshot, backup, restore, and do other lifecycle tasks on VMDK objects without requiring VM attachment.
An FCD is identified by UUID and human readable name. The UUID is globally unique and the primary identifier. The
UUID remains valid even if a snapshot is taken or its FCD relocated by XvMotion.
The VSLM API uses a SOAP-XML RPC protocol, modeled after the vSphere Web Services (VIM) API, and is included as
part of the vSphere Management SDK.
The VSLM API endpoint is
https://{domain}/vslm
For more information, see the following documentation.
• Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management API
Storage Policy Based Management API
The Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM) API is an extension of the Web Services (VIM) API. Storage policies
simplify the task of matching available storage to virtual machines.
A vSphere storage profile defines storage policy information that describes storage requirements for virtual machines and
storage capabilities of storage providers. You use the VMware Storage Policy API to manage the association between
virtual machines and datastores.
With appropriate policies, SPBM governs virtual machine placement into appropriate datastore, accounting for RAID
levels, pre-zeroed allocated disk, and space efficient thin provisioned disk. Storage policies may also request specific data
services for virtual disks, such as caching, replication, and deduplication.
The Storage Policy API supports the following capabilities:
• Access to vSphere storage profiles and to entities associated with profiles
• Compliance checking of profiles and entities
• Placement compatibility checking
The Storage Policy API uses a SOAP-XML RPC protocol, similar to the vSphere Web Services (VIM) API. It is bundled in
the vSphere Management SDK. The Management SDK provides RPC stubs for clients with Java language bindings.
Broadcom 7873

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The Storage Policy service endpoint is
https://{domain}/pbm
For more information, see the following documentation:
• VMware Storage Policy API
Storage Monitoring Service API
The Storage Monitoring Service (SMS) API provides methods to retrieve information about available storage topology,
capabilities, and state.
The vSphere API for Storage Awareness (VASA) permits storage arrays to integrate with vCenter for management
functionality. VASA providers expose features of the physical storage devices, such as storage health status, configuration
info, and storage capacity.
SMS establishes and maintains connections with VASA providers. SMS retrieves information about storage availability
from the providers, and clients can use the SMS API to perform the following operations.
• Identify VASA providers.
• Retrieve information about storage arrays.
• Identify vSphere inventory entities (hosts and datastores) which are associated with external storage entities on the
storage arrays.
The SMS API uses a SOAP-XML RPC protocol, modeled after the vSphere Web services (VIM) API, and is included as
part of the vSphere Management SDK.
The SMS API endpoint is
https://{domain}/sms
For more information, see the following documentation.
• vCenter Storage Monitoring Service API
ESX Agent Manager
You can add functions to vSphere by developing software applications that you register as vCenter extensions. A vSphere
Solution is an extension that registers with vCenter and implements some or all of the extension features of the vSphere
API.
You can deploy a solution as an Open Virtualization Format (OVF) package, with optional VMware vSphere Installation
Bundles (VIB). You can also install solutions by using an installer, such as Windows Installer (MSI) or RPM Package
Manager. Most of the extension functions in this API are independent of the technology that you use to deploy a solution.
If you deploy a solution by using OVF, you can use the vCenter Extension vService to simplify the registration of the
solution with vCenter.
You can create two types of vSphere solutions:
• A vService is a service that a solution provides to specific applications that run inside virtual machines and vApps. A
solution can provide several types of vServices. Virtual machines or vApps can have dependencies on several types of
vServices.
• A vSphere ESX agent is a virtual machine and an optional vSphere Installation Bundle (VIB) that extends the functions
of an ESX host to provide additional services that a vSphere solution requires.
The vService Manager and ESX Agent Manager are pre-built solutions that are part of the vCenter Extensions
functionality within the vCenter.
vSphere ESX Agent Manager is an intermediary between vCenter and a solution with two key aspects:
• provisioning agent virtual machines and VIB modules for the solution onto a scope in vCenter
• monitoring changes to the agent virtual machines and scope in vCenter, and reporting them back to the solution
Broadcom 7874

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
vSphere ESX Agent Manager exposes a SOAP-based API similar to the VIM API, that solutions use to register and
monitor agents. The SDK includes a Model-View-Controller framework and library functions for developing vSphere
extensions that interface with the vSphere Web Services (VIM) API. It is bundled in the vSphere Management SDK.
The EAM service endpoint is
https://{domain}/eam/sdk
For more information about using the ESX Agent Manager, see the following publication:
• Developing and Deploying vSphere Solutions, vServices, and ESX Agents
vCenter Management API
You can use the vCenter Management API to automate management tasks for vCenter. Instead of managing data center
infrastructure, these interfaces manage the vCenter instance itself.
Features of the vCenter Management API include:
• Installation and Setup
• Configuration
• Patching and Upgrade
• Backup and Restore
The vCenter Management API uses a REST JSON RPC protocol, associated with the Automation API. It is available for
download in the vSphere Automation SDKs.
For most operations, the vCenter Management API uses the following service endpoint, where is the name of
{service}
a specific service interface.
https://{domain}/api/{service}
During setup, until networking is configured and the service is available on port 443, the vCenter Management API uses
the 5480 service endpoint:
https://{domain}:5480/api/{service}
For more information about using the vCenter Management API, see the following publications:
• vCenter Management topics in the vSphere Automation REST API Programming Guide
• vCenter vCenterManagement topics in the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs Programming Guide
• Related interfaces in the vSphere Automation SDKs Programming Guide
vCenter Single Sign-On API
The vCenter Single Sign-On API is a programming interface for secure communications with vCenter Single Sign-On
service.
The vCenter Single Sign-On (SSserver provides a Security Token Service (STS). A token uses the Security Assertion
Markup Language (SAML), which is an XML encoding of authentication data.
vCenter Single Sign-On authentication can use the following identity store technologies:
• Windows Active Directory
• OpenLDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
• Local user accounts (vCenter Single Sign-On server resident on the vCenter machine)
• vCenter Single Sign-On user accounts
This API defines a set of request operations that correspond to the WS-Trust 1.4 bindings:
• Issue – Obtains a token from a vCenter Single Sign-On server.
• Renew – Renews an existing token.
• Validate – Validates an existing token.
• Challenge – Part of a negotiation with a vCenter Single Sign-On server to obtain a token.
Broadcom 7875

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
The vCenter Single Sign-On SDK includes Java bindings for the vCenter Single Sign-On WSDL. The SDK also contains
sample code that demonstrates client-side support for the WSSecurityPolicy standard. Security policies specify the
elements that provide SOAP message security. To secure SOAP messages, a client inserts digital signatures, certificates,
and SAML tokens into the SOAP headers for vCenter Single Sign-On requests. The Java sample includes a JAX-WS
implementation of SOAP header methods that support the vCenter Single Sign-On security policies.
The Single Sign-On service endpoint is
https://{domain}/STS/STSService
For more information about using the vCenter Single Sign-On API, see the following documentation:
• vCenter Single Sign-On Programming Guide
Virtual Disk API
The Virtual Disk API provides methods for backup and recovery, cloning, and other operations on virtual disks.
The Virtual Disk API can connect to local or network virtual disks, either for ESX or hosted applications.
The Virtual Disk API supports the following functions:
• Create, open, close, and delete virtual disks
• Read and write both data and metadata
• Grow, shrink, and defragment virtual disks
• Manage virtual disk snapshot chains
• Quiesce virtual machine access and flush buffers
• Clone virtual disks
The Virtual Disk API is provided as a C language library, running in-process as part of user-defined utility software. It is
often used in conjunction with Java-based vStorage APIs for Data Protection (VADP) for developing backup applications.
The Virtual Disk API is available as part of the Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK).
For more information about the Virtual Disk API, see the Virtual Disk Development Kit Programming Guide.
VKS (vSphere Kubernetes Service) Programming
VKS (vSphere Kubernetes Service) is included with VCF, providing self-service operations for developers working with
Kubernetes containers.
VKS provides self-service lifecycle management of Kubernetes workload clusters. VKS with Supervisor runs with vSphere
and integrates with underlying infrastructure including ESX, vCenter, cloud native storage, and virtual networking. Using
VKS, developers can provision standard Kubernetes clusters and can receive upstream package refreshes.
VCF Automation provides an additional layer for service administrators to make life easier for tenant organization,
especially DevOps programmers setting up Kubernetes clusters with minimal assistance. Although not documented here,
service administrators can deploy Terraform for further automation.
VKS management allows vSphere administrators to control VKS clusters, possibly of different versions, running on
various platforms. Admins download the VKS Management Proxy YAML manifest, upload it as a new service in vCenter,
enable it on a , and finally verify service health. DevOps programmers can request Kubernetes containers by
host:port
creating a YAML (example below) and running .
kubectlapply
kind: Cluster
metadata:
name: test-cluster
namespace: test-namespace
nodes:
- role: control-plane
extraPortMappings:
- containerPort: 30080
hostPort: 30070
Broadcom 7876

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
For developer-oriented reference documentation about VKS, see VCF 9.1 APIs > VCF Automation APIs > VMware
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) on the developer.broadcom.com website. The API reference documentation
is organized by packages and resource types, which describe the mandatory and optional fields that constitute the
declarative YAML descriptions for cluster management.
For administrator-oriented documentation about VKS, see vSphere Supervisor Services and Standalone Components
on the techdocs.broadcom.com website. You sometimes see the acronym VKSM, an abbreviation for VKS cluster
Management, which is the same thing as VKS.
API Design Standards
• Write APIs are usually declarative, supporting the command.
kubectlapply
• For read-only objects, write methods are rejected by role-based access control (RBAC).
• All APIs support pagination, and return generic read-only metadata fields, including UID, Generation, and
resourceVersion if applicable.
• Status follows the Kubernetes pattern of phase, conditions, and other fields as needed.
• All APIs support labels and annotations. System labels are in format:
mgmt.k8s.vmware.com/<key>: <value>
• APIs support standard Kubernetes label selectors (for 9.1) and field selectors (for 9.2). System labels should be added
for any fields that are commonly used for filtering.
– Fields in must be added as system labels to any filter resources that use label
spec.selector.matchNames
selectors. Example:
kubectl get clusterresources -l mgmt.k8s.vmware.com/cluster=cl-01
– Other fields in and that can be used as field selectors should be mentioned in documentation.
spec status
Example:
kubectl get clusters --field-selector status.health!=HEALTHY
– If set-based filtering is required on a field, a system label should be added for ease of filtering using a label selector.
Example:
kubectl get clusterresources -l mgmt.k8s.vmware.com/object-kind (Deployment, DaemonSet)

vSphere Add-On SDKs
Add-on API layers are available for some popular vSphere APIs. Open-source communities can contribute new language
bindings or usability improvements.
Additionally, Broadcom offers many stand-alone SDKs. Two prominent ones are the vSphere Client SDK, used to
develop plug-ins and user interfaces for the vSphere Client, and , the Python virtual machine object managment
pyvmomi
interface, Guest SDK.
Go Language with govmomi
For Go language programmers, is a library for interacting with the VMware Web Services API for ESX and
govmomi
vCenter.
The code in the package is a wrapper for the code that is generated from the vSphere API description. It
govmomi
primarily provides convenience functions for working with the vSphere API:
• Generated types, managed objects, and methods for the complete VIM API
• Client structure that abstracts a session and its immutable state
• Session Manager abstraction that allows a user to login and logout
• Wrappers for a selection of managed objects
• Generated coverage for some other SOAP-based APIs, such as SMS, SPBM, and vSAN
• Partial coverage for the vSphere Automation API
For more information about using , see the following documentation:
govmomi

Authentication with vSphere APIs
This chapter provides an overview of authentication options for vSphere users. You can use basic authentication or SAML
token-based authentication to access vSphere APIs.
Because it is the simplest method, this guide uses basic authentication to access vSphere APIs in the following chapters.
Broadcom 7884

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
You can use both the vSphere Management APIs and the vSphere Automation API to manage your vSphere environment.
With the VMware Cloud Foundation Java and Python SDKs, you gain access to a wider range of supported automation
features. Use the:
• vSphere Management APIs for host management, virtual machine provisioning, data center monitoring, virtual storage
management, and more.
• vSphere Automation APIs for configuration, authentication, certificate management, tagging, lifecycle management,
content libraries, Kubernetes cluster management, and more.
Choosing Your Identity Source
To administer vSphere users and groups, you must first choose your identity source. You can either:
Use the vCenter built-in vSphere comes with a built-in identity provider, called vCenter Single Sign-On. By default, vCenter uses
identity source the vsphere.local domain as the identity source (but you can change this domain during installation).
A vCenter Single Sign-On administrator can manage users and groups in the vsphere.local domain
from the vSphere Client. You can configure the vCenter built-in identity provider to use Active Directory
(AD) as its identity source using LDAPS, OpenLDAP, and Integrated Windows Authentication (IWA). Such
configurations allow customers to log into vCenter using their Active Directory or LDAP accounts.
Use an external identity In vSphere 7.0 and later, you can outsource identity management to an external identity provider through
provider as the identity federated authentication. You replace vCenter as the identity provider and the administration of users and
groups occurs on the external identity source. When you configure vSphere to use an external identity
source
provider, the external identity provider interacts with the identity sources on behalf of vCenter .
You can federate vCenter to the following external identity providers:
• Active Directory Federated Service (ADFS), starting in vSphere 7.0
• Okta, starting in vSphere 8.0 Update 1
• Microsoft Entra AD, starting in vSphere 8.0 Update 2
For more information on vSphere identity sources and identity management, see the topic "Authentication Mechanisms" in
the vSphere Automation REST API chapter.
Obtaining an Identifier and Unified Session
Before using the API services, principals must first obtain session identifiers for the vSphere Management API and the
vSphere Automation API. Valid session identifiers guarantee the identity of the principals and establish trust with the API
endpoints.
To obtain a session identifier for the vSphere APIs, you can use different authentication mechanisms, as covered below.
Once obtained, the session identifier is sent with every HTTPS request, or added to the security context for authentication.
Before vSphere 8.0 Update 3, separate sessions were required for vSphere Management API and for vSphere
Automation API. As of vSphere 8.0 U3, unified sessions are supported. Now, developers can re-use a vSphere
Management (VIM) session for vSphere Automation (vAPI) calls, and vice versa. See Unified Management and
Automation Session for details and code examples.
Starting with VCF 9.1, client applications can access vSphere APIs without first obtaining a session identifier. Instead,
pass a VIDB Bearer Access Token (VAT) directly in the HTTP header. Your existing vCenter
Authorization: Bearer
RBAC permissions apply when using OAuth bearer access token authentication. This approach eliminates the token-to-
session exchange step that is required in previous releases and is recommended for new automation workflows.
For APIs that maintain server-side state across multiple calls (for example, Property Collectors and Event Collectors),
vCenter returns a Server-side State Cookie ( ) on the first request. Include this cookie alongside
vmware-vsphere-state
the bearer access token in subsequent API calls to preserve the stateful session context.
Choosing Your Authentication Method
To obtain a session identifier, you can choose among several authentication mechanisms depending on your needs and
requirements. Simply stated, these mechanisms can be divided in two major groups: basic authentication and token-
based authentication.
Broadcom 7885

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Basic Authentication
With basic authentication, you supply your vCenter or external provider user name and password when connecting to the
vSphere Management or vSphere Automation endpoints.
• If you use the built-in vCenter identity source, you connect with your local domain credentials.
• With an external identity source, use your identity provider credentials to connect to the vSphere API endpoints. This
workflow is possible thanks to the OAuth 2.0 Password grant type.
For more information, see these topics:
• Authenticate to vCenter with vCenter Single Sign-On Credentials in the VMware vSphere Automation REST API
chapter.
• Authenticate by Using the Password Grant Type in the VMware vSphere Automation REST API chapter.
• Create a vSphere Automation Session with User Credentials in the VMware vSphere Automation SDKs chapter.
Note:
Use token-based authentication. It provides stronger security and greater flexibility for client applications.
SAML Token-Based Authentication
With token-based authentication, principals issue a token request to the vCenter Single Sign-On built-in service. In
response, vCenter Single Sign-On issues a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) token that principals use to
obtain session identifiers for the vSphere Management API and the vSphere Automation API.
Obtaining a SAML token You can obtain a SAML token by using either the Issue service of the vSphere Management API or the
AuthenticationToken service of the vSphere Automation API. For more information, see these
topics:
• "Authenticate to an AD FS-Federated vCenter by Using the Authorization Code Grant Type" in the
VMware vSphere Automation REST API chapter.
• "Acquiring a SAML Token from a vCenter Single Sign-On Server" in the vCenter Single Sign-On
chapter.
• "Retrieve a SAML Token" in the VMware vSphere Automation SDKs chapter.
Important:
If you are using an external identity provider as the identity source, you must first obtain a JSON
Web Token (JWT) from the identity provider and then exchange it for a SAML token. For more
information, see the topic "Authenticate to an AD FS-Federated vCenter by Using the Authorization
Code Grant Type" in the VMware vSphere Automation REST API chapter.
Creating a Session with After you receive the SAML token, you use it to obtain a session identifier from the vSphere API endpoints.
the SAML Token • For the vSphere Management API, use the LoginByToken service (in SessionManager).
• For the vSphere Automation API, use the CISSession service.
Once you have obtained a session identifier, you can use it for authentication in your subsequent calls or in your security
context.
Note:
Before vSphere 8.0 U3, you had to create separate authentication sessions for the vSphere Management API and
the vSphere Automation API. That is, you needed a separate session identifier for each of the APIs. With a unified
session, this is no longer necessary.
For more information, see chapter "Authentication Mechanisms" in the VMware vSphere Automation REST API chapter
and "LoginByToken Example" in the vCenter Single Sign-On chapter.
Unified Management and Automation Session
As of vSphere 8.0 Update 3, developers can re-use a vSphere Management (VIM) session for making vSphere
Automation (vAPI) calls, or re-use a vAPI session for making VIM calls. Examples follow.
Broadcom 7886

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Here is a Python code example to establish a vSphere Automation (vAPI) session to then invoke a vSphere Management
(VIM) call:
import requests
from pyVim.connect import SmartConnect
from vmware.vapi.vsphere.client import create_vsphere_client
vc_host = '10.168.203.112'
user = 'Administrator@vsphere.local'
password = 'NKCF_n4PagP0jmz_'
# vAPI setup
session = requests.session()
session.verify = False
client = create_vsphere_client(vc_host, user, password, session=session)
# Acquire session_id
session_id = client.get_session_id()
# Reuse session_id in SmartConnect
si = SmartConnect(host=vc_host,
port=443,
disableSslCertValidation=True,
sessionId=session_id)
content = si.RetrieveContent()
dc_moref = content.rootFolder.CreateDatacenter("TEST")
print(dc_moref)
Here is a Python code example to establish a vSphere Management (VIM) session to then invoke a vSphere Automation
(vAPI) call:
import requests
from pyVim.connect import SmartConnect
from vmware.vapi.vsphere.client import create_vsphere_client
vc_host = '10.168.203.112'
user = 'Administrator@vsphere.local'
password = 'NKCF_n4PagP0jmz_'
# Login with pyvmomi
si = SmartConnect(host=vc_host,
port=443,
user=user,
pwd=password,
disableSslCertValidation=True)
# TODO GetSessionId documentation
session_id = si._GetStub().GetSessionId()
# vAPI setup
session = requests.session()
session.verify = False
client = create_vsphere_client(vc_host, session=session, session_id=session_id)
print(client.vcenter.compute.Policies.list())

Here are example Curl commands to establish a VIM session via JSON, make a vAPI call, and then call the REST tag
API. The second and third are get requests and do not apply anything. The second command returns a list of folders. The
third returns a list of tags for folder .
group-d3
$ curl "https://$VC/sdk/vim25/8.0.2.0/SessionManager/SessionManager/Login"
-H 'Content-Type: application/json'
-d '{"userName": "Administrator@vsphere.local", "password": "$PSWD"}' -ki

-H "vmware-api-session-id: $VIM_SESSION" -k

$ curl "https://$VC/sdk/vim25/8.0.2.0/Folder/group-d1001/tag"
-H "vmware-api-session-id: $VAPI_SESSION" -k
The following caveats and limitations apply to unified VIM/vAPI sessions:
• Session timeout can be configured with property in file
config.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout /etc/vmware-
on vCenter, or using the vSphere Client UI.
vpx/vpx.conf
• Default session lifespan can be configured with property , also in , or
vpx.sso.sts.tokenLifetime vpx.conf
using the vSphere Client UI.
• The maximum number of inflight sessions can be configured with property
, also in , or using the vSphere Client UI.
config.vmacore.soap.maxSessionCount vpx.conf
• Session IDs from either endpoint work in the other endpoint. Clients that want the benefit of a single session should
adjust to accept variable-size Session ID tokens.

Basic Authentication Using pyvmomi
The SDK simplifies code for connecting to the VIM endpoint by using a function that accepts
pyvmomi SmartConnect
basic user credentials, opens a session with the server, and returns the object.
ServiceInstance ServiceInstance
contains references to specific managed objects needed to use VIM API features.
The object contains interface stubs for all Automation API endpoints. This code excerpt shows a
vsphere_client
function that connects to both the VIM endpoint and the Automation API endpoint and returns both the
vsphere_client
object and the object.
ServiceInstance
hostname = 'vc1.example.com'
username = 'administrator@vsphere.local'
password = 'TooSecret2C!'
from pyVim.connect import SmartConnect
from vmware.vapi.vsphere.client import create_vsphere_client, VsphereClient
import requests, urllib3
import sys
from pyVmomi import vim
def connect(host: str, user: str, pwd: str, insecure: bool) -> tuple[VsphereClient, vim.ServiceInstance]:
session = requests.session()
if insecure:
session.verify = False
urllib3.disable_warnings(urllib3.exceptions.InsecureRequestWarning)
print('Creating an Automation API session.')
vsphere_client = create_vsphere_client(host, user, pwd, session=session)
print('Creating a VIM/SOAP session.')
si = SmartConnect(host=host,
user=user,
pwd=pwd,
disableSslCertValidation=insecure)
return vsphere_client, si
(vsphere_client, service_instance) = connect(hostname,
username,
password,
insecure=True)
At this point, your session is established and the session ID is stored in a cookie that will be passed along with future
requests.

Tagging the Folder with Automation API for Python
To tag a folder, start by creating a tag category, then create a tag in that category, and finally attach the tag to the folder.
...
# Interface factory object:
stub_config = vsphere_client._stub_config
print('Automation API creating a tag category.')
from com.vmware.vapi.std_client import DynamicID
from com.vmware.cis.tagging_client import Category, CategoryModel, Tag, TagAssociation
import com.vmware.vapi.std.errors_client
category_id = None
tag_id = None
category_stub = Category(stub_config)
tc_create_spec = category_stub.CreateSpec(name='hello_category',
description = 'example of tagging category from pyvmomi',
cardinality = CategoryModel.Cardinality.MULTIPLE,
associable_types = set(['Folder']))
try:
category_id = category_stub.create(tc_create_spec)
except com.vmware.vapi.std.errors_client.AlreadyExists as oops:
print(oops)
print('Please delete category from Tags & Custom Attributes and try again.\n')
sys.exit(1)
print('New category created: ', category_id)
print('VAPI creating a tag in new category.')
tag_stub = Tag(stub_config)
tag_create_spec = tag_stub.CreateSpec(name='hello_tag',
description= 'example of a tag',
category_id=category_id)
try:
tag_id = tag_stub.create(tag_create_spec)
except errors_client.NotFound as oops:
print('Exception: \n', oops, '\n')
sys.exit(1)
print('New tag created: ', tag_id)
print('VAPI creating association of tag with Hello Folder.')
dynamic_id = DynamicID(type='Folder',
id=vim_moref_to_moid(hello_folder))
tag_association_stub = TagAssociation(stub_config)
tag_association_stub.attach(tag_id=tag_id,
object_id=dynamic_id)
print('Tag attached to folder.')

Tagging the Hello World Folder with the Automation API Through REST
To tag a folder, start by creating a tag category, then create a tag in that category, and finally associate the tag with the
folder.
1. Create a tag category.
echo 'Using REST to create tag category.'
BODY='{"name": "hello_category",
"description": "A tag category for custom folders",
"cardinality": "SINGLE",
"associable_types": ["Folder"]}'
CAT_ID=$(curl -k \
-X POST \
-H "vmware-api-session-id: $VAPI_SESSION_ID" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d "$BODY" \
"https://$VC/api/cis/tagging/category" \
| xargs -t)
The response contains the details of the newly created tag category, including its UUID.
2. Create a tag in that category. Use the tag category ID you created in the previous step.
Broadcom 7899

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
echo 'Using REST to create tag.'
BODY='{"name": "hello_tag",
"description": "example of a tag from Automation API",
"category_id": "'${CAT_ID}'"}'
TAG_ID=$(curl -k \
-X POST \
-H "vmware-api-session-id: $VAPI_SESSION_ID" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d "$BODY" \
"https://$VC/api/cis/tagging/tag" \
| xargs -t)
The response contains the details of the newly created tag, including its UUID.
3. Associate the tag with the Hello World folder. You must have the Hello World folder ID and the tag ID you created in
the previous step.
echo 'Using REST to tag Hello Folder.'
BODY='{ "object_id": {"id": "'${HELLO_FOLDER_MOID}'", "type": "Folder"} }'
curl -k \
-X POST \
-H "vmware-api-session-id: $VAPI_SESSION_ID" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d "$BODY" \
"https://$VC/api/cis/tagging/tag-association/${TAG_ID}?action=attach"
On success, the operation returns HTTP Code 204 - No Content.

Some Use Cases for VMware SDKs
VMware provides several stand-alone SDKs for specific use cases, including disk development for backup and restore,
interfacing with guest virtual machines, and developing feature plug-ins for data center management with the vSphere
Client.
Partners and customers can develop backup applications using the virtual disk development kit (VDDK). A code walk-
though of the Safekeeping application appears below.
The Guest SDK enables operations and communication with guest virtual machines. An example use of Datasets appears
below, to notify users of data synchronization status.
The vSphere Client SDK is for partners and customers creating a (remote) plug-in extension for the vSphere Client. This
is often recommended or required for third party extensions to vSphere or VCF. See Developing Plug-ins with vSphere
Client SDK for details.
Virtual Disk Development Kit
This SDK is most frequently used to implement backup and restore applications. This section is a walk-though of code to
restore a virtual machine.
The Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK) is a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create
applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks used for storage by products such as vSphere, Workstation, and
Fusion. VDDK is a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.
VDDK provides APIs for backup and recovery, cloning, and other operations on virtual disks. With VDDK, developers can
create applications that perform backup and restore operations for virtual machines, as well as applications that create
clones or snapshots of virtual disks. VDDK also includes utilities for converting virtual disks between different formats and
for creating virtual disks from scratch.
Safekeeping – a VDDK Use Case
Based on VDDK, Safekeeping is a "proof of concept" application to demonstrate backup and restore of vSphere VMs,
vApps, and first-class disk. You can find its source code on Github, as linked from the developer.broadcom.com SDK

VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs Developer's Setup Guide
The VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) SDKs help you develop management and automation applications for VMware
Cloud Foundation .
The VCF SDK includes components necessary to work with VMware Cloud Foundation APIs, including libraries, sample
code, and documentation. This guide covers SDK installation and setup.
Intended Audience
This guide is intended for anyone who wants to develop applications using the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs. Such
developers typically include software programmers creating client applications using Java or Python and targeting
vSphere and data center services.
Revision History
Date Description
February 2026 For VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1. Minor updates and corrections.
17 June 2025 For VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0. New revision, covering setup for vSphere Management, vSphere
Automation, and software defined data center management.
September 2023 For vSphere 8.0 Update 3. The last of previous versions for vSphere Web Services.
What to Know Before Using the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs
Application development with the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs requires programming knowledge, typically using Java
or Python. You should understand the following:
• Virtual Infrastructure Management (VIM) is a protocol for VMware's enterprise-targeted server products, ESX and
vCenter. Originated in the early 2000s, and intended for languages such as Java with Web Services methods, it is also
called the Virtualization Management Object Definition Language (VMODL).
• The vSphere Automation API (vAPI) is a suite of tools to build and test micro services in vSphere data centers.
Originated in 2015, it was designed to provide interfaces in multiple programming languages. Python and REST
interfaces proved to be most popular.
• VIM protocol communicates over the network with XML data encapsulated as SOAP, whereas vAPI communicates
over the network with JSON data. Both VIM and vAPI employ HTTP or preferably HTTPS connections.
• In vSphere 8.x, VIM was extended to allow JSON data communications, in an effort to unify the two APIs and simplify
development of automation and management applications.
• In VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, additional APIs are included for software defined data center (SDDC) management.
Broadcom 7904

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
Programming Language Support in the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs
Python and Java are supported with libraries and sample code. REST interfaces for data center automation are provided
as well.
The VCF SDKs support:
• Java developers
• Python developers
• OpenAPI specifications
• SOAP for legacy uses
Language and Toolkit Java Python OpenAPI
Development environment OpenJDK or JDK 11, JDK 17, Python 3.9 or later REST
and JDK 21
Web Services and/or open Maven central repository PyPI (Python Package Index) OpenAPI 3.0.1
source samples
Applications You Can Build with the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs
With the VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs, you can create client applications to manage and automate your VMware
Cloud Foundation installation, SDDC Manager, and vCenter instance workflows.
The following are some tasks that you could automate using the VMware Cloud Foundation SDK.
• Install VMware Cloud Foundation and manage it with the SDDC Manager API, SDDC Manager UI, or Cloud
Foundation UI.
• Create, configure, power cycle, or suspend virtual machines.
• Create, configure, and manage virtual devices, such as virtual disks and network devices.
• Connect, power cycle, and disconnect ESX hosts.
• Snapshot the state of a virtual machine, and later restore virtual machine state.
• Gather statistics about ESX hosts and virtual machine performance.
• Manage events generated by vSphere, such as alarms set for specific thresholds.
• Migrate virtual machines between hosts automatically.
• Manage load balancing and failover with vCenter using distributed resource scheduler (DRS) and high availability
(HA).
The following are additional tasks that you can automate using the vAPI.
• Manage the life cycle of hosts and clusters.
• Access the Content Library to access OVF packages and VM templates.
• Create a vSphere tag to add object metadata in the vSphere inventory.
• Configure the workload control plane to run Kubernetes microservices.
The vSphere Client is an example of a client application that was developed using VIM and vAPI. Many controls in the
vSphere Client UI call underlying vSphere API methods.
Scope of Changes from vSphere to VMware Cloud Foundation SDK
The VMware Cloud Foundation SDK supersedes both the vSphere Management SDK and the vSphere Automation SDKs.
A summary of the components follows below.
The vSphere Management SDK contained the following interfaces. All are Web Services, in the sense that they
communicate through a network endpoint in XML as defined by their Web Services Description Language (WSDL)
definitions. As of vSphere 8.x, applications can also communicate in JSON, for interoperability with vSphere Automation
APIs.
• ESX Agent Manager (EAM) SDK
Broadcom 7905

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Storage Management Service (SMS) SDK
• Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM) SDK
• Single Sign On (SSO) Client SDK
• vSphere Web Services SDK, also called VIM
• Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management (VSLM) SDK
The vSAN Management SDK, similar to the vSphere Web Services SDK but adding storage, is included in the VMware
Cloud Foundation SDK. The vSphere Automation SDK, also called vAPI, is also included in the VMware Cloud
Foundation SDK. Most developers use REST or Python bindings for vSphere Automation, although Java and other
language bindings are offered. The VMware Cloud Foundation SDKs includes libraries from the following:
• vSphere Automation SDK for Python and Java
• pyvmomi (Python VM object management infrastructure) for vCenter and vSAN
• Web Services SDK for Java
• vSAN Management SDK for Java
Note:
The VCF SDKs also include new interfaces for SDDC Manager and VCF Installer. SDDC Manager is a user
interface to manage a software defined data center. VCF Installer helps automate cluster setup.
Consolidated Contents of the VCF SDK
Various interfaces were bundled inside the vSphere Management SDK, including the Web Services SDK, which remains
available under folder (instead of vsphere-ws). Formerly available mostly on Github, vSphere Automation
sdk/vim25
SDKs are now bundled into the VCF SDK.
The vSphere Automation SDKs were originally provided on Github, but are now downloadable from the Broadcom
developer site. Zip files for Java and Python are available for download, however code repositories and release notes still
reside on Github.
The vSphere Management SDK contained the following packaged interfaces. All are Web Services, in the sense that
they communicate through a network endpoint in XML as defined by the Web Services Description Language (WSDL)
standard. In vSphere 8 update releases, applications can communicate in JSON also, which increases interoperability
with vSphere Automation APIs.
• The vSphere Web Services SDK is the most popular. It supports development of applications that call the vSphere API
to manage virtual machines and virtual infrastructure components such as data centers, datastores, resource pools,
and networks. See the vSphere Web Services API Reference for managed objects, methods, and data structures in
each release.
• ESX Agent Manager (EAM) offers support for vSphere solutions such as High Availability, NSX virtual networks, and
IO Filters.
• Storage Management Service (SMS) provides access to storage capabilities, associations, and space usage. SMS has
its own in-memory database manager (the SMS cache) that periodically synchronizes data with the storage information
provider database
• Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM) helps administrators use and define storage profiles that automate
storage provisioning for virtual machines. Client applications can manipulate storage policies with the API, and with the
vSphere Client.
• Single Sign On (SSO) provides a security service for vSphere authentication. Client applications call the API to obtain
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) tokens for logging into vCenter. For multifactor authentication, programs
must use vSphere Automation.
• Virtual Storage Lifecycle Management (VSLM) are APIs to manage First Class Disk (FCD), also called Improved
Virtual Disk. FCD is storage that exists independently of a virtual machine.
The vSAN Management API is a superset of the Web Services API, with additional methods and objects for handling
vSphere storage area network (vSAN). Java and Python language bindings are available and recommended.
Broadcom 7906

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
How to Access or Download the VCF SDK
The VCF SDK is provided as open source on the web. If you are a developer working inside a firewall on a limited access
network, or prefer Zip format, you can download equivalent Zip files.
Java developers can obtain the VCF SDK on the Maven Central repository. POM files are provided for build environments
Maven, Gradle, Kotlin, and others. The role of Maven Central is to ensure that dependencies are downloaded in a
standard way for the build process. The SDK itself is located in Github, or can be downloaded from the Broadcom
developer website.
https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/com.vmware.sdk/vcf-sdk-bom
https://github.com/vmware/vcf-sdk-java
Python developers can obtain the VCF SDK from the Python package index (PyPI). The role of PyPI is to ensure that
dependencies are downloaded in a standard way for the build process. The SDK itself is located in Github, or can be
downloaded from the Broadcom developer website.
https://pypi.org/project/vcf-sdk/
https://github.com/vmware/vcf-sdk-python
OpenAPI for REST operations and WSDL definitions for Web Services are available on Github.
https://github.com/vmware/vcf-api-specs
Alternatively, you can download the VCF SDKs from the Broadcom developer site. If you don't see VCF, click the SDKs
link for Cloud Management.
https://developer.broadcom.com/sdks
Sample Authentication with vCenter Single Sign-On Configurations
You can choose to authenticate your client with vCenter Single Sign-On (SS0). This topic explains how to do vCenter SSO
authentication with the SDK samples.
Currently, VCF install vCenter with an embedded Platform Services Controller, which includes vCenter Single Sign-On
Server, VMware License Service, and other features. This configuration combines all platform services into one vCenter
installation.
With this configuration, there is no need to provide the vCenter Single Sign-On URL (because vCenter SSO service is
embedded in the management node) and the SDK will continue to work as before.
The SDK samples have always had the option to explicitly specify the vCenter Single Sign-On URL. This was useful in
cases where the vCenter SSO service was deployed outside the vSphere management node.
When you log in to a vCenter SSO service, you must be in a domain that has been added as a vCenter SSO identity
source. If that domain is not the default domain, you must include the domain name as part of your user name, for
example administrator@vsphere.local. To learn how to configure vCenter SSO service, see the vSphere Security
documentation.
SDK Version Support and Limitations of the ESX API
VMware supports older versions of vSphere, although some features of VMC are not backward compatible, such as
SDDC Manager. ESX hosts have some limitations that vCenter does not.
The VCF SDK and vSphere Web Services support various versions of vSphere, including:
• ESX versions 9.x, 8.0 and update releases
• vCenter 9.x, 8.0 and update releases
For older releases of ESX and vCenter, VMware recommends using an older matching SDK.
The vSphere API is a Web Service that runs on vCenter and ESX hosts. The API exposed is the same in both products.
However, vCenter provides the following capabilities that are not available through ESX Web Service:
• Collecting historical performance data
Broadcom 7907

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
• Optimizing resources, including managing distributed resources
• Enabling migration from one host system to another by using VMware vMotion
• Providing distributed resource management, including recovery, across all host systems under its control
If you attempt to invoke an operation on an ESX system that is supported only on vCenter, the server returns a fault
saying “not implemented” or “not supported.” For example, the ExtensionManager API is available only on vCenter.
Attempting to register an extension to an ESX host returns a fault, “not supported.”
Setup for Java Development
This chapter explains how to set up an environment to develop VCF applications using Java.
Java Development Requirements for the VMware Cloud Foundation SDK
To develop Java client applications using the VMware Cloud Foundation Java SDK, you need Java SE and a Java Web
services development tool set.
The minimum Java requirement is to use Java platform Standard Edition (SE) version 11. For best results use one of the
Long-Term-Support (LTS) Java SE releases 11, 17 or 21.
Setup For Python Development
This chapter explains how to set up an environment to develop VCF applications using Python.
The VCF SDK for Python supports both VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) and its subset VMware vSphere Foundation
(vSphere Foundation). The VCF SDK supersedes vSphere Management SDK with pyvmomi, vSphere Automation SDK
for Python, vSAN SDK for Python, and vSphere Data Protection SDK for Python. It also contains interfaces for VCF
Installer and SDDC Manager.
Previously, Python libraries were shipped with the SDKs. Starting in VCF 9.0, these libraries are published to PyPI (https://
pypi.org) and must be installed locally for the SDK samples to work.
Note:
If you operate in an air-gapped environment off the Internet, you can download equivalent Python libraries from
the Broadcom developer site and install them locally.

Prerequisites for Python SDK
Before downloading the VCF SDK for Python, check that your Linux, Mac, or Windows system has the following items.

python

https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-

A Python virtual environment is highly recommended, although it is possible to work with the samples without one.
Installing the Python SDK
The easiest way to install the Python SDK is with the Python package index (PyPI) over the network, but you can also
install it in air-gapped environments.
The typical and recommended way to install the VCF SDK for Python is using . By default, install package
pip pip
fetches the latest version of a package from the Python Package Index (PyPI). The installation also gets its dependencies
from the PyPI artifactory. The vSphere Foundation SDK is a subset of the VCF SDK for vSphere-only development. Using
one of these commands, you can install the VCF or vSphere Foundation SDK from PyPI:
pip install vcf-sdk
pip install vvf-sdk
Fastpath:
Unless you have an air-gapped development environment, stop here.
Installation in an air-gapped environment is more involved, but helped by a requirements file. The Zip file includes only
the Python SDK deliverables. Third-party dependencies must be installed before installing the SDK from the Zip. In this
example, third-party dependencies are in a third party requirements.txt file. On a system that is connected to the Internet,
download third-party libraries from PyPI, and Zip them up.
pip download -r requirements_third_party.txt -d third_party_libs_pypi
zip -r third_party_libs_pypi.zip third_party_libs_pypi/
After moving that system into the air-gapped environment, unzip the downloaded third-party library dependencies, and
install from Wheel files:
unzip third_party_libs_pypi.zip
pip install -U third_party_libs_pypi/**/*.whl
Because the downloaded VCF SDK contains compressed folders, you must unzip again:
unzip v9.0.0.0.zip -d vmware-cloud-foundation-sdk-python
cd vmware-cloud-foundation-sdk-python
Now you can install the VCF or vSphere Foundation SDK, as above from PiPI over the network.
pip install -U lib/**/*.whl
pip install -U lib/vvf/**/*.whl
Running the SDK Samples
After you install the VCF SDK for Python, and have a VMware Cloud or vSphere installation, you can run the sample
programs and watch them work.
The VCF SDK for Python samples are distributed across three different Github repositories. The first one, VCF SDK for
Python, must be cloned. The remaining repositories can be fetched as submodules.
• vcf-sdk-python
• vsphere-automation-sdk-python
• pyvmomi-community-samples
After you clone the SDK samples, you can set up a Python environment to run them.
1. Clone the SDK to get all samples in one place.
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/vmware/vcf-sdk-python.git
Broadcom 7909

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
git submodule init
git submodule update
2. Update PYTHONPATH to use SDK samples and helper methods. On MacOS or Linux:
cd vcf-sdk-python
export PYTHONPATH=${PWD}:$PYTHONPATH
On Windows:
cd vcf-sdk-python
set PYTHONPATH=%cd%\sdk;%PYTHONPATH%
3. Using the VCF SDK repository, connect to SDDC Manager for samples execution. (If you have vSphere Foundation
instead of VCF, skip this step.) For demo purposes, this code uses password authentication and disables certificate
verification, which is not recommended in a production environment.
import requests
import urllib3
from vmware.vapi.sddc_manager.client import create_sddc_manager_client
session = requests.session()
session.verify = False
sddc_client = create_sddc_manager_client(server='<sddc_manager_ip>',
username='<username>', password='<password>', session=session)
sddc_client.v1.Domains.get_domains()
4. Using the VCF SDK repository, connect to vCenter for samples execution. See remark about "demo purposes" above.
import requests
import urllib3
from vmware.vapi.vsphere.client import create_vsphere_client
session = requests.session()
session.verify = False
urllib3.disable_warnings(urllib3.exceptions.InsecureRequestWarning)
vsphere_client = create_vsphere_client(server='<vc_ip>',
username='<vc_username>', password='<vc_password>', session=session)
vsphere_client.vcenter.VM.list()
5. Run the samples against SDDC Manager.
$ python create_domains.py --server <SDDC_Manager_IP> --user <username> --password <password>
6. Run the samples against vCenter.
$ python create_domains.py --server <vCenterServer_IP> --user <username> --password <password>

Setup for Development with OpenAPI
This chapter explains where to locate OpenAPI specifications for VMware Cloud Foundation interfaces, and how to set up
an environment to develop VCF applications based on OpenAPI.
VCF 9.0 provides officially supported ready-to-use component modules for Java and Python developers, along with
guidelines and code samples, available at Maven Central and PyPI respectively. For further development especially in
alternate languages, documentation and specifications might be needed.
Developers who use other programming languages can use API definitions under the specifications folder to manually
generate client code and server stubs in many languages. For example, Go language programmers could run
openapi-
(or an alternative also available on Github) to produce a Go client library and skeleton Go server, to be filled
generator
in with back-end Go language code. Actually Java and Python programmers could do this, but don't need to.
You can find specifications to browse at github.com/vmware/vcf-api-specs, or to download as a Zip archive on the
Broadcom developer website. The Github repository holds API specifications and documentation for VCF products,
replicated in the Zip file for developers working off-network.
The VCF 9.0 release contains JSON files conforming to the OpenAPI 3.0.1 standard. The following table summarizes
content of the repository.
documentation/vsphere/wsdl Zip files containing Web Service style API references for EAM,
PBM, SMS, VIM, vSAN, and VSLM.
scripts/java Folders containing unsupported Gradle 8.7-based projects
that you can use to generate client-side bindings. Intended for
backward compatibility with Java 8 now that vSAN and WS-SDK
moved to Java 11.
specifications/sddc-manager JSON file with OpenAPI specification for the SDDC Manager, for
fleet management.
specifications/vcf-installer JSON file with OpenAPI specification for the VCF Installer,
formerly Cloud Builder.
specifications/vsan-data-protection YAML file with OpenAPI specification for the Snap Service, a
vSAN feature new in 8.0 U3.
specifications/vsphere/openapi/automation YAML file with OpenAPI specification for vSphere Automation,
also called vAPI.
specifications/vsphere/openapi/vi-json YAML file with OpenAPI specifications for all the Web Service
APIs enumerated above for WSDL, including the popular VIM
(vim25).
These specifications are available:
• vSphere
• VI/JSON
• Automation - file dependencies, e.g. vCenter all depend on vAPI
• vSAN data protection (snapservice)
• Legacy use cases, before WSDL was superseded by VI/JSON
– JAX-WS / CXF generator / wsimport
Broadcom 7911

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
– CXF 4.0.5
– Old SDKs used JAX-WS RI 3.x
• SDDC Manager
• VCF Installer
OpenAPI Specifications for vSphere
Developers can use the OpenAPI specifications for vSphere to manually generate client code and server stubs in
alternate programming languages.
Under the folder reside two YAML files containing OpenAPI definitions:
specifications/vsphere
First, the VI/JSON file describes VIM (virtual infrastructure management, also called vim25) interfaces with JSON instead
of XML data transfer. This is a large file with all the former Web Services API categories, including EAM, PBM, SMS,
SSO, VIM, and VSLM.
Second, the vCenter YAML file describes vSphere Automation, also called vAPI. This is a more limited API focused on the
vCenter appliance, content library, tagging, and ESX host management.
Closely related, the vSAN data protection YAML file describes Snap Service, which provides support for vSAN native
snapshots.
Also for backward compatibility with legacy use cases, before WSDL was superseded by VI/JSON, the folder
wsdl
contains per-service definition files, XSD and WSDL. The previous VIM interfaces used JAX-WS RI 3.x and JAX-B
libraries. For code creation based on these definition files, you can use the CXF 4.0.5 generator, and/or the
wsimport
command.

Currently there are about 280 interfaces in the SDDC Manager API, also available as REST commands.

VMware Cloud Foundation Programming Guide
VMware Cloud Foundation APIs and SDKs are designed to help manage and automate various aspects of your cloud
infrastructure.
Introduction to the VMware Cloud Foundation REST API
Use the VMware Cloud Foundation REST API to manage your virtual infrastructure by using HTTP.
With the VMware Cloud Foundation REST API, you can manage vSphere components connected to authentication,
tagging, content libraries, clusters, internal and external certificates, namespaces, vSphere Trust Authority, vSphere
Supervisor, and more.
Broadcom 7914

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
This programming guide introduces the most important features and use cases of the VMware Cloud Foundation REST
API. You can use this guide in combination with the VMware Cloud Foundation API Reference that features all available
API services, as well as many code samples.
Components of the Virtualization Layer
At the core of VMware Cloud Foundation is vSphere, which provides the virtualization layer of the software-defined data
center. You can use vSphere deployment options for vCenter and ESX hosts to build virtual environments of different
scales.
Components and Services of the vSphere Environment
vCenter is a preconfigured virtual machine optimized for running the vCenter service and the vCenter components. The
vCenter service acts as a central administrator for ESX hosts.
Components Installed with vCenter
vCenter is a central administration point for ESX hosts. The group of components installed when you install vCenter
include the vCenter service, vSphere Client, VMware vSphere®Auto Deploy™, VMware vSphere®ESX™ Dump Collector,
VMware vSphere® Syslog Collector, and vSphere Lifecycle Manager service.
You can use the VMware Cloud Foundation API endpoint to access the following services running on vCenter.
Content Library You can use content libraries to share virtual machines, vApps, and other files, such as ISO, OVA, and text
files, across the software-defined data center. You can create, share, and subscribe to content libraries
on the same vCenter instance or on a remote instance. Sharing content libraries promotes consistency,
compliance, efficiency, and automation in deploying workloads at scale.
You can also create OVF and VM templates from virtual machines and vApps in hosts, resource pools, and
clusters. You can then use the OVF and VM templates to deploy new virtual machines and vApps.
Starting with vSphere 7.0, you can edit the contents of a VM template. You can check out the library item
that contains the VM template. After editing the VM template, check in the library item to save the changes
to the virtual machine.
Virtual Machine You can use the VMware Cloud Foundation APIs to create, configure, and manage the life cycle of virtual
machines in your environment.
Starting with vSphere 7.0, you can also clone, create an instant clone, migrate, register, and unregister a
virtual machine.
vSphere Lifecycle The life cycle of ESX hosts and clusters can be managed through the VMware vSphere®Lifecycle
Manager Manager™ feature. Based on the current state of the hosts in a cluster, you can easily create a desired
software specification by using the contents of a software depot. Then you validate the desired software
specification and you apply the specification on all hosts in the cluster.
vSphere Tags With vSphere tags you can attach metadata to vSphere objects, and as a result, make it easier to filter
and sort these objects. You can use the VMware Cloud Foundation APIs to automate the management of
vSphere tags.
vSphere Supervisor You can enable vSphere Supervisor on an existing vSphere cluster in your environment. Create and
configure namespaces on the Supervisors to run Kubernetes workloads in dedicated resource pools.
About vSphere
vSphere is the VMware software stack that implements private-cloud data center management and the on-premises
component of hybrid-cloud deployments.
A vSphere installation includes one or more instances of vCenter configured to manage one or more virtual data centers.
Each virtual data center includes one or more instances of VMware ESX.
Broadcom 7915

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x
About ESX
Each instance of ESX includes management agents and the VMware hypervisor layer, which runs several virtual
machines. Each virtual machine contains a guest operating system, such as Windows or Linux, capable of running IT or
user applications.
vCenter runs as a virtual machine on an ESX host. vCenter provides an independent endpoint capable of handling API
requests both for vCenter and for the vCenter Management API.
vCenter Management Overview
vCenter runs on a Photon OS™ guest operating system.
vCenter is a collection of services designed for managing and monitoring vSphere installations. vCenter responds to CLI
commands, requests from the vSphere Client, and API requests from custom clients. API clients can be written in a choice
of several software languages.
vCenter is managed by CLI, Web interfaces, or API requests. These requests help you manage vCenter configuration,
monitor resource usage, or back up and restore the vCenter instance. You can also use API requests to check the
health of vCenter. This programming guide explains how to use the VMware Cloud Foundation APIs that are available to
manage and monitor vCenter.
For more information about the capabilities of vCenter, see vCenter Configuration.
Understanding the VMware Cloud Foundation API
You can use the VMware Cloud Foundation REST services to automate many aspects of your vSphere environment such
as configuration, authentication, certificate management, tagging, managing the life cycle of clusters, content libraries,
Kubernetes cluster management, and many more.
• How Does the VMware Cloud Foundation API Work
• The VMware Cloud Foundation API in Context
• Which REST Clients to Use with the VMware Cloud Foundation API
• Why Use the VMware Cloud Foundation API Through REST
How Does the VMware Cloud Foundation API Work
The VMware Cloud Foundation API follows a resource-based REST architecture with JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
requests and responses. REST, an acronym for Representational State Transfer, is a software architectural style in which
programs use the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to exchange serialized representations of objects between a client
and a server. The client sends an HTTP request and receives an HTTP response from the server. Request and response
bodies are encoded using JSON, and must conform to the JSON schema associated with each operation.
The VMware Cloud Foundation API uses the main CRUD (Create, Retrieve, Update, Delete) functions over HTTP to
manage representations of the objects that the API defines. In the VMware Cloud Foundation API, these objects are
represented by a collection of JSON schemas.
You use:
• HTTP GET to retrieve a representation of an object
• HTTP POST to create an object
• HTTP PATCH or PUT to modify an object
• HTTP DELETE to delete an object
In addition, the HTTP POST operation is used for some custom actions outside of the CRUD framework such as
registering or relocating virtual machines.
The HTTP verbs are also called methods. Each API operation is identified by a method and a URL. Operations can
also contain a body that is composed of one or more data structures. The operation body contains parameters that are
structured as key-value pairs. For more information, see VMware Cloud Foundation API Requests.
Broadcom 7916

VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.x

automate many aspects of your vSphere environment such as vCenter configuration, authentication,
tagging, content libraries, managing the life cycle of clusters, managing internal and external certificates,
vSphere Trust Authority, vSphere Supervisor, and so on.
However, you cannot manage all aspects of your vSphere environment with the VMware Cloud Foundation
API as it does not cover all vSphere features. To expose the full set of vSphere functionalities you must use
both the VMware Cloud Foundation API and the vSphere Web Services API. For both APIs, VMware has
compiled SDKs that help programmers automate tasks.

Why Use the VMware Cloud Foundation API Through REST
You can choose whether to access the VMware Cloud Foundation API directly through REST or through the various SDKs
and automation tools binded to the API.
Possible use cases for using the VMware Cloud Foundation API through REST:
• There is no SDK available for your programming language. For example, you use PHP, JavaScript, Swift, Rust, and so
on.
• Your integration footprint is small and you can't justify the overhead of installing and maintaining the VMware Cloud
Foundation SDKs for Java or Python. For example, if you are designing a client application that fetches a few
parameters from your vSphere environment, you might decide that installing and maintaining the Java or Python SDKs
is unnecessary.

VMware Cloud Foundation API Requests
To retrieve or manage resources, clients make HTTP requests to a VMware Cloud Foundation API server.
An API request through HTTP must include a method (or verb), a URL, and headers. Depending on the type of operation,
the request might or might not include a body.
HTTP Method
The methods of the VMware Cloud Foundation API follow the logic of the CRUD (Create, Retrieve, Update, Delete)
functions used to interact with database applications.

PUT

PATCH

URL
You can reach each VMware Cloud Foundation API operation through a specific URL.
The URL is typically composed of:
• the vCenter IP address or FQDN.
• the base path

To determine what you want to do with the resource, you associate an HTTP verb (POST, GET, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE)
to the URL.

HTTP Headers
The HTTP headers transfer metadata associated with the API requests and responses. They are an integral part of HTTP
requests and responses as they convey information about authorization, request and response content type, response
caching, and so on.
You must typically set the following HTTP headers in your requests.
Authorization
All requests to create a VMware Cloud Foundation API session must include an
Authorization
header in the form prescribed by your identity provider. For vCenter Single Sign-On basic authentication,
you must use the base-64 encoded value of your user name and password separated by a colon
(username:password). For more information, see Authentication Mechanisms.
This is a custom header that you use to authenticate your subsequent calls after you obtain a session
vmware-api-session
identifier. Paste the session identifier as the header value.
-id
This header is used to indicate the data format of the request body.
Content-Type
Use application/x-www-form-urlencoded for requests to the Authentication Token service.
Use application/json for all other requests.
Request Body
The HTTP body must be in the JSON format.
Some VMware Cloud Foundation API requests contain a body and some do not. For example, retrieve (GET) operations
do not contain a body in the request.
To explore the request and response schemas, visit the vSphere Automation API Reference.
VMware Cloud Foundation API Responses
The VMware Cloud Foundation API responds to every HTTP request with either a success or an error status code.
The VMware Cloud Foundation API uses a specific set of HTTP success and error codes for the responses. The response
structure depends on the request type: some responses include a document body, some include a string, and some are
empty.
Table 1853: HTTP Success Codes
HTTP Code Message Type Message Description
200 OK The request is valid and was completed. The response includes a document body.
201 Created The request is valid. The requested object was created and its identifier is returned with the
response.
202 Accepted The request is valid and a task was created to handle it. The response usually contains a
task identifier.
204 No Content The request is valid and was completed. The response does not include a body.
Table 1854: HTTP Error Codes
HTTP Code Error Type Error Description
400 ALREADY_EXISTS An attempt was made to create an entity but an entity with the same name or identifier
already exists in that context.
400 ALREADY_IN_DESIR Indicates that an attempt to change the state of a resource or service had no effect because
ED_STATE the resource or service is already in the desired state.

HTTP Code Error Type Error Description
400 CANCELED Indicates that an operation was canceled due to an explicit request to do so.
400 FEATURE_IN_USE Indicates that an action cannot be completed because a feature is in use. For example, trying
to deactivate snapshots on a virtual machine that has a snapshot.
400 INVALID_ARGUMENT Indicates that the values accepted for one or more parameters are not acceptable. Examples:
• A parameter value that is not of the expected type.
• A parameter value that is not in the required range.
• A parameter value that is different from the specifically allowed strings.
400 INVALID_ELEMENT_ Indicates that an attempt to modify the configuration of an element or a group containing the
CONFIGURATION element failed due to the configuraton of the element. Examples:
• An attempt to move a host with a fault-tolerant virtual machine out of a cluster.
• An attempt to remove a host from a DRS cluster without putting the host into
maintenance mode.
400 INVALID_ELEMENT_ Indicates that the server was unable to fulfill the request because an element of a specific
TYPE type does not fit into a particular container type. Examples:
• An attempt to put a virtual machine into a folder that can only contain hosts.
• An attempt to attach an SCSI virtual disk to an IDE port.
400 INVALID_REQUEST Indicates that the request is formed in such a way that the server is unable to process it. For
example, sending an invalid JSON structure.
400 NOT_ALLOWED_IN_C Indicates that the requested operation is not allowed with a resource or service in its current
URRENT_STATE state. Examples:
• Trying to upgrade the virtual hardware version of a suspended virtual machine.
• Trying to power off, reset, or suspend a virtual machine that is not powered on.
400 RESOURCE_IN_USE Indicates that the operation could not be completed because a resource is in use. Examples:
• Trying to remove a datastore when there is a virtual machine registered on a host
attached to the datastore.
• Trying to add a virtual switch if the physical network adapter being bridged is already in
use.
400 UNEXPECTED_INPUT Indicates that the request body contains a parameter or a field whose name is unknown to
the server.
400 UNSUPPORTED Indicates that the operation is not supported by the underlying platform. Examples:
• Trying to hot-plug a CPU when the current virtual machine configuration does not support
CPU hot-plugging .
• Trying to change the memory size to a value beyond the acceptable guest memory limits
supported by the virtual machine's host.
400 UNVERIFIED_PEER Indicates that an attempt to connect to an unknown or untrusted endpoint failed because the
system was unable to verify the identity of the endpoint. Typically, the error data field of this
error contains information about the endpoint. If you decide to trust the endpoint, the request
can be resubmitted with an indication that the endpoint should be trusted. Examples:
• The client provides an IP address or an URL of an endpoint the system should
communicate with using a TLS connection, but the endpoint's TLS certificate is self-
signed, expired, or otherwise untrustworthy.
• The client provides an IP address of a host, with which the system must communicate
through SSH, but SSH does not recognize the host's public key.
401 UNAUTHENTICATED Indicates that the operation requires authentication and the user is not authenticated. For
example, if the session identifier in the request header is missing or if it identifies a session
that has expired.
403 UNAUTHORIZED Indicates that the user is not authorized to perform the operation. For example, some
operations might require that the user has one or more privileges over the operation or over
a resource identifier but the user identified by the operation does not have the required
privileges.
